Free lunches

Free lunches for Jewish families without a livelihood in Sosnowiec.
On the initiative of Mr. Asher Kleinberg a meeting took place in the premises of the Merchants' and Industrialists' Association, with the participation of a group of communal activists, at which it was decided to organise a relief campaign for the poor Jewish masses of Sosnowiec, who suffer want and need.
Dr. Hercman, president of „Dobroczynność“ [the charity society], described the catastrophic situation of the pauperised Jewish masses and pointed out the urgency of the planned campaign.
Mr. Kleinberg presented the plan of the campaign, which will be, first of all, to open a free kitchen and a distribution[?] of food products.
A committee was elected consisting of: Mrs. Dr. Jungster, Dr. Liberman, Dr. Żendrowski, Mordechai Reicher, A. Ostry[?], Sz. Chilczyk[?] and A. Kleinberg.
The committee has already set to real work. The list of donors will be published in the „Zaglembier Tsaytung“.

Rabbi Reb Yehoshuale, of blessed memory

Jewish Będzin lost, in the night from Tuesday to Wednesday [29–30 December 1936], its oldest moreh hora'ah (rabbinic decisor), Rabbi Reb Yehoshuale, whom the town had for decades called "Reb Yehoshuale Dayan". He died at a ripe old age, aged ninety; nevertheless, up to the last hour of his life he was in full possession of his mind and fulfilled his official duties as "podrabin" [?; deputy rabbi]; a few hours before his death he still managed to sign a document for the Magistrate (municipality).
Reb Yehoshuale of blessed memory died "by a kiss" (a peaceful death). He did not want to talk to anyone. When H.B.[?] Fridberg asked him something, he answered: "Do not disturb me in my last hour." Then he washed his hands, pulled [?] the skullcap over his head and breathed out his soul.
—
Reb Yehoshuale Dayan of blessed memory was a son of Reb Leibele Dayan of saintly memory, who was moreh hora'ah in Będzin. After his father's death Reb Yehoshuale took over his father's office until his last day. He was moreh hora'ah in Będzin for 49 years. Already as a young man he was regarded [?] as a prodigy (illui) and studied with the greatest scholars in Poland. The deceased was a great halakhic authority and a vastly learned man. Day and night he sat and studied.
—
The kehilla administration announced the mourning by means of klepsydry (death notices). At midday a mourning session took place in the premises of the kehilla administration, with the participation of rabbis [?], dozors (board members) and parnassim.
President Rubinlicht [?] opened the session with a short funeral speech. "None of us," he said, "can measure the great loss of the beloved moreh tzedek, who for 50 years fulfilled his office honestly and faithfully." His memory was honoured by rising and by a minute of silence.
President Rigski spoke about the request of the heirs of the deceased to put up an ohel over the grave. It was decided that the matter be decided by the rabbinate, the Chevra Kadisha and the kehilla administration, possibly by the Sochaczewer [?] Rebbe, may he live long.
In the funeral, which took place at 3 o'clock, many thousands of people from all strata of the Jewish population took part. A przodownik [?; police sergeant] with several policemen kept order.
The coffin was carried into the beit midrash, where hakafot (circuits) were made, and the morei hora'ah Fridberg and Lipszyc delivered eulogies. In front of the synagogue the moreh tzedek Lewin eulogized.
—
Many hundreds of people accompanied the eminent deceased to the cemetery, where at the open grave Rabbi Reb Shlomo Lipszyc, son-in-law of Rebbe Szapiro ("the beit-midrash [?] rebbe"), delivered a eulogy. The eulogy left a very good impression.
The grave plot of the deceased lies next to that of Rabbi Reb Tzvi Hanoch Lewin of saintly memory.
May his memory be blessed!
T.N.Tz.B.H. (May his soul be bound in the bond of life.)

On Sunday morning [27 December 1936] the first district conference of the Betar instructors was opened in the premises of the Będzin Ha-Tzohar (Revisionist Zionists).
The opening of the conference was conducted by the district commander Mordechai Lozyner [?], who spoke about [?] the Betar situation in the Zagłębie district and expressed the opinion that today's conference would bring about coordination in Betar work in the cultural and organizational field.
After the opening the commanders of the "nests" (local branches) gave reports on Betar activity in the local organizations, from which one can infer that the situation in most nests is satisfactory.

Prof. Messing in Będzin

The well-known telepath and phenomenal mind-reader Prof. W. Messing, who is well known in the scientific world, has been staying in Będzin for several days. As a man with an extraordinary mental power in the field of suggestion and telepathy, Prof. Messing is famous as one of the greatest authorities in this field. His experiments are conducted according to a strictly scientific system, and they are proof that the human intellect penetrates the most hidden and wondrous secrets of nature.
The séances that Prof. Messing conducts in the field of suggestion, i.e. influencing people through his own willpower, telepathy, or guessing the most complicated thoughts, and clairvoyance, i.e. the power to sense and see hidden things — are among the greatest wonders, and it is no surprise that they arouse enormous interest everywhere.
It is enough to mention, for example, that in his public séances in Warsaw and in all the larger cities of Poland Prof. Messing has always had outstanding[?] success both with the public and with representatives of science and medicine — not to speak of the private visits to him, in which he guesses the most hidden thoughts, recognises the character of the patient and of those around him, foretells the future and characterises people by their handwriting, etc., arousing the delight of all who visit him.
Professor Messing is no new face here; several years ago he stayed with us and aroused great interest among the public that attended his public séances.
Prof. Messing, who is staying in Będzin for only a few days, is lodging at the Hotel "Bristol".

Remarks on the Times

[Editorial — Sosnowiec, kehilla; Poland, relief for the unemployed.]
A ship without a rudder:
Several months have already passed since the elections to the new kehilla took place in Sosnowiec, and as we write these lines it is still not known when exactly our newly elected public delegates will sit down at the table of government.
The only dissatisfied party, which has gone with an appeal [rekurs] to the higher authority — to the voivodeship [województwo], is the Agudah, but the prospects are in any case quite weak.
It is as quiet as if nothing had ever happened.
The consequence of the situation created, i.e. of the indifference of the old, long-seated and the newly elected kehilla representatives, is that we voters find ourselves like a ship without a rudder.
One of the main questions at the present moment is drawing up the new kehilla budget, which is bound up with great difficulties in connection with the new ritual-slaughter law, because of which the revenues will be considerably reduced, and it will be necessary to go as far as raising the estimate [etat] or finding other sources of income.
But who is to carry out this responsible work?
The appointed administration of the old kehilla already regards itself now as "neighbours" and has no great desire to work for the newly elected kehilla representatives, who will have to be the actual executors of the adopted and implemented plans and decisions.
The newly elected representatives, on the other hand, are not coming to power for the time being, and consequently we, the voters, find ourselves like "a ship without a rudder" — neither able to sail there nor to come back.
We therefore hold that the newly elected kehilla representatives must intervene so that they become legal, consolidate themselves and fulfil their obligations towards the voters who sent them into the kehilla.
The winter campaign for the unemployed.
The campaign for the unemployed in Poland is being undertaken this time on a very large scale; all citizens who are more or less well-off must give for the benefit of the hungry poor in Poland. The principle seems to be: whoever does not take [relief][?] must give, and whoever really has[?] must give without evasions.
The budget of the campaign is to amount to tens of millions; the campaign will last a full 5 months of the winter season, and the campaign for the unemployed will surely have to be paid with great punctuality. There is a certain inner logic in this, since hunger is, after all, the king of human suffering in Poland, and to the degree that hunger is stilled, the other torments and needs will of themselves become smaller.
All this is on a general scale; and as far as it concerns us Jews, our communal guardians must stand on watch so that we are treated here according to the principles of elementary justice. Owing to various circumstances Jews are not represented in great number among the registered unemployed, because in normal times they were not registered among the poor workers; one must therefore pay special attention to the Jewish hungry, who are perhaps not registered but are no less unfortunate. And if other relief campaigns should suffer because of the winter relief campaign, the poor Jews would remain entirely without help or livelihood. Since the Committee for the Unemployed in principle makes no distinction between faith and nation, the Jewish participants in the committee should remember that their duty is indeed to care for all the afflicted. The Jewish communal workers must on the one hand popularise and propagate the campaign among Jewish donors, but on the other hand guard the interests of the Jewish needy, so that they are protected together with everyone.
Our "Patented" Intelligentsia

[Essay — the Jewish intelligentsia.]
It is a fact that our present-day diploma-holding intelligentsia is no longer popular with the public. If the simple Jew used to look upon a doctor of former times as a messenger from God, whom one must honestly respect — today the whole matter has become commonplace.
Moreover, in a conversation among "the common folk" one peers with a mockingly squinted eye into their intimate "private domain"[?]; people laugh at their empty arrogance, their estrangement from the community and, above all — their chasing after honour and money.
Let us take a look at what role the intelligentsia played among other oppressed peoples and among us.
A small comparison:
The intelligentsia of formerly enslaved Poland organised the Polish masses for the struggle for liberation; it went into the dark village, awakened and called and cultivated the mother tongue — Polish, so that she, the mother[?], should not be forgotten by the people, and it paid for this with the expected reward — with katorga [penal servitude] and Siberia.
The Russian intelligentsia was the backbone of the struggle against Tsarism.
The slogan "go to the people" accompanied the noblest children of Russia and created mighty cadres of teachers and educators of the masses.
And among us?
If the Haskalah movement, with all its shortcomings, broadened the horizons of Jewish life, tore [it] out of the ghetto and brought in a new current of European culture, paving[?] the way for a national movement and a workers' movement — we cannot credit today's Jewish intelligentsia with any positive achievements whatsoever.
The Jewish mass stands alone today in the struggle for existence, in the struggle for the right to work, in the embittered fight for elementary human rights — and where is this intelligentsia of ours that should help it carry the heavy burden, encourage it and not let it despair?
Our intelligentsia, which with its loyalty and devotion to the people's language and to Jewish culture, which with its conduct and behaviour should have been a model of self-respect and self-defence for the masses — runs away from the people, which is Jewish, and crawls submissively precisely to where it is spat upon and laughed at, dragging part of the unaware public along after it. —
Our intelligentsia!
At times it condescends to come down[?] from its heights and stretch out its hand to the masses for votes in elections to the city council, and then their election platforms are licorice-sweet, full of promises and of flattering the public.
But in everyday life you can search for it with a candle in the Jewish street.
True, a counted few of them still consent to let themselves be elected to a Jewish kehilla in a provincial town, where "intelligent" forces are especially needed, but for the most part the honorary office of representative of a purely Jewish institution no longer attracts them.
They are drawn far more strongly to the salons and clubs of the non-Jewish intelligentsia, and if these are closed to them, they segregate themselves among themselves like a foreign caste, they build a partition between themselves and the people from which they stem, and the needs of the masses do not interest them.
Their interests — the dancing, the poker table, their social activity — a mitzvah dance at a ball for a Jewish charitable purpose.
Because — let us say it openly —
today's intelligentsia is not the aristocracy of the spirit; this is not the type of the maskil of former times, for whom Torah for its own sake was the sole content and goal in life.
Today's Jewish intelligentsia are children of a war generation with its entire workaday-practical outlook on life, for whom school and education served a single purpose — a career.
And if from this materialised intelligentsia there still stand out types of idealists, purer and better types — for the most part "they don't make it". They fill up the kibbutzim, breaking off their studies, and thereby they sit in the boarding-houses on free board.
And only individuals among them, those truly blessed by God and endowed with courage and endurance, flash up in our dark life in the shape of great scholars and courageous leaders.
But I am not speaking of them here.

Sylvester (Impressions of the "Leyl Shimurim" Night..)

P. B—Z.
A panicky rushing about, an impatient [—] bustle, a giggling[?]. They chase about, Moshe as well as Maniek, Sala as well as Mania; one [—]s[?] the [—][?], one makes out invitations, runs to hairdressers, bathes, the girls telephone one another, one tries oneself out with cavaliers:
— New Year's Eve (Sylvester).
• • •
So Moshe sits with Sala and they drink wine[?] in style. There is no money: he earns 50 zł. a month, but one has to enjoy oneself, because others enjoy themselves too. So they drink brandy and smoke cigarettes. Sala, leaning on the chair like a drunken woman, crosses one leg over the other and smokes; she [chokes?]; not used to smoking, yet she draws the smoke deeper[?] into herself; one mustn't lag behind.
Both of them begin to feel [—][?] at heart: the brandy and the tobacco have [—]; Moshe sits with the cigarette in his mouth, [—], and looks at her with clouded eyes. Sala is afraid that she will throw up, right here in the middle, the little herrings she gobbled down at home. She smiles, supposedly, and Moshe imagines she is in love with him. Before her eyes everything starts spinning and dozing[?], and she smiles into the fog, weakly, half-forced, afraid that she might bring everything up here in front of everyone — with interest; but the main thing is that her girlfriends should think she is having a good time[?]:
— Sylvester.
• • •
There sits a "high-lifenik" (a society man), buying balloons and streamers, not taking his change ("forgiven"), and pouring liqueur into himself, gulping[?], and his face and his bald patch grow shinier, his movements — bolder, and his eyes — more lustful. Beside him — a Hasidic daughter; her father is a [—][?], careworn Jew, but she dreams, out of little books, that there is another life, a life of pleasure and forgetting, of fluttering romances, of flowers and travels, of knightly love; how the destined one first[?] sends roses every day and, at twilight in a [—][?], falls on his knees and whispers to her in a trembling voice:
— "Your eyes drive me mad[?], no woman has ever enchanted me so, you rob my soul of its peace."
So she sits with the "high-lifenik", and the old dreams take on skin and bones. He has a lot of money, is elegant, has [—] many women.
And the "high-lifenik" sniffs it out, moves closer, breathes heavily, his nostrils flare like those of a dog that has smelled meat; he touches her with his fat, lustful lips. All is going well. Only one has to get her out of here — [—] something in his head[?]. He pours her liqueur once, and again, and with trembling hands he pushes through the dancing crowd, whispering to her:
— "Rozkoszna jesteś!" [Polish: You are delightful!]
And she — drunk, with half-closed eyes, nestles up to him: surely he is the one she dreamed of in her restless girlish nights! And quietly, barely moving her lips, she answers:
— "Ty sokuszu[?]" [garbled Polish term of endearment].
And the "high-lifenik" is pleased with his quick conquest; he [—][?] contentedly[?], to himself:
— Ah, "cudowny" [wonderful] Sylvester!
• • •
Off to the side sits a couple: she a [—][?], triple-chinned Jewess; he a thin, worn-out man, his legs aching: rheumatism. He wanted to sit at home, begged for mercy, but she screamed at the top of her voice:
— That you won't get away with! I've blackened[?] my life enough with you. As a girl I didn't miss a single ball, I was chosen queen twice, and now you want me to darken my years!
So she sits with her husband at "Beyrsh-Shvang"[?]. He wants to sleep and she — to dance. In Krynica one pays the dance partner: let him [—][?]; but at home one has to be respectable.
She would gladly have "had some fun" (Polish zabawić się), but what comes of it? One starts talking (she talks) with resentment and jealousy:
— See that one there, that [—][?] and Don Juan! How he's slicked himself up[?], disgusting[?]. Oh, they're leaving!
And she feels vengeful towards that girl. After all he's a hundred-percent man, not like her schlemiel of a husband. She cannot bear the heartache and bursts out:
— With a husband like this one would be better off sitting under the stove!
— Maybe we'll actually go home — a hope of slipping away dawns on him.
— Not otherwise, because you want to!
He wanted to answer her: may it go dark before her eyes; "Big Bertha" [—] still wants to play a role! Give her cavaliers, the [—] Jewess! But he had to [—] her will. Two ladies came up; he looked "lovingly" at his wife and took several numbers for the election of a "Miss".
The ladies, with a smile, asked him to understand that no change need be given. He [—] his hands into his pockets and curses the [—][?] together with his "red heifer" with deadly curses; he looks at his wife as if to devour[?] her and [—]:
— A fresh plague, Sylvester, on their heads!
• • •
At the side sits a young man alone over a cold glass of tea; he hadn't wanted to go, he can't dance and doesn't understand the holiday, but he didn't refuse his fiancée, and she smiled radiantly into his eyes:
— "Śmieszny jesteś, lalku, wiesz!" [Polish: You're funny, dolly, you know!]
So he went; he sits in deep misery and she dances. She glides across the hall with a tall fellow, looks up at him and smiles happily; the fellow, reckoning that he has already "made it", holds her tight and laughs impudently in her face.
The young man strains not to look, he sips the cold tea and tries not to look; but the loud — dissolute, it seems to him — laughter of his fiancée reaches him. He turns his head and sees her at the buffet with the same tall fellow; she drinks the brandy like an old drunkard. He was dying to go over to the tall fellow and smash[?] his mug. She surely doesn't love him — a stab[?] in his heart — his money impressed her; for her he is the screen[?] behind which to [—][?] with strange young men.
He wants to get up and give the fellow one-two[?], but then he remembers her little smile:
— "Śmieszny jesteś, lalku!"
And he stays sitting in his place, superfluous, forgotten, and with a groan:
— Sylvester!..
The Successful Experiment

By Dr. M. Immerglück
When in France the Popular Front won the last parliamentary elections, and fate willed that the leader of the strongest party in parliament should be a Jew, the local "Yahudim" took fright; they were literally as if electrified when the chief of the strongest parliamentary party had the duty to ascend to the premier's portfolio. And they argued, by the way, that this fact should not roll up the Jewish problem in France and, God forbid, not awaken antisemitism, which in France since the Dreyfus affair, if not entirely vanished, had at least sunk into a lethargy; for even if Blum should succeed in dragging the heavy wagon out of the mud into which the world crisis had dragged it along, it would not be credited to the Jewish account, whereas if, God forbid, the experiment should not succeed, then the enemies of Israel would blow it up, and as is known all Israel are responsible for one another. Although no people mentioned in world history has ever yet had cause to complain about its Jewish statesmen — but on the contrary, wherever fate entrusted a Jew with the conduct of the state's interests, beginning with the biblical Joseph down to Disraeli, Crémieux, Rathenau and others, they always served their fatherland positively — French Jewry was nevertheless seized by a panic, and it went so far that the Grand Rabbi of Paris tried to influence Blum to refrain from forming the cabinet of ministers.
Fortunately the fear proved unfounded. The Blum experiment showed so quickly and so unexpectedly positive results both in external and internal affairs that it truly surprised all his opponents. In foreign affairs he consolidated with one stroke of the pen the delicate relations with England, strengthened a hundredfold the threads binding France with North America, secured the loyalty and friendship of Poland, switched off the danger of war by founding the Non-Intervention Committee for Spanish affairs, greatly raised France's prestige abroad, and lately also through the devaluation of the franc; and it is now no secret to anyone in France that Blum rescued France from a financial and economic collapse and set France back on the level of the Poincaré-era prosperity.
To get a clear picture of the good effects of his policy, it is enough to cast a glance at the stock exchange. As the stock-exchange reports say, domestic as well as foreign securities and raw materials keep rising. Copper has more than doubled its price; the exchange has lately been so swamped with demand for securities and for articles of primary use that it recently had to decide to postpone the closing of transactions for a few days; the banking houses and the stockbrokers have had to double their staff.
This boom ("hausse") does not, as some may think, run parallel with the devaluation, but is its result; for, as we see, the securities and products have risen in a much higher proportion than the devaluation amounts to. The banks and businesses too record a feverish activity, and it is a fact that many hoarded billions have lately flowed back into the banks, which proves the trust the masses have in Blum's government. The recruitment of tens of thousands of unemployed for public works has revived a large part of domestic industry, so that one gets the impression that the whole economic apparatus is again in full swing, and the first signs of a prosperity like that of the fine good times are already appearing in France.
To this state the Jew Blum brought a country that had stood at the edge of an economic abyss internally and of political isolation externally.
This striking victory is a slap in the face for the supporters of a protectionist and autarkic policy, which would in the end have had to lead to a national-chauvinist regrouping of the nations, lead them back to medieval sectarianism, overturn all cultural achievements and begin our history again from the beginning.
Fortunately two rays of light appeared on the horizon, two noble souls, two philanthropists and humanitarians in the full sense of the word: Blum and Roosevelt. Roosevelt too — who in fact served Blum as the prototype for his experiment — has, thanks to his liberal policy, brought back to America the prosperity of 1929.
We could learn much, very much, from the successes of Blum and Roosevelt, from the victory of liberalism over dark, blind chauvinism. Even if we take into account the particular characteristic socio-economic structure of each country, we must, after a thorough study of the two experiments, recognise liberalism as a positive factor externally and internally.
As we can also see, in the countries where the economy is based on liberal foundations and where reason of state triumphs over party sentimentality — in the countries where all citizens are children of the state with equal rights and are also treated equally as such — there indeed reign prosperity, peace, security and happiness.

The Board of the Jewish Kehilla in Katowice Must Render an Account to the Jewish Public.

(A letter to the editor).
From the New Zionist Organisation in Katowice we have been asked to print the following letter.
A short time ago Rabbi Gold gave a lecture in the local synagogue on behalf of the Mif'al ha-Bitzaron [defence fund], in which he put forward two demands: 1) money, in order to strengthen the Jewish "amer"[?] forces in Palestine, and 2) again money, for the damage done in the Land of Israel.
Although it was clear to the vice-chairman of the kehilla, Mr. Eliasz Abrahamer[?], to the board member Dr. Rapaport and to the member of the council of representatives Mr. Schlesinger, that this was not merely some sermon by a rabbi, and on a Sabbath evening[?] at that, but a large propaganda speech which they had already heard earlier in Kraków — the board permitted the lecture in the synagogue, bypassing all formalities in the process, and even co-signed the invitations.
When the writer of these lines some time later approached the board with the request to permit in the synagogue a lecture by President Ze'ev Jabotinsky, after long debates they came out with a refusal, which was at the same time also communicated to the representatives.
Such a one-sided and partisan act, which aroused the greatest indignation among those affected as well as among all neutral people, demands and calls for the strongest protest.
Even the opponents of the movement will have to admit that President Jabotinsky is a personality of such stature that ministers and statesmen of the whole world receive him with honour, and that he has at least the same authority, dignity and entitlement to give a lecture in the synagogue as any one of the many Zionist party agitators and fund-raisers.
With great astonishment one must ask: why did they not also, for the lecture of Rabbi Gold, consult the community bodies, and only in the exceptional case of President Jabotinsky did they hastily convene the board and the council of representatives?
The situation becomes even sadder in that those burdened with a bad conscience now want to use all sorts of methods to justify themselves and to wriggle out of such an embarrassing affair, which made such a depressing impression in our town.
Among other things it is also pointed out that President Jabotinsky's lecture was supposed to have a political purpose; now we must ask: did Rabbi Gold give a mere sermon? His lecture, after all, was also a political one, but in the view of the gentlemen of the board and of the council of representatives, one quite definite Zionist group has the right for its political purposes, and only that group has the right to hold public events of the general Jewry in Katowice.
In the very next few days people will come to the Jews of Katowice and demand of them large donations for the community building, and then, as always in such cases, they will appeal to their sense of solidarity.
But the gentlemen of the board and the council of representatives should be in no doubt: under the present circumstances and in such cases, the Jewish citizens of our town will regard the call for unity and self-sacrifice as very insincere and dishonest, and they will treat it with reserve.
Solidarity is not demanded only when money is needed; it must be proved by deeds, and these proofs the board and the council of representatives owe us.
Y. D.

Let Us Preserve the “Maccabi”!

(On the margin of the “fusion” question of “Maccabi” and “Nordia” in Sosnowiec).
The Jewish public of Sosnowiec that takes an interest in national sport already knows that the “Maccabi” finds itself in the same situation as the “Hakoach”, because the national circles have lost interest in the renaissance ideal of a re-awakening national life in the spirit of Nordau’s “muscular Judaism”, which ought to be cultivated by the national sports clubs such as “Maccabi”, “Hakoach”; and that as a result the so strenuous work of physical education and sporting achievement for the Jewish youth over almost two decades is, unfortunately, being destroyed; and this work, to which we once tied so many hopes, is being wrecked with our own hands, through negligence and public neglect.
Many are the causes of this state of affairs, but my present reflections aim to touch [?] on the already-mentioned fusion question.
I will therefore go straight to the heart of the matter:
Being unable to accept the thought that over the “Maccabi”, which has existed for over 20 years already, the “sword of Damocles” — eviction — should hang incessantly, the writer of these lines began to seek a way out of the situation and turned to the local Zionist organisation, as well as to all national youth organisations, with the request that they take an interest in the sinking “Maccabi”. Unfortunately, the action did not bring the proper success. I must add that, although [?] by agreement with the headquarters the organisations “Hashomer Hatzair”, “Hanoar Hatzioni”, “Nordia” [?], “Akiba” [?] and others had undertaken the obligation to cooperate actively with the “Maccabi”, we nevertheless received no material or financial support whatsoever from those organisations.
As a “Maccabi” activist of many years, president and lately a board member of the institution, feeling responsible for the institution which I served for so many years morally and materially, I endeavoured to save the “Maccabi” and its existence at any price.
Here we have come to the last and most important question in the existence of the “Maccabi”.
As is surely known, one of the reasons for the crisis in [—] “Maccabi” was the leaving of the “Maccabi” by many Revisionist sportsmen and the founding of their own Revisionist club, “Nordia”. Clearly, with joint work the “Maccabi” would have had an assured [?] sporting and material future. But in talks on this the Revisionists always put forward an unacceptable demand, namely that the “Maccabi” leave the World Union and adopt another name. Because of the latter, the attempts at unification came to nothing as long as a year ago.
A short time ago the former president of “Nordia”, Mr. B. Jasny [?], approached me in order to begin talks on the above-mentioned subject.
After a series of negotiations the following joint platform was found between the representatives of “Maccabi” and “Nordia”: 1) the name remains henceforth “Maccabi”; 2) “Maccabi” remains affiliated to the World Union; 3) “Maccabi” does not compel its members to collect for the national funds and for Tel-Ḥai, or to buy the shekel and the dinar.
Here, however, a storm broke out concerning my person in particular and the platform, on the grounds that I had thereby betrayed the national interests, etc. [?].
I therefore wish to make the following statement to the public from this place:
I do not wish in the least to defend the platform from the Zionist standpoint and from my specific party standpoint. I am fully aware that the proposed platform is a crime against our [?] national principles from the standpoint of prestige — I underline the word prestige, because in practice “Maccabi” has in any case contributed nothing to the KKL [Jewish National Fund], and the monies collected for that purpose under the name “Kfar Maccabi” have always been used for other purposes.
But let all those who criticise my step so sharply — especially those who only now remembered that they are “Maccabi” members and attack my person with such special zeal — remember that it is not I who am to blame for the “situation”, but first and foremost they themselves, with their apathy and indifference towards the “Maccabi”.
All those who shout that the KKL is being robbed in the “Maccabi” did not pay at all the 10 to 15 groszy for “Kfar Maccabi”, and also stood at a distance when I had an eviction for the “Maccabi”, and paid no membership dues to help the “Maccabi”. Now they make a racket, as if the existence of the “Maccabi” had really been on their minds...
I wanted and want further to save the “Maccabi”, dear to us all, from complete ruin.
By this thought, I am sure, all members will be guided who care [?] first and foremost that the “Maccabi” remain the one and only Jewish sports association in Sosnowiec where the Jewish youth will be able to develop physically.
The general meeting of “Maccabi”, convened for 3 January, will have the slogan: — “Let us preserve the ‘Maccabi’!”
Meir Lancman
Former president and current board member of “Maccabi”.
Strange Livelihoods.

It seems that in the whole world there are no harder and stranger livelihoods than precisely in our parts, where one person lies[?] practically on top of another and where most people do not know[?] in the morning where they will get the few groszy to get through the day.

And yet there exist in the wide world various strange livelihoods worth writing about.

Tea tasters make a good living. There are more than six hundred different kinds of tea, and the big tea exporters in England, France and other countries want to know which kinds are the best; so they employ tea tasters, who can tell from a little bit of tea, which they only take onto their lips, which tea has a fine aroma and will be bought by the public. Since such connoisseurs of tea are very few in the world, they are sought everywhere and paid as much as they want.

Another livelihood that pays well is that of the meat smellers. I saw them in Prague. Prague has many sausage factories, which send their sausages and smoked[?] meats to the four corners of the world; one must therefore know exactly which meats are fresh enough to be sent to distant places. But since one cannot cut open the sausage or the meat to see whether they will survive the long journey, a long thin needle is stuck into the meat, and the smeller senses from the smell of the needle whether the meat can be sent off and still arrive fresh.

In Sweden, the big match factories employ, at good wages, many people who have nothing else to do but take out of every batch[?] of matches that is finished a few little boxes of matches and slowly light them, to see whether the manufacture has succeeded — and for that they get themselves well paid.

In the Lyon silk factories various fatty substances are used in silk manufacture. If just one of the fatty substances is not fresh enough, the manufacture of the silk is spoiled. Therefore many people are employed there who must every day taste the various fats to see whether they are suitable for the manufacture.

In Japan many gas masks are manufactured and shipped all over the world. To test whether the masks are good, a few pieces are taken out of every lot that is finished and tested. In a room[?] filled with gas — a man goes in with a mask and stays there for a certain time. If he comes out alive, he gets an English shilling for it. There are hundreds of people in the Japanese factories who risk their lives every day for an English shilling.

In the last year of the war, 1918, a Viennese brought to the Leipzig fair "a vest for soldiers". He said that the vest could not be shot through even with cannon. He looked for people who would put on the vest and let themselves be shot at with real bullets, but no one was found who would be willing to risk his life.

Only years later, at the Chicago exhibition, were his vests tested. He paid 100 dollars to everyone who let himself be shot at; about a hundred people earned a hundred dollars each, only one was wounded, and nothing happened to the rest in this strange livelihood. A few years later he tested his vest on himself — and was shot dead.

Z. Haber, Vienna.
Oneg Shabbat — Parshat Shemot

Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion — collected and edited by Yehuda.
Parshat Shemot

a) "Now there arose a new king... And he said unto his people: Behold, the people of the children of Israel are more and mightier than we. Come, let us deal wisely with them" (1:9–10.)
The verse does not mention that the previous king had died; from the expression "arose" one may infer that he ascended the throne through an uprising, seizing power from the previous Pharaoh — and that all insurgents have always found the best means of staying in power to be the use of their influence over the masses through "let us deal wisely": through incitement against Jews, through feeding[?] the people with Jew-hatred, and through "when there befalleth any war" — through thirst for war... Imrei[?] Chen.

b) "But the more they afflicted them, the more they multiplied" (ibid., 12.)
Simply: had the Egyptians not tormented the Jews, and had they been able to assimilate, only a very small handful of Jews would have remained; but when "they afflicted them" — when Jews are tormented — "the more they multiplied": then the Jews increase, apostates come back, and no one deserts to the gentile camp.
Ta'alumot Chochma.

c) "And it came to pass, because the midwives feared God, that He made them houses"
What reward did Miriam receive? Wisdom. As it is said: "Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom." Midrash Tanchuma.
Because when one sees[?] a pious person, people say that he is pious[?] because he is not clever — therefore God gave Miriam, as a reward for her fear of Heaven, wisdom... Yalkut Yehuda.

d) "And he looked on their burdens" (2:11.)
He saw that they had no rest; he went and said to Pharaoh: Whoever has a slave, if he does not rest one day in seven, he dies; and these slaves of yours, if you do not let them rest one day in seven, they will die. He said to him: Go and do for them as you say. Moses went and instituted for them the Sabbath day to rest. Shemot Rabbah 1.
[unclear word; probably: Thus], Moses was the initiator of the Sabbath. He brought it about that Jews should rest one day a week, and so the Sabbath came into being; that is why on the Sabbath we say in prayer "Moses rejoiced in the gift of his portion", because Moses was the creator of the Jewish Sabbath... Shibbolei HaLeket.
• • •
No Jewish idea penetrated the gentile world as deeply as the Sabbath. A hundred years before the common era the Jewish Sabbath already dominated the world. Josephus Flavius writes in his book "Against Apion" (II, 39): "There is no Greek or barbarian city and no nation into which the custom of the seventh day, on which we rest, has not wished to penetrate." The Roman and Greek poets of that time mocked the Romans and Greeks, "the half-Jews", who light Sabbath candles. The satirist Persius (lived in the years 34–62 "before" our era) jeers bitingly at the Romans' adoption of the Jewish Sabbath custom of lighting olive-oil lamps on the Sabbath, eating fish and drinking wine (in his Satires 184–179). In a word: until the Christians exchanged the Sabbath for Sunday, the Sabbath dominated the gentile world. The famous Roman thinker Seneca writes: "Through keeping the Sabbath, which also spread among the Romans, the victors (the Romans) have been brought down under the yoke of the vanquished (the Jews)."
Sefer HaShabbat.
• • •
"Nothing in the world — writes Proudhon — can compare with the Sabbath, whose foundation is equality, freedom and above all religiosity. From the Sabbath, society began to develop morally, healthily[?] and happily."
I have to say: six hundred thousand Bismarcks, with all their attempts[?] to lighten the yoke of the worker, did not [—] the one [—] Moses, the creator of the Sabbath.
"...In the Roman theatres comedies were staged about Jews who keep the Sabbath, and yet the Jewish Sabbath was the cornerstone of human morality."
A. Jellinek ("The Jewish Race/Tribe").

e) "And God saw the children of Israel, and God took cognizance of them" (ibid., 25.)
When does God see a Jew? When things are bad for him he comes into the synagogue and pours out his bitter heart before Him.
"And God saw the children of Israel" — when He, as it were, saw the Jews coming to Him — "and God knew": He understood that things were not well with them... Tochachat Chaim.
• • •
"I will be with him in trouble" —
When trouble comes upon Jews, then they are with God, then they nestle up to Him. Leket Shmarim.

f) "Now Moses was keeping the flock of Jethro" (3:1)
A Hasid once asked the Ruzhiner:
— Rebbe, you have so many Hasidim, no evil eye, why do you not have such a disciple as Rabbi Simcha Bunem of Przysucha had: the Kotzker?
Reb Yisroeltshe of Ruzhin answers him:
The Gemara in Chullin relates that Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair's donkey was careful [printed: "guhar"] to avoid robbery. One asks: was Moses our teacher not as great a man as Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair? Then why did Moses have to lead his sheep "to the farthest end of the wilderness" — "to keep away from robbery, so that they should not graze in others' fields" (Rashi) — why were Moses's sheep not careful of robbery by themselves?
But the answer is: Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair had only one donkey, so he could imbue it with so much holiness that it would itself be willing[?]; Moses, however, had to pasture a large flock of sheep...

g) "And when he seeth thee, he will be glad in his heart" (4:14.)
Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai said: The heart that rejoiced in the greatness of his brother shall wear the Urim and Thummim. Midrash Rabbah.
What has this to do with the Urim and Thummim?
But in the days of the Second Temple there were no Urim and Thummim, because there were quarrels between the priests and the kings, who fought each other; and only a king can consult the Urim and Thummim, so there must be peace between the king and the priest who wore the Urim and Thummim.
That is what Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai says: the heart that rejoiced in the greatness of his brother — Aaron the priest, who rejoiced in the greatness of his brother Moses, who was a king — when there is peace between king and priest — "shall wear the Urim and Thummim".
R. Yehuda Leib Ginzburg.
An Important Week.

[Humour — satirical verse.] (Day-rhymes)
An important week has passed for the Jews,
a week of the noblest "kedushah"-yearnings...
The Jews have had their holiday, the greatest,
the true "holy" holiday "Sylvester" [New Year's Eve];
little Jews paid money without mercy,
ran to the holiday with "our" stubbornness,
pawned a pillow and sold their underwear —
just to celebrate together with the "Jureks" [Jurek: nickname for a Polish gentile]...
"Sylvester" — a holy "night of vigil" (leil shimurim)
for Jewish "pious" ones and free drunkards[?];
presumably, the Christian was driven out of "Sylvester",
and the little Jews remained there by themselves;
it's already come to the point, presumably — I mean it without joking —
that Christians are throwing "Sylvester" away in anger,
they no longer want the "Jewish" holiday
sitting together with Jews — they swear —
they'll turn round, the Aryan folk,
content — but to the other side:
they'll fill the kloyzn (prayer houses) densely
and eat a latke by the Hanukkah lights...
Shmerele.
Years.

[Humour — Zagłębie.] With the year 1937 everyone in Zagłębie has grown a year older except, of course, the girls, who never grow older. A year passes very quickly; in general a year is nothing much in Zagłębie nowadays — today you can stand a whole year in a shop and not see a grosz of takings. In the Będzin kehilla, before they deal with a petition, a whole year can pass as well.
A year contains no more than three hundred and sixty-five days; therefore all the local societies and institutions are indeed planning to submit a petition to the League of Nations that the days of the new year be increased, so that there will be enough of them to arrange flower-days (charity collection days).
Prophecies for the New Year.

[Humour — Zagłębie, kehilla.] [Page header:] "Der Kokh-Lefl" (The Cooking Spoon). Humour and satire. Compiled by Amotsli[?].
Prophecies for the New Year.
At the beginning of February ("Luty") the kehilla board will hold a meeting about a coal campaign. After a rather long discussion a coal commission will be elected, which will have to work out, within two[?] months, the project of how the coal campaign is to be organised.
—
The committee to build a mikveh in Sosnowiec will be taken for an examination by the doctors who take part in the fund-raising campaign for the Jewish hospital. If the examination turns out favourably, a competition will be announced for a brochure entitled "A Mikveh in 50 Years' Time".
—
In the month of April the president of the kehilla will begin writing memoirs of his kehilla activity. The memoirs will contain a special chapter entitled "How Urke Nachalnik's[?] comrade from Sosnowiec swindled me" [Urke Nachalnik — pen-name of a Jewish ex-thief turned writer].
—
The Jewish institutions will receive permits to arrange flower-days (charity collection days) only on Sundays. On the first of April 1937 the committee of winter[?] aid for the unemployed will issue support to all Jewish families who are registered at the gmina (municipality) to receive kimcha [Passover flour relief].
—
This year there will take place a consultation of all public activists in Zagłębie on the question of how to combat the Jewish informers (mosrim).
The Old Man.

[Humour — New Year poem.]
I met an old man,
with a parchment-yellow face,
and he walked nimbly,
with a bold step, and fast.
A heavy pack of belongings
he was dragging on his shoulders,
and his beard, the silver-white[?] one,
floated about in the wind.
I soon became curious
to find out who he is,
and I asked the people in the street:
who is this old giant?
Sly eyes, nimble his[?] steps,
and bent like an old man —
only a person who wants to run away
makes such giant leaps.
So I went straight after him, like a shadow,
followed him, tracked him,
I wanted to investigate thoroughly
what he carries in the bundles.
Suddenly his heavy pack
burst open on the way,
and out of the pack poured
whole bundles of life-days.
Such[?] days, dear, good,
pampered days, intimate.
My days — I recognised them —
the old man[?] was dragging with him.
Now everything was answered,
everything became clear to me:
the carrier of the suitcases
was the Old Year.
He who robbed me of the days
drags them off somewhere
in order to buy[?] a snail
made up like a little angel.
My days — to hell with them!
Let them go up in smoke;
I would already have forgiven him
if he took the crisis along too.
A. L. Wolfson.

Sosnowiec "Chesed shel Emes" in danger.
As "Der Kokh-Lefl" has learned, the Sosnowiec "Chesed shel Emes" (burial society) has received an invitation to come to Geneva soon.
Apparently this is connected with the Chinese-Japanese conflict, and the president of the League of Nations is of the opinion that the Sosnowiec "Chesed-shel-Emes men" are specialists in "smoothing out" [pun: "oysgleykhn" — to settle a dispute, and to lay out a corpse].

The Beautiful Benvenida (8)

[Serialized novel.] A novel that took place in the first Jewish ghetto and stirred up the governments of Spain, and Turkey.
For readers who have not read the beginning, we give the following summary:
Benvenida is the name of a Marrano woman of the Spanish Jews, whom the Inquisition had forced to convert, but who secretly went on living as Jews. Many of them fled Spain in order to be able to return to the Jewish faith. Because of this Benvenida and her father came to the first Jewish ghetto, in Venice.
The Spanish government demanded of the Venetian government that it catch such fugitives and send them back to Spain.
A hunt began in the Jewish lane to catch the Marranos, and Benvenida's father chose death[?] on the spot[?]: on Rosh Hashana[?] he jumped from a bridge.
Benvenida was caught, and they wanted to send her to Spain at once, but influential Jews of the ghetto obtained that she be held in the Venetian prison until they could look around[?] for what could be done for her.
Meanwhile Nathan Ashkenazi arrived in Venice, the son of Shlomo Ashkenazi, a famous Jewish diplomat in Turkey. He became interested in Benvenida's fate and undertook to save her.
Nathan Ashkenazi and the prisoner Benvenida were brought together in a side room of a hall where Roman aristocrats had arranged a ball for all the diplomats and royal people. The Jew Nathan Ashkenazi was there as the diplomat of Turkey.
When he caught sight of Benvenida he fell in love with her; her beauty and her education enchanted him, and he swore that he would not rest until he had freed her.
The closeness[?] with Benvenida was exploited by the ambassador of Spain, who denounced Ashkenazi to the Turkish court, claiming that he was disloyal to Turkey and that he was giving away state secrets.
Ashkenazi, however, did not want to break off relations with the Spanish ambassador completely, because he believed that he would help him free Benvenida, with whom he was very much in love.
And now read on:
Nathan Ashkenazi believed deeply that his hopes would be fulfilled, that his dreams would come true as soon as possible. On coming home he got his family interested, and with their influence at the Turkish court he expected[?] to get help from the whole court, which would foil every effort of the Inquisition in Spain to have Benvenida fall into its claws. So dreamed Nathan Ashkenazi.
Leaving Venice was hard for him; it seemed to him that he was abandoning Benvenida to the fate of death, without a protector. He consoled himself that it was not for long, that soon he would be back by the Venetian canals, and then he would come with his arms outstretched to receive a freed Benvenida.
A lovely dream Nathan Ashkenazi had as he set foot on the soil of Turkey after his sea voyage from Venice to Constantinople, in expectation that he would soon get the consent of the whole court to do everything so that his effort to free Benvenida would succeed.
And the dream went further[?] — Turkey sends a ship to Venice to bring Benvenida.
With this dream he entered the Turkish court, but soon sensed that he was given a cold[?] reception, not as friendly toward him as he had imagined; he even met with distrust.
At the Turkish court it was already known that in Venice he had clashed with the ambassador of Spain, and it was said that in Venice he had not behaved as a diplomat ought to behave.
A rumour of a different character also soon reached him — a rumour similar to the terrible talk he had heard in Venice from the royal representative of France, that the ambassador of Spain was hinting that he, Nathan Ashkenazi, was giving him secrets of the Turkish court.
Only in Turkey did he grasp the intrigue that the ambassador of Spain had spun against him in Venice.
As to whether Turkey would grant his request for Benvenida, he soon realised it would not come to that, because she is a prisoner on the order of the Spanish kingdom. Nathan Ashkenazi took it hard[?], as if he himself were a prisoner.
He applied to be received by the Grand Vizier, the chief head of the Turkish court.
At the same time he saw that Turkey was beginning to change toward the Jews, that the time when Jews played a great role around the Sultan's rule was disappearing.
Until he was received by the Grand Vizier, quite some time passed. This too was proof to him that at the Turkish court a hostile and distrustful attitude toward Jews was forming. He compared his present reception with the escort he had had when he left for Venice.
Then they had pampered him, whole staffs of officials had bowed before him; now he is barely greeted by simple servants. In the time until the Grand Vizier received him, he went to diplomats of other countries who were in Turkey and tried to get the ambassador of Spain at the Turkish court to inform his government that it need not demand Benvenida's extradition from Venice. Here he took on a struggle that was full of [—] for himself.
(To be continued)

The General Meeting of the "Gemilut Chesed" Fund Did Not Take Place.
The meeting is to be held in a month's time.

[Będzin — institutions; free-loan fund.] The important general meeting of the local Gemilut Chasadim (free-loan) fund aroused extraordinary interest throughout the town. Already several days earlier the meeting of this institution had been the talk of the day.
The climax was reached on Saturday and Sunday: on both days meetings and consultations were held by various sides on how to mobilise the "forces" that would help bring about the desired "victories".
In connection with the meeting there came specially the director of the "Joint" [JDC], Mr. Giterman, Inspector Pershtshevinski [?] and a member of the Ts.K. [central committee], Mr. Liberman of Zawiercie.
The meeting was to be held in the hall of the Merchants' Association. Even before the meeting began the hall was overflowing and could not take in any more of the large number of members who had come to the meeting.
In the presence of over 200 people in the hall, the chairman Mr. Rubinlicht opens the meeting and proposes as presiding officer the chairman of the Artisans' Association, Mr. Goldshtein. The proposal is accepted, and Mr. Goldshtein invites onto the presidium Messrs. Michał Lewin and Józef Rus, and as secretaries Rolnicki and Kaner [?].
After the minutes of the last general meeting were read, Mr. Rubinlicht is given the floor for the activity report, but in the middle of the report protests are heard that many members cannot attend the meeting because of the crush, and a motion is brought to break up the meeting.
The motion obtains a large majority, and the presiding officer announces that the meeting is broken off.
As we are informed, the supervisory authority has demanded that the meeting take place no later than 5 January [styczeń] of this year. Most probably, however, the meeting will be held only in a month's time.
— Later a session of the board of the free-loan fund took place with the participation of Messrs. Giterman and Pershtshevinski [?]. At the session the question of the fund's future board was discussed.
The representatives of the "Joint" demanded that at the next general meeting a provisional board of 7 persons be elected, which would act until the second general meeting, to take place no later than 31 March of this year — and, most importantly, that not a single member of the present board be elected among the 7.
Chairman Mr. Rubinlicht spoke out against this proposal, arguing that the members of the fund have the right to elect the persons in whom they have confidence, and that consequently those who have been on the board until now may also be elected.
The representatives of the "Joint", however, would not agree to any compromise on the matter and declared that if their demand were not met, they would be forced to withdraw the "Joint" funds.
Mass Meeting of Jewish Artisans

President Mr. Szajn is to build an artisans' school.
As we have already written, last week a consultation took place between representatives of both Jewish artisans' associations in our town. The aim of the consultation was to bring about peace between the artisans who belong to the association at Kołłątaja 45 and the one at Morawskiego [?] 4. The result of the consultation was that both sides agreed to call an artisans' meeting at which the "peace" would be proclaimed.
On the strength of this decision a meeting took place on Sunday morning in the "Nowości" cinema, with the participation of the president of the Central [union], Mr. M. Fiszer (Kraków).
The hall was packed full; on the presidium sat delegates from the neighbouring towns, the two [?] boards, and also representatives of the above-mentioned associations.
President Mr. L. Goldsztajn opens the meeting with a greeting to the guests and reports on the course of the peace negotiations, which were conducted at the premises of the Artisans' Union. At the same time Mr. Goldsztajn appeals to the representatives of the opposing side to state whether they are for the unification.
On this question Messrs. Zylbergeld, Tuchszneider, Drajter, L. Fuks, Kilsztok and Landner (president of the artisans' association in Dąbrowa) speak; all welcome the "peace" and call for a consolidation of the artisan masses.
Then Mr. Fiszer is given the floor for his lecture on the general Jewish situation in Poland as a whole, and on that of the Jewish artisans in particular.
The speaker deals with [?] a series of topical problems, among them the question of emigration, and comes to the conclusion that the Jewish artisans, who form a great force, will not abandon their workshops.
After the lecture the peace resolutions are adopted unanimously and received with enthusiasm by the assembled public; the members sitting on the presidium shake hands, and Mr. Fiszer kisses Goldsztajn — with this the official part of the meeting ends.
Then Mr. Fiszer gives a report on the World Jewish Congress; the report is delivered in the presence of President Mr. Chaim Szajn, who was the delegate of the town of Będzin to the World Congress.
Mr. A. Liter [?] speaks about the tasks of "ORT" for Jewish artisanry; in the name of Mr. Szajn he announces that Mr. Szajn will build an artisans' school; the announcement is received with great satisfaction by those assembled.
General Meeting of "Malbish Arumim"

Under the chairmanship of town councillor (Ratman) Mr. M. Hampel, the annual general meeting of the society "Malbish Arumim" [Clothing the Naked] took place on Tuesday evening at the premises of "Ahavat Chesed".
From the reports presented it emerges that the society has a deficit of 500 zł. from the last winter clothing campaign.
In discussing the budget for the coming year, Mr. S. Brat [?] proposes to earmark a sum of 300 zł. for renting premises for the society. The proposal is adopted. The "new" board was elected by acclamation.
"Heaven and Earth Have Sworn to Hide No Secret"

Slaughterer Radoszycki caught slaughtering "on the side".
As is known, the young slaughterers Radoszycki and Gerlic were taken on as kehilla officials after they had signed a written ban and herem [excommunication] undertaking that from now on they would not slaughter "on the side" [illegally].
But, as the saying goes, "as at 7, so at 70". Radoszycki did indeed give his signature on the written ban — and slaughtered illegally.
The kehilla official who was watching him caught him in a room slaughtering poultry.
As a result Radoszycki was suspended from his post; the poultry dealer, too, has had the discount he had until now been receiving from the kehilla withdrawn.
New Year Greetings

The Starostwo [district office] announces that the Starosta, Mr. Baksa, as representative of the government, will receive New Year greetings from the public and from organisations as well as institutions — for the President of the State, Marshal Rydz-Śmigły and the government — today, Friday the 1st of January [styczeń], at 12.30 o'clock in the Starostwo building.
"You Signed an Engagement Contract with Another — At Least Give Me Back the Cost of the Contract"

— cries a father-in-law-to-be to his former bridegroom...
A local young fellow signed tna'im [an engagement contract] a few weeks ago with a girl from Sosnowiec.
The bridegroom, however, came to regret the match, and without waiting until he had obtained a release, he became engaged [lit. "fined", by tna'im] to a second bride from Będzin.
When the Sosnowiec in-law found out about this, he summoned the "gem" to the rabbinate and argued: "You signed tna'im with another girl. At least give me back what the tna'im cost me."
The rabbinical court agreed with the claim and ruled that the former bridegroom must pay 50 zł. for the expenses of the first tna'im.
Nominated Kehilla Board Resigns

(Sosnowiec)
In recent days all members of the nominated kehilla board, headed by vice-president Dr. Hercman, notified the supervisory authority that, because they cannot work together with the kehilla commissioner Mr. Tencer, they are resigning.
As we are informed, the resignation came about for the following reason: a few days ago the kehilla commissioner called the nominees to a meeting about the new kehilla budget.
At the meeting some of the members raised the demand that, before one proceeds to draw up the budget, the subsidies that had been provided for in last year's budget should first be paid out; and since the kehilla commissioner categorically spoke out against this, all the board members left the meeting.
Later they held a meeting at which a decision on the resignation was adopted
Several Former Dozors, and the Slaughterers Too, Benefit from the Amnesty

In 1934, as is known, the kehilla books were taken away by the supervisory authority, and after they had been audited several dozors [kehilla board members], and the slaughterers too, were brought to court.
This week the accused received notices from the district court that a penalty of up to 6 months had been provided for them, but on the strength of the amnesty they are released from it.
A Theft in the Pogoń Beit Midrash

During the night from Monday to Tuesday several window-panes of the Pogoń beit midrash [Pogoń, a district of Sosnowiec] were knocked out, through which the thieves got inside, where they broke open the Holy Ark, tore off the mantles of the Torah scrolls and also stole the wall clock [?].
Weddings, Births and Deaths

According to statistical figures, last year in Sosnowiec there were 95 weddings, 330 births and 217 deaths.
The figures are interesting in comparison with previous years: for example, in 1935 there were 123 weddings, 376 births, and 184 died.
In 1934 — weddings 127, births 489, and 179 died.
As it turns out, in 1936 the number of dead rose sharply.
Suicide of an Apostate

On Saturday night the procurator [authorised signatory] of the firm "Oskar Spiegel", Józef Ginsberg, a baptised Jew, committed suicide in his own flat.
That same evening he had invited his acquaintances to his home, and in the middle of the "bibka" [party] he went out into a side room and shot himself.
The suicide's wife is Jewish, a daughter of the secretary of the Warsaw kehilla.
Punished for Insulting the Polish Nation

This Monday, at a certain moment, an exchange of words took place between the merchant Mr. Chaim Fiszel and a Christian. The latter later reported to the police that Fiszel had used insulting words about the Polish nation.
On the basis of the accusation Fiszel was arrested. After the investigation he was released the next day in the afternoon.
Hours of Slaughter at the Slaughterhouse Fixed

The manager of the municipal slaughterhouse has announced that from the 1st of this month slaughtering will take place at the following times: from 8 in the morning until 12 noon for treyf, and from 12 until 4 for kosher.
—o—
The Kehilla Commissioner Makes the Budget Alone
As we are informed, the kehilla budget for the coming year is being drawn up by the kehilla commissioner alone, without any participation of the nominated advisory council.
—o—
From the District Court
Before the local district court stood the local resident Józef Szwimer, in whose possession some time ago 200 cigarette lighters smuggled from Germany had been found.
Szwimer was sentenced to a fine of 14 thousand zł. and a month's arrest.

A Theft on a Bus
From Jankel Finsztemski [?] of [Jegrzet?], travelling on a bus to Sosnowiec, a wallet containing 200 zł. was stolen.
Will the Kielce Voivodeship Be Liquidated?

[Kielce — administration and state.] A letter from the Kielce city president to the Speaker of the Sejm, Car.
Lately rumours are again circulating in Kielce that the Kielce voivodeship is to be liquidated. Since these reports are causing an understandable unease among all circles of the population in Kielce and its surroundings, this very important matter was also discussed at the last session of the local city council, at which it was resolved to charge the city administration with checking whether the rumours correspond to reality, and to keep watch over this question.
In connection with this, the Kielce city president, Mr. Artwiński, has sent a letter of request to the Speaker of the Sejm, Car, who was elected as deputy for the Kielce district, asking that he exert his influence on the project concerning the liquidation of the Kielce voivodeship.
The said letter also recalls the attachment that the late liberator of Poland, Marshal Józef Piłsudski, had for the city of Kielce — he was an honorary citizen of the city of Kielce, into which he was the first to march in with his legionnaires.
The Quota Has Been Fixed

[Kielce — shechita.] For ritual slaughter "for the Kielce district.
This week the voivodeship office in Kielce fixed the quota of kosher meat for all the Jewish communities of the Kielce voivodeship. The city of Kielce has been allotted a quota of 227 thousand kilos of meat (live weight) for 3 months. That is, instead of the 175 head of cattle and 200 head of small livestock that were slaughtered in Kielce every week until now, from 1 January it will be permitted to slaughter only up to 60 animals a week, which comes to 2 (two) decagrams of kosher meat per head.
For Częstochowa, where there are some thirty-odd thousand Jewish souls, the "quota" was fixed at 345 thousand kilos a quarter — about 2½ decagrams per head.
Almost the same proportion has also been fixed for the other larger communities of the Kielce voivodeship, proportionally according to the number of Jewish souls in each town.
It has also been determined in which towns it will be permitted to slaughter according to ritual slaughter, and in which it will not be allowed to slaughter at all.
Of the 7 communities in the Kielce county, ritual slaughter will be permitted in only three towns: in Kielce (including Białogon), Chęciny and Bodzentyn, whereas in the towns of Łagów, Daleszyce, Słupia Nowa and Suchedniów it is not permitted to slaughter.

Laks, Henryk Wanijski[?], G. Sokołowski, Y. Nussbaum, Sh. Lejchter, Yosl Silberstein, Natan Białobroda, Y. Winiausz, Yeshaya Cukier, Y. M. Herszkowicz, Y. Białobroda and M. G. Bukszban[?].
Mr. Y. M. Rajzman was elected chairman of the committee, Messrs. Laks and Winiausz vice-chairmen, Mr. Fishl Herszkowicz treasurer, and Mr. G. Sokołowski secretary.

Why Did Jabotinsky Not Speak in the Katowice Synagogue?

(Concerning the open letter to the kehilla)
The writer of these lines does not belong to the Katowice kehilla bodies, nor has he been authorised by them to answer the New Zionist Org. But being a Zionist — not a "new" one, of course — and knowing the matter, I permit myself to explain the following:
First of all, the whole matter is no longer topical, because the Katowice Revisionists' application to the kehilla and the refusal took place several months ago; and at that time the kehilla refused to give the synagogue not only to the Revisionists but also to another party, whose leaders are likewise received by ministers and statesmen.
It is not true that Rabbi Gold [?], appearing in the Katowice synagogue on behalf of the "Hebron Fund" (Mifal Hevron), spoke in the name of a particular group; for a lecture given in the name of the Zionist World Organization and the Jewish Agency, which unite in themselves so many factions and currents of the Jewish people — so [?], which internationally and legally recognised bodies can claim more right than the N.Z.O.? — and that is what Mr. Y. D. Chisen did.
And one more thing: you surely know that [?] the kehilla building now going up in Katowice aroused [—] enthusiasm among the Katowice Jews, and that even before construction began, thousands of zł. in voluntary donations had already flowed in, apart from the fixed kehilla-tax surcharge.
And so it is also with the Jewish National Home being built in the Land of Israel, which you will no longer manage to obstruct.
L. Tenenbaum.
Rescue Campaign for the "Chofetz Chaim" Yeshiva.

The world-famous "Chofetz Chaim" yeshiva in Radun, which the world-renowned gaon and tzaddik the Chofetz Chaim, of blessed memory, founded and led for nearly 70 years, influencing it with his great, morally deep and pure soul, has in the course of its existence produced thousands of Torah scholars, geniuses of Torah and Musar, holding an acknowledged leading position in world Jewry.
Today the "Chofetz Chaim" yeshiva is under the leadership of the Chofetz Chaim's son, son-in-law and grandson, whose aim is to continue the holy teaching of their great father and rabbi with the 400 yeshiva students — a large number of them from Poland — making them steadfast enough against the corrupt "modern civilization", so that they may spread everywhere a Torah of life and true Jewish morality and ethics.
Unfortunately, the foreign support for the yeshiva has nowadays been greatly reduced, and there is a danger that the most esteemed, largest and oldest yeshiva in Poland will have to close altogether.
For this reason a rescue campaign for the "Chofetz Chaim" yeshiva is being conducted in Będzin, as in all the other larger cities of Poland, by the yeshiva's delegate, Rabbi Yaakov Karlsbrun, together with a local committee of respected local householders.
The respected local householders R' Mendel Rozenzaft [?] and R' Avraham Leib Grinwald have been appointed treasurers; they will send the collected money directly to the yeshiva.
It is to be hoped that the Jews of Będzin, who are famous for their refinement and generosity of heart, will receive the esteemed yeshiva delegate warmly and support the rescue campaign for the "Chofetz Chaim" yeshiva with an open hand.
2 Suicides of Young People.

The caretaker of the courtyard at Sandoszecher [?] 33 in Sosnowiec, going out into the yard at dawn, saw a young woman in night clothes lying unconscious. At the alarm, neighbours gathered and saw that it was Mrs. S., who lives in the same courtyard.
She was immediately carried up to her flat, where she was brought back to consciousness. As it turned out, she had attempted suicide by poisoning herself, and when the poison began to burn her badly she ran out into the yard in her nightshirt, where she fainted.
The reason is said to be that for a long time she had received no letter from her husband, who had left her, and, fearing that her husband had abandoned her, she committed the terrible deed.
The would-be suicide is in the Jewish hospital; as we are informed, her condition is serious.
— A second suicide, which also caused grief among the whole Jewish population, was committed by 23-year-old Simcha Paluszniecki.
On Sunday [?] S. P-cki came home as always and sat down with a book in the kitchen. Next morning at dawn, when his father went into the kitchen, he saw a terrible sight: Simcha had committed suicide by hanging himself.
The suicide was known as a steady and hard-working young man, and it is therefore difficult to discover what reason drove him to this desperate step.
A large crowd took part in his funeral, especially from the Revisionist organization. Mr. Lewinger spoke at the open grave.
