"A Public Kitchen".

(Sosnowiec's understanding of communal work. — The realization of a kitchen for free midday meals.)
The writer of these lines is faced every time with the question: why do we here in Sosnowiec treat every public undertaking with so much mockery, with such disdain? It is truly incomprehensible. A town that is in any case no worse situated than all the other towns in the country — and yet, yet everywhere there is more sense of responsibility for everything that is called "the community" than here with us at home.
It is no secret to anyone that we are, socially, the poorest of the poor. We are spiritually [?] backward. Proportionally, the smallest shtetl in Poland possesses more public institutions than we do, and what we do have — ah, how poor and limited it is.
We shall not even speak of our "sister town" Będzin, which has fallen greatly economically in recent years; yet there the public understanding is guarded at every step, and to its credit it must be said that not only is what exists maintained there, but one constantly strives [?] to renew; thus we hear that "Hakoach" is to build its own building, where it will be possible to raise youth according to the latest precepts of sport and gymnastics, while a certain philanthropist is himself to build a school for artisans. Of course these are all grandiose undertakings, of which we here cannot even dream. But when we compare ourselves with the small provincial shtetls, we will then come to the conclusion that even compared with them we are far behind.
The reasons for this? Quite simple: the Jews of Sosnowiec hold that everything that has to do with the community is in the form of a favour, and if it is a favour, then surely it is enough to give alms — why should there be any "yasher koach" [thanks]? No matter how much one gives, there is simply [?] no understanding among us for treating institutions as public undertakings which the people must care for and maintain; and as long as this does not change, as long as people will not want to understand that supporting an institution does not mean giving a burdensome charity from which one tries to wriggle out at every opportunity, but on the contrary, that thereby one pays a debt that one owes to society — as long as people here will not want to understand this thoroughly, so long will our institutions keep sinking.
Outside, the glitter catches the eye: there is trading [?], ostensibly, there is a bustle [?], people chase about — but only the upper part [?] actually makes a living; the rest do not have enough to get through the day. This should be remembered well and taken to heart at every opportunity.
Let it be known that a considerable number of residents live here — respectable, downtrodden people who are hungry in the literal sense of the word. People have already begun to see it, and from time to time it catches the eye of those who have an eye to see the need.
It is therefore to be welcomed that a group of intelligentsia have undertaken the initiative to open a kitchen where midday meals will be given out to respectable people.
The idea is a fine and highly useful one, and it is absolutely necessary to realize it.
In a number of larger towns such kitchens already exist, and we too need one here without any doubt, and the whole town must therefore help bring about the useful idea that certain communal workers have undertaken to carry out.
The creation of the planned kitchen is of enormous importance, because the midday meal sustains a person the whole day. In the morning and in the evening the poor man "scrapes by" somehow; in the morning he holds out hungry until midday, and in the evening one goes to bed without having eaten — so long as one knows that one has had a midday meal. But what happens when one does not eat a midday meal either, because a little warm food is impossible for the hungry to obtain? So with the opening of the free kitchen the initiators will achieve the most important thing that can possibly be done at the present moment.
But here one reservation must be made: that the midday meals be designated for the unemployed of all strata, and that the so-called professional "respectable" beggars should not push their way in.
This reservation must be taken into account even before the kitchen is set up, and then one will go to the town and say: we are creating such-and-such a kitchen, which will bring colossal benefit to poor, hungry people, and you must help us without any excuse. It will also be a sacred duty both of the Magistrat [municipality] and of the Jewish kehilla to subsidize this necessary [?] establishment.
It goes without saying that it is a duty and a sacred obligation of the aforementioned institutions to come to the aid in realizing the aforementioned kitchen. But that is not enough to release the Jewish population from its obligation; on the contrary, Jewish Sosnowiec must set the example, and then one can hope to receive, in the same measure, the further help and proper subsidies. Our citizens should remember this well already now, because if the scope is broader, if the initiators have an understanding for a large popular kitchen, where as many midday meals as possible can be given out, then accordingly one will be able to demand the subsidies.
One must therefore not make of the fine idea a miniature shop, where a few people will receive a couple of midday meals, and call that a "public kitchen".
The "public kitchen" must be created in proportion to the size of the town and according to the means of its inhabitants.
Dr. Papuri.
Communal Spirit and Abnormality

[Będzin — community and society; opinion.] When a general meeting of the Będzin “Gemilut Hesed” (interest-free loan) fund was called, so many people came, no evil eye[?], that because of the crowding in the premises of the “Merchants’ Association” the meeting had to be closed and postponed to another date.
We naturally[?] have nothing against the great interest of the members in the institution, about which we shall have occasion to speak separately; on the other hand we do have something against abnormal interest. With us it cannot be otherwise: either people take no interest at all, or — too much, and in both cases they are harmful.
The same week an annual meeting of the “Malbish Arumim” (clothing the naked) society took place; there the interest was so great that people had to be searched for[?] so that there would be a minyan.
The same goes for the general meetings of the orphanage; there too it is a rare occurrence that there is a minyan. And the question arises: what kind of modus[?] is this?
Why do people either take too much interest or, if not, then nothing at all? Are these not all signs of abnormality, of not knowing which way is in and which way is out?
Why should one take an interest in institutions only when they have already been broken, or when they are just about to be broken? Is it not high time to understand that one is obliged to take an interest in the fate of institutions at all times, and then catastrophes would have been avoided? Is this not a morbid phenomenon that keeps repeating itself, and that one never sees — or does not want to see? What value does such “interest” have? Does it bring any[?] benefit to the community, to the population, to society? Why should one “go and attend meetings only when they become “interesting” — just so that people can come to amuse themselves and enjoy it while one man curses the other back to his father’s father? What benefit can that bring to the community? Is this not destructive work of annihilation, which causes damage on all fronts of our withered[?] communal life?
It is high time to render an account of this, in order to try to find a way to repair the defects, already introduced far too much, which poison and make ugly Jewish public life more and more. Perhaps at last this thought will be considered seriously and sincerely!
Selekt.
We Are Guilty!

[Sosnowiec — opinion piece: the Jewish situation and communal disunity.] By P. Blumenkranz, Sosnowiec.
[—] we Jews began to exist for the sake of the idea of unity, of monotheism. For this idea we renounced a quiet[?] life. Jewish legislation strove, through various laws, to implant the concept of unity.
But grey Jewish life — the wandering, the changing and the having to adapt to the surroundings — has splintered our life. Instead of variety, which is a blessing for every people, with us it has become chaos; instead of different currents — unproductive division. And through this, dualism runs through various areas of our life — down to our two "New Years" in general. Twice a year we must render an account of where we stand[?] in the world, and therefore let us also use the second "New Year" and pause a little over our situation. But when one begins to reflect on Jewish life, on the Jewish situation in the whole world and on the internal relations among the Jews themselves, something begins to choke in the throat, the heart grows heavy, and the old Jewish cry of woe bursts out:
— "From whence shall my help come!" [Psalm 121:1]
• • •
Pseudo-cosmopolitans will ask:
— The world is shaking on its foundations, brothers wage war on brothers, they murder one another — and you are thinking about a handful of Jews!
A word from Turgenev's story "Fathers and Sons" comes to mind here, where the hero argues:
— True, a time will come when every peasant will have his own little house and a cow will graze in front of the house, but by then grass will be growing on my grave, and what will I get out of it all?
If democrats regard such[?] a person as an egoist, this bitter question nevertheless rightly arises with regard to a people:
— What will happen until the [?] of our world disappears; what will become of the spat-upon and the insulted until the world is purified?
The Jews who have reason to believe in the justice of the "great world" console themselves: England, the old "democratic" England, loves the Bible; in the Germany of Schiller and Goethe the truth [must win?]. In Romania the emperor [sic] received a Jewish delegation; Mussolini promised that Jews would no longer be hindered from keeping the Sabbath, etc.
But what does one say to the [?] Jew who does not believe in "biblical" England with Edward VIII, George VI and Baldwin together?
What does one say to this Jew, who looks at the Royal Commission [the Peel Commission] and at English good deeds as at splendid tragicomedies?
• • •
How do all creatures in the world behave in time of danger? — They band together! The instinct of self-preservation dictates the need for unification, for consolidation.
But that happens with everyone — but not with Jews. Jewish wisdom, alas, has in the course of time turned into over-cleverness, into "leave me be", and Jewish energy and collective aspiration — into small-town grabbing of [synagogue] benches and fights over aliyot.
Jews, with their scope[?] and enterprising power (for which [?] they used to be esteemed), have become, together with their little spice shops, "spice-shop communal workers", with all the cunning, begrudging and competition.
It is hard to write about these matters; besides, writing about these phenomena does not help. What is needed is a Jewish personality — a great one, a mighty one, a new Jeremiah — who would hurl the truth into the faces of our communal workers of all tendencies, show them their "penny-pinched lordliness"[?], their Lilliputian aspirations, and sweep the rubbish out of our life — purify it!
A person standing on the side is seized with horror; he would never believe that the very same Jews whom the enemies regard as a mighty force, as disciplined, as responsible, should in truth be so servile, [?], demoralised and atrophied[?] of every feeling of self-preservation!
• • •
And Jewish cultural work. The Jewish "book"? Optimists bring proofs from the number of Jewish newspapers, compile surveys, pat their bellies contentedly.
But these contented ones, for the most part professional comforters, do not know how ashamed the Jewish book is among the young "generation", how the older liberal Jew takes the Jewish book into his home the way one takes a [?] guest home for the Sabbath...
They do not know that Jewish writers have no possibility of printing their works in a daily paper; their writings lie in the drawer, [—].
And the Jewish book does not appear. The [—] who wants to read Yiddish must resort to foreign languages, and Yiddish is shoved into a corner. Shoved aside and ashamed, like the Jewish community as a whole...
• • •
But how long is the measure for saying lamentations? Among us it is the custom to end with consolation.
This time we want to depart from this fine custom.
Our life is so dark from outside and so gangrenous[?] within that the words of consolation get stuck.
But one thing must be remembered and impressed[?]: that we must at the very least sound the alarm about the social rottenness, about the cultural wasteland and about the burning necessity of consolidating our communal life.
For if the division that has prevailed until now does not stop, we shall with our own hands help bring about our [?] fall.
And then we shall lament in the [?] [possibly: the (5)690s, i.e. the 1930s] over the ruins of our life:
— "Our hands have not shed this blood!" [Deut. 21:7]
Behind the Coffin of the Great Rabbi R' Yehoshua'le Tellner of Blessed Memory

[Będzin — eulogy; rabbinate.] By Yehuda Yafet.
"And Joshua the servant of the Lord died" (printed: "servant of D'").
Joshua 24:29.
"R' Yehoshua'le the Dayan" — that is how he was introduced to me two years ago, when I came to Będzin. Casting a glance at that somewhat stern scholar's face, I somehow felt that the name "Dayan" was for this man not merely a plain title but a symbol, a symbol of the concept "din" (justice/judgment), which among us has still not been properly appreciated.
The title "Rav" is actually a rather[?] late one; it arose only in the medieval period, and the rabbinate as such arose only in the time of the Mahari Weil [R' Jacob Weil], as we find in his responsa, his Leket Yosher, etc.
The title "Dayan" existed already in the days of the Talmud. Whatever the Gemara says about the rabbinate it expresses in the form of "dayan", as in the fine[?] saying: "Every judge who judges a true judgment truthfully is as if he became a partner of the Holy One, blessed be He, in the work of Creation" (Shabbat 10) and other such[?] sayings.
"Rav" is the concept of eminence, greatness, haughtiness; whereas "Dayan" reminds us of the matter of justice and of the responsibility of "judging a true judgment truthfully", by which worlds are built — and if one strays a hair's breadth[?] from the path of the truth of the law, worlds are destroyed. "Rav" is the highest honorific institution of Jewish religious leadership; "Dayan" already means something like vice-rabbi, and because it is no longer stamped with haughtiness but only with the great responsibility of the bearer of Jewish law, on which worlds stand and which is so awe-inspiring — therefore its worth[?] in Jewish life is in a certain sense higher.
• • •
The first dayan among Jews was, it seems, J o s h u a. Moses the rabbi and Joshua the servant of Moses, the deputy rabbi. "The face of Moses was like the face of the sun, and the face of Joshua like the face of the moon" — and indeed in Joshua we already notice the dayan's zeal for truth.
Our great departed, too, who bore the name of the first dayan among Jews, the great rabbi R' Yehoshua'le Tellner of blessed memory, embodied in himself all the aforementioned qualities of a dayan. His face told me so at the first moment, and two years of acquaintance with him confirmed it: he was the embodiment of truth and uprightness. Throughout the whole 50 years in which he was dayan of Będzin, no one could point to the slightest deviation on his part from upright truth — and in our times that is a great, great strength. And not only that — this Jew would boil over at[?] any injustice done to someone. He organically could not bear a lie; "a true judgment truthfully" shone before his eyes like something holy.
Of a deceased person the Gemara says "his face toward the people — a good sign for him" (Ketubot 103). Our departed was always "his face toward the people": he conducted himself humbly, in a popular manner, did not think much of himself; he was also deliberate in judgment. Being a great authority in rulings, he was at the same time in awe of ruling, and with all his learning and saturation in the codifiers he approached every ruling like a young man just beginning to study.
• • •
For 50 years he was dayan in Będzin, and he carried within himself that typical Będzin atmosphere which I have noticed in no other town; he was bound up[?] with Będzin's half-century. Each time he told me about his former years, about the times of the rabbi R' Itshele of blessed memory, I felt how this Jew carried with him 50 years of Będzin life — that[?] portion of known life by which Jewish Będzin stands out in its distinctiveness.
The great rabbi R' Yehoshua'le of blessed memory was also permeated by a strong spirit of awe of God, truthfulness[?], piety and cleaving to the Creator. This found expression in the last minutes of his life: when the life in him had already almost ceased, when only faint traces of life could barely be found[?] in him — he still managed to pray the evening service and say the Shema with a tone of self-sacrifice, so that one can say of him that "his soul departed with [the word] 'One'".
Last Wednesday [6 January 1937] Będzin escorted to the grave 50 years of its history, of its former honest and Torah-true Jewish life.
Things Are Getting Dearer Again.

[Economy — cost of living worldwide; article.]
Year out, year in, in the month of December the economic policymakers in every country sit down and do a great deal of reckoning — whether things are already getting better or worse in their state. They calculate what all sorts of goods that the population uses cost, and examine closely[?] whether the population is living more cheaply or more dearly.
This balance is very important, because one can see from it how the population will be able to manage in the coming months, during which conditions will remain stable, since all agreements concerning the import and export of goods are concluded until roughly the next summer months; from January to June no new agreements whatsoever will be concluded anywhere.
It is therefore worth taking a look at a statistic of the Leipzig Fair, in order to see what is happening in various countries.
Only from South America is there better news. Of the largest factories in America, 245 have announced that they will pay dividends for the current year. For the year 1935 only 116 firms had profits and paid dividends. The 245 firms had in the year 1936 a profit of 792 million dollars, whereas in the previous years they had for the most part[?] losses or at best broke even. These firms possess a capital of eleven billion dollars and will pay ten[?] percent dividend. (It is worth noting that about half of the 245 firms produce goods that are used today for military purposes.)
In all other countries things have got worse lately. Only in Sweden, Austria and Czechoslovakia has not much changed. In England and in Italy it has become two percent dearer; in Finland one lives today three percent dearer than a year ago.
Foodstuffs have even become cheaper by one percent in some countries, as for instance Poland and Norway; on the other hand, however, clothing in Poland has risen by about five percent.
In Canada foodstuffs have become dearer by seven percent, although there are so many agricultural products there. Even in such an agrarian country as Hungary foodstuffs have risen by two percent, in Japan by four percent. In South America too clothing has risen by four percent and foodstuffs by three percent; in Hungary clothing has risen by six percent.
The prices of coal, wood, gas and electricity have also risen everywhere by one to eight percent.
Things have become very dear in those countries which in recent months devalued their currency. In Switzerland the rise in prices amounts to eleven percent: foodstuffs have become dearer by eight percent, industrial goods by 19 percent. In France the rise in prices amounts on average to fourteen percent; most foodstuffs have risen by eight per cent. Eggs have become dearer by 23 per cent, lard by 18 per cent, butter by 10 per cent, meat, fish and coal by 6 percent, milk, sugar and potatoes by 5 percent, industrial goods by 20 percent. One sees that the devaluation, too, has not brought the salvation that was counted on.
In this statistic it is also worth looking at the heading: wine. How much wine is drunk in each country?
In France every person accounts for 146 litres of wine a year; in Italy 108 litres of wine a year per head; in Spain 80 litres; in Portugal 71 litres; in Hungary 38 litres; in Romania 32 litres; in Yugoslavia 29 litres; in Austria 18; in Japan, according to the size of the population, only a tenth of a litre per head; in Poland barely four hundredths of a litre per head.
However one reads the reports from the individual countries — which are, of course, dressed up with various commentaries — this much is certain: in the coming months we shall live more dearly...
Z. Haber, Vienna.

Dorothy Lamour.
Until now she was known only in America, and even then in a quite limited circle. She used to appear on the radio, where she was employed as a singer. Among radio listeners she was very well liked and popular. A few years ago she met a certain Herb Kay, who is the conductor of an orchestra in Chicago. "On That Night..."

(How our brethren, the Children of Israel, celebrated the "holy" Sylvester)
Reported by Ben Amotz.

We went out into the street 2 hours before the old year departed from us to its eternal rest. The bustle is greater than ever, "humanity" is running, a rush at every step and stride. Older women and young girls are hurrying; the difference is that the former hurry into the butcher shops to "grab" a piece of meat for the Sabbath at the cheap price, and the latter — to the station, to "catch" the train to Katowice, to be the first on the Sylvester wagons[?]...

And as the immortal Sholem Aleichem says: "When one Jew runs, the other runs after him" — so I ran too (not into the butcher shop) but to the railway station.

Entering the "poczekalnia" [waiting room], packed full with holiday guests, it occurred to me at that moment that the crowd had probably come to see off a group of olim [emigrants to Palestine]; but it soon became clear to me that the crowd (mostly Jewish "pannes"[?]) were escorts of the old year and were travelling to Katowice for Rosh Hashanah. But — the devil's doing — the train was late. And they, poor things, have to wait...

And it was truly painful to look at the darkened[?] faces, who because of a "caprice" of the train might reach Katowice only after "Shacharit" [the morning prayer].

— "Nie martwcie się" [don't worry] — one of the young people travelling along consoles them — we'll still get there before the "blowing of the shofar"...

— "Co, to jest?" [What's that?] — asks a Jewish "Sylvester miss".

And no wonder she doesn't know what such a thing as "the blowing of the shofar" is: on the Jewish Rosh Hashanah there are no Sylvester wagons[?]..

After "dispatching" the "crowd", we take a stroll along the main streets — a meeting of acquaintances with whom one chats about the troubles and evil decrees pouring down on our heads, from Haman's slogan: "to destroy and to annihilate", and...

Suddenly the conversation is broken off; one of the gang cries out:
— "S'geyt"[?]! ["There they go!"]..

At first we thought that our friend meant to save us from a "mandat" [police fine] for standing on the pavement; later, however, it turned out that the "s'geyt" applied to our dandies, who were going to the Sylvester balls.

And we saw the unbelievable. To the right of Kołłątaja Street walked young couples, Jewish student boys, and to the left the "notables" of the town; and it was not only man and wife, husband and woman, who walked, but whole families, dressed up in silk and honey[?]. The mother in the middle and the children at the side — and why not? One must, after all, educate the children in a mitzvah; well, celebrating the "holy holiday" is a small mitzvah...

The young people turn into Sienkiewicza Street... and the householders head in the direction of the "Klub Stachruszyski"[?]...

The first to receive the guests is the doorman; he bows deeply before them and with a polite "Dobry wieczór" [good evening] he opens the little door of the entrance.

We strike up a conversation with him and ask:
— "Co za zabawa tu będzie?" [What kind of party will there be here?]
— "Sylwestra" — he answers — "a jakże, tu się bawią same Żydki, ale orkiestra to z goszych[?].. bo inaczej nie wypada" ["of course — only Jews ('Żydki') are having fun here, but the orchestra is from ours[?].. because otherwise it wouldn't be proper"]...

We welcomed the New Year with the Jewish academics, because, first of all, they do not dance for the sake of Sylvester but for the sake of profit[?] and "tashnit"[?]; after all, they are closer to us; after all, there are in their ranks a large number with a national colouring... So we squeezed ourselves into a corner, far from an "evil eye", and waited for the right minute when the shechita [ritual slaughter] law would come into force. Oh, to the devil! I meant to say: when the New Year would come out into the light of the world...

An abundance of light is poured over the hall. As the ball gets under way, dozens, dozens of couples dance to the sounds of a jazz-band orchestra; but not all are dancing yet — the "pious", the men of deeds, that is, will only begin to dance after the birth of the New Year.

The last minutes of the old year arrive, the lamps are put out, darkness in the hall, and in the darkness the "dance of death" is danced, and over the heads of the dancing couples hover the shadows of the Jewish martyrs, and sighs are heard from the students beaten in the past year...

And now the New Year strains with all its strength to live, bright rays flash up, but the darkness of the old year is stronger and does not allow it; so it repeats itself several times: the "new" wants to live and the old does not want to breathe out its last breath; and at the birth-pangs the orchestra plays[?] and the Jewish academics dance...

At last the hour of deliverance[?] strikes; the drummer beats out on his drum up to 12, and:
— Prosit 1937!...

———

From there we went on to Sosnowiec. The local "bachelors" this year arranged "closed celebrations" of Rosh Hashanah[?] not in public venues but at home, because to give up the "holiday" entirely — that one cannot do; as the saying goes, "habit is second nature" — so they arranged separate "clubs"[?] and celebrated the "holy night" to radio music.

Late at night, on Third of May Street, we met a group of our brethren the Children of Israel, dressed in their Sabbath clothes, wandering from one venue to another and nowhere finding a place of rest; hardly had they shown their noses in whatever venue it was, than they at once got the answer from the waiter:
— "Wszystkie stoliki zajęte" [all tables are taken]..

But since He, as it were, does not abandon even a little worm under the earth, He also had mercy on the wanderers (people from Będzin, Sosnowiec and Chorzów[?]..), who after midnight got a "tikkun" [a drink and a bite] at the "Savoy"[?]..
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Va'era)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Va'era
—o—
a) "And I appeared unto Abraham, unto Isaac and unto Jacob" (Ex. 6:3)
"...for I promised and did not fulfil" [?]. Rashi.
Why, then, did Abraham, Isaac and Jacob not protest when God did not fulfil the promise to them, whereas Moses our teacher did storm — "Why hast Thou dealt ill with this people?" — when it merely seemed to him that the redemption was not going smoothly?
Because with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob the promise about the Land of Israel concerned only themselves; there was as yet no Jewish people, and for oneself alone one may not [come] with such [?] audacity before God. Moses, on the other hand — with him it already concerned the Jewish people, and when it concerns Jews one must not show deference even, as it were, to God Himself... Yalkut Yehuda.
—o—
b) "To give them the land of their sojournings, wherein they sojourned" (ibid., 4)
It seems that even in the Land of Israel Jews will for a time feel like strangers, like foreigners; it will be for them "the land of their sojournings", a land of dwelling [?] — and yet there they will be regarded as strangers, as foreigners... Imrei Chen.
—o—
c) "And I will bring you out" (ibid., 6)
"For so I promised him: and afterward shall they come out with great substance." Rashi.
The promise can be fulfilled only together with the great substance. That is how it is: Jews must have great substance both for "I will bring you out" — for emigration — and for "I will bring you in"; both for leaving the exile and for the work of building up, Jews will have to make use of great substance, a large fortune — for what else comes so easily... [?] Leket Amarim.
• • •
When the foreign-currency restrictions began to be introduced, Rabbi A. M. Amiel [?] said:
Now I understand Rashi's words: "For so I promised him, and afterward shall they come out with great substance." It is a special promise from God that Jews will be able to take their property out of exile..
—o—
d) "And gave them a charge unto the children of Israel" (ibid., 13)
"Moses said: Bring the elders of the generation with me. The Holy One, blessed be He, said: Take a stick and strike them on the head. One spokesman for a generation, not two spokesmen for a generation." Tractate Sanhedrin.
When it comes to going to Pharaoh, various go-betweens [?] and various delegations always turn up. That is what God said: "Take a stick and strike them on the head — one spokesman for a generation and not two": with a stick over the head give it to those who always appear as "two spokesmen for a generation" and display Jewish fragmentation everywhere... Ateret Tzvi.
—o—
e) "And the houses of the Egyptians shall be full of the swarms" (8:17)
The Yalkut says that the ten plagues corresponded to the ten trials with which Abraham was tested. By this reckoning it turns out that the swarm of wild beasts corresponds to the trial of the kingdoms; it was hinted that Jews would one day find themselves among the kingdoms as among real wild beasts... Siftei Da'at.
—o—
f) "And I will put a division between My people and thy people" (ibid., 19)
"Pedut" is written defectively. Even when there will be a smaller difference between Jews and Egyptians, the redemption will nevertheless come... Tekhelet Mordechai.
—o—
g) "And the magicians could not stand before Moses because of the boils."
From then on we no longer find that Pharaoh strengthened himself, only "and his heart was hardened" — made heavy — because it was the magicians who had encouraged him, and since [?] they had got the boils, which no longer left them (Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer), and with boils on their heads they could not show themselves before Pharaoh... Panim Yafot.
Pen Splashes.

[Polemic — antisemitism and national dignity.] The antisemitic attacks on Jews in various towns provide a great deal of — unfortunately sad — material for assessing the culture, ethics and dignity not only of the attackers but also of the attacked.
For example:
An attacker shouts at a Jew: Are you a Jew? No. Give proof. The attacked man buys his way out with "siedem groszy" (seven groszy) and frees himself from the attacker — but his human dignity, his national consciousness, simply his self-respect — a wreck!
Quite differently, compared with this case, the Jewish student behaves, and even more so the woman student, at the universities.
— Are you a Jew? — shouts the attacker. — Yes, yes — is the answer.
— Back to the ghetto — to separate benches!
— No, no — we have equal rights.
Consciousness, dignity and also heroism.
———
In a railway carriage [?] or a tram someone sits with a Hitler look and hurls the most disgraceful insults at our brethren. But then he notices 2 pretty "żydówki" (Jewesses); a conversation starts, soon a flirt, they laugh and joke — and the Jewish passenger, often [?] a non-Jewish one too, asks:
Which of them is shameless — where is human dignity or self-awareness?
———
At the theatre: "Srub [?] Ogórek".. On stage a caricature of a "Moszek", monologues of mockery and contempt. The audience laughs, applauds. Somewhere in a corner a quiet, feeble heckle. Nobody protests, nobody leaves [?] the hall.
———
A newspaper: from every page and column peer out exclamations and supposedly scientific articles against everything that is not Aryan.
The latest news [?]: "Angnesn" [?] Ogórek, again Ogórek.
What is the point of such advertising?
There is no dignity, no self-awareness; plain common sense is lacking too.
With doctors, engineers, lawyers — no better.
The more hostile towards us — the more support; literally surrounded by Ogórek.
They boycott their Jewish colleagues — but the latter behave as if they did not know.
Human dignity? — better not look for it.
———
A record picture:
In one of the latest numbers of "Nasz Przegl." [Nasz Przegląd] there is the motion which the antisemitic lawyers submitted at the advocates' congress in Warsaw: to close access to the bar for Jews.
About 200 signatures: jurists, defenders of human rights, demand restricting the rights of candidates for the advocates' profession — because... they are Jews.
The motion was defeated — but the "Orędownik" [?] and "Jerne Karsa" [?] attack those who refused to sign (barely 6 persons): from Sosnowiec 4 exceptions: Adv. Pawelek [?], Haner [?], Marks, König; from Dąbrowa 2: Chilman, Chmielewski.
Dear reader! Do not be sad; learn [?] self-awareness; possess above all honour and dignity!
From the Book of “Job”

(For the shloyshim [thirtieth day] of my mother).
I.
Let me lay down my head and fall asleep,
until the cloud, darkened by the rainwater,
becomes empty[?] and bright again,
until your wrath flies past[?],
as the waves flutter over the stone,
until the waters depart from the sea,
from the place whence all rivers come,
and are dried up,
until —
my day of change shall come.
II.
I am frightened, because you do not cut me off from the world sooner,
before[?] you cover me with mists,
but you pour darkness over me
while I still live.
I am frightened, because you do not withhold from me
the darkness of the grave
until the time
when I shall be no more,
but you show it to me
on every day of my life.
I am frightened, because you do not pay me
according to my reckoning,
but according to your secret.
III.
Show me that my sin is greater than the guilt of others,
who rejoice in their exaltation[?].
And I will say: I alone have erred in this,
I alone have degraded my work.
Point out to me that my sin is as great
as the punishment you have sent upon me,
and I will bow my head, silenced and submissive,
point me out with your finger
why you punish,
why you make man perish in loneliness,
as a stone falls into the abyss.
Give me, God, to understand this,
before[?] you lay me in the grave,
and I will accept everything gladly,
and teach little children
to take a lesson from it.
Roza Jakubowicz.
Two Brothers

(A folk tale of olden times for all times).
There were once two brothers. One of them had a good, sharp head; the second was a bit dull, but he had a sense for reality.
The first studied and graduated as a doctor of philosophy, yet with all his diplomas he could not earn his basic necessities.
The second brother did not want to study, so he went off to a bigger city. Several years passed and nothing was heard of him. One fine morning the elder brother received a letter from him saying that he was doing very well.
And it came to pass that the elder came to visit the younger. The younger brother was dressed up “in vinegar and honey” [i.e. to the nines], while the elder wore old, threadbare clothes.
After a short conversation the elder brother learned that the younger was employed as a salesman in a large silk business and that he had a fiancée, the daughter of a rich manufacturer, whom he was soon to marry.
“And how are you, dear brother?” the younger asked. “Still an old bachelor? What did you need to study so much for — what good is your education to me? Look how I, without education, have achieved everything I wanted. I have amassed capital, I have a good position, a splendid flat, a fiancée with a very handsome dowry.”
The elder brother answered with a good-natured smile:
“No, dear brother, I have nothing to learn from you. Just try for one day to tell the truth to people’s faces, and then we shall see what comes of all your good fortune.”
The younger brother agreed to the proposal of his elder brother, who could not bear falsehood, the lie, in whatever form it might be.
The next morning the younger brother went into the shop with the firm resolve to tell only the truth. On entering the shop he found a customer who wanted to order a large lot of silk. To the customer’s question about the quality of the silk the salesman replied: “This silk is good for kapores” [i.e. worthless]. Naturally the customer withdrew from the deal.
To make a long story short, the salesman caused great trouble in the shop every day; he drove away all the customers with his answers. When the owner of the business heard what havoc his salesman had wrought, he raised an outcry:
“Are you drunk, or out of your mind?”
The salesman answered him quite coolly and calmly:
“I am not mad, nor drunk either; I merely told your customers the plain truth.”
“Go to the devil with your truth!” — and with these words the proprietor drove the salesman out.
In a desperate state the salesman ran off to his fiancée; she was astonished when her bridegroom burst into her room like a man distraught, without bringing her any flowers, as had been his custom.
“What happened?” the fiancée asked him — and he told her that the owner of the business had thrown him out.
In short, the bride and groom quarrelled[?]; she said to him:
“You don’t love me any more.”
To which he replied:
“To tell the truth, I never loved you.”
“It wasn’t me you wanted, but my dowry.”
“That is the plain truth,” he confirmed.
When the father heard of the scandal between his daughter and her fiancé, he at once called an ambulance from the municipal madhouse, and the young man was taken[?] to the institution for the mentally ill. The young man began to make a racket and shout at the top of his voice that he was not mad, but had only tried for one day to tell the truth; but all his pleas did not help him, because every madman — the doctors of the institution remarked — has his own truths, in which the clever world does not want to believe.
The next morning the elder brother came to the silk shop to see how his younger brother was faring after a day of truth-telling, and not finding him there, he turned to the proprietor with questions, to which he received a bitter answer: that his brother had been thrown out of the business.
To the question “Why?” came the answer: “Your brother yesterday drove away all the customers with his wild talk.”
The elder brother set off to the fiancée in the hope of finding him there. The rich fiancée replied that she did not know what had happened to her bridegroom; he had behaved so strangely during his visit that her father had been forced to hand him over to a madhouse.
When the elder brother came to the madhouse and tried to explain to the doctors what had actually happened to his brother, who had a sober and clear mind, and told them of their agreement that he would try to tell everyone the truth to his face, the doctors suspected that he himself was a lunatic.
Days and weeks went by until they finally succeeded in freeing the salesman from the madhouse, and when the two brothers were strolling in freedom, the elder said to the younger:
“Well then, now you could see for yourself that it was not through your intellect, not through your abilities, that you attained your so vaunted[?] happy station, but through lies, or at best through keeping silent about the truth.”
“What do you think now?”
“To tell you the plain truth, as you demand: I shall avoid telling the truth.”
Reuben Brainin.
“Der Kokh-Lefl” — Humour and Satire. / Ten Brothers Were We

[Humour — the “Kokh-Lefl” page; parody on the kehilla.] Der Kokh-Lefl [The Cooking Ladle]. Humour and satire. Compiled by Amotzli.
Ten Brothers Were We
(Parody of the song “Berl with the Fiddle”)
Ten nominees [government-appointed board members] were we,
in the whole wide world they were mine;
one of us ran away, so I was left with nine —
Berl with the fiddle, Shmerl with the bass,
play me a little song in the middle of the street.
Refrain.
When we were nine nominees, I laughed as well,
again one went away, so I was left with eight...
Berl with the fiddle, Shmerl with the bass,
play me a little song in the middle of the street.
(Refrain)
Eight there were, but all of them obedient to me,
suddenly half took offence and I was left with four...
Berl with the fiddle, Shmerl with the bass,
play me a little song in the middle of the street.
(Refrain)
Four we were already, but — great is the lament and the weeping,
they showed me a fig [a rude “nothing for you” gesture] and, poor me, I was left alone...
Berl with the fiddle, Shmerl with the bass.
Everyone plays the kehilla song on Modrzejowska Street...
(Refrain).
Questions for the Mind-Reader Prof. Messing in Będzin.

[Humour — “Kokh-Lefl”; Będzin and Sosnowiec — kehilla.] The editors of “Kokh Lefl” delegated their staff member to Prof. Messing [Wolf Messing], who is staying in Będzin, and put to him the following questions:
— How many parnasim does the kehilla board still have to “evict”?... And by what “power” did Agudah get the “Zionist” kehilla parnas in?...
— Has the present board of the Gemilut Hesed fund got the “little benches” back, or not?
— Which lady gave the apt name to the buffet at the ball in the Jewish gymnasium?...
— When will the Sosnowiec communal delegates get the kehilla benches?
— Will the artisans’ association survive, or must it be propped up with a couple of “patches” [flekes?]?..
— And also (only[?]) [he] wanted to put a few more questions, but the staff member remembered his childhood years, when the rebbe studied with him:
— Patach shin — sha [“hush!”]...
—o—
The Iron Wedding.
— I am going to celebrate my iron wedding anniversary.
— Have you gone mad?
— If I have held out with my wife for 25 years, I am made of iron.
Blessed People.

[Humour — “Kokh-Lefl”; jokes.] — You know, my wife has greater virtues than the sun.
— In what way?
— The sun pours out fire in Tammuz [midsummer], and my wife pours out fire in Shevat [midwinter].
— My son-in-law, too, has a greater virtue than the moon.
— For example?
— The moon is sometimes “full” and sometimes “waning”, but my son-in-law is always “full”...
Leib Shtabinski.
—o—
Rosh Hashanah and New Year.
— What is the difference between our Rosh Hashanah and their New Year?
— With us it is “on Rosh Hashanah it is written”
— On Rosh Hashanah things get written, and with them things get written (police reports) after New Year.
Leib Shtabinski.
There, in the Land of China...

[Humour — “Kokh-Lefl”; satirical poem — China.] There, in the land of China,
such a terror is going on now,
it’s a whole craziness[?]:
Chang Su Lang [Zhang Xueliang] and Chiang Kai-shek;
and when things get merry in China —
a terror falls upon “Europe”,
for the world is one country:
everywhere the same blows!
When they fight in China,
Chiang Kai-shek and Chang Su Lang,
it is bitter as quinine,
and the heart grows anxious;
it grows dark on the stage,
there comes the play of bullet and tank,
because they fight in China,
Chiang Kai-shek and Chang Khu [sic] Lang,
The “Order of Slaughter”.

[Humour — “Kokh-Lefl”; satire on the slaughter restrictions.] We have managed to find out the “order” of slaughtering an animal:
When buying a cow one may not feel her to see whether she is fat, or look into her mouth to find out her age — that is not gentlemanly. The butcher must make a curtsey before the animal, stand at a distance and contemplate it. If the animal pleases him, he must give her a kiss, as the verse says, “they kiss calves” [Hosea 13:2], and pay as much as he [the seller] wants; haggling is forbidden.
On a rainy day one must put galoshes on the animal when taking her[?] to the stable; on the way to the slaughterhouse one must take the animal into a café for a beer[?]; the animal may not be driven on foot, but must be transported in a luxury car.
In the slaughterhouse the shochtim must salute every animal. Before slaughtering, the ox must be laid down on a mattress and covered with bed linen.
After the slaughter the kosher meat must be delivered to the pharmacies and weighed out in grams.
The “Rush” in the Jewish Shops before the [Gentile] Holidays. / A Conversation Overheard on Modrzejowska Street.

[Humour — “Kokh-Lefl”; trade and the crisis.] On Modrzejowska Street, before the holidays [Christmas and New Year], I[?] overheard the following conversation between two merchants:
— Good morning, Reb Nute[?].
— A good year, Reb Yashe, what’s new with you? What did your takings look like before the holidays? Was there any “rush” [Polish ruch — trade, bustle]?
— Yes, there was a bit of a rush.
— Meaning?
— In the morning I came to the shop first, after me my two employees, the cashier, 5 creditors, 8 wholesale buyers and 12 communal activists with calendars from their associations.
— So I see you are bored in the shop?
— What do you mean? I play with my employees at “shop”, at “merchant and customer” — that is, we do [unclear word: tshkhitshegyes].
— And what do you live on?
— On habit.
— So as I see it, I can’t count on anything for the debt you owe me?
— Count you can — it shortens the time of waiting.
He Gets In First...

From the series "Train Stories."
Two Jews are travelling on the train. Both sit quietly for a while; at last one of them asks:
"Where is a Jew travelling to?"
"Kiss my ..." the other answered.
"Ha, how[?] does that occur to you? What have I done to you that you insult me in such a crude way?"
"I'll explain to you," the Jew answered. "If I tell you where I'm going, you'll ask me what my name is; and if I tell you what my name is, you'll ask me what I deal in; if I tell you what I deal in, you'll come to me to buy a parcel of goods, you'll give me promissory notes, you won't pay the notes, and when I come to you to demand payment, you'll say: kiss my ... So I'm telling you right away, now: kiss my ..."
Announcement

We hereby announce that we are taking in laundry for washing. In our "pralnia" (laundry) "laundry is washed" at half-price-for-nothing [Heb. "be-hatsi hinam", i.e. dirt cheap].

The Beautiful Benvenida. 9)

A novel that took place in the first Jewish ghetto and stirred up the governments of Spain and Turkey.

Absorbed in himself, immersed[?] in his fantasies, in the currents of his feelings of love, Nathan Ashkenazi, at home in Turkey, would not let himself be persuaded to come to his senses and look around him. Though he was being tossed about by a whole series of circumstances he had never been able to overcome, it seemed to him that his efforts would nevertheless bring him to his goal, and indeed very soon. Otherwise it simply could not be: Benvenida must be freed!
Besides, since he expected to be received any day now at last by the chief ruler of the Turkish court, he began to prepare himself to appear before the Sultan.
The Sultan at that time was Ahmed the First. Nathan Ashkenazi believed that it was his mother who would bring him to the Sultan.
The attitude of the Turkish court toward Jews in general was already not a good one at that time, but his mother still enjoyed great esteem there. His famous father was already dead, but the court's regard for the Ashkenazi family had not vanished with that; it was regard mixed with gratitude. The widow Ashkenazi had saved the Sultan's life: he had been struck by a severe smallpox illness, and no doctor in all of Turkey knew how to cure him, but Nathan Ashkenazi's mother did know; she tended the sick Sultan until he became completely healthy, and for that he rewarded her with much honour and jewellery. So Nathan Ashkenazi could surely believe that his mother would help him when he turned to her to obtain for him a meeting with the Sultan, in the interests of the captive Benvenida.
But Nathan Ashkenazi suffered a great disappointment.
First, his mother took his being in love with Benvenida as nothing serious; it was no more than a youthful flame that would go out — so she believed. He had been abroad, had seen the pretty face of a young girl, and it had attracted him; on top of that, a suffering girl — he had taken pity on her. But this was no deep love — so the mother reasoned, and so she told him, and she reproached him for having concerned himself with Benvenida at all.
The mother had already heard what others at the Turkish court had heard: that her son had had clashes in Venice with the ambassador of Spain, and that such rumours were going around about her son as would do him no good, which could even bring a catastrophe on him and on the whole family. And who is she anyway, this Benvenida? A captive girl of foreign Marranos[?] from Spain! Why had he forgotten his rank as a young diplomat, as one for whom great opportunities to enter royal courts still lay in store? And why, above all, had he forgotten who he is — a son of Solomon (Shlomo) Ashkenazi, such a famous father? He must not have Benvenida on his mind; she had other plans for him. So the mother argued with him.
Second, she set before him the situation of her other sons, his two brothers, who could expect connections precisely with people of the royal house of Spain, on which their future life, with a great deal of happiness, entirely depended. The two brothers expected to become physicians at royal courts in which Spanish princes and princesses played great roles — and he, Nathan Ashkenazi, seeks nothing but enmity with Spain!
The brothers argued with him just as the mother did; their words hurt him, and his heart in love was as if pierced through by them.
And it burned him, too, that his mother and brothers did not see the just side of the struggle he had undertaken for Benvenida, quite apart from his love for her.
She is, after all, a martyr, a sufferer for the Jewish faith — how can one allow her to be handed over to the Inquisition to be tortured to death?
Nathan Ashkenazi spoke in a moralizing tone to his mother and his brothers:
"We will not be worthy of our father's name, Ashkenazi, if we turn away from the voice of justice that comes to us from the Venetian ghetto[?], from Benvenida's prison. What will greatness and wealth be to us, and what will the luxury of royal courts give us, if we refuse to help the persecuted of our people? If it is our destiny to be exalted, to enter the halls of the mighty, of sultans, kings and lords, to sit at tables with princes — and we too are such a family, for whom this is destined — regardless of the fact that others of our faith are like sand[?] under the feet, like straw on the road — what joy will come into our life from it, if we are not in the service of our people? Will we protect ourselves by it? Will our own be kept safe while the whole people is being beaten? First, that is not true at all: here we see dozens of examples of Jews who today are allied with kings and tomorrow run through wild forests and across all the seas to save themselves. And second, even if we really were protected by buying ourselves favour in the eyes of this ruler or that — whom can that benefit, if tormented children of our people and our faith are wallowing at our feet? Jews in royal garments and with stains on their soul are creatures of Satan, not children of God. I do not want to be that; I would rather perish in poverty and be hunted like all our own, if I cannot, with my greatness, be like a messenger of God to answer the prayers of those who weep for help."
(To be continued.)
The Kehilla Budget on the “Workbench”...

[Będzin — kehilla.]
A coal commission elected. — The pensions of the morei hora'ah (rabbinic judges) raised.
On Sunday evening the kehilla administration held a meeting. On the agenda — the kehilla budget for the year 1937. Despite the fact that the new budget is being drawn up at a time when the ritual-slaughter law is already in force, owing to which a smaller income than hitherto is foreseen[?], the kehilla administration is not pessimistic and has raised the pensions of the morei hora'ah...
Also invited to the meeting was parnas (councillor) Goldsztajn, whom the Agudah faction wants to “bring into” the administration. Mr Goldsztajn declared, however, that he continues to hold[?] the office of parnas, and he left the meeting.
Before the agenda, on the proposal of Mr Manele, a coal commission was elected, which was joined by: Manele, Benhart [Bernhard?] and Hampel.
Then Mr Manele proposed that, in order to avoid in future the struggle that has gone on until now between the administration and the council over the budget question, a commission of representatives of the administration and of the council should be elected, and this commission might perhaps reach an understanding among itself on budget matters.
The proposal was put to the vote and was defeated. Then the pensions for the rabbinate were considered. Here the Agudah faction brought in a motion to raise the pension of the moreh tzedek R' Mendel Lewin from 2 500 to 3,800 zł.
The board members (dozors) Najmark and Hampel brought in a counter-motion to strike out the pension for M.[?] Lewin entirely; it goes without saying that the first motion obtained a majority and the second — was defeated. For the sake of “fairness” the pensions of the morei tzedek Lipszyc, Frydberg and Lewental were also raised, from 3,600 to 3 800 zł.
Then were fixed: for the widow Telner — 60 per cent of her pension until now; for the daughter of Rabbi Graubart — 1 000 zł.; and for the Rebbetzin Lewin — 6 000 zł.
Tragic Death of a Halutz

[Będzin–Sosnowiec — accident.]
Between Będzin and Sosnowiec a terrible incident occurred to the halutz (pioneer) Yisroel Zając from Kozł[?], who was travelling to hakhshara (pioneer training) in the Sosnowiec kibbutz. Mr Zając fell out of the train beyond Sosnowiec and was killed on the spot. His dead body was found later on the railway tracks.
—o—
The Szajn Brothers Declare 12 Thousand zł. for Winter Relief.
The management of the Szajn Brothers' factory in Sławków has declared 12 thousand zł. for winter relief for the unemployed in the Olkusz district (powiat).
—o—
An Appeal That the Registration Books Be Kept at the Kehilla
The national faction of the kehilla administration has applied with a request to the starosta that he order that the registration (vital-records) books, which are at the Rebbetzin Lewin's, be handed over to the secretariat of the kehilla.
—o—
For the Self-Help Fund
For needy pupils of the S. Fürstenberg Gymnasium a performance with a varied programme will take place this Saturday night.
Shochet Radoszycki Declared Fit Again.

[Będzin — kehilla, ritual slaughter.]
As we have already written, the poultry shochet Radoszycki was caught red-handed while slaughtering poultry in a little back room and causing the kehilla treasury losses in fees. As a punishment he was suspended from his work.
In connection with this, the local rabbinate also undertook to settle the matter, and since they “could not find any counsel for so difficult a question” — how to punish a shochet who had transgressed a prohibition — they brought in the rabbi of Trzebinia[?].
At the “din torah” (rabbinic court hearing), which took place on Tuesday, it was established that the above-mentioned shochet had sinned “under duress”, and he was declared fit (to slaughter) again.
One of the “kidnapped” young lads has again done a “Vayivrach” [fled]

[Sosnowiec — community; Ger Hasidim.] As we already wrote at the time [?], a few weeks ago two young Hasidic lads, Uriel and Yeshaya Ehrlich, disappeared. As later emerged, they had been “kidnapped” by the young married men of the local Ger shtibl and taken off to the Warsaw “Mesivta”, from where the family, only with great effort, managed to bring them back to Sosnowiec.
The father, Mr. Bezalel Ehrlich, fearing that the children would make another “escape”, kept them under his eye in a separate room and did not let them out into the open.
One evening — it was Motzei Shabbat — when Mr. Ehrlich had gone to the shop, Mrs. Ehrlich began to admonish her children: why do they cause her so much grief by wanting to run away from home? Is something lacking for you here? Can't you study in Sosnowiec? Why go off to a strange town?
And suddenly — the mother faints, [—] [?] a great outcry, neighbours come running and revive the mother. The scene made an impression on the children, so that the next morning they both declared to their parents that they no longer thought of running away, and that from then on, i.e. from Monday, they would spend half the day in the shop and half the day studying.
And so it indeed was. On Monday both were in the shop and did not arouse the slightest suspicion that they intended to run away from home again.
But the same thing happened as before. Uriel, who had gone home to eat lunch, disappeared, and to this day nobody knows where he is.
The police, to whom the whole story is already known, last Monday took the younger brother Yeshaya in for questioning; he stated that when they left the first time they were accompanied by a lad from the Ger shtibl, one Yehoshua Hanan Geigebauer [?], who hid them in Strzemieszyce; later, when he received word that they were being pursued, he travelled with them to Sławków and from there to Warsaw. On this basis the above-mentioned lad was also questioned. After the questioning he was released.
While the lads were “under arrest” at home, Mr. Ehrlich's flat was once broken into: a horde of lads burst inside and threw in hundreds of slips of paper bearing various slogans such as: “Remember that there is a God in the world”, “Remember in what surroundings you live”, “Do not obey your heretical guardians”, “Remember that you are the sons of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob”, “I sojourned with Laban” [Hebrew, printed “nartí” for “garti”], etc. [printed “o.ch.”].
As we are informed, the father has decided to hand the whole matter over to the public prosecutor.
A stormy meeting of “Maccabi”

[Sosnowiec — sport; “Maccabi”.] On Sunday a general meeting of “Maccabi” took place in its own premises. The meeting was to deal with the hitherto lamentable state of the association in general and with the ratification of the merger agreement between “Maccabi” and “Gordia” [Gordonia]. As we have already written, the agreement was brought about on the initiative of the former Maccabi president, Mr. S. Lencman [?], to which several persons in the present board do not agree. As a result two “fronts” have formed, for and against the agreement with “Gordia”.
The atmosphere in the hall was tense. The Maccabists, those who up to the last minute had taken an interest in the fate of “Maccabi”, gnashed their teeth on seeing the large number of new members who had come to have their say. The “fear” grew from minute to minute, the air “smelled of gunpowder”, the slightest utterance could have led to serious clashes; a passionate struggle developed between “pure” [?] old Maccabists and brand-new members, but both sides forgot that in the end nobody would suffer but “Maccabi”.
Before a packed hall the local president, Mr. Szwajcer, opens the meeting and proposes Mr. Jakub Lichtenstein (Będzin) as chairman, to which those assembled agree. The chairman appeals to the assembly to behave calmly and to help the meeting bring the desired result for “Maccabi”. Elected to the presidium are Messrs. Litman, Ehrlich and Mr. Schlesinger as secretary.
The calm, however, does not last long. Right after the chairman reads out the agenda a discussion begins, which leads to tremendous chaos and uproar.
The discussion again revolved around the proposal that, before proceeding to the items of the agenda, it should be established whether all those present are “Maccabi” members. Around this proposal the real conflict [?] between the “old” and “new” members began. Finally an understanding was reached that everyone would leave the hall and a special commission would check all the members.
The result was that after the “purge” more than half of those present remained outside, and the presidium took its seats in order [?] to conduct the general meeting. Here the “Satan” interfered again and another commotion broke out among some members. Then the policeman present would no longer tolerate the commotion and dissolved the meeting.
The kehilla presidents at the starosta about the present kehilla situation

[Sosnowiec — Jewish community.] As we have already written, the members of the commissarial kehilla board have resigned and no longer wish to cooperate with the kehilla commissioner. The situation is getting even worse, however, because to this day the newly elected kehilla representatives have still not been confirmed by the authorities, so that the entire kehilla economy is being run by a single individual — the kehilla commissioner, Mr. Tencer.
In this connection the presidents of the board and of the council, Messrs. Dir. Lewertowicz and J. Fitlis [?], conferred with the starosta [district head] on the question of when the elected kehilla leadership will finally be called to take over the kehilla's affairs.
The starosta declared that he would turn to the voivodeship office [?] on this question.
A petard exploded

[Sosnowiec — hooliganism.] On Saturday at about 9 in the evening a petard exploded in the courtyard of 3 Maja Street no. 3, which is in the vicinity of the police station. Several dozen window panes were smashed. The investigation established that it was the work of louts [łobuzy] who were amusing themselves.
Christians rescue a Jew from hooligan hands

[Sosnowiec — antisemitism.] Last Friday Mr. Ozer [?] Gertler of Będzin was spending time on business matters in the beer tavern of Mr. Urbański [?] in Pogoń. At that moment a young Christian came in, drunk, who, shouting “You little Yid [Żydziak], what are you doing here?”, made to beat Gertler. The enemy of Israel did not succeed: several Christians who were present, acquaintances of Gertler's, calmed the brawler [awanturnik] down and hindered him in his “work”.
A campaign to combat begging

[Sosnowiec — welfare; begging.] Several small-traders' activists have launched a campaign to combat professional begging; the appropriate statutes are already ready and will be submitted to the authorities in the coming days.
10th Anniversary Jubilee of the Gemilut Hesed Fund in Katarzyna [?]

The Jewish community in the suburb of Katarzyna [?] (probably the district by the Katarzyna steelworks in Sosnowiec), which numbers barely 70 families, last Sunday celebrated the jubilee of the local gemilut hesed (interest-free loan) fund, which was founded 10 years ago and exists to this day in the best possible way. It was started with 1,000 zł.; today the fund works with a capital of 10 thousand zł.
The jubilee celebration took place in the "beit midrash". The president [?], Mr. Nachum Baushikowski [?], opened the celebration and gave the floor to the moreh tzedek (rabbinical judge) Stark, who delivered a speech on topical matters.
On behalf of the gemilut hesed fund in Pogoń [district of Sosnowiec], Dr. Feierman brought greetings. Also speaking were Messrs. Yakel Stark, Leibel Karpelnik [?] and Buszgenfinger [?], who called for support of the institution. With this the festive and enthusiastic jubilee came to an end.
A New Lot Is to Be Drawn

As is known, a few weeks ago a lot was drawn concerning the 5th dozór seat [kehilla council member], about which the "Mizrachi" has a complaint.
As we learn, a new lot will be drawn among all 3 lists, i.e. 1, 2 and 3. Messrs. Pszapnik [?], M. Serin [?] and Kiwer will take part.
Delegation of Jews together with Christians asks for the abolition of the shechita ban

[Page header: "Life in Kielce" — Friday, 25 Tevet 5697 — piątek 8 stycznia 1937 (Friday, 8 January 1937).]
As of this Wednesday not one of the Jewish butchers in Kielce has yet obtained a concession for kosher meat. The kehilla has taken steps to have the issuing of the concessions speeded up.
Because no shechita is being carried out, an extraordinary[?] gloom reigns in kehilla circles, as well as among the religious functionaries.
Especially sad is the situation of the small kehillas in the Kielce district, where shechita has been banned altogether. The rabbis and shochtim there are simply left[?] to perish of hunger.
This Tuesday a joint delegation of Jews and Christians arrived in Kielce from the shtetl of Słupia Nowa, where ritual slaughter has been banned altogether. The delegation — consisting of the local rabbi, Rabbi Dichtwald[?], the cantor[?] Budzinski[?], Doctor[?] Heinrich[?], the sołtys (village head) Stępień, Prus[?] Finkelsztajn, school headmaster Jan Klimecki and two more Christian councillors — presented itself to the Kielce starosta, handed him a detailed memorandum on the shechita matter and asked that ritual slaughter in Słupia Nowa be permitted again.
The starosta promised the delegation to support its request with the Kielce voivode, before whom the delegation will present itself separately.
•
For the time being, as said, no ritual slaughter had taken place up to yesterday. Even of treyf meat very little was slaughtered. The kehilla therefore had no income at all from shechita this week. The municipal (magistrat) cashier, too, who used to collect several hundred złoty every day at the municipal slaughterhouse, collected this Monday... from 10 to 15 złoty...
• • •
Because of the non-existent[?] shechita, Tuesday's market day was a very bad one for the peasants. Buyers of cattle were quite few.
This is how the first results of the shechita decree look for the time being...
Important order of the Kielce Voivodeship Office on issuing concessions for kosher meat

The Voivodeship Office in Kielce issued this week an important order to all the starostas of the Kielce voivodeship, that they should immediately issue a certain number of concessions for kosher meat and not make any difficulties. This is so that there should be no shortage of meat for the Jewish population.
Christian butchers have applied for kosher-meat concessions
As we learn, several Christian butchers from Słomniki have applied to the Kielce Voivodeship Office for concessions for kosher meat.
Young Jewish man murders his fiancée

In the shtetl of Włoszczowa a horrifying tragedy took place on romantic grounds.
A certain Jankel Berkowicz had for several years been "going around" with Chana Zylbersztajn; a short time ago the girl finally agreed to sign the tnoim (betrothal contract) with him.
The wedding was due to take place shortly, but suddenly Berkowicz learned that his bride "is going around" with another man and wants to marry him.
The jilted bridegroom then went to the bride and, after a heated quarrel, dealt her such a blow that she had to be taken in a grave condition to hospital, where she died.
The bridegroom-murderer has been arrested.
Jews without a livelihood must benefit from the Winter Relief campaign

From the Winter Relief campaign, to which the Jewish population is assessed and gives quite considerable sums of money, very few Jews benefit.
Of the several hundred registered Jewish families without work or livelihood, barely a scant thirty persons have received anything.
We therefore call upon the Jewish representatives who sit on the committee of the Winter Relief campaign to demand that the several hundred Jews without a livelihood, who are perishing of want, should also benefit from the Winter Relief campaign.
Jewish milk dealer beaten up

The 55-year-old Jewish milk dealer Jankel Kamrat went on Monday at dawn to fetch milk in a village near Kielce. On the way he was attacked by a hooligan who demanded money from him "na wódkę" (for vodka). The Jew was badly beaten, but he [?] gave the attacker a blow back with the milk can and left a mark on his face; this enabled the police to catch the attacker, whose name is Jan Dedek[?], from the village of Dambowic[?]. About the Craftsmen's Unification

(A letter to the editors)
Mr. Editor! Allow us to print the following lines in your esteemed paper, for which we thank you in advance.
In the “Zaglembier Tsaytung” no. 2 there is a notice from the craftsmen's association at Sączewskiego[?] 1, calling on its members to re-register and to come and settle all craftsmen's matters. In this connection we, as former members of the “Klein-man Kredit”[?], wish to explain to the whole Jewish public, and first of all to the Jewish craftsmen, the role of this “association”.
When already 7 years ago the unified craftsmen's association (Kołłątaja 45) was split, and the many-thousand-strong body of craftsmen was turned into a ruin, careerists and seat-grabbers exploited it and turned the collective interests of the craftsmen into a tool of private interests.
Because of such a lawless situation we decided to put an end to it, and we said: enough! All honest and sincere craftsmen must reunite! This is no time for quarrels and splits!
And indeed, two weeks ago a big craftsmen's meeting took place, at which the act of unification was confirmed and enthusiastically welcomed by the craftsmen masses of Będzin. But those who are ready, for a little honour, to sacrifice the most vital interests of the craftsmen do not want to hear the call for peace, and are trying again with their last strength to split, in order to give the impression that something is still stirring among them, that they are still alive.
But know that you will not succeed, for do you have the right to call yourselves a craftsmen's association? Do you have members at all? The Jewish craftsmen masses, who have already felt on their own skin the taste of fragmentation, of fratricidal struggle, of competition, will pass over this with contempt to the order of the day, because we have a more important task before us — the unification of all Jewish craftsmen masses for the struggle for a new, better tomorrow.
(12 signatures follow.)
Open Appeal

To the Rabbinate and the Kehilla Board in Będzin.
Some time ago a certain young fellow, Mr. R.., forced his way in as shochet (ritual slaughterer), by force and against public opinion. It is superfluous to mention by what un-kosher means this happened — and precisely thanks to the Ger dynasty and the good “relations” between the Ger dozory (kehilla board members) and Mr. President Rubinlicht he managed to have the young fellow receive an additional raise of 30 zł. a month.
But the latest raise seemed too little to the “9-Pr'”[?] little shochet; he added to it himself and said “it is all mine”…, for, belonging to the Agudah camp, he knew that a permission had already been found for the prohibition “thou shalt not steal”.
Therefore we turn to the esteemed Rabbinate with the following question:
At a time when enemies from outside want, God forbid, to force us away from our faith, and when you, members of the Rabbinate, raise heaven and earth over kashrut — at that very time you yourselves help to tear down the prestige of kashrut? No excuses, no rationalisations and no “little permissions”[?] will help, nor bringing in a foreign rabbi from elsewhere (who settled such a question with a bit of moral reproof to the young fellow); no lifting of a prohibition will help: the young fellow, who with a quiet conscience fed treyf to a mother-city in Israel, ought to have been judged by the Jewish population.
We also ask the Kehilla board, with its president at its head: since when is kehilla money ownerless, so that one may take it for oneself as one's own? We know very well that when an official of the kehilla took what was due to him, he was immediately removed from his post, and as if that were not enough, he was not even summoned to a Din Torah but handed straight over to the public prosecutor (even the Rabbinate punished him through the court instead of a Din Torah).
So we ask the board with its president at its head: how do they intend to react to the grabbing of kehilla money, and not for the first time?
Does the board, together with the Rabbinate, have two measures — one for a Gerer Hasid and one for someone who is not a Gerer Hasid?
We expect a clear answer.

Theatre Notes

„Rachel's Children“, a play in 3 acts, performed by Lucy and Misha German and her ensemble.
Oh Americhke, Americhke! The Yiddish theatre is full of America: as soon as the curtain goes up, America speaks down[?] to us from the stage — it really gives the impression that without America no Yiddish theatre would be possible.
One must admit that in America a number of Jewish actors have grown up from whom we derive great pleasure when they come to us. But it is a different matter with the repertoire: the plays imported from across the sea speak little to our hearts and — this is the main thing — they are far from any literary-artistic value.
If we cast a glance at the repertoire played there, in America, one's soul feels a little uneasy: for example „A Wife for Everyone“, „Lost Children“, „Souls for Sale“, „Yone[?] Becomes a Bridegroom“ and the like.
Lucy and Misha German, too, have brought us a play of American production — „Rachel's Children“ the play is called.
It is about a woman (Rachel). When the husband (Max) left, their three children remained with her. The woman is a devoted mother and also very energetic; with her energy she brings it about that one son becomes a doctor and the other a lawyer. The children ought to be grateful to their mother — but it turns out the reverse: there is no gratitude from the children, for whom the mother sacrificed herself so much. „She worked hard and bitterly, just so that they would grow up healthy and educated.
As soon as the children hear that their father, who abandoned them, is a millionaire, they leave the mother and run to the rich father. For the mother this is a terrible blow and she suffers greatly from it; only at the end do the children turn back[?], because at the rich father's they miss — the mother, mother-love, and they run to her.
This melodramatic piece is poorly crafted even as a melodrama, but for Lucy German it is enough that she can pour out her tears — and of tears she has a treasure: she cries not only when she goes through troubles but also from joy; her tears can move stones.
Lucy German is a brilliant mother-role actress; her tone holds a wealth of maternal feeling, there is much simplicity and warmth in her playing; she does not merely play her role, she lives it.
Misha German (Max) does everything with great intent so that his wife (Rachel) should have as many troubles as possible; he cannot win any sympathy from the theatre audience for that, but he stands out strongly with his excellent acting.
H. Garik (Naftali) has in the play a rewarding role to bring out his talent on the broad road of theatrical art; it is a pleasure to see Garik in this role.
Contributing to the general success with their acting were: L. Yakubowicz (Hiera[?]), D. Rubina (Mary), Ch. Luksenberg (Reyu[?]), Basha Libgold (Sammy), Dawid Wasburger[?] (Leybish), D. Rybak (Dave), S. Weintraub (Kive[?]), S. Rarowski (Julius) and Y. Grinshan (Mike).
The scenery is very successful.
An Observer.
