A Few Words — About Our Będzin Gemilut Ḥesed (Free-Loan) Fund

About our Będzin gemilut ḥesed fund.
As one of the most effective means of weakening the sharpness of the heavy, lasting economic crisis, which brings ruin and pauperization in its wake, are regarded[?] the interest-free credit institutions that bear the traditional name: "gemilut ḥasadim" funds.
The idea of gemilut ḥasadim is no new phenomenon among us Jews. This beautiful moral virtue, which is a pure radiance of the soul, we inherited from our ancient[?] grandfather Abraham. For thousands of years the Jewish people has been fulfilling[?] this beautiful virtue of helping its fallen brother by means of loans, in order to set him back on his feet and not let him fall into the abyss of want and poverty. The Jew performs this deed with holy trembling and religious ecstasy as a great mitzvah, because he knows that "gemilut ḥasadim is greater than charity."
Jews always had free-loan funds, but they were in hidden corners and bore the character of "giving in secret" (matan beseter).
But then came[?] hard years of crisis; economic stability began to totter and collapse, above all among Jews, and impoverishment stopped sparing even the well-off among them[?]. When the ruin of Jewish livelihoods took on an epidemic character in the Jewish street, the secret-giving aid came[?] out of its hidden corner and dressed itself in a new, modern coat — that of an interest-free credit institution under the old traditional name: "gemilut ḥasadim" fund.
The question of making use of the help of the free-loan fund ceased to be a matter to be ashamed of. The fund is a public institution. It was created for the broad masses. Lives are breaking, and those lives must be saved. But together with the name "gemilut ḥesed" there was brought into the fund the essence[?] of soulfulness. Everywhere, the funds are led by devoted, sincere people who give much time and effort for the good of this cause, which they hold sacred. Often these public workers carry out their work with great self-sacrifice, and their only satisfaction is that[?] the fallen and needy man has been put back on his feet and did not fall into the abyss of despair and want.
The free-loan funds began to become a popular movement in 1926. Within a very short time free-loan funds were founded in almost all the towns and townlets of Poland. Today there are 800—900 free-loan funds in Poland with a share capital of about 12 million złoty. The funds serve a population of about 200,000 families; the great majority of these families, who make use of the funds' help, are completely dependent[?] for their existence on this help; without the help of the funds these families would have had to become beggars, door-to-door mendicants, or even, God forbid, perish of hunger.
Our fund in Będzin, too, belongs[sic] to the first shoots of this movement of 1926. Our best and far-sighted public workers sensed intuitively the time of trouble that was moving in on us and, with holy trembling, founded the Będzin free-loan fund.
Thanks to the energy of our public workers and the cooperation of the American "Joint", our fund grew quickly and its capital reached a sum of 120—130 thousand złoty.
Everyone found comfort in our fund — the poor craftsman, the poor small trader, and even the merchant who had come down in the world — who received loans of 100, 200, 300, 400 and 500 zł. without interest, for a term of 5—6 months, repayable in small instalments.
It is truly a blessing.
But Satan must stick his nose in everywhere. The managements at the head did not understand, or[sic: "to"] did not want to understand, how to safeguard this people's treasure and people's rescuer, and there, where "the mistress of the house is a shlimazl, the cook becomes the mistress of the house" — small, unworthy creatures who stood close to the work of the fund allowed themselves such deceitful deeds as must have no place in a public institution in general, and in a free-loan fund in particular. These criminal people threw the Będzin free-loan fund down from its lofty pedestal, darkened its good name, and reduced by a significant percentage its material strength and its ability to serve with loans the broad impoverished Jewish masses, who for their existence depend[?] exclusively on the help of the free-loan fund.
The "Joint", which always watches like a faithful father over the integrity and normal development of the free-loan funds, on seeing the collapse of our fund came to us this time too with its moral help.
For 6 months now an instructor-bookkeeper sent by the "Joint" has been putting the fund of our town in order. Much lost money has been collected back. Order has been established both in the bookkeeping and in the conduct of business. The great time and effort invested in the straightening-out have been crowned with success. Now society must[?] come forward and take into its own hands the child that has recovered but is still trembling — and here arises indeed the hard question: how will this be done?
We hope and believe that the general meeting of the fund's members will take place while it is still January. Interest among the public in this meeting is great; as one can observe, a huge crowd is getting ready [to attend]. It is worth knowing, however, with what intentions the public is coming to the meeting. Does it have in mind a scramble for seats? Does it mean only to get some pleasure out of sensations by "washing the bones"[?] (raking over) of those who neglected this important public matter?
My opinion is that the huge crowd gathering at the meeting must come with a clear and pure mind — not only to judge the deeds done so far, but also to find "men of truth who hate unjust gain" (anshei emet sone'ei vatsa), such people as know and deeply understand what our[?] public duty and public responsibility are, and what significance the free-loan fund has, in today's hard and bitter time, for the Jews, who are simply being crushed under the heavy persecutions of an endless crisis and of "zoological"[?] antisemitism; and only into the hands of such people must the leadership of this enormously important institution be handed over.
The persons, however, who have stood at the helm of the fund until today have unfortunately not shown[?] the abilities and qualities enumerated above, and therefore none of these persons may again be elected to the new administration.
A Będziner.
"Literarishe Bleter" in Its 14th Year

[Literature — press.] The "Literarishe Bleter" ["Literary Pages", the Warsaw Yiddish literary weekly] has entered its 14th year — something which, in our present conditions, undoubtedly deserves to be noted.
How many literary periodicals and journals have sprung up over the last 13 years here in Poland and in other countries, rich America included — and did not manage to last long; the "Literarishe Bleter" has appeared the whole time without a break, and 660 issues have already come out, containing a colossal treasury of important works on the various fields of Jewish and world creativity.
The most prominent writers and artists of the whole world take part in the "Literarishe Bleter". Every issue carries a rich and many-sided [?] chronicle, which is a mirror of our cultural life throughout the world. Not a single phenomenon on our cultural front, which stretches over dozens of settlements and communities, gets lost, thanks to the vigilance of the "Lit. Bleter". Everything that appears on the Jewish book market is recorded with special attention. The 13 years of the "Literarishe Bleter" are thus a piece of cultural history.
Greeting the journal, we call on all friends of the Jewish word, of Jewish creativity, to become readers and subscribers of the only Jewish literary journal.
The Firm "Khap-Lap i Spółka"... ["Grab-and-Snatch & Co."]

[Sosnowiec — feuilleton / humour.]
Y. Aberzhanek [?]
(Monologue of a man without a livelihood.)
I tell you, gentlemen, Sosnowiec hasn't dropped dead yet. Sosnowiec is a town that need not be ashamed even next to America. In America they snatch little children, and in Sosnowiec they snatch big ones.
I don't understand the whole story at all — what's all the hullabaloo? What's the noise about? They snatched a young man and transported him to Ger [Góra Kalwaria, seat of the Gerer Rebbe] — well, so what's the fuss? When did they not snatch in Sosnowiec? Our Sosnowiec folk are used to snatching: Jews snatch an interest-free loan, wives snatch a "mitl" [?], merchants snatch "peklekh" [little parcels]. In the shops the merchants snatch a nap, young women go to the dancing to snatch "powodzenie" [success], girls travel to Zakopane to snatch a bridegroom — people of Zagłębie in general are used to snatching. So what's all the hullabaloo about the story of the snatched son of Reb Bezalel?...
Reading every week the sensational, gripping story of how the 16-year-old child was snatched, how he was taken off to Strzemieszyce and then to Sławków, how the brother of the abducted "child" was treated — reading the gripping story, I caught a light nap and suddenly... the door opens and I feel somebody pushing a "sholem aleykhem" at me.
"Who are you?" I ask the stranger.
"I have come to you on an important matter."
"For instance?"
"I want to go into a partnership business with you, a little business by which one can get rich nowadays."
"Get rich? By all means, let's hear."
The stranger moved closer to me and began unfolding his plan:
"You've read the story of the 'kidnapped' young lads?"
"Yes, I've read it — well, so what? What has that to do with business?"
"Don't snatch; if you get heated it won't help [?]. Listen carefully with your head, and you'll see that I have an ingenious plan."
"Well, I'm listening."
"My plan is that the two of us found a 'spółka' [company], and it shall be called 'Khap-Lap i Spółka' [roughly 'Grab-and-Snatch & Co.']."
"What will be the purpose of the firm 'Khap-Lap i Spółka'?" I asked the stranger.
"Ah, if you talk like a merchant, I think well of you. The 'spółka' will have its own warehouses, so-called 'na przechowanie' [for safekeeping] — just as there are warehouses that take in 'for safekeeping' manufactured textiles, furniture, 'tuterwarg' [? probably furs] — so we will take in 'for safekeeping' live inventory."
"What does that mean? What is this live inventory for safekeeping?"
Here my stranger gave his little beard a tug and explained the following to me:
"Our firm 'Khap-Lap i Spółka' will have its own warehouses. Other warehouses take in goods 'for safekeeping': when a merchant wants to get rid of an off-season article, or [?] of defective goods, or of fur articles in summertime, the 'reject' is sent off to the warehouses 'for safekeeping' and storage fees are paid for it. In the same way we will take in live reject goods 'for safekeeping'. Take, for example, a Jew like you, at a time like now, when your wife is getting ready to welcome the Carnival: she sits whole days at the dressmaker's, at the furrier's, at the milliner's; then come the dressmakers, the milliners, the furriers with their little bills; at every bill black wheels spin before your eyes; and if that is not enough, from all the pleasures [?] she gets 'napady' [fits], and the doctor orders her to go to Zakopane, to the mountains. Well, what do you do then? You sign promissory notes, have them discounted and send your wife to Zakopane. But once there is such a 'spółka', 'Khap-Lap i Spółka', you will be rid of all these troubles."
"How so?"
"Quite simple: before the festivities [?] you ring up the spółka, and your wife is snatched off 'for safekeeping' into the warehouse. She will stay 'na składzie' [in storage] for several weeks — over the Carnival, that is — you will pay the 'składowe' [storage fee], and basta...
So it will be with other 'live goods'. Your missus, for example, will have a 'sarave' [?] sub-tenant, or at least a 'przyczepa' [hanger-on], and she won't be able to get rid of you — so she will do the same: a ring to the spółka 'Khap-Lap i Spółka', and hocus-pocus [?] — you are in the warehouse 'for safekeeping'...
You have a landlord, and he has been making your life miserable for years; every Monday and Thursday he calls you up with a 'yemur' [?]; now you will have a remedy against him: if he starts making a big fuss [?], you will say to him:
'Uncle, shut that saxophone, or I'll hand you over "for safekeeping" right away!'
You have dealings with your house-owner, and he keeps pressing you without a break:
'"Sreytl" [?], go to your purse!' — and if you don't pay 'z góry' [in advance], he threatens you with the 'begdl' [?]. Now he won't be a 'kunker' [?]; if he turns out to be a 'davar acher' [a pig], you'll hand him over 'for safekeeping', you'll pay 'storage fees' instead of rent, and be rid of the business. And if your daughters start pestering you [?]:
'Daddy, a coat!'
'Daddy, a dress!'
'Daddy, "vakn" [?]! Daddy this, and Daddy that' — you won't think long and will hand them all over, just as they walk and stand, 'for safekeeping'.
"You hear, this will be a golden business; the firm 'Khap-Lap i Spółka' will flourish, money will be raked in with shovels — a gold mine it will be!"
*
"Mendl! Mendl! What's the matter with you? What are you raking there with your hands?" — my missus woke me up.
"I'm raking in money with shovels."
"What shovels? What money? Are you mad or out of your mind?"
"Quiet! I'll hand you over 'for safekeeping' this minute!" — I answered my missus.
— May it not befall them, these wives: if not for my missus, who knows how much longer I would have been raking in money with shovels... If not for my missus, I would have become a partner in the firm 'Khap-Lap i Spółka'...
Greetings from America to the Jews of Zaglembie

By our contributor Shlomo Frohman.
Now that I am in America, I remember that I must not forget the promise I gave the editors at my departure[?]: that while in the distant lands I would, God forbid, never[?] forget the „Zaglembier Tsaytung“, and would regularly publish my impressions — what is heard, what is going on and how people live in faraway America — and pass on straight away the pulse, or the soul, of the giant melting pot („cooking kettle“) that the immigrant Jews, or[?] the „greenhorns“, call by no other name than „Ameritshke ganev“ [„America the thief“, a folk expression].
Yes, but the first thing I want to pass on here to the Jews of Będzin is a little greeting, and it will give them something to talk about. It was a few days ago. In the New York millionaires' hotel „Astor“, a few steps from the „New York Times“ building, where I attended the annual conference of the American „Joint Distribution Committee“. First of all I learned[?] here a new, quite original American custom, which, truth be told, I found quite sympathetic. At one o'clock in the afternoon, after we had listened for a couple of hours to the sermons of the conference preachers, so that[?] the delegates would not scatter to grab lunch each in his own way, tables were laid on the large ground floor[?] for all the delegates in the hotel itself. And something else: during the meal nobody came to pester us: „What would you like, herring or fish, duck or roast[?]“. Instead, without any questions, they at once served fish and herring, duck and roast[?] and delicacies with wine besides — just the way we Zaglembie Jews have always been „used to“. Each little table was set for 4 people. The 4 people at our table introduced themselves to each other[?] and shook hands firmly: Mister Lampert, Mister Rabinson, Rabbi Graubart, Shlomo Frohman.
— From your fresh[?] Yiddish one can tell that you have not been long in this[?] country — says a middle-aged man to me.
— If you understand mame-loshn! — I answer — then, thank God, one can talk the way the mouth grew, and one is spared for once from doing gymnastics and acrobatics with the tongue in English. I come from Pilica near Będzin and...
— From Pilica? Ah, then I knew your grandfather, Yisroel Frohman, with whom I and my father, the old Rabbi of Będzin of blessed memory, stayed when we were there for the funeral of the Rebbe R' Pintshe [Pinchas] of blessed memory. I can tell you more: when the first Zionists appeared, my father asked the Rebbe R' Pintshe „what to do with them“. The Rebbe R' Pintshe passed the question on to Yisroel Frohman, who soon found out that boys and girls go strolling together outside the town; whereupon the Rebbe R' Pintshe proclaimed and announced everywhere that „the Zionists are unfit by all opinions[?]“.
Our 2 neighbours, Mister Lampert and Mister Rabinson, lend an ear to our conversation, and Rabbi Graubart translates for them into English about the Rebbe R' Pintshe and R' Yisroel Frohman, and the two Jewish Americans marvel[?] and nod their heads: „Ah, yes!“ (Oh, is that so).
A few tables further on sit people who have something of a name in America: President[?] Governor Herbert Lehman, banker Felix Warburg, Henry Morgenthau. The toastmaster of the banquet, Alexander Kahn, asks the audience to take the trouble to shout 3 times „hurrah“[?] in honour of Felix Warburg, because he has once again donated for Jewish purposes something like half a million dollars... But that is not yet the main thing.
Upon my life, it was a pleasure to watch how our Rabbi Graubart waved[?] the whole affair away with his hand: that would suit „Sshusshpe“[?] [an unidentified small town] and not New York, because — says Rabbi Graubart — our Fürstenberg in Będzin has given more than Warburg, relative to his means; so why make such a fuss (tsimes) of him?
— Here somebody is criticising! — and at once people from the surrounding tables pushed over to us, and Rabbi Graubart began to drill[?] with them a „chapter“ on charity in Będzin in general, and about Fürstenberg, who gives with a generous hand, in particular.
— If that is so — I butt in — if one is already talking here about Fürstenberg of Będzin, then surely I may go up and snatch a chat with Governor Lehman.
— Just don't insult my Fürstenberg — Rabbi Graubart tugs me by the coat-tails — and here, in America, when you approach Governor Lehman you must know how to say in a few words what you want, because, as is the way of the world, he asks at once: „What do you want?“ (in English in the original).
— Just rely on me — I reassure Rabbi Graubart. But to tell the truth I must admit that this is exactly how it was: „What do you want“, Governor Lehman asked me.
— What I want from you — I answer him — is no less than fifteen minutes.
Hearing such a thing, he stops for a minute, looks me over well, eye to eye, and apparently did not have the nerve to refuse me.
— I'll give you an „appointment“ (rendez-vous) in my government office on Wednesday at two o'clock — Governor Lehman says to me, slaps me on the shoulders, and I walk away with his visiting card in my hand.
If my conversation with Governor Lehman has important consequences for world peace, I shall yet have the opportunity to report it in the columns of the „Zaglembier Tsaytung“. Meanwhile, Jews of Będzin, know truly that your former rabbi, Rabbi Graubart, has you in mind and remembers even Fürstenberg.
———
Yes, Mr. Jacobson, the president of the Pilica Society, came running to me and asked me to write that he himself and the Pilica Society send greetings to all of Pilica.
Winter in Former Years

If one can believe the various weather prophets, we shall again have a hard winter this year. They do not even say for certain that “the frost will break bones,” but there will be no talk whatever of a “warm winter.”
It is interesting that for more than a hundred years we have not had a wholly warm winter at all. In earlier years the winters in our parts were sometimes so warm that already in the first months of the year we had a new harvest, and sometimes it happened that the grain was reaped in the field twice a year.
If we look into the records of the Leipzig fair[?], we find for instance in the year 1328 a winter that was so warm that “in January the trees were already in bloom and in April there were already ‘fresh grapes’.” In 1383 there was already “new rye in April, and that year things were so cheap that one could get almost everything for nothing.”
Also in 1384 “the grain in the field was already reaped in April, but at the beginning of May it began to rain heavily and the water caused great devastation.”
In 1397, too, “there was new grain already in May.”
From 1414 to 1429 there was no winter at all. At the beginning of March every year one “already got cherries at the market.”
After that the records stop until the year 1514. Whether the year’s weather was no longer written into the archive, or whether until that year there was always a normal winter with cold and frost, cannot be said today.
Only in 1514 is a very warm winter recorded again. “Only from 14 to 25 March was it a little cold. Then came great heat lasting two months; from 24 May to 24 August there were such heavy rains that they utterly laid waste the grain and the fruit.” “That year there was real famine in our parts, and grain was brought from France’s colonies.”
In 1515 “the fruit trees bloomed twice; at the beginning of April almost all fruits were already at the market, and at the end of September one could again pick fresh fruit from the trees.”
In 1524 there was again heat in winter, but “people then talked of a new comet coming that would turn the whole world upside down. Everyone lived in great fear; luckily, however, nothing happened.”
From 1529 to 1537 “all the flowers in the gardens and fields bloomed in December”; in 1540 “the grain was already reaped at the beginning of April, at the end of October it was reaped a second time, and fresh cherries appeared once more at the market.”
In 1551 there was such a warm winter “as had not been remembered for a hundred years; that year the grain also grew twice in the fields.”
After that the archive records a warm winter again only in 1631: “the grapes were already ripe in May,” but at that time the Thirty Years’ War was raging, which destroyed everything.
Then the years 1721 to 1724 are also recorded with winters in which “in winter everything was already in bloom.”
From 1771 to 1783 the winter was so warm that “in March everything was green as in July, and in April there was already new grain.”
The last warm winter, in which “everything turned green, even almond trees in the open field,” is recorded in 1811.
Since then all winters have come with frost and snow. The harshest winters were in 1879 and 1928, which caused great damage, especially to the fruit trees of our regions.
Z. Haber, Vienna.
Our Kehilla Mess in the "Light of Science"... — A Conversation with Prof. Messing, reported by Ben Amotz

[Będzin — satirical feuilleton, kehilla.] A conversation with Prof. Messing, reported by Ben Amotz.
Having learned that the well-known psychologist Prof. Messing [presumably Wolf Messing, the "telepathist"] is staying in Będzin, we took the rare [?] opportunity and went to him with the request that he answer our few questions, which are wrapped in a cloak of "secrets".
We found him, the professor, on Małachowskiego Street ["Malakhovska gas"], very distracted, with wrinkles on his "professorial" forehead, and after a short greeting we introduced ourselves:
— We are from the press; we ask you for an interview.
— Spare [?] me now your press matters. My head is pressing on me enough as it is, because — he says — as I came out of the "Apollo", where Koussevitzky's concert took place, I was taken "captive" ["pleni"] by the management, since [—] [the words "hast buzl zey a'nf" not deciphered] and immediately replace the impresario, who had studied the Torah portion "Lekh lekha" [i.e. had cleared off] and had not "said goodbye" to the tax office ["finanska"]...
— And if you catch him — another one from the management shouts after me — would [?] you [—] [?] him in the [—] [?] and "replace" the "fountain pen" ["vietshne piura", Polish wieczne pióro] that the fellow "borrowed" from me for a while...
Therefore spare [?] me yourselves.
— the prophet Messing apologises to us — I am "finishing" ["skantshen", Polish skończyć] this "bit of work" not for the sake of the management but for my "friend" ["pushiatshel", Polish przyjaciel] Koussevitzky; he is, after all, a sort of old "client" of mine. Many years ago, when he was a little choirboy [meshorer'l], I foretold that he would grow up to be great. Well, you have seen a hunk of a man with an "instrument" in his throat, whom you may "describe" in your press...
The next day we went to the hotel and stood in the "queue" ["agonek", Polish ogonek] among the interested parties who had come to ask advice of the "guesser"...
Women, after all, have nine measures of talk [after the Talmudic saying], and a journalist — "thin ears"; and indeed they heard how the women were chatting meanwhile.
— What are you going to ask about? — one [?] asks a young wife, dressed in the latest fashion.
— I'll tell him — she looks around to see that no one is listening, and says: — I want to know what I'll have, a boy or a girl. My mother-in-law is "sure" ["pevne", Polish pewna] that "I have a boy on my hand" [i.e. the palm shows a boy], and my mother says I'll "take after" her...
— How much will he haggle for us [?] ["gipsig" — not deciphered] — asks a tall, strong young man whose face bears witness that he is a cattle dealer, and perhaps even an ox dealer?..
Now my "turn" comes. The professor again wants to wriggle out of the business: I hate — he says — advertising; a man like me, with such a name, and the scientific world does not occupy itself with such trifles.
— "Panie profesorze"! You call these trifles? The kehillas in Zagłębie play no smaller a role than the League of Nations; the only difference is that the states of the League of Nations, when they talk of peace and unity, of disarmament and other such nonsense, have in mind new territories, new colonies; and our communal delegates, when they talk of the revival of Jewish self-government, of draining the swamps of the kehilla — have in mind rabbis, rabbinical judges [morei hora'ah], shochtim and the like [?] — a "contribution" [levy]...
The argument "convinced" Mr. Professor, and he agreed to answer the questions we put.
— What can you tell us, Mr. Prof., about the state of the Będzin kehilla?
The professor lights [?] a cigarette ["papiros"], and after a few minutes' silence he says:
— It is hard for me to speak about the situation, because even the art of telepathy cannot [grasp] such a situation; I see only that your head of the kehilla [rosh ha-kahal] is a great medium; he is a man of firm character and "watches himself" [?] in serious business.., but apparently [?] there is among you a certain group that makes use of the holy names, and this group has a strong influence on him, so that with the best will in the world he cannot tear himself away from it..
As for your parnassim [kehilla councillors], it is also hard for me at the moment to give a clear answer. Lately they have been "isolated" from the public, because they are busy with the teaching of "chokhmat khir" [?] [unclear — perhaps a pun], which makes it hard for me to penetrate their psyche..
— Do the little poultry slaughterers forget themselves with "left" [i.e. illicit, on-the-side] slaughter?
— Yes, they will never give up any "side" earnings, for as Urke Nachalnik [the well-known criminal-turned-writer] says: "I play it safe". Even if they are caught red-handed, a beit din will surely be found to look for a heter [rabbinic permission], and not only will they not be fined, they will even be called out to:
— "Mutar lakh, mutar lakh" [You are permitted, you are permitted]...
— Excuse us, "Panie profesorze", we are truly delighted with your answers. You hit the mark just as if you were a Będzin resident; so give us now [?] one more answer, to the question:
— Will the stunning system before shechita be abolished?
— The law will become still stricter; I foresee that not only will the ox receive a blow on the head before slaughter, but the [—] system will also be applied between man and his fellow. The slap system will be abolished altogether; instead of a slap they will deal a blow over the head (here Mr. Professor falls into thought, rubs his forehead and says): my thoughts carry me to the Aleksander shtibl on Kołłątaja Street ["Kalantaya gas"], where I see a young man run up to an old Jew (incidentally a great Torah scholar) and deal him a blow over the head..
— And what else do you see?
— I see a great movement of our brethren, the children of Israel, especially on Sa-tshevska [?] Street. They walk in groups, and in their pockets there are materials about "seating" and "unseating" [i.e. appointing and deposing], as in "U-netaneh tokef": who shall be brought low and who raised up..
— My imagination — says Mr. Messing — carries me into the synagogue, where I see "two Hebrews quarrelling" [Exodus 2:13], how two Jews are fighting. Only one thing is hard for me to understand: why one of them uses, in a holy place, such an unsuitable word — "a kalba" [Aramaic: "a dog"]..
Our conversation is cut off in the middle by the announcement of the hotel servant that a delegation from Sosnowiec is waiting in the corridor.
Having received the promise that Mr. Professor will pass on to us the questions of the Sosnowiec delegation — we take leave of Professor Messing.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Bo)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Bo
—o—
a) "And that thou mayest tell in the ears of thy son, and of thy son's son" (Ex. 10:2)
Why is it said of no other plague that one should tell it to children and grandchildren?
Because the Ramban quotes Rabbeinu Chananel that to this very day, since [?] the Torah said "there remained not one locust in all the borders of Egypt", a locust swarm rarely comes to Egypt; and if locusts come to the Land of Israel and cross onto Egyptian soil, they do [?] no damage whatsoever there.
It is indeed a wonder with which later generations too will occupy themselves — which is why the Torah [says], at the plague of locusts, "that thou mayest tell in the ears of thy son, and of thy son's son": to pass on from generation to generation the reason why no locust does damage in Egypt today.. Siftei Daat.
—o—
b) "Speak now in the ears of the people" (Ex. 11:2)
"'Na' is nothing but an expression of request. I beg of you: warn them, so that that righteous man Abraham should not say: 'And they shall serve them and they shall afflict them' He fulfilled for them — 'and afterward shall they come out with great substance' He did not fulfil for them." Rashi.
A.
For them, for the Jews, even a little money would have been great substance — after all, until now they had been slaves. But "so that that righteous man Abraham should not say": Abraham, to whom it had been promised "and afterward shall they come out with great substance", was after all a very wealthy man, and since to him too "great substance" had been promised, he surely understood by these words truly great substance, a great fortune. Therefore they were told to take along, besides the spoil of the Sea, also vessels of silver and vessels of gold... Ktav Sofer.
B.
The Master of the Universe could have had an excuse not to give the Jews so much money from Egypt, since out of the money they would make the Calf. But Abraham would have [?] answered: "And they shall serve them and they shall afflict them" He fulfilled for them — because of the enslavement in Egypt the Jews after all also came to idolatry ("these are idol-worshippers and those are idol-worshippers"); nevertheless He did not, as it were, refrain from bringing troubles upon the Jews, although through them they became idol-worshippers — so He need not refrain either from giving them money and silver.. Yalkut Yehuda.
• • •
"Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life" —
God, blessed be He, has various ways of testing a person. One of them is wealth: will the person withstand the test, and on becoming rich will he also remain pious? Says [?] King David: if [I am to be] tested — "surely goodness and mercy shall follow me"; pursue me, then, and test me with good fortune and riches, rather than testing me with poverty, whether I will serve God even when becoming poor... Artzot HaChaim.
C.
The Torah is not speaking here at all about borrowing money and silver from the Egyptians; the Torah means here something quite different: "and let them ask every man of his neighbour, and every woman of her neighbour" — that Jews should lend to one another, that they should implant in themselves the quality of gemilut chasadim (loving-kindness), and therefore the verse concludes: "And the Lord gave the people favour in the sight of the Egyptians" — even the Egyptians liked this quality. HaMeiri.
—o—
c) "Moreover the man Moses was very great in the land of Egypt, in the sight of [the servants of] Pharaoh, and in the sight of the people" (ibid., 3)
The cheap popularity of a mass leader comes first from the people, and only afterwards, later, reaches the elite of society. The would-be leader finds it easier from the outset to win himself fame among the masses. The true, weighty [?] leader, by contrast, attains his fame first among the better people, and from them the fame reaches the common masses. So it was with Moses too: first he became famous in the eyes of "Pharaoh's servants", and only later "in the sight of the people". Meshech Chochma.
—o—
d) "Not a dog shall move his tongue" (ibid., 7)
"Dogs, of whom it is written 'yea, the dogs are greedy [lit. brazen of soul]' (Isaiah 56) — shall they merit to utter song?... Whoso keepeth his mouth and his tongue keepeth his soul from troubles." Yalkut Shimoni.
Come and see how great is the power of guarding one's tongue — said R' Eizel Slonimer to an insolent man — the dogs, who are a people [?] "brazen of soul", merit to utter song because they kept silent only one single time...
—o—
e) "Then he and his neighbour next unto his house shall take it" (Ex. 12:4)
Immediately upon the going out of Egypt they were taught to live together — unity. The whole matter of the Paschal offering was a matter of a family sacrifice. "And the whole assembly of the congregation of Israel shall kill it" — and therefore we learn at the Seder: "Let all who are in need come and celebrate Passover"... R' Yehuda Leib Ginzburg.
—o—
f) "And it shall come to pass, when your children shall say unto you: What mean ye by this service?"
"...And some say: they were given good tidings at that hour, that they would yet see sons and sons' sons." Mekhilta.
The verse speaks of the question of the wicked son; so what are the good tidings — that they will have wicked children? Rather: "that they would yet see sons and sons' sons". The good tidings are said precisely about the grandchildren: if the sons are wicked, the grandchildren will already be better... Imrei Chen.
—o—
g) [printed "b)"] "Whether he be a stranger, or born in the land" (ibid., 19)
From this verse one can learn about the Torah's concept of nationalism. Passover is, it would seem, a national festival, and yet a proselyte must celebrate it; whereas a non-observant Jew, "whose deeds have become estranged from his Father in Heaven" (Pesachim 28 [?]), may not take part in it — because what matters is not descent but conviction, faith.. Yalkut Yehuda.
Public Help

A group of public activists in Sosnowiec is setting up a free kitchen for poor people
(From the chronicle).
Political and economic upheavals force society to create relief for the victims struck by the crisis — in case of hunger, illness, etc.
Society [lies] in the individual; [when] society is filled[?] with good people, it creates and realizes useful institutions for the benefit of the poorer, weaker class, and each of them strives to satisfy that class of people which needs one or another kind of help. Since ancient times there have existed in the world in general, and among us in particular, public philanthropic institutions such as free-loan (gemilut chasadim) funds, hachnasat kallah (dowering of brides), etc. This proves that even in that period, i.e. in the "fat" years, there were also poor, weak people in the world, for whom hospitals, an orphanage, Talmud Torahs, etc. were founded and maintained.
Today, however, they exist in miniature form, because after the World War one must remember that not a small number of people, as in the past, but 75 per cent of the people of our society need help.
I will serve here with a few examples:
In the time before the war only a small number of children went to free schooling in the "Talmud Torah". Free books — but today everyone needs free schooling, books, clothing, food and medical help; and what about the children of the other cheders? And what is the situation of the children who study in the "folk schools" [Polish public elementary schools]? Look closely at the little faces of the schoolchildren, at the pale, weak[?], anaemic, scrofulous ones, and you will be convinced that they see very little of the sun. These are children from the "facjatki" [attic garrets] and cellars, where the dwellings are damp, badly heated and badly lit. Moreover they are fed badly and irregularly. Now imagine how the mental and physical development of our youth will look in the future? And today — what[?], what is the situation of the unemployed craftsmen? Of the poor small traders and of the Jewish poor sick?
True, the poor children in the cheders and schools are being fed, but is that enough for children of unemployed, hungry parents?
These are the thoughts that torment every thinking person, every society, today: that one must put out the fire, the want, alleviate the human sufferings that cause apathy, dejection, psychological depression.
At such a time the number of projects to provide help in the form of food-provisioning (aprowizacja) support for schoolchildren, the unemployed and needy[?] people grows.
Very nice!
For little children from the cheders and schools, when they come together it is a joy: they have the opportunity to warm themselves up, to amuse themselves, and when at the same time they also get something to eat, they forget everything. But what is being done for the great number of respectable householders who have come down in the world, who still stand[?] in their prestige, for the people who will not so quickly take off the mask of shame — what is being done for such people?
What is being done with the non-professional beggars, with those who deserve to be supported first? And there are so many of them: they will sell their last garment and keep silent — he will not go to eat a "soup", lest he never afterwards be able to wash himself clean.
Therefore it is urgent, and high time, that Jewish society find a suitable way, a dignified manner, to come to the help of this class of people in the form of money support as well as, often, with foodstuffs.
This, in my opinion, is the way out for the non-professional beggars, for the respectable Jews who have come down in the world in our present time.
Herman Szer, (Będzin).

P. Blumenkrantz (Częstochowa).
(In the margin of the splendid book "The Threepenny Novel" [Brecht's "Dreigroschenroman"]).
When Céline's well-known book "Journey to the End of the Night" appeared a few years ago, containing gruesome scenes of filth, many connoisseurs shrugged[?] their shoulders:
— Eh, too much dirt, too much nakedness, it has[?] a depressing effect.
And although Goethe's famous old saying ("I sing as the bird sings that dwells upon the bough") is today[?] really outdated (in particular, Goethe himself was far from abiding by it), these hyper-aesthetes still strive nowadays to erect the unnatural partition between life and literature.
They want to find — following the Schopenhauerian formula — an elevation above the everyday in literature. The shadow-sides of life are deliberately hidden from it; there, in the book, everything must be glorified. The sunny sides of our existence, rendered with exaggeration — but God forbid no filth, for we have enough of that in life itself, in our everyday existence.
• • •
But precisely grey life and its realities; precisely the sad realisation that across the barricades of our life the book is indeed used as a strong [unclear word: "fli-vin"?] — awakened some of the aestheticisers.
"The book must be the life of our time" (Belinsky). The book must react to what happens in our life, rouse and fight, illuminate our savageries artistically and in general combat them. "The root of evil — said Pudra[?] — is not knowing the truth."
A remark here for the sake of clarity.
To react to present-day injustices there are two ways: to describe today's life, present circumstances, relationships, etc. (Ehrenburg, Sinclair and others), or to turn one's face[?] to the past and choose an epoch that resembles the present time, and in that way draw attention to today's circumstances.
Some have chosen the second way. It gives the author perspective and freedom of movement. Treating a closed epoch, the author can reach certain conclusions and also analyse it better artistically.
This way was chosen by Feuchtwanger ("The Jewish War", "Jud Süß" and others). Along this way goes the conscience of Yiddish literature — Leivick. In one of his newest works, the splendid dramatic poem "Abelard and Héloïse", his hero of the 12th century (a cleric) says:
"My spirit was clear to me and bright,
I knew for what I need it,
it led me to my very own world,
to the knowledge of man — nature — and God —
to great reason — and through great reason
I saw the stumblings,
in errors and in injustices
that God — nature — and man perceive[?];
I saw pain, in poverty and tears,
in superstitious follies and wickedness,
and I nurtured within me a will
to free the world from injustice and from pain."
• • •
Brecht[?], the author of the work "The Threepenny Novel", also carries us somewhat into the past. The action takes place in the last years of the past century, among the lower strata of London. One of the main heroes manufactures beggar-cripples; a second, his son-in-law, owns a chain of cheap stores that receive goods from thefts and break-ins[?].
But these people advance, rise in society, occupy the top ranks and swindle together with the Navy Minister, buying old ships for heavy money, and with the chief police commissioner.
We do not wish to try to give even the smallest fraction of the content of this great (even in bulk) and clever book; it would take up too much space and pale the content. One reads this book, full of the most bizarre schemes, swindles, villainies, and a shudder runs through one!
— Ha, this is the homo sapiens of our time! That is how[?] one becomes great — by trading in war, in patriotism, in bribery! And where would the serious man put himself, he who cannot send off his duty of sewing shirts for the front-line soldiers, in order to get in among the philanthropic ladies and sell his [unclear][?] stolen linen[?].
We all remember Ehrenburg's famous book "Julio Jurenito"; he conquered us with his biting irony. But Brecht uncovers for us a larger area of our life and shows what gruesome scenes of lies, hypocrisy and baseness — which are a rarity in literature.
The author does not rage; he narrates calmly, he sets the contrasting scenes before us and we are shaken ("Only the quietest weathers[?] make the greatest storm." Nietzsche)
• • •
As we have already remarked, it is hard to convey even part of the content of this captivating, almost sensational and literarily rich book.
We only wish to draw attention to this document of the times, which is so topical for us.
From the whole book cries out Cato's well-known saying, "that small thieves lie in prison chained to a block, and the big thieves stroll about freely, adorned in gold and silver."
The book has not yet appeared in Yiddish (like many others), but we, the downtrodden and outcast of today's Hitlerite world, need to read such books, to recognise the lie that has seized a great part of mankind, in order to understand better that hundreds of years — as Jean Paul puts it — must pass before a truth is understood, and only then hundreds of years until it is carried out in life.
But realised it must be! We believe [unclear word][?] in the future truth, and that is our strength!

The Beautiful Benvenida (10)

[Serialised novel.] A novel that took place in the first Jewish ghetto and stirred up the governments of Spain and Turkey.
And Nathan Ashkenazi told his mother and his brothers of everything that was happening to Jews in various lands, in Germany in particular. Jews are driven out of the towns, and when they come to the villages they are robbed. In one place they are victims of killings [?], in another victims of plunder; and amid all these wanderings there appear among the Jews people of deep and lofty spirit, and [even?] in Venice new holy books keep appearing: printing houses work there and publish the Talmud and commentaries on the Talmud, and prayer books containing holy prayers — the most beautiful songs to God — of the Marranos, who keep escaping from Spain and Portugal and at once begin [?] to live as Jews. He spoke of the Marranos as of holy martyrs, and in the same way he spoke of Benvenida.
Such talk had already had an effect on his mother and his brothers. Since he hardly spoke of Benvenida as of his beloved, as of his bride, but rather as of a Jewish [daughter?], a martyr, they listened with great interest and deep feeling and had no doubts.
Once the mother even [?] said:
— We will contribute [?] to freeing the captives in Venice too, but never that you should bind your life to hers.
— Whatever I do about it will be on a condition from your side: that you will never make any effort whatsoever to meet her.
It was hard for Nathan Ashkenazi to hear such words from his mother, and he burst out in protest; but he calmed himself with the thought that he would, after all, have help to free Benvenida.
Meanwhile the time arrived for him to appear before the head of the Sultan's court, the Grand Vizier, and only then did he find himself in a situation as though his hands and feet had been bound.
In the Grand Vizier's circle the impression of a terrible event involving a Jewish woman at the Turkish court six years earlier was still strongly felt — an event that troubled the Jews of Turkey for several generations.
The story of Esther Kiera.
For fifty years on end she held a place at the top of the Sultan's court. She kept her prominent role under the rule of three sultans. This came from her being very gifted: she knew medicine and could show how to keep the Sultan's harem in a hygienic condition. She reached the height of her power [?] in the days of Sultan Murad. The most select of the harem, the Sultana Baffa, who came from Venice, was so intimate with her that she consulted her on every decision she had to make as the chief lady of the court. When a queen of another land wrote to her, she turned to Esther Kiera to answer for her; and through her closeness to the Sultana, Esther Kiera exercised an enormous influence on the Sultan. Her standing at court rose steadily. The Grand Vizier, who speaks in the Sultan's name, trembled before her. It came to the point that when the states of Europe needed to approach the Sultan, they first turned to the Jewish Esther Kiera, and in the manner in which one writes to a queen.
With her power she helped the Jews of Turkey a great deal. Constantinople, the capital, then had a large number of Jewish merchants. For all the recognition Jews received at that time at the Turkish court, the Jewish merchants were often tormented by city officials who took high interest (levies) from them. Esther Kiera stood up for her fellow Jews and always obtained relief for them and severe punishments for the officials. She was also a great lover of Jewish culture, of the works of Jewish writers, and supported them with money so that they could publish their books. Through her financial help the Talmud reached [?] the masses of Jewish communities in a number of countries; books that later became famous for generations would never have appeared without her help. In her later years she converted to the Mohammedan [?] faith and received the name "Fatima". But her interest in Jewish culture did not diminish because of this; as Fatima she became a character in many novellas of European literature. Her death was a terrible one; it shook all of Turkey. It was a result of her power at court, of her influence on the Sultan, of how she abused her power: she chose a remarkable field on which to turn her main interest — remarkable for a Jewish woman — the military field. In the same years other Jews were also active at the Sultan's court, first Joseph Nasi and later Solomon Ashkenazi, Nathan's uncle; but their domain was a different one, more understandable for Jews: with Joseph Nasi it was mainly finance, foreign trade and through it foreign policy; Nathan's uncle devoted himself entirely to diplomacy; while to the Jewish woman Esther Kiera fell the lot of the military, and it went so far that when she appeared in the military camps for an inspection together with other powerful figures of the court, the most important army officials bowed before her.

Bought a „Diamond“ Earring for 30 zł

However much has already been written not to buy any „bargains“, there are still naive people who buy „bargains“ in the street from strangers.
So on Tuesday, in broad daylight, the Altisker[?] Herszkowicz met, on Potocka[?] street, 2 strangers who came up to him and told him that they were from Romania, but since they had been left without money in a strange town, they had to sell a pair of „diamond“ earrings.
On seeing the „diamonds“ H.'s eyes even lit up; he went with the „merchants“ into a gateway, began bargaining with them and agreed on 60 zł for the „bargain“.
— Here, have 50 zł for now, — said Herszkowicz — and give me one earring, and he dashed off[?] to fetch the rest of the money.
The gang, afraid that the merchant might spoil the deal, made a „va-yivrah“ [took to their heels], and when H. came back he found nobody.

A 20-year-old son begs his mother to agree to be betrothed...

The story we are telling here took place in the home of Rabbi Szwarc. A young man 20 years old came to Rabbi Szwarc for a birth certificate, but on checking the registry books it turned out that the lad had never been registered at all. Why? Because his parents still have no „akt ślubny“ (civil marriage certificate)...
— Well, what is to be done about it? — the young man asks the official who keeps the registry books.
— One has to start from „In the beginning“: your parents must come here, and your father has[?] to betroth your mother in the presence of a rabbi.
The young man left, and it was not long before he came back with his parents, who[?] were to undergo „chuppah and kiddushin“...
When the mother heard that her husband was going to betroth her, she had second thoughts and was about to leave. When the son saw that his mother was claiming[?] regret, he began to beg her:
— Mama, don't go away, what harm can it do you if Father puts a ring on your finger and says „harei at“?
— My enemies should go mad! — the mother began to shout — What kind of betrothal? Isn't it so[?] that some twenty-odd years ago I married your father as God commanded, and whose are[?] the 6 children we have?
— Mama — the son begs her — you don't have to tell me that, I know best of all that you married Father, but this present betrothal is only „pro forma“..
— Let all this[?] fall on my enemies, what else will people nowadays think up! Chaim Moshe, why are you standing there laughing? Here, take my finger and say the words, because the shame is eating me up.
The son was content that his mother agreed to accept kiddushin, thanks to which at 20 he will at last appear in the registry books..

[Kielce — Zionism.] Last Sunday the annual general meeting of the “Mizrachi” took place in the premises of the Mizrachist “Beit Am” in Kielce.
The meeting was opened by Mr. Dawid Mendel, who gave a brief overview of the work of the Mizrachi in general and of the Beit Am in particular.
Mr. Ch. Ehrlichman was elected chairman of the meeting, and as assessors Messrs. Nachum Pasirman, Israelik Werszkowicz and Ch.[?] Pomeranzblum as secretary.
The activity report, as well as the treasury report, was delivered by Mr. M.[?] Nagle[?]. The report shows that the Kielce Mizrachi is active in almost all areas of Jewish social life, and above all in the Zionist field.
Following a rather long lecture given by Mr. Y. Bekerman on the ideological path of the Mizrachi, a discussion developed in which a fairly large number of those present took part.
After a vote of confidence was expressed in the outgoing committee headed by Mr. Mendel, a new committee (va'ad) was elected, consisting of Messrs.: D. Mendel, Chaim Zagajski, Y. Bekerman, N.[?] Pasirman, Shmuel Gutman, Fishel Kleiner, Ch. Ehrlichman, Israelki Rapaport, Ch. Pitetski[?], Barankiewicz and Y. Wenig.

To the party court — Messrs. A. A. Rosenblum, Ch. Ehrlichman, Y. Brawer and L. Wagsztajn[?].
Among the various resolutions, a resolution of confidence was adopted, among others, in the newly elected Mizrachi [representatives] in the kehilla, Messrs. Y. Bekerman and D. Tenenbaum, promising them full moral support in their work in the kehilla. At the same time the meeting expressed its astonishment that the newly elected kehilla has so far not yet been given the possibility of starting the kehilla's work.
The meeting was closed to the strains of “Hatikvah”.
Several Meetings Against Liquidating the Kielce Voivodeship

[Kielce — politics.] Last Sunday several meetings of the Christian economic organisations took place in Kielce, at which resolutions were adopted against liquidating the Kielce voivodeship. Telegrams were sent to Prime Minister Składkowski and to the Sejm Marshal Car, who was elected as deputy for the Kielce district, asking that he counteract the project of liquidating the Kielce voivodeship. Iron Hammer Breaks During the Mechanical “Slaughter”

[Kielce — shechita.] As has already been reported in our paper, the Kielce municipality (magistrat) has still not prepared the necessary devices for mechanical slaughter. For the time being the animals are struck on the head with a heavy iron hammer. This week, while stunning an animal, the hammer broke as the animal was given a hard blow on the head, and the animal went on living. Only afterwards was the animal given several blows on the head with an axe and killed.
What Has Become of the Committee of the Jewish Kehillot in the Kielce Voivodeship?

[Kielce voivodeship — kehillot.] As is known, a few weeks ago a conference of the Jewish kehillot of the Kielce voivodeship took place in Częstochowa. At this conference a voivodeship committee was elected, which was supposed to concern itself with matters of shechita, the kehilla budgets, etc.
The constituent session of the committee was supposed to take place in Kielce in the first days of the current month.

Ox Runs Away After the Mechanical Slaughter

[Suchedniów — shechita.] In the Suchedniów slaughterhouse an ox was slaughtered last Friday by the mechanical system. When a bullet was shot into its head with the pistol, the bull broke loose and started to run; on the way the bull went into the priest's yard and made a “not-so-kosher”[?] commotion there. A kilometre from the slaughterhouse several experienced butchers' workers caught “the lad” and led him back to the slaughterhouse, where he had to be slaughtered all over again...
Dabrach's[?] Peasant Party Dissolved

[Kielce voivodeship — politics.] On the basis of the order of the Minister of the Interior, the Kielce voivode Dr. Dziadosz has dissolved Dabrach's[?] peasant party in the territory of the powiats (districts) of Iłża, Kozienice, Radom and Stopnica, for conducting communist activity to the detriment of the state. Disaster with a Freight Train at the Kielce Railway Station

[Kielce — accident.] This week a disaster occurred at the Kielce railway station involving freight train no. 73. [Kielce — kehilla.] The renovation[?] at the kehilla has been completely finished. Work in the office is already being conducted normally. The large hall now looks splendid.

New Deputy Starost in Kielce

[Kielce — appointments.] The previous deputy starost in Kielce, Mr. Schneider, has been transferred to the same post in Mińsk Mazowiecki. Mr. Nowakowski, an official (referent) of the security department in the Łódź voivodeship, has been appointed Kielce deputy starost.
Boxing Match between „Maccabi“ and the Military Sports Club

Zelig Grosman, of blessed memory

[Kielce — obituary; community.] Jewish Kielce on Wednesday accompanied to his eternal rest one of the first Zionists in Kielce, Zelig Grosman, of blessed memory, who for many years was the shammes (sexton) of the Zionist beit midrash "Sha'arei Zion".
The late Zelig Grosman belonged to the type of fanatical and utterly devoted Zionists whom one rarely meets nowadays.
As long as 40–50 years ago he took part in all the clandestine Zionist meetings, which were strictly forbidden by the Tsarist authorities and for which one was threatened with being deported to Siberia.
Various stories are told about his love of Zionism. Thus, for example, it is told that 40 years ago Zelig Grosman dared [?] to slap the then Kielce magnate Litauer, who wanted to express himself in unseemly words about Dr. Herzl, of blessed memory.
Although all his days he lived in want and in [?] and was occupied with the worry of making a living, his love of Zionism did not diminish by a hair. He always shared in the sorrows [?] and joys of Zionism.
Zelig Grosman's funeral took place on Wednesday afternoon at the expense of the kehilla. In the Zionist beit midrash "Sha'arei Zion", into which the deceased was carried, eulogies were delivered by the comrades Rer. [?] Vilani [?] and Berl Moszenberg [?]; cantor Gornicki recited "El Male Rachamim".
It is a vexing fact that very few Zionists took part in the funeral, except for the older ones who had worked together with the deceased. His honour, however, was not diminished by this.
Honour to his memory!

Slaughter Revenue Has Fallen Considerably, but the Number of Supervisors Has Been Increased..

As everyone knows, since New Year, when the ritual-slaughter law came into force, the revenue from shechita has fallen considerably. For instance, according to statistical figures it has been shown to us[?] that the revenue of the Będzin shechita (is) lower by about 50 per cent compared with the previous months. It goes without saying that when revenues become smaller, expenses too must be reduced in parallel, in the same proportion. So common sense dictates; but it turns out that when one has to tear (a piece) off the kehilla's "nag" (klyatshe), it is might that rules, not fairness.
In Będzin, for instance, there is a "Va'ad ha-Kashrut" which, in connection with the slaughter law, has "afflicted" the town with several new — supervisors (ne'emanim); and it is surely as clear as day that "new supervisors are needed": for if earlier, when all the butcher shops sold kosher meat, the number of supervisors hitherto was sufficient, now that kosher slaughter has been reduced to a minimum, "one must take on new supervisors"...
In Sosnowiec too the "Va'ad ha-Kashrut" suddenly took up kashrut matters and also "established" that for the 4 kosher butcher shops "more new supervisors are needed"...
Against this, however, stands the kehilla commissioner, who does not permit the kehilla budget to be burdened with expenses for the "seasonal supervisors".
At the meeting held on Sunday at the Sosnowiec kehilla, the kehilla commissioner spoke out categorically on engaging fresh supervisors: if — he said — supervisors are needed, then the members of the rabbinate, who figure in the budget as supervisors, should supervise kashrut...
Gypsy "King" Kwiek Arrested and Jailed.

A sizeable group of Gypsies arrived in Sosnowiec — the "royal court" of the Gypsy king Michał Kwiek, together with his very own august person.
The Gypsy "monarch", accompanied by his suite and by the police, went off to the police commissariat. It turns out that the king is mixed up in a far[?] from royal affair.
In the middle of last summer[?], when the "royal" camp was staying in the fields beyond Mlachów[?], the "king" arranged a noisy party. A [?] group of village youth from the surroundings also came to this party and spent time together with the Gypsies.
During the zabawa (dance party) a brawl (awantura) broke out between the Gypsies and the village youngsters, which ended in bloodshed. The Gypsies, who were in the majority, carried the day; in the process they badly beat up several young village men.
The police intervened and arrested several Gypsies, among them also the sovereign[?] "king" Kwiek.
An Open Letter to the Esteemed Rabbi, Rabbi Chamaides.

The Jewish population of Będzin received with satisfaction the news that you, esteemed Rabbi, had been appointed temporarily to fulfil the functions of rabbi in our town, for we had reason to believe that you would fulfil your office objectively and impartially and that for you no parties and groups would exist, as befits a rabbi, a leader. But how astonished we were, unfortunately, to learn that already in the first days of your tenure in our town you bestowed your trust upon a "certain group" — upon those who from the outset fought your candidacy, upon those who never reckon with public opinion and with the real interests of the Jewish community, but always impose their own by force, for which they use various dishonest and improper[?] means, so as always to be able to rule over Jewish society.
And in this case too the said gentlemen (h"h), with the help of the "Neysraln"[?] kehilla president, who was the executor of the Agudist-Gerer[?] gang, seek (to carry out) a new assault on the Jewish kehilla in Będzin, and want to impose by force a young man as rabbi of Będzin, one who has no qualifications whatsoever to occupy so important a post as the rabbinical seat of Będzin.
And you, esteemed Rabbi of Katowice, have been drawn indirectly[?] into this important question and, against Będzin public opinion, have perhaps taken the side of this group.
We mean this in connection with the decision that the official registration books (meldungs-bikher) belonging to the kehilla are to be kept in the home of that young man, which gives the group and its candidate the opportunity to exploit this for their campaign purposes.
We ask: how can the official kehilla books be left in a private apartment and under the supervision of a private person?
Do you not understand, esteemed Rabbi, that this step of yours amounts to an official declaration[?]... and an internal[?] meddling in the most vital (literally: "bloodiest") interests of the Jewish community of Będzin, and to helping one side with your authority — whereby you arouse against yourself the resentment of the majority of the Jewish population?
Surely we have the full right to demand of you full and strict objectivity.
For all these reasons we demand of you unconditionally to remove all the official documents from the private house, and to give the Jewish citizens of Będzin the possibility of settling their affairs in the official kehilla office and not in the street, where one is[?] under the control and coercive agitation of the Agudah (more correctly: Ger).
This we expect of you.
Zionist Organization, the "Mizrachi"[?] and "Torah va-Avodah" organizations, Będzin.

[Sosnowiec — culture; theatre; Jewish gymnasium.] (On the performance at the Sosnowiec municipal theatre by the pupils of the Jewish gymnasium.)
It is long since the question of "Le'an?" — "Whither?" — has been so topical among us. We are now coming ever closer to the question: "Whither?" Whither leads the thorny road of the Jewish people? Is there for us a holy goal which demands, and is also worth, so many sacrifices, so much suffering? The question sits so[?] deep in our hearts, gnaws[?] at our minds — "Whither?"
