Current Affairs... (A sober voice: on the future of the Gemilut Chesed fund in Będzin)

(A sober voice. On the future fate of the Gemilut Chesed [interest-free loan] fund in Będzin.)
In the previous issue of the „Zaglembier Tsaytung“ I read the article about the Będzin Gemilut Chesed fund, written by „a Będziner“. That article truly touched on a very important question: from whom and how this important board is to be formed, so that the Będzin fund — which was created with so much effort and has truly helped many of our citizens out of severe hardship — will at last be run sensibly[?], so that the hands[?] of unworthy people will no longer have any control over it. It is truly a sin before God to take such an institution, which today is the only rescue for Jews, an institution that has every chance to grow and develop greatly, and to leave it ownerless — I say ownerless, because managing it the way it has been managed until now has not only brought the fund no fame and honour, but has actually caused much grief. Many members, for example, because of the indifference of the board, which failed to demand the debts in time from the ill-willed borrowers, now have to pay the debt, many of them as guarantors[?].
True, the debt can and must be paid; no Gemilut Chesed money may be lost. A means that keeps people alive must not be diminished or reduced. The fund's money is a people's capital, created in a time of trouble — and when has there ever been such a terrible time of trouble as today. It must be guarded like the apple of one's eye and must not be reduced by a single grosz; and all the more that lawless people should be raking from it into their own pockets — that is certainly, certainly not permitted.
Considering the situation of the fund until now, I come to the following conclusion: the people who have sat on the board until now did not understand their mission; the poor souls did not know what responsibility they had taken upon themselves; they probably did not know „what it's eaten with“; they understood only one thing: one must be filled with the attribute of mercy and satisfy[?] everyone who wants and everyone who needs. Mercy is indeed a very fine attribute, but where there is public responsibility and monetary law, one must also show „the attribute of strict justice“. A thing that is subject to weight and number must be guarded strictly, not merely as one's own thing but as a sacred thing, to the point of self-sacrifice. Possibly there was some understanding of responsibility, but it was a [wilful?] laziness about paying proper attention, relying on unscrupulous people; and the latter abused it in a criminal manner, while the board as well as the audit committee slept peacefully and did not bother to take a look whether everything was in order.
— It is clear as day that the management was an ill-starred one. The same householders must not remain any longer — not a single one of them. A new board of absolutely fresh people must come in throughout. Never mind — Będzin is still rich in human material: we have among [—] quite decent, conscientious people with heads on their shoulders, with a social sense and with a good, honest will to work for the common good. We also have very fine and honest people among the householders, merchants, artisans and small traders, Orthodox, Zionists, who know how to safeguard a communal grosz and how to bring benefit to the public, people who will not spare effort and time for the sacred cause and will work for its own sake.
Therefore, in order to emerge successfully from the situation that has arisen, one must apply, in my opinion, these 2 points:
1) Even before the general meeting, several gatherings of the best people from all strata may[?] be held, in order to work out a common list that will be imposing and acceptable to the general meeting; for if this is not done beforehand, the general meeting will never get to the end of the question.
And 2) the candidates who are put forward on the above-mentioned list must not come as representatives of groups or factions by which they are sent, but must be recommended and elected personally, according to their personal qualifications, so that these persons will not be compelled and bound by an obligation to repay their benefactors, who granted them the honour of becoming a member of the board.
Thus, and only thus, will we be able to achieve something worthwhile, and the Gemilut Chesed fund in Będzin will find its true and proper master.
Also a Będziner.
Tractate Kashrut...

When it began a year ago and was realised at the New Year [1 January 1937], so that the new slaughter law is a fact, it would have been foolish of us not to try to adapt ourselves to the new situation.

Last week we read a prohibition from the Sosnowiec rabbinate: "The hindmost part of the meat from kosher slaughter is treyf; Jews may not buy it."

In a number of regions of Poland, also in Galicia, people know nothing of these troubles; there they porge the hindquarter meat and sell it as[?] kosher lemehadrin min hamehadrin. The Jewish newspapers all over the country do not let up with the ...[?] [doubtful word] argument, and the practice of the second week of the slaughter bears witness[?] to how far the rabbis stand from the reality of life.

But we mention this only in passing, because it is connected with an appeal addressed to the so-called "freethinking" part of our Jewish society.

It is surely no secret that very many Jews do not think much of ritual slaughter. The rabbinate surely has no idea how far this matter has already gone. Were our Orthodox fathers with their long beards and silver atores [tallit collars] to ask their children, they would learn in which butcher shops Jews have bought meat.

We are not out to preach morals to anyone. We do not look into anyone's pots and do not teach anyone piety. We are not emissaries of the rabbinate.

But — allow us to paint such a picture:

On New Year's Eve [Sylvester night], that is, a few hours before the New Year, when the slaughter law came into force, three young Jewish intellectuals sat at a table in a night club. All three ordered dishes from the waiter. One ordered a dairy dish, the second — drinks[?], and the third — a pork cutlet.

It is not hard to understand that the one who ordered dairy is something of an observer of kashrut — at any rate he does not eat treyf meat; the second is a vegetarian altogether, and the third is — a "free" man.

A conversation developed at the table. The vegetarian condemned in general the tormenting[?] of living creatures and put the shochet and the slaughterhouse killer in one row. The kashrut-observer explained that although he is not pious, he has nevertheless grown organically together[?] with the old forms of Jewish slaughter, and precisely[?] as regards[?] meat he is unable to eat it if it was not prepared[?] the way his mother and his grandmother used to make meat kosher.

The third, touching the pork cutlet with his knife and fork, held forth as follows:

"I understand the vegetarian; he has a standpoint, perhaps even a worldview. But I do not understand someone who smokes on the Sabbath, shaves his beard, does not lay tefillin, does not refrain from other transgressions, and only when it comes to meat does he remember his grandmother. That is a weakness, a lack of character. And yet I think that tonight, on this Sylvester night, I am taking leave of the pork cutlet; in the near future such a thing will not enter my mouth, and not only that — from tomorrow on my wife will choose[?] specifically a Jewish and kosher butcher shop; not because I am suddenly becoming pious, but because kosher Jewishness is, after all, what I am after. I cannot imagine how a Jew, whoever and whatever he may be, can under present conditions consume meat knowing that it does not come from a Jewish butcher shop. To eat kosher meat means to support that part of the butchers, meat workers and meat dealers who have artificially been put in a worse position than others. To eat meat from a Jewish butcher shop is something of an answer to a great many things. To eat kosher meat is a question of national and human dignity for every Jew. Therefore tonight, on this Sylvester night, I say adieu to the pork cutlets.."

We believe that more than one Jewish "freethinker" speaks and thinks this way. This is how Jews now feel who perhaps their whole life made no distinction between a Jewish and a Christian butcher shop. Kosher meat takes on quite a different taste for them, and it depends on the prohibition or the hechsher of the rabbinate.

And if so, it is a wrong[?] when any rabbinate whatsoever comes out precisely now with a prohibition. It is liable to put every Jewish butcher in such a position that the kashrut committee [vaad hakashrut] will be unable to issue him any hechsher, and will push such freethinkers back[?] into non-Jewish butcher shops.

Y. N—m.
My Wife and I. (Monologue of a 'capitalist' immigrant)

I say to my wife: you know, Chaja, we have lived our life in all sorts of ways; we have stood on the horse and under the horse [i.e. known ups and downs]. But, thank God, to this day we have always had what we need at home, and precisely because I have a natural instinct, like a mouse on a ship: when the ship is sinking, it is the first to run away. I tell you, Chaja, the economic ship is going down for the Jews, and as long as one still can, let us go to Palestine. It is a free country, and as the Almighty helps, so we will settle in. One doesn't need a heavy household with whole sets of [?] furniture ["spanavinen" — doubtful reading], one doesn't need coal and warm clothes — there it is warm all year round and the air is good. In the sun one can bathe[?] all year; we will live in our own land free, as human beings and among human beings. But she is, after all, a Jewish woman like all Jewish women in the Diaspora: when the husband says day, she says night; and by the way, like all Jewish women, she is a little conservative. She knows[?] that a maid ["shikse"] like Stasia she will not have in Eretz Israel, and she fires off an argument: "Nie pojedę do Palestyny!" [Polish: "I won't go to Palestine!"].
A minute later she realised that the tempo[?] had been a bit too fast, and she says, now in a calm and practical tone: when Rabinowicz left for Palestine he got "odstępnego" [Polish: key money] for the flat and sold all the furniture at a good price, and I'll get nothing for the furniture, even if I give it away for free. So I say to her: Chaja, first of all, who says that in Eretz Israel you must cook on Primus stoves? If you like, I'll buy you an electric cooker on the very first day. Second, as for the furniture — you are a capable woman after all; don't look at anyone, start selling and sell everything. We won't drag any rags[?] from here; a złoty to a złoty, a hundred to a hundred, a nice sum will add up, and in Eretz Israel we will buy everything new and begin a new life. Then I tell her: one thing you must know, my wife — in Palestine I am free and you are free; I have decided and no force can hold me back; I am going to Palestine for sure; you can come along — think it over. I won't force you.
My wife is no fool. She heard such clear words from me, and also that she would not cook on gas burners and Primus stoves, because my wife believes me when I say something. To tell the truth, she had no great desire to go; she is bound up[?] with a whole town of acquaintances, "kumoszki"[?] [gossip-friends], pastry shops, cinemas, theatre, restaurants with dancing — everything was homely to her.
But it's a lost cause: when you can't get over, you have to[?] go under. She began to sell off our things; out of every little item she made money; a nice sum added up, and once you are left without furniture and without a flat, you leave gladly — and the sooner the better.
The send-off was a fine one, with flowers, chocolate and other gifts; on the train we travelled among halutzim [pioneers], it was merry, and the voyage on the ship was a real holiday.
In Eretz Israel we settled in decently: we went to a boarding-house and lived a couple of weeks quietly and pleasantly. Right on the morning after our arrival I went out with my wife and bought an elegant electric cooker, for which I paid almost as much as my wife had received for selling the period-style ["stylowy"] bedroom. We took a nice flat; my family was pleased with everything — the sea, the beautiful warm winter — but my wife was happy: everything new and clean[?], and above all an electric cooker. My energetic wife set about, with all her zeal, keeping house and cooking the first dinner in Eretz Israel, at home in our flat, on the electric cooker.
She put the soup on — and my wife runs every minute to the "licznik" [Polish: electricity meter] to check the calculation of the "prąd" [Polish: current]. The meter turns [?] ["mi a teytl" — doubtful reading] and every moment throws out another figure. She put the roast on — my wife runs to the meter; the meter goes "svigne"[?], turns and throws out figures; but my wife has lost her sense of humour — a small matter! — the power to cook the dinner costs more than the whole dinner is worth. I console her that one has to get used to it: an electric cooker, I say, is progress after all; in all the restaurants they cook only electrically, and it is cleaner[?] after all.
• • •
In her girlhood years my wife Chaja was young, pretty and very intelligent, knew languages and felt[?] a serious inner need to seek the ideal path in life; she sought it in young people's literary circles and in political parties.
By nature hasty[?] and full of temperament, she threw herself from one party to the next; no party gave her full satisfaction. The practical path in life she found in the party with me, in which she was sometimes the right wing and sometimes the left wing — but always in opposition. After the wedding she did not fall behind the intelligent circle, and took an interest in the newest problems and the newest literature.
She came to Eretz Israel with a firm resolve to learn Hebrew, so as[?] not to fall behind good society and to be able to follow the problems of Eretz Israel through the local press.
And indeed she soon took a teacher and began to study. It did not come easily to her: first, she is no longer so young, and learning is harder; second, in contrast to the European languages, Hebrew is read from right to left — so with her it comes out that Eliezer Ben Yehuda Street is called Yehuda Ben Eliezer Street.
Acquaintances asked my wife how she likes Eretz Israel. She answered: everything is good and fine, only she has two mortal enemies here: the electric cooker, for which she gave up a period-style bedroom, and the meter spins too fast; and second, the Hebrew teacher: the language knocks against the "trampl"[?] of a wall and bounces back — just like a pea against a wall: it knocks, rebounds and leaves no trace.
At the first "wieczorek" [Polish: evening party] that my wife gave, she decorated the table with some elegant cakes, exactly as if from a pastry shop — a capable woman, my wife! I ask her whether the cakes were baked on the electric cooker, and she answered that they were baked on a Primus and that she had also bought a gas burner.
Now my wife is completely acclimatised and content with Eretz Israel; the electric cooker she uses very[?] rarely, and Hebrew she studies a little, like this: on the couch ["tapczan"] doing the lesson — and as soon as she looks into the Hebrew, she falls asleep.
I suggested she buy a gas cooker ["gazowa"], but she categorically refused: she is comfortable with the Primus and the gas burner.
Sent in by P. Karnowski (Tel Aviv).
Clever Until It Comes to the... Jew

(Remarks on the times).
Three characteristic traits can be observed in our "good friends".
1) They weep, poor things, that they are suspected of antisemitism for nothing — it is simply a slander. They desire only the truth and indeed speak the pure truth.
2) They accuse Jews of hot-headedness and exaggeration. Especially the Jewish press — it blows up, they claim, every trifle. It cries out[?] hysterically, as Jews in general like to do, whenever someone allows himself to say a "[—]"[?] word.
3) In all matters they have a duty to acquaint themselves thoroughly, and the scholars among them in particular feel obliged to know the subject at hand. Where Jews are concerned, however, this duty does not exist. With the greatest levity people take up Jewish matters and talk about them like experts[?]. At the same time[?] they display ignorance and the crudest[?] notions about Jews, and they write about them in such a confident and authoritative tone that it[?] is bound to influence the uninformed.
• • •
We do not intend to engage in apologetics now. We think, by the way, that the efforts of Jews to prove with signs and wonders that our "good friends" are mistaken will lead to nothing. For every cheder child already knows one thing: all these sermons and scribblings are merely for rhetorical show, and the real reasons are entirely different — very practical and sometimes even purely personal.
We touch on the matter now in connection with a book that came into our hands in recent days, a book written by a Belgian[?] professor about Poland, in which he devotes a special chapter to the Jews as well.
Although the book appeared years ago and much has changed in the meantime, the motives concerning the Jewish question are the same ones that the enemies of Israel claim[?] today, and they contain the characteristic traits noted above.
But first a few words about the professor himself, for orientation.
Prof. Sarolea [probably Charles Sarolea], the author of this book, held a chair in Brussels, where he taught philosophy, and later in Edinburgh. He is also engaged in linguistics and literature, travels a great deal, and besides this he is interested in politics.
Well, it follows that such a person ought to approach a subject with certain preparation and objective assessments. But unfortunately it is quite the opposite.
According to Sarolea there are five million Jews in Poland! The Jews — he says — it would be very good if they wanted to assimilate, but the Jews have no wish to give up their jargon, which is in fact a broken "German tongue". Precisely because of this German tongue "Jews love the Germans" (!)
Sarolea tells of a dispute that threatened[?] to break out[?] between a well-known English "Sir"[?] and a Jew.
And he boasts:
When the polemic grew sharper and I wanted to soften it, I spoke up:
— Mr. D., [I am][?] ready to admit that the Jews are "the salt of the earth", but Mr. Leo Levinson[?] will also have to admit that too much of this salt has been poured into the Polish pot...
• • •
As we have already noted, as long as it does not come to the Jews, the professor speaks sympathetically. It is pleasant when a foreigner feels the joy of a liberated people and speaks warmly of the efforts (of the Polish people) toward its liberation.
But as soon as he comes to the Jews, he often displays complete ignorance.
"Besides the strange pretensions — writes Sarolea — of the Jews to have their jargon recognised, besides their German-Russian sympathies, there is yet another reason that causes Polish irritation: Bolshevism, spread by the Polish-Jewish 'Bund' (!), arouses revulsion among the honest people."
• • •
Strangely, this professor's arguments are almost the same as those of Budzyński[?] et compagnie. He also claims that the percentage of Jews in the towns is too large. The Jews hinder the creation of a Polish middle class, which is the foundation of a people's prosperity.
All Polish towns — complains the foreign guardian — such as Warsaw, Łódź etc., suffer from the Jewish inclinations toward trade, and they suffer from what may be called "Jewish congestion".
• • •
It becomes simply eerie to see[?] how people of stature acquire petty notions when it comes to a quite complicated people.
G. K. Chesterton, in the preface to that book, offers this piece of "wisdom":
"The Jew had his old accounts in Poland with the peasant (!) and even with the noble landlord, and when he changed into a Bolshevik he could openly show his hatred. From this standpoint one must regard[?] the passage of Jews into the Bolshevik and Zionist camp as a natural thing. 'The Bolshevik and the Zionist attack Europe openly and set out on their own path'."
• • •
Where are you, my experts on the Jewish people! [—][?] informants with the approval of clergymen spread very quickly among the simple masses. The professor gives his popular expositions a scientific, so to speak, face, and the simple public, which trusts such soothsayers — especially those seemingly disinterested (as in this case) — draws its knowledge about a people all of whose [—][?] and strivings are as foreign to these informants as the Yiddish language and Jewish creativity are foreign to them, the rises and falls of the Jewish people, its desires and its longing for a different, just life.
How much does the creator of "Mickey Mouse" earn?

[World — cinema; economics.] There is hardly a single country in the world today where people do not know the films with "Mickey Mouse". Even in countries where Greta Garbo is unknown, Mickey Mouse is a familiar figure; in Soviet Russia she was crowned with the title "Comrade Mickey".
Few people know that the whole "Mickey Mouse" turned eight years old only a few days ago, and in honour of this jubilee the creator of "Mickey Mouse" has published her "memoirs", in which he also describes how Mickey Mouse was born.
Walt Disney, an American from Kansas who now lives in California, is the inventor of Mickey Mouse. In his young years he read many descriptions of animals and birds, and since he can draw well, he used to send caricatures of various animals to American newspapers, and earned a meagre living [?] from it.
Eight years ago it occurred to him to draw a mouse and to make a little film of it, which was very well liked, because it was something new in the film world.
— Today two hundred of the best draughtsmen are employed making the Mickey Mouse films; a whole company of writers works out stories for Mickey Mouse. Every film comes with great difficulties. It has been calculated that if one man alone wanted to make such a film, he would have to work at it for five years, 24 hours a day. There are special schools in which the best draughtsmen study for a whole year to make Mickey Mouse pictures. Until such a draughtsman learns the craft, it costs the company a thousand pounds in tuition.
Because of the great expenses required for such a film, and because of the high salaries these collaborators cost, Disney does not earn much from the films, although up to today they have been shown no fewer than 468 million times. Disney has handed over the rights to the Mickey Mouse films to a company which pays him a sum of 120 pounds a month for them — and yet Disney is today a great millionaire.
He gets his income from the firms that manufacture articles with the picture of "Mickey Mouse". Disney relates in this connection that about seven years ago an English firm asked him to allow it to exhibit a Mickey Mouse doll [?] ("Puppe") at the Leipzig fair.
Disney gave his permission and asked 20 pounds a year for it. — He reckoned that perhaps 10 more firms would come forward afterwards, which would bring him a fresh 200 pounds a year.
Meanwhile so many firms came forward that Disney had to found a Mickey Mouse company of his own, to deal with granting concessions for making Mickey Mouse articles. This company today has 44 branches [?] in all the larger cities of the world.
Today there is not a single branch of industry that does not produce Mickey Mouse articles for children and adults, toys [?] and textiles — everything is made with the "Mickey Mouse" trademark, and the manufacturers do good business with it, because people buy the articles.
From these Mickey Mouse companies Disney has had an income in recent years of one and a half million pounds. On top of that come the fees from the newspapers, which constantly carry pictures and descriptions of the new Mickey Mouse films and pay Disney a handsome [sum — reading unclear] for it.
When such a Mickey Mouse film is finished, it is first shown in the Mickey Mouse clubs that exist all over America. The mothers and children who are members of the clubs give their expert opinion on the film — whether it is good or must be changed; only after that is the film screened in the cinemas of the whole world.
Once Disney showed a Mickey Mouse who smokes and drinks; but since the mothers and the children too did not like the drinking and smoking, the whole film was burned, and Mickey has never again been seen drinking or smoking.
Z. Haber, Vienna.
Our Panorama.

[Zagłębie — weekly satirical feuilleton; synagogue life and religious parties.] By Ben Amotz.
("Two" can be one thing. — "Reden" Jews have no time. — They travelled in partnership. — Forgotten: the Yekum Purkan. — An attack on synagogue gabbaim. — Must a gabbai wear a beard? — A delegate who is half Mizrachi and half Agudah. — Messiah's times.)

— "Time is money," says a proverb. — This holds for commerce in particular; at least there are still places where "Jews have no time"...
Take, for example, a Jew who lives in the "Reden" colony near[?] Dąbrowa [Dąbrowa Górnicza] — he will not spare you a single minute of time; time there is a piece of gold, not to mention[?] in the morning, when time is — diamonds...
And if you shrug your shoulders and do not believe that this is really so, then think for a while and strain your imagination: in the beit midrash at "Reden", where you see[?] how a minyan of Jews is "led" by prayer leaders — one stands at the lectern [amud] and the other — before the Holy Ark, and prays.
— What happened? — you will then ask; what does "trei kashtei[?] be-ḥad ḥarka[?]" mean? Well, ask the gabbai; he will make it clear to you, and you will then find out that both hold "concessions" on the "board" [the lectern]; the only difference is that the one standing at the amud has yahrzeit, and the one before the Holy Ark — is saying Kaddish.
In normal times, when time did not play such a great role as today, one would wait for the other; but today, in the age of technology and radio, when on the line of the once crawling "Iwangorod railway" run "motorówki" [motor railcars], one surely cannot demand that a Kaddish-sayer should first "let someone else up to the board" — a yahrzeit-holder? Is that possible? So there was truly no other way out but that both should "harness themselves to the wagon" and "travel" in partnership, because:
— "Time is money."
———
Because of a mistake by the musaf prayer leader at the minyan of the Sosnowiec [Sosnowiec] "Linat ha-Ḥolim", the worshippers also lost time, and not only time, but "their appetite meanwhile passed"...
The "occasion" happened precisely on the last Shabbat Mevarchim. The gabbai, as always, honoured one of the worshippers to bless the new month. This time the prayer leader did not wait, "so as not to lose time[?]", but at once took the book in hand and:
— Yehi ratzon milfanekha...
Suddenly there is a commotion; part of the congregation starts banging on the prayer books. Well, well, something has been forgotten.
— Forgotten what? — ask, curiously, those who were already in the middle of the "ḥayim"[?] [of the Yehi ratzon prayer]...
— Don't you know what? — The Yekum Purkan!...
— Of course! Such a sin on Shabbat Mevarchim! It is really an injustice to put to shame[?] such dear "guests"...
— But don't[?] make a commotion! — shouts the gabbai; there is a remedy for everything, never mind, "we'll go back"...
And so they did: they "appeased" the Yekum Purkan and then blessed the new month.
The advice was indeed "to the point", for[?] after all the congregation had left "the straight line" and saved a little time.
———
The "events" in the Będzin [Będzin] synagogue can be compared to the upheaval in Spain..., because both here and "there" the events break out at the same time and bear almost the same character. For instance, what do the Spanish fascists want? — To unseat the People's Government so that they themselves can climb onto the bench; and the "fascists" in the Będzin synagogue, what do they want? — To unseat the beardless gabbaim.
And lo and behold! The "victories" of the Spanish fascists look for the time being just like the "victories" of the "fascists" in the Będzin synagogue... Almost every "attack" fails to bring the desired result, and everything stays as it was.
The same fate befell the "assault" made last Shabbat on a "beardless gabbai".
— Down with him! — voices were heard from the "fascist" group, long live the beard!
The "neutral" public rose to its feet, thinking that any moment now "things will get lively"; but the weekly portion Bo had had its influence on him [the gabbai], and he fulfilled what is written in the verse, "and the heart of the gabbai was hardened" [a jocular twist on "and the Lord hardened Pharaoh's heart"], and did not budge from his firm position.
———
The Mizrachists in Sosnowiec are different: they are "weak natures" and have reason to make a "retreat" at every moment unfavourable to them.
Thus last Sunday the Sosnowiec "Mizrachi" organized a district conference, in honour of which a delegate arrived from the "government"[?].
Right at the first "reception", the connoisseurs of the Sosnowiec "Mizrachi" strained themselves to establish the "diagnosis" of the "in-law" [the guest]: he is somehow not quite... fit[?]; supposedly he comes from the Mizrachi central office, yet the "look" — somewhat Agudist...
But later, at the conference, the Mizrachists saw before them the same thing as once upon a time — Balak... [who sought a curse and got a blessing]. He, for example, delivered a sermon about Eretz Israel, such that it would be forbidden[?] — if R' Nisa[?] Friedman had said what the Mizrachi delegate remarked "me'ir ḥavira"[?]...
— Well, do you perhaps think the in-laws reacted properly? God forbid; they fell silent[?] and, like men flogged by one of their own — off they went from the conference.
———
— Different, you see, is the activity of the Będzin "WIZO". For example, the "Mizrachi" always leans toward the "Agudah", and at every opportunity it, the "Mizrachi", that is, gives way to the "Agudah"; whereas the "WIZO" has taken upon itself the mission of Mother Sarah — they "convert" women, but not just any women, rather such as already stood with one foot in "the other world"... And if the work continues further in this direction, then, without doubt, by the merit of the righteous women, there will come — the Messiah, "ve-tir'iya"[?], the Exodus from Egypt?
Last Saturday night the "WIZO" held a little celebration: a reading room ("świetlica" in the vernacular) was opened, and indeed at this modest celebration the footsteps of the Messiah were heard...
It was at the moment when, instead of words of Torah at the "tish" [the Hasidic table], one of the "członkinie" [members] recounted signs and wonders of all that the "WIZO" accomplishes in... Palestine.
Once, perhaps, Palestine was as treyf to this same woman as to a "Ger[?] Hasid", and today? Today she talks about Palestine with more enthusiasm than a Będzin Zionist. When one talks[?] of Messiah's times — surely it is "not out of place"[?]...
Ben Amotz.
A Word in Season.

[Trade and economy — the anti-Jewish boycott; article.] For the attention of the Jewish businessman.
The insolence that is being waged against Jewish trade and handicraft must draw the attention of our traders' and craftsmen's strata, so that they reflect on it together and individually, for this insolence has, after all, the aim of taking [?] the bite out of the Jew's mouth.
The insolent people keep persuading [?] the Polish customer that even if one can buy more cheaply from the Jew, the Jew gives worse goods, cheats [?] on the scales and swindles the customer.
In business there are no sentiments. We know that despite all the agitation the Jewish trader has not yet entirely lost his Christian customer. The Jew, too, buys even now from the Polish shopkeeper and places orders with the Christian craftsman. Every consumer buys mostly where the article he needs meets his requirements and is cheaper, where he is treated more politely and where an honest effort is made to satisfy his wishes and even his whims. Every seller will hand over his goods to whoever pays him more and will deal with him fairly.
These [?] elementary truths the Jewish trader and shopkeeper must remember well. At such a time every merchant and shopkeeper must reckon not only with the moment. Every mistake he has committed he must remember well will be written down to the account [konto (?)] of the whole of Jewish trade. [La-di (?) — unclear word], that one shopkeeper will lose his clientele — the community as a whole will also suffer because of him, for the slightest unserious act is immediately charged to the account of the community.
In the city as well as in the shtetl one must give up the antiquated methods of trade. In the matter of solidity, assortment of goods, cleanliness and order in the shop, the Jewish shopkeeper must lead the way. A national duty now lies on the shopkeeper: to content himself with the very smallest profit. He must treat the customer, and especially the peasant, the working man, as one of his own, enter into the psyche of the peasant and the worker who comes to him with a bitterly hard-earned grosz.
Every trader who permits himself a dishonest attitude toward the customer is simply a national criminal.
The contempt for the "simple customer" must disappear. The primitive person will become attached to whoever treats him humanely and seriously. No "ga-adiek" [?] will be able to drive the peasant away from the Jewish market stall [stragan] and shop, when the peasant feels that in the Jew he has a sincere friend who earns only a minimum from him.
We must use all our experience of long years in order to adapt to the present time, so as not to lose entirely the economic ground from under our feet.
Every merchants' organisation, craftsmen's association, small traders' union must carry out educational work among their members in this direction. Dishonest traders must be put in the pillory and expelled from their organisations.
Jewish merchants, shopkeepers, traders and craftsmen must remember that much can still be won — even [?] the Christian customer who has gone away [?] — if one competes with solidity, honesty and by contenting oneself with the minimal profit.

Reb Yisroel Dovid and the Bazaar.

[Będzin — Keren Kayemet (JNF); feuilleton.]
As soon as the first news came out from the Będzin KKL committee that they were already preparing for the bazaar, my neighbour Reb Yisroel Dovid became a frequent guest of mine.
Every evening Reb Yisroel Dovid is already waiting for me and inquisitively questions me: what's the news? How is the bazaar coming along? Will there be lots of exhibits and a big prize lottery?
On receiving from me the answer that the campaign is going exceptionally well, my neighbour simply comes alive and launches into praises and acclamations addressed to the KKL: what do you think, a trifle — the Land of Israel! The redemption of the Land! Why, it is one of the things that stand at the summit of the world! And he does not forget, while at it, to pay a compliment to our Zionist women activists. — Ay, ay, they stop at nothing and climb up floors and stairs in all the out-of-the-way places, just to collect for the prize lottery! Truly righteous women!
At first the whole business puzzled me: where does this sudden love for the bazaar come to Reb Yisroel Dovid, when for years he thought nothing of it at all!
Only these days did the matter become clear to me. When he knew that I could talk with him for at least a short while, he asked me: do you know that our manufacturers, merchants and craftsmen are donating valuable gifts for the bazaar? It will really be a booty of the most precious and best articles, and it falls exactly at the right time!
Here [?] I began to [—] and interrupted him at once — what, what do you mean "at the right time"?
— You understand me — answers Reb Yisroel Dovid — you know, after all, that the wedding date of my Rivkele, may she live, has been agreed for right after Purim, and apparently at the bazaar I will get at a bargain all the articles that I need for the wedding like an eye in the head.
Well, what do you say? Will buying 100 tickets in the prize lottery be enough?
When he gets my approval he goes off highly satisfied and wishes me success in the work.
Avromele.
A little feuilleton — The frost

[Feuilleton — winter and frost.] Long live the frost!
True, it is a cruel thing — it drives people off the street without any mercy, scorches the noses and nearly tears off the ears, blocks up the "shop windows" [?] and does not let you take in [?] a single grosz — but all the same, a frost is a good thing.
First of all, it makes proper people of us.
We no longer stroll back and forth along the pavements like idlers counting the cobblestones — you see no stones and you see no people...
And if somebody or other does run across a street, he runs like a real big-city man, as though business were hounding him at the neck, as though it were not his ears that were burning but his heels [?].
Secondly, thanks to the frost we can now catch our breath a little.
You will surely look at me as if I were mad — how does that fit? The frost doesn't even let you catch your breath!
On the contrary, ask those who are being choked by paying taxes, and they will tell you how they suffered in the mild weather: with them it was "one generation goes and another comes, and the earth abides forever" — one bailiff [tax distrainer] out and another in, and the shopkeeper always stood by the door looking out for a customer.
But now, when a bailiff slips in somewhere to warm up, he sits it out there until night, and the taxpaying fraternity has almost an hour of life.
Thirdly, the frost has raised certain little people to the highest rank.
Fourthly, the frost saves us money.
Who has cinema or theatre on his mind today?
And what does the public need amusements for, when the best amusement is to run out into the street, take a look at the barometer and run straight back?
This amusement costs not a grosz and the pleasure is great — your household and neighbours then listen with the greatest interest to your report on the expedition to the "North Pole" and back, and above all — how many degrees it is.
It makes no difference that between your looking at the barometer and getting back home the frost has risen a few more marks; you don't take money for the "report", after all, and if someone doesn't believe you, he is told to go himself...
Not to mention [?] even the people who don't need a barometer — they can sniff out with their nose what goes on in someone else's home, let alone [?] such a trifle as how many degrees of frost it is...
Fifthly... sixthly... seventhly...
I can no longer reckon up the frost's virtues, because it [?] has burst into the editorial office and given me a good one on the fingers...
And that, you see, is a real misfortune, because I cannot frighten the frost: at most you don't go out into the street, but the newspaper must, after all, "go out"...
May the frost burn [?]!...
Onkelos.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Beshalach)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Beshalach
—o—
a) "The Lord shall fight for you, and ye shall hold your peace" (Ex. 14:14)
The Jerusalem Talmud says in tractate Pe'ah:
Why, in the last period of Saul's kingdom, did the Jews suffer one defeat after another, although there were then many holy and pure men, whereas in Ahab's time, although there were then many wicked men among the Jews, the Jews won victories? Because in wartime there must first of all be unity among Jews; slander and informing are the greatest misfortune in a time of war. That is why the Jews suffered defeats in Saul's time: besides the righteous men there were then also intriguers and talebearers such as Doeg and others, whereas in the days of Ahab there were no informers at all.
Therefore: "The Lord shall fight for you" — but on one condition — "and ye shall hold your peace": you must keep silent, guard yourselves against talebearing and slander... Avak Soferim.
—o—
b) "Then sang Moses and the children of Israel" (Ex. 15:1)
"The ministering angels wished to sing a song. The Holy One, blessed be He, said to them: The work of My hands is drowning in the sea, and you sing a song?!" Midrash Rabbah.
The question is asked: why did God not let the angels sing, yet let the Jews do so? Surely "the work of My hands is drowning in the sea, and you sing a song?" applies to the Jews as well.
But the Jews sang not over the Egyptians' misfortune but over their own good fortune, over their liberation — "and He is become my salvation"; the ministering angels, however, had not toiled for Pharaoh, they had not now been liberated, and had they sung, it would have been purely over the Egyptians' misfortune — and to sing over anyone's misfortune, be it even the Egyptians', is not in keeping with the Jewish ethical conception... Gilei Hasrat [?].
• • •
God said to the Jews: "The Lord shall fight for you" — God will do the fighting for you. The Jewish victory could also have come about in the natural way, through a victory in war. But God did not want the first Jewish victory of liberation to be stained with blood, and therefore He had to [?] employ a supernatural miracle, so that Jewish hands should stay clean of blood — "the Lord shall fight for you, and ye shall hold your peace": you keep still and prepare yourselves for the highest morality: "Thou shalt not kill"... Ha-Me'assef.
• • •
And that is why Jews hate Amalek so much: because he was the f i r s t to force a b l o o d y war upon the Jews... Derashot Mahariv [?].
—o—
c) "The enemy said: I will pursue, I will overtake, I will divide the spoil" (ibid. 15:9)
Onkelos renders the word "said" here as "dahava amar" — "he was wont to say": he was in the habit of saying so. This is the favourite word of the enemies of Israel: "I will pursue" — I will persecute the Jews, in order to — "divide the spoil", to share out their plunder among ourselves... "Dahava amar" — a standing phrase with all the Pharaohs... Kol Yabasha [?].
—o—
d) "Who is like unto Thee, O Lord, among the mighty" (ibid. 15:11)
"There is none like Thee among the mighty [eilim], none like Thee among the silent [ilmim], for the Holy One, blessed be He, hears the insult offered Him by transgressors and keeps silent." Gemara.
Meaning [?]: the Master of the Universe [—] shows His might toward the Jews — by restraining Himself and not punishing the transgressors.
And that is what Jeremiah laments: "But My people hath changed My glory for that which doth not profit." The glory of the Master of the Universe is might; once [?] God used His might against the enemies of Israel, today He must hide it for the sake of the Jews, be mighty and not punish them for their sins... That is the meaning of "My people hath changed My glory for that which doth not profit" — exchanged My might for something useless... Panim Yafot.
—o—
e) "By the greatness of Thine arm they are as still as a stone" (ibid. 15:16)
At the sanctification of the month [i.e. the blessing of the new moon] it is the custom to rise on tiptoe and say the verse "Fear and dread falleth upon them; by the greatness of Thine arm they are as still as a stone." What is the sense of this custom?
Many Jewish scholars explain that it was introduced in the time of the Bar Kokhba revolt. As is well known, the signal that the court had sanctified the month was then given by torches on the mountains. The Jewish insurgents made use of this in order to give revolutionary signals the same way and to deceive [?] the oppressors into thinking it was only the sanctification of the month; and the insurgents' password was the verse "By the greatness of Thine arm they are as still as a stone", whose initials form "B-Z-Y-K" [?] — as Bar Koziba [?] was called...
—o—
f) "Today is a Sabbath unto the Lord" (ibid. 16:25)
Why do Jews in all their dispersions sing on Saturday night [?] the hymn "Elijah the Prophet, Elijah the Tishbite, may he soon come to us with the Messiah son of David"?
Because we know that "Elijah does not come on the eves of Sabbaths", and on the Sabbath Elijah will not come either — therefore, as soon as Saturday night arrives, we sing: "Elijah the Prophet... may he soon come to us" — let him come now: Friday and the Sabbath are over, he can come right away... Sefer ha-Manhig.
• • •
On the Sabbath we do not say "Who guards His people Israel forever" — because the Sabbath itself guards the Jews... it has guarded the Jews through endless [?] generations against assimilation... Shlit [?].
• • •
The Baal Shem Tov always made a point of being among Jews during the third Sabbath meal (shalosh seudos), saying:
Now the additional soul is departing, and the soul — [—] [text breaks off; the bottom of the page is damaged in the scan].

[Section heading:] "Der Kokh-Lefl" (The Cooking Ladle). Humour and satire. Compiled by Amutzli.

On the Ice-Slide

Sliding is in fashion today,
the whole world is sliding today,
young men, girls, ladies, gentlemen, —
everyone slides and beams with delight.

Children from the schools are sliding,
it's gymnastics, sport, a plaything[?],
and if the learning limps on crutches,
one [?] a hundred[?] on the skating-rink [ślizgawka].

Young fellows are sliding too,
already worn out by the years,
there is no work in the workshops,
so one slides, and calms one's anger...

Also sliding: [?] daughters,
already ripe for the wedding canopy,
because perhaps a destined match is sliding
among this whole group.

People slide also for this reason, therefore —
each one has his aims,
for one the day just passes by,
another means to play [?].

In short, in short, let the world know,
Będzin, Dąbrowa and Szczekociny[?],
and whoever wants to enjoy everything,
let him go sliding...
Sigulis.

[Humour and satire — "Der Kokh-Lefl": jokes and satire.]
After 25 Years.

Yona had lived with his wife for 25 years. It had been a bitter life, because she was a great shrew [arura], but nevertheless — they celebrated a silver wedding.
Late at night, when the guests had dispersed, the unhappy, somewhat drunk Yona remains sitting on the sofa, lost in thought.
— What are you thinking about there? — his wife asks him — you must be drunk as Lot[?], why don't you go to sleep?
— I'm thinking — says Yona with a heavy tongue — that here we have lived together 25 years, and we must go on living together.
— And what don't you like about that?
— Well — says Yona — I'm just thinking that if 25 years ago I had split your skull instead of marrying you, I would probably also have got 25 years in prison, but today I would already be a free man.

The Beautiful Benvenida

(1) — A novel that took place in the first Jewish ghetto and stirred up the governments of Spain, and Turkey.

The high military men knew that she could raise up this one and cast down that one. For it depended on her how the court would distribute honours in the army, who would be given a high rank and privileges, and who would be degraded and even brought before military courts. From this a widespread corruption developed; rumours and well-founded complaints began to circulate that people bribed with gifts and money either her, or her son, or all those close to them, in order to obtain the highest [—] privilege. Hatred of her developed in the highest [?] ranks of the army; dissatisfied generals incited their troops against her, and it came to an uprising. They demanded that she be [—]; they also made an attack on her house. To protect her and her sons, the Grand Vizier's deputy [—] them in his palace. The soldiers chased after them, caught them on the steps of the palace and murdered them. Their fury was not stilled by this: they tore apart the dead body of Esther Kiera, hacked off the hands and the feet, and hung her cut-up limbs on the doors of the military officials for whom she had obtained [?] privileges. A storm broke out in the whole court, throughout all Turkey. A rumour went about that the Grand Vizier's deputy, who had earlier called her to his palace to protect her, had himself stabbed her — he had met her with a spear in her breast. The Sultan then removed many of his courtiers from their offices. Among them, and above all in the Grand Vizier's circle, there was bitterness toward the Jews.
Echoes of the affair still resounded across Turkey when Ahmed the First was already Sultan — when Nathan Ashkenazi went to the Grand Vizier to ask protection for his beloved in Venice, the captive Benvenida.
Nathan Ashkenazi did not expect too friendly a reception, but neither did he imagine that he would be met with mockery.
“Thanks to your father, peace was established between Turkey and Spain,” were the Grand Vizier's first words to Nathan Ashkenazi, “and your father died proud of his achievement; and you, because of a love affair with a captive Spanish girl in Venice, are ready to destroy [printed “fargikhtn”] your father's achievement. How is one to understand you Jews?”
The Grand Vizier said it with laughter. Nathan Ashkenazi realised that the laughter referred to his father as well as to him [?], and also to Jews in general. Of course he knew that the peace between Turkey and Spain had been among his father's great diplomatic achievements, and it was precisely on this that his hopes [—] had been built that Benvenida could be freed: let only an official word come from the Sultan's court, and Spain would stop demanding that the captive Benvenida be sent back to the Inquisition. And now they were simply laughing at it.
“It is a simple [?] matter,” he tried to win over the Grand Vizier, “and the Grand Vizier must not misinterpret it: I have not come to ask protection for a chance sweetheart of mine; the honour of Turkey is involved in this. In Venice I took under my protection a persecuted Marrano woman from Spain, and I did it as a representative of the Turkish court, which for a hundred years in a row has offered persecuted Jews to come to Turkey and enjoy religious freedom. If [?] my action is ignored and Spain gets its way, the honour of Turkey will be diminished [?] in the diplomatic circles of Venice.”
The Grand Vizier resumed his speech with a laugh:
“In everything a Jew wants to accomplish for himself, he drags in the honour of the country in which he lives.”
“That is an insult!” Nathan Ashkenazi exclaimed.
“That is [—],” the Grand Vizier answered, now in anger, “for I had to inform you, you, second son of Solomon Ashkenazi, that an investigation is being conducted about you, as to how far your friendships with the Spanish ambassador in Venice went. Rumours are going about that in Venice you were not loyal to us, to your country, the empire of Turkey.”
As if he had been thrown into a blazing lime-kiln, with the flames devouring his limbs and him writhing, so Nathan Ashkenazi writhed in agony, bent and twisted, barely managing to cry out one word:
“A libel!”
At the same time the captive Benvenida was also being talked about at the Spanish royal court. Just as reports had gone to Turkey about what had happened concerning her in Venice between Nathan Ashkenazi and the Spanish ambassador, so reports had gone to Spain. It was no longer so much a matter of Benvenida's captivity and return to Spain, as of the fact that here an opportunity had arisen for all sorts of adventurers at the Spanish royal court to incite [?] the king concerning Turkey to shake off the peace agreement that Nathan Ashkenazi's father had established between Turkey and Spain several years earlier.

A quiet campaign for Jews without a livelihood

[Sosnowiec — relief; winter.]
A year ago, on the initiative of a group of Jewish intellectuals, a committee was formed which collects money at every opportunity; with the funds collected, coal is given out and in urgent cases also cash assistance.
This year the commendable campaign has been stepped up. Quietly, up to today, over 100 korzec of coal have been distributed, as well as a larger sum in cash for poor, respectable Jewish families.
Vocational courses at WIZO

[Sosnowiec — women; vocational training.]
On the first of next month vocational (household-economy) courses will be opened at the local WIZO; in the first period leather fancy-goods work will be taught.
As is reported, the courses have aroused wide interest; a larger number of girls and women who wish to take part in the useful courses have already registered.
Kajzer wins the lot for the second time

[Sosnowiec — kehilla; elections.]
As we have already written, the voivodeship office ordered that a second drawing of lots be held for the 5th mandate on the kehilla board, to which the national kehilla faction lays claim.
The "lot", which took place on Friday at the kehilla premises, for the second time brought a negative result for Rabbi Englard's list. The lot was again won by Moshe Yosel Kajzer.
Dąbrowa

[Dąbrowa Górnicza — kehilla; youth movements; sport; crime.]
Community elders come to blows...
On Sunday the local kehilla council held a session on the budget for the year 1937. The president of the council, Mr. A. L. Fuks, opens the session with a full complement of all the parnasim [council members] and proceeds to the budget. Parnas Y. M. Klajman submits a motion that, since the budget is too high and the income will not cover the expenditure, the budget be annulled and a new budget be drawn up on realistic foundations.
When the motion fails, Parnas Klajman leaves the session.
A great incident and tumult break out when Parnas B. Liberman demands that it be entered in the minutes that certain dozór members [kehilla board members] took bribes. Then come interjections of "You informer!", and from words they passed to deeds. A brawl began, in the course of which sticks, little benches, etc. were "active". When the police appear, it only then becomes quiet, and the opposition leaves the session. The continuation takes place with a smaller number of parnasim, and in a calm mood the budget in the sum of 46,500 zł. is taken up and is adopted.
From "Maccabi".
On the 24th of this month a ping-pong championship match of the Bielsko district will take place at the "Maccabi" premises, in which sports clubs from Zagłębie, Upper Silesia and Bielsko will take part.
"Free Forum".
At the premises of "Hashomer Hatzair" a "Free Forum" took place, at which dozór member Klajman gave a survey of the events of the week [?] and dwelt on the struggle in Spain. A. Weissulk [?] then spoke about the situation in Eretz Israel.

Will the Jews of Kielce allow a hundred poor Jewish children to lose their school? (From a press conference at the “Toras Chesed” yeshiva)

Among the existing religious schools in Kielce is the “Toras Chesed” yeshiva, which has existed for over thirty years and in which nearly a hundred poor children study.
In normal times, when the worry over a livelihood among Jews was not so great, the said yeshiva could exist [?]; its budget of barely seven hundred zł. a month was more or less covered. Now, however, when the economic situation of the Jews is so bitter, there can be no talk of a normal budget, and that is precisely why the yeshiva’s financial situation is getting worse from day to day. The deficit keeps growing, and there is a threat [?] that any moment now the yeshiva, which no longer even has premises of its own, will be closed, and the hundred poor children will have nowhere to study.
The chairman of the yeshiva committee, Mr. Y. Fiszman, therefore called a press conference of the local Jewish journalists this week, at which he described the sad situation of the yeshiva and asked the press representatives to alert the Jewish public to the threatening situation of this religious school.
Chairman Fiszman also explained to us that the yeshiva committee is now setting about writing a Torah scroll for the yeshiva. All the Jewish inhabitants of the town will be honoured with writing letters, and thereby give various donations for the yeshiva; from the letters campaign, which will have a popular character, Mr. Fiszman believes, a sum of several thousand zł. will be collected to cover the deficit, so that the yeshiva can continue to exist.
The celebration of the beginning of the scroll will take place in the coming [?] days in the “Linas Halaila” beis midrash (we shall announce the date separately), with the participation of all the local rabbis, the rabbinate, the kehilla and representatives of all organisations. The festive prayer at the celebration will be led by cantor Norniecki [?] with choir and orchestra.
“This,” Mr. Fiszman further explains to us, “is the last attempt by the yeshiva committee to preserve this important religious school, and we believe,” conclude Messrs. Fiszman and R’ Yudel Fajnsztat, “that our rescue campaign will succeed.”
We fulfil our civic journalistic duty and alert the Jewish public in Kielce to the danger of liquidation facing the “Toras Chesed” yeshiva, and we believe that the twenty-thousand-strong Jewish community of Kielce will without doubt heed the call of the yeshiva committee and will not allow the yeshiva to be liquidated, nor a hundred poor Jewish children [—], in such a hard and bitter time as now, to lose their school.
Everyone will come to the celebration of the beginning of the scroll. Every Kielce Jew will buy himself a letter — and the yeshiva is saved.
Voivodeship committee against liquidating the Kielce voivodeship

Under the chairmanship of the Kielce city president, Mr. Artwiński, a large meeting of representatives of Christian and Jewish organisations took place this week in the city-council hall, on electing a voivodeship committee that is to counteract the plan to liquidate the Kielce voivodeship.
After a short discussion a provisional committee was elected, which will come to an understanding with the territorial and economic self-government bodies and organisations of the Kielce voivodeship [?]; a united voivodeship committee will be created, which will take up the question of liquidating the voivodeship.
The Kielce city president Artwiński was elected chairman of the provisional committee. The provisional committee also includes the chairman of the kehilla council, Mr. Piotrkowski [?].
The committee’s first session also [?] took place on Thursday, at 1 o’clock midday, in the office of President Artwiński.
Constructive relief campaign for butchers and meat workers

Under the chairmanship of the local rabbinate [?], a large meeting took place this week in the kehilla premises, devoted to the constructive relief campaign for the butchers, meat workers and other religious functionaries who have lost their livelihood because of the shechita law.
After a detailed report by the delegate of the Warsaw Central Committee for Constructive Aid, Mr. Zaks, it was resolved to proclaim in Kielce a large relief campaign for constructive aid. In the coming [?] days large meetings [—] of the said relief campaign will take place.

A Large Coal Campaign for Poor Jews Proclaimed

[Kielce — winter relief.] On the initiative of the chairman of the Kehilla council, Mr. Piotrkowski, a large meeting took place this week on proclaiming a large coal campaign for the nearly one thousand poor Jewish families in Kielce.
A committee of the following gentlemen was elected: Rabbi Rapaport, Dr. Tojer, H. Goldberg, Sh. Bekerman, Y. M. Rajzman, chairman Goldman, vice-chairman M. Sternfeld, Y. Gutman, Sh. Lichter, N. Laks, Y. Zajączkowski, L. Finkelsztajn and B. Słowaticki.
Mr. A. Piotrkowski was elected chairman of the committee; vice-chairman — Mr. M. D. Zenberg [sic, probably Eisenberg]; and treasurer — Meir Eisenberg.
In addition, one and a half wagons of coal were provided[?] at once.
The members of the committee are visiting all the Jewish citizens of Kielce, from whom they collect suitable donations for the coal campaign.
We are sure that Jewish Kielce will help the campaign to be crowned with the greatest success, so as to be able at least partly to ease the distress of unfortunate poor Jewish families who are simply swelling from the cold.
Today — the Verdict in the Case between Editor Baczan and Director Akcentowicz

The Pińczów Rebbe of blessed memory has died.

At the age of 79, the Pińczów Rebbe, the righteous Rabbi Eliezer Finkler of blessed memory, died in Sosnowiec. He was the son of the old Pińczów Rebbe of blessed memory, and 8 years ago, at the request of his Hasidim in Zagłębie, he settled in Sosnowiec.
The deceased did not belong to the rebbes who also occupy themselves with [—] [?] politics; all his days he devoted himself to Torah and the fear of Heaven. He studied and prayed the whole day and only at the evening prayer (maariv) did he taste something. Because of this conduct his heart could not withstand the illness, which lasted about 2 months. All efforts to keep him alive were of no avail. Last Friday, a few minutes after candle-lighting, the Pińczów Rebbe of blessed memory breathed out his soul.
The Rebbe died fully conscious. Only a few hours earlier he would not let the doctor examine him, saying to him: "It is of no more use [?]; it is enough already."
The news of his death spread quickly through the region, and also to distant towns and townlets. [—] a large number of rebbes and rabbis arrived. Among others came the rabbis of: Kielce, Wolbrom, Kherszniece [?], Sędziszów, Wodzisław [?], the Będzin rabbinate, and the rebbes of Częstochowa and Khielon [?].
The ritual purification (tahara) was performed on a new board, and a new bier was also made. The deceased was brought into his beit midrash, where hakafot (circuits) were made with him.
Thousands of people took part in the funeral, which began on Sunday at 3 p.m. In the streets through which the procession passed there was a terrible crush. The procession went from Dęblińska [?] Street, where the Rebbe of blessed memory had lived, through Kołłątaja, Piłsudskiego and Deckerta Streets; there they stopped with the deceased in front of the synagogue, and the deceased's sons R' Pinye and R' Yitzchak, as well as the Miechów Rebbe (a brother-in-law of the deceased) and his son, the Wodzisław [?] rabbi, delivered eulogies.
Then the funeral went through Modrzejowska Street, 3 Maja Street and on towards the cemetery. Despite the severe frost, the number of mourners accompanying him to the cemetery reached into the thousands.
At the cemetery eulogies were delivered by: the Kielce Rebbe, the Khielon [?] Rebbe, the Sędziszów rabbi and the rabbinical judge (moreh tzedek) Glikman of Sosnowiec. The eulogies stressed the great righteousness and the good deeds of the deceased.
At the open grave the deceased is wished [?] mazal tov in honour of the fact that his eldest son, R' Pinye, takes his place.
The lineage of the Pińczów Rebbe of blessed memory stems from the Radoszyce stock. The deceased was a grandson of the Rebbe R' Ber of blessed memory. May his soul be bound in the bond of life.

What's New in Upper Silesia? — Children Murdered Their Father.

[Upper Silesia — crime and courts.]
In March of last year a horrible family tragedy took place in Karłowice [?] (printed "Karlovitse"; possibly Kochłowice). A certain Stula [?] lived "without a chuppah" [?] with a woman who bore him one child after another. Together with father and mother there were 11 souls in the house. The poor family occupied a small, cramped flat.
Under these conditions the father's treatment of the children was unheard of. He treated the children brutally and like a plain scoundrel [?]. Often coming home drunk, he used to beat them cruelly. He drank away the last hard-earned groschen. He therefore had nothing with which to feed and clothe the children, who had to go without shoes even in winter.
Once, when the father came home drunk, he drove his two eldest sons out of the house. The boys who remained then grabbed some utensils and with them seriously wounded their father. In a very grave condition he was taken to hospital, where he died the next day.
Both boys stood trial before the Katowice District Court, which sentenced the accused to 2 years' imprisonment, with the sentence suspended for them for 5 years.
The prosecutor appealed against the verdict, demanding a heavier penalty.
These days the appeal trial took place at the Katowice Court of Appeal. After careful consideration of the matter, the Court of Appeal upheld the verdict of the first instance.
