A Few Merry Hours...

(On last Purim's entertainments.)

"Purim is no holiday and fever is no illness" — so goes a folk saying. That was said in normal years, in golden times, when living meant living, when one felt good at heart all year round and the Purim holiday was not so keenly felt that one should [?] fuss over it [?] like a stuffed [?] guest, crammed and sated [?]. When life is dark and bitter, clouded and black as night, then even Purim is a precious holiday..

And indeed one saw this last Purim. In no year were so many children's entertainments held as this year. If the grown-ups no longer have any desire to amuse themselves, let at least the little ones rejoice.

A fine example of "gather us together" [?] was given by the teachers of the folk-schools in Będzin. They did the same as Queen Esther. Seeing the great danger lurking for the Jews, she issued an order to make [?] "Go, gather all the Jews" — go and gather all Jews; first of all, let us not be splintered. The teachers did the same. They gathered the children of all the folk-schools in one hall, where they amused themselves a whole day "until they knew not", danced and sang songs — it was Purim in the world..

So too [?] entertainments for adults took place, but with the "grown-ups" it is not worth bothering — for them it is Purim all year round..

—

In the secondary schools in Sosnowiec and Będzin, too, the Purim holiday was received with "open arms".

At the "Sz. Fürstenberg" gymnasium a children's entertainment in masks and costumes took place. Some of them distinguished themselves very nicely. The entertainment had an international character, for a number of "nations" took part in it, such as Persians [?], Arabs, Hindus, Japanese — with Queen Esther at their head. The little crowd already "understands" that without Queen Esther no joy can be complete...

At the entertainment a portion of the spiritual was also given. An artistic part was performed by the children of the folk-school under the direction of the teacher Elbojm [?]. The school orchestra, too, worked wonders, playing Jewish folk tunes and horas, to which the children danced like the [?] of old [?]...

And now [?] the material part: at the buffet various fruits and sweets were sold "at half price". The participants enjoyed themselves, ate and drank, and at the same time supported the Keren Kayemet.

—

Very successful was the entertainment at the "Mizrachi" school "Yavne". Under the direction of the kindergarten teacher (Fröbelist) Miss Rachel Karlin the children of the lower classes recited and gave Purim sermons; then they sat down at the richly set tables and together with their parents held a Purim feast. Amid the "four cups" the pupil Rewolich [?] recited A. Shlonsky's poem "Lishu Hidim" [?].

—

The "day of feasting and gladness" was celebrated magnificently at the "orphanage". To this day the little ones of that institution keep asking: "When will it be Purim again?"... The tireless Mrs. Wajnsztok took pains that everything be prepared properly; she also spent a whole day with the children and gave them of every good thing.

—

As always, this year too a Purim feast was arranged at the "Old Age Home" in Będzin. In the special dining room long tables were set up, served with "meat and fish and all delicacies". The old people also received "permission" from the management to drink "genuine" "Carmel wine" as much as anyone wanted. In honour of the feast the year-round servants were "dethroned" [?], and the Ladies' Committee of the society was invited as "waitresses" [?]; it "nursed" [?] the old folk... Particularly distinguished in this field were Mesdames Triger [?] and Szwarcberg.

After the feast the management together with the old people went into a little dance [?] — and how they lived it up...

Sz. L-st.
Planned Passover Relief Actions

[Zagłębie — Passover relief for the needy; leading article.]
The crux of supplying the impoverished masses with food for Passover. — One should give it serious thought.
Apparently we shall soon be past the hard winter, which got not a little [?] into the bones of the poor, and people will be able to breathe a little more freely; but for all that the situation remains difficult.
The chapter of livelihood is a very hard problem. Although the winter has ended and further [?] signs of spring are appearing [?], calling mankind to life and blossoming — in this beautiful season we have no way out for tomorrow.
But who can think about tomorrow, when today, the present moment, is so hard, and the broad strata of the Jewish population are downcast to the utmost degree and have nothing with which to get through the day — quite [?] literally, there is nothing to put in one's mouth, and the little children go hungry and swell from cold and from never eating their fill.
Jewish livelihoods are shrinking, branch after branch is torn away, and we grow economically weak in every field [?]; more and more branches dry up [?] for us, and we are falling behind in the economic field.
The economic situation of the Jews is now doubly hard. Formerly, when there was a relatively small percentage of impoverished people, one somehow helped. Society carried out a relief action, which almost always succeeded. The conscience of the people, merciful sons of the merciful, awoke, and the oppressed were set on their feet. Today the situation is considerably worse and the support many times more complicated, if only because those who are still holding on — that is, the average element, of whom the donors mostly consist — are themselves in much worse circumstances than before. That is one thing; and secondly one must not forget that the takers, the needy, the recipients, have increased enormously, while the donors have fallen in parallel, and therefore the procedure is a very, very hard one, a very, very complicated one.
We know that our readers agree with all our arguments; yet we cannot leave the question hanging in the air. In whatever way it may be — however heavy and burdensome the yoke may weigh — the problem must be solved.
If nothing is done for the community, which still somehow stays on its feet, if nothing can be done for it, if we are helpless and powerless here — that we must not be when it is a matter of saving hungry souls.
In the hard winter we came to help, at least with the minimum. Now Passover is approaching, and it is a tradition among Jews, at least in these days, not to let the poor brethren with their wives and children go hungry, and we do not doubt for a single minute that Jewish Zagłębie will do something before Passover for the hungry and the suffering. Certainly institutions will give produce, others — money, and the kehillas as usual — kimcha [de-Pischa]; then surely youth associations will come, religious and socialist, artisans' associations from this side and from that side, shtibl people of all kinds [?] and tendencies, who will provide for their members with whatever they will have the means to. It goes without saying that it is fine of these people when they devote themselves body and soul to the Jewish community, and they deserve thanks for their self-sacrifice and dedication; but we do not hold with it, because in practice it does not work and, incidentally, it does not bring the proper benefit. The distribution of money and produce by different institutions only introduces demoralisation, it costs the town money, and the poor man does not receive in equal measure: one gets more, double, because he pushes himself forward [?] — he knows his trade, let him be a „beggar“; and the other one, if he is shy or has not the courage to stretch out his hand properly, gets nothing and goes hungry precisely at Passover just as in the cold winter.
And therefore, if one intends to carry out Passover actions in Zagłębie properly, and for them to bring as much benefit as possible to the community, a unification must take place. Every town — whether it is Sosnowiec or Będzin, Dąbrowa [Górnicza] or Zawiercie, Kielce [?] or Olkusz — must set up a single Passover committee of its own, which should concentrate around itself both the donors and the recipients.
Too much demoralisation has lately entered the communal fabric [?], and the population knows it; that is why people often regard such events [„imprezy“] with contempt, since what is undertaken is not achieved.
Nor is it any wonder, for the population already knows the disgusting game that has accumulated [?] in these miniature associations, where the president strives to keep his armchair, so that he should not, God forbid, lose the president's seat.
And in these little circles the president's mission all year round is to maintain his „staff“ and to hire the servants and „servant-makers“ [?], so that they will secure his little bench for him. So the few guilders [złoty] collected from the members barely suffice [?] for the personnel and other expenses that this or that institution needs in order to exist for appearance's sake. And when one wants to show that one exists, that one is alive, one pushes to the front when an opportunity arises, such as carrying out some action or other, collecting money for a topical purpose, and the like.
But the population has lost confidence in the private little circles, which all together [?] claim to be communal, while in truth they are „firms“. There the president has his institution in his pocket together with the rubber stamp, and decides over it just as over his own capital.
When such „firms“ take on matters like a Passover action, it is doomed to failure in advance. One must therefore not allow large, worthy actions to be crumbled and broken up into miniature distributions.
The members are not versed [?] in the handing out of communal honours and therefore do not know that the activity consists solely of ringing the bells and advertising oneself as if one truly cared for the common good.
At the present moment no failure would be desirable, because it is a matter of supplying people with food for the eight days of Passover, and therefore order and trust are required, which can only happen when there will be no „my“ and „your“ poor, no „my“ and „your“ hungry sisters and brothers.
And therefore we are in favour of every town setting up a single central committee, where everything should be concentrated and from which the [needy?] should receive both the produce and the money support on as large a scale as possible.
If our arguments are not taken into account, a failure is to be foreseen.
We therefore consider the question serious and useful enough; the community workers should consult in good time and adopt a proper position, so as to gain the possibility of carrying out successful Passover actions for the impoverished Jews.
Let this important matter not be put off — as, unfortunately, is customary among us — until a few days before Passover; rather, let it be considered already now how the action can be realised as well and as finely as possible.
Selekt.
The Impressive Course of the Coal Campaign

P. Blumenkranz (Sosnowiec)
(From the series: "Social Tales").
Two weeks ago we reported on the meeting which the society "Ezrat Aniyim" [Help for the Poor] had decided to call in connection with the coal campaign.
Now we can joyfully announce that the meeting took place, and we also consider it [—] and instructive to relate the course of the meeting, so that other communal workers may take [?] an example from it.
It goes without saying that when one speaks of the society "Ezrat Aniyim", the first who comes to mind is its long-standing president, R' Michael Welinson.
He came to the coal meeting first; although his son-in-law from Łódź had come on a visit [?], he simply left him sitting at home.
The vice-president, too, arrived punctually, even though a meeting of the new society "Matan Beseter" [Secret Giving] was being held at the same time.
As always, the president and vice-president at once stepped aside to talk things over between themselves.
The president speaks up:
"R' Isaac, here I stand [?] — I have no more strength to work; for the sake of my life I would urgently need to recover a little. But how can I leave the society completely to its fate, especially in such a hard winter?"
"That's just what I keep crying out," R' Isaac replies. "Work, too, must have a limit. My wife argues with me many a time, and she is no fool at all. 'Isaac,' she says, 'why do you take the poor so much [?] upon yourself? You won't even get a thank-you for all of it.'"
"I feel indeed [?] that she is right, but I cannot, in such a hard and bitter time, abandon the hungry and the frozen and think only 'what's it to me' [?]. And unfortunately we must be objective and admit that all the existing societies (except 'Matan Beseter'), such as 'Ezer Dalim', 'Za'akat Aniyim', 'Lechem Le'echol' and all the others, do nothing; I have yet to see their pressure [?] [—]. What do you believe [?]?"
The presidents got carried away talking, as in Krynica while drinking at the "spring" [?], but as soon as the members began to gather they broke off. Modest people do not like to talk about themselves...
• • •
As we have already reported, the matter of the coal campaign stood, because of other more urgent questions, in 4th [?] place.
But before proceeding to the minutes, a proposal came in from the craftsman to move the seventh item to second place.
The president, not wishing to depart from his liberal principles, opened a discussion.
He took the floor first himself, defending the third item (a general meeting).
"Gentlemen, I regret to state that the board is not capable of working. The coal campaign I began to run together with the vice-president as early as the month of Tishrei. But it is not right that single individuals should bear the whole burden; I therefore consider it necessary to call the general meeting — one must absolutely be relieved somewhat of the work."
The vice-president, for his part, defended items 2 and 4 (the president's jubilee and the annual ball).
"Gentlemen," he exclaimed with pathos, "to be today one who faithfully attends to public needs is no small matter. The poverty is great and the means — nil, and what [—] satisfaction does an honest communal worker have! Our president has stood at the head of the society for 10 years already, one year longer than I (a hint that one should remember him, too), and despite all difficulties he has not abandoned his post.
But a communal worker is, after all, only human, and the modest jubilee celebration will give him courage for further strenuous work against all obstacles!
As for the ball, we must set to work on it already, for if we have no income we will not be able to run the coal campaign."
After the president and the vice-president, the floor was taken by the "aristocrat" Jozi [?] Schreier.
"Szanowne Zgromadzenie [?]! [Polish: Esteemed assembly!] We must react most strongly against the 'członek' [?] of the craftsmen; [Polish:] such [?] insinuations are inadmissible. Such outbursts [?] throw me off balance. I have finished."
I will not relate all the speeches to you. The "intellectual" spoke for half an hour and concluded in these words:
"Gentlemen, while not negating, in light [?] of the present situation and the hard winter, the absolute necessity of a coal campaign — for it is truly our categorical imperative — we nevertheless cannot ignore the rare opportunity to express our devotion to the president by arranging a modest celebration; we cannot pass on to the order of the day over the productive, self-sacrificing and intensive activity of the president" (a whole row of foreign words had slipped his mind).
"Yes," he concluded solemnly, "our president possesses many potential forces, that is, our society possesses vital forces. The joy of the honourable president is our joy, and also the joy of the starving [?] poor, who benefit from the generous hand of our society."
The president smiled discreetly, and the "intellectual" looked at everyone in triumph: let anyone try to refute so finely built a speech.
Finally the floor was given to the craftsman.
"Esteemed assembly! I ought not to have spoken at all, only to spit on the whole thing. I turn red with shame hearing that people are already [?] talking about jubilees at a time when the hungriest [?] poor are knocking at our doors. True, lately it has become a fashion to hold jubilees for doing nothing, but this could have been postponed for another five years, so that the celebration would turn out more impressive — '15 years of sitting on Jewish troubles' sounds finer..."
"Be silent! Whom are you insulting? Unheard-of insolence! Speak to the point!"
"Very well, I will not say much. I, as a poor artisan, unfortunately can do no more than talk; but I believe that when my words meet the tears of the hungriest [?] mothers, who warm the frozen little hands of their children with the breath of their mouths — we will not debate about jubilees."
The assembled now reacted less, and the president ordered the minutes to be read.
The secretary, a Jew in his fifties, began [—] [?] to read.
Just then the telephone rings. A woman's voice argues with the president; he says something, but she apparently does not agree. The president glances at his gold watch and says:
"Gentlemen, I wanted [?] to end the meeting earlier today. My son-in-law (my wife rang me this very moment) wants to see me 'koniecznie' [Polish: without fail]; but perhaps R' Isaac will continue to chair the meeting?"
"No, no," voices were heard, "at such an important meeting the president must be present; besides, it is already late, and we have not had supper yet..."
• • •
About the next meeting we will probably not write, because, as we have learned, the society "Ezrat Aniyim" is to set about a most premature [?] Passover campaign in these very days.
This report appears to be probable, for, as we have been told, even the president's jubilee has been postponed to Chol HaMoed Pesach, so that the full attention can be devoted to the Passover campaign.
We for our part are convinced beyond [?] doubt, from the activity to date of the [—] [?] society "Ezrat Aniyim", that the campaign will "certainly" pass with great success, because
— Israel is not forsaken!
Kehilla. / General and Local Aspects

[Sosnowiec — kehilla; article.]
With the taking over of the kehilla's affairs by the new kehilla board in Sosnowiec, one is compelled to reflect on two questions: what can a kehilla create nowadays, and how must it work in order to be able to function normally?
The first question is a general one; it depends on the legal part of our kehilla system, which forms the skeleton, the muscles, the heart and the soul of the kehilla organism.
The second question already bears an exclusively local character, since it depends on its elected councillors in the Jewish autonomous representation, who pour and breathe into the kehilla organism a spirit of life, so that its individual organs may be able to function healthily.
The limits on which our kehillas were built are no restriction on a kehilla activity that should embrace, besides the religious needs, also all the other needs of the Jewish public. Besides this it must be stressed that Jews in exile always lived in more or less organised communities, which helped them to wage the struggle for their threatened existence with various collective forces... Had every Jew been forced to fight for his existence alone, the Jews would long ago have perished; therefore the feeling of belonging to the Jewish collective is so extraordinarily strongly developed among Jews, because only with the help of the various organised communities or kehillas have Jews sustained their existence in exile over almost two thousand years...
In accordance with the above-mentioned standpoints, the organised Jewish community, or the kehilla, must embrace at the very least all the local needs of the Jewish inhabitants; the kehilla must strive to satisfy, as far as at all possible, all Jewish needs!
The kehilla must care first of all for Jewish national culture, for Jewish folk schools and for vocational education.
Further, a kehilla must care for the religious needs of the community. A kehilla must constantly think how to improve the hard conditions of competition in which antisemitism in fact places the Jew in his day-to-day struggle for existence. In the struggle in the economic field a modern Jewish kehilla must take first place!
Further, a kehilla must fight so that the injustices done to Jews in the field of social welfare on the part of the municipal self-government, on this or that formal pretext, be removed.
Then, among the basic foundations of kehilla activity belong the organisational and representative functions of a kehilla, which must be the centre of Jewish collective organisation and — the true, authoritative and devotedly self-sacrificing representation.
These are the chief foundations of a modern kehilla activity. A kehilla must satisfy this need of a Jewish community; there is no other body for this work!
As we have already seen, such a kind of activity stands in no contradiction whatsoever to the existing kehilla statutes. The said activity depends on the elected councillors who run the kehilla apparatus: if these are honest, devoted, capable representatives [—] (in the social sense) with a [—] record [?], with a definite [—], [—] the kehilla becomes a [—] collective organisation that satisfies all the specific needs of our society; otherwise it is not capable of fulfilling its tasks and becomes superfluous for the Jewish population — and as such it must die an unnatural death.
As for the present kehilla board, it consists of such public workers as possess the qualities enumerated above, and it is to be hoped that our Jewish representation will in reality become what it must and should be nowadays, i.e. a firm collective organisation that will worthily represent the Jewish community of Sosnowiec.

The Renewal of a Bank / (On Sunday's Meeting of the “Discount Bank”).

[Będzin — economy and institutions; article.]
Next Sunday the general meeting of the Będzin “Discount Bank” (Dyskonto-Bank) takes place, and it is worth dwelling on this phenomenon.
Suddenly, as if by a miracle, this “Discount Bank” has risen from among the ruins of the buried public financial institutions — a resurrection of the dead.
Nowadays we in Będzin have not a single public bank, and if we hear the call of the said institution, which stretches out its hands to the Jewish community for help, for revival, we must meet it halfway, because this is a public mission that comes to bring enormous benefit for the common good; for as soon as a Jewish public bank exists, the community benefits from it. The bank recruits [its members] from small traders, and for them it [?] is being renewed — solely for the broad masses of the population, regardless of whether one is a small trader or an artisan. It must serve the oppressed collective — the man who, receiving a bill of exchange for his goods [?] or [?] work, has nobody to trade it with because the doors of the banks are closed to him, so that he must come to the “thief” and take for the bill as much as one is willing to give him, since he has no other choice; it is precisely this element that the bank must serve, and only of him must it think.
But a bank is very complicated; it is a money institution where the “merchandise” must be stocky [?] — consisting of money, without which one can do nothing. Yet one needs something more, which incidentally plays no smaller role than money, and that is trust, full faith and sympathy; without all this it is very hard to manage and to exist — this must be taken well to heart.
It is still too little if the institution merely exists [?] and has a sign hanging announcing that the bank exists. It must get into operation and become viable, that is, obtain possibilities to discount bills, and collections (incasso) must also be entrusted to it — that is the most important thing in order to be able to exist. And if so, if one needs both money and trust, one must treat the institution with the greatest care. There must be a director and a board of honest and decent people; it need not necessarily have rich men, who perhaps will not want to commit themselves, but serious people who will have responsibility towards the community and [—] a warm attitude to the bank. I[f] [—] this will be, there are chances to exist.
Let this be well considered and heeded at Sunday's renewal meeting.
R. Les.
Inventions That Were Destroyed

[Science and technology — feature.] If one is to believe the various inventors and their exaggerated talk, then lately a number of inventions have been sold which the big industries bought up in order to destroy them.
Patents, however, are only granted for a number of years; after that they become free and anyone can do with them what he likes. So there is a bit of hope that some day these inventions will after all be of use to all people. Meanwhile, though, they are dead for a long time — even before they were born.
But whoever thinks that these are new inventions of our time is mistaken.
About fifty years ago an English shoemaker brought rubber heels and soles to the Leipzig Fair. He demonstrated that these soles and heels were cheaper and better than leather ones; nevertheless he did not do any big business. But hardly had he come home, in no great mood because of his bad business, when a representative of the big English leather manufacturers came to him and gave him to understand that he had already worked enough in his life. He should sell him [sic] his new inventions of the rubber soles, and in return the leather manufacturers would give him a "lifelong" pension. He would no longer need to work. The shoemaker agreed to it, and his patent was destroyed. Only about ten years later another inventor also [obtained] a similar patent, with which he began to produce rubber heels and soles, and he grew rich by it.
Many years ago it was already invented how to make milk from various plants. Plant milk is better and cheaper than cow's milk. For "agricultural reasons" the invention was bought up and destroyed, so that the farmers should not be ruined...
The "zip fastener" is already very old: the Chinese knew of it thousands of years ago, and on the European market too the invention appeared twenty years ago, but the button factories bought it up and destroyed it. Only a few years ago was it resurrected from the dead.
Razor blades have today become a big industry, run by the great steel concerns. A few years ago a Swedish engineer invented a razor blade that lasts ten years. The Swedish steel works bought the invention from him for a fortune and destroyed it at once, because a razor blade must not last longer than a week...
The "eternal match" has already been invented by several experts, but the great trust of the match factories has always bought up this invention, which could have ruined the big match industry...
The "eternal clock" too has been invented more than once, but every such invention was bought up and destroyed by the big factories; a clock must[?] be wound every day or at least every week. This leads to the spring being broken, and a little later the clock itself, and one has to buy a new one...
As said: only one consolation has remained — that patents cannot be lost forever. In the end they will after all appear on the market and will be used for the benefit of all people.
Z. Haber, Vienna.
Heard and Seen.

[Sosnowiec and Będzin — kehilla; satirical column.] By Ben Amotz.
1927 — 1937.
Those who stand at the helm of local Jewish politics, those who "make" the history of the rabbinate struggle in Zagłębie, must fulfil a sacred duty towards the broad Jewish masses and celebrate a 10-year jubilee...
The chief in-laws [of the celebration] should be the two well-known former representatives of the artisan masses in Sosnowiec, because they were the "pioneers" who carried out their holy mission in the democratic kehilla; they did not let themselves be influenced by any side, and in particular not by the national camp, which wanted at all costs to see the then rabbi of Lipno on the Sosnowiec rabbinic throne. But they acted according to their conscience, out of "justice and righteousness", and thanks to that brought "enormous benefit" not only to their voters but to the whole Jewish population of Sosnowiec...
This happened in the year 1927, when the elections of a rabbi for the Sosnowiec kehilla took place. Before the start of the session the writer of these lines turned to one of the leaders of the national politics with the question:
— For whom will the artisans' councillors vote?
— What kind of a question is that? With whom, if not with us? After all, we educated them politically.
And when the artisans' councillors then voted for Rabbi Brodt[?], it was indeed "a [—] total collapse".
— Ten years later, on 28 February [luty] 1937, the national camp in Będzin also saw for itself the same "truth"... The difference is only that in Sosnowiec the "democratic" representatives carried out their mission in one go: voted, and the matter was done with; the situation in Będzin, however, is different, where one has to go "from strength to strength". Step by step; the "business" does not come easily, the heart[?] is weakened[?] several times until one reaches the final goal... First one must elect a chairman of one's own. Then one must put on the candidate the hat of a moreh hora'ah [rabbinic judge], and if all goes well — seat him on the rabbinic throne...
But, as it were[?], "He who gives strength to the weary" — and the power of "truth" also stands by, and
— hands are shaken[?],
therefore we hold that both Jewish kehillas, Sosnowiec and Będzin, should celebrate the 10-year jubilee of the rabbinate history in Zagłębie in honour of the victories achieved in the years:
— 1927 - 1937.
A Living Moral...
In the session hall of the Sosnowiec kehilla a historic act takes place. Rule over the kehilla passes into the hands of the elected public delegates. The Jewish kehilla is freed from the unelected rulers — more precisely, from the one who at every opportunity brandished his "paper sword", on which was inscribed the verse:
— "For with a mighty hand will I rule over you"...
A festive moment. The Sabbath candlesticks on the green-covered table add to the holiday mood, and right in these "historic minutes" the outgoing ruler of the kehilla hands over the keys of the "royal treasures" to the new kehilla representatives, whose attention he draws with great intent that they should guard the "treasures" he built in the synagogue courtyard like the apple of their eye. Guard them well, honourable dozór members — he said — take care that the women have no control over the "treasures"...
Unfortunately the outgoing one did not hand over everything. What he left for Jewish society in Sosnowiec: he left behind him an inheritance that will be recorded to his account as a lament for generations. He not only built lavatories in the synagogue courtyard, but also founded a living lavatory, which pollutes the whole of Jewish public life in general and the Jewish printed word in particular. He took under his protection a beast in human form, whom he led around all the batei midrash and all the institutions, so that he should "write up" all the speeches and praises addressed to him.
And about this plague of leprosy the outgoing head of the kehilla did not say a single word, because he thinks that one of the new kehilla representatives, too, will be caught in the net of this unclean soul, this vile blackmailer, who later, when he can no longer blackmail, will come out with his disgusting insults against the new kehilla representatives as well...
But the "manoeuvre" will not succeed for him, because "the birds on the rooftops" are already telling of the ugly deeds of that disgusting creature; many months ago the present kehilla president banged on the table at the home of a well-known Zionist activist in Sosnowiec, [declaring] that this underworld figure must be removed outside the camp..
— Yes, Mr. ex-commissar of the kehilla, even if you did not reveal the deeds of this scoundrel, the latest insults against you by this person are
— a living moral...
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Vayakhel-Pekudei)

Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Vayakhel-Pekudei.
—o—
a) "And Moses assembled all the congregation of the children of Israel" (35:1)
"To tell you that the Holy One, blessed be He, said to Moses: make for them [printed: 'bread'] assemblies and expound before them [printed: 'bread'] the laws of Shabbat on Shabbat." Midrash.
The question arises: how does the Midrash conclude that this was on Shabbat?
But at every assembly, every time Jews were called together to a meeting, trumpets (chatzotzrot) were used, as is always mentioned in the Chumash. Only at this assembly are trumpets not mentioned — it must have been on Shabbat, when one may not sound trumpets... Perach Levanon.
—o—
b) "A Sabbath of solemn rest to the Lord" (ibid., 2)
"To rest on it and to rejoice in delight, eating and drinking — all the congregation of Israel shall keep it" — so it is said in the Sabbath zemirot. That means: the part of Shabbat that all Jews observe, of which "all the congregation of Israel shall keep it," is the part of "rejoicing in delight, eating and drinking" — this all Jews fulfil, consuming[?] the good dishes of Shabbat.. Sidurei shel Shabbat.
• • •
"Shomer Shabbat" means waiting for and looking out for the Shabbat ("but his father kept the matter in mind") — longing for the Shabbat... Ohev Yisrael.
• • •
The Baal Shem Tov made a point of being among Jews at the third meal (shalosh seudos) on Shabbat, and when asked about it he answered: at the third meal the extra soul (neshama yetera) departs, and a Jew wants the soul to depart among Jews...
• • •
"Woe to them who call evil good and good evil, who put light for darkness and darkness for light" (Isaiah 5:20).
This refers to those who stretch the weekday of Friday into the night — "who call evil good," "darkness for light": though it is already dark they say it is still day, just for one more stitch[?] into Shabbat; and they pray the Saturday-night prayers while it is still day, saying it is already night — they "put light for darkness," they make day into night. And of them the prophet says "For a small moment have I forsaken thee" (Isaiah 54:7): all in all it is a matter of moments, of minutes — and for the sake of these minutes one forsakes God... Shaar Bat Rabim.
—o—
c) "And they came, the men with the women" (ibid., 22)
The men came to see the wonder — how the women take off their jewellery and give it for the Tabernacle... Such an unbelievable thing they wanted to see with their own eyes... Imrei Chen.
—o—
d) "And the princes brought" (ibid., 27)
R' Eliyahu Chaim Meisel once needed a large sum of money for poor Jews for the holiday. So he called a meeting. To the meeting he invited all the poor people for a set hour, and the rich men (nagidim) of Łódź he summoned for an hour later. When Poznański and other rich men arrived, they asked how the rabbi was getting on[?] with the poor people. After the meeting, at which it had been decided how much money was needed and how to distribute it, he called in the rich men and demanded that they give the money, saying to them:
"I learned this from Moses our teacher. When it came to the Tabernacle, Moses did not want to consult the rich ('he did not wish to take counsel of the princes of Israel,' Avot de-Rabbi Natan 8:11), because he knew from practice that the princes prefer giving advice to giving money. So he took counsel with the poor — they know best how much is needed — and of the princes, in turn, he asked no advice, only money: 'And the princes brought'..."
—o—
e) "By the hand of Ithamar, the son of Aaron the priest" (38:21)
"Although Moses our teacher was appointed over everything, he had to appoint Ithamar with him, because authority over the public is not exercised by fewer than two." Baalei ha-Tosafot.
The same lesson — that in matters of charity one person may not handle it alone, so that no suspicion falls on him — the Gemara (Bava Batra 8) derives from the verse "and they shall take the gold." But here it is repeated once more to stress that not only an ordinary person must guard against suspicion, but even Moses our teacher... Yalkut Yehuda.
—o—
f) "As thou didst anoint their father" (40:15)
Moses himself had no reason to envy Aaron. Aaron was High Priest and Moses — a prophet. But on account of the children he did have reason to envy him: Moses's sons occupied no high office after him, while Aaron's sons remained High Priests. So God said to Moses: "And thou shalt anoint them, as thou didst anoint their father" — without a shadow of envy, just as you had no envy toward their father.. R' Meir Simcha ha-Kohen of Dvinsk.
From the World of Film.

A great film by a great director.
Cecil B. DeMille is without doubt one of the oldest and greatest film directors. He has been a director for 24 years already; he stood at the cradle[?] of film art in general; he was the first to create a feature-length film, and that was in 1913. Until then only short pictures in two acts used to be produced. Cecil DeMille was also the first to start using electric light in filming, and human hair in making wigs for the actors and extras. DeMille is one of the most important directors in Hollywood, and his films — whatever he may touch in them — are made with artistic verve and broad scope. He approaches every film with the greatest responsibility and reverence for the subject. The material is worked out and polished in every respect. His newest film depicts an interesting fragment of the life of a famous American hero, Buffalo Bill, but conceived quite differently from the historians and writers. Buffalo Bill himself is actually not the main hero here, nor the only one on whom the whole course of the picture rests; he is pushed somewhat aside, and up comes "Wild Bill" — Hickok, who is, so to speak, the other half of the legendary Buffalo Bill. The director DeMille has laid the whole weight of responsibility on Bill Hickok, because he is a more romantic and stormy[?] figure than the well-known Buffalo Bill. Thus[?] the director uncovers a new, unknown fragment of history, while casting a kind of enlightening light on a piece of the historical-romantic past. The part of Wild Bill Hickok is played by Gary Cooper; Buffalo Bill is played by the actor James Ellison. One of the main female roles is played by the actress Jean Arthur.
We sell the past.
This is the main motif of a new film that reveals what goes on behind the scenes of the American film paradise — Hollywood. We learn here of many truly interesting and very piquant stories; we are drawn into a web of intrigues and gossip, in which stars and directors, as well as the lowly[?] people of the film metropolis, are entangled and enmeshed[?]. What is interesting is that various well-known stars appear in the roles of extras: Elanor Weiss[?], Gary Cooper, John Wakirn[?] and others.
Director King Vidor and his newest film.
The American director King Vidor is no "new man" in the art of film. His name is known throughout the whole world — a reputation he earned thanks to his splendid film "The Big Parade". That was the first war film that treated the Great World War in a brilliant way, as seen and understood by the average man. Then came other films, such as "Souls of Blacks" and "Our Daily Bread", in which the director introduced larger mass scenes, while at the same time treating a topical problem of a social character. The individual and his relation to the collective, the collective as a socio-political factor — these are all questions that interest the director King Vidor. In his newest film, which depicts the hard struggles that the first[?] inhabitants of Texas, who came from all corners of America, had constantly to wage against Indians and plain bandits, King Vidor dwells on a series of quite interesting questions, such as the individual and the collective, love of the fatherland[?] and general human love, the white race and its relation to other races, etc. It should be noted that last year King Vidor received a medal[?] from the Belgian government for his film "On the Ruins of Happiness".
Safari.
What does this mysterious word actually mean? In the language of the Negroes of East Africa, "safari" means a kind of hunting caravan, with which the regions, and especially the jungles of Africa, teem.
That is also the name of a new film which is now[?] being prepared with the greatest care. The actual main idea of the film revolves[?] around all sorts of romantic adventures experienced by a couple in love who wander together with a hunting caravan.
The background against which all this takes place is the African jungle; countless black, permanent inhabitants of Africa also appear. "Safari" will be a colour film; special painters have been engaged. In the leading roles the well-known actors Carole Lombard and Randolph Scott will appear, the latter playing heroic-lover[?] roles in the film. The screen tests with this couple have given good results.
I Agree to Everything...

[Satirical feuilleton — Polish Jewry: shechita, market stalls, universities and emigration.] By Aron Luksenberg.
(Such a proposal from an ordinary Jew.)

I have decided to agree to everything, to become a loyal citizen; I no longer want to be a “backward one”, and above all I want the “good friends” not to show so much “understanding” for me. I want to help solve the Jewish question — possibly [?] the antisemites will show [?] me a lot of “gratitude” for it, or will honour me with gifts out of great joy — nothing of the sort! I will not let any difficulties stop me, because things are hard and bitter enough for me as it is. So I have nothing to lose in becoming good and pious according to the new Shulchan Aruch...
First — the painful shechita question. I shall make every effort so that the merciful Madame [?] can carry out fully, one hundred per cent, her large-scale plan for the shechita law, and let there be an end to it! I will also ask the honourable Madame [?] to put forward a bill that one should [?] forbid eating a limb torn from a living animal (ever min ha-chai) — that will be a great favour to us... I will even make every effort to introduce nikkur (porging) of the “zadki” [Polish: hindquarters], provided that in return they stop porging [“treybern”] other body parts. I guarantee that everything will be restored as it was before. The magistrates [municipalities] and the slaughterhouses will no longer have deficits, the peasant will remain a peasant, the butcher will not be left stuck with the “zadek” [hindquarter], and the oxen with the calves will let themselves be led to slaughter according to the new rite, as in the good old days..
Once I get out of the shechita business with whole bones, I shall turn to the market stalls [“straganes”, Polish stragany]. That is one of the most justified complaints — “The Jews have grabbed the stall, and it must be de-Judaized”! — Quite right! Enough have we been blackened at the stall, enough have we suffered from the cursed livelihood that the antisemites begrudge us! Let all the envious, who so badly crave [?] the fortunes at the stalls, come and take the bargain in good health — but on one condition: let the peasants [?] let the stall-Jews [?] up onto the land, and let the blockading [?] students hand over the universities, on the left and on the right, to the Jewish diligent scholar (matmid). We will not break any stalls, not post any pickets, not organise any blockades. The stall is yours, naive peasant and student, amen! We are too productive to have to remain forever at the wretched stall; take it for yourselves and for once feel the taste of the “anonymous państwo” [?] [Polish: “state” — apparently a mocking term for the imagined hidden Jewish power], which has grabbed the international “straganiarstwo” [stall trade]! Long live the new “straganiarz” [stall-keeper], who will take over the trade in boiled peas at every small-town fair! Let all the great and rich landowners, with their sons the students, take over all the stalls! But on the condition that they do not neglect the “golden” business...
And if it really came to solving the Jewish question, I would even give up all the liberal professions. If I have to crawl and drag myself through hard years at the universities and take part in the boxing matches, or even decree a fast upon myself and faint from hunger — it is much simpler to sit at home and do nothing, because it is a pity to waste time and health on such things. Blows I can catch in my own town too; and secondly, I do not want to be a doctor at all, and anyway one cannot [?] manage it at all. I have the choice [?] simply not to fall ill and to renounce doctoring altogether — but on one condition: that the antisemites do not later invent a libel against me, that I negotiated [?] with the “anonymous państwo” [?] that Jews should stop falling ill and the Polish doctors should thereby be impoverished. I want to know nothing — neither of any doctor nor of any illness! But I will not be to blame if Christians do not want to be treated by the “shlegers” [?] [brawlers, thugs], and if one-hundred-per-cent patriots themselves boycott their Polish colleagues and travel to be cured precisely abroad and precisely by Jewish doctors. I will remain loyal, I will not fall ill, I will not call a doctor in my whole life, and I will not even need to travel to foreign doctors abroad, although [—] from this “artisl” [?]...
To every doctor I will attach a lawyer — a Christian, naturally; we will become cheerful people, just as all the “friends of the Jews” wish for themselves. You demand seriousness [?] — by all means! Rather let our enemies rejoice! I have scarcely any time for such things. I want to be healthy, not to have a muddled head, and let my guardian [“struzh”, Polish stróż] be “Pan Mecenas” [Mr. Counsellor, the lawyer], with lawsuits [“sprawes”, Polish sprawy] and without lawsuits, or even with an “upadłość” [bankruptcy]...
— Piotr Kędziorek [?]! From today you become “Pan Mecenas”, but on one condition: that we Jews, with the whole “anonymous państwo” [?] at our head, shall know no more sorrow and from today on shall no longer know you. And one more condition: you must have no complaints against us that we boycott you, because we will have no lawsuits whatsoever; we will hand that over, too, to the impoverished peasant... All the economic [?] “placówki” [outposts, positions] — let them take them over, without distinction!
And if after all this you order me to emigrate, I will obey you in that too, because I want to be loyal and peaceably disposed.
I am ready for everything. To do for the good of the poor peasant! I will give up entirely the Jewish shechita, the wretched stall, all the liberal professions; I will even emigrate — if there is anywhere to go.
In a word: I agree to everything.

The Month of March

Winter has already
lost its impetus,
and dear Nature
already looks exactly
like a woman
who is about to give birth [lit. “has to lie in childbed”].

I sense in the air
a strange scent
of warm dampness [?]
and of heavy lightness..

The wet earth
lies heavy and damp,
and sweats and [groans?],
and thinks and ponders:
Hush! Don’t disturb!
The old [woman in labour?]
is again [?] on her feet [?].
She brings us a pearl [?]
for the street [?] and for people [?]:
dear [?] twins:
the sun and the spring.

So life goes on
year after year,
the world has not changed
by a single hair.
Born — buried,
such is the order

What Did the New Kehilla Board in Sosnowiec Take Over?

As we learn, the new kehilla board in Sosnowiec has taken over, besides the living “inventory” — such as gabbaim, cantors, shochtim, [—] [?] and the like — also a series of antiques which, in our opinion, ought to be divided into various categories, for example: correspondence, literature, mysticism, fantasy and pictures.

— I am unhappy — Leon wrings his hands — how am I to blame that my cursed livelihood drives me out of the house many times for several weeks...
— Well, is that why you're unhappy? — mutters [?] Selim.
— You understand me, that is exactly where my misfortune lies: when I go away, as a commercial traveller [?], for orders, my wife betrays me with another.
— How do you know it so surely?
— What do you mean “know” — how do I know? Am I blind? Have I no head left [?] — when I came back from the road yesterday morning, the maid told me (she tells me everything) that my wife is carrying on with a young fellow... Well, what do you say to that?
— Listen — he says to Leon — I have a plan how to make such a “fine fellow” harmless.
— How can one make such a fine fellow harmless? Murder him? Ah, no, not that, not that.
— Who's talking about murder? Nowadays people are cleverer and more careful.
— That is, little brother, what do you mean?
— At what time does your rival usually come to your little wife?
— Naturally, when I'm not at home.
— No, that's not what I mean. At what time, at what hour does he come?
— According to what the maid reports — he always comes around twelve — one at night.
— Excellent — Selim exclaimed — the plan is ready. Such a fine fellow will forswear [?] to the tenth [?] ever to crawl to other men's little wives...
— Well, tell me already! — Leon cried impatiently.
— Listen, go and hire two fine fellows who understand a wink, and let them wait for that rival of yours by the door. It's dark, after all; late at night hardly anyone goes up the stairs, and when the scoundrel is already standing by the door, let him catch a cold bucket of water. But [—] [?]? — such a cold bath that he'll have to dry himself for a year by a warm stove... He'll have to keep quiet, of course, because — go on, raise an outcry, so the neighbours find out that a strange young man knocks at one in the night at the door of a young woman who is all alone at home.
— Done! — Leon literally jumped up with joy.
— Ay, ay! — I'll teach such a fine fellow a lesson [?], but a lesson!
• • •
He hired two young men and instructed them that right after twelve o'clock they should come up the stairs of his flat. He would see to it that the janitor let them in. They must have with them a big cold bucket of snow-water, and when they see a fine fellow approach the door of his flat — then, little brother — splash!
He gave the two young men thirty zł. and was full of joy at the fine idea of his friend Selim.
One night passes, two nights, three nights and four nights — nothing! Not a sound, not a sight.
The young men declare that they have already stood four nights with the bucket of water and nobody shows up.
— Could the maid have fooled him?!
He decides that first of all he must check on these two helpers of his. Are they really standing there?
• • •
It is one o'clock at night; in the whole house it is deathly still, dark.
On the stairs of the second floor stand the two “guardians of morality”, listening hard for every sound; beside them stands a big bucket of water, waiting — for God's sake, let them empty it soon.
Suddenly — hush! — steps, careful, quiet steps. Someone is sneaking up stealthily; heavy breathing is heard.
— Berl, someone's coming, it's the culprit himself — one of the young men calls out.
Both lift the heavy bucket of water, ready to empty it.
The steps are already coming close, here is the figure almost next to them, they already feel his breath, they hear how he creeps quietly up to the door, now he stops, now he shuffles his foot, now...
And a sharp, loud [?] splash of water sprayed across the house —
and a loud, frightened shriek cut through the dark night air.
— Hooligans, bandits! What have you done? Brrrr, brrrr — someone's teeth chattered.
• • •
When the frightened maid ran out half-naked into the house [courtyard], she found her master standing there dressed [?] from head to foot, water literally streaming from his clothes...
Kehilla budget already passed by the Kehilla Council.

[Head of the local section; Będzin — Kehilla.]
[Page head: banner „What's new in Zagłębie?“; right: „Friday, 22 Adar 5697“; left: „piątek 5 marca 937“ [sic; = 1937].]
Będzin
Kehilla budget already passed by the Kehilla Council.
„Real“ [?] items adopted en bloc. — President of „Chalutz Baal Melacha“ votes with the „Agudah“. — National camp walks out of the session. — 3500 zł. budgeted to open a cheap kitchen. — Slaughter levy raised.
On Sunday the new Kehilla budget already received its „tikkun“ from the Kehilla Council, and this „tikkun“ did not last as long as it used to, when the debates over the budget took up several nights; all in all the spectacle lasted barely about 2 hours. Because the roles had been well rehearsed beforehand..!
One minute after the second deadline (6 o'clock) the chairman Mr. Ryński [?] declares the session open and proceeds to the agenda — the budget for the year 1937.
Vice-chairman Mr. Landauer proposes that, since the activity report for last year has not yet been prepared, the session be postponed by 8 days, and in that time the Council should acquaint itself with the report, so as to be informed for the future.
Mr. Ryński is against postponing the session, arguing that the postponement could harm the forthcoming kimcha [de-Pischa] campaign. Landauer's proposal is put to the vote and fails.
Then the parnas Mr. Szenberg makes a proposal that the „dział“ [section] covering the items for the Rabbinate be adopted en bloc.
Against the proposal spoke Messrs. Landauer, Herszletisz [?] and Rozynkier [?]. The last-named criticises the Kehilla administration, which in the budget cut by 22 per cent the subsidies for „dobroczynność“ [charity] and at the same time increased the items for the klei kodesh [religious functionaries].
Szenberg's proposal is put to the vote and obtains a majority thanks to the deciding vote of the artisans' parnas Mr. S. [?] Kajzer.
The Zionist parnasim, having received the unexpected „shot“, especially from one of their own, left the session in protest. In doing so they sharply condemned the deeds of the artisans' parnasim Klajman and Kajzer, who go together with the „Agudah“. The mutual „reckoning“, however, does not disturb the chairman; in one breath he reads out all the items of the „dział“ and calls out: whoever is in favour, raise your hand. And up go the hands of 7 parnasim: Ryński, Szenberg, Berysz Jakubowicz, Jechezkiel Fiszel, Moshe Leib Zylberfrajnd [?], Efraim Klajman and Moshe Kajzer. The „dział“ amounts to no less than 32 thousand zł..
Besides this the sum is increased by a further 2,400 zł. for the rabbi's „chamayres“ [?; unclear word], for which [?] the administration had set 200 zł. a month.
At this item proposals are brought in: 1) by parnas Abraham Issachar Rechnic, that the registration books be kept at the gmina [community office], and 2) that the income from the registrations go into the Kehilla treasury. Both proposals are rejected.
After this „victory“ the budget now runs „normally“. The items are read through and voted.
The same fate befell the proposal of parnas Rechnic that the pension of the shochet Radoszycki [?] be reduced by 500 zł. as a fine for having slaughtered „on the left“ [illicitly]..
The hall grows quieter. At the „national“ table sit no more than Rechnic and Kornfeld. The Agudah parnasim are already „tired“ of raising their hands, and they are displeased with the constant proposals brought in by parnas Kornfeld. The latter also protests that the „dział“ of subsidies for cultural purposes does not include the libraries named after „Bar Kochba“ [?] and „HaZamir“.
At this item a letter is read from the Small Traders' Association, which asks for a subsidy of 2000 zł. for Bażyrska's [?] commercial school; it is decided to subsidise 300 zł., the sum to be for 2 tuition-free pupils whom the Kehilla will maintain.
On the subsidy for the Talmud Torah Mr. Kornfeld proposes that, besides the 3 teachers for secular subjects, the Kehilla should also engage a teacher to teach Yiddish.
After a short debate it is decided to budget a further 700 zł. Half of the sum will go to the secretary of the Talmud Torah, Mr. Icchak Dreksler, for „teaching Yiddish“, and the other half to the headmaster Mr. Abraham Szapir.
A longer debate is provoked by the proposals of parnas Kornfeld: 1) to open a cheap kitchen and 2) an out-patient clinic. Taking part in the debate are the Kehilla president Mr. Rubinlicht, Szenberg, Ryński and others. It is decided to budget 3500 zł. for a cheap kitchen, and the subsidy for „Linas Cholim“ is raised by 1000 zł. with the aim of opening an out-patient clinic.
After the expenditure items of the budget are finished, the revenue items are „considered“.
On the revenue from shechita Mr. Rubinlicht declares that the administration has decided to raise the slaughter levy: instead of 5 zł. per head of cattle it will cost 8 zł., and a calf from 1,50 zł. to 3 zł.
Then Mr. Ryński thanks the parnasim for their calm and businesslike work on the budget, rebukes those who disturb the active [?] work and even insult the parnasim, and declares the session closed.

Saved from Death

[Będzin — road accident.]
Dawid Friedberg and Yankel Kastel were travelling on a lorry with matzot from Proszowice[?] to Będzin. Driving down from the “Soysn Barg”[?] the vehicle overturned and went into a ditch (“rov” — rów). The result was terrible: Friedberg's right arm was broken, and Kastel's eyes were flooded with blood. In great suffering they lay a whole night in the open field. Only in the morning, with the help of a group of peasants from a neighbouring village, was the vehicle put back in order, and then the injured were brought to the local hospital.
The Rabbinate Front Moves Forward... — The Competition Already Published

[Będzin — rabbinate, kehilla.]
This week the competition for the posts of a rabbi and a “podrabin” [assistant rabbi] in the town of Będzin was published in part of the Warsaw Jewish press.
Attached to the competition in the same issue was a notice from the “Agudat ha-Rabbanim be-Polin” [Union of Rabbis in Poland] that no one at all should put forward his candidacy for rabbi, because the rabbinical seat in Będzin, with all its rights, belongs only to R' Mendel Lewin.
As can be seen, the “Aguda” is working on the whole “front” to force through R' Mendel Lewin as rabbi of Będzin. To this end, as we have already written, a pact was concluded between the Ger and the Radomsko Hasidim. The latter undertake to vote for the candidacy of R' Mendel Lewin as rabbi; as compensation they receive the concession of the “podrabin”. The Kehilla Economy Is in the Hands of the Elected Representation — The “Farewell Ceremony”. — 23 zł in Cash and 35 Thousand zł in Debts. — Appeal to the Etat-Payers

[Sosnowiec — kehilla.]
On Sunday at 6 o'clock in the evening the president of the commissarial kehilla board, Mr. Tencer, took leave of the kehilla economy and handed it over into the hands of the elected kehilla board and council.
The handover took place in a festive manner. All members of the board and council are present. On the long green table stand candlesticks with burning candles. The head of the table is occupied by Rabbi Szwarc, president Lajzerowicz and Majslis; present is a representative of the supervisory authority in the person of Magister Mr. Kruszewski.
Mr. Tencer opens the meeting with a short introduction and goes over to the agenda — handing over the cash-box, the kehilla materials, the immovable property, etc.
Then the floor is taken by the parnas Dr. Liberman, who says that the commissarial kehilla board was active only in the field of satisfying religious needs and did not alleviate the sad situation of the broad Jewish masses. Dr. Liberman appeals to the new kehilla representatives to work out a broad relief plan for the benefit of the poor Jewish population.
Mgr. Kruszewski, in his reply to the previous speaker, appreciates the work of the commissarial kehilla board, which carried out its main task — to put the kehilla's finances in order, for which the speaker expresses thanks.
After secretary Mr. Flamner[?] delivers the report on the financial situation, the meeting is closed.
What does the financial situation of the kehilla look like?
On this question the writer of these lines turned to the new kehilla president, Dr.[?] Mr. S. Lajzerowicz, who gave us the following explanation:
“We were aware that it is a very hard task to take upon ourselves at the present time the heavy yoke of running the local kehilla apparatus, but compared with what we found in the kehilla, our fear looks like a dream beside the reality we found.
In the cash-box — says president Mr. Lajzerowicz — we found 23 zł in cash; besides that Mr. Tencer, in order to burden our situation to the utmost, sold the butchers' guild slaughter-tickets for 1,800 zł... He left kehilla debts amounting to 35,299 zł. So that in the present situation we are for the time being powerless to do anything for the kehilla's needs.
Our first task is to issue an appeal to the etat-payers [kehilla-tax payers] to come to our aid and pay the etat debts. The action will surely succeed: already in the first days of our term a number of etat-payers responded, who came and paid their etat debts (the first was Mr. Kandelis).”
The “Shtu” Has Entrenched Itself in the Premises of “Maccabi” — The Fourth General Meeting Again Failed to Come Off

[Sosnowiec — associations, sport.]
Last Sunday the fourth general meeting of this year took place in Maccabi's own premises. In the presence of about 100 members Eng. Szwajcer opens the meeting and proposes Mr. Berliner as chairman; the latter invites to the presidium Messrs. Kamrad[?] and Safer, and as secretary — Mr. Erlich.

After the elections, which did not bring the proper result, Mr. Lancman declares that he withdraws from further work; the same declaration is made by the representative of “Gordia”[?] [perhaps Gordonia]; because of this it is to be hoped that the 5th general meeting will soon take place.
The Chmielnik rabbi, Rabbi Epstein, arrested and put in prison.

[Page banner: “Life in Kielce” — Friday, 22 Adar 5697; piątek 5 marca 1937.]
Last Saturday, at about 2 o'clock in the afternoon, when the Chmielnik rabbi, Rabbi Epstein, was sitting at home in his apartment at the Sabbath meal, the local police commandant came in to him and informed him that on the basis of the order he had received from the authorities[?], he was under arrest. Rabbi Epstein informed[?] his family and the neighbours-householders present in the house of this, and took leave of them.
Rabbi Epstein was taken by car to Busko, and from there he was taken on a cart to Pińczów, where he was put in prison.
Rabbi Epstein's arrest is connected with the rabbinical dispute in Chmielnik between him and his cousin, Rabbi Silman[?].
A delegation of Chmielnik Jews came to Kielce to intercede for Rabbi Epstein to be released from prison. So far they have achieved nothing, and as these lines are being written Rabbi Epstein has not yet been released; when he will be released is not known.
Rabbi Epstein's arrest is also a result of the shameful disputes in the kehillas.

The old Rebbetzin of Chęciny has died.

[Kielce — obituary / Hasidism.] At the age of 100, the Rebbetzin of Chęciny, Sarah Horowitz, died last Friday night — the widow of the old Chęciny Rebbe, R' Chaim Shmuel Halevi Horowitz of blessed memory.
The Rebbetzin was regarded[?] as a great righteous and wise woman. After her husband's death hundreds of Hasidim used to[?] travel to her from every corner of Poland and give her kvitlekh [petition notes]. She was the only woman in Poland who conducted herself like a rebbe.
The old Rebbetzin of Chęciny came of great lineage. She was the daughter of the Kamin[?] rabbi, R' Heshele of blessed memory, a sister's daughter[?] of the great tzaddik R' Chaim of Sanz[?] of blessed memory, from whom she received a blessing for long life. She was also the mother-in-law of the old Grodzisk Rebbe, R' Elimelech Szapira of blessed memory, and a grandmother of the present Piaseczno Rebbe.
The deceased left more than 250 grandchildren and great-grandchildren, most of whom are rabbis and rebbes.
Two weeks ago she fell ill with pneumonia. On Thursday, Purim night, the Piaseczno Rebbe sent to Kielce the head of department (ordynator) of the Czyste hospital in Warsaw, Dr. Kapriner[?], who found that the sick Rebbetzin's heart was very weak.
On Purim she had the Megillah read and called her eldest son, the Olkusz Rebbe R' Heshele, to Kielce.
On Friday towards evening she lit the candles, received the Sabbath, made Kiddush and washed her hands for the "lechem mishneh"; then she fell asleep, and at 12 midnight she breathed out her soul.
On Sabbath morning prayers were held there with a minyan as always, and the Olkusz Rebbe went into the room where she lay, came up to the bed and said to her aloud[?]:
— "Good Shabbos, Mother!"
Later a tish was held as usual.
On Sunday at 4 p.m. the funeral began. The streets were black with many thousands of people, among them hundreds of Hasidim from every corner of Poland.
The Piaseczno Rebbe also came to the funeral; he is, as mentioned, a grandson of the late Rebbetzin. The Piaseczno Rebbe came together with his mother, the old Rebbetzin of Grodzisk, and with dozens of other rabbis from the large towns and small towns.
The late Rebbetzin was buried in the ohel in which her husband R' Chaim Shmuel and her two sons, who were also rebbes, lie. Kaddish was said by her son, the Olkusz Rebbe R' Heshele.
At the request of the deceased no eulogies at all were delivered.

Open Letter from the Będzin Artisans' Union to the Artisans' Kehilla Councillor Mr. M. Kajzer

[Będzin — kehilla; artisans.] At a time of severe economic crisis, which prevails among the Jewish masses and artisans, you find yourselves in a state of apathy and indifference and take no interest in the latest events in our public life here in our town.
We therefore wish to turn to the broad masses of artisans and enlighten them about the situation in the Jewish kehilla and the role of their delegates, who represent them and speak in their name.
At the last vote on the kehilla budget in the kehilla council, the so-called artisan representatives (Klajman-Kajzer) voted together with the representatives of the "Aguda", thereby betraying the interests of the Jewish population and especially of the artisan masses in Będzin. Instead of fighting for support of the special needs, they voted with the "Aguda".
The above-mentioned betrayal is only the beginning of the campaign being conducted by those who want to impose[?] a rabbi by force and stir up quarrels at this present hard time for the Jewish masses.
We declare in the name of the artisan masses, thanks to whom Mr. Kajzer has[?] the opportunity to be a kehilla councillor, that his above-mentioned deed is an ugly betrayal of the most vital[?] artisan interests and stains the good name of Jewish artisanry.
Fellow artisans! Mr. Kajzer has allied himself in the kehilla with Mr. Klajman — a person who was at the time publicly branded as a wrecker of artisan unity; not to mention that Mr. Kajzer unites with this very "artisan partner" and has harnessed himself to the wagon of the Aguda and its servants.
We therefore turn to you, Mr. Kajzer, as the one elected by the artisan masses, with the following demands: 1) to appear before the union's court and explain your deed, and 2) to lay down[?] the mandate immediately. We hereby declare before the broad public that as long as these two demands are not fulfilled, Mr. Kajzer will be regarded as a traitor to the artisans' interests and is consequently not entitled to represent the artisans' interests in the kehilla.
Board of the Artisans' Union, Będzin, Kołłątaja[?] 45.

A Branch of the B'nai B'rith Lodge Is Being Founded in Zagłębie

[Będzin — associations; B'nai B'rith.] On Tuesday evening, in the "S. Fürstenberg" Gymnasium in Będzin, a second meeting took place under the chairmanship of President Mr. S. Fürstenberg on the question of founding a Zagłębie branch of the B'nai B'rith lodge.
Taking part in the meeting were representatives of the B'nai B'rith institutions in Kraków and Katowice, as well as a number of public activists from Sosnowiec, Będzin and Dąbrowa.
After the chairman's introduction about the purpose of the meeting, the floor was given to Rabbi Chameides of Katowice for his lecture on the tasks of the lodge.
