The Living Corpse

[Serialized novel.] A. Zaglembier
THE LIVING CORPSE
(A most thrilling novel of Jewish life in Zagłębie before and after the World War.)

1. The Vanished Man.
It began on a gloriously wonderful evening, a few months before the outbreak of the World War.
From the Małobądz[?] meadows two armed Russian "strazhniki" [rural policemen] came into town late in the evening. Not wishing, apparently, to run into anyone from the "nachalstvo" [the authorities], they avoided the town, and right under the "railway bridge" they turned into the empty, uninhabited street on the other side of the rails, next to the barracks.
From there they took a straight road to the Będzin prison, which stands next to the big bridge leading to Dąbrowa.
At that spot, on the desolate, quiet road, sure that no one was overhearing them, the two "strazhniki" began talking between themselves:
— Well, Berko — said one of them, under whose glued-on black moustache blond hair was sprouting — so far everything is in order...
— Listen, Jędrek — answered the other, who apparently did not feel quite at ease in the strazhnik uniform — I've told you already: don't say "hop" before you've jumped over.
— Don't worry about that; with me every bit of "work" has to succeed...
Both had to stop[?] for a few minutes, because just then a freight train went past at full force and speed, shooting thick sheaves of golden sparks from its chimney; and when the whistling and clattering of the train could no longer be heard, Berko asked again, somewhat uneasily:
— Are you really sure that it's today they'll take him away to the Piotrków prison?
— If "Shmulek" has ordered it so, you can be sure: on his word you can build a wall. He has to "bastir" (escape) today. Without Shmulek our freedom is even worse than prison...
— If only it succeeds. How much time is left?
The other glanced at his little watch:
— A quarter of an hour at most.
— And Szostak?
— Szostak knows what he has to do. He's waiting on the other side of the "Banska Wszeka"[?]; everything is in order...
— If so, good.
And thus, talking quite quietly between themselves, both "strazhniki" reached the Dąbrowa bridge. Here they stopped[?] again, set off[?] with somewhat unsteady steps as though they were tipsy, and remained standing in the dark shadow of a tree quite close to the prison.
All around it was quiet. Only a few windows of the little houses nearby were faintly lit.
The two "strazhniki" did not have to wait long.
In the surrounding silence the creak and grating[?] of the opened prison gate rang out quite clearly.
Right afterwards three men came out from there: the "famous" Zagłębie thief "Shmulek Łapka", escorted by two armed Cossacks, who were to take him by train to the Piotrków prison.
At that moment the two "strazhniki" hid even deeper in the dark shadow of the tree, and when the Cossacks had already led Shmulek past, one "strazhnik" said to the other:
— It's good. They're taking him by the lower road too. They want to get him to the station as securely as possible, where everything is ready... I'll do the talking...
And lighting up cigarettes, both stepped out of the shadow, and two minutes later the two "strazhniki" drew level with the Cossacks and greeted them:
— Zdrastye...
— Zdrastye!
One of the "strazhniki", as if out of curiosity, glanced into Shmulek's face and at his bound hands, and then said to the Cossacks with a tipsy little smile:
— Well, you're escorting an important "bird" here!
— A bird indeed! — the Cossacks answer — the local prison is too weak for him, so he has to be transferred to Piotrków.
— Quite right too — the "strazhnik" pretends to rejoice, and hands the Cossacks a packet of cigarettes, saying:
— Smoke, brothers...
The Cossacks did not refuse.
And just as all five had stopped in the middle of the dark road to light up, a strange thing suddenly happened: while one "strazhnik" was giving them a light, the other "strazhnik" suddenly struck both Cossacks over the head from behind, whereupon both Cossacks fell to the ground.
Now the "work" went on according to the plan agreed beforehand:
While one "strazhnik" tied the Cossacks hand and foot and stuffed their mouths so that they could not shout too soon, the other "strazhnik" meanwhile pulled some tool out of his greatcoat and began tinkering with it at the little chains binding Shmulek's hands together. Shmulek "Łapka" himself was burning with impatience. His black, crazed eyes glowed; he was pleased with this bit of "work".
— You've done that nicely — said "Łapka" — I'll repay you yet... But why is it taking you so long? I see you've brought a bad pair of "shears" — you haven't cut through a single link yet?
— The devil knows[?] — the "shears" work fine.
Still, cutting through the chains on Shmulek's hands was hard going. Then the thought suddenly occurred to "Łapka":
— Just look in their pockets. The Cossacks must have the key to the chain on them.
And so it was. On one of the Cossacks they did indeed find the little key, and within a few seconds "Shmulek Łapa" [sic] had his hands free.
— Now let's do a "tik" [clear off], by the same road under the hill.
— You go first — the "strazhniki" told him — "Szostak" is already waiting for us by the "Banska Wszeka"[?].
Szostak was waiting at the agreed spot with a bundle of fresh[?] clothes. They tied the strazhnik uniforms together into one pack, poured enough sand into it to make it heavy, and then threw it into the nearby "Kanski Doł"[?]...
— And now let's split up — said "Shmulek Łapka", once he had dressed and also taken something along for the road — in the morning they'll find the Cossacks and things may get uncomfortable...
And the dangerous gang of thieves of Zagłębie parted here, on the other side of the "Przemsza", for a few days.
Both "strazhniki" with Szostak went back into town — now, however, no longer as "strazhniki"... "Shmulek Łapka" too went off on his own. It was now barely nine o'clock in the evening. After the "feast" Szostak had given him to take along, he would still be able to get a good sleep. He went out across the meadows onto the well-[?] road and from there into a little wood, to a cunningly concealed hiding place where years ago the well-known Będzin bandit Seler-ski[?] used to hide...
* * *
That same evening, and at the very same hour, dark-haired Sarahche, in despair, was running from house to house, to relatives and friends, to find out whether her husband had not been with them — the quiet, solid and universally respected collector of a large firm — Yosl Wertheim.
For such a thing was happening for the first time in Sarahche's life since their wedding.
And that is why she is now so frightened and desperate. For several hours she stood beneath her window, straining her eyes: "Maybe Yosl will come soon? After all, he's only human... Maybe Yosl had some difficult accounting with a merchant"...
So Sarahche talked to herself in the first anxious hours, and comforted herself with these words.
But when the late summer night began to fall, Sarahche could no longer sit at home, and in despair she began searching the town for her dear vanished husband.
For how could her husband suddenly have gone missing — he who today had not shown himself at home all day?
Family and friends began to console her.
— Come, Sarahche, be quite calm and don't wring your hands; look, [?] today Yosl is surely sitting somewhere settling accounts with a merchant.
— What's there to talk about — a person isn't a pinhead...
— And you should know that an edible[?] thing doesn't get lost; and secondly, it's barely 10 o'clock. Maybe Yosl has even gone to Dąbrowa or to Czeladź[?] to collect money from the customers?
But Sarahche's fright and despair grew from minute to minute. Somehow she would not let herself be comforted at all, and kept insisting:
— No, no, that's not Yosl's nature at all...
And Sarahche's heart, it seems, sensed best of all that something bad must have happened to her husband today, for it truly was not Yosl's nature. Always punctual and deliberate, and not wishing to cause his wife and children needless worry and heartache, Yosl always used to say beforehand whether he would be late for lunch or would only come home at night because he had to travel to the surrounding small towns. Then Sarahche would be calm and would not, God forbid, imagine anything bad.
Today, however, Yosl Wertheim left home for work very early, as always, and said nothing to Sarahche about whether he would be late for lunch. Sarahche had even wondered that on leaving the house he kissed her exactly the way he takes leave of her when he sometimes goes away. She had even asked him:
— Yosyeshi, are you going away?
And handsome, healthy Yosl answered her with a little laugh:
— And if one isn't going away, mustn't one kiss such a pretty little wife as you?...
Sarahche is ashamed to tell about this, but her heart pounds as if with hammers; the worst thoughts now come into her head. Perhaps Yosl really did unexpectedly go off to a neighbouring town? And the roads are so unsafe nowadays... bandits and murderers have lately been attacking merchants... and[?] did Yosl happen to have a lot of collected money on him?... Not long ago Sarahche herself had seen how the police and Cossacks chased the dangerous bandit Shmulek Łapka and his helpers over the Będzin rooftops, after they had tried, revolvers in hand, to rob a rich man's house...
— And tell me, Sarahche, what did Yosl's employers say? When did he leave the office today?
— I haven't been there at all yet — answers Sarahche, and a bright thought suddenly flashes through her mind — just see how dazed[?] a person can sometimes be: it didn't occur to me at all.
— So why are you standing there like a golem? Come, I'll go with you!
And at once someone else speaks up, wishing to give Sarahche still more courage:
— Believe me, in the time we've been standing here Yosl has already come home and is tucking into his lunch.
— Maybe he's already started looking for Sarahche... a couple in love, after all — they stick to each other like honey...
The owners of the office where Yosl Wertheim has worked for many years looked at Sarahche in great surprise and astonishment as they heard the strange story.
— Just today — said the employers — your husband left the office earlier than usual. We have, God forbid, no grudge against him for it, because when necessary your husband sometimes works an hour longer too.
— Did he perhaps have business money on him? — asks Sarahche, even more frightened.
— No. Your husband did indeed collect a lot of money today, but he handed it all in to the cash office, down to the last grosz.
— So what does one do? Where is my husband? I no longer know what to think... — Sarahche nearly burst into tears.
The owners of the firm calmed her, and her companions too gave her fresh courage:
— Come along now, don't brood over it, it's all for the good; Yosl is surely waiting for you. He's not a woman, after all, to go running around town at once looking for his wife.
But as soon as Sarahche crossed the threshold of her flat, everything went even darker before her eyes.
Her eldest daughter Blimke, a wonderfully beautiful, blossoming girl in her fifteenth year, was still awake; the two smaller children too, who had long been lying in bed, somehow could not fall asleep tonight, and before their desperate mother had managed to open her mouth, all three children asked at once, with trembling fear in every limb:
— Mameshi! Where is Tateshi? Didn't you find him?!
But instead of an answer, Sarahche could no longer hold back her anguish and broke into terrible weeping.
The relatives who had come with her began to console her again: it's only just 12 at night, maybe Yosl got held up somewhere?.. maybe a game of cards?.. after all, he's only human...
But Sarahche's pain and despair grew still greater when through her tear-filled eyes she saw Yosl's leftover lunch standing on the stove, untouched, and Yosl himself still not there...
— People, what does one do? Give me advice! — Sarahche wrung her hands.
(Further continuation of the thrilling novel — in the next issue.)
Our Haggadah — with a new commentary, by Ben Amotz

With a new commentary („teytsh"), by Ben Amotz [pen name].

The Seder Plate
The seder plate is arranged in this way:
Top right — a blown-up egg (a remembrance of the inflated desires).
On the left — the shank bone (a roasted bone — a remembrance of the times when people ate meat that was not rationed by quota).
Bottom right — the charoset (a remembrance of the muddy borscht[?] that the capitalist „vrashener"[?] left behind).
On the left — karpas — so that at the Four Cups we remember that we lie „nine ells" deep in poverty.
In the middle, in a place of honour — the maror; in a pinch one may also fulfil the duty with the front page of a Jewish daily newspaper...

Signs for the Seder.
The signs of the new seder are:
Kadesh — take in your hand the competition notice of the Będzin kehilla and the resolutions of the „National Camp" [OZN] and say the Rabbis' Kaddish...
U-rechatz — if you have touched the hands of a „neutral" parnas (community leader), go[?] wash and say „al netilat"...
Karpas — take the campaign for the Jewish hospital, the plan for the Sosnowiec mikveh, the project to build a gymnasium hall („turn-hale") in Będzin, and make the blessing — „borei pri ha-adamah" (Who creates the fruit of the ground)...
Yachatz — you take a „neutral" kehilla parnas and divide[?] him: give the first half away to the „Agudah" [Agudat Yisrael] and hide the other half as an afikoman.
Maggid — whatever your heart desires, but God forbid not the truth.
Rachtzah — you can be washed and become holy and pure...
Motzi — from all the rich men in Zagłębie one can „extract" something, but from the Sosnowiec ones it is impossible.
Matzah — because[?] most of them are war-profiteer rich men...
Maror — if you are a resident of Dąbrowa, you fulfil the duty when you recall who the heads of the kehilla are...
Korech — you take a good „orendovnik" [Pol. orędownik — intercessor][?], wrap him in a humanistic sermon together with a piece of dictatorship and democracy, and eat them together.
Shulchan Orech — according to the kehilla's „constitution", only those who sit at the kehilla's bowl may enjoy this item[?]...
Barech — thank and praise God for it — it could be even worse.
Hallel — to everything you are ordered, answer — „for His mercy endures forever".
Nirtzah — if you have done all this, you are a candidate for the old-age home.

Ha Lachma Anya
These are the matzot at which the rabbinate „fired" 42-cm-calibre prohibitions and bans. Kol dichfin — whoever is hungry can go into a restaurant or[?] eat — treyf[?].

The 4 Questions at Modern Daddy-Mommy's.
Together with introducing the new seder, the old questions are abolished. Only our Haggadah-master has 4 modern questions to ask.
The child asks the father:
1) Why, daddy, does mommy go to „Śląsk"[?] while you are at home, cooking lunch and washing the [—] (dishes?)?
2) Why does mommy go out whole nights to play „bridge" at the club while you mind the child?
3) Why does mommy smoke cigarettes and drink brandy while you eat „yushke" (thin broth)?
4) If mommy is the whole daddy, why do I ask you the questions and not mommy?
In accordance with the modern system, no answers are given to modern questions; therefore we proceed[?] straight to the Haggadah and make the beginning with the

Story of Rabbi Eliezer
To the story belong other rabbis too, „who were reclining". They held a meeting on urgent kehilla matters, „and were telling" — they talked about the situation of the Jews — „until their disciples came": Rabbi Elazar's[?] disciples said: „the time has come" — it is high time to publish a competition for a rabbi and a „podrabin" [deputy rabbi].
„Said Rabbi Elazar" — Rabbi Elazar said to them: Gentlemen, „behold, I am like a man of seventy", the experiences of the last months have weakened me greatly, so that I already feel like a ninety-year-old; therefore the rabbinate question should be left to the new kehilla. To this Ben Zoma did not agree and said: Mr. President, see what the sages say, that „the days of your life" — this world — is the main thing, that as long as one lives one must care for this world; whereas with the Zionists you will still[?] belong[?] to the world to come, „to bring the days of the Messiah"...
„Blessed" — praised be the Almighty „Who gave the Torah", Who gave His people Israel a little Torah with which one trades and closes deals; and praised also be the Haggadah-master for the

Four Sons.
The Wise — a Jew who peddles ideals and makes a living from it.
The Simple — one of the new trustees (ne'emanim), who looks at the ritual meat like „a rooster at people" [idiom: uncomprehending]...
The one who does not know how to ask — that is a non-party „dozor" (board member) of the Będzin kehilla.
Remark: We have not presented the Wicked son, because the number of wicked in the „Agudah" ranks has now grown greatly...
For practical reasons, also abolished are the „Baruch shomer havtachato", the „Tze u-lmad" (for wanting to learn you get the ten plagues) and the „Be-yad chazakah", because the Sosnowiec kehilla is no longer administered by a commissioner.

The Modern Ten Plagues
Blood — [unclear word][?], which is often [spilled][?] on the faces of the Jewish students.
Frogs — the enemies of Israel in Romania croak at us like frogs.
Lice — these are the „sashkes"[?] who crawl where they should not, and bite.
Wild beasts (arov) — the German refugees, poor things, wander about as if confused.
Boils — grow[?] on many upstart rich men.
Hail — a hail of bankruptcies, companies and other plagues.
Locusts — the Jewish merchants are starved for takings like locusts.
Darkness — when you look at who stands at the eastern wall in the synagogue, it goes dark before your eyes.
Slaying of the firstborn — the only thing left after the Jewish Cooperative Bank.
For reasons of principle the „Dayenu" is also abolished — there is no „Dayenu" — on the contrary, the parnasim say that however much one gives, it is too little.

And It Came to Pass at Midnight
In the Jewish clubs „they say Psalms" — at midnight...
The Ger–Radomsk agreement was concluded — at midnight...
Communal activists vote down a „fund" — at midnight...
The presidents of the free-loan (gmach) fund are „out"[?] — at midnight...
The kehilla treasurer, after handing over, drove off — at midnight...
Zagłębie „menzhatkes" (Pol. mężatki — married women) hold „chatzot" in the confectionery[?] — at midnight.
The Endeks [Polish nationalists] „care" for us day and night...

Who Knows One?
One we know: that with one „Zionist" vote R' Shlomo Yitzchak was elected parnas of the kehilla council.
Who knows two? Two we know: two artisan activists in Będzin have been „snatched" over to the Ger Hasidim.
Who knows three? Three we know: the three towns Sosnowiec, Będzin and Dąbrowa suffer from the „rabbinate disease".
Who knows four? Four we know: four Zionist parnasim are still on the kehilla council.
Who knows five? Five we know: five „dozores" ride the kehilla nag („klyatshe").
Who knows six? Six we know: six „old ones" have again entered the new management of the Gemilut Chesed fund.
The remaining „who knows" we do not give, because one may not tell everything one knows...

The „Secret" of „Chad Gadya"
A village Jew („yishuvnik") who was conducting the seder stopped at „Chad Gadya" and did not want to go on.
— Why did you stop? his wife asked him.
— I can't go on, because the story with the Chad Gadya is not „v porzhondku" (Pol. in order); it's a „chemne"[?] (Pol. ciemna — shady) story: how did the father sell a kid for two zuzim, eh?
— You're right, Moshe, — the wife agreed — truly a „pshikre" (Pol. przykra — unpleasant) affair.
One day the same village Jew comes into town; it was on the eve of Yom Kippur, and he saw his acquaintance going up into an attic with a rooster to do kapparot.
— Now here is a second secret: why did he go up with the rooster into the attic, of all places[?]?
The village Jew didn't hesitate and went to the rabbi to rule on the question: why did So-and-so son of So-and-so do kapparot in the attic.
— Because the rooster was a stolen one, — the rabbi explained to him.
— So, now I understand the „secret" of the Chad Gadya myself: why the father sold the kid for two zuzim — because the kid was stolen too...

The Bridegroom's Seder.
The Passover seder begins with „Kadesh" and ends with „Nirtzah".
The bridegroom's seder begins with „Nirtzah" (when he takes the dowry he is pleased) and ends with „Kadesh" (after the dowry he says the Rabbis' Kaddish).
Leib Sztapinski[?].
Inquiries — a Passover humour corner

[Humour — Passover; "Inquiries to the editor", anecdotes and dialogues.]
Before finishing [?] the Haggadah the editor received the following inquiries:
I have a daughter; she smokes [?], drinks vodka, runs to [football] matches — must she ask the Four Questions at the Seder?
———
This week I stood in the market and took in [?] "in the whites" [?] (meaning unclear) — must I still recline at the Seder on the left side?
———
I hold a patent [trade licence], have grown-up daughters and keep my mother-in-law with me — am I already exempt from maror?
———
My husband went to the Rebbe for Passover, and since I have a sublocator [subtenant], can he be "second to the king"?
———
I am a merchant and have already had eleven "breakdowns" [?] (break-ins/bankruptcies), am I already exempt from eating "farbrokts" [?] (soaked matzo; uncertain pun)?

Then and Now.
"Whoever tells at length of the Exodus from Egypt — is praiseworthy": once, he who told more of the miracles of the Exodus was worthy of being praised. Today, whoever counts more money — he is the one praised.
Leyb Sztabinski.
—o—
A Modern Interpretation.
The author of the Haggadah says: "In every generation a person must see himself" — that is, in every generation, at every time, a person must look at himself; let [?] him first see his own faults and only afterwards other people's...
Leyb Sztabinski.
—o—
Passover Dialogue
in the WIZO [?] premises.
— Tell me, Stefa, what sort of thing is Passover?
— I can't say exactly [?]; it's probably [?] the Jewish "święta maca" [?] (Polish: "holy matzo").
— Why do they hold a Seder?
— It's that kind of "wieczorek" [Polish: evening party] that lasts a "Wielkanoc" [Polish: Easter; literally "great night"]...
— I'd also like to know the reason for matzos.
— Well, it must surely symbolise the face of a beauty queen chosen in Egypt [?].

— Probably [?] it is meant to be an "starożytna" [Polish: ancient] holiday lipstick.

— Oh, it's a kind of menu card where [?] a menu [?] of various Seder dishes is listed.
— And what is salt water?
— Why, that's the Ciechocinek "solanka" [spa brine].
— Why [—] does one drink four cups of wine?
— Because the four well-known "sons" demanded so much.
— Can you perhaps also tell me the meaning of the ten plagues?

— What does afikoman mean?
— A hidden "gedn" [?] (undeciphered word).

A Pre-Passover Chat.
— Listen [?], Mendel, we should have whitewashed the house for Passover.
— Not necessary, my wife; [?] the two [?] walls [?] needn't be painted (meaning uncertain).
— Why?
— Because I am a "sposter" [?] and you — the "shlek" [?] (undeciphered words).

An Artist Wife.
Husband (to his wife, a pianist): Who knocked out a windowpane?
Wife: As soon as [?] I began to play, the neighbour threw a stone and knocked out a windowpane.
Intervention by “Agudas Yisroel” at the Ministry, that M. Lewin Should Fill the Functions of “Podrabin”

[Będzin — kehilla and rabbinate.]
The “Agudas Yisroel” in Poland has applied to the Ministry of Religious Affairs with an appeal, in which it is stated:
The kehilla board in Będzin adopted on 6 January 1937 a resolution to appoint R' Mendel Lewin as temporary “podrabin” [deputy/official rabbi] in place of R' Yehoshua'le of blessed memory.
The Starostwo [district office] forwarded [?] this resolution to the Województwo [provincial office], and Rabbi Chameides of Katowice was engaged as temporary rabbi.
For this reason we hold that: 1) it is absurd that so large a kehilla as Będzin should not have its own [rabbi], who would keep the registry books and be dependent on a neighbouring rabbi. 2) It is simply impossible that a rabbi in Katowice, who carries very many functions, should be able to perform the religious functions in Będzin as well. 3) It is almost [?] the will of the entire Jewish population that Rabbi M. Lewin should perform the functions of “podrabin”, since he possesses the spiritual qualifications for it; the best “proof” is that already many years ago he performed rabbinical functions with which the whole town was satisfied.
We therefore turn, as the representation of all religious Jewry, to the Ministry as the highest supervisory authority over the Jewish kehillas, to recommend that Rabbi Lewin be appointed “podrabin” in place of H. B. Selger [?].
A copy of the appeal was sent to the kehilla board with a covering letter, in which the Starostwo asks: 1) whether M. Lewin possesses the proper qualifications, and 2) at what times Rabbi Chameides officiates in Będzin.
In the reply of the kehilla board it is explained that: 1) M. Lewin possesses the proper qualifications, and 2) Rabbi Chameides officiates 3 times a week for 2 hours.

Festive Seders at the “Orphans' Home”
As every year, this year too the seders at the “Orphans' Home” are being celebrated in festive fashion. On Monday, Chol Hamoed, at 9 in the evening, a lecture will take place in WIZO's own premises by Mrs. Felicja Stendig (Kraków) on the theme [?] “How to educate” the parents.

They Did Not Hit the Right Address...

[Będzin — a swindle.]
Last Sunday afternoon Mrs. Kimelman, who was walking along Okrzei Street, was approached by an unknown person, who asked her in Polish “whether there are Polish shops on the street”. When Mrs. K. gave this person several addresses of Polish firms, he went away. At that moment a young Jewish man ran up to her and asked Mrs. K. to do him a favour and ask the Christian what he had to sell.
Mrs. K. realised that she had a fine [?] pair of swindlers before her; she gave the “broker” a good scolding, and he went away.
A Gabbai Who Dunns for “Shtibl” Debts After His Death...

[Będzin — Hasidim, curiosity.]
He came in a dream to a Hasid and demanded that he pay the debt.
Some months ago there died the Pilica Hasid Mr. G., who for 50 years had been a faithful gabbai of the Pilica “shtibl” in our town. Now it turns out that not only in his lifetime did he look after the welfare of the “shtibl”, but he looks after it also after his death...
When Mr. G. died, his successors found documents in the “shtibl archive” showing that the Hasid L. owed three zł. and 50 groszy.
When Mr. L. was called upon to pay the debt, he answered that “he had long since paid the debt to the gabbai”. Having no choice, they accepted the answer as “good money” and dunned him no more.
Last Wednesday, while Mr. L. lay sunk in a sweet sleep, the gabbai came to him with a stick in his hand and “said” to him: “If you do not pay the ‘shtibl’ debt, it will go very badly with you”...
— How much do I owe? — the frightened Hasid asked the dead gabbai.
— You owe no more than two zł. and 10 groszy...
At dawn Mr. L. came running to one of the Pilica Hasidim and paid the debt..
Now the Pilica Hasidim say: what a gabbai we had — even when he is already in the World of Truth, he still remembers the “shtibl” and collects the debts..
The “dream” cast fear upon the debtors, who hurried to pay, afraid of the “dead bailiff”..
There Will Be Dancing for All It's Worth

[Będzin — city council, taxes.]
Entertainments freed from the municipal tax.
The “stazh” [?] [highlight] of Thursday's session of the city council was the item — election of 6 delegates to the national congress of Polish towns. Because of the negotiations between the clubs (factions) on this matter, a recess was declared twice. Finally an agreement was reached that two delegates would go from each club. The Jewish delegates are: Dr. Weinzieher, and ławnik [member of the municipal board] G. Rabnitz [?] as deputy.
To the statute on the tax on entertainments, exemptions [?] etc., the motion of Councillor H. S. [?] Wilberberg [?] was adopted, that events for the benefit of cultural purposes shall be free of the tax. The motion was supplemented by Councillor Dr. Perl, that dance entertainments for charitable purposes, too, shall be free of the tax.
Sosnowiec — “Heads Up!”

[Sosnowiec — merchants and industrialists.]
President Safer calls out at the general meeting of merchants and industrialists.
On Saturday night the annual general meeting of merchants and industrialists took place. The meeting stood, as always, at the proper level; a series of reports was delivered, which made it plain that the board, headed by President [G.? ] Mr. Józef Safer, bears on itself the great burden of caring for the interests of its members.
The meeting is opened by President Mr. Safer, who dedicates a short but warm eulogy to the unforgettable honorary president Mr. Maurycy Wajger [?] of blessed memory, whose name has been perpetuated by the establishment of an annual scholarship for needy [?] pupils. Honour is also paid to the deceased members Henryk Oppenheim and Feldbaum.
At the general request Dr. Herzman takes over the chair, with Messrs. Ignacy Rajner, M. Klempisz [?] as assessors and Mr. Baloim [?] as secretary.
After honouring with a minute of silence the Jewish leaders R' Nahum Sokolow and Dr. Thon of blessed memory, the reports are heard with great attention: by Mr. S. Birman on the general report — the speaker addresses some words to those merchants who, even at the present time, have no interest in the most topical commercial affairs; on the housing (rent) question — Mr. Skszyna [?]; the regulations — Mr. Landau; internal activity — Mr. Feldman; tax affairs — Mr. Kleinberg.
The reports are supplemented by President Mr. Safer, who says that the work cannot be called economic expansion but only defensive work, to defend ourselves against the libels; but we must not lose heart — relying on the legal foundations of the Constitution, we call upon you, Jewish merchants — “heads held high”.
After the treasurer's report — Mr. Majtlis — and the auditing committee — Mr. Königsberg — a recess of 10 minutes is declared.
During the recess Mr. H. Terin [?] drew the presidium's attention to the shameful act of informing in the latest issue of the “Zaglembier Shlezish Folksblat” against the Zionist Organisation and against the Jewish Gymnasium. The outcome of this was that President Mr. Safer at once demanded that the “editor” of the rag, the “barrister” Symchowicz, leave the meeting forthwith.
After the recess Mr. Terin takes the floor, protesting against admitting to the meeting the “editor” of the “Zaglembier Shlezish Folksblat”, who demoralises Jewish public life with his informing and blackmail.
After the discussion, with the participation of Messrs. Ginsburg, Fiszel, Grandapel and others, an absolutorium [vote of discharge] is granted to the outgoing board.
After adopting the budget of 16,000 zł., the elections take place, and almost the entire previous board is re-elected.
The city council treats [us] in honour of the holiday with a new tax.

[Sosnowiec — city council, taxes.]
Last Monday a session of the local city council [of Sosnowiec] took place, which considered the budget for the year 1937/38.
The new budget provides for a new surcharge tax amounting to 60 thousand [?] zł. to build a public (elementary) school on Sucha Street. The tax will be levied as follows: 7 per cent on the tax [podatek] of house-owners, 5 per cent on the dwelling tax and 30 per cent on.. [trade] licences (patents).
The Jewish councillors spoke out against the tax, arguing that the merchants, and also the house-owners, who are already burdened enough, are not able to bear the yoke of new taxes.
The tax was adopted by a majority of votes.
After the vote the Jewish councillors proposed that the 4th trade category and the 8th [category of] artisans be exempt from the tax. The President [of the city] promised that the request would be taken into consideration.
A "Beit Lechem" department is to be created at "Bikur Cholim".

[Sosnowiec — charity.]
On the initiative of the well-known communal activist Reb Chaim Yosef Zoyants [?] [Zając?], a "Beit Lechem" [bread-for-the-poor society] is to be founded in Old Sosnowiec (Stary Sosnowiec), which will exist as a separate department of the "Bikur Cholim" society.

Public School No. 13 for poor children for the holiday.

President of the Zionist Organization in Poland, Adv. Hartglas, proclaims the Keren Hayesod campaign.

[Page banner: “Life in Kielce”; corner box: “Friday, 26 March 1937”]
On Monday, the first day of Chol HaMoed Pesach, Jewish Kielce will welcome the leader of Polish Jewry and president of the Zionist Org., Adv. A. Hartglas.

We greet the ambassador of the Jewish state-in-the-making, and together with the whole Zionist Jewish community in Kielce we wish this year's Keren Hayesod campaign an extraordinary success, to the glory and honour of the Jewish community
Sixteen hundred families asked for matzot for Passover.

How great the need is in the Jewish street can be seen from the enormous number of Jewish families who this year applied for holiday aid. Close to 16 hundred Jewish families, i.e. about 7000 souls, were registered with the kehilla for Passover support.
On Wednesday, the whole day, the kehilla office was besieged by thousands of poor Jews, who came with tears in their eyes to beg for at least a few kilos of matzot. Open Letter to Senator Mr. J. Trockenheim in Warsaw

[Będzin — Rabbinate.]
We have had the opportunity to acquaint ourselves with your memorandum, which you sent on the 10th of luty [February] to the Ministry of Education. Before we read this memorandum we were certain that your memorandum concerned the grave Jewish situation in all areas of Jewish life, or the grave situation of the Hebrew and Yiddish school system in general and of religion [teaching] in particular.
For otherwise we could not imagine that a Jewish senator would intervene at the Ministry of Education about other matters.
But how astonished and shaken we were when this memorandum says nothing more than that "the whole of Polish Jewry is interested in the confirmation of Mr. Mendel Lewin as temporary Będzin administrator [?]."
How, esteemed Mr. Senator, did your hand not tremble when signing this memorandum! Who authorised you thus to degrade the whole of Polish Jewry and to demand in its name the confirmation of some Mendel Lewin? Are these really the worries of Polish Jewry? Does even a part of it know who this Mr. Mendel Lewin is?
We ask you: by what right have you dragged the whole of Polish Jewry into a local struggle of a certain Ger [Hasidic] family, which wants by force to foist upon the Będzin kehilla a young lad who possesses not the slightest religious or secular qualifications and has nowhere served in the rabbinate — as rabbi of so large a Jewish community as Będzin?
By what right and on what grounds do you write about the proper performance of the functions by the temporary rabbi of Będzin, Rabbi Kalman Chameides of Katowice; do you know how those same functions were performed until now, when Będzin had a permanent rabbi.. Surely, esteemed [?] Mr. Senator, you should first have had yourself properly and objectively informed about everything, and not written according to the information of a few Agudah quarrel-mongers, then when you considered it such "an important question for the whole of Polish Jewry" and let yourself be drawn in this way into the ugly dispute in which a group of low politicians is interested. Who authorised you at all to meddle in the internal, bloody [?] interests of Będzin Jewish society?
We shall not dwell at all on the various other inaccuracies in the memorandum.
But one thing nevertheless surprises us: whence does the Senator — being in Warsaw — know of all the "great virtues" of Mr. Mendel Lewin, of which not a single Będzin citizen knows; on the contrary, they know something quite different...
All the Jews of Będzin, without distinction of party and tendency, as well as all Hasidic circles, will confirm to you that they regard it as extraordinary insolence when such a young man has the audacity to want to become the religious leader, the spiritual pastor, the representative of such a mother-city in Israel as Będzin.
Have you considered, Mr. Senator, to what compromising of the Będzin Jews you would have led, had your protégé young man been confirmed?
Esteemed Mr. Senator! We regard the intervention forced upon you as an assault on the rights of the Jewish population of Będzin. We advise you rather to devote yourself to the grave Jewish situation, and leave who is to be rabbi of Będzin to the decision of the Jews of Będzin.

The Seders in the Będzin Orphanage

[Będzin — Orphanage.]
I am still under the impression of the spiritual delight, of the great satisfaction, which we experienced during the festive seders in the Będzin "Beit Yetomim" [orphanage].
The finest concert, play, the finest film cannot give such moral satisfaction.
In the beautiful, large, splendid hall of the house, around several snow-white-covered tables on which there are candles, flowers and every good thing prepared, sit over 70 children (no evil eye), all dressed alike from head to foot in new clothes, all with festive smiling little faces, with shining contented little eyes, reciting and singing the Haggadah under the supervision of the teacher A. Nider [?] and the counsellor Miss Bras [?], in the presence of several board members with the chairman Dr. Weinzieher and wife, editor L. Szpigelman and wife, etc. Unfortunately, the number of "others" is small.
All the little children recite and sing the Haggadah — without fault.
And observing the wonderful picture, I think to myself: is there in the present time a greater moral satisfaction for every thinking person than seeing how children without parents are cared for, as far as possibility permits, with everything that human decency dictates: with a clean dwelling, clean linen, hygienic supervision, Jewish and secular education, medical help, etc., etc.
Who gives away their best time for the children of the house?
In truth, thanks are due to all those who support the institution, but merely giving money is still little; one must [?] work together, devote oneself with one's whole heart. Being the administrative machine — that is the main thing!
And who are they who carry out this meritorious work? They are: Mrs. Cesia Szajn and Mrs. Wajnsztok. They are the souls of the orphanage.
Mrs. Cesia Szajn is the so-called "mother" of the orphans' home. She practically lives there; the upbringing of the orphans — that is her heart, that is her theatre, cinema, her club, her bridge.
And with how much joy was her heart [filled], how her eyes shone when the seder was staged at the highest level, with which it could have impressed the greatest Jewish house?
The second — Mrs. Wajnsztok is her deputy; she is lit by the same spirit, she sacrifices the same time and work; in a word, no lesser pillar of the house, and no lesser thanks are due to her.
Herman Szer.

The Commandment of the Hour!

[Sosnowiec — small trade; opinion.] (In connection with the propaganda campaign in the Sosnowiec Small Traders' Association.)
We stand on the eve of the second [closing] days of our festival of liberation; the sky[?] is freeing itself little by little from its wintry clouds, and the dear sun is already beginning to warm a little — and yet, why am I in such a despairing[?] mood? What presses and torments my soul so? True, when the day[?] of freedom drew near, every Jew felt festive, a joy embraced everyone — and today? Today we do not feel the warm breath of spring; instead a leaden, clouded sky hangs over the Jewish world.
Some of the finest[?] Jews, who formerly still had a livelihood and supported the poor and needy with a generous hand, have unfortunately this year had to stretch out their hands for help.
Well, can the Jew of today, who sees all this, rejoice in the festival of liberation?
"Bitter and gloomy are the prospects for the Jews in the whole world in general, and for us Eastern Jews in particular.
But do we understand our situation as it is in reality? To this question the answer, unfortunately, is — no!
Unfortunately one must state a fact which is especially remarkable: at a time when all the organizations that wage an economic struggle against us grow stronger and mightier from day to day, at that very same time our defence organizations, which are our economic associations, grow ever weaker.
For example: in 1933 the non-Jewish small traders' association had about 70 members, and the Jewish small traders' association in Sosnowiec had over 700 members; today 2 Christian small traders' associations are already organized, with a total of over 1000 members. The Jewish small traders' association, on the other hand, has fallen to 500 members.
Therefore one would like to ask the weakened Jewish merchant: does he give himself an account of where such indifference can lead? Have you, Jewish merchant, considered what kind of situation you are in? At a moment when everything around us is organizing, and things have gone so far that at a gathering of non-Jewish merchants in Upper Silesia it was resolved to demand of the government that Jews be forbidden altogether to trade on Upper Silesian soil.
At a time of pickets being set up at Jewish shops, at a time of draft guild[?] laws, at that very same time such apathy has taken hold of the Jewish force[?], which does not even find it necessary to reflect on the extraordinary situation in which the merchant finds himself.
The merchant must take his own fate into his hands, he must break with the passivity that has prevailed until now; once and for all a strong, economically cemented organization must be created. This is the commandment of the hour: that the Jewish merchant be organized. Therefore every merchant and trader who has purchased a patent [trading licence] must be enrolled as a member, so that in this way, with united forces, a strong organization may be created.
In connection with this, the board of the Small Traders' Association has undertaken reorganization work by convening the representatives of the trade sections, so that all the leading members[?] should conduct a broad propaganda campaign among the members of their own trades, that they should enrol in the association en masse. We must be able, with united forces, to repel all the actions being waged[?] against us.
— To unite in a time of trouble — that is the commandment of the hour.
A. D. K-r, Sosnowiec.
The Deed Will Prove It

[Będzin — Zionism; Keren Hayesod.]
(On the "Keren Hayesod" campaign in Będzin.)
L. Herman.
Since [?] the beginning of our real Zionist work in Eretz Israel, after the Balfour Declaration, the Jewish people as a whole has not received any other opportunity for such great, productive [?] work as that through the Keren Hayesod.
True, one can still point [?] to the halutziut [pioneering] of our youth. It is they, after all, who actually created the fact. Their sacrifice is indeed the true sacrifice, and none greater than it exists. Halutziut means — blood and sweat, want [?] and pain, and personal sacrifice beyond measure; it stands above all symbols, it itself creates values, it personifies an idea that has been transformed into deed, and it, only it, halutziut, is Zionism in its purest form. But halutziut is, after all, a phenomenon of a special kind, which would be diminished in its stature if we were to clothe with its title every manifestation of ordinary egoism [?]; not everyone who ventures and stakes his life is a halutz. Here the motive and the thought are also important, because they often determine the character of halutziut. It happens [?], therefore, that those who have and who [ventured?] daring [?] instruments, who place their chief [?] new hope in the proven forces of economic egoism [?] and even create new paths for economic development, thereby placing themselves at the head of new economic achievements — do they not, after all, push forward [?] the development of the new social life-assets. And the realisation of Zionism in Jewish national [?] life. But since the true spirit of halutziut — which guards [?] it from whatever dangers — is not a matter of everyday life and is only a gift of the few, although it is a difficult educational task for the people — since this is so, we must take pains [to make clear] that halutziut is indeed an exalted goal, but not the foundation on which we shall rouse [?] the broad strata of the people and bring them to the deed. The sacrificial path of halutziut — since halutziut in reality is not only a matter of heroism but also a heavy sacrifice — is not the path on which the best of our people can go. The path of halutziut, as a model path, is apt to inspire and to uplift, but the path for the masses, for a new possible realisation, is a different one, and the sacrifice here is also a lighter one — and that is the Keren Hayesod.
Why precisely the Keren Hayesod?
Because the Keren Hayesod alone carries [?] within itself the right expression of the idea, the essence of sacrifice. A fine idea was realised by the second Zionist Conference in London in the year 1920 by creating the Keren Hayesod. From then on every Zionist Congress has underlined the duty of the Jewish people towards the Keren Hayesod.
It became clear that only the Keren Hayesod alone brought to expression and realisation the sacrifice and the will to act of tens and hundreds of thousands of Jews. The Keren Kayemet is endowed [?] with popular character and warmth; the Keren Hayesod, for its part, creates the form and realises the state and civic idea of the Jew who wants, by intention and by action, to contribute his share to the building of the land.
Precisely with regard to the Keren Hayesod the Jewish people has not proved that it is a politically experienced people, and today it is already clear to everyone that had we collected for the Keren Hayesod since 1920 not five and a half million pounds but twenty-five million, as we had originally calculated, we would have been much, much stronger in Eretz Israel as in the Diaspora. And would not strength have removed from us the worry that we carry within us regarding the near future?
True, we have neglected much, we have not made use of many opportunities, and they will never again return to the Jewish people. But there are still things that we shall be able to achieve.
The Keren Hayesod is now conducting its campaign in view of the political attacks by the Arabs on our work of construction and on our idea [?]. Which Jew, then, will not feel the great duty that lies upon him, the duty of giving a proper answer to all kinds of attacks and assaults. This year's campaign of the Keren Hayesod, which will surely be crowned with success, means more than a fund-raising drive. The campaign will serve as testimony [?] and proof that in the day of the gravest political danger, precisely this non-political people is ripe to commit the most correct political deed.
Let's Swap... (Monologue of a Sosnowiec Jew)

[Sosnowiec — satirical feuilleton; monologue.] (Monologue of a Sosnowiec Jew)
"There is no misfortune from which some good does not come" — so says an old Polish proverb [Nie ma tego złego, co by na dobre nie wyszło].
What am I saying this about? About the campaign "to transfer the peasants from the village into the town".
Reading this in the newspaper gave me a stab[?] in the heart: what[?], what does this verse mean? At first it would not go into my head, but on reflection my opinion changed for the better.
What does it mean — they will move the peasants from the village into the town and leave the villages abandoned? Who will plough? Who will sow? But don't fret[?] — there will be an exchange: the peasants will come into the town and the Jews — into the village. The peasant will become a "kupiec" [merchant] and I — a peasant!..
"Chanele," I said to my little wife, "get ready!"
"Get ready for what?" my missus asked. "Are we about to go on a journey[?]?"
"No, not that, my wife[?]; I mean you should get ready for a new life — we are setting out on a new life."
"What do you mean, a new life? What, do you think[?] it's the day after our wedding? What, we are setting out on a new life?.."
"Yes, Chanele, we are setting out on a new life: I become a peasant and you a peasant woman. The peasants are coming into the town and we are going into the village."
"You'll see, Chana-dear[?], my crown, what a bright[?] life we shall have: in the village I will plough and you will milk the cows — I will sow and you will reap..."
"Just imagine, Chanele, what a paradise we shall have: you will no longer need any 'liesgiskes'[?], you won't need pyjamas, no slips[?], no dancing, no theatre, no concerts, no poker[?]; you'll go to sleep together with the hens; you won't eat any cream[?] chocolates[?], only potatoes with borscht, 'ripiski'[?] groats[?], and you won't have any [—] on your nail[?], you won't know about high blood pressure; you'll be a peasant woman and you'll be healthy as a [?]!
I, too, will have a bright[?] life: I won't stand in mortal fear at the market stall [stragan], my feet won't swell. Standing[?] by my little '...'[?] shop, I won't be afraid of the sekwestrator [tax-distraint bailiff] any more; on the contrary, I'll harness the little horse and drive out with the little barrel of 'olive oil'[?] into the field. We'll have a 'shpepekhi'[?] — it will be all[?] blessing.
You'll see, Chanele, I'll wear cloth trousers, you a linen dress and a pair of 'trepy' [clogs]; you won't twist your feet in the 'kalisheveklekh'[?] with their hollowed[?] high heels like stilts; you won't wear silk stockings with 'strzałki'[?] [decorative clocks]; your body won't be squeezed and laced in; you won't need a shapely waist [zgrabna talia], and 'the line' [slim figure] you'll need like a hole in the head [lit. 'for kapores']; the hens will lay eggs, the cow will calve. We won't know of any bills of exchange, of any protests, of any 'obrotowe'[?] [turnover tax], 'dochodowe'[?] [income tax], 'lokalowe' [premises tax], of any appeals, of summonses[?] and reminders[?] — it will be 'for the Jews [there was light and gladness]'!..
And who knows, when the eve of the dacha season[?] comes, we'll whitewash the huts [chatki], we'll clean out the horse stable in order to let in[?] the summer guests [letnicy]; and who, do you think, will come to rent summer lodgings [letniska]? Precisely they, the former peasants who have become 'kuptsim' [merchants]; they will come to us to rent 'letnie mieszkania' [summer flats], and we will be living it up[?] in grand style.
'Co kosztuje to dworani[?]' ['How much does this ... cost?'] the summer lady will ask.
'[?] sto złotych z góry pła[—]' ['... hundred złoty, payable in advance'[?]] I will answer.
Later she will start [—] her nose: 'Fu[?], drogo' ['Ugh, expensive!'] — and I will lead her into the cowshed.
'Tu pani ma za dwieście złotych' ['Here, madam, you have it for two hundred złoty']...
The summer lady began to plead:
'Panie gospodarzu, nie mogę[?]' ['Mister farmer, I can't']; I live on Pańska[?] Street in a cramped little room, the children are suffocating from the [?], the doctor says they must have 'świeżość'[?] [fresh air]; and from the market stall there's no luck either — so will argue the former peasant woman and present 'kupcowa' [merchant's wife]; and I, a real[?] peasant, will stick to my opinion:
'Tak kosztuje!' ['That's the price!']..
"Only later, when the summer guests are living with us in the village, will we skin them alive: instead of milk she'll give 'bawerke'[?] [whey?]; for a little parsley, a carrot, one will charge a bit more; the summer ladies won't mind paying — the bit of 'świeżość'[?] [fresh air] will repay them[?] in [rosy] cheeks. One more[?] summer and we'll buy another head of cattle, another horse; the peasant will be a 'kupiec' and I — a peasant!..
"Chanele, don't worry, from every misfortune comes some good, and the transfer of the peasant into the town will also be a boon for me: I stop being a townsman — I'm going into the village!.."
My wife heard me out gravely[?] and in the end said:
"Yankele, you're right! When you were a merchant I was a merchant's wife, and when you are a peasant I'll be a peasant woman; when you take up the plough, I will milk the cows."
Having obtained my Chanele's consent, I went straight out into the village, to a peasant I know, where I have been staying for several summers on holiday, to negotiate with him:
"Panie Walenty [Mr Walenty], I have come to you with a proposition."
"Co [?]" ['What is it?'[?]] the peasant asked.
Then I laid out my plan before him: that I want to swap with him; I hand over to him my market stall, which is a 'złoty interes' [a golden business]; I cede to him the whole 'blessing'[?]: payment orders [nakazy], bills of exchange, protests, licences[?] [patents], reminders[?] and other '[—]-owe' papers; in return he hands over to me his farm [gospodarstwo]: he becomes a 'kupiec' in the town and I — a peasant in the village.
The peasant looked me over from head to foot and said:
'Panie, czy pan zwariował?[?] [—] jedź pan z Bogiem [—] basta[?]!' ['Sir, have you gone mad? ... go with God ... enough!']
I began to argue with him:
"Panie Walenty, przecież[?] tak piszą w gazetach" ['but that's what they write in the newspapers']...
'Niech piszą do jutra' ['Let them write till tomorrow'], the peasant answered, 'jak mówię, że chłop nigdy nie będzie kupcem, a kupiec nigdy nie będzie chłopem' ['as I say: a peasant will never be a merchant, and a merchant will never be a peasant']...
As you see, gentlemen, nothing came of the deal. I wanted to swap with the peasant, but he, with his peasant common sense, holds that a peasant cannot be a merchant and a merchant cannot be a peasant.
But I want to swap!
The Living Dead Man

A. Zaglembier
(A most thrilling novel of Jewish life in Zagłębie before and after the World War).

Summary of the beginning of the novel.
One summer evening [?] before the World War, when two Cossacks were about to transfer the dangerous bandit "Smulek Łamka" to the Piotrków [?] prison, they were suddenly attacked on the way to the Będzin station by two disguised "strazhniks" [rural policemen] — Łamka's comrades [?]. The Cossacks were later [?] found lying tied up, with their mouths gagged. Smulek "Łamka", set free [?], fled towards the [—] road [?] and hid somewhere.
That same evening [?], and almost at the very same hour, the widely known, respectable collector [?] (inkasent) Yosl Wertheim — a father of three children — suddenly disappeared. His wife Frumet runs about the town in terrible despair, searching [?] for him in every possible hiding place in all of Zagłębie, but Yosl Wertheim has vanished like a stone in water...

Now read on.
That was the first, most terrible, sleepless night Frumet had ever spent in her life.
And when Yosl did not come home the next morning either, Frumet in despair ran to report it to the police, whose strazhniks immediately set out across the town and all the surrounding villages. Inquiries were also made in the neighbouring towns and throughout the country whether the missing Yosl Wertheim might not be found somewhere. But from everywhere came one answer:
"In our town nothing is known of such a man."
Yosl Wertheim had vanished without a trace.
No one could understand what had happened here.
And Frumet's grief and despair helped [?] nothing at all. Within a single day she aged ten years...
Where indeed could her handsome, dear and faithful Yosl have gone [?], who had left home early in the morning hale and hearty and suddenly vanished like a stone in water?..

2. Who is the drowned murder victim?..
And Frumet grew even more desperate when the following day too passed with nothing.
All the efforts and searches had so far brought no result whatsoever.
Just as if into the water.
At the same time the police searched with even more energy and diligence for the vanished gentile [?] Smulek Łamka as well, and for the two "strazhniks" who had rescued "Łamka" from the two Cossacks.
Unable to catch any of the three, the police carried out a general round-up (obława) of all the thieves and underworld people in Zagłębie. Anyone on whom the slightest suspicion fell was promptly arrested. Among those arrested were also the two "strazhniks". In their present appearance, however, they were not recognised by the two Cossacks, who lay in hospital with bandaged heads.
And how could the Cossacks have recognised them, when on that night the two persons [?] had been dressed like genuine strazhniks with stuck-on moustaches, and besides, the night had been a dark one, and before they had even managed to look at their faces they had already been struck over the head with irons..
So all the suspects, after being held under arrest for several days, had to be released for lack of evidence.
But that still did not clear up the second [?] mysterious disappearance, that of Smulek Łamka, which happened on the same day on which Yosl Wertheim also disappeared...
In this case too, wanted notices (Steckbriefe) with photographs and descriptions of Smulek Łamka were sent out throughout the whole country, and abroad as well.
But Smulek's sudden disappearance was no smaller a riddle for his own comrades too, and especially for the two "strazhniks" — his chief helpers — with whom he had, after all, arranged to meet first thing the next morning at an agreed place...
And indeed they all [?] came to that place in the morning. But Łamka was not there. They set about searching for him in the surrounding forests, in every possible hiding place and thieves' "melinas" [dens]. But just like Yosl Wertheim, Smulek Łamka too had vanished like a stone in water. And Łamka mattered more than anyone to his own gang-mates. He was their "elder" — the ruler! Without Łamka all the other thieves felt nervous [?], small, lost and helpless too. For Łamka was bold; he could work out a plan for a big piece of "work" that would pay off for everyone. The two "strazhniks" were afraid that a split [?] might now begin within their own camp... Everyone would want to become elder in Łamka's place. Some might even start to "slikhe" [?] [unclear slang word] and to "shoot" [?].
That is why the thieves themselves also eagerly helped the police search for Łamka...
All the efforts and strenuous investigations, however, ended up hitting a blank wall, with no way out [?]..
And the whole strange [—] story would have remained from the very start completely dark and hidden, had it not been for one man who took the matter in hand with all his abilities and energy.
That was police inspector Chorecki [?].
This mysterious story, especially the disappearance of Yosl Wertheim, gave him no rest. During the initial tumult and noise, however, police inspector Chorecki always had the habit of standing a little at a distance.
— "Let [?] it cool down," he thought to himself, "and then they will let him work quietly on his own."
Chorecki considered himself a great specialist in this field. Almost [—] his nights [?] he [—] and did not sleep [?]. In his free time he was constantly studying criminology and read countless detective novels, from which he remembered very [?] well all the clever ruses and tricks that he would later use with success in his practice... He indeed regretted [?] that he was not being transferred at least to a gubernia (provincial capital) town — there he would really show what he could do..
In the present mysterious case too, police inspector Chorecki went his own way.
Only when all the police officials had already thrown up their hands and stood helpless, saying:
— It is a premeditated [?] job.
— Everything that could possibly be done has been done.
— This belongs to the kind of cases [?] that are seldom ever cleared up..
— only then did Chorecki set to work according to his own system. Weighing every step carefully beforehand, he [—] in order to get at the truth.
He too, the police inspector, on the first day looked for a close connection between the two missing men..
Soon, however, he discarded [?] the idea as false, one that could only hamper the investigation and lead it altogether down a wrong path..
Both cases — inspector Chorecki said [?] — may indeed have happened on one day and even in one hour, but that still does not mean that the two cases must be linked with each other.
And he made this clear to himself in the following way:
The dangerous thief and bandit Smulek Łamka, who had been rescued from the Cossacks, certainly had sufficient reason to hide in such a way that he could not be found so quickly. He knows, after all, what awaits him for such a thing — at the least, life imprisonment — and wishing to avoid the punishment, he took care [?], that very night after his escape, to slip across the border into Germany...
But where and why did Yosl Wertheim disappear?

After the „Seders“.

After the „Seders“.
(Impressions and expressions).
So here we are, then, already after the „seders“...
The order of the world [seder ha-olam] is admittedly still not in full order, but it doesn't matter; we have already grown so used to disorders that it now seems[?] to us that everything is in the very best order.
The „Four Sons“ look like the members of the League of Nations.
The Wise Son is, of course, the one who has armed himself „in secret“ with bullets and other bomb-capacities[?], because[?] now he plays and preaches all the time about world justice, about peace and suchlike fine things...
The Wicked Son long ago changed his name to „Righteous“[?]; what's more, he has submitted to the master of the Haggadah, to the creator of [—] the „League of Nations“, a protest against the name „wicked“, with which he was insulted[?].
The Simple Son doesn't do badly at all: when there is talk of disarmament, he is right there in the middle; when there is talk of rearmament, he too dances in the ring; in short — it isn't bad to be a simpleton...
But the best of all is done by the One Who Does Not Know How to Ask.
Ostensibly he couldn't bend[?] a cat's tail, but when you take a good look at him, you see that he is stuffed with all of today's political tricks.
And so piously stand[?] the Four Sons of „the Haggadah of...“ already for the [—] seder.
Sala.

The Będzin Shochtim [ritual slaughterers].
The restoration of the Sosnowiec kehilla's finances. The first meeting. — Departmental committees elected. — Pensions of the kehilla officials reduced. — The slaughter levy raised.

On Monday evening the new board of the kehilla in Sosnowiec held its first meeting. On the agenda were a number of economic questions, among them — incidentally the most important — restoring the kehilla's finances on the basis of the new budget, which the present kehilla board and council must determine.
The meeting — [—] [—] — was conducted with dignity; every budget item, especially of income and expenditure, was thoroughly[?] discussed, not for the sake of demonstration or out of "political" intentions, but with the good will to set[?] the kehilla's budget[?] on a realistic, sound basis.
Before proceeding to the agenda, honour was paid to the just-deceased "dozer"[?] R' Moshe Mordechai Wajnsztok[?] of blessed memory, to the leaders Sokolow and Dr. Kohn[?], and also to the holy martyrs who fell in the Land of Israel through the Arab terror[?].
Then the chairman, Mr. Lejnerowicz[?], read a declaration in which he set out his credo; after that he gave the report on the kehilla's situation since the takeover and until[?] now. It turns out that in this short time they managed somewhat to improve the kehilla's situation; for instance, this year's kimcha [de-Pischa, Passover flour] campaign was much larger than in the past, the officials received their salaries ("pensions") paid out for the holiday, etc.
A lively discussion took place around the new draft budget. The discussion was conducted in the direction of maintaining the balance of the budget, both on the income side and on the expenditure side, since the budget inherited from the commissarial board is completely unrealistic.
As a result of the discussion it was resolved to reduce the salaries ("pensions") of all kehilla officials, among them the shochtim (ritual slaughterers), to cut the retirement pensions considerably, and in general to restrict the kehilla's expenditure.
Because of the small income from ritual slaughter it was resolved to raise the slaughter levy by 100 per cent. The increase takes effect already from today.
Then the following committees were elected: Budget committee — D. Lewartowski and S. Warman.
Rabbinate committee — S. Wilczyk and J. Steinfeld.
Synagogue committee — Reuben Czapnik, Fajerman and Lewartowski.
Slaughter committee — Steinfeld, Wilczyk and Fajerman.
Cemetery committee — Warman, Czapnik and Lewartowski.
Public supervision committee — Steinfeld, Wilczyk, Szalom Pilc, Warman, Kajzer and Langer.
Audit committee — Czapnik, Wilczyk, Lewartowski and Warman.
At 11 o'clock the meeting is closed.
He bought the kettle with the... takings.

In the Będzin market halls ("hales") the following incident happened on the eve of the holiday: a Jewish woman dealer in kitchenware put her takings into a kettle. A crafty "customer" noticed this, bought the kettle without haggling and went off. Only later did the dealer realise that in the kettle she had sold there was also the whole of the holiday-eve takings...
For violating the foreign-currency ban.

Several months ago Mr. J. Winer (Będzin) travelled abroad to a wedding. During the inspection at the Polish-Czechoslovak border, three bills of exchange of two hundred zł. each, from Kina[?] "Ganaszczy"[?], were found in Mr. Winer's briefcase.
Mr. Winer's defence, that he had left the bills on his person through an oversight, was not [—] [—], and he was arrested. A few days later he was released, but a case was already drawn up against him, which took place in the Cieszyn court; the court sentenced Winer to 14 months' arrest and a fine of 600 zł. The sentence of arrest was suspended for two years.
The prosecutor appealed against the verdict, and the case was heard on Tuesday in the Katowice court of appeal, which confirmed the verdict of the first instance.
Will Jewish Sosnowiec allow the outpatient clinic of the 'Linas ha-Cholim' to be closed?

The question of renting a suitable premises for the outpatient clinic of the [?] "Linas ha-Cholim" in Sosnowiec has already been touched upon many times in the columns of our newspaper. But from the explanation we received from the board of the institution it turns out that the board has been trying for quite a long time to rent suitable premises; it is even ready to pay more than an ordinary tenant, but the Jewish house-owners have for some reason become "afraid" to let premises to the "Linas ha-Cholim".
Now the premises question has become much more serious, since the supervisory authority no longer permits the clinic to be located in its[?] present premises; the board has already received such an official notice from the voivodeship.
Therefore the question arises: will the Jewish public of Sosnowiec go on being so indifferent to the housing question and allow such an important institution to be closed?
The worshippers of the Old-Sosnowiec synagogue saw before them the first plague...

The synagogue in Old Sosnowiec, which is "famous" for its frequent brawls, has again been "enriched" with a brand-new "sensation", which took place during the past holiday and unfortunately caused a great desecration of God's name (chillul ha-Shem).
On Sabbath, the first day of the holiday, the gabbai Mr. Gershon Pikiewicz[?] was attacked[?] by several worshippers, who beat him murderously.
When the "dozer"[?] Mr. Reuben Czapnik learned of the shameful attack, he came into the synagogue and with great bitterness condemned the lawless deed. Mr. Czapnik declared on this occasion that if such outrageous acts are repeated, the guilty will be brought to court.
He fulfilled the commandment of eating bitter herbs...

The neighbours at Magduszew[?] Street 39 in Sosnowiec were startled on the first night of Passover by the cries carried from the flat of a local Hasidic tenant, whom the "bit of maror" (bitter herb) had choked. Thanks to quick rescue he was saved.
A young Jewish man stabbed.

Leybl Gastfraynt[?] was walking with his father on Sunday[?] along Lenishner[?] Street in Sosnowiec. They were met by several hooligans, who began to stab them. At a certain moment G. struck one of them with a bottle and ran away. The hooligans chased him as far as the gate of the house where G. lives; there they caught him and wounded him with a knife in the side and in the head. G. was taken[?] to the Jewish hospital.
A 6-year-old girl from Będzin burned to death in Stopnica.

Last winter the father of Mr. Chaim Yosef Wagner's[?] wife came from Stopnica to visit him in Będzin (Jasna Street). The grandfather[?], being acquainted with his son-in-law's material situation, took with him 2 little children, a girl of 6 and a boy of 4.
Once the grandmother went out of the house, leaving both children. At a certain moment the girl went up to a burning stove. Her clothing at once began to burn, and in the blink of an eye the child was engulfed in the flames. The little boy, seeing the terrible sight before him, ran out of the house and alarmed the neighbours. Unfortunately all means of rescue were already too late, and a few hours later the child died.

"Soul-snatchers" spread missionary pamphlets.
On the outskirts of the town of Będzin two ladies "patrolled" during the holidays, selling missionary pamphlets among the unaware Jewish masses.

The central office of the Small Traders' Union calls for founding free-loan funds.
The branches of the small traders' associations in Sosnowiec and in Będzin have been called upon by the central office in Warsaw to found separate gmilut-chesed (free-loan) funds for their members.
Nearly 500 poor children are fed by "TOZ".

On Monday morning, on the initiative of the "TOZ" society [Society for the Protection of Health of the Jews], a joint lecture was held on the tasks of the "TOZ" society. The hall of the Będzin "Orphans' Home", where the lecture took place, was overcrowded with listeners, drawn from the best strata of the Jewish population.
The first speaker, Dr. Weinzieher, dealt comprehensively with the causes of illness among the well-to-do and the poor population, and dwelt particularly on the situation of the poor neighbourhoods[?], where, together with hunger[?], need and poverty, the number of sick grows in general, and of tuberculosis in particular.
The esteemed speaker also dwelt on the psychological influence on the sick, which often works better than the prescribed remedies. It is also very important for a sick person to have confidence that he will recover. Our miserable[?] existence as a nation — says Dr. Weinzieher — is after all only thanks to the belief that we shall not perish.
On the merits and tasks of "TOZ" Dr. Liberman lectured. He gave a historical survey of the origin of "TOZ", its excellent programme and above all — what the work of "TOZ" looks like in general and of the Zagłębie branch in particular. It turns out that in Zagłębie about 500 children of the Talmud Torahs, the Mizrachi and Agudah cheders are fed by "TOZ". The children also receive medical help, such as quartz lamps etc.
The speaker therefore appealed to Jewish society to enrol as members and to help the "TOZ" society, so that it should have the material means to work for the protection of the health of the Jewish child.
Both lectures were rewarded[?] with warm applause.
It is desirable that such popular lectures should take place as often as possible.
Campaign for the Redemption of the Land during Passover.

As everywhere, in Sosnowiec too a vigorous campaign for the KKL [Jewish National Fund] was again[?] carried out during the Passover days. In the town synagogue the chairman[?] Dr. Melaristo[?] delivered a brilliant speech before the Torah reading, and those who received aliyot pledged larger sums for the KKL.
On Dr. Weinzieher's 40-year jubilee.

As we have already written, a committee has been formed in Będzin which is organizing the celebration in honour of the 40-year jubilee of Dr. Weinzieher's public activity. The committee is working very intensively so that the celebration should turn out impressive. As reported, a number of public activists and Jewish personalities from within and outside Zagłębie are being invited.
In the next number of our paper a special section will be devoted to the celebration in honour of the esteemed Dr. Weinzieher.
Enrol your children in the public schools.

From next Monday the children born in the year 1930 will be enrolled in the public schools.
Enrolments will also be accepted of children who for certain reasons have not been enrolled until now.
Passover food campaign at Public School No. 2.

The management of Public School No. 2 in Będzin carried out this year on the eve of Passover a large food campaign for the poorest children of the school. 125 kilos of matzot and 1200 eggs were distributed. 120 children benefited from it.
Conference on the working hours of commercial employees.

This week, in connection with the demands of the commercial employees, a conference between both sides took place in Będzin. After a lengthy discussion the delegates of the employees proposed that in the wholesale businesses the working time be extended by 2 hours relative to the official working time, but the wholesalers do not want to agree to this concession.

Festive Seders for the Jewish Soldiers of the Kielce Garrison

[Page banner:] Life in Kielce — Thursday, 20 Nisan 5697 — piątek[?] 1 kwietnia 1937 [Friday(?), 1 April 1937]
As already reported in our paper, the kehilla set up a Passover kitchen in the premises of „Maccabi“ for the Jewish soldiers of the Kielce garrison.
The first seder, in which close to 180 soldiers took part, went off very festively. The seder was opened[?] with a Polish speech [by] Meniga[?] Diuta[?] Pras[?], Grinbard[?], and the Kielce rabbi, Rabbi Rapaport, who conducted the seder.
Kiddush was made by Cantor Garnicki with the choir, which afterwards sang the Polish and the Jewish anthems.
Besides the numerous public, the first seder was also attended by representatives of the local administrative and military authorities, who expressed their appreciation to the Jewish community in Kielce, with the kehilla at its head, for its kind concern for the Jewish soldiers, which is also a sign of devotion to the Polish army in general.
The representative of the starosta and Capt. Brożek[?] made short speeches of greeting, thanked the chairmen Piotrkowski[?] and Goldman for their painstaking work for the Passover kitchen, and wished the Jewish community and the army a happy holiday.
The second seder was conducted by Rabbi[?] Herzberg; kiddush was made by R' Mordechai Chazan.
The soldiers feel very well in the kitchen and spend their free hours quite comfortably and cheerfully.
Both seder nights passed festively and left an exceptionally good impression on all present.
Festive Proclamation of the Keren Hayesod Campaign

This Monday night, at a festive tea evening in the Zionist club, this year's Keren Hayesod campaign in Kielce was proclaimed.
The campaign was proclaimed by the president of the Zionist Organization in Poland, Adv.[?] A. Hartglas, who, in the presence of a numerous public of the cream of Jewish Kielce, gave a very interesting lecture on the situation of the Jewish people at the present moment, calling on the Jews of Kielce to give a worthy answer to the latest events in Eretz Israel by strengthening the Zionist funds, and first and foremost the Keren Hayesod.
On the manner of the organizational work there then spoke Messrs.: Y. M. Geisman[?], Mrs.[?] Kizer[?], A. Grinfeld[?], Izush[?], Cukerman, and the honorary president of the Zionist Org., A. Ehrlich, who led the evening, and instructor Bram[?], the delegate of the Keren Hayesod directorate, who is conducting the campaign.
As we are informed, the most prominent and active communal workers of the Zionist groupings have joined the Keren Hayesod work, as well as other well-known Zionist sympathizers, with Director[?] Pozner[?] at their head.
The first two days of the campaign, i.e. Tuesday and Wednesday, gave brilliant results. A considerable[?] number[?] of pledges for appropriate sums has already been collected. The collectors are received everywhere with a friendly welcome.
We are certain that this year's Keren Hayesod campaign will be concluded with extraordinary success.

In Rybnik a founding meeting was held to open a branch of the cooperative named "Kredyt Kopiecki". The purpose of the branch is to be able [?] to compete with the local Jewish merchants.

On Saturday the local Jewish youth of Mysłowice held an entertainment evening. Two workers from the [?] "Karnga" [?] also came to the evening and began making communist speeches, for which they were arrested by the representative of the authorities who was present [?].

On Saturday afternoon a drunk was walking along Piłsudski Street in Katowice; at a certain moment he shouted "pierońskie Żydzi" [?] [Silesian curse: "damned Jews"] and smashed a window pane in a Jewish shop. The police detained the hooligan and put him in police custody.

This week the national Jewry and the Zionist Organization in Katowice celebrated the jubilee of 30 years of Zionist work of Mr. Alfred Miller.

Advice from an antisemitic newspaper.
The Katowice "Polonia" is very much afraid that mistakes may occur — that a Christian customer might, God forbid, still stray [?] into a Jewish shop, not knowing that it does not belong to a Christian.
