Strong activity is now demanded of the Jewish merchant.

Some remarks and suggestions.

In recent years the trade problem has become the main topic of public life.
Regardless of the tendencies that brought the question to the top [?] of the public discussion, the general interest [?] in the problem has created a special attitude toward trade and has produced conditions very characteristic of the present time.
In the given case the reasons for the factors that raised the question are not important, nor is it important whether the trade problem should actually become the main topic of the general economy; what is important, however, are the consequences [?]: the constant deliberations, the cries of alarm [?] and the atmosphere created around the matter were bound to find a resounding echo in the mind of every citizen, even of one who takes no interest at all in socio-economic questions.
The trade problem has thus been transformed from an economic question into a question of a psychological character. It is this transformation that interests us most at the present moment.
Until now trade was a stepchild; nobody took an interest either in its virtues or in its shadow sides. But from the moment trade became the favourite youngest child [?], everyone's eyes turned to it, and nobody let even its smallest flaw pass.
In this change in society's attitude lies the crux of the problem. The merchant who makes light of the newly created conditions will find himself eye to eye with the danger of ruin. There is no way back; there exists [?] only a way forward, to the new forms that life has called forth. This enormous general truth concerns first and foremost the Jewish merchant and shopkeeper.
What tasks, then, face us at the present moment? In my opinion a psychological driving force is now acting on the development of trade. All phenomena that carry a suggestive power easily reach the broad masses. This does not mean, however, that one should give up the content and diminish [?] the importance of the economic base on which trade is built. The psychological element shows that the broad strata of society can be won over only when the content is wrapped in a proper form.
The form of trade depends on inner [?] factors: artistic, aesthetic, civilizational and cultural. Until now little attention was paid to the importance of the problem of form. An understanding of this matter and the drive [?] to adapt to the newest achievements in this field can bring an upswing to Jewish commercial life and preserve many shaky economic positions.
Certain efforts to make use of the achievements of civilization in the field of trade can already be noticed today. This beginning must, however, be organized through appropriate propaganda, which should point out the necessity for the merchant and shopkeeper to take care of general and commercial education.
Trade is reproached that the choice of this occupation does not stem [?] from appropriate preparation and training, but from the belief in innate abilities and that work in trade is based mainly on improvisation and dilettantism, if not on chance.
The question of preparation for the commercial profession sets Jewish society two separate tasks: to train the youth, and to secure supplementary education for adult, independent merchants and shopkeepers.
The first task is less complicated than the second: the youth will adapt relatively quickly to present-day conditions. It is different, however, with the adult element. It will not be easy to convince them of the necessity of adopting the new forms; one will [?] encounter a number of obstacles, such as conservatism and above all the bad living conditions.
Clearly, little can be achieved by means of lectures [?]; the matter requires a long-lasting [?] effort and a great deal of tact.
Under normal conditions cultural needs develop after material needs have been satisfied. It is therefore no easy thing to develop among impoverished merchants the need to modernize their system of work.
The difficulties, however, must not deter us. At the beginning we will set ourselves very modest tasks. An important step forward would be the creation of clubs attached to the professional trade organizations, whose task would be to develop in the merchant a sense for public questions and for social life; they should [?] take an interest in questions they do not think about during the long "working day". Besides this, a network of supplementary courses should be set up at the organizations, and lectures, competitions etc. should be organized, to spread the most necessary education among the commercial element. The cultural institutions built up in this way can in time become an educational centre for the broad masses of retailers and small traders.
With good will, strenuous work and appropriate material support, significant positive results can be achieved in this field.
Y. G.
Literary-Musical „Wednesdays“.

[Będzin — culture; Yiddish literature.] The Będzin Jewish Club for Knowledge of the Country (ŻTK — Żydowskie Towarzystwo Krajoznawcze) holds[?] a literary evening every Wednesday, in the form of lectures on topical Jewish and general problems, as well as recitations from Yiddish literature.
The evenings are of a high standard and are gladly attended by the Jewish public, which longs for a better lecture and especially — for a literary-artistic recitation, something that has lately become one of the rarities in Zagłębie, because the proper circles that ought to concern themselves with it are lacking (our political parties of all kinds do not occupy themselves with such „idle“ things), and so it is no wonder that Yiddish literature and its creators are simply forgotten in Zagłębie. Here is an example: last Passover it was already 22 years since I. L. Peretz’s death — did any organisation in Będzin hold a public I. L. Peretz academy (memorial assembly)? And it is not so long ago that a number of parties were fighting over Peretz, claiming that he was entirely theirs!..
And do you know where people did take the trouble over a [—] word of I. L. Peretz? — In the Jewish Club for Knowledge of the Country!.. Although the evening was not dedicated specifically to Peretz’s yortsayt, it happened by chance that Peretz’s works took up the most important part. In the first[?] part the reciter Mr. N. Blum recited „Bontshe“ [Bontshe the Silent] and „In a Summer Residence“[?] very precisely and with pathos. It turned out that the other works by other Yiddish writers, set beside them, were as if put in the shade... And works were read by such writers as: Kulbak, Halpern, Moyshe Nadir and others. And yet the pure[?] Peretz appeared in all his gigantic stature!..
And although I. L. Peretz did not write in an easy style, his works were understandable to the listeners, thanks to the diction and mimicry of the reciter, which were the best interpretation and execution.
As one could observe, Nathan Blum is suited to more serious works, where he displays great abilities; on the other hand the l i g h t e r, so-called humorous-satirical works by Moyshe Nadir and others come out much weaker with him...
According to the head of the club’s culture committee, they are in negotiations with well-known personalities of the literary-scholarly world about reading their works in Będzin — and for that alone they deserve a true yasher-koach.
Elchanan Zider.

A Well-Deserved Jubilee...

[Będzin — satire on the kehilla leadership.] Quasi a report, by Sh. Libaszon.
Last Saturday night a jubilee was held in the great hall of the "Orphans' Home", in connection with the 80-year public activity of the kehilla president.
In honour of this rare jubilee a very large public gathered — the public that groups itself around the national camp of the town, and also from the surrounding places.
The tables were served with only [?] fruit and kümmel wines [?] (as is reported, this was the wish of the jubilarian).
High up — above the presidium table — hangs a large white ribbon with the following inscription:
"Thus shall be done to the man — this is how one treats a person who engages faithfully in communal needs and does not want to go in the ways of the Aguda."
Guests come, guests go; suddenly there is a stir in the hall, all eyes are fixed on the entrance. Through it the jubilarian enters, the choir of "HaNoar HaTzioni" sings "Od lo avda" and the official part of the celebration begins.
The vice-president of the kehilla, Av'hamel, is invited as toastmaster; he pronounces a "Shehecheyanu" and says that "today is the most beautiful day of his life."
After the public has enjoyed the soulful items [?], the greetings begin. The first to greet is the president of the Zionist Organization, Mr. Hinodoki [?], who points out the great benefit the jubilarian has brought the kehilla and says that the greatest in-law at today's celebration is the Zionist Organization, which is the first and only organization that discovered the pillar of fire, the meteor, that brings light into Jewish life and does not allow the darkness of the "Aguda" to rule..
The president of the council, Mr. Landner, relates some interesting details [?] of the struggle that the jubilarian waged in the gmina [kehilla] against the Aguda camp. "I could [?] — he says — go on telling a whole night how the president waged a stubborn struggle when the Aguda camp wanted, by various illegal means, to obtain the majority on the kehilla council.
We have before us — says Mr. Landner — a man of iron will; he fought like a lion so that the 'dollar slaughterers' would not be taken on as kehilla officials; in general, he carries out whatever he wants. When the 'Aguda' insisted [?] that Leibl Goldstein should enter the board, the president banged on the table and said:
— It shall not be! In my term of office comrade Goldstein will go on being a parnas, not a member of the dozór [kehilla board].."
After a series of representatives of the Zionist groupings enumerate the virtues and good qualities of the jubilarian, the "chatan dagan" himself takes the floor. The hall falls silent; with great respect they listen to what "he" says. First of all he shows that he flees from honour, because honour he has enough of among the gentiles, where every word he lets out of his mouth is snapped up like a roast.
— "Zasadniczo [in principle] I am against having a jubilee arranged for me, and several times I asked my colleague Avrahamle to drop it, because it is ogólnie [?] [in general] a bad time; unfortunately I did not manage to persuade my comrades from the Zionist camp, who arranged such an uroczystość [celebration] in my honour..."
Then the jubilarian turns to the rabbinate question. "I do not want to boast, but one thing I permit myself to declare: if at the head of the kehilla there did not stand a man such as I, who stands on guard and does not let himself be influenced even by the Jewish Sejm deputies and senators, there would be no other rabbi in Będzin than the one the 'Aguda' wants (loud applause).
Then the chairman reads a series of telegrams, among them also from the Zionist Central Committee and from the head office of the G"Ch [interest-free loan] funds in Poland.
The banquet programme also included a musical-vocal part with the participation of the parnas Hershlbovitsh [?], who scored a great success singing the well-known folk song "If I were a rabbi, I would surely know no Torah".
Very beautifully the representative of "Torah va-Avoda", Hillel Wszagner [?], sings Yosele Rosenblatt's "Amar Rabbi Elazar"...
With intent, Mr. Wszagner several times accentuates the phrase "Amar Rabbi Elazar", to which the public responds with stormy ovations.
On behalf of "Keren Hayesod" Mr. Landner greets; he gives a historical survey of the Maaseh Merkavah and reaches the conclusion that already in ancient times our sages said that the world stands on three things:
— on money, on money, and again on money..
After P"ns [?] Kornfeld draws a comparison between the victories over the fascists in Spain and the victory over the "Aguda" regarding the rabbinate question, the chairman closes the banquet with the announcement that, as a token of gratitude, the name of the jubilarian is being inscribed in the Golden Book of the "Yeshivat Chachmei Lublin"...
The public receives the news with extraordinary enthusiasm, and they break into a little dance,
Opinions of the great halakhic authorities on rabbis who "take" a town by the power of money

[Rabbinate — Jewish law and community.]
In connection with the "rumours" cast upon certain parnasim [community officials], that they allegedly took a "remuneration" to make possible the election of a rabbi and a "podrabin" [deputy rabbi], it is worth presenting the opinions of the great halakhic authorities about rabbis who "take" a town by the power of money.

"Any judge who gives money in order to be appointed — one may not rise before him, and it is a mitzvah to hold him in low esteem and to disparage him; and the Sages say: the tallit in which he wraps himself shall be in your eyes like a saddle on a donkey."
(Rambam, Laws of the Sanhedrin ch. 3, 9; Shulchan Arukh, Choshen Mishpat §8)

"A judge who is elected through bribery has the status of an idol: whoever benefits from him is like one who benefits from an idol, and whoever gives him a gift or honours him is as though he had given a gift to, or honoured, the idol."
(Pitchei Teshuva in the name of the Birkei Yosef, ibid.)

"One may not appoint a judge without the consent of the congregation, and if the judge has succeeded in acting through police factors [?] and in confirming a 'consent of the community' — every perutah that he takes from the community is outright robbery."
(Chatam Sofer, Choshen Mishpat §18)

"Those who took a bribe to elect a rabbi — even if they give the money back and take upon themselves, with a curse and an oath, that they will no longer take any money — may no longer vote and no longer have any right to take part in the deliberations on electing a rabbi."
(Chatam Sofer, Choshen Mishpat §18)

"The ban (cherem) that was issued in the year 5669 [1908/09], 26 years ago, under the name 'Moda'ah Rabbah' ['Great Proclamation'], which was issued 'in the name of the Lord God of Israel' on the initiative of the late Gaon of Sochaczew, R' Avrahamele, and the Rebbe of Aleksandrów, R' Yerachmiel Yisrael Yitzchak of blessed memory, both no longer living, and — may he be set apart for life — the present Rebbe of Ger [Góra Kalwaria], R' Avraham Mordechai Alter, may he live long and well.

This 'Moda'ah Rabbah' was signed, besides the above-mentioned great men of Israel, also by 281 rabbis and Rebbes from various towns and shtetlekh in Congress Poland.

The 'Moda'ah Rabbah' begins with the following words:
"Whereas in recent years, to our regret, scandalous things are being done among Jews, and in some towns the rabbinical office is bought for money from the kehilla, or from individual persons through bribery, and it has already come to the point that this epidemic has spread so far that in many towns it has become a rule that no rabbi is accepted unless he gives a bribe to the kehilla and to individuals, and people are no longer at all ashamed to transgress the law in the Shulchan Arukh, Choshen Mishpat §8, and in the Sma, where such rabbis are called 'gods of silver and gods of gold'."

Afterwards the introduction to the book "Vavei ha-Amudim" by the Gaon R' Sheftel of saintly memory (the son of the holy Shelah) is quoted there, who speaks out there energetically against the custom, which prevailed then as well, of buying rabbinical offices for money, in the following words:
"...And I praise the great Geonim of Poland, the holy ones, those already in Heaven and those still living among us, who placed under ban both the givers and the takers of bribes, not excluding even the agents of the transgression who carried it out."

Then the 'Moda'ah Rabbah' quotes the ban that was adopted at the Gromnice fair in Lublin in the year 5346 [1586] and was later reinforced in the year 5350 [1590] — which is found to this day in the pinkas [record book] of the Poznań Jewish kehilla and is printed in the responsa book "Minchat Eliezer"; there it says:
"...No rabbi whatsoever shall endeavour to obtain a rabbinical post through a loan or a gift that will be given, by himself or through others, and he shall not accept any rabbinate that comes to him through gold and silver, nor through other means and ways that bring monetary benefit. And everyone who stops his ears so as not to hear this ordinance shall never be forgiven, and this curse shall fall upon him (niddui, cherem and shamta), and we undertake to come out in battle against those who will not obey, to pursue them to destruction, to thrust them away from us with both hands. This ordinance we have enacted for all generations, until a priest arises with Urim and Thummim."

This prohibition and ban was signed by thirty great men of Israel.

After these quotations the authors of the 'Moda'ah Rabbah' — the Gaon of Sochaczew of blessed memory and the present Rebbe of Ger, may he live long and well — establish according to halakha that this prohibition and ban is valid to this very day, and they therefore conclude that from this day on "no one shall accept any appointment as rabbi or moreh hora'ah [halakhic decisor] through giving money, himself or through anybody, even one of his relatives; even for the greatest religious cause, such as building a synagogue, a beit midrash or a mikveh, one also may not give any individual [money] so that he should help, even merely as a broker."

"It is after all self-evident — it is said in the Proclamation — that the rabbi who, God forbid, transgresses this agreement and oath and abandons himself to being cut off from the Jewish community and from all its holy things and to remaining excommunicated from both worlds — one may not rely on his ruling even in the smallest matters"...

Then it is further stressed "that the prohibition applies both to the giver and to the receiver, and 'that upon this money there lurks a curse, and it is a terrible one, so that the guilty party loses the rest of his property too, as the verse says: "Neither shalt thou bring an abomination into thine house, lest thou be a cursed thing like it; thou shalt utterly detest it, and thou shalt utterly abhor it, for it is a cursed thing""...
News about Radio

We here in Europe, somewhat cut off from the tumult of the great world and sunk in our bitter affairs, have little by little stopped taking an interest in new inventions in general, and have even lost interest in the greatest invention ever made: the radio. We listen to our set only when there is occasion[?] to hear of some world sensation or to hear something extraordinary that will let us forget our worries for a minute; our nerves have grown dull in these hard times, and we have lost interest in almost everything.
And yet it is really[?] worth hearing how the radio has developed and what role it plays among the various peoples of the four corners of the earth.
According to a statistic of the Leipzig Fair, there are fifty-five million radio sets in the whole world. Of these, 25 million are in Europe and 25 million in South America [sic; probably North America is meant]; Asia has two and a half million radio sets, North America one and a half million, Australia one million, and Africa has only 266 thousand radio listeners.
In Russia there are twelve million sets, of which only about two million are in private hands; ten million sets are installed there in the various halls ("homes") where the government has organised collective listening — people gather to listen to the radio.
In Italy, too, there are today such halls where people gather to listen to the radio. Every village and every settlement (kibbutz) has such a hall, maintained by the government. The Italian government founded these halls only a year ago, when the public was eager to hear news of the Abyssinian war.
In Africa all the transmitters send only news that is of interest to the Europeans living in the colonies there; only the Egyptian transmitter also has a programme adapted to the needs of the native population.
Among the Arabs only the rich listen to the radio; the men are not interested in "such nonsense" — they prefer to sit in the coffeehouse or in the streets and listen to old wives' tales.
In Ireland the government guarantees everyone who buys a set that he will hear well. If the set breaks, an expert comes, even to the most remote village, and stays until reception is good.
In China there are to this day sixty stations, not a single one of which belongs to the government. Whoever wants one gets a licence there for a radio station.
The hardest struggle is that of the radio station in India. There some two hundred dialects are spoken, and the radio station does not know how to satisfy its listeners. In Norway and in Chile ever more new stations must be set up in the mountains there. The country is narrow and long, and it is very difficult to make it possible to hear everywhere there.
In the United States of South [sic; North] America there are seven hundred radio stations; of these 110 belong to the Broadcasting Company and 100 to the Columbia Company. Very[?] many stations belong to the big newspapers there; the "Hoysist" [probably Hearst][?] company, the largest newspaper enterprise in the whole world, owns 150 radio stations of its own, not only in all of America but also in many places in other countries. Through these stations of its own it immediately receives the news of all events in the whole world, and it indeed passes the news on, not only to its own papers, which appear in all parts of America, but it also supplies all the largest newspapers of the whole world with all the most important news it receives thanks to its own radio stations.
Z. Haber, Vienna.
When the Husband Lies in Childbed!... / Monologue of a Sosnowiec Jew.

[Sosnowiec — feuilleton/humour; monologue.]
Y. Aberzhanek [?]
May no one be punished, you hear, with a wife who is the breadwinner.
When a wife is the breadwinner, she wears the trousers — and woe betide the husband whose wife wears the trousers!
When the wife is the breadwinner, the husband is no husband, he is a rag, not a man. A servant he is, a slave. A nanny [?] — a nanny with a beard and sidelocks — may God protect you, men, from wives who are breadwinners!...
Yes, gentlemen, since my Yentele became the breadwinner I have stopped being a man; if you will [?], I am no man at all. Not enough that I lost my livelihood, my money, my business, my merchandise — I also lost, may it not happen to you or to any Jew, my manhood. We, I and my Yentele, have swapped roles: my Yentele is the husband and I — the wife. My wife is the breadwinner, travels to the "plansses" [?], and I? I sweep the house, polish [?] the floor, make the beds, light the fire in the kitchen, wash a child, shampoo the little heads, see to it that the baby lies dry... wash out a couple of "bits". I go out into the street [?], to the butcher's, and there one meets other men whose wives are the breadwinners, one stops for a chat [?], and when I come home my Yentele starts screaming: Schlemiel! Good-for-nothing! Spoiled soul!
— You sit that long at the butcher's for meat? Already had a little chat [?] with your pals [Polish przyjaciele]?
— What meat did you take: for soup, or for a stew?
— A black world [?] on you and the butcher together — what a cut he gave you, stones with bones — pure "khabis" [?]!..
I hear out my Yentele's screaming and keep quiet. Do I have any choice but to keep quiet? Since I became a housewife I must take everything with love. Every day she gives me a different job: once she gives me the laundry to mend, patches to sew on, the windows to clean, the floors to wax, the quilts [?] to re-cover, and if I happen to have nothing to do, she gives me the socks to darn.
The worst, though, is with the washerwoman; when there is a wash, I wish myself dead. If she starts talking "Holy Tongue" [Hebrew] to me, I want to run away to where the black pepper grows.
— Remember, she says, this one "toils well", but you must keep an eye on her hands, because this one is "a bit of a taker".
Remember, this one can "eat" for two horses and "understands every letter".
When my wife starts talking "Holy Tongue" to me, I want to run away to where the black pepper grows.
But it's no use: since I and my Yentele have swapped roles, since I have become a housewife, no clever tricks will help — I do everything a housewife has to do: I tidy [?] and wash, I bake and cook, I darn stockings [?] and wax the floor, I wash out a nappy and see that the baby lies dry. I talk "Holy Tongue" with my wife so that the washerwoman won't understand — I do everything a housewife has to do; but that I should also lie in childbed, that I should also have dealings with an obstetrician — that, you know, I, as a male person, had not reckoned with.
Hear, then, dear people, what happened to me here not long ago:
The other day I say to my wife: You know, Yentele, I don't feel quite like everyone else, I have strong stomach pains, my head is pounding as if with hammers.
Well, my Yentele did not play ignorant [?] and sent for the doctor.
— Go — she said to our daughter — to the doctor on Mała-Khazska [?; probably Małachowskiego Street] number... and tell him to come at once.
As bad luck would have it, two doctors live in the same building: an ordinary doctor and an obstetrician, and my daughter went in to the obstetrician — and here the real story begins:
I'm lying in bed like this with a compress on my belly, and I hear from the kitchen a conversation between the doctor and my daughter:
— Ill for long?
— Oh! Was healthy and fresh, tidied, cleaned, darned, washed, cooked lunch and supper, came back from the butcher's and started screaming about the belly.
— Aha — the doctor answered — came back from the butcher's as always and suddenly the belly... Be so kind [?], let there be hot water, and get ready a basin with soap and a towel.
Why hot water all of a sudden? What does he need a basin with soap and a towel for? But presumably he knows what he is saying, he is a doctor after all!...
Suddenly the bedroom door opens and in comes an old, hunched person in a white apron, with rolled-up sleeves, groping with his hands, half blind, shuffles up to the bed and begins to interrogate me:
— How long have you had the pain?
— Since today [—]
— How many children do you have?
— 7, may they live and be well.
— How old is the youngest?
— Half a year.
— Were all the births normal?
— But why do you need to know that?
— When I ask you, you would answer me: were all the births normal?
— Normal.
— Without complications?
— Without complications.
— Did you not once do some heavy work?
— Yes. Washed the floor.
— Aha.
So I saw that I had come upon an old fool — for what "connection of the Torah portion" does my stomach-ache have with my wife's births? What has my belly to do with childbed? So I turned my face away and let him talk to the "dashek" [?].
Seeing that I don't answer, he pulled off the quilt and began to press and tap, and meanwhile he said to himself:
— A hard belly!...
What happened next I unfortunately cannot tell you; suffice it to say that I jumped out of bed, grabbed the old doctor by the collar and threw him down all the stairs.
I knew that I had become a housewife, that I do everything a housewife has to do — but that I would lie in childbed and have dealings with an obstetrician — that I did not know...
You hear, Jews: may you be guarded and shielded from wives who are breadwinners!
Festive proclamation of the Keren Hayesod campaign in Będzin. — “Keren Hayesod is the soul of the Jewish people,” says Professor Schorr.

The festive jubilee in honour of Dr. Weinzieher is still fresh in memory, and once again Jewish Będzin celebrated a second joyous occasion, with the participation of Senator Professor Moshe Schorr, who came to proclaim this year's Keren Hayesod campaign in the town of Będzin.

The distinguished guest, who arrived on Sunday at 12 noon by the express train to Sosnowiec, was welcomed on the platform by the chairman of the Keren Hayesod committee, Mr. S. Fürstenberg, the well-known philanthropist Mr. Ch. Szajn, the Keren Hayesod instructor the writer Gross-Zimmermann, and N. Landner[?], who drove to Będzin in Fürstenberg's car. In the afternoon a reception for the town's notables was held at Mr. Fürstenberg's home.

On the evening of that day a festive banquet took place at the gymnasium. And once again it turned out that Jewish Będzin has an understanding for Jewish affairs; even when it is a matter of “out-of-pocket loss,” when called, people come.

The large, brightly lit hall is filled to the brim; the eastern wall is decorated with greenery and pictures of Jewish personalities; the head of the table is occupied by the “ten-thousand declarers” with their wives; on the right, at long laid tables, sits the “modern” company; on the left — [?], for the most part Mizrachi people, dressed “à la Warszawski,” in short[?] kapotes and spodik-like skullcaps on their heads. All in all — a picturesque scene.

Very active are the board members of WIZO; they fulfil the role of the material side and carry out their task to perfection, taking care that none of the “table-sitters” should suffer any wrong...

And now the celebration begins. After the gymnasium orchestra plays the Polish and the Jewish anthems, the chairman Mr. Fürstenberg opens the celebration with an introductory speech, in which he greets Professor Schorr and the writer Gross-Zimmermann on their mission to carry out the Keren Hayesod campaign in Będzin. Then — a solemn moment. Chairman Fürstenberg proposes honouring the martyrs of Eretz Israel with one minute of silence. A deathly silence reigns in the hall — honour and respect for those who perished for the sanctification of the Name and of the nation.

Then the greetings begin: the first word of greeting goes to Dr. Weinzieher, who points out that Keren Hayesod plays a dominant role for the liberation of the Jewish people.

On behalf of Keren Kayemet the delegate A. Liwer greets; from the Zionist Organisation — chairman Winadzki[?] (in Hebrew); from Mizrachi — L. Bobiszek[?]; WIZO — its chairwoman Mrs. Hisner[?]; from Labour Eretz Israel and Poalei Zion — Sołczowski[?]; from the Kibbutz — Grundler; the Friends of the Jerusalem University — Eng. Mangel (Sosnowiec); from the Hitachdut — chairman Rozenker[?].

Fine greetings for the campaign and for Prof. Schorr are delivered by Dr. Gusenblat[?] (Dąbrowa) and Advocate Kowalski (Sosnowiec), as former students of Prof. Schorr in Lwów.

After the greetings the chairman appeals for absolute quiet, because the distinguished guest, Senator Prof. Schorr, “takes” the floor.

The great scholar begins his lecture in Hebrew. “The honour and the praise that are spoken here about me belong,” he says, “not to me but to you, as part of those who help build the Land. The Keren Hayesod contribution must not be regarded as charity, but exactly as at the building of the Sanctuary, when the Almighty, as it were, told Moses to take an offering from every man whose heart moves him [printed: ‘yirbenu’ for ‘yidvenu’] — what the heart dictates to him, not by compulsion but with love, because Keren Hayesod is the soul of the Jewish people.”

He then switches to Polish and says that the Jewish people possesses four legitimations of its rights to Eretz Israel, and the fourth legitimation is the work created by Keren Hayesod. Prof. Schorr believes that Jewish Będzin, which has already made a name for itself in the Jewish world, will this time too pass its examination for the benefit of Keren Hayesod.

Prof. Schorr concludes with the words of the Talmud, that a dream seen at dawn, before the rising of the morning star, is a true dream that will be fulfilled; and our dream of redemption is surely the dream before the morning star of all mankind, and[?] it will certainly be realised, and Eretz Israel will remain our Old-New Land.

A storm of applause breaks out when the chairman announces that the floor goes to the brilliant speaker Mr. Gross-Zimmermann. Because of the late hour, however, the speaker must be brief; he points to the heroic moment that the Jewish people is now living through, to the debate that Prof. Chaim Weizmann is conducting before the Royal Commission, and he pleads, just as Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai once pleaded, that “Yavne” be given back to him...

Finally Mr. Fürstenberg says a few bitter words addressed to the Jewish intelligentsia, which stands aside, and also to the general public, which gives almost nothing for Keren Hayesod. “I have the right,” says Mr. Fürstenberg, “to admonish you, because I work [—].”

After certain “[—]” [—] (declare[?]) themselves ready to take an active part, the chairman closes the celebration at about half past twelve at night.
Aid circle for the Sosnowiec “Maccabi”.

The gymnastics and sports association “Maccabi” is in a very bad financial situation and is struggling with its last strength to maintain the positions that were won through hard toil and effort over the two decades of its existence.
Since the new board has taken the responsibility upon itself, it is seeking various means of maintaining the Jewish outpost, the “Maccabi,” which carries the Jewish flag high and proudly.
And one of the means is to open an aid circle, for which we have obtained the consent of the esteemed editorial board of the “Zaglembier Tsaytung,” and we are starting to run the circle in today's issue. We hope that our members and also sympathisers will respond warmly in favour of the campaign and help the “Maccabi” in its further development.
The Board.

Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Acharei Mot-Kedoshim)

[Oneg Shabbat — weekly Torah portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parshat Acharei-Kedoshim
—o—
a) "After the death of the two sons of Aaron" (16:1)
After the passing of a well-known rebbe, a dispute broke out between his two surviving sons. The rebbe in question had also been the rav (town rabbi) of his town, so it was understood that one of the sons would become rebbe and the other — rav. But each of them wanted the rebbe-ship, which brings in [printed: "ניט"] more money and more honour. So a din Torah (rabbinical lawsuit) over it took place before R' Yitzchak Shmelkes, the rav of Lemberg [Lwów].
When putting forward the claims, the younger son, who very much desired the rebbe-ship, gave the Lemberg rabbinate[?] to understand that the rabbinate (rabbanut) is a far more responsible and honourable post, and therefore it is due to the elder brother, while he himself would content himself with the rebbe-ship.
To this R' Yitzchak Shmelkes said:
— In Torat Kohanim it says: "After the death of the two sons of Aaron — that they did not take counsel with one another. And they died — just as[?] their death was equal, so[?] their sin was equal." But surely the question arises: their sin was not the same — one wanted to become king and the other High Priest (see Rashi). Rather, that is what "they did not take counsel with one another" means. Together, both of them indeed said "you and I will lead the generation." But when it came to the division, each one talked the other into becoming king — which is more responsible and honourable — so that the priesthood, which brings in money, the priestly gifts, would remain for himself...
—o—
b) "Fine aromatic incense" (ibid., 12)
A Masorah:
"ketoret samim dakah" (fine aromatic incense) and "kol demamah dakah" (a still small voice).
For in Arachin (15a) the Gemara says that incense atones for evil talk (lashon hara): "Let a thing done in secret come and atone for a deed done in secret." And this is what it means: the "fine aromatic incense" atones for the "still small voice" — for the evil talk that a person whispers...
Pele ha-Omer[?].
—o—
c) "And he shall make atonement for himself and for his household" (ibid., 13 [as printed; the verse is 16:17])
"His atonement comes first... before the atonement of the whole congregation of Israel." Yoma 34[?] [cf. Yoma 43b].
The question arises:
Everywhere a community takes precedence even over the greatest individual — so why should Aaron's atonement come here before the atonement of all Israel?
Rather, Aaron's atonement comes first here because he cannot atone for others as long as he himself is not pure and not atoned for. Therefore "and he shall make atonement for himself and for his household," and only then "and for all the congregation of Israel"... Imrei Chen.
—o—
d) "And he who burns them shall wash his clothes" (ibid., 28)
Concerning the priest who burns the red heifer, the same wording is also used, and there "and he shall be unclean until evening" is added. Why is "and he shall be unclean until evening" not found here?
Because here we are speaking of Yom Kippur, and on Yom Kippur it is in any case forbidden to eat terumah; and the Magen Avraham (Orach Chaim §612) says that even touching food is forbidden on Yom Kippur — so in law the "unclean until evening" makes no practical difference at all [printed "נארגיסט"].
R' Meir Simcha of Dvinsk.
—o—
e) "And they shall no longer offer their sacrifices to the goat-demons (se'irim)" (17:7)
As travellers relate, in many places in Africa (for example in Lower Guinea, South Africa) people still today worship se'irim — goats. When a tribe goes to war, it sends a goat ahead; if the goat walks fast, it is a sign that the tribe will win; if it walks slowly, it is a sign of defeat. In Angola (West Africa, belonging to Portugal) people still today bring sacrifices to goat-idols: they take the goat, tie it between two trees, and with dances and drumming bring it a sacrifice. The blood of the sacrifice is drunk by the people, and with the remaining blood they sprinkle the walls of the temples (see Moreh Nevukhim, Part III, ch. 46).
This makes it understandable[?] why precisely at the sprinkling of the blood the Torah adds "and they shall no longer offer their sacrifices to the se'irim" — because the worship of the se'irim was bound up, as far as is known[?], with sprinkling the blood on the walls of the temples...
R' Shimshon Bloch.
—o—
f) "And any man of the children of Israel... who hunts game, a beast" (ibid., 13)
In the Noda bi-Yehuda (part II) there is a question whether a Jew may go hunting. And R' Yechezkel Landau expresses his astonishment: how can a Jew find pleasure in the occupation of Nimrod and Esau...
The "Or Zarua" (Laws of Shabbat §17) and the Maharam of Rothenburg (Responsa part I §27) forbid a Jew to hunt with the help of hunting dogs, seeing in it a terrible cruelty.
Only learning to ride fast on a horse does the Mahari Bruna (Responsa §71) permit, because a Jew must be able to ride fast so as to be able to flee in time of danger...
And characteristically: hunting is the only field in which no Jew whatsoever has yet distinguished himself...
Dr. A. Berliner.
—o—
g) "You shall not go about as a talebearer among your people; you shall not stand by the blood of your neighbour" (9:15[?] [as printed; the verse is 19:16])
The juxtaposition comes to teach that sometimes one may indeed be a talebearer and reveal a secret — when it concerns your fellow's life; then "you shall not stand by the blood of your neighbour"... Toldot Yitzchak.
—o—
h) "You shall surely rebuke your fellow" (ibid., 7 [as printed; the verse is 19:17])
A maskil once reproached the Kelmer Maggid: why[?] does he take money for moralizing, for preaching mussar sermons — it is, after all, a mitzvah, and "just as I [do it] for free, so you [must do it] for free"...
To this he replied:
— The Master of the Universe can indeed afford to rebuke for free, because "Mine is the silver and Mine is the gold, says the Lord" — He has enough money; therefore "says the Lord" can preach mussar sermons for free. But a simple flesh-and-blood person must also take money for it...
—o—
i) "And whoever gives of his seed to Molech" (20:2)
That is why the section on Molech was said next to the section on forbidden relations: because only among those tribes that led an impure family life and did not themselves know whose the children were — only among them could such cruelty occur, that parents would burn children... Abarbanel.
A. Zaglembier — The Living Dead Man (5)

[Literature — serialised novel.] A. Zaglembier: The Living Dead Man. (A highly suspenseful novel of Jewish life in Zagłębie before and after the World War). 5)
Summary of the beginning of the novel.
On a winter[?] evening before the World War, when two Cossacks were to transfer the dangerous bandit „Szmulek Łapka“ to the Piotrków[?] prison, they were suddenly attacked on the way to the Będzin station by two disguised „strażniks“ (guards) — Łapka's helpers. At dawn the Cossacks were found lying bound with gagged mouths, and Szmulek „Łapka“, freed, had escaped towards the Gzichów road and hidden himself somewhere.
That same evening, and almost at the same hour too, the universally known, respectable debt-collector (inkasent) Yosl Wertheim — a father of three children — suddenly disappeared. His wife Sarahche runs about the town terribly desperate, searching for him in every possible hiding place in all of Zagłębie. But Yosl Wertheim has vanished like a stone in water...
Everyone stands before an extraordinary riddle. At last, on the seventh day, the freckled Wacek reports to police inspector Charecki[?] and tells him that on that day he saw Wertheim on the Gzichów road together with the Christian woman Wanda Komarska — a young, pretty shiksa whom Wacek had been courting.
Now read on.
Wacek lowers his head in shame and says:
— She also said that all my efforts were in vain, that I shouldn't fool myself, and that she would never become my wife, because her heart belonged to another...
— Did she mean Wertheim by that?
— I don't know, she didn't tell me whom, but I reckon so...
— It seems she's a decent girl...
— She is also a bad one. You could stretch yourself out at her feet and she wouldn't care at all.
— I see... And how did she look that evening? I mean her face... Was she content or agitated?
— I had never seen her so agitated as then.
— Why do you think she was so angry because of your proposals?
— Who can know...
— And she mentioned nothing about Wertheim?
— Not a word. I didn't have him in mind either.
— I understand. But don't you know whether Wanda also used to quarrel with Wertheim?
— How should I know that?
— And how long has she been carrying on the love affair with this Wertheim?
— Oh, it's been very long already, because it's nearly a year now since Wanda went cold on me...
— And you still love her?
— Yes. But I don't know myself why, she is so bad to me...
— And if she agreed[?], would you marry her?
— But she won't even let anyone talk to her...
— If so, I'll speak with her right away! Me she will answer all right... Where does she live, Wanda Komarska?
Wacek gave Wanda's address. At the same time he stood up, thinking that his interrogation was over, and asked:
— May I go now?
— No, not yet, you'll have to wait here. I will [—] need you.
— How long can it take? — Wacek asks uneasily, thinking that by coming here he had brought trouble on himself... Who knows whether the police inspector doesn't suspect him of something himself, and it might yet end in arrest...
— You will wait here in the other room.
Saying this, Charecki too rises from his seat and leads the freckled Wacek into the neighbouring room. Soon a duty strażnik also comes in there, with whom Charecki reaches an understanding by a wink. That is, the strażnik is to guard Wacek. Charecki himself goes back into his office, from where he at once sends a second strażnik to fetch Wanda and instructs him: if she does not want to come willingly, he is to arrest her.
For Charecki is certain that after the questioning of Wanda this possible[?] riddle will be cleared up for him..
But this time, too, a bitter disappointment awaited the conscientious police inspector, just when it seemed that any moment now everything would become so clear...
When the strażnik came for Wanda, she did behave as if she truly felt guilty of a grave crime... She was badly frightened, turned white as chalk and by no means wanted to go along to the police. She even hid under the bed and feigned a fainting fit, wanting thus to try[?] to force[?] the strażnik to leave empty-handed. In the end, however, Wanda realised that by putting up resistance she could only make her situation worse. Her parents also persuaded her; they accompanied her to the police station (komisariat) and comforted her on the way:
— Wandziu, what have you got to be afraid of?
— Surely a mistake has happened...
— Are you guilty of anything, then?
For even her own parents did not know about the great secret that their beautiful Wanda carries in her heart.
The parents had to stay and wait in the front hall[?].
And when police inspector Charecki saw Wanda in his office, he understood at once why she had so many „admirers“...
For Wanda was a shapely, healthy shiksa with a pair of fiery, laughing eyes, past which no man could pass by indifferently...
And because Wanda herself also knew and was able to appreciate her „virtues“ as a beautiful, alluring woman, she therefore carried herself haughtily everywhere, provocatively and very insolently.
Now too, as soon as she was left face to face with police inspector Charecki, she immediately asked in an angry, raised voice:
— What do they want from me? And why was I led through the street with a strażnik?
— First of all, sit down, miss — Charecki, as always at the start, began to smile mildly — presently, presently I will explain everything to you, and besides... is it then such a disgrace for an honest person to walk through the street with a strażnik?
— For me it is a disgrace! I haven't stolen from anyone...
— Nobody accuses you, God forbid, of any theft, oh no, with thieves one doesn't talk at all, one puts them straight into prison.. But above all you must calm down and sit, because our conversation may perhaps drag on a little.
And again[?] Wanda sees that with such people she will achieve nothing by anger. She shrugs her shoulders indifferently, looks around uneasily in the quiet, eerie room and at last sits down on the same chair on which the freckled Wacek had sat half an hour earlier.
— That's it — Charecki too settles comfortably in his seat and takes a fresh sheet of paper to put on record everything that Wanda will say.
The formal questions about first name, surname and age go very easily and quickly. But as soon as Charecki asks:
— And what do you know about the missing Yosek Wertheim? After all, you knew him well..
Wanda becomes momentarily uneasy and confused, and begins to stammer very unclearly, although she had of course expected that it was precisely for this that she had surely now been summoned to the police.
— Yes — she answers — I knew the man, but... I know nothing...
— What you don't know does not interest me, I want to know what you do know!
— I don't know what they want from me, some enemy of mine surely wants to do me harm...
— Don't talk about enemies. For a person can do himself more harm than the worst enemy! So don't think about others, but about yourself, and answer my questions clearly — Charecki at once adopts a sharper tone.
— But I really know nothing — Wanda pleads in such a pitiful tone, like a person who finds himself in a tight spot...
(To be continued).
The Cooking Ladle: A Pious Sports Ground

[The Cooking Ladle (Der Kokh-Lefl) — humour page.]
The Cooking Ladle

A pious sports ground.
And really, why shouldn't there be a Jewish, plain-pious sports ground? After all, we have a pious newspaper, pious colonies in the Land of Israel and even pious dance evenings.
As we learn, a pious sports club is to be founded for the current sports season.
We can already picture what such a sports ground will look like.
First of all, the engineers will have to make sure the ground is no farther from town than a Sabbath boundary (tchum Shabbat), and, of course, there will also have to be an eruv.
At the entrance comrade Pintshe will stand guard and check whether the sportsmen are wearing tzitzit; he will also take a look at the sports outfits[?], so that, God forbid, not too much shows[?].
The religious commission will send in a commissar, Elekhi[?] from the mikveh, to direct and supervise the women's race and high jump.
The footballers will have to wear skullcaps; mezuzot will also be nailed to the goals, and after every ball he stops the goalkeeper will have to recite the "Gomel" blessing.
At a football match the referee („sendzhevn", from Polish sędziować) will be the kehilla-board member („dozor") R' Eli Ber, Moshe Chaim will keep goal[?] and R' Nete will catch the ball.
Moshe Mendel will be in charge of the women's cloakroom („shatnye", Polish szatnia) (a fresh kehilla post), and R' Anshl, the [—][?] of the pious newspaper, will call the Jewish sportsmen — antisemites.

What Qualifications Must a Rabbi Have?

[The Cooking Ladle — humour; Będzin — the rabbinate.]
In connection with the rabbinical competition in Będzin, the editors of "The Cooking Ladle" (Kokh-Lefl) turned to one of the Agudah leaders with the question:

The Agudah leader slowly began stroking his pointed little beard and, after long deliberation, said:

How Can One Live to Old Age?

[The Cooking Ladle — humour; Sosnowiec.]
How can one live to old age?
A conversation overheard in the "old-age home" (moshav zkenim).
In the Sosnowiec old-age home two old men sit and talk:
— You see, Yisroel Bunem — says one to the other — tomorrow I turn, no evil eye, eighty years old. Thank God, I didn't drink, I didn't look at women, and that's why I have lived to such a fine old age.
— And with me — says the other — it's just the opposite. I did like a drop of vodka, I smoked cigarettes, I didn't hate what a healthy man loves, and I'm already, thank God, 75.
— But if you had lived the way I did — said the first — you would surely also be as old as me by now, 80...
Legal Advice

[The Cooking Ladle — humour; parody of a legal-advice column.]
— Give me advice on how to become slim. A woman.
Answer: How? Be good to your husband and stop "eating" him, because, as they say, all of a woman's fat comes from "eating" her husband...
* * *
— Is it true that unemployment has become much smaller?
Answer: Yes. Many people are already very busy looking for a summer apartment for their families.
* * *
— I have read that cattle, too, suffer from consumption; is that true?
Answer: Quite possible, for does one need to be a sage to catch consumption?
* * *
— I bought a new hat and it is too tight for me; can't you advise me how to stretch it?
Answer: There is no need to stretch the hat; I have a different piece of advice. Open a business without money, take a mistress, and that will shrivel your head so much that the hat will be wide enough.
* * *
— Explain to me why the earth is feminine in gender?
Answer: Because nobody knows exactly how old she is.
A Bookkeeper "Do Wszystkiego" (For Everything)...

[The Cooking Ladle — humour.]
The factory owner K. hired a new bookkeeper and agreed with him that he must know about everything. So he asks the bookkeeper:

The Keren Hayesod Campaign in Zagłębie.

[Page header: What is new in Zagłębie? — Friday 12 Iyar 5697 / piątek 23 kwietnia 1937 (Friday, 23 April 1937).]
Będzin
This year's Keren Hayesod campaign in Będzin and in Dąbrowa has taken on the character of a broad popular campaign. The events in Eretz Israel and the hard, decisive struggle before the Royal Commission in London have aroused in all Jewish circles feelings of solidarity and responsibility for the great hour. A large number of Keren Hayesod donors have this year contributed larger sums than last year, and dozens of Jews who until now have not paid to the Keren Hayesod are now reporting to the Keren Hayesod office or to the chairman Fürstenberg and are fulfilling voluntarily and generously their duty towards the upbuilding of Eretz Israel.
As every year, this time too the Będzin magnates, Messrs. Szajn, Fürstenberg, Jakub Gutman and others, placed themselves at the head of the Keren Hayesod campaign. Thanks to the energy and devotion of Mr. Chairman Fürstenberg the campaign has been brilliantly organized. To the festive banquet with which the campaign was opened, Senator Prof. Schorr came from Warsaw and delivered a masterly speech on the burning problems of the Jewish people at the present moment. The presence of Prof. Schorr in Będzin aroused strong interest among all circles of the Jewish population.
As director of the Keren Hayesod campaign in Będzin and in Dąbrowa the head office in Jerusalem has delegated the well-known writer Mr. Gross-Zimmermann.
Mr. Gross-Zimmermann, a brilliant man of letters and publicist and a witty speaker, is no longer a new face in Będzin. Already a year ago Mr. Gross-Zimmermann „conquered“[?] our town with his countless[?] lectures on various political and cultural subjects, and the impressive success of last year's Keren Hayesod campaign is indeed largely — alongside the influential work of chairman Fürstenberg — owed to the activity of Mr. Gross-Zimmermann.
Last Monday Mr. Gross-Zimmermann gave a fine, substantial lecture at „Yehua“[?] on „Our struggle before the Royal Commission“. As we learn, other societies and organizations too, such as the Ż.T.K., the League for Working Eretz Israel, Hanoar Hatziyoni, Gordonia and others, are preparing to arrange lectures by Mr. Gross-Zimmermann.
Provisions Campaign for the Orphanage („Beit Yetomim“).

After a rather long pause the so-called „kilo campaign“ for the „Beit Yetomim“ (orphanage) is being undertaken again. It is to be hoped that the collectors will be received as usual[?] and that every Jewish family will, according to its means, give provisions for the above-mentioned institution, where about 80 orphans are being brought up.

Next Sunday at 4 p.m. a meeting of bookkeepers will take place in the premises of the Merchants' Association. The purpose of the meeting is to discuss the new draft law and to elect delegates to the congress, which will take place next month in Warsaw.

At 8.30 the meeting will take place with whatever number of members is present.

Prof. Zaderecki Rebukes the Jewish Intelligentsia — Why It Does Not Know the Treasure of the Talmud

[Będzin — lecture, Jewish–Christian relations.]
The lecture by the well-known Christian Talmud expert Prof. Tadeusz Zaderecki in Będzin aroused great interest among all strata of the Jewish population.
The hall of the "Orphans' Home", where the lecture took place, was packed full with a varied Jewish public. Because of the heavy crush at the entrance many people went home.
The lecture, entitled[?] "If people knew the Talmud", brought almost nothing new to that part of the audience who had studied "Abaye and Rava", since even a "dardeki rebbe" [elementary-school teacher][?] knows that the Torah was given through Moses on Mount Sinai, that all the nations refused to accept the Ten Commandments, and that the Talmud is a treasure of learning, containing the highest measure of ethics and culture. Nevertheless it was interesting to hear how a Christian scholar displays so much erudition in Mishnah and Talmud, knows who our Tannaim and Amoraim were, and has the full audacity to deliver words of reproof[?] at the expense of the Jewish intelligentsia, which knows the foreign learning of other cultural treasures.
And Prof. Zaderecki is indeed right when he says that the various Hamans remind the Jewish intelligentsia that they are Jews...
The esteemed lecturer also settles accounts with the various "scholars" such as Pranaitis [Justinas Pranaitis, blood-libel "expert"] and the priest Trzeciak[?], who show that "according to the Talmud a shochet must have a craftsman's card"..
On the whole the lecture was interesting, but had the auditorium consisted of non-Jews, it would certainly have been worthwhile...

Life in Kielce — The cruel murder of 5 Jewish martyrs in Stawy before the Kielce District Court

[Kielce — trial; antisemitism.]
Life in Kielce
(Date boxes: Friday, 12 Iyar 5697 — 23 April 1937.)
The cruel murder of 5 Jewish martyrs in Stawy
before the Kielce District Court.
This Wednesday the trial of those accused of the murder of the 5 Jewish martyrs in the village of Stawy took place in the Kielce District Court.
In the dock sat: Józef Żembacki[?], Jan Pietras and Antoni Chmiel; all three accused are between 20 and 22 years old. Against the 4th, Stefaniak[?], arrested at that[?] time, the charge was dropped right after the first investigation for lack of evidence.
After the personal particulars of the accused had been established, Adv. Manela[?] filed[?], on behalf of the orphans of the murdered Szmulewicz family, a civil claim for a sum of 500 zł., and Adv. Rosner[?] — on behalf of the mother of the murdered melamed Königstein and on behalf of the sons[?] of the grandmother Chana Szmulewicz — 250 zł.
The court accepted the civil claim.
After the reading of the indictment, in which the exact details of the bestial murder are given, the court proceeded to hear the witnesses;
first to be heard was the one and only chief witness, the 12-year-old orphan Jankel Szmulewicz. As soon as Jankel Szmulewicz appeared in the courtroom, spontaneous weeping broke out among the relatives and [—] guests present.
Jankel Szmulewicz describes in detail how and in what circumstances the horrible murder was carried out. He relates precisely and clearly who of his family was murdered earlier or later. The 12-year-old orphan, who was a witness of the horrible tragedy, points to the three accused Żembacki, Pietras and Chmiel; he recognises them by face, build[?], clothing and voice. Szmulewicz repeatedly breaks off his statements because of the tears choking him. This moment is very dramatic.
Then the representatives of the Jędrzejów police command, Messrs. Petas[?] and Wasisla[?], who conducted the investigation, testify. As both state, already at the first investigation Jankel Szmulewicz pointed to the three said accused, whom he recognised among 30 peasants.
The court also read out the statement of the late Christian witness Kito[?], who had then reported that Żembacki did not want[?] to take back from him the old boots[?] he had given him for repair, because Żembacki had then told him that he now had a lot of money, was now a "good earner" and could buy himself new shoes... He had also seen a lot of silver money with him.
Then a series of witnesses, alibi witnesses, are heard, who declare that the accused are, poor souls, utterly innocent...
After hearing the witnesses and reading the autopsy report, prosecutor Wolnik[?] delivers the indictment speech. He pointed out that the orphan Jankel is mentally well developed, is fully convinced of his words, and demanded the harshest punishment for the accused.
After that the civil plaintiffs' counsel, Adv. Manela and Adv. Rosner, made lengthy speeches.
The last to speak was the defence counsel Adv. Czechowski, who says that the court cannot rely on the statements of a 12-year-old boy who was then badly frightened and could by no means have recognised the accused by the light of an electric lamp. He asks for an acquittal for all.
The same was asked by the three accused in their last word.
At half past five in the evening the court pronounced a verdict acquitting all the accused.
The grounds of the verdict state that the court cannot rely on the sole 12-year-old boy Szmulewicz, who changed his statements several times.

[Będzin — kehilla; Talmud Torah.]
Under the chairmanship of the president, Mr. Fürstenberg, a meeting was held on the situation of the Będzin Talmud Torah. On the agenda was the item: closing the Talmud Torah. Besides a larger number of the board, the rabbinic judges (moreh tzedek) Friedberg and Levin also came, before whom Mr. Fürstenberg pointed out the positive deeds he had performed for the Talmud Torah. Burned alive

In the building of the public (powszechna) school in Ligota the teacher Glrinska[?] occupied a room. Wishing to clean her clothes, Glbinska[?] had prepared a bottle of benzine, and at a certain moment she put the little bottle down near the burning stove; because of this[?] a strong explosion occurred and the benzine caught fire; the flames also seized the teacher's clothes. Her maid hurried over at the cries for help and began tearing the burning clothes off her, but the maid herself was so badly scalded that she lost consciousness. Both were taken to hospital, where the teacher died a short time later.

In the presence of 70 members, president Kiwkowicz[?] opens the meeting and proposes Mr. Turm as chairman, who is elected unanimously. Messrs. Kilsztok and Sengebojm[?] are then invited as assessors, Mr. Frejman[?] as secretary, and Miss Cukerman.
The activity report is given by Pres. Kiwkowicz, who points to the difficulties the board had when it took over the fund with a capital of 366 zł. The board then raised 12 thousand zł., which [unclear words] Pres. Kiwkowicz, Mr. Szpiner, Mr. Magdrer[?] and Mr. Szpigler, and thereby took into account the necessary[?] demands of the population.
The basic[?] capital amounts to 10,800 zł. This year 119 loans were distributed for a sum of 12,000 zł. "Frozen" debts in the year 1935/36 were 1,500 zł.; in the year 1936/37, 700 zł. were collected. The prospects are favourable, so that 75 percent will shortly be collected.
After the treasurer's report of Mr. Springer and of the audit commission — Mr. Z. Ten Years of “Gordonia” in Będzin

[Będzin — Zionism and youth movements.]
The pioneering youth organization “Gordonia” in Będzin celebrated last Saturday night (motzei Shabbat) the completion of ten years of its existence.
The celebration turned out very impressive; the youth rejoiced in the festive day and were in an exalted [?] mood, full of confidence in a better tomorrow — the 102 victims who fell through the Arab terror do not deter. Here lies the strength of our being here — “our hope is not yet lost”...
The hall where the jubilee was celebrated was packed with the celebrants; also a large number of the “father's family” — of the “Hitachdut”, which brought forth from itself such [?] a successful child, “Gordonia”; also present were some of the Zionist veterans, parents of the young people, and guests from Eretz Israel and from... the Diaspora. Among them the regular “ge-vodnik” [?] S. Gross-Zimmerman, who was given a warm welcome.
The numerous audience sat down at the richly laid tables (not at all in the pioneer manner...), and after a trumpet signal the jubilee celebration opened with “Techezakna”.
The opening was made by Mr. S. Zimmerman, who said that the festive day belongs not only to “Gordonia” but to the whole town. He also spoke of the efforts in the Diaspora, and especially in Eretz Israel, where 102 victims perished defending the Jewish settlements. Their memory was honoured by standing.
The chairmanship of the celebration was handed to the advocate Dr. Rechtman [?], who gave the first word to the guest from Eretz Israel, Dr. Yeshayahu Shapira. The speaker gave an assessment of various elements in Zionism and came to the conclusion that the most correct line in the Zionist movement is “Gordonia”.
Greetings were given on behalf of the Zionist Organization by Y. Migorucki [?]; on behalf of the Keren Kayemeth — A. Liwer [?]; of the “Hitachdut” — M. Rozenker [?]; of the Keren Hayesod — N. Lanerter [?]; of the Sosnowiec “Kibbutz” — Mirawnek [?]; of the Będzin “Kibbutz” — Morawski; of “Hashomer Hatzair” — Borowski [?], and others.
A greeting from Eretz Israel was conveyed by the instructress “of” [sic] Mrs. Rote [?]; many telegraphic greetings were also received, among them a telegraphic greeting from the local “WIZO”.
At the end came the highlight of the evening — the speech of the brilliant orator, the writer S. Gross-Zimmerman. He spoke with pathos about the tasks of Jewish youth at the present moment. Its main task — said the speaker — is to put an end to the “season of lamentation” that has lasted until now; enough lamenting, one must bring [?] restlessness into the Jewish camp and call it to a new life on healthy foundations in our old-new land.
Because of the late hour the second, artistic part was shortened; only the young members took part: Zilbergold (violin) and Kszenszywa [?] (recitation).
The chairman summed up all the opinions expressed in the greetings and, after reading out the list of the newly created patronage committee, closed the celebration at about 1 at night.
“Hatikvah” is sung, and afterwards hands are linked and a “hora” is danced.

Sanitary commissions and hygiene — Outward aesthetics and inner health hygiene. — Keeping clean according to the regulations and by educational methods

Outward aesthetics and inner health hygiene. — Keeping clean according to the regulations and by educational methods.
Spring has come to the world; the sun is beginning to warm with its reviving rays, which call forth a will to live and to enjoy the beautiful nature that is at the disposal of mankind.
Apparently, as a result of this, the sanitary commissions have begun to be active. Thus, for example, various regulations concerning hygiene are being issued, to which the population must conform. Shops selling products of prime necessity are inspected, and neatness and cleanliness are required.
It has also been ordered that the outer parts of the shops be refreshed, so that to the outside eye they make a clean and aesthetic impression. Then house-owners will be required to renovate their houses as well. Certainly the reforms are necessary — both for outward appearance, for the modern outlook, and for health, which finds expression in hygiene and cleanliness.
Certainly great attention must be paid to the outward appearance of the town, because it expresses the character of the inhabitants and their understanding of modernism, hygiene and aesthetic enjoyment.
When a visitor comes into the town, he judges the inhabitants by the look of the streets, houses, squares, railway station, institutions and so on. Therefore we indeed hold that great attention must be paid to making the outer parts of the town create as good and aesthetic an impression as possible.
But with this one is still far from having done one's duty, neither towards oneself nor towards others.
If only the outer parts of the town are cared for, it is merely for show. Great attention must also be paid to inner hygiene. Thus, for example, houses and courtyards must be kept clean inside, staircases must be washed often, and cleanliness in them must take the place of honour.
All possible means must be applied to educate the inhabitants on hygienic foundations; the idea must be implanted in them that cleanliness is health itself. For this purpose it would be absolutely necessary to make use of propaganda material that would enlighten the common people about the benefits of hygiene and the harmfulness of uncleanliness and dirt, from which epidemic diseases arise — diseases that are later hard to fight and that take countless human victims.
True, there are regulations that compel the inhabitants to live in hygienic conditions, but with law and statute little will be achieved here. In this case one has to educate the citizens, for whom laws play a rather meagre role. A mass can be educated only by speaking to the conscience, by using natural methods that will capture the heart and the soul. Otherwise there is no way whatsoever to penetrate there, and without this threefold cord the desired goal will not be reached. If it is a matter of inner hygienic education — that belongs to every housewife.
The "TOZ" [Jewish health-protection society] has great merits in this field, but it has to work under enormously difficult conditions because of finances, which unfortunately are not at its disposal.
Actually this is a civic question, and as such the municipal administrations must take care of the town and its inhabitants. To this end they must allocate funds and see to it that their town stands, in the hygienic sense, at the proper level.
Here we say one thing more: quite often house-owners are fined for trifles if they do not conform to the outward regulations, which in any case are of much less importance than inner hygiene.
And we come up against something else: we see public places, which perhaps belong to the town, that are neglected, and nobody cares that they be cleaned. So why should this not be dealt with as it should? If hygiene, if cleanliness and aesthetics — then they must reign in all parts of the town, without exception, under whatever authority they may be.
The sanitary commissions must be intensively active and strive to bring in cleanliness and order, both outwardly and inwardly; only then will it be possible to state that they aim at beautifying the town and making its inhabitants healthy.
In order to realise this properly, a planned, all-round, fruitful activity must be carried out intensively, one that can be crowned as useful work for the people.
R. Les.
"Linas ha-Cholim" and "Bikur Cholim"

(What benefit do they bring in the present situation, and what could they achieve [?] under different conditions?)

We have two philanthropic institutions here in Sosnowiec. Both have one and the same goal, one and the same ideal: to help poor sick Jews. And if both are one and the same thing — both are named after the "sick" (cholim) — one "Linas ha-Cholim" and the other "Bikur Cholim." And the question arises: if both have the same repair to make, why does one need the split portions [?], when neither is so rich that it could satisfy all the needy?

But the fact of the matter is that "Linas ha-Cholim" holds sway over the Modrzejów [reading uncertain] quarter and the neighbouring streets, and "Bikur Cholim" rules over old Sosnowiec.

And what shall we tell you — we, with our poor understanding, cannot by any means grasp why two separate institutions are needed. Granted, if they were rich, they could compete with each other for their "clients," so that one would offer better conditions, finer treatment; but there is not even that: neither the first nor the second has the means to fulfil its tasks in view of the prevailing want and sickness among the masses.

Nevertheless, relations of fraternal hatred prevail between the two. So there is no doubt that this disturbs the activity of the first institution as well as of the second. And the question arises: what is all this for? Why does one need this fraternal hatred? Surely [printed "azdai"] this is a groundless hatred? Who benefits from this hatred? Can one not manage without it? It brings harm and fragmentation even into the ranks of the sick, where the ideal is to help put the poor and suffering back on their feet?

Would it not be fairer, instead of having two institutions for the sick with barely sustainable means of existence, each of which is out only to fight the other, that they make peace between themselves and merge into one powerful aid institution, whose task should be to help all sick, helpless Jews, run by people who are truly out to work for the public good? Is this not more fitting [?]? Would not such a concentration bring more benefit both to the community and to the poor sick people who depend on the support of the above-mentioned [?] institutions?

There is no doubt that this would bring great benefit to the community, which would gain more trust in the heads of the institutions, because then one would see good will and a proper understanding for society.

We put forward the suggestion: let the heads of both institutions consider the question earnestly and sincerely, and they will find a language of peace for their ideal.

Dr. Papuri.
"A Room to Let Here". (Reportage).

[Reportage — hidden poverty in Jewish households that have come down in the world.] Y. Janasowicz.
(Reportage).

It seems that after one has walked through the "padoastshe" [? doubtful Polish word — probably the poor outskirts] and seen the poverty and want there, one becomes so hardened that nothing can move or affect one any more. And indeed, can one imagine stronger pictures of misery than those we see day after day in the poor quarters of the town? When one sees hungry children who sit a whole day in bed [?] and cry: "Mama, I'm hungry", when one sees old, sick people dying miserable and lonely in cold, empty rooms — it seems that nothing, no picture of want, can surprise one any more; one becomes somehow almost indifferent to all troubles.

And yet I did not remain indifferent when I met the spectre of hunger and want — and precisely on the main street of the town.

There is something touching and sad in the Jewish homes that have come down in the world. In those homes on the "principal" streets ["pryncypalne"], where from outside it still seems that rich men, wealthy people, live there — but as soon as one crosses the threshold one senses the specific smell of want and hunger.

There, on the street, on the stones [?], everything gleams like a mirror all around. Here, one thinks, rich men live. Here is a door, and on the door a brass plate bearing the name of a person well known in the business world. The bell by the door is even broken already. I knock, and it does not take long until they open for me. A long while I stand at the door until I hear in the corridor slow, unsure steps echoing with a hollow echo. The door opens and I am inside. It seems clean and nice, and yet I feel instinctively that something here is not in order; a familiar smell hits the nose. A smell that tells of poverty.

And on entering the flat my first impression was confirmed. Everything — the furniture, the walls and the people inside — everything tells of a great hunger that has spread itself out lavishly, tells of want; from everything there weeps down the sadness of a fallen fortune ["yordishkeit"], of former sated days that are like a distant dream, already belonging to the past. A heavy, oppressive gloom takes hold of me. Everything in this home speaks to me:
— This is how fate has played with us.

The poverty that has suddenly leapt out here, the destitution one did not expect to meet here, surprises and makes a deep impression, for if it is hard for those who were brought up in poverty, it is doubly hard for those who are only now getting used to poverty.

— What need I tell you — the master of the house says to me, a man dressed more than modestly and yet unusually clean — you have probably already heard a little about me, and why wouldn't you have heard? I ran quite fine businesses, and dozens of Jews made a living around me. Need I tell you what kind of house [?] was kept at my place? Eh! [?] It isn't worth reopening the wounds! It was one-two: only yesterday a rich man, and today already just as you see me. There had been bad times in business more than once before, and so, when the crisis came the last time and people stopped paying me, I kept thinking: it will pass, I'll steer my way through somehow. To the very last moment I paid my debts, wanted to remain an honest man, but it was beyond my strength; I had to withdraw from the "vis" [? doubtful word], life spat me out. I have already given up everything, but the shame, the shame I cannot bear; I would rather die of hunger ten times than have anyone find out what is going on with me and put on a pitying face over me.

I took my leave and went away from that home with a heavy heart.

I take stock: it is not the want that made such a heavy impression — perhaps I have seen greater want. It is the tragic picture of a human life ground down by the millstones of time; it is the tragedy of a man over whose head the wheel of fate has turned: downhill.

And on that very same day I happened to be in another such home.

I was looking for a room, and from an acquaintance I received the address of a respectable family that wants to let a room.

I knocked; an old woman with silver-grey hair and a refined face, on which lay traces of a former beauty, opened for me. She looked at me with sad eyes and answered my questions in a stifled whisper:
— Yes, a room is let here.

The woman invited me into the flat, and so, while we were talking about the room, I meanwhile managed to take a look around me.

We were in a large, spacious room. A sombre gloom looked down from the old furniture, which once had probably cost very much; a greyness looked down from the walls, and a sad wind blew from the pictures that hung on the walls.

One word led to another, and the woman, who at first had been so closed up in herself and talked only about "the room that is let here", began to grow more talkative and started to tell about her troubles.

— My husband — she told — was a big merchant, kept a large house; I did not meddle in my husband's business and never knew how things looked there. Only some two years ago, when my husband died and I had to take an interest in the business, did I see that we had been in arrears for a good few years already. There you see: as long as my husband lived, the little wheel kept turning, and when he passed away, everything collapsed like a house of cards.

— You see, about myself I no longer have any worry; there isn't much left to drag on to the end. But when I think about the children, everything goes dark for me. You understand, dear man, the children were brought up in luxury, not used to any worry at all — and what are they to do now? Even if they wanted to work — does one get work in present times? Meanwhile I do what I can. I have sold off from the house everything that is marketable. Now I am letting the room, and all of us will move into the kitchen. But what will be next? The children are growing up — what will become of them? Unless even "bushtovitz" [? unclear word]...

— "A room to let here" — does the chance passer-by who reads these words on a slip of paper know about the quiet tragedy that lurks behind this sentence?
