Why Must One Obtain a Journeyman's Diploma?

[Crafts — the Industrial Law; journeyman's diploma; article.]
The 1934 amendment ("novella") to the Industrial Law of 1927 was a victory for those craftsmen's activists and the chambers of crafts that strive to introduce, fully and one hundred per cent, the regulation of the crafts in Poland.
On 16 December of this year it will be 10 years since the Industrial Law came into force, and those craftsmen or craft workers who did not adapt themselves to the provisions of this law now deeply regret that they did not use the time when legalising one's position in the crafts was in practice liberal [the word "was" is printed twice] and was not bound up with so many costs and other formalities.
Now one can already see how well the craftsmen did [?] who in 1935 legalised their workshops. Today the situation is such that of those who seek a craftsman's card by way of "dispensation", at least 10 years of work in the trade are already demanded. If the applicant [?] lacks a few months of practice in the trade, or if he is younger than 25–26, he is not admitted to the qualification examination at all.
Some chambers of crafts already demand [—] from those who seek a craftsman's card by way of "dispensation" that they be able to write in their own hand a curriculum vitae, a quotation [?], an invoice, etc.
Today the situation is such that efforts are made to abolish entirely Art. 146 (on "dispensation"), and the aim is that those engaged in crafts should meet Art. 145, under which one must [?] show a journeyman's diploma and 3 years of practice as a certified journeyman.
When seeking admission to the journeyman's examination one must, under the regulations, show a written apprenticeship contract, as well as a certificate of completion of a vocational continuation school. Almost 80 per cent of the Jewish workers engaged in crafts, as well as young craftsmen who already hold craftsman's cards, do not meet these regulations. This great mass engaged in crafts (from the age of 18 upward) must therefore make use of the relief circular on admission to the simplified journeyman's examination.
Circular No. 28 of the Ministry of Industry and Commerce gives all those who do not yet hold journeyman's diplomas, workers and craftsmen alike, the opportunity to sit the simplified journeyman's examination, even if they cannot show a contract for the 3-year apprenticeship they completed at the time, even if they trained with masters who were not certified and not entitled to employ apprentices, and also did not finish any vocational continuation school — provided they apply for admission to the simplified journeyman's examination by 30 June 1937.
So in all only 2 months remain to make use of this important relief. Until this deadline every single person engaged in crafts can seek admission to the journeyman's examination and obtain a journeyman's diploma. Nor may one forget for a single minute that legalising oneself as a certified journeyman is not merely a private matter, but includes [?] in general the interest of legally preserving the Jewish stake in the crafts.
Under the conditions that have arisen and the prevailing tendencies, the journeyman's diploma is the only legal document that makes it possible to strengthen and secure the future influx of Jews into the crafts. Holding a journeyman's diploma gives a legal possibility of becoming independent and of increasing the number of certified craftsmen, thanks to whom Jewish youth will have the possibility of learning a trade in accordance with the provisions of the law.
The young Christian craftsmen take account of the new requirements and conditions, and they go to the journeyman's examinations. Unfortunately the Jews take no account of them and treat this matter lightly. Later, however, it will not be possible to put this right, and we will have no one to blame. We ourselves will be the guilty ones if we do not make use of the relief of admission to the simplified journeyman's examination.
Let us think it over while it is not too late. The few dozen złoty that carrying out the formalities and the journeyman's examination will cost must not be an obstacle to legally preserving the only productive position that we still hold now.
It is worth [?] carrying out at once all the necessary formalities connected with sitting the journeyman's examination. Do not put it off till tomorrow; submit applications with the necessary documents to the appropriate chambers of crafts.
We believe that the Jewish working man, with his usual good sense, will understand that we must not let ourselves be pushed down to a lower level in the crafts. We must be prepared for the new times and their hard requirements and conditions.
Let us therefore master all our weaknesses. Let us make the greatest efforts and provide ourselves with journeyman's diplomas. Thanks to this, Jewish working people will be able to pursue their crafts in peace and avoid fines for not conforming to the provisions of the Industrial Law, and will also be able to bring up the young Jewish generation in the crafts.
Chanan Hasman.
What One Can Get Rich From Today

[United States — feuilleton; report from Vienna.]
Which of us has not already spent his time solving the puzzles in various newspapers? One can always see people so absorbed in this work that, as soon as they enter a café where newspapers are lying about, they immediately set "to work" and do not rest until all the puzzles there have been solved — or until they realise that the effort is in vain: they cannot solve the puzzle.
In trains and trams they forget when they have to get off, because they are absorbed in the thought of how to find, for instance, a large body of water in North America with five letters...
But that one can make a living from these puzzles, or even get rich — not everyone knows that.
In the larger cities overseas there are special clubs and societies that occupy themselves solely with solving puzzles; they publish their own newspapers and announce prizes for solving difficult puzzles with quite large premiums — a thousand dollars, for example, for such a winner is no rare prize.
There is even one man, Frank Davis by name, from Springfield in North America, who now lives in New York, who is famous for the fact that for ten years no one has yet devised a puzzle that he would not solve. Yet this Davis is not an especially educated person: altogether he completed four classes of gymnasium; nevertheless he is so gifted at puzzles that he wins all the premiums at all the meetings, tournaments and congresses of puzzle-solvers, who are not few in America.
In Europe, a few years ago, there was a meeting of the European societies of puzzle-solvers in Leipzig, during the fair there. Davis was then in Europe for the first time, and we, the press people, had a conversation with him about his great "success".
Davis told us that he had come upon the idea of becoming a professional puzzle-solver once in a bar in New York, when he watched a young, pretty girl — it was the film actress Norma Shearer — struggling to solve a puzzle in a newspaper. He began to help her and within a few minutes the puzzle was solved. As a reward the girl gave him a kiss, and one of the gentlemen who were with her remarked: "The kiss is worth more than a hundred dollars"...
It was then that Davis got the idea of trying whether one could really receive a hundred dollars in cash for solving puzzles too, or at least something of that kind of value.
He began himself to compose difficult puzzles for newspapers, which almost no one could solve, founded puzzle associations and clubs, organised meetings and tournaments with larger premiums, and won almost all the prizes [himself]. He became known as the greatest genius in the "trade", so that for ten years he has been living quite well from it and has indeed become a rich man from the "profession"...
In the course of the last ten years Davis threw over all his business — he had been a farmer[?] — moved to New York and "now works only at solving and composing puzzles". During this time he has won forty thousand dollars in cash, ten automobiles, of which he sold nine and took in about fifteen thousand dollars in cash, two beautiful villas on the seashore, the finest furniture for the villas — even cows, horses and other animals that roam about in his stable were all won by solving puzzles.
As the American newspapers report, in the last year he won more than a hundred prizes, that is, two prizes every week. Prizes worth less than a hundred dollars (in cash or in kind) he does not even touch.
And the public in various countries invites him everywhere to demonstrate his skills, and everywhere he wins and grows rich from this livelihood.
Z. Haber, Vienna.

(Great victory of the Sosnowiec kehilla administration. — A new government in the synagogue in Old Sosnowiec. — A split in the "Mizrachi" minyan in Katowice. — Righteous women will bring the Redemption. — We ride a carousel. — R' Yaakov pays. — The Redemption stands at the door.)
The day of last Pesach Sheni should without doubt be written in golden letters in the history of the Jewish kehilla in Sosnowiec. Among the nations of the world such an event would have been turned into a national holiday and the heroes would have been immortalised — is it a small thing, to bring down a "government" that always threatened the peace of a whole town?
— "If all the waters were to become ink", it would not be enough to record all the events that took place on the premises of the synagogue in Old Sosnowiec. The walls of that synagogue are literally soaked with the blood of the victims who fell on Sabbaths and holidays in the field of the "distribution" of aliyot, hakafot and the like.
But as King Solomon says — to every thing there is a season, for everything there is a time, and the time has indeed come when the "walls of Jericho" fell, and together with them fell also the rule of the old gabbaim in the above-mentioned synagogue.
True, the new kehilla administration lost no small amount of strength until it managed to master the enemy camp, which, besides "human material", also held[?] a document from the former kehilla commissioner stating that the gabbai-ship belonged to them; but all these rights were rejected by[?] this[?] R' Dovid, who was entrusted with the portfolio of the kehilla departments for Old Sosnowiec, and at his stern call the old gabbaim abdicated.
This news — so we are told — was received with joy by the whole Jewish population of Old Sosnowiec, because with the abdication, they believe, the restless days so far come to an end and days of peace and unity begin.
— Would that it were so.
———
In the Mizrachi minyan in Katowice, where peace and calm always reigned, a "black cat" has run through and kindled a fire — may God alone protect and save us — let the fire not flare up any further.
And do you perhaps think that the quarrel flared up over earthly matters? You are mistaken. Katowice Jews (even the Polish ones...) are not yet as "cultured" as "ours"; there they do not have such foolishness in mind as we do, and the quarrel in the "Mizrachi" minyan of the holy community of Katowice, too, broke out over a "matter of principle".
And this is how it happened.
On the first Sabbath after Passover some of the worshippers got a better appetite and decided that the time of prayer on the Sabbath should be changed: instead of 10 o'clock, people should stand up to pray at 9 o'clock.
When the gabbai received the decision, he said "no" with an aleph. We Mizrachists — he declared — do not retreat, and the time of prayer remains as before, 10 o'clock as previously, and whoever has not the self-restraint to wait until 10 may go and look elsewhere.
The "left" camp, grouped around the so-called "9-ers", laughed at the gabbai's declaration and "let the train leave an hour earlier"...
When the gabbai arrived for prayers they were already at "Yekum Purkan". So he made them a real "Mi she-berakh", but the "9-ers" were not frightened by this and "kept on riding"...
As our correspondent assures us, the gabbai's position has become stronger, because the Mizrachi women — a large number of whom belong[?] to the "9-ers" — side with the gabbai that the prayer time used until now should remain unchanged; and since, as is known[?], the Jews were redeemed from the Egyptian exile thanks to the merit of the righteous women, it is to be expected that the gabbai's victory over the "9-ers" is also assured...
———
And that we live in "the time of the beginning of the Redemption" we were convinced at the last session of the Będzin town council.
As is known, the nations of the world are very busy with the Jewish question; naturally, the problem is not handled uniformly, according to one system, because it depends[?] on the conjuncture. We sit, for example, on the world carousel and the holders of power spin us around, and so the very "good friends" say "human beings" about us three times, and the moderate ones — make do with once.
Among the moderates are also counted the left-wing speakers of the Będzin town council; they too show their "friendship" for us only at certain times. For example, they are not against the Jewish "comrades" demonstrating together with them on the First of May, and also in the budget debate.
And when the municipal budget was discussed last Saturday night, the leader of the left actually demanded that the municipal fee on Jewish ritual slaughter be raised by 100 percent: if they want to eat kosher meat — he said — let them, the "Jewish bourgeoisie", that is, pay five złoty a kilo... Exactly as the verse says:
— R' Yaakov pays...
It does not matter whether the proposal was adopted or fell; what matters is the very fact, which gives us full certainty that "the Redemption is near", since the generation is already "wholly guilty"... Moreover, if we add that comrade Dr. P. came out against the proposal made by his comrade, then it is surely clear that all the sufferings that Jews endure are already the true birth-pangs and that we stand before "the beginning of the Redemption"...
Ben Amotz.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Emor)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Emor
—o—
a) "Speak unto the priests... There shall none be defiled for the dead among his people" (Lev. 21:1)
The preceding portion speaks of the necromancers and wizards (ov and yidoni), idolatrous priests who foretold the future with the help of the bones of the dead. Here comes the warning that Jewish priests may not occupy themselves with the dead... Ibn Crescas.
—o—
b) "And the high priest among his brethren" (ibid., 10)
"In wealth..." Midrash Tanhuma.
A German "maskil" asked the pious Baron R' Binyamin Wolf Rothschild: does the Torah, God forbid, also teach that great is he who has more wealth?
He answered:
Here the meaning is a different one. A high priest must be independent of anyone's opinion, and if one of the priests were richer than he, he would no longer be fully independent, for it is already man's weakness to be submissive [?] towards one richer than himself... Sometimes this finds expression in flattery, sometimes in a subconscious deference towards the richer man; in any case, fully independent can only be the richest man, and therefore the high priest must also be great in wealth.
—o—
c) "Neither shall ye do thus in your land" (22:24)
"This thing — to castrate any domestic or wild animal"...
"Whence do we know that castrating a human being is forbidden?" Rashi.
"Scripture says: neither shall ye do thus in your land — whatever is in your land is forbidden." Shabbat 110b.
For in biblical times it was customary to castrate people and animals, and this meant, as it were, handing over to idolatry the procreative power of man and beast; and thereby one understands what is said: "He that is wounded in the stones, or hath his privy member cut off, shall not enter into the congregation of the Lord." Why was a castrated man forbidden to enter the congregation of the Lord? Because the eunuch had been made so in honour of idolatry.
And thereby the words in Isaiah become understandable too: "Neither let the son of the stranger... neither let the eunuch say" (Isaiah 56:3), because the castrated are foreigners, servants of idolatry...
And in the Gospel (Matthew, as printed: 6 [?] 12–15 [?]) it is told that the first Christians castrated themselves for God...
Dr. Shlomo Rubin.
—o—
d) "Speak unto the children of Israel and say unto them, the feasts of the Lord..."
The whole portion is addressed to the priests ("Speak unto the priests"), and only here, concerning the intercalation of the years (see Rashi), is "Speak unto the children of Israel" emphasised, because the priests had no part in it, since the rule is indeed "A priest is not seated [on the court] for the intercalation of the month" (Rosh Hashanah, folio 11 [?]); and therefore this portion concerns only the children of Israel and not the priests...
R' Yehonatan Eybeschütz.
—o—
e) "And when ye reap the harvest of your land" (ibid., 22)
"I am the first and I am the last" — every beginning must be sanctified to God. With grain, at the beginning one brought the omer, and at the end of the reaping: "Thou shalt not make clean riddance of the corners of thy field when thou reapest, neither shalt thou gather any gleaning of thy harvest; thou shalt leave them unto the poor and to the stranger." And with bread too one must sanctify the beginning ("the first of your dough") and the end (Grace after Meals is commanded by the Torah); and on Passover, Shavuot and Sukkot, too, the first and the last day are sanctified...
R' Moshe Alshich.
—o—
f) "They shall therefore keep my charge, lest they bear sin for it" (22:9)
Yosef Rosenthal [?], the famous maskil, met R' Yashe Bern [?] and asked him:
The Torah states an explicit prohibition, "Ye shall not add", and the rabbis pretend not to know and keep adding stringencies upon stringencies, fences upon fences; does "ye shall not add" not apply to rabbinic commandments just as to the commandments of the Torah?
He answered him:
The Torah says "They shall keep my charge" ("make a guard for my charge", fences upon fences — the Sages), and to this an incomprehensible phrase is added, "lest they bear sin for it" — which means precisely that the sin of "ye shall not add" does not apply to these fences of the rabbinic commandments.
To what may this be compared? To a prescription that a doctor writes for a patient, telling him to drink tea after it. Of the prescription he may not drink a single drop more than the doctor prescribes; if he does take more, he may even poison himself. The tea, on the other hand, he may drink as much as he likes.
So too with the commandments of the Torah, which are in the category of medicines: one may not add to them a hair's breadth; it is different with the rabbinic commandments, which are like tea after the medicines — for them there is no longer any warning [?] not to add to them...
—o—
g) "As well the stranger as he that is born in the land, when he blasphemeth the Name, shall be put to death" (24:16)
It never occurred to Jews to suppose that a stranger should be treated worse than a citizen, that he should have fewer rights than him. The supposition might rather have been that he should have fewer duties than a citizen, less punishment; and this is what the Torah needs to state explicitly — that the stranger, too, must have the same duties and the same systems of punishment as a citizen, a burgher; but about rights there need be no talk at all — that the stranger has the same as a burgher. That is the Jewish morality of state.
Imrei Chen.

[Literature — feuilleton; diary pages.] By P. Blumenkranz (Częstochowa).
(Pages from a friend's diary).

Today I find myself in an extraordinarily strange and heavy mood. Something is pressing on my heart. I feel as cramped as an asthmatic. I stride up and down the room, try to read, to sing — and it doesn't work.
I want to find the reason and I don't succeed. Everything gets tangled in my brain. Reasons there are plenty — go figure it out.
Almost an hour ago I ran to the cinema; maybe I would forget myself. I watched a billing-and-cooing couple impatiently and walked out in the middle.
I tried strolling in the street, but suddenly I felt a tiredness in my limbs, a tiredness that comes from apathy — and back home...
Ha, isn't that really the main reason, that I am not capable of living? Ordinary people live, after all, without inquiries, without searching; they fit their desires to the possibilities — and I?
In the house it grows darker; the shouts of children absorbed in play penetrate to me, hammer [?] in my tired head and sound alarm calls. I want by all means to calm down, I want to divert my thoughts, think about something — and it doesn't work.
I take the calendar and leaf [?] through the pages as if I needed to find something, and read the notes aloud: "Tachanun and Lamnatzeach are not said; one stops saying Barchi Nafshi; before Mincha one says 'Avadim hayinu'; at Maariv 'Vihi noam' and 'Ve-ata kadosh' are not said." Once I read it louder, take fright at my own voice and break off.
I confess: in the face of today's life I would be ashamed to write about this publicly. Once people boasted of torments of the soul; Dostoevsky was admired, Przybyszewski — imitated. Moods were a kind of coquetry; for fashion's sake people even abused them.
Today people laugh at that. More just matters now fill the world; matters that have significance for the collective and not for the isolated, worthless creature.
And then again:
Sometimes I really doubt whether the concern for the unfortunate many [?] truly overshadows the suffering of the individual. It seems to me, on the contrary, that everyone's excessive concern for himself blocks the eyes from taking a look at the creature who is in agony [—] [?]; that the sufferings and torments of the individual have been pushed aside because of our [—] [?], vulgar, materialistic egocentrism.
And in these minutes I hate man.
I run into the street to drive away my loneliness, and tremble at the thought of coming near people — above all, of talking with them. Their banality, their self-love, peering out of their average, smugly bourgeois and smirking faces, disgusts me. I then feel a physical pain at every encounter with them.
But at that very moment a second thought always gets entangled, which mocks me:
— Perhaps your hatred of and disgust with people are a consequence of your own mediocrity. Perhaps it actually hurts you that you cannot rise above the great grey mass? Great men also had a similar feeling — Tolstoy, for example, in his young years, and others. They rose above it, and you crawl [?] on the earth like a worm!
• • •
In the house it is twilight-sad; I pace around like a prisoner in his cell. A little bird stood on the window sill, cast a roguish [?] glance with one little eye, hopped to a crumb [?] and fled. Others saw it, gathered on the window, snatched bits of bread in their beaks and flew off.
I come closer to the window. The drive of these little birds to keep themselves alive grips me! Two little birds chase each other with a twittering and fly into an opening in the cornice [?]; others chase each other among the branches — "she" pretends to run away and "he" chases with manly [?] stubbornness.
The yard with its bustle grips me. A dog, a big yellow one with drooping ears, stands by a window and barks [?]; his "beloved" is locked in, the match does not please the owners, and he looks up with his sad eyes and howls with longing.
A Jewish woman, with the help of her children, runs across the yard with outspread arms and drives the hens into the coop. They wriggle [?] out from under her hands and escape with a flapping of wings. Sweaty and dishevelled [?], she holds a fat goose in her lap and forcibly stuffs the food down its throat. The little ones hum like a beehive. Some play soldiers, each with a little stick on his shoulder, and march: one, two, three, four. Another group plays "klasy" [hopscotch]: one wants to get through with eyes closed and a little stone on his shoe; he walks carefully and steals a glance to see whether he is stepping on the line; the gang catches him and he is "disqualified".
A young wife, tearful and out of breath [?], shouts at the top of her voice at the maid:
— Kareli, Kareli.
She has come with the [—] [?] and to carry out of the [—] [?].
A young man stands at a window with a girl and talks and talks; her eyes shine. He says something; she pats him fondly on the hands and tousles [?] his "forelock".
— Ha, everything lives without calculations, and you sit twiddling your thumbs — I argue with myself. I want to persuade myself that it must be so for me too, and it doesn't help; I feel as if something is tearing inside me. I want to divert my thought, forget it with something, and something glimmers before my eyes.
The young man said goodbye to the girl and, going away, looked back every moment, as if they were parting for months.
I watch, and during this scene I feel even lonelier and more forsaken. I want to make light of it — and something knocks inside me stubbornly.
The young man has already disappeared, and the picture surfaces even more vividly. "You are no longer capable of all this" — a wild thought tramples [?] me — "you move away from life with every step, and life away from you — with three."
I stand as if glued [?] to the window. The "eye" opposite [the window across the yard] has already gone out. I stand and stare rigidly into the growing darkness.
Suddenly I feel something salty in the corners of my mouth. Have I really come to such brokenness?
Ashamed and hastily I wipe my face and run out of the house.
But where to? How does one run away from oneself?

A. Zaglembier — The Living Dead Man (6)

[Literature — serialised novel.] A. Zaglembier: The Living Dead Man. (A highly suspenseful novel of Jewish life in Zagłębie before and after the World War). 6)
Summary of the beginning of the novel.
On a winter[?] evening before the World War, when two Cossacks were to transfer the dangerous bandit "Szmulek Łapka" into the Piotrków prison, they were suddenly attacked on the way to the Będzin station by two disguised "strażniks" [guards] — Łapka's helpers. At daybreak the Cossacks were found lying bound with gagged mouths, and Szmulek "Łapka", set free, had fled to the Gzichów road and hidden somewhere.
That same evening, and almost at the very same hour, the universally known, respectable debt-collector Josl Wertheim — a father of three children — suddenly disappeared. His wife Sarah'tshe runs about the town terribly desperate, searching for him in every possible hiding place in all of Zagłębie. But Josl Wertheim has vanished like a stone in water...
Everyone stands before an extraordinary riddle. At last, on the seventh[?] day, the pockmarked Wacek reports to police inspector Charecki and tells him that on that day he saw Wertheim walking on the Gzichów road together with the Christian Wanda Komarska — a pretty young shikse whom Wacek had been courting as a match for himself.
Wanda is immediately arrested and taken in for questioning.
Now read on.
Charecki gives Wanda a sharp look in the eyes:
"What sort of memory do you have? You remember nothing?"
"Almost nothing..."
"And perhaps I should remind you?.."
"What?... What do they want from me?"
"The truth!" — Charecki suddenly springs up from his seat and cries out in anger — "The truth is what I want from you and nothing more! So answer: you were acquainted with the missing Jasiek Wertheim?"
Wanda turns red, confused. Her heart starts to pound harder and she answers quietly:
"Yes."
"And his wife, Sarah Wertheim, do you know her?"
"I saw her once.."
"And how long have you known him?"
"Not long.."
"And when did you last see Jasiek Wertheim?"
"Oh, quite a long time ago.."
"Roughly? A week, two, three?"
"About that!.."
"I asked you to 'tell' the truth! And you keep on lying!"
"I don't remember any more..."
Charecki bends very close to her face and looks her straight in the eyes:
"And last Wednesday evening you didn't meet him?!"
Wanda cannot bear his piercing gaze; she feels as if something were drawing[?] her into a faint, and answers still more quietly:
"No..."
"And I say: yes! You walked with Jasiek Wertheim along the Gzichów road, to the woods!"
"I?.."
"Yes, you with your beloved Wertheim!" — Charecki specially underlines the word "beloved" — "It was evening time. You went there together, but on the way back — it was already night — you walked alone, without Wertheim. And after that walk with you Wertheim vanished like a stone in water, leaving his wife and children like a widow with orphans! Only you alone must know what happened to Jasiek Wertheim, what took place between you that evening, and perhaps one more p e r s o n was with you then!"
But Wanda remains as stubborn as before:
"I know nothing.."
"It will be better for you if you tell the truth. I have witnesses who saw you walking with Wertheim that evening!"
"Me? I wasn't there and nobody saw me.."
Seeing that he would get nowhere with Wanda by kindness, police inspector Charecki tore himself from his seat, ran into the next room, came back with the pockmarked Wacek and asked Wanda, shouting very[?] agitatedly:
"And him, Wacek, did you see him that evening on the Gzichów road?.."
But now Wanda can no longer answer anything, because on catching sight of the pockmarked Wacek she lets out a terrible scream and falls into a faint...
Seeing Wanda Komarska collapsed and fainted, police inspector Charecki is sure that now at last the tragic disappearance of Josl Wertheim will be cleared up...
Otherwise Wanda would surely not have been so frightened and fainted instantly at the sight of a witness to the terrible event of that evening.
Yes, now she will certainly tell the whole truth, now he will at last get to the bottom of the tragic secret...
And therefore he at once called several more men into his office, who began to revive Wanda. Her parents, who were waiting outside, were told nothing about their daughter having fainted. To all their impatient and anxious questions came a gloomy answer from the duty officer:
"Lost[?] — it will[?] take a while, and if you have no time, go home; your daughter won't get lost..."
The pockmarked Wacek too helped bring Wanda round, and meanwhile he thought: perhaps Wanda will love him again now? Now, when she is accused of such a thing...
And after ten minutes they succeeded in reviving Wanda. She opened her eyes, and for the first while she was still in such a state as if people and things were hung with some transparent veil[?]. She also opened her mouth with its clenched teeth, which earlier the summoned[?] feldsher together with everyone else had not managed to do. And when she had sighed[?] and come to[?], and grasped where she actually was, she clutched her face with her hands and sobbed quietly.
Everyone moved away from her; only police inspector Charecki remained standing beside her and began to speak very gently, almost paternally:
"Well, Miss Wanda, are you feeling better now?"
"Yes."
"I myself would like you to go home as soon as possible[?], but you still have to answer me certain questions. Therefore... I mean... do you want to speak in Wacek's presence, or would you rather stay with me eye to eye?"
Hearing Wacek's name, Wanda turned her head and looked at the pockmarked man with boundless hatred, so that he was quite lost for shame — for it was he, Wacek, who had now brought this misfortune upon her... He surely came and spun[?] an invented libel against her... This is how he wanted to take revenge on her, because she does not want him as a bridegroom. But will they believe her that she is innocent and knows nothing? That it was merely a tragic coincidence that precisely on that evening, when Josl Wertheim — her beloved — vanished without trace, she was with him then on a date [randka] in the woods? Will they believe her that she too truly does not know where Josl Wertheim has got to since then?... Oh, if not for that cursed Wacek, the pockmarked one, who saw them both walking there, but on the way back saw only her alone, Wanda...
And sighing even harder after the heavy faint, Wanda struggles with herself over the question: "To tell the whole truth or not?" At last she decides: yes, she will tell the truth, only the truth! "For the truth one isn't beaten, after all"... In any case she will not be able to bear the "secret" within her much longer, a secret which in a few minutes will have to come out into the world anyway... Why[?] deny and perhaps make things worse. Yes, only the pure truth.
And still looking with hatred at the pockmarked man, Wanda answers Charecki's earlier question:
"No, I don't want any witnesses, I don't want to speak in their presence..."
"Ah, bitte sehr, with pleasure..."
(To be continued).

Painting Season.

With the coming of spring the painter's trade has come back to life; wherever one goes and wherever one strides[?], one bumps into white[?] benches[?] with the inscription:

May Day Appeal of the Flight Union.

Comrade "fleers" [members of the union of those who flee their creditors]!
On the 1st of May, as on every 1st [of the month], falls the day on which we must fulfil our duty towards dunning humanity. A "solidary" feeling pervades all our account-books, which show nothing but deficits; on this day we all go out into the street to look for an interest-free loan. We march "renowned"[?], our businesses closed, carrying in front of us the bills of exchange we have issued.
We all meet at the Notary (Rejent) Square. There we shout out our mighty protest and present our strong "[—]" against the printed and signed bills of exchange. From there we march in one flight-procession to the railway station.
Down with throwing oneself from the upper floors! Paying a debt is the business of the dunners themselves!
For the Flight Union ("Foot-makers")
Maske.
From "the Other World"

Greetings from a modest woman of Sosnowiec...
Mrs. Murenitshkova[?] fell ill. Before her death her husband says to her:
— Royzele, my crown, before you die tell me: have you never been unfaithful to me?
— Not even once. For every time that I was unfaithful to you, may I turn over in my grave once.
A few days later she died.
The husband took it very much to heart, and a week later he too "made skvartl"[?] [apparently: died].

— No, not here. Perhaps in Gehenna; go there, perhaps you will find her there.
Arriving in Gehenna, he asks the Gehenna shammes:
— Is my Royzele here?
— Yes, she is here — the Gehenna shammes answered — but I hardly believe you will recognise her.
— Why?
— Because she serves here as a — ventilator...

What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin: The Municipal Budget before the Plenum of the City Council

What's New in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 19 Iyar 5697 — piątek 30 kwietnia 1937 [Friday, 30 April 1937].)
Będzin
The Municipal Budget before the Plenum of the City Council.
A new tax of 75,000 zł. — A proposal by the Left to raise the levy on ritual slaughter. — Jews sell the "birthright" for 600 zł.
The last session of the City Council once again revealed the fragmentation and the lack of a sense of responsibility that prevail among the Jewish councillors. All the groupings come to the sessions with settled decisions on every question — and with us? A "generation of the dispersion" (Babel) mood: one says day, the other says night, and the upshot is that only the third party profits...
The session is chaired by the vice-president, Mr. Gac [?]. After several formal items on the agenda have been dealt with, the road tax (podatek drogowy) is taken up, on which alderman (ławnik) Mr. Rubinlicht takes the floor. After his speech sharp incidents occur between him and the president. By the majority of all the non-Jewish and left-wing councillors (Jewish ones too) the tax is adopted in the amount of 30 thousand zł.
Councillor Aron Hampel moves an amendment [?] that poor cab drivers (dorożkarze) and carters (furmani) who have only one horse be exempted from the tax. The vice-president promised to take this into account and exempt them.
By the same majority it is also resolved that the municipal bonds (obligacje; "Loan of 1918") be repaid over... 50 years.
"Appetite comes with eating": the Left moves a proposal to earmark a sum of 75,000 zł for building a school in Ksawera. Alderman Rubinlicht and councillor Silberberg speak against the proposal, but the majority decides. (For the new tax, which, by the way, will flow in from Jewish pockets, the councillor of the "Hitachdut" also votes.)
The "highlight" [?] of the session was the budget for the year 1937/38, to which a series of amendments and proposals are put forward, among them one from the Left to raise the levy on ritual slaughter by 100 percent. The proposal is strongly supported by alderman Laskowski (PPS), who "argues" that "whoever wants to play at ceremonies should pay 5 zł per kilo of meat".
The Left receives a fitting reply from Dr. Perl, Mrs. Z. Szajn, alderman Rubinlicht, H. S. [?] Silberberg, A. Hampel and Grunwald. The proposal is referred to a committee.
The whole discussion around the budget (already with "friendly words" [?] exchanged between one another) lasts about an hour and a half, and, presumably by prior agreement, councillor Grinwald proposes adopting the budget en bloc with the amendment that the subsidy of 600 zł for Jewish chadarim be raised to 1,200 zł.
The proposal is adopted with the votes of the B.B. [BBWR, the pro-government "Non-Party Bloc"] and their … [?] little Jews...
The total budget sum amounts to 1,853,761 zł, higher than before by 79,724 zł.
General Meeting of "Hakoach"

On Saturday the annual meeting of "Hakoach" took place in the premises of the Merchants' Association. With a very large number of members present, the chairman, Mr. S. A report on the activity is given by the secretary, Mr. Aleksandrowicz, who dwells in particular on the Maccabi–Hapoel [?] matter and comes to the conclusion that joint cooperation between the two associations is possible given good will on both sides. Despite all the difficulties the board fulfilled its task. During the past year the following sections were active: football, tennis, gymnastics, boxing, cycling, handball, athletics and music. Gratitude is also expressed to the editors of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" for their serious attitude to sports matters.
The treasurer's report is given by Mgr. H. Bauszykowski [?], from which a satisfactory state of affairs emerges.
After the report of the auditing committee, the board is granted discharge (absolutorium).
After the election of the new board, the question of building a sports building is discussed, in connection with which gratitude and recognition are expressed to the chairman, S. Fürstenberg.
Aid Fund for Jewish Craftsmen

In its own premises (Kołłątaja 32) the first general meeting of the Aid Fund for Jewish Craftsmen took place. After the reports on the activity to date, a board was elected consisting of: Szlama Zelinger (chairman), Lejzer Steinberg (vice-chairman), Jechezkiel Neugas [?] (secretary), Zajdel [?] Lewkowicz (treasurer) and Szmul Lejb Judkiewicz. The Industrialists' and Merchants' Association

[The Industrialists' and Merchants' Association] informs us that the Ministry of Education is now considering the possibility of exempting children who attend secondary and vocational schools from the obligation to wear on the left sleeve the number and initials of the school. It is therefore advisable for the manufacturers and dealers of these badges (tarcze) not to lay in large stocks.
Rabbi Chameides Studies Pirkei Avot with the Jewish Soldiers

On Sunday the first prayer service with the Jewish soldiers of the local garrison took place in the town synagogue, with the participation of Rabbi Chameides of Katowice. On the strength of the report in our newspaper a large crowd gathered in the synagogue, but at the request of the above-mentioned rabbi the civilian public left the synagogue.
The service proceeded in the following order: the cantor, Mr. Klagsbald [?], recites 10 chapters of Psalms with the soldiers; then Rabbi Chameides gives a short introduction about the plan [?] of the services that will take place every Sunday, and he begins to study Pirkei Avot from "Moses received the Torah from Sinai", in fine Polish, and explains the content from Moses up to the Men of the Great Assembly, who received the Torah.
At the end he points out to the soldiers that whoever has tefillin should bring them along. Prayer books and Chumashim are provided by the military authorities.
How “Aunt Tsvetl's son-in-law” swindled Feivel the gravedigger out of 90 zł. and a dollar bond

On Wednesday night, while Feivel Pieczacki [?], the community gravedigger, was busy at the cemetery, he was told that an unknown “traveller” [?] was calling for him. Both went into the tahara house, where the strange guest told Pieczacki to go at once to Dąbrowa, to Jakub Winer [?], Wiejska [?] 3.
— For what purpose must one go to Dąbrowa? — Pieczacki asked.
— For your own good — the “guest” answered with a smile — yes, something very important awaits you there.
Hearing such words, Pieczacki invited the guest to his home and treated him to a glass of tea. But the guest kept smiling, looked around the house and smiled.
At a certain moment the person asks Pieczacki: do you have sisters abroad?
— Yes, two sisters in Brazil [?]; one is called Rachel and the other — Tsvetl, but for a very long time now we have had no news of them.
— So? One is Tsvetl, you say? And I am in fact your sister Tsvetl's son-in-law — the person blurted out with a laugh — but at the same time I bring you sad news: Rachel is no longer alive.
— God in heaven! — Feivel clapped his hands for joy — you are my sister's son-in-law?
— Yes, yes, dear uncle [lit. “uncle, crown”], I have indeed come from America and brought the uncle 50 dollars; I for my part give you, uncle, 25 dollars; besides that I have brought clothes, which are in Dąbrowa at Winer's.
One can easily imagine the joy in the Pieczacki home — no small thing: a saving angel had brought so many dollars, and on top of that [promised?] to send 10 dollars every month, on condition that the uncle should be able to go away to a summer dwelling.
After chatting a little with the “family”, he proposed that the uncle and aunt go with him to Dąbrowa to collect the clothes, and in Będzin he would change the dollars.
All three did go to Dąbrowa, but on reaching Będzin he “remembered” that he had left his passport in Dąbrowa; so he told the aunt to go for the passport, while he and the uncle would wait in front of the bank on Kołłątaja Street.
When the “aunt” had gone to Dąbrowa, the person also “sent off” the uncle, and he himself went back to the Pieczackis, burst into the house in a hurry saying that “the clothes must [?] be redeemed at once”, and with various tricks he managed to cheat the Pieczackis out of a whole [?] 90 zł., and the Pieczackis' girl out of a “dolarówka” [dollar-loan bond], and vanished.
Until late [?] Pieczacki and his wife searched for “the aunt's son-in-law” with the dollars, but later they saw that they had fallen victim to a sophisticated swindler.
Sosnowiec — The deposit for buying a plot for a cemetery to be handed over to the community board

The chairmen of the community board and of the council intervened with the starost, Mr. Kędzierski [?], so that the 16 000 zł. for purchasing a plot for the cemetery, deposited in the Commercial Bank by the former community commissioner, be handed over to the control of an elected committee appointed by the community board.
The starost took note of the request and [will issue] the necessary order.

Dr. Maladysta [?], member of the audit committee of the Magistrate [municipality], received 245 zł. for his work on the audit carried out. General meeting of the Gemilut Chesed (free-loan) fund in Pogoń

On Sunday a general members' meeting of the local Gemilut Chesed fund took place in Pogoń. Certain seat-grabbers mobilised their “forces” for this meeting with the aim of coming to power, but they did not succeed, thanks to the energetic chairman, who in the “heated hour” broke off the meeting.

A bookkeepers' association founded.
In the premises of the Small Traders' Association the founding meeting of the Association of Jewish Bookkeepers took place. The meeting was opened by Mr. Rajchman; greeting the Central Committee member Mr. Wallach, he proposed Mr. M. Żurawanowski [?] as chairman.
After the budget was read and adopted, a board was elected consisting of: Żurawanowski [?], Rajchman, Lancman, Bronicki, Rozina, Bugner and Buksbaum. Deputies: Hamburger, Kerner and Strauch.
The propaganda for the Hebrew language

The local Jewish gymnasium this week held a propaganda campaign for the Hebrew language and for the Hebrew book.
The propaganda week began with a festive academy on Sunday afternoon in the great hall of the school. The academy was opened, in fine Hebrew, by the 7th-class pupil Yehoshua Mela-Dista [?], who briefly presented the programme of the Hebrew circle and asked his fellow pupils and also the parents to cooperate and to promote the Hebrew language and the Hebrew book. Then the school orchestra played “Hatikvah”, and the pupils of the elementary school performed a series of tableaux and recitations in pure, ringing Hebrew.
It was simply moving to listen to the recitations, performed by the youngest children of the second and third elementary-school classes.
The school orchestra closed the academy with a couple of lively Hasidic marches and with “Techezakna”.
Throughout the whole week performances were held for the children. Every afternoon pictures of Eretz Israel were shown through the epidiascope in the form of a journey through the whole country.
The propaganda week ended yesterday afternoon with a festive parade [report] of the school organisation “Tevuna” [?], to which the children's parents had been invited.
From the “Agniska”

The academic association “Agniska” [?], which last week organised the lecture by Prof. Worerecki [?], has decided to organise in the coming days a musical-vocal evening with the participation of the poet Moshe Broderzon.
Life in Kielce — Sensational News about the Murder of the 5 Martyrs in the Village of Stawy

[Kielce — Crime.]
(Date boxes: Friday, 19 Iyar 5697 — 30 April 1937.)
Sensational news about the murder of the 5 martyrs in the village of Stawy.
On Wednesday[?] a most sensational piece of news reached Kielce from Jędrzejów[?]: that the actual murderers of the Jewish Szmulewicz family in the village of Stawy beyond Jędrzejów[?] have been caught. The investigation is in full swing.
The official[?] communiqué on the result of the investigation will appear only today, Friday.
For the time being the following facts are reported:
Soon after the horrible murder of the Szmulewicz family, the house of the late Szmulewicz was sold by the relatives of the martyrs to a certain Krzyński[?], a young peasant from beyond [—][?]. Krzyński lived in the village together with his mistress. Two months ago the mistress quarrelled with Krzyński. Sharp conflicts broke out between them, and as a result the mistress, whom he had wanted[?] to leave[?], told the police that Krzyński had a connection with the murder of the Szmulewicz family in Stawy.
At the same time the police had been searching, ever since[?] the murder in Stawy, for a certain Chmielewski — Krzyński's brother-in-law — who had vanished from the village. Krzyński said that his brother-in-law had gone to Belgium to look for work.
Last Thursday towards evening the village fishermen in Stawy pulled out of the river a dead body that was already in a state of decomposition. They informed the police post in Moskowice[?] about it. The first investigation, as reported, [established that it] is the long-sought Chmielewski. A heavy 20-kilogram stone was hung on the neck of the body, which proved that someone had wanted to drown the body. Also, a piece of the dead man's nose had been bitten off.
The autopsy carried out has established, as people say[?], that Chmielewski was shot dead before being thrown into the river.
The police ordered the arrest of Krzyński and of several other suspects. Krzyński, however, had meanwhile fled, and on Wednesday he was caught in Kostowice[?] and brought to Jędrzejów[?].
The dead Chmielewski who was found, it is also said, is supposed to have been one of the murderers, and during the carrying out of the horrible murder one of the martyrs, probably the melamed Kenigsztajn, bit off a piece of his nose while they struggled. The murderers wanted to cover their tracks and so removed the inconvenient "comrade" from their way and dispatched him to the next world...
In any case, it is said, the tracks of the true murderers have already been found.
This sensational news spread with lightning speed in Kielce and the surroundings, and it is the main topic of the day. New reports are expected at any hour.
A Hen without a Gall... (From the 'Questions' at the Rabbinate)

[Kielce — Rabbinate; humour.]
A hen without a gall...
(From the "questions" at the rabbinate).
At the rabbinate the door opens and in comes a little woman with a slaughtered hen, from which the innards had already been taken out.
— Rabbi — the worried woman blurted out — the hen has no gall...
— Did you look? — the moreh hora'ah looked at her with his kind eyes.
— I looked, and the hen has no gall — and the woman began to dig[?] in the various parts of the hen's innards, where the gall should have been found, and while searching thus for the gall she meanwhile poured out her bitter heart:
— Meat is a costly thing, our teacher[?] Rabbi; now that the "quota"[?] has run out, meat will be dear, so I bought a little hen. Well, and to my bad luck it has to have no gall...
The rabbi rose from his chair and, without even looking at the desperate woman, who held the hen in her hand by the leg[?], said:
— It cannot be...
The woman insists on one thing:
— But you can see, Rabbi, that there is no gall.
— I tell you that a hen must have a gall. You were probably in a hurry, and in your haste you did not notice the gall.
— Have you[?] ever seen a hen without a gall? Go in good health — he said to the woman — go and cook it into a good dinner for your husband...
And the woman went home satisfied with the question about[?] the hen that had no gall..
—o—

In the village of Głowaczów[?], while a pit was being dug in the house of Mordechai Wismanowicz[?], a skeleton of human bones was found. According to what the doctors established, the bones had been buried for about 150 years.

Kielce without Kosher Meat

[Kielce — Ritual slaughter; kashrut.]
The quota for kosher meat for the city of Kielce has been used up. This week no more than 1 (one) head of cattle was slaughtered in the Kielce slaughterhouse according to ritual slaughter.

A Lover's Revenge...
For It He Will Sit 8 Months in the "Hidden Place"...

[Kielce — courts.] Before the district court in Kielce stood the secretary of the War Invalids' Association in Chęciny [?], who had been brought to criminal account for falsely accusing the teacher Helena Wapart [?] of Chęciny.
The accused had made the teacher's acquaintance at a dance venue [?], and at his very first meeting with her he fell in love with her head over heels.
When the teacher would not accept his declaration of love, the lover decided to take revenge on her; to this end he influenced the schoolchildren to report to the police that the teacher beats them and takes "la-pukhke" [?] [probably bribes, Polish łapówka].
The matter reached the ministry, which carried out an investigation that proved the accusations to be groundless.
The court sentenced the accused to 8 months' unconditional imprisonment.

What's New in Upper Silesia? — Katowice. A New Appointment for Rabbi Chameides

What's new in Upper Silesia?
Katowice.
A new appointment for Rabbi Chameides.
(Y.S.) The Katowice district court has appointed[?] Rabbi Chameides as an expert for the Upper Silesian court district, and in these days Rabbi Chameides has already taken the oath.
We wish the esteemed rabbi further success in his fruitful activity.
The Third of May Celebration

In honour of the state holiday of the 3rd of May, the Jews of Katowice visited the synagogue in great numbers on Monday morning, where Cantor Rosenzweig[?] with the choir sang Ma Tovu, and Rabbi Chameides delivered a speech in which — as he has always distinguished himself with his dignified[?] and courageous[?] words — he gave[?] expression to feelings of veneration[?].
The speech of the esteemed rabbi, delivered at moments in a very sharp tone in the presence of high civil[?] representatives and military men, made a strong impression on everyone.
Cantor Rosenzweig with the choir concluded the festive prayer by singing beautifully "Boże, coś Polskę".
"The Kehilla, Its Organization and Relation to Youth"

Last Thursday, at the Zionist academics' association "Herzliya" in Katowice, the vice-president of the Katowice kehilla board, Mr. Director Abrahamer, gave a lecture on the above-mentioned topic.
The speaker gave a detailed description of old times and of the various forms of organization, composition, competences and activity of the Jewish self-governing institution — how we would wish to see the kehilla, and how it actually[?] is under present conditions.
The lecturer devoted a special part of his lecture to the legal situation of the Upper Silesian kehillas, and especially of the Katowice kehilla.
The audience applauded Vice-President Abrahamer's interesting exposition, and Magister Mr. Haysztern[?] thanked him on behalf of "Herzliya".
A R O Y [signature].

What About a Jewish Library?

[Chorzów — culture; library.] A few words on the question — to the Jewish youth.
For several years now the writer of these lines has been concerned with the question of whether[?] a Jewish library should be created in Chorzów; unfortunately the matter has met[?] with "a voice crying in the wilderness", because most of the youth are, alas, cut off from the Jewish book, from Jewish literature; they spend all their energy and time on amusements and dancings.
But for the "activists" (ba'alei askim) it is already time[?], and one must give thought also to spiritual nourishment; the Jewish youth must continue to draw the golden thread of the People of the Book, whom the book has not left from the cradle to the grave.
The Jewish book has preserved our distinctiveness and was a protective wall against assimilation and destruction.
That is why I turn to you — Jewish youth in Chorzów: reflect and understand that without a Jewish library you will be almost as if torn away from Jewish life; the old and new Hebrew and Yiddish literature is foreign to you, and the treasures of the Jewish people will become foreign to you; and precisely for this reason I have the honour to call upon you to feel the holy duty that lies upon you, and to undertake to realise the command of the hour — to create a Jewish people's library in Chorzów.
The editorial board of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" will also help; it is opening a special tribune on this question, where everyone can express himself on the matter.
Menachem Bogomolny.

Apprentices Have One Month's Time

[Crafts — journeyman examinations; notice.] To apply for the journeyman examinations.
The Ministry of Industry and Commerce has issued a circular (okólnik) in which it is explained that all candidates who apply for the journeyman examination by 30 czerwiec [June] of this year will be admitted to the examination regardless of whether he completed his apprenticeship legally or illegally. The candidate must be 18 years of age. We therefore remind all interested parties, i.e. the masters, the journeymen, the apprentice boys and apprentice girls, as well as their parents, that everyone who has learned a trade and is older than 18, regardless of whether he worked for a master who has only a craftsman's card or a diploma, now has the right to submit applications to the Chamber of Crafts for admission to the journeyman examination.
We also point out that all far-reaching concessions are being made in the handling of the certificates (zaświadczenia) through the guilds (cechy).
Remember that the journeyman's diploma is the only proof that one is a journeyman, and it also gives the legal possibility of obtaining a master's diploma as well as a craftsman's card.
Whoever does not have a journeyman's diploma will never be able to become an independent master and will not be able to have his own workshop; nor will he be allowed to work for someone else. For example, in Upper Silesia it is already [very?] hard to get work in a workshop if one has no journeyman's diploma.

“Talmud Torah Outweighs Them All” — On the indifferent attitude of the Agudah to the Będzin Talmud Torah

(On the indifferent attitude of the "Agudah" to the Będzin Talmud Torah.)
It was a few months ago that President Fürstenberg took upon himself the mission of realizing and renewing the Będzin Talmud Torah.
We say "realizing", because in fact the institution hardly existed at all; for what kind of existence is it when every Monday and Thursday the melamdim [teachers] had to go on strike — not because they wanted to improve their situation, but simply because they were in no state to teach, since they were starving, and getting a coin of one gulden was a fantasy that could never come true. And when the melamdim did start teaching, the light was cut off, because the bill at the electricity works had not been paid; and even in the best case, when there was light and the melamdim had the strength to teach the children, the Master of the Universe stepped in at a moment's notice: He sent rain over the Będzin horizon, and since the roofs were in the same state as the institution, the books were soon soaked and the pupils had to be sent home — no more learning, no more Talmud Torah.
That, in brief strokes, was the economy and the material situation of the Talmud Torah when Mr. Fürstenberg took it on. It goes without saying that a proper renovation was carried out, and first of all rooms were fitted out that one could actually enter. Then the material situation was improved, so that the economy was set up as it should be: the staff receive their salaries on time, and all other expenses are covered, as among decent people.
Then President Fürstenberg goes to the rich, pious Jews and tells them: we have looked after[?] Y O U R Talmud Torah for you, we have brought it to proper order, we see to it that the 400 poor Talmud Torah children are not brought up as outright ignoramuses; we give money, we want[?] other, national-minded and non-pious Jews too to pay their increased monthly contributions on time — but where are you? What are you doing? Why won't you help us, when you have the same means as we do? True, you fed[?] us with promises, but further than that you did not go. More than the World to Come you did not want to invest in this business.
According to President Fürstenberg's statement in today's issue of our paper, he is laying down[?] his mandate and will no longer deal with the Talmud Torah. Only because for the pious Jews, the truly Torah-faithful, the whole matter "lies in the left side-lock"[?] [i.e. they could not care less] — can this be understood? Can the mind grasp it? It would seem[?] they ought to have been happy, as[?] a benefactor comes along and sacrifices himself for their ideal, and with such breadth[?] and abundance[?] as they would never have dreamed of.
And say what you will — is it not a paradox when a man comes along who, in any case, has better business to attend to, and is not religious, and devotes himself body and soul to the institution, which ought first of all to be maintained by religious Jews? And when he asks that people come to his aid, it does not befit the Torah-faithful — those who supposedly care for religious needs[?], those who are "the majority in number and in substance in Israel", those who have taken the Torah on lease, from which the 400 poor children of the people learn.
When it comes to the slightest trifle, they appear and declare that Judaism is in danger and that a fire is burning that must be put out, or else the root of Jewry will perish; and here, as soon as one has to put a hand in one's pocket — gone is the fear for Judaism, gone the fear for the holy Torah, of which they were entrusted to be the guardians.
Yes, they are, by the way, excellent at the art of putting on God-fearing faces; but as soon as they saw that money was being raised and that care was being taken to improve the condition of the institution — which ought above all to lie on their conscience — they, the guardians of the faith, threw off the yoke entirely and hid, so that, God forbid, they should not be called upon[?].
That is how much interest they have in the institution, to which they never used to admit any "free" elements, for fear these might, God forbid, profane its holiness; and now that the "free elements" do not touch the "holiness", they don't want to touch the whole Talmud Torah complex. Now we shall see what the state of the Talmud Torah will look like, what situation both the melamdim and the children will find themselves in, and above all the whole economy.
Afterwards they may perhaps see the mistake they made in refusing to lend a hand to the institution, which was run according to their instructions and according to their demands; but then it will already be too late, then it will be a blessing in vain.
It is only a pity for the Talmud Torah as such and for the children, who in a few weeks' time will surely be roaming the streets of Będzin, and who knows what will become of them; devoted Jews for their people and good citizens will certainly not be raised out of them; but then at least it will be known that the guilt is borne by the pious Jews of Będzin, the religious ones, who at every opportunity cry out that Judaism is in danger, that Judaism is perishing.
That is how people show understanding for their traditional-religious institutions.
R. Les.
The Sosnowiec Gemilut-Chesed (Free-Loan) Fund Must Get Back Its Former Resting Place.

This time it concerns the gemilut-chesed (free-loan) fund in Sosnowiec, about which we have written more than once.
The fund conducted itself, as usual, quietly and modestly and, of course, brought benefit to those who need to turn to it for help.
Well, nobody needs to be told that the situation has grown ever harder for the community, and in comparison with that the loan requests were[?], naturally, larger, so that it was not possible to relieve[?] all the needy; moreover, the fund found itself in ever harder working conditions, and one cannot say that it has been lifted up financially.
There are, as usual, various reasons, and first and foremost the fact that Jewish Sosnowiec was "blessed" at the time with a kehilla commissioner, who was not impressed by the old office. New premises were rented for the kehilla, enlarged and adorned, as they say[?], in vinegar and in honey.
And since the fund had had its resting place in the former kehilla premises, it was [now to] have[?] a more honourable place — but nothing doing [lit. "a day of yesterday"], "Jeshurun waxed fat and kicked" [Deut. 32:15]. They modernised and began to be ashamed of an institution that occupies itself with lending money to poor, fallen people.
But the board lived in the hope that the commissioner was temporary, and that as soon as we got back the elected representation, the kehilla leaders would remember the benefit of the institution for the community and would again give it a place there to continue its useful work.
The board [?] began to intervene in the matter, and the truth is that to this day it has not been refused; on the contrary, promises are made without end, but the upshot is that to this very day things are as before.
If the kehilla board is not able to subsidise such an important institution as the free-loan fund, it should at least come to its aid and ease its expenses. [The] fund could no doubt save 1500 zł. a year in this way, which plays a big role in the present difficult situation for Jews.
It makes no difference [to the kehilla]; the kehilla leadership[?] should meet the useful institution's request, as soon as it knows that it will save a considerable[?] sum with which it can also[?] bring benefit to the community.
In any case one must not treat this matter with indifference, because economy plays a very great role in our present life.
Dr. Papuri.
