How Reb Yonah Celebrated the 1st of May

[Satirical feuilleton — May Day.]
Retold by Y. Oberzhanek.
As is well known, I am a dry-goods (textile) merchant, and as long as no little war comes along, the dry goods really do lie in the ground and one is in great trouble.
But that is not what I am out to tell; I only want to tell how I, Yonah the dry-goods merchant, became a "tsitsialist" [pun: tsitsit + socialist] and how I celebrated the 1st of May.
I now admit and confess to you that I hated the tsitsialists just as a Hasidic factory owner hates a Jewish worker, as our "stinktelligentsia" hates to speak Yiddish. I knew that the tsitsialists were "akheirutniks" [heretics, from Aher], treyf-eaters, shaven-beard types, unwashed louts. That is why I was an enemy of the tsitsialists.
That was so until I found out that the tsitsialists actually mean my good, that they actually want to deliver me from my troubles and headaches, that they actually want to free me from all my blows and misfortunes. Yes, I heard it myself from a comrade with a black curled [?] forelock; he said clearly [?] that the tsitsialists want all people to be equal, that there should be no rich and poor.
The idea appealed to me — truly a fine thing: everyone should be equal, an end to Rothschilds and an end to paupers; or everyone should be a Rothschild; or the Rothschilds too should have to look for an interest-free loan for the Sabbath; or all paupers should live in 6 rooms with all the comforts; or the rich too should have to "khalyen na mshcharski" [?, unclear Polish phrase]; or we paupers too should be able in summer to send our wives off to bask in the sun and dip in the sea; or the double-chinned rich ladies too should be "zushne" [?] in "vglesbye" [?] together with the paupers' wives; or the paupers' daughters should all get fat dowries and not have to wait, and marry "z miłości" [for love]; or the rich men's daughters too should pine their souls out after some pair [?] — everyone should be equal!
And do you know, gentlemen, what else the comrade said? He said that this kind of [?] money must disappear entirely. Away with money! Do you even understand what wisdom lies in that?
Imagine, gentlemen, how good it would be for me if there were no money at all: if there were no money, I would not have, every [printed "yern"] morning, the "guest" with the yellow band [probably the tax collector or bailiff]; my little wife would not carry out an inspection of my trouser pockets, and she would not put questions to me:
Why does Yentl "di hale shtayern" [?, a nickname] have a sealskin coat while I must drag myself around in an old rag?
Why does pockmarked Zlate go to the spas every year, and I, with my [?] in the legs, don't?
Why can sallow Faytshe "afford" to be ill with gallstones, and I can't?
When I heard the words of the comrade with the black forelock, I thought to myself: if so, if that is what the tsitsialists want, then I myself am a tsitsialist too — so why do I still [?] hate them? Why shouldn't I celebrate the 1st of May together with all the tsitsialists? After all, they want to deliver me from all troubles and blows!
Well, so this year I really did celebrate the 1st of May together with all the tsitsialists. For me it was a holiday like all holidays.
On Sabbath morning I went to the mikveh, from the mikveh I went to the shtibl, and called out joyfully to everyone: "Gut yontev!"
And when the congregation asked me: "What holiday do you have today? Today is the Sabbath, isn't it?"
— Gentlemen, today is a great holiday, the 1st of May! — I answered.
— Reb Yonah, you've lost your mind! — the Jews looked at me as at a madman. — Since when has the 1st of May become a Jewish holiday? It is a holiday for sinners, for the shaven-beard types, for the unwashed louts — for the akheirutniks!
— Not true! It is my holiday, your holiday, all paupers' holiday, a holiday for all the oppressed and tormented, a holiday for all the persecuted and afflicted.
An uproar broke out in the shtibl; the crowd wanted to trample me, they shouted and cried "gevald": "Out, you sheygets! Sinners of Israel!"
Seeing that it smelled of gunpowder, I climbed up onto the bimah and said:
— Gentlemen, did you all have [what you need] for the Sabbath?
Everyone shrugged their shoulders.
— Gentlemen, do you have the means to pay your promissory notes?
Everyone shrugged their shoulders.
— Gentlemen, have you already put away dowries for your daughters?
— Oh, what an idea!
— Do you have a groschen to your soul?
— Forbidden! [on the Sabbath]
— But Rothschild does have something to bake for the Sabbath, eh? Rothschild has no evictions? Dowries for his daughters he has too, yes?
— That's why he's Rothschild! — someone answered.
— Gentlemen, I said, you should know that a time will come when everyone will be equal; there will be no Rothschilds and no paupers, everyone will be equal. There will be no money at all — there will be no envy; and if there is no envy, there will be no hatred; and if there is no hatred, there will be no war.
— Oh, good!... Oh, fine!... I really am a "zpasne" [?]! — and someone began to dance for joy.
— Gentlemen, you should know that all this that I have told you is what the tsitsialists want, and today is indeed the tsitsialist holiday, a holiday for all the oppressed and tormented, for all the persecuted and afflicted — understood?
From the synagogue I went home, made kiddush and told my wife to put on her holiday clothes in honour of the holiday.
My wife obeyed me, and [we went?] out into the street. I saw the procession, sneaked into the middle of it, sang along their "zmires" and helped shout "Niech żyje!" [Long live!].
That is how this year, for the first time, I celebrated the 1st of May, the holiday of the oppressed and the tormented, the only paupers' holiday!
My Appeal...

Sz. Fürstenberg.
Pierced by the incessant alarms and cries for help of the steadily sinking "place of refuge" for 400 poor children and orphans — the Talmud Torah in our city and mother-city in Israel, Będzin — and under the effect of the desperate "cry of woe" of the starved staff of melamdim (teachers), I, seeing [sic; a full stop in print] the general apathetic indifference to the matter, decided (where there is no man) on my own initiative to bring the institution back to life. But the most urgent "first aid" itself (the ruin of the building inside and out) did not allow waiting until people would call, wake up and act[?], and with my own means I gave the first aid. The rehabilitation too, thanks to a larger number of donors, succeeded to a certain extent. Thanks to the intervention[?] in the kehilla a teaching staff for secular subjects was engaged, and for 8[?] months now the melamdim have stopped starving. The Talmud Torah stayed alive and is on the way to recovery.
But if the illness once stemmed from not having the necessary means and possibilities to sustain itself and exist, — we now stand again before the same danger, and with the same dread we hear again: "SOS, SOS"[?] — and the terrible, familiar thing repeats itself.
And if [I appeal] now a second time — surely much more drastically and strongly — it is because in the 8 months in which I have fought tirelessly for the great (in my conviction) institution, I still did not manage to create the basis, the foundation, on which the Talmud Torah could securely hold out and exist. It is still far behind[?], when on a budget of about 2000 zł. monthly, the support from the main basic income, the membership dues, amounts to barely 400 zł. And I will by no means believe that the householders of our town would not want, or would not be able, to realise such a budget, and for such a great cause; and if this has not been possible until now — the fault is surely not with those who must "give", but with those who must be the "takers", with those to whom a Talmud Torah ought to be close and dear, with those who are the constant defenders, the [print: "of"] standard-bearers of everything connected with Torah; and above all the fault lies with those who almost by force seized the say of "others"[?] in[?] the administration of the Talmud Torah and solemnly declared their great self-sacrifice for the institution — they[?] did not fulfil their task, and the foundations of the institution are, even more than before, threatened.
And therefore, seeing no way out, I decided at the administration meeting convened last week — despite my great regret — to lay down my mandate as president of the Talmud Torah; but my sentimental feelings for the great cause did not withstand the moral pressure of all the administration members, who swore and fervently declared that with the greatest energy they would create, within 4 weeks, a proper pledge fund — and I granted their request and will try[?] my office as president for the next 4 weeks as well, because I want to believe that their present declaration is honest and sincere, and that their administrative work will, like every honest work, be crowned with success.
Jews of Będzin, givers and donors!
I appeal to you, I speak to your soul and conscience: when they come to you with the request to pledge, and if need be to increase, your membership dues for the benefit of the Talmud Torah, do not refuse. Whatever stratum, whatever class or conviction you may belong to, you must be among the members of the Talmud Torah. Remember that this concerns the only "place of refuge" in our town, where [—][?] very many spiritually forsaken, poor children, whose parents are unable to pay any tuition fee, and some of whose parents are no longer among the living, and only you become their providers. Let the feeling of love not abandon you today. Will[?] you, in today's hard times, give an account of the great responsibility of brother to brother, especially towards the poor, helpless and innocent orphan[?]. [—] Even[?] until today you gladly wanted to give, only no one demanded of you, no one dunned you, nor even reminded you. Remember that this is my last word on the matter, and if this present last appeal of mine too does not have the proper effect, and the requested 4 weeks do not realise the necessary budget — through the action[?] undertaken[?] by the administration — then my resignation is final, never again to be withdrawn; and despite my moral pain — watching how the Talmud Torah, the fortress of 400 poor children and forsaken orphans, is wrecked and annihilated — annihilated, never to be rebuilt, until "she is fallen, she shall no more rise" — my conscience will then be clean, but you will bear upon yourselves the great responsibility and will not be able to say calmly:
— "Our hands have not shed this blood"...
How Did People Cure Themselves 100 Years Ago?

[Feuilleton — folk medicine, history.]
One cannot say that a hundred years ago people doctored themselves less than today. True, the thousands of medicines, salves and powders that we have today did not yet exist then; nevertheless there were "natural remedies" for all illnesses, which were likewise not [—] [?].

Before me lies an archive [?] of the Leipzig fair of the year 1802, a "collection of select, best remedies", which all pharmacies sold" — and here we see that even then people already sought all sorts of means to be "beautiful"; but they did not want to smear their faces as today in order to look red and fresh — on the contrary, they sought a remedy so as not to have a red face. Here is the remedy:
"Take a pound of meat and mix it with wax, eggs and half a litre of wine vinegar", and with this remedy one smears the face, so that the red cheeks go away.

For various impurities of the face there was also a remedy: "Mix a lemon with several spoonfuls of sugar and add a little brandy", with this one rubs the face, and the skin becomes quite clean.

If one had a pale face, one got at the pharmacy "infused water", and from it the face became quite red. What this infused water was, we do not know to this day.

Showing women how to cut their hair was just like showing someone how to jump off a roof; nevertheless the pharmacist's book of that time had a remedy: women with red hair should "cut and rub the short hair with rainwater mixed with wine vinegar", and they will surely get black hair afterwards. The same remedy was used for red-haired children, when one wanted them to get black hair.

Remedies for various illnesses existed then, of course, in abundance.
Here is a remedy for all kinds of heart ailments:
"Take tsimping [?] water, this is the best means to strengthen the heart in all pains"...
"For all kinds of nervous illnesses, melancholy (except madness), one should use apple juice".
"Erysipelas [?] and even cholera are best cured with boiled worms, which appear after a rain".
Here is a very important remedy:
"Against various illnesses in which one gets fever, or against smallpox, measles and scarlet fever, the best is to [—] [?] mixed with vinegar"... This medicine expressly heals "old and young and even children in the cradle".
"To cleanse the blood, best of all is a plaster on the stomach"...
For liver ailments a special medicine was used, which "prolonged life by many years"...
This medicine is not described precisely and therefore it was indeed lost... just as we do not know today what the salve was "for rubbing the head when someone had the falling sickness, went mad, or was bitten by a dog"...
"The best remedy against all kinds of illnesses of the belly and the stomach" was "boiled rainwater from the month of May together with the worms that appear at that time after the rain"...
How these medicines, which were sold in all pharmacies a hundred and more years ago, actually helped against the various illnesses, has unfortunately not become known...
Z. Haber, Chin [?].
Heard and Seen.

[Column "Heard and Seen" — Będzin and Sosnowiec: May Day, kehilla, rabbinate.]
By Ben Amos.

Decency comes before Torah...
In no epoch, it seems, have we Jews demanded so strongly of the nations of the world that they treat us a little more tolerantly, may no trouble come. To that end, on every question with an antisemitic background, we use the eternal argument:
— "You are democrats after all, preachers of justice and truth, so take us too under the mantle of democracy and tolerance".
And if we demand of the outside world that they [—] [?] be more tolerant towards us — all the more so do we have the full right to demand this of our own... even more of those who also carry the banner of the new "Ten Commandments", among which is also the commandment of human tolerance, even towards those who stand outside the camp...
And how this is realised in life, we indeed convinced ourselves last Sabbath, the 1st of May, when the May demonstration of Jewish workers wound through the Jewish streets, headed by dozens of flags and banners. Very well, as for the demonstrators known in the Jewish street as avowed negators of national revival, who have nothing in common with the past, with Jewish history, and strive to uproot even the Hebrew language — we can have no complaints; but if the youth carrying the flag inscribed "Zion" and "Eretz Israel" permits itself such a public desecration of the Sabbath, especially in a Jewish town — to demonstrate at the very moment when thousands of Jews are going to pray on the Sabbath — that is, in our understanding, a reckless act [?] and a disregard of the religious feelings of thousands of Jews.
We know that the demonstrators are not religious, but it does not follow that the anti-religious may offend the feelings of the religious; this is after all a matter that falls within the bounds of tolerance and decency, and
— decency comes before Torah..

Make way ["wara"], the Sosnowiec kehilla is driving by...
On the "golden stretch" of Modrzejowska [?] Lane in Sosnowiec there is a great "bustle". If a stranger coming here for the first time saw the noisy life, he would not want to believe that those strolling up and down (people are afraid to stop — a złoty for a fine would be a pity) are pure Menachem-Mendels, building plans in the air, debating the outcome of the war in Spain, or who will control the situation in the synagogue in Old Sosnowiec — the kehilla or the present gabbaim..
Suddenly the movement slackens, all eyes turn east, from where a funeral is approaching. People step aside, let the funeral pass, and do not mourn [?] long, for "life is bustling again".
— "Four khapinkes [?] for 10 groszy"
— "A calendar for ten" — "A little mirror for five groszy", "The newest [?] hit songs for ten groszy, take your pick [?]..."
And in the throng — "Na bok!" ("Aside!"). A small cart drags along, harnessed to it a "horse" in human form, who shouts "Na bok!" so that the public in the street should move aside, for on his cart there are no ordinary implements, but the utensils of the dead [?]: a few minutes earlier the dead man was carried past, and now they carry the utensils with which the dead was ritually purified...
And these utensils are not among the "mute" either; true, their language is not understood by sinful humanity, nor by the rulers of the kehilla.. One hears no more than the clatter of the buckets, of the purification board and other implements lying "bundled together" [?] on the narrow cart..
At the building housing the modern office of the kehilla the clatter grows louder; apparently the "empty implements" too protest: why are they dragged on a rubbish cart and put to "shame" [?] before people's eyes...
And as we contemplate this "splendid" picture, which symbolises the "aesthetic" sense of the kehilla rulers, a proposal comes to mind: when the cart travels through the busy streets, a representative of the kehilla or of the Chesed shel Emes burial society should walk ahead and cry out loud:
— Make way, the Sosnowiec kehilla is driving by...

A look — a złoty...
For several months now, thanks to the Będzin rabbinate, a new occupation has come into being. This occupation consists of:
— "looking"...
The first experiment was made in the licensed butcher shops. These butcher shops are provided, besides a sign saying "Ritual meat is sold here", also with a "looker", who looks at the meat like a rooster at people and understands meat from "local slaughter" as much as Czapczak [?] knows what goes on in the Talmud; but that has no bearing on the matter itself — the main thing is a livelihood..
And since the first "experiment" succeeded, they started thinking how to employ new "lookers", and "I laboured and found": since bread is baked on the Sabbath on the strength of a bill of sale, every baker should also maintain a "looker", who comes on the Sabbath during the day to take a look in the "bakery" to see whether the owner does not work along.
The fee for such a "looker" is not large, in total 4 zł a month, so that it comes to
— a look — a złoty..

[Memoirs — the Hebrew press; Nahum Sokolow.] By Gershon Stawski [printed „סטאוסקי“].
(Recollections for his first yahrzeit.)

In the middle of the eighties [of the 19th century], when Dr. Kantor's [Judah Leib Kantor] first daily newspaper, „HaYom“, forced „HaMelitz“ and also „HaTsefira“ to appear daily — the Jewish world was then divided into 2 parts. For example, „HaTsefira“ had as its readers, for the most part, the older, more religious maskilim, and also the „kest“ sons-in-law [young husbands boarding with their in-laws]; all these were readers of „HaTsefira“, which fed them with „articles of wisdom“ (as „HaTsefira“ called them) by Ch. Z. Slonimski [Hayyim Selig Slonimski], such as: „Kokhva de-Shavit“, „Toldot ha-Shamayim“ etc. In questions of Jewish life „HaTsefira“ was then little interested, and [only?] later, when for the sake of „HaTsefira's“ existence Slonimski had to descend from the „heavenly questions“, adapt himself more to life, did he begin printing in „HaTsefira“ articles under the name „Tsorkhei ha-Ḥayim“ [„Needs of Life“].
For this kind of reader „HaMelitz“ was not quite kosher, especially when articles about the settlement of the Land of Israel appeared there from time to time — that meant one wanted to „hasten the End“ before its time.
The second part of the „world“, the readers of „HaMelitz“, consisted of younger maskilim, [doubtful word], less religious, who had already read Mapu, Smolenskin, Lilienblum and others. These readers were not interested in the „Needs of Life“ of „HaTsefira“, because other questions of life were on the agenda, and in „HaMelitz“ they sought answers to those questions. Among the readers of „HaMelitz“ were concentrated the „Ḥovevei Zion“, to whom I had the honour of belonging.
In that period „HaMelitz“ together with „HaTsefira“ were the pillars, the „Jachin and Boaz“ of the Haskalah. Both newspapers devoted a great deal of space to world politics. In „HaMelitz“ this was called „Hilkhot Olam“ [„Laws of the World“]. The writer of „Hilkhot Olam“ was the then head of the poets, Judah Leib Gordon. In „HaTsefira“ it was called „Divrei ha-Yamim“ [„Chronicles“], and the writer of that section was the young Nahum Sokolow of blessed memory. And here, with Sokolow's „Divrei ha-Yamim“, the borders between the two parts of the world became somewhat blurred, moved somewhat apart.
The greater part of the „HaMelitz“ readers simply licked their fingers over Sokolow's „Divrei ha-Yamim“, and it is interesting: the same Judah Leib Gordon who had so enriched[?] the Hebrew language with his poems „Bein Shinei Arayot“, „Birekh ba-Laylah“[?] and others, did not succeed with his readers with his „Hilkhot Olam“, because, firstly, the language was difficult and florid; whereas Sokolow's „Divrei ha-Yamim“ was read with relish.
Sokolow also illuminated West European politics in his „Divrei ha-Yamim“; through the „Divrei ha-Yamim“ one became more at home with French and English politics. No sooner had a cabinet crisis broken out in France than the „Divrei ha-Yamim“ already had material for several weeks to orient the readers, to acquaint them with the character and biography of every candidate for the cabinet. Not to mention when there were parliamentary elections in England and it was about to happen that the Liberal Party would take over the government from the Conservative or the other way round — then the „Divrei ha-Yamim“ had something with which to interest its readers, who were versed in every question more than a real Englishman. That is how we grew accustomed to the „Divrei ha-Yamim“, which became the political „Urim and Thummim“ and stood on a higher level than the greatest European newspapers.
(Conclusion follows)
What I Saw at the Będzin Gemilut Ḥesed Fund.

[Będzin — interest-free loan fund.] By chance the writer of these lines witnessed the following episode at the Będzin Gemilut Ḥesed [interest-free loan] fund:
A certain fairly well-off person, from whom the fund had demanded [a sum of?] 23 zł., paid 38 zł. instead, i.e. with various costs. The debtor, being an understanding man, did of course acknowledge that exclusively through his own fault the debt had increased by more than 65 per cent: when the G.Ḥ. fund had called on him 3 times to pay and he had not responded to any of it, extra special costs were, by necessity, added. Not everyone wants to understand this, and instead of [blaming] oneself one throws the blame on the Gemilut Ḥesed fund and even tries to create a hostile atmosphere around the fund, which is today a support[?] for more than 1500 families in our town, who thanks to the Gemilut Ḥesed fund have their livelihood.
As an outside observer I have found it necessary to bring the said fact before the public and to warn:
Remember that the Gemilut Ḥesed fund may not give gifts, only lend in order to be repaid, so as to be able to go on lending. It is in the own interest of everyone who receives a demand from the fund to see to settling his debt at once; otherwise money is lost, for which the Gemilut Ḥesed fund cannot bear the responsibility.
Kaem.

Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Behar-Bechukotai)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Behar-Bechukotai
—o—
a) "A jubilee shall it be... ye shall not sow, neither reap" (Lev. 25:11).
That is why the Torah forbade sowing and gathering the grain in the jubilee year: for in the jubilee one must give the land back to its original owners, and when the fields are full of grain a person will be loath to give the fields back... Imrei Chen.
—o—
b) "Or buyest aught of thy neighbour's hand" (25:14).
From this verse the Gemara (Kiddushin 26 and Bava Metzia 47) derives that backing out [?] once the purchase of a thing already binds — for a word also binds, and "He who punished the generation of the Flood and the generation of the Dispersion will exact punishment from one who does not stand by his word".
The question arises: what connection does the generation of the Flood have with one who does not keep his word?
But by Torah law one does not acquire a thing until one takes it home; yet there are things that are binding [?] by Torah law although they are not stated explicitly in the Torah — just as the generation of the Flood was punished for its crimes although at that time there was as yet no binding Torah at all. That means: such things too, which go against human morality, one may not transgress, even when there is no explicit prohibition in the Torah... Tikkun Shlomo.
—o—
c) "Thou shalt not give him thy money upon usury... I am the Lord your God."
Among the ancient nations lending money at interest [?] was bound up with their religion. The oldest bank in Greece was the temple at Delphi, which lent money at interest to various Greek communities. For a long time in the Middle Ages the bishops and churches were the chief lenders of money at interest. A synod (a gathering of Christian clergy) of the 4th century indeed raged against the priests over this, since the temple and the bank were one, as were the priest and the usurer. Hence comes the Torah's warning: "Thou shalt not give him thy money upon usury, I am the Lord your God" — you must, God forbid, not bind interest together with faith... Maor HaGolah.
—o—
d) "But over your brethren the children of Israel ye shall not rule one over another with rigour"
"One over another" — because if a Jew enslaves the other, he enslaves himself. For "he who buys a Hebrew slave for himself buys a master for himself": buying a Hebrew slave means buying a master over oneself.. Leket Amarim.
—o—
e) "And dwell in your land safely" (26:5).
"In your land you dwell safely, but you do not dwell safely outside it." Torat Kohanim.
The verse here speaks of blessings for the Land of Israel; so [?] what blessing is it for the Land of Israel to say "but you do not dwell safely outside it" — that we will not sit in peace outside the Land of Israel?
It is a blessing for the Land of Israel because, had we had rest in the Diaspora, we would long since have forgotten the Land of Israel... Yalkut Yehuda.
—o—
f) "And I will give peace in the land" (ibid. [?], 6).
"Lest you say: here is food, here is drink — if there is no peace, there is nothing. Therefore it says: And I will give peace in the land. This teaches that peace outweighs everything." Torat Kohanim.
In Wazirszak [?] the rabbi was once R' David, the author of "Galya Masechet". He had no surplus livelihood from the town, and so he had quarrel upon quarrel there.
Once there was talk of taking on a second rabbi, whom a certain faction particularly wanted to bring into the town. The head of the community came to him and laid before him a moral lecture on how great peace is, and that therefore, for the sake of peace, he ought to give up his rabbinate.
R' David answered him:
— The Torat Kohanim indeed says: "Lest you say, here is food, here is drink — if there is no peace, there is nothing." When there is even a livelihood and there is no peace, there is nothing at all. But when there is no livelihood either, then surely "there is nothing"...
—o—
g) "And I will break the pride of your power" (ibid., 19).
"And I will break the pride of your power — this is the Temple, and so it says: Behold, I will profane My sanctuary, the pride of your power. Rabbi Akiva says: And I will break the pride of your power — these are the mighty men of Israel, such as Joab son of Zeruiah and his companions." Torat Kohanim.
While the Torat Kohanim considers the destruction of the Temple the greatest misfortune, Rabbi Akiva comes and says: as long as there are heroes among Jews and there is heroism among Jews, the destruction of the Temple is not yet the greatest national misfortune. Here, the Temple had been defiled — the Hasmoneans came and re-sanctified the Temple. Worse, however, is when heroism among Jews ceases: then there is no more revival for the people; the destruction of the people is worse than the destruction of the Temple... R' Yehuda Leib Ginzburg.
—o—
h) "And ye shall be gathered together within your cities" (ibid., 25)
At the time of the great aliyah, when the whole stream of immigration went mainly into the towns, and in the villages people took to [?] seeking Arab workers, Rabbi Aronson of blessed memory, the former rabbi of Tel Aviv, said:
— It is a curse from the Rebuke, this running into the towns: "And ye shall be gathered together within your cities"...
—o—
i) "And they shall confess their iniquity, and the iniquity of their fathers, with their trespass which they trespassed against Me" (ibid., 40).
If they will confess, why then does the verse say further on that they will be [—]?
But the meaning of the verse is: "And they shall confess their iniquity... with their trespass" — while trespassing at that very moment, as criminals, they will confess "immersing with the reptile in their hand". A false confession, while at that very moment one goes on sinning... Be'er Yitzchak.
—o—
j) "And yet for all that, when they be in the land of their enemies, I will not cast them away, neither will I abhor them, to destroy them utterly" (ibid., 44)
"What then remained to Israel? Were not all the good gifts given to them taken from them? What remained to them — this is the Torah scroll, for had it not endured for Israel, they would not differ from the nations of the world." Torat Kohanim.
How does this discussion come to be on this verse?
But this is an addition to the curse: whenever [?] you will want to assimilate in order to rid yourselves of the curses — you will not be able to do that either; the Torah that was given you will make you different from the nations after all... Damesek Eliezer.

The Living Corpse

[Literature — serial novel ("The Living Corpse"), instalment 7.]
A. Zaglembier.
(A most thrilling novel of Jewish life in Zagłębie before and after the World War). 7
Summary of the beginning of the novel.
On a winter night before the World War, when two Cossacks were to transfer the notorious[?] bandit "Shmuelke Lapke" into the Piotrków prison, they were suddenly attacked on the way to the Będzin station by two disguised "strażniks" (guards) — Lapke's helpers. In the morning the Cossacks were found lying tied up[?] with gagged mouths, and Shmuelke "Lapke", freed[?], escaped to the Gzichów road in order[?] to hide somewhere.
That same evening, and almost at the same hour, the universally respected, solid [—] Yosl Wertheim — a father of three children — suddenly disappeared. His wife Sarahtshe[?] runs about the town terribly desperate, searching for him in every possible hiding place in all of Zagłębie. But Yosl Wertheim has vanished like a stone in water...
Everyone stands before an extraordinary riddle. At last, on the fifth day, pockmarked[?] Matek reports to police inspector Korecki and tells that on that day he had seen Wertheim walking along the Gzichów road together with the Christian Magda Komarska — a young, pretty shikse whom Matek had been courting.
Magda is arrested at once. At the beginning of the interrogation she denies everything, but when Korecki wants to confront her with pockmarked Matek, Magda suddenly faints...
Once she has been revived[?], she declares that she wants to tell the truth, but not in Matek's presence[?].
Now read on.
Korecki gives a sign that everyone should leave the room. Pockmarked Matek is led back into the neighbouring house, and he must go on waiting there; perhaps he will still be of use to the investigation.
"So you have finally decided to tell the t r u t h," says[?] Korecki, when he is once again entirely alone with Magda.
"Yes, I will tell everything... Evil tongues want to invent a slander about me..."
"What we are about to hear[?] — remember, consider well before you answer... Only the truth can save you, and this is not about some little game, this is about a human life! You were seen with Wertheim for the last time, and after that[?] he vanished without a trace. Do you know about it?"
"Yes," Magda heaves another heavy sigh, "I know about it... I myself searched for him afterwards wherever I possibly could..."
"What does that mean?" Korecki gives her a suspicious look. "What does it mean that y o u too searched for Wertheim? Don't you know what happened to him? Why are you again acting so naive[?] and childish?..."
"How should I know that?"
"Then why didn't you come at once to report to the police?"
"I was ashamed that people would find out about our..."
Here Korecki cuts her short and becomes very agitated:
"Say rather that you were afraid it would be found out who m u r d e r e d him and buried him somewhere — Wertheim! That is the only reason you were afraid!"
"What?! Wertheim has been murdered?!" Magda leaps from her seat in a terrible hysterical outburst. "Wertheim murdered?! Who says so?"
"God forbid that my words should prove to be lies; but if he has not been murdered, then you of all people, y o u  y o u r s e l f, must know where he has gone?.."
"When we parted, Wertheim stayed in the forest," Magda answers quietly.
"Magda Komarska! You said you would tell the truth! Remember! Only that, you say — that Wertheim stayed in the forest?"
"Yes..."
"What day was that?"
"Wednesday."
"Only then, when Matek saw you walking?.."
"Yes."
"And how long had you known each other until then, you and Yosl Wertheim?"
"Oh, a very long time already... We have known each other since childhood.. We once lived as neighbours."
"Yes, that is correct," Korecki says as if to himself, making a note on a paper. "Well, go on..."
"Later we were like strangers to each other for a long time, although I knew that Yosek was in love with me..."
"And you?"
"I was not indifferent to him either... Later I even loved him very much, and today I love him even more... But between us there always stood a firm iron[?] wall... Yosek is a J e w and I a C h r i s t i a n!..."
"But that has nothing to do with the matter," Korecki looks at her with ever more suspicion. "So you have known each other a long time. And you often used to go walking there, in the little wood?"
"Once or twice a week."
"And what did you do there?.."
Magda turns red, ashamed, and lowers her eyes. She is silent.
"You said you would tell the truth! What did you do in the little wood?.."
"We made love..." she answers quietly.
"Wait, I am too old and experienced for you to be able to pull the wool over my eyes with such nonsense. Dozens of witnesses, and Mrs. Wertheim herself as well, have established that he was the most faithful husband and father to his wife and children."
"That is true too... Nobody knew about our love, and nobody was allowed to know..."
"And for what reason did you do it? You are still quite young, and pretty too. And if you know that he also has a wife with children..."
"I love him too much, and if not him — then[?] no one..."
Korecki listens to all this with the greatest interest, and at the same time his suspicion of her grows ever greater and, so to speak, more decisive, more substantial. Well, yes, if so, then — it is already quite understandable to Korecki why Yosl Wertheim had to be r e m o v e d from the world. But to have confirmation of his terrible suspicion, he must after all hear such words from Magda's mouth. So he goes on asking, trying to conceal his extraordinary curiosity and suspense:
"So you love him so much, and he, Wertheim, too..."
"Too... He was ready to do anything for me. More than once he assured me that in the end he would leave his Jewish wife and children and go away with me abroad..."
"Why did he want to do that?"
"Because he sees, he told me, that it is impossible for him to lead such a d o u b l e  l i f e, and he cannot give me up — he loves me too much..."
"I see... And what did you do in the forest that Wednesday, the last one, when you went back alone?"
"We had words[?] then."
"What?!"
"Yes, we even quarrelled."
"You and Wertheim?"
"Yes."
Korecki rubbed his hands with satisfaction and at once said:
"And why did you quarrel then?"
Again Magda lowers her eyes in shame and is afraid to answer...
"Well, I am asking you. The more of the truth you tell, the better it will be for you; well, say it, why did you quarrel then?"
Without raising her eyes, Magda answers:
"Because of the c h i l d that I carry beneath my heart..."
"By whom?!"
"By Y o s l  W e r t h e i m..."
"What?!" Korecki jumps up from his seat in great surprise. "Yosl Wertheim is the f a t h e r of the child you are carrying?!"
"Yes, he alone..."
"Who else can confirm this?"
"No one but me — were there witnesses 'present', then?"
"That is not what I mean. But do your parents know about it too? Does Wertheim's wife know about it as well?"
"No one. Wertheim made me swear not to tell, and I kept the oath.."
"But why did you quarrel that evening?"
"Not at first, only when I began to speak about our child, who in a few months will have to come into the world.."
"Well, well..."
"Wertheim urged me, and not for the first time, to travel to Katowice to a doctor who would see to it that I would not have to give birth to the child..."

“Der Kokh-lefl” — Spring in Będzin

“Der Kokh-lefl” [The Cooking Spoon]
Spring in Będzin.

It is spring now, it is spring!
Who has not read at some time
of spring, of fields in bloom,
of little birds that sing and fly?
Just look: at the corner [“rog” — róg] stands a gentile woman
and deals in blue flowers..
—
The sun shines on Kołłątaja Street;
the sky throws gold[?] on the roofs...
Above us there is such a sky:
clear and blue, like a bluish little flower...
Not the sky of “Henetsh”[?]..,
that one is a little higher...
—
Ah! Come to the “Przemsza” to “ludken”[?] [refresh?] yourselves,
all you decent, cheerful couples!
One must enjoy something of spring,
and anyway greet the spring..
Come and bathe together with the frogs —
we have no better neighbours...
—
Rays fall from the sky
and make themselves baths in the Przemsza...
Only do not envy the rays!
We too will make ourselves such a bath...
It's spring... but the devil take it,
we know it, spring, from the calendar...
A. Jadek[?].

How I Got Married — Monologue of a Sosnowiec Bachelor

Monologue of a Sosnowiec bachelor.
In Mandelbaum's confectionery two young men are sitting and one of them is pouring out his heart!
— A few weeks ago a Jew comes up to me and asks me:
— Young man, do you have a couple of minutes?
— Yes, what is it? — I asked him.
— Would you like to earn 5000 zł.?
— What a question! Of course [literally: “everything means wanting”?].
— If so, then come with me.
— Where to?
— What's it to you, come.
He takes me into Lancman's and says to me:
— Take off your coat!
I took off first the coat, then the suit; they dressed me in new clothes and he paid. Then he gets into a droshky with me and we drive off. I ask the stranger:
— Uncle, where are we going?
— What's it to you, you want to earn five thousand zł., don't you?
— Yes, I do.
And before I can work out what and when, I am standing under the wedding canopy, they give me some sort of “parvenish”[?], and he says to me:
— Well, say the few words.
I say: Uncle, but...
— No buts at all, you want to earn 5 thousand zł., so do as you're told. — And I obeyed.

First General Meeting
of the Society of "Friends of the Hebrew University in Jerusalem".
On Tuesday the first general meeting of the Friends of the Hebrew University in Jerusalem in Zagłębie took place in the assembly hall of the S. Fürstenberg Gymnasium.
The meeting is opened by Chairman Fürstenberg; elected to the presidium are Messrs. Chairman Fürstenberg, Dr. Selarista [?] and Nachman Gutman, and as [—] secretary Mr. Y. Hingducki [?].
The floor for the activity report goes to Eng. Manges [?], who first gives, in Hebrew, a general overview of the tasks of the society and the [—] of the Hebrew University. The speaker then gives an exact [?] series of details on the organizational work of the branch and the results achieved.
To date about 250 members have been recruited (Będzin 100, Sosnowiec 120, Dąbrowa 28, Strzemieszyce 3); the treasury now holds a sum of over 900 zł. The one-time campaign for the University has so far brought in about 15 thousand zł.
Mr. Yaakov Magid then gives an interesting lecture on the work and plans of the University. The speaker begins in Hebrew and switches to Yiddish; he points to the colossal importance of the University for the development of the Land and to the great name that the institution of higher learning has already managed to earn in the world of science.
The administration has a grandiose plan to develop and enlarge the University.
Chairman Fürstenberg then turns to those assembled with a fervent appeal to strengthen the ranks of the "Friends": our nearest task must be to recruit 1000 members in Zagłębie. He points to the great importance of the University especially for Polish Jewry.
Dr. Selarista [?] points to the results already achieved and expresses the hope that the next general meeting will be much livelier.

With the singing of „Hatikvah“ the meeting was closed.
„That They May Know That in Sukkot...“

[Będzin — court; a brawl at Sukkot.]
It happened this past Sukkot, when during a brawl among shoemakers' heirs[?] Binyamin Rotenberg[?] got a knife in the side[?] from Yosef Fiszel. The epilogue of the brawl was played out before the district court in Sosnowiec, which sentenced Yosef Fiszel to a year and a half in prison and Chaim Rudaler[?] to 6 months. The verdict is being appealed[?].
„The Mister Doctor Is Not In“...

[Będzin — theft.]
A thief in the role of the doctor's servant.
On Sunday afternoon a thief got into the flat of Dr. Segal[?] and, taking advantage of the fact that nobody was at home, began to play the master of the house and packed the best household[?] things into a suitcase[?].
At that moment a Jewish woman, a patient, arrived and rang at the door. The thief, fearing he would be discovered, opened the door and politely declared:
— „Pana doktora nie ma“ [Polish: „The doctor is not in“].
But the declaration, especially from an unknown man whom she was seeing for the first time, made the woman suspicious and she raised an alarm; the thief then fled, leaving behind the whole loot.
The Site of the Cemetery on Zawale Street Belongs to the Magistrate

[Będzin — cemetery; municipality.]
As is known, the question of clearing away[?] the cemetery on Zawale Street has already been[?] on the agenda several times, but each time the matter was held back.
But as we are informed, there is in the possession of the local magistrate [municipality] a document according to which the plot on which the cemetery on the above-mentioned street lies belongs to the magistrate.
The „Bikur Cholim“ Women's Society

[Będzin — women's society; charity.]
In the premises of the „Beis Yaakov“ school a general meeting of the women's society named „Bikur Cholim“ [visiting the sick] took place. Before a packed hall the G.[?] president, Mrs. Chana[?] Zylberszac, opened the meeting and proposed Mrs. R. Damner[?] as chairwoman of the meeting.
The treasury report was given by the secretary Mr.[?] Mantzman[?]. It turns out that the society distributed aid to about 900 families.
After the report Mrs. Roza-Heitner[?] (Kraków) took the floor; she delivered a fine lecture which aroused enthusiasm.
Then the following board was elected: Mesdames the Rebbetzin Lewin, Zylberszac, Telner[?], Alter, Erlich, Waltzberg[?], Ferens[?], Damner[?], Fiszer, Rozen, Feinboim[?], Rinska, Lehmicz[?].
Suicide of a Couple in Love

[Będzin area — suicide.]
On Monday at midday the 36-year-old Wieczorkowa and the 35-year-old Grishka[?] [Gruszka] were found dead in the field behind Łagisza.
As it turned out, Wieczorkowa was a woman with 2 children; her husband is a railway worker. A year ago she had become acquainted with Gruszka, with whom she had intimate relations. The husband, however, found out about it, and she and her lover („kochanek“) decided to die. Both went out to the field, where Gruszka shot her and then shot himself.
Recitation Evening at WIZO

[Będzin — WIZO; culture.]
Next Sunday the 9th [of May], in the evening, a recitation evening will take place in WIZO's own premises, performed by the well-known reciter Yehuda Ehrenkranz[?] from Palestine.
On the programme: the pearls of Hebrew, Yiddish and German literature.
The 3rd of May Celebrations in Zagłębie

[Sosnowiec and Będzin — Constitution Day; the synagogues.]
Went off very impressively and with a great parade.
The [146th] anniversary of the Constitution [of 3 May 1791] was celebrated in Zagłębie with great splendour[?] and dignity.
The houses were decorated with national flags; in almost all shop windows the pictures of Marshal Piłsudski, State President Mościcki and Marshal Rydz-Śmigły were displayed.
Services and parades took place, in which the army and all military formations, societies, school youth etc. took part.
In the Będzin synagogue: after the Polish and the Jewish anthem had been played, Cantor Klagsbald conducted the festive prayer; on topical matters Rabbi Fridberg and Director Einhorn spoke. Very well received was the „Halleluyah“, which was performed together with the choir by the orchestra of Public School no. 2.
— In the Sosnowiec synagogue a huge crowd had gathered, mostly school youth. After Cantor Leichter[?] and the choir sang the appropriate prayers, speeches were made on topical matters, and the orchestra of the Jewish gymnasium played the Polish and the Jewish anthem, also „Hatikvah“.
The first appearance of the orchestra was received by the Jewish public with enthusiasm. Hundreds of people accompanied the orchestra all the way to the gymnasium building.
Ben-Gurion to Come to Sosnowiec

[Sosnowiec — Zionism.]
Ben-Gurion to come to Sosnowiec.
In the next few days a district conference of the League [?] for Labour Palestine will take place here, in connection with the Shekel campaign in Zagłębie.
As we are informed, one of the leaders of the Histadrut, Ben-Gurion or Baruch Zuckerman, is to take part in the conference.
District Conference of the Free-Loan Funds

[Zagłębie — free-loan funds.]
District conference of the gemilut-chesed (free-loan) funds.
This coming Sunday the local board of the free-loan fund is convening a conference of the free-loan funds in the Zagłębie and Zawiercie districts (powiats).
A representative of the "Joint" is also to take part in the conference.
The Dispute in the Synagogue in Old Sosnowiec Liquidated

[Sosnowiec — synagogue and community.]
The dispute in the synagogue in Old Sosnowiec liquidated.
Last Sabbath, before the Torah reading, there was again a great scandal in the sadly notorious synagogue in Old Sosnowiec, because the old gabbaim (wardens) did not want to step down from their "position".
To put an end once and for all to the lawlessness [?], the members of the dozór (community board), Messrs. Czapnik [?], Fajerman and Lewartowski [?], "deposed" the old gabbaim and appointed Messrs. Sztornglas [?] and Lakaj [?] to manage the affairs of the synagogue until new gabbaim are elected.
—o—
They did not look for big profits...
The local police have liquidated a factory of counterfeit 50- and 10-grosz coins.
The "manufacturers" were handed over to the judicial authorities.
—o—
"Festival of First Fruits".
Under this name a celebration with a rich programme is being organised at the Jewish gymnasium; it will be performed by the pupils of the gymnasium.
From a Dispute over a Cellar — the Same Story as with Potiphar's Wife

[Pilica — court.]
From a dispute over a cellar
the same story happened as with Potiphar's wife.
A certain M. of Pilica, an elderly Hasidic Jew, owns a small house in partnership with the local Jewish dentist A. Between the two householders there were constantly disputes over a jointly owned cellar. Once, when M. went down into the cellar, he met on the stairs the wife of his partner, who raised an alarm and cried out the same thing as Potiphar's wife..
The matter came before the municipal court there, which acquitted Mr. M.
The plaintiff was not satisfied with the verdict and appealed to the district court here, where the interesting trial was to have taken place last Tuesday; but because the plaintiff submitted her waiver [?] of all the witnesses, the trial was postponed.
The "Ulen" Debt Reduced by 4 Million Zł.

[Sosnowiec — municipality.]
The "Ulen" debt reduced by 4 million zł.
As is known, a number of towns in Poland went into debt through the "Ulen" loan taken at the time; among others Sosnowiec too owes a sum of 9 million zł.
Owing to the conversion of the loans the debt has been reduced to 5 million 600 thousand zł.
At today's session of the town council the question of the "Ulen" loan will be discussed.
Meeting of the "Lira" Members

[Sosnowiec — societies and culture.]
Meeting of the "Lira" members.
Today, Friday evening, a meeting of the "Lira" members takes place in the society's own premises. A number of current matters will be discussed on the agenda.
— Next Saturday the "Lira" society will stage "Der Goyel" ("The Redeemer") in the municipal theatre. The play, which has been directed anew, has been enlarged with a fourth act.
Forced His Wife into Prostitution

[Sosnowiec — court.]
Forced his wife into prostitution.
At the local district court the trial lasted 2 days of a certain Czajkowski, who was charged with forcing his wife into prostitution.
Czajkowski was sentenced to 6 months in prison.
—o—
A child thrown into the "Przemsza".
On Rybna Street the small dead body of a newborn child, a boy, was taken out of the "Black Przemsza".
The murderous mother is being sought by the police.
The Murderers Have Been Jailed

[Kielce — crime, courts.]
Life in Kielce — Friday, 26 Iyar 5697 — piątek 7 maja 1937
who carried out the horrific murder of the Szmulewicz family.

As we have already reported in our paper, the voivodeship [?] investigating authority in Kielce has issued an official communiqué about the new arrests of the murderers who carried out the horrific murder of the five Jewish martyrs in the village of Stachy.
The details are extraordinarily sensational.
The communiqué states [?], among other things, that even before the murder in Stachy the local resident Tadeusz Kaszyński was about to open a shop in Stachy, and that right after the murder this same Kaszyński indeed leased from Szmulewicz's relatives the house in which Szmulewicz had lived and kept a shop. Kaszyński lived together with his sweetheart, the sister of Roman Chmielewski, whom, a few days after the trial in the Kielce District Court, they pulled out of the river "Nida", where he had lain drowned for nearly 7 months.
It was then clear to the police that Kaszyński and his accomplices had carried out the murder in Stachy. All that was needed was material evidence.
From the bullets removed during the autopsy of Chmielewski's dead body, which were of the same calibre as those with which the 5 martyrs had been shot, the police were certain that, besides [?], Chmielewski had taken part in the murder, and that one of his companions had shot him and afterwards thrown him into the river, so that he would not be found and the wounds on his body, which he had received while struggling with one of the martyrs, would not be recognised.
On learning that Chmielewski's dead body had been found, Tadeusz Kaszyński fled to Katowice. There he was caught and brought in chains to Jędrzejów [?], where he was put in prison.
At the first interrogation, as soon as the arrested men were shown the material evidence, they all confessed to carrying out the bestial murder. Among the various pieces of evidence the bandits were also shown the revolver which Siemisław [?] had sold after the murder for 20 zł. to the Jew Yehoshua Goldberg of the village of Jakubów [?].
The investigation is being conducted with the greatest energy. For the sake of the investigation no exact details can yet be given.
The report that appeared in some newspapers, that among those arrested is also Wiśniewski [?], who had been acquitted by the Kielce District Court, does not correspond to reality. None of those acquitted has been arrested.
The 5 bandits face the death penalty.
This sensational trial will apparently take place in the Kielce District Court in the month of June of this year.
Have Pity on 40 Unfortunate Orphans!

[Kielce — charity, orphanage.]
This Sunday, at 6 in the evening, the annual general meeting of the local orphanage will take place in the premises of the Jewish kehilla.
The financial situation of the orphanage is an extraordinarily difficult one. Jewish society takes only little interest in the orphanage, and there is a danger that 40 unfortunate orphans may, God forbid, perish of hunger.
At the general meeting, therefore, ways will be sought to improve the situation of the orphanage and to secure a normal budget for the management.
Every Jew must therefore come to the general meeting; no one may be absent. Together we must deliberate on the situation of this exalted [?] institution, which must have [?] a secure existence.
Everyone must have pity on the 40 unfortunate orphans!
A Child Left at the Kehilla.

[Kielce — kehilla, welfare.]
This week a Jewish woman left a 6-year-old child at the kehilla and went away. As it later turned out, the child's mother is Rachel Fridman (née Tchórz) of Kielce. She left a letter to the kehilla asking that the child be placed in the orphanage, because out of need she must set off into the world in search of support [?].
The kehilla sent the child to the orphanage.
Correction.

[Upper Silesia — correction; Chorzów.]
In the Upper Silesian column it was reported [?], among the Chorzów news items, that Dr. Wierzbicki [?] would give a lecture in Chorzów this Saturday night (motzei Shabbat).
For personal reasons the lecture had to take place last Wednesday.
A detailed report on it in the next issue.
Kielce Rabbinate and Kehilla Took Part in the Funeral of Bishop Łosiński.

[Kielce — kehilla and rabbinate, relations with the Church.]
Last Friday afternoon the Bishop of Kielce, Augustyn Łosiński, died at the age of 70.
The bishop's funeral took place on Wednesday morning. The funeral, which was very imposing, was attended by a crowd of nearly 50 thousand people from Kielce and the surrounding area. Several hundred priests from all of Poland came to Kielce, as well as 10 bishops.
The funeral was also attended by the Kielce rabbinate headed by Rabbi Rapaport, as well as a delegation of the Kielce kehilla, Messrs. Rozer [?] S. R. Ajzenberg and the gabbai Hershl Goldberg, who were present during the solemn mourning prayer in the church.
The delegation was cordially received by a representative of the bishop's curia, who led it into the cathedral through the main ("parade") entrance, and they remained [?] there, as said, until after the mourning prayer.
Young Painter Kaminer

[Kielce — art; Zagłębie.]
Organises an exhibition of paintings in Zagłębie.
This week the young, talented painter-artist Dawid Kaminer left for Zagłębie with the aim of exhibiting his paintings in Zagłębie. Recently the President of the State has taken an interest in the young artist.
Dawid Kaminer is simply a child prodigy; his abilities have been recognised by the most eminent painters in Poland.
It is to be hoped that the Jewish population of Zagłębie will take an interest in the artist and help him to perfect himself in his field.
The Day of National Mourning.

[Kielce — state commemorations, schools.]
Programme of the ceremonies on the anniversary of Marshal Piłsudski's death.
As we have already reported, the school authority has issued an ordinance according to which on the 12th of this month there will be no lessons in the schools. The school youth, however, is obliged to come to the schools, where services will be held in memory of the leader of the nation, Marshal Józef Piłsudski.
On that day mourning services will take place in all houses of prayer.
[Continuation of “The Day of National Mourning” (2.56) — no heading in print; Kielce — Piłsudski anniversary.]
At exactly a quarter to 9 in the evening — when Marshal Piłsudski died — a 3-minute pause of silence is planned. At that moment all traffic everywhere will stop — all carts, trains, trams and the passers-by in the streets will stand still.
On the 12th of this month state flags will be hung out, lowered, as a sign of mourning, to half-mast and wrapped [?] in crêpe.
—o—
[Kielce — charity; old-age home.]
A Chain of Dinners for the Kielce Old-Age Home.
This week the following persons gave dinners for the Kielce old-age home, and the board thanks them:
Sunday, dinner, Abraham Szlomo Fridenzon [?]; Monday, dinner, Józef Machtinger [?]; Tuesday, dinner, Fiszel Korn; Wednesday, Welig [?] and Szelbzunok [?]; Thursday, dinner, Mosze Lindfeld [?]; Friday, a whole day, Mosze Lewensztajn [?] and sisters, for the yahrzeit of their father R. Chaim Jehoszua of blessed memory; Sabbath, dinner, Sindl [?] Szlomowicz [?] and children, for the yahrzeit of her husband and father Józef, may he rest in peace.

Ritual-Slaughter Law Adopted by the Sejm Committee.

[Upper Silesia — shechita, legislation.]
The agrarian committee of the Silesian Sejm, under the chairmanship of Deputy Polarczyk, held a meeting last Monday at which the shechita law was dealt with. After a lengthy discussion it was decided that the shechita law should also be introduced on the territory of the Silesian Voivodeship.
At the next sitting of the Sejm the question will be on the agenda.
Verdict in the Matter of the Mysłowice Railway Disaster.

[Upper Silesia — Mysłowice, court.]
Several months ago, as is known, a disaster occurred at the Mysłowice railway station in which 6 people were killed and several dozen injured.
A trial was held concerning those guilty of the disaster, and on Tuesday at 11 p.m. the verdict was announced, according to which the traffic dispatcher on duty is sentenced to a year and a half in prison and the head of the locomotives — to two and a half years in prison.
What's New in Chorzów? — From the Trial of the Empty JNF Box

[Upper Silesia — Chorzów; Zionism, JNF, culture.]
What's New in Chorzów?
From the trial of the empty JNF box.
On Saturday a trial of the empty box of the JNF (Keren Kayemet) was held in the premises of the Zionist Organisation.
Before a hall packed full of visitors the bench of the court appears. The presiding judge was Dr. Sternhel[?]; the associate judges — the president of the Zionist Organisation, Ch. Kapłowicz, Mrs. Bisner (WIZO) and Kakasz (Mizrachi); prosecutor — Mgr. Rastal; defence counsel — Dr. Kalberg; experts: Morsze[?] Jungster and Sz. Standorf; as witnesses: Miss Wegsztajn[?] and Comrades Bisner and Fojgelfang.
At the opening of the court the presiding judge honoured the leader Nahum Sokolow on his first yahrzeit by rising and one minute of silence.
Then Mgr. Rastal reads the indictment and demands the punishment of the communal workers who neglected the activity on behalf of the JNF. After hearing the witnesses and experts, Dr. Kalberg comes forward with a fine speech for the defence.
The verdict reads: guilty are that part of the Jewish population which avoids the box, and also the communal workers who did not conduct any broad propaganda.
To the strains of „Hatikvah“ the trial is closed.

The Necessity of Intensive Activity for the JNF in Chorzów

[Upper Silesia — Chorzów; Zionism, JNF — opinion.]
The trial held here of the empty JNF boxes, in which the wealthiest Jews of our town took part — who until now had been passive in their attitude to the JNF — gives full conviction that it is necessary to set about immediate intensive work in this field, if only because the JNF has taken upon itself one of the principal tasks: to buy up „the land“, to create the foundation without which one can achieve nothing at all in Eretz Israel; for what value do all the efforts, all the problems have, if the land lies in non-Jewish hands?
The trial also showed the way to adopt the means that will bring an improvement in the method of the work done hitherto.
Therefore it has now become clear to all friends of the JNF that the JNF's activity at the present time must be intensive, concentrated and strong, because the JNF is the foundation of our existence, of our entire national work.
The work must be reorganised, improved, systematised and calculated, and above all — conducted according to plan.
The time must be used, because too great is the present task which the Keren Kayemet has taken upon itself.
In every Jewish home there should be a box; the Jewish houses will be visited by senior communal workers, and then we shall see further who the guilty ones are.
Menachem.

On Monday a storm with heavy thunder and lightning passed over Upper Silesia. In Łaziska, Rybnik county, lightning killed a shepherd, and also 7 geese. In a number of places fires broke out from the lightning, causing considerable damage.
Mourning Ceremonies

[Zagłębie — state occasions; Będzin.]
On the second anniversary of Marshal Piłsudski's death.
On Wednesday, the second anniversary of the death of Marshal Józef Piłsudski, Zagłębie was wrapped in mourning. On all the houses national flags fluttered, lowered to half-mast and bound with black crêpe.
The culmination was the 3 minutes of silence, which began at a quarter to 9 in the evening — at the moment when, 2 years ago, the leader of the nation died.
The 3 minutes of silence were announced by church bells and the signals of sirens. Street traffic, and also tram traffic, came to a complete stop; passers-by in the streets stood still and conducted themselves solemnly.
In the synagogues mourning prayers were held in honour of the second anniversary of Marshal Piłsudski's death. In the Będzin synagogue Rabbi Friedberg spoke.

David Herman Has Died

The Jewish world has received sad news from New York: the well-known stage director David Herman has died there of a heart attack at the age of 61.
In Warsaw David Herman completed the Polish drama school as a director, and from 1903 he was active in various Jewish and Polish theatres in Poland.
In later years Herman led troupes of his own; after the war David Herman was director of the Vilna Troupe, and he made a name for himself above all with his staging of An-sky's "Dybbuk".
Among the Zagłębie Jewish theatre public, too, David Herman was beloved, and his appearances in Będzin always had the greatest success.
Honour to his memory.
Truth Shall Spring Out of the Earth...

At the hat-maker Meir Perlmuter's in Wazierske[?], a priest from a neighbouring village bought 30 caps for a youth organisation.
On receiving the caps, the priest saw that instead of 30 he had only 21. He at once sent a messenger to the hat-maker, from whom he demanded that he make up the 9 caps. Perlmuter, being sure that he had packed 30 caps, told the messenger that he was not responsible for whatever might have happened.
To the priest, of course, the explanation was not decisive, and he again wrote a letter to Perlmuter, demanding that he supply the 9 caps.
Over the affair a sharp quarrel arose between the two parties, until the awl came out of the sack [i.e. the truth came out]..
One fine morning a Christian boy comes in to Perlmuter and offers to sell him those same caps, at 50 groszy a cap.
Perlmuter began haggling with the "merchant" and meanwhile sent for a policeman, who arrested the juvenile thief.
As it turned out, the boy had stolen the caps from the parcel that was lying on a cart.
After the discovery, Perlmuter received a letter from the priest, who apologises for having suspected him without cause.

Before It Is Too Late.

(A few words about the Sosnowiec Talmud Torah.)
It seems that Jewish Zagłębie has no luck with its popular institutions, and first and foremost with the "Talmud Torahs".
Just last week the Jews of Będzin were alarmed — by the press[?], of course — that if they do not support materially this elementary popular institution, they will be the first to help undermine it.
The Sosnowiec "Talmud Torah" finds itself in no better state. There too the situation is serious enough, and the public relates to the institution very[?] apathetically.
It goes without saying that, finding itself in so serious a situation, the board must begin to take care how to rescue the institution from ruin. It must by no means sit with folded hands and wait for a steady deterioration and neglect, for in this way the situation can become more catastrophic from day to day, and then perhaps there will no longer be anything left to keep alive.
In our view, and as we observe the "Talmud Torahs", they do not stand today[?] at the proper height — not in the material sense, and still less in the educational sense; yet we cannot make peace with the thought that we shall remain indifferent to these institutions and watch them die out. We must not remain indifferent when we see institutions suffering, unable to pay their employees their meagre salaries. First of all, after all, one must have a budget that would be secured; otherwise one cannot conduct any planned activity at all that would secure its existence — and this plays the main role first and foremost. Otherwise there can be no talk at all of any future whatsoever for its maintenance.
And therefore: let the budget be secured, let the income be paid regularly into the T"T [Talmud Torah] treasury, and then it will be possible to plan various useful improvements, which are needed more and more.
The town must therefore take up the question more seriously and see to it that this useful popular institution can exist not on chance but on real foundations.
The board must therefore take upon itself the mission of reorganizing its activity; it must see to recruiting new members in town — such as pay nothing to this day — and as for the rich Jews who do pay a few groszy to fulfil an obligation, so that it may be said for appearance's sake that they are members, their commitment must be increased, doubled, each according to his means, according to his strength.
Some twenty-odd years ago, when Sosnowiec was small and insignificant, when for every trifle one had to come to Będzin, the Talmud Torah kept itself going; and today, when the town — and with it the Jewish population — has grown and developed, maintaining the Talmud Torah is harder than the splitting of the Red Sea.
Where, then[?], are the Jews who cannot remain indifferent when poor children are to be brought up in the street and remain boors and utter ignoramuses? Why do they not consider all this? There are, after all, Jews who have, or ought to have, understanding for a Talmud Torah — why do they not take an interest in the institution now, while it is not yet too late?
It is therefore worthwhile for the Jews of Sosnowiec to consider the question more seriously and to set about reorganizing the work of this useful institution before it comes to liquidation.
Selekt.
Let Us Pour Fresh Blood

Into the Arteries of Jewish Commerce!
At the centre of the most burning interests awaiting their radical solution, the painful Jewish question has also been placed.
Jewish trade in the sales stalls, which for years was decried as unnecessary intermediary "posts" (placówki) that bring no benefit, has been [—][?], and now[?] — owing to higher economic processes — is to go under; yet just now it is being so solemnly canonized and coddled as a source of livelihood and as coveted footholds for new Polish elements, who are to take it over into their possession and make a living from it.
At school, in the press, on the radio — everything calls and urges to storm "peacefully" the last Bastille, to seize the Jewish commercial enterprises, already so weakened, anaemic and sucked dry by burdensome[?] taxes.
The exalted thousand-year-old ideal of the Jews — to build themselves in it [this land] a pleasant, complete and full-blooded life — is so tastelessly distorted[?] into an impatient lust to be rid of the Jews, to have them emigrate, just to seize as quickly as possible the pieces of life, the livelihoods and establishments that they shaped over hundreds of years with blood and marrow.
With us, one-sidedly, there grows a dependence[?] — a tziduk ha-din [resigned acceptance of the decree] with glazed eyes; the process of pauperization spreads — genteel, householder poverty. Alongside this, the urbanist tendencies, still strongly rooted; alongside this, the urge to rise to the higher rungs of urban life, to make one's way into the pleiad of the free professions, into a half-prospering intelligentsia, to lead a clean, decent, elastic and dignified life.
Even today the most intimate ideal of every smaller or bigger merchant, of the Jewish petty bourgeois or manufacturer, is to see his son or son-in-law a qualified doctor, magister [pharmacist], court trainee (aplikant), engineer, etc.; and although all the doors and gates of offices and public institutions are shut to the educated Jew and to his sphere of action, as well as his place of work — and he jostles about and gets entangled in the narrow Jewish lane, around the wire fences of the Jewish enclosure, on the lean shoulders of the Jewish middle class — he nevertheless prefers to see, through the coils of cigarette smoke, an elegant office or a law chancery rather than a big business, a factory office or a goods warehouse.
Even today it still belongs to bon ton, to "better" society.
"Never mind me," the father, the merchant, thinks to himself, "I must already get through my few old years like this, in the dark Jewish livelihoods; but him, that young man of mine, him I will not let near the business — let him remain an intellectual, a man of the spirit, as I live."
A rewarding subject for a painter's picture: a Jewish yarn merchant holding up the "Alma Mater".
It is comical, if not tragic, when one considers that rooted, solid Jewish livelihoods, long-standing businesses and enterprises writhe in pain and die out, while the old merchant, with his broken Polish and outdated working methods, stands weak[?] and helpless, rebuffed, bare-headed, holding his hat with both hands, and whispers submissively to the wretched[?] "petition-writer" (prośba-writer) to save him from despair with an appeal (rekurs) — while his son, the "Viennese young gent", prepares for his intellectual profession.
Is it hard to understand that when the rag merchant goes under, the young man will be no "Viennese"; when the lanterns in the trading yards are extinguished, the chandeliers in the offices will not burn?
Would it not be more fitting if the fine army[?] of educated young people, armed with learning and knowledge, were to enter the still existing and prospering trade and industrial posts, in order to relieve and partly replace the fathers — the Jewish merchants — already weakened and estranged from the demands of the new time; for the young, after all, understand better the spirit of the time, the language, the customs and the art of manoeuvring "between" the new decrees.
In former years, it is told, a rich Jew used to pick an outstanding scholar for a son-in-law; when it was proposed that he become a rabbi, the father-in-law would shake it off — "the rabbinate buries those who hold it" — not a rabbi but a merchant he shall be, and conduct great commerce. And who knows whether we do not owe to those sharp Gemara minds the ramified expansion of Jewish trade and the greatest Jewish enterprises, which were a blessing for this country.
On the economic battlefield it is necessary to pour fresh blood into the arteries of Jewish commerce, to preserve the positions acquired over generations — Jewish livelihoods and existences.
S. Ivri.
