With the Heroes of the Book of Ruth...

By Y. Oberżanek.
A brilliant idea struck me: to snatch an interview with the heroes of the Book of Ruth, as befits Shavuot.
Without thinking long, I told my wife to hand me the pressed trousers with the new tie, grabbed my briefcase and set off to look up the heroes of the Book of Ruth.
First of all I went to Naomi.
I come up to the door, ring, and the door is opened to me by a shiksa [gentile maid].
— Co pan sobie życzy? [What do you wish, sir?] — she asks me.
— Czy zastałem panią Naomi w domu? [Is Mrs Naomi at home?]
Here a woman of middle years appears, wearing a [?] pyjama, with freshly waved hair, with[?] a cigarette between her freshly painted lips.
— Czym mogę panu służyć? [How may I serve you, sir?] — the lady asks me.
— "Is this Naomi?" — I ask her.
She says: "Nie rozumiem" [I don't understand].
— Aren't you the widow of Reb Elimelech?
— Owszem, tak [Indeed, yes] — she answered.
— And I am Editor Feinshmirer.
— I wanted to have an interview with you for my newspaper.
— Bardzo proszę [By all means] — she answered.
— Perhaps you can tell me, Madame Naomi, how come you speak Polish? After all, you were once a proper Jewish woman.
— Minęły się czasy [Times have passed] — she answered — zresztą [besides] — she looked around to see whether the maid was not listening — I can speak Yiddish too.
— Explain to me, Mrs Naomi, why did you send your daughter-in-law Ruth to Boaz in the barn; why didn't you go yourself?
— Don't ask, dear friend — she answered with a sour face — I regret it to this very day. Oh, today I would not be such a fool...
— By the way, perhaps you can tell me what your Elimelech died of?
— Yes, as you know, he was once a great merchant, a fine rich man.
— Yes — I say — I know.
— So he gave goods on bills of exchange, I got protests, the "Skarb" [Treasury] chased him with podatki [taxes], and the rest you surely know already?
— Yes — I say — I understand now. And tell me, then, what did your two sons die of?
— They were treated at the "Kasa Chorych" [sick fund]...
— Excuse me for asking you one more question: you are, I see, a modern lady, and in the Megillah you are presented as a modest Jewish woman?
— Go on, go on — she burst out laughing — do you believe everything that is written in the Megillah?
I thanked her for the interview granted and went off to Ruth.
— Is Madame Ruth at home? — I asked the shiksa who opened the door for me.
— Yes — she says — that is me myself; what do you want?
— I am — I say — Editor Feinshmirer; I want to have an interview with you for my newspaper. Would you be so kind?
— Bitte sehr — she answered me politely.
— If so, I will ask you questions and you will answer me.
I: How come that you, a Christian woman, decided to marry the Jew Boaz?
Ruth: Did I mean Boaz, then? I only meant his majątek [estate].
I: Then why did you first go out to the field to gather ears of grain?
Ruth: Quite simple: just as all other women go into the forest in summer "na jagody" [berry-picking] and [?] they mean something else...
I: Aha, I understand. And how did Boaz receive you at night in the barn?
Ruth: No worse than other men when such an "okazja" [opportunity] comes their way.
I: But the Megillah says he was frightened?
Ruth: What else should the Megillah write? Besides, I don't understand why the whole Megillah was written at all; as if few such [?] stories happen nowadays with the "straw widowers" when their wives go off to the dachas?...
I thanked Mrs Ruth and set off to Boaz, to his estate.
— Can one see the master? — I asked one of the farmhands (parobki).
It doesn't take long, and from the [?] comes a short, pot-bellied little Jew with broad shoulders, smoking a long cigar.
— Who is it, a Jew? he asks me.
— I am Editor Feinshmirer; are you Reb Boaz?
— Yes — he says — [?].
— I wanted to have an interview with you for my newspaper.
— An interview? — he stares at me wide-eyed — what for? Better that people don't know that Jews own estates in times like these.
— Excuse me, Reb Boaz — I say — I don't mean your estates; I only want to know a few interesting (ciekawe) details that were written about you in the Megillah.
— If so — he gave his belly a stroke — then with the greatest pleasure.
I: Tell me, Reb Boaz, how come that a fellow like you — you were, no evil eye, a rich man, with your own fields and forests — how did you come to the gentile woman?
Boaz: Excuse me, I did not come to the gentile woman; the gentile woman came to me.
I: Could you not have got a kosher Jewish daughter for a wife?
He: Here's a penny for all your "kosher" daughters — before the wedding they are all kosher, and after the wedding?
I: Explain to me, then, Reb Boaz: did you know Ruth already before?
Boaz: What an idea!
I: But it says in the Megillah that you ordered the young men not to bother her.
Boaz: And so what if the Megillah writes it? As if various newspaper rags don't write plenty of cock-and-bull "megillahs".
I thanked Boaz for the interview granted and went home to eat kreplach.
Shavuot — the Feast of Harvest — the Day of the Firstfruits

[Holiday — Shavuot; historical essay.]
"And the feast of harvest, the firstfruits of thy labours, which thou hast sown in the field."
Exodus 23:16.
"Also in the day of the firstfruits, when ye bring a new meat offering."
Numbers 28:26.

The celebration of the festival of Shavuot is based mainly on the natural phenomena with which every agricultural people is blessed [?]: the cutting of the harvest and the picking of the ripe fruit from the orchards. It is therefore self-evident that the Torah commands the Jewish people — as a former agricultural people — to celebrate the festival of Shavuot as "the feast of harvest," when the grain is reaped [?] from the field, and also as "the day of the firstfruits," when [?] the fruits ripen.

But the festival of Shavuot is also based on "the time of the giving of our Torah," according to the verse in the Torah "In the third month (Sivan) etc., and Moses went up unto God etc." — and it was then, on Shavuot, that Moses received the Torah on Mount Sinai.

In the course of time, however, the natural character of Shavuot was entirely erased and almost forgotten, and during the long time of exile it has been celebrated only as a purely religious festival, as "the time of the giving of our Torah"; and so the question arises: how could it happen that so important a moment in the life of the people — one based on a logical [?] and special content and connected with the splendid tradition of terumot, the tithe, gleanings, the forgotten sheaf and the corner of the field, the fallen grapes and the gleaning of the vineyard, etc., which had such [?] enormous value and significance for the broad poor masses of the people and for the unfortunate, such as the stranger, the orphan and the widow — how is it that so important a symbol of a former agricultural people should be entirely erased and forgotten?

It goes without saying that a strong cause of this was the cruel fate and terrible tragedy that befell the Jewish people, which after the destruction of the Second Temple was driven out and torn away from its mother-soil and no longer had either the physical or the moral possibility of cultivating its old traditions. But that still does not resolve the question, because the Jewish people, having a cult and reverence for its traditions and sacred things, still marks at least with certain symbols the memory of its feast of harvest and day of firstfruits — and the question arises with full sharpness: how did this happen?

But in order to answer this question we must turn back [?] a page of our bloody, tragic history of two thousand years ago. We must reflect upon and look deeply into the development of the historical events after the destruction of the Second Temple — or, better said, at the end of the period before the Second Destruction, when the Jewish people fought with its last strength for its freedom and independence against the mighty Roman enemy.

That was shortly before that terribly tragic time, before the despotic enemy plunged his bloody sword into the deep heart of the Jewish people, before the drunken soldiers of Titus set fire to and burned the Holy Temple, which had been the soul and the pride of the people. The bloody war of [?] a handful of Jewish heroes and mighty men against the powerful, gigantic armies of the Roman legions was still in full swing, and the Jewish heroes still did not want to yield to the terrible thought that the dreadful destruction was approaching with giant strides, that their days were numbered and that their fate was already sealed. But the great spirits of the people held a different opinion about the outcome of events: their perspective was more far-reaching and clearer, and they saw the great danger threatening the very existence of the Jewish people if its cultural centre, the Torah, were not rescued.

And among those far-sighted spirits the place of honour was taken by the famous tanna Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai, who risked his life and by a certain stratagem was smuggled through the Jewish military post [?], because the Jewish heroes watched every single person, and whoever wanted to make contact with the enemy outside was regarded as a traitor and condemned to death. And there [?] he presented himself before the Roman field marshal Vespasian as the representative of that party among the Jews which capitulates and surrenders to the enemy voluntarily.

And when Vespasian asked him what reward he demanded for this, Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai answered him: "Give me Yavneh and its sages!" — give me "Yavneh" with its scholars; and the request was granted.

As is known, shortly afterwards Jerusalem fell; the Holy Temple — the spiritual centre that had united and cemented the whole people — was burned; the best sons and daughters were driven from their homeland and sold as slaves and into the houses of shame.

And then Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai sets about fulfilling the historic task that fate had cast upon him, and begins to realise the idea of exchanging the lost political independence for a spiritual and cultural independence. To reach this goal he takes various measures: first of all he proclaims that "Yavneh" takes the place of Jerusalem with its holiness; then, that the Sanhedrin of "Yavneh" possesses the same authority as the Sanhedrin of Jerusalem [abbreviation unclear]; then he sets about ordering social and even private life on the foundations of religion, so that the whole life of the community and of the individual becomes closely bound together and organically grown together like one indivisible being, and everything came to be founded on the principles of the Torah. In this way [?] the whole life of the people acquired a religious colouring.

It is therefore no wonder that a festival like Shavuot, founded on logical [?] grounds as "the time of the giving of our Torah," was in the course of time transformed into a purely religious festival, and its age-old traditions were completely erased and forgotten.

We, the present generation, whom fate has called to take part in the wondrous historical process of the resurrection of the Land of Israel — let us hope that we shall yet be privileged to celebrate it:

The festival of Shavuot — as "the feast of harvest" and "the day of the firstfruits"!..

Y. Wygodzki.
Fifty Years Ago

[Feuilleton — world and technology.] The present President of America, Roosevelt, never gives interviews to any newspaper. "By the time — he says — my conversation is printed, the world will meanwhile look different and everything will be outdated." He is somewhat right. In quite a short time the world changes so much that we marvel[?] at what could so excite us only yesterday...
Let us look a little at the events of some fifty years ago, a time that many of us still remember — how much has changed in the course of that time!
In the year 1879, for example, one could see at the Leipzig fair the first carriage that travelled without a horse, by steam. The newspapers wrote then that it was by no means possible to travel without a horse: one would travel a few kilometres an hour and would not be able to go on, because uphill and downhill one can steer only with living creatures... Besides that, the newspapers of the day prophesied that there would never be a person who would pay some three thousand dollars for such a carriage or fifteen thousand dollars for a bus without a horse... Today horses have almost entirely disappeared.
In the year 1881 trains on several lines in England began to travel at fifty kilometres an hour, and the then railway minister of England said he hoped that one day people would travel by train at seventy kilometres an hour... What an uproar there was in all the newspapers of the whole world!... All the experts and engineers and all the "lender"[?] laughed: seventy kilometres an hour — they argued — is altogether impossible... Today one already travels at more than a hundred and forty kilometres an hour..
Collecting stamps was regarded fifty years ago as a madness or as a pastime of idlers who do not know what to do all day... When in the year 1850 the first stamp shop opened in Brussels (Belgium), the newspapers said that within a few weeks the shop would go bust[?]. People laughed even more when the New York conductors of the local omnibus company founded in the year 1850 the first society of stamp collectors... The newspapers asked whether the omnibus company had nothing better to do, that its conductors had such empty nonsense on their minds. Today millions of people all over the world collect stamps, and tens of thousands make quite a nice living from it...
Big fees for actors were paid in the past: the actress Sarah Bernhardt of Paris played 50 years ago about 4 months in New York, and for 141 performances she received net, without expenses, 421 205 dollars — no single star of the acting world earns that much today.
According to the latest Hollywood tax statement, Marlene Dietrich earns "only" 400 thousand dollars a whole year... The other film stars (except Greta Garbo) earn a great deal less a whole year: Colbert[?], Marshall[?] and even Jan Kiepura earn "only" up to a hundred thousand dollars a year, little Shirley Temple earns only 75 thousand, Menjou[?] and Wallace Beery "only" up to 50 thousand dollars a year...
Radio is a new invention; nevertheless, already 50 years ago one could transmit operas from distant places by telephone. In the "Times" of the year 1882 there is a letter from a reader who heard through his telephone a performance of the London opera. He tells what a pleasure it was to hear the opera at home while he was eating supper. He even writes which instruments he heard well and which badly, and advises composers to write operas only with instruments that are heard well through the telephone.
As one sees, it is indeed true that everything has already been in the world, and that everything passes from today to tomorrow.
Z. Haber, Vienna.
Heard and Seen — by Ben Amotz

[Sosnowiec — satirical feuilleton; kehilla, merchants.]
The first exam...
A short notice in bold letters we read in one of the latest numbers of the "Literarishe Bleter". In this little notice it is reported that "the Jewish kehilla in Sosnowiec has refused henceforth to subscribe to the said publication".
And so that one should not suspect it, the kehilla board, of evil intentions — that the refusal came because the contents of the "Literarishe Bleter" do not satisfy the gentlemen of the kehilla board — no, it is "for reasons of budget economy".
Plain and simple: the kehilla budget of the city of Sosnowiec, amounting to barely a hundred thousand złoty, cannot bear the burden of subscribing to the journal, which costs no less than — 30 groszy... a week, i.e.[?] 12 zł. a year...
And truly, one cannot have any complaints against the gentlemen: the "Literarishe Bleter" are after all not an "article" one cannot do without; that "article" cannot even be compared with a kehilla [—][?]. If the journal appeared in a foreign language and its contents were foreign too, one might still have overlooked it; but such a thing as the "Literarishe Bleter" — what do I know — "the matter is not worth the effort"...
Therefore we say that the editors of the above-mentioned journal can have no great complaints against the kehilla board of Sosnowiec, may God protect it; on the contrary, they even hold that their tactic (in this, poor thing, materially) is a "consistent" one, and they deserve a yasher koyekh for — the first exam..
We are still at Bereshit..
In the Jewish street the trumpets blare, the bells ring, people call out and rouse — unity, strengthened ranks, self-defence and several more "heavenly" slogans at the expense of the Jewish merchant class.
And the stronger antisemitism grows — the louder the calls are heard.
And we say that all this drumming and rousing goes to waste, because they do not touch the important questions: the Jewish people possesses a host of petty hawkers[?], but no merchants.
We want to illustrate this with living facts that we have seen and heard in the secretariat of the Small Traders' Association in Sosnowiec.
Into the secretariat comes a member, a well-to-do merchant, and asks for a certificate[?].
The secretary gives him the certificate and asks for 50 groszy.
— What? — the merchant turns red with anger — a członek [member] — he says — has to pay for a certificate? I am a członek after all...
— "True, you are indeed our member, but for the certificate you have to pay, because we too pay for the printing, and secondly — those are the orders I have from Warsaw[?]."
— "Who ever heard such a thing — the członek starts preaching his sermon — that to be a członek one has to pay, and for a certificate too; so what do I need the związek [union] for?"
The dialogue between him and the secretary lasts about half an hour. The merchant makes various proposals as to how he could wriggle out of the "eygl" [lit. "calf"] so as not to have to give the fifty groszy: for example, he wants to borrow the certificate to take home, where he will copy down the prices; if not, let the secretary tell him who in his branch has such a certificate, and he will copy it from that person...
At that moment the association's collector arrives and pours out his bitter heart about the members, who have absolutely no understanding of their vital interests.
— We — he says — were invited by the price commission at the local Magistrat to a meeting on fixing prices for articles of first necessity. One would think our association ought to have been represented by a proper delegation, but from morning till evening I could not find a single member willing to take part in this important meeting for merchants.
And listening to the collector's report and to the haggling of the rich Jewish merchant with the secretary over a certificate for 50 groszy, we come to the conviction that the call to the Jewish merchants to be organised and strengthened is groundless, because first of all one must educate the Jewish merchant, start teaching him the alef-beys, because
— we are still at Bereshit...
The Teaching of the Deed (Shavuot Reflections)

[Essay — Shavuot; thought and ethics.] By P. Blumenkrantz (Częstochowa).
(Shavuot reflections)
Na'aseh ve-nishma — "We will do and we will hear"!
The aggada relates:
When the Jews said "we will do" before "we will hear", a heavenly voice went forth and said: Who revealed this secret, which the ministering angels use? For they strive through deeds toward perfection, toward the highest degrees of perfection.
And remarkably:
At the time of the Jews' entire enthusiasm[?] for learning, at the time of the glorification of knowledge of the Torah, the sages warn:
He whose wisdom exceeds his deeds is likened to a tree with many branches and weak roots, and the wind comes and uproots it.
And the great Jewish sage R. Yohanan ben Zakkai, he who at the time of the Destruction asked only for Yavneh, the great leader who at the time of the Jewish catastrophe [—?] asked first of all for a little corner for the Torah, says to his five disciples:
— Go and choose for yourselves a way to keep to. And when the disciples come back with their answers, the old, wise R. Yohanan likes best the answer of R. Eleazar ben Arakh: a good heart, because this answer contains within itself all the others.
A good heart!
We have never overlooked anyone's bad deeds because of his learning.
The nations took pains to justify the contradictions often observed between "teaching and deed" in their great men. And when their spiritual leaders behaved differently from what they taught, this was explained away, and the contradictions were sometimes even made into an attribute of genius.
Among Jews, by contrast, the "Aherim" [the "others", i.e. those like Elisha ben Abuya] were condemned. There is no duality; on the contrary: "Not study is the main thing, but the deed." And when the proselyte comes to Hillel to be taught the whole Torah on one foot, he tells him:
— "What is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow; that is the whole Torah"...
• • •
Only an absolute harmony between idea and deed could bring into the world, already thousands of years ago, in an age of general savagery — a [? word unclear], which has remained in its greatness to this very day — the idea of the End of Days!
And it is precisely this attitude, that the main thing is a person's deeds, that set its seal on Jewish ethics, which is based on life and is distinguished by its realism and practicability.
The opinion of the Talmud, that one does not impose a decree unless the majority will be able to adapt to it, shows absolutely[?] the realistic view of our sages on the precepts of life. In contrast to Christian ethics, account was taken of human needs, inclinations and capabilities. No self-renunciation for the sake of another is demanded of a person; you need only love him as yourself, truly, warmly.
This realistic attitude to man, imbued with a deep love for the chosen one of creation, consequently had to produce such opinions as express it vividly: the Sabbath is the foundation of the Jewish religion, but to keep a person alive, even for a single moment, one may desecrate the Sabbath. The four death penalties of the court exist, but the Sanhedrin that carried out a death sentence once in 70 years was looked at askance.
• • •
With these deeply human concepts of life the Jewish people began to wander among savage and half-savage peoples, among peoples demoralized by prosperity[?] and enslaved ones.
It began to wander, penetrated among them and unsettled them with the invisible, incomprehensible God and a modern ethics.
And when the idolatrous, pleasure-loving Romans saw that Jewish ethics (in a popularized and extreme form) was beginning to penetrate their lives, they first resisted and afterwards took it over — at the same time taking revenge on us for the gift...
• • •
These thoughts — old ones, many times pondered and written — surface in moments of reckoning.
We were not, when creating our precepts of life, exaggerated in ethics — [we were] realistic and deliberate, not separating it from everyday life. We strove to root the ethical concepts so that they would grow organically together with man and his conduct.
And precisely because of this we succeeded, earlier than others, in restraining the wild instincts, in mastering ourselves and becoming masters over many destructive human inclinations.
And if we see that the unrestrained beast in man wants to break out of the frames built up over centuries, we must not despair, nor [recoil?] from the "man of the fist", but go on believing in the unshakeability of our truth.
When the Rebbe of Kock saw — so it is told — that the Hasidim did not understand him and that his Torah teaching of the well-known Friday night had been badly understood, he was disheartened by the narrowness of the Hasidim, but, God forbid, did not doubt his truth.
And if the question steals[?] into our aching[?] hearts — "Is this the Torah, and this its reward" — we must take to our aid the warm hearts scattered[?] across the whole world, which bleed together with us.
Sodom would not have been destroyed had there been ten righteous men in it; perhaps today's merciless Sodom will not be destroyed for the sake of its noble sons?
— "I will not destroy it for the sake of the ten"..
• • •
We must believe in the victory of our truths, for that is the secret of our existence.
"Had you not believed, you would not have seen..."
Nahum Sokolow of blessed memory (Recollections on his first yahrzeit) — 2

[Memoirs — Nahum Sokolow; part 2.] My trust in Sokolow's "divrei chimim" [?] later caused me much grief and also did me harm. It was before the outbreak of the war, in 1914, when people began to talk of war between Germany and Russia. For me this was the whole world turned upside down, because my entire business depended on both countries. And listen to this: two days before the mobilisation Sokolow writes in "Ha-Tsefira" an article entitled "Milchama lo tihye" ("There will be no war"), which shows [?] that even if — so he wrote — the cannons were already heard "talking", there would still be no war.
Soon after the end of the World War I had the opportunity to meet Sokolow and told him what damage I had suffered because of the article "There will be no war". To this he explained to me that the reason for his conviction had been that he was then influenced by German policy (he was living in Germany at the time).
My first acquaintance with Sokolow was in 1899, at the first conference of the Polish Zionists in Warsaw. I was there as a delegate of the Sosnowiec Zionists.
At that illegal conference it was decided to send Sokolow, together with the Wkrasszym [?] rabbi, R. Yona Wlatnik [?] of blessed memory, to the "Gerer Rebbe", so that he would give his consent to the Zionist movement. After 2 days they came back with nothing.
Ten years later Sokolow took part in the 25th jubilee of the Katowice conference of the "Hovevei Zion". In honour of the "jubilee festival" a banquet was arranged in Katowice, at which Sokolow was the principal speaker.
At the end of my recollections of Sokolow it is worth relating the following episode:
Last winter, a few months before Sokolow's death, I happened to spend a Sabbath in the town of Wshichlin [?]. There I learned that Sokolow had spent many years there with his grandfather and with the local rebbe, with whom he studied, and that there was an old Jew there who had studied together with him under the Wshichlin rebbe. This Jew is today the synagogue beadle in Wshichlin. On the Sabbath I went to the synagogue, sought out the beadle and asked him: Is it true that you studied together with Nahum Sokolow?
— Yes, — the beadle answered me — I studied together with him under the old Chinan [?] rebbe. A great, decent man could have grown out of that Nachumke, but for our many sins he threw away his learning.
Hearing this, I recalled Reuben Brainin's article about Sokolow when he turned 40: among the thousand virtues that Brainin found in Sokolow, he even found that he is the cleverest Jew of our generation — but his fellow pupil from the same rebbe is, poor thing, such a fool, begging his pardon...
In honour of Shavuot — Torah sayings and remarks in honour of Shavuot; collected and edited by Yehuda

[Shavuot — Torah sayings; anthology.]
a) Torah and charity.
On no other festival is "the tribute of a freewill offering of thy hand" ("missat nidvat yadkha"; printed "missat nivat yadkha") said, only on Shavuot, because Torah without charity is no Torah...
R. Eliyahu Chaim Meisel.
b) Grass on Shavuot.
Where does the custom of spreading grass in the houses come from?
Because in Eruvin 22 the Gemara relates: R. Abba bar Matana went to the house of study. His wife said to him: Yours — what shall I do for them? He said to her: Have the reeds in the marsh run out?
And this is what the grasses spread on the day of the Torah symbolise: to show that whoever wishes to take upon himself the yoke of the Torah must be ready, like R. Abba bar Matana, to content himself even with grass...
R. Asher Zvi of Ostroh.
c) Na'aseh ve-nishma.
The giving of the Torah — said R. Yaakov Aharon of Volozhin [?] — was our wedding with the Holy One, blessed be He, and when a match is made, equal obligations are demanded of both sides. We put "we will do" before "we will hear" — so the Holy One, blessed be He, must do likewise, and even before the "we will hear", before He has heard from us that we will be good and pious, He must first of all do good to us...
d) A festival without sin.
Shavuot is every year pure, without sin, like a little child that is born. A proof:
On all festivals a he-goat for a sin-offering is mentioned, except on Shavuot, because on the day of the giving of the Torah every Jew is like a newborn child and no sin-offering is relevant — at that time there is no sin among Jews...
R. Levi Yitzchak of Berdichev.
e) Shame and Torah.
"It is a good sign when a person has a sense of shame — and whoever has no sense of shame, it is certain that his ancestors did not stand at Mount Sinai."
What has shame to do with Mount Sinai?
Only that at the giving of the Torah it says: "And all the people answered together: all that the Lord has spoken we will do and we will hear." Surely there were some Jews who did not want to accept the Torah, but they were ashamed to stand out and shouted along with the whole community "all that the Lord has spoken we will do and we will hear". So here shame was precisely a virtue, and whoever has no shame in him — it is certain "that his ancestors did not stand at Mount Sinai"...
Ktav Sofer.
f) Together.
When people do something with ulterior motives, they are not of one mind, for each has a different motive: one is after honour and the other is after money. It is different, however, when one does something without ulterior motive, purely for the sake of truth — then there can be "together", because truth is the same for everyone...
Dersh [?].
g) The Ten Commandments.
The Ten Commandments were spoken in the singular, so that a person should not think: Who needs my commandments anyway? If I do not keep the Torah, others will be found who will keep it. That is why the Ten Commandments were spoken in the singular: you need not look at others, whether they keep the commandments or not — to you, the individual alone, they were spoken...
Zer Zahav (printed "Zer Vahav").
h) The Tablets.
Why did Moses bring the Ten Commandments engraved on tablets of stone? Would the people not have remembered just ten commandments?
The people would indeed have remembered them, but each would have interpreted them differently: one would have said, this is how I heard them, and another would have said, I heard them differently... Therefore the ten commandments had to be engraved in stone, so that nobody could twist them...
R. Samson Raphael Hirsch.
i) "Thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God."
Ruth first said "thy people" and only afterwards "thy God", because one cannot have a share in the God of Israel if one is not part of the people, if one does not acknowledge the national foundation of the Jewish people...
R. Zvi ha-Levi Horowitz.
j) Six measures of barley.
In Ruth it is told that Boaz gave her six [measures of] barley, "and he measured six measures of barley" — what did he mean by that?
In former times barley was given before a wedding as a sign of marriage (Ketubot 8, as printed: "ayin-zayin 8"), and by this Boaz wished to hint to her that he would marry her.
Megillat Sefer.

The Living Corpse. (A Most Thrilling Novel of Jewish Life in Zagłębie Before and After the World War). (8)

[Literature — serialized novel; instalment 8.] By A. Zaglembier [pen name].
(8)
Synopsis of the beginning of the novel.
On a summer evening before the World War, when two Cossacks were to transfer the dangerous bandit "Szmulek Łapka" from the Piotrków prison, they were suddenly attacked on the way to the Będzin station by two disguised "strażniki" [rural policemen] — Łapka's helpers. At dawn the Cossacks were found lying bound with gagged mouths, and Szmulek "Łapka", a famous [?] one, had fled to the Gzichów road and hidden himself somewhere.
That same evening, almost at the same hour, the everywhere-respected, solid collector [Inkassent] Josel Wertheim — a father of three children — suddenly disappeared. His wife Sara'tshe runs about the town terribly desperate. He is searched for in every possible hiding place in all of Zagłębie. But Josel Wertheim has vanished like a stone in water.
Everyone already believes [?] it an extraordinary riddle. At last, on the fifth day, the business clerk [?] Maciek reports to police inspector Charecki [?] and relates that on that day he saw Wertheim walking on the Gzichów road together with the Christian woman Magda Komarska — a young, pretty shiksa whom Maciek had been courting with a view to marriage.
Magda is arrested at once. At the start of the investigation she denies it, but when Charecki wants to confront her with the [?] Maciek, Magda suddenly faints...
When she has been revived she declares that she wants to tell the truth, but not in Maciek's presence.
Magda then explains to Charecki that on the very day Wertheim disappeared they quarrelled, because Wertheim demanded that she go to Katowice to have [?] an operation, so that their unfortunate child would not be born.
Now read on.
— What? — asks Charecki.
— Yes, he himself, Wertheim, wanted to go with me. But I don't want that.
— Why?
— I am afraid... I have heard that many women have already died of such an "operation"..
— Only for that reason were you afraid?
— Yes.
— Perhaps you were also afraid that after freeing yourself of the pregnancy Wertheim would throw you over?
— I thought about that too, but I was not afraid of it; I know he loves me too much...
— Well, and that, it means, is why you quarrelled then?..
— Yes.
— Did the quarrel last long?
— The whole time of our conversation, ever since we went into the forest; it had already become night...
— Well, and then?
— I became very angry, I was also a little agitated, but his stubbornness had completely driven me out of patience.
— Well, so what did you do? — asks Charecki with bated breath, leaning still closer [?] toward her across the table.
— Nothing... I ran away from him, offended.
— That's "nothing"? And he didn't try to hold you back?
— Yes, he ran after me, shoved money into my hand, for the doctor... But that upset me even more; I insulted him, cursed him and ran out of the forest [?].
— And he, Wertheim?
— He, apparently, stayed in the forest; I didn't even look back at him, although he called me back.
— Why?
— Because at that moment I was very angry with him...
— And you went straight away, not even wanting to know what happened to him?..
— I couldn't imagine that anything bad could happen to him; after all he is not a child who can get lost...
— And tell me: perhaps somebody else besides you was in the forest then?...
— Certainly not!
— Are you so sure? Look me straight in the eyes — perhaps you took someone along then as a witness... you do have friends...
— But I would never want such a conversation between us to be overheard by anyone. Neither I nor Wertheim would want that.
— That means that apart from the two of you there was nobody?
— No...
— And when did you learn — Charecki now asks with a barely noticeable venomous little smile — that Wertheim had disappeared and was being sought by the police?
— Only three days later. Indeed I wondered why he hadn't let me hear from him right away [?] the next morning.
— Who?
— Jasiek Wertheim.
— And why didn't you come to the police to ask about him?
— I didn't want it to reach the public about our...
— Well yes, you are indeed right, and also cunning and clever enough. Of course you didn't want it to come out, but, you know, it has come out without you too...
And suddenly, banging on the table, Charecki asks in a stern, threatening voice:
— And now tell me, Magda Komarska! What did you do then with Wertheim?.. Where is his dead body?..
— What!! — Magda tears herself from her place and she flares [?] with flames of terror — his dead body?!
— Surely you murdered him! Alone or with someone else!.. I pretended to listen calmly to the "pretty little story" which you made up quite nicely! Precisely because of the child you are carrying by him you removed Wertheim from your path!.. I hear he also had money on him! It certainly paid off! Now tell me, where did you put him?!
Hearing the terrible accusation hurled into her face, Magda fainted once again. When she had barely been revived, they put little chains on her hands and led her off to prison, under the terrible suspicion that she, she alone, had murdered Josel Wertheim and hidden his dead body somewhere...
And in order to make the strange, mysterious case still clearer, police inspector Charecki decided at once to hold a second interrogation with Sara'tshe and to see how far Magda had told at least something of the truth.
And burning with impatience, this time he went himself to the flat of the black-haired Sara'tshe.
After all he must also know what [?] the lawful, deceived and betrayed wife of the vanished Josel Wertheim will say to it.
And perhaps the wife knew about her husband's "love" with the pretty Christian woman, but, wishing to avoid shame and disgrace, kept silent and pressed it down inside herself?..
In any case Charecki was now very hopeful and in good spirits. He no longer had any doubt that he had finally succeeded in clearing up the terrible mystery.
True, the most important thing is still hidden for the time being: he does not yet know where the vanished Wertheim is, where one must search for his dead body; but when he takes her a second time for a cross-examination, she will have to confess everything; let her suffer a little in prison meanwhile, later she will start talking differently, she will have to tell the truth... one way or another, by fair means or foul...
With just such thoughts police inspector Charecki now entered the flat of the black-haired Sara'tshe.

“Der Kokh-Lefl” (The Cooking Spoon): Greens and Dairy (Shavuot Couplets)

Ah, how green it is — a delight,
green, wherever you just look around,
green the long Małachowskiego [street?],
which smells to us like a tree.
Green run the tramcars,
merrily they ring, cling-clang,
and the wives, though painted,
also turn green without difficulty...
• • •
But if it is still too little green,
the “tel”[?] must be bigger still —
the summer lodging will help
to make the men green and yellow...
Dairy, dairy —
[?] everyone is drawn to it [?],
sour milk has the taste of paradise,
not to mention a little sour cream.
And with it a bunch of onions
and chives, cold sorrel soup —
all of it tastes[?] like an emperor’s meal
and that of a high-placed count.
Dairy! Dairy! — the women shout,
eating meat is not in the plan now;
if not meat, then at least dairy,
rather than be fasting[?]... the husband!
• • •
Ruth and Naomi, Ruth and Naomi,
one young and one old,
and Boaz of the Scroll
is a young man — not cold;
so he takes a liking to the Moabitess,
the Moabitess, Mrs. Ruth.
— It is no foolishness, upon my life,
it is not such a great folly...
Here, we know a young fellow,
very handsome and very fine,
who says — if Ruth is no longer around,
a young Romanian girl will do...
Yakl ben Flakl.
Why Do Jews Eat Dairy on Shavuot?

Jews eat dairy on Shavuot because until the Giving of the Torah Jews were neither dairy nor meat, so the Master of the Universe made them a dairy feast.
— Why didn’t He make them a meat feast instead?
— Quite simple: because to eat meat one would have needed slaughterers; the Gerer [Hasidim] would have wanted Gerer slaughterers and the Aleksanderers — Aleksanderer slaughterers; so as not to spoil the holiday, there was nothing left but to eat dairy.
Benyele Zalts[?].
Green and Yellow

When the Zionist faction watches how “their” kehilla councillors vote with the Agudah, they turn — green and yellow.
—
When one looks at a session of the Będzin town council and sees our “mute fish” sitting there, one turns — green and yellow.
—
When the elected board of the Sosnowiec kehilla acquainted itself with the budget the commissioner had left behind, they turned — green and yellow.
—
When one rides in the train or in the tram and sees how our “intelligent” ladies[?] light up cigarettes, one turns — green and yellow.
—
Będzin kehilla councillors “set” prices for their votes in the rabbinical elections, but until they see the coin before their eyes they will turn — green and yellow.
—
When a Jewish shopkeeper goes in the morning to open his little shop and sees how on the “merchandise …”[?] hangs a poster “Nie kupuj u Żyda” [Don’t buy from a Jew], he turns — green and yellow.

Shavuot, a Lovely Holiday.
Why is it held that Shavuot is the loveliest and merriest holiday among Jews?
Because right after Shavuot the Jew is rid of his wife for the whole summer...
Leyb Shtabinski.
The New Scroll of Ruth

Translated according to the latest fashion.
By Leyb Shtabinski.
“And Elimelech died” (Ruth 1:3): Why did Elimelech die before the whole family? The meaning[?] is that as long as Elimelech was rich, he was a good husband and Naomi — a good wife; but as soon as Elimelech became impoverished, his wife Naomi began to make his life a death, until he died before his time.
“And rebuke her not” (Ruth 2:16): Boaz instructed his workers not to shout at Ruth. Evidently in those times there were already unions which did not admit a new worker to the job.
“And he said, Let it not be known that the woman came to the threshing floor” (Ruth 3:14): Boaz told Ruth that no one should find out that a woman had come to him at night in the barn.
— Why?
— Because every night a new bride would have come up to him in the barn, so that he would have been at his wits’ end, not knowing whom to marry.
“And she told her all that the man had done to her” (Ruth 3:16): After the visit to Boaz in the barn, Ruth told everything to her mother-in-law; but had Ruth had a husband, she would no longer have told her mother-in-law about such a night visit...
The Ten Commandments from a Husband to a Wife

“I am” — I am your destined one, I said to you “Behold, you are [consecrated to me]”, I make clothes and buy hats with [?] — I am your husband and no one else.
“You shall have no” — there shall be no lodgers with you, no “friends” and no other scoundrels.
“You shall not make” — do not make [?] before my [?].
“You shall not lift” — do not raise your hand to all [?] loves.
“Remember” — remember that you have a husband [?] with grown-up daughters.
“Honour” — the best honour for such a Jewish woman is to sit at home, not to gad about at five-o’clocks.
“You shall not murder” — do not kill with your eyes.
“You shall not commit adultery” — (this you must remember when I travel to the Rebbe).
“You shall not steal” — do not steal your way into strangers’ hearts.
“You shall not covet” — do not lust after what I lust after.
—o—

What is the difference between a footballer and a member of the Będzin kehilla board (dozór)?
A footballer works with his feet, and the Będzin board members “work” with their hands.
Będzin: “Kind-hearted” ladies as swindlers

[Będzin — crime.]
The incident took place last Sunday evening, during a heavy rainstorm.
Mrs. Fajgla (Feigele) Flesner, who was walking on the new [?] pavement of Małachowskiego Street, was approached by two young, unknown, finely dressed ladies, who politely offered to accompany Mrs. Flesner home because of the bad weather.
“Thank you — it isn't necessary, I'll go alone. But who are you?” Mrs. F. asked them.
“We... are...”
As she said these words, one of the “escorts” took Mrs. F. by the arm and began to cover [?] her face with a kerchief, while the other began fiddling with Mrs. Flesner's hand, meaning to pull off her 2 diamond rings.
Mrs. F., however, instantly grasped the situation, tore herself free of the escorts, and in doing so gave one of them “a present from her hand”...
Accident to Mr. Stopnicki. — A cyclist knocks him down on the pavement and he is injured.

[Będzin — accidents.]
On Tuesday towards evening, as Mr. Hershl Stopnicki wanted to cross Czeladzka Street, at that very moment a young man on a bicycle rode into him. From the force of the blow Mr. Stopnicki fell onto the roadway and was badly bruised.
S. was taken to the hospital, where it was established that a bone in his chest (rib cage) was broken.
“Joint” delegates hold a consultation on constructive aid.

[Będzin — relief.]
On Monday a delegation of the “Joint” (American Jewish Joint Distribution Committee), Messrs. Bernstein and Sowbin [?], stayed here and held a consultation with the board of the local Gemilut Hesed (free-loan) fund on a plan of constructive aid for the broadest Jewish masses.
Mr. Bernstein related a number of interesting facts on the question; among other things Mr. B. reported that a large firm in London wants to create a cartel for Jewish furrier workers in Poland,
Delegation of market traders at the city president's

[Będzin — trade.]
On the 8th of this month a delegation of the trading halls [?] — as representing [?] the local Market Traders' Association — in the persons of chairman M. Fridman, board secretary S. Jura [?], together with the association's manager M. Manesa, was received in conference by the city president, Mr. Izydorczyk. The representatives raised a number of painful [?] questions concerning the interests of the market traders and the local [?] [illegible-meaning word] trade carried on by various elements, the occupying of the stalls by shopkeepers who come in from outside on market days, etc. The president, having listened attentively to the representatives' demands, promised to investigate everything thoroughly and to issue appropriate regulations.
Constitution of the Gordonia patronage committee.

[Będzin — youth movements.]
At the premises of “Gordonia” (the Zionist pioneering youth movement) a meeting was held of the patronage committee, which was recently [?] created. The meeting was also attended by the guest from Eretz Israel, Mr. Lewin.
The meeting is opened by Dr. R. Rechtman, who gives the floor to the above-mentioned guest, who speaks about the tasks of youth at the present moment and about the support to which the patronage committee can commit itself.
A discussion then develops, after which the presidium is constituted of Messrs.: Y. Wygodzki [?], G. Landner, Dr. R. Rechtman, editor S. Lewkowicz, Mrs. Rozenker, Mrs. Frenkel, Mrs. Edith Litwer and Mr. S. Cymerman as representative of the “Gordonia” leadership.
A child born in... a sausage shop

On Monday evening[?] a young Christian woman accompanied by a man came into Mr.[?] Gutenberg's sausage shop on Rybna Street. Both went into the adjoining room of the shop, and suddenly the cry of a newborn child was heard. When the shop owners went into the adjoining room, they saw that the woman, lying on the floor, had given birth to a child...
The sensational news was telephoned to the police station, from which an ambulance (pogotowie) soon arrived, in which the mother[?] and child were taken to hospital.
The most urgent midwifery work at the birth, before the ambulance arrived, was performed by the caretaker woman[?] (stróżka) of Gutenberg's building.
The news spread like lightning through the neighbouring lanes, from where hundreds of people came running to see the 'happy' [word unclear — new mother?][?].

Kosher-meat licences returned.
Some time ago the supervisory authority withdrew the kosher-meat licences of the butchers Hochberg[?] and Ferstenfeld. Thanks to the interventions of the local rabbinate and of Rabbi Kamer[?] Tsers[?], the licences have been returned.

Sokolow academy.
In connection with the first yahrzeit of the Jewish leader Nahum Sokolow, the local 'Hitachdut' is holding today, Saturday, in its own premises, a festive academy dedicated to the memory of the deceased. Mr. D. Liter[?] will speak on his life and work.

A memorial in the synagogue.
On Sunday evening a hazkara (memorial service) in honour of the memory of R. Nahum Sokolow of blessed memory was held in the town synagogue, conducted by cantor Klagsbald. Mr. Higarucki[?] spoke about Sokolow.

In the premises of the W.S.K. in Będzin, next Wednesday, 9 p.m.[?], there will be a lecture by editor M. Borochowicz (Kraków) on the topic 'The storm of racism on culture'.

In connection with the stay in Zagłębie of comrade[?] [—][?], of the A.K. (Actions Committee), Mr. Baruch Zuckerman, a regional rally of the [League for?] Working Eretz Israel will take place in Będzin, in the halls of 'Hapoel', at which Mr. B. Zuckerman will take part with a lecture.
Kaminer's picture exhibition at 'Chiza'

As we have already written, the young painter Dawid Kaminer of Kielce is staying in our town and will exhibit his pictures in the premises of 'Chiza'.
Dawid Kaminer is one of the child prodigies; the President of the State took an interest in some of his drawings and, through the Kielce voivode, ordered[?] the Kielce municipal administration to take an interest in this child prodigy.
The exhibition opens next Tuesday in the premises of 'Chiza' (Kościuszki 13) and will be open every day from 4 to 9 in the evening.

On Sunday the general meeting of 'Tze'irei Mizrachi' took place, at which the following committee was elected: Israel Szwarcbaum, Hercl Lask[?], Szlama Stobnicki, Abraham Szwarcbaum and M. M. Lensszner[?].

An interesting trial over 65 thousand złoty

The local K.K.K. [probably the municipal savings bank] gave the cooperative 'Legiona'[?] a credit of 100 thousand zł. on bills of exchange endorsed by the members of the cooperative's board. The unpaid bills from the year 1932 amount to 65 256 zł., which the K.K.K. has claimed through the court.
This week the trial took place before the District Court in Sosnowiec. On behalf of the 'baalei-khoyves' (debtors/creditors) Advocate Rylman appeared, who established the amount of the debt. The verdict is to be handed down on the 24th of this month.
Recruitment drive for the Talmud Torah

Under the chairmanship of President Mr. Fürstenberg, a large meeting took place in the premises of the Talmud Torah, attended[?] by delegates of all the minyanim and shtiblekh, who pledged to take an active part in the recruitment drive being conducted this month for the benefit of the Talmud Torah.
It was also decided that on the festival of Shavuot the gabbaim should urge [worshippers] to pledge larger donations.
Again wild scandals in the synagogue in Old Sosnowiec

It was believed that after the kehilla board had appointed Messrs. Sturger[?] and Lokai[?] as gabbaim of the synagogue in Old Sosnowiec, the wild scandals that take place every week during prayers would finally stop; but it turns out that most of the worshippers 'are not living badly at all', and their only concern is to stage a new 'spectacle' every Sabbath.
Such a 'spectacle' also took place last Sabbath. The leading roles were played by the old gabbaim, who would not allow the new gabbaim to take over 'the power', and it came to a wild scandal, because of which a large number of worshippers left the synagogue.
— Perhaps the kehilla board will finally put an end to the lawlessness in the above-mentioned synagogue? It is high time!
Regional conference of the free-loan (g"ch) funds

As we have already written, the 'Joint' organised in our town a regional conference of the gemilut-chesed (free-loan) funds.
We cannot, however, give the report of the conference, owing to the decision of the representatives of the Jewish press, among them also of 'Haynt' and the J.T.A., that if the sadly notorious 'editor' of the [—][?] 'Folksblat' were present at the conference, all would leave the conference.

On this occasion we declare that we shall take the same steps against all social and philanthropic institutions that will have any[?] dealings with this creature.
General meeting of the “Shomrei Shabbat” society.

Under the chairmanship of Mr. Chaim Unger, a general meeting of the “Shomrei Shabbat ve-T[almud] T[orah]” [?] society took place here. After the report by Michał Francuz on the activity in the field of Sabbath observance, family purity and the building of a mikveh, a heated discussion developed, after which a number of resolutions were adopted, among them to buy at once the suitable plot on which to build a modern mikveh.

On the strength of an ordinance of the Kraków school curatorium, the local Jewish gymnasium is opening, for the new school year, a general-education lyceum with a humanistic department.

“The False Messiah.”
This year the dramatic group of the local “Lira” is staging Bernhardt's well-known work “The False Messiah”, which has aroused great interest among the broadest Jewish strata in Zagłębie.

Simcha Estreicher, of blessed memory

On Friday evening the well-known haberdashery merchant R' Simcha Estreicher, of blessed memory, died of a heart attack in Sosnowiec at the age of 64. The deceased was one of the most respected Aleksander Hasidim, distinguished himself by his fine character and was a great giver of charity.
The funeral, which took place on Sunday afternoon, was attended by many thousands of people from all strata of the Jewish population.
May his soul be bound up in the bond of life.

Second Yahrzeit of Marshal Józef Piłsudski

[Kielce — memorial.] A solemn mourning commemoration in the synagogue.
On Wednesday, the day of the second yahrzeit of Marshal Józef Piłsudski, a solemn ceremony took place in the municipal synagogue. Present at the ceremony were representatives of the local administrative, military and municipal authorities, Jewish soldiers of the Kielce garrison, pupils of all the Jewish schools, as well as several hundred people.

With the singing of the Polish and the Jewish anthems the solemn mourning prayer came to an end.
A Sensational Trial

[Kielce — trial.] In the Święty Krzyż prison.
At the end [?] of May of this year the Kielce District Court, at its visiting session in Święty Krzyż, heard a sensational case concerning an attack on the governor of the local prison.
The attack was carried out by one of the prisoners, who had been sentenced to life imprisonment. During a conversation with the governor in his office, the prisoner threw himself upon the governor and tried to cut his throat with pieces of glass.
With his last strength the governor managed to press one of the electric alarm buttons and alerted the prison guards, who tore him out of the attacker's hands.
The governor's state of health requires a lengthy cure in Kraków.

When the Husband Came Home

[Kielce — street life.] Passers-by saw two men running along Bodzentyńska Street, one in front, in one shoe and without a jacket, and behind him a second with a stick in his hand. The mystery was cleared up later.
Mr. Z. has a wonderfully beautiful little wife, and when he came home one evening, there happened to him what (may he be the last, as he is not the first) happens to more than one man. In the wardrobe he found an unknown young man with one shoe on his foot and without a jacket.
"Tell me what you are doing here, but don't tell me a story that you are waiting for the bus... Don't tell me either that you came to polish the floor, because people go around the houses with floor-polishing machines on Fridays, and not young men, and in the daytime, not at night; I have already 'cooled down' three such 'polishers' in my home."
The hero in the wardrobe, however, had no desire to carry on a discussion: he came out of the wardrobe, smashed a pane with his shoulders and jumped out of the ground-floor window.
Then the chase through the streets began. Thanks to a 'sweet-smelling' barrel that stood across the width of the street in his way, the husband managed to catch the fleeing hero, whom he 'honoured' in such a way that he will tell ten others that one must not be a swine..

New “Albaril” Soap-Powder Factory

[Szopienice — industry; advertorial.] The chemical soap factory and laundry-products works P. Strahl & Co. in Szopienice (Upper Silesia), known for 60 years at home and abroad, which thanks to its good production has won a series of high prizes at domestic and foreign exhibitions, has built and put into operation a new, independent factory of “Albaril” soap powders. The task of this new branch of industry, equipped according to the latest technique, is to satisfy the growing demand of the domestic market, and also that the well [?]-tested chemical product should give the maximum to the household.

Thus the importance of the new “Albaril” powder establishment becomes apparent, bringing thrift into the household budget: by buying “Albaril” one gains money and time, and besides that one provides work for a large number of people.
We therefore wish the new establishment much luck.

The Brisk affair was mentioned at the town-council plenum. The investment tax of 75,000 zł. adopted

On Wednesday evening a meeting of the Będzin town council took place. The most important item on the agenda was the statute of the investment tax in the amount of 75 thousand zł. With this sum a public (elementary) school is to be built in Ksawera.
On this question alderman (ławnik) Rubinlicht took the floor; he came out energetically and factually against the project. At the end of his speech Mr. Rubinlicht declared that he would make efforts so that the project should not be approved by the supervisory authority.
Councillor Wabłazik[?] (P.P.S.) wonders why the Jewish councillors are against the project. Speaking of the importance of the public school, he mentions in passing the Brisk affair, in the sense that if youth had been well brought up, the Brisk events would not have happened. Here councillor Silberberg jumps up and calls out: „School youth, too, is not entirely clean in what happened in Brisk“.
The sharp moment, however, is quickly liquidated by the presidium, which points out that the matter has no bearing on the question itself.
The statute is put to the vote and is adopted by the majority of the Polish councillors.
Then the question is discussed whether the town of Będzin should be represented in the committee to defend[?] the position that the Kielce voivodeship should not be merged with Upper Silesia. After a discussion it is decided that Będzin shall not be represented in this committee.

Nothing Good Comes of Haste...

On Wednesday at 10.40 a.m. the passengers travelling on the Katowice—Warsaw train witnessed the following scene:
At the station in Szopienice, while the train was already in motion, Miss Paula Abramowicz of Sosnowiec tried to get on; at the same moment a young man also came running, and both grabbed hold of the handrail of the carriage. Suddenly the girl lost her balance and, holding on with one hand, was dragged along about 15 metres, after which she fell under the carriage.
At the signals of the stationmaster and the conductors the train was stopped at once, and everyone started running to the scene of the accident. As it turned out, the girl had been saved from death by a miracle. She only badly bruised her side; she was taken aboard the same train, and in Sosnowiec a report was drawn up with her.
An Impressive Shavuot Sermon by Rabbi Chameides.

On the second day of Shavuot, after the Torah reading, Rabbi Chameides delivered a rich and impressive sermon in the Katowice synagogue, in which the esteemed rabbi said, among other things, that one must sometimes also mention our non-Jewish friends, the Righteous among the Nations, who do not abandon us; thus in the dark Middle Ages we had a number of princes who protected us against the blood libels, and in more recent times these were the great spirits such as Émile Zola, Leo Tolstoy, the unforgettable Lord Balfour, President Masaryk and others. As we see, Israel is thus not forsaken ("lo alman Yisrael"), and so one must hope for better times.
The encouraging sermon made a colossal impression on the worshippers who filled the synagogue. (L.S.)

Chorzów — The Jewish Communities and Their Tasks

[Chorzów — community.] (For the attention of the community-tax ("etat") payers in Chorzów).
How often one hears criticism: the community ("gmina") has not done this or that, and how varied are the Jews' opinions about the community's duties towards Jewish society. But no one has yet given any thought to whether the community is in a position to do anything at all.
In brief strokes I want to sketch what the kehilla is and what it ought to be.
By law, the community must first of all maintain the religious institutions, such as: the cemetery, the synagogue, the slaughterhouse, the mikveh, and make efforts so that all Jewish children of school age receive religious instruction.
To cover the expenses connected with the above-mentioned institutions, the income from real estate, from renting seats in the synagogue, from ritual slaughter, the mikveh etc. is meant to serve.
Besides its religious activity, the community has taken upon itself part of the duties that belong to the territorial municipality or the government, namely: care of the poor and the sick, education, maintenance of a Hebrew school, buying books for poor children, summer colonies for the poorest schoolchildren, a kosher kitchen to feed poor children, feeding vagrants and the poor population on holidays, as well as prisoners and the sick, etc.
For these expenses there is no income in the budget, and therefore the "etat" (community tax) is assessed. Naturally, this involves great difficulties: maintaining a staff of officials to draw up the tax lists, dunning[?] the payers, who make great demands that the community build schools, hospitals, an old-age home — but taxes they do not like to pay, because of which the community is burdened with new expenses such as enforcement (distraint) costs and paying usurious interest[?] in order to cover the community budget. Because the etat is not paid on time, the communities fall into debts that they cannot repay so quickly. Most payers make light of the payment deadlines, and many do not pay even for whole years, arguing that "there is no such thing as a poor community"; but in fact this is not a healthy phenomenon, and in time such a state of affairs can lead to the financial collapse of the community in question.
Very many payers who out of "carelessness" pay no etat lose, in time, their active and passive voting rights. By paying the instalments regularly they support the foundation[?] of this public-law institution, which represents Jewish society also towards the outside.
With a little good will one can make it possible for the communities to stand at a proper level, in order to regulate life in Jewish society.
Yehuda.

A School That Teaches One to Think About the Future

[Poland — economy, PKO.] (JTA) At the house-warming celebration of the new PKO (Postal Savings Bank) building in Poznań, the deputy premier and finance minister, Eng. Kwiatkowski, delivered a greeting speech on behalf of the government, in which he declared, among other things:
What is PKO? Were it merely a bank and one of the institutions that collect money and transfer[?] it in certain directions, it would truly have been a meagre occasion for celebrations. PKO, however, is the guiding star[?] for shaping the public mind in thinking about the future. It places us in the field of the economy and knows how to answer us[?] what is more important: today, or the material future of the nation. If PKO now informs us that it has two and a half million depositors, this means that under its influence there are in Polish society 10 million citizens with their families. This is thus an enormous school, the like of which no university in Poland possesses; it is an institution that teaches 10 million people daily that important problems lie ahead in the future and that they must be solved.
The president of PKO, Dr. Henryk Gruber, gave a report on the construction of the new PKO building in Poznań, stating in the second half of his speech that the total of savings deposits in PKO amounted on 30 April 1937 to 605 million zł, and that the number of active savings books comes to two and a half million.

A Jewish gathering in Sosnowiec.
We have already had occasion to say a few words on this subject. Non-Jewish society finds itself in a state of intensive organizing and consolidating work, and precisely we, who must gird our loins enormously for self-defence, have let our hands drop, and the work of social organization proceeds among us at a considerably slower pace than in the years of the so-called "prosperity".
And therefore we were very [?] glad to see how Jews from several dozen small towns came together in Sosnowiec to discuss the state of Jewish livelihoods.
Jewish gatherings often have a specific aftertaste which always, to a certain extent, impairs [?] the seriousness and matter-of-factness of the subject under discussion. Over it there hovers some evil spirit of artificially inflated ambition — no longer party ambition, but organizational, which is in essence even much worse; consequently they do not work creatively.
In this respect the gathering of the gemilut hesed (interest-free loan) funds in Sosnowiec bore an entirely different character. Here really nobody asked, and nobody was interested in another's social "passport". The "CEKABE" has not yet managed, for the time being, to impose on the individual funds its specific Hasidic-shtibl seal.
Gemilut hesed delegates.
One might have expected the delegates from the small towns to consist of Jews with red [snuff] handkerchiefs, because — who in a small town is interested in lending someone an interest-free loan? Who works for this great mitzvah? The youth? Today, after all, it is stormily seeking other ways of self-help. Interest-free lending is the concern of the quiet, easygoing Tevye the Dairyman. And bad is the state of a society whose youth forgets tomorrow and must occupy itself with the affairs of today.
With us, unfortunately, it is indeed so. At the gathering in Sosnowiec we saw a quite different type of gemilut hesed activist. A large number of young people who, instead of working for all sorts of principles and "isms", have become absorbed [?] in gemilut hesed work.
What happened here? The young generation, after all, had been taught that "such things" smack of philanthropy, of pity, of charity, and that its task must be to devote itself [?] to constructive work. Has the [?] young generation of activists, then, rejected that teaching? No. Something else happened here. Delegates related how "fine Jews" had plundered the funds. Instead of the World to Come, those Jews preferred that their gemilut hesed work should give them this world; instead of [their money?] supporting such a fund, they saw to it that the funds should support them — and not only themselves, but indeed also their children and relatives...
The small towns have already once lived through such a plague, may it not be recalled today: the cooperative credit banks, which could have played so great a role in sustaining Jewish existences and livelihoods, were, after all, plundered by such "town notables" and destroyed. In the small towns the gemilut hesed funds became the only place where one could help oneself out with a groschen of credit, and so that that plague should not repeat itself, the young generation — in the interests of social self-protection, of moral and ethical cleanliness — flung aside those "benefactors" and took the gemilut hesed funds into its own hands.
—
Gemilut hesed has ceased to be a ladder to paradise, and has become a tool in the hands of Jewish firefighters. One may now, and one is now allowed to, not be ashamed of such work; if the socially healthy element must now take it up — that is certainly no misfortune.
Worse is that borrowing an interest-free loan has ceased to be a disgrace: people do it openly, they demand it loudly, and there are already such as "use" an interest-free loan, and for them it is exactly the same as using a product made in Łódź.
This is a phenomenon not only in the small town; even in Sosnowiec it is no different. Not only when a cab-driver's horse falls, but also when a merchant wants to rebuild his shop window in the town centre, or when craftsmen want to save their livelihoods — the gemilut hesed fund is for them the rescue bridge.
Yes, the gemilut hesed fund today bears such a burden and such a responsibility that, if it has become the centre toward which toil-worn hands stretch from all sides, then those in it who dispose of monies intended for rescuing Jewish positions must also remember this.
Reconstruction work.
This slogan took the place of honour at the gathering.
Reconstruction work, strengthening shaky positions, etc. — and on this point things limp badly, precisely at the "top".
It is a ship without a rudder, or rather the opposite — a ship with 18 captains: a merchants' delegation comes to the minister and presents him with certain demands, and next morning a petty traders' delegation hurries in with quite opposite demands. "TOZ" does some work — "CENTOS" competes with it; "ORT" is active "in a certain aspect" — the "CEKABE" jumps in here too; Jewish agriculture in Poland must be saved — "ICA" keeps its sabbath to itself: the heirs of the rich Baron can hardly fraternize with every pauper; and soon one no longer knows where "CEKABE" ends and where the central office of the credit cooperatives begins. "Down below", in the towns and small towns, the hands of the same faces get entangled — hands that want and must [—] of common work.
In our present tragic situation a unified leadership is more important than ever, at least in those areas where the tasks of the various central offices are common. And because this is not done so, and because at the common fire everyone still tries to bake his own separate pastries, the result is such that millions of złoty, which have already been sent for Polish Jews, have been frittered away and will not give any creative strength to the Jewish population.
Economic reconstruction — the representative of "CEKABE", Mr. Borgsztejn [?], gave a brilliant report on it, a thousand times right, clever, sensible, realistic and practical; everyone understood it and agreed — but all this will remain words, and even the funds already available will go to waste, if the reconstruction work is not the result of a well-thought-out plan and of a unified leadership.
Y. B-m.

The Problem of Public Health (On the Occasion of Sunday's General Meeting of "TOZ" in Sosnowiec)

[Sosnowiec — public health; TOZ.]
It is no accident that the nations which play the leading role in the history of mankind also distinguish themselves by a high level of health. It is no accident, because a good state of health of a people, low mortality and a longer life span are the expression of its well-being. It is therefore quite understandable that the state of health of the broadest Jewish popular masses is so low.
Must we, then, fold our hands and wait for the health of the Jewish people to improve together with its economic situation? — That would be more than naive; it would be a policy of suicide!
Of course, the best way of raising the state of health of the Jewish masses would be to provide them with proper dwellings, so that they would not have to live 8–10 persons to a damp, dark cellar room. They would have to be provided with a livelihood, so that they would not have to "perish" of hunger ten times a day, and so on.
But as long as we cannot achieve this, everything that can be done under the present conditions must be done. It must be done, because what is at stake is the health of the Jewish people and, as a consequence — its future.
And what can be done? — No one will deny that healing institutions for the sick are a very important thing. However hard the situation of the common man may be, it becomes truly unbearable when someone in the family falls ill. And it is not for nothing that the greater part of the philanthropic institutions are occupied with support for the sick.
But from the perspective of the people's interests, care for the sick is not the most important task. More important from this standpoint is care for the healthy — that they should not fall ill. What is important for a people is the prevention of disease, more important than the curing of the sick.
Here we must turn our gaze first of all to the youth, for in order to safeguard the health of the broadest Jewish masses, care must be taken of every individual from the moment of birth. Moreover: care must be taken even before the child comes into the world, and for this purpose there are advice centres for pregnant women. Later, when the child is born, it must remain under the constant supervision of the advice centre for mothers and infants. It goes without saying that the child will not develop on good advice alone, and therefore the task of these advice centres is also to distribute milk products to those children whose parents cannot afford them.
In the course of the following years the child ought to be placed in a children's home, so that it should spend as little time as possible in the dirty dwelling of its parents, often without any supervision at all. The schools in which the majority of the children of poor parents are found, such as Talmud Torahs, schools, heders, etc., must be under constant hygienic-medical supervision. In this connection it is very important that the children who come to school hungry (unfortunately the overwhelming majority!) be fed, and that every child should at least once a year enjoy the fresh air at the colony.
All this for the youth.
For the adults, war must first of all be declared on the greatest plague of mankind — tuberculosis! Here too care must first be taken to prevent this terrible disease, through broad hygiene propaganda and through the organisation of tuberculosis dispensaries.
These, in brief, are the tasks to be fulfilled in the field of improving the state of health of the Jewish population.
In Poland these tasks have been taken on by the society "TOZ" [Towarzystwo Ochrony Zdrowia Ludności Żydowskiej — Society for the Protection of the Health of the Jewish Population].
How does it fulfil these tasks?
There are cities in Poland where the programme sketched above is carried out fully, 100 percent, and the institutions of "TOZ" are held up as a model for the Polish population. Unfortunately this cannot be said of our Zagłębie, although here too much has been done in recent years: the state of cleanliness of the poorest Jewish children has risen, the schoolchildren are under constant medical-hygienic control, they are bathed and given haircuts, hundreds of children are fed and sent to the summer colony, and so on.
But all this is a drop in the ocean compared with what needs to be done. For everything depends on the interest, on the support on the part of the Jewish community in Zagłębie.
Let us hope that the general meeting of "TOZ", which will take place next Sunday [23 May 1937] in the hall of the Jewish kehilla in Sosnowiec, will bring a change for the better in this respect.
M. Fr.
Będzin "WIZO" and Its Social and Cultural Activity

The Zionist activity of the women's organization "WIZO" in Będzin is known for its intensity and energy, both in the form of the large collections for the building of the Land of Israel and in the arranging of events, which also carry a strong propaganda character — such as the so-called "banquets" in honour of meritorious public workers and Zionist activists, as well as the successful KKL [Jewish National Fund] bazaar in our town. In all this work "WIZO" occupies the most respected place. It can also show to its credit the "Gan Yeladim" [kindergarten], which it has maintained for a number of years and which helps to develop the Hebrew language in the mouths of our children. "WIZO" also engages in cultural activity, such as arranging literary-scientific lectures every week, which are very well attended. This proves that such lectures are very much needed as spiritual nourishment after the grey daily occupation. The greatest success, however, was had by the latest recitation evening of the artist Mr. Yehuda Ehrenkranz [?], who recited the classic pearls of Sholem Aleichem ("Hotels in Kasrilevke", "To the Dacha in Boiberik", "Getting Some Air"), I. L. Peretz ("Chaim the Porter"), M. Rosenfeld ("In the Shop at the Machine"). The reciter enthused the listeners with his mimicry and intonation, so that every character came out truly as if alive; and although all these pieces were read from the book, they nevertheless came out precise and polished [?] in the highest manner.
Ehrenkranz also recited finely the Hebrew work of A. Shlonsky "I went down into the ship going up to the Land of Israel", and in Yiddish a translation by Dor [?] Stegowicz of "The Jubilee of the Wagon-Drivers", which came out very beautifully; but in our opinion the piece would have come out more beautifully in the original and would have been understood just as well as in the Yiddish translation, owing to the great artistic means the reciter possesses — and it would also have been a great merit on his part for the Hebrew word..
Not bad either was the novella by K. Čapek "Vierbach" [?] (in Yiddish translation) — excellent was the feuilleton by Tunkeler "An Interview with Pharaoh in Egypt", which is still as topical today as it was thousands of years ago. — It would be desirable that our Będzin cultural workers and organizations arrange such evenings more often; they would thereby themselves prove their right to exist on the Jewish street.
Meanwhile the organization "WIZO" in Będzin, with its energetic president Mrs. Husger [?] at its head, has honestly earned the greatest recognition and thanks for its useful cultural and social activity in our town.
Elchanan Zider.
