In August the 20th Zionist Congress will convene, closing a period of 40 years of struggle for the Jewish revival and for the upbuilding of the Land of Israel.
Had the past year in Eretz Israel been a normal year, we could have told much about our work and achievements; we would have assessed our efforts in creating and building the Yishuv of more than 400,000 Jews in Eretz Israel, which already reaches 30 percent of the country's total population. The present time, however, is not suited to the summings-up that are usually made when celebrating a jubilee. Since the bloody events in Jaffa we have stood without pause in a hard struggle, forced upon us by our enemies — the enemies who strive with all their might to tear apart our work of construction and to block our road to redemption.
Since that bitter day one day chases the next. When the attacks on the roads and in the towns ceased, when the number of attacks on our settlements and on our youth diminished — the youth who defended our positions with heroism and endurance and for the most part beat back the weapons — then began the struggle of words and arguments before the Royal Commission; and even before the Commission has finished its work, we already stand before the third, decisive struggle, in which the Mandatory Power will determine for a certain time the fate of our enterprise on the basis of the conclusions and proposals of the Royal Commission.
From the first two assaults on us we emerged with honour. We proved by deeds how firmly the Jewish Yishuv has taken root in the country, how strong its power of resistance and creation is. We repelled all attacks on all our settlements, and the attackers did not manage even once to penetrate even the smallest and weakest of them. The course of our economic, social and cultural life was not interrupted for even a single minute. And not only that: we can also record new achievements and conquests in this period, the most important of which are the port in Tel Aviv and the penetration of Jewish labour into our orange plantations. In our testimonies and declarations before the Royal Commission we demonstrated the greatness of our work, which enlivens and makes fertile the wastelands [?] of the country for the good of all its inhabitants, and we stressed with full determination our demands to build a homeland for our people, which is perishing in torment in the lands of exile, and to transform the country into a national home open to all those cast out of exile. We unfolded before the Royal Commission the whole chapter of our sufferings and torments, of our complaints and demands.
And soon the last, decisive struggle will begin; it will be the hardest of the struggles so far. We must gather all our forces, unite and strengthen them, so that we do not fall in this struggle, so that from this struggle too we emerge with honour. We must enlarge our camp, mobilise all sympathisers of our liberation movement together with the Zionists, who have stood for years in the front ranks. And let no one have even a shadow of doubt that our popular masses have recoiled in the face [?] of the dangers lurking for our work, that they are not ready for all the efforts and sacrifices needed to attain our goal!
We came to the 19th Congress in the name of a million shekels, which called upon us to continue further, with still more courage and self-sacrifice, to carry on our work of construction and our struggle for liberation. To the 20th Congress, which will have to decide fateful questions of our people and our movement, we must come in the name of a far greater camp, one that will show that all the creative forces of our people are uniting in the war against those who want to close the road to redemption before it.
Everything depends only on us and on our strenuous work. Our hard, unbearable situation in almost all the lands of exile strengthens among our masses the conviction that there is no other way for us except the way of liberation and revival in Eretz Israel. The Jewish masses are only waiting for the call to join the camp of builders and fighters for our revival.
Let us therefore go to the people with the tidings of our struggle for revival. Let us call all the tormented and the afflicted, let us gather all those who hope and yearn for liberation and redemption, and bring them into the camp that builds and fights. Let us increase the number of shekels, the number of citizens of our Jewish-State enterprise. Let us create the strong force that will remove all the obstacles that lie, and that will yet be laid, on the road of our revival and redemption!
Our Great-Grandmothers Already Knew About Cosmetics Too

[Magazine — women and beauty; history of cosmetics.] By Z. Haber, Vienna.

If anyone thinks that only in recent years have women begun to look for means of becoming "young and beautiful", he is wildly [?] mistaken. It seems to me that Eve herself already sought means of pleasing Adam...

That our great-grandmothers, 150 years ago, had, exactly as today, means "to make themselves beautiful" — of this we have proof in hand.

In the archive of the Leipzig fair there lies a small brochure from the year 1798, published by the Parisian doctor André Harrishen [?], who was then the best cosmetician and specialist in skin diseases. The brochure bears the title: "Best Rules of Beauty for Ladies and the [most essential?] Means in Life". This brochure is a collection of articles that had earlier been printed in the "Paris Fashion".

There various pieces of advice and remedies for women are printed, in case they "want to be beautiful and become young"...

True, the notion of beauty was different then from today. The brochure says that a woman was then beautiful "when she is at least 170 centimetres tall, walks upright, has a clean, coloured [?] skin on her face, a high forehead without wrinkles, a round face, large, lively eyes, a small little mouth, red lips, soft plump hands, broad hips, and is a little stoutish in body"...

To be beautiful there are various rules, which we pass on without any comment:

"Young women should not go about [?] in the cold, because from that one gets a red-black, thick skin on the face."

"Sharp, and especially peppered, dishes should not be eaten, because from them one gets a yellow face; from honey one gets spots on the face"...

"The face should not be washed with warm water, because from it one gets wrinkles; soap is very harmful to the face"...

"If one gets wrinkles on the face, one should use this remedy: boil a little barley and add to the water a few drops of 'pearl balsam', which must [?] be strained [steeped?] for ten to twelve hours... One washes the face with it, and soon, surely [?], loses the wrinkles"...

"For freckles the best is brandy [?] mixed with [—?], or one makes an ointment of fresh butter mixed with turpentine, four egg yolks, and in addition a few drops of orange oil [?].. The face must be smeared with it in the morning and at night, then washed off with a 'clean little cloth' — that is the best medicine against freckles"...

"A good means of getting a clean face is also to wash with milk or with lemon water."

How to paint the lips so they are red — this, too, our great-grandmothers already knew; they did it with "Florentine lacquer or nutmeg oil". — Of lipsticks they knew nothing.

"White lead mixed with rose water and horseradish root [?] is the best means of getting a young, beautiful and fresh face"...

"The hair of the eyebrows was dyed with 'ash of burnt almonds'"...

"Grey hair is best dyed with nut oil and vinegar. That turns it black"... Of blonde or red hair nothing was yet known then...

"The sun harms the face. If someone must go out in the sun, he should smear his face with nut oil mixed with boiled wax."

"Corns should be smeared with garlic, or with the gall of a pike, and they fall off by themselves."

"For a sluggish memory the best thing is to inhale the smoke of boiled raisins"... "From it one can also sleep well."

"If something gets into an eye, one should hold a pearl or a diamond by the eye, and the dirt will fall out by itself."

How [?] the best remedies... A pity only that we do not possess them today... Our great-grandmothers lived long with them and felt fine, just like a fish in water...

Z. Haber, Vienna.
Who Has Not Made Me...

[Satirical feuilleton — religion and society; the "shelo asani" blessings.] By "Leyzer der Tsudreyter" [Leyzer the Muddle-Head]; passed on by A. Z.

I want to record here [?] a conversation that I had with a Jew, perhaps also a bit of a muddle-head like me. The Jew, a poor embittered soul, whom the depression had itself squeezed hard and who is very embittered over the troubles of the Jewish people, asked me a question as heavy as a log — more precisely, three log-heavy questions at once.

We say — he says — every morning three "shelo asani"s: "who has not made me a gentile", "who has not made me a slave" and "who has not made me a woman". Every Jew thanks God that He did not create him a gentile, a servant or a woman. So all these blessings are pointless blessings, blessings in vain; blessings that make no sense.

What — asks the Jew with great bitterness — is so good for me in having been created a Jew? What is so good for all Jews in being Jews? A great fortune has befallen us — we are not gentiles! We are persecuted and given no place of rest, and after all is said and done — "Blessed... who has not made me a gentile". Thank you, dear God, for not creating me a gentile!

It is — perhaps one must not say so — to distinguish, like in the old days, when a squire had a peasant flogged, and the flogged man, after the lashes, had to kiss the squire's hand and say: "Dziękuję" — I thank you, dear squire.

And the same — the Jew argues on — with "who has not made me a slave". What, for instance [?], would be so bad for me if I were now a slave, a servant, a domestic with someone? I would gladly be a "stróż" [caretaker] for a Jewish landlord, something of a cleaner, a [slop-pail?] [?] carrier, or whatever — I would have something to eat! So what would I lack? A thousand times better than wandering about aimlessly, languishing [?], hungry, barefoot and naked, with nowhere to earn a penny, a thousand times better than blackening one's face [shaming oneself] and turning to the "Beys Lekhem", to the "Gmiles Khesed" and the like. In the end — "Blessed... who has not made me a slave", thank you for not creating me a servant; once again: "Dziękuję panu" [thank you, sir].

And so too with the third "shelo asani", with "who has not made me a woman". Thanks to Him for not creating me a woman! And what, God forbid, would it have harmed me, for example, if I were not a man but actually a woman? The whole point is that I would not have so many commandments, so many duties on my head — well, so be it! For what, so to speak [?], do I get from all those many commandments? Eh [?], what — the World to Come? Well, are women then barred [?] or excluded from the World to Come? Even gentiles are, after all, assured [?] of the World to Come. Our Gemara says: "The righteous of the nations of the world have a share in the World to Come." So surely gentile righteous women too. And now I ask as well: what would it matter to me if I were not a Jew and not a man, but simply a gentile woman, an honest gentile woman?

If I were not what I am, but an ordinary "areylis" [uncircumcised (gentile) woman], I could surely perhaps earn something; a woman is given more attention, and they would give me something to earn [?]; I would wash laundry, scrub floors, and earn my bit of bread honestly. But the story is this: accept for the good that you are a man, and make the blessing: "Blessed... who has not made me a woman".

Now — the Jew concluded — I have asked you three questions; give me an answer.

And I, the humble one, called Leyzer der Tsudreyter, first of all justified the first "shelo asani", but without lofty explanations and arguments that we Jews are indeed the "treasured people among all peoples", the very top of the bowl among all nations, the true "Thou hast chosen us" — but in an entirely simple way.

For "who has not made me a gentile" — I said — the Almighty deserves a great "yasher koyekh", and you must thank and praise His dear name for having created us Jews. In our present time, when antisemitism rages [?] in the world, and the gentiles carry on [?] as wildly [?] as one can imagine.

It is hard — people say — to be a Jew, and to be a gentile is perhaps harder still. If someone shows himself an antisemite, he is given pepper to smell [is punished]; if, on the other hand, someone is a good gentile, he becomes hated and persecuted by other gentiles, by friends and even by his own brothers, and is branded a "Shabbes goy", a "żydowski pachołek" [Jews' lackey].

Nevertheless, I said, it sometimes happens that a gentile speaks out as a friend of the Jews; it happens before elections, when a gentile candidate in a Jewish electoral district proclaims himself in his speeches a friend of the Jews and is not rebuked for it — but that is only to win Jewish votes. But should someone really be a friend of the Jews, he loses favour [łaska] with many of his co-religionists, and that often causes him a great deal of unpleasantness.

Between ourselves, it is hard to be a gentile; a Jew can fulfil his duty with his Jewishness more and more easily than a gentile with his gentileness. Here we have among us a Jew, a "kol-bo" [a jack of all trades], who is accused of various disgraceful sins, yet he insists on being our head of the kehilla. But the kehilla has had enough of him; a Jew, no evil eye, advanced in years — he had better rest, study, recite Psalms.

That is precisely why the blessing "who has not made me a gentile" is right: because, firstly, gentiles, to distinguish, would not have agreed to such a head of the community, and a gentile, to distinguish, would not even have had the audacity to want to become a community leader.

The questioner was satisfied with my answer; he will — he said — come once more so that I answer the other two "shelo asani"s for him, but that I will do, God willing, another time.

Leyzer der Tsudreyter.
Passed on by A. Z.
Two People Are Dissatisfied — With the Jewish Gymnasium in Sosnowiec

[Sosnowiec — education; the Jewish gymnasium, statement of the parents' committee.] With the Jewish gymnasium in Sosnowiec.
Dissatisfied man number 1 is Mr. "Editor Dr. Jakobi".
The man cost a mere 3 zł., and for 2 years he was a satisfied man.
3 zł. was the cost of the advertisement which Mr. "Editor" received from the school, and with that his satisfaction was bought. But as soon as Mr. "Editor" again got an appetite for an advertisement, and the school had no desire to advertise itself in Mr. "Editor's newspaper", he became dissatisfied and took pen in hand.
Dissatisfied man number 2 is the "well-known communal worker and activist", Mr. Feigreich.
As long as the "well-known communal worker and activist" Mr. Feigreich enjoyed a reduction in tuition fees at the school, as long as his daughter attended the school and received her matura, so long was the "well-known communal worker and activist" Mr. Feigreich satisfied; but as soon as the school demanded of the "well-known communal worker and activist" Mr. Feigreich that he pay a debt of 90 zł., which the school had exceptionally extended for him, our "well-known communal worker and activist" became dissatisfied.
Dissatisfied man number 1, that is Mr. "Editor Dr. Jakobi" (3 zlotys), met with dissatisfied man number 2, that is the "well-known communal worker and activist" Mr. Feigreich (90 zlotys), and they began — as such little people usually do — to spit on the school and to sling mud at those who stand at the head of the institution.
Neither our gymnasium, nor the director and the professors [?] need our defence. Mr. "Editor Dr. Jakobi" will have the opportunity to present his "doctor's diploma" before a different authority; there his moral qualifications for meddling in school affairs with dirty criticism, over not getting advertisements for 3 zł., will also be examined.
The same authority will probably also call Mr. "Editor Dr. Jakobi" to account for blackmailing the gymnasium.
The "well-known communal worker and activist" Mr. Feigreich, against whom the school holds a court judgment, must absolutely pay the debt as quickly as possible; if not, the school, being a public institution, is obliged to use all legal means to obtain the debt from the "activist". Since the "activist" permits himself to slander orally persons who have great merits for the school, we are of the opinion that Mr. "communal worker" must absolutely be brought to judicial account — not for the sake of the private honour of the persons he slanders, but for the good of the school. The "activist" must be taught a proper lesson: one must not spit into the well from which one drinks water.
We repeat: neither the gymnasium nor those who stand at its head need our defence. But if we take the floor in this matter, we do so because Mr. "Editor Dr. Jakobi" and the "well-known communal worker" Mr. F. (both together 93 zł.) have permitted themselves to speak in the name of the parents. Here we must say to both gentlemen: hands off our clean work!
We, the parents of the pupils of the Jewish school, who are organised as the "Parents' Committee at the Jewish Gymnasium and Elementary School in Sosnowiec", are the only representatives who have the right to speak in the name of the parents. Not only do we have nothing whatsoever to do with the unethical conduct of the two gentlemen, not only do we reject them with disgust — but we are proud of the imposing development of our gymnasium, and for this we have only the energetic school management and the board to thank, to whom we hereby express our warmest thanks for their untiring work for the development of the Jewish gymnasium and elementary school in Sosnowiec.
In the name of the Parents' Committee
The class patronage committees.
A Little Feuilleton. "I'm Satisfied"

[Feuilleton — Polish Jewry; the "Aryan paragraph" in the doctors' association.] "I'm satisfied"...
My neighbour Shloyme Yoyne, the perpetual optimist, takes nothing to heart; the greatest decrees — may they never come — do not make the slightest impression on him. On the contrary: after reading the projects of the various "benefactors", the resolutions of the "kosher Aryans", a smile spreads over his face and he says to himself pleasantly:
— "I'm satisfied."
Last week he had already driven me out of my wits with his optimism. It was on a fine spring day, the sun was sending out its tender rays, the little birds were singing hymns — in comes my neighbour with a newspaper in his hand, laughing out loud.
— Good news for sure — I think to myself — the Royal Commission [the Peel Commission] has probably already issued its decision, and "the English government strives to build the Jewish national home in the Land of Israel"...
— Here you are, read — my neighbour says to me, and hands me the report of the doctors' congress, at which a resolution was adopted to introduce the Aryan paragraph into the doctors' association.
— A strange death on my enemies, have you, God forbid, lost your mind, Heaven save us? What is so great about it for you?
— Calm down, Panie Libason, don't get nervous; here, sit down and I'll make you understand why I am perhaps the one and only Jew who does not fall into a mood of despair, but accepts with love all the troubles that pour down on our heads — more than that, "I'm satisfied."
— Let us first consider — he says — the latest resolution of the doctors' association. It seems that the resolution has aroused much bitterness in Jewish circles, but when you examine it "in small change", you come to the conclusion that it isn't worth getting upset; on the contrary, the Aryan resolutions may perhaps bring some good to us Jews.
For let us look the truth in the face — one will surely say that, were it not for the present "love" for us, thousands of ours, and perhaps tens of thousands, would not have known until their death that they are Jews...
Why, it would simply have been a tragedy for our shmendriks if the non-Jewish maid had found out that her breadwinners — who ape every foreign ceremony and, God forbid, never fail to light a "choinka" [Christmas tree] for the Christmas holidays — are also "Zhids"...
And so I am "very satisfied" that our Jewish intelligentsia, who always cast "eyes" where they were not gladly seen, have been shown the door and told:
— Do excuse us, go in good health, we prefer the Orthodox Jew to those who want to be "Jew-Poles"...
— Wise words, with which I am very satisfied...
Sh. Libason.
Oneg Shabbat (Sabbath Delight)

[Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings on the weekly portion.]
Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes around this week's portion
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Naso

a) "All that enter in to perform the service (lit. 'to wage the host')" (4:23)
How does the expression "tzava", which means military, come to be applied to the Levites, who have only holy work before them?
Rather: undertaking a sacred service is also called "litzvo tzava", because one must then stand in a hard war for the purity of the people, and at times one must also take the sword in hand, as it was at the Golden Calf... Yalkut Yehuda.

b) "And every offering... which they bring unto the priest, shall be his" (5:9)
Earlier the Torah speaks of trespass (me'ila) and robbery. Now comes the warning that everything[?] a person gives the priest, gives to charity — "shall be his" — must not come from dishonest money...
Imrei Chen.

c) "If any man's wife go aside." (ibid., 12)
"What is written above this matter? — 'And every man's hallowed things shall be his.' If you withhold the priestly gifts, by your life, you will have to come to him to bring him the sotah." Rashi.
If he was stingy and did not give the priestly gifts, what is the wife guilty of? Why must she become a sotah?
It appears that in not giving charity the wife always has a great say, and if the husband is a miser, the wife is to blame...
Migdal Oz[?].

d) "He shall separate himself from wine and strong drink" (ibid., 3)
The "Iron Head", the Lublin rabbi R' Azriel Horowitz, once asked the Seer of Lublin:
— When one sees[?] a Jew getting drunk, he is an outcast, he is regarded as a common man — yet your Hasidim drink and get drunk and are considered Jews of high spiritual rank!
He answered him:
In parashat Naso Rashi says: "Why is the section of the sotah juxtaposed to the section of the Nazirite? To teach that whoever sees a sotah in her disgrace should abstain from wine."
So wine is a bad thing; yet further on, on the verse "for that he sinned by reason of the soul", Rashi says that the Nazirite's sin consisted in his being a Nazirite and separating himself from wine; so it turns out that drinking wine is, on the contrary, a good thing — does Rashi then contradict himself?
But in truth drinking wine is not at all such a bad trait — "wine maketh glad the heart of man"; wine is bad only for one who is bad in his essence, and therefore "whoever sees a sotah in her disgrace should abstain from wine" — such a person may not drink any wine...
— But Rebbe, this does not speak of a man who is bad, only of one who "sees a sotah in her disgrace" — the "Iron Head" retorted.
— That is just it — the "Seer" gives him a smiling[?] answer — one who sees bad in another is a sign that he himself is also not in order...

e) "He shall come at no dead body" (6:6)
That is why a Nazirite may not come near a dead body: a Nazirite is holy ("he shall be holy"), and "the Divine Presence does not rest amid sadness"; one can be holy only when one is in joy...
R' Yehuda Leib Ginzburg.
* * *
And therefore the Gemara says in Berakhot 5:
"A person should always incite the good inclination against the evil inclination. If he defeats it — good; if not — let him engage in Torah. If he defeats it — good; if not — let him recite the Shema. If he defeats it — good; if not — let him remind himself of the day of death."
The question arises:
Why should he not remind the evil inclination of the day of death right away?
Because recalling death evokes sadness, and that is not at all able to drive away the evil inclination... Therefore it is more fitting first to study Torah, which gladdens a person: "The precepts of the Lord are right, rejoicing the heart."

f) "The Lord bless thee" (ibid., 24[?])
The blessings were said in the singular, because a single blessing for the collective is not apt. For one person money is a blessing ("bless thee — with wealth"), while for another it is actually a curse... For one, children are a blessing ("bless thee — with sons"), and for another a curse... Therefore the blessings had to be in the singular: each has his own blessing, the one he needs...
Dan mi-Daniel.

g) "The Lord lift up His countenance upon thee" (ibid., 26)
Rav Avira expounded:
The ministering angels said before the Holy One, blessed be He: It is written in Your Torah "who regardeth not persons, nor taketh reward", yet it is written "The Lord lift up His countenance upon thee"?
He said to them: And how shall I not show favour to Israel, for I wrote for them in the Torah "and thou shalt eat and be satisfied, and bless", and they are strict with themselves to bless even for an olive's bulk or an egg's bulk!
Berakhot 20b.
God praises the Jews in that "they are strict with themselves": the fact that they are strict with themselves and say grace even over an olive's bulk is expressed as "strict with themselves" — for themselves they count even an olive's bulk as a meal, but not for a stranger[?]; there one need not count an olive's bulk as a meal.
Ksav Sofer.

The Living Corpse

[Literature — serial novel ("The Living Corpse"), instalment 9.]
A. Zaglembier [pen name].
(A most thrilling novel of Jewish life in Zagłębie before and after the World War). 9)
Summary of the beginning of the novel.
On a winter night before the World War, when two Cossacks were to transfer the dangerous bandit "Szmulek Łapka" into the Piotrków prison, they were suddenly attacked on the way to the Będzin station by two disguised "strażniks" (guards) — Łapka's helpers. The Cossacks were found the next morning lying bound with gagged mouths, and Szmulek "Łapka", freed, fled to the Gzichów road and hid somewhere.
That same evening, and almost at the same hour, the universally respected, solid collector (inkasent) Josl Wertheim — a father of three children — suddenly disappeared. His wife Sarah'tshe runs about the town terribly desperate, searching for him in every possible hiding place in all of Zagłębie. But Josl Wertheim has vanished like a stone in water..
Everyone stands baffled before an extraordinary riddle. At last, on the fifth day, pockmarked Matek reports to police inspector Karecki and tells him that on that day he saw Wertheim walking on the Gzichów road together with the Christian woman Magda Komarska — a young, pretty gentile girl whom Matek had been courting.
Magda is arrested at once. At the beginning of the interrogation she denies everything, but when Karecki wants to confront her with pockmarked Matek, Magda suddenly faints...
When she has been revived, she declares that she wants to tell the truth, but not in Matek's presence.
Magda then declares to Karecki that on the very day Wertheim disappeared they had quarrelled, because Wertheim had demanded that she go to Katowice to have an operation so that their illegitimate[?] child would not be born. Magda is arrested, and Karecki goes to Wertheim's wife, Sarah'tshe, for questioning.
Now read on.
He barely recognised her, because in the course of those ten days Sarah'tshe had become a shadow... It was truly a mystery how Sarah'tshe could bear it. Neither does she eat nor can she sleep. The boundless despair and pain had broken her completely; at times it already seemed that any moment she would lose her mind... for whole hours could pass while she buried her head in the pillow and, with hysterical, pitiful weeping, endlessly repeated one and the same words:
— Dear God! Why has this befallen me, why has this befallen me — to become a wretched agunah [abandoned wife], and my children — living orphans!.. Why.. why?..
And the children wept along with their despairing mother. Neighbours stopped coming into their home, because it was hard for everyone to look upon the misfortune. Besides, Sarah'tshe would not let herself be comforted at all.
And now, suddenly seeing police inspector Karecki in her home, Sarah'tshe sprang up from the place where she had been lying, as if a new hope had suddenly awakened in her heart... Trembling all over with expectation and with wide-open eyes, she ran up to Karecki and cried out breathlessly:
— What news? Found?!.. Do you know something already?!
— Certainly we know; the matter is in any case moving forward..
— But my husband! The father of my children! — Sarah'tshe wrings her hands — where is he?!
— In a moment, in a moment — Karecki sits down himself and asks Sarah'tshe to sit as well.
— Please, sit down, Mrs. Wertheim; if I have now come to you myself, you must understand that I have come about a very important matter...
— But my husband... — Sarah'tshe does not stop lamenting — just look what has become of us!
— Of course I have come about your husband, but patience, and above all, calm yourself. You must understand well what I am going to ask you, and you must give me clear answers, because I have already found out a great deal.
— But..
— In a moment, in a moment; first answer me — I have even asked you this once already: did you know about it, or do you know, that your husband was in very intimate, close relations with another woman?..
The question strikes Sarah'tshe like thunder. Everything even begins to get mixed up in her head; it looks as if she had not heard, or as if she had not understood at all what was being said to her.
— My husband... my Josl...; — she murmurs, dazed[?] — I don't understand...
— I understand — answers Karecki — that this is no pleasant news for a woman who loves her husband dearly and believes in him firmly...
Karecki suddenly breaks off, because, seeing that the pretty Blimke and the other two children too are listening to his words with great interest, he suddenly says to them:
— I must ask you, children, go into the other room; you need not hear this, it is not for you.
Blimke blushes, becomes ashamed, and together with the other children runs, weeping, into the other room.
Only now, left alone with the utterly astonished and gaping Sarah'tshe, does Karecki continue:
— But so it is, my dear woman; in life anything happens, the most honest man sometimes wears a mask on his face.. And in spite of the fact that your husband had such a good reputation in the whole region and among all his acquaintances, he nevertheless carried on a secret love affair with another woman as well, and that love has even already begun to bear fruit...
Though[?] Sarah'tshe does not yet understand exactly the meaning of what Karecki is telling her, she instinctively leaps up from her seat, as if suddenly seized by flames:
— What?! What did you say?! No! No! That is impossible!..
— It is a fact — Karecki answers calmly; he does not understand why this Jewish woman makes such a tragic affair[?] of a husband's betrayal, for what husband does not betray his wife at least once in his life?.. Karecki knows this from his own experience too...
But Sarah'tshe will not at all admit such a terrible thought. It is not enough that her husband suddenly disappeared — now they also want to invent such things about him..
— No! No! It is some slander by an enemy — Sarah'tshe cries in despair — my husband!..
— But calm yourself, Mrs. Wertheim; I have told you that anything can happen; unfortunately it is a fact, a proven one... I have come to you precisely to establish whether that woman is really telling the truth about it.
— Who is she, who?!
— Magda Komarska. They used to meet often outside the town...
— What?! With a Christian woman?! No! That is impossible!..
— So it is, my dear woman; you must get used to the thought, however terrible it may be, for that woman, the Christian...
— A slander! A vile slander against my husband! Some enemy wants to take revenge!
— Calm yourself. That woman is already carrying your husband's child under her heart...
For a while Sarah'tshe loses the power of speech on hearing the last words.. She feels she is losing her mind; within one minute she starts crying and laughing; but when Karecki tells her that this same Magda Komarska has already been arrested on suspicion of knowing what happened to Sarah'tshe's husband, and she hears further details of Magda's interrogation, Sarah'tshe begins to sob in a choked voice and convulse[?].
— Oh, why did you tell me this? Why! I would have been better off not knowing it — it is so terrible!... My husband with..
And again she starts up from her seat and begins to scream hysterically:
— No! No! I don't believe it! It's a slander! A slander!..
Karecki waits a while until she calms down, and then he goes on:
— Forgive me very much, but please understand: unintentionally I may have caused you grief... But it is my duty after all, I must get to the truth... And you yourself surely want to know where your husband has gone... and who?..
— No! No! I cannot understand it at all!...
— But calm yourself, for God's sake! From you I can learn whether this Magda Komarska is telling the truth, and it is only for that that I have come now.
— I am supposed to know that?!
— Of course you knew nothing about their "love". I only want to establish one thing. Everyone, and you too, say that on that day your husband had no money on him.
— He handed everything over to the firm, down to the last grosz!
— And now Magda says that precisely on that evening your husband wanted to give her several hundred roubles for a doctor, so that she might "destroy" the "forbidden fruit"..
— It cannot be! No!!
(To be continued).

Reply from “Kokh-Lefl”.

Sosnowiec / After 6 Years a Mother Finds Her Child Who Had Been Kidnapped by Gypsies

[Sosnowiec — orphans, kidnapping.]
It happened 6 years ago, when the 2-year-old child Reuven Machower suddenly disappeared, leaving no trace whatsoever. Some time later the police in a village beyond Warsaw took the boy away from a band of gypsies. Not knowing to whom the child belonged, the child was placed in one of the municipal shelters (przytułki) in Warsaw, from where he, together with other Jewish children, was sent to be brought up in the local „Orphans' Home“ [in Sosnowiec] at the expense of the Warsaw magistrate [municipality].
All this time the mother of the lost child did not rest; she wandered from town to town, but without success. One can easily imagine the despair of the mother, who for 6 years already has not known where her Reuvele is, whether he is still alive.
And finally, at a certain moment, when the mother poured out her bitter heart about the fate of her unforgettable child, she was asked at the Warsaw magistrate whether she could say what mark her vanished child had.
— He has — said the mother — a birthmark ("flame") on his neck.
The magistrate reported the „mark“ to all orphans' homes in which there are children from Warsaw, and it turned out that the vanished Reuven Machower, who is already 8 years old, is in the local orphans' home.
These days the boy, accompanied by the secretary of the local „Dobroczynność“ (charity society), was taken to Warsaw, where he was handed back to his mother.
The scenes that took place between the mother and the child are almost indescribable.

In the classes talks are held on the significance of the Galilee, and the children collect money in the boxes („pushkes“). In some elementary-school classes 5 minutes of the Hebrew lesson are dedicated to the „Mifal ha-Galil“. The campaign is also conducted among the teachers: every teacher signs a declaration „for the Galilee fund“.
The „Birth Pangs“ of the Kehilla Budget

[Sosnowiec — kehilla, budget.]
As we have already written, the kehilla board, in agreement with the supervisory authority, set about drawing up a new kehilla budget that should correspond to the needs of the kehilla.
The deadline for drawing up the new budget was the end of March. But we are already nearly at the end of the month of May, and the budget is still in its „swaddling clothes“.
The reasons for this are various, but as we are informed, the main reason is that both bodies, the board and the council, cannot come to any agreement on the question of the establishment (etat, staff and salaries), which according to the new budget project has to be raised; and since there is a group which holds the position of not raising the establishment, the budget question is therefore at a dead point.

Mintze Kalichstein, may she rest in peace

On Friday Mintze Kalichstein died in Kraków at the age of 70, the wife of the well-known Kielce Zionist activist Moshe Kalichstein, of blessed memory.
The late Mrs. Kalichstein came from a large family of distinguished lineage; she was a sister of the old rabbi of Pińczów, R' Shabtai Rapaport, of blessed memory, and a granddaughter of the Shach, the Keter Kehunah and other famous rabbis.
Despite the strictly religious upbringing she had received from her parents, as long as 40 years ago, after the first Zionist Congress, she joined the Zionist Organisation and, together with her late husband Moshe Kalichstein, of blessed memory, took an active part in Zionist work. Her house was always a meeting place for all maskilim, Lovers of Zion and later also for many Zionist gatherings. All her children (three of them are in the Land of Israel) were raised in a genuine national-Zionist spirit, which was the main content of her life.
Mrs. Kalichstein also distinguished herself by her good qualities in the other spheres of Jewish public life.
With the death of Mrs. Kalichstein one of the noblest and finest types of womanhood has departed this world, of a kind that seldom comes again.
Her funeral took place in Kraków, and therefore Jewish Kielce did not have the opportunity to pay her the proper honour that she had honestly earned.
Honour to her memory!

When there is money,
one loves as well...

In town they are now telling a legend-like story.
Two years ago the Kielce young lady L. married the Warsaw young man Z. for love. After the wedding, however, the young wife learned that her husband had earlier had a fiancée in Warsaw, who had afterwards emigrated to a rich uncle in Mexico.
The first year the couple lived happily.
Later, however, the husband changed completely; more and more often he began to mention his former fiancée and to tell how rich she is now, in what prosperity and luxury she lives in Mexico, and how happy he would have been had he married her.
A few months ago Z. vanished from home, and no one knew what had happened to him.
This week the mystery was cleared up. The wife suddenly received a letter from Mexico from her runaway husband, in which he informed her that the desire to lead a rich and comfortable life had overcome his feeling of love for her, and that he had decided to marry his former fiancée.
He therefore proposes to his wife that she accept a get (divorce) from him, and he will also give her a large sum of money.
The abandoned wife, who, incidentally, has been left with a small child in her arms, has had no choice but to accept this proposal, and in these days the Kielce rabbinate is to carry out the divorce formalities between Kielce and Mexico.
A Successful Visit

[Zagłębie — Zionism; shekel campaign and Congress elections.]
Of Mr. Baruch Zuckerman in Zagłębie
These days the vice-chairman of the A. K. [Actions Committee?], Mr. B. Zuckerman, stayed in Zagłębie.
The distinguished guest was received[?] in Sosnowiec by the comrades of [the League for] Working Eretz Israel in Zagłębie. After a reception in the café "Reks" and a lunch at Sarn[?]. On behalf of "Maccabi", ch. Lancman, a consultation took place with the participation of all Zionist groupings on the plan of the shekel campaign.
At 3 o'clock in the afternoon a large public meeting took place in Warman's[?] courtyard.
Ch. Y. Goldberg opened the public meeting, devoted to the shekel campaign, greeted the distinguished guest and leader and gave him the floor. Ch. Zuckerman was received by the audience of over a thousand people with stormy applause.
In a long, finely constructed speech ch. Zuckerman described the situation in Zionism and in Eretz Israel, and unfolded at length the history of our struggle[?] in the fight for a Jewish Eretz Israel.
Towards evening a glass of tea was held in the guest's honour at the home of ch. Lancman.
From Sosnowiec ch. Zuckerman went to Będzin, where, on the initiative of "Poale Zion", a gathering of all Zionist groupings took place in the premises of "Chiyuv"[?].
Before a packed hall ch. Małczowski[?] opened the consultation and greeted the comrade guest. A lively conversation developed, after which ch. Małczowski thanked the comrade guest for his instructive remarks.
On Monday a regional conference [of Zagłębie] took place in the premises of "Poale Zion" in Zagłębie.
Ch. Sobkowski was elected chairman, and to the presidium the comrades: Krzesiwa[?], Wborowski[?]. Meten[?] (Będzin), Lenczner (Sosnowiec) and Sztimpfer[?] (Dąbrowa).
After the report of ch. Małczowski and after a discussion, ch. Zuckerman gave a long, substantive lecture on the most topical questions of Eretz Israel and Zionism.
Mr. Sobkowski closed the conference and called on all to a vigorous shekel and election campaign.
At 3 in the afternoon a large open-air public meeting took place, attended by over two thousand people. Ch. Lichter[?] opened the meeting and gave the floor to ch. Sobkowski, who called on the Jewish masses to buy and spread the shekel and also to vote for Working Eretz Israel. Then ch. Zuckerman gave a major political lecture on the current problems of Jewish life, in Zionism and in Eretz Israel.
With the singing of Hatikvah the public meeting was closed.
Tsvi.

Recitation Evening by Yehuda Ehrenkranz

[Upper Silesia — Katowice; culture.] (L.S.) Last Thursday the Katowice "Chinuch" and the Zionist academics organised in the Zionist premises a recitation evening by the artist Yehuda Ehrenkranz, who recited with great success a series of works by Sholem Aleichem, Peretz, A. Shlonsky and others.
Ehrenkranz excelled in three languages (Hebrew, Yiddish and German), especially in the pieces[?] he performed — and so naturally, both when he lived a serious work and in the lighter children's conversations in an Eretz-Israel kibbutz.
The evening drew many new faces from among the Katowice Jewish intelligentsia, which warmly applauded the brilliant artist.
General dissatisfaction was caused by keeping the audience a full 2 hours in the closed hall — that is, no window was allowed to be open and the door was locked until the interval; many visitors left because of this.
General Meeting of the Gemilut Chesed Fund

[Upper Silesia — Katowice; aid institutions.] (L.S.) On Sunday the annual general meeting of the Katowice Gemilut Chesed (free-loan) fund took place in the Zionist premises.
The chairman, Dr. Kaufmann, opens the meeting and gives a general report, and Mr. Herbstmann the treasurer's report, from which it emerges that in the course of the year credit loans of over 18 thousand zł. were granted. From the previous year 9,700 zł. remained to be collected. 14,700 zł. were repaid. Members' dues — over 1,700 zł. Various donations — 1,600 zł. Expenses for administration and other items — over 1,400 zł.
In the year 1935/6, 95 loans totalling 13 thousand zł. were issued, and in the year 1936/7, 136 loans totalling over 18 thousand zł.
The fund's capital consists of: deposits[?] 8,500 zł.; "Joint" 4 thousand zł.; private debts 1,700 zł.; and a loan from the bank [unclear abbreviated name] 700 zł.
In the discussion Messrs. Heignraub[?], Pineshevsky[?], Erler and others took part.
Mr. Erler says that the house-owners[?] have too much influence on the activity and the small traders too little. Rabbi Fogelman appeals not to bring any party politics into the institution. Mr. Manele reads the minutes of the auditing committee, and a vote of discharge (absolutorium) is expressed to the board.
It is resolved to elect from among the board a loans committee, which will represent all economic groups.
Mr. Freund expresses thanks, in the name of those assembled, to the chairman Dr. Kaufmann.
Elected to the new board were Messrs. Dr. Kaufmann, Bruno Freund, Herbstmann, Gangerelman[?], J. Ritmant[?], Schlachter, D. Ehrlich, Almer[?], S. Kaufmann, Milner[?], Willer[?], H. Blumenfrucht and Popiel.
To the auditing committee: Messrs. Manele, Schiff and Meitlis.
The institution today numbers 250 members, and for such an important institution that is few. Katowice Jews should therefore enrol as members in large numbers.
Police at a Bris

[Upper Silesia — Katowice; police.] On Sunday a circumcision (bris milah) was celebrated at the home of Mr. Shimon Goldstein in Katowice (3 Maja 38). While the company, numbering about 30 men besides the women, was assembled, several policemen came in and demanded that the company go with them to the police station. At Whose Expense?

[Będzin — Kehilla; opinion piece.]
At Whose Expense?
Can the Będzin kehilla allow itself such a gesture? It would be worth hearing an answer.
The state of affairs in the Będzin kehilla is a grave one; the situation is becoming ever more critical and serious. What more is needed: a large number of officials have still not been paid their pensions for the year 1936; and that officials are not rich men and are in no position to hold out [?] for further years of pensions is self-evident; and that subsidies are not being paid out is also no longer any news. On the contrary, if once in a while some institution succeeds, thanks to the merit of the forefathers, in getting an a-conto payment on a subsidy, that is a notable [?] occurrence.
And who knows, perhaps this is no wonder either, because, as each of us knows, the revenues keep falling steadily, while the expenses — not only does one make no effort to reduce them, but on the contrary, they keep on rising, keep on climbing [?], because hardly does someone come along with good "protekcja" [connections] that gives him a chance [?] of being taken on, and this worsens the situation, increases the expenses and makes the outlook for continued existence harder.
True, there is a saying among Jews that "there is no poor community", but it has to be understood in the old-time sense, when it was a matter, for instance, of buying an etrog for the community or of repairing the synagogue, which was a one-time expense.
It must be understood quite differently, however, when it concerns permanent expenditures; here one can by no means argue that "there is no poor community".
If we want to look with open eyes, if we do not want to fool ourselves, we must come to the conviction that nowadays the community is indeed poor, and that one indeed cannot allow oneself unlimited expenditures at its expense.
And here we now stand before an accomplished fact: the gmina [the kehilla] has rented new premises, apparently because it is too cramped for it in the old premises — never mind that it does considerably less for the public than in previous years. Why, people say the gmina has turned back into the old-time plain shtibl — so what has precisely [?] now become so cramped and stuffy in the present premises? And something else: if change it must, then it should have been to the best advantage of the public, so that it would be in a separate house with a large courtyard and the rent would not go up much. Meanwhile we see the very opposite. They have taken up quarters in a large house, where the location will be very [?] unfavourable for the Jewish members, for various understandable reasons, and moreover the rent costs more than a hundred percent more. So — neither convenient nor cheap; then what was it needed for? Whom will it benefit? And where will they get the money for the more-than-doubled expenses, when the rent alone comes to more than 100 gulden [złoty] more? For once one expands, one must also buy furniture and sofas [?]; surely it doesn't do to move [?] into empty rooms when one wants to be modern and elegant! Where, then, will these monies flow in [?] from — monies which, incidentally, have a hundred other places to go?
How hard-pressed the gmina is can be illustrated by this one fact alone: the synagogue beadle is owed several years' pension. On top of that he is dangerously ill, so that an operation is unavoidable, and urgently so — and he cannot get the few hundred zł. paid out, because of which he cannot be operated on.
Does one need further arguments to show that we are crawling ever deeper into the swamp, from which later we will no longer be able to get out?
Yes, we understand that it is more comfortable to have more rooms, modern furniture, elegant premises, but the question arises: are we able to afford it, is one permitted to do what one is in no position to do? From whom did they get the power of attorney (koach harsha'ah) to make this grand gesture, which in this way will lead to considerably greater expenses besides the rent?
We have not yet forgotten Metzer's commissarial dictatorship over the Sosnowiec Jewish kehilla, who did everything so that not a grosz would remain in the kehilla treasury. Are they not starting to do the same here? Are they not going down the same road here too, are they not striving to drag the kehilla ever deeper into debts from which it will no longer be able to crawl out? Otherwise it simply cannot be understood: when one takes upon oneself burdens one cannot bear — how can one take on fresh expenses, when one is simply bankrupt and cannot drag along what lies on one's neck? At whose expense is all this being done — really at the expense of the poor kehilla treasury, which incidentally is dried out and parched enough as it is, so that there is no one to lean on?
And has the Jewish public not become impoverished enough in the course of the last years? From whom, then, do they reckon to tear it out? And even if there were someone to tear it from, the question then arises: is it worth it, when the public gets no benefit from it and society is not helped by the money? Must one really strive by all means to enlarge the budget for one's own use, only to then torment oneself [?] over how it is to be covered, at a time when one is burdened with so many debts on every side? Is this well-considered and logically justified? Upon my life, it would be worth hearing in this case the opinion of our kehilla representatives in general and of the president [prezes] in particular.
The kehilla board is a public body, taken from the public and belonging [?] to the public; therefore a sacred duty lies upon the kehilla representation to stay in contact with the population and to give it an accounting of everything that goes on there.
After all, in critical moments it demands that people come to its aid; therefore we have the right to demand an answer when something is done that the public does not understand.
R. Let.
Jews in Old Sosnowiec

[Sosnowiec — Feuilleton.]
Jews in Old Sosnowiec.
Jewish Old Sosnowiec [Stary Sosnowiec] truly lives like God in France. Who has it as good and pleasant as when the Sabbath comes? And never mind a holiday — one girds one's loins and sets off to the synagogue. And there one helps the Master of the Universe with His handful of little Jews, and there is no lack [?] of work. During the week there is indeed nothing to do. On a weekday one waits for a customer, who seldom shows up. On the Sabbath, on the other hand, there is work, as they say [?], over one's head..
And the work is done for its own sake, not just to discharge an obligation. One might [?] think, without doubt, that [—] [?] one risks one's life — life, after all, is not [—].
And when Jews become energetic, when Jews get carried away with enthusiasm — may He whom I am not worthy to name guard and save us.
The kehilla delegates its representatives to these Jews, who take upon themselves the mission of standing guard and seeing to it that the crowd does not run too wild and that the wardens [Vorsteher] keep to their duties. But what comes of it? As soon as the "holy work" is rehearsed in a planned way with rare [?] enthusiasm, so that no one is in a position to disturb them, there is no choice but, as in a catastrophic moment, to call in the third party, which already knows what to do...
When strange Jews come there, to the synagogue, on a Sabbath day, they certainly envy their brethren, watching what they are engaged in, because these Jews are sure that their brethren lack nothing all week, if they can arrange themselves so nicely on the Sabbath and live in such "raskosh" [Polish rozkosz, delight].
These people have their own little world, their "idyll", their pleasures; beyond that nothing concerns them; beyond that the world may turn upside down — it is none of their business.
Can one imagine that such a whole little corner should exist at all in the vicinity of our bustling Zagłębie, where everything is measured out [?] precisely and diligently!
And when we meet these Jews face to face, we truly do not know whether to pity them or envy them. Should we pity them because they are so blind and dull and do not see what is going on one glance beyond themselves, or should we envy them, that they want to see only what is happening beside [?] them, and one step further no longer concerns them — they absolutely do not want to see, not to feel, not even to take it into account!
What is this — strength or weakness, egoism [?] or self-control?
And who knows, perhaps it is better so; it may be that in today's cruel times for Jews narrow-mindedness, dullness and egoism [?] are better than pondering the troubles of the whole world and of the Jewish people and falling into feelings of despair? Perhaps it is better — healthier in any case — not to know, or not to want [?] to know and feel, what is going on one step, one glance beyond one's personal self.
Dr. Papuri.

Papers in Spring

[Sosnowiec — feuilleton.] Told by a Sosnowiec Jew.

Coming home for lunch, I found on the table a demand regarding the local tax; my wife handed it to me with displeasure. I looked for a while at the familiar treasury [„skarbowy“] paper and hid[?] it in my pocket. Ten days — I thought — must I really pay already now? But I was mistaken: it was not the only surprise;
— What are you talking about — my wife handed me a second [—] — this one is for „sekurecja“[?] [distraint / enforcement?], here you are and enjoy...
I had not yet managed to make peace with these thoughts when a fellow with a briefcase under his arm brought me another present: the „Ubezpieczalnia“ [social-insurance fund] is dunning me for a debt for a maidservant from three years ago. Here my wife really got angry[?];
— What, you still haven't paid Marysia? All my misfortunes are because of you! You're a good-for-nothing, a schlemiel.
My arguments that I did pay Marysia, that it is probably a mistake that will be cleared up, were of no help — „mine“ sticks to her own. I see no lunch on the table, and instead of in the pots she is rummaging in papers. Papers and [little papers?] she does indeed find:
— And this one you surely forgot?
I take a look and again everything starts spinning before my eyes: no more and no less than a hundred gulden! A gift from the „Bank Kupiecki“ [Merchants' Bank], a souvenir of long-forgotten times — a bonus for May.
Now „mine“ starts spitting fire: „Where have you squandered[?] the money? You're a worm, a disaster!...“
I swear to her by all that is holy to me that I owe no money; I argue from the eleventh paragraph of the cooperative law. I explain to her precisely and clearly Article 53, which says plainly that when a bank, a „spółdzielnia“ [cooperative society], a cooperative, a savings fund, a company and the like goes bankrupt, all members bear the liability; and since I, the humble Moshe Meir of the holy community of Sosnowiec, had the great honour of belonging to the late „Bank Kupiecki“, I shall unfortunately have to suffer it with great heartache..
We were already worked up to the highest point and had forgotten about eating... Unnerved[?], I jump[?] in bitter[?] trembling, and suddenly another trouble: a new paper is handed to me: „wo-do-cią-go-we“[?] [water-supply charge].
— What kind of a visitation is this, my God! — my boiling wife screams her justified complaint — there's hardly any water from the „wodociąg“[?] [waterworks], so what's this news? In short[?]! When I take a bucket [„wiadro“] of water I pay a „two-groszy piece“ commission[?] anyway.
— Precisely for that the [—] — I answer — for that you have the tax. They want you to install running water, sewerage; they want to make your life comfortable, modern — to beautify, improve and ease your life is what they want! Understood?
— If so — my little daughter, who has just come from school, picks up my words — then let them ease my life. Like[?] having a teacher for the matura, a „pensak“[?] for Latin, a tutor for mathematics, a [?] for Polish and an assistant for physics, and without[?] it I have no matura...
And by the way she slips me a note, a letter from the headmaster, that since they are going to build their own school building, it is the duty of the parents... he most politely asks them to come to a [meeting?]..
And an errand boy brings me from the notary [„rejent“] news of my[?] bill of exchange, which goes to protest tomorrow; and the grocer brings a bill; and Keren Hayesod[?] calls for paying the debt to the old-new homeland; Keren Kayemet announces that tomorrow the great campaign of [?] begins; and the „Red Cross“ sends me a declaration and [—] to remember the consumptives...
—
..I am tired, exhausted; I feel my legs won't carry me any more, my head is spinning, everything swims before my eyes. Let there be an end — I think — to all this; I want to be alone, alone with myself. To forget for a while the day-to-day worries. I flee to my study, to cut myself off from my own family circle with its petty demands. Here it is, the newspaper, the daily report from the great, wide, beautiful [vast?] world — let me find consolation here.
On the front page, in big „Kiddush Levana“ letters, I read the headlines of the world news:
— Great outrage in the world over the barbaric attack on the holy Basque city [Guernica]; thirty German aeroplanes bombed the city with ferocity, hundreds dead and wounded.
— Three hundred thousand women seek shelter in Bilbao.
— All Jewish philanthropic institutions in Germany dissolved.
— The „Völkischer Beobachter“ writes that it is time to do something again regarding the Jewish question.
On the other side — unrest again in Palestine.
— Great mass arrests going on in Russia. Over three hundred people arrested.. In Moscow they are preparing for a new trial...
1000 victims in Brisk [Brześć], help urgently needed.
I fling the newspaper away. My God, where can one run to?... Tired, I fall onto the sofa; heavy thoughts chase one another... One thinks of the good, the naive[?], the gentle[?] that still remains in man...
And through the open window the sun smiles, bright, warm; she sends us her first dear spring rays, and one longs, one wants so much to rejoice in the beautiful spring. But it is so hard... want[?], pain and misery, troubles and hatred, sword and fire rule over the world, and the best years, the youngest, slip away in bitter doubts and despair...
And one wants to drive far, far away the shattered belief that... that's it!.. everything is over!... and so it will go on. — — —
Z. Mitsznik.
More on the Chapter of Jewish Labour

[Poland — Jewish labour; article.] In this place we have already dealt with the question of the right to work in the Jewish factories. Among other things we also remarked on the difficulties of a psychological nature that one comes up against in the practical application of the struggle for the right to work. With today's article we aim to bring in a little clarity and to penetrate the sphere of the so-called psychological obstacles in the struggle for Jewish labour in the Jewish factories and the larger craftsmen's workshops.
The main claims that the Jewish factory owners put forward against Jewish workers are the following: first, that the Jewish workers are not physically strong enough to be able to match the non-Jewish workers in the intensity of the work; and second — the Jewish worker, because he is more [class-]conscious, agitates the non-Jewish workers in the factory. With these two main claims the Jewish factory owners try to defend themselves; the claims just mentioned are as old as the struggle for Jewish labour in Jewish life is old.
If we try to confront these claims with our present-day reality, they do not withstand the slightest [?] criticism. The first accusation, about the supposedly lesser physical endurance [?] of the Jewish worker compared with the non-Jew, falls apart completely on a broader look at reality. As a classic example of Jewish parity with non-Jews in respect of working capacity, the new Land of Israel can serve us. In the light of the achievement in the Land of Israel, where Jews perform the hardest Jewish [?] labours under the burning sun, the reproach of the Jewish worker's physical incapacity sounds like an outright slander [?]; and not only in the Land of Israel but also here in this country: whoever is acquainted with the pioneers' (halutzim) work knows that many thousands of Jewish workers and young people, as soon as they have the opportunity, perform the hardest work in sawmills, stone quarries, factories, etc. The living fact is the large number of [Jewish] workers in Fürstenberg's factory. These examples definitively refute the reproach of the Jewish worker's physical unfitness.
Let us say [?] that it is true that the Jewish worker is for the most part a more [class-]conscious element — and it would be an affront to the Jewish worker's dignity if one wished to deny it. But, first, this "shortcoming" has at the same time the great merit that the conscious worker does his work better and more precisely [?] than the non-conscious one; second, with the great growth of professionally organised workers there is in practice no difference in this respect between Jewish and non-Jewish workers. (Incidentally, when there were still large sections of unorganised workers, one could have spoken of the fact that in the specially organised part of the workers Jews play a significant role. Today, however, when unorganised workers are hardly to be found, especially in the larger factories and workshops, the exclusion of the Jewish worker is nothing more than a prejudice cut off from real life.
As we see, then, the so-called psychological difficulties we mentioned at the beginning are nothing but old, outlived prejudices, which are both false and unreal when confronted with our present-day Jewish and general reality.
(Y. H. K.)
The Coronation, Then and Now

The coronation of the English king [George VI] is over. Everything went off nicely and punctually, and, heaven forbid, no mishap whatsoever occurred. Lord Norfolk, the chief master of ceremonies, did not shut an eye for months and had only one worry: would everything be in order, and would he, heaven forbid, forget to invite one of the important persons, or, heaven forbid, invite someone who did not fit into the company... Besides that he had to know the pedigree of the invited guests, so that, heaven forbid, during the ceremony nobody should walk later who ought to walk earlier, or the other way round, nobody should walk in front who ought to walk behind...
The banquet gave him a great headache. Who may sit at the king's table, and whom should he seat at the side[?]? Who should sit next to whom? In general it is no easy job with the conservative Englishmen – what quarrels can come of it?...
No less fright had the police president of London. What if, heaven forbid, a bomb at one of the distinguished guests, or even a disrespectful word... one cannot imagine what that might cause...
And the chief baker together with the chief butler – they did not sleep either. If what the newspapers write is true, they had to make 1243 different dishes so that the guests would get their food "just like at home"... and for that one needed a minister's head[?]. This one does not eat pork and that one does not eat meat with milk – everything had to be watched, to make the distinction, like kashrut with a pious Jew...
But, thank the dear Lord, this time everything went all right... The newspapers report that "this time there was no incident whatsoever"... One must stress the word "this time", because at the earlier coronations not everything went as it should.
Mister Stoops[?], the all-knowing editor of the London "Times", once told us at a press meeting at the Leipzig fair what "terrible things" had happened in the past.
King George the Fourth, for example, ordered the doors of the church closed at his coronation so that the queen could not come in... that is how much he hated her. And so as not to have to think about the queen, before the ceremony he drank a fair amount of brandy and took a smelling bottle along.
At the banquet, when all the guests were already seated at the table, they had to wait over an hour for the king, who had suddenly vanished. Later he was found naked, with only the crown on his head, in one of his rooms... he had been too hot, so he took off the coronation robes.
At Queen Victoria's the ceremony also had some faults. She took the sceptre herself a quarter of an hour before the bishop wanted to give it to her... Then he put the ring on the wrong finger and she had to hold her hand in ice water for an hour until the ring came off the finger. Besides, she left the church early, because she thought it was already over, and when the bishop turned round to finish his prayers before the queen, he stood before empty benches.
At the coronation of Edward the 7th, the bishop of the day, who was almost blind, wanted to put the crown on a priest who was standing beside him. The king took the crown from him and put it on himself. The sword could not be found at all, and the Lord Mayor of London had to lend his sword so that it could be girded on the king.
Besides, at almost all coronations quarrels arose between Indian[?] princes, and [?] one never knew who was more worthy than the other.
Today one can indeed be happy that everything passed smoothly, and who knows, perhaps we will soon hear of some quarrel between England and an Australian state whose ruler was not received so nicely at the coronation?.. Who can know already today what may still come of it?
Z. Haber, Vienna.
A Wealth of Winnings in the First Ten Days

In the first ten days of the drawing of the fourth class of the 36th State Lottery many larger prizes fell. Two prizes of 75,000 zł. fell, on the numbers: 72,737 in Przemyśl, and on number 84,967 [printed "967, 84"] – Łódź. The owners of the individual quarter-shares of the tickets were workers, artisans, teachers and officials. Prizes of 50 thousand zł. were won altogether by five numbers, namely: 103,949, 31,656, 39,291, 24,518 and 172,413.
A quarter of the last number was owned by Mrs. Pelagia Staralna[?] of [unclear place]. And among the six prizes of 30,000 zł. we note number 167310, a quarter of which belongs to Miss Władysława Strowna[?], a housemaid at Sienkiewicza 1, flat 26, in Warsaw.
That the capricious goddess of luck, Fortuna, bestows her favour on those who have faith in her is shown by the following case:
Mr. Józef Marchal[?], the son of a farmer from Rybnik county (Upper Silesia), came to Warsaw to look for work. The 10 hectares of land could not feed his numerous family, consisting of his parents and 9 children – five daughters and four sons.
On coming to Warsaw, Mr. Marchal acted quite boldly: out of his limited money – so limited that he had to sell his last suit – he bought himself a whole ticket for the 1st class of the current lottery. With great toil[?] he held out to the fourth class, and lo, on the 9th day of the drawing a prize of 10000 zł. fell on his ticket number 63,475.
What such a sum means for him will be understood by those who, just like him, have no steady work and must live on temporary earnings.
Mr. Marchal intends to pay off his family and take over the farm on his own account.
On the 31st of this month the drawing of the grand prize in the amount of a million zł. will take place. The drawing will be transmitted by radio.
Besides that, there still remain a prize of 100,000 zł., 75,000 zł., fifty thousand zł. and many others.
Heard and Seen.

[Będzin — weekly feuilleton; the two-hour protest strike, the matriculation certificate, the kehilla council and the Talmud Torah.] By Ben Amotz.

Dlaczego! [Polish: "Why?"]
A beautiful May day. I go out into the street; life goes on at its everyday pace, but the Jewish faces are full of sadness, gloom-ridden, despairing. In the busier streets Jews stand with their watches in their hands, waiting for the twelfth hour. "It reminds me of how Jews in the little shtetl used to look at the sky like this on Tisha b'Av, whether "three stars are already out", whether one may already pray Maariv.
The factory whistle sounds[?] — 12 o'clock, the "holiday" begins, shops are closed and the merchants pour out into the street.
— Another fresh holiday — one says to another — no nation in the world has as many holidays as we do, because besides religious and national holidays we have[?] in recent years also…!
— Beating-holidays"…
The movement in the streets grows and draws[?] attention. What has happened! In the very middle of the day the Jewish shops close and people set out for a "stroll".
— Co się stało! [What happened!] — a Christian woman turns to a Jewish owner of a shop on Kołłątaja Street.
— Święto [A holiday] — answers the Jewish shopkeeper.
But the Christian woman is astonished: "Co za święto! [What kind of holiday!]" Evidently she knows that Jews have "Wielkanoc" [Passover], "Zielone Świątki" [Shavuot], "Trąbki" [Rosh Hashanah], "Sądny dzień" [Yom Kippur], but of a "żydowskie święto" [Jewish holiday] right after the "Zielone Świątki" she knows nothing.
— Pani ma rację[?] [You are right, madam] — the Jewish shopkeeper explains to her — this is a new holiday, w rodzaju[?] [a kind of] Tisha b'Av, only there is a small difference in the dates: the destruction of Tisha b'Av falls in the month of "Sierpień" [August], while the "[?]" of this "holiday" took place in the month of May, when nature bursts into bloom in all its splendour.
Soon a second questioner comes along; this one actually belongs to the Jewish people, her father prays in a "shtibl", but her words sound just like the first questioner's:
— Co się stało! — asks the modern Jewish young lady — Dlaczego zamykają sklepy! [Why are they closing the shops!]
— Dlaczego? — a young man answers her sarcastically — from all of Brisk[?] [Brześć] you'll find out "dlaczego".
— Don't take it amiss — an elderly Jew chimes in — you have a complaint against a Jewish daughter, why[?] she knows nothing about the two-hour protest! Firstly, a Jewish daughter is not obliged to know everything; it is enough for her that she knows how to read antisemitic newspapers, to run everywhere[?] where they mock the Jew, and to be well versed in the family life of every actor; and secondly, it is not at all modern for a Jewish daughter to read and think in Yiddish, for one depends on the other: if she lived in the Jewish world, she could not play the role of the Simple Son of the Haggadah, who stands up and asks "What is this?"
— Dlaczego!..

Matu-ra. [pun: "matura" (school-leaving certificate) — Hebrew "mat ve-ra", "weak and bad"]
On the street leading to the Jewish gymnasium I met an acquaintance, with whom I struck up a longer conversation:
— Where are you coming from? — I ask.
— From the gymnasium, he has already received it.
— I don't understand! What do you mean, who is "he" and what has "he" already received!
— My son, I mean, has already received the matura certificate.
— Well, and that is why you are so gloomy! You ought to be happy that your son has been privileged to it. A small thing —
— M a t u r a!
— True, so it was indeed once; I still remember today how great the joy was in our house when I received the matura: my mother could not stop weeping for joy, feasts worthy of King Solomon were held, the whole family rejoiced along and kept wishing one another mazel tov; the presents I received cost a fortune; such "luck" was granted, after all, to "one in a town and two in a family". But today, when I take a look at my son with the matura in his hand, my head begins to spin and sad pictures with a big question mark rise before me
— What do you mean?
— Yes, once such a certificate was called matura, and today
— matu-ra.

Talmud Torah — everyone.. against. [inversion of "and the study of Torah outweighs them all"]
A day before Shavuot the kehilla council in Będzin met in session to approve the report of the past budget year.
And since the parnassim [communal leaders] also belong to the people called "a hasty people" [Talmud, Shabbat 88a], and since the session took place, after all, before the Giving of the Torah, the parnassim (we mean the Agudah ones) were simply in a hurry, did not even listen to the "Ten Commandments" of the chairman[?], but at once said: — "We will do and we will hear", and accepted the "Torah" by "spirit".
It is hard, however, to establish by whose "spirit", for all of them, both the members of the kehilla board and the parnassim who raised their hands, are "heart and soul devoted" to the Talmud Torah, for one must not, God forbid, sin with the thought that such Jews as R' Dovid, R' Bunem, R' Yechezkel, R' Berish, R' Moshe Leib and the like would, God forbid, want to harm the "Talmud Torah", where 400 poor Jewish children study, and yet —
And yet those very same Jews raised their hands and gave their consent that the subsidy debt in the amount of 1700 zł. (1800 had been preliminarily budgeted, and over the whole year a hundred-odd[?] was paid out..) be null and void..
— 1700 złoty struck out!
And come to think of it, "such a sum plays no role" for the Talmud Torah — the scholarly strikers-out know that well, and incidentally, by their deed they have established that in matters of Talmud Torah everyone is against, as it "says" in the Mishnah:
— And Talmud Torah — everyone — against..
