Oneg Shabbat — Parshat Beha'alotcha

[Oneg Shabbat — Parshat Beha'alotcha.]
Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes around this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parshat Beha'alotcha
a) "Toward the face of the menorah" (8:2)
The Sages say that when the Temple was destroyed, the menorah was hidden away, and no foreign hands ever gained mastery over it.
For the menorah symbolizes Jewish wisdom — "He who wishes to become wise should face south, and he who wishes to become rich should face north; and your sign: the table in the north and the menorah in the south" — and this is what the saying of the Sages means: over the table, which symbolized Jewish wealth, the enemies of the Jews gained mastery; only over Jewish wisdom did they have no mastery, and it remained unvanquished [?]... Yalkut Yehuda.
b) "And he shall minister with his brethren" (ibid., 26)
R' Nachumke Horodner was a great giver of charity; his whole life he devoted to collecting charity. In his old age it was already hard for him to go round the houses collecting for the poor, so he called several young men [—] [?], [spoke?] with them about the mitzvah and gave them to understand that with this holy work [—] he was honouring them.
Says one of the young men:
— R' Nachumke! With such a great and holy thing one honours old, distinguished Jews, not such young [whippersnappers?] as we.
R' Nachumke answers:
— We see in the service of the Tabernacle that whoever reached the age of fifty "shall return from the service of the work": he may no longer carry the boards of the Tabernacle on his shoulders. Although this too is holy work, and the older the kohen becomes, the more fitting he should be for this very holy work — yet because one simply has to carry boards on the shoulders, one needs young strength..
c) "With matzot and bitter herbs they shall eat it" (9:11)
It was taught: Rava said: matzah nowadays is from the Torah, and maror is rabbinic. Pesachim 120 [?] a.
Why are we nowadays not obliged by Torah law to eat maror? Because maror is a remembrance of the embittered [?] Jewish life in Egypt, and today, in our time, we have more than a remembrance — we feel the maror in life itself.. R' Yehuda Leib Ginzburg [?].
d) "And it came to pass when the ark set forward" (10:35)
Our Rabbis taught: for this passage the Holy One, blessed be He, made markers above and below. What is the reason? Rabbi said: because it is an important book in its own right. Shabbat 116.
In what way is the passage "And it came to pass when the ark set forward" a distinct important book?
— Because in this passage one of the principles of Judaism has been given expression: that one must not strive for the annihilation of one's enemies, but "Rise up, O Lord, and let Your enemies be scattered, and let those who hate You flee before You" — we pray only that they be scattered, but not that they perish...
e) "We remember the fish which we ate in Egypt for free" (11:5)
Rav and Shmuel disagree about it: one said actual fish, and the other said forbidden relations. The one who said fish — because it is written "which we ate"; the one who said forbidden relations — because it is written "for free". Yoma 75a.
How does the word "for free" point to forbidden relations?
Only he who keeps a household with a family must work hard for it, whereas the one given to illicit relations is without a yoke — therefore he is designated "for free". Leket Amarim.
f) "And Moses heard the people weeping by their families" (ibid., 10)
"By their families" — over the relations that were forbidden to them. Rashi.
Why does the Torah state explicitly that they wept wanting to eat meat, whereas about the prohibition of forbidden relations the Torah speaks only by way of hint?
Because about meat they themselves were not ashamed to say it explicitly, whereas about the prohibition of forbidden relations they themselves also spoke only by way of hint... Imrei Chen.
g) "Every man at the door of his tent" (ibid.)
Each one wept over his own sorrow; each one cared only about himself... Torat Moshe.
h) "And let me not see my wretchedness" (ibid., 15)
He should have written "their wretchedness", but Scripture used a euphemism; this is one of the scribal emendations in the Torah, for euphemism and refinement of language.
It may be, however, that Moses said it thus: if the Jews are [?] bad, it is not possible that I alone should be good; if it is "their wretchedness", it is already also "my wretchedness". The environment must affect even the greatest person. "For this let every pious one pray... surely the flood of waters shall not reach him" — even when he is pious, he is not sure that the "flood of waters", the current, will not sweep him along.. LeBeit Yaakov.
i) "Six hundred thousand on foot" (ibid., 21)
For the verse does not count six hundred thousand people, but six hundred thousand feet; it does not count by heads but by feet, because now they were in the state of [standing?] feet.. R' Moshe Alshich.
j) "Are you jealous for my sake?" (ibid., 29)
Moses asked Joshua:
That you take my honour so much to heart [?] — do you really mean only me, or do you mean yourself? That is to say, you want your rabbi to have competitors [so printed, without a negation], because if my honour is diminished, your honour too is thereby diminished... Ktav Sofer.
At the Border... — The Troubles of My "Żołądek" [Stomach]

[Humorous feuilleton — a trip to Karlsbad; a currency search at the border.]
By I. Oberżanek [?]
As you know, I am already a seasoned[?] spa-goer. Every year I go off to a spa. In former years I used to go to Germany; now I am afraid to put my stomach into a German's hands, so I go to Czechoslovakia — to Karlsbad [Karlovy Vary], as it's called. Every summer I pack up my stomach, take it off to Karlsbad, they rinse it through[?], wash it out, mangle it out, press it out, I bring it home — and it is no longer the same stomach. It doesn't flare up at every idle[?] trifle, doesn't boil over and doesn't play wild[?] crazy tricks; it sits quietly, decently — I know I have a stomach, not a cripple!
This year I got a partner for Karlsbad. My Irene has begun "dealing"[?] in stones and sand, and the doctor said that with this bit of merchandise one has to go to Karlsbad.
Well, never mind — we both had foreign passports made. I threw myself into a short "ubranie" [Polish: suit], with a stiff "bekher"[?] on my head, put on a stiff collar with a bow tie, combed my beard into two points like Franz Joseph [?] — a whole "datsh"[?] with a "kushk"[?]...
My Irene had thirty dresses made for herself, coats, [—][?], stockings, hats, besides silk underthings and other rags.
Before Shavuot we got ready for the road — I with my stomach and my Irene with her sand and stones. Who would have wanted[?] to know that now there is this business with foreign currency [dewizy] — what one may take out and what one may not take out.
We arrive at the border, and they "invite" [zaprasza] me and my Irene into a special room.
I ask the gentleman[?] official[?]:
— My dear sir, why are you taking us into a cabinet? Do you think we are strangers? We are husband and wife — why are you leaving us in "yichud" [seclusion of a man and woman]?
— Inspection! — he answered.
Well, so be it — an inspection is an inspection, and what do I have to fear? My property [majątek] they won't take from me. I stand and wait my turn; finally they call us both into a second room, and he asks me:
— Co pan ma? [What do you have, sir?]
— Kram żołądkowy. [a stomach "kram" — i.e. a stomach complaint; pun: kram = stall, goods.]
— Kram? Co to za[?] kram? Niech pan pokaże. [A "kram"? What sort of kram is that? Show it, sir.]
— Heh... heh... what does that mean? Co znaczy "show"[?]? Jak to można? Co mam pokazać? [How is that possible? What am I to show?]
— No, ten kram. [Well, that kram.]
— E, pan się wicuje[?] [the gentleman is joking] — you are joking, sir.
He looks at me and asks me:
— Co jeszcze pan ma? [What else do you have, sir?]
— Tak, mam troubles. Na luksusy[?] — I answered.
— Co? Luksusowy towar? Proszę pokazać. [What? Luxury goods? Please show them.]
— Heh, znów ta sama bajka [the same old tale again], the same story again — to... to nie można pokazać! [that... that cannot be shown!]
— Jak to nie można? [How can it not be shown?] — the other got angry[?] — W tej chwili pan ma pokazać! [You must show it this minute!]
I give him to understand that this "luxury merchandise" is kept inside. I gave him to understand that this luxury merchandise and that "kram" I would have registered[?] down to every single gas[?]. I talked, explained it to him, and he shrugged his shoulders, wrote "luksusowy towar", "kram", and I pointed to my belly:
— "O, tu wszystko[?]. Mam... tu, w brzuchu, proszę pana" [Here is everything. I have... here, in the belly, sir]...
When he had finished with me, he turned to my Irene:
— "Co pani ma?" [What do you have, madam?]
— "Nic, proszę pana". [Nothing, sir.]
— "Jak to nic? Coś pani ma?" [How, nothing? You have something, madam?]
— "Co ja mam? May it be said of all the apostates, co ja mam!..." [What do I have? ... what I have!]
— "Walutę pani ma?" [Do you have foreign currency, madam?]
— Shlomo Mendel, what is he asking?
— He's asking whether, besides the sand, you have another [—]?
— "Tak, tak... tak... mam" [Yes, yes... yes... I have] — answered my Irene.
— "Wiele"[?] pani ma? [How much do you have, madam?]
My Irene stood there bewildered[?] — what does "how much" mean? How would she know how many stones she has? So I answered:
— "To się dowiemy w Karlsbadzie" [We'll find that out in Karlsbad], "jak Pan Bóg da" [God willing]... when they take them out, they'll know "how many" [—].
He keeps standing and looking at me, looks at me and looks at my "so-and-so" [missus]; I see he wants to say something but isn't "śmiały" [bold enough] to ask, so I took pity on him and helped him out:
— "Ma pan jeszcze pytanie, niech się pan nie wstydzi" [You have another question, sir? Don't be shy] — we are our own people.
— "Tak" [Yes] — the other piped up[?] —
— "Czy wy jeszcze macie[?] srebro, złoto?" [Do you also have silver, gold?]
— "Tak, ja mam[?]" [Yes, I have] — answered my Irene.
— "O, tu proszę pana" [Here, sir] — and she showed him her mouth and showed three gold crowns.
— Aha... złoto [gold]... and the other grew cheerful. His face began to beam; I thought my Irene had cooked up a mess[?] here — I saw it from his expression as he sat down to write a report.
Again he stood there, looked at me and at my Irene, and after some deliberation he asks my Irene:
— "Może pani jeszcze coś ma? Brylanty? Drogie kamienie?" [Perhaps you have something more, madam? Diamonds? Precious stones?]
— "Tak... tak... mam, jeszcze jakie kamienie" [Yes... yes... I have — and what stones!] — answered my Irene.
— "No proszę, niech pani pokaże". [Well, please, show them, madam.]
— "Pokazać?" [Show?] If only I could show them, I wouldn't need to go to Karlsbad.
My Irene, seeing[?] that he had "touched on"[?] her stones, grew bolder with him and told him straight out:
— "Wie[?] pan, ja mam piasek też!" [You know, sir, I have sand too!]
I went on explaining to him, and only then did he see[?] what kind of "majątek" [property] we were taking out, and we got the permission to travel — I with my stomach, my Irene with her gold, with the precious stones, with the "luxury merchandise" and other "luxury articles"...

The Living Corpse

[Literature — serial novel ("The Living Corpse"), instalment 10.]
A. Zaglembier [pen name].
(A most thrilling novel of Jewish life in Zagłębie before and after the World War). 10)
Summary of the beginning of the novel.
On a winter night before the World War, when two Cossacks were to transfer the dangerous bandit "Szmulek Łapka" into the Piotrków prison, they were suddenly attacked on the way to the Będzin station by two disguised "strażniks" (guards) — Łapka's helpers. The Cossacks were found the next morning lying bound with gagged mouths, and Szmulek "Łapka", freed, fled to the Gzichów road and hid somewhere.
That same evening, and almost at the same hour, the universally respected, solid collector (inkasent) Josl Wertheim — a father of three children — suddenly disappeared. His wife Sarah'tshe runs about the town terribly desperate, searching for him in every possible hiding place in all of Zagłębie. But Josl Wertheim has vanished like a stone in water..
On the fifth day pockmarked Matek reports to police inspector Karecki and tells him that on that day he saw Wertheim walking on the Gzichów road together with the Christian woman Magda Komarska — a young, pretty gentile girl whom Matek had been courting.
Magda is arrested at once. During the interrogation she declares that on the very day Wertheim disappeared they had quarrelled, because Wertheim wanted to give her money to go to Katowice for an operation so that their illegitimate child would not be born. Karecki then goes to Wertheim's wife Sarah'tshe and tells her about her husband's love affair with Magda, but Sarah'tshe does not believe it and declares that her husband had no money on him.
Now read on.
"That is exactly what I came to establish, and it is, after all, one of the most important things, because if your husband really did have money on him, it is very likely that it was precisely because of that money that Magda, perhaps together with someone else, killed him. Several hundred roubles — that is a large sum, after all, [?] you say.."
"No! No! That cannot be, no!.."
"But it is possible, isn't it, that he perhaps also had money of his own on him; did your husband not have some money of his own put away somewhere?"
At that moment Sarah'tshe turns her wide-open eyes to the wall cupboard, and a terrible thought suddenly flashes through her mind: and perhaps?.. perhaps?..
Until now it had not occurred to her, she was even afraid to think about it, but after Karecki's last words... yes, one must take a look... There in the cupboard, in a little purse, lie the few hundred saved-up roubles that Sarah'tshe always kept for a "black hour" — may it never come; and Karecki did mention money of his own...
And as if in madness[?] Sarah'tshe suddenly runs to the cupboard and starts rummaging and searching. Karecki follows her every movement with great curiosity. And now Sarah'tshe pulls out of the cupboard the little purse that lies [—]. She unwraps it, searches inside, shakes it out, and as she draws out an empty hand her face becomes deathly terrified and she collapses onto a chair with a bitter[?], heart-rending cry:
"Gone!.. The money is gone!!"
"Really gone?" Karecki asks again, and at the same time he is pleased that the terrible mystery is after all beginning to unravel. "Just let me search, you are too agitated now."
But Karecki too finds in the purse only various slips of paper, documents — no money...
"So, Magda Komarska told the truth," Karecki rises to leave, "but she has not yet told everything..."
"Ah," Sarah'tshe sighs heavily, "you had better not have told me, I had better not have known... My husband with her... with a Christian woman..."
And as he leaves, Karecki says triumphantly — for Sarah'tshe's suffering matters little to him, so long as his investigation is on a good track:
"Don't worry, Magda will also tell us where your husband is; I will make her do it!.."
When Sarah'tshe is left alone, for a good while she cannot come to herself after the terrible news and the discovery that together with Josl their emergency money has also vanished from the purse...
Until all at once she tears herself from her place like a wild woman, runs after the police inspector and begs him with tears in her eyes and with stifled sobs:
"I beg you.., at least let no one know of my shame... I beg you..."
"I will do that for your sake, but the court... before the court one must, after all, tell everything..."
"But until then at least let no one know..."
"Good, I promise you."
And so, left standing all alone on the stairs, Sarah'tshe is suddenly overcome by a terrible thought; something draws her to the window... she wants to jump out into the courtyard... to fall headfirst onto the sharp stones... One leap and she will be freed of all her sufferings..
But she does not do it, remembering at the same time her children, who are in any case already left half-orphans; what fault is it of the poor children if their father... must they now also be left without a mother?..
"No, no!" everything in her begins to cry out. She must live; for the children's sake she must live; she will hide their father's shame from them...
She goes back into the house, more crushed and desperate than before, and the one[?] tormenting[?] thought scratches[?] in her brain like a rusty[?] [—]:
"Why has this befallen me?! He, Josl, my Josl, for whom everyone envied me, he could commit such a thing? Live in secret with a gentile woman, from whom a bastard will surely also come into the world — he could do that? Was I too little for him? He, for whom I was ready to lay down my head, he masqueraded like that before me?.."
And the longer she ponders the terrible event, the more she begins to look at the whole matter with quite different eyes; she begins to see her Josl in quite a different shape than until now.
If he really is such a "bird" and besides his wife also had a gentile woman, then why should she be so desperate and so [—] herself over his disappearance?.
And if so, he must surely have deceived her from the very first minute... Ah, yes, now Sarah'tshe understands his frequent excuses in the evenings, when he used to say that "today I have to settle accounts[?] with a customer" — this gentile woman, she was the "customer", and she believed him so... And to whom could the slightest suspicion have occurred about such a quiet, solid and loving husband? He had always been such[?] a faithful husband and an even more faithful father to the children — no! If this could happen, Sarah'tshe now sees that one cannot believe anyone, not even one's own father and mother..
Thinking this and coming to such conclusions, Sarah'tshe feels it becoming easier for her, as if the terrible nightmare had been lifted from her all at once.
And perhaps it is in fact good that it happened this way?.. She does not know whether Josl ran away somewhere on purpose, or whether perhaps he really was murdered and his body buried somewhere, but it is better indeed that it happened this way, and so she need lament no more — it was God's judgment... And it is good that her shame is not carried out into the street; meanwhile, after all, nobody knows yet.. And let her imagine that her husband really died — does it not happen that one is left a young widow with orphans?.. And is it not better to be a widow or an agunah than to have a husband whom one must share with another woman, and on top of that with a...
Yes, it is really better that it happened this way!..
And giving herself courage and hope to be able to go on dragging the heavy yoke of life, Sarah'tshe "pinched her cheek so that the colour would stay" and finally made peace with the thought: it is really better that it turned out this way...
And wishing also to free her children once and for all from the terrible predicament, a few days later she told them this:
"Listen, children, you no longer have a father..."
And together with the children she once again had a good cry over her unexpected misfortune...

When Does One Become a Jew?

[Humour — “Der Kokh-lefl”; Sosnowiec — converts.] The convert in a fix.
In a family of Sosnowiec converts, little Staszek asks his father:
— Daddy [tatusiu], at what age does one become a Jew?
The father looks the kid [“bnak” — doubtful reading] over from head to foot:
— I don’t understand, why are you asking that?
— I’ll explain it to you — little Staszek let his father understand — I am 6 years old, so I am a Catholic; uncle [wujaszek] Leopold is 40 years old, so he is an Evangelical; and grandpa [dziadek] is 70 years old, so he is already a “Żydek” [a little Jew]..
On Urke Nachalnik’s Visit to Będzin.

[Humour — “Der Kokh-lefl”; Będzin — lecture.] Last week Urke Nachalnik appeared in Będzin with a lecture. The lecture had no success. As we are told, the reason for the flop is that for Będzin Urke is no interesting “number”: in this town there are such Urke Nachalniks by the dozen; what is more, they also take a lively part in Jewish public life...
The Second Meeting Will Take Place in Chol ha-Moed.

[Humour — “Der Kokh-lefl”; Sosnowiec — kehilla; Będzin — slaughter and mikvehs.] From a well-informed source we learn that the second meeting of the kehilla board in Sosnowiec will take place no later than the coming Chol ha-Moed Sukkot...
It is interesting to add that the first meeting, too, took place during Chol ha-Moed Pesach...

Everything Will Be Stamped
As is known, on the basis of the slaughter law every animal slaughtered as kosher is stamped all over.
As we are informed, it is also planned that the identity cards of the Będzin mikvehs be stamped after every “visit”, so that one may know which “beast” is kosher...

Perhaps Something Cheaper?
In the Old Market a sanitary commission goes round checking whether the shops are clean. In one shop, where not everything was in order, the official says:
— Sir [Panie], you will be fined 100 zł.
— Please, sir [Proszę pana] — said the merchant — perhaps you could knock something off; after all, I am a regular customer of yours!..

What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin: Rabbi Chameides administers the oath to the Jewish soldiers

[Head of the local section; Będzin — Jews in the army; religion.]
What's New in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 18 Sivan 5697 — piątek 28 maja 1937 [Friday, 28 May 1937].)
Będzin
Rabbi Chameides administers the oath to the Jewish soldiers
Festive divine service in the synagogue.
On Tuesday the oath of the Jewish soldiers of the local garrison took place, conducted by Rabbi Chameides.
In connection with this, a festive prayer service was held in the synagogue with the participation of all the Jewish soldiers, before whom Rabbi Chameides delivered a fine speech in Polish, in which he pointed out that the Jewish commandment of the Ten Commandments is not to swear falsely. Rabbi Chameides calls on the Jewish soldiers to be loyal to the fatherland, because the Jewish community is always the guarantor for the deeds of an individual.
The protest strike in Zagłębie.

[Zagłębie — protest over the Brześć pogrom; Będzin, Sosnowiec.]
The protest strike in Zagłębie.
The Monday [?] two-hour protest strike against the events in Brześć was complete.
At the appointed time, 12 noon, all Jewish shops, the bank and the offices were closed; work was also stopped in the Jewish institutions, establishments and organisations; there was great movement in the streets, and in the shtiblekh psalms were recited.
In Fürstenberg's factory all the workers, Jewish and non-Jewish, joined the protest and stopped work for 2 hours; the workers decided to donate the wages for the 2 hours to the victims in Brześć.
In Sosnowiec the shops were closed. Also [—] [?] were [?] open on the public day [?]. But there were also such as did not show solidarity with the Jewish community and kept their shops open; these are: a shop on Jekerska [?] Street and Deutsch's shop in Old Sosnowiec.
Regional conference of the 'Hitachdut' in Zagłębie.

[Zagłębie — Zionism; Hitachdut.]
Regional conference of the 'Hitachdut' in Zagłębie.
On Sunday a large regional conference of the Zagłębie district will take place in the premises of the local 'Hitachdut'. A large number of organisations from all of Zagłębie will take part.
On behalf of the Central Committee of the 'Hitachdut', Comrades Pinchas Lubianiker and Dr. A. Sternberg will take part; they will lecture on the topic [?] 'The situation in Zionism and in Eretz Israel'.
The participation of the above-mentioned delegates has aroused great interest in progressive Zionist circles.
Swindlers at work.

[Będzin — crime; fraud.]
Swindlers at work.
Mrs. S. Wajn [?], who lives on Małachowskiego Street, was approached by an unknown gentleman who asked her where a cooperative [?] was.
When this person had left her, a second gentleman, very elegantly dressed, came up straight away and asked the woman [what] the first one had asked her.
Mrs. Wajn, realising that these were swindlers, gave the second one a good scolding [?] and went away.
Trial of the president of the Jewish combatants.

[Będzin — courts; veterans' organisations.]
Trial of the president of the Jewish combatants.
Next Tuesday an interesting trial will take place in the local municipal court.
In the dock sits the president of the Jewish combatants [veterans], who is accused of having insulted a high state official.
The story is as follows. The accused, who is the gospodarz [manager] of the 'Sadzawski [?] Club', dismissed [?] a Christian servant of the club several months ago. Because of this she turned to the authorities with a complaint, in which she reported that at a general meeting of the combatants Dr. Rechtschaft had used an insulting word about one of the important leaders of the state.
On the basis of the complaint the prosecutor's office brought a case, which will be heard next Tuesday at 12 noon.
A larger number of witnesses have been summoned to the trial.
From the 'Brit Nashim Leumiyot' organisation.

[Będzin — women's organisations; Revisionists.]
From the 'Brit Nashim Leumiyot' organisation.
On Sunday evening a tea evening was held in the organisation's own premises in honour of the founding of the branch of the women's organisation 'Brit Nashim Leumiyot' [League of National Women].
After the lecture by Miss M.A. Grünstein (Bielitz) there were declamations and recitations, among others 'The Last Word' (Bialik) and 'Sand and Stone' (Frug), performed by Eckstein.
Then Mr. A. Diament spoke about the events in Brześć, and it was decided to undertake a fund-raising campaign in the town.
After the singing of 'Hatikvah' the chairwoman, Mrs. Szarf, closed the evening.
A craftsmen's activist before the court.

[Będzin — courts; artisans.]
A craftsmen's activist before the court.
On 4 June the trial will take place in the local court against Mr. Efraim Kleinman, who is accused of having, as a craftsmen's activist, taken 100 zł. from Mr. D. Silbernagel [?] to settle [a matter] at the tax office, and of not having carried out his mission.
Delegation of the Biała kehilla.

[Będzin — kehilla; synagogue; accident; Revisionists.]
Delegation of the Biała kehilla.
Last Monday a delegation of the kehilla of Biała stayed here, together with the rabbi, Rabbi Dr. Hirschfeld.
The purpose of the delegation was to become acquainted with the paintings in the local synagogue and with the installations of the municipal mikveh.
Rabbi Hirschfeld, and also the other members of the delegation, were delighted by the beautiful artwork of the eastern wall in the local synagogue.
—o—
Little girl run over and killed.
On Reymont Street in Grojce [?] [Grodziec?], 5-year-old Janina Matejka [?] wanted to run across the street; at that moment she fell under a cart loaded with coal and was killed.
—o—
A new kehilla office.
The office of the local kehilla has been moved to new, large premises at Santszewska [?] 29.
—o—
Meeting of the Revisionists
Today, Saturday, at 2 p.m., the annual general meeting of the local Revisionists will take place in their own premises. Editor Josef Klarman will also take part in the meeting.
Sosnowiec — Committee Formed to Carry Out the Relief Campaign for the Jewish Victims in Brisk. Message of Sympathy to the Brisk Kehilla

On Monday evening an extraordinary meeting of the board and council of the local kehilla was held in the kehilla's premises.
The meeting was called for the purpose of organising a broad relief campaign for the Jewish families who suffered in Brisk [Brześć nad Bugiem].
After a lengthy debate on the question it was resolved: 1) to adopt a protest resolution concerning the sad events in Brisk, 2) to send a telegram of sympathy to the Brisk kehilla, 3) to organise a fund-raising campaign for the victims, and 4) that the kehilla itself should contribute to the campaign.
In accordance with the last point, the gmina [Jewish community] contributed 500 zł for the victims in Brisk.
For the same date a larger meeting of representatives of all the political, cultural and economic organisations in our town was also called.
The meeting took place in the kehilla's council hall. About 60 delegates took part, among them the most respected public figures of our town.
At the meeting, which lasted about 2 hours and proceeded in a serious manner, the first question dealt with was in what form the collection should be conducted. Several plans were put forward on this question, but the majority was in favour of the collection being carried out by delegates who will visit every Jewish home.
On the spot 1023 zł was collected from several persons.
Then a committee was elected, which includes 2 representatives each of: the club of city councillors, the merchants and industrialists, the small traders, the house-owners, the artisans, the charitable societies[?], [—], the Zionist Org., Mizrachi, Torah va-Avoda[?], the Revisionists, Brit ha-Hayal, Agudah, the League for Working Eretz Israel, Betar, the Hitachdut, and others.
The fund-raising campaign in the town is to begin as early as next week.
Annual General Meeting of "TOZ"

In the premises of the local kehilla the annual general meeting of "TOZ" [Towarzystwo Ochrony Zdrowia, the Jewish health-protection society] took place in the presence of 25 members. The report we have received reads:
The meeting is opened by the vice-president, Adv.[?] Kahn, who asks those present to honour by rising the deceased members of "TOZ", Moryc Rajner and Ferdynand Patak.
Director Lejzerowicz[?] is elected chairman of the meeting; he invites Mr M. Lancman to serve as secretary.
After the society's manager, Mr Fried, reads the minutes of the last general meeting, the secretary, Dr Liberman, delivers the activity report.
From Dr Liberman's very successful address, given in a fine Yiddish, it can be seen that "TOZ", despite various obstacles and despite the indifference of Jewish society in Zagłębie, expands its useful activity every year, caring for the state of health of the Jewish masses. Thus, for example, the work in the field of school hygiene has been enlarged; it currently covers over 800 children of the religious schools, which receive no support from the magistrate. This year, too, up to 450 children of the poorest strata were fed, and at the same time received cod-liver oil and quartz-lamp irradiation treatments. At the Talmud Torah schools in Będzin and Sosnowiec school out-patient clinics are active, employing a doctor and a hygienist. An important part of "TOZ" work is also devoted to the summer colony, which 116 children enjoyed free of charge last year.
Adv.[?] Kahn supplements the report, highlighting organisational matters. Then Dr A. Lewental gives the treasurer's report and at the same time presents the budget for the coming year, adapted to the expanded activity.
On behalf of the audit committee, which found the books in perfect order, Dr Wercman[?] moves to grant a vote of discharge (absolutorium) to the outgoing board. After a discussion, in which President Rubinlicht, Dr Trakewer[?], Dr Wercman and others take part, the motion is adopted.
The newly elected board includes: Dr Weinzieher, Adv.[?] A. Kahn, councillor Mrs Z. Szajn, Dr Liberman, Dr Lewental, Mrs Dr Grodzińska, Binder, Dr Rotsztajn, Adv.[?] Perbrystal[?], Zamberg, Szer, Zylberszac, Eng. Białska, Dr Gruszkiewicz, Goldfeld, Dr Taraszejski[?], Dr Mittelman, Dr Sternberg, Dr Szmidel[?]. Audit committee: Director Grodziński[?], Dr Wercman, Rajchman, President Rubinlicht and Dr Trakewer[?].
Shots Fired after a Fleeing Ruffian

On Tuesday morning a well-known ruffian (awanturnik) accosted Jewish passers-by in Old Sosnowiec, among them the iron merchant Icchak Fiszel of Old Sosnowiec, whom the ruffian wounded with a razor.
At the alarm a policeman came and detained the ruffian. On the way to the municipal lock-up he started to run away and went into Wiejska Street. Then the policeman, after calling on the fugitive several times to stop, fired several shots from his revolver and wounded the fugitive.
The ruffian has already been punished several times for various crimes.
Debtor Threatens Revenge

A resident of Old Sosnowiec, Mr Suchecki, had a distraint (zajęcie[?]) levied on a debtor of his, over a debt of 130 zł.
On the same day, in the evening, the debtor came into Suchecki's place together with an unknown man, where the stranger introduced himself as the president of the "Narodowcy"[?] [the nationalists] and demanded of Suchecki that he withdraw the judgment (wyrok) from the bailiff (komornik); if not, he would take revenge on him.
Fairs Should Take Place on the Sabbath — So Wants the Polish Merchants' Association

Last Monday the annual general meeting of the Polish Merchants' Association took place here.
The meeting is opened by the president, Narliński[?], who welcomes the representatives of the administration and of the tax office.
From the reports it emerges that the association intervened in a number of matters; among other things, the association came out with a proposal that the markets and fairs should take place on the Sabbath.
The report also stated that the association has been allotted the sale of wine, which had been entirely in Jewish hands.
Hooliganism. —o— Mizrachi's Siyum ha-Sefer. —o— Price of Water for the Synagogue Reduced. —o— Budget of the Commissarial Kehilla Board Sent Off

The 50-year-old Lejbisz Wrocławski[?], walking on Sunday along Kołłątaja Street, was attacked by a hooligan who "honoured" Wrocławski with blows.
—o—
Mizrachi's Siyum ha-Sefer.
Next Sunday the local "Mizrachi" celebrates a siyum ha-sefer [completion of a Torah scroll]. In connection with this the committee held a meeting at which it was decided that the siyum should take place without any publicity.
—o—
Price of Water for the Synagogue Reduced.
Following the intervention of the kehilla representatives in the magistrate, the price of the water to be used in the town synagogue has been reduced by 25 per cent.
—o—
Budget of the Commissarial Kehilla Board Sent Off.
As we are informed, the local starostwo wanted[?] to send to Kielce the kehilla budget according to the draft of the commissarial kehilla board.
Why Is No Relief Committee Being Formed for the Jews of Brisk?

Everywhere relief committees are being formed, which have already set about the collection campaign.
Regrettably, nothing at all is yet heard about founding such[?] a relief committee in the city of Kielce.
Yet it would be an unforgivable moral and social wrong if no relief committee were formed in Kielce.
Brisk must be rebuilt! No excuses whatsoever may be sought[?]. Nor are there any legal difficulties, since the relief committee for the Jews of Brisk has already been legalised by the Ministry.
All kinds of public work must be set aside for a day or two, and the Brisk relief committee must be formed as quickly as possible[?]!
Every day, every hour counts. The Jews of Brisk cannot and must not wait to rebuild their ruins.
It is therefore the duty of the public activists, and first of all of the kehilla, to call as soon as possible a larger meeting on founding a relief committee for the Jews of Brisk!
The Protest Strike of the Kielce Jews Against the Brisk Events.

Jewish Kielce protested this Monday against the anti-Jewish events in Brisk. All Jewish shops and artisans' workshops were closed, with the exception of one single Jewish [business?][?], the “local German” on Sienkiewicza Street. The conduct of this “Yekke” aroused bitterness among the Jewish population of Kielce.
Who Received the Matura?

The matura examinations at the Jewish girls' and boys' gymnasiums in Kielce have now been completed. At both gymnasiums 18 Jewish pupils, girls and boys, received the matura.
At the girls' gymnasium:
Miss Ch. Eisenberg[?], S. Salomonik[?], M Kaner, Ch. Lewi, Sala Lewis[?], G. Beinhal[?], St. Dżukiewicz[?], Hela Oksenhendler and G. Grinsztajn.
At the boys' gymnasium:
L. Szmulewicz, Ch. Rapaport, L. Werszkowicz[?], L. Wikinski[?], J. Waksman, E. Knobel, K. Goldszleger, M. Eisenberg[?] and Sz. Zuszech[?].
Gambled Away a Diamond Ring and a Bit of Cash...

Passing along Piotrkowska Street this week, the young woman Z. noticed a few fellows playing “hit or miss” [a street guessing game]. The young woman, it seems, has a hot temperament; she felt like having a game, and she liked the game very much. In the course of a few minutes she gambled away a tidy couple of złoty and a diamond ring, hoping[?] for such[?] a windfall. Then the fellows ran off, and Mrs Z. was left standing as if dazed.
The Great Disaster in Działoszyce.

A delegation from Działoszyce, headed by Mr Akiva Duszpieniecki[?], came to our editorial office to give the details of the great natural disaster that took place there last Saturday night.
Our town — says Mr Dżepieniecki[?] — was utterly destroyed within 5 hours. 90 per cent of the Jewish population were left naked and destitute. The water, which came with a terrifying storm, swept away iron bridges, houses[?], multi-storey houses, and caused enormous destruction; up to 10 buildings were carried off entirely by the water, and the winter synagogue was carried off too.
The natural catastrophe unfortunately also caused human victims; they are: Avraham Kleiner, 56 years old, Leah Werszdinska[?], 65 years old. In Werszdinska's[?] house, besides the drowned, were her daughter, son-in-law and 4 grandchildren. At the critical moment they all went up to the attic, leaving in the house the grandchildren Aharon, 5 years old, and Elchanan, 8 years old. When the grandmother went back down from the attic to fetch the remaining grandchildren, it was already too late, and she and the grandchildren drowned. Pesil[?] Nowotna[?], 58 years old, Leah Konduktor, 90 years old, and Reizl Rejtfeler[?], who died of a heart attack in the attic on seeing how her whole property was carried off by the water.
The funerals of the victims took place on Sunday.
The delegation appeals to the Jewish population of Zagłębie to hasten with help for the sufferers; clothing is especially needed.
Campaign for the “Galilee Fund” (Mif'al ha-Galila)

This Sabbath the campaign for the “Mif'al ha-Galila” (to redeem the land of the Galilee in Eretz Israel) is being proclaimed in Kielce. The campaign is being proclaimed by the well-known Zionist activist Mrs Baruch[?] from Eretz Israel. The most active workers of all Zionist groupings are taking part in the campaign, headed by the women of WIZO.

Supplementary enrolment at the Hebrew University in Jerusalem for the year 1937—38.
The Society „Friends of the Hebrew University in Jerusalem“ announces that the University has ordered[?] a supplementary enrolment for candidates from Poland for the academic year 1937/38.
The supplementary enrolment will last until 20 June. Within this period all candidates are obliged to submit all their documents and the tuition fee.
All candidates who are obliged to take an examination in the Hebrew language will sit the examination at the beginning of September of this year. Until they pass the examination, these candidates will be accepted by the University provisionally.
It is in the interest of all candidates to submit their applications as quickly as possible, because the period of the supplementary enrolment will in no case be extended.
The branches of the Society are located in Będzin in the „Sz. Fürstenberg“ Gymnasium, and in Sosnowiec in the Jewish Gymnasium, Sadowa[?] 6.

What's New in Upper Silesia? — Katowice. Roskowska Sentenced to 3 Years in Prison.

[Upper Silesia — Katowice; courts.]
On Tuesday the Court of Appeal in Katowice heard the case against Janina Roskowska, the murderess of her husband Roskowski, a mortgage-registry judge in Sosnowiec.
As is known, the District Court in Katowice had sentenced her to 2 years in prison, suspended.
The prosecutor appealed against the verdict, and last Tuesday the Court of Appeal handed down its judgment, under which Roskowska is sentenced to 3 years in prison, without suspension of the sentence.

“We Do Not Take You for Fools” (On the Margin of Our Disintegration).

[Będzin — city council; article.] Not once and not twice have we had occasion in this place to deal with the question of the splintering of the "Jewish councillors" in the Będzin city council. At every session and consultation, at every debate and conflict, one feels the loss caused by our disintegration[?]; thanks to the rift we lose, at such moments, position after position, because one pulls to the right and another to the left, and no one[?] will after all be so naive as to give in [—][?]; so that at every opportunity one finds a way to do exactly the opposite, and excuses are found in such a case on the spot; just so as not to give in to one another — one gets one's bearings, thank God, quickly. If only the conjuncture were used to our advantage, for the benefit of the community.
The non-Jewish councillors in the city council already know Jewish disintegration[?] excellently and exploit it a great deal. At every opportunity they put forward such proposals and projects as are to bring them benefit if the Jews do not hold together united — which they know excellently in advance. Not a single such position have we lost this way, and more. Every failure — when[?] we [—] the damage the community suffers thanks to our splintering-obstinacy, which leads to nothing but rift and ruin.
A non-Jewish councillor, no great lover of Israel, once[?] said to the writer of these lines: Say[?] what you will, but it is after all impossible for us to understand you. For example — he argues — it is known all over the world that you go into fire for one another; among us Christians one does not see[?] such unity; thanks to your loyalty you have existed in exile for two thousand years now, still[?] the same Jewish people, as if you had your own land and your own state. And yet, as soon as one works with you in the public sphere, it is by no means possible to understand you; one then[?] has to change one's opinion of you, and at such a moment, at such a time, you become for us a sphinx, a riddle that cannot be answered.
Here I am, one who sits[?] together with your citizens in the city council and watches closely, and I have a nature to investigate and follow every movement, every trait of yours — I must tell you the truth, that I do not understand you, I by no means comprehend you. In any case, as I see it, no unity reigns among you, and we gain a lot by it. I would after all not [—] that this is done by you for our good, since it brings you so much[?] damage. I am, after all, not so naive, and I take no one for a fool; therefore there must be some hidden essence[?] in it, secrets[?] — is it then any wonder that we cannot have any trust in you, when you are even more as if veiled and concealed? Can we then treat you as equals with equals, when you do not let yourselves be known, you do not let yourselves be explored?
What could we answer him, when it simply did not sink into his mind[?] that this should be a genuine rift; as we know it, what, what — he went on, helping himself with his convinced[?] opinion — only we do not take you for fools, that you would do yourselves harm so that some good should come of it to us. No, that — you see — we will no longer believe from you!
And you, dear brothers, our city fathers, what do you think[?] of these arguments?
R. Les.
Is the Campaign for the Jewish Hospital Under Way?

Oh, a good few months ago — perhaps it is already nearly a year — when it dawned on people in Sosnowiec that philanthropy was not being pursued very vigorously, and since they began to fear that everything might fall asleep all at once, they wanted first of all to rescue the great and useful institution called the Jewish Hospital.
And the truth must be told: the matter was not approached merely — let us say — to discharge an obligation, to support some little society and be done with it. No, it was done somewhat more finely, more grandly, in a most [?] modern manner. In short, there was a commotion in the Jewish [—]; a great campaign for the Jewish Hospital was undertaken; a special committee was elected for the purpose, an executive, with great fanfare and with the whole noise-making apparatus [?]; but after all that shouting, rattling the collection boxes and agitating for the long-desired campaign, it suddenly went quiet. Apparently it fell asleep; neither [?] we nor the public — so we believe — know what became of it all. Is the campaign still under way, or has it been completely finished?
Be that as it may — whether it is under way or some kind of slumber has set in — why is the public not roused to fulfil its duty to the hospital and finally complete the campaign? For a campaign must have a deadline [?] and must, after all, come to an end. And if, who knows, it has long been finished and we are troubling ourselves with this question in vain and for nothing, then surely, most surely, one should say so; surely, most surely, one should render an account, so that the public knows what it has achieved for this useful people's institution.
If money and a collection [?] are demanded, one must surely say "well done" to the donors and at the same time tell them what has been accomplished with the funds collected. Unless — what? People did not want to support the campaign? They wanted a fiasco [?]? Jewish Sosnowiec did not want to understand its tasks at a time when it was called upon to fulfil an elementary duty? — then this must be said to it plainly [?] and it must be given to understand: if the best-situated Jewish residents do not want to hear the bitter cry of the poor sick man who must be rescued, one may without any doubt reproach them [printed "him"].
On the other hand, such a campaign must on no account be left hanging in the air, with no one knowing what became of it and whether anything came of it at all.
Dr. Papuri [?].
Sosnowiec Is Building Itself Up

[Sosnowiec — municipality and sanitation.] And what about conveniences?
Sosnowiec is at a stage of development. They keep modernizing the town, taking pains[?] to enlarge and beautify it, paying attention to everything that has to do with aesthetics and splendour. The city fathers keep considering how the town may have a decent appearance, so that it should not make a "fatal" impression when compared with the city of Katowice, which lies only[?] a few kilometres away.
Certainly orderliness[?] is a very fine virtue and benefits the inhabitants, but when one is already speaking of the welfare of the citizens, one must not forget that it is still not enough that a new street is built wide and a new house is already put up; on the other hand too little attention is paid to the sanitary condition being satisfactory. The streets are covered with dust to the point of being unbearable; in the respectable commercial streets the smell[?] is "fatal", so that one could faint[?] and throw up. Why does one not see to remedying such defects [printed "refects"] radically? Aesthetics — very nice; modernism — quite respectable; but the most important thing of all is surely to be able to walk in the streets in a normal[?] way, in hygienic conditions. That plays the first[?] and most important roles for human health, and it is this that must be dealt with first and foremost. True, outward appearance counts[?] for a great deal, but no less important is the convenience of human life, which our city fathers must take care of.
Now they have made us a "convenience" as of the 1st of this month: the gates [of the courtyards] are open until 11 o'clock. You understand — two months a year we have the gates open until 11 o'clock, but ten whole months only until 10. So in the greatest heat and on the longest days, as in the past month of May, the public had to run home before 10 if it wanted to have the gate open. Is that really such a great "convenience"? Why can [the gates] in neighbouring Będzin be open until 11 in May, while here, where the traffic is livelier, they have to be locked no later than ten o'clock?
The councillors (ratmani) should raise the question in the city council and decide once and for all that the gates are to be open until 11 o'clock the whole year round. After all, one cannot be so tied down the whole year, when the traffic in the street is quite large enough.
The same applies to the hygiene and the pavements in the streets: care must be taken that one can walk through the streets, and that they too be in a sanitary condition. Great attention must be paid to this, especially in the important[?] summer months, when it is so hard to breathe in the Zagłębie district[?].
Selekt.
On the Fourth Floor (Reportage)

[Będzin — reportage; daily life.] Y. Janasowicz
(Reportage).
Dirty, winding stairs lead up to the fourth floor. As one walks on them, it is somehow as if they were annoyed[?], as if they were angry that nobody leaves them in peace.
The stairs that lead up to the fourth floor and down from the fourth floor are constantly in motion — a walking, a running[?] — they groan, the stairs, and from anger they turn quite black.
The walls beside the stairs are, self-evidently, scratched and scribbled on; they have a faint look, and on top of that they are densely[?] covered with inscriptions, with slogans, with whole speeches, in which find expression the [—] instincts[?], the whole difference of opinions of the writers — for whom writing on the walls is at the same time a discharge of energy and also something like a school matter. The wall, that is, is a kind of school blackboard on which one learns[?] to write, for from the inscriptions one sees clearly that the writers are still at the stage of learning.
On the fourth floor it hums and roars with children's shouting, [—] and crying[?]. They, the children, with their pale faces, their rickety little legs, their trachoma[?] eyes — they want to know of nothing; everywhere is their world, everywhere they make it known that they exist.
On the fourth floor the room is not bounded by the door that leads into the corridor. On the contrary, the corridor is a continuation of the narrow room. Why torment oneself in the stuffy room, crammed with all sorts of broken odds and ends[?], when there is a wide corridor here, eh? Those who have many rooms have the choice of letting the corridor be empty, free, tidy; but those who live in narrow little rooms on the fourth floor cannot allow themselves such a luxury.
Of course it is not like this everywhere — not on every fourth floor, that is. There are places where the neighbours do not like to meddle in each other's affairs; the doors are locked, and from the polished[?] doors shine the little brass plates showing that So-and-so son of So-and-so lives here, and if you have some business with him, be so kind as to knock, and if you are asked in — go in. The corridor serves only for passing through, and not for anything else.
Take, for example, a well-known house on Kołłątaja Street: when you sometimes go up to the fourth floor there, you fall into a thick, damp fog of steam, so that you do not know where to go. What has happened? Nothing — they are doing the laundry. And where does one do the laundry? In the corridor, of course; where else should one wash?
It often happens that you come into the corridor of the fourth floor and are assailed by a biting smoke that eats at your eyes and brings forth tears. It is not, God forbid, from any fire — it is the ordinary smoke of a kitchen stove that precisely in summertime refuses to burn; and where should the smoke go, if not into the free, empty corridor?
In summertime, when the great heat sets in, the „private domain“ of the fourth floor is transferred to the „public domain“. It sometimes happens that a person who is not used to it comes there — and he is simply startled[?] and dumbfounded; he does not know where to go. And walking along the corridor of the fourth floor in summertime is something you must know how to do. First, you must know how to walk with your eyes shut, because what with the smoke and the steam you see nothing anyway; and then you must know how to walk so as not, God forbid, to trample the little ones rolling about underfoot.
One really has to be an artist to push one's way through such a crush without stepping on a child's little hand or foot; and if you are not such an artist, better not go, because you will imagine that you are walking by all the rules and regulations[?], and suddenly a scream will be heard, a squeal, „himl shtalt zikh“[?]! You will want to sink into the ground from fright, because you have [—] stepped on a child's little hand. Where does a child come from here? Don't ask — the gang of little ones on the fourth floor: wherever you don't look[?] for them, there they are.
And now — careful! That is not all. In the darkness of the steam you must also take care not to knock over a tub of water or a pot of rainwater that stands waiting to be used for the laundry. You can also overturn a rolling board with rolled-out[?] meat[?], or even step with your foot into a noodle board on which lies flour waiting to be kneaded into dough — and then your[?] life is not safe: the housewives may come running and give you a real dressing-down[?]. No arguments and counter-arguments help. Have you got eyes, or haven't you got eyes? And in general, why does one crawl in here, to [?] the black year [= to the devil]? — and no excuses help here, for with agitated women it is better not to conduct a discussion.
Thus, for example, an acquaintance of mine told me the following story.
He had come to Będzin from another big city — let us say from Warsaw. Having come, he learned here in Będzin that on Kołłątaja Street, of all places, there lived an aunt of his whom he had not seen for a long time — for a good many years. So he went to Kołłątaja Street, and there he asked and asked: his aunt lived on the fourth floor.
So he went up to the fourth floor, and as soon as he entered the corridor he stopped, because he did not know where to go. Smoke, steam. But what — would he stand there and gape? He began to feel his way, and, groping like that, he knocked over something that fell with a loud bang. A Jewish woman came running out, and it turned out that he had knocked down a small rolling board with meat[?]. Well, what went on there! The [—] woman nearly wanted to swallow him alive, and since my acquaintance was not used to such things, he answered something — probably a bit too sharply — and before he knew what was what, the woman landed[?] him a slap that simply rang out.
So what?
It turned out later that the woman who had landed[?] him the slap was none other than his aunt, whom he had come to visit.
A Craftsman Must Also Be Able to Read and Write!

On the importance of short-term preparatory courses.
As is well known, all those who sit for the qualification examination in order to obtain a craftsman's card [karta rzemieślnicza], or for the journeyman's examination in order to obtain the journeyman's diploma, are required — besides professional knowledge — to have a certain measure of general education as well.
Even though both at the qualification examinations and at the eased journeyman's examinations only elementary knowledge is required — for instance, writing and reading Polish, or writing out a bill or a simple letter [?] in one's own hand — there is nonetheless a considerable percentage who do not possess even this elementary knowledge and fail the examination. These candidates are given a period of 6 months to prepare for a second examination. In such cases, apart from the fact that those concerned lose time, they must also, according to the regulations, pay for a second examination. The candidates who failed have complaints; it somehow seems to them that special difficulties are being put in their way, and they do not want to understand that whoever engages in a craft must also possess certain elementary knowledge, and that the time is long gone when a craftsman had to know only his trade and a little general education was a "superfluous, unnecessary" thing.
But even 40—50 years ago, when attending a primary school was not compulsory, when the existing laws on crafts did not provide for any minimum of [school?] education for those engaged in a craft, there were already craftsmen who understood that a craft also requires a little general knowledge, and thanks to that such craftsmen or workshop workers got on better and were not dependent, for every little thing, on turning to a private or office scribe, etc.
To our regret we must state that nowadays, in a time of struggle against illiteracy, in a time when the demands — both of the law and of society — are much stricter with regard to crafts, there is nonetheless among Jews a considerable percentage of those engaged in crafts who do not possess the elementary knowledge of general education, which is so necessary, especially now, when everything is "regulated" and hemmed in by constantly growing demands. From this it is clear that even if the law did not require craftsmen to possess such knowledge, it would anyway be a demand of the new times, of the new conditions created in the last few decades, to which every craftsman must adapt if he does not want to fall behind and be pushed into an economic back alley [?].
All the more must those reflect on this who, in accordance with the relief [?] circular No. 28 on eased journeyman's examinations (even when they learned the trade under non-certified masters, did no [—] and attended no school), will be able to seek admission [?] to the eased journeyman's examination, if they submit their application to the Chamber of Crafts [Izba Rzemieślnicza] by 30 June of this year.
This relief concerns tens of thousands of workshop workers and young craftsmen.
Although from the time of submitting an application for admission to the eased journeyman's examination until presenting oneself for that examination takes approximately 4 to 6 months, all those concerned must already think about learning, during that time, to write and read Polish, to do arithmetic, and to be able to answer all the other questions put at the examinations.
The United Committee for the Affairs of Jewish Crafts has in good time sent to all committees and craftsmen's organizations a brochure of the "ORT" society [?] on organizing short-term preparatory courses; according to the programme of these courses, anyone can within 3 months learn and acquire all the necessary knowledge of what is required at the examinations.
These short-term courses involve no great expense and can be organized with the help of the local teachers of a "powszechna" [public primary] or private school. Taking such a course will, first, remove the fear of failing the examination, and second, it will also achieve that all those engaged in crafts will possess general knowledge, which is needed nowadays in order to hold on in the trade and rise to a higher level.
There is therefore a duty incumbent upon the entire organized Jewish community, upon the Jewish intelligentsia and upon ordinary public activists to take up this important matter and to enable all those concerned to obtain the minimum of education that everyone must possess. If we do this, we ourselves will have passed the examination, and to a certain extent we will ease the lot of those engaged in productive work.
Chanan Hofman.
Bad and Good Pupils

[Essay — education; pupils and schools.]
Soon, soon school will be over, and father and mother have troubles and headaches: what to start doing with the children who are now finishing their studies. How can one find them some possibility of having the most necessary and most urgent things in their lives. The enormous [?] worry is very great today, and unfortunately there is for the time being no cure for this plague...
But many parents — and this is what we want to talk about today — poor things, rack their brains over how the children can get a better report card. The children do not want to learn, or they simply do not have a good enough head to grasp what the teacher teaches them, so the parents spend a fortune. They hire various tutors for them, so that the children should not, God forbid, have to repeat the year.
It is therefore worthwhile [?] to dwell on the question: do bad pupils have less success in life than good pupils?
Mister Stoops [?], the [presiding?] [?] director of the London "Times", once spoke about this at a press meeting of the Leipzig Fair. He told us that, for example, the great mathematician Giusan [?] was the worst pupil in his school. Another mathematician, Agukh [?], could not read or write at all until the age of 28.
The great natural scientist Lige [?] only began to study at twenty, and the famous chemist Liebig failed in almost every class. His father took him out of school and apprenticed him to an apothecary, who, however, also soon threw him out, because "he was good for nothing"... The same was true of the natural scientist and philosopher Darwin, who also had to repeat almost every class of his school.
Pasteur, the famous medical researcher, did not finish gymnasium, because he did not want to study, and the famous physicians Koch and Billroth were the weakest pupils in their school. With toil and trouble they got their matriculation.
Stephenson, the inventor of the locomotive, did not go to any school, because he did not understand what the teacher was saying, and the great physicist Robert Mayer was the worst pupil in his school and indeed failed physics twice; nevertheless he later became the greatest genius in physics...
Edison, the greatest inventor of all time, did not go through any schooling at all. In the first grade the teacher threw him out, because "nothing will come of him anyway"...
Napoleon was a bad pupil in all his schools, and even at the military war-school the officers, his teachers, said: "he will never become a decent soldier"...
Even Bismarck, Metternich and other great politicians and world-changers were very bad pupils, and failed more than once in their schools and had to repeat classes.
Among the great writers there are quite a large number of the best names who failed in their schools because they "knew nothing". We will mention only a few well-known names among them, who could not get into the universities or could not finish their schools, because "they were not capable of it"...
Thomas Mann, Heinrich Kleist, Jonathan Swift, Gottfried Keller, Otto Julius Bierbaum, Oliver Goldsmith, Gerhart Hauptmann and more names of very great poets and thinkers who were bad pupils.
We do not, of course, mean to say by this that bad pupils grow up to be great geniuses. But we only want to show that if a child fails at school and has to repeat the year, there is still no reason whatsoever to despair; it is not yet the worst thing, and it proves nothing yet that this pupil no longer has any hope of great success in his life in the field in which he has resolved to achieve something.
Z. Haber, Vienna.
Our Panorama.

(A fire is burning. — Bachelors past "thirty" do not want to marry. — Hidden fires. — Back from Ger mourning and with heads covered. — Fire from both banks of the Jordan. — Questions and answers.)
A fire is burning!
— Where is it burning? Everywhere it burns, the whole world is in a [?] fire; the only difference is that this fire is hidden from the human eye, and only a chosen few, the elect, who have the merit of enjoying the hidden light, the "concealed light" [can see it]. Thus, for instance, not one of the "ordinary" Amshinov hasidim in Będzin saw that a fire was burning in the shtibl; only a single one saw it, who has a very [?] hot gaze and a mighty [?] sense, and this seer, on Shabbat before the Torah reading, banged on the table and let out a cry:
— "Jews, there's a fire!"
— Where is it burning? Gevalt! all the worshippers threw off their tallitot and started running to the door.
— Where are you running? the "seer" laughed at his hasidim — right here in the shtibl, around us, the fire is burning! Don't you see that among us there are bachelors who are already past thirty and still haven't married?..
The congregation, hearing that the fire "is to be found among the thirty-year-old unmarried bachelors", breathed more freely and had a "Mi sheberakh" said for the far-seer of the Amshinov shtibl, who had perceived the great danger arising from the bachelors' not wanting to marry...
We cannot yet assess the significance of this discovery, nor whether the bachelors will change their "standpoint", but be that as it may, one thing must be admitted: in the Amshinov "shtibl" there is a hasid with a hot gaze, and he has perceived that
— a fire is burning...
Among the "hidden fires" are also the Ger hasidim in Będzin, who spent this past Shavuot in Ger.
What such a journey costs, and what trials one has to endure nowadays when travelling to Ger — after all, even the session of the Będzin kehilla council got nervous a few years ago over the trip to Ger — and suddenly such a slap in the face...
Not in the face, but across the whole face, so to speak: hasidim of our own circle, the kind who were always drawn close in Ger — one at the "tish", another with a zemer, a third with an aliyah and an honour — and now pushed back [?]! And why not? They do earn the honour "in the middle of the night"; they are, after all — one may say — busier with local politics than with their own affairs, and here suddenly, without a word either way — they were given a "Rückzug" [retreat]...
And what is more: had the displeasure fallen only on individuals, one could still bear it — so what, I say, it can happen; but to take the whole "Będzin colony" and keep it at a distance on both days of Shavuot and not honour it with:
cantor,
zemer,
"tish",
aliyah —
such a thing has not happened since its founding until now. Evil tongues interpret this to mean that the "Rückzug" hints that they should set right what they have not managed to settle to this very day: not only has the rabbinate affair not moved forward, but they have even allowed the business to move backwards...
And the punishment was accepted with love; they swallowed the bitter pill and kept silent, but in their hearts burns "a fire", a "hidden fire", so that, God forbid, none of their enemies should find out about it...
In the synagogue in Old Sosnowiec (Stary Sosnowiec) there is a worshipper in whom a "hidden fire" is also smouldering. As is well known, there is no lack of "fire" in that synagogue; especially every Shabbat things happen there on the tables and on the benches; but that fire is not hidden — even babes in their cradles already know that in Spain, and also in the Old Sosnowiec synagogue, a civil war is going on, one citizen fighting the other over power; the only difference is that in Spain they fight over the crown, and on Wiejska [?] Street — over the gabbai posts...
But that a foreign "fire" should also be found in that synagogue — of this surely none of the worshippers knew.
And the "fire" was revealed when a delegate of the local "Keren Kayemet" committee went up onto the bimah and began to speak about the redemption of the Land.
At that moment there suddenly appeared the "fire from both banks of the Jordan", which went for the speaker for his impudence in speaking about the redemption of the Land not according to the programme of "Malkhut Shri" [?]...
At first the speaker took a bit of a fright, but soon he came to himself, because the "fire from both banks of the Jordan" quickly cooled off, for fear that one might in truth "not grow cold"...
It was also "hot" this past Shabbat in the "shtibl" of the Aleksander hasidim here in Będzin.
As in all the "shtiblekh", in this "shtibl" too there was talk about Shabbat observance. There will probably be some plain obstinate people who will ask:
— In the Aleksander "shtibl" one needs to talk about Shabbat observance? Can it be?
The answer is — Brisk (Brześć).
Then the question becomes even bigger: "What has the Sabbatical year to do with Mount Sinai?" What connection does Shabbat observance have with the events in Brisk?
To the second question the committee of the Shomrei Shabbat society answers that since the events happened because of the sins of the people, one must after all do repentance, and hasidim and men of deeds cannot be an exception.
But we mention this only in passing; the main thing we are after is this: when in the said "shtibl" they began to talk about "sins", a great "heat" arose... It came from the question-askers... who asked many questions at the expense of our rabbinate, which consists of hundred-percent democrats who say "it is permitted to you" to a shochet who is caught even at theft...
And since the member of the rabbinate who was present refused to give answers to the questions, the temperature indeed rose and it became very "stuffy" [duszno]...
Ben Amotz.
The Jewish Public Has the Floor! (In Connection with the Closing of the Będzin Talmud Torah).

It is incomprehensible and unbelievable; it is sad, yet nonetheless an accomplished fact — a fact that shakes the soul, a fact that Jewish society must brand as a shameless[?] act on the part of our kehilla administrators. Too glaring, too provocative is what has happened, and, to the great shame of Jewish Będzin[?], it cries out by itself: "Has such an outrage been done in Israel?!"
Listen and be amazed: at the board meeting of the Talmud Torah (T.T.) held 4 weeks ago, when I agreed[?] to the board's request to keep my mandate as president for another month, one of my main conditions was that within that time the 1000 zł. subsidy for 1936 be paid out, which the kehilla was supposed to have legally secured[?] for the T.T. (the balance left: 1,700), and the Agudah kehilla representatives (at the same time members of the T.T. board) solemnly promised me this. To my constant interventions with the president of the kehilla board I received promises from day to day that the 1000 zł. would be paid out; moreover, when I proposed to the kehilla president that I would personally intervene with the supervisory authority to permit payment of the sum, the esteemed president declared that it was not necessary, explaining that all the legal safeguards were in perfect order and that the payment was a matter of a day or two. When the T.T.'s material situation worsened and I again categorically began to demand payment of the subsidy, the soap bubble then burst, and — "neither bears nor forest" — the T.T. cannot be paid the subsidy, because there is no [—] at all for the T.T. How so? Quite simply: the kehilla submitted to the supervisory authority a list of all the town (even out-of-town) institutions and obtained permission to pay them a few thousand zł. out of the unrealized subsidies of 1936, and no[?] small sum; — and precisely[?] the T.T. they simply "forgot".
Do you hear? They forgot the T.T., where 400 children study. All the societies and little associations, even the lowest-ranking party stalls, they remembered — only the institution that holds the place of honour throughout the Jewish diaspora, the institution that is found and must be found wherever a Jewish community exists, and of which the rabbinate declared at the last T.T. meeting that a town without a Talmud Torah ought to be destroyed — that very institution they forgot. They forgot to subsidize an institution whose budget item even the gentiles (the supervisory authority), who year after year strike out the items of all other institutions, leave untouched, appreciating the necessity and importance of the institution; and here come kehilla representatives — and not just anybody, but the very Agudah kehilla board with the presidents at its head — and "forget" to secure the subsidy for the T.T.
This fact cries out to heaven and is unforgivable, and its consequence is that the T.T. is closed. By your sorry deeds you have confirmed my long-expressed opinion about you, that the T.T. is for you, as the saying goes, "a bone in the throat" — which must not die but by no means live, for fear of competition; and the Torah, with which you trumpet at every holy war, is for you merely a weapon, "a spade to dig with". And therefore, when I decided to close the T.T., it was, first, from a purely material standpoint, because you dealt the T.T. the final death blow by striking out the subsidy; and second, as an expression of protest before the Jewish public against you, for you and only you have hammered shut[?] the doors of the Będzin T.T. And let Jewish Będzin know that the responsibility for the 400 poor, forlorn children who roam abandoned on the pavement because the T.T. doors are closed, and who are exposed to growing up as illiterates, street urchins and morally corrupted, and at the same time the responsibility for the 12 hunger-tormented families of the T.T. staff — you bear it upon yourselves.
Let the Jewish public judge you.
Sz. Fürstenberg.
A Little Feuilleton. A Bit Too Early...

[Feuilleton — humour; early heat and summer life.] A Little Feuilleton.
A Bit Too Early...
Last week our "faithful reader" came into the editorial office, exhausted[?]. He wiped the sweat from his brow; this time he had no complaints for the editor, but just talked to himself:
— Oh, bitter[?], it's nasty, it has turned hot[?], the heat is unbearable — who ever heard of such May[?] heat!
— What's wrong with you[?], my faithful reader? On the contrary, when it's warm[?], Jews earn money, women snatch up goods for "see-through" dresses, for pyjamas, the seamstresses are [?] [—] [rest of line undeciphered]... Now it is the season for cold things, such as: ice creams [lody], [—][?] water and other "chłodniki" [cold soups], and above all — this year the wives will leave a month earlier for "[unclear Polish phrase]"[?].
— Well, well... that's just what it's about[?], that's exactly what I mean! That's why it really is nasty, just nasty — the "faithful reader" replied — my summer-resort (letnisko) troubles always began a month later, and this year already now, in May, I could find no rest. This year I already hear in May the familiar little tune[?]:
— Henek, a [—][?]! Henek, a [—][?]! Henek, a [—][?]! Henek, [—][?]! Henek, [—][?]! [calls to the waiter Henek; the Polish food/drink names are undeciphered.] This year people started "Henek-ing" a month earlier. That's why I tell you it's nasty, it's very bitter for me, poor me; for the Jews who deal with women[?] it is indeed an advantage, but for me it's a misfortune, a great misfortune.
— Who, I ask you, needed the May heat, [—][?]
We calmed our "faithful reader":
— Don't take it to heart, Reb Mendl, rest assured that in June [czerwiec], when people have to go to the summer resort (letnisko), they'll swell up from the cold.
— If only, sweet Father! — the man replied[?] with a sigh — and went off dejected.
Ab—nek.

Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Shelach)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Shelach
—o—
a) "And Moses called Hoshea the son of Nun Joshua" (Num. 13:16)
1.
"And when Moses saw his humility, Moses called Hoshea son of Nun — Joshua." Targum Yonatan.
Seeing Hoshea's humility, Moses added a "Yod" to his name, for the "Yod" in Hebrew indicates "I" (a final Yod means "me": "shelaḥan-i"[?] — meaning "me", etc.[?]); and a leader must have in himself a bit of "I", a bit of independence; otherwise he constantly falls [—] under alien, harmful influences. Yalkut Yehuda.
2.
He said: "May the Lord[?] save you from the counsel of the spies." Sotah 34b.
As the verse goes on to tell, "And all the congregation said to stone them with stones" — they were simply threatened with death. To be stoned — and yet Moses did not pray about that for Caleb and Joshua; never mind, Jewish stones are not so dangerous... What he prayed for them was "from the counsel of the spies" — from petty Jewish intrigues; for that one really must pray that the Holy One, blessed be He, guard and save. R. Yonatan Eybeschütz.
b) "Whether there be wood therein" (ibid., 20)
"Whether there be trees therein" — whether they are not such vandals[?] who in battle would uproot trees; those are the most dangerous people. Alshich.
c) "And surely it floweth with milk and honey" (ibid., 27)
That is surely only praise —
But the spies used it as something bad about the Land of Israel, for the main tactic of wars of old was to encircle a city, besiege it, starve it out, and so force it to surrender.
But [?] if it is a land of milk and honey, it will surely be hard to starve it out and take it. Ketav Sofer.
d) "And they brought up an evil report of the land" (ibid., 32)
At first the spies told the truth about the Land of Israel. But seeing that Caleb opposed them, there awoke in them, as is the way of things, the desire to stand against the opponent, and this very[?] desire to defeat the opponent already brought them to tell lies and to speak lies about the Land of Israel. That is what the human lust to defeat the opponent can lead to... Be'er Mayim Ḥayyim.
e) "The Lord is slow to anger" (14:18)
When Moses asks God to forgive the spies and the people's revolt against the Land of Israel, he calls to God and mentions all His attributes[?]; but one thing, which he always mentioned on such occasions, he did not mention here: the merit of the forefathers.
For the forefathers had loved the Land of Israel, and God gave them the land as a gift, and now the Jews were disgusted with this very gift. Therefore Moses did not want to mention the merit of the forefathers now... Leket Amarim.
f) "I have pardoned according to thy word; but as truly as I live" (ibid., 20—21)
Thus God answered Moses:
"I have pardoned according to thy word" — I forgive the Jews, for I am in no hurry at all to take revenge, since "as I live" — I live forever, and revenge will never escape Me; I always have time... Ha-Ketav ve-ha-Kabbalah.
g) "One statute shall be both for you and for the stranger" (15:15)
After God told the Jews that only after forty years of wandering in the desert, after forty years of roaming, would they enter the Land of Israel, [came] the proclamation "One statute shall be for you and for the stranger" — that the minorities will have the same rights as the conquerors of the land; for such is already the way of the world: the more a people is tormented before it conquers its land — the more it later oppresses the minorities of the land... Imrei Ḥen.
h) The man gathering sticks on the Sabbath (ibid., 32)
There is an opinion that the gatherer "intended it for the sake of Heaven", that by his transgression he meant only a heavenly matter; yet he was condemned, because we, simple flesh and blood, do not know the criterion of "for the sake of Heaven"; every criminal can say that he means it for the sake of Heaven, and we are called to judge not by intention, but by what our eyes see... Imrei Yirmiyahu.
i) "And that ye go not about after your own heart" (ibid., 39)
If someone has a good heart, may he too not "follow his heart"? Why is it not said "and go not about after your evil hearts"?
To this Reb Mendele of Kotzk [Kock] said that even good one may not do out of the heart's caprice; even good must be done not merely because the heart is drawn to it, but after long study and inner toil; good that is done light-mindedly is no true good...
