The Living Corpse

[Literature — serial novel ("The Living Corpse"), instalment 11.]
A. Zaglembier [pen name].
(A most thrilling novel of Jewish life in Zagłębie before and after the World War). 11)
Summary of the beginning of the novel.
On a winter night before the World War, when two Cossacks were to transfer the dangerous bandit "Szmulek Łapka" into the Piotrków prison, they were suddenly attacked on the way to the Będzin station by two disguised "strażniks" (guards) — Łapka's helpers. The Cossacks were found the next morning lying bound with gagged mouths, and Szmulek "Łapka", freed, fled to the Gzichów road and hid somewhere.
That same evening, and almost at the same hour, the universally respected, solid collector (inkasent) Josl Wertheim — a father of three children — suddenly disappeared. His wife Sarah'tshe runs about the town terribly desperate, searching for him in every possible hiding place in all of Zagłębie. But Josl Wertheim has vanished like a stone in water..
On the fifth day pockmarked Matek reports to police inspector Karecki and tells him that on that day he saw Wertheim walking on the Gzichów road together with the Christian woman Magda Komarska — a young, pretty gentile girl whom Matek had been courting.
Magda is arrested at once. During the interrogation she declares that on the very day Wertheim disappeared they had quarrelled, because Wertheim wanted to give her money to go to Katowice for an operation so that their illegitimate child would not be born. Karecki then goes to Wertheim's wife Sarah'tshe and tells her about her husband's love affair with Magda, but Sarah'tshe does not believe it and declares that her husband had no money on him. But when she goes to the cupboard, she finds that the several hundred roubles of savings are gone, and she gives up hope for her vanished husband.
Now read on.
People had already gradually begun to forget the tragic affair; there was no longer so much talk about Josl's disappearance. Only police inspector Karecki went on busying himself with the investigation, and the trial of Magda Komarska was prepared, as the accused in the robbery and murder of Josl, because all the evidence available so far led to her alone. Although Magda, without stopping, with bitter tears, denied it "by stone and bone", she kept repeating the one thing: she had indeed met Josl on that day, but she had run away from him after a quarrel and did not know what had happened to him...
But then something extraordinary suddenly happened, which confirmed the accusation against Magda even more...
It happened some weeks later, on a very hot Sabbath day.
As always, today too the Cossacks of the Będzin regiment went in the afternoon "under the hill" to bathe in the deepest spots, showing off various swimming tricks.
One of the best Cossack swimmers dived down under the water at the deepest spot, at the so-called "Koński Dół", wanting to reach down to the ground[?]. As proof that he had reached the bottom, he had to bring up from under the water a handful of sand or clay. This time too the Cossack dived into the water head down, reached the "bottom" and grabbed something in his hand. But when he came back up, head first[?], and showed what he had brought up from under the water, everyone stood trembling with fear and astonishment, because in his hand the Cossack was holding a whole tuft of hair from a human head...
"Gospodi pomiluy!" [Lord, have mercy] several Cossacks cried out at once in dreadful[?] fear.
"There must be a drowned man lying down there!.."
The swimmer flung the tuft of hair away from himself in fright and said:
"Yes, yes, I really felt something, as if I had touched something round.."
"A man's head!"
"Surely a drowned man!.."
"Kovirev[?]! Are you afraid? I'm not! Who's going down under the water with me? We have to get the drowned man out!"
"Me!"
"Me too!"
"And me!"
And so six Cossacks at once dived down at that spot. But a minute later they came back up empty-handed[?], boasting:
"I held a foot!"
"I a hand!"
"And I the head!"
"But you can't move him from the spot!.."
"Not true! I did give him a tug from the spot, but I ran out of breath!"
"Me too!"
"That's why[?] it's impossible!"
"We need a rope! A long rope!"
"Somebody should go into town!"
And with lightning speed the news spread through the town and the surroundings that a drowned man had been found.
Police inspector Karecki soon came down[?] to the scene with several strażniks. The firemen came too, and after them a crowd[?] of youngsters[?] and plain curious people, who wanted to see with their own eyes. But no outsiders were let near the spot itself.
The news about the drowned man also reached the black-haired[?] Sarah'tshe. Instinctively she gave a sort of [—] shudder, as if it had a very close connection with her... But she soon stopped thinking about it. Did she lack other troubles?.. After Josl's disappearance she had been left as if on the wind. Especially since Josl had also taken the saved-up cash... And what does one take up?.. How does one earn a living for oneself and for the growing children?..
Meanwhile a long, thick rope was brought to the place of the strange discovery — to the river. The good swimmer, the Cossack Kovirev[?], made a kind of loop at one end of the rope, went down under the water again with it and laid the loop around the drowned man's body; the other end of the rope was held by those standing on the bank. And when Kovirev came up again and reported that he had done it well, they began pulling the rope until they had dragged him out together with the heavy burden.
Only now a terrible cry burst at once from many mouths:
"A man!.."
"He must have been soaking in the water a long time!"
"Don't you see, he's already rotting!"
"The fish must have eaten up his face!"
"Serves him right! He shouldn't have gone bathing in 'Koński Dół'.."
"He surely couldn't swim either!"
"What nonsense you're talking! A man doesn't go bathing in a frock coat!.."
"And maybe he was drunk and fell into the water!"
"Make way!"
This last order was given by Karecki when the drowned man was laid on the grass. He looked like one soaked mass; the clothing was decent, and he was also wearing whole shoes. But his face could not be recognised: it was both thoroughly rotted and as if bitten up, by the fish indeed...
When Karecki examines his clothes, he says:
"This man was surely thrown into the water!"
"He shouldn't have let himself be!" a Cossack calls out mockingly.
"But he was surely murdered first.."
"What? You think so?!"
"I am deeply convinced of it," says Karecki firmly and triumphantly to the commissioner and the other police officials.
"You have already worked that out, two minutes after the drowned man was dragged out of the water? How?"
"Quite simple," answers Karecki. "Take a look at the corpse's[?] pockets — you see how full they are?.."
"With water!.." several answer with ironic laughter.
"But with sand too!.." Karecki calls out seriously. "The murderer surely did it on purpose, so that the burden would be as heavy as possible and would surely sink to the bottom.."
(To be continued).
A Victim of the Heat... (Weekly Chatter).

I must, dear Jews, blab to you a true story that happened these days (read: these nights) with my wife.
When the "nadzwyczajne" [?] (Polish: extraordinary) tormenting, oppressive [?] heat waves set in, she began to feel "dushen" (from Polish dusić — to stifle), and in the middle of the night I got from her a "dushikh" [?].
— "Hartsneshpan" [?] mine, "khver udishes" [?] (apparently garbled Polish: "I'll suffocate")! she says [?] to me anxiously.
I understood that she meant "samitsushe" [?], so I gave her a speech:
— "Kileshi" [?] my crown, you feel stuffy ("dushne", Polish duszno)? And which Jew doesn't feel "stuffy" nowadays? So many Jews lack "pavye-tshe" [?] (Polish powietrze — air); [—] would you [?], "kileshi" my crown, [—] [?]?
And secondly, what kind of air does a Jew have today on the rubbish dump ("smietniske", Polish śmietnisko), when the "pregurotnik" [?] comes there — what kind of clean air can there be, [?] so to speak?
My sermon had an effect on her.
And when I finished my "speech", she clapped her hands:
— Shimshe, [?]!... Shimshe, almost [?]!...
I got truly frightened, went to the window, was about to open it, but I became so flustered [?] that I could not find the latch. Suddenly she lets out a shriek:
— Shimshele, what are you hesitating for [?] — knock out a pane! So I did.
Tr-a-kh, tr-a-kh — and the pane was smashed to bits.
Then [?] my wife caught her breath and came to herself, drew in "świeże" (Polish: fresh) air — she remained, praised be the Lord, alive.
* * *

What's New in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 25 Sivan 5697 — piątek 4 czerwca 937 [Friday, 4 June 1937].)
Będzin
Relief Committee for the Victims in Brisk
Under the chairmanship of Dr. Weinzieher, a meeting of the relief committee for the victims in Brisk [Brześć nad Bugiem] took place on Monday evening in the premises of the Gemilut Hesed (interest-free loan) fund.
At the meeting a number of questions concerning the technical work of the committee were dealt with.
After a lengthy discussion it was decided to invite a large number of public figures from all strata of the Jewish population to the meeting which will take place this coming Saturday night (motzei Shabbat) in the premises of "Chiyuv"[?].
— In the kehilla premises a meeting of the board and the council took place, which decided to create a relief committee for the victims in Brisk.
The kehilla contributed 300 zł. to the campaign. The sum has already been sent off.
Meeting about the Reconstruction Fund

[Będzin — reconstruction fund.]
On Tuesday a meeting about the reconstruction fund ("Oyfboy-fond") in our town took place in the premises of the Gemilut Hesed fund, in connection with the Million Campaign that was organised at the time.
Taking part in the meeting, besides the board of the fund with its president Mr. M. Szejn, were also members of the Million Campaign committee with its president Mr. Fürstenberg, delegates of the artisans, merchants, small traders and others.
During the deliberations various plans were put forward as to how to use the money that will be placed at the disposal of the reconstruction committee. The greatest support was won by the project to build jointly-owned stables for cows and horses outside the town, because the stables in the town will have to be removed, and this could undermine the livelihood of a large number of families of cow and horse owners.
It is therefore very important that the interested persons come to an understanding with the reconstruction committee at the Gemilut Hesed fund and put forward their plans, which will be finally decided by the committee in the shortest time.

Sosnowiec — A "Bargain" Bought "to the Last Hair"...

[Sosnowiec — crime; fraud.]
Sosnowiec
A "bargain" bought "to the full hair"[?]...
Mrs. Sh., a resident of Old Sosnowiec, was walking last Saturday towards evening along Piłsudski Street when an unknown man came up to her and asked her whether there was a jeweller's shop on the street.
Meanwhile a young Jewish man came up and asked her what the "katsap" (Russian) had asked her, and in doing so he told her that the katsap had wanted to sell a diamond brooch to his father, who has a jeweller's shop at Modrzejowska[?] 32, but because of a "trifle" the katsap had changed his mind[?]. If she wants to earn a couple of hundred zł. — said the young man — let her go over to the katsap and buy the diamond brooch.
The naive woman grabbed at the deal as at a stroke of luck; since she is no expert — she said — she wants to show the brooch to an expert.
As if out of nowhere[?] there at once sprang up a Jew with a pious face, who appraised the brooch as a rare bargain.
The woman, hearing the expert opinion of the "Hasidic" Jew, ran quickly home and brought 160 zł., and with the "bargain" she went to Modrzejowska[?] Street to sell it in a jeweller's shop, but there the terrible secret was revealed to her.

Eliezer Epsztejn, stayed in Kielce and gave the kehilla detailed particulars of the terrible devastation that the flood catastrophe wrought in the towns and shtetls of the Kielce voivodeship and especially in Działoszyce, where several hundred Jewish families were left[?] naked and destitute. Michał Hager: The Destruction of Działoszyce — Jews of Zagłębie, Respond!

[Działoszyce — disaster; appeal for aid.] Whoever wants to have his breath taken away by the description of the great destruction — let him visit the little town of Działoszyce, and everything will become clear before your eyes. Human imagination is unable to grasp, the pen cannot at all express, how much horror and despair the Jews of Działoszyce are living through because of the elemental disaster that struck the town so[?] heavily and bitterly.
"And He blotted out every living substance" — has been said[?] here in the full sense of the word. Of the once proud[?] Działoszyce only a geographical point remains; at the present moment Działoszyce belongs — to the past.
One's hair truly stands on end when speaking of the Działoszyce tragedy. But it is not reportage that I want to convey to the Zagłębie public; I write these lines, in the columns of the Zagłębie tribune — our newspaper — only because I want to fulfil the obligation I left[?] in Działoszyce: to give their Zagłębie and Silesian brothers and sisters a sincere greeting, and to convey to you the whole bitter and naked truth about their tragic and desperate situation.
But it is simply impossible to dwell in detail on the horrifying particulars of their tragedy; I believe that the Działoszyce people living in Zagłębie certainly have the opportunity to learn about the tragic fate of their Działoszyce dear ones and relatives, and it will suffice merely to report that yesterday's respected, wealthy Jews stand today in line for a piece of bread and a spoonful of cooked food.
Fate spared no one, made no distinction; 300 Jewish families are exposed to death by hunger.
There are not the few groszy for a living, there is no garment for the naked body, Jews go naked and barefoot, there is no roof over their heads.
In a word: such a destruction as that of Działoszyce we could have seen only on the battlefield in the Great War. The situation grows more desperate from day to day. Had the state of affairs continued a short while longer in the form in which the writer of these lines found the town, the Działoszyce people who remained alive would have perished from an epidemic that threatens to break out there.
The Działoszyce community in and around Zagłębie is a large one. On these Jews, therefore, lies the duty more than on others to help the Działoszyce sufferers, and you can help with whatever is possible: with a pair of shoes, a dress, a shirt, food, money and whatever is possible.
A broad relief action must be undertaken immediately in our Zagłębie territory for the Jews of Działoszyce — out[?] into the street[?] with a fervent appeal: Jews of Zagłębie, respond! And the Jews of Zagłębie will, as until now, this time too faithfully and honestly fulfil their duty toward a desperate Jewish community whose tragedy is called: the destruction of Działoszyce.

The poet Z. Segalovitch in Zagłębie

The well-known Yiddish poet and writer Z. Segalovitch, who is staying in Zagłębie, visited our editorial office yesterday.

(On the decree against the Yiddish theatre.)
In Upper Silesia and in Zagłębie the Yiddish theatre posters have for [?] a long time now disappeared from the walls, and all [?] is quiet; nobody reacts against the unheard-of decree, the Jewish cultural activists keep silent, as if nothing had happened.
True, all our attention and energy has lately been directed toward bringing help to the ruined Jews in a number of places, but that does not mean that nothing at all need be done, and one must not let so important a Jewish cultural position in our region as the better Yiddish theatre disappear.
The central Jewish Actors' Union must intervene.
The kehilla representatives, too, ought to have taken the initiative; and if in Zagłębie this is not possible (unfortunately the majority has little understanding for such a matter), we propose to the Katowice kehilla leadership — since its vice-president, Mr. Dir. Abrahamer, has a genuinely serious attitude to Yiddish stage art — we propose that the Katowice kehilla representatives undertake an energetic intervention with the supervisory authority and thereby win a [?] precedent.
L. Tenenbaum.

Manufactured "pure" Aryans

The Court of Appeal in Katowice last Tuesday heard the following sensational case: in the dock sat the f[ormer] municipal officials Krashni [?] and Gawęda [?], as well as the merchant Kutsch and his wife, all of Katowice, who are accused as follows: in 1934 a certain Adolf Rosenblum of Berlin tried to obtain a licence to import Polish films into Germany. When [?] Rosenblum could not obtain the licence, because he was not an Aryan, he turned to the above-mentioned officials with a request that they issue him a document as a Protestant. A "conflict" between France and Germany over a Jewish worker

A group of workers numbering 600 men is travelling to France for work, but among the group there is one single Jew, a certain Welishewicz [?] of Będzin, and here the Jewish tragedy begins.
The point is that German law does not allow any Jew to benefit from the collective visa for the whole group, but demands a separate visa for him. France for its part "argues" that the Jew, who is included in the group, needs no separate passport. The same old story of "two verses contradicting one another".... But then came the third party, the Jewish party, in the person of Mr. B. Chameides, who intervened so that an exception be made for the single Jew and he could travel along with the group. It is to be expected that the intervention will bring the desired result.

What Must the Small Trader Do?

A hard time is being lived through today by the small traders, and they must overcome enormous difficulties in order to hold on to their hitherto sources of livelihood. In this hard and bitter struggle, however, the Jewish small trader must not let himself be ruled by moods of despair; he must stand his ground.
Endurance and stubbornness — yet that is still not enough today. The Jewish small trader must adapt himself to the changes that the new circumstances bring forward, and must run his business with methods that correspond[?] to today's trading needs.
This adaptation is the command of the hour. The Jewish shop must acquire a different appearance than until now, both outwardly and inwardly — the rules of hygiene must be observed in it, and it must acquire an aesthetic appearance; more than until now, attention must be paid to the proper treatment of the customer, in order to keep him and draw[?] him to the shop. The small trader must take care always to have in stock the necessary quality and quantity of goods, and to be able to sell them as cheaply as possible. The small trader must raise the level of his business and become competitive.
It is clear to everyone that carrying out the necessary reforms involves considerable expenses, which often exceed the means of the individual shopkeeper. This can, however, be achieved through a collective effort on the part of a few retailers. It is therefore a necessity to carry out a consolidation (komasacja) of small trade. Instead of several smaller shops that are located next to one another and lead a vegetative existence, a larger partnership store must arise, equipped with modern fittings. Such a partnership enterprise will, relatively speaking, save to a considerable degree on administrative expenses, which today make up a very large percentage of the small trader's budget; it will have a larger capital at its disposal, enjoying much higher credit than each individual merchant separately; it will be able to make the necessary investments and abolish[?] the undesirable competition that today wears out small trade.
We know that the idea of consolidation will have to overcome many deep-rooted psychological habits of the Jewish shopkeepers before it gains full rights of citizenship in Jewish society. But it is a necessity, and the sooner it breaks its way into the shopkeepers' consciousness, the better for Jewish small trade.
As a first stage towards full consolidation, the principle of joint purchasing must be put into practice. The professional organisation of the Jewish small traders must take upon itself the initiative of organising joint purchasing according to the particular branches, in order to procure[?] for the members the necessary goods from the first source at the lowest prices.
In this[?] striving to renew his working conditions, the small trader must find support from Jewish society. Under normal conditions the state would have had to take upon itself the task of supporting such undertakings[?]. What is involved here are long-term credits, which could be used for investment purposes and would allow the small merchant to get through the hard time. It must be stressed here with sorrow that many Jewish manufacturers and wholesale merchants have found[?] it fitting precisely at the present moment to refuse credit to the Jewish small trader and to divert it elsewhere.
Jewish society must be vitally ("bloodily") interested in the restoration to health of small trade. The appropriate social circles, which have the necessary means at their disposal, must, in their own interest, come to the aid of the small trader and strengthen the economic positions of the Jewish middle class.
P. Liberman.
The Relief Campaign Has Been Proclaimed

[Będzin and Sosnowiec — relief for the Brest pogrom victims.] The Brisk (Brześć) relief campaigns have already been officially proclaimed by the newly created Jewish committees in Sosnowiec and Będzin.
At the meetings there was long debate about how to carry out the relief campaign technically; they wanted to make sure that the campaign would really yield a substantial result, that the Jews of Zagłębie would give — money.
One said that a fixed minimum should be set; another said that one should rely entirely on the honesty of the givers.
But all agreed on one conclusion[?]: the Jews of Będzin, the givers of Będzin, can be relied upon.
Będzin in particular needs only hands to take and feet to go to the donors [printed "m'dvim"]. They will surely not go away empty-handed.
One may complain that Będzin lacks a proper Jewish milieu, intellectual cultural activists. Artists who come here complain that the social atmosphere here is very narrow, that the Jews of Zagłębie lack the necessary sentiment, that the social-cultural milieu is very poor.
All these complaints are unfortunately largely justified; even the party activist complains of a lack of the necessary warmth towards his own comrades. But all this concerns the thin stratum which has to create a milieu in limited corners. It is quite different with the ordinary Jew in Będzin. Whoever loves the masses and can bear them — finds a milieu, warmth, sentiment and even enthusiasm. People do not spare[?] their own pockets, and often do not check at all whether the purpose of the collection fully corresponds to their own party convictions; if only the thing smells of — let us call it — Yiddishkeit, they open their purse and give with a full hand.
Apart from those individuals, who are censured in their own circles [unclear words: "bazayn taki"[?]], Jewish society as such has a warm heart and open hands.
And when it is a matter of helping the Jews of Brisk, who fell victim not because of their sins but because they are Jews, we have every reason to expect that the Jews of Zagłębie will not disappoint; it makes no difference — whether the committee carries out the campaign in this form or another — it will no doubt meet warm hearts.
Brisk lies deep in our blood; Brisk has struck us in the soul, in our honour and in everything that is holy and dear to us as human beings and as Jews.
To rebuild Brisk [printed "Brist"] is our just ambition; the joy of the antisemites that the historic Jewish town of Brisk will cease to be Jewish will prove groundless.
We can be at ease about the Jews of Zagłębie: of their own free will they themselves will come with bricks to rebuild the ruined town.
The campaign has been officially proclaimed.
Y. N—m.

I'm a Fabric Manufacturer!...

[Humour — comic monologue.]
Retold by Y. Aberzhanek.

Jews, I warn you: don't go to any boarding-houses! If you do, go alone, without your wives; and if, God forbid, you are already caught up in the business and you come with your better half, go to a "Jew-only" boarding-house [lit. "Jew-clean", i.e. with no gentiles]. If not — if you won't listen to me — you'll have such a debacle [?] as I had.
Listen, gentlemen, to the debacle I had:
Looking at me, you surely think I'm a strongman who can break iron — well, from the start [?] you are making a big mistake. I am — may it not be thought of you — beset by great, terrible troubles; mind you, I'm no dangerously ill man, God forbid; I have only one trouble [?] — the stomach! It's a stomach like all stomachs: quiet, modest, not pampered, takes what is due to it, doesn't insist on this yes and that no — it is content with its lot... But what then? One little thing: it is a burner — it burns!.. No how, no when, it just starts to burn.
Recently, during one such "fire", my wife says to me:
— Hertskeshi, my crown, what will be the end of your burning?
— Well, what am I to do?
— What do you mean? You must go to a doctor, let him "zbadać" [examine] you — what you've got there in your stomach.
So I obeyed my wife and went off to a doctor, a specialist in "fuels" [?].
The doctor "examined" me, felt and listened, tapped and squeezed, and after the listening, tapping and squeezing he began questioning me:
— How old are you? Are you married?
— A fine question, upon my life, from a doctor! If I were a bachelor I'd be burning with love... panie doktorze [doctor, sir]. Have you ever met a bachelor with a stomach? All the troubles and blows stick to us married men.
— Do you have children? Do you live normally? Do you eat on time? When?
After the examination he puts away the stethoscope [słuchawka] with which he had listened to me, and the little hammer with which he had tapped me, and finally he says to me:
— Uncle, your heartburn comes from there being too much acid [lit. "sour-stuff"] in your stomach; the first thing you must do is a diet.
And he wrote me a slip of what I may eat.
I listened attentively, and as soon as I left the doctor I went straight into a bar, snatched a little glass of "clear" [vodka] and chased it with a good piece of herring. I tell you, never did a little glass of brandy taste so good to me as that time; I felt all the flavours of the world in that piece of herring...
Well, who do you think won out? The doctor, of course. The end was that I had to start living on a diet.
It was last summer; my wife says to me:
— Hertskeshi, I have no strength left for your burning. Listen to me and go to a boarding-house for dieters; there you'll get used to it and you'll stick with it.
I obeyed my wife — but how does one go alone to a boarding-house? How can one be such a swine, go off to a boarding-house and leave the little wife in town? First, the whole boarding-house [?] won't do me any good; and second, it's almost [?] a dangerous thing to leave a wife within four walls — who knows what can happen!..
So I took my wife along to the boarding-house, and here the story [?] begins!
The boarding-house was not "Jew-clean", that is, among the guests there was one shaygets [gentile youth]. Well, needless to say, my little wife, bless her, tracked him down at once, the shaygets. They quickly became very chummy [?]; she and the uncircumcised one became thick as thieves [lit. button to button], he told her jokes and they "held their sides"...
But all that wouldn't have bothered me — with whom else should she have shown herself [?], with me perhaps? "Na łonie natury" [in the lap of nature] with one's own husband? You'd have to be crazy! All that wouldn't have bothered me if she hadn't talked to him about my heartburn.
Recently he asks her:
— "Mój mąż ma shtofn" ["my husband has shtofn" — she meant the "stuff", the stomach acid; but in Polish sztofy = fabrics] — she answered.
— Fabrics? For long?
— Some ten years.
— Really? Ten years? A w domu kto jest? [And who is at home?]
— W domu mamy teściową nieruchomą [at home we have a mother-in-law who can't move] — a mother-in-law who doesn't stir from her place.
After a month on a diet I came home from the boarding-house like a dried-up lulav, skin and bones, barely a soul left in me. I had weaned myself off eating. Before, it used to burn after I'd eaten a quarter of a roast goose, and now — after semolina porridge with milk...
But that is not what I set out to tell; I only want to tell about my after-pains from the boarding-house.
A few months later I am sent a "wezwanie" [summons] to present myself forthwith at the "urząd skarbowy" [tax office] for a "wyjaśnienie" [explanation].
— Explanation? What business do I have with the tax office? What am I, a manufacturer or a merchant? All in all I'm a matchmaker, so what "explanations" does a matchmaker have to give the tax office?
I come there, and the official, sir [?], asks me:
— Do you have a licence? Do you keep books? How long have you been manufacturing?
— Who, me?
— Who else, me perhaps? — the gentleman got angry.
— Who said that I manufacture?
— You yourself.
— Me? That's not true, how could I have said it? I'm only, by profession, a... matchmaker.
— Co pan mówi? Co to jest za interes? [What are you saying, sir? What sort of business is that?]
— Shadkhan [?], shadkhan... the kind who turns young ladies into married women [?]...
— Co pan gada? [What are you babbling, sir?] — the gentleman boiled over — przecież żona sama powiedziała, że... [but your wife herself said that...]
Hearing "żona" [wife], it dawned on me. I started "playing him the cymbal" [?] — and he showed me a whole megillah in which it stands written clearly, black on white, that my wife had "wyraźnie" [clearly] explained to the sequestrator [bailiff; misprinted "sekdestrator"] Staszek that I've had fabrics for 10 years already and that at home I have a "nieruchomość" [real estate]; that is, that I run an illegal manufacture, I keep no books, I pay no "podatki" [taxes], so I have, so to speak, been cheating the treasury for 10 years; for that... well, for that you know what's coming.
It didn't help — my talking, my proving that I am, may it not befall you, a pauper "on seven coat-tails" [?], that I'm poor and destitute and wretched [?], a beggar in his own good name; my "explaining" that I'm a "professional" [zawodowy (?)] matchmaker didn't help — I said "gate" [?] and he answered "attic" [we talked at cross-purposes], and I've had plenty to sing and tell about it to this very day. To this day they come to carry out inspections, to see whether I haven't hidden [?] my "fabrics" and how my "nieruchomości" [real estates] are doing...
All this I owe to my wife's "słabość" [weakness] for shkotsim. Therefore I say:
If you go to a boarding-house, go alone, without a wife; and if you take the wife along, then go to a Jew-only boarding-house, without shkotsim.
A clarification on the lyceum question — From the Board of Supervisors of the „S. Fürstenberg“ Jewish Gymnasium in Będzin

From the Board of Supervisors of the Jewish Gymnasium named after „S. Fürstenberg“ in Będzin.
In connection with the communiqué of the management of the Jewish gymnasium in Sosnowiec in „Zaglembier Tsaytung“ no. 23, which misleads public opinion and in consequence of which many parents turn to us for clarification, we declare the following:
1) The claim of the management of the above-mentioned gymnasium that the humanistic type, as the only type of lyceum being opened at the Jewish gymnasium in Sosnowiec, is the most suitable for our youth, is false, because:
a) among Jewish youth there are pupils with various abilities and interests, and therefore lyceums of various types are required, and in no case only of the humanistic type.
b) The best proof of this is the fact that in the most important and largest Jewish schools, e.g. in Kraków, Łódź, Lwów etc., separate lyceums of various types are being opened.
2) The claim that abroad only a certificate from schools where Latin is taught counts is meant solely to frighten the parents, and moreover it degrades the dignity of an educational institution, for:
a) the claim is not based on any regulation, but is plucked out of thin air.
b) Foreign universities admit without difficulty graduates (abiturients) of the gymnasiums existing until now, which have no Latin.
c) Graduates of every type of lyceum must, after all, in any case first complete a gymnasium of the new type, in which they will have had to go through the Latin course.
3) As to the claim that opening lyceums of various types is no privilege at all — we state that the plan of the State School Curatorium in Kraków provides for the Będzin gymnasium the opening of three types of lyceum, and for the Sosnowiec gymnasium only one single type of lyceum.
4) The claim of the management of the Sosnowiec gymnasium that every gymnasium is permitted to open any type of lyceum at the request of 3 pupils is simply ridiculous, because only the state school authority can decide on opening a lyceum.
This last claim degrades and trivialises the concession right of a lyceum, by implying that the right to open a lyceum does not even require the will of 3 parents, but that the request of 3 pupils suffices.
We must therefore state that the communiqué of the Sosnowiec gymnasium misleads public opinion, and that it is beneath the dignity of a gymnasium's management to issue such a communiqué.

Who Invented the Sewing Machine?

It seems that no invention of the last hundred years has brought about so great an upheaval as the sewing machine. There is practically not a single country in the world where it is not found in almost every home. But when one asks who invented the sewing machine, and what it looked like at first — three nations quarrel over it: Austria, France and America. All three want to prove by signs and wonders that it was their own countryman who was the first to bestow this invention on the world.

The first to hit upon the idea that clothes cannot be sewn by hand and that a machine is needed for it was — so it appears — the Viennese tailor Josef[?] Madersperger. For 30 years, from 1807 to 1837, he toiled to devise a model of a machine for sewing with a needle, as we still have it to this day.

Exactly a hundred years ago he took out a patent on his machine, which made 100 stitches a minute. When one knows that today's machine makes 4 thousand stitches a minute, 100 stitches are certainly a trifle, but with it this invention stirred up the whole world.

Had Madersperger had money, he would surely have manufactured sewing machines and become a rich man. But he was a great pauper. The 30 years of work on the machine took from him his last strength and the last bit of money he had; he badly neglected his tailoring, and when he had at last finished his invention he was poor and sick, and indeed soon died in the Vienna poorhouse (hekdesh).

The Parisian tailor Thimonnier bought the machine from Madersperger's widow and improved it somewhat, so that he brought it up to 200 stitches a minute. In 1841 he exhibited the sewing machine at the Leipzig fair, and indeed he soon succeeded in finding a partner, with whose help he began to manufacture sewing machines. But hardly were the first machines finished when Parisian tailors with their journeymen fell upon the "factory" and smashed the machines. Thimonnier barely managed to escape with one machine, with which he used to travel around the French provinces looking for work. In 1850 he died in want and penury.

Elias Howe, a weaver in New York, then created, after Thimonnier's model but on the system of a weaver's shuttle, a sewing machine that already made three hundred stitches a minute. In 1850 he too received a patent for it and indeed began to manufacture sewing machines, but his fate was no better than Thimonnier's. Tailors fell upon his factory and smashed everything. He fled to London, where he managed to get a position with a tailor and to work there for two years.

When he afterwards came back to America, he learned that a company had meanwhile[?] begun to manufacture sewing machines according to his system, only of iron instead of wood, as his machine had been. He brought a lawsuit against the company, which would not hear of him at all, and by the time he had carried on the lawsuit for several more years he was already so broken and battered that he no longer had any pleasure from the money the company had to pay him for his patent... At 47 he died of a heart disease.

When the sewing machine afterwards made its way back from America to Europe, it was said to be an American invention, and people quite forgot that the real inventor of this important machine had been an Austrian. Now, for the hundredth anniversary of the sewing machine, Austria is preparing to hold a great celebration in honour of its countryman Madersperger, who was the first to have the idea of a sewing machine.

Z. Haber, Vienna.

[Będzin and Sosnowiec — satirical feuilleton; shechita, kehilla, free-loan fund, aid for Brześć.]
Whom do the feathers belong to?..
An original din-torah took place before the Będzin rabbinate: summoned to judgement were the poultry slaughterers so popular among us [?].
Actually it is no sensation that the poultry slaughterers should be summoned to judgement — more than once they have stood before the "green table" over their good deeds; only this time the accused is not the kehilla representation, but the leaseholder of the poultry slaughterhouse.
So let us give him the floor.
"For decades now the feathers of the poultry slaughtered in my slaughterhouse have belonged to me. Once there were golden times: the goods were in the feathers, they 'flew high' and brought me an income of 4 (in words: four) gulden a day. Later, however, a crisis set in, there was no buyer, and I abandoned the feathers as ownerless.
Now — he says — there is a better 'conjuncture', the feathers 'are flying higher again', so I have a new trouble again. What is it?
— The poultry slaughterers have cast an 'eye' on this article, and they pluck.. and they pluck on purpose: while the bird is still twitching they are already tearing out the feathers... and when one has in mind to tear out a few feathers, one surely cannot keep strict [?] supervision over the slaughter.."
Thus argued the old leaseholder of the slaughterhouse, together with his wife, before the Będzin rabbinate, and put various questions to them.
The rabbinate was "in an embarrassment" and did not know what ruling to issue. Had the Czebin [?] rabbi also sat in, they would all, as always, have said to the slaughterers:
— Permitted to you, permitted to you..
And the rabbinate hit upon an invention and decided that the feather affair should be handled by an arbitration, which shall issue the ruling:
— Whom do the feathers belong to?..
A modest town...
Sosnowiec excels in one field — in the field of modesty. And in recent days the ten-year jubilee of a public institution was celebrated. Do you perhaps think the institution is a "raiser of the bowed" [—]? Then you are greatly mistaken: the institution bears on itself the emblem:

Oneg Shabbat — Parashat Korach

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion; followed by a film item.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Korach
—o—
a) "And Korah took" (Num. 16:1)
In Kiddushin, folio 2, the Gemara says that every "taking" means "with money", by money. So "And Korah took" also means "with money": that is, Korah bought himself with money all the intriguers who helped him stir up the dispute. Where there is a dispute, there is already a smell of bribery.
Ugo shel Yosef.
—o—
b) "Two hundred and fifty men, princes of the congregation" (ibid., 2)
The Torah even finds it necessary to enumerate the chiefs of Esau; the Torah would [?] not publicise any names. Here, however, with the 250 men of dispute, the Torah names no names at all, because the Torah does not wish to publicise sinners; thus the wood-gatherer is not called by name, nor are so many other transgressors.
In Sanhedrin 43b the Gemara says: when God told Joshua that the Israelites had sinned, Joshua asked: Who among the Israelites? The Master of the Universe answered him: Am I then an informer, that I should tell you who the sinners are? Cast lots and find out for yourself...
R. Levi Yitzchak of Berdichev.
—o—
c) "Princes of the congregation, called to the assembly, men of renown" (ibid., 2)
All titles that have no connection even with the slightest [?] deeds; titles of "honourable Jews" who receive the titles for everything, but not for deeds — and it is precisely these who always become the men of dispute and the intriguers.
Leket Asher.
—o—
d) "For all the congregation are holy, every one of them" (ibid., 3)
R. Yaakov David of Slutsk had no great joy in his town: always dispute upon dispute, and above all a certain Moshe made his life miserable. Once, when this strongman quarrelled with R. Yaakov David, he said to him:
— It is a miracle for you, Rabbi, that Slutsk has only gentle people; otherwise you would have been driven out of here long ago.
R. Yaakov David smiled and said:
— But that was exactly Korah's claim: "You take too much upon you" — that you stand at the helm and are leaders is only because "all the congregation are holy", because Korah's people are good and pious people; had you come up against others, they would long ago have taught you some manners. Only, Korah's people are, after all, decent [?], quiet and pious folk...
Imrei Chen.
—o—
e) "And what is Aaron, that you murmur against him?" (ibid., 11)
"You and all your company who are gathered together against the Lord" — you who rebel against God do not want sacrifices to be brought to Him; "and what is Aaron, that you murmur against him?" — why are you jealous of Aaron? For one who believes in God, the priesthood is a great honour worth fighting for; but for you, who rebel against God — what is there to fight for: the privilege of slaughtering an animal and cleaning out the ashes?
Chavot Daat.
—o—
f) "Do not respect their offering" (ibid., 15)
According to its plain meaning: the incense. Rashi.
In Yoma 44b the Gemara says that the incense atones for slander. So here, too, the incense should have atoned for the slander; therefore Moses turned to God: "Do not respect their offering", for the sin of slander is forgiven only when the person about whom the slander was spoken forgives it...
Yalkut Yehuda.
—o—
g) "Neither have I hurt one of the people" (ibid., 18 [?])
With those who are only supposedly humble one sees [?] a characteristic trait: they draw near little people, whom it would never occur to anyone to compare with them, while they keep at a distance people who stand on the same level as themselves — those they fear...
Moses, the truly humble man, was humble even towards the great: "Neither have I hurt 'one of the people'" — "one of the people" is a designation of a highly placed person (Genesis 26); even to them, the great ones, Moses did no harm...
Meshech Chochma.
—o—
h) "And all their goods" (ibid., 32)
This is why Korah's wealth was swallowed up: only thanks to his wealth did he have the audacity to wage disputes against Moses; had he not been rich, he would not have had the audacity for it...
R. Yehuda Leib Ginzburg.

At the Home of the Poet Mordechai Gebirtig (From a Visit)

By Heszel Danziger. (From a visit.)
A fine Jewish folk poet, in the great folksy city of Kraków; to this day our grandmothers tell wondrous tales, legends of old Kraków with its great rabbis, rebbes and miracle-workers who blessed and cursed... To this day our mothers lull the little children to sleep with songs: — "Great you will grow, in Kraków you will live, charity you will give" — Kraków is beloved, baked into the hearts of the masses, has become a thing of the people.
Day after day tourists and travellers[?] stream to Kraków, to see the museums, relics, sights[?], to soak up the dust of olden times.. Kraków breathes old age — but antiquity has a specific smell..
It is our lot, in this old folksy city, to have a spring of life, of refreshment; if you want to refresh yourself, come into the Jewish quarter, to the heart of the old ghetto, to the thoroughly Jewish street Berek Joselewicz [ul. Berka Joselewicza], where for 26 years now a strong spring of Jewish folk song has been flowing — come to the Jewish folk poet Mordechai Gebirtig.
Here you will find:
"In the quiet little lane
Stands, lost in thought, a little house;
There, in the little attic room,
Lives my dear Reyzele."
Here you are in the Jewish courtyard with its attic and cellar dwellings, with a long wooden gallery (ganek), where Reyzele's sweetheart used to come every evening to whistle up to the little window — which pained the father and the mother: how[?] does such goyish whistling come into a Jewish courtyard? And the father, the folk poet, sang out:
"Whistling is not Jewish,
It suits only them;
Call me 'Reyzl', simply in Yiddish,
One, two, three."
And a great, great many sorrows has he sung out in these 25 years — —
* * *
In the home of the administrator of the Jewish hospital, spending time in pleasant company, we met — in an idyllic room, in the evening glow of the May sun, its walls shaded by the acacia trees under the window —
Mordechai Gebirtig — a white-haired little Jew[?], a tender, a noble man, a white quiet dove fluttering about the Jewish spaces with a written song in its mouth — Mordechai Gebirtig, the folk poet.
For 25 years he has been creating the Jewish folk song with so much fire and zeal (25 years — actually a jubilee; where are the celebrants?); he is already close to sixty, and soon we shall have to celebrate his sixtieth jubilee. He is still fresh and healthy; his popularity, which began with "Kinder yorn" ["Childhood Years"] from "Di rumenishe khasene" ["The Romanian Wedding"], does not yet end with "Reyzele", which made Lola Folman famous, and "Avreml der marvikher" ["Avreml the Pickpocket"], which, poor thing, gets "friendly-pickpocketed"[?] in the repertoire of many Jewish actors. His work will yet go further than "Motele" and "Arbetloze" ["The Unemployed"]. His song "Arbetloze" has already given work to more than one Jewish actor.. Gebirtig's songs want first of all to solve the social question; meanwhile, one sees, his songs solve this problem only for Jewish actors, while for him himself his material situation is not solved by them. His royalties are paltry.
Recently all his songs, with music, have appeared in book form, in a splendid edition, and nobody will dare to "lift" them, because Gebirtig's wife will rap them over the knuckles. She is already in a lawsuit with a Warsaw film[?] company, because they "butchered"[?] some stanzas of one of Gebirtig's songs.
But Gebirtig himself laughs at all of this. He does not seek material success, he does not need publicity; by nature he is retiring and modest, a hidden saint of sorts — for how many people are there here in our Zagłębie who know of a Jewish folk poet, Mordechai Gebirtig, who lives not far from here — in neighbouring Kraków?
He seeks no enthusiasm and applause; it is enough for him to hear how the masses of the people, tailors and shoemakers, sit whole days at work humming his songs to the beat of the machine and the hammer. It is enough for him to see how Malwina Rapel brings Avreml the Pickpocket to the stage through her brilliant creation, complete[?] with the fingers, just as he, the father, conceived[?] him... His Avreml the Pickpocket cries out his bloody protest to the world that made a thief of him:
"Abroad, nothing to live on,
I grew big, a [—][?] would still give,
But those people who are always sated
Often drove me off in anger,
A thief grows up[?] [—][?] became"
And he takes revenge on the sated world in his own peculiar way:
"Though not at markets[?] like those
Ugly thugs[?],
But only from stingy, filthy
Magnates".. 
* * *
Besides all this, Gebirtig composes the music for his splendid songs; he creates his music very originally, without notes, without conservatories — it bursts out of the depths of his soul; he himself is music, himself a song.
A mightily strong spring, flowing with genuine Jewish folk creation, and the soul wearied by the daily turmoil of life wants to drink from it more and more — — —
We believe that we Jews of Zagłębie will have the good fortune to enjoy his splendid folk melody at a concert, which will probably take place here soon.
Kraków derives true delight from the folk concerts held there with the participation of the folk poet Mordechai Gebirtig and his young, well-known daughter Lola, who is already today a gifted artiste and first-class singer; perhaps Zagłębie too will have the pleasure of seeing them?

A. Zaglembier — The Living Corpse (12)

[Literature — serial novel ("The Living Corpse"), instalment 12.]
A. Zaglembier [pen name].
(A most thrilling novel of Jewish life in Zagłębie before and after the World War). 12)
Summary of the beginning of the novel.
On a winter night before the World War, when two Cossacks were to transfer the dangerous bandit "Szmulek Łapka" into the Piotrków prison, they were suddenly attacked on the way to the Będzin station by two disguised "strażniks" (guards) — Łapka's helpers. The Cossacks were found the next morning lying bound with gagged mouths, and Szmulek "Łapka", freed, fled to the Gzichów road and hid somewhere.
That same evening, and almost at the same hour, the universally respected, solid collector (inkasent) Josl Wertheim — a father of three children — suddenly disappeared. His wife Sarah'tshe runs about the town terribly desperate, searching for him in every possible hiding place in all of Zagłębie. But Josl Wertheim has vanished like a stone in water..
On the fifth day pockmarked Matek reports to police inspector Karecki and tells him that on that day he saw Wertheim walking on the Gzichów road together with the Christian woman Magda Komarska — a young, pretty gentile girl whom Matek had been courting.
Magda is arrested at once. During the interrogation she declares that on the very day Wertheim disappeared they had quarrelled, because Wertheim wanted to give her money to go to Katowice for an operation so that their "illegitimate" child would not be born. Karecki then goes to Wertheim's wife Sarah'tshe and tells her of her husband's love affair with Magda. But Sarah'tshe does not believe it and declares that her husband had no money on him. Yet when she goes to the cupboard she sees that the several hundred roubles of savings[?] are gone, and she gives up hope for her vanished husband.
Some time later the Cossacks, while bathing[?] in the river, found the dead body of a man. Karecki established that the drowned man had first been murdered and then thrown into the river.
Now read on.
— This really is a discovery! Oh, what's this, there is something in the trouser pockets too!
— What?
— Clods of earth! Torn out together with the grass...
— So you see, first of all[?] we are dealing here with a murder...
— Right, so it is, Mr. Inspector.
— A pity his face is no longer recognisable, but first[?] just take a look at what he is...
Two men pull the soaked[?] [—] shirt off him, and then several cry out at once:
— A Jew! A Jew!
— You see!
— A "circumcised one"!..
— Now just look in his pockets. Perhaps some slip of paper, a document has remained there, although I doubt the murderer would have left traces behind him... Well, do you find anything? — asks Karecki, and goes himself to search in the [—] pockets.
— There is! There is! — someone suddenly shouts — a little booklet! Surely a passport!
— Careful! Careful! Oh, how soaked it is, but perhaps one can still make something out of it.
— In the sun it will soon dry.
— Very true.
It was indeed a black-bound booklet, a Russian passport. Nothing else was found on the drowned man apart from it[?], but Karecki needed nothing more now; this very booklet, which the murderer had forgotten to take from his victim — so Karecki thought — would clear up everything for him...
And very carefully, as if he were now holding a rare antique[?] in his hand, Karecki began to [—] the pages[?] of the passport, which were as if glued to one another.
But under the effect of the hot, glowing rays of the sun, the pages first began to [—] and then came apart from one another. The writing inside was smeared and stained, but still remained legible. Straining his eyes as much as possible, Karecki began to spell out the document, and suddenly cried out, surprised and utterly astonished:
— My God! It's him!
— Who?! You know him?!
— You know him too! It is the mysteriously vanished Józek Wertheim!..
— Impossible! That's him?!
— It is the vanished Jewish collector!
— You're not mistaken, inspector?
— Here, read the document yourself, the writing is still legible enough — answers Karecki triumphantly, since he was the first to discover it.
Within a few minutes the passport passes through dozens of hands, and everyone who hands the document on exclaims just as surprised as Karecki:
— Really! It's him!..
Some, however, still doubt the correctness of the identification, and the first to express his doubts is the commissioner himself:
— But I think this is still too little... Can you still[?] recognise Wertheim by his face? I never knew him.
It turned out that nobody in the police had known him so well as to recognise him in his present condition.
— In any case it is impossible to establish that now — says Karecki — you can see how his face is eaten away or rotted... The most important thing is the document, and it is easy to see that the man has been lying in the water for several weeks, that is, exactly the time since Wertheim disappeared.
— Nevertheless it must be established precisely — the commissioner insists — just call here a few Jews who knew him well, only don't make a crowd, call only a few men here.
— Ah, that's the simplest thing — others agreed too.
— If so — says Karecki — then surely the simplest thing is to call Wertheim's wife, she will certainly recognise him best!..
— Certainly that must be done at once, but you are a bit mistaken, Mr. Inspector, if you think she will recognise him best; she will be too shaken to be able to look at him calmly and establish whether this is really her vanished husband, whereas a mere acquaintance will look at the dead man with more sober eyes. Therefore we should first hear what Jews say; after all, a protocol has to be written.
Karecki had to admit that the commissioner was right in this case, and while one strażnik went off to Sarah'tshe to bring her the evil, dark news, a second went up to the crowd that had gathered out of curiosity, which was standing far away from the dead man and talking loudly:
— Hey, yevreichiki (little Jews) [Russian: еврейчики], which of you knew Józek Wertheim well? Whoever did, raise a hand!
The assembled Jews remained standing a good while in mortal terror, and from mouth to mouth they asked one another in fear and dreadful anxiety:
— Can this really be Josl Wertheim?!..
— Can it be that they murdered him and threw him into the river?!
— All because of that treyf[?] little shikse?!..
— Who knows?..
— Anything is possible...
— Perhaps she had helpers, such a shikse!
— Well, who will go up? I would surely recognise him, but I can't look at a dead person, I faint right away...
— I'll go...
— Me too, who else?
— And you, Perlman? You're Josl's neighbour, after all!
— Of course I would recognise him.
And at once dozens of hands went up together. Among those who volunteered to identify the murdered man there was also one of Josl Wertheim's best friends.
When the strażnik led them to the scene of the incident, they remained standing, trembling, and tears appeared in the eyes of some.
— Well, you are not women, after all! — Karecki calls to them — the question is whether you recognise in the murdered man the vanished Josl Wertheim.
(To be continued).

Then and Now.

Once merchants travelled to fairs — today they have travelled off [are finished].
Once, when the gold watch "crawled" [ran slow], it crawled to the watchmaker; today, when it crawls, it crawls off either to the pawnshop or to the sequestrator [bailiff].
Once a landlord gave a Jew alms — today he gives him — an eviction.
Once a Jewish student received the title of doctor — today he receives the title — invalid [patient].
Once Jewish manufacturers had plenty of zakazy [orders] — today they have — nakazy [payment orders].
Once people said: what you lack in your head, you make up for with your feet; today they say: when you have nothing in your pocket, you stretch out your feet [die].
A. Iskin.

What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin: A United Relief Committee Formed for the Jewish Victims in Brisk

[Będzin — Relief; Kehilla.]
(Date boxes: Friday, 2 Sivan 5697 — piątek 11 czerwca 1937.)
Będzin
A united relief committee formed for the Jewish victims in Brisk.
In the previous number of our paper we reacted, in a short notice, to the fragmentation in organising the relief action for the Jewish victims in Brisk [Brześć nad Bugiem]; but we note with satisfaction that common sense has prevailed, and out of the various so-called committees a united relief committee has been formed, in which sit representatives of all the political and economic organisations, and also the editorial board of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung".
On Sunday [?] evening a meeting took place in the kehilla hall under the chairmanship of President Mr. Fürstenberg, with the participation of representatives of the kehilla board, the council, and also of all the above-mentioned organisations.
In the opening speech the chairman stressed the importance of unity, and at his proposal the martyrs of Brisk were honoured.
The president of the kehilla, Mr. Rubinlicht, reads the minutes of the meetings in the kehilla about forming a relief committee, and he proposes that the committee formed should bear the name: "Relief Committee at the Jewish Kehilla in Będzin".
Mr. Fürstenberg opposes this, saying that the action may end in a fiasco if it bears the stamp of the gmina [the community], because the gmina is compromised.
That was the first "shot" aimed at the kehilla board; then comes a second. Mr. Fürstenberg, in the name of those assembled, expresses the sharpest protest against the kehilla, which only two weeks after the Brisk events first called a meeting about creating a relief action, at a time when communal activists of the town had already formed a relief committee several days earlier.
After a discussion Mr. Rubinlicht's proposal is rejected, and it is decided to form a "Będzin Relief Committee for the Jewish Victims in Brisk".
After a heated discussion, during which very drastic moments of personal insults occur, the election of the presidium of the relief committee takes place.
The struggle centres on the person of President Mr. Rubinlicht, whom the Agudah board members ("dozores") and Mr. Piekarski in particular absolutely want to see elected among the vice-presidents.
The strongest opponent of this election is Mr. Liwer [?], who declares that if Mr. Rubinlicht is elected to the presidium, the whole committee, which does not want to work together with Mr. Rubinlicht, will be dissolved.
After this declaration Mr. Rubinlicht leaves the meeting.
The following list was formed: S. Fürstenberg (chairman), Dr. Rechtszaft, S. Manela, N. Langner, Ch. Malczadzki [?], P. L. Buchweitz [?], N. Rechnic and Ed. S. Lewkowicz.
Contributions to the action can be paid in: at all Jewish banks, at the editorial office of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" and at the Gemilut Hesed (G"Ch) fund.
With great satisfaction the announcement of Mr. Fürstenberg is received, that the Jewish and Christian workers of his factory have given away, for the benefit of the victims in Brisk, the wages of 2 hours' work. The office staff also gave 2 percent of their salaries for this purpose.
Finally, the question of a second relief action is dealt with, for the victims of the natural [?] disaster in Działoszyce. After the discussion it is decided to create a sub-committee, which will immediately collect for the Jews of Działoszyce.
— The technical commission held a meeting on Monday, at which it was decided: 1) to issue a public appeal (kol kore) to the Jewish population, and 2) the collection is to embrace the whole town, poor and rich.

Another Victim of "Diamonds"... / Discount Tickets for the Gdynia Fair / From "Brit HaTzohar"

[Będzin — Crime; Będzin — Commerce; Będzin — Zionism.]
Another victim of "diamonds"...
The latest victim of buying "diamonds" is the poultry dealer B. of Modrzejowska[?] Street. On Monday at dusk she arrived here by train from Mysłowice. Not far from the railway station she is stopped by a "Russian", who asks her to show him a reliable jeweller's shop. The Jewish woman becomes curious and demands that he tell her what he has to sell. At first he "did not want to say", but later he revealed the "secret" to her, because "he knows that he has before him an honest Jewish woman": he has — so he says — a precious diamond, but finding himself in a strange town without money, he wants to sell the diamond.
Having confided the "secret", the "Russian" went off; at once a young Jewish man popped up who, introducing himself as the son of Balimowski[?], told the woman that since he cannot come to terms with him, she should buy the diamond from him, "and for her trouble she will get 50 zł."
The woman went along with the deal and began to bargain over the "item". At a certain moment the "Russian" demanded that she leave him a deposit of 200 zł.; he would then entrust the diamond to her so that she could ask an expert...
The merchant woman ran home quickly, but as she had no more than 80 zł., she took various gold articles of her late husband and handed them to the "Russian", who gave her the "diamond" so that she could show it to an expert...
It goes without saying that "a fool remains a fool and a bargain remains a bargain"...

How Does One Attain Happiness?

[Advertisement — Polish State Class Lottery; Kapłan's lottery office. Advertorial.]
People worn out with toil, careworn, who look as though sunk[?] [—], often ask themselves the question: why does one work so hard when one enjoys so little of human life, and [—] in danger [—], when he sees how his neighbour is suddenly blessed with fortune and begins to live differently, to breathe more freely, to enjoy rest and pleasure — in such a case a person begins to believe in luck.
He sets about energetically looking for luck, but the thing is[?] that one does not know where it is to be found. We know that more than once we simply pass luck by and do not bend down to pick it up.

For Jewish journalists “entry is forbidden”...

On Sunday a peasants' rally of “OZON” [Camp of National Unity] of the Kielce voivodeship took place in Kielce.
The Jewish journalists who wanted to hear the public address of General Galica received an answer from Deputy Długosz, in the presence of Deputy Kib [?], that “for the Jewish journalists entry is forbidden”.
It is worth noting that Mr. Kib was elected deputy thanks to the thousands of Jewish votes. On the eve of the Sejm elections he spoke in the Kielce synagogue, and the rabbi then issued an appeal to the Jewish population to vote for Mr. Kib.
But all these things already belong to the past...
Great fires in the Kielce voivodeship.

In a number of villages in the Kielce voivodeship great fires broke out this week, causing great damage amounting to hundreds of thousands of złoty.
In the village of Oleśnica (Stopnica county) 50 houses and 100 barns burned down; in the village of Sudół (Pińczów county) 6 farmsteads burned down, and in many other places as well. The damage amounts, as said, to colossal sums of money.
8 Tammuz — the yahrzeit of the Kuzmir Rebbe of blessed memory.

On Thursday, 8 Tammuz (the 17th of this month [June]), falls the yahrzeit of the famous Kuzmir Rebbe, Reb Motele of blessed memory.
As we are informed, on the day of the yahrzeit several thousand Hasidim from all corners of Poland will arrive in Kielce, as well as many rabbis and rebbes of the Trisk dynasty.
The 39th Class Lottery.

In accordance with the law of 9 July 1936, which repealed [?] the previously binding law of 26 March 1920, the Polish Lottery Monopoly was brought into being; it holds the exclusive right to organise lottery undertakings on the territory of the Polish Republic. We note that the question of granting permits to organise a one-time prize (“fant”) lottery for philanthropic or public purposes is regulated by the ordinance of the Minister of Finance, published in No. 21 of the “Dz. U.” [?] [Journal of Laws] issue of the current year.
The Polish Lottery Monopoly has thus [?] remained the heir of the General Directorate of the State Lottery, and it also continues to run the class lottery, so popular in the country, on the organisational foundations in force until now.
In the first class, whose drawing begins on 22 June and will last 5 days, there will fall [?], among others, the following prizes: one prize each of a hundred thousand zł. and 50 thousand zł., two of fifteen thousand zł., five of ten thousand zł. and [—] of five thousand zł., fifteen of two thousand zł., thirty of a thousand zł., etc. Independently of those listed above, there will also fall the so-called daily prizes — four of five thousand zł. for the first tickets whose numbers are drawn each day, and five of twenty thousand zł. for the tickets whose numbers are drawn from the wheel after all the prizes of each day have been drawn. Altogether thirteen thousand prizes totalling 1,448,600 zł. will be drawn in the first class.
Those who begin playing not from the first class but in the later classes must, when buying a ticket, pay not only for the current class but also for the preceding classes; and it goes without saying that it is most practical [?] to start playing from the 1st class, since every class gives a chance to win a handsome sum. So one should not lose these chances.
One should obtain tickets in advance, since in this way it is easiest to get the desired number and generally to avoid various unnecessary complications. The ticket must be kept carefully, since only with the ticket can one collect the prize; and especially now, when we already have the economic crisis behind us, the ticket opens wide horizons before us.
Supervisory authority confirms the elections of the kehilla presidium

This week news arrived that the supervisory authority has confirmed the elections of the kehilla presidium and board.
As we learn, the newly elected board members (dozorcy) and parnassim will take over the management of the kehilla within the next few days.
Campaign for the “Mif'al ha-Galila” proclaimed.

Today, Friday, the well-known Zionist activist, the leader of “WIZO”, Mrs. [?] Miriam Baruak [?], is coming to Kielce; she will proclaim and at the same time lead the campaign for the “Mif'al ha-Galila” [Galilee Fund].
Tonight at 9 a meeting of activists takes place at the Zionist club, and tomorrow, Saturday evening, a meeting in honour of the distinguished guest will take place (also at the Zionist club). About 300 guests have been invited to the meeting.
Conference of the Zionist organisations of the Kielce voivodeship.

As we are informed, in connection with the elections to the 20th Zionist Congress, a conference of the Zionist organisations of the Kielce voivodeship will take place in Kielce in the next few days.
The vice-president of the Central Committee, Dr. M. Kleinbaum, will take part in the conference.

The activity of the Gemilut Chesed fund in Grodziec

Last Thursday the annual general meeting of the local [?] Gemilut Chesed (free-loan) fund, which has existed for [?] 2 years, took place in Grodziec [?]. The meeting was opened by Mr. M. Drozwik [?], who pointed to the gravity of the moment and proposed Mr. Yisroel Fertig as chairman; as assessors Messrs. Meir Ehrlich and Y. L. [?] Pelta [?], and M. Feuerman [?] as secretary. Mr. Fertig gave a lengthy speech in which he called for unity, in order to mobilise all energy in the defensive struggle for the preservation of the economic positions against the attack of the elements that have threatened our existence. He calls on the deserting [?] wealthy individuals, in view of the latest events, to take more interest in their suffering brethren and to rejoin as dues-paying members.
From the general and treasury report delivered by Mr. Drozwik [?] we learn that the capital is twelvefold higher than 2 years ago. 92 per cent of the members benefit from loans; the largest loan amounts to 150 zł. During the debate Mr. Gotlib criticises the management [?], which — he says — has no initiative. After the reply of Messrs. Weinrib and Drozwik [?], an absolutorium (vote of discharge) is granted to the outgoing management.
By secret ballot the following are elected: Weinrib, Drozdik [?], Izbicki, M. Yaridson [?], S. Wals [?], Ehrlich, Schneirman [?]; deputies: Freilich [?], Schweitzer [?]. Audit committee: Fertig, Winger [?], Friedman; deputies: Berkowicz [?] and Erdinast [?]. Then a series of resolutions is adopted, e.g. [?] a sharp protest against the Będzin Jewish kehilla for rejecting [?] the request [?] for a subsidy, although it collects the local [kehilla tax] assessment with very strict means. The management is therefore instructed to take energetic steps with regard to the kehilla so that it should allot a subsidy of a thousand [?] zł.

Session of the Będzin town council

[Będzin — town council.] Session of the Będzin town council.
Question about the smeared signboards.
At Wednesday's session of the town council in Będzin a series of economic questions were dealt with, among them [?] the project of the municipal power station on introducing 'block' tariffs. Alderman (ławnik) Rubinlicht pointed out that the tariffs are relatively more expensive than in other towns, and on his motion the project was sent back to a committee.
Later the report of the vice-president [?] on the congress of Polish towns was heard. Dr. Weinzieher supplemented the report.
Finally Dr. Weinzieher, among other things, put a question to the president: whether he knows that on the night from Saturday to Sunday a number of signboards of Jewish shops were smeared. To this the president replied that he knows about it and will consult on the matter with the appropriate authorities, so that such deeds will not happen again.

Against Antisemitism.
In the "Powstańców" [?] hall in Katowice a large youth meeting took place, convened by the P.P.S. [Polish Socialist Party]. About 1,000 people took part. After the speeches of Dr. Wszałkowicz [?], Janty [?] and others, a resolution of protest against antisemitism was adopted.

In connection with the fact that a municipal "pływalnia" [swimming pool] has been created at Bugla-tiona [?], the activity of the swimming section of "Bar Kochba" has been renewed. Training sessions take place on Tuesday and Friday from 17 to 19. Members pay only 30 groszy admission. Registrations for the exercises are accepted by Mr. Berger.

The board of the Small Traders' Association in Katowice announces that the secretariat is open every day from 1 to 9 midday [sic], Sunday from 10 to 12. The association's premises are at Kochanowskiego 11.

(L. S. [?]) The "Mishnayot" society existing in Katowice, which has renewed its activity: study takes place every Sabbath and holiday afternoon for three hours, and on weekdays before Minchah for one hour.

Needless to add that Jews who have an interest in the age-old Jewish study of Torah should enrol as members of the society.

Life in Chorzów. From the Small Traders' Movement.

At the plenary meeting, held under the chairmanship of Mr. Szpinger, the following board was constituted: Mr. Sandrer (president), Mr. Buchbinder (vice), Mr. Baldinger (secr.), Mr. Kac (treasurer), Messrs. M. M. [?] Kipkowicz, Szpigel and Barimherzig, who are also on the court of honour.
The secretariat is open every Monday and Thursday from 7 to 9 in the evening, where members are given any necessary legal information.
Incidentally, it is worth noting that the new board shows great intensity. Last week the market stall-holders came to the board with an outcry, because they were not being allowed to come to the market in Szarlej, which threatened many Jewish families with losing their livelihood. Thanks to the prompt intervention of the board, headed by Mr. Sandrer, with the Chamber of Commerce in Katowice as well as with the police authority in Szarlej, coming to the markets in Szarlej has been permitted again.
It is, however, also desirable to note that the members should also fulfil their duties towards the association by paying the monthly dues punctually, on which the existence of the association depends, it being the apparatus defending its members.
Relief Campaign for Działoszyce.

The Jewish community in Chorzów has undertaken a collection campaign for the stricken Jews of Działoszyce. The community has also issued a special appeal to the Jewish inhabitants, in which it describes the great distress of the Jewish flood victims in Działoszyce, who are threatened with perishing from hunger and various diseases.
On this occasion we draw the attention of outside collectors to the fact that collecting money for Działoszyce without the permission of the community is forbidden. As for those persons who do not hand over the sum to the community or do not come for permission, the matter will be reported to the local police authority.
"Corner" Shochet Fined.

Before the local district court an interesting trial took place on the basis of the indictment brought by the local Jewish community. In the dock sat the Mysłowice shochet Mendel Wasman and the local butcher Icchak Dawidowicz. The former was accused of engaging in illegal ritual slaughter, and the latter of bringing in meat from outside.
After hearing the witnesses [?] from the local rabbinate, the court fined Wasman 200 zł. Dawidowicz was acquitted.
From the Free-Loan Fund.

Dozens of Jewish families cannot obtain any loans from the Gemilut Chesed fund, because the borrowers do not find it necessary to repay the money they borrowed, and because of this other Jewish families suffer, who are struggling with a hard existence. If the borrowers felt for those needy Jews, they would come at once with their instalments, so that others could be helped.
Because of the board's very desperate situation, it was decided at the last meeting that those who do not pay their instalments will be published on the "black list".

On the Credit Bank

This Sabbath the general meeting of the Kredytowy[?] bank takes place, in which all members must take an active part, above all the small traders and peddlers.
For 3 years the bank's management has been pursuing such a "policy" as to push out all small traders, peddlers and market-stall keepers. Now a struggle is under way between the management and the small traders and peddlers, who find themselves in the most desperate situation because of the antisemitic pressure that pushes every single one of them out of their positions.
It is worth noting that the bank holds 140 thousand zł. of "frozen[?] capital", which brings no benefit at all. When a small trader or peddler wants to discount a couple of customers' bills, they are so "checked" that in the end the director Lipszyc declares he cannot accept the bills — while at the same time the "top of the heap"[?] receive discounts on tens of thousands of zł.
It is therefore high time that all small traders and peddlers come to the meeting.

When the heat is great...

(Yt"a) When a hellish fire burns from the sky and a heatwave beats from the blazing walls, gloomy thoughts take hold of the city dweller who did not take care in good time to be able, if only for a short while, to hide away in the forest shade or to dip in the refreshing waves of our sea. And yet only a little forethought[?] would have sufficed to be able to afford these pleasures.
It is enough to obtain a PKO savings book, so that from small deposits one will after a while have saved a little money, enough to leave the city walls and spend one's holiday pleasantly. Owning a PKO savings book is the guarantee of a pleasant holiday and allows one to enjoy many conveniences. One is spared guarding one's bit of cash on the road, and there is no need to fear thieves. Without any trouble, at any post office one can withdraw[?] a small sum from the savings book for current expenses.
While one is away, depositing cash, valuables and securities in a PKO safe also gives many guarantees of security.
First Yahrzeit of the Late Maurycy Rajner

Last Sunday, on the day of the first yahrzeit of Maurycy Rajner, a memorial service was held in the synagogue of the old-age home in Sosnowiec — where the deceased and his wife had been immortalised by a marble tablet — with the participation of the deceased's family and a large number of friends and public activists. The service was nicely arranged by the director of the old-age home, Mr. Mordechai Pargasl[?].
Later, at the local cemetery, the unveiling of the tombstone took place. Cantor Leichter with the choir sang a chapter of Psalms and recited an "El Male Rachamim". At the end Mr. Abraham Branicki gave a short speech about the virtues of the deceased.
The academy (commemorative assembly) in the hall of the Merchants' and Industrialists' Association turned out impressive. The large meeting hall was packed full. In front of the speakers' platform stood a portrait of Maurycy Rajner; the burning candles were decorated with fresh flowers.
In a solemn mood the chairman Mr. Józef Safer[?] opened the academy and in a longer speech pointed to the unforgettable loss of the person who embodied in himself the humane, the noblest and the most honest.
On behalf of the Charity Society Dr. Herzman[?] and Mr. A. Landau spoke. After each speech the memory of the deceased was honoured by standing.
In the musical part Miss Perczik (piano) and Mr. Fridman (violin), with piano accompaniment by Eng. Lejbowicz, took part.
From the Gemilut Chesed Fund in Pogoń

On Sunday the continuation of the annual general meeting of the members of the Gemilut Chesed (interest-free loan) fund in Pogoń took place.
Before proceeding to the elections Mr. Rozencwajg (of the Zawiercie G"Ch fund) called upon the sides to make peace and proposed that the general meeting adopt by acclamation a joint peace list of candidates from the existing board and the so-called "opposition"; but several persons from the "opposition" did not agree to this and demanded that elections be held at all costs, evidently wanting to achieve a complete victory.
The members then voted en masse and showed that they want the G"Ch fund, the only institution in Pogoń, to go on existing and not fall into the hands of those who want to destroy it.
By an absolute majority a board was elected consisting of Messrs. T. Altman (president), Fajerman (vice), Bradelski (treasurer), Harszwic[?] (vice), Blajcher (secretary), Kurland, Szykman, Skóra, Wasznica; deputies: Jakubowicz, Sztern and Najman. Audit committee: Glidman, Blum and Klajnberg; deputies: Abramowicz and Litmanowicz.
