We must take counsel about urgent aid.

(What will be done with the money collected in the Million Campaign?)
As is known, the „CEKABE“ [Central Society of Interest-Free Loan Funds] undertook in the winter[?] a broad drive to collect throughout Poland the „Million Campaign“, the sum of which was designated for productive aid to ruined and fallen people.
Regrettably, the drive did not catch on as it should have, and the desired result was not achieved.
For this very reason the moneys collected are lying untouched to this day and have not been used for any purpose whatsoever.
If the times were bad, if the situation was hard and catastrophic when the collection for the Million Campaign began, today the condition of the helpless and the hard-hit has become simply appalling, and it grows from day to day worse, harder, more catastrophic — literally to the point of having no way out.
And therefore, if it was bad and catastrophic then, now it is bitter and simply appalling, not knowing where is the way in and where the way out, so[?] that one must begin to think seriously about how to save people from ruin in the literal sense of the word.
As is known, the collected moneys were set aside only because the drive did not catch on. We do not know what the central office in Warsaw intends to do with them; in any case it would have been worthwhile to give the matter some thought and to hear an opinion. Surely no one will agree that because the Million Campaign did not catch on at all, the moneys that were collected should also lie untouched, and the community and the hard-hit Jews should get no benefit from them at a time when so much misery and poverty prevails among the broad masses.
Let us say, for example, Zagłębie and Upper Silesia — we did, after all, collect a quite respectable sum here, and it would certainly be worthwhile to take up this matter seriously.
We do not know whether we are right with our conscience if one can tolerate that at such a difficult time money should lie untouched and the community should derive no benefit from it?
In the winter[?] we heard that as much as the town would give, the Joint would add of its own, and also from the government an addition was supposed to come [as printed: „צוגעב-קומען“], so that we here in Zagłębie and Upper Silesia could have realised a sizable sum, from which the community would have had the chance to benefit greatly in one form or another.
As is known, the drive was created for productive aid to artisans, who can make their living from their trade only when one comes to their aid with the proper tools or machines they need for their trade. Certainly this is for a craftsman an invaluable help, thanks to which he can support himself and his family and not become a burden on society, if he does not want to start going hungry.
Certainly much would have been achieved with such support, since it is no small thing when one helps make productive a mass of common people who cannot help themselves for material reasons; and yet we do not say that it must stay this way. Above all, we do not want to impose our opinion on anyone. It may be that people will come with other plans, better and more realistic, and if they prove more practical and necessary, they can also be changed[?] for the good of the community.
It is therefore important, first of all, to confer about this question and to hear how the situation stands. We hold that Warsaw has enough practical experience and expertise in this field, so that one can listen to and perhaps also accept their proposals and projects, provided[?] they will bring benefit to those who need productive aid.
When people come together, they will hear — perhaps there are chances to create with the Zagłębie and Silesian moneys some kind of collective enterprises that could provide a living for a large public, common people who have been pushed out of their trades — would such a project, for example, then be a small gain?
On the other hand, we must not remain indifferent and helpless towards the question. We must push it to the foreground, lecture about it, give it a push[?] and make it urgent and topical.
The matter must not be postponed, because we find ourselves today in all too difficult living conditions. Moreover, the outlook is so pessimistic that we see before us no better and brighter tomorrow. We must not fool ourselves and say that we will just leave things as they are, because things as they are — each one of us sees it — are not good; and on top of that comes the drawback that things do not even stay as they are, but get steadily worse and worse, and the middling people, especially the middle-class people, are beginning to lose the ground from under their feet.
And if we live in such hard conditions, people's funds must be created, with which one would be in a position to help people, not to let them sink down into the deep abyss from which they will no longer be able to rise up again as human beings.
Money — if it was created by the people and from the outset was designated for the people — must not be left lying untouched when the Jewish situation is so depressed. One need only consider how to bring the community as much benefit as possible with it and, if possible, to enlarge it, in order to create something grandiose for the masses.
R. Let.
Morai verabotai, let us have a little talk — in Będzin the Talmud Torah has been closed

[Będzin — kehilla; Talmud Torah.] Two weeks ago the chronicle in our paper reported that the Talmud Torah (T.T.) in Będzin had been closed.
Much has already been written about the situation of the Talmud Torah. Well, is it worth writing at such length about such a matter?
Yes. It is not only worthwhile but indeed very necessary to have a talk about it and to draw certain conclusions.
We do not intend to put the question on a principled basis, and certainly not on the plane of secularism versus religion. Let us assume that such a religious need must in fact be satisfied. First of all, the kehilla may have duties in this direction; but let us also not deny a second, indisputable truth: that a large part of the Jewish population has other cultural needs, and these too must be satisfied, and towards them too the kehilla must bear certain duties.
But how does this look in the light of reality?
There is an orphanage. "Apikorsim" [heretics] run it; our kehilla is almost entirely free of any worry about it, and the "apikorsim" really do beat their heads against the wall, drag money out of the walls, cross the ocean — while our Orthodox activists have not given it even a moment's thought.
There is the TOZ society [Society for the Protection of the Health of Jews], again an institution for all Jews — and only the secular take care of it. A "flower" in the street [charity flower day], membership dues, knocking on the doors of all kinds of offices, dancing at the club, extracting [money] from Warsaw[?], the budget is covered — and the kehilla has not[?] the slightest worry.
And if we talk about libraries and all the other cultural institutions and cultural needs of the Jewish masses in Będzin — the kehilla has not the slightest connection with them.
Tens, if not hundreds of thousands of złoty a year Jewish Będzin pays for all sorts of needs of Jewish society, and all of this has not the slightest connection with the kehilla.
Talk to the Orthodox — after all they are the "rov minyan verov binyan" [the great majority] of Będzin's Jews, and if it is a matter of respected Jews, wealthy men — one finds them too among the Orthodox. So let them show us in which religious-social work these people are engaged.
Several times already there were threats to close the Talmud Torah, the melamdim [teachers] are off the staff[?], because it has not yet happened that, in the merit of "Talmud Torah outweighs them all", Orthodox activists should really try to take care of the Talmud Torah.
But rebbes and rabbis, "morai verabotai" [my masters and teachers] — for two weeks now the T.T. has been closed, and you have not let out a single groan lest poor children fall victim here.
And one more thing:
The secular activist can hope that for all his worries and cares, for all his toil and trouble, for the strength, time and money he sacrifices for the good of Jewish society, they will put up a tombstone for him after a hundred and twenty years; whereas the religious-Orthodox activist — he believes, after all, in a great reward, the World to Come awaits him, the gates of the Garden of Eden stand open before him; the mere size of that "honorarium" alone ought to turn our Orthodox activists into the boldest[?] in social work!
So why does it all look so upside down?!
—
It is also worth taking a look at the kehilla's budget book — who pays how much. We take the liberty of asserting that the main burden of the kehilla and of its budget is borne by the secular part of Jewish society. Such a tradition has been established for many years in the Będzin kehilla.
Gentlemen — on the contrary, let someone point out from which Orthodox Jews one receives voluntary[?] money for social purposes! Even the specialists in collecting money, the Zionists, do not find their way to such doors.
—
With this article we are not driven by combative motives — this is not the place for that; but some kind of accounting must surely be made at some point, the question must surely be raised, and so we thought it good to use the occasion of the closing of the T.T. to summon our Orthodox activists to a public "din Torah" [rabbinic trial].
The opposing party — if he has and wants to say something, by all means — the columns of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" are open and free to him.
Y. G—m.
In the Hot Days.

[Feuilleton — summer and leisure; Będzin and district.] By Y. L. Lawa [J. L. Lawa?].
(From the local "plaża" [beach]).

In the very middle of spring, when the "better" ladies' society was very busy [?] and preoccupied [?] with the dressmakers, the milliners and with choosing a spot far removed from the everyday places — to "rest" in the coming hot days and nights — a burning summer suddenly set in, with a deep-blue, clear sky and a naked sun. One had to throw off the just-sewn "hipsiuan" [?] costume, coat and "deszczówka" [?] [raincoat?], and simply put on last year's "deseniowa" [patterned] little dress...
So the hot spring really got on the modern woman's nerves, and she went about gloomy and cross with the whole world.
What bothered her was not so much that she was unable to make use of the spring season, as the hard question before which she had suddenly been placed. What does one do then [?] — and, as if out of spite, no winter fashion [?] has yet been seen [?] in town. At every opportunity, wherever and whenever young doctors' wives, patrons' wives, engineers' wives and directors' wives gathered — in the cinemas, the pastry shops, at the tailors' and milliners' — the only topic was: the hot spring, which had turned into a philosophical inquiry: what is more important? Or better said: what must a modern woman reckon with more? Is the main thing the weather, i.e. that a woman must dress only according to the weather, even if it does not agree with the newest fashion — or does fashion alone, la mode, play the leading role, even if it does not suit the weather.
This dispute went on so long until Madame Vernfas [?] came from Paris and she was the arbiter — not with any facts or arguments, but with the single word "Paris" she settled the question.
If women went about in woollen-cloth costumes and sweated not a little in those hot spring days — it was a sign that they were the "small-towners" [?] of the city who dress according to the "Parisian" fashion...

Quite differently did the broad masses greet the spring heat. They did not think about dressing, but kept on undressing. Men stayed in unbuttoned workers' blouses on their bodies, the women — in thin chintz dresses, through which, in the sunshine, the nakedness of the body shows through. Doors and windows are flung open [?] like the clothes on people, which gives the impression that they are opening their hearts and revealing their secrets to the dear and honoured guest who has come to gladden them [?].

A free summer — say the old folks — is a gift from God. You are [?] not tied to the narrow little bed with the short blanket; you can stretch out in length and breadth as much as your heart desires, straighten your bones, your back and all your limbs on the free floor, in the yard and in the forest, and above all feel for yourself [?] that you are a person equal with other people...
Right on the first Sabbath, from early morning, whole crowds of people streamed [?], young and old, some with baskets, some with bundles, bigger and smaller, in their hands, and some with [—] [?] — to the "Babske" [?]. Every little tree and wherever even a bit of shade shows itself is quickly occupied, as in a musical-chairs dance [?], where the one who is not nimble always remains without a chair.
Here, lordly, smaller and larger groups of people have spread themselves out on the grass [?], some in a waistcoat, some in a nightshirt, some with a stud [?] at the neck and some with a décolleté. One woman is burning her feet, another — her shoulder, and others — even their face. All [?] as at a [—] [?]; barefoot, not laced in, not embarrassed and free as at home...
Here a young woman [—] turns somersaults one after another and stays standing for a second on her head with her feet in the air. Here young fellows steal past with [—] [—] shouts [?], singing and whistling; they too look for shade, but [—]...

"Now," says a sparse-bearded man in blue spectacles, "a fragrant [?] cucumber with bread would be good, mmm, mmm, a fragrant [?] sweet [?] little cucumber. They (meaning the rich) eat [?] the young radishes with the cucumbers, and we have to wait until Tisha b'Av."
"On the other hand," a second one breaks in, with rolled-up sleeves, lying with his shoulder to the sky in a white nightshirt with brown speckles — a sign of the "night battles" that take place on his bed — "on the other hand, this winter [?] we were the first 'dacha-folk', not they."
"I," says a third, who was lying in blue underpants and looking for something in a basket, "I very much doubt who [?] draws in more — we the field air, or the trees the damp and bitter [?] sweaty smell of our heated bodies?"
And now their conversation was interrupted by a choral [?] song, which carried from afar and was soon taken up by many neighbours:
Merry, joyful, friends, let us sing
In honour of the summer, the beautiful one,
Mighty, splendid let our voice
Ring out,
High, far, together with the birds.
The talkers too forgot for a while about "us" and "them" and quietly hummed along:
Merry, joyful...
New Problems of Our Life

[Opinion — Polish Jewry; problems of the day.]
In the present hard times that we are living through, not only has the source of livelihood dried up among us, but also the source of problems, of thoughts about the further [?] organisation of our life. Not for nothing was it once said to the prophets, after the Jewish destruction, in the form of an imperative: "Comfort ye, comfort ye my people!" In our present-day destruction, too, the prophets, the spokesmen [?], do not know how and with what to comfort the people, how to find a foothold on the slippery downhill slope that is pushing us, it seems, impetuously into the abyss.
Brisk [Brześć] is not our problem. Upon Działoszyce there came a destruction by the hand of Heaven whose ruins [?] weigh ten times more than Brisk, and for Poland it is indeed a great national misfortune, but not a problem.
Our Jewish problem is not Brisk, which can be rebuilt, but that which must [?] torment us — the political-economic pogrom that is dragging us down.
And not only do we have no remedy for it, we are not even looking for one.
Our terrible misfortune is that we, an Eastern people with conservative moods and traditions, are still stuck quite deep in our national fatalism; and if the individual is still able to do something for himself, to seek a gulden's worth of livelihood so as not to perish from hunger, the community, the collective, is entirely dependent [?] and stripped of any worry for tomorrow. A people wanders in the dark and seeks no way out at all.
Fatalism dominates not only the Orthodox Jews, who carry in their psyche the belief in higher powers and the dreams of the Messiah, but also the national intelligentsia, who have turned secular, popular messianism into a practical movement, which inspires [—] millions of Jews, but creates opportunities for struggle, for victory and for advancement only for small groups — the whole bulk [?] of the people remains outside the influence of this movement and must watch, with staring eyes, the hopeless state of slow decline before it.
And even our hundred-percent materialists and nationalists, who want to forge the future of mankind only with the strength of the broad masses of the people, are not free of fatalism either; for while their comrades of the majority nation think about the future and at the same time consolidate their position [?] in unison with the nationalist circles, our socialists are at present complete political vegetarians: they get no pleasure whatsoever from the world, they stew in suffering and pain together with all the Jews, and console themselves only with ephemeral dreams of some distant future, whose contours nobody yet knows and which may perhaps come about only through some miracle..
And this dream-state, which has gripped almost all circles of our people, holds us captive as if under a spell and frees us from worrying and thinking about [?] our communal life.
A systematic tendency is advancing against us; racist consciousness is strong enough in the surrounding society and — why fool ourselves? — partly among ourselves too. We are in any case woven into general life by such thin threads that the slightest breezes [?] can tear them. One can almost state that the change is coming [not?] in reality, but in the world of beliefs and hopes. Instead of our gaze being turned, as until now, from what is near outward, we must now turn it back towards ourselves and into ourselves.
But our ghetto of today is no longer, and can no longer be, what the ghetto of old was, from the Middle Ages to the nineteenth century. Back then we had a terrible poverty, an old-time way of life, backwardness with respect to secular culture and civilisation — our spiritual fortresses were only the beth midrash, the cheder, the yeshiva and two or three old-fashioned societies of a social-philanthropic character. We may perhaps take pride in this, because our neighbours did not have even that.
But what use to us is the pedigree of the cemetery? Now the world has been turned upside down, and we too are becoming entirely different. Our neighbours have climbed with giant strides up the ladder of freedom, prosperity and civilisation, and we have dragged ourselves along after them; and if they push us back into the ghetto, we shall take with us the rays of light we have caught, the sensations of prosperity experienced or enjoyed, the concepts of secular civilisation, of progress, of social reconstruction. Our social baggage is considerably [?] richer and entirely re-formed; our medical care, school system, child welfare, spread of crafts, credit institutions and the like are no longer ghetto stalls, but fortresses of a well-founded sovereign [?] communal life.
Our own face, too, has changed [?] completely. There has grown up among us a youth, an intelligentsia, a society that can no longer be laid into the Procrustean bed ("Sodom bed") of the ghetto of old. All the vital and creative forces that seethe in the modern Jewish collective will not be content with the present organisation of the Jewish community, but will rebuild [?] it after their own image and likeness; even into the kehilla and the cemetery new people will come and create new conditions.
But the main thing is to adapt all our energies and potentials, the whole growth of our power of resistance and our zest for life, so that we can live in the newly created conditions.
P. K.
Underwear in Former Times

[History — the history of clothing and underwear; article from Vienna.]
It cannot be denied that shirts were worn even in very ancient times. There were[?] even times when only a very rich man wore a shirt, because it was more expensive than the other garments people wore.

At the beginning of the 16th century, when men's shirts appeared at the Leipzig fair, one cost no less than 10 pounds[?], and women's shirts too were still very expensive then, so much so that Queen Anne of France owned only 17 shirts in all.

True, these shirts were trimmed with silver and gold collars. King Charles the First, too, owned only a dozen shirts, which were adorned with a thousand metres of the finest and most expensive lace.

And even from the year 1739 it is known that for 12 shirts made for the wedding of a French princess, lace costing 625 thousand francs was used.

Shirts were worn only by day; of nightshirts nobody knew anything. In no list whatsoever up to the 18th century are nightshirts to be found, just as we rarely find socks[?].

Only later, in the 18th century, did people begin to wear shirts, but only on top, over the other clothes. Indeed, not many shirts were needed, since people rarely put on a new shirt. If the shirt got very dirty, a piece of clean linen was stitched on over it. Charles the Second, for example, owned only 3 shirts, and the chronicle of that time reports that he used to put on a new shirt every month.

It is a fact that Empress Eugénie vowed not to change into a new shirt until her husband had taken Ostend. She kept this vow from 1601 to 1604.

Women's drawers were worn only by old women or by maidservants while cleaning the windows. Later, in Holland, drawers were introduced for women when they went skating on the ice. These drawers were made of coloured velvet[?], mostly green, red and brown.

On the other hand, women wore a great many undergarments. In Spain, for example, it was the custom until the year 1870 that women wore eight petticoats in summer and ten to twelve skirts in winter. The outer skirts were of the finest velvet and satin with costly embroidery. The very lowest skirt was of linen.

Only at the beginning of the nineteenth century did people begin to wear linen underwear. At first it was made from the same linen that was woven at home and used to make sacks for grain. Such shirts could also be bought, and they cost about half a thaler apiece. Very refined people wore shirts of better linen, which cost up to twenty thalers apiece. Fine shirts for women were sold for up to forty thalers apiece.

In those days the greatest fashion was for the bride to weave linen and then sew shirts for the groom, and if a groom wished to give the bride a really fine present, he had six fine shirts made for her, which were the most beautiful gift...

Only around 1850 did people gradually begin to wear underwear as we still wear it to this day, with the high collars for men, which were always a source of jokes and of sweat[?], and which more than once made life a misery...

Z. Haber, Vienna.
Our Panorama.

[Zagłębie — weekly feuilleton; synagogues, Hasidim, mikvehs.]
"The sun also rises, and the sun goes down" [Eccl. 1:5] — the sun rises, sets and rises again. Such is the order of the world "from above", and so the winds[?] "go round". Thus, for example, the shul in Old Sosnowiec [Stary Sosnowiec][?] always held the top place in our "kingdom". If all the waters turned to ink, it still would not suffice to describe all the events that played out there over several years — a real Spanish war in miniature.
But the "Bastille" fell and everything went hush-quiet, so we feared that "the sun had set on our horizon". It turns out, however, that the fear was groundless: the sun did indeed set in the shul in Old Sosnowiec, but it rose in the beit midrash in the "Reden" colony.
And in that beit midrash the sun spread out in all its splendour and warmed[?] the limbs of the local worshippers, especially those who pray with the first minyan.
And the heat at "Reden" is so strong that the Jews there have completely forgotten their outside and home troubles — that the "Talmud Torah" is closed and several dozen poor Jewish children are taking "vacations"... O.Ch.[?], practically every Sabbath a public spectacle takes place in the beit midrash. The programme is varied. Sometimes the programme of such a spectacle is a "humorous" one: a Hasidic Jew steps up[?], whom they honour with revi'i [the fourth Torah call-up], and then the agitated man starts singing a little song entitled "Nie pa-yaren"[?]... Or one of the prayer leaders, if a great "scholar" takes a fancy to play a "joke", proclaims three days of Rosh Chodesh...
A "dead inhabitant" also takes part in the "performances" — that is the table that stood along the whole length of the above-mentioned beit midrash.
The "experts" even say that the table plays a large part in all this: the long "table" is the reason why the worshippers have acquired "short heads" and short-sighted eyes that do not see what is going on around them...
So the sages of the holy community of Reden began to think: what is to be done with the "wicked table"? A meeting was held, at which it was decided to apply the same verdict that King Solomon handed down in his day in the dispute between two mothers over a child — "Divide it"...
And that is indeed what they did: they cut the table through. Whether the experiment will have any effect, it is still too early to say. But that the Jews of Reden have nothing in mind but to stage spectacles in the beit midrash every Sabbath — that is a clear matter...

———

"In Pińczów it is already dawning" — there is such a folk saying, and among the Pińczów Hasidim in Będzin it is already "broad day": it is already so bright there that from the strong light "their eyesight has been ruined"[?], and they, poor things, do not see what is going on in the Jewish street. Among the Hasidim there is one who arouses sheer pity, because "he, poor man, does not see", and so he sometimes stumbles. His latest stumble happened on the day of the Brześć events: during the clash that took place at the "shulchan" [the bimah] he fulfilled the "ruling" of "a Jew who is a sagi nahor [blind]"...
Those in the know say that what worked on him was his love[?] for the aliyah to which he had been called; and when[?] the "sagi nahor"[?] — the special "caller" — honoured someone else with that same aliyah, the Torah-lover paid him for it "according to the law of Moses and Israel"[?]...
True, the rest[?] of the congregation was very indignant at the blind man's deed and stopped him. But the striker is not greatly to blame either. After all, he prays in the Pińczów shtibl, and "in Pińczów it is already dawning"...

———

The partnership agreement between the owners of the bath-houses (mikvehs, in the holy tongue[?]) in Będzin is also already "dawning".
The representatives of "Family Purity" [Taharat ha-Mishpacha] in Będzin thought very hard about how to "draw" the public in[?] — or rather, into the mikveh...
And "you have laboured and found": they thought and thought for a long time. Suddenly one of those present spoke up:
— I've got it!..
— What have you got? — everyone asked curiously.
— I have a plan that will without doubt[?] win over the whole world in general, and the men and women of Będzin in particular, and they will have to go...
— Wait: my plan is that a concern should be set up of both mikvehs, a sort of small joint-stock company, which will issue monthly coupons on which there should be no more than these three words:
— "Kupon do łaźni" [a bath-house coupon].
— I am sure[?] — the author of the proposal cried triumphantly — that "everyone will go". Why[?] — monthly tickets to the theatre, don't people take them? And when bread was handed out, didn't people stand for hours in the queue [ogonek][?]? That's how it is: where you need a coupon — people go...
— Psh-psh, oy-va[?]! — everyone went into raptures over the proposal. Wonder of wonders...
And writers have written that Reb Chaim ben.. and Reb Shlomo ben.. are forming a mikveh "concern", which will issue "coupons" for both sexes. They will go into the...
Among the points of the agreement it is also stated that the "Family Purity" society must be the driving force, the locomotive, which is to lead the coupon-holders into the...
But "Satan" too is not sitting with folded hands and is "working deeds", so that the holy flock should stop going, as a protest... And Satan is not short of excuses with which to catch them on the fishing rod, and he is indeed working deeds. People say that he has gained the largest number of followers among the "Torah-loyal".
The initiators want to justify it by the great heat, but be that as it may, the partnership agreement is already "dawning"...
Ben Amotz.

Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parshat Chukat

a) "This is the law: when a man dies in a tent" (19:14)
"This is the Torah — a man": man is the whole Torah; all worlds are included in him, the whole Torah..
•
R' Mendele of Kotzk [Kock] — so it is told — spent long years writing a treatise on man, which was to contain the entire Torah of man; he indeed called it "Torat ha-Adam" (The Teaching of Man). The treatise contained a whole... "smur"[?]; in the end it did not satisfy him, and he burned it.

b) "When a man dies in a tent" (ibid.)
"You are called adam, and the idolaters are not called adam." Yevamot 61.
In Hebrew[?] man is called by different names, such as adam, ish, enosh, gever. The last three mean: ruler. "Ish" and "enosh" mean householder, owner; "gever", again, derives from gevura, strength; only "adam" means — a human being.
"The idolaters are not called adam": among the idolaters there is no adam, simply a human being; there is only either a ruler or a ruled one. Only among Jews — "you are called adam". Only Judaism created the concept of a human being who is neither a slave nor a master.
Rabbi A. M. Smial[?].

c) "Hear now, you rebels" (20:10)
It is told that when the late Rebbe of Munkács [Mukačevo] was in the Land of Israel a few years ago, he paid a visit to R' Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld, who, as is known, was also a great opponent of Zionism. The Munkács Rebbe, as was his habit, began to curse and revile the Zionists. Noticing how this troubled R' Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld, he asked him:
— But you too are an opponent of the Zionists, aren't you?
To this R' Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld replied:
The Yalkut says that Moses our teacher was punished because he reviled the Jews: "Hear now, you rebels." The question arises: had[?] Moses already forgotten the punishment, when a short time later he said "You have been rebellious against the Lord" (Deuteronomy 9), and why was that not counted against Moses as a sin? The difference is this: when Moses said "You have been rebellious against the Lord", the tone of the words bears witness[?] that he was rebuking the Jews — and that is no sin; on the contrary. The tone of "Hear now, you rebels", however, speaks of anger. When wrath is mixed[?] into it, it is already a sin, even for a Moses...

d) "And he struck the rock with his staff twice" (20[?]:ibid.)
R' Chaim of Sanz [Nowy Sącz] was a great zealot; when he was told something bad about someone, he would immediately flare up in anger. Once R' Yehoshuale of Dzików[?] said to him:
— Is it possible, Rabbi of Sanz? Anger is, after all, a bad trait.
— The Master of the Universe also gets angry — answers the Rabbi of Sanz — in Berakhot, page 7, the Gemara says: "The Holy One, blessed be He, is angry every day, as it is said: 'a God who has indignation every day'"; well, one must walk in the ways of the Blessed Name...
R' Yehoshuale of Dzików[?] answers him:
— If you get angry because the Blessed Name is also angry every day, [—] make use of it[?] how briefly[?]. The Gemara says there: "And how long is His anger — a moment." So then, one gets angry also only for a moment a day...
And that is indeed Moses's wrong, that he struck "with his staff twice": for the first blow could be forgiven him — a moment; sometimes a person may fall into anger; but striking the rock a second time — that is already beyond the permitted measure of anger...

e) "With a heavy people and with a strong hand" (20:ibid.)
"And with a strong hand — through my grandfather's blessing: 'and the hands are the hands of Esau'." Rashi.
Esau too sometimes makes use of the merit of the forefathers — "through my grandfather's blessing"; but first of all he arms himself with a "heavy people", and only then does he come to the merit of the forefathers...
Imrei Chen.

f) "For the border of the children of Ammon was strong" (21:24)
"See[?] the love with which the Holy One, blessed be He, loved the Ammonites more than the Moabites. Concerning Moab He says (Deuteronomy 2) 'Do not distress Moab', but impose forced labour on them [kuti?]; but concerning Ammon it is written (ibid.) 'Do not distress them and do not contend with them'. And why all this? Because of the deed: the elder daughter named [her son] Moab brazenly, but the younger, who named her son modestly Ben-Ammi — to teach that the Holy One, blessed be He, does not withhold the reward of a fine utterance." Pesikta Zutrata.
Even a fine utterance, a good word, gently and beautifully expressed — a thing which has nothing to do with breaking one's traits, with fighting bad traits — this alone[?] is also a great thing; it can have historic consequences; a beautiful word can make history...
R' Simcha Zissel of Kelm [Kelmė].

g) "Come to Heshbon" (ibid., 27)
"Come, let us make the reckoning of the world." Bava Batra 78.
It is easier to make the reckoning of the world, the world-reckoning[?], than one's own reckoning, the reckoning of the individual... It is easier to criticise the corruption of the world than one's own corruption.
R' Mendele of Kotzk.

Things that happen...
That night on Okrzei Street.
In the middle of the night on Sunday, some residents of Okrzei Street were frightened by loud cries heard from one of the houses on the said street.
Only later[?] did it become clear that the whole fright was due to a "stray": one[?] of the most respectable householders had "paid" a visit to a lady acquaintance while her husband was paying visits elsewhere..
But Satan is an accuser, so he, Satan, that is, "egged on" the husband to go home already.
The night was a bright[?] one; the moonlight "peeped in" through the window and smiled at the loving couple...
Suddenly — a knock. Oh, woe is me, now I'll have a real scandal — said the little wife — but she quickly collected herself, pushed the "friend" into another room and opened the door.
— Why so late? — she asked her husband —
The latter, however, answered nothing to this, locked the door of the room in which the "friend" was, and began "counting out" to his wife, one by one.
The "arrested" man, hearing the cries of the beaten wife, called for help through the window. As is reported, the police wanted to draw up a report for disturbing the night's rest.
Ploni [So-and-so].
Z. Segalovitch (On His Visit to Zagłębie)

[Literature — a visit; Zagłębie.] Heshl Dantsiger.
We met in the editorial office of the „Zaglembier Tsaytung“. Yes, it is he, Z. Segalovitch! From his large beer-coloured[?] eyes the „eternal lonely one“ looks out and searches for himself; his fresh, brown-skinned face brings greetings from slopes, fields, [?] and flowers. Only the silver hair on his head reminds one: fifty-odd years; his slim, tall figure tells nothing of 35 years of work in the Yiddish literary field. His step is still a light one, his chest a proud one, though the shoulders are already a little bent — and yet one feels that this man still has far to go and to reach along his broad, far-reaching literary working path. He is full of literary plans and very productive. Recently his books appeared: „Dem habers[?] tokhter“ (The …'s Daughter), „Hoy-ganif“[?], „Lider far eynem“ (Poems for One); soon to appear: „Brider gemol“[?] and „Shures akht“[?]. The poems „Shures akht“[?] are splendid, original creations, which will be an ornament of Yiddish poetry — a new genre.
But when one begins to talk about new Yiddish books, it calls forth unhappy reminiscences about the Yiddish reader. And so indeed our conversation with Z. Segalovitch turned to Yiddish.
Through Segalovitch's softly coloured, lively conversation, heated with bitterness, the whole hard, fateful path of Yiddish runs like a kaleidoscope; at those years of the heroic rise of Yiddish Segalovitch's sad eyes light up[?]. In the bygone distance[?], in the pre-war and post-war years, when maskilic[?] assimilation received its first hard blow, he says, Yiddish was the most glorious dream, the strongest faith. People were ready to kill (with pen and ink!) for Yiddish. People believed, hoped, that Yiddish would get its true tikkun, would become the language of the whole Jewish people, and .. today such a disappointment that perhaps it is not worth killing a fly for the sake of Yiddish..(?)
Today's youth, which has merely had a sniff of a Polish elementary school, already turns up its nose at Yiddish. Yiddish books on the dusty shelves of the publishing houses, and the manuscripts — in the writing desks. Only a very small part of the conscious youth reads Yiddish. The leftist youth element, the working youth, seeks[?] only the „topical“, the Soviet, and reads — of course — Polish, because the supply of this sort of literature comes only in Polish — a small percentage in Yiddish.
With Yiddish today it has happened — so Segalovitch makes one understand with a parable — as with a beautiful woman, ten years after the wedding, barren. The husband and the relatives long for a child. They run to rebbes, to doctors, and, poor thing — God helped — she became pregnant! Joy, great delight for the grandmother[?]... but; oh, a misfortune happened: the beautiful woman, God save us, miscarried. And the same happened with Yiddish: it had already developed nicely, great values had been created in prose and poetry, young talented forces had joined — fine, very[?] fine, but one wants a child — a future; a campaign began, propaganda, agitation; Segalovitch himself has to his account a huge propaganda tour for Yiddish in several dozen places. Good hopes began to show — a pregnancy! But what did it turn out to be[?]? The youth is far from Yiddish — a stillborn child! The future is fog[?]!..
The Yiddish book has become a „khoyzer al hapsokhim“ (a beggar going from door to door); one knocks on the doors of Jewish homes: buy a Yiddish book! If the reader does not come to the book, the book goes to the reader. Woe and alas to such a path..
Segalovitch waves his hand: eh, why talk so much, why pour salt on the wounds...
Less talk, more action!
Is it possible to accomplish something in our Jewish Zagłębie, for Yiddish, for the Yiddish book? Let those called to it come (if they dare [?]...) and try.. because, after all, the situation is not yet so bad. More effort, responsibility, can lead out of this situation to broader, brighter horizons. — — —

A. Zaglembier — The Living Corpse (13)

[Literature — serial novel ("The Living Corpse"), instalment 13.]
A. Zaglembier [pen name].
(A most thrilling novel of Jewish life in Zagłębie before and during the World War). 13)
Summary of the beginning of the novel.
On a summer evening before the World War, when two Cossacks were to transfer the dangerous bandit "Szmulek Łapka" into the Piotrków prison, they were suddenly attacked on the way to the Będzin station by two disguised "strażniks" [guards] — Łapka's helpers. The Cossacks were found the next morning lying bound with gagged mouths, and Szmulek "Łapka", freed, fled towards the Gzichów road and hid somewhere.
That same evening, and almost at the same hour, the universally respected, solid collector [bill-collector] Yosl Wertheim — a father of three children — suddenly vanished. His wife Sore'tshe runs about the town terribly desperate, searching for him in every possible hiding place in all of Zagłębie. But Yosl Wertheim has vanished like a stone in water..
On the fifth day the pockmarked Matek reports to police inspector Charecki and tells him that on that day he had seen Wertheim walking on the Gzichów road together with the Christian Magda Komarska — a pretty young shiksa whom Matek had been courting with a view to marriage.
Magda is arrested at once. During the interrogation she declares that on the same day on which Wertheim disappeared they had quarrelled, because Wertheim wanted to give her money to go to Katowice and have an operation so that their "illegitimate" child would not be born. Charecki then goes to Wertheim's wife Sore'tshe and tells her of her husband's love affair with Magda, but Sore'tshe does not believe it and declares that her husband had no money on him. But when she goes over to the cupboard, she sees that the several hundred roubles that had been saved are gone, and she gives up hope for her vanished husband.
Some time later the Cossacks, while bathing in the river, found the dead body of a man, on whom a passport in the name of Yasek Wertheim was found. Wertheim's wife is sent for, and several Jews are taken [?] to identify whether this is Yosl Wertheim.
Now read on.
It took several minutes before each of them had mastered within himself the feelings of horror and disgust at the sight of the thoroughly rotted, drowned dead man. Two of them indeed could not bear it and immediately, on the spot, began to faint, and they had to be led aside.
Charecki took the others by the hand and, together with each of them, went up to the dead man, asking:
— Well, do you recognise Yasek Wertheim in him [?]?!
Not wishing to meet the same end as those two who had fainted, and also unable to bear the dreadful stench that rose from the drowned man, three men answered at once, without any scrutiny:
— Yes, that is he..
— Yosl Wertheim...
— I recognise him quite precisely..
And they left the dreadful spot at once, not themselves believing in their identification; it surely looked as though the three Jews had merely wanted to satisfy their earlier curiosity — to take a look at the drowned man.
Among the "identifiers", however, there were also several Jews with stronger nerves, who were not frightened by the sight of a dead man, and whom the dreadful stench did not drive to fainting either.
And it was precisely these Jews who voiced the first doubts concerning the identity of the dead man..
By the face it was quite impossible to establish any resemblance to the vanished Yosl Wertheim, because it was no longer a face, only some peeled, decayed, bloated [?] mass with a half torn-off nose. Yet certain facial features had still remained in a normal state.
— No, it is impossible for me to recognise him — one finally says.
— And you, what do you say? — Charecki asks a second one.
This was indeed one of Wertheim's best friends, and he answers with certainty after a longer look:
— No, in this dead man I recognise no resemblance whatsoever to my vanished friend Wertheim; he had a much shorter forehead.
— One cannot rely on that alone; can you point to further signs?..
— Yes, the hair of the head is different too; Wertheim did not have such dark hair...
— You know that for certain?
— Quite certain.
— Wertheim was also not as tall as this one — another of the Jews speaks up — he was even shorter than me.
— One cannot yet go by that; a man who lies long in water always becomes bigger and longer.
— Bigger perhaps yes, but not longer.
— In any case, you know — now the commissioner too addresses Charecki — that one cannot always rely on a mere document; above all it is hard to believe a document when it is found in the hands of a d e a d man.
— Do you seriously think that this is not the vanished Wertheim?
— I do not say that, but we have not yet heard from anyone who would say for certain that it is he..
— And I am convinced that it is, because I know precisely the whole course of the tragic event; I shall also bring Magda Komarska down to this spot, and then she will surely remember what she did with Wertheim that evening...
— That is a separate matter.
— And I think it is one and the same matter. Besides, here is Wertheim's wife herself already. It seems, Mr. Commissioner, that her identification can be believed.
— Yes, if she recognises him, one can believe it, because a wife always knows some special mark on her husband that others do not know about...
— Step aside, let her through!..
With her head deeply bowed Sore'tshe approaches that dreadful spot. She strains all her strength not to fall off her feet, which from time to time give way...
She already knows what she has now been called here for... On the way the strażnik [guard] told her everything. Her heart gave a painful tremble, a cold shiver ran through her body, but she no longer wept and no longer had convulsions as in those first days, before Charecki told her of the dreadful secret that had bound the father of her children to the shiksa.
For since that day Sore'tshe had begun to look with quite different eyes at her own misfortune...
Yosl's shameful betrayal — and with whom, at that! — had at one stroke torn out of her all the love and faithfulness she had always borne her husband, and therefore she was not so terribly shaken now either, when she was called to identify her dead husband. She thought that really only God's judgement had taken place here, the judgement that must strike all those fathers of children who want to bring shame and mockery upon their wife and home.. And perhaps it is better that it happened this way; better that an abscess be lanced at once than let it grow...
Yet, on reaching the spot and bringing the dreadful [word uncertain] figure close before her, Sore'tshe sprang back with a stifled wild scream, and she had to be held under the arms so that she would not fall.
And it took a long time until she finally calmed down. Charecki and the other policemen too spoke to her such gentle, soothing words, just as one soothes a crying child.
— For God's sake, Mrs. Wertheim, you are not a child, you must calm yourself.
— Well yes, it is very unpleasant to look at such a sight, but you yourself must surely also know whether you still have to wait for your vanished husband, or whether you have already found him, unfortunately, in such a state...
— Look more closely, you need only confirm whether this is h i m, or...
At long last Sore'tshe overcame within herself all those evil and at the same time loathsome feelings. After all, the people are right; never mind herself, she must also know what to answer the children at last: "Do they still have a father somewhere or not?"..
And boldly, quite unlike her nature in such painful cases, Sore'tshe walks up very close to the dead man, who lies on the grass with a packed little mound of sand at his head. For a long time she studies the man of whom she must say that this is her former husband Yosl Wertheim... and longest of all she looks at the dead man's face, which is so mangled and torn that it is truly hard for her to recognise whether this is really Yosl's face..
(To be continued).

A Delegation of Będzin Synagogue Worshippers at the Rabbinate.

[Humour — "Der Kokh-Lefl"; Będzin — religious life.]
This week a delegation of the worshippers of the Będzin [Great] Synagogue came to the rabbinate to ask a question: when does Rosh Chodesh Tammuz fall?
The religious judges (morei hora'ah), hearing the strange question, grew angry and cried out:
— Jews, what is with you [?]. Don't you know that Rosh Chodesh Tammuz was on Wednesday and Thursday of the week of parashat Korach?
— Don't hold it against us, — the leader of the delegation explained — we were misled by the shammes.
— How so?
— The present shammes did indeed bang on the table (bimah) on Tuesday at Maariv and call out: "Ya'aleh ve-yavo".
At once a second bang was heard from the old shammes, who sang out in the Gemara chant:
— "It shall neither go up nor come"...
— Ah... hm... — the dayanim mumbled, and told the delegation to go home.

Barukh: What don't you understand, Noah? God afterwards gave Job back twice as much of everything; [?] had He taken Job's wife as well, He would have had to give him back two wives — and He did not want to punish him that severely...

At the Butcher's.
Customer (to the butcher): Reb Itzik, give me a good piece of meat, but without bones.
Butcher: Every beast has bones, you yourself too..
What's Happening in Zagłębie? — Będzin: Dozens of Jewish Shop Signs Smeared with Tar.

Friday, 9 Tammuz 5697 — piątek 18 czerwca [1]937.
Będzin
A delegation of the Jewish merchants' associations at the deputy starosta's.
On the night before Sunday dozens of signs of the Jewish shops on Małachowskiego and Kołłątaja streets were smeared [with tar]. The hooligan work was carried out especially on the freshly painted walls around the shops.
The smearers by mistake also smeared the sign of a Christian shop.
In connection with this a meeting of representatives of the merchants and small traders took place, who decided to go in a delegation to the starosta and hand him a memorandum on the matter.
The delegation, consisting of Messrs. Rubiglicht [sic, for Rubinlicht], Michał Lamin[?] and Goldsobel[?] (of the Merchants' Association), Y. Ross and D. Gitler (of the Small Traders' Association), was received by the deputy starosta, who promised to issue the appropriate order on the matter.
Exhibition of Pupils' Work.

At the A. N. Sh. Fürstenberg Gymnasium an exhibition has been opened of various practical objects made by the pupils of the gymnasium.
The exhibition will be open until next Tuesday.
Summer Colonies of 'Ognisko'.

Following the pattern of past years, the Society of Jewish Academics 'Ognisko' in Kraków, together with the Jewish Medical Circle, is organising summer colonies in Zakopane and on Hel. Both colonies are situated in the most beautiful surroundings, with splendid villas and comfortable premises. The colonies also have a social character: the programme provides for a series of excursions into the Tatras, the Pieniny, an excursion to Gdynia, Danzig, etc.
The price for 4 weeks in Zakopane is 88 zł., on Hel 140 zł.
Registrations and information: the secretariat of 'Ognisko', Kraków, Przemyska 3, tel. 107 64.
A 14-Day Excursion to Paris.

The Society for Knowledge of the Country is organising: 1) a 14-day excursion to Paris for the International Exhibition, in July and August, for 395 zł., with all expenses already included; 2) summer colonies in Druskieniki, 205 zł. (a month), Karwia[?], 225 zł. (a month) and Zakopane (170 zł. a month); 3) a 21-day excursion to Yugoslavia in the months of July, August and September, for 495 zł.
Registrations and information: the secretariat, Kołłątaja 45, from 16 to 17 o'clock.
—o—
Permitted to Collect 50 Per Cent of the Budget.
The supervisory authority has permitted the kehilla board to collect one half of the kehilla budget for the year 1937.
—o—
Window Panes Smashed in the Middle of the Night.
On the night before Monday several window panes were smashed in the apartment of Dr. Volkovisky[?].
—o—
Jews Among Themselves...
On Wednesday morning two young Jewish men beat each other bloody on Satchevka[?] street. The brawl made a dreadful impression on the passers-by.
—o—
From the Second Floor onto the Pavement.
In Grodziec[?] the 26-year-old sportsman Zagórny[?] jumped from the second floor onto the pavement with the aim of committing suicide.
Zagórny, who was seriously injured, is fighting for his life.
Agudah More Moderate on the Rabbinate Question

This week the president, Mr. Fürstenberg, received a delegation of the Agudah leaders on the rabbinate question.
The delegation declared to Mr. Fürstenberg that they are ready to give up the rabbinical seat, on condition that their candidate Levin becomes 'podrabin' [deputy rabbi].
As we are informed, the national camp is putting forward a second proposal, namely that R' Mendel Levin be accepted as moreh hora'ah [religious decisor], on condition that he withdraw his candidacy as rabbi.
Dispute Between the Ne'emanim [Supervisors] and the Butchers.

In connection with the reduced meat quota, the butchers plead retraction and want to rid themselves of keeping the ne'emanim [kashrut supervisors], who receive 15 gulden a week each; at best they want to cut the wages by half.
Since the ne'emanim do not agree to this, a sharp dispute has broken out between the ne'emanim and the butchers.
As we are informed, the local rabbinate has handed the matter over to Rabbi Kh-a-m-y-y-s[?].
Head of the Tax Office Dies Suddenly

On Tuesday, while on duty, the head [naczelnik] of the local tax office, Mr. Plavak, died suddenly.
The doctors who were called established that Plavak died of a heart attack.
He was 55 years old.
The Existence of the Talmud Torah Depends on the Kehilla's Subsidy.

Under the chairmanship of the president, Mr. Fürstenberg, a meeting of the board was held on Tuesday in the premises of the Talmud Torah, which considered the question of its further existence.
A discussion developed on this, in which the kehilla board and council, which had struck out the subsidy for the Talmud Torah in the amount of 1,700 zł., were very sharply censured.
Finally a resolution was adopted to turn to the kehilla representatives with a protest that, if the subsidy is not paid out, the whole responsibility for the 400 poor Talmud Torah children falls on the kehilla.
Important for housewives.

[Będzin — advertisement set as news (advertorial).] The incomparable booklet of recipes by Dr. Oetker A.G., “The Good Housewife Bakes Herself”, is available in all grocery (colonial-goods) shops, bookshops and from the representatives of the Oetker firm. The price has been reduced to 30 groszy. The booklet is invaluable, containing [?] a great number of recipes for baked goods and the like.
Sosnowiec — Concentration of all relief committees for Działoszyce

[Sosnowiec — relief; Działoszyce.] The local relief committee for the afflicted Jews of Działoszyce has, through the YSA [?], approached all similar relief committees in the country with a proposal that all the committees concentrate their efforts in order to work out a common plan of work in general, and above all that the money collected be used for constructive purposes.
Committees that understand the proposal should apply to Bernard Jaski in Sosnowiec, Targowa 15.
— The local committee has sent 4 crates of linen and clothing to Działoszyce. The money collection has so far reached 2000 zł. There is, however, still a large part of the local Jewish population, among them well-to-do Jews too, who have not yet fulfilled their duty toward the hundreds of homeless, hungry and naked sisters and brothers in Działoszyce.
Midwife sentenced to a year in prison.

[Sosnowiec — court.] The trial of the midwife Gnurkowska [?], who had performed a forbidden operation [abortion], took place before the local district court. The midwife was sentenced to 1 year in prison and to pay 100 zł. The patient too was sentenced to a month's arrest.
When did work on the orphanage begin?

[Sosnowiec — orphanage; correction.] In the previous issue of our paper we reported that work on the building of the orphanage had begun on Saturday afternoon. As it turned out, however, we had been badly informed, because in fact the first work began on Friday.
7000 zł collected for Brisk.

[Sosnowiec — relief; Brisk.] The relief committee for the afflicted Jews of Brisk (Brześć), under the leadership of Advocate Kowalski [?] and Dr. Meladyssa [?], is working intensively. By the end of this week the collection has reached 7000 zł. There is, however, still a large number, among them well-to-do people too, who have not yet fulfilled their brotherly duty.
Theft at the flat of notary Sałak. Two hours later the stolen goods were found.

[Sosnowiec — crime.] Through the open window a thief got into the flat of the notary (rejent) Mr. Sałak and stole clothing and valuable objects from there. The police, on receiving the news of the theft, undertook an energetic action, and 2 hours later the stolen goods were found.

A victim of the beach
[Sosnowiec — incident.] In broad daylight a naked young woman suddenly appeared on Wiejska street. It later turned out that the woman was a victim of the beach: from the extraordinary heat she had suffered a fit of madness.
—o—
Successful campaign for the Hebrew University.
[Sosnowiec — Zionism; Hebrew University.] The campaign for the Hebrew University in Jerusalem was conducted by the energetic activist, the chairman [?] Mr. Józef Tafer. The campaign brought an unheard-of result: about 5 thousand zł was collected for the purpose.
—o—
Out of jealousy...
[Sosnowiec — incident; suicide.] [—] Górski (Piłsudskiego 29) suspected his wife of infidelity. This week he had words with her, and when the woman went out of the house he hanged himself.
The baby is born, but it is not alive — the “sulking dance” between the kehilla board and council.

[Sosnowiec (?) — kehilla; budget.] As our readers know, the kehilla board has drawn up a new budget project. The work on the budget took nearly 3 months, but as the saying goes: “better late than never”. At last the budget was completed and also adopted by the board, but despite this the budget is for the time being not alive, because the presidium of the kehilla council does not want to call a meeting of the parnassim [councillors]. Why is hard to say, but according to the rumours going around the matter has to do with a certain party which wants to have the influence over kehilla life.
From the Bookkeepers' Association.

[Sosnowiec (?) — associations; bookkeepers.] On Tuesday the first information and discussion evening took place at the association's premises, with the participation of a fairly large number of members, at which the board informed those assembled about its activity to date and the association's plans for the future. A number of topical bookkeeping questions were also dealt with, on which a very interesting discussion developed that showed clearly how useful it is to introduce such discussion meetings.
— In the near future a lecture by the architect Wilczyński will take place at the association's premises.
Punishment for insulting the President.

Before the local District Court the trial took place of a certain Machura of Dąbrowa, who during a conversation on the tram insulted the President of the State.
Machura was sentenced to 8 months in prison. The sentence is suspended for 3 years.
In honour of the end of the school year.

On the initiative of the local Jewish gymnasium a festive prayer service was held in the synagogue with the participation of Rabbi[?] Beger[?], who delivered a Hebrew speech to the Jewish student youth.
Great applause was evoked by the pupils' procession with its own orchestra at its head.
Tragic accident with an 88-year-old Jew.

In the house of M. Haberman in Zawiercie[?] lived the 88-year-old Yankel Silberberg. Last Sabbath at dusk he went down to the cellar for sour milk, but while going down into the cellar he fell from the stairs and suffered a concussion.
A few hours later Silberberg died.
Life in Kielce

[Kielce — section; a true story.] Friday, 9 Tammuz 5697. — Friday, 18 June 1937.

The husband "shoots" with... a chocolate revolver, and the wife confesses to betrayal.

When Gutsze G—n got on the bus with her two children to go off to the summer lodgings, she saw the summer sun for real for the first time; she felt comfortable and free — for several weeks she would lead an independent life, she herself would work out the plan of the day and would not be so harnessed [?] in chains as she is all year long with her husband.
God forbid, she does not hate her husband — on the contrary, she is very faithful and devoted to him. But it is hard for her to bear his groundless jealousy: he comes in — doesn't say a word, he is already angry. If something has been going on, and if the "something" happens to be a young man — he torments her with questions: Who? After what? What for? And she must always "confess" that this one told her this, and that one — that. And if she came back from a walk, she found him nearly mad with rage: where had she been? With whom? Is she telling the truth?
All this, however, did not prevent Gutsze from really having [?] a close friend, with whom she shares all her sorrows and joys and without whom it would be very hard for her to get through the days and the weeks.
That is why she was so glad when she left for the dacha. Her husband armed himself [?] with his mother, who became the guard of her daughter-in-law.
On Friday afternoon the husband went out to her. His mood too was a very good one. The first week his wife and children spent [?] in the forest, far from Kielce, under his mother's supervision. So in town he bought various presents, among them a chocolate revolver for his 7-year-old little son.
Coming into the house, the husband put down his briefcase, took out the "revolver" and went to look for the boy, who meanwhile was playing outside among the trees. Then the husband took a fancy to imitate a scene from a film. When his little wife came running in from the forest to greet her husband, she found him standing with a revolver in his hand.
"My death or your death," he cried out, imitating the actor in the film, "and perhaps the death of us both — tell me what happened! Who is the traitor?"
Gutsze was truly frightened.
"Put the revolver down."
"No, I know everything and only want to hear what you have to say."
"But I'm not guilty, I didn't know he also lives here... I met him by chance in the forest, we walked a bit of the way together, he asked me to come in for a moment to see his room, my children were with me, nothing happened at all."
Only after this "confession" did the husband really begin a thorough investigation, and — may such days be said of the enemies of Israel — such days as this couple's first Sabbath turned into.
Little by little everything was cleared up: both the chocolate revolver and the paper betrayal.
Sunday morning the couple packed their things and, with the mother-in-law and the children, went back to Kielce. Gutsze declared that her husband would have no peace in town, and the husband too agreed that it would be best if Gutsze were beside him in Kielce.
And so, because of a chocolate revolver, a dacha season and a Jewish family were wrecked.
A thousand złoty "compensation".

[Kielce — a true story; divorce.] From a nearby small town a young woman came to Kielce to look for a job. Here she began to play the part of an intellectual and flirted with her good looks and romantic air. Young men desired her company, but she declared that she was untouchable — she was a married woman, she had a husband who was mortally in love with her. That was indeed true: she really did have a husband, but she had run away from him. Here she went walking properly with a strange young man, whom everyone took to be her husband. But this was her lover, with whom she had already prepared in good time, even before divorcing her first husband. The kosher married woman wrote to her husband that he should come to Kielce and everything would be good and fine again.
The husband came, and here she introduced him to his future successor — a big-boned fellow, a hero, a "surowy chłop" (Polish: a rough brute), before whom the husband simply trembled. He saw that the matter [?] was settled, and he had to — under the "rozkaz" (Polish: order) of his stormy-tempered little wife and under the harsh word of the lover — give a get (divorce bill) and on top of that pay her, for the 12 lines [of the get], a thousand złoty "compensation".
Jewish Youth!

[Piotrków — education; vocational training; public appeal.] The day is drawing near when you will leave the "powszechna" [public elementary] school for good.
In the present, extremely difficult time of crisis, which is pregnant with great social upheavals; in the epoch of the most terrible antisemitism — this is for you, young man, a very responsible turning-point.
You must now decide by which road you will go consistently towards your independent tomorrow, and the roads are various:
The old trade-and-dealing of your grandfathers and fathers, from which you are being mercilessly pushed out, and which history has in any case condemned to die out.
The morbid striving among Jews for a doctor's diploma, for the free professions, which in our times are already a sheer surplus and unemployment. For example: the Association of Jewish Engineers in Poland has registered barely 5 thousand engineers, of whom a thousand work in various branches of trade — not in their profession — and 4 thousand engineers are completely unemployed; the same is true of doctors, lawyers, teachers and the like, not to mention that attaining secondary and higher education is bound up — under present conditions — with colossal formal, material and social-Jewish difficulties. Secondary and higher education is nowadays an expensive luxury, accessible only to the very rich.
There remains therefore for you, youth of the broadest masses of the people, only the one consistent and healthiest way out — learning a trade. In the course of 3 years of study you become an independent, productive person, for whom the whole world is open, because your hands, which can create and build, will stand in for any language.
But a trade must today — in the times of [—] — be learned not in an old-fashioned, primitive, unhygienic private workshop, but in a modern craftsmen's school, which teaches the trade both practically and theoretically and also supplements the necessary amount of general education.
Therefore, young man —
Do you want to become a productive and thereby useful working person in society?
Do you want never in the future to be a burden to anyone?
Do you want the wide, beautiful world to be open to you?
Become a pupil in a craftsmen's school!
Society for the Spreading of Crafts and Agricultural Work among Jews in Piotrków [Piotrków Trybunalski].
The Necessity of Life

[General — class lottery; promotional piece.] We are living through extraordinarily complicated times. Whether in the field of international politics or in the economic field — wherever one may turn, we see that mankind is seeking, with titanic efforts, new ways and forms of life[?], because the existing reality no longer satisfies it.
On a smaller scale individual persons live through the same thing, and to this are added personal worries and troubles, from which no one, not even the best situated, is free. How[?] hard is the situation of those who with difficulty earn the means needed to maintain their existence and who lose their strength in the struggle for "the right to a place under the sun" for themselves and their own...
New forms of social order — that is the goal of our most secret strivings. It is still far off[?] today, and we do not even know what shape it will take. But each of us must remember the necessities of everyday life, what he must have already today or in the near future, if he wants to exist at all.
Hard, exhausting work awaits him, and it can be eased by possessing certain relief funds and drawing on them at particularly difficult moments. Thus the striving of every person to create such relief funds for himself is natural, and to this end very enterprising individuals use every opportunity to settle the most urgent problem, such as, for example, playing in the class lottery.
The said opportunity exists now too, because the drawing of the first class of the 39th lottery already begins on Tuesday. One must therefore hurry to buy a ticket.
After the Blessing "Borei Minei Besamim" — a Stink Bomb

[Koziegłowy[?] — wedding; incident.] In Koziegłowy[?] a wedding took place last week, and [—] as a wedding in a shtetl is one of the rarities, there was indeed merrymaking at table and bench. But the joy was somewhat disturbed.
On Saturday night, after Havdalah, a stink bomb "flew in" through the open window.
The General Zionists and the 20th Congress

[Poland — Zionism; 20th Zionist Congress; elections.] The Central Committee (C.C.) of the Organisation of General Zionists in Poland (Group B, "Velt-Farband" [World Union]) has lately developed a great work of unification for the election campaign to the 20th Zionist Congress: [e.g.[?]] a large number of circulars sent to all towns in the provinces about the shekel campaign, and a series of visits made by members of the C.C. and the party council.
A very great impression was left in Radom by the visit of the President of the C.C., Mr. L. Lewite[?], who at a closed meeting of the most respected Zionists lectured on the most topical problems in Zionism and Eretz Israel.
Eng. Yosef Swan[?] took part in a district conference of Zagłębie, at which there were representatives of Sosnowiec, Będzin, Dąbrowa Górnicza and a number of smaller towns.
The member of the C.C. presidium, Adv. B. Płotucki, set out in a big lecture in "Soyon"[?] the election platform of the Velt-Farband for the Congress, and on the spot an organising committee was formed for a branch of the Velt-Farband in Poland[?].
A number of towns were also visited by members of the C.C. and the party council: A. Y. Zeitlin (Brisk [Brześć], where a district secretariat for Polesie was formed), S. Barman (head of the district secretariat for Volhynia), Y. Grawewicz[?]. In the near future larger meetings will be organised in Białystok, "Birnatsh"[?] and Volhynia.
According to reports received, the members are taking a very active part in the shekel campaign, and everywhere energetic preparations are being made for the election campaign, which will ensure the success of the list of the General Zionists (Velt-Farband).
Appeal of the Chamber of Commerce to Help the Victims of the Flood
[Sosnowiec — Chamber of Commerce; flood.] The Chamber of Commerce in Sosnowiec has published an appeal to help the victims of the flood in the Kielce voivodeship.

In Częstochowa it is quiet.

Yesterday at 4 o'clock in the afternoon we were informed by telephone from Częstochowa that it is already quiet there. The streets have regained their normal appearance, the Jewish shops are opening, except on Warszawska[?] street. A committee has been formed to help the victims. Some 300 victims are being registered at the kehilla.

„Treyf“ butchers intervene so that the shochtim should not take the „kishkes“ from the kosher butchers...
It has been the custom since olden times[?] that from every animal found kosher in the slaughterhouse[?] the shochtim receive the so-called „kashrut“, i.e. a little fat, intestines and the like.
This[?] week a delegation of the Jewish butchers in Sosnowiec — those who have no licences (concessions) to sell kosher meat — applied to the kehilla administration[?] with the request not to allow the shochtim to take from their „kosher“ colleagues the above-mentioned „gifts“ (matanot).

Income from the badge sale for „TOZ“.
On Tuesday in Sosnowiec and on Wednesday in Będzin badge sales were held for the „TOZ“ society [Society for the Protection of the Health of Jews]. The income was 255 zł. in Sosnowiec and 264 zł. in Będzin.

100 poor Jewish children to a summer colony.
Next week the „Dobroczynność“ [Charity] society in Sosnowiec will send some 100 poor Jewish children to a summer colony.

Rabbi Chmiedes accosted.
On Monday at about 8 in the evening, as Rabbi Chmiedes was walking to the railway station in Będzin, he was accosted not far from the station by a hooligan, who gave the rabbi a shove.

Swallowed 4 teeth.
Yesterday, while eating lunch, Mrs. Landauer, Będzin (3 Maja [street] 7), swallowed 4 [false] teeth.

„Pages[?] of Life“.

On meat for the Jewish colony in Sławków.
As is reported, there is a slim[?] prospect that the Jewish summer colony in Sławków will [—] receive kosher meat, because the quota (contingent) in Sławków is small even for the local Jewish population. Life in Chorzów. A General Meeting Must Be Called (Addressed to the Present Board of the Artisans' Association in Chorzów)

[Upper Silesia — Chorzów; artisans' association, letter of criticism.] Recently an extraordinary general meeting was called, to which barely 7 persons came, because the board was afraid to invite more, since they know that their "little benches" [seats] may fall.
As is known, an incident occurred between one member and several board members, over the deceiving of the members with lies.
In general the board has lately brought disharmony into the ranks of the best members.
It is therefore high time that the board resign by itself and convene a general meeting of all members who were still there 2 years ago — at that time the general meeting strengthened the existence of the association — and if a board is elected again with the first founders at its head, the association will regain its former standing in the whole town as well as with all municipal authorities.
At the same time all former loyal members are advised: if you have not received any invitation by post, you will have a sign that the board is afraid of you and wants as few members as possible to come to the meeting.
It is therefore desirable that the members who are artisans talk over the question of raising the artisans' association into a powerful Jewish organisation in our town of Chorzów.
This is the demand of the great majority of the nationally-minded artisans, who also have an understanding of providing for the [needy?] journeymen in the future.
Menachem.

Less Use of the Wagon — A New Circular from the Finance Ministry

[Taxes — Finance Ministry circular.] The Finance Ministry has recently sent out a circular to all tax offices, No. 1-37 3503, in which it points out that officials of the offices [urzędy] carry off the goods on which a seizure [zajęcie] is made into the office's warehouses, although there are no justified reasons for it.
The Finance Ministry points out that goods on which a seizure is made must be left on the spot, in the premises of the taxpayer, under his own supervision ("nadzór").
Carting away the various goods with the wagon immediately after the seizure may take place only when the taxpayer refuses to take on the supervision over them, or when the tax authority has a well-founded fear that the taxpayer will carry the goods away or damage them.
Officials who transgress this will be duly punished.

A Hardworking Woman Is More Charming than the Frivolous Women (On today's performance of “Kariera” at the Sosnowiec Municipal Theatre)

[Sosnowiec — theatre review.] A phlegmatic big-city girl, a typical Viennese[?], poor as a church mouse and who must still support a mother, is looking for a post. She is a capable office worker, knows steno-typing, stenography, correspondence and all seven things. She only needs an office where she can apply her knowledge and abilities. She has even already “organised” the [?] of all sorts of enterprises, and as soon as a post opens up somewhere, or somebody “flies out” of an office, she is to be told at once. And the longed-for day comes.
In a big bank the director's secretary “flies out”, because she can flirt better than work, and Tony Katz (as our heroine is called) has the opportunity to demonstrate her abilities in all fields, for Tony Katz proves to be not merely an efficient secretary to her boss. Just as she got in first and, over the heads of the 100 job candidates, sneaked in first to the director in his office and won the vacant post, so she also manages to steal first into her boss's heart, although some[?] 100 candidates stood in line; and Tony Katz makes, of course, the true career that millions of girls, church mice all over the globe, dream of. From a poor office girl who gets [unclear passage], she becomes the [?] of a huge banking concern, before whom the doors of the biggest jewellery shops stand open.
That, in short, is the story of “Kariera”, whose moral is, after all, not a very clear one; as far as one can infer, the author sets out to show that precisely a modest and hardworking woman is more charming to men than the frivolous women who are puffed up with themselves.
