Within Our Own Four Cubits — On a Very Unpopular Subject

On a very unpopular subject.
It is topical and necessary — a talk on a very unpopular subject: the kehilla and the "etat" [the kehilla tax assessment].
We do not belong to the protectors and defenders of today's kehilla. We have, it seems, already wasted [?] a fair amount of ink and paper to shed light on the dark sides of the kehilla and its leaders. Our readers also know that we by no means belong to those who sing serenades under the windows of most of today's communal workers, although more than one bigwig of greater and lesser calibre clenches [?] his fists at us for it and would with pleasure throw us into the devil's mouth.
But — such is our path, and we accept everything with good grace, finding satisfaction in the awareness that we are fulfilling our journalistic duty.
We make this proviso because in the present article we shall have to defend the kehilla.
It is not the interests of the shochtim, nor the rabbinate either, that we set out to defend, but a certain principle: that there exists a little Jewish world with specific internal relations, needs, conflicts and quarrels, which must not be settled otherwise than within our own four cubits, by our own measure of truth and justice.
In other words: the principle of defending the autonomous positions which we have, somehow or other, attained.
In short: whoever waives his autonomous rights is easily turned into a no-man's thing, from which anyone may and can tear off pieces.
———
If we think that every reader agrees with this reasoning and these arguments, then let us go a step further and deal with a similar matter.
People are not ashamed to run with appeals against the etat assessments.
No one contests the right of the authorities to reduce in such cases, but we do contest the moral right of Jews to run with such appeals.
In this respect people of various strata and circles sin, with beards and without beards.
It is not the poor and the average, simple taxpayers who run; it is precisely the richer ones who run with appeals, and not always when they suffer an injustice. With them the appeal is a prophylactic measure: if I do not shout today, next year they will hand me double... With others it is merely coquetry — let people see that they know which door-handle to open. And there are yet others, for whom a hundred plays not the slightest role, yet they will oppose the etat with the greatest zeal, because it vexes them that "a few Jews there" should "rule" how much they are to pay; and still others simply think [—]: to wriggle out [?] of a few zlotys is always worthwhile.
We hold that the kehilla has not sufficiently clarified this question before the competent authority; the supervisory authority surely does not want a bankruptcy of the kehilla's finances. But the crux lies in the etat, and if the doors are open to etat appeals, it becomes a morbid mass phenomenon, and as a result the existence of the kehilla is in fact undermined.
Shlomo or Baruch, Yosl or Nachman — the name plays no role; what matters is the principle that kehilla affairs be settled by the kehilla itself.
If we want the possibility and the freedom to give expression ourselves to our demands, we must first of all prove one simple thing: that there, where nobody compels us, we can ourselves create [?] our own town [?].
———
Here a comparison suggests itself between the situation of the Jewish kehillot in Poland and the situation of the kehillot in Germany in former times — soon after the first "Crusade", i.e. at the end of the eleventh and the beginning of the twelfth century. Let us be permitted here to use a quotation from the well-known Jewish communal leader in Vilna [Wilno], Mr. Dr. Jakub Wygodzki.
In the book entitled "Sefer ha-Torah veha-Chayim be-Artzot ha-Ma'arav bi-Yemei ha-Beinayim" [Torah and Life in the Western Lands in the Middle Ages] by Dr. M. [?] Güdemann (Chief Rabbi in Vienna) it is said: The Jews took great care that the lords and bishops should not interfere in their internal affairs, and every member of the kehilla who brought this about was punished as a traitor and informer; and in the takkanot laid down by the rabbinical assembly in Mainz (1120) severe penalties were imposed not only on the informer, but also on anyone who sought, through the mediation of the authorities, to free himself from the yoke of the kehilla or from the ban or tax which the kehilla had imposed on him.
We condemn the method; but if we condemn it in social and in political life, if there we find in it demoralisation and informing [?], is it any different when one sets out on such a path for the sake of a few guilders, the success of which is more than once doubtful?
I hear a voice:
— Don't make fools of yourselves with these words, it is a voice crying in the wilderness. You want Jews to accept the kehilla etat [—] with love — that you will not achieve. Declamations about national rights, prestige, honour, character, consistency, not to submit [?], not to give in [?] — those you will hear at every step, those everyone will repeat to you by heart; but to pay a few zlotys for it — not with Mosie! [i.e. nothing doing!]
And yet it was necessary to speak out this truth, because we believe that things are not yet so bad with us. One need only remind, enlighten, clarify, teach, make people understand — and more than one will realise that the path of tearing down the kehilla's means of existence is a crime, and that certainly those circles which are not in the worst situation must not do it.
We must prove that we are capable of managing our own affairs, that we are worthy of autonomy. Other peoples do something more for their autonomous rights than pay a few zlotys of etat, even when the assessment is not accurate. Let one overcome the evil inclination, and instead of running somewhere, come to the kehilla and only to the kehilla, and its decision in such cases must be final.
And therefore — let there be an end to etat appeals outside the kehilla.
Y. N—m.
In Times of Danger There Is No Yerida.

[Article — Zionism; Eretz Israel, the partition plan and the 20th Zionist Congress.] As we write these lines, the partition of Eretz Israel [E.I.] is not yet here. But Zionist reality is already dominated by it; it is darkened by its black shadows.
For 40 years now Zionism has created out of a graveyard a living Yishuv with an independent[?] source of life, encircled by a strong network of colonies, towns, highways and roads, which were created and built by national capital and national pioneering.
The history of the present time is the finest page filled in by this generation, a generation imbued with the deep sorrow and suffering of its people, which is tormented without any "why".
The new Jewish generation threw itself onto the sands of Eretz Israel and with song built houses and highways.
Now, when the people is clouded over and black clouds have drawn across Jewish life, we must, as always, bring out the people's heroism and the enduring[?] national defensive struggle[?]. There must not now be found any laggards or indifferent ones.
The first central mobilisation point must be the 20th Zionist Congress, a congress of soul-searching (heshbon ha-nefesh). A congress that will have to show the whole world its will and striving, its unbrokenness and its courage to defend itself[?] outwardly and inwardly. However great the danger may be, it must not overwhelm[?] us with any feeling of yerida (decline, emigration from the Land) and despair. Precisely now, when the fate of Zionism lies in the balance, the call is addressed to the masses of the people and above all to the Jewish youth.
The youth must now equip itself with all the necessary tools on the hard road of struggle that lurks around us. Your brothers and sisters, the stone-breakers and road-builders, stride[?] with their bare feet in the depths of the swamps, threatened by the wild and incited[?] Bedouins. Children of rich parents have already, for the umpteenth time, set out on the riskiest new conquests, lain under a hail of bullets and for months in wet, cold tents.
To create a second Emek [the Jezreel Valley] — that is the highest ideal of the new generation! And the best answer for defending ourselves[?] in times of assailing dangers, and thereby the thought of yerida will vanish from many.
The new generation and the new Emek will lead us to the victory of our just struggle.
Yerachmiel Zelewiański[?] — Warsaw
(Member of the party council of the General Zionist Halutz Youth ["Ha-Noar ha-Tsiyoni"]).
Risers and Fallers ("Olim and Yordim").

[Będzin — reportage.] By Y. Janosowicz[?]. (Reportage).
This is one of those stories of which the world says that, regardless of their great age, they always stay new.
I mean the story of the ones who go up and the ones who go down. Very often[?], almost[?] daily, it happens. One goes up and the other goes down. In colloquial speech it is called: one becomes rich and the other — poor. Just like the buckets of a village well: at the moment when one goes down[?] empty into the mossy, damp darkness of the well, the other rises full of clear water towards the dazzling sun.
We humans call it luck, and we shake our heads regretfully when we happen to hear of, or ourselves witness, such an occurrence; and thanks to forgetfulness, so characteristic of the human race when it comes to someone else's sorrow and joy, we pass on to our own affairs and cover with the dust of indifference everything that has no connection with the interests of our own four cubits.
Sad is the situation of the "yordim" (those who have come down), a hundred times sadder than the situation of the perpetual born paupers, [—] from them and from their homes melancholy and gloom beat out, we feel their sorrow. On the other hand, from the one who goes up, who becomes rich, there beats an unpleasantness (lack of sympathy), and it is hard to establish why that is so.
I know, on Modrzejowska Street [printed "Mandzhshever[?] gas"], a shopkeeper — a small shopkeeper he was, and this shopkeeper had always been a pauper squared; that means he died of hunger every day not three times but a full twelve times, and together with him his wife, and "bit by bit" also the children.
Why the children only "bit by bit"? Because they [people] are known as merciful sons of the merciful, as people with soft hearts who cannot swallow a bite while a hungry person looks them in the eyes; whereas my acquaintance's little ones not only stood by the neighbours and looked them in the eyes while those were eating, but, if only they were allowed, they literally snatched from their hands... They hated waiting until someone would give them food; it might have turned out a bit too long for them to wait, and hungry people are, as you know, impatient by nature.
That is why the children of my acquaintance, the pauper shopkeeper, went hungry only "bit by bit".
He himself, this acquaintance of mine, was in great trouble, and on top of all that he was quite a nice person, quiet, modest and decent; he did not consider himself a wise man, did not voice his opinion with a hundred-percent certainty, and in general listened more to what the other was saying and kept silent himself.
But they say still waters dig deep. My acquaintance did not dig. He traded and went hungry; but a Jewish gut ("kishke") truly cannot be estimated. It turned out that he went hungry not so much because of [?] [printed "mishum goys", doubtful], as because he was saving up a groschen, and in the end he did indeed amass a tidy sum of money.
And so it happened that the more my acquaintance's gut shrank, the bigger and more packed his little shop became. The less flesh on his bones, the more goods on the shelves; and all quietly, modestly, bashfully, silently, putting on a face that one could pity, he became a rich man.
When I was told for the first time that Moshe Boym — that is the acquaintance's name — was already "making a veksele" (discounting bills of exchange) and charging a handsome percentage for it, I looked at the man as if he wanted to persuade me that at the heavenly fair they sell gypsy donkeys[?] made of butter, and that the gypsies cook tea on the donkeys[?] in kettles made of stone. But it did not last long at all, and I learned that Moshe Boym was indeed a rich Jew.
And from then on Moshe Boym was unrecognisable, as if a new skin had been pulled over him. Moshe Boym, when he talks to you, no longer lowers his eyes to the ground; Moshe Boym has stopped being a silent one, and since he rented a flat of three rooms with a kitchen he has become quite a different man, one of those[?] who already voice their opinion on various matters, and in general he already considers himself a wise man.
And it has gone so far that lately I avoid him, although, to tell the truth, what do I have against him that he became rich? He took nothing of mine. Would I have been better off if Moshe Boym had been a poor man? But that is how it is: from people who go up there blows an unsympathetic smell, and people do not like them, although, fundamentally, this goes against logic.
In contrast to the "risen", the world sympathises with the "fallen"; their grief and their pain find an echo in human hearts.
I will tell you of a story which resembles the first one in that it is exactly the opposite.
The landlord of Kołłątaja Street number... was hated by everybody with a deep hatred, and there was a reason. This Jew, who was stuffed with money, had a heart of stone wrapped[?] in steel; a Jew — a bully, an arrogant and insolent man. People older than he, if only they were poor, he addressed with "du" (the familiar "you") and generally abused them like little boys. His entire household[?] was as if rescued from burning Sodom — pure poison, gall and malice.
Then it so happens that the Jew becomes poor, that is, not all at once, God forbid: first his wife fell ill — he spent a fortune[?] on her illness, and she died; afterwards other troubles came, and little by little, little by little, the Jew became a pauper; his houses were sold at auction, and altogether it came to an end — may it so befall those who wish us ill.
Do you think the Jew has changed? No[?]! The same nasty, capricious old man. He walks about and still puffs himself up; but on the other hand people's attitude towards him has changed. Of the former hatred nothing has remained, and instead people now support him and put up good-naturedly with all his caprices, and meanwhile they shake their heads:
— Poor man, a "yored" (one who has come down)... he had such great wealth, and now he has come down so[?]...
The "Logic" of Emigrationism

[Poland — antisemitism and emigration; Sosnowiec.]
The word emigration, emigrationism, is popular at the present time; the word is mentioned almost daily in the Polish press, in which the opinion is expressed that Jews must emigrate from Poland.
According to the mood and the main mood [?] of the present hour, this is [?] the first commandment "in honour of" us Jews.
But the question arises: is this proposal [?] logically founded, and can it be realised at the present time, even with emigration committees and commissions that have been created?
For as long as we Jews are here and must exist, earn our bread and must be properly provided for, socially as well as by the state, equally with everyone, life must lead to a peaceful and productive coexistence for the good of the country, which must also strive that all citizens be equal in rights without exception — that is the spirit, the ABC of the logic of today's "emigrationism".
Here is a fact of Jewish emigration.
In "Środula" there lived for many years a Jewish tailor who had always barely had enough to eat with his family, even before the war and later after the war. When he was left without a stitch of work [?], he took up a grocery shop, and in the end he had to flee, because day after day they smashed his windowpanes and caused him great trouble so that he would emigrate. And he did indeed emigrate — he pushed himself one kilometre further, that is, from Środula to Będzin.
But it is truly worth noting the joy of the "Kurier Zachodni" of the 11th of this month, in which the "popular patriotism" is expressed against a Jew who sold his goods very cheaply and gave credit for long periods, and yet had to leave — and, what is more, as the last one — his place, in which he had lived almost all his years. The same thing — writes the same "Kurier" — is noticeable in Pogoń, a suburb next to Środula, where the number of Jewish shopkeepers grows smaller by the day, and it is wished [?] that this should happen throughout the country.
This is what the logic really looks like, in the light of the unfounded "emigrationism", for Jews!
Herman Szer.
It Is Worth Knowing

[World — wars and crisis; statistics.]
Little by little we are beginning to forget the great wounds that the World War inflicted on us. The present generation, born shortly before the war, in the war years themselves or even after the war, cannot form any idea at all of the great troubles and suffering that people in almost all countries had to go through from the terrible war in the years 1914 to 1918.
It is worth knowing that this war claimed no fewer than ten million 542 thousand dead and 20 million 816 thousand wounded, of whom a great part later died as well, or in the best case are still going about crippled to this very day.
Only afterwards did the years of inflation and crisis begin, which made a heap of ruins of the whole world. To this day the world cannot recover, because it still suffers from the consequences [lit. causes] of the World War.
According to a statistic of the Leipzig Fair, the economic crisis of the first five years, from 1930 to 1934, caused exactly as much financial damage as the war itself. That is to say, in other words, the whole world is bankrupt today. England alone lost in the crisis years no less than 24 billion Swiss francs.
It is further worth knowing that in the last sixty years we have not come out of the various wars at all: no fewer than 40 wars have we lived through in the last sixty years.
In the year 1876 there was the first war between Serbia, Montenegro against Turkey. In the years 1877 to 78 Russia and Romania also clashed [?] in war against Turkey.
In the year 1878 Austria occupied Bosnia and Herzegovina. In the same year England waged war against the Afghans. One year later England again waged war against the Zulus.
1879—82 Chile [printed "Shtile"] waged war against Peru and against Bolivia. England again fought with the "Ashungen" [?]. In the years 1880 to 1884 England waged war against the Boers, and France occupied Tunis.
In the year 1882 Austria fought in Dalmatia, Russia against the Turkmens and England in Egypt. From 83 to 86 the French waged war in Madagascar and in other colonies, the English in the Sudan and in Burma, the Serbs against the Bulgarians.
In 1892 the French occupied Dahomey [printed "Dahamer"]. From 93 to 96 there was a civil war in Brazil and a war between Germany and South Africa. From 94 to 95 there was a war between Japan and China, and France against Madagascar. In 1896 Italy fought against Abyssinia; from 56 [sic, for 96] to 98 England fought in the Sudan, Greece fought with Turkey and Spain with America. — From 1899 to 1902 wars were waged by England with the Boers and with China. 1904 to 1905 was the Russo—Japanese war. In 1900 [sic] the Spaniards waged war with the Rif Kabyles [?]; in 1911 Italy waged war with Turkey over Tripoli.
In the year 1912 the first Balkan war broke out (Serbia, Montenegro, Greece and Bulgaria against Turkey), and a year later there was the second Balkan war (Serbia, Montenegro, Greece and Romania against Bulgaria).
From 1914 to 1918 the World War lasted. In the year 1920 Russia fought with Poland. 1921 to 1922 was the Greco-Turkish war. From 1926 to 1932 there were wars between Japan and China. From 1934 to 1935 the war between Bolivia and Paraguay lasted, and from 1935 to 1936 there was, for the time being, the last war, between Italy and Abyssinia.
Perhaps a time of peace will now at last begin, which we need so urgently.
Z. Haber, Vienna.
An End to Communal Business!

[Satire — communal activists; relief drive for Brześć.]
(Monologue of a communal activist).
"Listen [?], Fania dear," a respected communal activist said to me on his way from a meeting, "let all the communal work come to an end! You hear, with a ... [?]! You know, since I threw off the communal business (he still has a couple of little seats left [i.e. posts]), I have become a person like other people. I eat my lunch on time, I take a look at how my children do their lessons, I have a chat with my wife, with acquaintances. I have become a free man. I can run my business as one should. After all, before I had no time at all. From early morning until lunchtime, at the offices [urzędy] — with everyone you have someone to intervene for; there are troubles enough in town [?], and people come to you with an aching heart seeking help in need, he pours out [?] his mind to you and you feel that you can help him after all — well, can you refuse? You know how it is — so what do you understand? When the children are waiting for you? And after lunch? Aha? After lunch! That's how it is with the meetings and consultations of the 15 societies and institutions, and where are all the various campaigns? And now a brand-new campaign for the Jews of Brześć and the 'Duipla-shitser' [?]! I'm telling you, it's dangerous! You have no head at all! True, the Brześć campaign must be helped, since [?] everyone will understand that by himself. — And indeed a committee was created to collect the money. And with that, it seems, everything is in the best of order?
But when it comes to the main thing, it turns out to be a flop [lit. an attic]. When one has to go round, nobody is there — 'no time'! And if you do want to help with something, you must be ready to listen to abuse, because as soon as you start talking about a larger donation, he gives you to understand at once that he knows it himself, only he cannot give any more, because he has — that is, not he, but a female relative of his has in Brześć an in-law of a first cousin, and it may be that if he does not forget, he will send something... And you must not have any complaints against him, when he knows it himself! And if you don't like it, he himself sends it to the 'Zaglembier Tsaytung', and then everyone will read that Yaakov son of Shmerl gave such-and-such! And if you like, he tells you quite simply: since I hold that the misfortune is not so great at all, I am not at all obliged to make Brześć richer than it was, and besides one can rely entirely on the American brothers — they [?] will arrange everything themselves. And if you get worked up [?] and say a word, you get as much abuse as you like...
Well, I ask you, should one meddle in communal affairs?
That is why I'm telling you: let communal business come to an end!"
S. Wilbawiański.
10 Years of the Bank Spółdzielczy (Cooperative Bank) in Chorzów

On Saturday, with 62 members present, the 10th general meeting of the Kasse-Bank (bank-fund) in Chorzów took place.
The first member of the council [?], Mr. Ernst, opened the general meeting and gave an overview from the founding to the present day. The chair was taken by Mr. Szpelc [?], who invited to the presidium Director Lipszyc, Messrs. Hejgrojb [?], Ernst, Dr. Herlich, Posłuszna [?], and as secretary Mr. Turm [?]. The chairman described what the bank looked like from 1927 to 1933; only thanks to the energetic and solid management of the leadership did the bank succeed in raising itself to the height at which it stands today.
Then the president of the board, Mr. Hejgrojb [?], took the floor; he gave a report on the whole 10 years of the bank's activity, made a comparison between 1927 and 1937, and expressed thanks to several gentlemen for their efforts for the bank's existence.
Then Director Lipszyc spoke; he described what the Jewish people is living through all over the world and came to the conclusion that, despite the hard, bitter years, the bank had risen. Whereas in 1930 the bank had 37.000 zł and deposits [?] of 8.000 zł, today the bank holds deposits [?] of 400.000 zł, and discounted credits of 1,715,851,06 zł.
After the report, confidence was expressed in the council and the board.
Then the chairman Szpelc read out the subsidies that the bank grants to the institutions of Chorzów, among others handsome subsidies for the KKL, Keren Hayesod, the summer colony, poor children, the kitchen, the gemilut-hesed (free-loan) fund and the merchants' association. A heated discussion developed, in which the president of the small traders' association, Mr. Mandrer [?], criticised the board for not granting any subsidy to the small traders' association, which has existed from the very first minute that the bank has existed; it is thanks to the small traders and peddlers that the bank has attained its present splendour — and from it the small traders today receive no credit and are being broken [?] in every field. It is sad enough how the small traders and peddlers struggle with everyday need; broken [?] and dejected is [?] the association — so the board of the bank ought to have granted it the first and the largest sum, and not pretended to forget that there still exists a small trader; and he came to the conclusion that the board should allocate a sum like that for the merchants' association.
Then the president of the gemilut-hesed fund, Mr. H. Springer [?], spoke, demanding that the meeting allocate a thousand zł for the gemilut-hesed fund. Others spoke against this, and the meeting allocated 100 zł for the small traders' association and 1000 zł for the gemilut-hesed fund.
Then Dr. Sternhell took the floor and proposed that the meeting express its most heartfelt thanks to the tireless workers of the bank over the 10 years — Messrs. Hejgrojb [?], Director Lipszyc and Kołodziej [?]. After the fine closing speeches of Messrs. Hejgrojb [?] and Director Lipszyc, the meeting was closed with the singing of Hatikvah.
Menachem.
Heard and Seen. By Ben Amotz

Questions without answers..
There is, it seems, no other people that asks so many questions as we Jews; and especially in recent months we find ourselves asking only one single question:
— What's the news?.. What's heard here and what's heard there? Is it really true that our martyrs' history has been enriched with a fresh chapter?!
Saturday at dusk I went out into the street and met Jews I know, but their strange looks [?] — a darkness lies poured over them; people don't greet each other with "Gut Shabbes", but the first question is:
— What's the news? Did you get any word?
And a second question bursts from a Hasidic Jew; he wants to know: "On whose account [?] are we indeed becoming — he says — such an unfortunate people, that is held responsible for the mad act of a single individual?"
———
Another question I happened to hear on Monday morning. A group of Jewish parents stopped me in the street and asked:
— Why do we Jews, the poor and tormented people, become "in-laws at every wedding" (i.e. involved in everything)?
— What do you mean by that? — I ask the group of parents — but instead of an answer they point me to the great number of Jewish children, pupils of the public schools, hurrying with bouquets of flowers in their hands into the schools.
— What sort of holiday is this?
— Today is the last day of the school year, today the children receive their school reports, and in honour of the occasion the children bring "first fruits" to their teachers..
— That is indeed fine and good, why not? But excuse me: in normal years one could still understand it; but when we Jews find ourselves in such a time of trouble, when hundreds of Jewish families in various places cling on in pain and misery, when children long for a piece of dry bread — it is the duty of Jewish teachers to plant feelings of compassion in the children and tell them:
— "Children, instead of flowers, give the złotys to hungry children"..
— "Questions and answers"...
A far-sighted look...
At the cemetery in Sosnowiec.
Accompanied by a local communal worker, we look at the tombstones of the fully and half-assimilated Jews, whose memory survives only in the cemetery.
We stop at the family grave of a well-known Jewish family in Sosnowiec. Their father was, it seems, head of the kehilla in Sosnowiec; perhaps that is why his tombstone bore, besides a Polish inscription, also a Hebrew one.
And here we come to the main point.
A few years ago the monument, which spans about 8 graves, was renovated. But the stonecutter was told that all the Polish inscriptions should be refreshed, except the single Hebrew inscription...
— Perhaps remove the Hebrew inscription altogether? asked the stonecutter.
— No, that's unnecessary [?], because if the letters are not refreshed, in a few years they will wear away by themselves...
— And I'll show you one more thing — said our guide — you see this corner? This place was meant to be the grave of the one to whom the Hebrew inscription was a thorn in the eye, and he did indeed have the "privilege" of not lying in the "żydowski cmentarz" (Jewish cemetery)...
— Possibly he did not intend that, but his place remained empty, and one can say that even while he lived he had
— a far-sighted look...

Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Balak)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Balak
—o—
a) "And he went with the princes of Moab" (Num. 22:21)
In Sanhedrin, folio 105, the Gemara says: "Balaam was lame in one leg." Balaam limped on one foot. The question arises: from where do the Sages infer this?
But it is meant figuratively: that he kept wavering[?] — to go, not to go — and that is what is meant by his being lame on one foot... Igeret Maharshak[?].
b) "And the Lord opened the mouth of the ass" (ibid., 28)
A well-known Prague antisemite once mocked the Torah and the Jews in the presence of Rabbi Yehonatan Eybeschütz. Among other things he asked Rabbi Yehonatan:
"In your Torah it says that God opened the mouth of a donkey. I ask you, have you ever heard a donkey talk?"
"Yes," answers Rabbi Yehonatan, "I am hearing one right now..."
• • •
The Austrian Jewish deputy Joseph Bloch, as is well known, waged a great and hard war against the "Talmud-devourer" and antisemite Professor Rohling. Bloch deliberately insulted Rohling, called him a Talmud forger and abused him publicly, in order to force[?] him to sue him in court and thereby expose his ignorance.
In one of his Talmud "researches" Rohling happened to translate the Talmudic expression "hamar-gamal" (meaning a [?] that goes in two opposite directions[?]). Not understanding the sense of the expression, he translated it "a complete donkey" — he thought it ought to read "hamor gamur".
Bloch wrote an article about this and remarked mockingly[?] that not only had Rohling mistranslated a Talmudic expression, but he had illustrated the expression ("a complete donkey") by his own person...
But Rohling did not take offence at this either and did not want to sue Bloch in court, fearing that his scholarship would be unmasked.
c) "I have sinned, for I knew not" (ibid., 34)
The brother of the Rebbe R' Naftali of Ropshitz [Ropczyce], R' Yakl of Bolechów[?], was a misnaged. Once he fell ill. Being on bad terms with his brother because of his Hasidism, R' Naftali had for some time had no news of him and did not know that he was ill. When he found out, he came at once to Bolechów[?] to visit his sick brother.
R' Yakl asks him: "And why did you not come until now?" He answers him: "I did not know that you were ill."
Says R' Yakl to him — he was as sharp-witted as his brother:
"Balaam said, 'I have sinned, for I knew not.' The question arises: if he did not know, then surely he did not sin? But for a man who sees[?] prophecy, not knowing is also a sin; a prophet must know everything. And you are, after all, also some kind of rebbe — why did you not know that your brother was ill?..."
d) "He hath not beheld iniquity in Jacob, neither hath he seen perverseness in Israel" (Num. 23:21)
Jacob is a higher[?] level. If the great and fine[?] Jews do not become sinful — "neither hath he seen perverseness in Israel" — then the common people are not sinful either. In Midrash Rabbah, Genesis 26, R' Shimon bar Yochai says: "Every breach that does not come from the great is no breach" — everything depends on the great. If the great do no damage[?] — no harm is done... Yalkut Yehuda.
e) "And he saw Israel abiding according to their tribes" (Num. 24:2)
"He saw that the openings of their tents were not facing each other." Rashi.
The chief curse, the first curse, the curse of Adam, came from envy, lust and honour, which are among the things that "remove a man from the world", that destroy a person; where envy does not rule, a curse cannot prevail... R' Pinchas HaLevi Horowitz (the "Haflaah").
f) "Whose eye is opened" (ibid., 3)
In the piyyut of Parashat Shekalim there is the following wonderful passage: "Ein otzem mispar afarim mi mana u-fakad ba-helesh u-furim" [roughly: "the closed eye, who said 'who can count the dust', sought by casting lots"].
R' Ephraim Zalman Margolies said that this means Balaam: "ein otzem" (the blind one, "shetum ha-ayin"), "mispar afarim mi mana" (who said "who can count the dust of Jacob"), "u-fakad ba-helesh u-furim" — he wanted to destroy the Jews by lot, by watching for the moment when God is angry with the Jews...
g) "As cedars beside the waters" (ibid., 6)
"But the wicked Balaam blessed them with the cedar: just as the cedar does not stand in a place of water, its roots are few and its stump does not sprout again, and once the south wind blows on it, it immediately uproots it and turns it upside down." Ta'anit 20a.
"He who wishes to become rich should turn south" (Bava Batra 28[?]) — the south means wealth. "And once the south wind blows on it, it immediately uproots it and turns it upside down" — the south wind, the wind of wealth: when it gives just one blow among Jews, it turns everything into a ruin-heap...
R' Yehuda Leib Ginzburg.
h) "And Israel abode in Shittim" (Num. 25:1)
"Rabbi Yochanan said: wherever it says 'and he abode' it denotes nothing but distress."
Where Jews regard themselves as permanent residents, where there is "and Israel abode" — they believe they are settling permanently — that is a term of distress. From this follows at once the misfortune[?] of today: that everywhere they are uninvited guests. Torat Hayyim.
From the World of Film

[Cinema — Hollywood.]
"Angel."
For more than two months now the shooting of the film "Angel" has been going on, with the famous star Marlene Dietrich in the leading role. For the first time she is acting in a film supervised and directed by one of the greatest film directors — Ernst Lubitsch. He has been working on the screenplay for more than a year. While being [?] last year in the autumn [?], Lubitsch recalled this film, which he already had as a project. But he did not yet know for sure whether Marlene would take part in it, since she had various plans at the time. The screenplay is based on a stage play by the gifted Hungarian dramatist Melchior Lengyel. Lubitsch worked on the screenplay with the participation of the English playwright Frederick Lonsdale. Marlene plays here the role of the wife of an English diplomat, who is not happy in her family life. She is utterly disillusioned. She travels to Paris in order to forget everything and everyone there. Meanwhile she meets a young painter, with whom she falls in love, experiencing only now the one love of her life. The actual action, however, takes place in England, after the woman returns home. This content is very well suited to the character and [—] of Lubitsch's directing manner. He is, after all, a true master of splendid ideas, which he weaves through with his specific, good-natured humour. The family life of diplomats, seen in a kind of crooked mirror — that is surely first-class material for the director Ernst Lubitsch.
Hathaway.
Hathaway is nowadays a byword in cinematography. Henry Hathaway now displays a style and character in film. This unique film director has altogether 3 films in his directorial baggage, but that is fully enough to achieve originality and uniqueness, for in the end it is not a question of number but of the quality of the films produced.
Hathaway's films so far are: "Bengali" [The Lives of a Bengal Lancer], "Peter Ibbetson" and "In the Shadow of the Lonesome Pine" [The Trail of the Lonesome Pine]; the last is a colour film. Each of these films is in and of itself a work of art, in which problems of varied character are treated in accomplished [?] form. Each of them has a deeper content, to which Hathaway also fits an appropriate form. "Bengali" dealt with moments of heroism and love of the fatherland; in "Peter Ibbetson" the emphasis was laid on the motif of love that is stronger than death. The colour film "In the Shadow of the Lonesome Pine" stressed the special [?] attachment to mother earth and the upheaval that civilisation brings with it. Besides that, this film represents a great step forward in the field of the colour film in general.
In his new film "Souls at Sea" Hathaway touches on the breakdown of human souls during a shipwreck at sea. Here, face to face with the horrible catastrophe, human souls are revealed to us in their unveiled truth. A very hard but rewarding task for a film [?] director of the cut and scale of Hathaway.
King Vidor and His Newest Film.
Who does not know the director King Vidor? Still engraved in everyone's memory is his first war film "The Big Parade" (from the days of the silent film), which to this day serves as a model for war films. Then comes into consideration Vidor's interesting film "Souls of Blacks" [Hallelujah] with the participation of Negro actors, and finally the special film "Our Daily Bread", in which the director places the emphasis on the economic needs of the workers' and peasants' class. Now, as the foreign newspapers report, King Vidor has finished a film, "The Legion of the Fearless" [The Texas Rangers]. It is already being shown with extraordinary success in New York and in Paris. The action of this film takes place in the border area of Texas. It depicts the heroic battles which the border guards [?] had to endure against the Indians. Woven into the action, very discreetly and subtly, is also a romantic love motif between a young border guard [?] and the daughter of the garrison commander.
The role of the guard [?] in love is played by the beloved actor Fred MacMurray. His love partner is Jean Parker. Also appearing [?] in this film is Benny Bartlett [?].
The Wanderer

[Literature — in memory of Leib Malach; essay.] By P. Blumenkranc, Sosnowiec [?].
(For the first anniversary of the death of Leib Malach.)
To measure the world in its length and breadth, not to sit in one place, to wander without end, to observe the many-coloured life of lands and peoples — and to describe it.
And not merely to describe, to aestheticize, but to penetrate the dark sides of life, to get to know the oppressed and despised and bring it out into the light — that was Malach.
And Malach wandered: North America, South America, Eretz Israel, Europe — and shared it all: about the life of the Negroes in Harlem and the bullfights in Spain, about Paris [?] and about pioneering Eretz Israel, about Buenos Aires and about a remote little town in Brazil.
He travelled, saw and told — both in his reportages and in his picturesque "pralektsies" [?], and last but not least — in his belletristic works.
Yiddish literature, in contrast to the wandering ("na-venad") Jewish people, held for many years to the settled, the stable. Even when already sitting in New York, one could not forget the shtetl with the pump in the middle of the market-place and the water-carriers.
In noisy New York one did indeed live, but in spirit one was bound with all 248 limbs to Yehupets and Kasrilevke, and the shtetl dominated Yiddish literature, because it drew all its vitality from there.
But life does not stand still. Jews, driven by pogroms, want and pain, began to wander.
At first they had Buenos Aires as their goal — and got stuck in a little town in Italy; they wanted to go to Eretz Israel — and were pushed off [?] to Persia; they set out for New York — and "were turned into a far-off vek [?]" [doubtful reading; perhaps: drifted far away] in Canada; they were chased by pogroms to China, driven by hunger to Manchuria.
Everywhere there are Jews — from recent times, and already from ancient times, driven by earlier [?], forgotten troubles. Jews who speak Yiddish, and Jews who look like Indians, Arabs, and sit at the nargileh with crossed legs, etc.
Several Jewish writers have set out into the wide world and come upon these remote Jewish communities. And we have only a few such writers — pushed by restlessness, wandering and drawing ever further artistic nourishment from their wanderings.
The representative, so to speak, "veyerer" [?, perhaps a misprint for "vanderer" — of the wanderers], is Peretz Hirschbein, about whom Pilnyak expresses himself so warmly (Pilnyak, "O.K.").
Peretz Hirschbein began to wander and wrote splendid reportages. His travel book "India" reads with bated breath, and some chapters are suffused with a poetry of awe [?]. Hirschbein says, for example, about India in the first chapter:
"Indian eyes are a mystery, their gaze — a riddle, their fire — as from a flint; they glow and want to tell about themselves in silence."
And after him Melech Ravitch, who sings:
Seven worlds and seven seas
and two-and-forty years —
nightmares about the white
nights on the equator.
The eyes open, the heart kissed [?],
in the blood a mosquito drinks
and buzzes, buzzes, buzzes
in the head its nightmarish song.
Well, and our Leib Malach, who died so young, the author of "Mississippi" and "Don Domingo's Crossroads".
• • •
Leib Malach did not content himself with writing reportages. His great work "Don Domingo's Crossroads" is a novelty in Yiddish literature; he tore himself out of the four cubits of the Jewish shtetl and gave us a new life, a new milieu. In a short time Malach managed to penetrate Jewish life in Brazil and give us an impressive work about life there.
His drama "Mississippi", the cry of pain of the Black people in America, in the supposedly democratic United States, is a work that shakes one up and moves by its artistic authenticity.
Malach wandered, suffered want, wrote and wandered again. He was still young, full of plans. Before his death he made a journey across Europe and wrote vigorous reportages about Spain.
The fate of the Jewish wandering writer did not deter him.
His restlessness and artistic curiosity drove him from land to land and from continent to continent, with faith in his heart that the world would become better.
"After all — relates Yaakov Beler [?] — Malach told him soon after the World War — the world is big; we have so much faith and courage — we will conquer it."
And in the midst of weaving his hopes, in the midst of [—] life, Malach was torn away from us.
The restless wanderer has halted his steps for ever...
A. Zaglembier: The Living Dead

(A most thrilling novel of Jewish life in Zagłębie before and after the World War) (14

Summary of the beginning of the novel.
One summer evening before the World War, when two Cossacks were about to transfer the dangerous bandit "Szmulek Łapka" to the Piotrków prison, they were suddenly attacked on the way to the Będzin station by two disguised "strazhniks" [rural policemen] — Łapka's pals. The Cossacks were found at dawn lying bound, their mouths gagged, and Szmulek "Łapka", the bandit [?], escaped to the Gzichów road and hid somewhere.
That same evening, and almost at the very same hour, the universally respected, solid debt-collector Yosl Wertheim — a father of three children — suddenly disappeared. His wife Sore'tshe runs about the town, terribly desperate. He is searched for in every possible hiding place in all of Zagłębie. But Yosl Wertheim vanished like a stone in water..
The next day the pockmarked [?] Wacek reports to police inspector Chodecki and tells him that on that day he saw Wertheim walking on the Gzichów road together with the Christian woman Wanda Komorska — a pretty young shikse whom Wacek had been courting.
Wanda is arrested at once. During the interrogation she declares that on the very day Wertheim disappeared they had quarrelled, because Wertheim wanted to give her money to travel to Katowice to have an operation, so that their "illegitimate" child would not be born. Chodecki then goes to Wertheim's wife Sore'tshe and tells her about her husband's love affair with Wanda. But Sore'tshe does not believe it and declares that her husband had no money on him. Yet when she goes to the cupboard, she sees that the several hundred saved-up [?] roubles are gone, and she gives up hope for her vanished husband.
Some time later the Cossacks, while bathing in the river, found the dead body of a man, on whom was found a passport in the name of Yosek Wertheim. Wertheim's wife is sent for, and with several neighbours [?] they are to identify whether this is Yosl Wertheim. No one recognises him [—] Yosl's wife, Sore'tshe.
Now read on.

"Well, Mrs Wertheim, is it he?" asks the commissar.
And seeing that she does not answer at all, because everything inside her is screaming: "No, no, this is not my husband"... Chodecki becomes somewhat alarmed and at once forestalls the commissar with another question:
"It is true that the most important identifying features of his face are unfortunately so deformed that it is really hard to recognise him, but going by other signs, and apart from the document that confirms Wertheim's identity. I mean to say: did your husband leave home on that tragic day in the same suit he is wearing now?"
"Yes," answers Sore'tshe.
"Well, there you see," Chodecki triumphs again.
The commissar, however, is still not satisfied.
"Not always," he says, "can one rely in such a case on external signs alone. Tell me, Mrs Wertheim, did your husband have some special mark on his body, such as the scars [?] many people have?.."
"No, he was quite normal."
"Naturally I do not mean that he had a hunchback or anything like that; I mean such small marks as scars [?], for example, a little spot on the skin, on a leg, or on another part of the body..."
"I never noticed that on him," Sore'tshe answers quietly and also abashed.
"You need not be ashamed here; the matter is too serious."
"I really never saw anything special on him."
"And by the face, as it is by the forehead?.."
"I find much resemblance," Sore'tshe answers after a moment's thought, wanting by now herself to be rid of the dreadful scene...
"And by the height?"
"My husband was not shorter."
"Wait! Wait!" Chodecki suddenly cries out. "In a moment we shall have another good sign!"
"What? What?" several ask him at once.
But instead of answering them, Chodecki turns again to Sore'tshe:
"Tell me, Mrs Wertheim, did your husband wear marked linen?.."
"Yes, every piece of linen in my house is marked."
"Did you mark it yourself?"
"Yes."
"How?"
"With a monogram 'Y. W.'"
"Very good. The dead man is wearing a shirt, after all — we shall see at once! Well, well, just get the shirt off him!"
The order is carried out at once, since the clothing on the drowned victim had already dried somewhat in the course of time. Chodecki snatches the removed shirt, searches it greedily with his eyes and, indeed spotting an embroidered monogram, brings it up to Sore'tshe's eyes and asks aloud:
"Is this it, Mrs Wertheim? Is this your work?"
"Yes. This is his shirt," Sore'tshe answers in a choked voice. "I marked it..."
"Well, it seems that after such proofs one can no longer doubt," Chodecki turns to the other police officials.
"Well, yes, most [?] of the proofs speak for this being indeed the missing man..."
"I was convinced of it from the very first minute..."
"Perhaps you are right..."
And, considering the investigation of this painfully tragic affair thereby concluded, the body of the deceased victim was handed over to Wertheim's family. The next morning the funeral took place. No one was surprised that Sore'tshe followed the bier so indifferently, without weeping, without crying out, as though it were not her husband she was now accompanying to eternal rest... After all, no one knew that the terrible secret about Yosl, which Sore'tshe carried deep in her heart, had robbed her of all the feelings of love with which she had formerly endowed her husband... Others, again, said that everything has its limit, and in the course of those several weeks Sore'tshe had already wept, lamented and grieved so much that she had run out of tears...
That is why the heart was cut by the desperate, squealing little voices of Blimke and the two smaller orphans, who were surely certain that it was their father being carried in that black box..
And a grave was dug, and in it was laid the victim, in whom everyone had by now recognised him... And over the filled-in grave, after the last three shovelfuls, a lettered board was stuck in, saying that here lies buried Y o s l  W e r t h e i m..
And right after the funeral Sore'tshe sat shiva with the children. Family, relatives and plain acquaintances came to comfort the mourners; they consoled her that God would help. Death, after all, lies in wait for every one of us. They also talked about the trial of Wanda Komorska, which would take place very soon before the "okruzhnoy sud" [district court]. It was as clear as day that she, she alone — perhaps with accomplices too — was the murderess of Yosl Wertheim, although she denies it through thick and thin...
Sore'tshe listened to all the words of consolation; she was grateful to all those who did not abandon her in so hard an hour. Yet all the while she could not free herself from the very painful thought and feeling which, like a worm [?], gnawed away at the strength in her heart... And to herself, in silence, she asked herself incessantly:
"Was that really Yosl, the father of my children, the one who was buried in that black, dark grave?.."
Even at night, in her dreams, the terrible question often tormented her...
(To be continued).
You Don't Send a Cat for Butter...

[Humour — "Der Kokh-Lefl" (The Cooking Ladle), story.]
"Write to me!" said the wife [?], sticking her head out of the railway carriage.
"I'll write, darling," Max shouted, waving a handkerchief.
The train moved off and Max went home.
"All the same, she does trust me! Not once did she tell me not to betray her!.. But now I am a straw widower!"
For two [?] days Max behaved most decently; he sat at home. But on the third day he said to himself:
"Whatever happens, one is a straw widower only once... I'll take a little stroll and see whether there are still young women in the world.."
Saying this, he shaved [?], bathed and put on his finest suit.
It was pleasant in the street.
Suddenly Max spotted from afar an alluring blonde.
"May I accompany you!" he asked, not boldly.
"I don't make acquaintances in the street," the lady answered proudly.
"Then let us go into a confectioner's!"
And they went into a confectioner's.
After that they went to the cinema.
And after that...
After the first kiss the alluring blonde suddenly clutched her forehead.
"Oh, I completely forgot that I wanted to take care of an important matter here."
"What matter?"
"I have just come from the summer resort of Kzimshiralki [?]."
"Kzi... Kzimshiralki?" Max gave a start; that was exactly where his so-and-so was.
"Yes... two days ago a woman arrived there, with whom I quickly made friends, and she asked me to travel to Sosnowiec and keep an eye on whether her husband was behaving decently..."
Max nearly died of fright.
The next day Max's wife received the following little letter:
"Dear Madam!
I have carried out your request. I can inform you with satisfaction that your husband performs his manly duties excellently. I simply envy you for having such a husband.
Regina Mishumatshke [?]."
The wife breathed more freely and kissed her husband's photograph.
A. B.
They Say...

[Humour — "Der Kokh-Lefl"; Będzin and Sosnowiec — kehilla, gossip.]
That out of the Agudah's peace proposal a fresh war will soon break out..
—
That the Sosnowiec "dozors" [kehilla board members] are ready to give a certain sum to a good cause, provided they are freed from the kehilla seats..
—
That a registration is being carried out of those injured by the drastic [?] "barricades" on Małachowskiego [?] Street in Będzin..
—
That a well-known butter merchant in Sosnowiec has received from the local Brześć committee [relief committee for the victims of the Brześć pogrom, May 1937] a "Mi she-berakh" without the "because he has pledged"..
—o—
My Own Dacha.
"Reb Shakhne, why don't you go to a dacha?"
"I have my own dacha. Da-tshe stands for:
D'ages (worries),
A'rbetslozikeyt (unemployment),
T'apn [?] a khoyv [?] (groping for a debt [?]),
Sh'tayer (taxes),
E'gmas nefesh (aggravation)."
Leyb Stabinski.
—o—
A Fitting Inscription.
In the new premises of the Będzin kehilla there is a department where the affairs of the staff budget [?] ("etat") and the cemetery are handled.
We think a more fitting name would have been:
"Here they fleece the living and the dead"...
—o—
Sosnowiec—Ostrava.
A Faithful Wife.
Mrs. Anna Furernitshka [?] travelled to Ostrava the other day. The next day her husband sent her a little letter:
"Andushele [?], just don't forget on the beach that you are a married woman. Samuel."
To this Samuel received a telegram:
"Shmuelshi [?], have no fear: a minute afterwards I always have you in mind. Anka [?]."
—o—
The Straw Widowers Don't Sleep.
This [?] week, after the wives had left for their summer lodgings, the first night-guests were seen on 3 Maja Street, walking about "aired out" [?]. One asks the other:
"My dear fellow, what are you doing in the street so late at night?"
"I'm looking for... a flat."
"A flat? So late at night?"
"Yes... I'm looking for... my own flat."
—o—
Important for Capitalists.
Not far from Czeladź a morg of land is for sale, with a pump with water on it, suitable for a dairy business,
Hymn — To the Straw Widower.

[Humour — "Der Kokh-Lefl", poem.]
O straw widower,
You widower of straw,
You're doing fine now
And so much to your wish [?]..

In Krynica, in Rajcza,
Or in Bystra,
You can now [?] go sniff
Your "lovely" wife [?]..

She sits there at her dacha,
She burns in the sun,
And in the pleasures of this world alone
She's wholly immersed...

And fatter and broader
She grows from a chicken [?],
And the guests there
Enjoy it all..

Your wife is living it up now,
She doesn't sleep — she's awake...
With her girlfriends
She has fun and laughs..

So don't think, O "widower",
Don't ponder and don't think,
If [?] she lives it up by day now,
Then you live it up by night..

O straw widower,
Don't be a fool,
For your peace and quiet now
You've paid not badly..

So let yourself have a good time
On electricity and steam
And get ready in good time
For the victorious [?] fight!

Go do "tshkhitshenies" [?] now
With plenty of women,
And do it properly,
Get down to the business..

Remember that your so-and-so,
Who has such fine [?] charm,
Is not writing [?] tefillin now,
I swear to you — oh no.

Iksigrek.
Wanted to Become Inspector of Clandestine Slaughter — What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin

And he himself, poor fellow, got caught.
A few weeks ago Zysza Gerlic, son of Abraham the shochet, approached the kehilla administration with a proposal to appoint him inspector of clandestine slaughter in the town. He asked for no salary, only a payment per "piece" he would catch.
Meanwhile the very same candidate for inspector was himself engaged in clandestine slaughter. After lengthy observation they succeeded in catching him while he was slaughtering calves.
Reb Zysza the "inspector" was taken to the police station, where a report was drawn up against him for illegal slaughter.
Departure of the First Group of Children to the Colony

Next Wednesday the first group of children (boys) leaves for the municipal colony in Sławków.
Parents whose children have qualified for the summer colony must report on Sunday the 27th of this month at 4 p.m. at the premises of "Piast".
Prayer Books and Chumashim for Jewish Soldiers
For the Jewish soldiers of the local garrison, the military rabbi in Kraków has sent prayer books, Chumashim and Bibles (Tanakh), which are needed for the prayers held every Sunday in the synagogue.
Delegation of the Działoszyce Kehilla

A delegation has come here from Działoszyce, in the persons of the kehilla president Mr. Sternberg and the shochet Friedberg, in connection with the relief campaign for the 300 afflicted Jewish families in Działoszyce. A collection of linen and clothing is also being organized.
A Prayer Service for the End of the School Year

On Monday a prayer service was held in the town synagogue in honour of the end of the school year. It had been arranged that Ch.B.[?] Chamieres[?] would give a speech to the children, but for "certain reasons" he announced that he would not take part.
A Commercial School and Courses — for Jewish Merchants

On Sunday a conference was held at the premises of the local Merchants' Association on the question of opening a commercial school for Jewish school-age youth, as well as supplementary courses for young people already engaged in trade.
Representatives of the Jewish merchants' associations in Sosnowiec and Będzin took part in the conference.
A discussion on the question followed, after which it was decided to elect a temporary committee to carry out the project.
The temporary committee comprises: from the Merchants' Association, Messrs. M. Lewin, Markus Gertner and Jekel Sandauer[?].
From the Small Traders' Association: Messrs. D. Gitensztajn[?], B. Brasa[?] and J. Rus.
From the Merchants' and Industrialists' Association in Sosnowiec, Messrs.: Dir. Landau, M. Rajcher and Ch. Felerman[?].
From the Small Traders' Association in Sosnowiec, Messrs.: Kajfer[?], Feuerman[?] and Ojfner[?].
It was also decided to send a delegate to the convention to be held shortly in Warsaw.
A Big Theft in Broad Daylight

On Monday, at one o'clock in the afternoon, thieves got into the flat of Mr. A. M. Szwarcbaum (Kołłątaja 17), from which they stole several fur garments and fur goods. The damage from the theft is estimated at a few thousand złoty.
School Year Ceremonially Concluded at the "Yavneh" School

In connection with the end of the school year, a festive siyum [completion ceremony] was held at the local Mizrachi school "Yavneh" for[?] the pupils of the sixth grade. The headmaster Mr. Berkowicz and the educator Mr. Pesachson[?] stressed in their speeches the great importance of the specific education the school had given them.
Mrs. Sztarchman ([—]), on behalf of the parents, expressed heartfelt thanks to the teachers of the school for their hard toil and work, which had indeed been crowned with success.
Finally the pupils made merry for several hours with singing and little dances, and ended with "Hatikvah".
General meeting of the tailors' guild

On Sunday the annual meeting of the Jewish tailors' guild took place in the premises of the Jewish Artisans' Union (Sączedska [?] street). The meeting was opened by the elder (starszy) Mr. Abraham Klejman, who proposed the union's president, Mr. Moshe Hampel [?], as chairman. The latter invited Messrs. Moshe Kajzer and L. Fruchtzweig to the presidium, and Mr. S. Sanest [?] as secretary.
Mr. A. Klejman gave the report on the year's activity and at the end appealed for the election of a viable, capable board.
M. Hampel [?] spoke about the good development of the guild and stressed that the guild's chief merit is that its members are people [?] who do not exploit the guild for their own interests.
Then the secretary, Mr. Sanest [?], reported on the guild's main tasks, especially on the obligation to conclude an agreement with the apprentices.
After the budget was approved, elections were held and the following board was elected: M. Kajzer (starszy — elder), Moshe Sterner [?] (podstarszy — deputy elder), M. Hampel [?], A. Klejman, G. Rapszyk [?], A. Handelsman, Sh. H. Gelbhojer [?] and Wolf Yaakov Krzeszywa [?].
Deputies: M. Rapszyk [?], Y. Goldbring [?], B. Pergricht [?], L. Rudzin [?], D. Wigrheim [?] and L. Fruchtzweig.
Audit committee: B. Warszawicz [?], Avigdor Drewniani [?] and Yosef Szyfetisz [?].
Summer colony for sportsmen and tourists.

The society [?] "Gwiazda [?]-Shtern" ("Star") is arranging [—] colonies for sportsmen and tourists as well. The colonies are being set up in the most splendid areas of Zakopane and the Beskids.
Fee [?] — 8 zł a day. Registration at the secretariat, Kołłątaja street number 34.
Arlosoroff memorial evening.

In connection with the fourth yahrzeit of the unforgettable Dr. Chaim Arlosoroff, the Będzin "Gordonia" is arranging, on Saturday the 26th of this month at 9 p.m., in its own premises, a festive academy dedicated to his memory.
Taking part in the academy is Mr. Zeev Goldberg, member of the chief leadership (Hanhagah Rashit) of Gordonia in Poland, who will deliver a lecture on the life and work of Dr. Chaim Arlosoroff, of blessed memory.
The number of shekels sold

In our town 2,358 shekels were sold. Of this number, Hitachdut–Gordonia sold 585, "Mizrachi" — 550, Kibbutz — 400, P.Z. (Poalei Zion) — 330, General Zionists "A" — 164, General Zionists "B" — 106, Hashomer — 113, Hapoel — 40, "Frayhayt" — 36 [?], "Haoved" — 33.
—o—
3000 zł to Brześć.
This week the relief committee sent to Brześć the first sum of the money collected, amounting to 3 000 zł.
The collection is still under way.
—o—
Inspection at the kehilla.
This week representatives of the supervisory authority carried out an inspection (lustration) of the kehilla's activity in the past year.
Instructions of the "Związek Polski" for Christians going on vacation.

The Sosnowiec branch of the "Związek Polski" has published in the "Kurier Zagłębia" a series of instructions on how the Christian population should behave towards Jews during the vacation season.
After an introduction about the Jewish "hatred" of the Polish people, attention is drawn to the following: the boarding houses should have Christian suppliers; one should choose boarding houses that do not accept any Jewish guests; on excursions one should not spend time with Jewish elements; at the kiosks one should ask only for the anti-Jewish press; one should take care that Polish youth have no dealings whatsoever with Jewish youth; and one should be treated only by Christian doctors.
In addition the "Związek" appeals to the motorists [?] to distribute the booklet entitled "The Jews in the Time of the Struggle for an Independent Poland".
A citizens' committee to inspect conditions in the shops.

On the initiative of the Chamber of Commerce a citizens' committee has been created, whose task is to inspect the sanitary condition and other matters in the commercial premises.
On the proposal of alderman (rajca) Mr. Kajzer it was decided that the merchants should first be informed what it is about, and the inspections should take place later.
In this connection a mass meeting is to take place on Sunday afternoon in the premises of the Small Traders' Union, at which Mr. Kajzer will report on the question.
Official liquidation of the "Bank Kupiecki".

The department for banking affairs at the Ministry of Finance has delegated here the liquidator Mr. Giberman, with the aim of carrying out in the shortest [?] time the liquidation of the inactive cooperative banks.
Mr. Giberman is making the start in Sosnowiec, with regard to the liquidation of the former "Bank Kupiecki". In this matter the liquidator is calling an extraordinary meeting on Sunday in the premises of the Small Traders' Union. At the meeting Mr. Giberman will give a report on how the liquidation is to proceed according to his plans.
Did Professor Tyski die a natural death?

Three months ago the mathematics professor at the Bolesław Prus gymnasium here, Józef Tyski, died suddenly. The cause of the sudden death was supposed to have been a heart attack. Soon afterwards, however, rumours began to spread that Prof. Tyski had died in mysterious circumstances. The professor's pupils informed his sister, a teacher in Wilno, who came to Sosnowiec last week and looked into the matter. After a careful examination of the professor's apartment, the sister established that a savings book [?] had disappeared, as well as various documents, among which were the inheritance papers for his property in Bessarabia. Professor Tyski, who was a bachelor, lived with a certain Mrs. Piecha [?].
The sister therefore came to suspect that her brother had been murdered for the purpose of robbery.
The sister is demanding that an exhumation of the body be carried out, in order to establish the truth about the mysterious death.
Wanted to Introduce the “Aryan Paragraph” in His Own House

[Sosnowiec — court, antisemitism.]
Before the local municipal court stood the landlord Jan Herfel, who had been charged by his tenant Miss Maszenberg [?] with harassing her in an unheard-of manner. During the proceedings Herfel declared that he had wanted at least in his own house to introduce the “Aryan paragraph” and to be rid of the tenant. “I hate the Jews and do not want to have them as tenants,” he said.
The court, however, did not agree with Herfel's “methods” and sentenced the Hitlerite landlord to one month's arrest, the sentence being suspended for 5 years.
The “Hanukkat HaBayit” of the Pogoń Synagogue — Postponed

[Sosnowiec — kehilla, synagogues, economy.]
Last Sunday the “Hanukkat HaBayit” [dedication] of the newly renovated synagogue in Pogoń was to have taken place. For certain reasons the celebration was postponed to next month.
The celebration was postponed — but the report on the celebration we read in Tuesday's issue of the Warsaw Jewish-Polish newspaper “Piąta Rano”.
The report relates that “the celebration was attended by representatives of public institutions, the board of the Jewish kehilla, Jewish councillors, etc., and that the memorial plaque of the martyr Rozenglum [?] of blessed memory was also unveiled”...
—o—
Session of the Kehilla Council
Next Monday the kehilla council convenes for a session at which the new kehilla budget will be discussed. The gallery will be admitted to the session only against entrance cards.
—o—
Aftermath of the “Bank Udziałowy”
On Monday evening a meeting of the “victims” of the bank Ltd. “Związek Kredytowy”, which at the time was supposed to become the “heir apparent” of the “Bank Udziałowy”, took place on the premises of the Small Traders' Association.
At the meeting the outcry of the “udziałowcy” [shareholders] found expression; from whom the syndic is demanding [payment on] the obligations they gave at that time so that the bank could become active.
After a lengthy discussion a series of resolutions was adopted.
Jewish Kielce — Be Ashamed!... (A few words on the catastrophic situation of the Jewish institutions)

[Kielce — editorial; welfare institutions.] What has happened lately with Jewish Kielce is truly beyond understanding. A town of nearly 20 thousand Jews, a town that still has a few well-to-do Jews who could, without any excessive effort, ease the bitter plight of the Jewish institutions — and yet the situation of the Jewish institutions grows from day to day ever more threatening [?].
There is no end to the social irresponsibility in Kielce! Every interest in public responsibility has been lost; meetings, however urgent they may be (lately Brisk, Dwight-Łaszyc [?], etc.), are attended by a handful of individuals; one does not even see [?] the certified public activists.
And not only has the interest in public work been lost, but, regrettably, the public sense for the very greatest needs has also been blunted; people simply do not want to give for the most urgent Jewish needs.
There live [?] here in Kielce a certain number of rich Jews, among them also such as even hold honorary posts in certain Jewish institutions — and these Jews will not give even a single dinner for the old-age home.
A town like Kielce has to this very day not given a single grosz for Brisk! Is this not one of the greatest public scandals?
Kielce has a splendid orphanage, housing some forty-odd orphans, and an old-age home, where nearly 30 old people are maintained, and every day Jewish Kielce is alarmed that any moment now the two institutions will be liquidated; one hears [?] that any moment now they will go under. Forty-odd orphans are starving, nearly 30 old people suffer want! And Jewish Kielce keeps silent! Is this not a disgrace and a shame?
And one must tell the truth: were it not for R' Moshe Pfeffer, of blessed memory, Kielce would to this day have had no synagogue; were it not (to distinguish, for life) for the Zanaysk [?] family, there would be no orphanage and old-age home in Kielce; and were it not for a few individual activists, there would be nowhere to obtain a decent [?] donation.
Yes, that is how it is. It is a disgrace and a shame!
Meeting on Building Our Own School Building in Kielce

[Kielce — education; school building.] We wrote in its time about the founding meeting held several months ago on creating a fund to build a building of its own for the Jewish secondary gymnasium. For various reasons the project could not be realised, and beyond buying a plot of its own for the building — which was indeed done — nothing more could be achieved.
But "what reason does not accomplish, time accomplishes." In the course of these few months much, very much has changed in Jewish life. In particular the whole structure of Jewish economic life has changed, and under the sign of these colossal changes the idea has been revived of creating a proper fund to build a large building of our own, and this time not only for the secondary gymnasium but also for a whole series of public Jewish schools which, under the regulations, must have special premises.
In this connection a large meeting of a number of public activists took place, at which it was decided to set about energetically realising this splendid plan and to proclaim a broad fund-raising campaign among the Jews of Kielce for this purpose, i.e. to build a large building of our own for Jewish elementary schools, gymnasiums, craftsmen's schools and lyceums.
A committee was elected, consisting of: Dr. M. Pelc (chairman), L. Rajzman [?] (treasurer), Eli' Wilner, B. Cynier [?], Inusz [?] Cukierman, Dr. Harkawi, A. Ch. Hofer [?], D. Tenenbaum, Adv. Dr. Pruks [?], Y. Edelsztajn, Sz. Markowicz, editor Wisłagi [?], Dr. Sojfer, Sz. Lichter, Dr. Fajt [?] and Professor Growald [?].
The committee has already set to work.
Suicide in the Jędrzejów Jail

[Jędrzejów — crime; suicide.] The Jewish poultry dealer of Jędrzejów, Abner Garfinkel, was arrested by the police this Monday for buying several stolen geese. On coming into the jail, it was discovered that Garfinkel was dead. He had hanged himself in the cell by the sleeves of his jacket.
Garfinkel was some forty-odd years old; he has left a wife bereft with several small children.
The cause of the suicide is not known.
He Sensed His Death

[Olkusz district — village; strange case.] In the village of Rodaki, Olkusz county, an unusual case occurred. The 76-year-old Władysław Wabrik [?], for many years the village head (sołtys), sensed his death and went to the priest and declared that he wished to settle all the formalities connected with his death. To this end Wabrik gave the priest 250 zł. The priest at first did not even want to hear the old man's words, but the old man forced him to take the money.
Coming home, the old fellow put on his holiday clothes and wanted to go to Olkusz to order a coffin. But on leaving the house he collapsed and died.
Solemn Herzl Memorial in the Kielce Synagogue

[Kielce — Zionism; Herzl anniversary.] Next Tuesday, 20 Tammuz, the 29th of this month, at 10 a.m., on the yahrzeit of Dr. Herzl of blessed memory, a solemn memorial service will be held in the town synagogue, conducted by Cantor Górnicki with the choir.
The same day at 8 p.m. a Herzl academy will take place at the Zionist club.
The Jewish population is requested to take part in the memorial in large numbers.
Chain of Dinners for the Kielce Old-Age Home

[Kielce — old-age home; donors.] Last week and this week the following persons gave dinners for the Kielce old-age home, for which the management thanks them:
Last week:
Sunday, breakfast, Kalman Frydman; dinner, Moshe Zelkowicz; Monday dinner, Shmuel Lewartowski, on the occasion of the wedding of his daughter Ester in [?] Chpat [?]. Tuesday, dinner, Moshe Elbirt [?]; Wednesday, dinner, Moshe Frymer, on the yahrzeit of his mother Yuta [?], may she rest in peace. Thursday, dinner, Mrs. Hirszhorn [?], on the yahrzeit of her son Yechiel, may he rest in peace. This week:
Sunday, dinner, M. Prybilski, on the occasion of his daughter's wedding. Monday, breakfast, Eli' Zylberberg, on the yahrzeit of his father Yechiel, may he rest in peace; dinner, Avraham Rechtman [?]. Tuesday, dinner, Eli' Piotrowski; Wednesday, dinner, Mrs. Partyńska [?]; Thursday, dinner, Israel Wajberman [?]; Friday, dinner, the brothers Chaim and Moshe Dembski; Sabbath, dinner, Moshe Tenenbaum.

Kehilla Council Raises the Budget by 10 Thousand Zł.

[Kielce — kehilla; budget.] On Tuesday a plenary session of the old kehilla council took place, at which, over the course of several hours, the budget for the year 1937 was approved. The budget amounts to about 160 thousand zł.
No special changes were made in the budget, except for the single change that this year's budget will be raised by 10 thousand zł., and this because the main income has been considerably reduced on account of the ritual-slaughter law.
Great Success of the “Ha-Galil” Campaign.

[Kielce — Zionism.]
The campaign for “Mtel ha-Galila”[?] [probably “Ma'ale ha-Galila” — a drive to redeem land in the Galilee], which is being led by Mrs. Baruach[?], is being conducted with great success. When One Wants to Overcome the Evil Inclination.

[Kielce — Swindle.]
Ch. K. is a young married man not only God-fearing and modest, but also of strong character. A cold heart. What he sees and what he hears makes no impression on him. Apart from his grandmother and his mother he knows no other woman in the world; the evil inclination has no power over him, and when it happened that on Warszawska Street a young lady offered him “a wedding” for only 2 zł — as long as they were not counterfeit — he ran away from her like [unclear phrase: “vi der fefer hekst”[?]]. Counterfeit dollars, glass diamonds — you may offer him the most golden deal, he will always answer you with a sideways shake of the head that it doesn't suit him!
But someone offered him to try his luck at cards. Just 3 cards, 2 black and 1 red. At that very moment the evil inclination seized him, and he went off into a side alley to try his luck. He tried and lost 6 zł — and already regretted it, but getting out of the evil inclination's paws was no longer so easy, and he lost another 21 zł. He paid 20 zł and remained owing 1 zł, so he wanted to leave a pledge. The evil inclination, however, declared that with him there is no pawnshop (“lombard”), and served him with his fist and with stones.
Only now has Ch. K. sworn seven times that henceforth he will not stop with anyone at all in the street, and if he feels the urge to play cards, he will go off to some establishment where there is no stone paving.
