Conference on a Reconstruction Fund

[Katowice — economy and mutual aid.] The headquarters of "CEKABE" in Warsaw called a conference last Sunday on the reconstruction fund (Aufbau-Fund) that was collected at the time during the million campaign.
The conference, held at the "Concordia", was attended by representatives of the free-loan funds in Silesia and Zagłębie; on behalf of the headquarters — Messrs. Bernsztajn and Kagan.
The opening address is delivered by Dr. Kaufman, who greets those present and gives the floor to Mr. Bernsztajn for his lecture on productive branches for the declassed Jewish masses; in doing so he presents various plans that the CEKABE headquarters has worked out.
A heated discussion develops over the lecture, during which Mr. Kryszpak[?] (Bielsko) sharply attacks the headquarters: "Where is the money the headquarters received from our brothers abroad?" — exclaims Mr. Kryszpak.
Mr. S. Kagan proposes that part of the fund be given to the poor small traders, who are forced to make investments in their shops.
After the discussion a resolution was adopted expressing thanks to the headquarters for its initiative, and all delegates are called upon to see that the associations in every town send the plans worked out to the headquarters.
Among the more serious plans and several[?] of the speakers it is worth mentioning Mr. Głogic[?] (Sosnowiec) on creating a district office; Eng. Wajsman speaks at length on various plans; Milner (Katowice) on a school for artisans; Dr. Firsztajn (Bielsko) on concrete support from the headquarters in general and a faster pace in settling matters; Cymberknopf (Tarnowskie Góry) on an artisans' cooperative, etc.
Mr. Bernsztajn replies at length to all speakers and finally gives some figures that characterize the Jewish situation, namely: a few years ago the Jewish cooperative banks operated with a hundred million zł., today — with thirty million zł. The "ideal" monthly budget of a Jewish family in the small towns is eighty zł. You understand how one lives on such a budget, and that — he says — is still an ideal.
A r o y.
Life in Chorzów / On the Day the School Year Closes for the Jewish Children

[Chorzów — education.] Already at 8 in the morning, columns of Jewish children march in closed, brotherly ranks to the school, under the direction of the head teacher[?] ("g. leyter") Mr. S. Fiber, who leads all 6 classes.
The children are escorted by their teachers, men and women, to the synagogue, where Rabbi Dr. Kalberg gives an address to the hundreds of children; then the chief cantor Mr. Kahn performs a prayer with the choir.
From the synagogue the children go back to the school, where the report cards ("cenzurki") are [—] festively handed out.
It is, however, worth saying a few words about the esteemed teaching staff, such as Mrs. Felicja Frisz, Miss Langner, Miss Gizela[?] Frisz, Miss Werner, Mr. Jan Gorik/ Miss Anghirt[?], Mr. Szlamkowicz, Dr. Czaczkes, who fulfil their tasks perfectly, sincerely and honestly, and for this they deserve the heartfelt thanks of the parents.
Meeting of the Cooperative Bank. / Jewish Children Beaten. / Lecture by Dr. Tartakower.

[Upper Silesia (probably Chorzów) — economy.] On Tuesday the annual general members' meeting of the "Bank Handlowy Spółdzielczy" (Cooperative Commercial Bank) took place. With 30 members present, the president Mr. Szpigler opens the meeting and proposes Mr. Turm as chairman; Mr. Turm invites Messrs. Bencłowicz and Adolf Klasner as assessors, secretary — Richter.
After the reading of the minutes of the 9 years, the bank's secretary Mr. Wajgryb gives a survey of the 9 years of activity and concludes that, despite the difficult situation of Jewish commerce, the bank grew compared with 1934 by 109 per cent in 1935 and by 50 per cent in 1936.
The report is supplemented by the chairman, who proposes expressing confidence in the management and the council. The proposal is adopted by a majority of votes; especially warm thanks are expressed to the director Wajgryb for his activity, who keeps watch over the good interests of the bank.
The meeting sets a credit for each member in the amount of 3000 zł.
The same gentlemen who had dropped out of the council and the management by lot are re-elected.
It is also decided to subsidize the local free-loan fund with 100 zł.
Unfortunately the meeting ended under unpleasant circumstances, because 2 members, Messrs. Lura[?] of Kazimierz and Richter (Sosnowiec), were beaten by hooligans on their way to the train; the same happened to Messrs. Adolf Klasner, Bencłowicz and Herszhajm[?], who were dragged by the hooligans into a gateway and badly beaten. After an intervention at the police station, police came and managed in good time to prevent further excesses. The remaining members were taken[?] home with a [—].
—o—

The funeral took place on Tuesday. After the memorial prayer by the chief cantor Kahn, Rabbi Dr. Kalberg speaks; then Mr. Wajgrojb spoke, describing the life path of the young deceased. At the open grave a representative of the headquarters and several close comrades spoke.

Sosnowiec in Fourth Place among the Relief Committees for Brisk

[Sosnowiec — relief; aid for the Brisk victims.] In the list which the Central Relief Committee for the victims in Brisk [Brześć nad Bugiem] published this week in "Der Presse", the town of Sosnowiec occupies fourth place.
And indeed Jewish Sosnowiec has passed[?] the first test of the campaign. As the chairman of the relief committee informs us, 7,700 zł have been collected to date. The money has already been sent to the central office.
As one can see, the committee is working very intensively on the campaign for the suffering Jews of Brisk.
"Unfortunately, however, there are also," declares chairman Arch.[?] Ch. Kozałski[?], "such individuals, rich Jews of all people, who refused to give to the campaign with the excuse that they had already given in Katowice. These are Szmuel Nute Szlachis[?], engineer[?] of a bank in Sosnowiec, and the big merchant Ch. Skapecki. It turned out, however, that the two had got off with lame excuses, because we, the committee, were informed that the above-mentioned gentlemen had wanted to use the same[?] excuse in Katowice."
But in general the whole Jewish population took part in the campaign; the best proof is the above-mentioned sum collected.
Support the „Galepkes“ Campaign of „Beys Yaakov“!

[Sosnowiec — education; Beys Yaakov.] From Sunday a campaign begins in the form of a sale of "galepkes" for the benefit of the Sosnowiec "Beys Yaakov" school.
Some 300 girls study at the school; most of them are recruited from the poor Jewish masses, who pay minimal school fees or study entirely free of charge.
Therefore the campaign must be supported, so as to make it possible for the religious school for girls to have its right to exist.

[Będzin — tourism; Jewish Society for Knowledge of the Land.] The Society for Knowledge of the Land [ŻTK, Żydowskie Towarzystwo Krajoznawcze] in Będzin is organising: 1) a 14-day excursion to Paris to the International Exhibition, in July and August [lipiec, sierpień], for 395 zł with all expenses included; 2) summer colonies in Druskieniki (205 zł a month), Karwia (225 zł a month) and Zakopane (170 zł a month); 3) a 21-day excursion to Yugoslavia in the months of July, August and September [lipiec, sierpień, wrzesień] for 495 zł.

To Unify the Campaign for the Działoszyce Victims

[Sosnowiec — relief; aid for the Działoszyce victims.] As we have already written, the relief committee in Sosnowiec for the Działoszyce victims came forward with a proposal that all sums collected throughout the country for this purpose be unified, so that the funds should not be fragmented by the separate committees.
In this matter a delegation of the Sosnowiec relief committee, in the persons of chairman H. Berg[—]-gi[?] and R' Becalel Erlich, stayed in Będzin and held a consultation with the representatives of the Będzin committee on the question of unification.
The outcome of the consultation was that the proposal will be dealt with at "a meeting of the whole committee in Będzin.

Our Endurance and Trained Merchants

[Opinion — economy and commerce; Zagłębie.] (Notes toward remarks on the past, the present and the future.)
Polish Jewry is living through hard days. We live in extraordinary[?] conditions; at the slightest rustle everyone becomes[?] nervous[?] and shaken; the act of a single irresponsible individual can cause the most terrible consequences, and then nothing remains but to take up the beggar's sacks and wander across the world[?] as professional beggars.
True, at every misfortune we console ourselves that we are a tried and tested people: we have suffered no small amount of trouble and pain on our long road of exile, yet each time we came out as victors, and without losing the image of God. In the dark times of Torquemada and the Crusades, in Chmielnicki's periods of 1648 and 1649, the Jewish people did not lose its hope, and in today's times, so hard for Jews, we do not let our wings droop either. We start from the standpoint that we are a people with duties and citizens with demands; we have the right to want to live as human beings among human beings.
And yet we feel in our hearts[?] that we are broken by the troubles and pains which have poured down on Jewish heads in every corner, wherever [—] Jewish hearts[?]. To tell the truth, we too, the older generation, are composed[?] at such moments. We tell ourselves: never mind, we'll somehow push through these few years — but our children, how hard life's road is becoming for them, with no way out[?] in sight at all and no good signs whatsoever for the future.
More than once, when the Jewish public considers a question concerning the future, one wonders how people have the courage to think of tomorrow, of the future, when today, the present moment, is so serious.
What would you have — we are beside ourselves; we say that then the Divine Presence rests upon people, and such an[?] attitude, perhaps a divine power, guides their deeds.
We do not hold with the argument[?] that we must justify[?] ourselves; on the contrary, for the most part we say that we ourselves are to blame, because we do not want to recognise in time our real shortcomings, from which we suffer and make the whole people suffer. That is a truth which we must take well to heart on every occasion; but the moral[?] also has a second side, and that is that we ought to admire ourselves. We ought to admire[?] our patience and our forbearance — that in the time of the greatest destruction we are courageous and do not forget to keep drawing the thread from our tangled ball.
* * *
We are, as is known, a people of merchants; as such we have been characterised, and on occasion even crowned[?], just as on another occasion we stumbled; hardly was that not to the liking of our enemies. Be that as it may, efforts of the most intensive kind have been made to wrest this tool out of our hands.
We therefore welcome the fact that Zagłębie merchant activists have come together to deliberate on founding a school for merchants which would educate the merchant of the future; courses will also be arranged there for the merchants active today.
True, we are merchants; we know how to give a twist and a combination[?], how to be energetic and to find our bearings on the spot and in the situation, which is one of the most important virtues in commerce; but one must not forget that this is still far from everything. Let us not fool ourselves at all[?] into thinking that this is everything. Nowadays a merchant must be intelligent and educated; he must be able to speak and know how to speak to the customer; then he must be able to calculate and be [?] — this plays no smaller a role than orientation. Professional training is also[?] required, without which one simply cannot exist today — let that be taken well to heart.
All the nations of the world, especially the cultured ones, must train themselves as merchants if they want to prosper[?] as such. Until they have such a[?] certificate in their pocket, they will not be able to take up commerce. We too must remember this well, if we want to go on earning our living from this branch; that is precisely why we attach so much importance to the deliberations of the Jewish merchants in Zagłębie, and we feel compelled[?] to say that this must not remain on paper alone, but that resolutions must be adopted which will turn the projects into deeds. For we know how far it is from starting projects to realising them.
We live in too serious a time; we are too hounded and tormented to be able to allow ourselves to pass the time with mere proposals and fantasies.
When projects are put forward that prove useful to the people's interests, all possible means must be taken to realise them.
We have always boasted[?] in the arena that we are gifted for trade, and therefore we have neglected a great deal. Now, when[?] others have begun to imitate us in everything and to overtake us, we must see to repairing what was neglected and learn to trade according to the newest conditions of existence. We must, therefore, have trained merchants, who will surely bring benefit to the community.
ELES.
Dąbrowa Needs a Gemiles-Khesed (Interest-Free Loan) Fund.

[Dąbrowa — relief; interest-free loan fund.]
In all the towns of Zagłębie there are gemiles-khesed (interest-free loan) funds, and not only in the towns — even in the villages they exist too, and everywhere they develop and prosper, and of course they thereby already bring benefit to the masses. But there is one exception: Dąbrowa [Dąbrowa Górnicza]. This little town possesses no gemiles-khesed fund whatsoever, and the question arises: is Jewish Dąbrowa really so well situated that none of its merchants, traders and craftsmen ever needs a loan, that they all have [—?] so much money for their businesses that they do not lack [?] a penny?
A stranger who does not know the town could think so. We, however, know how great the poverty among the masses is; we know that poor Jews could make a living if they received even a small loan, but of that a Dąbrowa Jew can only dream; it goes no further.
So the question arises: if so, if a loan is such a great thing, why is there no gemiles-khesed fund?! To that there is one answer: there was one — and it is no more!
Of course, if other towns need a gemiles-khesed fund, such an institution would simply have been a salvation for the masses of Dąbrowa.
We do not know exactly how it happened, why the institution was liquidated at the time, but we believe that indifference and apathy gained the upper hand, so that this is surely the reason for its disappearance. But why search in the archives for why it closed? Better to search for ways to set the institution up again. Jewish Dąbrowa has become impoverished, and the public must have somewhere to get a guilder on loan. The institution would bring only [?] a certain revival among the masses, who have nowhere to take a loan and who would thereby obtain further possibilities of making a living — which today is one of the hardest things.
Yes, it must become a live issue that Dąbrowa get a "gemiles-khesed fund"; every means must be used to realise the institution, which would be a very important event for Dąbrowa Jewry.
As a well-known communal worker in Dąbrowa informs us, the town collected about three thousand zł. for the "Million Campaign". We are sure that in that case the "CEKABE" [central of interest-free loan funds] would agree that this [?] capital be handed over to the fund, which would thus rise from the dead.
It is simply a command of the hour: the communal workers of Dąbrowa must not rest as long as they have not realised the gemiles-khesed fund in their town.
We hope that our call will be heard, if only because the institution is an urgent necessity.
Selekt.
Thieves, Have Mercy!

By Y. Oberżanek [?].
(Monologue of a summer holiday-maker [letnik]).
As you see me, gentlemen, I never thought much of any "letniska" [Polish: summer resorts], and my missus also laughed at the "śmietniska" [pun: śmietnisko — rubbish dump].
Who mostly, she said, goes to the "śmietniska"? The very rabble, the whole old market. "Lepsze" [Polish: better] people go to Krynica, Szczawnica, Truskawiec i tak dalej [and so on]. In the "kuracyjne miejscowości" [health resorts] one meets "better" society; one goes [?] to the "źródło" [?] [spring] to grab a glass of "Naftusia" [?] [Truskawiec mineral water], and in between [?] one grabs a little flirt; one starts chatting about "stones": he tells how many stones he has shot... out, and she tells miracles about her "woreczek" [gall-bladder]; one starts with "stones" and "woreczek", and it ends with... "gdzie pani mieszka" [where do you live, madam], "gdzie się [?] zatrzyma" [?] [where are you staying] — a "kuracyjna miejscowość" is something altogether different from a "śmietnisko" [?] of Zagłębie.
You should count the stock [?] of stones. The doctor knows exactly how many are missing and how many [?] stones have been added; and since only handsome young doctors go to Krynica and Truskawiec, specialists in "damskie woreczki" [ladies' gall-bladders], people do stand in line at the "specialists".
The spas were made not only for young women with gall-bladders [?], but also for older women who bring along other parcels, which are — daughters! That is to say, supposedly. And the daughters go to look after the mothers, and in truth the mothers bring their "parcels" to the fair — perhaps a buyer will turn up for the goods...
And so every summer my missus dressed up the "goods" — the two daughters, that is: hung them from head to foot with trinkets [?] [świecidełka], painted them and powdered [?] them, with "wieczne ondulacje" [permanent waves], [?] "per-navyes" [?], packed them in velvet and [?] took them out to the fair:
— Here, buyers, what golden goods I possess!.. No shoddy goods, God forbid, but extra!..
So indeed every summer she went, once to Krynica and once to Truskawiec. Every summer she packed her "parcel", every summer she took the "goods" out to the fair, showed her "collection", and every summer she brought the parcel back again, having found no takers for the "golden goods".
When my missus saw that salvation would not come from Truskawiec and Krynica, she decided to "lower" herself to the "rabble", to the letniska. What do you say? If you can't go over, you must go under; and my missus gave in, having no choice.
That was two years ago. After bringing the "parcel of goods" back from Krynica, she said bitterly:
— Listen, Leizer, I'm not going to the idiots any more; I'm going black and dark [with grief]. Smear today, smear tomorrow, ondulations here, ondulations there, the girls dance their feet off at the dancings, the poor things no longer have the strength to stand on their feet. The idiots at the spas make eyes, pay compliments, and when it comes to the "point" — they've croaked... I'm not going to the idiots. From today I'm going with the girls to a letnisko, precisely to the rabble; there you meet "chłopcy" [lads] with "kunak" [?], fellows like bears, and when a girl pleases them they don't play those crazy tricks, they say straight away: "Panienka [miss], you please me" — and one, two, they say the couple of words. I'm going with the girls to a letnisko, and basta!...
And again three years went by. For three years she has been taking the "goods" to letniska. Every summer they get a new trousseau, as for a bride going to the wedding canopy: silk dresses and "kompletne stroje" [complete outfits], red pyjamas and blue pyjamas; in the morning they "opalają się" [sunbathe] on the "plaża" [beach], swim in the pool; towards evening their mother takes them "na piwo" [for a beer], lads "zapraszają" [invite] them to dance, "na lody" [for ice cream], they are treated [?] to "ciastka" [cakes]; in the evening one goes "do lasu" [to the woods]. They have tremendous "powodzenie" [success], but luck they have none. Everything yes: sunbathing together on the beach, swimming in the pool, doing "jaskółka" [swallow] dives in the water, treating them to ice cream and cakes, inviting them to dance, going to the woods in the evening — everything yes; but when one starts a conversation with them about "eighteen and thirteen" [?], about a serious matter, that is — they vanish... as if [?] they had been chased.
My missus had even already considered [?] giving up the letnisko too this year. What does one need it for? If one gets no "korzyści" [?] [benefits] from the letnisko anyway, why torment the children for nothing? Why should they sunbathe for nothing? And indeed my missus had already decided to give up the letnisko this year, but suddenly she changed her decision because of a completely new plan. Listen, gentlemen, to my wife's new plan:
A few months ago a Jew comes in wearing a soft hat, with a briefcase under his arm. He has, he says, a business for me.
— Namely, what sort of business?
— Since I go every summer to a summer lodging, therefore he has a plan for me to insure myself against theft, and my wife and I will not have to tremble that, while I lie stretched out on the "leżak" [deck-chair], someone is meanwhile doing a "search for leaven" in my cupboards.
The plan appealed to me, and I insured myself against theft.
And just as I have no success with my daughters, just so I have no success with the thieves. Every day another neighbour is robbed, and nobody touches my door. If I were robbed, I would get the real bit of "mamona" [money], I could marry off a daughter; but with the thieves too I have no luck. So my missus hit upon a plan: we shall go away to a letnisko, we will leave the flat unguarded; well, how could there not be found at least one compassionate thief who would be so kind as to take... my daughters!
In short, these days I am leaving for a letnisko, I am leaving the flat unguarded, and therefore I turn with a warm appeal to the worthy thieves:
— Dear, kind-hearted professionals, I am going away, my door is at your disposal; there is even a lock hanging on it, but that is only "na pozór" [?] [for show], so people will think one is afraid; in truth one need only lift a finger and the "gates of mercy" will open for you at once!
I therefore appeal to your human conscience: visit me! Have pity on a father of two grown-up daughters who are waiting to be helped thanks to you!.. I await your early visit, and good luck to you..
In Those Days

[Częstochowa — anti-Jewish riots.] P. Blumenkranc.
(Pictures from the Częstochowa "events").
1. The destruction of the Beit Midrash.
Monday, the third day of the attacks; the [—] gangs set off into the Jewish quarter. The Jewish inhabitants, having seen the sad events of the previous two days, gathered in front of the Beit Midrash in order to drive the hooligans away.
But the enraged[?] mob ran riot and began to "work over" the Beit Midrash, the synagogue and the slaughterhouse.
In the Beit Midrash named after the late Rabbi of blessed memory, a [splendid?] building, everything was smashed. Whatever came to hand — the parochet [Ark curtain] was torn down.
The thugs took the holy books and threw them into the water (the "Warta" flows through there); Jewish young men jumped into the water and pulled the books out.
When you enter the Beit Midrash, your heart begins to beat faster. The Holy Ark burst open, the [—] smashed, glass mixed with [the] Tablets lies strewn everywhere — witnesses of human bestiality...
2. Devastation.
Opposite the synagogue, at Mirowska 10/12, lives a poor Jew named Nachtigal; there the hooligans vented their rage in particular. We enter the flat and see how all the chairs and belongings lie smashed in the middle of the room.
They did the same in Warszawska Street 136, 186, at the Czarny[?] family's. Toiling people, who work hard for a piece of bread — their whole meagre property the beasts destroyed.
One of the Czarnys has a well in the courtyard — they destroyed the well too.
The same elsewhere. For example, a Jew comes to the kehilla, stands there and weeps. He cannot speak; all who stand there get wet eyes, and he tells:
Hooligans broke into his flat on the Sabbath, smashed the furniture, took away the trousseau of his daughter, who was soon to be married, and left him naked and destitute.
"Master of the Universe," the Jew cries out, "what have they made of me? My daughter is left with a single dress. They did not leave me even a spoon."
3. At the farm.
The gardening farm, where there are over a hundred halutzim and halutzot [pioneers, men and women] in hachshara [training], lies just outside the town, in a [—] area. We were alarmed about the danger; for the time being there are no police, and the young men together with the young women decide to defend themselves.
The hooligans approach, cut their telephone line — and are repulsed. They try to force their way in and are not let in. For an hour and a half they defended themselves with their own strength, until the police came.
* * *
Częstochowa is still under the impression of the sad "events". It is still hard to take stock of what was done; one thinks it was a calamity, but "things start to stir"[?] and people forget a little.
But already Jews come to the kehilla to tell that they are fasting and have not even a piece of bread for their children; others — that they have nowhere to lay their heads. Day by day the destruction takes on a clearer shape, and a bitter question bursts from the mouth, the question: how long will we be trampled?
— Until when? — — — —
Disregard or Other Intentions?

[Sosnowiec — the Jewish hospital; open letter.] (Addressed to the committee for the rehabilitation of the Jewish hospital in Sosnowiec).
It is an accepted rule that committees founded for public affairs must give reports — an account of their activity — to the public. Just such an account the Jewry of Zagłębie demands from the active or inactive committee in Sosnowiec for the benefit of the local Jewish hospital, because it concerns those who respond to brotherly suffering and want to come to help, for they feel that they owe their brotherly duty to the family of their stock, which they are obliged to save, especially in today's time, when nobody's fate is secure and we do not know what tomorrow may bring. We clearly see what Jewish life looks like: whoever wants mocks[?] at it, and whoever wants can trample[?] his bit of property and still declares himself a hero; in such an insecure time a building like the Jewish hospital in Sosnowiec is surely one of the most important social adornments. But what does it look like in reality?
The mere apathetic attitude of the committee, the silence for a long time, the giving of no account to the public, the ignoring of the demand — is unfortunately a sign of limited responsibility, a desecration of the holiness — a Jewish hospital, which one must respect. It would be a hillul ha-Shem [desecration of God's name] if such a building as our hospital were so orphaned, cut off from all that ought to be in the memory and in the heart of every Jew.
Such a building, which should at the very least have stood on the same level as the [—] Jewish hospitals, will still have to wait long until it reaches the goal, and who knows what may happen to it until then, with such indifference of the committee?
It is no secret to the public that the financial situation of the hospital is a critical one and stands on [shaky?] little legs.
It is so poor, and even with a better situation of the hospital — must the committee then demand of the public such inactivity, which does not agree with the very first letters of the most elementary [—] of social ethics[?]?
Nobody has any complaints against the committee, even if it has done nothing until now; but let it come forward openly and tell the truth — what has its activity yielded during its existence?
For those who fear for the fate of the Jewish hospital are worried; their worry is for the sick, who are not able to be cured at their own expense and must have the hospital.
Therefore we hold that the matter is urgent and cannot be ignored. A clear position must be taken towards the hospital; otherwise it is simply a crime!
Here, the injustice cries out from those who cannot understand[?] [how] all the sick can be satisfied[?] nowadays, since a hospital can afford only according to its expenses and also according to its income!
We sum up: either give an account of the activity so far, a precise[?] open report, or[?] let it hand over the holy work into other hands!
That is the demand of the hour, at the present moment, when the hospital lies in the balance.
We therefore expect from you a quick but clear answer.
Herman Szer, Będzin.
Who Made the First Will?

[Article — history; wills.] In the archives of museums and libraries in almost every country there are wills from various generations. In the British Museum in London, for example, there are wills beginning from the years 1396 — these are the oldest wills that exist at all.
In those times one did not make a will at home. One had to go to the town hall (community house) with two trustworthy witnesses, and there it was entered in a "testament book" that after 120 years the property belongs to So-and-so son of So-and-so. In this testament book [the testator] signed and sealed with his seal, together with the signatures of both witnesses. If someone had no seal, three witnesses had to sign in the testament book.
After the death the relatives went to the town hall, and only there did they learn of the "last will". The "testament book" kept in the British Museum contains no fewer than twelve thousand wills from the years 1396 to 1526.
It is interesting that in almost every one of the wills a part is bequeathed to various religious or charitable societies. Whether this was already [a custom?] or whether the "well-known [ones]" [?] received "a hint to act" so that part of the property would be given away "for the world to come" — that cannot be known today.
Only from the year 1526 could one in all countries make a will at home. For this one needed only at least four witnesses. But most wills were signed by seven to ten witnesses, so that they should have certain force... Only from the year 1583 were the regulations everywhere settled that no more than two witnesses are needed. So that no more than two witnesses should sign, a 16 [?] fee was at first introduced on every testament signed by more than two witnesses.
The first Jewish will about which anything is known is known through the archive of the Leipzig fair. A Russian Jew, Pinchas Levi, fell ill in Leipzig in the year 1620; he called together three Jewish merchants and dictated a will to them. This was the first will that begins with the words "being of sound mind". Since — so it says there [?] — man does not know whose tomorrow it is, he therefore makes a will and bequeaths his whole property to his wife Esther and his two children Yisroelik and Leah. His son Aharon Avraham shall receive nothing after his death, because he did not walk the straight path and brought shame on his house when he married...
It is not known whether Pinchas Levi really died in Leipzig, or whether he recovered and travelled home to "his own". Perhaps he later changed his "last will"... This much is certain: the testament, in which is recorded from A to Z all that he owned, was later translated from Hebrew into German and was sealed by the Leipzig authorities.
Among others, another will from the same archive is worth mentioning, also translated from Hebrew. This will, it seems, was made by a great joker.
He bequeaths his property of two thousand roubles ("kerblekh") to his wife Sarah, on condition that on Yom Kippur before the memorial prayer she announce in the kloyz where he always prayed that she knows her husband died because she shortened his years... If she does not announce this before the whole congregation, she shall not receive even a single penny; and besides, he is sure that of the two thousand roubles she will distribute at least fifteen hundred to the poor..
This will dates from the year 1804, from Berish Lekhtnert [?] of Dragushge [?]; what happened to the will is likewise not known...
Z. Haber, Vienna.
Nothing Has Changed.

[Impressions — summer holidays; Bystra.] (From a visit "on the line").
By S. Libaszon.
When I went out into the street at 5 in the morning, I already found myself under the impression that "Jews are travelling" and that people really are leaving. It just isn't right that those who are not travelling should still be able to sleep — for that we are Jews, after all, and all Israel are responsible for one another...
On a balcony on Małachowska [Będzin] a whole family is saying goodbye to the "child", who is going to the summer colony in Szczyrk; far, far away the cries can be heard:
— Yosele, see that you write; eat the berry [?] cookies today still, so they don't go stale.
At the station it hums like a beehive, everyone talks out loud; here a flustered [?] Jewish woman comes running, shouting, "My Toybele, where are you" — a disaster has befallen her: her Toybele has gone ahead, perhaps, to the train and not said goodbye to her, my Toybele...
Panic breaks out when the train arrives; everyone wants to be first and pushes with his hand luggage; the passengers who need to get off defend themselves — how can it be that they are not let off? A just complaint, with which all agree. But no one gives up his "seized position" and everyone wants to be first in the train.
The mother of the "lost" Toybe-Reynele [?] shouts even louder until the train leaves. At every station it takes in masses [?] of passengers; most are going out "to rest" — and actually they worry not for themselves but for the children.
— Bystra! — the conductor calls out, and we, exhausted and squeezed together, crawl out of the "herring barrel" and breathe in the fresh mountain air...
Barely does one step onto Bystra ground and it seems one is at home. Zagłębie "strikes the eye": wherever you [—] and wherever your eyes look — only "locals". Many of them, however, are hard to recognise at once — they have almost changed their form. The faces [—] [?] in their dress — "[—]" [?], the upper ones up and the lower ones down.. But what are you surprised at, foolish man — that is why one goes to a "letnisko": at home, on the Old Market in Będzin and on Pańska Street in Sosnowiec, that Tsipe will surely not parade in trousers.
— Greetings, Bystra, you have not changed at all; your green slender mountains, which look like giant lions' heads, have not lost their charm. Mankind has become wilder, more bestial; wickedness, murder without measure. But the works of Creation do not change. It says in the morning prayer, after all, that every day the works of Creation are renewed.
Our "little folk" [?] has not changed at all either: the same impudence, the same commotion [?]; they yell in the streets, "make scandals" before the whole congregation, without shame before their own or strangers; the heavyweight women lie and "roast" themselves; little Hasidic yeshiva boys in skullcaps stroll with older bearded Jews and probably debate [?] some difficult pilpul, perhaps only about a hint that we are indeed living in the era of birth-pangs [?]..
— We stride along the long highway between mountains and trees and more trees, and we are laughed at —
— "You've come just now [?] to rent a flat?" — a young woman from Będzin laughs out loud. — "What, you still don't have a lodging?" [?] — wonders a five-pood Jewish woman from Sosnowiec. — We are people too...
— "Do you know when I rented my 'mieszkanie'?" — a third one breaks in — "right after Wielkanoc [Easter]."
— "Madam, you are mistaken [pani się myli]" — retorts [?] the first — "we went to rent together, after all; it was, excuse me, madam [przepraszam pani], if I'm not mistaken, a few days after the Brisk [Brześć] events..."
— "A curse on these years," philosophises the five-pood Jewish woman, "today's young women, so to speak, don't even know when the Jewish holidays fall. She says that a few days after Wielkanoc, a few days after the Brisk affair, they rented a flat — and that was, after all, a day before Shavuot; that's how today's women are, they know everything, only not a speck of Jewishness; that is the very calamity." Oy, I think to myself, the shoulders are already breaking...
— "What's the use of you hunting for such foolishness," a flat broker says to me, "come with me, maybe we can still 'do something' for you."
And we, that is, I and my companion, set off on the way with a prayer on our lips:
— "God in heaven, do not shame me before people's eyes and send me a 'letnie mieszkanie' [summer flat]"...
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Pinchas)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Pinchas
—o—
a) "Phinehas the son of Eleazar the son of Aaron the priest" (Num. 25:11)
"The Holy One, blessed be He, said: It is right that he should take his reward; therefore say: Behold, I give unto him My covenant of peace." Bamidbar Rabbah 21.
There is no reward for commandments in this world. God does not want to pay the one who performs commandments, so that he should not turn bad by growing rich — "But Jeshurun waxed fat, and kicked".
It was different, however, with Phinehas. He was, after all, one who brought merit to the many, and "whoever brings merit to the many, no sin comes about through him". So he was already assured that he would never sin — and so God was indeed already permitted to pay him a reward in this world, and therefore "it is right that he should take his reward"... Torat Moshe.
—o—
b) "The covenant of an everlasting priesthood" (ibid., 13)
"He who has relations with an Aramean woman — zealots strike him. It was taught: not with the consent of the Sages, and Phinehas [acted] not with the consent of the Sages."
Jerusalem Talmud, Sanhedrin ch. 9, halakha 7.
Our Sages did not hold with taking the law into one's own hands, even where it concerns such "matters" as "zealots strike him", because the person who takes up the cause of God never has the certainty whether with his zeal he really means it purely for the sake of Heaven, or whether subconscious self-interested motives do not sometimes move him to wage the war of the Lord of Hosts...
Yalkut Yehuda.
—o—
c) "Now the name of the man of Israel" (ibid., 14)
"Just as the Holy One, blessed be He, takes care to publish the praise of the righteous in the world, so He takes care to publish the disgrace of the wicked in the world. Phinehas He made known for praise and Zimri for disgrace. Of them (Proverbs 10) it is said: The memory of the righteous is for a blessing, but the name of the wicked shall rot." Bamidbar Rabbah 21.
In blessing the righteous man it is said in the singular ("The memory of the righteous is for a blessing"), and in cursing the wicked it is said in the plural ("but the name of the wicked shall rot"), because the wicked, whom one must [?] curse, are far more numerous than the righteous, who deserve to be blessed... Imrei Chen.
—o—
d) "For they vex you with their wiles" (ibid., 18)
"With their wiles" — with the thoughts they made you "yirshenen" [inherit? — doubtful reading], with the spiritually alien baggage they loaded onto your shoulders — by that they are your worst enemies... If you have learned bad deeds from them, that is still only half a misfortune; deeds can be shaken off, worse it is with thoughts, doctrines, which penetrate the brain. R' Elimelech of Lizhensk [Leżajsk].
• • •
A famous Jewish professor once asked R' Eisel Charif:
— How is it that the Jewish rabbis of old were not so afraid of secular education, and besides being geniuses [of Torah] were also great secular scholars, like Maimonides, Gersonides; why were they not so afraid of external wisdom?
R' Eisel Charif answers him:
— I too am troubled by a similar question: how is it that the great Jewish secular scholars of old were at the same time also well versed in the Babylonian Talmud and the Jerusalem Talmud, like, for example, Maimonides, Gersonides — and why are today's Jewish scholars such ignoramuses?..
—o—
e) "Then drew near the daughters of Zelophehad" (27:1)
The section of inheritances, the laws of inheritance, was given through women. For inheritance comes after a dead person, and it was the women who brought death into the world... Rabbeinu Bachya.
—o—
f) "My offering, My bread for My fire-offerings" (28:2)
"If you should say that there is eating and drinking before Me — learn from Moses; see what is written of him: And he was there with the Lord forty days and forty nights; he did not eat bread, etc."
In Bava Metzia folio 86 the Gemara says that a person should not deviate from the custom of the place where he finds himself — a proof from Moses, who was forty days up in heaven and did not eat. The question arises: why is this not deduced from the fact that he did not sleep in heaven those forty days? After all, it is harder to refrain from sleep than from food (see Nedarim 15).
To this the Maggid of Dubno told an episode from his wanderings through the Jewish towns and shtetls.
Once he went astray [?] in a village; he goes in to a villager and asks for something to eat. It is late at night; the villager tells him that he has nothing in the house. He asks at least for a dry piece of bread, but he receives the answer: nothing at all. So he asks at least for a place to spend the night. The yishuvnik [village Jew] shows him to lie down on the stove ["piekelik"]. Late at night, when the yishuvnik thought that the Maggid was already asleep, he takes out of a little sack the "orims" [?] and holds a feast..
This [?] episode — the Maggid of Dubno used to say — answered for him the question mentioned. For if one says that Moses did not eat in heaven because the angels also do not eat, then it necessarily follows that he did not sleep either; for had he slept — how could he have been sure that the angels do not eat? Perhaps while he sleeps they set about holding a feast.. Sfat HaYerua [?].
—o—
g) "The Lord's Passover" (ibid., 16)
Before Passover R' Eisel Charif once came to a rich man about maot chitim [Passover wheat-money for the poor], and the rich man gave nothing at all. R' Eisel says to him:
In the Gemara there is a dispute about what the Tree of Knowledge was, from which Adam ate — whether wheat or a fig. Therefore, instead of maot chitim ["wheat money"], you give maot te'enah ["fig money"], that is to say — a fig [in Yiddish also the "fig" gesture: nothing at all]..
From the Book Table

“Women Rebbes and Famous Personalities in Poland” — by Moshe Feinkind, of blessed memory, Warsaw 1937.
If Moshe Feinkind’s first book, entitled [?] “Gute [?] Yidn in Poyln” (“Good Jews [i.e. Hasidic tzaddikim] in Poland”), stood out for its popular character and its historical truth and was warmly received by the critics — then the second book, which has now appeared under the title “Women Rebbes”, deserves to be treated with even greater attention, because of its rich, interesting material, which at first glance looks sensational, but in reality consists mostly of historical facts that the author succeeded in discovering and finding in old pinkasim and in archives; and therefore the book reads with a gripping flavour, just like thrilling novellas, because the author has breathed a living flavour into the dry facts, and the “dry bones” rise before you in resurrection of the dead..
The book is divided into four parts. In the first part, in 50 pages, the women are described who became famous as rebbes from the Baal Shem Tov’s time onward (from the end of the 17th century [sic]) and who had very many... Hasidim and followers. Such were: Yente the Prophetess [?], Khitniu [?] the Chernobyler [?]; “the Maid of Ludmir”; Perele of Kozienice; Rokhele, the Apter’s [daughter]; Khayele of Ger; Sore’le of Chęciny (who passed away in 1937, aged 99); Leah’le [?] of P[—]ane; Malke of Trisk. The descriptions of them are very interesting, considering the specific piety that prevailed among Jews in those times, especially with regard to women — and yet it was possible that there should be women who possessed such strength to distinguish themselves so much by their religious way of life that they drew to themselves camps of Hasidim, who travelled to them from the most distant places..
The second part already deals with “famous Jewish women writers and heroines” and takes up a very large part of the book. Here the author treats facts dating from the 12th century up to 1905/6.
This part is, in our opinion, the most interesting of all, because a whole gallery of heroic women in the fullest sense of the word appears before us, and the most interesting thing about it is that the majority of the heroic women lived in Poland in the 17th—18th century.
Interesting, for example, are the chapters: “Judith — the heroine in Jan Sobieski’s times (17th century)”; “The Golden Rose”; “The Grete [?] Katarzyna Weigel”; “Sahom Gegie [?] — the Jewish Joan of Arc (13th century)”; “Miriam the Conspirator”; “Esther the General’s Wife”, and other chapters on the activity of Jewish women in the 19th and 20th centuries, such as “Gitele [?] Pakhstaniek [?]”; also “Khane-Sore Gaots [?] — heroic leader of the ‘Bund’ in Łódź”.
All these interesting facts will surely later be used as material for great novels and dramatic works. For example, some of the facts have already been used as material for literary works: “Pulcelina the Martyr” has appeared in Hebrew as a drama, and “Esterka, the Polish Queen” has already been described many times in great historical novels. But all the facts the author describes in our book are so attractive [?] that they demand [?] to be exploited literarily in larger creations.
The third part deals with “Łódź [?] street stories” from Napoleon’s times up to now. Here too the author succeeded in assembling rich, interesting material concerning Jews in general, which sounds like a sensation with its thrilling content.
The fourth part deals with stories “from the old past”.
Very fine stories are: “Frederick the Great and the Jewish rag dealer”, “A Polish Jew — a Russian Tsar in 1607-10” (by the way, that is how the date should be, because in the book there is an annoying error, 1907 — besides other orthographic errors, especially in Hebrew words, which absolutely must be corrected); “The great controversy between R’ Yaakov Emden and R’ Yonatan Eybeschütz”; “The first pioneer of the Haskalah in the 18th century”.
In conclusion it is worth remarking that, having read the book through, one has the satisfaction of having also been enriched with much historical knowledge, while at the same time enjoying the fine tales — and that is the chief merit of this very interesting book.
Elkhanan Zider.
A Wife Tells Her Husband — About Her Past, and Nothing Good Comes of It.

[Feuilleton — morals and family; a story from life.] By B. Lerner.
About her past — and nothing good comes of it.

The question is as old as the hills: should one tell the husband the whole truth, or should one not tell?

A girl who, through some accident or other, or for one reason or another, fell in love with a young man and gave herself to him; later, however, he had regrets, and they parted. The girl came to love a second young man, and the second one wants to marry the girl. Should she tell him about her first love? Should she tell him that she has already loved once and given herself to her lover?

A hundred and one wise men came and answered that for heaven's sake she must [?] tell, because not telling is not honest, not nice, not decent, and if the husband should later learn the truth from someone else, there will be darkness and it will come to misfortune.

But then a hundred and one wise men came and cried out "gevalt!", that for heaven's sake the girl should keep silent: nobody is asking her and she need not speak, and even if they do ask her, she must have the sense to answer in such a way that the husband will not know what happened to her before, before she met him, before they fell in love.

There were those who followed the one side or the other. And if it turned out well, all was well, and people went along with the reasoning that this side had given good advice. But if it turned out a flop, they said that the other side's advice was good for nothing [lit. "fit for kapores"] and one should follow the advice of the other wise men.

The real truth is that it depends on the person himself. There are men who will not make a fuss [a "tsimmes"] about it and will understand that the woman did not have to be faithful to them back then, when she did not even know whether such a person as he existed in the world; and there are, on the other hand, egoists who go with the notion [?] that the woman should have waited for them and meanwhile been shut away in a convent.

About one such man we shall now tell a sad story:

His name is not important. He came here with his parents as a young boy soon after the revolution in Russia. Here he grew up, and here he met a girl who lived in the neighbourhood.

The girl and her mother had only just moved into that [?] area. Already at their first acquaintance the girl fell in love with him and gave him every opportunity to declare his love to her and propose marriage. The young man went to his parents and told them that he had met "the most beautiful and best girl in the world", that he was in love with her, and that if they said "yes" he would talk with her this very evening about the wedding.

The parents knew the girl, knew her mother too, and agreed to the match. So they began to prepare for the wedding.

And only then did the girl come out with it: she called her bridegroom aside and told him that before him she had loved another, and that she had lived with that man as man and wife for several months.

The young man went wild on the spot, but she calmed him, quieted him, and the wedding took place as God commanded.

But already in the second week a terrible [?] jealousy of "that man" awoke in him. At first he tried with kindness to prevail upon his young wife to tell him who that man was, what his name was, where he lived and what he did. The young wife did not want to tell. That irritated the young man even more. Now he was already certain that she had not forgotten that man, that she still loved him and wanted to protect him.

Of course the wife denied it, but it did not help; quarrels began in the young, newly married couple, and the quarrelling grew ever sharper and uglier.

They had lived together barely a year; at the end of the year she gave birth to a child and went straight from the hospital to her mother with the child. The young man came running like one scalded and demanded that she return to him, but she refused.

The young woman said to her husband: "Let us be apart [?] for a while. If you come to see that you still love me, that you cannot live without me, and you are ready to swear an oath to me that you will never again in your life remind me of my past, I will come back to you. But I think that you no longer love me. I once loved another man for a few weeks, and you cannot forgive me for it. To you I am a sinner, an outcast; you have come to hate me. The best thing is that we part [?] now."

But the husband is a hot-headed fellow: he flared up, shouted, raised a racket, ran to his parents, pleaded with her mother, and — everyone advised the young woman to go back to her husband. The end was that she listened to no one, took the child one evening and went off with it to a relative at the other end of town.

When the young man came and did not find his wife and child at his mother-in-law's, he was sure in his own mind that it was the mother-in-law who had played this trick on him — although the mother was in fact on his side and had begged her daughter to go back and live with her husband.

The mother told him that she herself was worried too and had even wanted to call the police to help her find her daughter and grandchild; but the son-in-law did not believe his mother-in-law and even insulted her so badly that she opened the door, told him to leave and not to come again.

In the end the young man came to the conclusion that a woman has no right to tell her husband about [?] her past.

B. Lerner.
The Living Dead Man (15)

[Serial novel — Zagłębie, before the First World War; chapter 15.]
A. Zaglembier.
(The most thrilling novel of Jewish life in Zagłębie before and after the World War).

How did it happen?..

Life meanwhile went on in its natural course, which forces people to forget "yesterday" so as to be able to occupy themselves with "today".
In the world, terrible events began to approach, which foretold nothing good.
Here and there, on some [?] evenings, people suddenly saw strange signs in the sky, in which pious believers saw most dreadful omens...
Something is coming upon the world, which has become wicked and corrupt. Who knows what? A plague, a flood or a war.. and perhaps all of it together?.
And very soon indeed "the shot in Sarajevo" echoed across the world. It was a warning and at the same time also a [—]:
War!..
Least of all did Sorele (Sarah-she) think about all this, for she had more pressing [?] worries. She was left a forlorn [?] widow with three children, two [?] of them still quite young fledglings [?]. What does one do? What does one turn to.. And as with every poor man [?] whom misfortune strikes, so all her former good friends gradually began to draw away from Sorele too.
She was left dependent on herself alone...
And on top of all that, she could not for a single minute free herself from the tormenting doubts: "Did she really escort Josel to his eternal rest?.. Was it really him?.."
The mind did not admit any other thought even for a moment, but the heart.. Sorele's heart kept telling her something else all the time, something that no human being would want to or could understand, something she could not confide even to her own children, for they too would have seen madness in it...
And even in her sleep the tormenting doubts did not leave her. Almost every night Josel comes to her in a dream and tells her some strange, uncanny story of why he had to vanish from home... She sees him alive and hears his living voice... He tells her that none of this is true... he did not die, he is alive.. and that [?] man whom they dragged out of the river is not he, but a strange man...
More than one night Sorele would wake up during such a dream with a terrible scream, and the children [?] too burst into tears from great fright.
Sorele was even ashamed to tell about her evil, dark dreams...
But a dream [?], it seems, never deceives [?]...
For Josel Wertheim really was alive and is alive to this day... And at the time when Josel was being "buried" and mourned here, he was walking about fresh and healthy, but quite far from his home..
But in order to clear up this strange, mysterious riddle — that at the time when everyone was sure that Josel Wertheim was already dead, he was in fact alive — in order to clear this up, we must go back to that dark night when the dangerous bandit "Szmulek Łapka" escaped from the Będzin prison.
And as the readers remember, "Szmulek Łapka" that night, after taking leave of his comrades, fled in the direction of Gzichów [?] and kept himself hidden in the forest; but in vain did the Zagłębie "guvim" [?] search since that night for their [—] [?], for just like Josel Wertheim, "Łapka" too vanished as if into water...
And it happened under the following circumstances.
On coming into the forest, "Łapka" decided to rest here a little and afterwards to [—] across the border and wait until the danger had passed.
He lay down among thick trees, where he could not be seen, and began to enjoy the parcel of food that his "comrades" had given him.
Suddenly, however, "Łapka" froze, trembling; the morsel stuck in his throat as he suddenly heard footsteps and human voices..
He mechanically snatched out his revolver and a knife, sure that the police were in pursuit and had already reached the place where he had fled. A moment later, however, "Łapka" breathed more freely and calmed down, hearing that people were speaking Polish, and about things that had nothing whatever to do with him...
Nevertheless Szmulek "Łapka" pricked up his ears, wanting to hear what the people were talking about. Moreover, the two people stopped very close to "Łapka's" hiding place, so that the bandit heard every word of theirs quite precisely.
And the two people were — Josel Wertheim and his beloved shiksa, Wanda Kosarska...
Josel had long been seeking means to free himself from the "Rejnbur" [?] shiksa, who had lured and bewitched him. He somehow felt that no good would come of it; after all, he was the husband of an honest woman, a father of children. But once entangled in the dangerous net, he could no longer get himself out of it...
And how many times had he already decided to break off with Wanda at last, even if a great scandal should break out, which is unavoidable in such a case. More than once, too, he had thought of telling Sorele the whole truth... She would surely understand him and also forgive him, perhaps not so much for his sake as for the children's. But each time he put it off until later; something, apparently, was still not in order within himself... And each time he again answered Wanda's call, and could not tell her the truth either...
Particularly, Josel had no wish at all to meet her that night. As if he had a foreboding that this would be their last "meeting". After all, he felt how far things had already "got", and moreover [?] Wanda had summoned him today..
As always, they went to the forest, to the agreed spot, by separate ways, so that nobody should see them.
In the forest they only then met and greeted each other. And as Wanda took him in her arms, Josel at once forgot his wife and all dangers. He pressed himself into her juicy lips and let himself be carried away by the stream of passion...
So it had gone on for a long time already, and so it was that evening too...
And when a quiet night set in, when the earth had already grown damp and began to seep into one's bones, they rose and, arm in arm, set off strolling deeper into the forest.
And so they reached the very spot where Szmulek Łapka had lain down to rest. They kept talking about one and the same thing, which gave Wanda great pleasure, while Josel was seized with horror at her words...
"Well, what will happen, Jasku?" Wanda asked.
"What should happen?.. It will [?] be good.."
"You're not a little boy, after all — why do you pretend not to understand?!"
"I really don't understand..."
"You know very well that in a few months I'll be a mother... I'm carrying your child under my heart..."
A cold sweat came over Josel. Actually, it was not from today that he knew of it, and precisely because of this he had met her today, in order to settle the matter in a peaceful, good way...
"You don't answer me at all, Jasku?"
(To be continued).
“Der Kokh-lefl” — Tammuz Thoughts...

[Humour and satire — “Der Kokh-lefl” (The Cooking Ladle); poem.]
Heat-waves, heat-waves, mighty heat-waves
Have [?] come upon the world;
People panting, people sweating —
Air to breathe costs real money.

And here are a few nice cases
That happened these days;
I saw them with my own eyes
And I even noted them down.

A merchant, from the heat,
Got his brain so thoroughly sweated
That he went off at once — it's no joke [?] —
And bought up a load of chaff [Häcksel].

A young lady on the Sosnowiec
“Trusheczak” [?]
Shouted out loud and clear:
“People, know that these very days
I turn forty years old!...”

And in the tram that same week
There was a big antisemite
Who didn't stab a single Jew
And didn't shoot [?] anybody either...

A local “rich man”
From the great heat got a “tongue” [?]
And stopped a poor man
And gave him five groszy..

I met my daughters —
Listen, what a wonder:
I can't stop laughing —
They were actually speaking Yiddish!..

And even that group...
Was seized by the heat,
And [?] Turkow's [?] troupe
They watched and gaped at everything...

The writer of these lines, too,
The heat has enslaved.
“You may make ‘stores’ [?] of him”,
Because he created this little song
In the heat...
Shlomoke.
When Yente Brone Goes to Krynica.

[Humour — “Der Kokh-lefl”; joke.] At the station the husband takes leave of his wife, who is going to Krynica. Before the train departs she says to him through the window:
— Yankev [Yakev] Feyvish, write more often — remember, it costs altogether only 60 groszy... out of a 100-złoty cheque!!...
Suddenly Gone Blind.

[Humour — “Der Kokh-lefl”; joke.] An incident in a boarding house in Bystra.
In the boarding house “The Merry Spring” [?] in Bystra the guests get “narrow” portions. One of the guests, when he was served a portion of meat, suddenly began to shout:
— Help, Jews, quick, get a doctor, I've gone blind! I feel that next to me stands a plate of cutlets, and I can't see them.
The next day the boarding-house keeper served him a big portion of meat covering the whole plate, only the meat was as thick [?] as paper.
— Well, and now? What's new with your blindness?
— It's quite beyond understanding — the guest replied — my eyesight has improved so much today that I can even see the plate under the meat.
Since the First Destruction.

[Humour — “Der Kokh-lefl”; joke.] A summer-holiday scene in the woods.
A couple is sitting in the woods. He is called Moniek and she is called Feygele, and they are arm in arm. Suddenly he puts his arm around her and gives her a kiss.
— Oy, a khurbn [disaster], what are you doing? — the girl cries out.
A while later he puts his arm around her again and gives her another kiss.
— Oy, a khurbn... — the girl cries out again — what are you doing!
Suddenly the young man turns round and notices that behind them sits a Jewish woman, and he is curious whether the woman hasn't seen all this. So he asks the woman:
— Tell me, madam, have you been sitting here long?
— Since the first khurbn — the woman replied.
When the President Goes to Palestine.

[Humour and satire — “Der Kokh-lefl”; Sosnowiec — society life.] A moving farewell speech at a local association.
The president of a local association left for Eretz Israel these days, and the board arranged a farewell banquet. One of the board members gave a speech, in which he said among other things:
...Our esteemed president first saw the light of day here among us in Sosnowiec; here in Sosnowiec his cradle stood, here he grew up, here he went to kheyder and here he got married. We therefore had the right to demand that here, too, he should come to a Jewish burial [kever Yisroel]; unfortunately it was not destined for us — l'chaim!
—o—
[Humour — “Der Kokh-lefl”; joke.] They Missed the Train.
Both of them, husband and wife, were hurrying to the train to Bystra to rent a summer cottage. She had done her toilette, put on make-up and dyed herself.
On reaching the train, he says:
— You see, Karolcia [?], if you hadn't spent so long dressing, we wouldn't have missed the train.
— If you hadn't been in such a hurry, we wouldn't [lit. “one wouldn't”] now have to wait for the next train — the wife answered.
—o—
[Humour — “Der Kokh-lefl”; joke.] Like His Wife.
In the boarding house “Der Fresser” (The Glutton) in Wisła one guest says to another:
— You look very much like a relative of mine.
— Like whom?
— Like my wife. The same face, the same eyes, the same figure; the only exception is the moustache.
— What do you mean, I don't have a moustache!
— Well yes, not you; I mean my wife has a moustache.
Summer-Cottage Comparisons

[Humour — “Der Kokh-lefl”; jokes.]
What is the difference between a merchant and a lady summer-holidaymaker (letniczka)?
The first takes [“nemt tsu”, i.e. grabs money] and goes to sit [in jail], and the second sits and puts on weight [“nemt tsu”].
—
What is the difference between a lady holidaymaker and today's livelihoods?
Both are up in the air [“oyf der luft” — outdoors / without foundation].
What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin — Memorandum of the Merchants' Association on the Investment Tax
