Festive End of the School Year at the „Beys Yesoymim“ (Orphanage)

[Będzin — Orphanage, education.] On Tuesday, 20 Tammuz [29 June 1937], in connection with the end of the school year at the „Beys Yesoymim“ (orphanage) school, a celebration took place with the participation of members of the board. On this occasion Mrs. Ts. Szejn spoke warmly to the children and drew their attention to the importance of education in a person's life. „Therefore, children,“ says Mrs. Szejn, „you must strive to distinguish yourselves in every respect, and especially to take care to behave in an exemplary way, so as to find favour in the eyes of God and men.“
Mr. Yitskhok Winogrodzki, in connection with 20 Tammuz [the anniversary of Herzl's death], dwelt on the significance of Dr. Herzl and Ch. N. Bialik, of blessed memory, for the Jewish people and the Land of Israel, and calls on the children to take these great personalities as a model, with their self-sacrifice[?] for the idea of redemption.
The teacher Mr. Elkhonen Zider pointed to the grave times we are now living through; but on the other hand the rising sun in the East shines for us, which comforts us and gives us courage to endure.
On behalf of the children the pupil Brayndl Trajman thanked Mrs. Szejn, Mr. Winogrodzki and the teacher A. Zider, and also the teacher Miss Bras, for their effort and work in educating the children.
After the distribution of the certificates in the Judaic subjects the celebration was closed with the singing of „Hatikvah“.
Cantor Schwarzenberg Leads the Prayers Again This Sabbath

[Będzin — synagogue, cantorial music.] Last Sabbath the Kalisz cantor Mr. S.[?] Szwarcenberg led the prayers in the Ashkenazi[?] synagogue and made a great impression with his praying. For this reason the synagogue committee has invited him to lead the prayers this Sabbath as well.
Rabbi Chameides' Leave

[Będzin — rabbinate; short items.] On 20 July Rabbi Chameides leaves for abroad on a 4-week leave.
In this connection we are informed that all those who wish to draw up marriage certificates[?] but[?] do not yet have the required documents should already report to the registry (metrical) office at the rabbinate, since during Rabbi Chameides' leave no marriage certificates will be signed.
All other matters will be dealt with as usual at the rabbinate office.
—o—
The Talmud Torah Is Already Open.
On Sunday the kehilla board held a meeting with the participation of the president, Mr. S. Fürstenberg, who came specially on the question of the Talmud Torah. At the meeting the board resolved to give 700 złoty, and on that basis the Talmud Torah has been opened.
—o—
Delegate of the Central Relief Committee.
Yesterday Mr. Moyshe Mrozka, delegated by the Central Relief Committee for Brisk [Brześć], stayed here and held a conference with the local committee about the further collection[?] for the victims in Brisk.
—o—
With the Husband's Stick...
The 67-year-old Yitskhok Hersh Starowum[?], walking along Gzichowska[?] Street, was met by a Christian couple; the husband was drunk and the wife „sober“. The latter, on seeing the Jew, became very angry and with her husband's stick „honoured“ Starowum[?] with heavy blows.
—o—
A Poor Man Foiled the Theft..
During the midday hours a thief got into Epsztajn's flat (3 Maja [Street] 4) and began to make himself at home. When the thief had already packed up the few household belongings, a poor man came in asking for alms. The thief, thinking[?] that the owner had arrived, made off[?] through a window, taking with him only a purse[?] with 25 złoty.
—o—
At Public School No. 4
the distribution of school certificates for the 7th grade took place in a festive mood, in the presence of the parents and [—] [probably: guests].
The celebration was organised by the pupils; the programme of the academy (festive gathering) was also written by the pupils.
With sincere emotion the pupil (Wiberman) bade farewell to the school.
The teacher Mrs. Paleńska[?] bade farewell in moving words to the 47 pupils who have completed the school.
„Where Is the Bus Going?“ — „He Invited Her into a Hotel“...

[Będzin — street incident.] The scene took place in front of the house at Sa...szewska[?] [Street] 29. Opposite a passenger bus stands a woman, to whom a strange Jew, a Hasid, goes up; thinking she is Jewish, he asks her in Yiddish where the bus is going.
At that moment the woman's husband arrives. When the woman tells him that the Jew asked her something she does not understand, the husband goes up to the Jew and gives him a punch in the face, claiming that he had proposed to his wife that she go with him to a hotel..
A Story of a Tarred Sheygets

[Będzin — street incident.] On Monday on Kołłątaja Street a quarrel broke out between 2 gentile youths (shkotsim) over 50 groszy, in the course of which one smeared the other's face with tar. The smeared one then went up to the policeman on duty in the street and reported that a Jew had smeared him. „Witnesses“ were soon found who confirmed this. The policeman, however, believed the Jewish witnesses, who explained the whole affair to him, and paid no heed to the statement of the smeared youth.
Memorial Services for Dr. T. Herzl and Ch. N. Bialik

[Będzin — Zionism, memorial services.] On Tuesday morning a memorial service took place in the town synagogue (Shtot-shul) on the 33rd yahrzeit of Dr. T. Herzl and Ch. N. Bialik, arranged by the New Zionist Organisation.
The service began with the singing of „Ma Tovu“ and some chapters of Psalms by the cantor Mr. Klagsbald with the choir under the direction of the conductor Mr. Dawidson.
Then Dr. Lipman, representative of the Central Committee (Ts. K.), gave a lecture, which was listened to with suspense by the assembled public.
At the end „El Male Rachamim“ was recited, and with the singing of „Hatikvah“ the service was closed.
— On the same day in the evening a memorial service of the Zionist „Organisation“ took place in the synagogue; the synagogue was packed full; Mr. Winogrodzki spoke on topical matters.
— In the morning a public meeting devoted to the above-mentioned anniversaries took place in Marman's[?] courtyard in Sosnowiec[?].
Mr. M. Lewinger opened the meeting and gave the floor to Dr. Lipman for his lecture „The Destruction of Jerusalem“.
In the evening a festive memorial service took place in the town synagogue, at which Dr. Malodiska[?] spoke.
The loss of the “Bank Kupiecki” amounts to 217 thousand zloty.

[Head of the local section; Sosnowiec — economy, bank liquidation.] The members must, however, avoid it coming to an “upadłość” (bankruptcy).

As we have already written, Mr Józef Giberman was delegated here by the State Cooperative Council in Warsaw, for the purpose of carrying out the liquidation of the “Bank Kupiecki” (Merchants’ Bank).
In connection with this, Mr Giberman called an extraordinary meeting of the bank’s “udziałowcy” (shareholders) on Sunday, in order to explain to the members the true state of the bank and the possibility of liquidating it, so that it should not come to an “upadłość” (bankruptcy).
In his opening speech Mr Giberman declared that the liquidation is being carried out by him on the basis of the decision of the District Court in Sosnowiec; Mr Giberman then reports that the previous supervisory board did nothing at all to speed up the liquidation, and he appeals to the members to pay their obligatory shares voluntarily; if not, everyone will have to pay tenfold under the law on the share.
After the report was presented by Mr Yosl Grabadina [?], the balance-sheet report is heard, and it turns out that the bank’s loss amounts to 217 thousand zloty, besides a further 31 thousand zloty of liquidation costs claimed by the previous liquidators: Messrs Katz and Ch. Felcman.
A new supervisory board is then elected, consisting of: Gershon Stazski [?], Dawid Shmeitser [?] and Y. Grabadina [?].
Under the item “free proposals” a discussion develops, in which reproaches are made against the previous liquidators. The accusations [?] are answered by Mr Katz, who declares that their activity so far has been in accordance with the binding regulations.
At the end Mr Giberman speaks about the importance of the members settling their obligations amicably, so that they may spare themselves large money expenses for nothing.
It is also announced that the liquidation office operates in the premises of the Small Traders’ Association, from 9 to 1 and from 3 to 7.
Don’t leave your flats unguarded.

[Sosnowiec — crime, burglaries.] On Sunday night, when the Glejcer family (Prez. Mościckiego St. 23 [?]) was not at home, thieves got into the flat and stole fur garments, linen and other valuables.
— In the night to Monday thieves climbed up onto the balcony of the 2nd floor of Janelewicz’s flat (in the same street) and from there tried to get into the flat. At that moment a resident happened to pass along the street, and he informed the police about it. The thieves, seeing that the police were coming, ran away. One of them, however, fell into the hands of the police.
— In broad daylight the flat of L. Lencman (Stróża [?] St. 4) was broken into, from which a large number of garments, linen and valuables were stolen.
The first meeting of the kehilla council did not take place

[Sosnowiec — kehilla.] On the basis of the demand of the supervisory authority that the kehilla budget must be adopted by the council by the 1st [?] of this month, the council was called last Monday to a meeting on the budget question.
The meeting, which is the first of the present term, was “supposed” to take place on Monday at 4.30 in the afternoon (why the meeting was not called for Sunday, or alternatively for Tuesday, remains a puzzle). Everything was prepared (even the “permanent” kehilla buffet was supplied with all good things), but no more than six parnasim (councillors) from Englard’s side came (8 from the national camp did not come), so that after several hours of waiting the chairman, Mr Majtlis, declared that since there was no quorum, the meeting could not take place.
“It’s not the Haggadah they’re after, but the kneydlekh (dumplings).”

[Sosnowiec — petty trade.] On the citizens’ commission being set up at the Chamber of Commerce.
On Sunday a meeting of several sections took place in the premises of the Small Traders’ Association, before which councillor Mr Kajzer [?] explained in a lengthy lecture the aims of the citizens’ commission being set up at the Chamber of Commerce. The commission will from time to time carry out inspections in the shops and establish whether the sanitary condition is satisfactory, and also whether the text on the signboard is identical with the patent (trade licence); the point is that every signboard must bear the full first name and surname of the owner of the business.
Precise explanations are given at the secretariat of the above-mentioned association.
Sunday — unveiling of the memorial tablet of the martyr Rozenblum, may he rest in Eden.

[Sosnowiec — commemoration, religious life.] This coming Sunday the unveiling will take place of the memorial tablet of the 14-year-old martyr Rozenblum, who perished on the threshold of the beth midrash in Pogoń in a bomb attack.
The tablet, which was made on the initiative of the Jewish councillors’ “Koło” (caucus) in Sosnowiec, will be placed in an honourable spot in the beth midrash.
At the same time the synagogue will be reopened after its renovation, together with the dedication (hanukkah) of the new Holy Ark.
The ceremony, which takes place at 3 o’clock in the afternoon, is to be attended by Rabbi Hager, the presidium of the kehilla board and council, kehilla representatives, town councillors and public activists.
A Great Thing Is Being Created!

[Kielce — education; community.] On the campaign for a "bank" [so printed; probably for: building] for Jewish public schools in Kielce.
Without tumult, without noise, a colossally important Jewish undertaking has been started in Kielce.
Only a week ago, in the very columns of this newspaper, there was talk of the neglect of Jewish public life in Kielce.
Today we are in a position to record a welcome fact — may it be a good beginning of a new era for Jewish Kielce.
On the initiative of a group of responsible communal workers, a start has been made on a building for Jewish public schools — vocational-technical, commercial and general.
They have set about it really and practically: we attended a consultation and heard a report on the first ten thousand zł. that have been raised, heard of a large, valuable gift made by the heirs of the late Kielce Jewish communal worker Jakub Gawak [?], and we also saw the strong will and eagerness of the several people devoted to the cause, which they want to carry through in full.
This time the praise must be addressed to the Jewish university-trained intelligentsia. It is a good sign that the wall between them and Jewish society has been broken through.
We sat and saw the enthusiasm of the committee members Dr. Felc [?], Dr. Chowewi [?] and others for the work begun, and we believed that these people will achieve it.
God willing [?]: with the help of the whole Jewish community, such shameful facts must not recur as the answer of a Kielce rich man to the committee's appeal: "We don't need to have our own schools [shkoles, szkoły]."
Our answer to all persecutions is: in spite of everything we want to develop and improve our life and also to provide for the future of our youth.
And the answer also concerns those Jews who still learn nothing [?] from life. Yes, gentlemen, if we do not build buildings for the Jewish community as a whole, your own buildings will be in great danger.
Jewish Kielce now has an opportunity to show its maturity and understanding.
A great thing is being done! A building is being created for the young Jewish generation.
All of us will build this building!
L. R.
—o—
Festive Herzl and Bialik Memorial.
[Kielce — Zionism; memorial.] On Tuesday, 20 Tammuz, a festive Herzl and Bialik memorial took place in the Kielce synagogue. The prayers were conducted by the choirmaster Gornicki (son of Cantor Gornicki) with the choir. Speeches were given by Ed. [editor] Wiflani [?] and Rozenblum. The academy closed with the singing of "Hatikvah".
A Chase after Love with... Disturbances.

[Kielce — local incident; humour.] It is a dacha story, although it happened in Kielce.
The hero of the story is a well-known merchant, who had sent his family off to the dacha and took a fancy to a new love.
After closing his shop the young merchant went out into the street and [—] [?] to find someone [?]. A couple of hours later the young merchant was already on his way home accompanied by a young woman.
He quietly brought her up to his flat and wanted to amuse himself.
When, while amusing himself, he ran a bath, he forgot after bathing to turn off the tap. The water soon filled the tub and began to pour out onto the floor, soaked through the ceiling and began to flood the flat below, where a real flood ensued.
Hearing a knock at the door in the middle of the night, the man concerned felt deathly ill. He thought his wife had come in the middle of the night on an inspection.
He made his lover dress as fast as possible, let her out through the back entrance and only then opened the front door.
Seeing the neighbours, a stone fell from his heart.
But with that the love adventures with disturbances were not over.
The next morning the nocturnal partner, decked out "in vinegar and honey" [dressed to the nines], came into the merchant's shop.
He at that moment reckoned that she had come to arrange [?] a new "randke" [Polish randka, a date]. But how disappointed he was when she explained to him:
— You forgot to pay me..
— What? Pay? I thought that, that, that this was love..
The "Fräulein" then made him a real "vimsta-ve" [?] [scene] in the shop, and only when the merchant took a 50-gulden [złoty] banknote out of his pocket and handed it to her did she calm down.
—o—
A Round of Lunches for the Kielce Old-Age Home.
[Kielce — charity; old-age home.] This week the following persons gave lunches for the Kielce old-age home, whom the management [?] thanks:
Sunday, lunch, Hilel Gusineaicz [?] and wife, on the birth of their daughter Dina; Monday, lunch, Szmul Klajman; Tuesday, lunch, Rojze Tenenbaum, side dishes [beylagn] (through R' Dawid Manels [?]); Wednesday, lunch, Mosze Eli' Laks; Thursday, breakfast, Boruch Slamatycki [?], on the yahrzeit of his father Mosze of blessed memory; Thursday, lunch, Jeszaja Rubiniek, on the yahrzeit of his father Meir of blessed memory; Friday, lunch, Mrs. Dr. Krauze, on the yahrzeit of her father Szmul Kamrat [?] of blessed memory; Sabbath, a whole day, Icchak Nertler and wife.
Threatened with a Revolver..

[Kielce — crime.] This week, when the Kielce resident Szepsel Cajgel was passing the Plac Wolności with his wife, the postman Leon Metryka [?] ran up to him and wanted to shoot with a revolver. Cajgel managed to wrest the revolver away and to hold the postman. Cajgel's wife ran for the police, who took the revolver from Metryka and led him off to the police station, where a report was drawn up against him. The postman was handed over to an investigating judge [?].
A Festive Reception

[Kielce — politics; state visit.] In honour of King Carol and Prince Michael at the Kielce railway station.
This Wednesday, at about 3 o'clock in the afternoon, the Romanian King Carol and Prince Michael, together with the high state dignitaries of Poland and the royal suite, passed through Kielce in a special train on their way to Kraków.
At the railway station, which was splendidly decorated with Polish and Romanian flags, a crowd of several thousand people gathered, who enthusiastically greeted the royal guests and raised cheers in honour of Polish-Romanian friendship.
When the train arrived, the orchestras played the Polish and Romanian anthems, and the high guests were greeted by the Kielce voivode Dr. Dziadosz and by the city president.
The train stopped at the station for several minutes.
On the “Kielce History”...

[Kielce — local history; press, rejoinder.] In the “Radomer Lebn” [a Radom paper] a certain Y. Ts—r is printing historical notes about Jewish Kielce. Well, never mind — the “literary” value of the notes we will leave to the readers themselves (if there are any). On the other hand, it is impossible to pass over in silence the ignorant errors of the author.. since this concerns so delicate a matter as historical facts, which can lead people into error.
When one sets out to write a “Kielce history”, one must know, for instance, that the present Rabbi of Kielce is a son of R' Tuvia Nisen (not “Nisme”, Mr. history-writer!) and not a grandson. One must also know a great many other things.
If you don't know it, then you don't write any history!..
The Reliefs on the Old Tax “Arrears” Will Not Be Extended.

[Taxes — arrears and reliefs.] It is important to point out that the tax “arrears” [Pol. zaległe] dating from the years 1933 and earlier can be paid off with securities and under the large reliefs only during the current budget year.
These important reliefs will not be extended. On the basis of the reliefs, 70 percent of the debt is cancelled if one pays the old tax arrears of those years by means of the state securities.
After the current budget year the tax authority will already demand the old taxes in the full amount, with interest [?].
The Chełm Rebbe, R' Moshe Leibele Twerski of Blessed Memory, Has Died.

[Kielce — Hasidism; obituary.] At the age of 64 the Kuzmir [Kazimierz] Rebbe, who lived in Chełm — R' Moshe Leibele Twerski of blessed memory, a grandson of the Trisk Maggid — died on Wednesday evening in Warsaw.
In his will, which has been found, the Rebbe asks to be buried in Kielce, in the ohel of his father R' Motele of blessed memory.
Yesterday the deceased was brought to Kielce. The funeral will take place in the afternoon. As we write these lines, the exact hour of the funeral is not yet known. Hasidim are arriving from the whole country.
Only two weeks ago the deceased was in Kielce for the yahrzeit of his father R' Motele of Kuzmir of blessed memory; here he became weak and could no longer be at the ohel. Nevertheless he went to Warsaw to a doctor — and now the news of his passing has arrived.
Not Every Beard Is a Jewish One...

[Kielce — antisemitism; railway station.] A fact characteristic of the present times took place this week at the Kielce railway station.
Before the departure of the Częstochowa [?] train several passengers were sitting on a bench; one of them wore a beard, and this caused him to become the object of excessive “attention” on the part of some young Christians (apparently with “narodowy” [nationalist] [?] blood in their veins), who duly honoured the bearded man with insults.
Suddenly the victim rose from his seat and paid one of the attackers back in kind [?]. There was a commotion; the fellows could not understand the impudence of the “brodaty Żyd” [“bearded Jew”] [?], and they wanted to throw themselves at him again. But here a policeman arrived and did not allow “hotter blows”. The whole crowd was taken [?] to the railway police station. The attackers justified themselves, saying that “the Jew was insolent” [Pol. bezczelny].
But when the “Jew's” identity was checked, it turned out that he was a Viennese [?] knight (Ritter).
A report was drawn up on the whole brawl.
Resigned from His Post as President of the Craftsmen's Association.

[Kielce — craftsmen; followed by: Poland — economy, cartels.] Because of internal frictions, and also because of various intrigues, the long-standing president of the Craftsmen's Association and chairman [?] of the Builders' Guild, Mr. Y. Gutman, has resigned from his post.
—o—
The cartels continue to be liquidated.
This week the government liquidated the glass cartel and also all the conventions of the glassworks with the foreign glassworks.
Glass, especially window glass, will now become considerably cheaper.
The government has also liquidated 3 cartels of chemical articles — of potash [?], soda and chrome alum [?] — which will also make all these articles cheaper.
The material concerning the liquidation of a further series of cartels is also being dealt with.

Zagłębie under the impression

[Zagłębie — Palestine: the Peel Commission report; local news.]
...of the English declaration on the Jewish state in Palestine.
The news in the press that the Royal Commission [the Peel Commission] would publish on Wednesday evening the declaration on the Jewish state in Palestine somewhat cheered up the depressed mood.
Yesterday morning the Jewish press, which carried the full report of the Royal Commission, was awaited with great suspense.
In the streets Jews wished each other mazel tov in honour of the new Jewish state.
Around the question there were also discussions between the „yes“ and the „no“ sayers, but on the whole the report produced a holiday mood. „So as not[?] to get into discussions — says an elderly Jew — one thing I do know: better a smaller apartment, one's own, than a big apartment as a tenant [lokator]“..
—o—

What's New in Upper Silesia?

[Upper Silesia — short news items.]
A Convention.
On Sunday a convention was held of the independent shoemakers'[?] guilds[?] of the P.P.S. [Polish Socialist Party]. About 30 thousand men took part in the convention, before whom [spoke] Dr. Wolkiewicz[?], Ciołkosz[?] and Stańczyk[?]. In their speeches they sharply condemned[?] antisemitism. The convention passed off quietly.
—o—
A Year in Prison for Forging Bills of Exchange.
Moshe Altman of Przemyśl[?] stood before the Rybnik court. Altman was charged with putting into circulation 4 bills of exchange with forged signatures. For this he was sentenced to 1 year in prison.
—o—
Not Satisfied.
At the state gymnasium in Mysłowice a Jewish teacher (professor) from Sosnowiec has been appointed.
The „Polonia“, bringing the news, knows that „among the Catholic parents there is dissatisfaction that a Jew should hold this post“.
—o—
The Customs Office to Be Moved.
It is planned that the office of the customs directorate in Mysłowice be moved to Katowice.
The date of the move has not yet been set.
A Hebrew Teacher of No Means Congratulates the English King on His Coronation. / A Big Fire Beyond Bielitz. / The Clothes „Exchanged“.

[Katowice and Silesia — news; three items.]
A great sensation was caused here by the news that a Hebrew teacher of no means from Katowice has received a letter from the English king.
The story is as follows. Before the coronation of the English king, a local Hebrew teacher, a certain Włoszczowski[?], sent a letter of congratulation in the Hebrew language. In the letter Włoszczowski wrote that he is a Hebrew teacher, the father of a large family, and since he has relatives in England, he asks the king to help him emigrate to England, where he wants to occupy himself with giving Hebrew lessons.
These days Włoszczowski received from the king's civil chancellery thanks for the congratulation, and also an instruction to report to the nearest British consulate about obtaining a passport [visa] to England.
Włoszczowski did indeed turn to the local English consulate, where the necessary formalities are being dealt with.
—o—
A Big Fire Beyond Bielitz.
On Tuesday a heavy rainstorm accompanied by thunder passed over Bielitz [Bielsko] and the surroundings. Lightning struck the storehouse of the „Lenko“[?] factory in Aleksandrowice, from which a huge fire broke out. The damage to the burnt raw materials is estimated at three million złoty.
About 1,000 workers were employed at the factory.
—o—
The Clothes „Exchanged“.
The dentist Fluksman of Katowice went on Monday to bathe at the stadium[?] in Bogucice, leaving his clothes in the cloakroom.
How astonished he was, though, to see later that his clothes, in which there were various documents, had been stolen; the thief, however, left his „client“ his old clothes.
A Former School Head in Court.

[Katowice — courts; education.]
Before the Katowice district court a trial took place against the former head of the „Berek Joselewicz“ public school, who was charged with not depositing the 712 złoty of the children's savings in the municipal savings bank, but keeping it himself. Although the head had returned the money, he was nevertheless charged with causing the loss of interest[?] that the children would have had if the money had been in a bank.
At the trial the head declared that he had borrowed the money for himself and that he considers himself innocent. For lack of incriminating evidence the court passed a verdict of acquittal.
A Theft at a Jeweller's Shop.

[Upper Silesia — crime.]
On Sunday afternoon a theft was carried out at the jeweller's shop of Chaim Feller in Chorzów[?], from which a large quantity of jewellery items and 894 złoty in cash were stolen.
Demands for Increases by the Mine and Steelworks Workers.

[Upper Silesia — labour and trade unions.]
All the trade-union organisations in Upper Silesia sent a few days ago to the Association of Iron Works in Poland a demand for an increase of 20 per cent. They set a deadline for a reply by the 31st of this month.
— The trade unions of the coal-mine workers have put forward a demand to reduce working hours to 40 hours a week. In this way labour would become 18 per cent more expensive.
A Brawl at a Market.

[Upper Silesia — antisemitism; trade.]
In Lubliniec a brawl broke out between non-Jewish and Jewish stall-keepers. The brawl broke out because the non-Jewish stall-keepers would not allow the Jewish ones to trade at the market.
The police broke up the brawl and restored order.
Two of the ringleaders were detained.
The CEKABE Reconstruction Fund and the Zagłębie Free-Loan (Gemilut Hesed) Societies

The readers of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" surely know of the time when CEKABE [Centrala Kas Bezprocentowych, the central of interest-free loan societies] proclaimed a million-złoty campaign among Polish Jewry as a reconstruction fund for constructive aid. Besides the million złoty that was to be collected, the "Joint" promised another million złoty and the "Fundusz Pracy" [the state Labour Fund] — the third million; that is, great plans to help the déclassé [Jews], etc.
As delegate of the Czeladź free-loan society at the district conference of free-loan societies in Sosnowiec, and hearing the reports of the delegates from various small towns, as well as the lecture of Dr. Bornsztajn, head of the economic-statistical bureau at CEKABE, one came away with the impression that "the mountain gave birth to a mouse".
True, the "Fundusz Pracy" has not paid out the promised million, and the collected bonds of the National Loan[?] have not yet been realised either, but the "Joint" has already given a considerable sum to the reconstruction fund. Unfortunately, however, the Zagłębie societies cannot benefit from this fund, although the Zagłębie societies worked intensively in the collection drive — because of CEKABE's attitude towards the towns where it is not possible to create new livelihoods. For instance, in Zagłębie one cannot carry out all those experiments in rabbit breeding, basket weaving, medicinal herbs[?], etc.; but the societies in Zagłębie need more money in order to strengthen the old livelihoods. This is exactly what the delegates of the Zagłębie societies demanded of Dr. Bornsztajn: that in Zagłębie, where it is not possible to create new livelihoods, it [the society] should at the very least get back its own collected money, which was gathered with such difficulty from poor people, who had been promised that for every złoty they would receive 3 złoty on loan. Dr. Bornsztajn, however, rejected the proposal and declared that the collected money will go to the towns where it IS possible to create new livelihoods.
CEKABE's conduct reminds us of the following anecdote: a Polish rosh yeshiva begins to study with his pupils the Gemara "one who is seized by kordiakos". One of the pupils asks the rosh yeshiva what kordiakos is; the rosh yeshiva answers him that kordiakos is a kind of illness, and they study on. But when the teacher at the rabbinical seminary studies the same Gemara with his seminarists and one seminarist asks the same question, a search begins in the old medical books, and the teacher explains that the first case of the disease occurred in the 18th century, and 20 years later Professor Hans Blumenthal found the bacillus of the disease, and 40 years later Professor Otto Steinbach invented a serum against it, and 50 years later again a serum from a Professor So-and-so, etc. Meanwhile the teacher remarks that it is already lunchtime; they close the Gemaras and go to lunch. That is the difference: by the time the Polish rosh yeshiva goes to eat lunch he has already studied 3—4 folios of Gemara with Tosafot, while the seminary teacher goes to lunch still in the middle of studying the disease...
The same I want to say to the esteemed comrades of the statistical bureau at CEKABE: we are hungry, we want to eat, and you are still busy studying the disease.
Abraham Epsztajn.
A Sound Method for Learning the Hebrew Language

Staying in Będzin[?] is the well-known gymnasium director Mr. A. Lipman, who has acquainted us with the new sound method for learning the Hebrew language.
Director Lipman demonstrated to us his newest sound method for learning the Hebrew language.
In 30 lessons — Hebrew — by means of gramophone records, "Fonaglot", "Sfat Ami" is truly an outstanding achievement. The purity of the sound, the clarity of the diction and the [?] Sephardi [pronunciation] make an excellent impression.
It is certain that the language records will help a great deal in bringing Hebrew to life among adults too.
The wall-chart[?] and dictionary that go with it are made by a master hand, so that the vocabulary of over 3000 expressions is easily absorbed by the pupil.
One can see here both great professional knowledge and a knowledge of the soul of learning.
This is no accident: Director Lipman is, after all, the founder of the Jewish gymnasia in Pińsk, Pułtusk, Chełm and Lublin, and of the Warsaw Jewish teachers' seminary, in which he was also a language teacher and lecturer in pedagogical psychology.
For this new deed for the spread of Hebrew among adults, in keeping with the newest technical achievements, Director A. Lipman deserves a great yishar koach.

How the Premises Tax Is Assessed on a Flat That Has Been Divided

A question has arisen as to how the premises tax (lokal tax) should be assessed on a flat that consisted of more than 2 rooms and was divided into 2 smaller flats: should the premises tax in such a case amount to 12 per cent, as for a large flat, or 8 per cent, as for small flats.
The tax authority therefore clarifies that if the premises have been divided in such a way that each flat has a separate kitchen, and one flat has no connection with the other, has a separate number and is occupied by a different principal tenant, they are to be counted as separate premises, and the premises tax must be assessed at no more than 8 per cent.
Food shops will have to carry out thorough renovations

[Economy — commerce; sanitary regulations.] In merchant circles great attention has been aroused by the new circular of the Ministry of the Interior, which lays down what arrangements and repairs must be carried out in shops selling foodstuffs.
The authorities are determined to keep strict supervision over food shops, restaurants, butcher shops and sausage shops, so that they are clean and hygienic and the products are protected from dirt and dust.
The merchants and shopkeepers will now be forced to make larger and important repairs in their shops. For the sanitary and hygienic condition of the population these required repairs are [?] necessary. Unfortunately this comes very hard for many shopkeepers and merchants, since it involves larger expenses. It will [?] therefore be necessary for the merchants' organisations to organise a special credit campaign, so that the less well-off merchants will be able to carry out the repairs and investments.

Where Will This Lead? (On the rift in the Sosnowiec kehilla).

Twenty years ago great hopes were aroused by the kehilla statute with which the German occupation authority favoured us, and which was afterwards supplemented and improved by the Polish government in 1919.
True, the kehilla statute limited the competences of the kehilla bodies and did not satisfy the demands of the Jewish national circles, who wanted to see in the kehilla the core of Jewish national autonomy, which ought to have embraced the whole of Jewish life in all fields and not been limited only to duties and functions in the religious field.
But even within the framework of the kehilla statute, it was hoped that the influence of the Jewish kehilla over the whole of Jewish life could be increased and broadened, and that the independence of the Jewish kehillot could also be broadened after obtaining[?] the Supreme Religious Council which the kehilla statute provides for.
In the first years of the new kehillot's existence, a little fresh air and also a fresh spirit did indeed penetrate the dusty, neglected and — largely through assimilation — mouldy [?] houses; it was reckoned that the kehillot could be built up and brought to a good state, that they would again be able to occupy their proper place in the positions of authority they once held in Jewish history, and that they would be able to embrace and heal the whole of Jewish communal life.
But what do the Jewish kehillot look like today, after 20 years of their existence?
Not only has it not succeeded to build up the competences and broaden the rights of the kehillot, but we must unfortunately note a great ruin in all the Jewish kehillot, from the largest kehilla in Warsaw down to the kehillot of the smallest shtetlekh. The Jewish kehillot have become nests of party quarrels, of personal ambitions and of the private interests of various strongmen (takifim).
Because of the rifts, constant quarrels and internal fights within the kehilla bodies, the financial situation of the kehillot has been brought to a catastrophic state. Officials' pensions go unpaid for months on end, so that the officials find themselves in great want. Even the smallest sums for social aid are lacking, to relieve in the least measure the great want and poverty that reign in the Jewish street and grow from day to day — not to speak of constructive aid, which ought to have been organised by the kehillot.
What causes have brought about this state of affairs?
There are many causes, but one of them is the main cause: the rabbinate question, and the quarrel did not permit normal, healthy activity, and things were run according to the discretion of various strongmen, whose only aim was to be able to go on riding the poor Jewish nag.
And is it any wonder that under such circumstances the kehilla bodies here in Sosnowiec, which took over power several months ago already, are still almost inactive?
Are not the same forces still at work here, in order to go on maintaining the chaos in the kehilla?
— Where will all this lead?
D. Ersler.
Calm and Restraint.

It is an old rule that when an epidemic breaks out, the number of victims who fall from fear of the epidemic is always far greater than the epidemic itself swallows up.
When an epidemic reigns, the first and best condition — if it cannot be defeated entirely, then at least to reduce the number of victims to a minimum — is calm and cool-headedness.
One must, with clear thought[?], coolly handle the situation that has arisen and seek means of removing it, and if it is impossible to remove it at the given moment, then at least to reduce it, to limit the area of its activity.
One must remember well that the base[?] ("dek-") elements do their work in a heated and incited atmosphere, where everything guarantees them, as it seems to them, impunity.
At such a moment, more than ever, there must be no panic, which disorganises not only ourselves, but even those who have not yet been poisoned with the shameful hatred of humanity, with the human poison, and who are ashamed of such deeds as degrade human dignity.
At the present[?] moment calm and restraint are more important than ever.
Panic — is the best accomplice of the dark element.
On the other hand, calm and cool-headedness on our side will also greatly ease the task of the organs of authority, which are called upon to protect life, property and the citizens against attacks, from whatever side they may come.
The Jews must understand once and for all that it is not in the interests of the state to hand over to the street, so that it should become the judge.
The state is strong enough to punish those who take upon themselves functions that are not theirs.
The state is firm enough not to allow interference in its competences.
And therefore, however strong the pain may be, there must nevertheless reign among the Jewish population the firm conviction that the state, which protects all its citizens without distinction of faith and nationality, will with a firm hand mete out the proper punishment to the guilty and will not permit outbreaks by irresponsible base[?] elements.
R. S.
Back to Free Trade

[World economy — international trade.]
The question of reintroducing free trade between the states has now become topical on the world's agenda: that all the restrictions and quotas ("contingents") on the export and import of goods be abolished, and that the closed roads for [?] and money be reopened.
President Roosevelt recently declared officially that the revival of international trade in goods will bring prosperity to the economic situation in all countries and will at the same time work to curb the war moods that have grown so much stronger in many countries.
Even Germany, which is carrying out at home a Four-Year Plan of self-sufficiency (autarky), has already set about introducing free trade.
The whole world has already become convinced that trade between countries cannot develop if it is bound by all sorts of restrictions and burdens.
It is also the opinion of the economists that without free trade in the wide world the crisis will quickly return. If the borders are not opened to free export and import, this will without doubt lead to a terrible dearness of all goods.
It is now everyone's opinion that if the artificial trade restrictions between countries were abolished, this would quickly bring a great relief to the international situation, economically as well as politically. It goes without saying that success depends on the methods by which the reforms of world trade will be carried out.
For one must know that it is not at all so easy to reintroduce free trade as it was 10—12 years ago, because in the years of the crisis enormous radical changes were made in the economic order of the countries, which make it simply impossible to reintroduce complete freedom in trade with foreign countries.
Even England, America and France will likewise not reintroduce complete freedom in trade and in foreign currency, because it is already impossible to do so that quickly; for in recent years very much has changed in the world — the forms of trade and of foreign-currency payments abroad have become highly complicated, and it is simply impossible to change this quickly.
In official circles, in all the countries of Europe, very great hopes are placed in the negotiations that President Roosevelt is conducting with his economic advisers.
The Park of Youth.

[Będzin — reportage.] By J. Janasowicz.
(Reportage)

Summer has already set in — as the saying goes — in all its splendour. The little trees have already drawn on their greenish veils. The "park", for form's sake, has also decked itself out with green grass, which gives the impression as if it had fainted[?]; and above all the mercury of the barometer has begun running madly upward, announcing thereby that it is summertime[?] in town.

If not with greenery, then the town has blossomed with clouds of dust, which drift in billows over the streets, to spite the house-caretakers, who must, as if possessed[?], constantly pour water on the town's stone, sun-baked pavement — the dust drifts, driven together with the smoke-fog, and the two in partnership make a thorough ruin of the city-dweller's lungs, which are not healthy even so.. The town's stone walls have also blossomed with... soda-water[?] kiosks[?], "chłodnie"[?] [cold-drink/ice stands], ice-cream[?] booths and the like — peculiar products of the summer harvest[?] in town.

Hot days have set in. The air is scorching and heavy. In the hot, scorching air the hot tram wires glitter and the tram rails gleam against the sun; the meagre shade that falls from the houses is a transparent grey, and has no strength to protect those who wish to shelter behind it from the glowing sun.
The city-dweller's dream these days is air, greenery, forest and field. But for the great majority of the urban population this is no more than a dream, which is hard to attain. [word unclear]. Livelihood is the scissors that cut the thread of the dream. Lost. —
But the summer sun does its own thing. It really ought to be put on trial, because it acts "demoralizingly" upon the established "good manners", which we naturally regard as an expression of our civilizedness. On the promenade, for example, and in other places too, the hot sun has forced people to set aside[?] all the "regulations" concerning dress, and indeed one sees men and women going about in a [garment — word unclear], which is no longer so far from Adam's attire. When the heat burns, one does not think about whether it is proper or not; only then does one realize how much in our wardrobe is superfluous.
Not to mention the children. For them summer is indeed a joy; [?] the hot sun, for which they have done everything[?]. First of all they have thrown off everything that has any connection with the textile and leather trade, and just so, as God created them, they turn the world upside down and make wild noises that can deafen.

Summer in town.
But those who cannot attain the dream of travelling somewhere outside town and enjoying the air, the forest and the field — they must content themselves with what is accessible to them: if not a forest, if not a field, then at least something of the sort that is reminiscent of all that.
That means the "parks".
And the parks really do everything they can to create the illusion of nature-corners outside town. The trees, which seem themselves to long to go away for a bit of summer holiday, strive with all their might to create a little shade. The grasses and flowers, which beg not to be counted[?], so that no evil eye may harm them and perhaps the blessing may also come into them — strain themselves, poor things, enough to create a little cosiness that should have a refreshing effect on the weary senses.
And the city-dweller, it seems, appreciates the good will and fills the "parks" as is proper. On a day off, a bench in the "park" is a dream for tired, harried[?] feet — a dream which not everyone is privileged to see realized.
But never mind, it does not, God forbid, disturb anyone; anything is better than sitting in the cramped, stuffy homes, in the dusty, smoky lanes. One finds a way. Especially when a group of young people comes into the "park", then they sit on the bench in instalments. One sits and the rest stand, and afterwards they swap, and the same thing comes out again — one sits and the rest wait.
And the next day[?]:
It seems everywhere the same parks, and nevertheless every "park" has its "Hasidim", who give the "park" a distinctive face and a distinctive colouring.
The "Góra Zamkowa" [Castle Hill in Będzin], for example, is chiefly the park of the growing-up youth, whose it indeed is[?]; in every corner young voices ring out with clear, silvery laughter, with carefreeness and joy.
There is the refuge of the 15- and 16-year-olds, who are only just beginning to mature, who are only now feeling the first great tremor of a mighty feeling of love. There you will find them, those who are growing before your eyes out of their children's shoes. There is something particularly touching in the helpless glances, in the blushing[?] faces, in the whole shy, unbold bearing of the maturing youth — something touching, because it recalls the time that we ourselves went through.
Here you see before you the familiar schoolboy types. Here walks a young gymnasium pupil with his cap in his hand. The cap he holds in his hand is going through a real black year: it gets crumpled and broken without mercy. The lad casts shy glances about him. Here two young schoolgirls come towards him, laughing[?], playful; their glances meet, the girls walk on and burst out laughing; the lad turns red, and now it seems to him that he is as ugly as a cripple.
The first youthful tragedy.

Not all the young are so timid; on the contrary, there are quite a lot who are distinguished by "boldness". They come with a definite aim: they strike up acquaintances, "accost" girls, trade words, the girls answer back, a quarrel breaks out, they tell each other off properly — but in the end one realizes that an acquaintance has been made.
And that is how it begins. Young hearts beat, the young red blood rises into the face — the beginning of sleepless nights, the beginning of sorrow and joy...
The "Górka" [the hill] belongs to the youth, to those freed from a whole year's yoke of studying at school. Now they frolic like young colts let loose from their hobbles. The bit of greenery adds to the young, cheered-up mood.
Here begins the road[?] that perhaps costs so much health; here, through the merry, senseless chatter, the great feeling crystallizes — the feeling that plays such a dominant role in our life, the feeling that leads a person to the knowledge of joy, but still more to the knowledge of suffering: love, which kindles in a person the energy to climb the ladder of life up the mountain, and still more often pushes him down from the ladder of life, down into the abyss of tragedy.
Not Philanthropy, but Constructive Help for the Small-Town Jew

By P. Blumenkranc (Sosnowiec)

Those born in the larger Jewish settlements, who have had no opportunity to become acquainted with Jewish life in the small towns, still have a kind of romantic attitude towards the small Jewish shtetl.
And no wonder. Their knowledge in such a case is drawn chiefly from literature, and there, after all, the shtetl has been sung in the most varied ways.
After Mendele, who painted [?] the poverty, the hopelessness and the degeneration [?] of the Kabtsansk folk, the shtetl was for the most part later celebrated in Yiddish literature.
And therefore, of itself, when one speaks of the shtetl, the idyllic "pictures" float up before us: the little houses [?], the enamoured couples, the leisurely, expansive Sabbath, the strolls outside the town along the highway, the forbidden love of the shochet's son for a poor man's daughter, etc.
Yes, we have forgotten the healthy carter types and the "village-goers" [Jewish pedlars who made the rounds of the villages], who were awaited impatiently by their wives from Sabbath to Sabbath. At home everything good is prepared, and the village-goer brings presents for his wife and little daughter. Later he secures [?] himself a good son-in-law and gives him kest [board], and one thanks and praises the Creator...
True, the life is a limited one, but on the other hand a tranquil one, a healthy one and, economically, however modestly [?], a stable one; not much was lacking.
• • •
We therefore decided to become acquainted with life in a number of small towns nearby, to look a little into the life of these Jews, from whom we have lately been receiving uncomfortable greetings.
We do not want to fall into a Job-like tone; the weeping has already become almost banal. Nevertheless we cannot avoid saying that we came away from the small towns shaken.
Outwardly all the towns have almost the same appearance: in the middle a market square and a few streets around it with darkened little Jewish shops that are in their death throes — and so too the situation of the Jews is almost the same everywhere.
Those who stand on the steps of their shops and yawn are counted everywhere among the rich men of the town: they have, after all, a shop, a "loan-penny" [?]; but the majority stand in the corners of the market or in the beit midrash and lament their own fate.
In Kshepits [Krzepice?], already a relatively larger Jewish settlement, several Jews come to us in the name of the village-goers and complain of their bitter lot.
A Jew in his fifties, a stoutish man (a remnant of better times), begins to tell about himself:
— I was a confectioner, I carried baked goods to the villages and supported my household by it. Today it is bitter as death: one cannot go to the village, and for weeks on end I have not earned a single grosz.
— In the morning I sit longer in the beit midrash to get by [?] without breakfast; later I go home and lie down to sleep, and afterwards back to the beit midrash.
The Jew stands and weeps, and something chokes us in the throat; nothing is as piercing as the tears of grown men.
A second one tells:
— Today I went to the village. My wife says to me: Leyzer, don't go alone, I'll come with you; whatever happens, I want to be with you. We went to the village and barely escaped with our lives: they pelted us with stones; we were saved at the house of an elderly Christian.
• • •
And the same cry of woe everywhere from the largest, the most desperate [group] — from the village-goers.
In every small town there are up to 20—25 per cent Jews who make their living by going to the villages. One buys up a little grain, another — butter and eggs, a third — a calf. All these Jews used to make a living.
A Jew from Panki (near Truskolasy) tells us that he supplied geese to the Częstochowa "paszarnie" [goose-fattening houses]. Lately he has stopped trading: a calf one can buy and quickly get out of the village, but a flock of geese has to be driven, and they make a great racket — so trading is impossible.
— Last week — the Jew tells — I bought [?] a hundred geese. A Christian woman wanted to sell to me, but she warned me not to come into the village.
And the same lament everywhere.
On the day we were in Kłobuck, the Jews there told us of the following case.
A Jew drove with his wagon to the village of Bukidua [?]; there he was attacked by a gang of "łobuzy" [hooligans]; they overturned [?] the wagon and wanted to throw him into the water; the police rescued the Jew. On the way back he was attacked again and ransomed himself from the attackers [—] by handing them the only gulden he had on him.
• • •
And so these Jews are dying away. Because of the constant worry about how to get a piece of bread, they fall ill and do not think at all that they must be cured; they suffer from contagious diseases (tuberculosis; the children — from "mazus" [?], etc.) and have no idea that they must isolate themselves (incidentally, the Częstochowa "TOZ" [Society for the Protection of the Health of the Jews] has done a great deal in this respect in the surrounding small towns, for which the society truly deserves recognition).
Apathy [?], indifference, despair, hopelessness look out of the eyes of every Jew.
These Jews, who possessed so much that was sound and robust, who were such a well-spring of Jewish energy and of folk character — are dying before our eyes.
We are witnesses to an extraordinary tragedy of dozens and perhaps hundreds of small Jewish communities which are expiring before our eyes. A Jew tells us that if he had 6 złoty a week he would make a living. Well, you understand how far the economic decline of this Jew has gone! In one town there are 6 bakers — the Jews there assured us that not one of them has the money for 20 (twenty) kilos of flour.
• • •
The conclusion we draw from this:
If our situation in general is desperate, the situation of the small-town Jews is hopeless; and therefore, if the societies that trumpet so much about aid and productivisation do not concretely take up the occupational restructuring of the Jews in the small towns, complete ruin threatens them.
And although some attempts have not succeeded (the "TsBSh" [?] with the knitting machines in "Barystn" [?] in Truskolasy), the "Joint" must see to it, with the help of Polish Jewry, to work out certain realisable projects that will at least partly solve the question of the Jews in the small towns, especially of the village-goers.
The competent bodies, which occupy themselves — so they say — with constructive aid, must take an interest in these dying Jews, who find themselves on the brink of economic decline.
Something must therefore be done for these Jews! Not philanthropy, but something concrete, productive, in order to save these Jews from complete destruction!
A Happy Piece of News

[Humorous feuilleton — cost of living.] (A little feuilleton)
Matches are becoming 20 per cent cheaper.
(From the press)
Our "faithful reader" came to the editor yesterday with a complaint.
Already from the fact that his cap was twisted [?] with the peak ["daszek"] to the back, one could infer that he was "nervous".
— Please [?], Mr. Editor, what kind of good fortune are you telling me about in the paper?
Did you ever hear such a thing! Matches have become 20 per cent cheaper — some luck for my grandmother! [ironic: "big deal!"]
Tell me, I beg you, how much will the "profit" [?] come to, say, for a little man like me? Go ahead, take a pencil and work it out.
In the course of the day my wife [?] strikes 3 matches: one in the morning, a second for lunch and a third for supper. If a box holds 43 matches, that means the box lasts me two weeks. 20 per cent makes 2 groszy, which means that in the course of 2 weeks I will save [?] — 2 groszy.
Well, I ask you, is it worth talking about? On the contrary, say it yourself: if you had brought, for instance, news that potatoes had become 20 per cent cheaper, flour, groats ["kashe"] — that, you know [?], Mr. Editor, would have been something. But matches — leave me in peace with such good fortunes...
Ab-Nek.

[Feuilleton — summer-resort life.] (Sketches from "the Line" ["der linye" — the line of summer resorts])
By Sh. Libazon.
2.
And my prayer was "accepted". Accompanied by several "landslayt" [fellow townsmen] we went into a peasant hut ("hiltsi blan" [?]), where there was still a "free" flat to be found; to tell the truth, this flat too was "zajęte" [occupied]. But the deal fell through because the landlord's female cousin [?] would not agree to having a "Żyd z brodą" [Jew with a beard] [?] living in their house...
Apparently I did find favour with the villa owners after all, and we got down to the business itself. How much is it [?] — I ask him.
— I have — he explains to me — one more "pytanie" [question], namely, he wants to know how many children I have, because the tenants ["lokatorzy"] in his villa may not have more than one child.
Hearing such talk from my "one-child-system man", my head begins to spin and I start arguing with him:
— Is it possible? A worse decree than Pharaoh's! Pharaoh once decreed that the newborn boys be thrown into the water, but let the girls live — and you, sir ["panie"], decree against girls too?
— You have only girls? — he asks me.
— Of course, just girls.
— That's no good either. "Nie ma różnicy" [no difference] [?], girls or boys, as soon as there's more than one child I don't let.
— But dear sir [?], I swear by beard and side-locks that from this day on no more than 3.. But my promise did not help at all. He said "nie …" [an unclear Polish phrase] [?] — and go do something about it.
The end was that he stayed with the "mieszkanie" [flat] and I with my daughters... Still I remained "satisfied", because I felt on my own shoulders the power of civilization, which has by now "stepped" [?] into the village too...
They play [?]...
An important branch of dacha life is taken up by card playing. Everybody plays, and when we say "everybody" you understand, of course, that we mean — the women.
But the "species" must be classified, because there are three species of women in Bystra.
The first "species" plays poker, the second "species", the monarchists, play "Red King", the third makes do with "Sixty-six" and "Thousand". The rest of the women, who occupy themselves only with their children and have food on their minds — are no women at all.
The three species of women are divided into two sorts: one part, women who play for big money and in mixed company; the second sort play for small money, but also with men. And women who play only among themselves — those "are no women". But...
Such views we heard from the little women themselves, between one "kon" [round/pot] and another, when one snatches a moment [?] of fun with a bit of gossip ["plotka"].
At the dacha it is the custom to play three times a day, i.e. from morning till lunch, from the afternoon until "kolacja" [supper], and afterwards until midnight — but altogether no more than 3 times a day... Often changes are made, especially on Sunday, when some of the tired, sick women, worn out by a whole year, "work" a few hours in the evening at the dancing...
The "work" begins right after breakfast. "No, co, będziesz?" [Well, will you play?] [?] — one neighbour asks the other — "Don't you see any 'min'?" [?]
The neighbour does not hesitate long, pulls her pyjamas on and asks:
— Where's the full set?
— We'll go to Halinka and to Bela, then "to będzie komplet" [that'll make a full table].
— An "instrument"? [?]
— "The cards are with …" [a garbled Polish sentence, perhaps "someone from Będzin has the cards"] [?], he will play too, one only needs to "zaciągnąć" [drag him in].
And the "frajer" [sucker] lets himself be easily "caught"; they sit down [?] on the open veranda and "smakert" [?] — and all this is "done" [?] for the children's sake. The little women are good ones, the very "cream of mothers" [?], adherents of free upbringing — not that they want, God forbid, to bring up the "frajer", but to bring up their little children freely; for what won't one do for the poor, miserable little babies [?]? One literally sacrifices oneself and simply lays down one's life so that the little children may have proper freedom and the watchful maternal eye may be busy with the "poker"..!
The biggest "season" plays out on Saturday and Sunday, when men arrive "from the four corners of the earth" to their wives. Between us, on their part it is just an excuse; they [?] do not come to their own wives, but come to hold wrestling bouts with the cards...
And really, why not? A whole week they toil in town, poor things — surely they may at least on Saturday and Sunday indulge [?] themselves with the cards.
A company sits down [?] — not in the forest, the noise there is too great — on a veranda around a makeshift table, and they start "min".
In the middle of the game one also "snatches" something into the mouth; the women serve their husbands all kinds of "delicacies" [?]. They play until the clock shows that in half an hour the train leaves.
"More cultured".
Dacha life has a special virtue; the virtue consists in this, that most of the dacha-folk, more precisely — the dacha-women, become "more cultured". At home, between the stuffy ["duszne"] walls, "culture" too is kept within limited frames — it's the town after all; but as soon as one comes out into God's free world, one only then becomes a "human being", drives the "darkness" away and becomes a free person. Better said — an "intelligent".
But in this field too, the "cultural" one, there are various sorts which must be divided and classified, because with the same measure with which we must measure the "cultured" women of Zagłębie one cannot measure those from the Silesian side [?].
But we shall have a talk about that in the next number.
