A Letter to the Editor.
Dear Editor!
In connection with the report of the relief committee for Brisk [Brześć] in Sosnowiec concerning my person, I have the honour to submit the following clarification:
1) It is not true that I spoke to the delegation in such a way as could have meant that I want to wriggle out of the campaign — I expressly declared to Messrs. Advocate Kozalski[?] and Mr. Czapnik that I take part in all Jewish campaigns and therefore I also gladly wish to take part in this important campaign, — only, since I live in Katowice and money is being collected for Brisk there too, I shall give there.
2) As regards Katowice: I declare categorically that up to today nobody at all has approached me to donate to the A. R.[?] campaign, and as I am informed I am not the only one; there are many givers in Katowice who have not been visited, and they, understandably, have not given, despite being ready to give, — on the other hand, as I had only just returned from my journey and learned that no one had yet been to me, I immediately sent a larger sum of money to the Jewish kehilla in Katowice for the victims in Brisk.
3) It is true that Mr. Adv. Kozalski said on the spot that I want to wriggle out of taking part in the campaign, — to which I answered him on the spot: „What I give for philanthropic and charitable purposes in the course of a few days, Mr. Adv. Kozalski does not give in the course of a whole year“.
At the same time I have the honour to declare that there is truly no campaign in Sosnowiec in which I do not take part, despite being a resident of Katowice.
Respectfully,
Shmuel Nota Szlamowicz.
Rebbetzin Feigl Lewin, of Blessed Memory

At the age of 65 Rebbetzin Feigl Lewin, of blessed memory, widow of the Rabbi of Będzin, the great Rabbi R' Tzvi Hanoch, of blessed memory, died in Warsaw. For formal reasons the funeral took place only on Sunday. At the request of the deceased she was brought for burial to Ger [Góra Kalwaria]; although the funeral began at half past 5 in the morning, some 3 thousand mourners took part. In Ger the Gerer Rebbe, who was her brother, eulogised the deceased.
The deceased was of great lineage, a daughter of the Sfas Emes and a great-granddaughter of the Chiddushei HaRim; she was regarded[?] as a wise woman. In Będzin she took an active part in a number of philanthropic institutions and was honorary president of the women's society „Bikur Cholim“ and of „Hakhnasat Kallah“. May her soul be bound up in the bond of life.
Fundraising Campaigns in General and the Collection for Brisk in Będzin

[Będzin — fundraising; the collection for Brisk.]
We are still in the midst of the fundraising campaign for Brisk [Brześć nad Bugiem]. The writer of these lines also takes part in the collecting work, and therefore I think it is worthwhile to share with the readers my impressions of how Jewish Będzin collects and gives money for Jewish public causes.
—
Jewish Będzin runs fundraising campaigns almost all year round.
Among [?] all sorts of collectors, first place is held by the group of Zionist activists, which collects for the Keren Kayemet and especially for the Keren Hayesod. For the funds, tens of thousands of zł are collected year after year.
For many years the Zionists have intensively developed among Jews a kind of cult of giving money for Palestine causes, and they have also taught such things to the Jews of Będzin.
—
What does the collection for Brisk look like?
One of the Jewish householders of Będzin, whose name the collecting group had on its list, happened to walk into the premises of the kehilla just as the delegation was standing ready to go out into the street. One of the committee turns to this householder:
— Honoured sir, make a start right here and wish us [?] success on our way; why would you trouble so many people to come to your home?
The man was almost [?] "insulted."
He did not like the tone in which he was being spoken to. He does not want to be lectured; he can insist that they do come to him; he already knows himself what he has to do, too [?].
In short, the gentleman left. The delegation group had already had its first "start" [?], which was not capable of spoiling its mood, and it went off on its further mission.
By the way, the above-mentioned gentleman hurried [?], no longer waited until the delegation came to his home, brought a few złotys to the editorial office and — "discharged his duty."
The delegation came in to one of the Orthodox rich men.
When the Jew heard that they had come about Brisk, he delivered himself of these words:
— What is Brisk to me and who is Brisk to me, when I have such pogroms every day!
— What sort of thing do you have? — asks one of the delegation.
— I am pogromed every day!
— We do not understand.
— Here: I had hoped [?] that on the first [of the month?] [?] some 30 thousand zł would flow in to me [?]; they brought me barely 14 thousand zł. You understand my loss [?]! And such losses I have every day...
Not one of the delegation found himself [saying]: would that such "pogroms" were said [of us] [?]. Arguments begin; one talks, one persuades, one appeals to the mind and to the heart, to this world and to the next — the rich man dug in [?] that he gives 50 złotys and —
— I fear no one, only God, and you can do to me what you will.
And if God commanded him to give 50 zł., it is surely out of the question for the delegation to change a divine decision...
From this rich man the delegation went to an intellectual, who, God forbid, has not lost out in Będzin, and "may his loss be said of all Jews."
He received the delegation with a "barukh haba" [welcome]:
— Finally! A whole month has already passed since the events in Brisk, and Będzin has still not responded! Why, I have been literally waiting for you; I already wanted to send my money off to Warsaw!
The delegation was very glad: now these are words! This is the attitude of an intelligent Jew!
One delegate wrote out the receipt, and the intellectual rich man began to count. He counted out a few złotys in small coin [bilon] and —
— More I don't give!
— At least 50 zł. You can surely afford it.
— Not a grosz more.
— Then we won't take it.
— Then don't.
— Dozidzenia [goodbye — do widzenia].
— Cześć [?].
In fairness one must add that a few minutes later this gentleman reoriented himself and sent the 50 zł. after us.
—
I observe the Jews who bring smaller donations to the various collection points. The fact strikes the eye that very well-known rich men pop into a bank, or send a few small zł. by messenger — as though they were thereby ordering the committee not to trouble itself to come to them. Others bring a few zł., and it is evident that they have waged a struggle with themselves. The evil inclination stood by the pocket, the weak good inclination could not cope with it, but the Jew could not fall asleep and got rid of [?] a few ten-groszy pieces (groszy), so that it would seem to him that he had bought himself a few charity-box [pishkes] "kwitek" [receipts].
—
The action for Brisk is not yet finished, and we do not yet intend to draw up any totals.
We have brought these few facts so that they illustrate for us the mood in which the Będzin committee has to conduct the fundraising campaign.
Should we judge the Jews of Będzin unfavourably?
Why, above we brought other facts that tell us something quite different. The Jews of Będzin do have open hands and do not lock their pockets; and if one should accept [?] that only the ineffable Name of Eretz Israel is capable of opening the Jewish purse — we nevertheless have other, conspicuous facts that tell how gladly the Jews of Będzin give large sums of money for local causes as well — the Jews of Będzin deserve to be judged favourably.
So what is the matter with Brisk?
Why are the results so small?
Why has the collection not yet taken on the character of a true popular action?
We stand before a riddle, and since with this article we do not aim to set our readers riddles, but to talk things over frankly, to describe the true state of the action, so that Jews will read, know and help reach the proper results — therefore we shall leave the final total until after the collection is completed.
Y. N—m.
Small Traders Demand an Extension of the Lump-Sum (Ryczałt) Turnover-Tax Term.

[Economy — taxes; small traders.] In December of this year the term ends up to which all the smaller commercial and industrial enterprises with a turnover of up to 50 thousand zł. a year paid on it a lump-sum (ryczałt) turnover tax at the rate of one and a half per cent.
This method of lump-sum turnover tax was introduced in 1936 for a term of 2 years, i.e. 1936 and 1937. Subject to the lump-sum turnover tax were the commercial enterprises of the 4th and 5th category and the industrial enterprises of the 6th, 7th and 8th class.
In this connection, as the end of the term for paying the turnover tax by ryczałt is approaching[?], the Central Union of Small Traders has sent the Union of Chambers of Commerce a memorandum in which they [printed "ווי"] propose to leave this system in place for a further two years; moreover, the enterprises with a turnover of up to a hundred thousand zł. a year should also be subject to this system, and it should also cover the gastronomic establishments. This question will be dealt with already this Thursday at the session of the Chamber of Commerce.
Three Summer Holidaymakers. What Each of Them Tells.

[Humorous feuilleton — summer holidaymakers.] By J. Oberżanek [?].
(What each of them tells)
In summertime, when the wives go out to the meadows ["lonkes" — łąki] to "poprawić się" [recover their health], the husbands become "gospodarne"[?] [thrifty housekeepers]. The husbands, it seems[?], take over the wives' mission. Each does it, of course, in a different way. The other day I overheard a conversation of three such "gospodarze" [householders]! Each told how he "gospodaruje" [keeps house]... I render the conversation almost word for word:
Letnik [holidaymaker] number 1
— I, when my missus goes away — said the first letnik — become a regular "gospodarz". I don't eat in the restaurant; I have no patience to sit down at a table and wait until the waiter deigns to come over, and when he does come over, he pours out at me a bundle of soups: zupa francuska, zupa włoska, zupa hiszpańska, zupa wiedeńska [French, Italian, Spanish, Viennese soup] — a whole "International"!... — and when he finally brings me a zupa włoska, it is a plate with a soaked bottom in which a consumptive little carrot floats about with a whiff of parsley — that is a "zupa włoska".. — if Mussolini eats such Italian soups, woe betide him...
And with the meat, is it any better? After the soup you sit for a whole hour, you knock with the knife on the plate, knock here, knock there, shout: "panie ober" [Mr. Head-waiter], "panie starszy", and when he does come over, he again reels off[?] a whole "composition" at you:
— kotlety, klopsiki, mostek, ozór, gęsiny, kaczka, pieczeń cielęca [cutlets, meatballs, brisket, tongue, goose, duck, roast veal]. He pours out his composition in one breath like the ten sons of Haman, and in the end I again don't know what to order. One mustn't think long, because if you change your mind just once, the "pan ober" turns into a wild beast, slaps with his napkin and [—] ["vild inzu" — doubtful reading]!
The same with the "janoszinkes"[?] in my "kompas"[?]; when I get through such a restaurant lunch, I am as hungry as a wolf...
Therefore, you understand me, I do it all myself. How do I do it, you want to know? Well, listen then!
I have my shikse [gentile maid], who comes to me every morning with milk; then I set about cutting kindling, lay one chip next to another, stuff old newspapers and candles into the kitchen [stove], pour paraffin, light a bundle of zapałki [matches], blow into the ash, and after an hour of striking matches and blowing into the ash it comes "out of business"[?] — luckily there is fire; and by the time I come back from the shop with the rolls, the milk is — on the podłoga [floor]... not a trace of any milk — boiled over.
Well, if there is no milk — what of it, a letnik must drink milk for breakfast. I take on the lunch: I go into the jatka [butcher's stall] and say to the butcher:
— Reb Leyzer, give me a good portion of meat, but without any bone-makeweight.
— What do you want? For soup or for a stew[?]?
— It can be a bit of this and a bit of that.
Says the butcher:
— What does that mean, a bit of this and a bit of that? Either you cook a soup, or a stew[?]?
— Let it be, say I, a piece for mincing.
I come home with the piece for mincing, take the chopper and get down to work. At every blow the windowpanes tremble, at every thump[?] of the chopper pieces fall from the sufit [ceiling], I have more plaster-and-wood than meat... You see, sir, the bandaged finger? That's from chopping meat. Instead of the meat, I put my finger under...
I hate the restaurants; I do it all myself. I am very — "gospodarny"... I do it exactly like my wife, only a little differently.
Letnik number 2
— And I — says the second letnik — don't hold with such things. I say that a man who puts on his wife's spódnica [skirt] is a rag, not a man. A man who makes the fire, who boils milk and goes into the butcher's for meat and makes klopsikes [meatballs] with his own fingers — degrades the prestige of the whole of male humanity. Someone like you is no "mężczyzna" [man] at all!..
— I, you see, don't boil milk, don't go into the butcher's for meat, don't chop klopsikes with the chopper. But I also don't go to eat in the restaurants, I don't wait for the waiter, don't knock with the knife on the plate, don't shout my throat out: "panie ober", "panie starszy", I don't eat any Italian soups — I do it differently. I bought myself a "tygodniowy" [weekly] ticket and I travel every evening to my wife at the letnisko [summer resort]. She shouldn't have such an easy[?] life: a wife must not be given so much "wolności" [freedom]; when a missus has too much "wolności", she becomes "rozpłoszczona"[?] [spoiled?] — and I don't want a "rozpłoszczona" wife!
— So I decided to buy a "tygodniówka" [weekly ticket] and I travel out every evening to my missus at the letnisko.
I have a bright life: I am the only male in "Moskiwa"[?], the only "mężczyzna" in the whole villa, the women besiege me from all sides, my little wife triumphs:
— See what a faithful husband I have, he can't live a single day without me!
The women envy her her faithful husband, and I live like God in Odessa. True, I do get all sweaty, I do get worn out, I do drag myself every evening on the trains, but I feel[?] that I am a "mężczyzna": I don't boil milk myself, I don't make fire, I don't go into the butcher's for meat, I don't chop off my fingers over the klopsikes — I am a man as God commanded.
Letnik number 3
— And I, you see, gentlemen — says the third letnik — do it quite differently! I neither become "gospodarny"[?], nor do I travel every evening to my wife at the letnisko — I don't go out of the house. And do you know why I do so? I'll tell you:
— A year ago in the summer I behaved like this: lunch I ate in restaurants, and every evening I travelled out to my wife at the letnisko. I hold that a woman, if she goes out for "świeże powietrze" [fresh air], must have "odpoczynek" [rest], she mustn't have any "kłopoty" [troubles], she mustn't have to guard the little pot for her husband — it is enough that she guards the pot all year; in summer she must "erholen" [recuperate], come to herself. So I ate lunch in a restaurant, but since she is a bit "nervous" and afraid to sleep alone, I travelled out every evening so that she could sleep "spokojnie" [peacefully].
Well, so I really wasn't at home the whole summer. In the morning I went straight out into the street to sniff out what's new, at lunchtime I went to a restaurant, after lunch again into the street, to a cukiernia [café-patisserie], and in the evening — flew off on the "sprziwonek"[?] [train?] to my wife at the letnisko.
So it went the whole summer, every day the same, and since my wife left, I did not set eyes on my flat in town.
I saw the flat only when my missus came back — and I saw such things that everything went dark before my eyes.
Together with me, the inkasent [collector] of the elektrownia [power company] came into the flat and handed me a bill for 182 zł.
— What? What? 182 zł.? Where from? How? I wasn't at home the whole summer! How does such a swollen bill come about?
Later it turned out that he was right, not I. How did the swollen bill come about? Quite simply: before leaving I had left the big lamp burning in the dining room, and it burned "bez przerwy" [without a break] for three months...
Now you understand why I don't go out of the house — I am guarding the "licznik" [electricity meter; a pun on "letnik"]!
This Is the Hour of Destiny.

[Article — Palestine, the Peel Commission partition plan.] By P. Blumenkranc (Sosnowiec).

We do not want to make revelations in the following lines. Enough has already been said, and clearly, about England's "yachloku" policy ["yachloku" — "let them divide it", the Talmudic ruling for two who hold one garment], and much more will be said between the time these words are written and their publication.
Nevertheless one cannot keep silent; one feels an irrepressible[?] need to speak out, so that it should become a little easier.
Unfortunately we have no other weapon. Napoleon, it seems, said that he does not set an ultimatum if he has no armies behind him. We must content ourselves with mere shouting — especially since when it hurts one shouts, and does not ponder whether it will have any effect.
*
One is reminded of the well-known Jewish joke (which also has several variants):
A Jew comes to his good friend on a Friday and is warmly invited to stay for the Sabbath. The traveller agrees and leaves his money with his good friend over the Sabbath. On Sunday[?] morning, when he asks for the money back, the host tells him "neither bears nor forest" — that he never gave him any money to keep.
The Jew raises an outcry:
— How can it be, what's the matter with you? Don't you remember that I gave you the money?
— Nothing of the sort — the host answers coldly.
— What do you mean? It cries to heaven!
In short, back and forth, they go to the rabbi. The mara de-atra heard out the claims, rubbed his forehead, dissuaded [them][?] from taking, God forbid, a "kabbalah"[?], and issued a ruling that the host must give the guest half of the sum.
After the ruling had been issued, the host returned the whole sum to the guest, adding:
— As you know, I did indeed take the money; I only wanted to show you what a decent rabbi we have...
*
The joke came to mind in connection with the "yachloku" policy. Yes, there is only one difference between the rabbi and England: the rabbi did it out of innocence, and England out of cunning (too weak an expression).
After 20 years of the Balfour Declaration, after the well-known letter to Weizmann, after various assurances on festive occasions, they suddenly begin doing favours to the Arabs[?] and to the Jewish people by giving away (for the time being not yet) one sixth of Eretz Israel.
And English diplomacy, mixed[?] with compassion, with kind-heartedness, has embraced all living creatures.
The Arabs "sympathise" with the tragedy of the Jewish people — says the Commission — but after all they cannot be so over-compassionate as to give up the whole of their own land for the benefit of the Jews.
What does the Jew think about it?
True, there really is no justice in the world, might makes right; but how can one so mock the hopes of a people that has brought so many sacrifices on the strength of these pledges, that sent its youth into fire and despair, that for generations held back from resignation because of these promises?
And not only do they mock, they also resort to methods like those of the "enlightened times": if you too want to live, you must pay a kind of poll-tax to the Arabs, who must consent to live with you as neighbours (a sort of constitution).
*
The English are by nature very cautious in diplomacy, even cowardly. Not to speak of her conduct regarding Spain, where it is mainly the interests of the rich that dictate[?], England showed much cowardice towards Italy in the Abyssinian affair, and shows much servility towards Germany. The German minister sulks, and England flatters and apologises.
A characteristic fact.
Peretz Hirschbein relates that when he returned from Sarnath[?], where there are ruins of Buddha temples more than 2 thousand years old (from the time of King Ashoka [printed "Asaka"]), he stopped by a gathered crowd, where a young blonde girl was speaking about the Christian religion. Suddenly someone in the crowd asked aloud:
— How much did Christ get from the English government for standing on the broad road leading to Benares[?] and telling the people these clever words?
And before she had even finished[?] her speech, a second man tore himself out of the circle of people and spat the blue-eyed missionary in the face, and so did a second, a third.
And Peretz Hirschbein relates at the end of the chapter ("India" — a spit in the face) that when, some time later, he met the Englishwoman, she turned to him in these words:
— You surely wondered how I can bear a spit in the face so easily; know that English blood flows in me, that is the strength in me; you do not know what English blood means!
And Hirschbein concludes:
Apparently one must also let oneself be spat in the face when one wants to rule the weak, who can do no more than spit back in one's face.
And I think to myself that the last among the rulers and the ruled will be those who can one time display armed force and another time — let themselves be spat in the face.
The English let themselves be spat in the face too, but towards the Jews they are haughty: you don't want certificates in the number I give? — I'll distribute them myself.
And only with regard to Jews could such an idea be born — to create a "Jewish state" without Jerusalem.
After the World War small nations were given back their state independence, and it did not occur to anyone at all to take from them the "heart" of whatever country it was.
One need not be a Zionist, nor sentimentally Jewish[?], to understand what an absurdity it is to demand that Jews give up the most [?] Jewish city, the city where every stone tells of Jewish sorrows and joys, toward which for thousands of years the faces of millions and tens of millions of Jews have been turned, in times of joy and in times of mourning, the city where rivers of Jewish tears and Jewish blood were shed — and at the same time to speak of a "Jewish state" and have the audacity to talk about [?] liberating the Jewish people; something like that only such politicians as the English can do.
*
They perform an operation on the Jewish Eretz Israel: they give the Jews a sixth of Eretz Israel and take away from them the Negev, Rutenberg's station, the Dead Sea and Jerusalem; they want to calm the Jews, the starved, tormented Jews, with a sweet, a toy. The tactic of all seafarers and travellers towards savages: oil wells, coal treasures — for little watches that chime, for glass beads that glimmer.
The Jews are needed — a safer element, they are loyal, provided they are only allowed to live; of the Arabs one is afraid, so one tells the Arabs who have grown rich: — Throw the Jews a bone; you have 5 times as much as they; we will give you money, the Jews will pay you, and it will be all right..
And the Jews swoon[?] — everyday Jews and even wise and learned Jews; the word pleases them. A cousin a minister (until now barely a cousin a doctor). Our own money, our own locomotives!
But the naive Jews forget that Monaco is small and exists and its inhabitants are well off — and that is because there is no "Monacan" question in the world; whereas against us all the evil forces have set themselves[?], and the accursed Jewish question does not leave the agenda for a single minute.
And if until now Jews were angry with England because they are not let into Eretz Israel, then after the creation of the "state" within the projected borders they will be even angrier with the cousin-ministers, the Jews, who will be unable to let [them] into that "dew-and-rain" [i.e. tiny] Eretz Israel.
*
Jews are living through moments of upheaval, when the fate of 50 years of work is being decided; and if Jews do not use the means of other peoples, they must make use of their influence, which is so exaggeratedly portrayed, [and raise] a mighty outcry, so that the work of tens [of years], hopes of thousands of years and the hard, sacrifice-filled work of camps of young people who wanted to plough over[?] this land should not be destroyed.
Not only every people but every person has moments of submission[?] [probably meant: decision] that influence his further life. And woe to the person who misses these moments in his life — doubly woe and alas to a people that cannot make use of these fateful minutes.
“Nothing Has Changed”.

(Sketches from the “Line”.) By S. Libaszon.

3.
“Culture” and “Civilization”.
Life at a dacha [summer cottage] has a great virtue: not only does the body get a “tikkun” [repair], but the soul too. It, the soul, that is, then becomes “crystallized” and takes on its true face, because at home, on the Old Market in Będzin, or on Pańska Street in Sosnowiec, the prevailing “darkness” of Jewish life hinders[?] the soul from acquiring a free spirit; but when one gets out into an entirely free world, free senses develop in a person, by which the human being is raised to the epoch before the Creation, to the time when Adam and Eve were in the Garden of Eden...
Nevertheless there are certain changes — after all, we live in the twentieth century. The changes are: 1) Adam and Eve covered their naked bodies with fig leaves, while today’s Eves make use of “modern costumes”... 2) Eve of primeval times was ashamed, even though in the Garden of Eden there was nobody apart from her husband (granted[?], there was also a serpent there...), whereas the Eves of the epoch of “culture” and “civilization” are no longer ashamed; on the contrary, they demonstrate their nakedness on the promenade, while shopping and even in company at lunch in the boarding house...
— So have no complaints against her, the modern Eve; she did not come to the dacha for matters of the soul — that is a business for the “ciemna hołota” [Polish: the ignorant rabble] — but only to spread and propagate the idea of today’s “culture and civilization”...

T r o u s e r s.
Of men’s garments the one most often mentioned is — trousers. The “trouser article” is used [?] in various folk sayings[?]; for example, a bridegroom without any livelihood whatsoever is called “a fellow in a single pair of trousers”; when one tells of a culprit, a villain[?], one says: “He has a guilt[?] — sew[?] it into the trousers.” But since the dacha fashion has got into the “cobbler’s bench” [i.e. down to the common folk], when people run into debt over their heads just to go to a summer lodging — the trouser article has lost its former sharpness and has also got “into the cobbler’s bench”...
You surely remember what a “sensation” the first “trouser-wearers” caused; young and old talked of the new women “culture-bearers” who made a breakthrough in the “trouser world”: — “You men will no longer strut so; in the name of women’s emancipation we are shaking the foundations of the old world: men’s trousers, alcohol and smoking papirosy [cigarettes]”...
But the new cult gradually lost its glitter and splendour, and the “dacha trousers” have become “workaday”. When a Jewish matron drags herself along the highway in cultured trousers, she can barely move, the poor thing barely has a breath left in her [lit.: owes God her soul]; and when for ten months of the year her appetite is by no means bad — no wonder one quickly[?] reaches the scales...
From afar it seems a circus clown is coming; when the “coloured lady” draws near, only then do we see with whom “we are going to table”: why, it is the well-known supplier of wampelekh[?] [probably tripe, flaki], a well-known “brand” — the best wampn[?] you get from her.
* *
— “[—] this?!” [roughly: “How does this look?!”; doubtful reading] — she bursts out talking, so that one hears it[?] in the tenth villa — “what do you say[?] about my trousers? If my husband[?] saw me now, he would run off to where the pepper grows” [idiom: to the ends of the earth].
— “It is not at all bad[?], only the trousers on you[?] are a bit tight” — our compliment.
— You hear, all my children have put me up to this. This year they felt like going to a “letnisko” [Polish: summer resort]; so — I answered[?] them — if you mean a letnisko, then go to Sztwer[?] or to Slovakia[?], why Bystra of all places? They gave me to understand that there is simply no other way, only to Bystra must one go: the whole “yentelligentsia” of Zagłębie goes to Bystra. Well, never mind, I thought to myself, what pleases the Almighty suits me too. Who knows, girls nowadays — maybe help will come to them from Bystra...
So they really went, but it was not long before my children began bombarding me with letters that for heaven’s sake I should come to them at once; they also wrote that I should come “like respectable people”. Guess, dear guests[?], what they meant by the word “respectable”? — Simply that I should bring along coloured trousers...
— Mama — wrote the youngest girl — don’t you dare come without trousers, you could blacken our faces in people’s eyes; here we play the role of “better ladies[?]”, “lepszego domu” [Polish: “of a good family”]; so let people know that we told no lie, that we really have a “modern mama”.
And the “modern mama” — sighs the poor Jewish woman — must keep up appearances: even when I go to the market [targ], into the butcher’s [jatka], the children don’t let me out until I put on the trousers...
Oh, may this fashion of going to the “letnisko” burn up already; there is a whole upheaval going on at the “letniskos”: wives turn into “men” and the Sabbath turns into — a weekday...
What more shall I tell you? — My daughters don’t let me light candles in honour of the Sabbath; it does not suit them — they say — before the neighbours, that they have a fanatical mother. You surely think they are ashamed before the Christian neighbours — you are greatly mistaken; they are ashamed before the women “intelligentsia” of Będzin, of Sosnowiec and of Sandrusze[?]...
— “Excuse me, I have poured my heart out a little in Yiddish. At home — I mean at the letnisko — my girls won’t utter a single Yiddish word; they give me to understand that I myself must also avoid speaking Yiddish here, because I too am already a “yentelligentka”: I no longer light candles in honour of the Sabbath, and I go to the market — in trousers..

Destruction and Redemption

[Essay — Tisha b'Av; reflections.]
(Tisha b'Av thoughts).
"The night of the first day of Passover is the night of Tisha b'Av... and over this Jeremiah lamented: 'How doth the city sit solitary'..." (Petichta of Eikhah Rabbati).
Those who know the secret of combinations, of the connections in Jewish history, have noted well that already with the very first steps of redemption the "stigma" of our destruction was marked, and that the symbol-day of the first redemption — Passover — is fatally bound to the symbol-day of destruction — Tisha b'Av. Just as destruction is closely bound up with redemption.
* * *
Redemption within destruction, destruction within redemption — that is the red thread that runs through [?] our whole history; and if over the first, the strange [?] beginning-road of the people, the lamenter mourns: "How doth the city sit solitary," then comes the comforter, who sees the second stage of the historical road and says: "Comfort ye, comfort ye my people!".
Not as a fatum do we regard the day of Tisha b'Av, which became "the day prepared for calamities." True, we are despised [?] by all nations, but that does not touch our spirit.
Our history is a perpetuum mobile, which does not stop at one point.
For the nations of the world it is either-or: either destruction or redemption. For us it is, as everyone knows, "recurring," which always joins the beginning to the end and the end again to the beginning. We join the "Eikhah" to the "Nachamu," just like the "Chazak" [?] to "Bereshit," because we do not want to stop, and we always seek a tikkun for our greatest historical sin — our stubbornness to live.
When the people already finds the way to itself in [—] and is already, it seems, at the end, one must begin anew from "Bereshit," from a long, hard road from oneself to the world. And it, the world, still wants our destruction..
"Jews are the [?] (uncertain word) of all nations, and the [?] are trampled underfoot..." says Sigmund Freud. We carry on with our work, because the sated and contented smile is foreign to our faces...
We want once and for all to break a way through for ourselves and not to live forever in fear.
We do not rejoice too much at Passover, and we do not [?] (probably: mourn) excessively on Tisha b'Av, because we believe in our future, and we are the people of past and future.
In our ancient books it is told that in the hardest times of the wars around the walls of Jerusalem the whole national treasury was spent, and the daily (tamid) offering was still brought at that time, because we have always regarded destruction as something temporary, which must on no account set aside the perpetual (tamid) work.
* * *
Destruction and Building.
Other nations take pleasure in going to visit the places where they won victories, hold celebrations, put up [?] monuments, and they are afraid to recall their defeats. We, however, go to visit the "Western Wall," because we know that in it lies the seed of our rebuilding; and if for certain reasons we shall no longer be able to visit the "Wall," we shall visit the port in Tel Aviv, the source of song and life for our whole future.
Hard is our road, the road of constant movement, but the more struggle, the more zigzags — the more refined and strengthened we shall emerge.
Yerucham Bachrach.
Interesting Things We Don't Know

[Miscellany — around the world; Turkey, history of objects.]
1) The Taster.
Among the strange livelihoods that exist in the world, worth recording is the livelihood of the Englishman Frederick Egzon [?], who now lives in Ankara, the capital of Turkey.
He is the taster of the dishes cooked for the Turkish dictator, the minister-president [sic] Kemal Atatürk.
Atatürk rules Turkey with a strong hand. He introduced reforms in matters that had been rooted there for hundreds of years through religion, through customs and ceremonies that had prevailed there since time immemorial. He abolished the harem — no one may now have more than one wife; he ordered the fez taken off and ordinary hats put on, or going bare-headed. He abolished the Turkish script and introduced the international Latin letters, and he abolished the veil for women — they must now show [?] their faces in the street.
Of course, especially the older people raised a [?] (uncertain word; probably: an outcry), but it did not help them at all. Nonetheless Atatürk is indeed afraid of being poisoned. So a trustworthy man was taken on, an Englishman who formerly had a carpet business in Constantinople, and he was made overseer over the "chief baker and chief cupbearer." His work consists in this: an hour before the food is brought in to the Turkish minister-president, he has to taste it; the doctors say that every poison, even the strongest, must take effect within an hour.
For this work he receives 250 pounds a month. In the 10 years he has had this livelihood, it has happened only once that the taster began to vomit after half an hour. Doctors and chemists were called together, the food was examined closely, but nothing was found in it. To this day it is not known why he vomited; in any case the whole meal was thrown out, and the staff employed in the kitchen too.
2) How Old Is the Spoon?
It is hard to believe when one hears that only in the year 1737, that is exactly 200 years ago, were spoons brought for sale for the first time at the Leipzig fair. They were carved by hand and indeed had the shape of a human hand. True, in Holland "lepels" had already been made some years [sic] earlier — this was a kind of vessel with which one could scoop water (in Dutch it was called "lapel" [?], and from this indeed comes the word "lefl" [spoon]).
But this vessel was very large and could not be used at table. At most one could "ladle" with it from a barrel, but not from a plate.
Exactly 200 years ago a spoon appeared on the table for the first time, more or less in the shape and size in which we use it to this day.
Z. Haber, Vienna.
Free Medicines for the Poor Unemployed Population

[Poland — welfare and health; Ministry of Social Welfare.]
The Ministry of Social Welfare has embarked on a broadly conceived campaign of distributing medicines and remedies free of charge to the poorest and unemployed population that is under the care of the hygiene-medical health centres. This [?] will make possible the treatment of the poorest and unemployed sick, who cannot buy any medicines and cannot obtain them from the insurance fund (Ubezpieczalnia).
The free distribution of medicines is part of the general campaign of the Ministry of Social Welfare, which aims to raise the state of health of the broadest masses of the population.
The voivodeship offices and the district (powiat) doctors throughout the country are now preparing data concerning the consumption of remedies in the various regions and the number of people who need to receive the remedies free of charge.
The medicines will be sent directly to the various health centres in such a form that they can be issued to the persons who need them. According to an estimate [?], the total value of the medicines and remedies amounts to 950 000 zł.
The list of medicines intended for distribution comprises about 93 kinds, among them cod-liver oil for 300.000 zł.
Interesting Promotion of „Enrilo“ Coffee at the „Work and Culture“ Exhibition

[Lisków — exhibition; advertorial.]
With an interesting promotion, the largest domestic factory of coffee products, the firm Henryk Franck and Sons [Henryk Franck i Synowie], joint-stock company, known throughout Poland for its good coffee for enjoyment[?] under the name „Enrilo“, appeared at the exhibition „Work and Culture of the Village“ in Lisków.
We go up onto the exhibition grounds at midday, when the packed crowd is now eating the truly cheap lunch, which costs no more than 55 groszy, served by the exhibition committee and the field kitchens. After eating this lunch comes something unexpected.
Next to[?] the kitchen pavilion a booth of the firm Henryk Franck and Sons, joint-stock company, has been set up, in which the visitors to the exhibition are treated to the extraordinary „Enrilo“ coffee.
With great effort we get into the firm's booth, around which large gathered crowds are pushing and tasting the good coffee. We too taste the „Enrilo“ coffee, which comes easily, because it all goes very quickly. We learn that „Enrilo“ coffee owes its popularity to its [?] domestic raw materials.
As we learn, the firm Henryk Franck has considerably helped to strengthen the domestic agricultural economy thanks to the large orders that the firm places.
Noting on the spot the great success of, and the interest in, this original promotional event, we become convinced that in connection with the exhibition the followers of „Enrilo“ coffee among the broad masses will grow — those who until now have not had the opportunity to become acquainted with the extraordinarily good beverage that is „Enrilo“ coffee.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Devarim)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Devarim
—o—
a) "And it came to pass in the fortieth year" (Deut. 1:3)
"This teaches that he rebuked them only close to his death." Rashi.
The Baal Shem Tov's disciple, R' Yaakov Yosef of Polonne [Połonne], once argued with R' Leib the Preacher (Mokhiakh):
— The Midrash says that even Moses did not rebuke the Jews except close to his death, and you preach at and rebuke Jews day in, day out.
R' Leib answered him:
— In Avot it is said, "Repent one day before your death" — do teshuvah a day before your death — and it is interpreted: reckon every day that tomorrow you may die, and so you must do teshuvah every day. I too reckon every day that any moment now I shall die; it follows that when I rebuke Jews, I am rebuking them before death...
• • •
"He that rebuketh a man after Me shall find favour" (Prov. 28:23) —
People don't mind being preached at about piety; on the contrary, it is pleasant to hear a sermon, it somehow soothes the conscience, one even sighs over it. It is different, however, with matters between man and his fellow — in such matters it already annoys people to be preached at...
That is the meaning of "He that rebuketh a man after Me shall find favour": whoever preaches to people only "after Me" — in matters of piety — "shall find favour", he does find favour in people's eyes... R' Israel Salanter.
—o—
b) "Wise men and known" (ibid. 15)
"But men of understanding I did not find." Sifre.
Why did he find no men of understanding?
Because "men of understanding" means "one who understands one thing from another", one who foresees a matter. Apart from wisdom, it is a special cleverness to foresee a thing; and those who were men of understanding could foresee what would become of leaders, how the people would treat them — and so they hid from Moses. That is the meaning of "men of understanding I did not find": I could not find them, because they had hidden themselves... Imrei Chen.
—o—
c) "Ye shall not respect persons in judgment" (ibid. 17)
"Ye shall not respect persons in judgment" —
In Nitra there was a famous rabbi, R' Avraham P.K.[?]. He once said about the rabbis who show partiality, once to this one and once to another:
The Gemara says: "If the rabbi resembles an angel of the Lord of Hosts, let them seek Torah from his mouth; and if not, let them not seek Torah from his mouth." In what must a rabbi be like an angel of the Lord of Hosts?
Only this: an angel is single-faced — "an angel does not carry out two missions". The angel is the embodiment, the symbol, of single-facedness, and that is what a rabbi must be too... Melitzei Esh.
• • •
At a great din torah [rabbinic court case] there once met R' Eizel of Słonim, R' Yitzchak Elchanan [Spektor of Kovno] and the Rabbi of Kobryń. Just on that day there was a great heat, so that it was hard to sit it out.
R' Eizel made a joke:
The Gemara says: "A judge should always see himself as if Gehenna were open beneath him" (Sanhedrin 7) — that a rabbi during a din torah should be as though Gehenna were open beneath him. Today[?], when three rabbis have come together for a din torah, it is no wonder that it is so hot...
—o—
d) "Go up, possess it" (ibid. 21)
The whole portion is said in the plural; only when it comes to the conquest of the land does it change to the singular: "Go up, possess it!" — because one can conquer the land only when all are like one man; that is the first condition for the conquest of the land.. Yalkut David.
—o—
e) "Ye shall pass over armed before your brethren the children of Israel" (3:18)
The children of Gad were heroes — this is told about them many times — and therefore they were appointed as the vanguard. But the children of Reuben — about them it is nowhere told that they were heroes — so why were they made "armed men passing before the camp"?
But however unheroic they may have been by nature — once they had left wives and children across the Jordan, they could already become heroes... Mishenet Moshe.
—o—
Eicha (Lamentations).
—o—
f) "Judah is gone into exile because of affliction and because of great servitude" (1:3)
With other peoples poverty is a symptom[?] of unemployment; with Jews, alas, both are present together: "great servitude" — harriedness[?] and drudgery up over one's head, and "affliction" — poverty. Jews get nothing from their toil and labour[?]; everything goes to strangers... Avodat HaLevi'im.
—o—
g) "Her adversaries are become the head, her enemies are at ease" (ibid. 5)
How many different kinds of enemies Judah has, and nevertheless they can all unite, make peace ("her enemies are at peace") and have one head over them, when it is a matter of doing harm to Jews; whereas for Jews it is hard to make peace even when it is merely a matter of defending themselves... Derashot Maharib.
—o—
h) "He hath filled me with bitterness" (3:15)
R' Avraham Yehoshua Heshel of Apta [Opatów] was an opponent of fasts; he used to say:
— If I had authority in Heaven, I would abolish all fasts except Tisha beAv and Yom Kippur. Yom Kippur — because who needs to eat then? And Tisha beAv — who can eat then?..
—o—
i) "Our fathers have sinned, and are not; and we have borne their iniquities" (5:7)
"Our fathers have sinned, and are not" — whoever raises a bad generation sins even when he is no longer alive; for when the young generation sins, it is after all because of the bad upbringing by the older generation. That is the meaning of "our fathers have sinned" — our parents sin, "and are not" — even when they are no longer here...
R' Israel Salanter.
—o—
j) "Servants rule over us" (ibid. 8)
"Over us" [Heb. banu, also "through us"] — through us: with our own hands we have brought it about that servants should rule over us... Pri Tzaddik.
The Living Dead Man (17)

[Serialized novel — "a most thrilling novel of Jewish life in Zagłębie before and after the World War"; installment 17.]
A. Zaglembier [pen name].
(A most thrilling novel of Jewish life in Zagłębie before and after the World War).

"Łapka" ran after him, shouting in anger:
— So "bird" helps you [?], remember [?]. Now you won't get away from me dry! A devil in your...
Because of the thicket and the darkness they lost sight of each other for a moment; all that could be heard was further [?] stifled [?] breathing [?] and the pounding of Yosl's heart. He ran zigzag, hoping in this way to shake off "Łapka", but the bandit was after him, now with the knife already in his hand...
— Stop! Or else you'll pay with your life!

But Yosl no longer heard any further words. He ran on and on, forward. Suddenly his foot caught on a thick broken branch; he fell, got up at once and, without accounting [?] to himself why he was doing it, snatched up the pole [Yiddish "drang", Polish drąg]; but a moment later it was already clear to him: the pole could come in useful to defend himself. And indeed he was not mistaken, for "Łapka" was afraid to shoot — lest it be heard from nearby, and that could give him away [?] himself — and so he chased Yosl only with the knife. But now Yosl already feels that he will not hold out, any moment "Łapka" will catch up with him, and he feels that his end is near... And indeed, like a man who has nothing left to lose, Yosl decided to take the risk. In a very dense spot he suddenly stopped short under a big tree, raising the pole high, and just as "Łapka" went past, thinking that Yosl was still running on — the pole suddenly came down with an extraordinarily hard blow on his head... At that very moment "Łapka" fell to the ground with a split skull, groaning and gnashing [?] horribly, trying to get up again and throw himself at Yosl:
— You've split my head...

And as if in madness [?], not knowing himself where such strength came to him from, he again raised the pole up and down, until he no longer heard any groan at all, until "Łapka" was left lying dead...
Only now did Yosl Wertheim see [?] what he had done, and he shuddered with terror even more. Already, it seemed to him, everyone knew that he had killed a man.. The police are coming, he is being arrested...
But that was only in the first minute, as he looked at his still-warm victim. A little later, however, he calmed down and began to look for a way to wipe out the traces of his terrible deed, how to save himself...
And since need and despair are often the best counsellors, a strange plan suddenly occurred to Yosl too — how to be rid of all his troubles at one stroke.

For after all he had more to fear from Wanda's threat than from what he had just done; from here [?] he could quietly walk away [?] and no one would know who had killed "Łapka"; the dead "Łapka", on the other hand, could now help him free himself of Wanda... So, at any rate, Yosl believed.
And having considered the whole plan carefully, he at once set about carrying it out.

After waiting a little until "Łapka" had gone cold, Yosl set to work...
First Yosl took the knife out of Łapka's stiffened hand. With fear and disgust at once he also took the revolver out of the thief's pocket. Both things Yosl buried near the spot, deep in the earth, not yet knowing himself why he was doing it.
But at the last minute, when he also had to remove the traces of the murder itself, Yosl Wertheim saw [?] that his idea was not so simple at all: he would have to drag the dead man a long way, somebody might just pass by, somebody might just see him [?] then...
And heeding [—] his conscience, Yosl again seized on the very first thought he had had right after the terrible deed...
"The simplest thing is to go to the police and tell the whole truth, just as it happened"...

Lost... for every man in life good as well as bad lies in store... In truth he is no murderer, he only defended himself...
— And Wanda.. — the thought at once strikes him on the temples too — that misfortune he will not escape... And he imagines how they will start to question and interrogate him: "What [?] were you doing in the forest, and why did you go there?" And who knows what else they might pin on him; it has happened before that for nothing at all one can be dragged into the greatest misfortune...

No, no! Better to be rid of all of it — he seizes again on the earlier thought — only that will be the one salvation.
And now he is already decided on anything, just to escape the terrible disgrace and shame...
Better to disappear [?] himself than to show himself to his wife and children as a murderer.
And just at this moment the whole plan finally ripened in his head.

He bent over "Łapka", who lay cold and stiff, pulled his clothes off him and put them on himself, and his own suit, with everything that was in it, he pulled onto "Łapka". Heavy drops of cold and warm sweat ran down Yosl's face as he worked and fell onto his victim... At moments it seemed to him that he was going out of his mind... At the slightest breeze, at the slightest rustle, it seemed to Yosl that "Łapka" was moving, that he had come alive and would at once throw himself at him.. At moments he was so gripped by this ghastly thought that several times he kicked the dead man with his foot, thinking that any moment now he would get up.

At last he was finished with everything. Then, already without any fear, with cold calculation, he took the dead man on his shoulders, went out of the forest and, in the dark night, by side roads, carried him to the river...
Here, on the bank, he rested again; he wanted to make sure that nobody was watching, for the splash [Yiddish "pliosk", Polish plusk] of the water could be heard; and so that the dead man would be as heavy as possible, the thought prompted Yosl to fill "Łapka's" pockets with sand and earth... He did just that, and afterwards, bending [?] the dead body a little, he flung it with all his strength into the water and himself took to his heels as if from a blazing fire...

The roads of Zagłębie that led to the former German border were very well known to Yosek [i.e. Yosl]; more than once he himself had "smuggled" something over from the other side; so now he indeed ran without rest, for he was still pursued by the chasing [?] "Łapka" with the outstretched knife in his hand...
But at last, together with daybreak, he safely reached the other side — Germany, where for the time being he was beyond all danger...

„The Cooking Spoon“ — A Letter from the Dacha.

My dear husband, I am fine,
I walk around naked, bare [?],
and I roast myself in the sun
and grow even prettier from it.

You wouldn't recognise me at all,
I've shrunk [?] as if burnt,
I feel I'm gaining weight,
I'm putting on [?]... from day to day.

My neighbour is a nasty fellow (paskudniak),
he always rocks me in the hammock,
only he whispers [?] quietly —
do you perhaps know what he wants?

He often calls me to go into the woods,
be it hot, be it cold,
and he keeps groaning, it seems to me —
do you perhaps know what he's looking for [?]..

As soon as he sees a bit of grass
he runs straight to it like a hare,
his eyes burn wild and sharp —
do you perhaps know what he needs?

He can't find himself a place
and he sighs at every word
and pays me many compliments —
do you know what his aim is?..

[Humour — “Der Kokh-Lefl”; Będzin — merchants.] An exchange of letters between two Będzin merchants.
Grinshteyn writes a letter to Rozenblat:
— For 8 years you have owed me 100 zł. Will I yet live to see you pay me back the money?
Rozenblat's answer:
Dear Chaim, I don't know how your health is, but if you keep away from alcohol, don't eat “alte takhlir” [?, unclear — perhaps rich dishes] and live normally — you too may live to see it one day.
—o—
A Slander, Poor Thing!
Husband: I've been told that you were unfaithful to me in Krynica.
Wife (indignant): That's a vile lie! That's a base slander (podłe oszczerstwo) — why, that was actually in Szczawnik!
P.P.S. and Jewish Councillors Walk Out of the City Council Session

[Będzin — City council.] The city council session held last Thursday was dissolved because of the interpellation by the "OZN" club against Alderman (ławnik) Mr. Rubinlicht.
The story is as follows: Alderman Mr. Rubinlicht is accused of having related that during a conversation with the Sosnowiec city president, Mr. Kaczkowski [?], the latter had wanted to use an insulting word about the city council.
Although Mr. Rubinlicht declared publicly that he had not said this, the "OZN" club submitted an interpellation stating that, since [?] Alderman Rubinlicht is spreading insulting rumours at the city council's expense, the city administration should take the trouble to investigate the matter, and until then Mr. Rubinlicht should be suspended as alderman.
After the interpellation was read out, Dr. Weinzieher took the floor and pointed out that legally the motion could not be put to a vote.
On this question Alderman Laskowski asked for the floor, but the president would not give it to him, citing a point of the standing orders according to which no discussion is allowed on such questions.
Then the workers' club left the session, and after it the Jews as well, so that, since no quorum remained, the chairman dissolved the session.
New Prices for Bread and Flour

[Będzin — Prices.] On Tuesday, under the chairmanship of Starosta Mr. Baksa [?], a conference of the county (powiat) price commission took place, which fixed the following prices for bread and flour.
Rye flour, 70 per cent: wholesale 32 zł. per 100 kilos, retail 36 groszy a kilo. Rye flour, 82 per cent: wholesale 30 zł. per 100 kilos, retail 33 groszy a kilo.
The prices of bread have also been reduced: for a kilo of bread from 75-per-cent flour, 34 gr.; from 95-per-cent flour, up to 26 groszy a kilo. The prices of other articles are unchanged. The above-mentioned prices are in force from yesterday.
"The Mouth That Forbade Is the Mouth That Permitted"..

[Będzin — Kashrut; children's summer colony.] The meat at the Jewish colony was declared forbidden and then made kosher again.
Strictly kosher meat is sent for the Jewish children staying at the summer colony in Sławków. Now it so happens that someone comes to the local rabbinate and relates that at the colony "geshakhn" [?; reading doubtful — apparently meat not ritually slaughtered] meat is being used.
What did the rabbinate do? Without investigating the matter properly, it issued a prohibition on the meat and also on the vessels in which this "geshatene" [?] meat had been cooked.
When the head of the colony learned of the prohibition, she immediately came here and told the guardian (opiekun), Mr. A. D. Balisowski [?], about it; he went to the rabbinate and showed that the meat sent to the colony is genuinely kosher. Then the rabbinate sent a second notice that the meat is kosher...
—o—
Hanged Himself in a Lavatory
In the lavatory of Grochodziak's [?] house the caretaker of that same house hanged himself.
—o—
Day Camp for Jewish Children
On the 20th of this month the day camp (półkolonia) for poor Jewish children from the public schools will be opened. The children can be registered with the school guardians.
Conference on Founding a Commercial School

[Będzin — Commerce and education.] In the premises of the Merchants' Association a second conference took place on the question of creating a school for merchants. After a discussion it was decided that one school should be created for the towns of Zagłębie; in addition, commercial courses should be set up at each merchants' association in its own town.
It was also decided to conduct a propaganda campaign among the interested circles.
Lecture by Dr. A. Lipman

[Będzin — Brit HaChayal; lecture.] On Saturday a meeting of Brit HaChayal members took place in the hall of Brit HaTzohar.
Dr. A. Lipman gave a lecture on the origins and experiences of the Jewish Legion. After the lecture Commandant Nigal gave accounts of experiences on the various fronts during the World War.
After a discussion, in which members of Brit HaChayal and ex-servicemen (combatants) took part, it was decided to create a recruiting committee and a secretariat.
Suicide of a Jewish Girl

[Będzin — Suicide.] On Tuesday at dawn 28-year-old Hinda [?] Szaładzisz [?], intending to commit suicide, drank a sizeable dose of vinegar essence. Miss Szaładzisz was taken at the expense of the health fund (Kasa Chorych) to the hospital in Dąbrowa, but she died on the way.
A few weeks ago the suicide had received from her sister in Brazil a travel permit to "Brazil". Since then she had been nervous, and this was apparently the cause of the suicide.
The Discount Bank Is Developing

[Będzin — economy, banks.]
In the premises of the Discount Bank (Małachowskiego 2) a meeting of the board and council took place on Sunday, at[?] the bank's honorary president, Mr. A. Trapojer[?]. The purpose of the meeting was to hear the statistical report of the bank over the last months. The report shows that the bank is developing very nicely and is gaining the confidence of merchant circles.
After the report Mr. Trapojer declared that he would help to keep the bank at the proper level. In conclusion it was resolved that such report meetings should take place often.
A Vows Campaign for “Ezrat Menahamei Avelim”

[Będzin — charity.]
As every year, the board of “Ezrat Menahamei Avelim” [Aid for Comforting Mourners] is organising this year too a vows (nedarim) campaign over 4 weeks, i.e. all vows from the portion Devarim to the portion Re'eh belong to the above-mentioned society.
It is possible that in our town there are institutions that are as popular as “Ezrat Menahamei Avelim”, but one must take into account that in the present hard times the society fulfils a great task for the poor mourners, who during the seven days of shiva, God forbid, have not a single grosz for their livelihood and are dependent on the support of the said society.
A “Gedud Ivrim” Founded

[Będzin — Zionism, Hebrew.]
On the initiative of Dr. A. Lipman, a “Gedud Ivrim” [Hebrew Battalion] has been founded in Będzin by the N.Z.O. [New Zionist Organization — the Revisionists], whose task is to spread Hebrew literature among the local Jewish youth by introducing Hebrew courses according to Dr. Lipman's new system on gramophone records, and a Hebrew library with a reading room of all Hebrew publications from this country and from Eretz Israel.
The Gedud numbers today 30 members; shortly a propaganda and recruitment campaign will be carried out.
On Remarks on the New Timetable

[Będzin — trade, transport.]
The Chamber of Commerce in Sosnowiec has turned to the local Merchants' Association [to say] that in connection with the new [railway] timetable, which will be introduced on 6 September[?] of this year, the Merchants' Association may submit proposals or remarks concerning the timetable.
Proposals can be submitted at the association's secretariat at the latest by Monday the 19th of this month.
For the Sake of Peace “Mizrachi” Gave Away 75 Votes

[Sosnowiec — Zionism, Congress elections.]
Rabbi Hager — delegate to the Zionist Congress.
In connection with the elections to the Zionist Congress, a meeting of all Zionist groupings took place here, which resolved that in our town no elections should take place at all, but that the distribution of mandates should be according to the number of shekels sold. On the eve of the elections, however, the League [for Labour Palestine] — as we are informed — came forward with a proposal that “Mizrachi” should give it 75 votes... The proposal was accepted for the sake of peace.
Out of the total number of mandates which “Mizrachi” received in the whole country, Rabbi Hager was elected as delegate to the Zionist Congress.
The Orphanage Will Be Ready in the Coming Days

[Sosnowiec — welfare, orphans.]
As we have already written, a building for Jewish orphans is being built on Kongreda[?] Street, next to the Jewish hospital. The work is proceeding at a fast pace, so that in the coming weeks the building will be finished. It should be noted that the entire building is being financed by Mrs. Rena[?] Spiegel. In general Mrs. Spiegel takes part with larger donations in all Jewish public causes.
The Kehilla in Its Fight Against the Back-Alley Slaughterers

[Sosnowiec — kehilla, ritual slaughter.]
In our town there is a “bumper crop” of... back-alley slaughterers [unlicensed shochtim]; they literally grow like mushrooms after rain, so that up to the present day about a dozen petty shochtim practise the “craft”, causing thereby great material losses to the kehilla treasury.
In connection with this the president of the kehilla has turned to the supervisory authority with a request that the back-alley slaughterers be brought to administrative account.
The Budget Commission “Is Wrestling”...

[Sosnowiec — kehilla, budget.]
As is known, at the last session of the kehilla council a commission was elected which is to deal with the new kehilla budget according to the board's draft.
As it turns out, however, the commission's work is meeting certain obstacles, because each member of the commission, who incidentally[?] represents a certain group, wants to push through his own proposals.
—o—
They Got “Walking Pay”...
[Sosnowiec — violence.]
On the way to the cemetery hooligans attacked the second cantor[?] Mr. Anisman[?] and Karn[?] Stark[?] and beat them badly.
—o—
It Didn't Pay Off...
[Sosnowiec — crime.]
In the office of the “Helena” coal mine a burglary was carried out.
The burglars, however, found in the cash box no more than 30 zł. in cash, postage stamps worth 18 zł. and a summer coat.

Kaminer's Exhibition at the Kehilla.
[Sosnowiec — culture, art.]
Next Monday the pictures of Dwal[?] Kaminer will be exhibited in the kehilla hall. Jewish society should visit this exhibition in order to become acquainted with the work of the young talent.

Hurricane Storm
[Zagłębie — weather.]
On Tuesday at about 3 in the afternoon a great storm accompanied by strong thunder and lightning passed over Zagłębie. Several times lightning struck the running trams, but it did not cause any damage.
Because of the heavy rain, cellars were flooded in some places.
Windowpanes Smashed.

[Sosnowiec — antisemitism, violence.]
The brawl between Dymarskin and Hirszfeld in Pogoń was exploited[?] by shady elements, who incited the mob to anti-Jewish outbreaks; but thanks to the prompt, energetic intervention of the police and [—][?], it did not come to any serious incidents.
The mob, which was dispersed, smashed on its way the windowpanes in Jewish homes, also in Shelce[?] [Sielec?] and Katering[?] [Katarzyna?].
The kehilla is registering a series of cases[?] of Jews who suffered in the suburbs.
In this connection many of the guilty have been arrested; among those arrested is also the [—] [leader?] of the Endeks [National Democrats], Frankowski.
A New Public Elementary School.

[Sosnowiec — education.]
By order of the school authorities, a new public elementary school [szkoła powszechna] for boys will be opened in our town from the new school year. The school, which will bear the number 5, will be located on Mościckiego Street.
It should be stressed that the Sosnowiec school inspector is staffing[?] the school personnel — the head as well as the teachers — exclusively with Jewish teaching staff. (G.)
11-Year-Old Girl — Killed by a Tram.

[Sosnowiec — accident.]
On Tuesday at about 5 in the afternoon a tram disaster occurred on Feliksa Perla Street, which cost the life of 11-year-old Zosia Rydunik[?]. The girl was playing with a ball, and at a certain moment, when she ran after the ball, she fell under the tram, which seriously injured her. A short time later she died.
Abolish Jewish Ritual Slaughter Entirely.

[Sosnowiec — shechita; Polish press.]
So demands the "Kurier Zachodni".
In the "K. Z." of the 14th of this month, a short note deals with the situation in the local slaughterhouse owing to the slaughter law, which "is being sabotaged by the shochtim [ritual slaughterers]".
Our opinion is — the editors declare — to abolish ritual slaughter entirely.
Off to Polesie for Work.

[Sosnowiec — unemployment.]
Last Monday a party of unemployed men left from here for Polesie to work.
From the Będzin county [powiat] a total of 400 unemployed men have left.
The Old-New Kehilla (On the Change of the Kielce Kehilla Leadership)

[Kielce — Kehilla.]
Last Monday ought to be something of a date in the history of Kielce kehilla life. At Leonarda [?] 23, at 5 o'clock in the evening of that day, a change-over of the leaderships took place. The old leadership stepped down and its place was taken by the council and board that were elected a year ago.
Among decent people, when a cabinet change occurs, one bids farewell to those departing in various ways. The satisfied draw up a fine balance of deeds and achievements [?], and the dissatisfied express their [?] satisfaction at the newly arrived rulers.
In the present case we are in a strange position. We can neither play the role of the former, nor can we feel like the latter. What kind of bottom line can we draw from the five-year work of the outgoing kehilla leadership, when we have before us not a single real, useful item [?] that the kehilla has left us. Five years is a long time in the life of such an institution as a kehilla, and even taking into account all the understandable and known difficulties, we surely did not expect that a leadership would leave without leaving behind even the slightest legacy [?] [—] for the town.
Nor can we be full of joy over the new leadership that is coming, when the situation is such that the "new" gentlemen are, in fact, the old ones, and the "old" gentlemen are the new ones. "It's the same Yente", and even veiled she is no different, since in the presidium posts there are no changes whatsoever.
We will have to [?] take into account the several new parnassim and dozors [board members] from the political parties. It is rather hard to believe that they will succeed in reforming kehilla life in Kielce. But it is to be expected that these gentlemen will, at the very least, liquidate the [—] chaos that reigns in the Kielce kehilla. They will curb it and not let it turn into a chronic disease. In time, perhaps, positive and useful work will begin that will arouse satisfaction.
On the contrary, it is now useless to dwell on and criticize what is already past. Nothing more than a [—] [—] or a few articles will remain to us of it. But no one can take from us the right now, when a new page of kehilla history is opening, to call out loudly to the old-new men to whom such a respected Jewish representative institution is being entrusted:
— Gentlemen, we want no more chaos! When from outside they want to throw us into chaos, we must keep a clear head within. We demand the highest measure of responsibility and vigilance from our representatives.
Jewish Kielce is poor in every respect. Spiritual poverty cries out from every corner. There is a broad field here for serious, useful public work. A very great deal can be done.
But on one condition: that the people who take up such work should feel that there is someone who keeps account — the public must keep watch.
The time has come for the kehilla leadership to understand this well.
For if the first 5 years of neglect can be called frivolity, the continuation of such a system is already — a scandal.
L. Radal.

Post Office Branch Opened on Chęcińska Street
[Kielce — Post.]
A few days ago a new post office branch was opened on Chęcińska Street.
—o—
Kielce Young Man Drowned in Włoszczowa
[Kielce — Accident.]
This week 17-year-old Dawid [?] Rozencwajg [?] of Kielce drowned in the river at Włoszczowa.
We Did Warn!... On the Liquidation of the Homeowners' Bank

[Kielce — Economy.]
Barely two years ago, at the general meeting of the Homeowners' Bank, seeing that the bank could not be rehabilitated, we warned not to prolong its death throes but to carry out the liquidation at once. Some persons then dug in their heels and would by no means make peace with the thought that the bank would sooner or later have to be liquidated. For two years they kept up a needless administration for nothing and increased the bank's debt.
And after two years a Christian liquidator has finally been installed, and the town will now have something to talk and gossip about.
The responsibility is borne by the obstinate board members, for we warned in good time...
Jewish Engineer Discovers a Historic House from the Year 1767

[Kielce — History.]
This Tuesday the construction workers under the direction of Eng. M. Cukierman, who are employed in renovating the house of the Kahane family in Kielce, discovered in the middle of the wall on the first floor a splendid [?] white marble stone, on which there is a carved Polish eagle with two inscriptions, in Latin and in Polish.
The inscription reads:
"This house was built in the year 1767 (17th [?] c.). God protect its inhabitants from all evil."
Hundreds of people gathered at the spot to look at the historic stone, as well as representatives of the authorities, who ordered that the stone be safeguarded until after the renovation.
In town people say that one of the Polish kings lived in this house for a certain time, and that after the partition of Poland the stone was covered up until the present day.
It is told that when the Polish Legions entered Kielce in 1914, they rested in front of this house.
It is also possible that the house in question, which has historic significance, will be purchased by the state.
On Monday the newly elected dozors and parnasim take over the management of the kehilla.

[Kielce — Kehilla.] The taking over of the management of the kehilla by the newly elected dozors [members of the community board] and parnasim, which had been set for last Sunday, the 11th of this month, has been postponed because of the „Nine Days“ (on the proposal of the Agudah dozor Mr. Rotenberg[?]) to Monday the 19th of this month.
Last Reply — The Ignoramus „Editors“.

[Kielce — Press, polemic.] I declare that it is beneath my dignity to enter into a polemic with youngsters, ignoramuses and boors, the „contributors“ of the Kielce branch of „Radomer Lebn“ [„Radom Life“], who want to become „popular“ as „editors“ through the polemic. It is also a great wrong[?] on the part of the actual editor of „Radomer Kielcer Lebn“ [„Radom-Kielce Life“], Meir Herc, that he gives room in his paper to vile[?] lampoons of a personal character against his former co-workers and good friends.
I am sure that comrade Herc certainly[?] regrets[?] his ill-considered deed, which was brought about[?] by two irresponsible youngsters who have the cheek and the insolence[?] to want to touch the sanctity of journalism.
This is my last reply!
Ch. Zielony.
R' Tsvi Hirsh Zagajski, of blessed memory.

[Kielce — Obituary.] Last Wednesday Jewish Kielce accompanied to his eternal rest one of its most respected and prominent Jewish citizens, R' Tsvi Hirsh Zagajski, of blessed memory.
His funeral, which took place at 2 in the afternoon, was attended by a crowd of several thousand people, among them numerous delegations of all Jewish political and social organisations, as well as the children of the Talmud[?] Torah, the orphanage and the old people of the Kielce old-age home, for whom the deceased had been like a good and loving father.
Eulogies for the deceased were delivered by the Kielce rabbi, Rabbi Rappaport, and Rabbiner[?] H.[?] Harberg[?], who in warm words recalled the rare virtues of R' Hershl Zagajski of blessed memory, his charity and his kind-heartedness.
For 20 years R' Hershl Zagajski was president of the society „Achi-Ezer“, long-standing president of the Jewish kehilla and a councillor of the Kielce city council, and of many other Jewish institutions.
Together with his late brother R' Yaakov Zagajski of blessed memory he founded in Kielce some years ago the orphanage and the old-age home, donating two splendid buildings for these institutions, which are an ornament of Jewish Kielce.
R' Hershl Zagajski of blessed memory also set up a beit midrash in his house and helped both with money and with work in the development of the Jewish institutions in Kielce.
With the death of R' Hirshl Zagajski of blessed memory Jewish Kielce has, as said, lost one of the finest and noblest figures among the most distinguished and best householders of the town.
Honour to his memory!
Ch. Zielony.

Meeting of „Brit ha-Hayal“ in Będzin.
This Sabbath a members' meeting takes place with the participation of Dr. Lipman.

Mr. Moszkowicz reported at the office of the Będzin kehilla that on Tuesday, while he was travelling with a deceased (bar-minan), the hearse wagon was pelted with stones.

Appeal of the Committee of the Construction Fund to Public Institutions.
The committee of the construction fund (Aufbau-Fund) in Będzin resolved at a meeting that all associations[?] that took part in the meeting must send in, by the 25th of this month, concrete projects for further activity.

As we are informed, the dramatic circle at the local[?] Bar-Kochba[?] kibbutz is preparing a performance on a topical theme from Jewish life: suffering and redemption.

The administrative authority has imposed rather large fines on several landlords in Będzin for the unsanitary condition of their houses.

These documents the finance officials must show at every request of the taxpayer.

The "kidnapped" child was found in a garden

[Upper Silesia — Katowice.] On Thursday afternoon a rare incident occurred at the corner of Andrzeja [?] and Mikołowska streets. A woman came up to a nursemaid who was pushing a child [in a pram] and told her she should go home at once, because her employer had suddenly fallen ill. At the same time the unknown woman offered to go on wheeling the child herself. When the nursemaid realized she had been tricked, she ran back to the place where she had left the child, but found no one there any more — neither the woman nor the pram with the child.
In the evening the child was found in a garden on Mickiewicza Street. The child, which was wrapped in rags, was carried by the finder [?] to the police station, where the mother, who had been called in, recognized it as her child.
Historic Sejm session

[Upper Silesia — Katowice.] On Friday the 16th of this month, at 10 a.m., a plenary session of the Silesian Sejm took place in Katowice. Present at the session were representatives of the authorities, headed by Voivode Dr. Grażyński.
Sejm Marshal Grzesik opened the session with a speech in which he stressed the historic significance of the session in connection with the fact that from the 15th of this month the legal-political conditions under the Geneva Convention no longer apply.
At the end of the session the bill was passed in third reading providing that on the territory of the Silesian Voivodeship the official language is Polish only. To make outward [?] use of the German language one must have a permit from the authorities.

Life in Chorzów — 10 years of craftsmen's activity

[Upper Silesia — Chorzów; craftsmen.] For 10 years now a Jewish craftsmen's association has existed in Chorzów, and it is worth giving an overview of how this association was created.
In 1927 a large influx of Jewish artisans, petty traders and peddlers began; at that time a few people were found who wanted to create something in the public sphere.
At that time Messrs. Izydor Rozenberg, Gabriel Ernhart, Fridman, Pilk, Eichel, Schichter and Sala Fridman called the first illegal [i.e. not yet registered] meeting at the home of Messrs. Schichter and Pilk. In time the above-mentioned drew a larger number of supporters to themselves and also obtained legalization from the central office.
The first founding meeting took place in the Cooperative Bank (Bank Spółdzielczy), at which the first board was elected, headed by Mr. Izydor Rozenberg, which tirelessly reorganized the association and drew in members to a number of up to 180.
A short time later elections to the kehilla took place, in which the craftsmen obtained 4 seats in the kehilla.
Some time later a new board was elected, headed by Mr. Fridman, which helped to create the Gemilut Chesed (free-loan) fund, from which the craftsmen, petty traders and peddlers received much assistance.
The association carried on fine activities, among other things enabling [?] its members without means to receive medical aid, etc.
In a word, the association was a model for other towns; but when the association had reached the highest level, Satan meddled: over a "little bench" [i.e. a seat/post] disputes began which led to the present state of the craftsmen's association in our town.
Menachem.
