Tisha B'Av in Zagłębie

[Zagłębie — Będzin; holidays.] This year's Tisha B'Av fell, because of the Sabbath, one day later. But this did not take away the traditional character of this national day of mourning. And although [?] the shofar of the Messiah can be heard — the birth of a Jewish state is at hand — it nevertheless changed nothing at all in the Tisha B'Av mood among Jews.
In the houses of prayer people sat [on the floor] in their socks, recited kinot (lamentations), threw prickly burrs at one another and wept [?] while reciting.
At the old cemetery in Będzin hundreds of Jews gathered and recited Psalms at the ohel (tomb) of Rabbi Grinberg [?] of blessed memory.
At the new cemetery too there was no lack of people who came to pour out their bitter hearts at the graves, as well as at the ohel of Rabbi Lewin of blessed memory.
The only novelty was the talk about the Jewish state. But Jews did not feel the redemption. The Jewish state is somehow not yet quite right: everyone from right to left rejects the English gift; nobody thinks much of a British Messiah... Meanwhile everything stays as of old.
A Shabbat Chazon and a Shabbat Nachamu. Of things to lament and things to pray for, a Jew today has no shortage.
May it be better a year from now.
A tenant's chase after... a cat

[Zagłębie — Sosnowiec.] This is no invented tale but a fact that happened in Sosnowiec on Charnaza [?] Street.
Through an open window of a ground-floor flat on the said street a cat came in. A black, frightening cat, which quartered itself not simply as is proper [?], but [—] [?] on a mattress [?].
At first the owner of the flat did not offer the cat much resistance; his wife is at the dacha (summer cottage), so [?] who has time to bother with a silly cat?
But when several days had passed and the cat still had not left the occupied mattress [?], a chase after it began. The owner of the flat called together several of his neighbours, who came armed with poles, brooms and other "stratagems of war", and the real offensive began.
Finally, after several hours of "battle", the cat gave up and left the neighbourhood [?].

The groom has a wife and two children, and the matchmaker is his sister.

When a girl turns 18, she already dreams of [—] a knight in the shape of a footballer, a boxer — he may even be a law clerk (aplikant) — as long as he is handsome, well built and pleases her girlfriends (koleżanki).
When she reaches 27–30 and her dream has still not come true, she will settle for [—] some sort of suitor with whom she can live. Let us call it her longing.
But once she leaps past 30, one had better be careful with such a one: such a fire burns in her eyes and in her heart that, for safety reasons, it would be good if she were always dipped[?] in the firemen's rubber hose[?].
In just such a 35-year-old [?] state was Krajndl B. of Kowalska Street, who moreover had a handsome purse (motnia) ready to buy herself a husband.
A matchmaker came to Krajndl.
— Krajndele, my crown, I have a groom for you[?], a real jewel! You will be grateful to me your whole life, Krajndeleszki — as soon as you just see him, you won't be able to tear yourself away from him, what can I tell you — a treasure! Besides, he has golden hands!
The matchmaker brought the groom — truly a fellow with golden hands, the proof being that he managed to take Krajndl's money and vanish.
Later it became clear that the young man has a wife with 2 children and the matchmaker is his sister.

Dr. Abraham Koralnik

In New York, at the age of 54, the well-known Jewish publicist and contributor to the American “Tog”, Dr. Abraham Koralnik, has died.
The deceased was born in Uman in 1883 and, having received a thorough Jewish education at home, he later, after finishing gymnasium, studied at the universities of Kiev, Florence, Berlin, Bern and Vienna and obtained a doctorate in philosophy. Dr. Koralnik began his literary and journalistic activity in the central organ of the Zionist Organisation, “Die Welt”. Later he contributed to a number of Yiddish and Russian newspapers, and from 1915 he was a contributor to the American “Tog”.
The deceased was also active in the Zionist Organisation and for a time was a member of the Greater Actions Committee.
It Is High Time!

[Będzin — children and welfare; article.] (On the opening of the half-colony [day camp] in Będzin)
Such, then, is the fate of the poor Jewish child, who lives and is brought up[?] in present times, more than ever, in extremely hard conditions because of the sharpened economic need, because of the increased Jewish poverty. The Jewish child has only one hope[?], one joy, one radiant[?] minute and one better, brighter memory. That is the minute when our little Moshes and Shloimes get the chance — after many efforts and endeavours — to leave the town and go away for the summer to the colony!
The colony is the only bright ray in the great, dark, stuffy[?] life of our growing generation. Therefore, when summer comes, the poor child already longs for the minutes when it will leave, if only for a short time, its poor, unhappy home and travel together with many other children to the summer [women's?] colony, where it will be able to breathe more freely, where it will be able to rejoice the whole day long with the little green trees and grasses, where it will be able to play a lot, play freely and romp in the lap of nature, for which it has longed so sadly throughout the long, frosty, hard winter.
• • •
When do all of Będzin's poor children have that pleasure? When do they have the chance to enjoy at least 4 weeks of fresh air? When do our little Moshes and Sarahs eat on time and their fill for 4 weeks, staying in the summer colonies under good supervision? Will we forget for 4 weeks the children from the homes where there is so much sadness, poverty, doubt and worry? Will we take from the eyes of the unhappy mothers their emaciated, pale little children with big dreamy eyes? So as to send them off to the summer colonies?
Everyone knows that the Magistrate [the Będzin municipality] sends out parties of Jewish children to Sławków, and for the schoolchildren who remain[?] in town, 1,800 zł. has been allocated to set up a half-colony. But the sum (1,800 zł.) is too small for the large number of children who want and need to benefit from the half-colony, and for that the Jewish community in Będzin must help — it must do much more in this field.
And — to do much more — means giving many more little children the chance to forget their sad reality for a few weeks. To do much more — means — fewer sad, pale little faces in our growing generation.
Therefore one must not neglect the time, and one must set about at once organizing a large-scale[?] campaign for the half-colony for the poor children.
The kehilla administration is called upon to do so, and it is its duty. We hope that it will fulfil its duty completely and begin making the necessary preparations, because — it is high time.
Yosifon.
In Vacation Time.

[Education — children's summer holidays; article.] After a year of hard work our school youth has been set free, in order to rest and draw fresh strength for further strenuous work.
The summer holidays — that is one of the important achievements of modern life. Together with the social conquests for all working people, such as an 8-hour working day, paid leave, etc. — the weakest of all the weak and the most suffering[?] of all the suffering — the poor Jewish child — also receives his well-deserved holiday.
But what does this year's[?] children's holiday look like in the Jewish home?
Happy are the children who can spend their holiday time at a summer colony, in the lap of nature, in the company of children, under the supervision of an educator, amid songs and games. But how does the Jewish child who stays in town get through the vacation months?
The situation in our Jewish home is hard. Oppressed under the yoke of earning a living, perhaps never having had in their own whole life any chance to free themselves from the shop or the craft — father and mother are always nervous, irritated, and look upon their child's return home for a whole day — as upon a heavy plague, exactly as the immortal Sholem Aleichem depicts it in "The Fair on the Eve of Passover".
Children are sensitive, they sense it at once, and that is precisely why they go out and wander about the streets in groups, without any supervision, without any daily plan, and not seldom the vacation time turns for the child into days of severe over-exhaustion, of unruliness and wildness.
But what should be done about it?
Every father and mother must know that merely thinking the question over is already a gain. All parents must give a little time from their toilsome hours in order to organize the children in vacation time.
God forbid, not to diminish the children's freedom; on the contrary, as much as possible in the open air, but it must all be planned. Let the parents objectively help the children to put together a group and to fix the time in the enclosed courtyard where the children will play. The parents must also help the children's groups acquire play equipment such as a ball, a hoop and the like. In vacation time the parents must help more and pay attention to their children, because they are in their charge and under their sole responsibility.

Which Premises Are Exempt from the Housing Tax

[Poland — taxes; premises tax.]
The Ministry of Finance has distributed to its subordinate offices a detailed instruction concerning the premises tax (lokal-shtayer, podatek lokalowy).
According to the said instruction, premises used as houses of prayer are exempt from the obligation to pay the premises tax. In this case it makes no difference whether the house of prayer is in a special building or merely in a special room. Likewise there is no difference how often prayers take place, whether every day or only once a week, and whether the shtibl belongs to a private person or to an association.
Also exempt from the premises tax are the premises of educational, scientific and charitable institutions — but not the premises where these institutions have their legal seat, i.e. the premises in which the associations concerned keep their secretariat, where the meetings of the board take place and where all the so-called organisational work is conducted.
Only the premises in which the philanthropic activity, or purely scientific and educational work, is carried on enjoy the exemption.
When premises are used partly for trade and partly as a dwelling — even if together they consist of 1 or even two rooms (a shop, or a shop and a room) — the premises tax must be paid on the whole premises. If, however, it is a matter of premises in which a work enterprise is run together with the dwelling, only the dwelling, if it consists of more than 2 rooms, has to be taxed; whereas the part where the workshop is located, regardless of the number of rooms it occupies, is indeed entitled to the said relief.
As for the tax on premises of two rooms and a kitchen in which people both live and work at the same time: it is charged[?] only if the workplace is not in a special room; as soon as a special room is in fact set aside for the work, the whole premises is not subject to any premises tax.
"Premises in which work is done" means in this case premises in which a workshop[?] is run on the basis of a work patent (trade licence).
Unemployed persons occupying 2 rooms and a kitchen are exempt from the premises tax. As soon as they occupy larger premises, however, they no longer enjoy the relief.
To be exempted from the premises tax, one must attach to the application at the tax office a certificate from the labour exchange at the Labour Fund and a certificate from the house administrator[?], stating how long the tenant concerned has been unemployed, what his occupation is and whether he keeps subtenants.
Certainly[?] an unemployed person who has subtenants is not exempt from the premises tax. Parents, brothers and sisters (unmarried[?]) cannot in such a case be regarded as subtenants; but if married brothers and sisters live together with their households at the tenant's, they are indeed recognised as subtenants, and consequently the occupied premises are not exempt from the premises tax.
As regards the right to exemption from the premises tax as an unemployed person, it makes no difference whether he is a mental or a manual worker, nor whether he receives a pension (rente) or not.
With 4 Children Free on the Train

Shlomo Yona Naydhorim[?] heard the news that one can travel on all railways with 4 children completely free of charge, so he — Shlomo Yona, that is — decided to make use of the golden "opportunity" and really travel to Warsaw with 4 children — other people's, of course.
He began to negotiate[?] with the neighbours, men and women: in that case, if they would chip in for a return ticket to Warsaw, he would take their children along; he would look after them so that, God forbid, they would lack nothing on the way.
The first to join the plan was Yente the coal-dealer, and she at once began getting 5-year-old Mendele ready for the trip. She packed him a heavy[?] bundle of provisions and told him, for heaven's sake, to hold on to the flap of the light-coloured sack in which[?] Shlomo Yona was travelling to Warsaw. He was to give the food to no one — and little Mendele swore, in baby-talk: "May I be as healthy[?], Mummy, as I'll eat it all up"..
The second partner in the journey was Yankev Yosef the grocer. He sent along his Veligl, a scrawny little boy of 7. The father, too, told the little one not to lean his head out of the carriage window and, God forbid, not to get lost in Warsaw.
The last two free passengers to Warsaw were sent by Hinde the goose-dealer. She gave both her boys — Zaynvele, aged 9, and Fayvele, aged 11, both of them "regular fellows" — clean handkerchiefs and told them to behave quietly on the way. "Remember," she threatened, with her thick thumb under their wet little noses, "if Shlomo Yona comes home and has anything to report about you, cholera will strike the two of you"...
When the camp with its "herd"[?] and the bundles of provisions was ready to march, Shlomo Yona set off to the station with his camp.
When the train pulled in, Shlomo Yona got into a carriage packed with nothing but children. He barely found a place to stand, and began shouting and calling "his" children to stand next to him so that he would not lose them.
The train went on its way. The dealer's two sons began pushing toward the window to get a better view of the fields spinning past — but right at the window another[?] boy had been standing from before and would not let them near. A shoving match broke out at the window, and 11-year-old Fayvele snatched that boy's cap and — whoosh[?] — threw it out of the carriage window. That boy then [—] grabbed Fayvele's cap and threw it out of the window too, whereupon that boy's guardian (opiekun) started making a racket. At this the conductor came running and ruled that Shlomo Yona must pay 2 złoty for the cap Fayvele had thrown out; otherwise he would have to put him off at the first station and take away his guardianship (opiekuństwo) over the children.
Having no choice, Shlomo Yona settled the 2 złoty, already regretting his whole enterprise.
Meanwhile the gang started tugging at him: food! Shlomo Yona untied the bundles of provisions and handed out portions. Meanwhile he got everything mixed up[?] — the small fry raised such a din, oy, that Shlomo Yona could not hear a thing. When the train stopped at the first station and several passengers got out of that same carriage, among them one with a light-coloured sack, little Mendele grabbed the light-coloured flap of that man's sack (as his mother had told him) and got off the carriage together with him.
Later Shlomo Yona sees that he is missing a child and starts raising a hue and cry on the train. The train was stopped in the middle of the line, and the first station was telephoned about the mishap with the child, with a description of what the boy looks like. The answer came back that such a little boy is indeed standing on the platform crying: Mummy... At the second station Shlomo Yona got off with his three remaining children, but a conductor got off with him too and led Shlomo Yona to the station master (naczelnik), where a report was drawn up against him for stopping the train in the middle of the line, and a second report — for "niedbalstwo" (negligence).
After all these troubles Shlomo Yona still had to wait until a conductor brought little Mendele back from the first station on another train, and only then did he resume his "wycieczka" (excursion). Just before midnight Shlomo Yona and his 4 children finally arrived in Warsaw.
Midnight on Marszałkowska. Shlomo Yona is wandering with his 4 children; Yankev Yosef's Veligl starts crying that he needs to do what even an emperor must do in person... Shlomo Yona runs with his "retinue" from gate to gate knocking, but not a single caretaker lets him in. Meanwhile little Veligl could not withstand the "trial" and...
That portion was the last straw for Shlomo Yona. He decided to give it all up — go to the station and travel home on the first train.
Meanwhile the goose-dealer's two sons had again stopped to gape at a shop window (wystawa), and Shlomo Yona walked on, crestfallen, [?] a stretch of the way. Then he sees that Zaynvele and Fayvele are not following — he runs back and shouts at the top of his voice:
— Fayvele[?]! Fayvele[?]!
— Zanvele[?]! Zanvele!
At the shouting a policeman comes running and writes Shlomo Yona down in his notebook for disturbing the public peace.
Shlomo Yona runs back, flustered[?], to look for the children, and finds[?] them standing at a window full of dolls (lalki); he grabbed them both by their little hands and started running as fast as he could[?], as if chased by demons of destruction, to the railway station (dworzec).
On the first train Shlomo Yona, sleepless and dishevelled[?], travelled home from the excursion with his 4 exhausted children.
Well, you can imagine the "welcome"[?] he got from his neighbours, and what Yankev Yosef said when he saw the "state" of his Veligl, and how he had "cheered himself up" after his ailment..
The real "mi-sheberakh" was given him[?] by Hinde the goose-dealer when she saw her firstborn without a cap. "If you can't do it," she squealed at the top of her voice, "you don't take it on".. — — — — — —
Now Shlomo Yona is waiting for the fines on the reports, and spits on all excursions and railway discounts. All of "Warsaw" has become as treyf to him as pork, and he cannot look at children. He has sworn that for this very reason he will never get married...
A.
Protest or Accept with Love?

[Article — Zionism; the Peel Commission and the 20th Zionist Congress.] The only question that interests every Jew today is: how will our delegates to the 20th Congress [the 20th Zionist Congress, Zurich, August 1937] deal with the problem of our present political situation? What way out will they find, and will they be in the clear[?] before history, before the conscience of the people?
The[?] mission at so important a political moment is a very serious one and demands that the answer to be given be well considered and thought over, so that it should not, God forbid, bring any harm upon the whole of Israel with the words "yes or no".
The present political situation is like the situation of a gravely ill patient: however you lay him down and however he may lie, he is still not comfortable; bad, but for want of any choice he must put up with it. And what choice do we Jews have today?
Do we have a way out for our real, topical, logical demands?
Will our honest demand, our honest voice, reach the diplomatic English surgeons, and will they refrain from the amputation of 5/6 of the limbs of our territorial body, with our heart at its head — Jerusalem, which is our spiritual wellspring of thousands of years, which strengthens our spirit in exile, which is mentioned day after day in our prayers and in our symbol, our emblem and our pride?
A patient is shaken when he learns that he must be amputated; and what should a whole people say of such an inheritance, when 5/6 of the parts of its territorial body are to be amputated?
But what answer should the whole of Israel give to the proposal of the Royal Commission [the Peel Commission]? To stake everything on one card and say "No", or to commit political suicide, turn ourselves into a caricature of a human figure and say "Yes"?
And yet, however pessimistically one may be disposed, 7 July 1937 (28 Tammuz 5697) [the day the Peel Report was published] is a historic day in Jewish life. A new epoch, a new page in Jewish history, which awakens our land from an almost[?] 2,000-year lethargic sleep, so as to become[?] once again part of the pantheon of all states and to work for the good of the land of our forefathers — to whose spirit we owe today the invitation of the Royal Commission, which we did not compel either by sword or by cannon, but only by the power of our spirit, which unites us and binds us together; and so it has not perished but lives — which has lived and now lives again also in the land of our forefathers — the spirit that is not afraid of any artificial[?] borders, which the slightest political wind can destroy.
The Jewish people has not risen in a resurrection of the dead. Its political [—] reawakens only back in its own land; but its culture lives, triumphs everywhere, dominates in all corners of the world.
This strong spiritual position we owe to our forefathers, and it must also strengthen the [—] of our delegates to the 20th Congress, so that with their answer they will blunt[?] the English diplomatic lancet, which wants almost[?] to destroy the Balfour Declaration.
And our answer to the English must be: you may permit yourselves to amputate someone else's body, but we will not renounce our thousand-year-old oath: "If I forget thee, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget."
Herman Szer.
How Much Does the King of the Jazz Players Earn?

I met him a few years ago. He had come to Leipzig at the time of the fair there to give one [?] of his concerts, with which Paul Whiteman, the jazz king, conquered the world.
And he told me:
If you ask me since when jazz music has been played, I will tell you that in 1915 a small-time musician, one Joseph Garman [?], gathered 20 Negroes in New York who could play a little, gave them saxophones and wanted to give a concert with them. None of the players could read music; they could only blow and make a racket. So their concert was such a dreadful thing that the musicians and their manager had to flee in good time, before the audience wanted to trample them.
I was one of the guests at that concert, and it occurred to me then to arrange good pieces of music for saxophones and so create good jazz music. I worked at it for three years, and when I already had a larger repertoire I put together the best players and began giving jazz concerts, first in smaller and larger venues.
In a short time there was no hall in New York big enough for all the people who pushed their way into my concerts, but no "better people" came to the concerts. Only in 1924 did it occur to me to hire the biggest hall in New York, give a concert at high prices only and invite the "upper ten thousand", so that [?] the real American snobs [?] would hear the new jazz music.
It was a test of life or death. Had the concert not been a success, I would have thrown away the whole work. I must confess that I had never trembled and sweated like that at any concert in my life as I did then. We had such a great success as no musician and no band had ever had.
And since then nothing but jazz music is played in America. I am now making a tour of Europe, and I believe that here too people will soon hear nothing but jazz music. We have, of course, the means to take on the best musicians and pay them salaries they never even dreamed of. While a good musician earns 50 dollars a week in America, we pay up to 800 dollars a week. The son of the banker Kahn, who plays with us, gets a thousand dollars a week, and we have other players who get 50 thousand dollars a year.
In America today there are 35 thousand jazz bands with 250 thousand musicians. A few years ago America spent 600 million dollars a year on music, of which about 10 percent on jazz music. Today America spends 750 million dollars a year, of which about 85 percent on jazz music. I myself pay taxes on an income of a million dollars a year.
In America today there are about 17 million saxophone players. You can imagine what that means for the saxophone factories. Add to that the gramophones, records [?] and radio musicians, who also play jazz music for the most part.
Not to forget the poets, composers, music publishers and many other people who have new sources of livelihood. One can safely say: in the last 15 years jazz music has brought about a complete upheaval in the musical world..
Z. Haber, Vienna.

"Nothing Has Changed"

[Feuilleton — summer life; Będzin.] Pictures from the line.
By Ben Amotz.
3.
"Dobry dzień" [Polish: "good day"]...
There is a saying:
"The Almighty, as it were, said: I have a precious treasure — Sabbath is its name; I will give this precious treasure to the Jews."
And Jews always had pleasure[?] from this treasure; pious Jews already on Wednesday began preparing in honour of the Sabbath — what a thing to say — Sabbath! Heine, after all, compared the Sabbath Jew to a prince.
The coachmen at the summer-cottage (dacha) resorts, too, greatly praise the Sabbath day: the single Sabbath day — so they say — brings in more earnings than all the weekdays.
For, when "culture" had not yet penetrated so deeply into the broad masses of the people, it happened that riding out to the dacha on the Sabbath was only "one in a city and two in a family." As they say: only "individuals" [jednostki] rode. But today, in the epoch of the Nuremberg laws[?], everyone has eaten of the "tree of knowledge" — everyone rides: almost the head of the kehilla rides, the "sagreyter"[?] rides, the (woman) teacher rides and the "kabte"[?] (perhaps Pol. kobieta — the maid) rides — for if not, one is, after all, not "intelligent."
I am told the following little story:
One Sabbath morning the Jewish public is riding from the railway station; one droshky chases the other, they "race"[?] each other exactly as once in a small shtetl — you would think[?] they were driving out to meet the bridegroom...
On the droshky — the whole family. "He," who has come on a visit; "she," the dacha wife, who rode out to welcome "him"; and the little children — let them, too, enjoy this world; first of all, one must after all educate the children in the commandments, since they are "fed" [Pol. paść] on "koytsh"[?] meat, so to speak. Besides, when one is "wytsapane"[?] (dressed up?), one takes the children along on the droshky — all the more so, let the "sasheshi"[?] (perhaps Pol. sąsiedzi, the neighbours) see that he has a one-hundred-percent intelligent wife.
But we mention this only in passing, by the way; we only intend to relate the mishap that befell a Będzin Jew.
— Who is he? It is not necessary that you should know; it will be enough that we describe him euphemistically. All his days he prayed in a "shtibl"; when he had put on a few "feathers" [grown a little rich], he began to trim his little beard, and later he had already become a full-fledged "postępowiec" [progressive] and came on the Sabbath to his family in Bystra.
Suddenly the little horse with the droshky on which our "guest" was riding stops and will not go any further.
The coachman whips it mercilessly, but the horse neighs, as if to say:
— Beat me to death, I won't go any further...
Later it turned out that the cause of the horse's strike was the prayer "Keter," which could be heard from a well-known villa standing close to the highway; for as soon as the prayer leader had finished "Keter," the horse became "brutskhi"[?] and ran on with the former shtibl Jew...
— A fine day, a precious day is the "żydowski szabes" [Jewish Sabbath] — the coachmen chat among themselves — the whole week there is hardly anyone from whom to earn a gulden, but the Sabbath brings the greatest "ruch" [traffic].
— "Dobry dzień"...
In honour of the Jewish state...
Tisha B'Av in "Azus"[?].
In the "minyanim" "Eicha" has already been finished; those who "remained" sit on the low benches and talk about the destruction of old and of today — a real comparison between the Kamtzas of old and today's informers.
Suddenly a loud whistle is heard, and at once — a man's voice carrying through the stillness of the night:
— Stefa!
— Who's that, Józek? [Kto to, Józek?]
— Yes, Józek. Are you going to the dancing? [Tak, Józek, idziesz na dancing?]
— But it's Tisha B'Av for us. [Przecież mamy Tisze Baw.]
— Silly, we already have a Jewish state. [Głupia, już mamy państwo żydowskie.]
The magic word "Jewish[?] państwo" swept along us Eicha-reciters too, and we also go off to the place of entertainment.
But we came too late: outside stood [—] couples who no longer had the possibility of getting a "stolik" [table] and had to wait for an "okazja" [opportunity], when there would be a bit of "miejsce" [room] to set a foot.
To the strains of the jazz orchestra various couples move elegantly; the waiters run from one table to the next with cold and hot drinks; a fair-like[?] mood prevails.
But my companion is pessimistic; he looks around — and draws my attention to the fact — that the "Aryan paragraph" has been introduced in this establishment: there is not — he says — a single non-Jew here...
— Crazy, fine partners! Such a strange thought occurs[?] to me: how is it that pure Aryans should take part together with Jews on Tisha B'Av?..
And do you perhaps think that the dancing was for the sake of Heaven? You are greatly mistaken. You heard explicitly from Józek that he is going to dance — "in honour of the Jewish state"!
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Va'etchanan)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Va'etchanan
—o—
a) "Neither shall ye diminish ought from it" (Deut. 4:2)
The verse says earlier: "And ye shall come in and possess the land which the Lord God of your fathers giveth you." [So?], where it speaks of the commandment that Jews settle the Land of Israel, there follows a warning: "Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you [this day], neither shall ye diminish ought from it" — meaning: you may neither add to nor take away from the commandment of settling the Land of Israel "which the Lord God of your fathers giveth you"; you may not give up a single foot of the soil of the Land of Israel, whose borders God has fixed: "From the wilderness and Lebanon, from the river, the river Euphrates, even unto the uttermost sea shall your coast be" — of these borders you may not give up a single foot, "neither shall ye diminish"!.. Imrei Chen.
—o—
b) "Keep therefore and do them; for this is your wisdom and your understanding" (ibid., 6)
It is not as people think — that the fear of Heaven needs no great wisdom and that any fool is capable of it; "for this is your wisdom and your understanding" — "keep and do" in fact demands wisdom and understanding. R. Moshe Chaim Luzzatto.
• • •
R. Naftali of Ropshitz [Ropczyce] once said to his intimates:
— Hell I do not fear so much. I am only afraid that they may lay me in Paradise next to a foolish Hasid.
— But — he immediately corrected himself — on that score I can rest assured, for no fool has yet crossed the threshold of Paradise...
—o—
c) "Statutes and judgments so righteous" (ibid., 8)
"Chukim" means laws whose reason is hidden; and just as there are commandments that are "chukim" — commandments whose reason is unknown — so there are also transgressions that are "chukim": sins that people love to commit without sense or reason, as they are called in the portion Acharei "abominable customs" (chukot ha-to'evot). If it must be statutes — better then "righteous statutes"; if one must do something without reason or sense, far better that it be commandments... R. Amram Blum.
—o—
d) "For ye saw no manner of similitude" (ibid., 15)
In the Talmud and Midrash God is, so to speak, often called by the term "Makom" (Place). Where does this come from?
An interesting explanation is offered by the young scholar Dr. Menachem Stein in his new book "Philo of Alexandria".
The Greek translation, the Septuagint — the first translation of the Torah into a foreign language — renders the verse "And they saw the God of Israel" (Ex. 24:10) as "They saw the P L A C E where the God of Israel stood", thus removing any anthropomorphism. God cannot be seen — only the place around Him; hence the Talmud and Midrash call God "Makom".
—o—
e) "And make you a graven image, or the likeness of any thing, which the Lord thy God hath forbidden thee [lit. commanded thee]"
You will make yourselves idols "which the Lord thy God commanded thee" — and moreover claim that God, so to speak, told you to do so, and that you are even performing a commandment by it. Dan Madgiel [?].
• • •
"Horror hath taken hold upon me because of the wicked that forsake thy law" (Psalms 119[:53])
I fear the wicked who, for their vile deeds, "forsake thy law", and still help themselves with the Torah — bringing proofs from the Torah for their evil deeds and believing that they are doing nothing but commandments... Leket Amarim.
—o—
f) "When thou art in tribulation, and all these things are come upon thee, even in the latter days, if thou turn" (ibid.)
Two things bring a person to repentance:
"When thou art in tribulation, and all these things are come upon thee" — troubles that befall a person; or: "in the latter days" — old age, when the passions already cease... Dorshei Maharsha [?].
• • •
The Chiddushei HaRim was once asked: why is there no "Laws of Repentance" in the Shulchan Aruch, while in Maimonides' "Mishneh Torah" there is such a section?
The Chiddushei HaRim answered jokingly:
— As is well known, the Shulchan Aruch deals only with commandments that apply in our time, and since repentance, for our many sins, is not popular in our time, the Shulchan Aruch does not include that law. Maimonides, on the other hand, as is known, deals also with matters that do not apply in our time — therefore he includes the Laws of Repentance.
—o—
g) "Honour thy father and thy mother, as the Lord thy God hath commanded thee" (Deut. 5:16)
"As He commanded thee" — they were commanded about honouring father and mother already at Marah. Rashi.
What difference does it make where they were commanded the precept of honouring father and mother?
Because ordinarily the natural respect a person shows his parents stems from the fact that they give him food, drink and clothing until he earns his own living. Such respect is a natural feeling with which a person repays his parents.
The commandment of honouring father and mother, however, is not based on this egoistic feeling. Precisely at Marah, where there was manna and "thy raiment waxed not old upon thee", where children did not need to come to their parents [—], precisely then the commandment of honouring father and mother was given, which has a higher meaning. Ksav Sofer.
—o—
h) "And thou shalt love the Lord thy God" (Deut. 6:5)
A Hasid once asked R. Yehuda Tzvi of Stratyn, a famous master of segulot (charms), to give him a segula for the love of God.
He answered him:
— The segula for the love of God is the love of Israel...

But in the city — in the city it is a pleasure.
Nobody chirps, nobody caws.
You sleep like a count — till six o'clock, till seven, till eight.
And if a gramophone or a radio wakes you a bit earlier, at least there is something to listen to...
Jazz, classical music, a fine speech.
It is not chirping, it is not some foolish birds.
—
All right, by day the dacha can still somehow be endured.
At least one does not have to drag oneself around.
It is cool, one sits and contemplates nature.
Not to mention, if the cards are running well, it is a real pleasure.
At night — that is when the dacha is a torment.
Nowhere to go.
Either you go to sleep three times a day, or you lie sprawled [?] in a hammock and chase flies.
And people call that: what a life!
Swimming in a river — like a fish — they call: having a good time!
[—] [?] at least: simple people — they would not call it anything better.
Do you know who these people are?
People from the very „highest windows“ [the wealthy upper class].
People who have the best comforts in their homes; people who, had they stayed [?] in Sosnowiec or in Katowice, could truly have enjoyed themselves on a summer day.
And saved money as well.
But where have you ever seen pleasure entirely without a bit of trouble?
Well, so one suffers a bit.
Still better than splashing about in a river, like a fish, a whole day.
Or chasing [?] flies without end.
—
Hush. And what about the food?
Much do I relish [?] the food they give you at the dacha!
They tear muddy plants out of the earth and shove them straight into your mouth [?].
But eat the plants they give you in the city.
That is a pleasure.
It is scraped and washed and cut and garnished.
And it is not given [?] to you as to cattle, straight out of the mud.
One takes it out calmly from an intelligent tin, a nice one.
And one need have no fear at all.
On every tin the name and address of the manufacturer are expressly printed.
And if, God forbid, one upsets one's stomach, one knows at once whom to claim damages from.
It is not „hefker petrushke“ [a free-for-all].
—
Therefore I say that I do not understand why one needs to go to a dacha at all.
It really is a torment.
Y. Pershelik.

The Living Dead Man (18)

[Serial novel — Zagłębie, before the First World War; chapter 18.]
A. Zaglembier.
(The most thrilling novel of Jewish life in Zagłębie before and after [?] the World War).

The only bad thing was that he had been left without documents, a man without a name.
But to stay here, close to the border, Yosl Wertheim did not dare either; every day, after all, acquaintances, Jews from Będzin and Zagłębie, cross over here — smugglers and gold [?] dealers — and what if he were seen?
And most of all he was tormented by the thought that over there they already knew everything, that they had already pulled "Łapka" out of the water... that they had recognised him as the escaped bandit [?], and since Yosl's documents had been found on him, they had at once understood what had happened here and were already searching for him in every country...
Nevertheless Yosl tried as far as possible to control himself and calm himself down. One must only [?] be far from the border, and since he did have money on him — what he had not given to "Łapka" — he went straight to the railway station, although it was not yet clear even to himself where he wanted to go.
Having changed the money into marks, he went up to the ticket window, and only when the cashier asked him:
— Where to?
did the word burst out of Yosl against his will:
— To Hamburg!
Fifteen minutes later he was already sitting on the train...

* * *

On a gloomy evening, though it was a very [?] hot summer, Yosl Wertheim arrived in the wild, foreign port city.
Dead tired as he was, the countless "Hotel" signs beckoned to him like a deliverance. Yosl did indeed turn at once towards one of the buildings, but on reaching the door he suddenly stood still as if driven back [?] and asked himself bitterly:
— Where to?.. Where are you now, who [?] knows?.. Without documents they won't let you in...
So he went into side alleys, thinking that perhaps something could be arranged in a smaller hotel.
Everywhere, however, the first question was:
— Your documents?..
Yosl began stammering out a different excuse in each place, but the German knew no tricks: without documents he was let in nowhere.
In one little hotel he was advised to go to the police and meanwhile take out a temporary registration. Yosl said he was going to do so... but on hearing the word "police" the ground began to burn under his feet... That was all he needed — for them to start asking him: "When, where?" One careless word and he would bury [?] himself...
— No, no, better to stay and spend the night in the street.
And that is just what Yosl Wertheim did. First he went into a cheap restaurant near the port, ate, drank and rested a little, and late at night, when the restaurant closed, he again began wandering through the streets, went into the station and so pushed through the night, which dragged on for him like an eternity.
At dawn he was among the first to buy a newspaper and look for news from Poland. He understood that about such an affair, if it is discovered, foreign newspapers also write. Finding nothing about it, he felt a little lighter at heart. At the same time, however, the thought of his wife and children did not stop tormenting him...
What are they doing now?..
What are they thinking about him? Perhaps they are saying for certain that he has perished; perhaps they are already mourning him...
And Yosl Wertheim ponders how to find a way to let Sarah'tshen [?] and the children know about him after all, that he is alive.
Perhaps write a little letter and send it from another town without a return address?
But what to write, and how to tell Sarah'tshen [?] the truth?.. Besides, she has surely already reported his disappearance to the police, and what if his letter were intercepted by the police?..
What does one do?.. — Yosl racked his brains in despair, seeking a way out of his desperate situation.
And suddenly, in the middle of the night, sitting in the station, another thought occurred to him. He will go to the local rabbi and confess to him, he will tell him everything: he is no murderer... he did not want to kill a man; the other one wanted [to kill] him... and he had to defend himself.
Soon, however, he also considers the other side of the plan. Surely the rabbi too will have to inquire whether what he tells is true, and then it will turn out that he has given himself away...
No, no, he must wait for news from home; money to live on for the time being he still has; perhaps some opportunity will turn up...
And such an opportunity did indeed turn up a week later, when Yosl could already come among Jews, among emigrants who were travelling through there to America.
In the first days he had been afraid that he might meet an acquaintance here, or simply be recognised. But now, when he had already grown a decent little beard and a moustache, Yosl went into a barber's, had himself shorn and trimmed [?], and his face took on a completely different look. To be safe he also put on a pair of dark glasses, which many emigrants wore here because they had diseased eyes and had to wear them until they were cured.
And coming among Jews, Yosl too passed as an "emigrant" who had to wait because of his eyes...
And now, coming in once to the cheap eating-house, which was full of Jews from Poland, Russia and Lithuania, Yosl saw among them all a familiar face from Zagłębie. He knew the Jew but did not know his name. Yosl was at once drawn to that spot, and having waited until a guest vacated the place, he promptly sat down on that chair, close to the Jew from Zagłębie.
He orders food, but he has no appetite; his heart is pounding, his head is buzzing: this man could, after all, bring him greetings from his nearest and dearest — but how does one start talking to him?..
The Jews meanwhile were chatting among themselves about various things:
— If only one manages [?] to get on board the ship.
— What do you mean, "manages" [?]? Can you miss anything in the "...[?] camp"? If not this ship, then another ship.
— Ay, my dear Jew — the man from Zagłębie speaks up again — you evidently don't know what is going on in the world today.
— And if something is going on, so what? When wasn't something going on?
— You don't read any newspaper, I see...
— You mean the talk about a war? What else should emperors talk about?.. They should have our worries! Believe me, all these scare-stories aren't worth a pinch of snuff.
— You really know [?] your politics!
— And you know them — the other replies, offended.
— I tell you, things are happening today that were never heard of — messianic times...
— What? — several ask curiously.
— You haven't heard about the affair that happened in our Zagłębie? I tell you, a lawless world! Life just isn't safe! You haven't read it in the paper?
— Do tell!
Involuntarily Yosl Wertheim pricks up his ears even more, and his heart begins to pound harder...
— Well, let's hear it then...
(To be continued)
We Have Invented New Livelihoods.

At the suggestion of „CEKABE“ [the central association of interest-free loan funds], the editors of „Kokh-Lefl“ [„The Ladle“] have organised a scientific expedition with the aim of searching out new sources of livelihood for the declassed Jewish families in Zagłębie.
The members of the expedition first of all visited the ramified industrial areas such as Gzichów, Podzamcze and Małobądz, as well as Pańska[?] and Stara-Wiejska streets in Sosnowiec.
The results are simply astonishing. According to the radio reports from the leader of the expedition, it turns out that there are great opportunities to provide employment in the regulation of the „Przemsza“, at the tunnel that is to connect[?] the town of Będzin with.. Bushevadik[?], catching flies on the „Nurka“[?] and supplying bath-brooms to the mikveh concern in Będzin...
We believe that the sources of livelihood we have discovered will evoke a proper response from all the committees of the Reconstruction Fund (Aufbau-Fund) in Zagłębie.
At the Deathbed. The Far-Sighted Husband.

In the last minutes before her death she calls her husband over and says with her last strength:
— Dudl... I'm dying... a home.. a household.. children.. need upbringing[?].. need to be[?] in a woman's hands.. marry.. but don't look among strangers.. marry the maid.. Gutshe.. she already knows.. she's attached to the children, and the children to her.. marry her... do you promise me?
The „deeply grieved“ husband stands by the bed, the tears falling like beans, and finally he says:
— Lakhshi[?] Kroyn, what do I need to promise you.. I already thought about that 3 years ago.
Once Upon a Time...

Once, when a girl gave a kiss
the paint did not stay on the lips,
once, when one opened a business,
one did not carry the earnings to the treasury (skarb).
Once there was no talk[?] of human rights
and one was sure of one's life.
Once a young man did not take so much dowry,
and could provide a living for a wife.
Once, when one took a wife,
there were not so many „silent partners“.
Once the streets were not so dressed up,
but from the pocket one gave a rouble (kerbl).
Once the government was not democratic,
and Jews did not have their windowpanes smashed.
Once there were not so many „ignes“[?] and philanthropists
and one did not nab them „on the job“.
Once, when a merchant issued a bill of exchange,
he was not ashamed to pay it.
Once, when a woman went about her housekeeping
she was not forever busy with — painting her face.
Kaprizner.
He Doesn't Bathe with Jews.

A „Narodowiec“ [a member of the nationalist camp] comes to the Katowice „plaża“ (bathing beach), where people bathe, goes up to the cash desk to buy a ticket, and in the middle of it he notices Jews going in to bathe; he turns round and wants to walk on.
The cashier asks him why he is leaving.
— I don't bathe together with Jews; perhaps you can show me where Jews don't bathe?
— Yes, the cashier answers — in the gutter.
Sh. Reles.

What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin: 6 Jewish Families Knock About Under the Open Sky

What's new in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 15 Av 5697 — piątek 23 lipca 1937 [Friday, 23 July 1937])
Będzin
6 Jewish families knock about under the open sky.
In the courtyard of the house at Modrzejowska 81 there are 6 poor Jewish families who were forced to leave their flats. The evicted tenants are: Gedalia Pszestazski[?], Icchak Cymbler, Chaim Pelupnowik[?], Jakob Ber Wilkam[?] and Kopel Krakauer.
What do the evicted say?
This week the above-mentioned came to the editorial office and related the following:
For decades we have been living in house no. 81 on Modrzejowska Street. The moment the old landlord, Mr. Kukienik[?], died, the house passed to a new owner, a certain Chaim Jaskierowicz of Sosnowiec. The new landlord first of all[?] began oppressing the tenants by raising the rent; when we offered no resistance and paid the rent as he demanded, he hit upon a new trick, namely: he submitted a request to the local Magistrat [municipality] to have all 6 tenants put out of the flats of an entire[?] "oficyna" [rear/annex building], on the grounds that the annex is dilapidated…
A commission came, which granted his wish, and on 15 July[?] all 6 of us tenants had to vacate the dwellings and lay down[?] all our belongings in the courtyard.
The fact is a very sad and bitter one, because not a single tenant has the means for a flat, and on top of being in the street, we also have no bread, because we are poor unemployed people and have nowhere to work. From knocking about, several children have already fallen ill, and they have nowhere to sleep.
The terrible deed of the above-mentioned landlord — cry the desperate tenants — must not be passed over in silence by Jewish society.
Protest Demonstration of the N.Z.O.

On Sunday a protest meeting called by the N.Z.O. [New Zionist Organization, the Revisionists] took place in the packed hall of the "Apollo" cinema.
Mr. Nigel opens the meeting and calls on those assembled to a persistent[?] struggle against any partition of Eretz Israel and for a Kingdom of Israel on both sides of the Jordan.
Then Dr. A. Lipman[?] is given the floor for his lecture; he gives a thorough analysis of Eretz Israel and of why the N.Z.O. fights the project of partition or cantonisation.
In conclusion Mr. Nigel speaks again, calling on all those assembled to take part in the demonstration, which takes place immediately upon leaving the cinema, with banners (transparents) and black flags. Brit HaChayal and Betar were represented in their uniforms. At the town synagogue the procession disperses.

The "Customers" Stole Several Pieces of Goods

In Ginzberg's cloth and "kort" [woollen fabric] shop a theft was carried out in the following manner:
In the middle of the day an elderly Jewish woman came in to look at material for a costume (suit). It was not long before an elegantly dressed couple came in, a man with a woman. The latter told Ginzberg that she needed material for a costume but had no time to wait long; meanwhile the gentleman asked to see[?] various "samples" of the goods he wanted to buy.
And since at that time only Ginzberg himself was in the shop, the "customer" began looking for the "samples", and finally they all left, supposedly unable to agree on the price.
Later Ginzberg realised that the "customers" had stolen several pieces of goods worth a few hundred złoty.

A “Night of Vigil” at the Sosnowiec Kehilla Council

[Sosnowiec — kehilla, budget; followed by an item: the “Beit Lechem” campaign.]
The kehilla budget raised by 27 thousand zł.
As we have already briefly reported, on Thursday evening a meeting of the local kehilla council [Sosnowiec] took place on the question of the budget for the year 1937. At the meeting, which lasted from 8 o'clock until dawn the next morning, the parnassim [kehilla board members], in[?] setting the first kehilla budget, “unloaded” their whole arsenal of various explosive[?] materials, which caused a number of drastic moments during the discussion. At the meeting the principle of “guard mine and I'll guard yours” found expression: every faction pushed through its proposals. The result — the kehilla estimate will be raised by 27 thousand zł.
Almost all parnassim are present. Chairman Mitlis opens the meeting and announces that at today's meeting the kehilla budget must be adopted, since this is the demand of the supervisory authority.
Before the agenda, parnas Goldberg takes the floor and proposes adopting a protest resolution against the partition of Eretz Israel; a similar motion is put forward by the vice-chairman of the council, Mr. Jasny, with the amendment that the resolution be sent to the English [British] consulate.
Parnassim Dalisman and Sibemski[?] speak against the resolution, arguing that the matter does not fall within the competence of the kehilla.
During the discussion of Goldberg's motion it comes to a sharp exchange of words between the mover and Dr. Lieberman on one side and Messrs. parnassim Dalisman and Sibemski[?] on the other.
Dr. Lieberman supports the motion with the amendment that a drafting committee be created to work out the protest resolution; the motion is adopted. The committee comprises: Mitlis, Jasny and Liwertowicz[?].
After the “storm” over “an egg not yet laid”, they proceed to the budget. The rapporteur Dalisman points out that the budget committee, going through each item, raised the budget from 199 thousand zł. (according to the board) to 216 thousand zł. Out of the 12 thousand zł. a number of subsidies were raised, e.g. the subsidy for the Jewish hospital from 10 to 13 thousand zł., winter relief 3000 zł., for poor emigrants to Eretz Israel 2 500 zł., Talmud Torah from 2 to 4 thousand zł., the craftsmen's school from 600 to 5000 zł., for families without means to marry off [their children] “aksn”[?] 1000 zł., “Menuchi”[?] from 500 to 1000 zł., Beit Yaakov from 300 to 1000 zł., Keter Torah and “Yachal”[?] from 100 to 500 zł., Keren Hayishuv 500 zł., “Nechipodai”[?] 100 zł. on condition that they do not play on the Sabbath, “Ognisko” from 150 to 500 zł., etc.
Only after the report did a long discussion begin, which led to the council adding a further 10 thousand zł., so that the budget amounts to 226 thousand zł., i.e. 27 thousand zł. higher than the board's draft.
The increased sum includes: for trade licences (patents) for poor merchants — raised from 600 to 2000 zł., for craftsmen from 600 to 1000, for the Talmud Torah an additional 1000 zł., Keter Torah 500 zł., winter relief from 3 to 5 thousand zł., urgent aid from 12 to 16 thousand zł. (printed 16—12), etc.
At six o'clock in the morning the night session was closed.
As we are informed, the majority of the board is of the opinion not to accept the budget raised by the council; instead the board's budget will be sent to the supervisory authority.

From the “Beit Lechem” campaign.

[Sosnowiec — abandoned child.]

5-Year-Old Jewish Boy Killed by a Car

[Sosnowiec — traffic accident.]
On Friday at about 10 a.m. a car accident occurred at the corner of Piłsudskiego and Stara [streets], which cost the life of 5-year-old Josele Szwarcbaum[?]. Scandals and Brawls — At the Revisionist Protest Meeting against the Partition of Eretz Israel

[Kielce — Zionism.] On Sunday, the 9th of Av, towards evening, the Kielce Revisionists convened a large protest meeting against the partition of Eretz Israel, against the “destruction of the Third Temple”. The meeting was to have taken place in the synagogue courtyard, but at the demand of the moreh hora'ah (rabbinic decisor), Rabbi Holberg[?], the meeting was moved into the synagogue, where, because of Tisha B'Av, a large crowd had gathered.
The first protester was the head of the rabbinical court (Raavad) Horberg[?], who is against the partition because of Jerusalem, which is not included in the Jewish state.
Second, the leader of the Kielce Revisionists, editor[?] Rozel[?], began to speak.
During his speech the kibbutzniks present and others heckled him, and when the Revisionist stewards tried to remove the hecklers from the synagogue by force, a great tumult broke out, which led to wild scandals and brawls, so that part of the synagogue furnishings was wrecked.
The crowd began to shout: “Long live Weizmann.” “Long live the Zionist practical workers[?].” “We accept the Jewish state,” etc.[?]. And the Revisionists in turn raised cheers in honour of Jabotinsky and protested against the partition.
The Revisionist protest meeting, which had turned into a Zionist demonstration, broke up in panic[?] to the strains of “Hatikvah” and “Techezakna”.
Writing Doesn't Help, Warning Doesn't Help.

[Kielce — crime.] Miss T. was a poor girl; she lived together with a cripple on Bodzentyńska[?] Street (printed “Bodzentiger”), and made her living by carrying vegetables into rich houses, from which she barely scraped together her bit of food[?].
And indeed Miss T. felt herself superfluous in God's world, complained of her bitter fate and saw no future for herself, no way out of her sad situation.
And [...] [doubtful passage: “avchn, voser mitish ... mukhbk zayn” — apparently: she would have liked to withdraw from the world[?]], but she has no money. But there is, after all, no Jewish convent, — and suddenly some shrivelled Jewish woman drops in on her and introduces herself as a neighbour. The visitor begins to lay out whole heaps of stories about how, through her lucky hand, hundreds of ugly orphan girls had grabbed their right match, and that for her too she had brought, in a lucky hour, her true destined one.
A young man, truly worthy of a blessing, and moreover already once married[?]. He is not even a bachelor, but a divorcé, but with such a one she will[?] after all have a bright life.
The girl was completely bewildered[?]. It seemed to her that the scene taking place here in her room was no more than a dream. Until now she had already considered herself lost, forgotten — and now such happiness should suddenly befall her?
The sly neighbour apparently understood into what confusion her news[?] had thrown the girl, and to drive away every doubt she suddenly[?] opened the door, and at her wave of the hand a short, elderly person slipped into the room.
The guest bowed down to his knees, planted a fat kiss on her hand, placed himself in a “kor'im” (prostration) position and declared eternal faithful love.
A while later the cavalier had already brought along 2 dressed-up Jewish women and introduced them as his mother and sister. The neighbour immediately set to work, and after an hour's labour she brought matters, that very same day, to a “vort” [engagement].
The bridegroom did not step away from the bride; he even followed her when she went off to trade at the market stalls.
Thus passed 1 day, 2 days. On the third day the mother-in-law comes along and declares to the bride that for her, as an old-fashioned God-fearing[?] Jewish woman, today's conduct is not fitting; let her set up a chuppah with the bridegroom. The girl agreed to fulfil the wish, and the very next day a quiet wedding was prepared.
Well, love is indeed a fine[?] thing, but it doesn't bring a livelihood after all. The young wife, poor thing, had to get up early in the morning, harness herself to the two baskets of vegetables and stride through the town for a living. The young man felt somehow not quite himself and wanted to stay at home during the day.
The young wife hurried home to her husband — after all, it is the honeymoon. But how surprised she was when, coming into the room, she did not find her husband; she began to rummage in every corner and indeed established that together with the husband the little bundle with over 100 zł. had also vanished.
Only then did she realise that she had fallen victim to a refined swindle, that the neighbour, the bridegroom and his so-called sister are one gang of swindlers[?], and that the whole wedding had been nothing but a trick to scrape out of her the little bundle with the few guilders.
To Blazes with It!.. (Monologue of a Kielce Communal Activist)

[Kielce — Feuilleton.]
(Monologue of a Kielce communal activist.)
"Listen, Panie redaktorze [Mr. Editor]," a former[?] communal activist said to me this week, "to blazes with the whole communal work! Do you hear me or not? Since I threw the kehilla business off my back I have only now become a human being. A human being like other people. I eat my dinner on time, I take a look at how my child does his lessons, I have a chat with my wife, I go out with[?] her a little to the stadium, and I can do what I want and when I want. Before, I never had any time: from 8 in the morning till 3 in the afternoon I was busy in the 'urzędy'[?] [government offices] (in fact[?] boards and corridors alike) with interventions. There are[?] troubles enough in town, and people come to you with aching hearts seeking help, and you feel that you can help them somewhat — well, can you refuse? So you go — and what[?] do you think? Will the wife and children wait for you? And what about the meetings, the consultations of other institutions, and what about all kinds of campaigns? And now the campaign for Działoszyce? I tell you, it is terrible!
True, the Jews of Działoszyce must[?] be helped. But with what? It seems, at the very least, with several thousand złoty, and indeed a committee was elected right away. So everything is in the best order? But it all comes to a bluff. The committee is no committee. Since there is nobody to go out [collecting], you cannot gather more than 5—6 people. 'There is no time!' And if you do want to help somewhat and you do go out to collect a few złoty, you must be ready to hear all sorts of abuse, for as soon as you start asking the rich to give a 'początek' [opening donation], they answer: I know one must give. But today I need not give much, because I have near[?] Działoszyce a relative, an in-law[?] of a first[?] cousin, and it may be that, if she doesn't forget, she will send something... and more such hollow excuses.
And you can have no grounds to answer him anything, when he knows it himself; and if you like, he tells you quite simply and quietly that one can safely rely on our American 'brethren'[?], on the 'Joint' — he knows it will arrange everything itself; and if you happen to dare and cannot bear to hear it and say a word, then you get abused with a smooth tongue[?] and they even threaten you too...
Well, I ask you: should one meddle in kehilla matters? In short, I will no longer occupy myself with any communal work; I am fed up — 'to blazes with it!'.."
Sh. H.

(Concerning a small incident in the Katowice synagogue).

What actually happened?
The wife of the parnas and Chevra Kadisha member Mr. Grinfetzter [?] died; the cantor Mr. Rosenzweig, who incidentally had only just returned from leave, owing to a misunderstanding did not take part in the funeral, and for that the severe verdict already came, not permitting the cantor to be "mekabel shabbat" [to lead Kabbalat Shabbat]; and here one should have taken into account that the synagogue worshippers were guilty of nothing — and indeed the synagogue public wondered, firstly at the harshness of the verdict and secondly at the attitude towards public opinion.

[Upper Silesia — Chorzów; refugees from Germany.]
Our town was the first to take in the first refugees from Germany, numbering 50 families, but these families are literally struggling with death by starvation. At the time they turned to the "Joint", which sent 7,500 zł. to Katowice, to Dr. Kaufmann, for the above-mentioned Jews.
At the general meeting of the refugees, which took place last Wednesday in the hall of the Jewish community in Katowice in the presence of 120 refugees, the sufferings of the Jews in general and in particular of the German refugees who are in Upper Silesia were heard. The Chorzów refugees were represented by Mr. Abba Shteynik, who was also elected to the distribution committee, but the chairman Mr. Sachs did not allow this, because he is not a Katowice resident but lives in Chorzów, and the money — so he said — is only for Katowice. After this statement Mr. Shteynik left the meeting.
During the discussion the needy refugees protested against the committee, which keeps the money sent by the "Joint" in the iron safe, and it is not distributed to the refugees, and they are threatened with dying of hunger.
A resolution was adopted to turn to the "Joint" that a representative be delegated here, who should help in a proper [?] way the 50 Jewish refugee families in Chorzów.

On Pinkasim (Record Books) of the Jewish Kehillot in Zagłębie

[Zagłębie — history; kehilla.] It perhaps smacks of idleness to come to the Jewish public with a plan precisely today, when in these times of enormous depression — economic as well as moral-spiritual — its signs are becoming ever more pronounced and stronger. And nevertheless the plan is a topical and a burning one.
Whoever has had the opportunity to talk with older inhabitants of Będzin knows that a piece of history is floating around in Będzin that needs to be worked up and immortalised. Another ten years and this material will be completely forgotten, and at best it will exist in the form of old legends and, as is the way of things, with a good[?] dose of heated fantasy. Already today people tell stories that border on the world of imagination...
Unfortunately, the Będzin Jewish kehilla to this day has no pinkas [communal record book] whatsoever in its possession. Several years ago the proposal of the vice-president, Mr. G. Lagrer[?], concerning a pinkas was adopted, but to this day the proposal has remained on paper. In the kehilla there are, according to my information, certain materials which could serve the historian as a source for reconstructing those generations; these materials, however, have to this day not been looked through by anyone, nor sorted[?]. In all likelihood there is an abundance of interesting archival material there — but one has to set about it and start looking into it.
Sosnowiec too is a place where considerable documentary material ought to be found on the origins of the Jewish community in Sosnowiec. Here too everything is, unfortunately, [lamentable?], and the whole matter is virgin soil.
The Sosnowiec Jewish community is relatively young, but in the course of time societies, associations and institutions arose and were wiped[?] off the surface without echo and without resonance; people great and small were active here for the good of Jewry and to its detriment.
But it is not only a matter of the older[?] past; it is also a matter of the recent past, which is not shrouded in the secrets of withered minute-books and mouldy archival materials.
Here too the things must be researched scientifically, and beyond all that a systematic attempt must also be made to immortalise the present-day community in all its currents[?] and phenomena; and since this will be[?] the mirror of today[?] or of the very recent yesterday, it proves to be an extremely responsible task. The necessary distance and the necessary time-perspective to be able to evaluate all events and deeds properly are not yet there; in this section of the work there may well be partiality and vested interests, and in this kind of work — historical in essence — the main thing, after all, is objectivity.
As said, the whole matter may seem an idle one, but it is not so. At a time when it is argued incessantly from all sides that we Jews are a people that has come in from outside[?], that we must emigrate, we must avail ourselves not only of polemics and discussions, which in the end influence no one, and of interventions and petitions to bodies that [deserve the same?]; we must prove that for long generations we have been naturalised here in this country, each in his place. The Jewish community of Zagłębie, however young it may be, also already counts several hundred years. We have our merits in the growth of the economy in the town; we have laid a brick in the development of the towns in general; we have taken part in the volunteer[?] struggles, in the Polish uprisings and in the fights for freedom[?] for Polish independence. Documentarily and on the basis of archival materials we will prove that we are on this territory as conscious citizens, who suffered together, wept[?] together and rejoiced together in all the sufferings, sorrows and joys of the Polish people.
That is the external aspect. For us Jews ourselves such a pinkas is of first-rate importance, for one must, after all, someday draw up a summing-up of our life and work; nothing at all may be lost.
This work is not a work for a single person; it calls for a collective effort of several qualified commissions which are to conduct the work jointly. Certain sums of money are also [needed?] to make the work possible — the search[?] for archival traces of Jewish Zagłębie, which costs not only energy and toil but also actual money. The body called upon for this, which must finance such a project, is the Jewish kehilla.
It would be worthwhile for the administrations of the Jewish kehillot in Zagłębie, during their work on the annual budget, not to forget this matter and to give their contribution, and thereby also the impetus, to this colossal work.
Y. M. B—man.
With the Pencil in Hand.

[Dąbrowa — Kehilla.] (For the attention of the new kehilla representation in Dąbrowa [Górnicza]).
At a very difficult moment fate fell upon us to take over the representation of the Jewish population of Dąbrowa. At a time of general crisis in general, and for us Jews in particular, and on top of that comes the ritual-slaughter law, which has considerably reduced the kehilla's income, and with such a fatal deficit as the kehilla has left behind, we are to be the ones who must repair what the outgoing[?] leadership neglected.
I speak of the deficit. It is generally known that every institution, if it conducts activity, may have a deficit. But that holds for activity that creates something good. With us in Dąbrowa that is not the case: nothing was created and nothing was built[?]; the only thing that did remain is debts in every field. Possibly this was the result of the fact that "life is stronger than the possibilities", or perhaps economic light-mindedness, and perhaps even economic incompetence...
The [—] and the proclamation, which was called to conduct its activity, must work very[?] intensively so as not to repeat what has been done until now. Last Sunday saw the end of the activity of the old kehilla representatives, and at the same time the activity of the new ones begins.
The beginning of our activity in the kehilla must be under the motto "with the pencil in hand". If we manage that, then it is to be hoped that what has been done until now will not be repeated.
Everyone who has a public past knows that where there are people with full awareness, means and aims, where at the top stands a person psychically[?] young, the results are always[?] good; whereas where at the top stand people who operate with yellowed[?] initiative, the results are not good even with the greatest efforts. It is to be hoped, however, that the present kehilla leadership will no longer belong to the latter.
Public activists are divided into several kinds: conscientious people with awareness of means and aims; in [—][?] are also divided the activists "with the pencil in hand" — they[?] measure and calculate precisely the plans and the possibilities of realisation, which is so necessary in public life. Others do not measure, do not calculate, but live with "optimism" and, waving a hand, "it will be fine somehow" — this leads to various fictions and misfortunes.
Therefore caution [printed 'farnikhtikeyt'] must penetrate everywhere, in every field and in every initiative — "with the pencil in hand" must be the starting point of every activity.
We must achieve much, and the possibilities are not wrapped in miracles, in hidden secrets, in pilpul; quite simply — live realistically, "with the pencil in hand", calculate precisely the available means, to which the activity in the kehilla must be adapted.
S. Jakubowicz.
(Member of the kehilla council in Dąbrowa).
