Commercial courses for merchants.
The question of educational centres for merchants and shopkeepers.
The question of modernising trade and shops.
The question of adapting the goods to the taste and demand of the customer, and finally the question of receiving, serving and treating [the customer] decently, has become a question of first-class importance, to which Jewish merchantry must at long last thoroughly adapt itself.
The Jewish economic organisations have long been occupied with finding a radical solution to all these questions, and first and foremost the Central Merchants' Association in Warsaw is seeing to it; for this purpose it has recently already held a series of conferences.
In connection with the above, commercial courses for merchants and shopkeepers have been established in a whole series of towns, where the merchant is taught, besides general subjects, also the modernisation of the business and the cultured treatment and serving of the customer.
The Zagłębie merchants' associations are not lagging behind and are also concerned with improving the economic situation of Jewish merchantry in Zagłębie.
In this connection, as we have already written, commercial courses for merchants and shopkeepers are being organised for the beginning of the new school year.
We are fully aware of the great, hard work that lies ahead in connection with organising such commercial courses, but the call of the hour demands that we take this responsible work upon ourselves, and right away, without putting it off till later.
The merchants' associations, however, expect moral support from the mercantile public, which should understand that this is not a personal whim but matters that demand a quick and radical solution.
The boards of the Zagłębie merchants' associations will therefore already set about the organisational work for the above-mentioned commercial courses, which will open in the coming weeks.
It is, however, highly desirable that the initiators organise large public meetings for merchants, at which all these questions would be discussed from every angle.
At these meetings lectures should be given on the topic "The general situation of merchantry", and in particular the situation of Jewish merchantry.
A start must be made now.
Important Decisions of the Supreme Court

[Law — Supreme Court rulings; tenancy law.]
The legal value of a tenant's ["lokator"] declaration made outside the court.
The court cannot order the eviction ["eksmisja"] of a tenant solely on the basis of his having declared, outside the court, that he does not need the flat he occupies.

Relations between tenant and sub-tenant ["sublokator"].
The circumstance that the tenant's lease of the flat has been terminated by notice has no bearing on the lawsuit the tenant conducts with the sub-tenant, regardless of whether it concerns an eviction, a claim for rent, or the fixing of the basic rent.

Grounds for evictions.
The circumstances that the landlord needs the flat because he himself lives in a damp, unhygienic flat, that he needs the flat for a watchman [probably the building's caretaker], or that he needs the flat for a daughter who is getting married, give a [word unclear: "vey-nign", perhaps "valid"/"sufficient"] ground for eviction.
On the other hand, changing the designated use of the premises ["lokal"] gives a ground for eviction, but only in the case where the change harms the landlord's interests or creates competition with a tenant who was living in the same building earlier.

Deposits ["kaucje"].
When the tenant has deposited a security in order to guarantee the rent owed, there is nevertheless a ground for eviction if he misses payment of the rent in 2 instalments ["raty"].

Postponement of evictions.
A postponement of an eviction is granted on account of unemployment and extraordinary poverty.
Extraordinary poverty means having no earnings, means of subsistence or any property apart from the necessary household goods.
In the case where he is employed but is not paid his wages and one has no other income, or one works only a few weeks a year, this means that one is in a state of extraordinary poverty, which entitles one to a postponement of eviction.
On the other hand, it does not mean that one is in a state of extraordinary poverty if one is supported by one's children.
The plea of extraordinary poverty may be invoked only when it concerns a dwelling, but not a business premises.
The "Garden" of the Old Market. (A Reportage)

[Feuilleton — reportage; the life of poverty and beggars.] By J. Janasowicz.
(Reportage).

On one [one word illegible under a blot] summer evening, after a hot, muggy day, three Jews with tangled beards sit on a bench in the "Garden" on the Old Market [Stary Rynek?]. The faces of these three Jews, and the clothes that hang on their bodies like sacks, bear witness that these are three representatives of that stratum which lives on human pity.

The "Garden", as on every summer evening[?], is packed full of people. Most of those sitting here are a working-class crowd, but you soon recognise that these are not factory workers, but, as usual, Jews — workers from small, stuffy ["duszne"] workshops, who come here to the "Garden" to rest after a whole day of hard toil ["harówka"] in the heat of the pressing iron, or in the dust of [word unclear].

People come here to "draw" air, air that is heavy and saturated with smoke and dust; people come here... because one meets acquaintances here and there is always an opportunity to hear what is going on in God's great world; incidentally, one can snatch a chat about this and that and about such[?] great things that weigh on the heart, and it becomes easier once one has talked it out. Here workers meet workers and also their own masters, who also come to the "Garden"[?] to draw "fresh" air of the [words unclear: "privies'(?) sort"]..
And upon my life, at first glance it is hard to tell who is the master and who the worker; both have the same gloomy appearance.

To the "Garden" on the market come Jews about whom one need not be a great psychologist and judge of people to establish that they do not belong to those who have married off their children "in joy" and are, besides, already provided with a livelihood. You can immediately read on each one's face the worry about tomorrow; you can see how each one's shoulders bend under the heavy burden of earning a living. Every Jew who sits here so comfortably drawing air has — as the saying[?] goes about a Jew — a bundle, in which lie various troubles.. troubles with the children, a sick wife, the rent, afflictions, and plain livelihood troubles.

The "Garden" is full of "needy citizens" ["noyt-birger"]; around every bench, and also at the sides, circles of people stand and chat; the men "politicize" and the women — as is the nature of women — talk, and above all gossip about whatever they can. Nevertheless it seems to me that if a writer were to note down these chance conversations being conducted here, the result would later be a naturalistic drama (or comedy) that would tell a great deal about the life of poverty.

And if this were by chance to survive for a long time, later generations could, thanks to such a manuscript[?], obtain a picture that would certainly agree more with historical reality than hundreds of written articles and history books.

Thus, for example, I am convinced that in order to get an idea of the psychology and way of life of so huge a stratum among Jews as the beggars, one would need not much — only to take down in shorthand and record the conversation that the three Jews with beggarly faces, sitting here on the bench, are conducting among themselves.

Naturally I do not have the possibility of rendering their conversation with full accuracy; I shall render only part of what I overheard.

Of the three Jews here on the bench, who exploit human compassion, whose main source of livelihood is the feeling of pity — two are cripples ["kalikes"]. One of them, with a red tangled beard, has a wooden leg — among beggars that is reckoned as half a livelihood; the second is blind in both eyes — that is already a tool with which a beggar can attain a very high rank; and only the third Jew is healthy in all his limbs — nothing at all, he has no better business — in begging, too, a business!

— And I say — the blind Jew speaks up — that begging would not yet be lying in the ground like this, were it not that the "fine Jews" are burying it; like [word unclear, perhaps vermin] they crawl around, overnight new ones and more new ones spring up. Where has it ever been heard of that anyone who merely has a respectable beard should go round the houses... a real impudence.

— That's not all — the lame one replies — the [word unclear] women, the slatterns ["shlumpers"], should be rooted out; they make a ruin of everything, they band together a whole gang of "shlakhtes"[?], and however much one gives, they take.. They go in threes and fours, and when one gets a grosz they share it — a black year on their heads — they have made themselves a partnership business.

— What do you mean — says the healthy one — neither the "fine Jews" nor the women are to blame. The ruin is something else altogether: the courtyard singers, the musicians — they finish us off, the "hat-makers"[?] ["kapelusz-makher"]; for the grosz that is thrown up to them they give a whole concert — and go do something about them.
— That's it — confirm the other two.

— And I say — the healthy beggar speaks up — that if we old beggars were united among ourselves, something could still be achieved. The first thing — not to let in any new ones, to put an end to the "stulkes"[?], and not to take bread, bits of sugar and other such [word unclear]; you want to give money — fine; if not — break your head; and with the musicians, too, we would find a remedy. The main thing is to be united — would that it were so! The shoemakers and tailors have a union ["farayn"] — don't they achieve something?
The Rent Reduction Must Be Extended

A long and hard struggle had to be waged for the reduction of rent. The gain for the tenants, taken purely materially, was a paltry one compared with the efforts invested and the hopes attached to it, especially in view of the general fall in business takings[?] at the time, the inability to pay and the burden on the broad masses; in any case it stood in no proportion whatsoever to the considerable benefit that the compensation granted brought the landlords.
The reduction amounts in all to 10 or 15 per cent, and incidentally only a small part of the tenants benefit from it, namely the better-situated, and therefore those who pay their rent punctually and are absolutely independent of the landlord's ill or good will; on the other hand, the said miserable relief[?] obtained[?] was compensated to the landlords many times over by removing shops and furnished[?] premises from tenant protection; likewise the new tenants are, as it were, handed over to them as well — not to mention the unheard-of enforcement rights for securing owed rent debts, substantial concessions in the case of rebuilding, and also the switch from quarterly to monthly rent.
It must, however, be stated quite specifically that all the enumerated concessions recognised[?] for the landlords are stable, permanent, whereas the rent reduction was fixed for barely 2 years.
Now, at the end of November, the said 2-year term thus expires, and it must be established as a fact that the very conditions which moved the deciding factors at the time to reduce the rent have not changed during this period; on the contrary, in the course of this time the cost of living has risen considerably, earnings, by contrast, have shrunk, and consequently the population's ability to pay has worsened beyond comparison.
In such circumstances the rent reduction ought not only to have been extended, but even widened and deepened; and yet one cannot so lightly launch a campaign for the further validity of this concession, because it is truly hard to say what surprises the policy of equilibrium will bring this time.
One must, after all, have the courage to admit that the whole campaign for the rent reduction, which was waged with such fervour two years ago, has, in view of the results achieved, very bitterly disappointed every responsible tenant, since on the whole they brought the tenants far more harm than benefit.
Nevertheless, the struggle for the extension of the rent reduction must unconditionally be taken up, and no circumstance whatsoever may hold it back; and if the practical benefits of its victory are not so substantial, it nonetheless has a significance of principle.
The question arises, however, who will undertake the campaign and how it must be conducted so that it is crowned with success.
First of all it must be stated here that immovable „property“ has powerful protectors „in the high windows“ [in high places], and its interests are tenderly[?] guarded; besides, the landlords form a strong, unified front, united to such a degree that even the „race fashions“, which demoralise all civic organisations, have no hold whatsoever in those ranks.
And the tenants?
The broad masses of tenants do not appreciate the necessity of organisation and show not the slightest understanding for it.
In Zagłębie there are no tenants' associations at all, and therefore the struggle for the extension of the rent reduction — and incidentally also for postponing the abolition of tenant protection for new tenants — must be taken up by the craftsmen's, the small traders' and all other interested organisations, in order to measure up against the influence of the landlords.
Y. A.
On the Zagłębie Pinkasim.

[Zagłębie — local history; a reply (the almanac of Zagłębie Jewry).]
In the last issue of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" Mr. M. G. B—man comes forward with a proposal to the Zagłębie kehillot that they support the publication of pinkasim [record books] of the local kehillot.
Reading Mr. B—man's article one gets the impression that this gentleman does not live in Będzin. Had Mr. B—man lived in Zagłębie, he would surely have had to know that for more than a year now work has been going on on an illustrated almanac of Jewish Zagłębie, which has already found such a strong echo in local society that it is unthinkable that Mr. B—man should have heard nothing about it.
In the said almanac there will indeed be printed — besides the history of the Jews in Zagłębie — also the history of all the Jewish public institutions in the region. Apart from that, all the pinkasim of the Będzin chevrot [societies] have for months been carefully worked through, and this work is already in print.
According to Mr. B.'s information, important historical materials on the history of the Jews in Będzin are supposed to be found in the local kehilla. As a member of the local kehilla board, however, I can state that no such materials exist in the kehilla.
As for Sosnowiec, the historical material is being worked on there too, and among other materials the local kehilla pinkas is also being used.
Mr. B. thinks that this is not a matter for an individual but for commissions. But it is the whole luck that the work is in the hands of an individual, because had commissions dealt with it, the almanac would never have seen the light of day. It is an old rule that "commissions" are created only in order to bury a matter, not to bring it to life.
If one also takes into account that this individual is the editor S. Rozenberg, who possesses all the qualifications for this kind of work — broad erudition, a splendid style and, above all, perseverance and objectivity — one can already be sure that the almanac will be a lasting achievement.
Not only the local press but also the Jewish press in America has written about this publication. Thus, for example, the New York "Morgen Zhurnal" of 2 May and "Der Tog" of 30 May this year carried substantial notices about the almanac.
Before me also lies a letter from the former Rabbi of Będzin, Rabbi Yekusiel Zalmen Grojbart (now a rabbi in New York), to the editor S. Rozenberg, dated 10 Iyar 5697. In the letter Rabbi Grojbart confirms receipt of the first 2 printer's sheets of the almanac, and he also writes there [?] the following:
"In general I must tell you that you are doing a wonderful work. One can see the warmth and earnestness that hover over every page. You have approached the publication with much soul and feeling and are carrying it out with magnificence, splendour and masterly brilliance. You have made of Będzin 'a city of perfect beauty', and you deserve a sincere yasher koach, especially in our present time, when the Jew must so often legitimise himself and show his pedigree, his bond with the land where he has lived for hundreds of years — such a work is an important contribution to the historical security of the Jews in Poland and to his awareness of his rights."
As for Mr. B—man's appeal to the Zagłębie kehillot to support such a work vigorously, we can reassure B. that the kehillot did not wait for his advice and had already earlier decided to subsidise the almanac.
So, Mr. B., the work is being done. Taking part in it, besides the local forces, are also such historians as Prof. [Majer] Bałaban, Dr. [Emanuel] Ringelblum and others, and it is expected to be a fundamental work in this field.
Judging by the tone of your writing, it seems you consider yourself something of a specialist [?] in historical research. If that is true, the editors of the almanac are ready to make use of your collaboration.
Moshe Manela.
Who Are the Ten [?] Greatest Rich Men in the World?

[Miscellany — world economy; the richest men.]
One reckons someone to be a great rich man — and after his death it turns out that he was mostly [—] [?]; almost all the richest houses go to ruin as soon as the master of the house passes away.
Something similar happened with Rockefeller's fortune. Hardly had he died when it turned out that this very "richest man in the whole world" died a "pauper"...
True, may such poverty be the lot of all our readers; but with 25 million dollars one is, among the richest people in the world, a veritable beggar...
If one casts a glance at a statistic of the Leipzig Fair on the ten richest people in the world, one sees [?] only then that not a single one is left of all the rich men who in the twenties were considered the richest people in the world.
Today the richest man in the world is the Englishman Andrew Mellon, who owns fifty department stores in England, has his own banks and mines, and owns two billion dollars.
The automobile king Henry Ford owns not much less and is therefore in second place among the world's rich men.
The third-greatest rich man in the world is the Frenchman Pierre du Pont, the noblest man in the world, a great French manufacturer, who keeps the noblest house in the world.
Young Rockefeller, with the fortune his father gave him while still alive, is the fourth among the rich men. After him comes the newspaper king Hearst, who has his own papers in every larger city in America, with a circulation of millions of copies a day.
The sixth among the world's rich men is George Baker, a bank director in New York, who holds — as they say — the "sack" [?] of all the banks in his hand. He earns on all bank speculations, knows when to buy cheap and when one must sell dear...
Frederick Prince, the great sportsman, is the seventh rich man. His horses always come in first. Besides that he is the chief shareholder of all the Boston banks.
The New Yorker Arthur James is the eighth rich man. Where his money comes from, nobody knows. His father was already rich, but the great fortune he made himself. What kind of business he has, nobody knows...
In ninth place stand the Weyerhaeuser brothers, who came from Germany to America only thirty years ago. Both brothers came without a cent and bought up old paper, old rags. From these goods, which are spread throughout America, they made their great fortune.
The last of the ten richest people in the world are the two brothers Vorstord [?]. They too came over from England to America some thirty years ago without a penny. Today the brothers, with their department stores, are so rich that they are counted among the richest people in the whole world.
Z. Haber, Vienna.
"Nothing Has Changed"

[Feuilleton — Zagłębie, summer 1937.] Sketches from the "Line" [?]. By S. Libaszon [?].
Back to nature...
When one looks more closely at "dacha life" [life in a summer cottage], all the theories about "the happiness of mankind" become pitiful [?] — that things cannot get better until the time comes of "and the earth shall be full of knowledge" [Isaiah 11:9], or of the fraternisation of peoples; the only means that could radically solve the problem of the peoples is
— back to nature.
Strong is the power of nature; the greatest hero cannot overcome it, and what is more [?], nature receives everyone equally, makes no distinction between rich man and pauper, recognises no numerus clausus, and no anti-Jewish excesses can happen there; even the wild beast makes no distinction as to who shall be its victim.
And so [?] it has come to show in full force the "freedom" that already exists in the bosom of nature: the city man becomes a "free bird", casts off everything connected with "Europeanness" and is transformed into a "man of nature"...
Here they show us a "villa" where several groups of "poker players" are firmly entrenched [?], each group at a separate table, playing.
But in this case we are not interested in the card-playing, because in today's modern times, when card-playing takes first place in what is called pastime, it is simply a mitzvah to play cards at the dacha; what interests us is who the players are.
At home, that is in the town where one lives, such an idyllic picture would have been [—] [?] — a trifle! The wife of a magistrate (town-hall) official playing cards together with... Ger Hasidim. But here it is an ordinary phenomenon. "Slebs" [?] with nature — you can also, for example, find a Hasidic Jew, with beard and sidelocks, grazing cows, because the Jew here has been conquered by the rich nature...
Therefore we say that the most radical means of solving the race problem would be for mankind to return to the primeval times
— back to nature...
From town to the village...
This year the Zagłębie public has "occupied" the Beskid resorts. In Rajtsze [Rajcza?] — I am told — there is "all of Będzin"; in Bystra — Sosnowiec, Będzin and a bit of Częstochowa and Zawiercie [?]; if one wants, for instance, to meet a Będziner or a Sosnowiecer, one "must" [?] travel to Rajcza, Bystra and Szczyrk.
In certain [?] [circles] people rack their brains over how to explain the "why is this day different from other days"? Why is this year's dacha season so Purim-like [?], that everyone has gone away? [—] because in [—]? We already have enough of everything, only the bit of fresh air is lacking for our [—]..
— Fools that you are — a Jew calls out. [—] [?] stands "San ha-bi" [?] and turns to the [—] [—] — Rosh Chodesh. Among the "parpers" [?] there are a great number who are racking their brains where to get the expenses to "pack up" the household back home. It is even told that one of the "letniki" [summer visitors] sold a piece of merchandise he had set aside for winter suits for his children, and with the "proceeds" sent his household off to a dacha. "Let her be equal to all the wives," said the loyal husband. And secondly, since the newest policy is to resettle the peasants from the village into the town, our brethren the Children of Israel do exactly the opposite and run
— from town into the village...
Peace is here...
At the "depot" [?] [station] in Bystra the following scene takes place:
One of the "letniki", a Jew already on in years, walks with quick steps and shouts:
— Jews, peace is here!
— Peace? What is the meaning of this verse? Perhaps Japan has made peace with China, or the Arabs with the Jews?
Well, and if so, who here gives a hoot about the matter [lit. "whom does it lie in the left heel"]?
Later the matter became clear: peace had indeed been concluded — not between states, but between a "dachnik" [male summer visitor] and a "dachnitsa" [his female counterpart]...
And this is how it happened.
For more than 1 year now there has been no domestic peace between this couple (between us — the couple lives in Zagłębie; for certain reasons — after all the "peace" may still be spoiled — we do not give the names or the exact place..). Good friends had already moved heaven and earth so that peace would be made between them, but they did not succeed, and the "war" went on until..
until just last week, on the morning after the blessing of the new month of Elul, the little wife was seized by thoughts of repentance and.. (the rest you can surmise for yourselves..)
The peace had such a strong effect on the "dachnik" that out of great joy he went out for a stroll, and to whomever he met he announced the good tidings:
— "Peace is here"...
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Re'eh)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] (Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes etc. on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Re'eh
—o—
a) "Behold, I set before you this day" (11:26)
In Goraj, the birthplace of R' Mendele of Kotzk, there were many Lublin Hasidim who used to travel to the "Seer" [of Lublin]. R' Mendele, however, never wanted to travel to Lublin with the crowd. He went his own way, and an elderly Lublin Hasid scolded him:
"Is it possible? Such a young man as you travels[?] where the whole crowd travels — what, are you some kind of separatist from the community?"
R' Mendele answered him:
"The verse says 'Behold, I set before you this day a blessing and a curse; the blessing, if ye hearken'... So the verse begins in the singular and ends in the plural, because when it is a matter of 'Behold' — of choosing a path — one must go alone, not let oneself be swept along with the many, with the current, but go one's own way. Only once the path has already been chosen can one, and must one, go with the many..."
—o—
b) "Unto the place which the Lord shall choose out of all your tribes" (12:5)
Which place is meant by "which the Lord shall choose out of all your tribes"? It means Jerusalem, because the whole Land of Israel was divided among the tribes, only "Jerusalem was not divided among the tribes"; that is the meaning of "which the Lord shall choose out of all your tribes" — what God chose out of all the tribes belongs to God and to no one else. Binah ba-Mikra[?].
• • •
When in 1929 the English parliamentary commission arrived in the Land of Israel, and the Mufti with his cronies stirred up[?] incidents over the Western Wall, it came[?] to the point that the leaders of the Yishuv were about to agree to a proposal to give up the Western Wall entirely, [—][?], and since the Temple Mount with the Omar mosque would always remain danger points with which the Arabs could be incited — certain Zionist leaders held that it was worth renouncing the Western Wall, if only not to provoke the Arabs' wrath.
Rabbi Kook, of blessed memory, was ill at the time. But on hearing how matters stood, he invited several Zionist leaders and told them:
"Who gave you the right to renounce the Western Wall? 'Jerusalem was not divided among the tribes'; Jerusalem with the site of the Temple belongs to God, and no Jew has any right to renounce anything of it. If you do anything of the kind in this sense, I will come out with a protest and proclaim to the worlds that you have betrayed your people and your God..."
This declaration held the Jewish politicians back from a dangerous step.
—o—
c) "And ye shall rejoice before the Lord your God... and the Levite that is within your gates, for he hath no portion nor inheritance with you" (verse 12)
You will rejoice with the tithes you bring from your produce, and the Levite will rejoice in the fact that he has no inheritance. That too is a joy — not to bear the yoke of property... The Dubno Maggid.
• • •
In Jerusalem no Jew at all had a share. It is God's city, and before God all are equal; therefore the Levite too will rejoice, "for he hath no portion nor inheritance with you", because together with him you have no portion and inheritance there[?] — for in Jerusalem you, too, have no portion and inheritance; there he is equal to all. Pnei Yafot.
—o—
d) "Then thou shalt kill of thy herd and of thy flock" (12:21)
R' Yitzchak Dembo, the well-known fighter for Jewish ritual slaughter in Russia, attended the first Zionist Congress in Basel. When he was asked what he was doing there, he answered:
"In case a Jewish state is founded, I will secure[?] Jewish ritual slaughter there..."
—o—
e) "And there shall cleave nought of the cursed thing to thine hand" (13:18)
"And there shall cleave nought of the cursed thing to thine hand" — let nothing of the ban cling to you, nothing of the cruelty you must show toward the condemned city. After every war a brutalization remains in people; against this spiritual legacy of wartime the verse warns. Imrei Chen.
—o—
f) "Thou shalt surely give him" (15:10)
"Whoever averts his eyes from charity is as though he worshipped idols."
How does charity come to idolatry?
But "poverty drives a man to transgress the will of his Maker", and if one gives no charity one turns the poor man into a sinner and into one who rebels against his Maker; therefore the Gemara calls it [i.e. withholding charity] idol worship. R' Chaim of Sanz.
—o—
g) "And the Lord thy God shall bless thee in all that thou doest" (verse 18)
The Rebbe R' Zusha used always to laugh at those who give the Master of the Universe advice on how to help them. "A fine God that would be," he used to say, "if I, Zusha, had to give Him advice..."
In These Historic Days... (On the opening of the 20th Zionist Congress)

[Zionist Congress — article.] (On the opening of the 20th Zionist Congress)
One may believe that with religious ecstasy and with the prayer "Grant success to my way, the emissary of the congregation", our emissaries boarded the ships and trains on the way to Zurich, to the 20th Zionist Congress, which opened last Tuesday and at which the question of the English government's partition plan will be decided and an answer given: "yes" or "no".
As the emissaries of the people of Israel crossed the threshold of the session hall for the first time, there surely rose before their eyes the picture of the past and present situation of their peoples[?] — a picture full of all manner of calamities and evil decrees, in which the Jewish people finds itself today — at a time when a ray of hope begins to show itself in the form of the report of the English commission, which wants to give the Jews back a part of their ancient home, of the land of their fathers, but without Jerusalem, without the Negev, without Rutenberg's electrification, with a shared port of Jaffa and Tel Aviv — only a small piece of land without life-giving water[?] to nourish it; and on this the emissaries are asked to answer "yes" or "no".
And the question arises: what can and will the emissaries answer? Say "yes", so as to be inscribed again in the political book of life, or say "no" and renounce the English favour? Agree for the time being to a resting-place for a sixteenth part of the Jews, or not? Shall we, like the man who is about to drown with the ship, grab hold of the point of a sharp knife, or not?
These are the questions that must be answered from the rostrum of the 20th Zionist Congress.
We believe that the delegates must treat these hard questions according to the qualities of the Jewish merchant, who is known in the world for the fact that, on approaching a deal, he does not ask what he can gain by it but, on the contrary, what he can lose by it?
For even a small state in caricature form, or ministers[?] in the form of proud[?], capable politicians, with a legislating parliament, an administration, schools, representation in the world — has that no value?
And that is why the eyes of all of world Jewry are turned to Zurich, where the fate of our future will be decided: to become a people equal to all peoples, or to go on existing as eternal wanderers[?]...
Herman Szer.
Zionist Youth Colonies

[Zionism — youth, summer colonies and tourism.]
(From an outing to "Hala Boracza".)
You live in a valley. And all around you, on every side, you are ringed[?] by high, gigantic mountains with deep, dark forests, and near them fields spread out looking like brightly coloured carpets. It seems to you that it is all so close that after a few minutes' walk you will reach the forest and be swallowed up[?] in it; and something draws you there[?], and your feet carry you off by themselves, and you walk as if bewitched... You cast a glance back[?], upward[?] and further — and you are astonished: you have already been walking for two hours and still have not reached your goal. The mountains fool you, they "tease" you: little human[?], how you look beside us giants in God's beautiful world! And you cast a glance downward: oh, what deep abysses!... And the gigantic, tall trees cling to the rocks on the mountainsides, and it is a wonder how a person can get close[?] to them[?] from the [—] and the "[—]"...
Songs of Eretz Israel in the Forest.
Suddenly you hear familiar strains of singing — and which ones: songs of Eretz Israel! You are amazed. The singing grows ever stronger and clearer — strains[?] of Hebrew songs. Meanwhile the forest comes to an end, and you are already on the mountaintop, and before your eyes a blue-and-white flag flutters on a tall mast next to a Polish flag. The riddle is solved when you see enthusiastic young men and women marching in a long line with heads proudly raised, the joyful singing bursting from their throats. Quickly approaching them, I learn that here on "Hala Boracza", 854 metres high, there is now a colony of "Gordonia" of more than a hundred persons from all over Poland. We are soon noticed by a young man from Sosnowiec, a pupil of the Sosnowiec Jewish gymnasium, Perlsztajn, who leads us and shows[?] us all the buildings they live in here on the mountain, and he and other comrades from Częstochowa inform us about their daily schedule, which is very rationally put together. Afterwards we have a conversation with the leaders of the colony — persons with higher education from Eretz Israel, who lived through the recent events in Eretz Israel and themselves took part in the defence of the guard [Hagana / Shmira], and who now take care that the training of the youth be adapted to the reality of Eretz Israel. The programme therefore contains a great deal of sport and gymnastic exercises and Hagana training, and at the same time cycles of scholarly lectures: geography of Eretz Israel, Hebrew literature, sociology, etc. And since the majority here understands Hebrew perfectly, Hebrew holds[?] the upper hand, and some subjects are taught in Yiddish as well. The comrades feel very good here; bread and other food they get from Milówka[?], a two-hour walk from here, but they lack nothing here.
A week earlier there was a Betar colony here on the mountain, of youth from Upper Silesia and Bielsko, but since they consisted mostly of such as had been brought up in non-Jewish schools, they used other languages, and only a small part spoke Hebrew as well. Their programme also included the subject "prayer", and before going to sleep they all said a prayer composed by Jabotinsky himself...
The "schronisko" [mountain hostel] on the mountain helps them with part of its facilities and buildings; thanks to it the Jewish youth of all Zionist parties can properly train to be good sportsmen and loyal Zionists, and at the same time enjoy God's beautiful world.
Bravo Będzin!
We walk up to the beautiful white[?] building, which is still quite new and gleams in the sun with wonderful[?] window panes, and in the courtyard we meet "sunburnt" Będzin and Sosnowiec townsfolk and [—] and [—], who refresh themselves with white milk after the long trek through the forests; and although the sun is shining, they cry that they are cold here and wrap themselves in coats and sweaters. We therefore decide to go into the "schronisko". Right at the entrance a beautiful mezuzah[?] is fixed, with the inscription "Jerusalem", and on the wall by the stairs hang 2 marble[?] tablets, and on one of them is a Hebrew inscription: "Nordau Hut on the summit of Borac[?], at an altitude of 854 m. Erected by the 'Maccabi' association in the year 1932 under the presidency of Engineer Oskar Deutsch, through the architect[?] (?) Eng. Feliks Koren; ceremonially opened in December[?] 1932."
In short[?], the "schronisko" is named after Dr. Max Nordau of blessed memory, who preached the spreading of sport among Jews together with their national renaissance.
Elchanan Zajder.
A Little Letter from Rajcza...

[“Der Kokh-Lefl” — humour; poem, summer resort.] I've been four weeks now at the dacha [summer cottage],
I even got sunburnt [?],
Thank God, I have lost
No more than two and a half kilos...

I've climbed no mountain,
Bathed in no sea...
At nine o'clock here in Rajcza
They already keep the shutters closed...

Children cuddle up to mothers,
People go to sleep in good time,
Soon it turns quiet as a cemetery,
One hears [?] only barking from afar...

Flirting is not in fashion
Across the whole Rajcza area,
At most one catches a little flirt here
With a bread roll [?] and a radish...

And above all — the company,
Most refined and successful.
The “Vayishman” [the fat ones] and the “Panska” [the ladies, pańska]
Are quite well represented here...

“Boxing matches” take place here,
And may the Creator protect us,
Women tear at each other's hair
Over the children — the little bandits...

The screaming and the racket
One hears constantly, on and on,
The wonderful voices
Are surely heard throughout the Zagłębie region.

But on the other hand, when Sabbath comes
It gets really merry, a delight,
At the baker's, after the cholent,
There stands a long queue of women.

And one catches the right “sutl” [?]
In the sweet aroma of cholent...
And the “letnichkes” [female summer guests, letniczki] feel
How they draw fresh strength.

On Sabbath guests come over
And are gladly treated,
Some with coffee, milk, a little [?],
Some with kvass and “bani” kernels [?]...

Only the young soon slip away [?],
The impetus carries them off [?]
Somewhere between forest and grain field,
Surely not to recite Psalms...
G. K.
The Analysis. (A True Little Tale of a Nouveau-Riche Woman)

[“Der Kokh-Lefl” — humour; story.] A true little tale of a nouveau-riche woman.
Until the war Alte-Masha [“old Masha”] was [?] as healthy as a Don Cossack and never knew of any illnesses at all.
But to Alte-Masha's misfortune a war broke out, and poor Alte-Masha was fated in her old age to ride in a “samokhod” [motor car, samochód] with a “trombke” [horn, trąbka].
Ever since she rides in a car she behaves like a rich woman. Under the left [?] she suffers as if from the “tsal” [?], in her right ear she has “sugar”, in her jaw [“gombe”, gęba] she suffers from arthritis [“atretizm”, artretyzm] [?], and at the ankle of her left foot there are signs of a lung defect.
Alte-Masha decides to have herself examined [“zbaden”, zbadać] by a doctor, to know which spa to go to.
After Alte-Masha laid out her collection of ailments before the doctor, the doctor explains to her that she must have an analysis done.
— That, panie doktor — says Alte-Masha — I already have in my bag.
— Where did you get it?
— From a “makher” [fixer, agent].
— A makher? — wonders the doctor — you had an analysis made by a makher? What has a makher to do with an analysis? Perhaps you can show me the analysis?
— No — answers Alte-Masha — it still has to be confirmed by the German consul.
— What are you saying, madame — the doctor is already beside himself — what consul?
— What, you don't believe me? — Alte-Masha is getting angry — here, read.
— What are you showing me? Why, this is a visa!
— Well, did I lie to you when I said I already have it?
— But this is a visa!
— Well, you did say I need to get myself a visa [?].
— Not a visa, an analysis.
— But what is the difference between a visa and an analysis [?]?
— A visa is made by the consul, and an analysis you make yourself.
— How does one make it, this “lene-lize” [?]?
— Be so kind as to bring me your urine; after 24 hours I will establish the diagnosis from it.
Having agreed, Alte-Masha crawls out of the car, dragging a heavy bucket [“vyadre”, wiadro] to the doctor.
— Panie doktor, I am “slavge” [?]! I have it from a whole 24 hours.
Pouring from the bucket into a little bottle, the doctor explains to her: Madame, tomorrow at this time the analysis will be ready.
Next day the doctor explains to her: Madame, you are completely healthy, the analysis shows no signs of illness whatsoever.
Hearing the good news, Alte-Masha runs to the telephone and phones: Zerach, you are healthy, Yankele is healthy, Feygele is healthy, Mother is healthy, the mother-in-law is healthy, the cook is healthy, the shikse [gentile maid] is healthy too!..
—o—
A Dacha Interpretation.
Our forefathers say that on the Sabbath eve at twilight the demons were created.
But with the dacha-wife [“dachnitse”, holidaying wife] it is exactly the reverse: on Friday evening, when the husband is due to arrive, her demons die out...
Leib Stabinski.
A Dreadful Tale (How a Będzin Jewess, an Eternally Barren Woman, Was Blessed in Her Old Age with 4 Children, No Evil Eye)

[“Der Kokh-Lefl” — humour; Będzin.] How a Będzin Jewess, an eternally barren woman, was blessed in her old age with 4 little children, no evil eye.
We are informed of a wonderful and simply unbelievably happy case that happened last week to Mrs. Keyle-Beyle Flignapt.
The extraordinary miracle came about thus: this Jewish woman was known from always as childless, and, alas, nobody could help her — not her husband, not the doctor, not even the remedies and “shpeles” [?]; moreover she is by now a person on in years, over fifty, and if, for instance, someone had told her a year ago: “Keyle-Beyleshi, you'll see, you will still have a child” — she would have looked at him or her as at a madman. And yet, despite everything, the great miracle happened: last month she suddenly had 4 children at once: 3 boys and 1 girl... And the “having” of the “quadruplets” took place nowhere else but on the train... travelling from Będzin to Łódź for merchandise... As she herself relates, even before leaving, while she was at the local railway station, she already felt that the journey would not go smoothly for her... And indeed, suddenly [“naglie”, nagle] they pushed in one after the other — 4 little schoolchildren, whom she had to take along to Łódź on her ticket... And that is how, all at once, in her old age she became a “mother” of four children, may they live...
The Riddle Has Been Solved.

[“Der Kokh-Lefl” — humour; Dąbrowa.] A few weeks ago a storm passed over Zagłębie. Suddenly people in Dąbrowa [Górnicza] saw the wind carrying aloft an “ovalkhes” [?] that resembled a human being.
Only last Sunday did the matter become clear, during the speech of Pines of [?] the Krimilov [?] Hasidim, who declared that “evil winds once carried [someone] by force into the gmina [municipal council]”...
A Good Pupil.

[“Der Kokh-Lefl” — humour; jokes.] Rebbe: — Well, say it, Moishele: ishah — a w... [hinting at “a vayb”, a wife]
Moishele: — A vaser [water].
Rebbe: Oh, you peasant, you! Ishah — a w...
Moishele — Vants [bedbug].
Rebbe: Oh, you thickhead. An ishah is a thing that your father has, your rebbe has, and you too will have when you grow up.
Moishele (after thinking it over): — A gelding [“merin”].
—o—
The Clever Son-in-Law.
The father-in-law from Kielce [?] writes to his son-in-law in Sosnowiec:
— Dear son-in-law, if a son is born, telegraph at once; if a girl is born — write a letter.
God helped, twins were born, and the son-in-law sends the father-in-law this telegram:
“Mazel tov, a boy — a letter is on its way”.
—o—
[Dąbrowa — Women's Association; greeting (humour).]
Greeting.
We the undersigned at last greet the local president [?] of the kehilla board in our town for his courageous demand that we, the righteous women, should have a say in the kehilla. Upon my life, it is high time that we women had a say in the gmina, which after all is nothing more than a „religious union“ [?] („yonagye religini“ as printed).
In the name of all our members (członkinie),
the Board (Zarząd) of the Women's Association in Dąbrowa.
The Living Dead Man (20)

[Serialized novel — "A most thrilling novel of Jewish life in Zagłębie before and during the World War"; installment 20.]
A. Zaglembier [pen name].

And all at once Yosl Wertheim found himself [?] as if cast away somewhere on an island, without any prospect. Ah, why had he held on to the letter for so long? People say — even the newspapers write it too — that the war will last at most three months... And later, longer?.. It will really look as if he had come from "the other world"...
But the danger for Yosl himself began only [—] after the outbreak of the horrific world war.
A bitter life began for every foreigner. Every alien was regarded as an enemy of the German people, as a spy.
Within a counted few hours firmly established [?] livelihoods were shattered; all foreigners were expelled from the country by force.
Yosl Wertheim was in the fortunate position of having no fixed lodging, but in the streets too, in the restaurants, people with spying [?] eyes hung about, looking for suspicious faces. Yosl understood what awaited him if he were suddenly detained — a man without documents, without a name; by his accent they would know at once where he came from, and they would send him back.
No, he must save himself at any price.
And as if his heart had told him that only here could he expect help, he no longer stirred from the port. He watched the feverish work of the sailors and porters, who were ceaselessly carrying cargo up onto the ship, which was due to sail in a few hours.
With painful envy he watched everyone being let up onto the ship, showing their documents and ship tickets — he alone..
And suddenly an idea came to Yosl which he could no longer give up; in any case he had nothing to risk.
And seeing that the tumult and hubbub around the departing ship was growing ever stronger, ever louder [?], everyone rushing, no one seeing the next man — Yosl decided to do it.
There, where the cargo was being loaded, sailors' jackets lay on the ground, which the sailors had thrown off because of the terrible heat.
Yosl edged closer and closer to that spot. No one noticed how he flung off his coat and nimbly pulled a sailor's jacket on himself; under it he even heard someone shouting why he was standing about dawdling, evidently taking [?] him for a real sailor. That gave Yosl courage. He snatched up a huge bundle, which hid him completely. Because of the load he had to walk with his head bent down, so that in any case his face could not be seen, and so Yosl crossed safely — though with a hard-pounding heart — the gangplank that finally brought him up onto the ship.
Seeing what the other sailors were doing, he too went with his bundle to the same place — to the baggage holds. Just like the others, Yosl too flung his load onto the floor, from where others then put it away in its proper place.
But Yosl Wertheim did not go back. Taking advantage of the tremendous [?] hubbub that reigns in the last hours before an emigrant ship sails, Yosl went down to the lowest deck of the filthy cellars, burrowed like a mole among barrels and crates, and lay with bated breath as if dead.
And all at once his heart gave a leap of joy as he felt something toss him and he began to rock to and fro..
He understood that the ship had already begun to move from its place and was sailing out onto the broad open sea. Yosl Wertheim — hunted and tormented by his own conscience — did not know whether to rejoice or to mourn, for he did not know where the ship was taking him or where fate would carry him...

Years Later...
It happened many long years later, after the tragic events, in the "promised land" [lit. "the praised land"] — America.
Together with the stormy time that passed over the world, our heroes from Zagłębie were as if wiped away and fell silent [?].
It was a horribly bloody world war. With hunger, epidemics — a time when human life in Europe did not play the slightest role.
And first of all the weakest fell, those who could put up no resistance.
The war struck dark Sorele [Soretshe] with her children just then, when that terrible wound was still bleeding deep in her heart. How could she manage, all alone?.. She grabbed at all sorts of earnings, just to feed her "swallows"; but when life takes to punishing someone, everything is too little... And Sorele was indeed among the first victims whom the war epidemics cut off [?] from the world...
(To be continued).
Będzin — Deadline for Removing Cattle Stalls from Będzin's Main Streets Postponed

[Będzin — Trade.]
Deadline for removing the cattle stalls from Będzin's main streets postponed.
In connection with the order of the Będzin Starostwo (district office) to remove the stalls for cattle from the entire Będzin area as of 1 August of this year, a delegation of the Będzin Retailers'[?] and Small Traders' Association, together with Councillor[?] Mr. Dechnik[?] Grasz[?], presented itself to the Starosta.
The delegation handed the Starosta a memorandum drawing attention to the difficult material situation of those concerned, who are threatened[?] with the danger of losing their livelihoods.
The Starosta listened attentively to the delegation and promised to look into the matter more closely.
As a result of the intervention, Dr. Mr. Riedel, the chairman Mr. Ros and the secretary Mr. Kager were summoned to the Starosta on Tuesday. After a lengthy conference they succeeded in having several streets exempted from the order and, in general, in having the deadline for carrying out the order postponed by several months.
The Floor Shook During the Reading of the Ketubah / Miraculously There Were No Human Casualties

[Będzin — Events.]
The floor shook during the reading of the ketubah.
Miraculously there were no human casualties.
On Sunday evening a wedding of the Markow[?] family took place in the house at Kołłątaja 37. The officiant at the ceremony was the Komarno Rebbe Bambach[?]. Just as the ketubah (marriage contract) was being read, the floor shook, which caused great fright among the wedding guests.
After the chuppah the whole crowd indeed left the room in haste; only later did people see that a great miracle had happened in that there were no human casualties, for the floor had broken through and remained hanging in the air.
A Jew Stabbed by... Jews

[Będzin — Crime.]
A Jew stabbed by... Jews.
On Saturday towards evening a boy came into the apartment of the 26-year-old carter Israel Dąbek and told Dąbek that he was being called and should come outside. When Dąbek was in the gateway of the house where he lives, he was attacked by several young men, who wounded him seriously with knives.
As reported, this was supposedly an act of revenge over a quarrel between Dąbek's wife and the wife of one of the attackers over one [—][?].
The knife-stabbers have been arrested.
The Night-Watchmen's Company Staged Fictitious Break-ins

[Będzin — Crime.]
The night-watchmen's company staged fictitious break-ins.
In the previous issue of our paper we already reported on the arrest of the director of the night-watchmen's company, Mr. Wincent[?], together with 3 inspectors.
As we learn, the director together with the inspectors carried out fictitious break-ins in shops etc.[?] that were not insured with the company. Naturally, after such a break-in the director turned up with an offer that the owner should insure the shop; if the person concerned did not accept the offer, the same thing happened again within a short time.
The affair caused a great sensation.
Marshal Rydz-Śmigły an Honorary Citizen of the City of Będzin

[Będzin — Municipality.]
Marshal Rydz-Śmigły an honorary citizen of the city of Będzin.
On Tuesday evening a special festive session of the City Council took place. At the session, attended by representatives of the administrative, police and military authorities as well as of civic organisations, it was decided to approach Marshal Śmigły-Rydz with a request that he accept the title of honorary citizen of the city of Będzin.
A Planned Attack on a Girl?

[Będzin — Crime.]
A planned attack on a girl?
This week, in the evening hours, as Miss Róża Brandweinhendler was walking home from Siewierska[?] Street to Ogrodowa[?], she noticed a car driving slowly in the middle of the road and a young man following behind her. At a certain moment, when she reached the corner of Ogrodowa[?], the stranger seized her by both hands and stopped her mouth. With her last strength the attacked girl began to scream, whereupon the dogs of the house where her parents live started barking loudly. When the landlord of the house came out, the person got into the car and quickly drove off.
Everything Depends on Luck...

[Będzin — Events.]
Everything depends on luck...
A well-to-do Jewish woman from Sosnowiec lost a string of pearls this week. She reported the loss to the jewellery shops, among them also to Mr. Galisowski[?].
A few days later a poor Jewish woman came into Galisowski's[?] shop with a string of pearls and asked whether the "beads" were worth anything. It has been a few days already — she said — since my children found the "beads" in the street. I am no expert in such things.
The woman in Sosnowiec was immediately notified of the find, and she established by identifying marks[?] that these were her pearls.
The woman who handed in the find received a proper monetary reward.
Briefcase Workers' Strike Settled

[Będzin — Labour.]
Briefcase workers' strike settled.
The strike of the briefcase workers, which had lasted barely 3 weeks, was settled this week.
The workers obtained an 8-hour working day and higher wages.
The Revisionists are holding a "dancing"...

[Będzin — Revisionists; the town synagogue.] In several public places in the town notices have been posted by the local Revisionist organisation that this Sabbath a "dancing" (dance evening) will take place in one of the halls.
A new conductor engaged.
In place of the dismissed[?] conductor of the local town synagogue (Stadt-Shul), Mr. Dakhiruzn[?], the choir conductor Mr. Frenkel of Warsaw, already known in our town, has been engaged.
A juvenile thief.

[Będzin — crime.] From a pram in the courtyard at Małachowskiego 15 a 14-year-old Christian girl stole a little dress. When she was [—], she threw away the stolen item and ran off.
—o—
Summer colonies of the Ż.T.K.
[Będzin — holidays.] The local branch of the Jewish Society for Knowledge of the Country (Ż.T.K. — Żydowskie Towarzystwo Krajoznawcze) is organising summer colonies for the month of August (sierpień) in Karwia[?] (by the sea)[?], Druskieniki and Zakopane. Prices are reduced; details at the secretariat from 4 to 5 in the afternoon.
Last date for paying turnover tax.

[Taxes — turnover tax.] The 15th of August (sierpień) is the last date for merchants who keep no commercial books to pay an advance (zaliczka)[?] on the turnover tax.
One must pay one fifth of the turnover tax that was assessed for last year.
When one goes after an inheritance...

[Będzin — the town mikveh.] On Friday morning Ch. Berman came out of the town mikveh. He saw that his tallit and tefillin, which he had left "for safekeeping", were gone. People began to investigate until they found out where the "theft" was.
The injured party[?], together with the mikveh keeper, went to where the lost property had turned up and began to argue with the Jew that he should give back the "lost property"[?] — "For this," the mikveh keeper proposed to him, "you will get a whole month of free entry to the mikveh."
That man, however, would not agree to it and demanded a reward of 20 zł.
Then Ch. Berman went for a policeman, who took the tallit and tefillin and drew up a report (protocol) about it.
Petitions of the kehilla officials about their pensions.

[Sosnowiec — kehilla.] As is known, the kehilla board in Sosnowiec reduced the pensions of the kehilla officials; the council could not bear the "injustice"[?] and restored the pensions according to the budget of the previous year.
In connection with this the kehilla officials have turned to the supervisory authority with petitions that their pensions be confirmed according to the council's draft.
For robbing 9 zł. 27 gr. — a year and a half in prison.

[Zawiercie — crime, court.] Two beggars, Aron Dawid Grinberg and Hirsz Steinkeler, were walking from Zawiercie to Żarki[?]. While going along the road Grinberg struck Steinkeler on the head with a knife and then robbed him of 9 zł. 27 gr.
Grinberg was sentenced by the district court to a year and a half in prison and to the loss of civic rights for 5 years.
A new street named after Rydz-Śmigły.

[Sosnowiec — municipality.] On Friday evening[?] a festive session of the local town council took place here. At the session two proposals of the town board were adopted: 1) to confer the title of honorary citizen of the town of Sosnowiec on Marshal Rydz-Śmigły, and 2) that the new street, which links up with 3 Maja and President Mościcki streets as far as the town hall (ratusz), be named after Marshal Rydz-Śmigły.
14-year-old Jewish girl jumps from the second floor with intent to commit suicide.

[Sosnowiec — suicide attempt.] On Tuesday at midday the 14-year-old Tania[?] Bekermajster jumped from the balcony on the second floor of a house on Kołłątaja Street, with the intention of committing suicide.
In a serious condition she was taken the next morning to Kraków.
Distributors of “literature”...

[Sosnowiec — antisemitism.] On Modrzejowska[?] Street 2 young “Nara-people” [members of the ONR] stationed themselves and hawked the “literature”, such as the “Grunwald”[?] and similar anti-Jewish weeklies.
The city councillors[?] Messrs. Klinger and Majerczyk intervened about this with the city president, who declared that he would come to an understanding about it with the police authorities.
Hacked up the furniture and then doused it with petrol

[Sosnowiec — court.] The trial took place in the local district court of building technician H.[?] Soll[?] (Będzin), who was charged with having, when the tax bailiff wanted to remove the furniture for a tax debt, hacked up the furniture with an axe and then doused it with petrol.
S. was sentenced to one month’s arrest, with the sentence suspended for 3 years.
Already muttering about a competition for a rabbi.

[Sosnowiec — kehilla.] Regardless of the fact that the kehilla treasury is empty and the officials have not yet received their salaries (lit. “pensions”) for czerwiec [June], the question of the rabbinate in our town is again being pushed forward.
According to the rumours circulating here, Rabbi Englard’s side is in favour of the kehilla board, after the budget has been settled, applying to the supervisory authority for permission for a competition for rabbis.
New labour inspector.

[Sosnowiec — appointments.] The labour inspector until now, Eng. Wesołowski, has been transferred to the same post in Radom, and the Radom labour inspector, Eng. Rosten[?], has taken over the same post in Sosnowiec.
The kehilla board’s budget has been sent off.
[Sosnowiec — kehilla.] Yesterday the kehilla budget was sent to the supervisory authority, according to the draft of the kehilla board, with the amendments of the kehilla council.
Drunk droshky driver runs over a Jewish woman.

[Sosnowiec — accidents and crime.] On Monday during the day, on Targowa[?] Street, Mrs. Krajman was run over by a droshky; she was taken to the Jewish hospital. The droshky driver was drunk.
—o—
The stalls on Niemiecka Street remain standing.
[Sosnowiec — trade.] The Jewish stall owners on Niemiecka Street had received an order to remove the stalls; after an intervention by city councillor Majerczyk, permission was given for the stalls to remain standing.
—o—
An attack in broad daylight.
[Sosnowiec — crime.] As St. Płuczyński[?] was walking along Dęblińska[?] Street, three persons came up to him and demanded money from him for vodka. When P. declared that he had no money on him, the attackers threw themselves on him, robbed him of a gold ring off his finger and ran away.
1,500 zł. in the Rabbeinu Tam tefillin...

[Kielce — local incident.] A beggar's original idea of where to hide money...
For several months now an elderly wandering beggar from a small town in Kielce province has been roaming about Kielce. Day after day one sees him walking through the streets with his tallis bag under his arm, going from house to house asking for alms. He has no permanent place to sleep; sometimes he sleeps in the old beis-medrash, at a baker's on the oven, and sometimes — at... at the cemetery. He never lets the tallis bag out of his hand. While eating he hides it under his caftan, while sleeping — under his head, and he takes it along even when he goes to relieve himself...
This strange behaviour of the beggar aroused great astonishment among all his fellow beggars, and they decided also[?] to see the tefillin bag and what was in it.
This Monday night, when the beggar was already sleeping soundly on a bench in the beis-medrash, two young beggars opened the window and climbed inside. They pulled out[?] the tefillin bag and began to search it.
The Rashi tefillin were "nor-mal", whereas the Rabbeinu Tam tefillin were heavy, and as soon as they opened those tefillin a good deal of silver money began to pour out of them — 5- and 10-zł. coins — as well as 2 banknotes of 500 zł., altogether a sum of nearly fifteen hundred zł.
At the ring of the silver coins falling on the floor the beggar woke from his sleep and began to make terrible noises. [—] the surrounding neighbours came running together, who were [—] to know what had happened. The two young beggars told the whole story and demanded that the money be taken from him and handed over to the rabbinate for a good cause, as a punishment for the old man having desecrated the tefillin...
To the question of those gathered why he had hidden the money in the tefillin, the beggar answered that nowadays one cannot trust anybody, and the "best" and "safest" place to hide a few gulden is only in the tefillin...
The old man got the money back, and before dawn he had uprooted himself from Kielce in an unknown direction.
Sat 8 years in the Święty Krzyż prison and became a famous writer.

[Kielce — people and letters.] The sensational life story of Sergiusz Piasecki.
By an act of pardon of the President of the State, the said prisoner Sergiusz Piasecki was released this Monday from the Święty Krzyż prison.
Fifteen years ago Piasecki was sentenced to life imprisonment, which was later reduced for him to 15 years. He sat three years in various other prisons and 8 years in Święty Krzyż.
During his stay in the Święty Krzyż prison he wrote several works — interesting stories, which were recognised by the best literary critics. Thanks to his literary abilities the prisoner Piasecki became very popular, and his release from prison found an echo in the whole press.
Several well-known Polish writers, as well as some publishing houses, turned with a request to the President of the State to pardon Piasecki, so that he could devote himself undisturbed to his important literary work, and, as is known, the President of the State granted the request and pardoned Mr. Piasecki.
Sergiusz Piasecki made his first visit to Kielce, where he met the staff of the Polish and Jewish press, to whom he gave very interesting details of his sensational life story up to his present career.
From Kielce Piasecki left for Warsaw, where he handed his new works to a publisher for printing, and he will continue his literary work, which will give him a secure existence.
A Divorce Because of the Card-Playing Plague — At the Summer Lodgings

Among the dacha crowd a story is now being told that took place these days in a dacha resort beyond Kielce, where a lady lost at "telefon" [?] (a card game) the most precious thing a woman possesses — her honour.
As is well known, at the letnisko (summer resort) the main occupation of the locals [?] is — cards. Wherever you go and wherever you stand, people "pasze" [?] (play). The poor play small and the rich — big, but everybody plays.
Among the women players is also Madame K., the wife of a rich local merchant.
Then something happens: a young man from Kraków comes to visit. A fellow strong as a tree, and an expert besides. He knows how to conquer the hearts of the fair sex.
Seeing the "pike" (the catch) [?], Madame K. cast an eye on him; first she "invited him for tea" [?] (in Polish), and then she asked him:
"Sir! Do you play rummy?"
"Rummy I don't play; telefon [?] — gladly [?]!"
Here the tragedy begins:
At daybreak, when everyone is still asleep, it is lively in Madame K.'s villa. In front of the young gentleman [?] from Kraków lies a pile of "czupki" [?] (chips?), and she keeps on losing. When she noticed that her purse was running short, she began to bargain with the man from Kraków:
"Panie Władysławie, what am I to do now?" (in Polish)
"Panie Władysławie, have pity, lend [?] it back to me."
"Not with me! From the cemetery nobody is brought back. There is only one way out: you will come home with me."
"What do you mean? At daybreak?! And my husband? I assure you I'll come to you in the afternoon."
But the Kraków man remained cold as ice, and having no choice she agreed.
When the husband woke up around daybreak and did not see his wife, he looked for her and indeed found her at the Kraków man's.
In the morning the summer guests were woken by a terrible scandal. Old K., in a dressing gown, with a thick stick in his hand, was chasing a tall, elegant young man in blue trousers.
As people are saying, the affair will also lead to a divorce.

New Regulation on Bicycles

The Ministries of Communications and of the Interior have issued a new regulation on bicycle traffic on public roads.
It is forbidden: for young people up to 12 years of age to use bicycles on the highways; to ride "in the middle of the highway" instead of on the right; for two or more bicycles to ride abreast in one line instead of one behind the other; to carry another person if the bicycle is a single-seater; to ride without holding the handlebar with the hands or without the feet on the pedals; to hold on to other vehicles. Nor may one use the highway if there is a separate path for bicycles. An exception is made for little carts driven by the feet, bicycles with motors and motorcycles.
Every bicycle must be equipped with at least one brake, a white lamp, or [?] a red glass (reflector) three centimetres in size, and [printed: "of"] a bell.
Bicycles must be registered at the municipal office (magistrat) or the village commune (gmina) and receive a registration plate valid for 2 years. In the first year 1 zł. is charged for such a plate, in the second year 3 zł.
Exempt from the fee are: the gendarmerie, the police, the border guard and lower state and municipal officials, if it is certified that the bicycle is used for official purposes.
The regulation came into force on 31 July.
Draft Law on Certified Accountants

The Ministry of Finance is drafting a bill on certified (diplomaed) accountants. A certified accountant will be able to sign the balance sheets of commercial firms, and his balance sheets will be recognised by the tax authorities as authoritative.
The title of certified accountant may be obtained by a Polish citizen who has never been convicted and possesses a commercial education and a secondary-school matriculation certificate (matura). The aspiring candidate will receive the title of certified accountant after 5 years of practice as an accountant. Candidates with higher education will receive such a title after three years of accounting practice.
Every accountant who wishes to obtain the title of certified accountant will have to pass an examination at the Chamber of Commerce before a commission in which delegates of all the ministries will also take part.
For accountants already practising [?], the bill provides a period of 5 years to adapt and obtain the title of certified accountant by means of an examination. Where the candidate has no matura, he must show accounting practice of 10 [?] years, and 5 years as an independent accountant. Holders of the matura need show only 5 years of independent practice. The law will come into force in January 1938.

From the Będzin Small Traders' Association

[Będzin — trade.] We learn from authoritative circles that inspections will be carried out in the shops, to check whether they comply with the sanitary and hygienic regulations, and also what the condition of the shop looks like in the aesthetic sense.
Since a large part of our Jewish shops are not at all aesthetically fitted out, and because of this — apart from paying, all year round, at every slightest opportunity, fines upon fines — they may be closed altogether at this inspection, the board of the Small Traders' Association has resolved that it is necessary to create a capital fund from which long-term loans (for 3—4 years) can be granted, which the trader shall use exclusively for renovations and investments in his shop, in order to improve its outward aesthetic appearance.
We therefore call on all our members to report to our secretariat by the 20th of this month what sum they need to improve their shop, submitting at the same time in writing an exact plan of the works they wish to carry out.
We point out that those who do not register within the stated deadline will later not be able to benefit from our investment fund, as we will not have surplus money at our disposal.
— We draw the attention of the tobacco dealers to the fact that the deadline for registering ends definitively on the 20th of this month.
During this time every trader dealing in tobacco products must register at our secretariat and write a properly justified application to the Directorate of the Tobacco Monopoly. For the consequences of not keeping to the above deadline we disclaim all responsibility.
Exact information on all the above-mentioned matters is given by our secretariat, Małachowskiego 2, during normal office hours.
