“Cucumber Season” in the Jewish Artisans’ Organization

[Article — Zagłębie, artisans and their organizations.]
In the little world of the Jewish artisans it is now quiet, calm. One hears almost nothing from any organization whatsoever; it has become completely quiet — “cucumber season” [i.e. the dead summer season, sezon ogórkowy].
The silence and calm at the present moment are, however, a highly abnormal phenomenon, one that has never occurred until now: that at a time when clouds are gathering on the horizon of the Jewish artisan, people should keep silent.
We still remember the times when, over any matter at all, even a trifle, that concerned the artisan, an uproar arose; when the Chamber [of Crafts, Izba Rzemieślnicza] set about creating the inspection commission [komisja lustracyjna], an uproar arose, a hullabaloo. All the artisans’ organizations held meetings, assemblies and joint conferences; the same happened with other questions too, even less important ones.
And now, when it is a matter of questions that may threaten the existence of thousands of artisans and perhaps of the whole community too, now, when there is talk of making changes in the industrial law, such as abolishing the “kazns” [?] [probably the licences — koncesje], compulsory guilds [cechy przymusowe] and similar “good things” for the Jewish artisan — the artisans’ representatives have taken a mouthful of water; all is quiet.
Besides this, a number of trades have now been added to the artisans’ [sphere] which have become obliged [?] to hold the artisan’s card [karta rzemieślnicza]; is anything being done to help them obtain the card?
Does anyone ask whether all these artisans — who, incidentally, consist solely of poor people — are able [?] to buy out the card, whether a fund will some day [?] be created for this purpose? No, all is quiet; nothing at all is done even in the direction of helping and removing the difficulties in obtaining the card.
We have several times appealed in the columns of the “Zaglembier Tsaytung” concerning the question of the linen seamstresses, a trade made up of poor home-workers [chałupnicy], of people who cannot even afford to cover the expenses for the card — that something be done in their matter; and yet this had no effect whatsoever.
And what the outcome will be — everyone understands that: later one will throw the blame on the other, and the third, the individual, will be the one who suffers.
But the question arises: what is the cause of the “silence”? To that one can give only one answer: the despair, the apathy that has torn its way into the ranks of the Jewish artisan. The representatives have given up [?] in their struggle, knowing that in many cases their effort is in vain.
That, however, can no longer excuse the situation; one must on no account stop, even without looking to what the outcome will be — the situation must be changed. A remedy must be found to remove the despair. The energy must be created that will carry on the struggle of former times. That can come only through a union of all the artisans.
Quietly, calmly and modestly the Warsaw Jewish artisans have set about negotiations for a union, and precisely during the “cucumber season.” They have at last found the cause of the backwardness prevailing among the Jewish artisans — it is fragmentation. There they realized [?] and arrived at the plain conviction that a broken body cannot fulfil the functions that a whole and healthy one can, and therefore they are trying to make the body whole, and now they are setting about making it healthy.
The same sickness exists in the Zagłębie artisans’ movement. As long as all the Jewish artisans will not work together under one body and one organization, the above-mentioned state of affairs will prevail, the “cucumber season” will always prevail; and even if from time to time some organization does try to do something, it will be able to achieve nothing, it will not be treated seriously, because it will always come in the name of only half a body. And if the organization does already want to do something, it will do it without courage. —
The only way for the Zagłębie artisans to still be able to rescue the little that remains — to be able to come forward united. Then the representation will be able to come forward in the name of the whole mass of artisans, and no one will ask any more “in whose name do you come,” as is the practice now. Then it will be possible to remove the excuse “you want it this way, and the other side wants the opposite.”
The only way left to the Jewish artisans of Zagłębie to remove the despair and apathy that have eaten so deeply into their ranks is: to make the body whole and to make the organization healthy. Then the “cucumber seasons” will cease to prevail.
Y. Redlus.
The Face of Our Intelligentsia

[Essay — the Jewish intelligentsia and assimilation.] To accuse a large part of our present-day Jewish intelligentsia is a very thankless task. To take a particular part of the people, hurl accusations at it, make it swallow the bitter pills of complaints which on the surface look as if made out of spite — that is not an ordinary thing. We know that every people takes pride in its intellectuals and its intelligentsia; in every matter [?] they are the initiators and the givers of opinion — and precisely among us people are not satisfied with them; more than that, they accuse them... We must make an analysis of our own and other peoples' ways. We know that a people cannot consist only of scholars and experts; every people divides into 2 parts: the larger part — the masses; the smaller part — the intellectuals, the givers of opinion and guides, and everywhere they are the pride, the glory of the people. Thus we see among the Russians the Decembrists, who came almost exclusively from the upper spheres; among the French, the pleiad of Danton, Marat and company; among the Americans, the Lincolns — and whatever their path of ideas may have been, good or bad, it was always for the people. And precisely for that reason the masses gained trust, and they, the intelligentsia, saw to it that the idea of national unity and national pathos penetrated into the complicated corners of the mass soul. That is how it is among the nations of the world; with us it is the reverse. Today we are living through the most terrible moments of our 4-thousand-year history. In such a situation as we live in today, it would seem — so it appears! — that the only way out is to despair; but the core of the masses is sound, and we do not raise a hand against our own life. We only ask: in such hard times we should have been able to rely on the help of our "intelligentsia"; they should, after all, have given us moral support to endure the hard hours — but instead we see a different, surprising [?] picture: although assimilation has received a death blow, since more than 100 years of intermingling in Germany did not save the Jewish community there and, on the contrary, fascist race hatred triumphed — they, our "protectors" [?], are walking away from us. At the present time, when we must join the ranks of those who fight for life and rights, who boldly [?] knock at the world's doors [?] that we want to live under a roof of our own, and not give every king our best sacrifices — they, the "intelligentsia", put stones under our feet, although they themselves stumble over them [?]. At a time when we must rise to the pathos of the national-social struggle for life — they block our way and blunt our will; although they themselves are living through a shattering tragedy, although they are losing the ground under their feet — they embitter our life with their cowardice, they try to save themselves by clutching at a straw, and they disturb our life.
Today, when the leitmotif of our tragic life must face the sorrows and joys of the masses — they tear themselves away from us and destroy our hopes.
We do not want the help of the Tuwims, the We-mars [?], the Bergsons [?]; but we will stand up against the destroyers in their criminal, degenerate [?] work. The Polish people had a Rejtan, the American people — a Lincoln, a Washington; we do not have that. Our intelligentsia dances a wild dance before the downfall; they feel they are already drowning, and still they do not look over to our side. But we do not need them; we will "keep our shtetl going" without them too. We are indeed insulted, humiliated — but proud. We fight — but they? They are marionettes dancing on a string. We suffer for our land, and they for their sugary [?] cowardice; they see the sad reality and pretend not to know. They look for new homes and do not see how their own home is being destroyed. They want to find new ways for their children and do not see that they themselves have long been dead... They dig graves for themselves and sew shroud-shirts for their children; they walk away from us in order to display their heroism [?] and to duel [?] with the non-Jewish environment. Therefore one must say to them, the Jewish intelligentsia: although the masses have no pretensions to intellect, our masses nevertheless kept the Hitler boycott, while the Elunergs [?] and Guidiners [?] treacherously broke it and desecrated the holiest principles of the people. Therefore now, in the time of "All Israel are responsible for one another", one must shake off the traitors and cry out with pride: we are ashamed of you! You do not belong to us; but when you one day make a reckoning of your souls, it will already be too late...
J. Szwarc.
A Balloon of Soda Water

[Literature — reportage; Zagłębie.] By Y. Janasowicz.
(Reportage).
The story of an ordinary copper balloon of soda water.
It seems a dead thing — as the saying goes — without body, without life; and yet this balloon has a history behind it, a past, in which one can see the footsteps of fate.
And this story of the balloon may be described as a story of descents, of a fall down the ladder of events.
Every descent holds a tragic kernel and is moving in itself; even the descent undergone by such a dead object as a soda-water balloon has a moving moment, because in it — if one only wishes — one can find the traces of the bony fist of fate that pushed it down; and in that respect it has much in common with a person whom fate has played out and led ever deeper and deeper down the rungs of the ladder of life.
And this, in brief, is the biography of the hero, who never lived, who was always a dead object — nothing more than a copper balloon filled with the cool drink that is so gladly drunk on hot summer days — soda water.
The beginning — it began even before the World War — was in a foreign metal factory. There, after the balloon was finished, it was polished, scoured and rubbed so that its copper belly would shine. From there it was packed together with a whole row of other balloons and sent here, to Zagłębie.
Here it fell into a "Litvak" soda-water factory, one of the first and best in town. Here it was filled with the cool, fizzing drink — and off, onward.
It rode on a rattling little cart through the streets of the town and arrived at a fine building[?] which housed a night club. Here, in the night club in Sosnowiec, it found a refuge for the night. It was set up behind the buffet in a wooden box bedded with ice.
And so it went on for a long time: by day it rode back to the factory, where the water with gas was poured into its copper belly, and at night it rode back to the night club, where the half-sleepy buffet girl[?] drew soda water into thin cut glasses, mixed with [—] syrup, for the guests.
Yes, what did it not see there in that night club, where the light was coloured and dimmed and came not from the ceiling but from the walls and the floor; music played there and the fiddle wept wondrously sweet; slender dancers danced, gliding like legendary figures, and beside them elegant gentlemen and officers always fluttered about, tenderly kissing the ladies' white little hands.
It looked like life in paradise.
But once, it remembers, there was a commotion in the night club, an uproar; a revolver shot was heard, and then[?] the waiters carried one of the elegant guests out of the hall. People said then that he had taken his own life because he had gambled away his fortune on the Hungarian dancer whose black eyes flashed so wondrously. Taken his own life, because she had betrayed him.
Then came the World War. The balloon wandered off to a large confectionery on the main street. It too[?] stood there behind the buffet, and an elegant young lady with delicate fingers drew soda water from it.
Someone used to come to the young lady, a tall young man; the pretty, delicate young lady would blush whenever he drew near her, her hands would tremble nervously, and more than once, while drawing water from the balloon, she forgot to take her delicate hands off the tap, so that the water overflowed the glass.
The last time it saw the young lady there was likewise some strange commotion in the confectionery. The young lady had drunk some strange liquid from a little bottle and collapsed. Then they drew soda water from it and poured it into the young lady's clenched mouth.
Later it was its lot to stand in kiosks on various streets. It saw many vagabonds with brown faces, and every time a vagabond came up for a glass of water it heard the squeaky voices of the girls who belonged to the vagabonds.
And so everything went, ever further down, down.
Recently it came into the hands of a Jew. The little Jew drags it, hung on a rope in front of him, and crawls about with it through the dusty streets, shouting:
— Something cold and something good!
Here, with the Jew, the balloon first feels how deep it has fallen. First, the running about whole days, never standing still in one place, some strange running about on this Jew's part; [?] he runs as if he were being chased, and perhaps he really is being chased. Besides, it cannot bear the Jew's sighs and groans. The balloon feels it is to blame for being so heavy, and the Jew has no strength to drag it. But worse still is the night, when it comes home with the Jew into the stuffy flat where sick children lie. The Jew then counts the takings, the small groszy and two-groszy coins. He counts and sighs, counts and groans:
— Those who wish us ill — he says hoarsely — let them trade in soda water; let the soda-water balloon be their only provider...
Only then does the balloon feel how deep it has sunk, how great the extent of its descent is...
In German Upper Silesia — The Anti-Jewish Agitation Intensifies

[German Upper Silesia — persecution of Jews.] (A letter from Upper Silesia)
Across the whole length and breadth of German Upper Silesia, Germany's greatest Jew-baiter, Julius Streicher, has now spread himself out [?]. On every street corner his famous newspaper "Der Stürmer" is pasted up, specially devoted to the newly created situation in Upper Silesia. Wherever one goes and wherever one stands, one sees the "Stürmer", stuffed with the bloodiest abuse and blood libels against the Jews, and especially against the Jews of Upper Silesia. But Streicher has not contented himself with that. He has had giant placards hung over the houses of the Upper Silesian towns, in which he exults with joy that at last "the land has been freed from Jewish hands". Here is what is said [?] in the giant placards of the "Stürmer":
"German fellow-countrymen (Volksgenossen), the days of shame are over. Upper Silesia has been freed from the Jewish disgrace. For 15 years the Jews ruled here in the land and did not let our newspaper, the 'Stürmer', come out. That time is past; now at last the truth can be told here. Upper Silesians, buy the 'Stürmer' and learn the truth!"
And it is not only with placards that the agitation against the Jews is now being waged here. Already on the very first day of the "liberation", 15 July, a mass meeting took place in Hindenburg (today Zabrze) on a public square, where the highest party leader of the district delivered a bitter antisemitic speech in the presence of the highest government representatives. In this speech the Nazi leader Jagas [?] said:
"Today, 15 July, is the day on which Upper Silesia has been completely freed from Jewish influence. In recent years you, Upper Silesians, still had to endure what is no longer tolerated anywhere in Germany. It is now already clear that the Jew is the enemy of the German people and that the Nazi movement must wage a bitter struggle against the Jews and against everything that is Jewish. Besides that, it is necessary that all officials know that they may no longer have any connection whatsoever with Jews."
And this took place, one must remember, on the first day, 15 July. It is simply astonishing to see how in the course of a few days this land, Upper Silesia, has pulled the Nazi cloak over itself. It is hard to imagine that only a month ago one did not yet see here a single Nazi placard or a single anti-Jewish slogan. That is German "thoroughness".
But not only outwardly has Upper Silesia become a Nazi province; with the same German thoroughness and punctuality all the laws and decrees from which the Jews in all of Germany now suffer have already poured down on Jewish heads. The list of the Nuremberg anti-Jewish laws that came into force for Upper Silesia on 15 July is a very long one, and it would be very hard to bring it here in full; but we shall point here to some of the bitter decrees that have an immediate effect on Jewish life in Upper Silesia.
First of all — the anti-Jewish boycott. Already earlier, in the time of the minorities protection, the Nazis boycotted the Jewish shops, but this was done quietly and nobody was forced into it. Now, however, the boycott is conducted quite openly, intensively, with compulsion and threats. There is no doubt that the few Jewish businesses that still remain will have to liquidate.
The Jewish professionals will also suffer very severely — teachers, notaries, lawyers, doctors and all who worked directly or indirectly for a public institution. All Jews, and also partial Jews, who hold government posts will be removed on 31 August of this year. Lawyers who began to practise after 1 August 1914 will not be admitted to plead in the courts. All Jewish notaries are dismissed, also Jewish doctors, dentists and druggists who began to practise. After 30 September of this year Jewish doctors, regardless of how long they have been practising, lose their posts in the hospitals, the sick funds and other public institutions.
The dangerous decree of "race defilement" (Rassenschande), because of which the Jews of Germany now have so much trouble, has also fallen upon the heads of the Jews of Upper Silesia. It is hard to imagine the inquisition the Nazis conduct against the Jews under the pretext of "race defilement".
This is, as said, only a small part of the persecutions the Jews in Silesia began to suffer on 15 July, and one can very easily understand the feelings of the local Jew who said to me:
"The worst of all is that all these troubles come upon us at once. The Jews in the rest of Germany at least took the bitter medicine spoonful by spoonful, but we must swallow it all at once. All the anti-Jewish decrees that were devised against the Jews of Germany over the course of 4 years we are now getting all at once."
It will not be long before the Jews in Upper Silesia begin to feel the Nazi laws on their shoulders.
When I travelled by train from Breslau (today Wrocław) to Upper Silesia, several hundred Nazi party leaders, who filled several carriages, travelled on the same train. In every town of Upper Silesia some of the Nazi officials got off, who will already see to it that Upper Silesia too becomes a hell for Jews.
Beuthen (Bytom), Upper Silesia.
A. S.
Which Newspapers Do People Read Today?

[Press — international survey; article.]
We know this [?]. We tell ourselves that culture was born in Europe and from there spread to the four corners of the world. But when we look closely at the many treasures that modern culture possesses and try to find out where these treasures come from, we find that many, many years earlier wild Asians or African tribes already knew of them, and we copied them, or simply took from them and passed them off as our own...
If we look at a statistic of the Leipzig Fair on newspapers, we see that the first newspaper in the world was not born here in Europe, not in some land of culture, but precisely in the then half-wild China.
Already eight hundred years ago, at the beginning of the twelfth century, a daily paper was published in Peking called "Ki Pao", which in our language means "Daily News". This newspaper, of which [—; printed "sumen"] complete annual volumes have been preserved to this day, had seven columns, each column having sixteen lines. The paper measured fifteen [?] centimetres and had twelve to sixteen pages a day.
In this paper, which was distributed all over China, the government announced all its laws and in general everything it wanted the people to know. The paper also brought quite important news from Russia and from Japan. As to how far this news reached China, and how far it mattered [?] that the Chinese readers should learn of it.
[—] already at the chapter of newspapers, it is worth taking a look at how little interest there is in the world today in serious papers. Only sensational papers do the business today. Good serious papers, with which before the War worlds were shaken [?], today have very few readers.
The London "Daily Mail", which before the War had about three million readers, today has a circulation of barely a hundred thousand.
The serious world paper "The Times" has a circulation of barely half a million copies. Meanwhile the sensational paper "Daily Express" comes out in two editions a day and has a circulation of nearly four million copies, and on Sunday about six million copies. The "Daily Chronicle" together with the "News Chronicle", with their sensations, print more than one and a half million copies a day, while the "Morning Post" had to [?] be sold...
It is the same in other countries. The Paris "Figaro", which once almost turned the world upside down and before which all governments trembled, today has a circulation of 60 thousand copies, while the sensational paper "Paris-Soir" together with "Paris-Midi" print over 2 million copies a day and are spread everywhere.
Mussolini's "Giornale d'Italia" has barely 100 thousand copies a day, while quite small Italian sensational sheets have a circulation of half a million copies a day.
In Japan too, it is not the serious papers, which pay a fortune for staff and correspondents all over the world, that have the large print runs, but the sensational papers "Asahi Shimbun" and "Nichi-Nichi", which are printed in millions of copies every day.
In New York the "Daily News" prints more than one and a half million copies every day, and the serious "New York Times" prints only 400 thousand copies. The largest paper in South America, the Buenos Aires "Prensa", prints only 240 thousand copies a day.
The Moscow [?] "Pravda" [?] prints 2 million copies, and "Izvestia" 1.7 million copies a day.
Z. Haber, Vienna.
“Nothing Has Changed”

[Bystra — feuilleton; summer-resort life.] (Little pictures from the “Line” [the resort line])
By S. Libaszon [?].
After all, one must dance...
The Saturday night after this year’s Shabbat Nachamu has remained for the Jewish youth spending their holidays in Bystra — a lament for generations, because that very night, on that night, in the heat [?] of the “service”, a pure Aryan reminded the Jewish youth that they are not the chief proprietors of the dance hall and that there are also visitors of another race who also wish to fulfil the commandment of dancing...
And indeed the youth was obedient, and out of the hall [it went]. Well, the first days, while the youth was under the impression of the “incident”, they stood “on guard” [?] and said:
— No dancing!
But once they had sobered up a little and the question arose [?] in all its breadth: what does one do? Is it even conceivable — to be at a summer resort [“letnisko”] and not dance every evening? Well, the days one spends at cards, but the nights?
Over this question a “hot” discussion began. The moderates [?] said that “the adversary is the ... [?] not pigs”. So what if some gentile [lit. “uncircumcised one”] shouted “now Jews are not dancing”? So what — it is no worse than when signs are hung in front of certain places saying “entry forbidden to Jews”, and nevertheless — don’t Jews go in there? That is plainly a “Jewish brain”: on one side, to get thrown out, and on the other — principles [?]...
Against this “argument” spoke out dancers of the “right-wing camp”: if our last “tango” has been taken from us, we can no longer dance in this place.
— Well, what does one do then? “A congregation that has no etrog does not say the blessing”, but to be at a dacha and not dance?! And so indeed a search began for a remedy. The first category went off to the “Cyganeria”, the second — to Szczyrk, and the third makes do with piano music, simply [—], in the peasant cottage (“Zile Glav” [?]), and set up [?] a piano there (in a pinch one makes do with a gramophone too) and
— they dance...
And the greatest “recognition” must — in our opinion — be expressed to the dancers of the first category, since they are in fact atoning [?] for all Israel and, poor things, stayed awake [?] until the grey dawn in... the Gypsy Forest [Cygański Las] (in the new version: in the “Cyganeria”).
This week we visited one of the new ... [?], of the “Cyganeria” visitors. The people (a very [?] well-known Jewish family from Sosnowiec) aroused feelings of pity in us as we listened to their sighs [?] and groans.
— What is the matter with you? we asked them; the clock already shows nearly midday and you are still in bed?...
— Oy, my feet! cries out the “pani letniskowa” [Mrs. Summer-Guest].
— Your feet, and mine are any better? — retorts the “pan letnik” [Mr. Summer-Guest].
— Why are you muddling my head with your feet? — I say to them — tell me rather: “where were your heads?”...
— You are quite right, we really have no sense, letting ourselves be talked by our friends [“przyjaciele”] into going dancing at the “Cyganeria”. Well, dancing is one thing, but walking back at three o’clock at dawn in a downpour from the Gypsy Forest to Bystra — that is worse than the parting of the Red Sea... But we had no other way out, because “here one doesn’t go”, to Szczyrk we didn’t want to travel, because there we were afraid of the “evil eye”, so we made a pilgrimage to the Gypsy Forest, because
— after all, one must dance...
Where are our husbands?..
The greatest hit being “played” in the present dacha season in Bystra is:
— “Where are our husbands?”
The main [?] heroines are two “letniczki” [female summer guests] from Zagłębie (for certain reasons we do not give the names or the town where the leading [?] actresses live), and the play was staged last Friday after candle-lighting.
On Friday, the whole day, they — the little wives of whom we are “speaking” here — were busy with the preparations [?] in honour of the Sabbath and especially in honour of the distinguished guests, their dear husbands, who were coming out to them.
Having finished [?] the work, both of them, dressed up “in vinegar and honey” [?], went out onto the highway [“szosa”] in the direction from which the droshkies come with the passengers arriving on the evening train.
On the first droshky came acquaintances, who greeted the dressed-up little wives warmly and announced to them the happy news:
— They have come!..
But what happened? Already the last droshky, and “they”, the “hubbies” [mężulkowie], are nowhere to be seen. With uneasy minds the wives went back home — perhaps they had walked on foot through a side alley?
But coming home and learning that they were not there, the unease only grew more, and they ran to acquaintances with the question:
— Where are our husbands?
Only when “Kiddush” was heard from many “Jewish” villas did they come home.
As it turned out, the two “hubbies” had found a “third hand”, went into a strange villa and before Kabbalat Shabbat “snatched” a “wiszek” [?; apparently a card game]. Playing, they completely forgot their wives and children, to whom they had come, and caused their little wives to ask themselves in fright:
— Where are our husbands?
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Shoftim)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Shoftim
—o—
a) "And thou shalt not take a bribe" (Deut. 16:19)
1.
In Lemberg [Lwów] there was a judge (dayan) of whom it was said that he took bribes. Outwardly, however, he was very pious, shouted while praying, and above all shouted "Shema Yisrael" loudly.
Rabbi Yaakov Orenstein said of him:
"Every judge who judges a true judgment truthfully becomes a partner of the Holy One, blessed be He, in the work of Creation." But one who takes bribes surely does not become a partner in God's work of Creation, and therefore he shouts aloud "Hear O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is O-N-E (echad)" — for him God is indeed an "other" (acher); he has no connection with Him whatsoever...
2.
"Every judge who takes a bribe does not depart from the world [until] he rules righteousness in his ruling." Yalkut.
What does the Yalkut mean to say by this? —
The meaning of this seemingly strange Yalkut is: every judge who takes a bribe — at the beginning he knows full well that he is ruling falsely; he still has some pangs of conscience; but in the end he becomes so used to it, "until he rules righteousness in his ruling," that he already thinks he is ruling truly, that this is in fact righteous judgment... Karnei Re'em.
• • •
"Once a man has committed a sin and repeated it — it becomes to him as if permitted." —
When a person commits a sin "and repeats it," and on top of that he is a Torah scholar and "learns" his way into the sin — it becomes to him as if permitted: he already finds a permission, an explicit law, that he may commit the sin, that it is actually permitted... the Seer of Lublin.
• • •
"If you saw a Torah scholar commit a sin at night, do not suspect him by day — surely he has repented (asah teshuvah)."
If you see a Torah scholar commit a sin — "surely he made a t-e-s-h-u-v-a-h": he has probably already written a teshuvah [a rabbinic responsum] stating that the sin may be committed...
—o—
b) "Thou shalt not plant thee an Asherah" (ibid., 21)
"Whoever appoints an unworthy judge is as if he plants an Asherah."
There is idolatry in the form of a graven image: that is idolatry which everyone recognizes. It is different with an Asherah. An Asherah is a blossoming tree, and no one can know that inside this blossoming tree an impurity is lurking. It is the same with an unworthy judge...
—o—
c) "And thou shalt come unto the priests the Levites, and unto the judge" (17:9)
Kraków was a city full of rabbis. One of the rabbis also wanted to act as a town rabbi, so the Rabbi of Kraków, Rabbi Akiva Kornitzer, sent for him to come to him.
Coming to Rabbi Akiva Kornitzer, he says to him:
"In Kraków there are so many rabbis, and none of them calls the other a trespasser (masig gvul), and there is barely a single rav. May no second one act as rabbi already?"
Rabbi Akiva answers him:
"The verse says: 'the priests, the Levites, and unto the judge.' Priests and Levites are referred to in the plural, whereas the judge is referred to in the singular, because there can be many priests and Levites in one town, but a judge — a rav — there is only one..."
—o—
d) "And he shall read therein all the days of his life" (ibid., 19)
All his life long he should read in the Torah.
Ktav Sofer.
—o—
e) "That his heart be not lifted up above his brethren" (ibid., 20)
"A haughty stride takes away one five-hundredth of a man's eyesight."
A haughty stride — a single step in arrogance already takes away the light from a person's eyes, so that he does not see where he stands in the world. Rabbi Aharon of Kaidanov.
• •
Rabbi Dovidl [?] of Talne used to say:
"One must not play too much with humility. Once, after the passing of my father of blessed memory, a great magnate came to me and brought a large pidyon [a gift for the rebbe]. I ask him: why do I deserve such a pidyon? He answers: I gave your father such a pidyon too. I say to him: why do you compare me to my father, who was a supremely holy man — and how do I measure up to him? So the magnate thinks it over and takes back the pidyon... From then on I saw that one must not play too much with humility..."
Paris Notes.

[Paris — correspondent's notes; French Jewry, aid for Poland's children, ORT, the High Holidays.] (From our Paris correspondent).
1) The campaign for the Jewish child.
It is very regrettable [?] that such [?] an important campaign as supporting the growing-up [?] Jewish generation in Poland, which found an extraordinary echo in Jewish Paris and was received with enthusiasm by the general Jewish public — regardless of the trend and party each one belongs to — [has suffered] through petty behind-the-scenes politics, in that each of the 2 federations which, thank God, we have here (the Federation of Jewish Societies and the Federation of Polish Jews) wanted to take it as its monopoly, and each wants to be able to write afterwards that only thanks to it were the Jewish children helped. Precisely because of this, such a fine and important campaign, which could have produced the best results — we unfortunately have to state the negative [?]: after passing through various committees, where each committee neglected rather than worked, a liquidation committee was finally set up recently, whose task consists of: 1) introducing a little order and collecting the money itself, and 2) then sending that same money to Poland; and according to what the present treasurer, the respected public worker and very punctilious [?] Mr. Berkow [?], told me, 52 thousand francs have come in so far.
2) The ORT conference.
On the 24th of this month [?] a world conference of the ORT organisations takes place in Paris.
Prominent parliamentarians and representatives of many Jewish and French local organisations will take part in the conference. The chairman will be the French Minister of Education, Jean Zay. With speeches that will be of special value and in which such important and topical questions will be discussed as concentrating Jewish reconstruction work in the near future, there will appear among others the well-known French social politician Prof. William Oualid, the president of the executive Dr. Bramson, Dr. Syngalowski, Dr. Lvovitch, Jaszunski and others.
Of special interest will be the lecture of Y. Tsuzelnitski [?], who will report on Jewish reconstruction work in Russia.
Besides many delegates from the French provinces and colonies, many foreign guests from Europe and America are expected at the conference, and for the 1st time also delegates from South Africa and Argentina.
This year's conference will be of quite special value, since [?], owing to the seriousness of the general Jewish situation in the world, the opinions will be heard of those who lead the great and important work of ORT, and also of various statesmen who are interested in solving the Jewish economic problem.
3) The pious season.
The first blast of the shofar is in Paris the signal that the great season of Jewishness is beginning: from the four corners of the earth arrive various rebbes, rabbis, cantors and plain religious functionaries.
In the Jewish press the familiar advertisements begin to appear in double-eight-sized letters with “to hearken unto the song and the prayer”, and beside them the photograph of the cantor, which has great importance in choosing [?] a “seat” in a synagogue, especially among the fair sex...
Many synagogues for the holidays are set up in theatres, cinemas, clubs and simply empty flats, and even in restaurants and dance halls. It has even happened that the owner of a well-known dance hall asked the cantor at Ne'ilah to speed up the “Open the gate for us”, so that he could open the hall to the couples thirsting for another little dance...
In general it is to be expected that this year's season will be an exceptionally good one, and as the gabbai of a synagogue in the Jewish quarter assured me, the demand for places is now enormous and he even intends to raise the prices of the “seats” according to the dollar-franc [?] rate, so that the “High-Holiday Jews” — he says — should at least know of a truly “dear” holiday.
The synagogue beadles too, who all year long go about with sulky faces and look at you with an expression as though you were to blame that he became a beadle — and not a vice-minister — will now receive [?] you with a smile on their lips and a beaming face, and generally feel like a fish in water.
From Rosh Chodesh Elul until after Simchat Torah, when he says “The angel who redeemed” with all the little boys, he is on the level of a Parisian “concierge” (stróż [watchman] in the vernacular), and then he looks at everyone from above.
But every worshipper seeks by all means to be on the best terms with the beadle, because thanks to him you can enjoy various privileges, such as snatching a little “pesichah” [opening of the Ark], getting through his mediation a “fine” aliyah, and not being called to order while you chat with your neighbour or read a French newspaper during prayers. Knowing that his reign is a limited one, he seeks to exploit it to the utmost [?]; this gives him heart and courage for the whole year.
Salomon Lewkowicz [?].
—o—
Before an operation the doctor must warn
[Law — Supreme Court ruling; health insurance.] The Supreme Court has recently confirmed once again that the “Ubezpieczalnia” [social insurance fund] is not responsible for the scientific errors which the doctors commit in treating the members of the “Ubezpieczalnia”.
As regards the responsibility of the doctors, the court establishes that it is not enough to ask the patient whether he agrees to the operation, but one must warn him of the complications that may arise after the operation. If the patient was not duly warned and complications occur after the operation, the patient has the right to compensation from the doctor.
Old Acquaintances

[Feuilleton — a humorous letter from the mountains, summer holiday.] (A little letter from the mountains)

Dear friend!
I am in the mountains this year, in the same pension where I stayed last year, and I have met here this year my good friends, old acquaintances.
To tell you that I was not [?] very glad of them — I cannot; I would be telling a lie, and telling a lie I hate like death.
You can surely imagine that I met here the same women or girls — well, I want to tell you that you are mistaken; I would not be ashamed to tell you the truth.
I am no great devotee of the vampish [?] ladies who amuse themselves here in the mountains.
So hear about my old acquaintances — hear, then:
As soon as I sat down at the table I at once recognised last year's tablecloth: the same yellow stains, the same red wine stains, the same little fish bones still sticking [?] — they have not washed it yet; I also saw the same dirt, the same little hole burnt by a cigar.
And as soon as I took the salt cellar in my hand I recognised it at once: the same rust, the same clogged little holes; [even if?] you slaughter [?] it on the spot, it will not give out any sign of salt; it is damp and stuck to the lid like a lover to his beloved, and when one needs to salt something it comes really with death — one has to bang the salt cellar on the table for half an hour until one is convinced that it is no use.
I also recognised the same eggs as last year, the same stench, the same blood spots. Even the same unwashed plates and glasses and spoons and knives and forks.
On my plate I recognised, too, the waiter's fingerprints. How do I know they are his? Because the waiter has only four fingers on his left hand, and on the plate there were also four fingerprints — I recognised them at once.
I also recognised the bitten spoon, which [—] already completely bent; it complained to me bitterly — ever since it came into the world it has suffered from human mouths. What do people want of it? Why do they bite it so!
I also recognised the butter and the herring — old familiar dishes.
And as soon as I [—] opened the sugar bowl I recognised at once the four dead flies, left over from last year — dead flies who had died a sweet death.
I also recognised several hairs in the soup: black curly hairs from the waiter and a couple of red hairs from the cook.
The same hair, the same soup and the same cook.
I feel so good, so at home; it seems to me that I have been there the whole year, that I never went home to Zagłębie at all.
And when I went into my room to sleep, there too I met my old acquaintances.
The same old bed, the same mattress and the same creaking, even the sheet and the little pillow.
And when I closed my eyes there came the barking of two dogs — the same old dogs from last summer, the same voices.
And when I fell asleep I woke up at once: a bedbug had bitten me.
The same bedbug, the same bite and in the same place.
How a bedbug remembers it.. I tell you, the memory of the local bedbugs is simply to be marvelled at; iron heads they have — they could have sat in Berlin...
And when I opened my eyes I found on the walls the same nails for hanging clothes, the same curtains at the windows, begging to be washed.
I also found the same little washstand with the same tap that will not turn, which you have to hold with all your strength with your fingers, and when you let go of it the whole pension shakes as if from an earthquake.
I even found an inscription on one tap, "warm", but the tap swore to me that as long as it has lived it has never yet set eyes on warm water.
I also found on the floor the same old piece of "chodnik" [runner rug], the torn one, which catches your feet so that you are bound to fall.
I also found the same limping chair, badly in need of a pair of crutches...
I even found in the drawers the same Jewish newspapers as last year, and in one drawer I found a newspaper from 1913 — it was still dealing with the Beilis trial..
And the prices [?] — also the same!
Old acquaintances have met here — how good, how homely!
B. K-r.
The Living Dead Man (21)

[Serialized novel — "A most thrilling novel of Jewish life in Zagłębie before and during the World War"; installment 21.]
A. Zaglembier [pen name].

Before long Sarahtshe "took" her two younger children to herself [i.e. they too died]. Left in God's world, lonely as a stone, was only Blumke, who, despite the hunger and want, had nevertheless blossomed, grown into a wonderfully beautiful girl and drew ever more attention from men's eyes.
Only now did the family — which had also become poor and ruined in the war — remember [?] the orphan and help [?] support her, so that she would not be carried off [?] onto bad, slippery paths. And since Blumke was growing more beautiful from day to day, it was simply a danger to let her out alone on the street: the slightest glimmer and promise in her need could intoxicate her and make her forget...
And seeing that here there would in any case be no future for her, the family, as soon as the war had ended, began bombarding the relatives in America with letters, asking them to have pity on Sarahtshe in her grave and save her only remaining child.
And so the beautiful Blumke came, soon after the war, to America, to the giant city of New York. And since she had no documents, she was brought in on ready-made "papers" in the name — Betty Grinwald.
But in the "golden land", too, her family was not exactly among those who had made their fortunes [?]. At first Blumke had to go from house to house; after hopping [?] for a while to an uncle's, an aunt then took her in for a while... So it went on, until Blumke at last "stopped being a greenhorn" [?], was no longer afraid of the giant city and decided to earn her own living.
But she had no trade in hand; her prospect [?] was to get a job in a shop as a saleswoman.
And here luck played into her hands.
Searching among the advertisements, her eye stopped at the following notice:
"Wanted: young, beautiful models; those engaged can expect good earnings for light work. Ready-made clothing firm John [printed "Dushan"] Flank."
More than at all the others Blumke stopped at this advertisement, as if her heart were telling her that here she would find...
And taking the newspaper with her, she went straight to the address given.
And her heart indeed did not deceive Blumke, although on arriving at the place she saw that plenty of candidates were already waiting, being let in one by one to the owner of the huge business — Mister John Flank.
And at last Blumke's turn came.
When she was let into the owner's magnificent office, she remained standing by the door, frightened, not knowing herself why.
"Please, come further in," she hears a strange but firm and confident voice.
It was Mister "John Flank" speaking to her, who had not yet properly looked at her.
But when he sees her beautiful, charming little face, he suddenly lifts himself from the desk and almost runs up to her.
"Please, sit down," he points to a chair and gazes at her ever more intrusively...
Apparently already used to being devoured by men's eyes, Blumke moves back a little and says, showing the newspaper:
"I have come about the advertisement."
"I understand, but sit down. What is your name?.."
"Betty Grinwald," answers Blumke, knowing that she will surely also have to present a document.
Only now does one see the momentary tension vanish from Mister Flank's face... It gives the impression that he regretted something, and, looking at her now with quite different eyes, appraising ones — whether she will be fit for the business or not — he says at last:
"Yes, I engage you. From tomorrow you can already come to work."
Blumke thanked him. With great joy she ran home to tell her relatives the good news. At last she would no longer feel so fallen [?]. She would earn her own living and no longer need to depend on anyone.
Together with Blumke Mister Flank did take on more models, but in none of them was he as interested as in the one everyone called "Betty".
Those, too, who had worked in the business from before noticed something: since Betty had arrived, the boss had become a completely different man. Always a sullen, scowling and silent man, his eyes hidden behind large glasses, he suddenly began to show himself in the shop among the employees, and mostly there where "Betty" was. A smile had already been seen on his withered [?] face. It was a simple matter. "Mister Flank is in love with the beautiful 'Betty'," everyone thought [—] and even said it aloud among themselves. And although Mister Flank was a mysterious figure to all — nobody knew where he came from or who he was — one thing was known: he was a lonely man, who spent his time nowhere but in his business or at home, where an elderly Black woman served him. Whether he had once had a wife, children — about that nobody knew.
In all the time that Mister Flank had been in New York and had bought the large ready-made clothing business, he had not formed any closer acquaintance with anyone; even with his nearest neighbours he had exchanged no word beyond a greeting.
No man leads such a secluded life for pleasure; "Mister Flank", too, apparently had reasons to guard himself from the world... More than once he could not fall asleep, thinking about those from whom he had at last freed himself, in order [?] to be able to start a decent, human life again. Ah, how many years had passed since he had made the first false step in his life, which had taken such heavy revenge on him..
Now he sees himself in New York, the same New York years ago, arrived from abroad, all alone, struggling, grabbing at all sorts of jobs, just to have a piece of bread; there was even a time when he too had to stretch out his hand for alms... And just then, when he once stood like that with outstretched hand, they drew him into the net. At first it was one, then several; they told him that such a young man must not beg, they had "work" for him at which he would earn well.. Only later did he understand what they had made of him: an easy living indeed, but bound up with how many mortal dangers... He had become a gangster.. He worked a long time for the gang, but he never grew at home with them; before his eyes always stood his former decent life and his nearest ones, whom he had had to abandon in such terrible circumstances...

„Yes“ or „No“

[Humour — „Der Kokh-lefl“; the partition plan.] Our survey among the great men of Zagłębie
By order of the editor we conducted a survey among our great men [word „פארגעבן“ unclear], whose names resound from Małobądz[?] to Katarzyna, to hear their opinions on the partition plan of the Land of Israel.
First under fire goes
Advocate Ka-elski
— What do you say, „panie mecenasie“[?] [Mr. Attorney, in garbled Polish], to the creation of a „państwo żydowskie“ [Jewish state] in Palestine?
— „Owszem!“ [Certainly!] Go, you Żydki [little Jews], to Palestine, if you simply[?] feel like being crazy; I will send along with you a few[?] „fanning“[?] chłopcy [lads] who will „air“ you „od czasu do czasu“ [from time to time], because there are great heats there.
— What's the use, panie mecenasie, of talking about heat; you're not [—] after all. Tell me rather: why are you a supporter of a Jewish state? When the Żydki leave Poland, you won't have a stroke[?] of work?
— „Jak to?“ [How so?] There will still remain a Jewish ambassador — we'll have one Jew „for a remedy“.
— „Racja!“ [Right!] You're right. Oh, you need, panie mecenasie, a remedy for your brain-box!
With a Sejm deputy.
— What do you say, „panie pośle“ [Mr. Deputy], to the creation of a Jewish kingdom? Which do you like better: the first plan — the Balfour Declaration, or the second plan — the Peel Declaration?
— As a Sejm deputy I am always a supporter of the „first“...
— And what do you think of the Mandate?
— Yes, that yes — a „little mandate“ is a fine[?] thing. Even for my Sejm mandate I did not sink the whole inheritance.
Chackele Klabunik
Our last visit we paid to our darling Chackele Klabunik.
Seeing the „Kokh-lefl“ representative, he stuck his hands in his trouser pockets and started talking [in coarse dialect]:
— So they ask me what I say about the Jewish kingdom? I say the same as all the fellows from Podzamcze[?] and from [—] [—][?].
— I'm no fool; [—] one doesn't ask questions; I say: [—] water[?]; if we are to have our own kingdom, one must already know what to do; nobody needs to put a finger in my mouth [i.e. I'm no simpleton]. I know how they sing in the theatre, and in [—] they sing like this:
— One shoves someone. Whoever is clever shoves someone too; whoever is no fool shoves someone himself.
With Chackele we finished our survey.

Then and Now.

[Humour — „Der Kokh-lefl“; youth.] The youth of old, who studied in the heder, knew that the world stands on three things: on Torah, on worship and on acts of loving-kindness.
Today's youth learns that the world stands on flirting, cards and eating.
Elul.

[Poetry — „Der Kokh-lefl“; Elul; Palestine.] The shofar has sounded —
Elul has already come —
and its „tekiah“ with the „shevarim“
has seized our hearts.

Somehow it weeps, this shofar,
this year, it seems, stronger, softer,
as if it felt that now
the cup is truly full.

Now it seems as if it laments
with its weeping „shevarim“:
God in heaven, how long now
will Jews be counting graves?

How long yet will they murder
us — the dark Arabs,
with the quiet little consent
of the Englishman, „his friend“?

How long yet, really,
will our human rabble
make the Jew everywhere
the exile's scapegoat-chicken?..

Now the shofar lets out
[—][?] a sad „tekiah“ —
is the shofar not sounding the alarm
over the holding-back of aliyah?..

Elul, shofar, after the summer —
who can read the papers now —
every line — exile and tears,
barbarism, fratricidal wars;
the heart bursts, one cannot listen;
one would wish that the shofar
with its lamenting teruah
would at last bring down from heaven
salvation for the people.
Szmerszle[?].

A “Wywiad” for the Magistrate and a “Wywiad” for the Jewish Gmina

[Będzin — kehilla, municipality, welfare.]
It is the practice that whoever applies to the magistrate [municipality] for some sort[?] of support, whether material or medical, has a “wywiad” [inquiry, means investigation] made into the material situation of the applicant (petent).
The same procedure is carried out when an etat payer [kehilla-tax payer] submits an appeal (rekurs) against the etat sum which the kehilla has assessed him.
How the “wywiads” of the two authorities turn out can only[?] be seen from the following examples:
The “wywiadowiec” [investigator] of the magistrate comes in to a poor man who has applied for support, looks around in every corner, asks various questions and arrives at the conclusion that the person concerned “does not qualify to receive any support”...
It is different, however, when the “wywiad” concerns[?] the gmina [Jewish community]. When the same “wywiadowiec” “does not see” that the etat payer occupies a flat of 4 rooms and kitchen, which [has] separate servants for the children, and[?] even knows that the etat payer is entirely kept by the family...
Such is the face of the “wywiads”, on which[?] human lives often depend..
Jews, Have Pity — a Midwife Is Needed..

[Rajcza — summer resort, incidents.]
Last week[?] the following case occurred in Rajcza. A young[?] Jewish woman, who had been staying there in summer lodgings, set off home, because by her reckoning she was already “due”. On the way to the railway she was seized by labour pains and[?] a midwife was already needed..
The end was that the persons who had travelled together with her to the railway went back with the woman to her dacha lodgings, where she gave birth to the child.

For weeks they prepared for the wedding, but when it came to "Harei at", the groom took to flight...

[Sosnowiec — daily life.] Sosnowiec
For weeks they prepared for the wedding,
but when they had already reached "Harei at" [the betrothal formula], the groom did a "vayivrah" ["and he fled"]...
Pańska Lane is in a whirl because of the story that happened there in a respectable[?] Jewish family.
Last Sunday a wedding was supposed to take place in the family. The wedding was meant to be a "quiet" one, because the groom's parents had not consented to the match. The parents tried many times to influence their son to break off relations with the bride, but as they say[?]: "Love is strong as death"; the young man, who had been going out with the girl for several years already, rejected his parents' proposals and swore "eternal love" to his future companion.
And indeed they began preparing for the wedding, even though they knew that the groom's parents would not come to the wedding. But not only did the parents not come — the "gem" himself also "disappeared" on the day of the wedding canopy, and he is no more.
At the appointed time the guests gathered, candles burned and they waited for the groom. They waited an hour, another hour — and the groom is not there. Messengers went to the "gem's" parents and started shouting: how can one so[?] shame a Jewish daughter? "What do you want of him? — the parents answered — we ourselves don't know where he is."
The end was not a happy one: the candles went out and the guests dispersed, and as we write these lines it is still not known where the groom in question is.

In its own premises the local Zionist Organization held on Tuesday evening an "academy" devoted to the 40th anniversary of the First Zionist Congress and to the "jubilee" [so printed] of the 20th Congress, which is taking place in Zurich.
Speeches were delivered by the chairman Dr. Maladista[?], the chairman of the Zionist Org. in Będzin Mr. Y. Winogrodzki[?], the Zionist veteran Mr. Gershon Stawski and Mr. Kupermintz. The academy, which was well attended, closed with "Hatikvah".
In honour of the Sabbath...

[Sosnowiec — daily life.] In honour of the Sabbath...
The Jewish tenants at Dekerta 12 complain that the rubbish of a whole week is carted away every Friday towards evening. The tenants do not know the reason for it. Perhaps — they say — the house-owners brought along the custom from [—]?..
The first thirty...

[Sosnowiec — economy; banks.] The first thirty...
The liquidation committee of the "Bank Kupiecki" [Merchants' Bank] has proceeded to use legal means against the bank's debtors. These days the first 30 members who have not settled their obligations towards the bank are being handed over to the court.
In the middle of the Kedushah the landlords come in demanding rent

[Sosnowiec (Katarzyna?) — community.] In the middle of the Kedushah
the landlords come in demanding rent.
We receive[?] a delegation from Katarzyna[?]. They came into the editorial office to pour out their hearts about the spiritual decline of their community.
Since the moreh hora'ah [rabbinic decisor] Shtark — they say — went away to Sosnowiec, bad management has entered our Jewish life. There is no strong hand to govern; rather, whatever anyone wants he does, and consequently everything goes down and down, and if no improvement comes there is a prospect that what we have built over 40 years will be destroyed.
As an illustration may serve what happened last Sabbath. In the middle of the prayers the Christian landlords came into the beit midrash with an outcry[?]: why are they[?] not being paid rent.
— What do you ask? — we ask.
— We have come to you so that through the newspaper you appeal to the heads of the Sosnowiec kehilla to take an interest in us. After all, we are their budget-contributors ["etat"-payers]. The Sosnowiec kehilla board should also call on the transferred[?] moreh tzedek [rabbinic judge] to come, as he promised before leaving, to Katarzyna twice a week, so that we shall not be like sheep without a shepherd.
Praying, Too, Must Be Done at a Fixed Time...

[Sosnowiec — kehilla.] At the last meeting of the kehilla board the question was discussed concerning order in the municipal synagogue in the field of... praying. The point is that in the synagogue people used to pray almost the whole day.
It was decided that from today onward the following prayer times shall apply: in the morning from 7.30 to 10.30, and Mincha and Maariv from 6 to 8 in the evening.

Life in Kielce — Do Not Sell!

Friday, 6 Elul 5697. piątek 13 sierpnia 1937 [Friday, 13 August 1937].
Do not sell!
To the attention of the Supervisory Board of the former[?] Folksbank (People's Bank).
Rumours are circulating in town that the building of the Folksbank is to be sold to private persons.
Should this be confirmed, the Jewish community of Kielce will receive the fact with the greatest dismay, since[?] at the time when negotiations were being conducted with the „Joint“, it was said that the building would pass to the Jewish community of Kielce — naturally upon covering the debt to the „Foundation“; this was meant to be a satisfaction for what the community had suffered from the Folksbank affair.
We are convinced that we express the opinion of the greater part of Jewish Kielce when we say that for the time being the building must not be sold. The Folksbank affair cost the Jews of Kielce blood, and if it is a matter of raising a certain sum of money to cover the debt to the „Foundation“, it will be raised, so long as the building remains in the possession of the Jewish community of Kielce.

The Jewish Cemetery Must Not Be Desecrated

In the month of Tishri of this year Jewish Kielce was shaken by the desecration and defilement carried out at the old Jewish cemetery, where about 80 tombstones were destroyed.
In order to ensure that in future no such sad cases of desecration of the place where our holy martyrs and sages lie will occur, a special cemetery committee has been formed, headed by Dr. Fleszler[?], which has set itself the goal of bringing the cemetery into the best order and raising it to a proper level, as befits the holy place of a great Jewish community.
In this connection the committee must first of all carry out the following tasks: 1) raise the fence (parkan) around the cemetery, 2) introduce a planned arrangement of the graves, and 3) engage special attendants to guard and tend the cemetery.
In order to create the necessary fund to carry out the said tasks, the committee appeals to the Jews of Kielce — and to those who live outside Kielce but whose relatives rest in the Kielce cemetery — to support the collection campaign for these important tasks.
The committee is convinced that the Jewish population of our town will not permit the eternal rest of our dearest ones lying in the Kielce cemetery to be disturbed, and will receive its representatives warmly, taking part in the campaign that has been undertaken.
Hooligan „Pranks“ by Kielce Jokers

A gang of Kielce jokers have lately hit upon new hooligan „pranks“. They telephone the local doctors in the name of well-known Kielce Jews, asking them to come there „at once“ because someone in the family has suddenly fallen „ill“..
This week, while a certain Mr. K. was sitting at supper, two doctors came in to him with a feldsher holding the stretcher in his hand.. To the question of the household as to why they had come, the doctors answered that they had been called by telephone...
If this goes on, then in a genuine case no doctor at all who is called by telephone to a sick person will be willing to go.
It is therefore everyone's duty to expose these hooligans and to put an end to such deeds.
Rabbi Shmuel Hagerman, of blessed memory

Hasidic Kielce accompanied to eternal rest a few days ago one of the most interesting Hasidic Jews, R. Shmuel Hagerman (called „R' Shmuel the Little“), of blessed memory.
The deceased belonged to that kind of Jewish figure that no longer comes after us. All his days he occupied himself with Torah and the fear of Heaven. He used to travel to Ger [Góra Kalwaria, i.e. he was a Gerer Hasid]. At the same time he was an exceptionally humble man. In Hasidic circles he was regarded with the greatest reverence.
The deceased left no children. After the burial Kaddish was said by R' Pesach David Ajnberg[?].
Eulogies for the deceased were delivered by: the Kielce rabbi, Rabbi Rapoport; the head of the rabbinical court (ABD) Harberg[?]; the dayan Grynszpan; and R' Mordechai Rozenberg, the deceased's best friend.
May his soul be bound up in the bond of eternal life.
Rabbi Yaakov Tenenbaum, may he rest in Eden

Last Sunday R' Yaakov Tenenbaum, of blessed memory, died in Otwock at the age of 60.
The deceased was a Torah scholar; he was a son-in-law of the first rabbi of Kielce, R' Tuvia Gitman[?] Rapoport, of saintly and blessed memory, and a brother-in-law of the present rabbi of Kielce. R' Yaakov Tenenbaum was a Pilica Hasid.
Recently he suddenly fell ill with a heart disease, and on Sunday towards evening he died in Otwock.
The funeral took place the next day, Monday, in Kielce, with a large crowd taking part. He was eulogised by the Kielce rabbi, Rabbi Rapoport.
May his soul be bound up in the bond of eternal life.

On Acquiring Real Estate in the Border Zone

In connection with the entry into force of the regulation of 1 July this year on the state borders (Dz. Ustaw no. 12 of 22 February 1937), the Będzin starosta [county head] announces:
Matters connected with the purchase of real estate in the border zone are to be treated as urgent and must be dealt with first.
The starostwo [county office] reminds those concerned that when wishing to buy a house one must submit an application to the 2nd[?] instance, i.e. to the województwo [provincial office], through the local starostwo. The application — which is exempt from stamp duty — must state exactly what kind of transaction is involved (purchase, exchange, lease etc.; exact designation of the house or plot, mortgage-register no.).
The following must be attached to the application:
a) a certificate of Polish citizenship.
b) if one does not have such a certificate, one must attach such documents as entitle one to obtain such a certificate.

Dr. Yehoshua Rapaport — 50 Years Old

[Upper Silesia — Katowice, Zionism.]
The president of the Katowice Zionist Org., Dr. Yehoshua Rapaport, has turned fifty.
On this occasion it is worth mentioning that the esteemed Zionist public figure is active not only in the Zionist movement but takes part in a number of leading bodies of important public institutions; namely, as a member of the community board („dozór“) the jubilarian heads the school department, and he is a member of the Bank Udziałowy S.A.
As a token of thanks and recognition for his merits, the Katowice Zionists have resolved to inscribe the jubilarian in the Golden Book of the Keren Kayemet, and this Saturday night, 21 August, a festive evening [?] in honour of the meritorious Zionist and public worker will take place [?] in the „Concordia“ halls.
We wish the esteemed jubilarian many more long years of fruitful activity in the revived independent Jewish state in Eretz Israel.
A R V Y.
Will the „Berek Joselewicz“ School Be Moved to Bogucice?

[Upper Silesia — Katowice, education.]
At the Katowice Magistrate a session of the so-called „Dozór Szkolny“ [school board] took place. On behalf of the Jewish population of Katowice the local rabbi, Dr. Vogelmann, was present. On the agenda, among other things, was the question of moving the elementary school named after „Berek Joselewicz“ in Katowice to Bogucice. The question was presented by the vice-president, who explained that the Magistrate's initiative that the school should have a building of its own is a very good one, but he cannot agree to it for reasons of safety, because the new school building in Bogucice is far from the town. After this explanation it was resolved that a special commission should acquaint itself with the question on the spot, and within two weeks the commission is to issue its decision.
A Debate on Jews in the Katowice City Council.

[Upper Silesia — Katowice, city council.]
The gallery visitors who make anti-Jewish outcries are removed.
Last Friday a session of the city council took place in Katowice, at which the Jewish councillor Mr. Ludwig Zmigrod raised the question of the well-known communiqué issued by the Magistrate about Jewish visitors to the municipal bathing establishments at the Bugla [?, „Bugla-Khyune“]. Mr. Zmigrod's interpellation was met with antisemitic outcries from the gallery, so that the chairman was compelled to order the gallery to be cleared. The gallery visitors, on their way out, shouted various antisemitic slogans.
In his speech councillor Mr. Zmigrod criticised the author of the communiqué. „It is a pity — says Mr. Z. — that the author did not state in his communiqué how many cubic metres of water at the Bugla belong to Jews and how many to non-Jews. In the municipal bathing establishment there is also the notice that ‚with a beard, entry is forbidden‘; so how will the vice-chairman of the city council, Mr. Dr. [?] Ligoń, who wears a beard, be able to enter the municipal bathing establishment?“ — asks councillor Zmigrod.
In conclusion Mr. Zmigrod appealed [?] to the Magistrate that the communiqué be corrected; if not, the Jews will be compelled to turn to the Voivodeship or to a higher instance (interjection of councillor Mr. Kapacz: to the League of Nations).
In the discussion some councillors expressed their satisfaction with the communiqué. An exception was the speech of councillor Janta (P.P.S.), who criticised the communiqué in a satirical manner.
A Cunning Swindler Cheats a Young Child.

[Upper Silesia — Katowice, crime.]
To 8-year-old Lucja Mandel [?], who was walking along Kościuszki Street in Katowice carrying a briefcase with papers, there came up an unknown woman, who gave the girl 20 groszy so that she would bring her down a parcel of laundry from a house on Ligonia Street. The investigation against the Prince of Pszczyna (Pless) („the Younger“) has already been completed, and in the near future the Katowice prosecutor's office will serve the indictment. A Street Sank 18 Metres Deep

[Upper Silesia — Disaster.] In Rozhrusheniye[?] [probably Roździeń] near Szopienice a "story of Korah" happened — an entire street sank into the ground.
Within an hour[?] "the mouth of the earth" opened there, as the Pentateuch puts it, and an abyss 15 metres deep and three metres wide appeared!
Fortunately there were no human victims — it happened, as it were, on a street that was by chance empty.
As it turned out, the catastrophe with the street happened because beneath it there is a coal pit, which is now being worked out.
