An Old Question

[Będzin — public life and communal activists; opinion piece.] — Old questions —
Będzin is blessed with an abundance of public organizations, associations, societies. They have more or less important tasks of greater public significance. Every society or organization is, according to its nature and character, designed for a membership that ought to be the organizational, financial and social foundation and support of the given organization. The more members, the more active the membership, the more purposeful the division of work among the more active ones — the healthier the activity of [—] organization, the more substantial its achievement.
So it is according to reason and according to theory; but so it is not in reality in the public life of our town.
With us you will find everything upside down.
With us you will find that around the few minyanim[?] of societies and organizations there revolve a few minyanim[?] of "epaulette-wearers" ["shlifes treger", from Polish szlify], who "govern" 5–10 organizations simultaneously (of course there are exceptions). Well, what can such an "epaulette-wearer" do, when he has so many organizations on his head? ("[doubtful reading:] tsale minste na — grab little glasses[?]").
And one rule applies: if one serves as gabbai in several organizations, one merely occupies the place of someone else who might perhaps have managed[?] to accomplish something. Every such[?] board, when it consists of the same activists in several societies, is[?] in the nature of a burial society (chevra kadisha) for the organization.
And — let us be frank — it is already very hard to understand[?]: when you find among the activists some who have "sat themselves in"[?], and you try to give them a temporary leave, you are "not sure of your life"; such an activist becomes your mortal enemy, exactly as if it were a question of life for him, or at the very least a matter of livelihood.
And now a second scandalous, truly fatally acting phenomenon.
These same activists, for the most part, have either a dismissive attitude or an aversion toward the "plebs", who ought to be the "flesh and blood" of the organization, the foundation, the milieu of the given society.
The result?
Most institutions have a negligible membership, it does not come to the meetings, people take no interest, and so the institutions look pitiful, moribund, half or complete fictions.
The public answers the activists' unwilling attitude in the same coin.
An old question remains:
How long will this scandalous state of affairs last?
How long yet shall such irresponsible conduct by a handful of honour-seekers be tolerated, who to a great extent are ruining the public life of our town?
How much longer?
L. H.
In the fight against carelessness — An appeal to the Jewish population on the state of kashrut in Będzin

(An appeal to the Jewish population concerning the state of kashrut in Będzin).
Among the few[?] positions that Jews have preserved through all the hardest times of spiritual and material decline, the position of kashrut undoubtedly occupies — a chief place.
In all the hardest and most tragic moments the Jewish people has lived through, moments of violence[?], religious persecutions and evil decrees, in moments of elemental upheavals[?], in all these moments kashrut — that is, keeping a kosher kitchen and guarding against forbidden foods — was observed most strictly by all circles and strata of the Jewish community.
With the introduction[?] of the shechita law, there has unfortunately come a breach in this so very firm position of kashrut, and the lawlessness reigning in this field threatens to undermine the foundations of kashrut, for which Jews have always been ready to sacrifice themselves.
And remarkably: while the shechita law was still at the stage of a bill, voices were heard from all circles, even from the non-observant, who are not so careful about kosher meat, that now, when they want[?] to strike at the Jew, they would not [?] use any non-kosher meat. On the contrary. It was promised in all freethinking circles: if the law is meant to strike at the Jew's economic foundations, we shall all use only kosher meat.
Unfortunately this has turned out to be merely good promises, and the lawlessness in this field is taking on serious forms.
For the sake of a few groszy cheaper, people do not withstand the temptation and buy meat in unsupervised butcher shops that sell nevelot and treifot as kosher.
Every Jewish heart trembles when one sees[?] Jews buying "shot" meat [from animals killed by shooting], or meat slaughtered in cellars by lawless[?] people. Meat not purged of forbidden fat (chelev), and nobody gives any account of the great and grave prohibition of eating nevelot and treifot, which is a prohibition punishable by karet, just like eating chametz on Passover.
And let us speak about our own town, Będzin. Będzin belongs to the few towns where the rabbinate, with the help of a large number of householders, managed to recognise the threatening danger in time and with great effort created the system of ne'emanim (supervisors). In every butcher shop without exception that sells kosher meat there is a ne'eman of the rabbinate and of the Va'ad ha-Kashrut, who has supervision and control over every piece of meat there. Thereby[?] every Jew who wants to buy kosher meat is given the assurance that what he buys is truly kosher.
The system of ne'emanim is actually nothing new. Even back then, when kashrut was entirely normal and nobody yet knew of such lawlessness as today, the slaughter and sale of kosher meat required special trustworthiness. Everyone understood that one cannot entrust the sale of kosher meat to just anyone; it was understood that a butcher, be he the most honest and the best — in view of the loss he faces if his animal turns out treif, this [great?] loss may give rise to the thought of ascribing the intention to the shochet and thereby justifying[?] concealing or erasing the traces of a sircha (lung adhesion) or other treifot.
The task of the rabbis and of those concerned with kashrut has therefore always been to keep a watchful [?] eye on all those in whose hands kashrut lies, from the shochet to the butcher, and above all to create the conditions in which they would feel the responsibility bound up with kashrut, and then to create a situation prevailing in this field such that nobody would want to ruin his trade: a shochet or a butcher knew that with the slightest abuse in matters of kashrut they risked[?] losing their bread and giving up their trade, being at the same time branded by the Jewish community as criminals. That was enough to maintain kashrut in its proper form and to prevent breaches.
With the coming into force of the shechita law, by which the price difference between kosher and treif meat has grown many times over — especially treif meat from a kosher slaughter, which has to be sold very cheaply because of the propaganda among the non-Jewish population not to buy such meat — the trustworthiness of the butcher has been entirely undermined, and daily experience proves that there is no means of preventing pitfalls in matters of kashrut other than the system of ne'emanim, which has succeeded brilliantly here in our town.
Unfortunately not everyone understands this, and many go on buying, for a few groszy cheaper, "kosher"[?] meat without any supervision and control.
We therefore appeal to all the Jews of Będzin not to buy any meat as kosher except in the butcher shops in which ne'emanim of the rabbinate are stationed.
Strong enlightenment must reach the careless consumers who buy meat in shops without ne'emanim, where there is no control whether the meat is slaughtered or shot, kosher or treif, purged of forbidden fat or not purged.
A great, broad[?] campaign must be undertaken to enlighten all these careless Jewish customers in general[?] and bring them to the awareness that they are being fed nevelot and treifot.
This enlightenment must embrace all circles of the Jewish population, not excluding the progressive elements, for we must remember that apart from kosher meat being one of the most cardinal foundations of Jewishness and of guarding the purity of Jewish food, one must also ask the progressive Jew to take into account the general Jewish economic situation, which obliges everyone without exception to work together for the sake of kashrut.
This was, after all, the chief motive that compelled our modern spokesmen to declare "pathetically" and solemnly that after the shechita ban they would demand of their followers that they keep kashrut from a national standpoint as well; so now is the moment to demand that this promise be fulfilled.
Using meat that falls under the suspicion of being "shot" must be declared national treason.
All Jews, without exception of trend and conviction, must help in this struggle — in the struggle to preserve one of the most cardinal Jewish foundations! In the struggle to guard the purity of Jewish food! In the struggle against the plundering of Jewish positions!
One of the rabbis.
A Little Fresh Air...

[Sosnowiec — humour; monologue.] By Y. Oberzhanek [J. Oberżanek?].
A monologue of a Jew from Sosnowiec [Sosnowiec].

You see my face, yellow as wax? The bags under my eyes? The sunken cheeks? I got all that from fresh air...
As you look at me — I used to be a "makhgl" [?]. When I could "viln" [?] with highway gravel ["shose" = szosa], in all my life I was never sick, I knew nothing of doctors, medicines, pharmacies. Rather than carry the money to the doctor and the pharmacist, I preferred to give it to the baker, the butcher, the fishmonger, the milk-woman.
In a word, I laughed at blood pressures, at diets, at spas, and if ever my stomach wanted [?] to play a farce on me, I took half a "gegul" [?] and "kleyn kleyne khibie" [?].
You'll ask, of course: if I'm such a giant, such a "makhgl" [?], how did I come by such a yellow face? Such wrinkles on my forehead? So listen to this:
It was at the beginning of summer. On Shabbes for lunch I wolfed down a fat cholent, brown potatoes, a metre of fat kishke with farfel, followed it with half a "gegul" [?], washed it all down with a dozen glasses of beer and then threw myself into bed. Suddenly I woke up: my stomach was "playing" me a concert, the gases [?] in my belly had risen from the dead and told me the whole story.
— Perele, what's [?] happening with the second half of the "gegul"? You know the first half pushes itself into the belly on its own.
— No, you won't get anywhere with me — my wife answered — you should have gone to the doctor long ago.
— To the doctor? Ha, ha, ha, me — to the doctor? Do you suspect I'm going to "moyvln" [?]?
— Don't joke — my wife answered — you should have gone to the doctor long ago. You're not a child after all; a man of your years, when a thing like that happens, has to go and get himself "looked over" by a doctor.
Well, so be it. When a wife digs in her heels no clever tricks help, and off I went to a doctor, a stomach specialist, where the moment you step over the threshold you have to pay the shikse [the maid] 20 złoty.
After three hours sitting in my queue ["koleyke" = kolejka], the gases [?] in my stomach had meanwhile "unpacked" [?] and I was already about [?] to run away, but I begrudged the 20 złoty. Why should he get 20 złoty for nothing? Let him work for the money.
When I came in to the doctor, he started questioning me, asking blockhead questions: how old I am, what I do for a living, what I'm complaining about ["nazhekn" = narzekać], what hurts me.
— Nothing hurts me — I answered — you've taken 20 zł. It won't make you sick [?] to find out for yourself what's wrong with me.
So he really got down to work: felt me, listened, squeezed, tapped with a hammer, kneaded my belly the way a baker kneads dough, and after half an hour of squeezing he says to me:
— I find nothing wrong with you.
— What do you mean you find nothing? That's an excuse for grandma. You took 20 złoty, and now you tell me you find nothing? Things like that don't go with me. Either you find something, or you give back the 20 złoty!
The doctor got scared and said:
— I'll give you a note to another doctor, he should do a "psheshvyetlenye" [prześwietlenie, X-ray] for you.
— A what?
— A psheshvyetlenye, a "durkhshayne-len" [screening], a... a "vryentshe" [so printed — a mangling of "Röntgen"].
— A photograph, you mean?
— Yes, a photograph.
— Perele — I said to my wife — go to the hairdresser, have a fresh permanent wave done, get your hair curled, put on the new dress with the gilded brooch, put on the ring with the chain, wash [?] and comb the little children, and give me my Shabbes kapote too and a clean collar with the tie.
— What's happened? Why dress up all of a sudden on an ordinary Wednesday?
— The doctor said that I have [?] to have a "vryentshe" done, a photograph; for the same money we can all have ourselves photographed. A family photograph, that's what it is!
So we really all went off [?], the whole family, dressed up "in vinegar and honey" [i.e. in our finest], to have ourselves photographed. Arriving there, I hand him the note from that other doctor; he looks at me and asks:
— What has the whole family come for?
— To have ourselves photographed!.. You'll be doing a "vryentshe" anyway, so what do you care if you "snap" the whole family in one go?
The doctor burst out laughing:
— I'm no photographer but a doctor; you need to be "psheshvyetlen" [X-rayed], shone through, to see what you've got in there inside.
— Only [—], before one does the X-ray — he says — be so good as to take a little "bitter water" [mey ha-meorerim], to rinse out the intestines; when the stomach is full one can't see what's going on inside.
When I'd gulped down that bit of bitter water I saw all my forefathers resting in bright Paradise, and once I was empty he did the "vryentshe" — psheshvyetlenye, that's what it's called.
Well, do you think he found anything? He looked at a "shpaktiv" [?], turned it this way and that, and in the end he says to me:
— No, uncle ["feter"], the X-ray shows nothing; but you know what? I'll give you a note to a nerve doctor, you must be nervous.
So off I went to a nerve doctor. Again a doctor with a name, where you have to pay the shikse 20 złoty in advance ["zgury" = z góry]. Again he started asking me blockhead questions, told me to work out how much 6 times 6 is, whether there are any madmen in my family, and other such clever questions. Well, and what do you think was the end of it? After an hour of tapping, feeling, listening and asking questions, he says to me:
— Uncle, I find nothing wrong with you, I won't prescribe you any medicine. The only thing you need to do is — go away for fresh air.
Believe me before God — as long as he found something!
So I promptly rented a summer flat, packed the things, sent my wife and the children off for fresh air. My wife was in the fresh air, I was in town, eating "three-course" lunches in restaurants, and after every lunch of "three courses" I had seven "goings" [pun: Yiddish "geng" = courses / trips (to the lavatory)]... and after the first month the fresh air "took effect" on me. I'm sick in my stomach and my nerves; the doctors no longer need to search long, no need to tap and knead — one glance at my face, yellow as wax, the bags under my eyes, the wrinkles on my forehead, and right away you know that I'm dangerously ill, that I'm gasping [?] my last breath —
The fresh air helped...
Yordim (Those Who Have Come Down)...

[Zagłębie — Jewish public life; article.] In the turbulent[?] times in which our generation lives, we happen often, very often, to meet in life the well-known type of the "yordim" [people who have come down in the world].
A yored — that is like a person with whom fortune has grown angry[?], whom the evil winds of life have carried downhill. Such a person lives only on memories of his former wealth and happiness, when he too "shook the world", back when the street, the town, did not yet know today's upstart rich men.
But it is not only among people that you meet them, these unfortunate yordim; there are also yored-countries and yored-towns, and among those few towns in Poland that belong to the category of yordim one can without any doubt count our Zagłębie as well.
Zagłębie is a yoredet. For years now its public life, especially the Jewish one, has been steadily going downhill, and nobody makes the slightest effort or exertion to halt and stop this decline by anything at all.
Even a visitor staying a short while can establish with proof that of all the once so lively political parties there remain only tombstones in the form of rubber stamps, going mouldy somewhere in a drawer of this or that former activist, who today, unfortunately, can in no way remember what office he holds[?] in the organisation — is he the chairman or perhaps merely a secretary?..
And how long ago was it that the Zionist groupings were active to such an extent that even quarrels and strife were not lacking; and today it is as quiet as in an old, closed cemetery, and the question involuntarily arises: where are they, all these "politicians" and public workers? What has transmigrated them into public impotents — the rummy and bridge in the Jewish club, or the glass and the dancing in a gentile restaurant!
No better, and perhaps much worse, is the situation in the philanthropic institutions, from which one hears something only once in a while, when people get heated[?] at a meeting.
People who like to plead in mitigation will attribute all this to the prevailing poverty, but that is completely wrong: in the first years of the crisis poverty and helplessness were greater, and yet Jewish public life in Zagłębie stood at a certain level and did not roll about in the nethermost pit as it does today.
What Zagłębie lacks today is a sense for public affairs. There remain very few capable and valuable individuals, but they are apathetic towards every kind of communal work, and thanks to that everything goes downhill in every respect.
Zagłębie is a yoredet.
P. Lazer.
Letters That Never Arrived

[Feuilleton — the post; undeliverable letters.] Today in every country there is, at almost every larger post office, a special department in which skilled people sit, who study the exact[?] addresses and try by various means to find out whom the letter-writer meant with his clever addresses. Today almost no letter gets lost any more. Somehow one finds out to whom the writer wanted to send his letter.
But some hundred years ago, when writing was still "a hard thing" and the post had only just "started to run", a large part of the letters really did get lost, especially when the letter-writers did not write exact addresses and one could not know whom they meant.
Mostly the letter-writers wrote only the initials of the names and of the towns and reckoned "they'll find it somehow [jakoś]"; the over-clever used to write "Ni, Gi and Ni", as one says: you already know whom I mean.
In the archive of the Leipzig post office lie letters of fair visitors[?] from a hundred years ago that could not be delivered to the people to whom they belong, because one could never know who was meant.
How, for example, could the post know to whom to deliver the letter addressed: "To the late Rabbiner Shmuel in M., to be delivered to his widow". How many rabbis were called Shmuel, and how many towns are there in the world that begin with M.? Or:
To the esteemed daughter of the late master builder.
To the royal gendarme G. G. in S
To Mrs L., widow of the royal Galician officer N.
To the pretty girl who once was in service in Leipzig.
To Mrs Lemer, who got divorced[?].
To the tavern-keeper whose wife has just had a baby.
To the journeyman tailor Fritz in Warsaw, only not the red-haired one, that's a different one...
To the peasant Nikolai from Russia. I ask the post to deliver the letter at once..
To the handsome "reyngder"[?] who comes into town every time..
To the maid of the inn, who also milks the cows..
To Miss Gina, who studies with the children and takes them for walks...
To the tailor Christoph, born in Vienna, who is now a "Negro"[?] in a circus...
To the shoemaker G. G. If he has died, it doesn't matter, we all must die...
To the fine washerwoman who washes only for rich people.
To the madam who weighs more than three hundred pounds.
To Martha Kühne, who lent me 28 groschen.
To my brother, with a thousand kisses.
To the pretty washerwoman who washed my trousers last week...
To Wern Heber, who has just come out of prison...
And many, many hundreds more such letters were left lying, and nobody knew where to send them or to whom to return them.
Z. Haber, Vienna.
Elul.

[Feuilleton — reflections for the month of Elul.] By B. Pertshuk.
(Reflections.)

The people of Israel sins..
It sins throughout the year.
It wants fresh air, it wants to eat, it wants a garment — sheer sins[?]!
The Jew wants to be left in peace, to be allowed to live on God's earth — a Jew[?]!
The Jew strives for education, for fruitful productive activity — a sin that shall not be forgiven!
And so the Jew sins a whole year, sins against his fellow man of another faith, another nation, sins by the single fact of his existence...
He sins until the month of Elul comes!
A trembling seizes the sinner!
Satan, the accuser, works on deeds[?]; the scales are being tested...
The record books are being prepared, where each one's deeds are written down separately[?].
So that he shall not be able, shall not dare to deny...
The Judge is getting ready...
— — — — —
The Judge is getting ready to judge not only the Jew.
He is getting ready to judge peoples and countries; not only the Jew has gone bad[?] — something is wrong with all of humanity...
For Satan boasts that catching souls has come easy to him lately.
Free souls — are not to be found...
They are all sold, or getting ready to sell themselves...
— — — — —
Every morning a bright sun rises.
The sun bathes in seas of blood, in rivers of tears.
Spots appear on the shining sun — dark spots.
Spots of the blood of people who slaughter, who murder one another.
The scholars aim their telescopes — they study the spots on the sun.
They sit, the scholars, in their studies, and devise poison gases...
Let people murder one another, let the murders multiply — but let it be done cleanly — without blood — let the sun not be stained!
To put to sleep in eternal sleep, without blood, without torn limbs, without suffering!
It is so progressive, after all, so humanitarian, so humane!..
— — — — —
And a hell burns in Spain, skies flare up in the Far East..
— The shofar sounds, announcing the day of judgment..
And congresses hurry, trumpets blare: culture is being carried, progress is being carried to the backward, to the stubborn!
— — — — —
We have trespassed more than any people!
We are the real sinners, we are the real guilty ones!
We do not think of humanity, we have ceased to be bearers of culture, spreaders of culture.
We do not exterminate the recalcitrant with bombs from three-engine aeroplanes, with poison gases..
We are selfish, we want to live in peace, to trade, to study!
And that is why our sin is great, that is why it is heavy!..
That is why it comes, Elul, to announce to us that the Day of Judgment is drawing near..
And every day the shofar sounds, sounds and spreads terror..
And we tremble and we cry out:
— "Behold, the Day of Judgment!"
A Belated Letter.

[Short story — summer-resort life.] (A dacha story.)

Rachel Doroshkin's husband was a small earner, and so she could not afford such a luxury[?] as going to a dacha for the summer. Only ten years after her wedding, after a serious illness, when the doctor ordered[?] her to go to the fresh air, did Mrs. Doroshkin set out for a dacha.
She loved her husband and their three children; she was always together with them and had grown so close to her family that she could hardly imagine herself alone without them. Her husband and the children saw her off, and he, Aaron, asked her to write frequent letters.
— Let me know about everything you will see and hear, and about what will please you best of all.
She promised him to do so.
—
A strange, refreshing feeling came over her on arriving at the place. The open space and the lush[?] quiet all around gave her new strength; she felt like running, jumping, laughing...
She saw people dressed very lightly and comfortably; she too was already[?] in her dacha clothes, but her face remained serious, and, as in town, when she met people she wanted to avoid them.
But here something happened that she had not expected at all. The holidaymakers smiled at her as at an old acquaintance, and she answered them shyly with a yielding[?], gentle smile.
They asked her in a homely way whether she could swim, what was new in Zagłębie, and for how long she had come to Bystra.
She was quickly drawn into the warm, homely circle, and in the evening, at the dance, she became so friendly with one holidaymaker that she already had a feeling for him as for someone of her own. He was no younger than her husband. He became unusually attentive to her, looked at her with enraptured eyes and every so often discovered new virtues in her. She was intoxicated, and [he] carefully held her small, weak hand in his.
And together the holidaymakers danced in the brightly lit dance hall. Through the open door and through the large open windows a dark-blue, quiet night looked in. The music played merrily, and he, the new acquaintance, put his arm around her and whirled her around him. She had the feeling that the floor[?], the walls and the ceiling — everything, everything was dancing along with her. All at once she stopped and said to him:
— I can't dance any more.
He bowed to her and led her to the bench, a[?] bench by the wall, but she did not want to sit; she could not sit down there, because he would immediately sit down next to her..
Something began to annoy her, as if[?] she had been drawn into a game, and so she went outside.
— Allow me to accompany you — he offered politely.
She wanted to tell him to stay and not follow her, but the strange, unusually quiet darkness frightened her, and although her room was close to the casino[?], she was nevertheless afraid to walk alone. He gladly followed her outside, took her arm and tenderly led her down the few wide steps of the casino.
— To bed so early? — he asked her.
— Yes, I must — she answered.
— Yes, you must — he repeated after her — but let us take a little stroll.. may I?
She wanted to refuse him and could not. He led her along the half-lit, narrow and crooked dacha road, suddenly turned left, and it became dark. The dense trees blocked out all the light from the other side, but here the starry sky flared up even more brightly.
— Where to? — she started.
He sensed fear and unease in her voice and at once led her back to the lit road.
And that is how it began.
He gave in to her in everything and thereby won her trust. She let him embrace her and even kiss her, but the next day she could not write a letter to her husband; for a whole day she went about angry at her own wantonness, reproached herself for her frivolity, and decided to go to bed early and not to show herself to him, to her new friend.
But the splendid evening lured, drew... She went again, he met her with joy, he continued the game; she did not understand herself, did not believe herself, and he — he was very tender to her, and he emphasised his gratitude more and more with extraordinary attentiveness.
On the second and on the third day she again did not write to her husband. Only when she had let herself be mastered by the night-time[?] feeling, and when that which she had feared had already happened, did she wake at dawn and, still half asleep, write her husband the following little letter:
"My dear Aaron!
Forgive me for not writing to you at once; I was so taken by the new, wonderful, rustic surroundings that I went about like a drunk woman... I thank you very much for sending me to the dacha; it has so many virtues that one cannot count them all, but its chief virtue is that people make friends here very quickly.
Be well, I kiss you and I kiss the little children.
Your Rachel."
S. Tarczyński.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Ki Tetze)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] (Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Ki Tetze
—o—
a) "And thou wouldest take her to thee to wife" (Deut. 21:11)
"The Torah speaks only against the evil inclination: for if the Holy One, blessed be He, did not permit her, he would marry her in transgression." Rashi.
"Is it conceivable?" asked the Seer of Lublin — how can the Torah suspect a Jew that, if the beautiful captive is not permitted to him, he will marry her in transgression?
But here it speaks of Jews who persuade themselves that they have no sins, for "he who fears because of the sins in his hand" — he who is afraid that he has sins — does not go to war at all (and here, after all, it speaks of wartime: "When thou goest forth to war against thine enemies"); and a Jew who is so sure of himself that he has no sins — of him one can believe anything, him one may suspect...
• • •
"The Torah speaks only against the evil inclination" —
If "thou wouldest take her to thee to wife" — if you must toil hard for a living for wife and children, you will thereby already stand against the evil inclination: you will no longer have any "birdies"[?] in your head..
Toldot Yaakov Yosef.
—o—
b) "But he shall acknowledge the firstborn... by giving him a double portion" (ibid., 17)
Why do firstborns get a double share of the inheritance?
Because in olden times the firstborns were the priests; they were the holy ones and performed "the service". Therefore they took a double inheritance — just as later the priests were given gifts so that they would have something to live on, for they are not engaged in the settlement of the world, only in the service...
Sh. B.
—o—
c) "If a man have a stubborn and rebellious son" (ibid., 18)
Yechezkel Hoge, before he converted, was with the Seer of Lublin. The Seer called him[?] and foretold about him that his end would be that he would convert.
Once Count Czartoryski came to the Seer. The Seer honoured him greatly and received him almost as a [—] nobleman and a lover of Israel.
When the Count had driven off, the impudent Yechezkel says to the Seer:
"Rebbe! You persecute me because you fear that I will convert and become a gentile — yet the Count is already a gentile, and you honoured him so."
The Seer answers him:
"A stubborn and rebellious son is judged on account of his end. Because his end will be that he will rob people, therefore stoning is due to him. The commentators ask: why should so harsh a death as stoning be due to him? After all, the whole punishment comes to him only[?] because one day he will become a murderer and kill people — and then, even when he is a murderer, he would only[?] get death by the sword, which is much lighter. It must be, then, that becoming bad is much worse than the bad itself; it blemishes the soul more than the bad thing itself."
—o—
d) "Thou shalt not wear a mingled stuff (sha'atnez)" (22:11)
Reb Yisroel Salanter once met at a spa with Reb Shmuel of Lubavitch. The Rebbe, as was his custom, rode in a droshky to drink the water of the spring, surrounded by Hasidim and intimates, while Reb Yisroel went on foot.
Once the Rebbe, from the carriage, saw Reb Yisroel walking, and invited him up into the carriage. Reb Yisroel did not want to: there is a suspicion of the prohibition of sha'atnez in sitting on an upholstered carriage. The Rebbe, believing that this is Reb Yisroel's reason, says to him:
"The Shvut Yaakov permits it and holds that there is no suspicion of sha'atnez, and believe me, it is much easier to rely on the Shvut Yaakov than to go on foot."
"Yes," answers Reb Yisroel, "regarding the suspicion of sha'atnez one can indeed rely on the Shvut Yaakov; but what about the suspicion of pride? On whom can one rely there?..."
—o—
e) "And the damsel's father shall say" (ibid., 16)
Before a well-known Polish rabbi and gaon there took place a din Torah between a present-day Rebbe and his wife. At the din Torah the wife enumerated her husband's faults; the Rebbe stood up and said to the rabbi:
"On the verse 'And the damsel's father shall say' Rashi says: 'A woman has no licence to speak in the presence of the man.' So why do you allow the woman to speak out against me like this?"
The gaon answers him:
"You have forgotten another verse. On the verse 'And they shall say unto the elders of his city' the Targum Yonatan says: 'And they shall say to the sages of the city: [he is] a transgressor[?] against the word, the decree of God.' [—] there it is said 'And they shall say' — both of them said it, she too. So you see that a woman may indeed enumerate faults in her husband's presence."
—o—
f) "A perfect and just weight shalt thou have" (25:15)
Truth is naked — writes Rabbi Aharon Shmuel Tamaret, "one of the sensitive rabbis" — and people are modest; that is why there are so few willing to be bold enough to approach it.
• • •
"Truth springs out of the earth" —
And what is the sowing of truth? — the old Kotzker [Rebbe] was asked.
"Falsehood!" he answered. "When falsehood is buried — truth grows out."
“The World Is Turning Upside Down”..

[Essay — "the end of the world"; social psychology.]
A "terrible" piece of news appeared last week in the newspapers: "this month the world turns upside down". The news aroused an impressionable mood in society, and looking at people's faces the question arose: what do they say? Do they recall Rodin's picture, which represents protest[?] — with goggling eyes, a half-open mouth and widened nostrils — and asks in a tone of half-resignation: will his light be extinguished? Or perhaps the faces express great enthusiasm and smile[?] as if to say: enough! Let the world turn upside down already!
Yes, the faces expressed the second eventuality, and they reveal a deep psychological background. People wish that the world would perish, and in that they see a satisfaction for their suffering and pain — because they are weak. For what is the psychology of a weak man? To react to the blows he receives; and since he cannot hit back, he must seek a moral satisfaction. He prays that the whole world turn upside down, as long as the stronger one also falls.
And indeed, people are already — it seems to me — [weary?] of suffering; they waited for a satisfaction, but it did not come. In this case too we can find a gladdening phenomenon: it is still good that people want the world to turn upside down — it is, after all, a sign that they believe that what exists is bad.
Yes, how many years must one sometimes wait until people acquire an awareness of their situation...
Tsimuki.
A. Zaglembier — The Living Corpse (22)

[Serial novel.] (A highly gripping novel of Jewish life in Zagłębie before and during the World War.)
And now, when an opportunity arose — when he "earned" a larger sum in a bank at one stroke — he was at last able to get back [?] into his former skin. He left his bloody gang, went off to distant New York, hid his eyes behind a pair of big glasses and began the new life...
But he still remained lonely. Despite all his searching he did not manage to find a single one of his closest relatives, with whom he would so much have liked to share his present wealth...
And so it went on for a long time, until he noticed his newly hired [—] [?] — Betty Grinwald [?]...
And although "Mister Plank" was already past his sixties, he suddenly felt his heart stir with so many new, long-forgotten feelings... All women had been indifferent to him, and precisely those who tried to match themselves to him — from them he ran away. But regarding "Betty" the other employees made [?] no secret of it, telling [?] her, not without envy:
— Betty, she'll yet be our boss's lady...
"Betty" was embarrassed, though she too was drawn to "Mister Plank", precisely because he treated her quite differently from all the others: he never got angry at her, never made the slightest reproach, and once, when "Betty" felt a little unwell, Mister Plank came over to her. "Betty" stood frozen in fright, thinking the boss would shout at her. But Mister Plank asked her in a fatherly way what was wrong, and she could stay home another day if she still felt weak.
And then for the first time their eyes met with that unique look that draws one in...
— Today I'll drive you home in the car — Mister Plank said to her — you'll wait until everyone has left, all right?
Blumke did not answer; her heart began to pound, but not from fear — something told her that this man wished her well.
But why? — she asked herself — doesn't he also mean "such a way"?. [sic]
And with an even more fluttering heart she got into the car that evening, in which "Mister Plank" wanted to drive her home. She sat beside him. But halfway there the boss suddenly addresses her:
— Miss Betty, I have long wanted to invite you to my place.
Blumke takes fright. She trembles [?] from head to toe and, not knowing what to answer in the first minute, said as though she had not heard his words:
— What?..
"Mister Plank", holding the steering wheel of the car in his hands, leans a little toward her and repeats:
— Miss Betty, I would like you to visit my house.
— What? Now.. Her heart does not stop pounding.
And evidently understanding her fear, the fright of a young girl before an older, unknown man, "Mister Plank" hastened to reassure her:
— Don't think that I am out to do you any harm. There are indeed many people who are only out to exploit another's loneliness [?], but believe me, I am not one of them, I am not one of those lechers who mean to take advantage of their female employees that way. Believe me, Miss Betty!
She becomes even more confused, stammers something:
— Yes, but...
And he goes on speaking, words one feels come from the depths of the heart:
— I simply want to sit with you a little at the table and talk, nothing more. I don't know whether you can understand me; you are still a young lady and perhaps not very experienced. I am also not as old as I look, but life does that... I am rich, I have a big business, I lack [?] nothing [?], people envy me — but if you only knew how lonely I am in the world and how often I feel so unhappy. Simply [?] because of that...
— Why? — asks Blumke, and instead of her earlier fear she is overcome by pity for the man she had been afraid of.
— Why? — answers "Mister Plank" with a heavy sigh — Not here; in the car is the place to tell about it... [sic; presumably "is not the place"] Certainly [?] I once had a wife, children; my daughter, the eldest, would by now have to be your age — but where are they?.. Ah, the accursed war tore my life apart too...
— I don't understand — says Blumke naively — you don't know?
— Believe me, I have spent plenty on it already, I have done everything, because I often think: I work, I amass a fortune, but for whom? For whom?..
And suddenly, turning into another street, "Mister Plank" exclaims:
— [—] [?], Miss Betty, we are already approaching your house; you can still decide, and we will turn toward my place.
But Blumke has not yet made up her mind. She answers:
— Forgive me very much, Mister Plank, but not today, I'm not feeling quite myself...
— God forbid, I won't force you, but consider, Miss Betty, you are the first whom I would like to have as a guest at my home, and perhaps more.. I don't know why, but one doesn't question the heart...
And they parted not as a boss with his chosen employee, nor as with a sweetheart, but really as friends, though they still knew each other so little.
Like one born anew, "Mister Plank" came home to his rich apartment, from which so much gloom and loneliness weeps — but not now... Somehow he now felt cheered and more at home; the thoughts of his hard past suddenly left him, because he had begun to see some unknown but bright future thanks to the meeting with "Betty"...
(To be continued.)
“The Ladle” — Then and Now:

[“Der Kokh-Lefl” (The Ladle) — humour page.] Once a bride and groom were not allowed to see each other before the wedding, but they could see each other after the wedding. Today they see each other before the wedding, and after the wedding they don't look at one another.

Once a boy put on tefillin for the first time at his bar mitzvah. Today a boy puts on tefillin at his bar mitzvah for the last time.

Once the wife used to search in the husband's [?] trousers; today the husband searches in the wife's trousers.
—o—
Unhappy Women, Poor Things!
A Justified Complaint of a Jewish Woman
In a Hasidic boarding-house [?] a woman says to a man:
— For us women it is always worse than for you men; even in the Ten Commandments we women were wronged.
— In what way?
— You men were given 10 commandments, and we only 9.
— How so?
— Well, yes. What has the commandment “Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's wife” to do with us women? It means only you, men!
—o—
Tragic Incident in Krynica.
The park keeper in Krynica found a couple in an unconscious state. As it turned out, the couple were a bride and groom who had gone into the park to enjoy a little fresh air. The sharp air took the couple's breath away so badly that they collapsed...
The summoned doctor of the emergency service [pogotowie] revived the couple and drove them in the carriage to the rabbinate, where they received marriage certificates [?]...
—o—
Angina Once Again!...
The Boss's Advice.
The bookkeeper of a Sosnowiec firm telephones the boss that he is sick with angina and will not come to work.
That same evening [?] the boss meets the bookkeeper in Katowice with a pretty young girl. He calls him aside and says into his ear:
— Sir [“Panie”], when one has such an angina, one doesn't go out with her...
Coming Back from the Dachas.

[“The Ladle” — humorous poem.] Gone is the summer, over the dachas [summer cottages],
Over the joy, over the love and the luck,
Carters stream in from all the highways —
O straw widowers [husbands whose wives are away on holiday], enough of your merriment,
The wives are coming back...

They come back with sunburnt faces
Just like the copper pots..
They come from Bystra, Ustroń and Rajcza
Back to their dear husbands..

They have even put on themselves
This one a couple of “rekl” [?] and that one also a hernia [“kile”; perhaps a pun on “kilo”]..
Strolled in the woods in trousers, in pyjamas,
Daughters and mothers flirted...

The bright summer has already flowed away,
Its charm and its beauty are already past,
And woe to him who did not enjoy
The beauty of summer, the magic of May...

The poor husbands, the straw widowers,
Prepare an excuse with sense and reason,
When the bright [?] wives put the question [?]
As if summoning to the Day of Judgement.

When the little wife [—] a heavy list
Of questions, of harsh demands [?]:
Did a neighbour come over [?] as a guest,
Did he take a “ponczoszka” [?, stocking — pończoszka] from her,
And when did you go to sleep?..

O husbands, remember what you have to bluff:
Tell them that you haven't slept a single night
From longing for your wife... What do you care?
It is, after all, a mitzvah to fool a little wife,
Because one thing — this you should keep in mind:
That at the dacha she fooled you even more..
Graf Koli.
The Zagłębie Staff Is Ready

[Zagłębie — satire, Zionism.] Zagłębie does not sleep, does not rest; it works, toils, sweats and helps to set up and revive the Jewish state [after the Peel partition plan].
There are even some who still have on their minds a livelihood, rent money and similar trifles, but these are “lost crooked heads”. The whole of Jewish Zagłębie needs nothing more today; it has forgotten all worries and only one thing interests it: how best to safeguard the Jewish state, how to make sure it has a lasting existence, conducts itself decently, in order, and is a model for the world! And thinking so, one came to the conclusion that it would be best to safeguard the Jewish state with our own home-grown staff.
Prime Minister — Comrade Yakub Volbert [?]. He has a far-sighted view and a broad scope; proof [?] — the victory of his Et Livnot list in the Congress elections, his wise advice at every meeting; a cabinet may be entrusted to his hands.
Foreign Minister — Madame [?] Dok-torda [?] Niewarżyuska [?] (Sosnowiec). She possesses elasticity [?], is no stubborn one, is as if born for diplomatic negotiations; indeed there is no woman foreign minister in Europe.
Minister of the Interior — the young town councillor Mikhl Zelig, if at the End of Days “and a little child shall lead them” must also come true.
Minister of Justice — one of the arbitrators of “Helena” [?], Reb Dovid Lererman. For years he has been studying this kind of arbitration, and he is the best and cleverest of the legal experts. He will take his whole staff with him, even Reb Avrom Malkhn.
Minister of Finance — Reb Zalmen Polk. He studied it as a long-time authorized agent [?] of Keren Hayesod.
Minister of Education and Religions — Reb Leybish Heytsbikh [?]. This famous leader of Mizrachi stands out for his enormous [?] tolerance, and therefore foreign religions may entrust their fate to him.
One of the ministerial posts [?] could have been entrusted to Reb Mendele Maligevats [?], but he must be kept in reserve, because later an assassination attempt will have to be carried out in the Jewish state — and that is his specialty.
Comrade Shteynerlibt [?] is designated minister without portfolio; his work will be to calm tempers, conclude compromises and in general bring about consolidation, as he has been doing successfully for so many years in Będzin.
Having put together this staff, we hold that Zagłębie has thereby saved the Jewish state.
A Shvartser [“A Black One”].
“Yes” and “No”.

[“The Ladle” — humour, politics and taxes.] These two words play a very important role today.
If, for example, one were to ask the 20 million Polish citizens: who wants a partition [of Palestine, per the Peel plan — enabling Jewish emigration]? 19,999,999 votes will answer “yes” and 1 vote “no”. (That one will also have to be photographed.)
Should new taxes be introduced? 20 million citizens will answer “no”.
Do we need the tax-assessment commissions? 99 per cent of the population will say “no” and 1 per cent (the assessors) “yes”.
Do the Zagłębie kehillas exempt the needy among the Jewish population [from the kehilla tax]? Everyone will answer “no”, and the bench-squeezers [?] — “yes”.
He Only Wants to Listen!..

[“The Ladle” — joke, Będzin.] A Będzin Jew in Paris.
An elderly Jew from Będzin travelled to the Exhibition [the 1937 Paris World Exposition]. While in Paris, one day he wanted to have a peek into one of the Parisian cabarets. Coming up to the box office, he asks:
— How much is a ticket?
— Thirty francs.
— What? Thirty francs? A relative of mine was here two years ago and paid only ten francs for a ticket.
— Yes, that's true, but back then there were no such performers [?] as today. If you want to go to such a famous artiste, you must pay thirty francs.
— Don't talk impudence [?], I only want to listen! — the Jew answered.
A Lightning Flash Costs No Money.

What they tell about a stingy Sosnowiec rich man.
The Sosnowiec rich man B., who is known as a great miser, is now staying with his family at a summer residence in the Beskids. One of these days[?] he is sitting with his wife on the veranda; suddenly it began to thunder and lighten. The wife took fright and out of fear dropped[?] 10 groszy; she takes a wax candle and wants to light it to look for the coin. B. grabs her by the hand:
— Wait a minute, don't go lighting wax candles; any moment there will be a flash of lightning and it will be bright in your eyes. A wax candle costs money, and a lightning flash you can have for free.
Poor Summer Holidaymaker, Alas!

Arriving safely in Rajcza on Friday evening, the holidaymaker says[?] to his holidaymaking wife:
— Listen, wifey, what a journey I had! On the train I stood on my feet the whole way from Sosnowiec to Rajcza.
— Really? And your feet don't hurt you at all?
— Silly, was I standing on my own feet?..
A Cantor for the High Holidays

An advertisement by a hotel owner in a Jewish newspaper, in large letters:
Cantor wanted!
The cantor must be an ordinary man and a very[?] cheap one. He must be, if possible, a widower or an old bachelor. He must be physically strong. He must weigh from 180 to 190 pounds; his voice must be a strong one, a baritone. If he is a Litvak, he had better stay at home — we want to hear the proper Hebrew; our worshippers are Polish. He must have a little beard, a pointed one; he must also be tall; he must be a jolly fellow with a gentle smile on his face and not very pious; he must know how to sing songs, dance with the fair sex and tell peppery jokes; he must also be able to tinkle a little on the piano, and above all he must be a handsome person, someone worth taking a look at.
If such a one can be found, let him reply at once and state his price. We cannot give much, because we do not charge our guests for tickets[?]. The most we can give is 100 zł. with board and lodging.
Respectfully, Yaakov Moshe Dalfon, owner of the Hotel „Grandiose“. Answer at once.
On the fourth[?] day the hotel owner received the following letter from a cantor:
Esteemed Mr. Dalfon!
I have read your advertisement and cannot make head or tail of it. You say — just a cantor, but you do not say what sort of cantor you want: a leader of Shacharit, of Musaf, a shofar-blower or a Torah reader. Since not every cantor possesses all the qualities I have listed here — but I do possess all these qualities. I am a leader of Shacharit, of Musaf, a shofar-blower and a Torah reader. With me you can plug all the holes, as you see.. And handsome I am, and healthy I am, and dancing with women and girls I can[?], and playing a good game of poker I can too, and telling a „treyf“ [dirty] joke I can too, and as for weight — I weigh 200 pounds, I am six feet tall, I have a baritone voice, I am strong, a giant. Besides praying, reading the Torah and blowing the shofar, I can also wash floors[?], chop wood, heat the stove, carry out the rubbish, and, as you see, Mr. Dalfon, I am a useful man.
But one thing I must tell you, what I am not. I am very far from knowing Hebrew; that is the plain truth. I want you to know this: I make more mistakes in the prayers than you can imagine. From all the mistakes I make one could publish two festival prayer books, and there would still be enough left for a small one.
And if your guests know Hebrew well, you must look for another cantor; and if they themselves make mistakes, I will be a great success with them...
As for the price, we shall come to terms, of course. 100 zł. is no price at all. The main thing is whether you are[?] happy to have a cantor who makes a lot of mistakes in his Hebrew.
Let me know at once what you think of me, because I do not want to lose any post and[?] another position.
Respectfully: Binyamin the Cantor.
P.S. — Let me know too whether you have a good cook; if not, I will bring along my wife, with whom I have been sweating it out[?] for six years now. A pretty little wife and a great homemaker.
„The same“.
Four days before Rosh Hashanah the hotel owner answered the cantor:
„Esteemed Cantor!
I accept your candidacy; I like you already, although I have not yet seen you in person. I like your frankness, your telling the truth.
That you make a lot of mistakes in your Hebrew is nonsense [lit. „mud“]. In truth our guests do not pray at all. They run away from prayer as from a fire, and those who do pray come out only to fulfil the obligation and then run off at once for a stroll. Others sit and play cards, others clean their fingernails, still others sleep like the dead — so you need not be afraid of mistakes...
What I like most is that, besides praying, you will also be able to be a servant: wash the floors[?], heat the stove and carry out the rubbish...
That quality matters more to me than the whole art of cantorship. As long as you are a handsome young man, tall, strong, and can dance with women and tell off-colour [lit. „left-wing“] jokes.
Come at once, and we will not go to the rabbi [to haggle]; ten gulden more plays no role, as long as I have the real cantor, the proper prayer-leader.
Respectfully,
Chaim Dalfon“.
P.S. — Bring along a couple of packs of cards, new ones, not marked, and if possible bring a good quantity of schnapps, thin[?] and watery; and you may bring your wife along too — I want to have a look at her; perhaps she will be able to stay with me at the hotel through the whole winter.
„The same“.
If you want to know how it ended, I will tell you that this cantor had a great success — not, God forbid, with his praying, but with his mistakes, his dirty jokes and his dancing.
G. K-r.
Conference with the owners of the hairdressing establishments about keeping the Sabbath.

The rabbinate called the owners of the Jewish hairdressing establishments to a conference on the question of having the „rezures“[?] (apparently: the salons) closed on the Sabbath.
The owners of the hairdressing establishments gave their consent to this on condition that the rabbinate exert its influence on Jewish youth to come for their shaves on weekdays, not on the Sabbath.
During the conference the hairdressers raised the conduct of Jewish women: not only those of „better society“, but also daughters of Hasidic parents avoid the Jewish hairdressing establishments.
The outcome was that it was resolved that the rabbinate should issue a proper public proclamation (kol kore) on the matter.
Struggle between poultry dealers and the rabbinate over supervisors (ne'emanim)

For two weeks now the struggle has been going on between the rabbinate and the dealers in slaughtered poultry. The struggle is taking place because of the rabbinate's decision that at every point of sale of slaughtered poultry there should be a ne'eman [kashrut supervisor], to which the poultry dealers do not agree.
Support the holiday campaign of „Beit Lechem“.

As every year, the society „Beit Lechem“ is this year too conducting a flour[?] campaign, which begins already in the first days of next week. One must, however, take into account that this year's holidays will be very[?] hard for the less well-off part of the Jewish population; therefore everyone who is able should support the campaign, so that the society „Beit Lechem“ has the necessary means to fulfil its task towards the large number of families who have already applied for support for the coming holidays.
Bought a „bargain“.

The day before yesterday[?] an unknown Jewish woman came into Balizar-ski's[?] jewellery shop in „Nevags“[?] to sell a few diamonds which she had happened to buy as a „bargain“.
Only in the shop did she learn that such „diamonds“ can be bought even cheaper in any jewellery shop.
Trying to save a bicycle, he himself drowned.

A terrible accident happened here which cost the life of the worker Stefan Dzienecki[?] of Warsaw. Dzienecki, riding home from Będzin on a bicycle, fell on the bank of the „Przemsza“ on Podzamcze[?] street, and the bicycle fell into the water.
Trying to save the bicycle, Dzienecki went into the water and drowned.
The half-colony — solemnly concluded.

The half-colony (day camp) for Jewish children was concluded in a festive manner.
Present were: the committee, the school guardians[?] (opiekunki), vice-president [deputy mayor] Mr. Gak[?], alderman (ławnik) G. Rechnik, director Mr. Wachyrowski[?] and others.
In the name of the colony committee Mr. D. Gutensztajn welcomed the representatives of the municipal administration and delivered a report on the activity.
The report shows that about 220 children from the poorest strata received food 3 times a day for 20 days.
In conclusion Mr. Gutensztajn appealed to the representatives of the magistrate that a larger sum be earmarked in the new budget for the half-colony for Jewish children.
Vice-president Mr. Gak[?] expressed his satisfaction with the work of the committee and staff and declared that next year a larger sum will be earmarked for this purpose.
After the children's performance Mr. Gak[?] donated 10 zł. for sweets, and at his request a photograph was taken.
Support from relatives in America.

We draw the attention of all those interested who wish to receive support from family or friends in America: they should apply at the premises of the local kehilla during office hours, from 8 to 3, where they will be informed about the way to make their applications to their relatives in America.
A burglary at a summer residence.

In the night from Friday to Saturday thieves got in through the open window on the first floor of Mrs. Dąb's[?] apartment in the villa „Szelonka“[?] in Bystra, from where they took several suitcases with clothes. The damage amounts to about 1 200 zł.
Convention of Small Traders.

[Będzin — small trade.]
This coming Sunday a convention of all the small traders' associations of the entire Kielce voivodeship will take place in Częstochowa.
The small traders' associations of Sosnowiec and Będzin will be represented by a large number of delegates.
From Brit HaTzohar

[Będzin — Revisionist Zionism.]
In the Brit HaTzohar's own premises a lecture will be given on Saturday afternoon by Mr. D. Wasser[?] (Katowice) on the subject “On the Threshold[?] of the Jewish State”.
50 Percent of the Jewish Population Eat “Shot” Meat. So the Shochtim Declare.

[Sosnowiec — ritual slaughter, kashrut.]
The local shochtim [ritual slaughterers] came to the premises of the kehilla on a visit[?], [declaring] that they can prove with glaring facts that 50 percent of the local Jewish population eat “shot” meat [from animals killed with a stunning gun, i.e. not ritually slaughtered], which is sold in the butcher shops as kosher.
In connection with this a conference took place between the kehilla administration and the local rabbinate, which decided that this Sabbath the matter should be spoken about in all the larger local houses of prayer, and the Jewish population should be warned to buy meat only in the licensed butcher shops.
—o—
A Trade School at the Talmud Torah.
The administration of the local Talmud Torah has decided to undertake a campaign to create a trade school at the Talmud Torah. As the chairman, Mr. L. Szwajcer, informs us, a fund-raising collection is being undertaken for this purpose, and if the Jewish public shows its goodwill, the plan will be realized in the near future.
Don't Go Where You're Not Wanted... A Defeat for Our Shmendriks at a Local Night Spot.

[Sosnowiec — social life, antisemitism.]
There is a night spot here where the Jew is not a welcome guest — plainly and simply, the Jew is not gladly seen. But our shmendriks [good-for-nothings] take pleasure precisely in pushing their way in there, where they are not wanted, and waiting until they are asked to kindly leave the premises.
Just such a scene took place in recent days with a couple of shmendriks who were sitting in this night spot and had settled down[?] at a table. Then one of the waiters came up to them and pointed out that “this is not a waiting room”. When one of the Jewish guests reacted to this, he received a clear answer: “What are you coming in here for? We don't want you here...”
—o—
Appeal to the Supervisory Authority to Increase the Meat Quota for the Holidays.
In connection with the approaching holidays the kehilla administration has appealed to the supervisory authority with a request to increase the meat quota for the Jewish population and also to permit the butcher shops and grocery stores to be open from 8 to 10 in the morning on the Sundays that fall on the eve of a holiday.
From a Woman — to a Man.

[Sosnowiec — courts.]
In the legal circles of Zagłębie a great sensation has been aroused by the case of a certain woman, Bednarska, a resident of the Niemce[?] colony, who is endeavouring to be recognized as a man, and to this end she applied to the District Court in Sosnowiec concerning the change of her first name and surname.
The woman was examined by doctors. Professor Dr. Olbrycht, director of the Institute of Forensic Medicine in Kraków, sent a detailed explanation according to which the woman's demand to be recognized as a man is legally justified.
As planned, the interesting case is to take place in the civil division of the local District Court and is to begin next month.
A Housewife Seeks a Jewish Maid. The Husband Comes to the Editorial Office with an Interesting Question.

[Sosnowiec — society, domestic servants.]
In a local Jewish family a Christian maid is in service; they keep her there like the apple of their eye, she lacks nothing in food and drink and a good bed, and the lady of the house treats her gently and does not drive her at work.
And the house there is a real find — guests almost every day[?], they play poker and bridge, and a few groszy fall to the maid.
In short, the lady of the house assures us that the girl lives with her as in paradise, which can be translated into prosaic language: she does not have a bad position.
Now a black cat has run between the maid and the lady of the house.
The lady of the house had been away[?] at a summer residence, and on returning she brought the maid a present: a pair of silk stockings and some other trifles.
But the girl was not satisfied — too small a present; she had guarded the house faithfully and honestly, so she had expected something better.
And the girl and the lady of the house fell out.
And the lady of the house made up her mind that she would now like a Jewish servant girl.
But where does one get a Jewish servant girl? At the placement agents' there are only Christian girls, and in any case she does not take anyone from an agent, only on a recommendation — and nobody knows of any Jewish maid; this species has died out!
So the husband comes to the editorial office to ask a question:
The Jews in the small towns are in such dire straits, after all; there are families who have been left without bread — why shouldn't a girl from such a suffering family come to the city? She would provide for herself and could even send something to her father and mother.
Formerly[?], before the war, in the time of good fortune and prosperity, before one knew of today's troubles, Jewish girls from the small towns of the Kielce voivodeship used to come to Zagłębie, take positions as maids and save up a little money for a dowry; and today this is not to be found — people starve at home and do not go into service with strangers. Why?
We publish this question and believe that it concerns not only that family of the pair of stockings, but many Jewish housewives and even more so poor Jewish girls.
Perhaps the local Jewish Women's Association might take an interest in the matter.

The “Probation Period” for Employees May Last Only 3 Months

[Law — labour law; Supreme Court ruling.] A very important ruling was handed down these days by the Supreme Court on the question whether an employer may engage a white-collar employee on a probation period lasting longer than 3 months.
In a concrete case, after one month of probation, the boss kept the employee on probation for another 6 months and then dismissed him without compensation.
The Supreme Court recognised that the second agreement was binding for only 2 months, and that thereafter the same laws apply to him as to other employees.
A Landowner's Wife Instructs Before Her Death That a Jew Should Bury Her.

[Kielce — from the region.]
In the Kielce area there is an estate (majątek), Janowice [?], belonging to a rich landowner. The landowner's mother-in-law, already a very old woman, fell ill and her days were numbered.
A few days before her death the old woman dreamed that she would go straight to Paradise if her grave were dug by a Jew. With her last strength she told her daughter about her dream, and shortly afterwards [?] she died.
The landowner decided to fulfil the wish of his late mother-in-law. He called a poor Jew [?] to the cemetery (cmentarz), who dug a grave in which the deceased was buried; on the Christian public present [?] the sight of a Jew digging a grave in the cemetery made a strange impression.
After the “pogrzeb” [funeral] the landowner paid the Jew 18 gulden [złoty], a litre of vodka with a [—] [?], and thanked him very much [?].
The pious Jew went home satisfied, with a few gulden in his pocket and with the [—] [?], and he did indeed pray to the Almighty that the landowner's mother-in-law should have a bright Paradise.
The House of the Kielce Bank Ludowy Is Being Sold! — Stormy General Meeting of the People's Bank

[Kielce — economy.]
A few days ago the general meeting of the former People's Bank (Bank Ludowy) took place. The meeting was a very stormy one. During the discussion, which lasted several hours, various painful incidents occurred between some of the members, the liquidators [and] the supervisory board [?].
By a majority of votes it was decided to sell the large house at Leonarda 23, in order to cover part of the debt to the “Joint” [JDC].
Present at the meeting was a representative of the Auditing Union, Mr. Szpigler.
Peasants' and Workers' Demonstration in Kielce, in Honour of the Holiday of the “Miracle on the Vistula”.

[Kielce — politics.]

On the market square (Bazaar Square) a large rally was held, at which several speakers appeared, among them the secretary of the Kielce PPS, Mr. Śliwiński, who spoke about antisemitism.
Several Endek students, who tried to disrupt the demonstration and began to stage an anti-Jewish demonstration, were driven away by those assembled.

All Jewish Apprentices Must Enrol in the Vocational Supplementary Schools.

[Jewish crafts — announcement.]
On the 25th of this month enrolment in the vocational supplementary schools will already begin.
All apprentice boys and apprentice girls from the age of 15 upward who are employed in workshops must enrol in these schools.
It is superfluous to stress the importance of enrolling in and attending the vocational supplementary schools. It is enough merely to mention that according to the law only those who present a certificate from a vocational supplementary school are admitted to the journeyman's examinations.
In this connection the United Committee for the Affairs of Jewish Crafts has already sent to all localities in the country where united committees, artisans' associations, guilds and trade associations are active all the necessary materials, legal instructions, as well as a larger number of posters calling on the Jewish working youth employed in workshops to enrol without fail in the vocational supplementary schools.
The United Committee for the Affairs of Jewish Crafts calls on [?] all local committees, as well as all trade associations, guilds and artisans' associations, to influence all their members, the parents and the apprentice youth itself, not to miss the deadline and to enrol the apprentice boys and girls en masse in the vocational supplementary schools.
Localities which for whatever reason have not received the materials sent out must immediately notify the United Committee for the Affairs of Jewish Crafts in Warsaw (Zilka [?] 23, flat 4).

A kohen married a divorcee... — the finale of the fictitious weddings

We are written from Olkusz:
Some years ago, at the very height of the aliyah to Eretz Israel, a young man came here from Eretz Israel who, for a certain payment, betrothed (by kiddushin) the daughter of a respected local Jewish family, so that she could emigrate to Eretz Israel.
After the "wedding" the young man went back to Eretz Israel, promising that he would soon send for her; but as it later turned out, she was deceived, and instead of emigration papers she received a "get" (bill of divorce) from a certain "rabbi" in Petah Tikva.
A few weeks ago the girl married... a kohen, and here the question arises: are the first, fictitious kiddushin valid or not? For if the kiddushin are valid, a kohen may not marry a divorcee.
With this question the local rabbi has turned to several of the great halakhic authorities; meanwhile the whole town is in a whirl...
The First Appearance

[Będzin — culture and theatre.]
(On the staging of the play "The Voice of Blood".)
There were times when various music and choral societies existed in Będzin, drama groups which from time to time "staged theatre performances and concerts. Every appearance of a "Muza" [?], of a "choral society", was a holiday for progressive Jewish society. Of all that a heap of ruins is left. There is no institution at all in Będzin that would conduct broad social-cultural activity; a complete lack [?] prevails in this field. A lax [?], easy-going mood prevails today in the Jewish street. If one can speak at all of some cultural activity in our town, there is the Society for Knowledge of the Land (Landkentenish) and the Kibbutz; apart from these two bodies absolute quiet reigns.
• • •
The management of the drama studio at the Kibbutz did well in choosing Y. D. Berkowitz's play. The play is not a new one, but the problems are always old and eternally new.
We shall briefly give the plot: in a town there lived a bad Jew, whom they called Moshke Chazir ("Moshke the Pig"). For various reasons he converted and married a village shiksa, who bore him a son. He married the son off to a Jewish girl from the town. Although he lived on good terms with his peasant neighbours, deep in his heart he was their enemy; within this same Moshke Chazir a hidden love lay dormant, a feeling for his people. Once, on Yom Kippur, the peasants of the surrounding villages fell upon the town, slaughtered women and old men and made a ruin-heap of the little town. Then the "pintele yid" (the Jewish spark) awoke in Moshke Chazir, and a feeling of pity seized him for the whole people, hunted, tortured and murdered. To him, to Moshke Chazir, into his house, two Jews escaping the Russian pogrom burst in, a father and his daughter, and Moshke hides them in his cellar. The peasants of his village learn of it, and his best friends and neighbours come with a whole gang of peasants and by force break open the cellar, and the two Jews, the father and his daughter, together with several more Jews, are butchered; Moshke's son too takes part in the "holy work". In Moshke's soul a struggle takes place between Jew and Christian, and when the peasants want to settle accounts with Moshke as well, he sets fire to the house and all his property, and with the siddur [?] on his heart he is burned in the fire.
• • •
As for the staging, one must understand that it is the first play, and all beginnings are hard. Despite this the first performance was not bad, and some scenes were even good. We saw before us young working people who after a working day devote themselves heart and soul to their own artistic formation.
Fine characters were created by: the Russian peasant woman Akhinat [?] (Gitl [?] Steinman), Moshke Chazir (Ts. [?] Wilgerman), the priest Piatak (Ratskazich [?]).
The director M. Mielnik [?] invested much effort and work. It is his first debut; we await further ones, and above all a topical play.
Tsvi Paliwoda.
