[Dąbrowa — kehilla; followed by three short items.]
Meeting of the Kehilla Council.
Last Sunday afternoon a meeting of the local kehilla council took place; on the agenda were a number of “urgent” questions which, no doubt, “must” be resolved in the days before the holiday, for example, acquainting the new councillors (parnassim) with the regulations, the report of the former kehilla board, and the like.
The chairman of the council, Mr. Y. Rozenboym, opens the meeting and warns the “gallery” to keep quiet; if not — he warns — the gallery will be abolished at the next meetings.
Before the agenda, councillor Eisenman (Agudah) turns to the chairman with the question whether it will be permitted to read declarations of the factions that did not read [theirs] at the first council meeting. A lengthy discussion follows, with “yes” and “no” speakers, but since the chairman had promised at the first meeting that the “non-readers” would be able to read at a second meeting, the promise is kept and they read...
In the name of the Zionist organisation, councillor Dr. Steinberg reads a declaration in which the Zionist demands in the kehilla are set out, in particular that it will not be permitted for the kehilla machinations practised until now to be carried on under the cloak of hypocrisy.
In the name of “Agudat Israel” — councillor Ch. M. Eisenman; the “gist” [?] of his declaration is that Dąbrowa needs a rabbinical authority...
After the “reading”, the item concerning the regulations is dealt with. On the motion of Dr. Steinberg it is resolved that a copy of the regulations be sent to each councillor so that he may acquaint himself with it.
The second item, the report on the activity of the outgoing kehilla board, remains “hanging in the air”, because none of the board members present, headed by the vice-president, were authorised to deliver the report to the plenum of the council. The task is, however, carried out by the chairman, who relates a series of facts about the “good” kehilla management. Among other things, Mr. Rozenboym reports that the lamps of the synagogue were used in the kehilla office, and the synagogue was dark.
Under the item of free motions, councillor Jakubowicz [?] raises the question of creating a council (va'ad) of the Zagłębie kehillot, with the Dąbrowa kehilla to take the initiative upon itself. It is resolved that the proposal be dealt with at the next meeting.

From Year to Year — A Survey of Jewish Communal Life in Zagłębie in the Year 5697

A year of hard experiences we bid farewell to the day after tomorrow. The Jewish settlements in Zagłębie are links [?] in the chain of Jewish settlements throughout the whole country and the whole world, and therefore our Zagłębie account, too, cannot look any different from the balance that the entire Jewish people is drawing up today.
This year sad events took place in Brisk [Brześć], Częstochowa and other towns and shtetls. In the year 5696 the Endecja [National Democrats] began to try out [?] its antisemitic claws, set up "pickets" around the Jewish shops [?], terrorized the Jewish merchants. The period of throwing [?] stones and petards into Jewish shops, which did not spare even the health of peaceful Jewish passers-by in the suburban streets, intended in this way to force [?] the Polish population to take the Endek path and deepen the antagonism — to build up artificially the hatred between the Jewish and the Christian population.
Today, looking back, we can state with satisfaction that that well-known Endek campaign achieved only outwardly a partial effect. In depth it did not strike [root], and, despite the poisonous [?] incitement, the Polish population was scarcely carried away by it and did not let itself be thrown into a sea of hatred towards its fellow citizens.
In merchant circles the idea was born of creating a body that would represent Jewish Zagłębie. To this day the Jewish public does not know what these attempts looked like: they managed to seat [?] at one table the very top of the Jewish civic (bourgeois) parties and organizations, a series of legal and organizational steps were taken in order to set up such a representation — and yet they got stuck in a narrow corner, and for half a year already the matter has not budged.
Evidently such an institution cannot be created artificially, even when [?] the will of individuals may be the very best.
—
One feels [?] a great many [?] of the Jewish economic positions in Zagłębie slipping away; but how shall we protect [?] these positions? There are hardly any. Jews trade, trade — but as if in the air. No merchant knows on whom and on what he relies; Jewish commerce vegetates, receives no support in the form of credit and depends exclusively on its own strength; there is nowhere to obtain statistical information on the state of Jewish economic life here; our Jewish economic organizations take no interest in such things — so we do not even know where we stand in the world. The Jewish councillors (radcy), both in the Chamber of Crafts and in the Chamber of Commerce, have ever less influence; the Jewish artisan, too, did not make use of the credits theoretically earmarked for him at the B.G.K. [Bank Gospodarstwa Krajowego], as a result of which the Jewish position in the economic institutions has been weakened still further.
The Discount Bank in Będzin has been saved, but it has still not managed to arouse towards itself the necessary interest that such an institution must have in order to be able to fulfil completely its credit tasks for the Jewish merchant and artisan.
Sosnowiec is still under the effect of the deep blow of the Merchants' Bank, which further [?], through a lack of responsibility among people, was brought to compulsory liquidation. The Sosnowiec merchants unfortunately still do not understand that a slaughterer's knife is stretched over their necks, and if, God forbid, everything is not done to remove the danger, hundreds of Jewish merchants may, God forbid, be wiped [?] off the face of the earth.
—
In the year 5696 the new governing bodies of the Sosnowiec and Dąbrowa kehillot took over power.
The new kehillot, which were born under very difficult conditions — the Jewish public and communal workers paid for them with a great deal of nerves, ambition, effort and struggle; many forces were spent in order to give Jewish Sosnowiec and Dąbrowa a better kehilla, around which the whole Jewish population is now grouping itself, wanting to see in it the protector and defender of its needs and interests.
We now stand on the threshold of the new kehillot, and the only thing we wish them for the time being is that they rise to such a height that no artificially created representative institutions will be needed — that the kehillot become the true and worthy representatives of the Jewish population in Sosnowiec and Dąbrowa.
—
The year 5696 made itself felt among the Jewish workers too, with its unemployment and want. In hundreds of Jewish workers' homes hunger and cold settled broadly and deeply. No one took an interest in this want, there was no one to turn to and no one to cry out to; yet no loud groan came [?] from there — people learned to suffer and keep silent. No one set up free kitchens, no relief campaigns were organized; "Bontshe Shvayg" [Bontshe the Silent, Peretz's hero] asked nothing of anyone and accepted his own fate lovingly, displaying tremendous steadfastness — the proof: his organizations and institutions, which have not broken in the slightest. The Jewish worker managed to carry the Polish worker along with him, and this year we witnessed public actions by Polish and [Jewish workers] in the struggle against antisemitism.
A general fragmentation prevails in Jewish life, and this is the main reason weakening [?] our defensive struggle.
The same can be said of the Jewish artisans' movement, which in the departing year showed an increased tendency towards quarrels and splits — something the Jewish artisan cannot allow himself today, since the conditions of existence drive him to concentrate and unite his forces.
—
Philanthropic activity in the Jewish street in Zagłębie has all but perished. People who could usefully have worked in this field have begun to climb the ladder of a lofty public career and strive to seat themselves up there, where they can only do harm.
Unfortunately, we also have no positive results to record so far from the campaign for the Jewish hospital in Sosnowiec.
For weeks on end there was commotion at tables and on benches, committees and executives [?] held dozens of meetings, the fund-raising campaign even actually began — but what result was achieved, and in general what the hospital's situation looks like, is still not clear, and the matter is marking [?] time.
The only plus in the past year is the new building for an orphanage. The building will soon be finished, and Jewish communal life in Sosnowiec will be enriched by a very useful institution; dozens of orphans will receive a home of their own.
—
The balance is a sad one, but all that remains for us is to wish that 5698, the year we welcome the day after tomorrow, will bring a happy balance for the whole Jewish people, and consequently also for the Jews of Zagłębie.
Y. N-baum.

After Tashlich

[Feuilleton — Rosh Hashanah.] Rosh Hashanah, after the afternoon (Minchah) prayer.
On the bank of the Przemsza, by the Talmud Torah grounds, men and women, older and younger, stand lined up in long rows.
Jewish children have come to the water to perform Tashlich.
They are all dressed in holiday clothes, some hold festival prayer books or prayer books in their hands, and with bowed heads they say "Mi El Kamocha" and other Tashlich prayers or supplications.
Having said them[?], one finishes by shaking out the coat-tails, the hems of the garments, as it is written in the mahzor, "and shaking out the hems [printed: shukei] of their garments" — one must shake out, shake off the hems of one's clothes.
Afterwards people disperse with lighter spirits, with merrier hearts — some to the synagogue to say or hear a word of Torah, some to exchange "Gut Yom Tov" greetings, and some to their homes.
And the water begins to bubble[?] with a rustle; little wavelets come up onto the surface of the water and sink down again, rise and sink and swim like a swarm of flies or bees.
These are the sins and little sins that Jewish children have shaken off into the water.
Here they get acquainted, introduce themselves to one another and tell how they were used and what role they played with their sinners.
"My name," one introduces herself, "is 'Iniquity' (Avat). I was kept by an ignoramus, by a coarse lad, and through me he became a respectable man; with my strength he pushed himself in everywhere, even where he does not belong[?]. He always used me as a tool to be the leader in a synagogue, in a Talmud Torah and in other Jewish institutions, and he ruled with a strong hand, ignored everyone and carried out whatever he wanted — however crooked, however tactless and impractical, so that certain things should not happen. If not for me, 'Iniquity', who would have so much as looked at him?!"
"And I," another spoke up, "am called 'Flattery' (Hanifa). I had my lodging with a rabbi, right in the synagogue where comrade Iniquity, the passionate one[?], is president, and one may say that I held the rabbi by the neck. He, the rabbi, licked up to and flattered the head of the community, humbled himself before him, showed him favour, said with his mouth not what he thought in his heart, was two-faced — all to win the favour of his overlord. Had the rabbi not had me to help him, he would not have lasted even a single day."
"And me," said a third, "people call 'Tzvuyestva' [hypocrisy]. I lodged with scoundrels, with sinners, with unbelievers, who think it right to do every forbidden thing, but they put on a pious face, made themselves out to be supposedly righteous men, and that helped them a great deal in their livelihood, with credit and in other matters. It won them honour in the synagogue, in the street and everywhere. If not for me, what kind of face would they have had?!"
"Deceit and Falsehood" (Kahash ve-Kazav) also introduced themselves and told what they had done for the people they had lodged with.
"We, 'Deceit and Falsehood' — or, in short, call us 'Bluff' — played a very important role indeed. Many a person, many an empty-handed pauper made use of us and bluffed about big deals, about big earnings; many a one denied his poverty, because that suited his purposes[?], and many a rich man, on the contrary, denied his wealth, passed himself off as a beggar, as one badly hit by the crisis, in order to wriggle out of the 'coat-tail pullers' [fund-raisers], out of the alms-beggars..."
"Pride", "Gossip", "Slander" and other sins, greater and smaller, also rose up and dipped in the water, and they all had something to tell: how, and for what purpose, they had been used.
"And yet," the shaken-off sins and little sins spoke with resentment and bitterness, "and yet they throw us away! We do them so many favours, and they go to Tashlich and fling us into the water! Ungrateful people they are, those little Jews! They get so much out of us, and it counts for nothing with them. This is a scandal, this cries out to heaven!"
Suddenly a rustle is heard in the air: it is the Evil Angel flying, the heavenly prosecutor Samael, beating his clumsy, terror-choking[?] wings.
He comes down lower and bursts out in devilish laughter:
"I heard," he says, "how you complain about your lot[?], and I must laugh at you, children. You are no youngsters any more, you are already quite respectable elders. Don't you know from your own experience that you have nothing to be afraid of! Calm down. You are not yet killed, not cast out, not homeless; you will be taken back into your homes and you will again play the same roles you played before."
"Year in, year out, at the same time," Samael goes on, "the little Jews perform the same ceremony of Tashlich. Year in, year out they supposedly shake their sins off themselves, and nevertheless I always have respectable bundles 'to bring before the Heavenly Household 'for their Day of Judgment. Don't worry, little children: you have only been given a little leave — just let their 'days of repentance', as they call them, pass. And I will find you all again in your homes, at your posts, and perhaps you will not even have to wait that long, and you will be serving your sinners even during the days of repentance. I still relish Tashlich and the whole theatre they put on."
Samael wants to say something more, but a voice like thunder cuts him short!
"Hush, accuser!" cries out from heaven the Jewish advocate, the good angel Michael. "Shut your mouth and do not dare to speak ill of the people of Israel. This very thing — that they hold on to the traditions of their parents and great-grandparents for so many generations, this very thing — that they do not give up the custom of their fathers after so many persecutions and oppressions they have endured — this covers everything.
"Don't you know, you scoundrel, that more than once antisemitic hooligans have thrown stones at Jews as they stood at Tashlich?! And don't you know that my dear Jews have been persecuted, tormented and plagued for many hundreds of years in exile, and nevertheless they keep, more or less, to their Torah, to their laws and customs, often with true self-sacrifice? Another nation in the same circumstances would long ago have been wiped off the face of the earth — and little Yisroelik lives. He runs to the synagogue, if not all year round, then at least on the High Holy Days, and for that alone great credit is due to him.
"You boast, you old fool, of the bundles of sins that you bring before the Heavenly Household — and what do you achieve[?] with those bundles? The merits of the Jews always outweigh them, and you remain a fool; this time too you will remain a fool: the 'verdict' of the heavenly court will be in favour of the Jews, and in your disgrace you will have to answer 'Amen'."
Samael lets out a heavy sigh, spreads his black wings and flies away in shame.

Where Chance Reigns

(Impressions from the Zoppot [Sopot] casino).
P. Blumenkranz (Sosnowiec)

11 in the morning, the sun is blazing, the "Steg" [the pier] is almost empty, thousands of people are sunbathing on the kilometre-long beach, hundreds of children jump into the sea and fill the surroundings with their joyful voices.
And right at this hour of sun, sea and bathing, the little ball is already beginning to run over the roulette board, and the croupier is already letting his monotonous word be heard: "Nichts mehr" ["No more"], as a sign that no more stakes may be placed.
Every day at 11 in the morning the eyes of the casino gamblers begin to sparkle — those who renounce the beach, the sun and the sea in order to seek out a few gulden from [?] chance.
The first to start playing are the impatient ones, but from hour to hour the movement grows, until it reaches its peak.
In the evening hours old Germans go to the concert of the spa orchestra, couples in love to the woods, old Jewish fellows with some ailment to the "Steg" (the molo, the pier), and the "high life" [? printed חיי-לייץ] — to the casino.
There one sees in the evening hundreds of elegant women with glittering stones on their hands and silver foxes on their bosoms, sunburnt, thoroughly "beached", sitting at the roulette tables, drawing, noting, calculating and smoking.
They forget then about flirting, forget to gossip about one another; they are absorbed in the little ball, which the croupier sets in motion every single minute.
• • •
12 at night, the casino halls are flooded with light. At the tables one hears only single words from the players:
— Last six!
— One—three!
— Carré premier!
— Black!
— Red!
The casino official rakes in the chips [?] (the casino coins) as if by magic. Eager [?] people sit absorbed in noting down the numbers, calculating, combining.
Every two or three minutes the croupier is heard:
— Nichts mehr.
The crowd stares at the little ball.
One man has dug in his heels and plays only on black; he stakes 200 gulden at a time and loses continually; outwardly he is calm, keeps taking out his wallet and laying down 200 gulden at a time, and precisely on black. His wife stands beside him biting her lips with agitation; he loses everything and calmly walks away; the wife remains standing and tears appear in her eyes.
Meanwhile a crowd of Englishmen and Americans bursts in noisily, with tall, thin women in long evening [?] gowns. They all set to playing at once.
One of them, an American woman with a face a bit of a silly goose [?], laughs out loud; she turns by chance to an acquaintance and asks whether he would not like to play for her.
He does not grasp what she wants, so she sits down herself, loses and laughs, loses and laughs.
She changes her dollars and loses; the laughter vanishes; my acquaintance, who had already begun to become [?] her escort, also lost his good mood.
Another evening, the attendance of players and onlookers was especially large. Hundreds of eyes were riveted to one table; one player held all the people in suspense; he played with relish [?], staked 500—600 gulden at a time, won continually 1000—1500 gulden; the guests [?] became somewhat unsettled [?], and so, in the middle of the whole commotion, an old German woman comes up to me and asks: since she has lost 50 gulden, she does not know what to do — to go on playing or to wait until tomorrow.
Having heard out her doubts, I answered her with an air of authority [?] that she must wait until tomorrow and play not on numbers but on colours.
I gave her to understand this like a scholar in the wisdom of roulette, and the "Kriechsin" [?] went away somewhat consoled.
But not everyone obeyed my "authoritative" advice. A little Jewish woman from Warsaw, who also asked my advice but did not much believe in my roulette wisdom, did indeed become [broke?] [?]; afterwards she went on a "głodówka" [a hunger diet], ate potatoes with salt for lunch and telegraphed her husband to send money.
The husband sent it, and she gambled that away too; later she set out [?] in search of a small loan, so as to be able to travel home...
• • •
In the chase after winnings people create theories, combine, calculate, compile tables. A few days before my departure, in a Jewish restaurant, there lay on every table a notice written in German, in which the author announces that he has invented a new system that gives a hundred-percent guarantee of winning.
He is not — the author stresses — some bluffer; his system is tried and tested.
He can, however, reveal the system only to a person who pays 864 gulden. With this person he is ready to talk and to demonstrate the correctness of his gaming system.
If a person with 864 gulden turns up, he may apply to post-office box number, etc.
Faith expresses itself in various forms.
Women believe even in the croupier, in the movement of his hand, as if he were a dentist; some of the women hold, on the other hand, that the croupier has more luck, and they have him [?] place the stake [?], so that he picks the number, etc.
So I am sitting one evening in the reading room of the casino, which is supplied with all newspapers except, naturally, Jewish ones, and an acquaintance says to me:
— It is well known that when a woman comes home in the evening [?] [—] [?], flushed, from the... dressmaker [?], and [—] to her husband's pillow, it is a sure sign that she has betrayed him. True? But then again, if a woman comes home early from Zoppot with a wail that she has been longing terribly [?] for her husband, it is a sign that she has gambled away her few złoty, and that is where the longing comes from...
That is what I learned in the Zoppot casino.
Since When Do We Write Postcards?

[General — history; the postcard.]
Postcards have been written among us for so long that it seems they are already thousands of years old. Very few of us know that postcards may be written only since the year 1869.
True, as early as 1777 Paris introduced a kind of „open card". On that card, however, one could only send congratulations to relatives, friends and acquaintances on a joyous occasion. Nothing more was allowed to be written on it, and the post strictly watched the content of the „open card".
In 1865, during the fair in Leipzig, representatives of various countries held a meeting at which it was decided to petition [„proshenye"] the post offices of all countries to introduce a postcard on which one would be allowed to write short messages from one place to another, and for which the post would charge a smaller postage than for a letter.
These petitions were shelved for 4 years; only on 1 October 1869 did Austria, first of all, introduce postcards, or, as they were called, „correspondence cards", on which one was allowed to write whatever one wished. On these cards the post printed that it assumed no responsibility whatsoever for the content of the correspondence card.
Only in 1872, when the World Postal Union was founded, did all the other countries also agree to introduce the correspondence card.
In 1881 the picture postcard appeared for the first time. The city of Basel issued a kind of advertising picture to promote the beauty of Basel, with a „pretty Swiss girl" on it. For years no other country imitated the city of Basel.
Only in 1890 did the great picture-postcard industry begin to develop, which embraced the whole world. Thousands and tens of thousands of people made quite a nice living from it.
First they brought out pictures of cities, then of individual buildings, of various animals and beasts. Later they also brought out pictures of beautiful women and men, of actors and artists — in a word, it became an industry that flooded the whole world.
A few years later people began to collect picture postcards; thousands of societies existed all over the world, with hundreds of thousands of members, who used to send each other picture postcards. Many thousands of matches (shidukhim) were born of it. For years the collecting of picture postcards was more widespread than the collecting of postage stamps.
Today the collecting of picture postcards has stopped, but the picture-postcard industry, which today is mostly busy with advertising pictures, still provides a livelihood for tens of thousands of people in the four corners of the world.
Z. Haber, Vienna[?].

Yehuda Yafet: Rosh Hashana (Reflections).

„Pakhad“ (awe) — that, after all, is the origin of the divine aspect [?] of judgment, of the boundless [?], fearsome and splendid gaze upon [the world]. The world he did [?] want to create [by the measure of judgment]. And although his gracious [?], gentle gaze of mercy did after all have to shine forth in the creation of the world, beneath the soft silken veil of mercy the primordial judgment always lay in wait; from time to time awe [?] tore open the light silken weave, and out peered the endless, trembling, heaven-and-earth-splitting abyss of awe [?].
When he wraps himself in the attribute of mercy, he is Israel's father — an indulgent [?], forgiving, compassionate father. True, even then „His mercies are over all His works“: he casts his merciful glances over all his creatures, even upon the tiniest worms [?], and when his human „handiwork“ drowns in the sea, he does not want song to be sung before him — but when he is wrapped in a smile of mercy, Israel is after all his beloved only son, his „darling child“, the most indulged [?] child.
But when judgment and awe surge [?] and pour down [?] — „Today the world was conceived; today He brings to judgment all the creatures of the worlds“ — the whole world, the entire cosmos, is torn open by the pre-creation gaze of awe. „And so, put Your awe, Lord our God, upon all Your works, and Your dread upon all that You have created.“ Israel's chosenness grows pale for a moment, is thrown into the great endless cosmos over which hovers [?] the eye of Elokim.
No Hallel is said on Rosh Hashana, on the day when awe erupts: „Is it possible that the King sits on the throne of judgment, the books of life and the books of death open before Him, and Israel sings song?“ Not a day of praise, of song to God, but a day of trembling, of merging into the universe, of opening heart and ear to the name [?] of Elokim.
It is the day of the greatest elevation: to rise to the level of a human being, of a child of the world. To have in mind not only the „I“, and not even only one's own people, but „Reign over the whole world in Your glory, and appear in the splendour of Your majestic might over all the inhabitants of the earth.“
Great is [—] elevation, [—] dizzyingly high: to tear oneself out of the narrow cages [?] of petty [?] egoism, and even out of the large but fenced-in field of nationalism, up to the infinity of humanity. The „Inscribe us in the book of livelihood and sustenance“ and even the „Because of our sins we were exiled from our land“ grow pale and wan before the „And so, put Your awe, Lord our God, upon all Your works.“ „All you peoples, clap your hands, shout to God with a voice of joy.“
The day when the Jew feels bound up with all, with all human beings and creatures of the world, because at the same time, just like everyone, he is judged today by the „Judge of all the earth“. „And all who come into the world pass before You like sheep“ — all the little lambs and even the great terrible wolves...
* * *
„Mishpat“ (Judgment).
The highest prophetic concept. Nothing is done without a reckoning; for everything you will have to give account, whether individual or nation. It would seem that this sober [?] concept must follow from the very idea of faith: if one believes in the Almighty, it is clear that nothing is done without a reckoning. But our prophets raised the concept of judgment higher than a self-evident consequence of the idea of faith. It is the nerve of the Jewish world-view. And through all the transformations of Jewish thought about God, the concept of judgment has remained intact, not displaced even from its top place.
And among all the heaped-up edifices of human thought there is no doctrine so anti-Jewish as the preaching of purposelessness, the starkest contradiction of the idea of Judaism.
At times the idea of judgment appears in national garb. When Abraham — as we read on Rosh Hashana — said to Isaac, „God will provide Himself the lamb for a burnt-offering, my son“, he had already then designated him as the „lamb for the offering“, as the eternal world-sacrifice who would have to bear all the sins of the world... And when Isaac endures [?] this most tragic of roles, it is because he knows that for all this they, the nations, will have to give account. The day of reckoning will come, sooner or later; and when we say that faith sustains the Jew in his harsh exile, [it sustains him] above all through the awareness that the world will give account for its deeds against the Jews.
On Rosh Hashana, however, the idea of judgment is raised [?], just like the Godhead itself, to the level of humanity.
The judgment over nations and countries will come on that great day. Today, however, every individual is judged, every individual of every nation. Judged not at the end of the year for the past one, but at the „beginning of the year“, in order to trace the coming year out of the past; not at the balance sheet for the sake of a total, but in order to draw up the new bookkeeping.
Three books are opened on this day: of the wholly righteous, of the wholly wicked, and of the beinonim, the middling ones. The righteous, like the wicked, are judged at once; only the middling ones remain „suspended“.
And if [?] suspension is our tragic fate, if the term for our tragedy is „to be [?] suspended“, if we hang between redemption and destruction, and if neither the abyss nor the elevation [?] swallows us up or spits us out — it is because the level of our generation is middling. „The son of David comes only in a generation that is wholly guilty or wholly meritorious“ — night or day; [ours is] twilight and only a ghost, when a ghost can neither set nor rise.
Are the Jews sinful today? Leaf through Jewish history from the Bible to the era of Shabbetai Zvi and you will see much deeper mires and swamps into which Jews sank spiritually. In many generations Jews were more sinful than we are, but we are worse than sinful — we are middling...
We have sinned [?]; today's sinners are not wild [?] and reckless, with sky-reaching aspirations; theirs are the sins of weaklings [?], of the middling.
And the era in which we live is by no means a middling one, but rather [?] an era of „the world being conceived“; yet we, the generation, are a generation of middling ones. That is why we have the hardest [?] fate, the fate of being suspended, of hanging between redemption and destruction.
And characteristically: with the middling ones one does not wait until they are raised to the righteous or lowered to the wicked — no. The middling ones always remain in their role; they lack courage for either. Our sages put it well [?]: „If they merit, they are inscribed for life; if they do not merit, they are inscribed for death“ — it all hangs [?] on merit alone, on whether they will be worthy.

I have some news to tell you. I am quitting as a newspaper writer — enough making a laughing-stock of myself, writing and erasing [?]...

Dear Uncle!

In Honour of Rosh Hashana — Torah sayings and remarks

[In honour of Rosh Hashana — Torah sayings.] Torah sayings and remarks in honour of Rosh Hashana,
collected and styled by Yehuda Yafet.
—o—
a) The eve of Rosh Hashana.
In the "Tur", at the start of the laws of Rosh Hashana, it says: "On the eve of Rosh Hashana the great ones fast." The "Shulchan Aruch" already says: "On the eve of Rosh Hashana everyone fasts." The question arises: why does the "Shulchan Aruch" say "everyone" instead of "the great ones"?
Because in the time of the Tur there were still "great ones" and people who did not consider themselves "great ones"; today, after all, everyone considers himself one of the "great ones" — for who in our time is not a great man? Therefore — everyone fasts. Let them be counted as great ones also when it comes to fasts...
—o—
b) "Blow before Me with a ram's horn so that I may remember for you the binding of Isaac" (Rosh Hashana 16).
If it is to recall the binding, surely one should have laid down a slaughtering knife (chalaf) and not a ram's horn?
But with the shofar we remind Him, as it were, that He does not want human sacrifices. Just as He did not then want to accept Isaac as a sacrifice — so let Him inscribe us in the Book of Life and not demand human sacrifices.
R' Zvi Hirsh of Zydaczow [reading uncertain].
—o—
c) "The books of the living and the books of the dead are open on Rosh Hashana."
Why are the books of the dead opened on Rosh Hashana? Are the dead judged too?
But with every accused person, when he is brought to judgement, one also takes into account his descent — what upbringing he received; therefore the "books of the dead" are also brought in [reading uncertain] — [—] for each person, who his parents were...
Chefetz Shlomo.
—o—
d) "He who knows the inclination of all creatures."
What does that mean?
Every person has his own inclination. "Whoever is greater than his fellow, his inclination is greater than his", and that is what the liturgical poem means: God knows and understands each person's inclination, and He judges everyone according to his inclination...
R' Avremele of Sochaczew.
—o—
e) "Be surety for Your servant for good; let not the arrogant oppress me."
"All Israel are guarantors for one another." All Jews are guarantors one for the other; in good and in bad alike we are responsible, one Jew for the other. But because of this very mutual responsibility more than one pogrom has already been carried out against Jews.
Therefore: "Be surety for Your servant for good" — Father in Heaven, let only good come of this mutual responsibility; "let not the arrogant oppress me" — let them not make pogroms on us and rob us under the pretext [?] of this very mutual responsibility...
Imrei Chen.
—o—
f) "And so, put Your awe upon all Your works."
Why do we pray for the fear of Heaven for the nations? Do we ourselves already have enough fear of Heaven?
But "he who prays for his fellow is answered first" — whoever prays for another is himself helped first.
R' Chaim of Sanz.
—o—
g) "Our fathers sinned and are no more, and we have borne their iniquities."
"Our fathers sinned — and are no more": their sins no longer count against us [?]; "and we have borne their iniquities" — we suffer and tolerate it, that what was a sin for them, for us is nothing but mitzvot...
Otan [?] Imrei Shefer.
• • •
R' Naftali of Ropczyce went with the Seer [of Lublin] to Tashlich. When the Seer had emptied his pockets, R' Naftali bent down and splashed his hands in the water.
"What are you trying to catch there in the water?" asks the Seer.
"The Rebbe's 'sins' — for me they would be true merits..."
—o—
h) "And the angels hasten, and trembling and dread seize them."
It is no such easy thing to plead in defence of the Jews; even the angels are seized with trembling when the Day of Judgement comes and they have to plead in defence of the Jews. Rabbi Shlomo of Belz.
—o—
i) The Fast of Gedaliah.
"The fast of the seventh [month] — this is the 3rd of Tishrei, on which Gedaliah son of Ahikam was killed; and who killed him? Ishmael son of Nethaniah. This teaches you that the death of the righteous is equal to the burning of the House of our God."
Have few righteous men been murdered? Why are no fasts held in their memory?
The tragedy of Gedaliah's death at the hands of Jews lies in the fact that it happened right after Rosh Hashana — that a Jew should think it right [?], straight after the Holy Days, to kill another Jew.
Yalkut David.

The Crisis before the Heavenly Court.

[Feuilleton — humorous fantasy for Rosh Hashana; the economic crisis.] By Y. Vaynshteyn [J. Wajnsztajn].
(A Funny Fantasy).

And it was on the day of Rosh Hashana, when all people are brought to judgement and for each of them his verdict is pronounced, for good or, God forbid, for bad.
One of the accusing angels stood up before the Heavenly Court and began to pour pitch and brimstone on mankind, and especially on the people of Israel.
— How much longer, Master of the Universe, will You suffer these sinful people? See how they have laid waste[?] Your earth, soiled Your world and desecrated everything holy that You gave them! Make an end of mankind, create a new world!
Michael, the old advocate for the defence, rose and argued thus:
— Your little Jews, dear God, are surely not guilty at all... Not enough that You put into man an evil inclination, which accompanies him from childhood to his last minute — You have also sent a bitter crisis upon them... and this very crisis drives them to all kinds of sinful thoughts and deeds... Just let the crisis stop, and You will see how they all become fine and good!
— Crisis? — called out an oldish[?] judge[?] of the Heavenly Retinue. — What sort of creature is that?
They began to leaf and rummage, searched in old holy books and found nothing about a crisis...
Couriers were sent across all the heavens, into all the worlds, to inquire whether anything was known about a crisis, but nobody could say a word about it!
So it was decided to send a special envoy down to the lower world, to find the crisis and bring it before the Heavenly Court..
They sent down a young little angel with a pair of clean white wings and a crystal-pure heart..
The young angel came down to earth and flew straight, as is the custom, to a synagogue...
And he arrived at a synagogue just on the first day of Rosh Hashana...
He looks around on all sides — nothing but dressed-up Jews, and when he cast his glance at the women's gallery, his head began to swim before his eyes; he had never seen such luxurious clothes.. In every world[?] they all come in brand-new clothes, yes indeed[?]. It dazzles the eyes: the finest silks, [unclear word, perhaps necklaces?], precious stones on the fingers and in the ears; alluring hats — a sea of luxury and wealth.
So he asks one of the worshippers:
— Perhaps you know, Reb Jew, where I can find the crisis here?
— You're looking for a crisis among us? Wasted effort! Go to the paupers!
He went off to other synagogues, but there too he did not find it.
And he went back up to heaven and reported that there is no crisis...
— Who wants to go and look for the crisis? — a voice was heard from the elders[?] of the Heavenly Court.
— I do! — called out a textile (manufaktura) dealer, who considered himself a victim of the crisis and hoped he would find it.
— Go! Go and fulfil your mission perfectly!
And the textile man began to wander from lane to lane, but at once several shop assistants came running toward him and showered him with the most expensive fabrics, with the finest and best goods.
— Very nice — murmured the envoy — but where is your crisis? I wanted to see this personage that everyone talks about so much in all the worlds.
— Wha-a-at? Crisis? We textile merchants have no such article; perhaps among the textile market stalls [straganes] you will get that article.
So he went off to the market and approached the first trader.
— Dear uncle, could I perhaps get from you at least a little piece of crisis..
— You mean something like that? For outer shirts[?]...
— No, crisis...
The second envoy, too, came back empty-handed.
— I'll go — called out the soul of a poor wretch — I'll search among my own kind, among the beggars...
He came upon a Jew who goes from house to house begging alms.
— Uncle, would you like to earn a few fat groszy?
— Earn? But I'm not used to working... Thank God, I earn my bread easily..
— You go round the houses, it seems to me, right?
— Yes!
— Well then, surely you know what crisis means?
— Well, well, some knowledge that is!
— Then come along[?], if you please, with me for a couple of hours to a place where you will tell what you know about the crisis, and for that you'll be well paid.
— Far from here?
— Not near, but it's worth it, you'll be satisfied.
The beggar pondered for a while and in the end gave his consent to go.
— But first I must go home — he said to the stranger — to have a look at my bit of poverty, to secure it so that thieves won't snatch it, and then I'll go with you.
And the two of them went off.
The beggar dragged out a small bundle and hid it.
— What have you got there? — the envoy asked.
— Nothing! Gold rings! I've saved them up for my old age.
Then he spread out a [unclear word, perhaps silk] tablecloth and began throwing together shoes, suits, socks and all sorts of almost new things..
The envoy saw all this and at once was uprooted [went up] to heaven and reported that among the beggars too he had not seen the crisis.
— — — — — — — —
After a long investigation and inquiry the Heavenly Court decided that there is no crisis in the world.
So where is it, after all?
When they started to search well and look around, they saw that the crisis was lying hidden — in heaven itself, under the chair of one of the judges who judge mankind.
And there was an uproar, a tumult in all the heavens, in all the worlds, in all the heavenly halls!
— Watch out, the crisis has sneaked in among us!

A Jewish Commercial School

Instruction will take place for several hours a day, given by well-known specialist teachers and pedagogues under the direction of an experienced headmaster.

Small Interest with a Side Benefit Is Also Usury

[Rulings — Supreme Court; Sosnowiec — news items.]
A most interesting question came before the Supreme Court: if one takes the legal interest for lending money, but besides that a special benefit for the creditor is also agreed upon — is that usury?
The Supreme Court ruled that usury is when one takes for lending money such a profit as is more than the law permits. It makes no difference whether the profit is in the form of a small interest with the addition of a special benefit.
If, therefore, one takes a small percentage and besides that procures [?] another benefit for making the transaction, that is usury and it carries a penalty as for usury.

Kielce ONR Hooligans' Failed Attempt to Introduce a Ghetto in the Market Square

[Kielce — antisemitism.] Last Thursday night a fairly large group of ONR (National-Radical Camp) hooligans gathered in the market square [of Kielce], where the fairs are held, and with lime divided the market square into two parts. The right side they assigned to the Christian merchants and the left — to the Jewish ones.
On Friday at 5 in the morning the hooligans set up on the right side large posts with placards on which was written: "Strona chrześcijańska" [Christian side], "Swój do swego" [?] [each to his own — the boycott slogan] and the like.
When the Jewish traders arrived with their goods, the ONR gang, armed with thick sticks, began to terrorize the Jewish traders and forced them to move their stalls to the left side, into the Jewish ghetto. Out of fear "lest something happen", the Jewish traders moved their stalls to the left side. Some of them did not unpack their goods at all and went home.
For some time the hooligans lorded it over the market freely and openly; the mood among the Jewish traders was a depressed one.
It is interesting that even some Christians did not want to move their stalls to the right side, but the ONR men terrorized them too.
The head of the Kielce investigation office, Commissioner Zdankiewicz, arrived at the market square with a fairly large police detachment. He at once ordered the placards taken down and demanded that all traders take up their former places again.
Several ONR hooligans were arrested and their weapons [?] were taken from them.
The whole day the police kept order in the market. The fair passed quietly.
Thanks to the energetic action of Commissioner Zdankiewicz, the attempt to introduce a ghetto in the market failed.
Great Funeral of the Suchedniów Rebbe, of Blessed Memory

[Kielce — mourning.] Last Saturday night, at about 1 o'clock, during the recitation of Selichot, the Suchedniów Rebbe, R' Elimelech Rabinowicz, of blessed memory, died in Kielce after a long illness, aged 73.
The deceased, a born [?] rebbe, was a son of the famous Końskie [?] Rebbe, R' Pinchasl, of blessed memory, and a grandson of the Holy Jew [of Przysucha].
The Suchedniów Rebbe fell gravely ill during his stay in Krynica, where he had gone for a cure. The Rebbe was therefore brought to Kraków and from there to Kielce.
It is characteristic that during his illness the Suchedniów Rebbe several times expressed the wish to live at least until the yahrzeit of his father, which fell on the first day of Selichot. It is even more remarkable that the Rebbe died on the very same day and even at the very same hour as his father.
The funeral of the Suchedniów Rebbe took place on Sunday at 8 in the evening in Kielce. It was attended by a crowd of nearly 10 thousand Jews from Kielce and the whole Kielce region, among them many rabbis and rebbes headed by the Ostrowiec Rebbe.
At the grave eulogies for the deceased were delivered by the Kielce rabbi, Rabbi Rapaport, and others.
As successor the younger son of the deceased, R' Yosele, was appointed, whom the crowd wished mazel tov at the Rebbe's grave.

[Kielce — antisemitism.] This week the 'Naro' people (the National camp, Narodowcy) smashed the windows in the apartment of the Christian Świetlik [?], who last Friday, too, did not allow a 'ghetto' to be introduced in the market square.

They also smashed the windows in Pikes's [?] beth midrash and in the photographic studio of Mr. Kisler [?].

On Saturday night, as people were going to Selichot, they attacked several Jews and beat them up.

Rosh Hashanah in Katowice.

(L.T.) Although the Jewish situation in exile in general, and in Poland in particular, has unfortunately not improved lately, the Jews of Katowice were nevertheless able, on the threshold of the new year, to record a new item among the community's assets, namely: last Saturday night they festively celebrated the opening of the new synagogue.
In the presence of all the parnassim, the kehilla councillors (dozors) and a large crowd, Cantor Rosenzweig sang "Ma Tovu" with the choir, and speeches for the occasion were delivered [?] by: the kehilla president Mr. Altman [?] and both rabbis; and with the singing of "Hatikvah" the festive dedication was concluded.
Festive Rosh Hashanah sermon by Rabbi Chameides.

On the eve of Rosh Hashanah, after the evening prayer, Rabbi Chameides delivered the festive New Year sermon in the overcrowded Great Synagogue. He gave a survey of the Jewish situation in the world, spoke with grief and anger and protested sharply against the ever-growing wave of hatred and enmity against Jews, and argued that despite everything our will and our vitality are not broken, citing as an example the gigantic work of construction in the Land of Israel and depicting [?] in glowing terms the realisation [?] of our ancient dream, as before our eyes the Jewish state begins to take on real form in our old-new land.
The speech, which was distinguished by particular rhetorical force and pathos, made an unforgettable impression. (L.T.)
Sermon by Rabbi Fogelman.

(L.T.) On the first day of Rosh Hashanah, after the Torah reading, Rabbi Fogelman delivered a sermon in the Great Synagogue, speaking about the past year in Jewish life and also about the refreshing effect of the coming year on the Jewish person.
On the second day of Rosh Hashanah Rabbi Chameides again spoke in the Great Synagogue, mentioning among other things [?] the speech of Lord Samuel in the English House of Lords during the Palestine debate, and speaking about the territorial significance of the Land of Israel in the past and today, arguing that the size of the territory is by far not as important as its effect as a point of support for the Jews and its influence on Jewish life.
Cantor Rosenzweig, too, led the prayers [?] beautifully and with great feeling, with the well- [?] rehearsed choir.
The fine, warm weather contributed to the better mood, awakening good hopes for the new year.
The Katowice Jewish Choral Society

is resuming its activity after the summer holidays. Yesterday, Thursday the 9th, the members of the society's board met to discuss [?] the new plan of activity.
Perhaps the society will at last become Jewish not only in name but will also include in its programme the so very rich Jewish folk music. And let us be fair towards the leaders of the society and say that it is not so much their fault as the fault of the Jewish national intelligentsia, which unfortunately has no interest in the society. A pity. (L.T.)
Riding "na gapę" was not enough for him — he also wounded two officials.

On Saturday night a certain Szykora of Czeladź, who had travelled from Kraków without a ticket, was detained at the railway station in Szopienice.
When the station duty officer [?] came to check the passenger's papers, he threw himself at him with a razor.
At that moment two railway officials ran up to the passenger, wanting to tear the razor out of his hands. This, however, was not easy, and they were wounded.
The "na gapę" passenger has been arrested.

Deep Suffering — of a Young, Educated Woman in Lipiny.

P.L. Irma was well brought up by her father. Irma was a decent child, always occupied with her studies. When she grew older, rich young men, doctors, engineers and the like sought her hand; she turned down these chances, until time brought it about. Her parents died, and she, left an orphan and burdened besides with the business and with keeping up 2 [houses?], was matched with a young man, a certain P. from Sosnowiec, whom she married.
Several years passed, and the husband cast a crooked eye on his faithful wife, began to treat her badly, talked the tenants out of paying rent, etc., and in the end ran away from her.
A few weeks ago the "gem" came to his wife together with a cousin of his. The husband explained that he had come because of the child; the woman received the guests very well and with tears began to work on him to forget [?] quickly [?] and make peace again. "I forgive you everything — she said — for all the time of troubles you caused me, all [?] so that our child should not be left without a father."
The husband told her he would still think it over, and took his leave. 15 minutes later the cousin who had been introduced comes back with a small parcel in his hand and says the husband is sending bananas for the child; he put the parcel into the woman's hand and went away again.
Half an hour later the woman opened the parcel to take out the bananas, and to her great misfortune she also took out... a get [bill of divorce]. The woman went to rabbinic authorities, who declared that the get is not valid.
What will come of this tragic story is not clear, but meanwhile Lipiny is seething, and the indignation at the young fellow — A.B., the son of very pious parents — is very great.

From the Past Rosh Hashanah.

This year's eve of Rosh Hashanah stood under the sign of the present hard times, and in general the mood was a depressed one; the enthusiasm and the usual holiday-eve atmosphere were missing, so this year the New Year was not greeted in a cheerful frame of mind. Only thanks to the fine weather was there at least a bit of comfort for the dejected spirits. For many years Jews cannot remember such a beautiful Rosh Hashanah. That the sun should shine and warm as in the middle of Tammuz, and a [—] [?] breeze should blow and refresh the spirits — such a beautiful and warm Rosh Hashanah will surely mean a beautiful and good year, people wished one another — may it be so!
The synagogue, the study houses, shtiblekh and minyanim were overfilled, and when a Jew runs into the synagogue it strikes him deeply to the heart.
In the synagogue in Będzin on the first day of Rosh Hashanah a mishap [?] occurred: the cantor suddenly felt faint [?] during the "loud" Shmoneh Esreh [the reader's repetition] and had [?] to be taken away [?] from the lectern, and the choir under the direction of its conductor Mr. Frenkel completed the Musaf with the prayer leader Mr. Beri.
On the State of Kashrut in Sosnowiec.

As we are informed by authoritative rabbinic circles, the state of kashrut in Sosnowiec is very [bad?]; the lawlessness is very great, and in various places treyf meat is openly sold as kosher.
It is therefore a sacred duty of the rabbis to draw attention to this, and especially in the Shabbat Shuva sermon to rouse the public to the importance of extraordinary care, so as not to stumble into eating carrion and treyf, forbidden fat and the sciatic nerve. One should believe absolutely no one in this matter, and everyone should buy meat only in the licensed butcher shops.

We Must Create a Sound Financial Institution.

[Sosnowiec — economy; cooperatives and banking.]
(On the reorganization of the Sosnowiec Small Traders' Bank)
We live in a time when the policy of exterminating the Jewish population — on the part of both the rulers and the opponents — is celebrating its triumph. The Jewish leaders who foresaw the tragic moment and told the Jewish population to be ready for the phenomenon have for [?] years propagated the idea of self-help, which was to consist in creating cooperatives. One — and indeed the most important — of the institutions of cooperation are the Schulze-Delitzsch [?] banks [cooperative credit banks], which help the Jewish population by granting small credit.
Unfortunately, most of the cooperative banks here in Zagłębie did not withstand the trial by fire and left the scene, leaving behind a very bad name and at the same time stripping away [?] the public's trust. They went under because they served not the idea of constructive help but, sadly, the aims of various politicos, both groups and individuals, who very lightly traded with the public's penny and who with such "management" destroyed relief points for the Jewish population; the members and savers [?] of those banks still suffer the grave consequences to this day.
But there is in Sosnowiec a genuine cooperative bank which neither the "rgot" [?; probably: rabbinate] struggle, nor the party wars, nor the crisis could destroy: the Artisans' and Small Traders' Bank in Sosnowiec, which at its last general meeting changed its name to "General Cooperative Bank", wishing thereby to express that, together with the signboard, it has decided at the same time to change its field of activity — to embrace all sections of society: the artisan, the stall-keeper [?] (straganiarz), the small as well as the big merchant, industrialists, etc.
The bank has existed for 14 years already. Its activity was strongly limited by a lack of financial means; nevertheless in that time it managed, by granting credits, small ones though they were, to keep alive more than one Jewish position, thus winning the trust not only of a very large part of the Jewish population in Sosnowiec but also throughout Poland, the best proof of which is the great number of collection (incasso) documents the bank receives from the whole country.
Seeing the activity, seeing the rational management that is being conducted and the benefit the institution brings to the Jewish population, the American Committee [the Joint], the Audit Union [of cooperatives], and also the rehabilitation (sanacja) commission of the Kielce voivodeship decided to help the small institution by creating a large bank that will in future be able to serve not only Sosnowiec but all of Zagłębie. To that end the "Joint" has taken over all the liabilities of the bank and is granting long-term credits.
Today the fate of this institution depends on all of us — on the Jewish population of Sosnowiec in the first place, and of all Jews in Zagłębie, because the "Joint" holds to its eternal motto: "Help yourselves and we will help you threefold". We Jews have no "Bank Polski", no "P.K.O."; we can rely only on our own strength — and who today does not need low-interest credit? Whether it is a shop owner who, because of the authorities' ordinance, must bring his shop to an aesthetic appearance; or a craftsman about to buy a machine; or a house owner who must properly repair his house — all of them can obtain credit only in their own cooperative bank.
In the name of our own interests, in the name of preserving the Jewish positions, we must help create a sound financial institution. So all Jews should enrol as members of the cooperative and deposit their savings in the General Cooperative Bank. Let us create our own "P.K.O.", our own position, where in this so difficult present time of struggle for our existence we shall find help.
Let us look [?] at nearby Częstochowa, where two cooperative banks exist, working with capitals of millions. Are we Sosnowiecers any worse? Let us become local patriots and create the same thing that our brothers in Częstochowa, Wolbrom, Pułtusk and other towns in Poland have created.
A Sosnowiecer.
The Beginning of the School Year.

[Editorial — education; start of the school year.]
A week ago the gates of the school opened for all the children who more than 2 months ago were let free in order to rest and throw off the yoke that, after all, every pupil carries, from the youngest to the oldest.
Since then the youth together with the parents have taken upon themselves the worry about the future. This worry is borne quite especially by Jewish youth and their parents. Already at the very beginning, when one has to put the child into school, the parents' worry begins: which school?
For others this is no question at all: the school is a normal one, a state school in the mother tongue, a national one, and a continuous one from the elementary school up to the university.
With us, however, the question is a hard one from the start. Jewish parents must have a Jewish-national school, must think about the continuity of schooling, and must already think about the purpose. Purpose means future — and of any future for our youth we know nothing. The children already see it and feel it; they themselves already have no rosy prospects, and more than once they put questions to their parents to which there is as yet no answer.
Even greater worry is borne by the parents, who are responsible for the child's future: what will happen when the child finishes elementary school, secondary school and even university — what hopes [?] have we of settling our children in life?
That is the way most parents think. But it must not be so; pessimism and hopelessness must not be allowed to press into our lives. At the beginning of the school year we must, full of confidence and faith in better times, send our children to a truly Jewish school, not cloud our children's faces with melancholy, but preserve as long as possible their naivety and childhood, their faith in people and their confidence in the future.
Now, at the start of the school year, when the children again take the burden upon themselves for a whole year, we wish them the will to learn and to education, which has always sustained us through our long history. They must remember their belonging to their people; they must remember that upon them we are building our future.
Y.
Prices Are Rising Again.

Newspapers all over the world proclaim that salvation has already come. Any moment now [?], just a little longer, and the crisis will be gone and we are already beginning to live better and more cheaply.
There is only one piece of luck: figures and statistics cannot be twisted; they tell the truth. If serious people in every country undertake to compile true figures on life in their country, one soon learns whether things are getting better or worse. In every country there are statistical bureaus that report accurate figures, which can always be checked.
When we look at a statistic from the Leipzig Fair, we arrive at accounts that are not very cheerful.
Everywhere, in every country, things have become dearer in the past year.
In Poland, for example, the cost of living has risen by about 8 per cent compared with the same time last year; individual items have risen even more. Foodstuffs, for example, became dearer in Poland in the past year by 13 per cent, clothing by 9 per cent. Only rent and heating have not risen; add to this that for several months the Polish government has been trying to keep foodstuffs from becoming any dearer. Textile goods in Poland rose by only 1 per cent.
Things are no better in other countries. In France meat became dearer by 15 per cent, fats by 11 per cent; clothing and shoes rose there in recent months by 7 per cent, sugar by 5 per cent, and so on and on.
In Switzerland the rise in prices compared with last year amounts to 6 per cent, in Holland 5 per cent; clothing in Holland has risen lately by more than 30 per cent.
In England the rise in prices amounts to 5 per cent. This rise set in only in the last few months; before that, prices there had been stable. Compared with the same time last year the cost of living in England, as stated, rose by 6 per cent, but compared with the year 1933 it amounts to 15 [?] per cent.
In Italy things became dearer in the past year by 5 per cent, in Hungary by 7 per cent — although this agrarian country has so much food that it does not know what to do with it; clothing there became dearer by 19 per cent, heating by 5 per cent.
In the lands overseas, too, things have lately become dearer, but in North America it amounts to "only" 3 per cent. In Japan, even before the present war with China, everything had become dearer by 14 per cent.
Only in Czechoslovakia, Austria and Denmark is the rise about 1 per cent, in Sweden only half a per cent.
This much is certain: in no country in the world did things become cheaper in the past year, although, according to the newspaper reports, things are going better and better for us.
Z. Haber, Vienna.
My Blessing for the New Year.

A good year to you, gentlemen!
What kind of good year shall we all wish one another? For Reb Yisroel I have a simple blessing: "A life of livelihood, a life of peace, a life of plenty [?]!" — all good lives; but for Klal Yisroel, the Jewish people as a whole, I am afraid it is no blessing yet...
For tell me yourselves, on the contrary: how would it look if up there they [?] were for once to make a stroke of the pen and erase [?], make vanish like a fog [?], all Jewish troubles — no Hitler, no "Nesharim", no Aryan paragraph, no excesses [?], no decrees, no persecutions, no oppressions; an abundance of livelihood has poured down on Jewish heads, all shopkeepers are taking in money, all factories are humming, all weavers put up cholent, all men buy aliyot!
And peace has come to the land: all the nations have shaken hands, we [—] sign a pact not only on the East but also on the West and the North and the South, and Russia with Germany with Japan with America have taken each other by the hand and, with moist eyes, [sworn] friendship in the League of Nations; and America has shortened the working hours of the day and the working days of the week and raised wages, and unemployment suddenly vanished, and all the continents and all the nations learned from America, and eternal peace came about between worker and employer, and the crisis is gone and all the nations live in contentment and tranquility, and we little Jews among them too!
How then, gentlemen, would things look with our increased aliyah to Eretz Israel?
It is even said [?] that a strong Diaspora must exist in order to be able to build a strong Eretz Israel; so far, however, we have not seen it. So far the strong Diaspora has built itself, and only once it grew weak and drowsy did it set about building the national home.
In the Gemara there is a saying [?] that from the destruction of Jerusalem Rome was built and from the destruction of Rome Jerusalem will be built. That is too deep a philosophy for my plain householder's head. If the literal meaning is intended, I know after all that Rome was built earlier, before Jerusalem was destroyed, and after the destruction of Jerusalem Rome too was destroyed a little later, and for fifteen hundred years now Rome has lain in ruins and Jerusalem is still not rebuilt. If, again, the cultures and cults of Jerusalem and Rome are meant, I also do not know how to square it with chronology.
But never mind — let the preachers come and interpret the verse as they understand it; it will be more correct, however, if we apply the saying to the Diaspora and Eretz Israel: from the destruction of Jerusalem the Diaspora was built, and from the destruction of the Diaspora Eretz Israel will be built.
So what should I wish after all? What does a good year mean among Jews today? That the Diaspora should run out [?] like a cracked raw egg? That all Diaspora organizations, both the economic and the political, should burst like a soap bubble? That there should be thick darkness in Egypt, so that you can grope it with your hands, so that the light of Goshen should shine more sharply and visibly [?]?
That might indeed be a blessing for the ten thousand certificate-holders, but what will the 16 million 950 thousand Jews who have no certificates say to it?
I recall the "Hanoten teshua" [the prayer for the government; printed "Hoten"], where it says that the same God who makes a way in the sea and a path in the stormy waters shall bless and guard and protect the lord, the emperor. One asks a question: what has the stormy sea to do with the blessing for the emperor? And the answer is: the hardest thing for the Master of the Universe is to fulfil the Jews' prayer for the emperor. For suppose, for example, there is a war between Japan and Russia: the Japanese Jews will pray for the success of the Mikado and the Russian Jews will pray for the success of Stalin — what is the One in heaven to do? But He is already used to it; He had the same dilemma earlier with the sea: at one and the same time passengers board a ship from Europe to America and another ship from America to Europe, and here and there they pray for favourable winds. How can one make the wind blow both this way and that?
There is one remedy for it: one does not ask the wind at all; one runs the ships on steam, and with that power every ship goes its way and whistles in the wind's face.
The same goes for the "Hanoten teshua". The only remedy is not to ask Him [?] at all: whoever has the stronger army and the cleverer strategy will win the war.
And exactly so, probably, will it be with my wishes for the New Year. Eretz Israel and the Diaspora will surely wait until I choose which blessing to give them! They will build themselves, and whoever has the true vital force will live and grow strong.
And after all [?] there was once a time, in Babylon, when the bright, brilliant Diaspora did in fact build a fine Eretz Israel. So let us indeed wish for the coming year: that all Jews be capitalists and tourists, have shops on Zagłębie's "Nalewki" and orange groves in Tel Aviv, and that Jews give with a full hand to all the funds — but the capital should always remain with them as an iron capital.
That is my blessing for the New Year 5698.
Argus.

For Sins Never Committed

[Essay — Yom Kippur and the Jewish fate.] There is in the Yom Kippur festival prayer book (machzor) a prayer that is said before Kol Nidrei, a prayer that each person says for himself, in a whisper, not in public. This is the Tefillah Zakah.
I do not know whether there exists anywhere else in the world a similar people that possesses so remarkable a prayer as the one just mentioned.
The remarkable thing about this prayer is that the Jew who recites it confesses to every kind of sin in the world — so many that even if he were the greatest villain on earth, he still could not have managed to sin that much.
And he does not so much confess to all kinds of sins as he abases himself utterly and exalts on high the One to whom he prays.
This prayer was composed by the author of "Chayei Adam" [R. Avraham Danzig], who, according to tradition, ordered that he be buried not among the righteous and the learned but among simple folk, street people, and that his body be thrown into the grave like a carcass, head down.
Only when one becomes acquainted with the Tefillah Zakah does one truly understand the state of mind of its author.
It is a prayer, as said, in which a person completely debases himself before the whole people and congregation, in the synagogue and before the Master of the Universe; he spits in his own face and says of himself everything imaginable.
The person stands and reviles himself before the Creator:
Two inclinations of thought Thou gavest man, a good one and a bad one, so that he should have the free choice to pick the good or the bad thought — and I chose the bad one; a brain and a heart Thou gavest me to think and to feel about good deeds, and I defiled them with alien thoughts; Thou gavest me eyes to look into the Torah, and I looked at women; ears to hear words of holiness, and with them I heard obscenity and slander; a mouth and a tongue and teeth and a throat and a palate and a gullet to speak words of learning, and I spoke filth, lies, mockery, gossip, strife, curses, false oaths; hands to do good things — and with them I killed people; feet to run to do a mitzvah — and I ran to commit sins, etc.
When we reflect on how a person could have composed such a prayer, the thought occurs to us that such things often happen in life.
Often the accused have admitted and confessed before the Moscow court.
If such people can so abase themselves before an earthly court, how much more so a simple mortal before the heavenly court. Only then does it become understandable to us how the author of "Chayei Adam" could have composed such a Tefillah Zakah.
For sins never committed one always confesses in moments of despair, in moments of fear [?].
In such a state we Jews find ourselves almost our whole lives. It is this state that has made such prayers possible among us. Were our situation a normal one, as with the other nations of the world, I am sure it would never have entered the mind of the author of "Chayei Adam" to compose such a prayer, in which a person should debase himself so much.
In normal times Yom Kippur would be among us the most joyful of holidays, as it indeed once was while the Temple still stood. Jewish daughters used then to put on their finest clothes and go out into the gardens to dance with young men and snatch themselves bridegrooms. Only in the times after the Destruction did Yom Kippur become Days of Awe, days of fear, days of self-abasement, of declaring upon oneself all kinds of sins — even ones never committed.
Will this abnormal condition last much longer for us? We hope that there will one day come for us Jews, too, days of forgiveness and pardon, days of satisfaction for suffering for sins never committed. Those days will come when the world around us, too, stops sinning against us and against its own conscience.
These will be days when all nations will be made equal and will live in peace and tranquillity, not divided by borders and territories, by patriotism and nationalism, by hatred of one another; in those days we will have satisfaction for the suffering for sins never committed.
A. Y. G—ski.
A Short Feuilleton

[Feuilleton — Yom Kippur; satire on communal activists.] [Sins that even Yom Kippur does not atone for.]
"For You know that man's heart is evil by nature; therefore You have appointed a day of pardon and forgiveness, a day when the 'niger'[?] (apparently: the sin) is wiped away"...
Yom Kippur! But we Jews are blessed with such a day, which by itself automatically atones for transgressions. Only one small thing is needed: make yourself, Jew, a little soul-searching, and with your whole heart cry out "Al Chet"!
The great prayer that ushers in this day, "Kol Nidrei", has in all times been misunderstood and falsely interpreted by our enemies. In Kol Nidrei the Jew tries to free his conscience of various vows, promises and obligations that he took upon himself.
Yom Kippur. A fine, faithful[?] thing this day has, even more so the night of Kol Nidrei, when one can, just like that, with one throw, cast off from oneself the whole little bundle of vows, promises and oaths. A fine thing first of all for our Jewish town councillors, who sinned with promises of support for ruined merchants, poor small traders, exhausted artisans and hungry workers — all this one can, after all, annul so easily today with a "our oaths are not oaths".
The same applies to our activists, the "councillors"[?], who swore heaven and earth, assuring us that, God forbid, it was not seats they were after, not party "pickings"[?], but that "the plight of our brothers and sisters" lay on their hearts; and now, when the seats are already firmly under their feet — well, call me "nutcracker" [i.e. who cares], for there is a Yom Kippur and — "nidrana la nidrei" [our vows are not vows]...
And so it goes from top to bottom. Shochtim who go into partnership with back-alley shochtim and butchers; Zionists who reproach others for not paying to the Keren Kayemet and the Keren Hayesod; Shomrei-Shabbos men who know the rule that "the small ones are hanged and the big ones are pardoned"; "t[?]got"-people [perhaps "ta'avot", lusts], who are big shots at someone else's expense; small traders with big delusions, and wholesalers with petty little ambitions — all of them feel truly so calm and secure, because Jews they are and they know the rule that Yom Kippur atones for everything.
I have deliberately passed over only the important big-shots — our deaf-and-dumb representatives in the Jewish kehilla; for them, poor things, there is now bitter pity, for the New Year will bring them the true Day of Judgment — kehilla elections, and who knows how the "kvitl" [verdict] and the seat in general will look. They will surely, without my moralising, at Kol Nidrei pray and cry more heartfeltly than anyone — "Forgive us"!
Yes, Yom Kippur is indeed capable of washing the greatest sin clean, like an innocent child, like a little white angel. But there is one condition: whoever thinks to himself "I will sin and repent" or "I will repent and sin" — his repentance is not valid... For such people even Yom Kippur does not atone.
Yankele.
