„Long Live Marienbad!“..

[Feuilleton — humour; the Agudat Israel Knessia Gedolah at Marienbad.]
The other day a Jewish woman came to me and laid out the following story, in these words:
— Good — she says — that I've found you, because you writers can never be found at home. At night you work and in the daytime you sleep.
Now that I've found you on a weekday, I must tell you a story. Whether you want to or not, you'll have to hear me out.
— You, Mr. Aberżanek — the woman began — always laugh at the spas, [?], which, you say, have been made into places for pleasure-seekers. What does going there mean? Not so much [?] to put a patch on the stomach, to dissolve the calcification, to drive out the stones; you say our womenfolk go to the spas not for the „czyszczenie" [purge] and the „woreczki żółciowe" [gall-bladders][?], but to snatch a [juicy?] little flirt — that the womenfolk go to the spas not to preserve their lives but to have a good life. Well, I've come to you now to plead[?]: a spa is a great thing. A friend of mine (my „koleżanka"), for instance, was barren for fifteen years, may it not befall us, and she travelled from one „good Jew" [Hasidic rebbe] to another — and „ani rusz" [not a budge]; then she went to Karlsbad and there she really was helped... My friend was helped by Karlsbad, and now I have been helped by... Marienbad.
You think that I am, God forbid, a sick woman? [?]. I am healthy, as may be said of all Jewish daughters. I am quite a [?] woman; I know nothing of diets, [?]; I don't hold with all these modern medical „[?]" that turn certain people into cripples.
So you'll ask: since I'm as sound as a nut, how do I come to Marienbad? Then I'll tell you the story in order[?]:
— From time immemorial there has been hell in my house. My „shepsl" [„little lamb" — her husband] was forever squabbling with the children.
— As you know, my shepsl is a die-hard Agudah man, and today's children — well, you know them: they are „postępowe" [progressive] and laugh at father and mother; each has his own „programme", and their father is of the „stara data" [old school]...
— Well, my house turned dark; an eternal war raged between father and son. Above all my shepsl was angry with my eldest son, Shlomele.
— You, Father — my Shlomele said — believe in the Torah of Moses, and I — in the Torah of Vladimir [Ze'ev Jabotinsky]... You, Father, hold that redemption will be brought by the one „poor and riding upon an ass", and I say that redemption will be brought by the little sword. Father — only the fist!..
The real war broke out between father and son when my Shlomele came home dressed like a full-fledged general, „lehavdil": a military suit, a cap with a shiny peak, with epaulettes[?] and medals with cords, ribbons, whistles, bells and other trinkets. My shepsl asks him:
— Shlomele, what is this?
— Daddy, I've joined Brit HaChayal [the Revisionist soldiers' league]!
— What?
— This is the future Jewish army, Daddy, which will liberate Eretz Israel from the occupiers — my Shlomele answered proudly.
— My bad wild dreams on my enemies' heads! — my shepsl answered. — You're going to fight the mighty British lion?
— Ha ha, hee-hee — my Shlomele burst out laughing — Nicholas [the Tsar] was a lion too; well, isn't he now lying in the ground baking bagels? Didn't little David lay low the giant Goliath?
So my shepsl got angry:
— Take off that military uniform at once! Take off at once the epaulettes[?], the ribbons, whistles, bells and the other rags, do you hear? That is no Jewish way; a Jew does not go with the sword; a Jew asks, a Jew appeals to justice — but to fight?
Such „wars" were forever going on between my shepsl and my Shlomele — whole days of quarrelling and strife.
But we have a great God, who performs miracles. One miracle He did for my friend, who was helped by Karlsbad with a male child, and I have been helped by... Marienbad.
— Just listen, Mr. Aberżanek, to what happened:
Two weeks ago my shepsl comes home well pleased:
— Chava Leah, pack me the elegant kapote, the velvet hat, the shoes and socks, the tallis bag and clean linen.
— What's up? Are you going to the Rebbe?
— Not to the Rebbe — to Marienbad I'm going!
— To Marienbad? Why on earth Marienbad? Are you ill, God forbid?
— I'm not ill, thank God I'm healthy, as may be said of all Jewish children.
— Then why are you going to Marienbad?
— I have been, you understand, elected as a delegate to the Knessia Gedolah [the Great Assembly of Agudat Israel].
— What kind of new plague is that?
— A plague, you say? You silly woman! It's a kind of great assembly, a congress, „lehavdil". Do you know, Chava Leah, who goes to the Knessia? The very greatest sages, pure olive oil, the finest of the fine. It concerns the very foundation of our people's existence — to secure Jewish rights in the Jewish land on the foundations of the Jewish faith. Do you understand, Chava Leah, what it's about?
— I don't even begin to understand; I only understand that it's probably an important matter, so as far as I'm concerned — go in life and peace. Arrange everything well, and while you're at it, once you're in Marienbad, grab a few baths too — what harm can it do you...
— Now I tell you, Mr. Aberżanek, that Marienbad is a precious spa. My shepsl came back a different man, not the same at all — you simply cannot recognise him. As soon as he came into the house he asked straight away:
— Where is Shlomele? How is Shlomele? And as soon as he saw him, he fell upon him and started kissing and hugging him:
— My dear, [bright?] child, in vain did I quarrel with you, in vain did I cause you grief. Now I see that you are right — I heard it with my own ears from the [holy?] mouths of great Jews. Forgive me, Shlomele; what was, was; from now on there is peace between us; you and I are now „brothers in distress". Give me your hand, Shlomele; from now on we are both — Revisionists...
— Well, what do you say now, Mr. Aberżanek? You laugh at the spas — so I've come to plead with you[?]: you are not right; a spa really is a good thing, and the best spa of all spas is Marienbad.
— Long live Marienbad!..

Jewish Youth, Language and Literature.

1.
Day after day [?] people write and speak about the economic ruin of the Jewish masses, about the economic decline of the Jewish people, etc. [?]. True, these are all problems of the first rank, which decide our national existence, but it is a mistake not to speak, or to speak little, about our cultural tragedy, about the tragedy of our language and literature, because just as great as our national-economic ruin is, our cultural ruin is no smaller.
2.
The economic crisis, which has already lasted 3 years, has thrown all of humanity into a state of hopelessness and despair; hunger, want and unemployment have become everyday accompanying phenomena in the life of humanity.
The well-known economist Jacob Lestschinsky characterises the economic decline of the Jews thus: "From wholesale trade one passes to middle trade, from middle trade to retail trade, from retail trade to street trade, and from street trade to beggary." That is what our economic situation looks like. And what about culture? Is culture, then, a matter torn away from grey everyday life? Culture does not float in the air; spiritual problems are not [sic] interwoven with material interests; therefore, because we live in such a hard time, when all our care and thought are directed only at how to obtain work, bread and a livelihood for ourselves or for the family, the man without a livelihood has no desire [?] to think about spiritual problems; where there is economic decline, cultural decline follows too. In all countries where the crisis has struck deep roots there is an enormous decline in the field of literature and culture. Therefore we do not wish to blame anyone for not buying Yiddish books, Yiddish publications, because there is simply no money, every grosz is precious and one cannot allow oneself a luxury such as a book; but we do wish to blame them for not reading a Yiddish book, for the disdainful [?] attitude toward the Yiddish language and literature, for the stepmotherly, belittling attitude toward everything that is called creating Yiddish culture and living Yiddish culture.
3.
After Hitler's coming to power, when thousands of Germans were made into Jews overnight, people thought that assimilation had already been buried forever, but we were mistaken, true [sic]. An assimilation with an ideological content perhaps no longer exists; an assimilation with a vision [?], with pathos, is no longer to be found; but in everyday life assimilation is at work even more than before, and above all linguistic assimilation.
We hold that never before has the Yiddish language been so foreign to Jewish youth as now; Yiddish is treated with contempt, people are ashamed of Yiddish — and on whose part? On the part of those who have always been, and perhaps will later also be, the bearers of our national culture. Rarely does anyone read a Yiddish book; at home you will find books in all sorts of languages, only not in the Yiddish language.
When you walk in the street, two thirds of the strollers do not speak Yiddish, and the same is true at home.
We have in Będzin one single Jewish library, the Sholem Aleichem Library, which owns several thousand books, the best and newest works of Yiddish and world literature; this library has only 150 readers, while at the same time Jewish youth fill the non-Jewish libraries, where 90 per cent of the readers are Jews.
Things are no better with the press. The Yiddish press is read mostly by the older public. Most of the youth buy and read the non-Jewish press.
Together with linguistic assimilation comes cultural shallowness; the youth in Zagłębie, and above all in Będzin, idle about [?]; they fill the dance halls, card houses and cheap places of amusement. Let us say it to our disgrace and shame! A large part of the Jewish youth, [—] the girls [?], cannot even sign their names in Yiddish.
The works of the Yiddish classics are gathering mould; people do not know Mendele and do not read Peretz; they have not even heard of a Leivick or of David Pinski; the youth is being torn away from Jewish folk creation and folk treasures. The youth is demoralised and petty [?]; it pains the heart to see how the young, growing generation has not the slightest notion of our past and future.
4.
Many causes have brought about this situation: not having a national life of our own, being constantly harassed in the press, the suppression of national cultural needs, the non-Jewish schools, the environment — the outer one, which to a great extent has split [?] the inner environment too, the home. But a people with ideals must not succumb to the environment of the street; it must go its own way.
And what must we do? Create first of all cultural institutions, courses, which can educate the youth in our spirit. That is the task of a Jewish kehilla.
Unfortunately we have a kehilla that is deaf to all the social and cultural needs of the Jewish population in Będzin, and in general we cannot demand anything positive from it, and we ourselves must create something.
We know that there exists a People's University at the Szul-Kult in Będzin; let it take upon itself the initiative of creating courses in the Yiddish language and literature, and the work must begin now.
The wave of illiteracy on the Jewish street is growing; the youth, which is becoming spiritually foreign to us, must be rescued from cultural destitution; it must be educated, a new soul must be poured into it, a soul with a faith — a faith in the existence of the Jewish people; it must be made into loyal and proud Jews and human beings, who will be called to fulfil their task in life.
Tsvi Paliwoda.
Make Possible the Study of the Jewish Economy

(An appeal to the Jewish industrialists in Zagłębie.)
The unhomely tidings from Jewish towns and townlets that reach us day after day through the Jewish press certainly give us much to reflect on regarding the specific Jewish economic structure and Jewish economic policy in general. They also remind us of the urgent necessity of research and constructive help for Polish Jewry.
* * *
Purposeful[?] economic help, however, cannot be conceived[?] without a prior and precise study of the economic situation.
Those who still held an indifferent or dismissive attitude toward Jewish economic research have surely changed their minds under the pressure of recent times. The turbulent[?] economic processes taking place lately among us, and chiefly around us, must first of all be researched by us.
* * *
In line with the arguments cited above, the Yiddish Scientific Institute (YIVO) has strengthened the activity of its economic-statistical section.
After the successfully conducted study of Jewish commerce, which also yielded relative[?] results, the economic-statistical section at YIVO has proceeded to a study of Jewish industry in Poland.
* * *
Jewish economic research is hampered mainly by the fact that it has no official bodies behind it that regulate economic life and that would be obliged to supply it with the proper information and figures. Jewish economic research is therefore wholly dependent on the proper understanding and good will of Jewish society.
* * *
Just as throughout the country, YIVO has set out to study Jewish industry in Zagłębie as well.
This study has been entrusted to the writer of these lines, who has undertaken to carry it out, trusting in the healthy instinct of Jewish society and in the proper understanding of the Jewish industrialists.
From these columns we therefore appeal to the Jewish industrialists in Zagłębie that this time, too, they express their already traditional positive attitude to every public cause and show their good will when they are visited in the above-mentioned matter during the study of Jewish industry, which is one of the pillars of the Jewish economy in Poland.
P. Lejner.
In the Days of Repentance

Torah sayings and remarks in honour of Yom Kippur.
Collected and styled by Yehuda Yafet.
a) The Eve of Yom Kippur.
"On the ninth of the month" — do we fast on the ninth? Do we not fast on the tenth? Rather, this tells you: whoever eats and drinks on the ninth, Scripture accounts it to him as if he had fasted on the ninth and the tenth. Berakhot 8b.
Why is it a mitzvah to eat on the eve of Yom Kippur?
Because for sins between man and his fellow, Yom Kippur does not atone "until he appeases his fellow." Therefore it is the custom on the eve of Yom Kippur to go to friends and ask them to forgive the sins one has committed against them — and appeasing a friend is best done over a little feast. "Whoever is mollified by his wine has something of the mind of his Creator," says the Gemara in Eruvin 65. So it is indeed the custom on the eve of Yom Kippur to go to good friends, to taste something at their home and exchange good wishes. It is about this eating on the eve of Yom Kippur that the Gemara speaks.
Yalkut Yehuda.
* * *
Eating on the eve of Yom Kippur has such importance because when a Jew lets himself enjoy[?] the eve of Yom Kippur, eats and drinks — he surely has trust that his sins will be forgiven, and such trust is a great thing!
R. Moshe Leib of Sasov.
b) Yom Kippur Will Not Be Abolished.
"All the festivals will be abolished except Yom Kippur." Midrash Mishlei.
Because — said Rabbi Levi Yitzchak of Berdychiv — Jews will never stop sinning, and the Blessed Name will never stop forgiving...
c) The Day of Amnesty.
The blowing of the shofar on Yom Kippur — say the Rishonim — derives from the fact that Yom Kippur recalls the Jubilee, for the Jubilee year began on Yom Kippur and on the Jubilee the shofar was blown.
And just as the Jubilee is a year of the land, Yom Kippur is a release of sins, an amnesty for sins. In the Jubilee the fields return to their owner even when he has no money to redeem them, and Yom Kippur releases the sins even when one does not repent...
R. Shlomo Leib of Łęczna.
d) Avinu Malkeinu.
"Our Father, our King, we have no king but You" —
Strictly speaking we cannot ask forgiveness of the Master of the Universe, because "a king who forgoes his honour — his honour is not forgone": a king has no right to renounce his royal honour, for his own honour he may indeed forgive, but the honour of other kings, of the estate of kings, he surely cannot forgive.
But You say "we have no king but You" — You are, after all, our only King, and in Your kingdom there is no estate of kings; therefore You may indeed forgive us.
R. Eleazar Fleckeles.
e) A Sin for the Second Time.
"Sins one has confessed on this Yom Kippur one should not confess on another Yom Kippur; but if he repeated them, he must confess again." Yoma 86b.
Why does the Gemara need to say that if one commits the same sin year after year one must confess it again on Yom Kippur — what supposition[?] would there have been that a repeated sin should need no atonement?
— Because every sin that is committed again no longer has any taste of the forbidden, of transgression. One feels a taste in it only the first time; the second time one already feels disgust for it...
Sama de-Hayye.
f) Silence the Accuser and Take the Defender in His Place.
Take the defender "in his place" — you, defender, take as your means of defence "his place": the Jew's place and situation in which he finds himself, the hard conditions in which Jews live. How is it possible in such a situation to remain honest and to keep the Torah?..
Re'ah[?] Levanon.
g) Kittels.
That is why on Yom Kippur one dresses in white kittels, as a sign[?]: "Though your sins be like scarlet, they shall be white as snow." Maharshal.
h) "I Have Forgiven, as You Have Spoken."
Just as you speak, just as you plead — so do I forgive you..
R. Nachman of Breslov.

Were you there with your heart

If not, you still have time — quick,
cleanse your thoughts!
Between today and the Day of Judgement

Quicker, Jews, grab your chance,

Grab it, oh, grab it,
cleanse yourselves of the mud,
as long as there is still time

and its end — hidden,

hard to picture —

and with a thousand "what-ifs"
every single second is pregnant.

If a man wants to be a man,
let him be it n o w.

Women.

[Feuilleton — impressions from Safed; women and holidays.] By P. Blumenkranz (Sosnowiec).
(Impressions from Safed).

That women readily sacrifice themselves for the commandment of "fashion" is a thing known since the ancients. From all the commandments that depend on time women are indeed exempt — but not from the greatest and holiest commandment of all, the one that is renewed, recut[?] and altered[?] by the Paris tailors. This commandment was given to them, apparently, for the sake of balance[?], and they fulfil it in all its details and fine points.
For example — let it not be said aloud — let us take just one example. That most women have legs which, God spare us, are not in order, every young man or old man knows; nevertheless not one of them transgresses the positive commandment of short dresses. The legs, the log-like ones, are indeed displayed in all their "splendour", but what can you do — it's in fashion, so: "be killed rather than transgress".
Women bring even greater sacrifices to this idol.
In every town or shtetl you will notice at dawn or early in the morning how [—] fattened, heavy-limbed women run. One meets them in the parks, the suburbs and generally wherever there is room[?].
What this poor running is about — everybody knows, namely: these running women eat a lot and eat[?] a lot, do not work — and at the same time not to grow fat is a hard task. So one has to run in order to keep the figure.
So, poor things, they run to be able to eat, and eat to be able to run — and so round and round.

• • •

This year Safed has become the fashion in Warsaw and Łódź.
We can imagine how, after the Shavuot season, the women began to "interest" their [—] husbands in that suitable[?] "gar-morush"[?] [unclear], and the little mouths surely chimed one to the other:
— Bolu, wiesz, jadę do Safat! [Polish: "Bolu, you know, I'm going to Safed!"] And you — na [?]!
— No, dzieckiem jesteś [Polish: "Well, you're a child"], ja [?] do Safat.
And so the Salas, Balas, Balbinas and Jadzias[?] gave up Michalin, Śródborów and Wiśniowa Góra and went to Safed.
Which is just what one of the "[?] season" ladies complains to us about:
— A few years ago one used to see at least[?] distinguished, elegant people here, mostly foreigners; you never saw a woman without a "lis" [fox fur]; today it's different — a stampede...
We cannot say that this "bitterness" was entirely without basis[?]. Warsaw girls — office clerks and "daughters of the house" — scraped together[?] a few gulden and went to Safed; women from Nalewki[?], from the Iron Gate. [—] came to "play a role".
And when you talked to such a lady, she would first of all tell you two things: about her love for her husband and about her [—].
For example, one conversation:
A young woman sits in a restaurant, twirls the menu and does not know how to tell the waiter that she wants wine (she was afraid to let on[?] that she knows Yiddish).
Well then. One helps her out. One starts a conversation. She tells at once (no exaggeration):
— Yokh [I] didn't love my husband before the wedding. Yokh was a "piękność" [a beauty], quite extraordinary "powodzenie" [success with men]. Yokh "strasznie" [terribly] didn't love my husband, but he was "idealnie" [ideally] good, bought me presents[?]. "Wyobraź sobie, pan" [imagine, sir][?], on the day of the tna'im [betrothal agreement] yokh dug in my heels that yokh wouldn't go to the "zaręczyny" [engagement party].
My parents "rozpaczali" [despaired], they begged me:
— Zosieńko[?], what are you doing to us! He's so good for you, you'll be a "księżna" [princess][?]! But I — no and no.
Now I love him, he is very good to me, works hard.
— Yokh must go soon — she adds — yokh must talk to him on the telephone. Every day yokh talk to him. He "tęskni" [pines] very much; yokh do[?] nothing. Yokh haven't the slightest "pojęcie" [idea] what the maid cooks for lunch. Yokh know nothing about a kitchen. But yokh "szalenie" [madly] love the sun; yokh must go home "opalona" [tanned][?], "jak z brązu" [like bronze].
And she talks and talks.
— Yes, she didn't "zdradzić" [betray] her husband; her "koleżanka" [girlfriend] married "z miłości" [for love] and cheats right and left; she "potępia" [condemns] that. Why laugh? Because[?] they have nice teeth... One may still love someone besides one's husband, but to jump from one to another is "karygodne" [reprehensible]. "Dlaczego ... pan ..." [Polish, unclear] she. They have already had such "[?przeżycia — experiences]". Interesting, it is, that...
And besides[?] — one could easily recognise a woman from those Warsaw streets. She didn't understand a word of Yiddish; she told at once that all year she does nothing, and about her great love for her husband.
Again, it was almost plainly obvious that the girl was from Łódź, since she powdered herself every two minutes (even on the beach).
For that Łódź women are elegant even the Warsaw women admit — only they add at once, and rightly, that they are no natural beauties and that they paint themselves too much.
In the casino sits a girl — elegant, made-up, sun-tanned, with blackened brows and [?]. We start talking and it turns out that our guess was right — a Łódź [?]. Every couple of minutes she looked into the mirror and powdered herself.
She went up to the roulette table and soon sat down again, laughed loudly, straightened her [?], "poprawiła" [adjusted] her fox fur and "[?]" herself.
— Before leaving she had a shoemaker make her 10 (ten) pairs of slippers — all to fit[?] her foot.
The 10 pairs of slippers we did not count after her, but we can testify that the next morning she came to the casino with a bandaged foot...

• • •

Now a few words about the ugly sex. The men may take fright and think that one has to be very supple in body[?]. But — a question on a story: here you meet a Jewish woman from [—], there a girl from Lwów, later a painted one from Sosnowiec, then a woman with her own car!
Let us then reassure all the young men and tell them that they need to know only two things: joking and dancing — and above all the second.
The Łódź lady with the 10 pairs of tight[?] slippers will give up an excursion because of the slippers, but not a "[?]" — dancing opens all the doors of the lower Garden of Eden.
A woman who already has to leave confesses[?] to her acquaintances on the beach:
— When I came to Gdynia by ship I had a partner — "bosko tańczył" [he danced divinely]! I'd gladly have stayed on a few more days.
It's true, it's hard to dance; one doesn't really dance at all, one only treads on each other's [—] — but dance one must.
So the good dancers feel like Casanovas in their young years. Such a dancer casts an eye on the prettiest girl, walks up to the little table, makes an elegant bow, kisses her hand, mumbles his name and his [—] — and that's that.
Such a dancer doesn't go out with girls in a way that he would have to pay. He wants a free hand — it's cheaper and more practical. He goes alone, and his feet already provide him with company.
It is therefore no wonder that one hears[?] a bit of "Kedushat Levi" [the Berdichev rebbe's book] and martyrs all those who toil every day in the [—] with the dance teachers. What indeed, poor things, should the wretched people do? There is, after all, such a hell too, where all good things are set out before you, but you can't reach them.
These young men, or old ones with a young evil inclination, could simply rake in "powodzenie" [success] with women[?] — only this little matter of not dancing stands in the way.
So they work, toil, sweat — and meanwhile time passes; that doesn't hurt either, everything runs away like that anyway, as Shmuel said[?] to Rav Yehuda: "Grab and eat, for the world we are leaving is like a wedding feast" [Eruvin 54a].

• • •

And since it is proper to part with a word of Torah, we will say no more about Safed today.
How a Crafty Character Tricked the Będzin Synagogue Beadle Out of the Holiday Baking

On Monday[?], the first day of Rosh Hashanah, in the morning, an unknown Jew in his fifties appeared in the Będzin town synagogue, went up to the beadle Szabsi Brasten[?] and introduced himself:
— "I am from Lublin, my name is Zylber. You have heard of the big firm Zylber in Lublin? I am that very man. Besides a [—], I own[?] several houses in Lublin, and since it has fallen to me to spend Rosh Hashanah away from home, I ask you to give me a seat in the synagogue; for this you will be well rewarded by me right after the holiday, and if you like, I can pay at once."
The beadle, impressed by the "speech" and even more by the promise, gave the "rich" guest a proper seat and took his coat and hat from him, as one does for a householder.
During the prayers the guest calls the beadle over and asks whether he could get a few pieces of cake for his son, who is lying in hospital, because — he says — bought pastries from a confectionery my son will not eat, since he is a student of the Yeshivat Chachmei Lublin; if you can get this for me, you will receive a proper recompense from me right after the holiday.
The beadle accepted this proposal too at face value and sent a messenger home to his wife, telling her to send cake and also apple cake.
When the beadle's wife heard that her husband was sending home for cake, and in these important[?] weeks at that, she took all the baking prepared for the holiday and sent it with the messenger to the synagogue — why ask questions, perhaps he wants to treat the synagogue wardens or the community leaders.
When the messenger came back to the synagogue with the cakes, they were saying "Shir ha-ma'alot mi-ma'amakim"; having no choice, the beadle handed the "parcel" to the "Lublin" guest, who indeed vanished from the synagogue within a few minutes and was not seen again.
Not Bronisława but Bronisław / Court Accepts a Woman's Claim That She Is a Man

As we have already written, a year ago a petition was filed with the District Court in Sosnowiec by the 23-year-old Bronisława Bednarska to change her first name and surname, because — she is in fact a man.
The trial, which has now taken place and which naturally caused a great sensation throughout Zagłębie, had been postponed for the second time because the court wished to hear the opinions of the medical world on the matter.
For this purpose Ms Bednarska was examined by Professor Olbrycht in Kraków, who established that "she" is in fact a "he".
On this basis the court changed the name from Bronisława to Bronisław.
"Bednarska" came to court already dressed as a man.

Suicide of a Young Woman.
On Tuesday evening the 22-year-old Zofia Kotna[?] in Sosnowiec committed suicide by cutting her throat.
K. committed the suicide after an incident with her husband.
—o—
"There, Where the Devil Cannot".
This Sabbath, to mark the opening of the theatre season, the comedy "There, Where the Devil Cannot" will be staged at the Sosnowiec Municipal Theatre.
—o—
Child Falls Out of a Window.
Three-year-old Nute[?] Rozenberg fell out of the open window on the first floor of the house at Krakowska 11 in Będzin, and the child was taken to hospital in a serious condition.
—o—
A Burglary.
On the night from Friday to Saturday various goods were stolen from Gitler's stationery shop in Sosnowiec. The thieves have been arrested.
On the Way to a "Zachor Brit" She Met the Vanished "Bird" in the Street

On Modrzejowska[?] Street in Będzin lives a certain Jewish woman, H., whose husband went away a long time ago, and there was no news at all of where he was.
The woman tried various means to find him, but he had vanished like a stone in water.
Last Saturday night, when the woman was going to a "Zachor Brit", she met her "faithful" husband.
— Mendel! Is that you?
But Mendel, surprised by the unexpected "encounter", quickly realised that he might fall into the "trap", and quickly vanished.
Drunkard Causes a Panic

Thanks to the fine weather, the "park" on Saczewska[?] Street in Będzin was full of children and adults too on both days of the holiday. But on the second day of the holiday, towards evening, the promenade in the "park" was disturbed because a drunkard suddenly began throwing stones. There was indescribable commotion and running about, and it only became calmer after the "hero" had been taken away by the police to the police station.
Rabbi Chameides's address in honour of the new school year.

In honour of the "new school year", which began last Wednesday, a prayer service was held at the Będzin school with the participation of the Katowice rabbi Ch. B.[?] Chameides, who delivered an address (in Polish) to the school youth, in which he pointed out the mission of the Jewish people in general and of Jewish youth in particular.
For the first time the Jewish children heard warm words from a spiritual representative at school.
Jewish young man carries a wounded Christian boy to hospital.

On Piłsudski Street in Będzin a boy, [son] of the house caretaker Chyras[?], was run over by a cart. At that moment a Jewish young man was passing by, who carried the unconscious Christian boy in his arms to the municipal hospital.
The "white foxes" gang jailed.

Recently[?] a great sensation was caused by the uncovered fur swindle, which was carried out by well-organised swindlers.
The swindle was carried out as follows: customers came into the fur shops, dressed[?] as railway officials, and bought the most expensive fur goods, especially white foxes. For the goods they bought, these persons paid half in cash and half in bills of exchange. Later the same persons sold the furs at low prices.
As a result of the investigation, the railway official Janas of Mysłowice and Izydor Kern of Katowice were arrested.
This week the fur merchant Pollak of Katowice was arrested. The latter is said[?] to have been the leader of the gang.
The merchants who suffered[?] are mostly from Zagłębie.
Where did the wallet go?

Before the Sosnowiec district court the trial took place of Mr. Abramczyk[?], who is accused that in his shop the wallet of L. Kasen, containing 2,830 zł, 5 pounds and various documents, disappeared.
Because Mr. Kasen is abroad, the trial was postponed.
Railway disaster beyond Strzemieszyce.

On Friday towards evening a railway disaster occurred beyond Strzemieszyce. A coal train travelling from Dąbrowa left the rails; 14 wagons were smashed.
The cause was that the wagons broke away from the train, which consisted of 100 wagons.
The hard living conditions caused...

Before the district court in Sosnowiec stood 2 assistant dentists of the Social Insurance Office (Ubezpieczalnia), who had committed abuses in their posts.
The accused were sentenced to a year and a half in prison.
The man killed at the Zawiercie railway station was a Jewish tailor from Sosnowiec.

In the previous issue of our paper we reported a telephone message from the Zawiercie kehilla board that a Jewish man had been found killed on the railway line there.
As it later turned out, the tragically deceased man is from Sosnowiec; his name is Abraham Wachs, a tailor. Wachs was travelling to Częstochowa. Under what circumstances he died has not been established.
Poet Bistritzky is coming to Będzin.

As we are informed, the well-known national poet Mr. Natan Bistritzky is to come to Będzin on behalf of the Keren Kayemet.
In honour of the visit a regional conference is to be held with the participation of all KKL branches in the Kielce voivodeship.
Sentence Reduced for the Demonstration in the City Theatre

[Sosnowiec — Courts.]
As we wrote at the time, during the performance of the "Cyrulik Warszawski" [the Warsaw revue theatre] in the city theatre, under the title "Alfa and Omega", rotten eggs were thrown from the gallery onto the stage. The throwers were Nara people [ONR, the National-Radical Camp], who used this as a demonstration against the play performed, which was written by the Jewish-Polish poets Tuwim [Julian Tuwim] and Hemar [Marian Hemar].
The gang stood trial before the municipal court in Sosnowiec, which sentenced two of the accused to 3 months and the rest to 2 months of arrest.
Against the verdict [?] the convicted lodged an appeal, and in these days the case was heard by the district court, which reduced the sentence.

Great Fire in Kielce.

[Kielce — disaster.] 40 poor Jewish families left without a roof over their heads
On the second night of Rosh Hashanah, at about 1 o'clock, a great fire broke out on Nowy Świat ["the New World"], in the first Jewish quarter of Kielce, which lasted a whole night. 8 houses burned down completely; 40 Jewish families, of the very poorest, were left [?] naked and destitute.
During the fire heart-rending scenes took place. By a miracle they managed to rescue the women and children, who had been sunk in deep sleep.
The situation of the unfortunate fire victims is an exceptionally bitter one: they are wandering about under the open sky and are simply "oys fun goys" [?] [apparently: utterly ruined].
On the second day of Rosh Hashanah relief committees for the fire victims were founded in all the houses of prayer.
In the synagogue, before the blowing of the shofar, Rabbi Rapaport called on the Jews of Kielce to help the unfortunate Jews.
On Wednesday a meeting of the council and the board of the Jewish community took place, at which it was decided to carry out a large fund-raising campaign. Rabbi Rapaport was elected chairman of the general committee and treasurer.
We too, for our part, appeal to the Jews of Kielce to take part in the fund-raising campaign and to donate appropriate sums for the 40 unfortunate poor Jewish families who have suffered such a bitter decree.
Monday — The Great Political Trial over the Events in Racławice.

[Miechów — trial.] As has already been reported in our paper, the Kielce District Court, at its visiting session in Miechów, will on Monday the 13th of this month begin hearing the great political trial over the events in Racławice.
Sixty persons will sit in the dock. 29 of them are under arrest and are being held in the Miechów prison.
Over 200 witnesses have been summoned to the trial. Close to 20 well-known lawyers will appear.
The trial, which will last barely two weeks, has aroused great interest throughout the country.
All the newspapers have delegated their correspondents to the trial.
Rosh Hashanah in Kielce.

[Kielce — holidays.] This year's Rosh Hashanah passed for the Jews of Kielce in a very depressed mood. The holiday began and ended under the sign of an intensified anti-Jewish wave, boycott, pickets and other Jewish troubles.
All the houses of prayer, especially the Great Synagogue, were overfilled with thousands of worshippers, who between one prayer and the next talked about the terrible troubles that pour down incessantly on Jewish heads. Jews hoped that perhaps in a year's time, at Rosh Hashanah, they would already find themselves in the built-up Jewish state.
60-Year-Old Jewish Woman Hangs Herself on the Eve of Rosh Hashanah over a... Stolen Goose.

[Kielce — suicide.] On Sunday, the eve of Rosh Hashanah, the 60-year-old Jewish woman Nispel [?] of Kielce (Old Warsaw [Street?], [—]) committed suicide.
The suicide had suffered for several years from a nervous disease. On the eve of Rosh Hashanah at dawn she went into the pantry for the goose, wanting to send it to the ritual slaughterer. Learning that the goose was not there, she took it very much to heart and hanged herself.
The funeral of the suicide took place on the eve of Rosh Hashanah towards evening.
Kielce Jews Had an Unhappy Holiday.

[Kielce — antisemitism.] The Jews of Kielce lived through two difficult holiday days.
On the first day of the holiday "Nara" [?] [ONR?] hooligans went out into the street with sticks in their hands and tried to provoke excesses. They went off to the park, where they formed a procession. There was panic among the Jewish women and children, who were in the park in large numbers.
On leaving the park the "Narowcy" [?] ran into a group of Polish workers. It came to a brawl; the Endek Duda was taken to hospital, and the SN members [?] Śliwiński [?] and Winer were arrested.
In the evening hours Jews were attacked again. The chalutz Gruszewski of the Borochov kibbutz was seriously wounded.
Windows Smashed at the Kielce Old-Age Home.

[Kielce — antisemitism.] On the second night of Rosh Hashanah a group of unknown "Nara" [?] [ONR?] people gathered in front of the building of the old-age home on Poniatowski Street and there threw in quite a number of large stones and smashed the windows.
The stones were thrown with such force that they actually fell into the beds of the sleeping old men and women. Among the old people there was an understandable commotion; the house staff went out into the street and began chasing the hooligans, who were not caught.
The police were informed of this, but when the police arrived none of the hooligans was there any longer.
The police drew up a report.
A Comic Story of 30 Złoty and a Pot of Potatoes.

[Kielce — local life.] At the landlord [?] Mr. G.'s, on Bodzentyńska Street, a poor tenant, Mr. B., has been living for years. The landlord recently obtained an eviction order against the tenant. At the same time he agreed with the tenant that if he moved out a day [?] earlier, at exactly 9 o'clock in the morning, i.e. last Monday, he would receive 30 zł. The money was deposited with a third person.
On Monday, however, Mr. K.'s wife took a fancy to cooking potatoes. The potatoes, however, knew nothing about the 30 zł., and at 9 o'clock they were not yet ready, but only around 10 o'clock. The landlord would not hear of anything and carried out the eviction. All the poor tenant's efforts to get the 30 zł. were of no avail.
All — because of a... pot of potatoes; but the landlord had no mercy on him in this either and gave him an "eviction".
Two Cousins Fight over a Bridegroom.

[Kielce — local life.] Miss R. of Działoszyce [?] was offered a match — a bridegroom from a neighbouring village. While in the town, the said young lady introduced the bridegroom to her cousin, Miss K. The latter, however, pleased the bridegroom more, and with good luck the engagement contract (tenaim) was concluded on Saturday night.
Miss R. found out about this, and during the signing of the tenaim she came in with her parents and made her cousin a "black wedding" [a scandal]. A brawl broke out, but the tenaim took place all the same.
Rosh Hashanah in a Night-Club

[Kielce — Society; Jewish–Polish relations.]
It is already an old rule: the bigger the antisemite, the more he "likes" "Żydóweczki" [little Jewesses], and the closer he is with "Żydóweczki", the deeper his hatred of Jews flares up.
Queen Esther left behind other grandchildren than[?] Mordecai the Righteous[?].
The "Żydóweczki", however[?], face no danger anywhere; they feel splendid in the company of uniformed and non-uniformed pure-Aryan cavaliers.
It is worse, though, with the Jewish young men who come in the company of "shiksas".
Jewish young men are very tolerant when they see Jewish girls or women of their acquaintance in the company of Christians. The latter, however, do not answer with such tolerance.
On this ground an ugly[?] scene played itself out on the night of Rosh Hashanah in one of the local night-clubs.
A. B. G—n, one of the most popular among the Kielce "better youth", who seeks out[?] all the novelties of the street, sports matches, and is a respected guest in all the establishments, a daring young man, with success among the fair sex regardless of nationality and religion, invited on Rosh Hashanah night his[?] brand-new acquaintance, a young Christian girl, and went off with her "into" one of the local night-clubs to wish himself a ketivah va-chatimah tovah [a good inscription and sealing].
At the little tables there happened to be sitting a few young "narodowcy" [National Democrats], who know this Jewish young man and envy him his successes, and this time it came to a sharp incident.
One of the "narodowcy" shouted loudly at the "Żyd" that he should leave the Christian girl alone.
— "Today is your Nowy Rok [New Year], isn't it, so go off to the bóżnica [synagogue]."
Another narodowiec went up to invite the shiksa to the Polish couple[?].
The Jewish young man stood up to them boldly, but one of the hefty narodowcy informed the young man through a waiter that he had better take himself off[?] as quickly as possible, otherwise he would be carried out of the place.
The owner of the place and the older waiters intervened; the Jewish young man declared categorically that he was ready for all the consequences — let them carry him out, but he would not take himself off voluntarily. He has a right to a shiksa, just as the narodowcy have to "Żydówki".
In the end a compromise was reached: the Jewish-Polish couple got a small table in a corner of the hall, where they indeed remained sitting obstinately, but in return they were not allowed to dance.

Merchants and Manufacturers Must Keep the Receipts for Rent

[Taxes — Rent.]
According to the new implementing regulation to the tax ordinance, merchants and manufacturers who do not keep commercial books will have deducted from their income (dochód) the sum that was paid as rent for the shop or for the factory premises.
The deduction will be made only if one has certified documents of the rent paid.
It is therefore necessary that every merchant and manufacturer, when paying the rent, should obtain a receipt for the rent bearing a stamp and the signature of the landlord or of his administrator, and with the date when it was paid and for what period the rent has been paid.

Yom Kippur in Zagłębie

[Zagłębie — Będzin, Czeladź, Sosnowiec: holidays; community; short news.]
[Yom Kippur] passed quietly; the synagogues and prayer houses were packed. Those called up to the Torah pledged large sums for the „Keren Kayemet“ (Jewish National Fund); the record in this field was set by the Ashkenazi synagogue in Będzin. In the Będzin City Synagogue Mr. Hibarocki[?] delivered a speech in which he called for pledges for the redemption of the Land [of Israel].
In the Będzin City Synagogue there was an extraordinary crush. The cantor Mr. Klansbald[?], with the choir under the direction of the new conductor Mr. Frenkel, led the prayers very beautifully; the worshippers took great delight. The choir does still sing with some strain, but „all beginnings are hard“...
— The report in yesterday's Warsaw Jewish press that „anti-Jewish excesses took place in Czeladź on the eve of Yom Kippur and that all the windows of the synagogue were smashed — does not correspond to reality; only in the Ger shtibl were two window panes smashed, which happened at about 9 in the evening.
—o—
Appeal of the Będzin rabbinate for the fire-brigade campaign.
In connection with the campaign being held this week for the Będzin Fire Brigade Association, the rabbinate asks all local Jews to support, as far as possible, this important and necessary campaign, which concerns the common good of our town.
It is to be hoped that the Jewish population will take proper part in this campaign.
—o—
Caught at the critical moment...
On the night of Yom Kippur Miss Wszebner[?] (Będzin, Kołłątaja 12) saw thieves break into Walcberg's[?] glass warehouse. The young lady notified the police, who arrived at once and caught the thieves.
—o—
A new security company.
In Sosnowiec a new company for protection against theft, named „Hipros“[?], has been legally registered. The new company is under the supervision of the police authorities, who issue instructions to the night watchmen. The „Hipros“ company is earning the public's trust because at its head stand Messrs. Piasecki, head of the waterworks office at the Sosnowiec Magistrate (town hall), and Mr. Rakitsch[?], both well known in Zagłębie.
As reported, the number of subscribers of the „Hipros“ company, Sosnowiec, 3 Maja 22, grows from day to day.

A Jewish-German Refugee Wants to Solve the Jewish Question

[Będzin — personalities; refugees from Germany.] He considers himself a second Columbus. Meanwhile, poor fellow, he needs a few złoty.
This week a Jew came to us at the editorial office, a refugee from Germany, Emil Spangler, who introduced himself as one who feels capable of "solving" the Jewish question. He is ready to write a book about it within 4 weeks that will cause a worldwide stir. The greatest trouble — he says — lies only in the fact that he has no one to finance it. He has been wandering about for years now, begging people to hear him out, but nobody wants to take an interest in him.
Besides the solution of the Jewish question, he also wants to publish a book that will utterly demolish the whole race theory. Here he comes forward with geographical proofs that are supposed to confirm his claims that the European peoples do not belong to the Aryan race, that the white race in general has nothing whatsoever to do with it, and that, rather, it is the Semites who stand closer to the Aryans. In this field — he says — he is able to make a revolution and even to show the greatest scholars and professors that they are living in error. But again the same story: he has no money to publish the book, and someone to finance him — that he does not have either.
In further conversation with the German refugee we learn two things: by origin he comes from Lesser Poland (Galicia), he is a native of the little town of Rymanów, and he is illiterate — he cannot write down a single word. He can only read, and he has read a great deal, chiefly history, but above all he considers himself an expert in the science of geography. Here — Spangler gets carried away[?] — he can turn worlds upside down; here he feels like a new Columbus who can astonish the world. He lacks only two things: a publisher, or a Jewish patron, to bring out his books, and a person to write down what he thinks and researches. In a word, he is capable of bringing the Jews "redemption".
In Poland — he says — I now wander from town to town and can in no way realize my plans. In Będzin I am looking for an atlas, and I want to demonstrate here, before all who know geography[?], the falsity of the race theory. I will point out great errors in the big atlas that was published in Germany in 1920. The same in [—] Römer's[?] atlas. In a word, I want to give culture a push.
We look at the great man and know only one thing: that he is in trouble, that he stands in the wilderness, that he is a wanderer[?] and must go to sleep in the hostel for wayfarers (hachnasat orchim), and then think about where to get a few złoty in order to wander on.

[Dąbrowa — Kehilla.] A deal remains a deal, and the kehilla “seat” belongs to the buyer.
In kehilla circles in Dąbrowa [Dąbrowa Górnicza] there is a seething dispute between one of the present kehilla parnassim and a candidate who figured first on the electoral list of “Beit Yaakov”.
The story is as follows: for the last kehilla elections in Dąbrowa, besides the “Agudah”, “Beit Yaakov” too put up a list of candidates headed by the parnas Kalman Epstein. The latter, wishing to secure his candidacy, turned to the Pilica [Pilica] Hasidim with the proposal that they unite with his list, and in return their candidate, Mr. Meir Lustig, was to figure in first place.
The Pilica Hasidim accepted the proposal, and an agreement was concluded between them and the above-mentioned parnas, according to which Kalman Epstein figures in first place on the electoral list and in second — Meir Lustig. If the list “draws” 2 candidates — well and good; if not, Epstein will cede his place to Lustig. As a guarantee, a few hundred zl. and also valuables were deposited.
The list, however, “drew” no more than one mandate, and Epstein was elected parnas.
And here the tragicomedy begins. Parnas Epstein would already have agreed to keep the points of the agreement and cede the “seat” to Lustig, but the “Agudah” leaders are against it, because that would weaken their “strength” on the kehilla council. So what now? They are trying to negotiate in fairness with the Pilica Hasidim that they return the “withdrawal money”. The latter, however, will not hear of it, arguing “a deal remains a deal” and...
Meanwhile Epstein does not attend the meetings of the kehilla council until the agreement is dissolved. Be that as it may, Dąbrowa is boiling over the “seat” affair.

Perhaps After All...

[Zagłębie — communities; opinion.] (On the proposal to create a Council of Communities — Va'ad ha-Kehillot.)
However much has already been written and said about a united representation of the Jewish population, its realisation has nonetheless remained stuck at a dead point.
And it is no wonder that such[?] an elementary idea of the hour cannot be realised, because however many virtues the authors of the projects may possess, they also possess one "small" defect, which must not be covered up at all; on the contrary, one must always point a finger at it.
The defect lies in this: whenever one begins to talk about centralising the Jewish forces, one always starts with the parties — and it is self-evident that the extreme left cannot agree with the postulates put forward by the extreme right, and the progressives can never agree with the religious, and vice versa; and if each party gets one representative for itself, the next one comes and demands for itself absolutely two representatives, etc.
So, from experience so far we know that if we start from the parties, the united force will come to nothing positive. The question arises: at such a responsible hour we may not be distracted for even a single minute — we must create a union; but how[?], and of whom should the union consist? In my opinion the union must come from the Jewish communities (kehillot). They are, after all, the elected representation of the Jewish population in every town. A Council of Communities must be created on the model of the communities abroad (England, America, etc.), where it is perhaps not so much of a necessity as with us. The tasks of such a council would be very great; among other things, a certain place must be given to the struggle against racial antisemitism, by publishing various educational pamphlets and undertaking various interventions on Jewish matters with various government authorities, with the cooperation of the Jewish parliamentarians, etc.
The Council of Communities must, and will be able to, dispose of larger financial means. As to where the money will flow from — the council will find[?] means; one of them could be that every community, when fixing its budget (etat), adds a surcharge to each budget, let us say 2 per cent, for the Council of Communities. Thus the community (gmina) treasury will not suffer from it at all, and it will not burden the taxpayer much, while it can bring large revenues through which the Council of Communities will be able to accomplish a great deal.
As for the statutes, which a special commission will draw up for it, in my opinion the authorities will certainly legalise them, because the authorities prefer centralised communities (gminy) to disorganised ones.
Now the question arises: who should take the initiative? Properly, the mission ought to be taken on by the Jewish community of Warsaw, as the largest Jewish community in Poland. Unfortunately Warsaw has no elected [—]; Łódź the same; and another community would not have the proper authority. So who then? At a meeting of the Community Council in Dąbrowa on the 29th of last month, the writer of these lines, after reporting on this, [—] as a council member, submitted a proposal that the Dąbrowa community administration should send a questionnaire[?] to the other communities in Zagłębie, so that they would state their views on the matter. For formal reasons the proposal will be dealt with at the next meeting; and if the answer of the other communities is positive, the Zagłębie communities can then set up a temporary organising committee which will be able to convene all the communities of the entire Kielce voivodeship, and then one may hope that, following this example, all the other communities in the other voivodeships will do the same. In this way[?] perhaps a central body can be created — after all, every institution, whether political, economic or philanthropic, has its central body.
Only one thing must be remembered: "What you must do today, do not put off until tomorrow." Perhaps after all...
S. Jakubowicz.
Member of the Community Council in Dąbrowa.
The Role of the Shop Window

[Commerce — advice to traders.] (For the attention of retail merchants.)
In today's article we shall dwell on the importance of displays in the retail shop.
For display one uses both the shop window and the interior of the shop.
The most popular and most effective means of advertising is the shop window, and therefore the retailer must put a great deal of [—] into its proper fitting-out; at the same time one must take into account the size of the shop window and the branch of trade.
The shop window must first of all stop the passer-by, draw his attention to itself, and finally interest him in the articles on display.
The passer-by's attention can be drawn first of all by proper[?] cleanliness of the shop window, then by the lighting[?] of the display, by a harmonious play of colours and by appropriate tastefulness of the light.
If the shop window and the conditions allow, it is desirable[?] that the advertised articles be placed on stands[?] that are in constant motion. In this case too the articles must be aesthetically arranged[?] and well[?] lit.
The scientific observation of various advertising firms has shown that the passer-by stops very willingly at shop windows dressed in various colours. The base on which the articles are displayed should be covered in white.
The articles in the shop window must be changed often and systematically, since mostly the same people pass by the shop, and the shop must keep them in constant suspense and interest them with articles of various kinds. If the passer-by becomes convinced that the shop window is often changed, he will stop by himself every time in order to become acquainted with the new articles.
Besides the shop window, one must make proper use of the interior of the shop for display purposes. The rule must be that as many articles as possible catch the customer's eye. A customer often comes in for one article, but precisely thanks to the display he also becomes interested in a second article, which he had not at first intended to buy.
A very bad impression is made on the customer when the window shows the same price on a better sort of article than in the shop. This happens most often in grocery ("colonial") and fruit shops, and therefore we not infrequently hear from the customer: "Give me cherries or oranges from the shop window." The merchant justifies himself that these are the same fruits, only in the window they are laid out more nicely, but the customer will not hear of it and moreover[?] loses his trust in the merchant. From this one must learn that the interior display must be arranged with the same care[?] as the exterior one.
In any case, every merchant must realise that the effort and the expenses for a display and for the decoration of the shop window are not things thrown away, because in the struggle for the customer the winner is the one who can better exploit the means of advertising.
Kelum.

A Young Couple

[Literature — sketch; family life.] By M. Goldenberg.

Half a year after the wedding. He is busy with business all day long, and she keeps house. Both young, fresh as two "shehecheyanu" fruits [new-season fruits over which the shehecheyanu blessing is said].

In the evenings they receive guests. The electric lamp pours out rays of light, the hanging [?] mirrors smile in rainbow colours, the sideboard sparkles — mahogany set [?] with crystal — the many-coloured [—] [?] on the wall smile, and the flowers in the room look as if just picked in the garden. On the divan lie handsome cushions of wonderful workmanship — all of it ready to delight the eye and to bear witness to prosperity [?]. And in case all that is too little, on a handsomely carved little table [?] there also stands a gramophone, and on the table — this is the main thing — stand all sorts of fruit bowls [?] and trays, pure Japanese work with geishas in flowered kimonos, full of pastries, fruit, preserves — all the work of the young housewife's golden hands. The guests enjoy themselves [?], are not bored [?], and send words of praise [?] to the woman of valour, and she glows [?] like a ripe rose, and her eyes — two little smiling flames — "Eat, eat!" — she begs them, young Madame Sheingold [Szajngold], while the hospitable host winds the gramophone. A cantorial "Kevakoras" [a cantorial piece from Unetaneh Tokef; printed in the diminutive "kevakoresl"] curls upward in high trills, but the company of guests is absorbed in weightier things: conversations about the season's clothes, chatter about cakes and preserves and freshly baked bits of gossip about close acquaintances — and so it goes on until well into the night. Then, as if by magic, the light goes out, the talk falls silent, and a quiet calm wraps everything in the dark cloak of sleep.

So days and weeks go by, and apparently the Sheingolds lead a fine life. The circle of guests grows and the gramophone gurgles. People say that such a fitting assemblage of everything bears witness to taste, to the capital of a good home — and with her own hands, too! A young housewife — and a real one!

Sometimes there comes a "yoma de-pagra" [a day off], a holiday, and young Mr Sheingold happens to be at home; he wanders about all day long and does not know what to do with himself. He has a chat with his wife — well, how much can one chat? He meets a customer, finds himself an errand — but the day drags on and on. After lunch one would gladly lie down — but how [?], like a robber, mess up [?] such royally made beds; he would be in heaven stretching his legs out on the divan — but how can one trouble such wonderful embroidered cushions, lying there so spaciously?

Mr Sheingold wanders about the beautiful rooms, tired, neglected [?], and waits [?] for the evening [?], when guests will come, his wife will set refreshments on the table, and he will wind the gramophone until it grows late and the quiet calm takes pity on him and puts him to bed.

A few more months go by, and a new little living creature makes its little voices heard in the quiet, comfortable flat, and because of the new little creature a whole commotion arrives: an old nanny with a wrinkled face, diapers and swaddling bands, [—] [?] and friendly, cheerful mazel-tovs, and also the troubles of young breasts that yield more milk than the tiny little babe needs.

The gramophone is left standing as if forgotten, the lamp sometimes looks out with one single eye and sometimes it is completely blind, no refreshments are set out any more in such order and hospitality on the beautiful laid table. Quite other figures now bustle about the house: old women, advisers, experienced since their own young womanly years, who want [?] to give advice though no one asks them...

Young Madame Sheingold is truly at her wits' end, not knowing whom to listen to. Her mother comes to visit — how could one not come to a daughter with a firstborn? — a Jewish woman of the older generation. She sticks a knife into a prayer book and lays it in the cradle at the head, a charm against a "good eye" [a euphemism for the evil eye] and against — may it not be spoken. And Madame Sheingold — a woman with a city gymnasium education, with literature — obeys [?], because what won't one do when the child has a tummy-ache and "plays on its little head"? — The doctor says the milk is to blame; but if mother has a charm — perhaps that is good too!

And Mr Sheingold — busy as he is with business all day — and at night, right in the middle of the best sleep, a thin little squeal breaks out and simply pierces the ears; sleep is lost. One [—] [?], gets out of bed, wakes the nanny, turns on the lamp, and the night flies out as if up the chimney. The little one wriggles and chokes with crying. The young madame weeps [?], [—] [two very doubtful lines: "16 [?] ... wet-nurse [?], a former singer [?]"], and her mother, [full of] dreams [?]: — "I know what it is [?]: your fine guests have devoured the child with their eyes!" And she goes over just as she is, in her bodice, only in her underslip and with the quilt [?] over her head, licks the baby's little forehead with fasting spittle and spits three times, muttering with her lips, and then she says: — "I've learned enough by now; you'll see, there's nothing wrong with the child!" And from all this Mr Sheingold goes about with a headache, his face unshaven, and Madame — in a worn-out dressing-gown, her hair dishevelled, and everything in the house, even the cushions on the divan, everything tells of a new [?] dictator who rules the house — the new little squealer.

And sometimes one of the former guests comes into the house — and carries out a freshly baked bit of gossip: "At the Sheingolds' — God preserve us [?] — [—] [?] in every little corner!"

Sukkot Thoughts.

[Essay — for Sukkot.] By Y. Wygodzki [J. Wygodzki].

"You shall dwell in booths seven days."
(Leviticus 23:42).
"...Therefore they go out of houses full of every good thing at the time of ingathering and dwell in booths, in remembrance that they had no inheritance in the wilderness and no houses to dwell in." (Rashbam, ibid.).

Sitting in the sukkah should remind the Jew that Jewish property, goods and chattels, which he acquires and possesses in the wilderness, that is, in exile, has no real and factual value whatsoever, and just as a sukkah is in danger of collapsing at every gust of wind, so too Jewish property in exile is in danger of being destroyed at every mishap."

The content of the above-cited quotation has never yet been so topical and so aptly fitted to Jewish reality as to the present-day Jewish situation. When the Jewish people is living through a period of enormous sufferings and catastrophes, when not only is its property ownerless prey, when not only does the enemy tear the last morsel from its mouth by force, but its very life is in danger of being destroyed and annihilated. For a long, long time the waves of hatred, enmity and annihilation against [?] us Jews have not reached such an enormous tempo and character as now — in particular the antisemitism of recent times, which in its hatred surpasses even the most tragic times of sad Jewish life in exile; and that is indeed [?] why we celebrate this year's [?] Sukkot in a depressed mood and in a spiritual depression.

But "the Divine Presence does not rest amid sadness etc., but amid the joy of a commandment" [as printed: "amid commandments of joy"] — we must not fall into any mood of despair nor be dominated by any depression. The latest period in our history is — despite the enormous sufferings and catastrophes — a period of extraordinary historic events, a period of struggle and heroism, of ascents and victories, and, to spite our enemies of all times, they have not [?] and will not succeed in destroying the Jewish people. For the Jewish people, even though in its exile life it no longer exists as a political and territorial community, has never ceased and will never cease to exist as a spiritual people; and even when it is "not by might, nor by power," it is nevertheless a people "by spirit" — no physical force whatsoever is able to break it. What is more, the effect is the opposite: "But the more they afflicted them, the more they multiplied and spread"; the more [?] our enemies oppress and persecute us, the more national pride and national consciousness grow in us — the instinct of self-preservation, of "auto-emancipation," the struggle for existence — and with the strong, stubborn force of the "stiff-necked people" we overcome all sufferings and persecutions and are strengthened and encouraged for the continued, final and victorious struggle.

And when we leaf through the book of Jewish history of the last fifty years, we are simply dazzled and amazed [?] by the colossal, gigantic successes and progress that we have achieved in this relatively short span of time. It is truly simply astonishing what gigantic historic transformations [?] we have gained [?] during this time. The last years have been an epoch of enormous struggle and sacrifices, of heroism and victories with regard to the building of the Land of Israel. The stubborn battles around the building of Eretz Israel have been turned into a "front-line struggle" and into central pillars of Jewish life, and they continually govern ever larger Jewish masses, for whom Eretz Israel has turned into the one and only point of support and centre, where they can escape from the heavy, unbearable sufferings of exile and find work and a livelihood there, and above all live their lives as politically free human beings and proud national Jews in their historic, renewed fatherland.

And therefore, when we celebrate the festival of Sukkot, we must not fall into any mood of despair, and the sukkah must not serve us merely as a symbol of the sufferings of exile; it must also remind us of the revival of Eretz Israel and of the renewal and rise [?] of our cultural treasures and of the rebirth of "for out of Zion shall go forth the Law." The sukkah must also remind us of the joy of the "Festival of Ingathering," when the Jewish people lived in its own free land on its own soil, "every man under his vine and under his fig tree," and was in those [days] joyful [?] at the time of the harvest and the gathering-in of the grain from the field and the fruits from the trees.

But above all, today's sukkah must remind us — as thousands of years ago, the Jews in the wilderness — that we are once again building our old historic land, Eretz Israel; and that despite our sufferings and catastrophes in exile, we have nevertheless had substantial [?] ascents and victories in the building of Eretz Israel, and that we have already been privileged to see the great historic miracle that the British Royal Commission has decided to propose to the League of Nations the creation of a Jewish state in Eretz Israel; and we must exert ourselves for the further struggle, sacrifices and endurance until we bring about the final victory — and then we shall celebrate Sukkot only as "the season of our rejoicing"...
Treasures That Lie in the Seas

The newspapers have just reported that the company founded in England and America to raise the English ship "Hussar", which sank in 1782 with a sum of three and a half million pounds in cash in gold, has given up its work. For about twenty years people toiled to bring up the ship, which had sunk into the abyss, and it did not succeed. So they stopped the work, which had cost many millions of dollars.
Such[?] companies have been founded more than once. Just as people search[?] for gold in various countries, so they try with all of today's technical means to bring up ships that carried gold and sank for various reasons.
In the archive[?] of the Leipzig[?] fair many ships are recorded that went down carrying gold or jewellery. At the same time one must also reckon with the fact that on some ships chests of gold and [—] [—] stones were insured. In the past the insurance companies did not take over the goods themselves through their own trustees; they relied on the shipping agents (expediters), who were mostly also "gainers"[?] and used to take a share of the insurance.
Such a[?] case happened many years ago with a French ship that sank about five[?] hundred miles off Tunis. The ship carried precious pearls insured for one million pounds. For years the ship was searched for and not found, and the insurance company paid out the million pounds. About twenty years later the ship was nevertheless raised – and in the chests there were no pearls at all, only lead... and of the insurance swindlers there is by now not a trace[?] left.
But such[?] things have happened once or twice; about the sunken "gold ships" it is known for certain what they carried. For example, the Spanish ship "Don Pedro", which sank in 1812, had pure gold worth two million pounds. That ship has not been found to this day.
In 1707 the Dutch ship "Wilhelmina" sank with thirty chests of gold; thirty years later, 1817[?], the "Kreinstein"[?] sank with 1,250 small boxes of gold.
Not far from Biscay the ship "Wengro"[?] went down with gold worth ten million francs, and in the seas of Mexico lies the ship "Islander", which carried gold worth five million pounds.
If one adds up all the gold sinkings[?] about which it is known for certain that there was gold aboard, a sum of a billion gold pounds lies in various abysses of the seas.
It certainly pays to invest [—][?] and to try with every possible means to bring up the sunken ships with their treasures. All over the world there are many companies with large capital, but they seldom manage to dig anything out; mostly they lose their money in the long search. For "what the sea swallows, it has almost never given back"...
Z. Haber, Vienna.
Heard and Seen.

[Sosnowiec and Będzin — weekly feuilleton.] By Ben Amotz.

The committee is still waiting...
At the first meeting of the Sosnowiec committee for Brisk [Brześć nad Bugiem] he — a man of society and, God forbid, no pauper either — took the floor and spoke thus:
— "Brisk lies on my heart; we Jews will show our stubbornness and our character; Brisk opens not only our hearts but also our pockets; the greatest sacrifices will not be too hard for us for Brisk's sake."
The meeting ended, a committee was elected and the collection began. Our man of compassion, on whose "heart Brisk lies," inquired from time to time how much had already been collected. "It's little — he sighed — too little; the Jews of Sosnowiec must give much more."
He himself had not yet given, but that is a trifle: when you go in to him, he will gladly hand over[?] the several hundred złoty; in fact you need not go at all, he will surely bring it himself — why should you trouble yourselves? Why? He knows very well that a relief action is being carried out for the victims in Brisk; he will not wait until the collectors come to him either, he will bring his donation himself.
But what happened! Our "philanthropist" left for a "summer residence" — abroad, it seems — and gave nothing for Brisk! But don't hold it against him and don't suspect him; he probably forgot — after all, a trip abroad involves considerable[?] worries, above all the worry of getting a permit to take a few złoty abroad. So in his great haste he surely forgot about the Brisk action; but rest assured that when he remembers it there, the warm baths will do him no good, and he will probably send his donation by telegraph.
Our "philanthropist" has already come back, thank God, and he is surprised — no, he is angry: the relief committee has not yet been wound up! "I thought that when I came back, God willing, the committee would already be past its liquidation."
— But, honoured sir, what about your contribution for Brisk?
— What a worry you have! About me[?] — a joke, upon my life[?]. You know from the very first moment that "Brisk lies on my heart"...
— And the committee is still waiting...

When the heavens split open...
— "Gevald, Jews, the Messiah is coming! — not only coming, he is already walking, one can already hear his steps, the redemption is drawing near!" — with these "glad tidings" a couple of Jews came into the editorial office with the request that we publish the "tidings" in the paper that "the Messiah is coming."
At first we had the impression that the group had escaped from the asylum in Bushavits[?]; but later, when the matter became clear, we too had willy-nilly to admit that it is indeed so, that:
— "The redemption is indeed near, and the first to have been privileged to sense the time of redemption are the Będzin Revisionists.
And it is no wonder that precisely this organization has been privileged to be the herald of the redemption: first, its motto[?] is to fight until the realization of "Malkhut Shaddai" [the Kingdom of the Almighty], and second — the power of the match just concluded with the "holy Agudah" [Agudath Israel] in Marienbad is so great that the above-mentioned organization is arranging a dance evening precisely on the night of Hoshana Rabbah.
— "When the heavens split open"...
And to their credit it must be said that as soon as "the heavens split open" the music will stop playing and the couples — stop dancing, for after midnight the true[?] "tikkun" for the whole of Israel begins; this is also how "Hapoel" in Będzin acted recently, which arranged a dance evening for the first Selichot and "Zekhor Brit," but the dancing went on only until after midnight..
The same custom is not altered by the followers of "Malkhut Shaddai" either, who have decided to dance on Hoshana Rabbah until — "the heavens split open"..

The youth says goodbye...
We accepted our friend's suggestion to take a stroll through the town in the evening hours. The town clock had struck the 21st hour, but there was still lively movement in the streets; strolling couples argued out loud — and why not, "let others also hear what we are talking about" — so, probably, think to themselves those who make the "hundred-times march route" along Małachowskiego Street back and forth. But that we do not care[?] to know; we want to dwell on one matter that demands attention. Namely: among the strolling crowd we came across 10–11-year-old children from the public schools and also from the secondary schools; they stroll in closed ranks almost every evening, the "qualified" ones light up a cigarette, and those who are not short of a grosz "pop" into the cinema and "live it up."
Later we happened to go into a Jewish confectionery shop, where we witnessed the following scene:
A Jewish school head came into the shop and asked for chocolate. The shopkeeper, without the slightest suspicion that the customer "has an Aryan stomach," handed him chocolate from a Jewish firm.
— "I don't want this chocolate" — declared the head — give me another chocolate (naming at the same time a firm known as very "Judenrein").
— "Panie [Sir]" — the shopkeeper began to work on the Jewish customer — the chocolate I am giving you is one of the very best firms, apart from the defect that the manufacturers are Jews. But no argument had any effect; the Jewish customer did not buy, because the shop did not have the requested chocolate of the non-Jewish firm.
Seeing this scene, the question was answered for me at last why most of the Jewish school youth in the public schools have a negative attitude to Jewish national matters: if their teacher boycotts products of Jewish firms, the pupils surely cannot be better — "If Rabbi did not teach it, whence would Rav Hiyya know it?"...
When we came out of the shop, the strolling in the streets had already thinned out; the night stillness was broken from time to time by the "Servus" that the "youth" shouted as they took leave of one another...
— Hush, the youth is saying goodbye...
