Sukkot — The Holiday of Contrasts

[Feuilleton — Sukkot.] Yehuda Yafet.
(Reflections).
Sukkot is the Festival of Ingathering. The true nature-holiday. More precisely: the holiday of nature. Not of nature's joyful blossoming, of spring [?], and not of nature's first fruits, of bikkurim, but of the generous [?], sated [?] blessing of nature, when Mother Earth has already given out everything she had to give her children. "On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, when you have gathered in the produce of the land."
Which holiday could express the Jewish attachment to the soil more than Sukkot? "Any man who has no land is not a man." A person who has no land of his own, who treads on foreign soil, is no person — and what is a people that has no soil of its own?
The Festival of Spring, the spring holiday, is lived through even by the wanderer. With us even [?] the spring holiday is a holiday of "going out," of [—] evacuation [?]; first fruits are brought even by the exile, for what exile does not try to root himself in the earth again, and every fruit is in any case blessed with first fruits, with bikkurim — but the Ingathering is the fullest and ripest expression of attachment to the soil and of rootedness.
And therefore —
"In sukkot you shall dwell seven days — leave the permanent dwelling for a temporary dwelling."
Therefore demonstrate that there is no rootedness, that all is temporariness; therefore demonstrate it with your wanderer's tents...
Could any other people display more contradictoriness [?], more disharmony in its character, in its thinking and in its feelings?
Ze'ev Jawitz once wrote:
"One of the most essential [?] character traits of our people, which distinguishes us from all peoples and makes us an exception, is unity. Let us compare our people with the Spanish people, which sits on its own land and strives above all to be conservative in spiritual matters. Was it possible for that people to maintain unity? It almost [?] never could, because just as its fatherland and language are a jumble of the Visigoths, Arabs, Armenians [?] etc., so too its culture is a mixture of the spirit of distant [?] peoples, who will never bind themselves together in one union."
To which Micha Josef Berdyczewski wrote:
"When was this great thing [?] ever with us [?]? When did there not reign among us family quarrels, a war of ideas, and a complete divergence of opinions on the most important questions of life, which still reign within us and among us?"
But — what does unity mean? Unity means a fusion precisely of contrasts, which are brought into harmony. Had there been no war of ideas among Jews, there would have been no unity. That is precisely the wonder of the Jewish spirit, which unites extremes, creates a harmony out of them, crystallizes them into a whole, while letting the particular hue of light of every element [lit. "object"] taking part in the process of harmony shine through.
In this way Sukkot can be both a holiday of the temporary dwelling and a holiday of land, of rootedness.
Sukkot — the holiday. Of joy, of "and you shall rejoice in your festival," "and you shall be only joyful."
At no other holiday is joy so demanded.
And Sukkot — the holiday of Ecclesiastes, of "vanity of vanities"...
"And you shall be only joyful."
And —
"And of mirth, what does it accomplish?"
Sukkot — the holiday of exile. "For I made the children of Israel dwell in booths when they went out of Egypt." Sukkot, which recalls the first Jewish wars with the Egyptians, with the eternal Amalek.
And —
Sukkot, the holiday on which seventy bullocks are offered for the welfare [?] of the nations of the world...
Ulu Ushpizin Ila'in (Enter, Exalted Guests)

[Sukkot — essay.] L. Serner.
Ulu, ushpizin ila'in, kadishin! [Enter, exalted guests, holy ones!]
Come in, holy, exalted guests, to us in the sukkah!
Not into rich palaces shall we invite you, dear guests, not to richly laid tables do we call you, because there [?] — we know you very well — there is not your place; there, in the big houses with many rooms, you do not feel well, you feel cramped — you can barely catch your breath! And you do not go there very gladly...
To our poor sukkot — "temporary dwellings," the symbol of our life in exile — we ask you to come on the night of Sukkot. Poor they truly are, our sukkot, the walls put together from thin boards, just enough to fulfil the obligation. They can barely withstand an "ordinary wind"; let a slightly stronger breeze come, and they can no longer hold out.
But we feel overjoyed in our poor sukkot. They remind us of our freedom of old, which we finally reached after long wanderings [?] in the cruel desert..
Ulu ushpizin ila'in..
• • •
Tivu, ushpizin ila'in, kadishin! [Be seated, exalted guests, holy ones!]
Be seated, holy, exalted guests, at our common [?] table!
There is no rich, laid table here, for the holiday of Sukkot has long ceased to be for us in exile the "Festival of Ingathering" of old. Quite involuntarily other thoughts come to mind: a hard, unbearable situation, the approaching winter...
But on the "Festival of Ingathering" of old we want today to forget all this. "One who is distressed is exempt from the sukkah" — Rabbi Reb Bunem interprets: if you are "distressed" in the sukkah — in the sukkah, which is the only commandment into which you can enter with your whole body and life, even with your boots... if [—] in the sukkah you can also be "distressed," then you are exempt from it — so you had better go home!
We want, however, to spend today with you, dear, exalted guests, in our joy, a true joy of a commandment.
On the night of Sukkot we want to forget all our accounts of the whole year. Whatever trend and current [?] you may belong to, dear neighbour, however you may think and feel — as long as you are no traitor to our so suffering people and you have come to us in the sukkah with honest intentions — then you are a member with equal rights and have the right to take part in our joy...
"Happy is the lot of Israel" — let us all rejoice together in our holiday, let us bind the happy past to the so promising future!
Tivu, ushpizin ila'in..
A Little Feuilleton.

[Feuilleton — Sukkot; a Jew's thoughts in the sukkah.]
Sitting in the Sukkah.
A Jew sits, a simple Jew, in the sukkah and thinks...
What does a Jew think about as he sits in the sukkah?
He thinks that it is a bit of luck that you do not always see the sky before your eyes. It is good that a sechach (the sukkah's leafy covering) covers the roof[?] over your head and makes a partition between you and the sky, where the stars twinkle so brightly, so luminously, that it grips you[?] at the heart...
How can one, in such a time, allow oneself to shine like that[?]?
And something else a Jew thinks about in the sukkah...
He does not feel overly at ease: what if the sechach suddenly up and falls right into the Jew's soup? After all, the sechach grew out in the open, and the Jew took it and brought it into town, laying it on top of his sukkah...
And the Jew sitting in the sukkah thinks further:
— What a state of affairs it would be if someone were to drop in on him in the sukkah now and see how he and his household are celebrating the holiday — that person would run off at once, for nowadays it is better to sit in the sukkah without neighbours, so that the other fellow does not see what is going on with you...
And the Jew in the sukkah thinks about many other things nowadays, but who can tell and pass on everything?
The Jew sits in the sukkah and thinks. Let him think — one may think about everything, as long as one does not speak.
Rebus.
From the World of Film.

[Cinema — China and Japan; Spain.]
China Is Topical.
Now, when present-day China never leaves the newspaper columns in every country, when, besides that, people speak of the Sino-Japanese conflict in the Far East, from where the flame of war may flare up over the whole world, everyone's eyes turn there in suspense, and one is bound[?] to show[?] a certain interest in literary works that depict China or Japan. Film too, the most topical of all branches of art, is beginning to take an interest in China—Japan. Lately films about China are being made; Chinese and Japanese actors, even extras, are being sought out with a candle. At present a film, "Shanghai Daughter" [Daughter of Shanghai], which depicts the latest events in China, is in the works in Hollywood. The lead role is played by the well-known Chinese actress in Hollywood, Anna May Wong. Her partner will be the actor Akim Tamiroff[?], whom we know from the China film "The Yellow Treasure".
The Film about Spain.
"The Last Train from Madrid" — that is the name of a film about present-day Spain, which stands in the fire of a bloody civil war. At its centre are several foreigners whom the civil war has made witnesses to cruel events, when Madrid is being evacuated and they travel off to Valencia.
In Honour of Sukkot.

[Sukkot — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes; by Yehuda Yafet.]
Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes about Sukkot, collected and styled by Yehuda Yafet.
a) The Etrog.
"And why the etrog? Because it resembles the heart and comes to atone for the thoughts of the heart." Midrash Aggadah.
And that is why people are so particular that the etrog should have no blemish: all the limbs can bear blemishes, only the heart cannot endure the slightest defect, the lightest blemish.. R' Naftali of Ropshitz [Ropczyce].
b) The Gentiles and Sukkot.
"And the Lord will smite the nations that do not go up to celebrate the festival of Sukkot." Zechariah.
Why should the nations go to Jerusalem to celebrate the festival of Sukkot? Is it their holiday?
But on Sukkot the Jews used to offer seventy bulls for the seventy nations. Jews bring sacrifices to God and pray for the welfare of the nations, and therefore Sukkot is their holiday too.
c) One Who Suffers Is Exempt from the Sukkah.
The law is that "one who suffers is exempt from the sukkah," and therefore one does not sit in the sukkah when it rains too hard. R' Velvele[?] of Strykov [Stryków] did sit in the sukkah even during a heavy rain, and when he was asked why he did so, he answered:
On the verse "and rest under the tree" the Midrash says: "Your children will merit[?] the shade of a sukkah." Abraham our father was also engaged in a mitzvah[?] — he was waiting for guests — and yet he sat even "in the heat of the day," in the fiercest heat. It follows that even one who suffers is merely exempt from a mitzvah, but he is not obliged to exempt himself...
•
The Shulchan Aruch says that whoever sits in the sukkah during rain is called a hedyot (a simpleton).
Said R' Chaim of Sanz [Nowy Sącz]:
— A simpleton I want to be, and in the holy sukkah I will sit...
•
The Chiddushei HaRim said about this:
— What does "hedyot" mean?
— Simple, straight, without knots ("senkes")..
d) Hoshana for the Sake of Our Creator.
When a craftsman makes a vessel that is no good, people do not talk about the vessel, but about the craftsman. Hoshana — help us, God — for the sake of our Creator, for Your sake, our Maker. We have sinned, we have committed follies, but the fool is, after all, Yours.. R' Yechiel Meir Sanelnitser[?].
e) Oppression in Exile Teaches Fear of You.
When Jews are oppressed in exile they become pious, they study; troubles make them God-fearing and devout... Ateret Paz.
f) Hoshana for the Sake of Your Covenant [printed "lema'az"].
R' Shlomo Leib of Lentshne [Łęczna] once stood up to argue with the Master of the Universe:
The Gemara says: "A covenant is mentioned with salt and a covenant is mentioned with suffering; just as salt sweetens meat, so suffering sweetens the body" — just as salt gives meat its flavour, so suffering gives life its flavour. But, Master of the Universe — R' Shlomo Leib exclaimed — too much salt is no good either!. "Hoshana for the sake of Your covenant" — the "covenant" compares suffering to salt; but salt is good only when there is a pinch of it, too much spoils the meat. So too suffering is good only when there is a little of it, a pinch...
g) And to Lay Hold on Folly (Ecclesiastes 2:3)
The Midrash says on this: "What is 'in folly'? — 'besikhluta'." What does the Midrash mean by that?
But in the portion Ki Tisa (31:6), on the verse "in wisdom and in understanding," the Targum says: "bechokhmeta uvesukhletanu"; thus "understanding" means "sukhletanu," and here too "and to lay hold on folly" means to grasp, to consider with reason, for otherwise the verse makes no sense. Gishmei Berakhah.
h) I Made Me Gardens and Orchards (ibid., 5)
The Targum says on this: "and its boundaries from the wall of the city of Jerusalem" — I built the orchards outside the wall of Jerusalem. The question arises: what does the Targum mean to say here?
But in Bava Kamma 82 it is said: "Gardens and orchards are not made in Jerusalem," and that is what the Targum means: that the gardens and orchards were made outside Jerusalem.. Megillat Sefer.
i) Then I Saw That Wisdom Excels Folly as Far as Light Excels Darkness (ibid., 13)
"Or" (light) means both day and night (see Pesachim 2a). So it is with wisdom: the wise man can make himself out to be a fool as well, whereas the fool cannot make himself out to be a wise man.. The Vilna Gaon.
j) He Has Made Everything Beautiful in Its Time.
"Rabbi says: even for a matter of sin." Midrash.
What does that mean?
But with a sin too there is a difference according to the time. When a young person sins, it does not provoke so much anger[?] as when an old man sins.. Avodat Elokim[?].

Shaking. (A Lesson)

[Humour and satire — “Der Kokh-lefl”.] [Section heading:] “Der Kokh-lefl” [The Cooking Ladle] — humour and satire in honour of Sukkot — by Amotsl.
The matter of shaking is one of the “shakiest” problems. In our time it has counted as the most important and the shakiest.
It is a problem over which the clever shake their heads “no” and the fools nod “yes”...
For instance, when it comes to a certain Zagłębie communal activist, people say:
— “A fool, a fool, and he sways”...
Such swayers can be counted in Zagłębie by more than a “shok” [threescore].
Zionists say that the word “shoklen” [to shake] derives from “shekel”.
The Shlomei-Emunim types say it derives from Sh"K (Shabbes Koydesh, the holy Sabbath), which their sons and daughters “shake off”.
Our left-wing parties are shaky themselves and stand on chicken legs.
Whatever you touch here — everything shakes — it is a shaky situation...
And to tell the truth, it is better to shake than to stand completely[?] still.
So let us shake, and by this merit may we have a Sukkot that is all holiday!
Not a Sukkah Conversation

[Humour — “Der Kokh-lefl”; joke.] He: Last night I dreamt I was sitting like this with Maniek.
She: (curious) Really?
He: Yes. So we're talking, and he says to me: I'll show you right away a woman who is a terrible seductress of men. When she gets to know a man — married or not — she already turns his head, and he must already come to her, and he must already sin, he must.
She: Interesting.
He: And he takes out the picture and shows me. So whose picture do you think he showed me?
She: Whose?
He: Your picture.
She (agitated): When Maniek comes here, I'll slap him and throw him out.
He (alarmed): What, he has your picture?
She: (catching herself) No, no, what do I know? How would my picture get to him? But why does he have to come to you in a dream?

Prophecies for the New Year

[Humour and satire — “Der Kokh-lefl”.] The magistrate [town council] will take a fresh loan and prolong the old debts. The streets in Warpie and Kazader[?] will be paved and beautified.
What the Jewish councillors achieve in the magistrate for the Jews will still remain a secret.
The kehilla will take on several more officials to supervise the "corner" (unlicensed) slaughterers; the rule of the presidium will last long; the petitions for aid will be distributed as fuel in the coal campaign; and the kehilla council will undergo a rejuvenation operation.
The "Peretz" Society will still not have finished the statute[?] for the workhouse, and the plot will be overgrown with grass.
In the Sosnowiec "Linas ha-Kholim" there will still be no general meeting.
In the rabbinate there will be a civil war with the newly arrived rabbis and rebbes.
President Ritski[?] will deliberate a whole year whether to call a plenum of the kehilla council.
To the club of the Sh.T.K.[?] the same members will come, only with new evening dresses and new gossip.
Yosef.
Satan's Complaints

[Humour and satire — “Der Kokh-lefl”.] The Days of Awe are already gone, when Jews begged to be forgiven their sins and threw the whole blame for their sins on me.
Jews, what do you have against me? How am I guilty towards you?
Once, when I was young, I used to have to work hard and bitterly to talk an honest Jew into a sin; but today — who needs me at all? Before I even stir, everyone has already sinned ten times.
Here I spent this summer at a dacha in the mountains. My God, how sinful are[?] Your mountains! Oh, what went on there!
When I look at today's women, I say that every one of them is more dangerous than a hundred Satans. Short, thin little dresses, entirely without stockings! What does one need a Satan for?
Therefore I pray to the Master of the Universe:
— Merciful God! You surely see that the world needs me “for kapores” [i.e. not at all]; they sin without me much faster and harder, and I am already old, I cannot watch people sin so hard. Give me some other occupation.
Every Rosh Hashanah I pop into a synagogue and look for a penitent there. Well, righteous men one cannot find — so I wanted at least to see a true penitent who regrets his sins for at least one day. And what do I find? Nobody thinks of stopping sinning. Looking into their prayer-books, they plot sinful thoughts in their heads; they only want to wheedle a good verdict-note out of the Master of the Universe, and afterwards they'll carry on with their old tricks.
Master of the Universe, have pity on the old Satan who has grown weak, and give him some other livelihood, where he would have something to do and not take a pension for nothing.
I Have All of Sukkot at Home!

[Humour and satire — “Der Kokh-lefl”; poem.] [Subtitle:] Told by a contented Jew.
Don't worry, brother,
don't worry that you're a pauper,
listen closely to my plan,
and you'll save yourself from everything.
Sukkah:
High up on the 4th floor,
there's no lack of wind and rain,
[—?] I have a [—?] there,
so my flat is “first class”.
Etrog and lulav:
My wife is yellow as an etrog,
the children — green as willows,
my skin trembles like a lulav —
so I have everything according to the law...
Challah:
Challah is collected for me, truly,
by my neighbour going here and there,
just like a communal charity bowl...
so I have challah sweet as a tart.
Meat:
From my landlord I hear coldly
[—?]: “The bailiff is on the spot!”,
till my very flesh splits from me —
so I have meat aplenty.
Fish:
My wife thrashes about like a pike,
I, like a fish, don't say a word,
in my heart I grant she's right...
so I have fish of that sort.
S.
He Makes Himself at Home

[Humour — “Der Kokh-lefl”; joke.] Asher: I tell you, when a person doesn't understand [—?], he can bring himself into the greatest misfortune.
Binyomin: Meaning what?
Asher: Last year at Sukkot Akiva was my guest. Of course I received him very warmly and told him, as is customary, to feel at home. And what do you think happened? It didn't take even five minutes before he quarrelled with my wife, threw the cat out of the house, dismissed the cook, beat the child black and blue, broke half a sideboard of dishes and called me the worst names.
What Jews Prayed For

[Humour — “Der Kokh-lefl”; joke.] A husband — that he be the only man of his wife.
A neighbour — that as many girls and boys as possible be born.
A lawyer — that husband and wife keep on fighting.
A doctor — that people be ill the whole year.
A dentist — that mouths rot.
An aviator — that he not fall to the ground.
A weather prophet — that he guess the weather correctly.
A barber — that women too grow beards.
Sayings.

[Humour and satire for Sukkot — sayings and jokes.]
It is better to be beautiful than to be good, but it is better to be good than ugly.
• • •
The only people who never make any mistake are — dead people.
• • •
One must beware of a person who is quiet and of a dog that does not bark.
• • •
Some people get up in the morning and suddenly become famous; others, on the other hand, stay awake[?] a whole night and become sadly famous.
• • •
With the white[?] cloak of charity one can cover whole mountains of sin.
• • •
A beautiful figure is better than a beautiful face, and beautiful conduct is better than a beautiful figure.
—o—
A brilliant idea.
As we learn, the “Bund” has taken over the sale of etrogim from Arab orchards. Every Bundist is obliged to buy an etrog with an Arab kosher certificate from the Grand Mufti [“hoypt-mufti”], so as in this way to harm the Jewish Yishuv and support the Arab pogrom-makers.
—o—
The sukkah and tenant protection [“lokatorzy-shuts”, from Polish ochrona lokatorów].
An explanation from our lawyer.
In answer to the many inquiries we explain that the law on reduced rent does not apply to Sukkot; the question will be settled together with the rent reductions for commercial enterprises.
Sholem and Yisroel

[Humour and satire for Sukkot — jokes; Sosnowiec.]
Two friends, Sholem and Yisroel, were walking home from the field, and they had to cross a muddy place. Sholem says to Yisroel that he must carry him across the mud, because it is written in the Torah “and peace [sholem] upon Israel [Yisroel]”.
Well, no choice — Yisroel took Sholem on his shoulders and carried him through the mud.
Having gone half the way, Yisroel goes and throws Sholem down into the mud and smears him from head to foot. Sholem asks him what that means. Yisroel answers that he too remembered that it is written in the Torah “and I will give peace in the land [in the earth]” [printed “ותית”, for ונתתי] — so you have to be in the earth [“in drerd” — also: go to hell].
—o—
The worry of a Sosnowiec “crisis magnate”
Lately it has become the fashion for rich men to go for the holiday to the guest-houses in Rajcza and Bystra.
One of the Sosnowiec upstart “crisis magnates” [those who got rich during the crisis] also went to Bystra for the first days of Sukkot. On arriving there he asks the guest-house keeper:
— Sir [“Panie”], when does one eat here?
— Breakfast from 9 to 11, second breakfast from 11 to 1, lunch from 1 to 4, afternoon tea [“podwieczorek”] from 4 to 6, supper from 6 to 9[?].
At this the “crisis magnate” scratched his little beard and said:
— I don’t understand, so when will I have time to pray?...
Long Live the Pole!

[Humour and satire for Sukkot — poem.]
Yom Kippur, thank God, is gone,
the weeping. Sitting whole days
saying “Ma’avar Yabbok”...
The shofar has long been silenced,
Sukkot goes, Sukkot comes,
already one must carry poles [“drenger”, from Polish drąg]...

There is no lack of poles among Jews,
they grow here at every step
like mushrooms after rain...
The pole — he is the hero of the day,
he has a great field of work
on almost every road..

In short, gentlemen, bring here
all the poles, as many as can be,
let no one get away.
I am building a sukkah now — a treasure!
For everyone there will be found
a place, a spot with me...

Wedding ring — “who has made me a slave”.
A modern man — “one beloved and one hated”.

Subtenant [“sublokator”] — “a plague in the house”.

Divorce (get) — “who frees the bound”.

“Randke” [Polish randka, a date] — “sick with love”.
The Four Species

[Humour and satire for Sukkot — dialogue; parties.]
A conversation between party men
— There is one thing I cannot stop wondering at.
— Namely?
— About the four species.
— What do you mean by that?
— It really is a wonder past understanding: four Jewish species, and they can stay united for seven whole days — how is that possible?
— I really don’t understand...
At the Selichot.

[Humour and satire for Sukkot — jokes.]
In the women’s gallery at the Selichot a Jewish woman sits and prays: “Dear Father, Master of the Universe, see to it that my sister-in-law in America becomes fat and broad.”
A neighbour asks her: — Why on earth are you praying for your American sister-in-law?
— She sends me a parcel of old clothes every year, and they are narrow and tight on me.
—o—
Overheard and caught.
During the Days of Repentance a widow sits on her husband’s grave and wails aloud:
— My dear husband, you have gone and left me desolate and lonely; one comfort remains to me — at least now I know where you spend your nights...
Sweet and Bitter.

[Humour and satire for Sukkot — short poem and aphorism; Zionism.]
Working for yourself is sure [so printed; perhaps for “sweet”],
working for someone else is bitter,
writing cheques is sweet,
writing appeals [“rekursn”] is bitter,
having one’s destined match is sweet,
having a master [“hersher”] is bitter,
taking money to the bank is sweet,
wearing torn shoes is bitter,
hearing music is sweet,
hearing curses is bitter.
—o—
A kind of aphorism.
The various rich so-called Zionists betroth the Land of Israel “by money” — with money they intend to give up to the [—] [“ka-shne”?]; “by deed” — with promissory notes which they issue for the “Keren Isur” [so printed — “Fund of Prohibition”, a pun on Keren Hayesod] and let them be protested; but not “by cohabitation” — coming to Eretz Israel, that not.
Open the Gate for Us...

[Subheading:] The gates of the houses must stay open until 11 o'clock
Two weeks ago the board of the Merchants' Association in Będzin adopted a resolution to approach the competent authorities so that in the winter months, too, the gates should be closed at 11 o'clock in the evening.
Welcoming the resolution, we pointed out that other economic organisations, too, should support the resolution and take an interest in the question; but, as we learn, nothing at all positive has been done to have the head starosta's decree rescinded[?] by the local organs of authority.
There is, however, still time to do something in this direction: the Jewish merchants' associations, together with the artisans' associations, must not neglect the matter, but should make every effort to have the gates stay open until 11 o'clock in the evening.
Paid a Vow Because He Had a Dream...

One of the gabbaim of the minyan at the Artisans' Association in Sosnowiec was approached in the street by an unknown Jew, who gave the gabbai 3 and a half złoty, which he had pledged a year ago in the above-mentioned minyan.
"Why I have not paid the vow until today," the stranger said, "you had better not ask. Perhaps I would not have paid the vow even now, were it not for the terrible dream that if I do not pay the vow, a great misfortune hangs over me..."
The gabbai is very pleased with this and wishes that all those who do not pay their vows should have such dreams...
Lecture by Prof. Fodor in Sosnowiec.

The society "Friends of the Hebrew University in Jerusalem", Zagłębie branch, is organising next Saturday a lecture by Prof. Dr. Fodor, professor at the Hebrew University in Jerusalem, on the subject "The Hebrew University and Its Cultural Tasks".
The lecture will take place in the premises of the Merchants' and Industrialists' Association, Sosnowiec, 3 Maja [Street] 11, at half past eight in the evening.
The person of the lecturer and the subject have aroused an understandable interest among Zagłębie Jewry.
One Jew Against Another

On Sunday, in broad daylight, when Henech Wechsler of Sosnowiec was standing in front of his shop on Mandzhev [Modrzejowska?] Street, an employee of Rożański's [?] shop in Katowice ran up to him and with a blunt[?] object struck Wechsler's right eye.
Zionist Organisation in Sosnowiec Celebrates a House-Warming.

The Zionist Organisation in Sosnowiec has moved to large, splendid premises on Wspólna Street. During the High Holidays a minyan was organised in the new premises, which proved very successful. A larger sum was also collected for the KKL [Jewish National Fund] during the vows [pledges].
The festive opening of the premises is set for Saturday night of Chol HaMoed. Advocate Hartglas has been invited to the celebration.
Impressions of the Zionist Congress.

On Saturday night, a fairly large audience gathered in the premises of "Tehiya" in Będzin for the lecture by Dr. Weinzieher on the subject "My Impressions of Switzerland".
The speaker, as a member of the Jewish Agency at the Zionist Congress, gave a series of descriptions of the general life in Switzerland and its magnificent natural scenery, and went on to the contested "yes" and "no" question at the Congress; in this connection Dr. Weinzieher characterised a few personalities of the Zionist Executive and President Weizmann himself[?], who made a strong impression on him.
The lecture, which lasted 2 hours, was heard by the audience with great attention.
Będzin Has Won...

[Subheading:] Jabotinsky's lecture will take place in Będzin.
For several weeks the "struggle" between the Revisionist organisations in Będzin and Sosnowiec went on. The "struggle" was over Jabotinsky's coming to Zagłębie, where he will give a lecture soon after Warsaw[?].
The two towns competed with each other, and in the end Będzin "won"; this week the local organisation has already paid the full amount for Jabotinsky's lecture.
Extraordinary Meeting about the Commercial School in Sosnowiec.

Under the chairmanship of city councillor A. D. Kajzer[?], an extraordinary meeting was held on Sunday evening in the premises of the Small Traders' Association in Sosnowiec on the question of creating a commercial school for merchants.
After the chairman had welcomed the representative of the Merchants' and Industrialists' Association, Mr. H. Feldman, Mr. Feldman spoke on the importance of opening a commercial school as quickly as possible in connection with the new commercial laws for merchants.
Messrs. Feldman and Kajzer[?] then spoke on the question, and an appeal was made to all Jewish merchants in Sosnowiec to enrol as members of the commercial school, so that the matter can be realised as soon as possible.
Intensified Campaign of the “Shomrei Shabbat” Society in Będzin — A Signal When Candles Must Be Lit — A Demonstration in Front of the Shops That Are Open on the Sabbath

[Będzin — religion, Sabbath observance.] On Sunday a meeting took place in the premises of the Będzin rabbinate with the aim of strengthening Sabbath observance in the town of Będzin.
The meeting adopted a series of regulations, among others that every shop should display a plaque of the “Shomrei Shabbat” society. The plaque is to bear the inscription “Remember the Sabbath day” (Zakhor et yom ha-Shabbat). An appeal is also to be issued to the Jewish population to buy only in shops that are closed on the Sabbath.
It was then decided that a “siren” should be installed in the building of the municipal mikveh, which is to give a signal when the shops must be closed and the candles lit.
On one of the coming Sabbaths several hundred religious Jews will demonstrate in front of the shops that are open on the Sabbath.
The Swindle Did Not Succeed — But One Should Not Change Money in the Street

[Będzin — swindle.] As Mr. Mordechai Dafner [?] was walking along Małachowskiego [?] Street in Będzin, an unknown Jew came up to him with a request that D. change a 20-złoty banknote for him into small money. When Dafner had changed the banknote into 4 coins of 5 zł., the Jew asked him for small change: “If you haven't got any, here, take back the fives.” Dafner, however, saw that instead of 4 the Jew was throwing back into the [purse] only 2 coins of 5 zł. Dafner then held him and wanted to call a policeman, but at once a second Jew sprang up, who begged Dafner not to do it. “After all, it is — he said — just before Yom Kippur...”
“Jewish Youth Spreads Germs of Demoralisation...” — So the “Związek Polski” in Sosnowiec Has “Established”

[Sosnowiec — antisemitism.] In the Sunday issue of the “Kur. Zag.” [Kurjer Zagłębia], the “Związek Polski” in Sosnowiec addresses Polish parents with an appeal in which the “Związek” expresses its “concern” about the future of the young Polish generation.
And what is the remedy? The youth must have no dealings whatsoever with Jewish youth, which “is always an element of destruction and spreads germs of demoralisation”.
The “Związek” also expresses its great sorrow that Polish children play with Jewish ones, and it warns Polish mothers to keep watch over this... and that [the children] should not play with the little Jews (małych żydków — Ed.).
“The Dybbuk” and “Tkies Kaf” in the Będzin Cinemas

[Będzin — cinema.] The “Nowości” cinema in Będzin, which had been closed during the summer months for a thorough renovation, reopened at the end of Yom Kippur. This cinema is showing a film work that has not yet been seen in Zagłębie.
As the cinema management announces, the newest film hits will be shown in succession, among them also the Yiddish films “The Dybbuk” and “Tkies Kaf” (The Handshake/Vow), which will be shown during the days of Sukkot.
Commercial Employees Who Must, After All, Be Registered with the “Ubezpieczalnia”

[Poland — social insurance, employees.] Until now there is still a difference of opinion on the question of which employees one must register with the Ubezpieczalnia [social insurance fund] and which are not subject to it.
According to the law, one must register with the Ubezpieczalnia those commercial employees who have completed 6 classes of a secondary school, or a secondary vocational commercial school, but also those who, apart from the work of selling in the shop, are also constantly occupied with keeping the books, with the cash desk, or with purchasing the goods.
On the other hand, a commercial employee or shop assistant (ekspedientka) who does not have the above-mentioned education, but who, apart from the work of a shop assistant, is occasionally, but not constantly, employed in such work as is performed by a white-collar (intellectual) worker — need not be registered with the “Ubezpieczalnia”.
An “Orthodox Section” Founded at the Keren Kayemet in Będzin

[Będzin — Zionism, Jewish National Fund.] On Saturday night a meeting of gabbaim and religious activists took place in the “Beit Torah ve-Avodah”; it had been convened by the local KKL (Keren Kayemet le-Israel) committee, with the participation of Rabbi Hager (Sosnowiec). The meeting aroused great interest in religious circles. A larger number of gabbaim from synagogues and shtiblekh came, [and] the most prominent activists of Mizrachi and Torah ve-Avodah.
The head of the KKL, Mr. Malczarski [?], opened the meeting and welcomed the distinguished guest Rabbi Hager, as well as the well-known activist who was present, the KKL delegate in Sosnowiec, Mr. W. Koszuch [?], and handed the chair over to Mr. P. L. Buchweitz [?].
After a short introductory word by the chairman, the floor was given to Rabbi Hager, who delivered a certain report on the last Zionist Congress and on the meeting of the session of the Jewish Agency. The speaker dwelt in particular on the plan to create a Jewish state in a part of Eretz Israel and related details of how the plan had come about.
The speaker also described the achievements of “Mizrachi” in Eretz Israel in all fields, and [—] the Agudah and its followers, who know only how to criticise but cannot show any deeds.
He ended with a call to religious Jews to devote themselves to the holy work of the redemption of the Land by strengthening the work for the KKL and penetrating all strata of the people. During the Days of Awe one should not content oneself with praying for life and livelihood, but should also emphasise the prayer “U-vekhen ten kavod le-amekha ve-sasson le-artzekha” [And so grant honour to Your people... and joy to Your land]...
Finally an “Orthodox Section” (Mahleket ha-Haredim) was elected from among gabbaim and members of Mizrachi and Torah ve-Avodah, whose first task is to strengthen the KKL work in the houses of prayer by carrying out the pledges (nedarim) and Yizkor campaign.
The chairman, Mr. Buchweitz [?], thanked the esteemed rabbi for his spirited lecture and closed the meeting with the assurance that the work for the redemption of the Land would thereby be greatly expanded.
The “Beit Lechem” Holiday Campaign

[Będzin — relief.] In the course of this week the “Beit Lechem” society in Będzin supported for the holiday some 200 poor Jewish families, who received meat, flour, sugar and other products.
—o—
Big Railway Scandal
[Sosnowiec — crime.] The railway authorities have uncovered a big railway affair which took place on the Sosnowiec—Częstochowa line; some 100 persons took part in the affair. A larger number of railway officials from Sosnowiec and Częstochowa have been arrested.
—o—
Tram Runs into a Cart
[Będzin — accident.] On [?] Street in Będzin a tram ran into a horse-drawn cart. From the violent collision one horse was killed and the carter injured.
—o—
Counterfeiters Arrested
[Sosnowiec — crime.] The police in Sosnowiec have arrested Janina Jaszerowska [?] and Michalczyk on suspicion of making and circulating counterfeit 5-zł. coins.
—o—
Strike at the “Helena” Mine — Settled
[Zagłębie — labour.] The strike at the “Helena” coal mine has been settled; for the period of the strike the workers received 160 thousand zł. as a one-time compensation.
—o—
Shechita Income Down by 50 Percent
[Będzin — community, ritual slaughter.] According to the statistical figures it can be seen that the community's income from the slaughter of cattle (shechitat gassot) in Będzin has this year decreased by 50 percent.

The trial over the events at Racławice

[Miechów — trial; the Racławice events.] On Monday the trial over the events at Racławice began in Miechów, in the large hall of the Christian Craftsmen's Association.
First the 29 defendants who are held under arrest were brought into the hall; they were brought under police guard. This group was seated separately, and opposite them sat the remaining 31 defendants, who are [illegible word; presumably: at liberty].
Altogether, then, there are 60 accused.
Among the accused are 4 women, including a 17-year-old village girl, the most heavily accused of calling on the peasants to follow her example: "I am a woman — she shouted — and nevertheless I am not afraid; so come with me!"
Immediately after the defendants were brought in, the court entered: presiding judge Wysocki and associate judges Wędrychowski and Chmielowski. Appearing as prosecutors are Bogranowicz [?] and Lejtman.
Appearing for the defence are the Warsaw advocates Alfiński [?], O. Jaworski [?] and Szczerbiński, and from Kraków: Grodzicki, Mierczyński and Ławarczyk [?].
The former Marshal of the Sejm Rataj and other leaders of the peasants are to appear at the trial.
The reading of the indictment took 2 hours. It runs to 80 pages.
After the reading of the indictment, the examination of the accused began.
The first to be heard is the accused peasant Bisag [?]. He answers in a trembling voice. He can barely stand on his feet. He asks to be taken back to prison immediately, because he is ill. His request is granted.
The first three accused, who are questioned next, do not admit to the charge of attacking anyone. They declare that they took part in the Racławice rally because they did not know that the rally had been forbidden by the authorities.
The hearing of witnesses continues.
Scenes that took place during the fire in Kielce

[Kielce — disaster; the fire and relief for its victims.] We have already reported on the terrible fire that broke out in Kielce on the second night of Rosh Hashanah. The fire appeared at one o'clock at night in the house of the Jewish baker Rozenholc [?] on Nowy Świat (the largest Jewish quarter in Kielce). All the tenants were sunk in deep sleep. Within a few minutes the fire had seized the neighbouring houses on two sides [?]; 10 houses stood in flames.
During the fire scenes from hell took place; the cries rose to the heavens. Only with the greatest effort could the old people and the children be rescued. The fire could be seen throughout the whole town, and it seemed as if all the streets were engulfed in flames. Gangs of thieves also appeared at the scene of the fire, taking advantage of the disaster and starting to plunder. Some of them, however, were caught at once and arrested.
The fire lasted until 7 in the morning. The damage amounts to over 150 thousand złoty. Some 300 Jewish souls were affected, who are now left naked and barefoot under the open sky.
In connection with this a relief action was created; a meeting was held in the kehilla premises, at which it was decided that pairs would visit every home.
Last week the delegate of the Warsaw relief committee, Mr. Riuszazy [?], stayed in Kielce and declared that the relief committee would support the action with the same sum as the Jews of Kielce will give.
— Jews! Remember that winter is coming; let the Jewish feeling of compassion awaken in you for the dozens of unfortunate Jewish families, and contribute for the homeless, who have no roof over their heads.
Yom Kippur in Kielce

[Kielce — holidays; Yom Kippur.] Kielce has not seen such attendance on Yom Kippur for a long time: the great town synagogue, the batei midrash, the shtiblekh and even the minyanim were full — a sign that Jewish sorrow has already reached its utmost limit.
The misery and bitterness also found their expression on the eve of Yom Kippur in desperate weeping at the graves in the cemetery, and on Yom Kippur in the synagogues themselves during "Yizkor", "Unetaneh Tokef" and the Ne'ilah prayers.
In all the houses of prayer speeches were delivered in which the worshippers were called upon to donate to the Keren Kayemet.
In the town synagogue there was a great crush, but it was worth spending several hours in the great crowding in order to hear the sweet prayer of the cantor Mr. Gurnicki [?] with the choir.
On the whole, the day of Yom Kippur passed in the synagogues and batei midrash quite calmly, without any incidents whatsoever.
Grand holiday dancing at the Zionist premises

[Kielce — Zionism; holiday entertainment.] On Tuesday, at the close of the first days of Sukkot, a grand holiday dancing evening with a varied entertainment programme will be held at the Zionist premises.
Theft at the 'Renesans' photographic studio
[Kielce — crime; theft.] On the eve of Yom Kippur thieves got into the establishment of the represented [?] firm "Renesans", where they forced open the drawers and stole a few hundred złoty.
Bandit attack on a Jewish family

[Miechów — crime; robbery.] In Miechów three masked bandits broke on Sunday night into the flat of the local wholesale meat dealer Szymon Feldman. Having tied up Feldman and his wife with 2 children, the bandits robbed 2 thousand zł. in cash and jewellery worth several thousand zł. Before leaving they beat Feldman murderously. The alerted police immediately organised a round-up and arrested all 3 bandits, who are from Miechów: Antoni Skadrek [?], Rasiński and Łubowski [?]. They were put in chains and locked up.
Rail discounts for spa guests valid until 31 October

[Poland — transport; discounts for holiday-makers.] By an order of the Ministry of Communications, the railway discounts for spa guests on their return journey have this year for the first time been extended until 31 October.
Until that day, therefore, anyone who spends just 14 days in one of the 30 Polish spa and rest resorts will be able, on travelling back home, to enjoy a discount of 33 per cent on the railway ticket.
Security chief — vice-voivode

[Kielce — official appointments.] The hitherto head of the security department at the Kielce voivodeship office, Mr. Łuszczacki [?], has been appointed vice-voivode in Kielce.
The previous vice-voivode has been transferred to the same post in Brześć.
Mr. Krakozin [?] has been appointed head of the security department.
Jews of Kielce!

[Kielce and Olkusz — public life and local news.] Jews of Kielce! On the festival of Sukkot, when you are called up to the Torah —
pledge for the Keren Kayemet!
—o—
A ceiling collapses onto a worker.
During work in the house of Mr. Dawid Szpinler [?] at "Talbers" [?, reading and place uncertain], the ceiling caved in. An assistant worker was seriously injured.

From Yehoshua Oksenhendler's textile (manufaktura) shop a "customer" stole a piece of goods worth 200 zł.

L.O.P.P. Week in Olkusz.

For this purpose a local committee has been set up headed by the starost, Mr. Buszastyński [?].
A series of events will take place.

Give Education to Jewish Youth!

An appeal by Rabbi Chameides on behalf of the J.N.F.
(L.S.) In his Yom Kippur sermon in the great, overflowing synagogue, Rabbi Chameides devoted much attention to the problem of Jewish youth education, declaring among other things that the educated Jewish parents who are nationally and religiously indifferent and do not cultivate Jewish traditions — do a great wrong to their children, not giving[?] them the proper spiritual strength for the hard road of life that lies before them, from earliest childhood, in exile.
In the second part of his speech the esteemed rabbi dwelt on the holy duty that the Jewish people must fulfil: to be inspired on behalf of the J.N.F., redeeming the soil of the Land of Israel and thereby coming to the aid of the heroic efforts of the pioneering camp.
As always, this time too Rabbi Chameides's inspiring speech made a strong impression.
Lecture by Dr. Y. Schwarzbart

Last Saturday night Dr. Y. Schwarzbart gave a lecture in the new large community hall on the topical subject: "On the way to the Jewish state in the Land of Israel".
The chairman, Dr. Rapaport, greeted the lecturer and those present and explained the significance of the first Zionist event in the new community building, stressing the great difference in the attitude of the Katowice community towards Zionism then and now.
Dr. Schwarzbart explained in detail the community of interests of various political factors with Zionism and, [—] answering[?] personally the opponents of granting full powers to the Zionist Executive, he justified the necessity of the majority decision of the last Zionist Congress.
After the lecture the Katowice Zionist intelligentsia gathered with the lecturer in the "Opera", and over a glass of tea various questions were put.
Special attention was drawn by the question of the Zionist activist present, Dr. Strasan[?] (Group B): whether it was not already time to unite both General Zionist groups, Group A with its 128 mandates and Group B with its 44 mandates; and, as was unfortunately to be expected, Dr. Schwarzbart in a lengthy statement gave a negative answer.
The good will is still lacking in the World Union, unfortunately. (L.S.)
Life in Chorzów

The situation of the Jewish market traders and home-workers (chałupnicy).
Lately the situation of the market stallholders[?] in all the surrounding villages where Jews used to come to the markets has grown much worse. This is because the non-Jewish village merchants demand[?] of the gminas (rural communes) not to allow any Jewish merchants from other places to come to the market.
It is high time for the market stallholders[?] and peddlers to organise in the Small Traders' Association, so that the hungry Jewish families do not lose their bread in Upper Silesia.
The situation of the Jewish home-workers, too, has grown much worse compared with last year, and their existence can be improved only by joint work towards the winter season.
It is high time to reorganise in the Craftsmen's Association in Chorzów. If you come with an appeal to the newly elected board of the Craftsmen's Association, the board will be compelled to do something for you, as well as for all branches of the association.
If the board takes an interest in your situation, the causes of the decline[?] and the means to improve your situation will be found.

[Chorzów — representatives' congress.] In connection with the Representatives' Congress of the Jews in Poland, which is to take place at the end of October this year in Warsaw, meetings of all communal, economic and professional institutions must be called in Chorzów, to explain to their members the importance of such a congress. The meetings must form an organising committee, which is to get in contact with the Main Committee for Galicia and Silesia in Kraków.

“The Dybbuk” on Film

[Będzin — cinema.] (On yesterday's premiere at the “Nowości” cinema, Będzin)
The greatest sensation of the current season will undoubtedly be An-ski's immortal work “The Dybbuk” on film. No motion picture, of course, arouses such interest as the Dybbuk film, for which preparations were made and which was created with the reverence that An-ski's masterpiece demands. Only now, in the era of the talking picture, will we have the opportunity to admire “The Dybbuk” on the cinema screen.
The “Dybbuk” film was directed by the well-known film director Michał Waszyński[?], from the screenplay by Mark Arnshteyn and Alter Kacyzne, who adapted An-ski's work as befits it and fitted it for the screen, without losing in the process the main idea and the spirit of An-ski's “Dybbuk”. To play the leading roles as well as the second- and third-rank roles, the best Yiddish actors were engaged, headed by Morewski, Samberg, Lipman, Dina Halpern, Liebgold, Ligna[?] and Bożyk[?]. The music was written by Henech Kon, who in his work kept strictly to the line of An-ski's dramatic legend. The dances and crowd scenes were staged by Judith Berg.
After long months of hard and responsible work, the Dybbuk film was finally completed, and it is in and of itself an important event in Jewish cultural and cinema life throughout the whole world.
“The Dybbuk” has been showing since yesterday in Będzin at the “Nowości” cinema.

Later it turned out that a hooligan had thrown stones and smashed several windows of the orphanage.

Free Credit for All — On the Membership Drive of the Gemilut Hesed Fund in Będzin

By Nute Landber.
Some 10—12 years ago, when the Jewish population in Poland was hard hit by the general economic crisis, a ramified network of various Jewish cooperative banking institutions was set up throughout Poland with the help of the American "Joint"; they formed the financial apparatus of the Jewish merchant class. At the same time a large network of gemilut hasadim [interest-free loan] funds was also created, whose task was to relieve the terrible distress of the pauperized Jewish masses, who could not obtain any credit at the cooperative banks. Thanks to the gemilut hesed funds thus created, thousands of Jewish livelihoods were saved from ruin.
Because of their popular character these institutions developed very quickly and won the sympathy of the broadest Jewish masses; they gradually took an important position in Jewish economic life and became a very important factor in our struggle for existence.
The gemilut hesed fund in Będzin was also one of the finest funds in Poland. In its heyday it counted over 2 thousand members, with monthly payments of over 2 thousand zł., and over several years it succeeded in building up its own capital of twenty-odd thousand zł. Together with the "Joint" capital, the fund had at its disposal a capital of over a hundred thousand zł.
Unfortunately, in recent years the fund began — for well-known reasons — to wither badly: its foundations began to shake, the capital was frozen, the Jewish population lost its trust in the fund, and the number of members fell to 700, with monthly payments of 400 zł.
A year ago, thanks to the energetic action of the central board in Warsaw, the fund was reorganized. A thorough audit of the books was carried out, and people deserving full trust were placed at the head of the institution. The fruits of this reorganization are already noticeable: the number of members grows from day to day, the monthly repayments keep rising, the old frozen loans are becoming active again, new loans totalling 12000 zł. are issued every month, and they are also repaid properly [?] on the appointed dates.
We are now living through a very hard time. Antisemites of every kind have openly declared a war of extermination on us, the economic boycott has taken on the most horrible forms, all of Jewish life is being undermined, the number of Jewish families pushed out and declassed grows from day to day, and the poverty in the Jewish street is taking on dreadful forms.
The former cooperative banks, which did so much for the Jewish merchant, have almost all gone under; what remains is only the one relief fund, the "gemilut hesed," where the fallen merchant and the impoverished Jewish craftsman can still find a point of support [?], and where with a loan of a few hundred złoty he is saved from ruin.
The present board has set itself the question [?] of restoring the fund to its former glory, making it a true people's institution, increasing the number of members to the maximum, strengthening its financial means, enlarging its own capital and, finally, being able to issue loans free of any charge. A small beginning in this direction has already [—] been made: after acquainting myself with the fund's present situation, I proposed reducing the charges on the loans, which are already lower by 50 gr. per hundred zł. My proposal was accepted by the entire board, and now the board strives to free the loans entirely of any charge, so that the name "interest-free fund" will match reality. All this can be achieved if Jewish society knows how to appreciate the importance of the fund, which already serves 1,500 families today — and no one knows what a day may bring, who will need the fund's help tomorrow. It is therefore the duty of every single person to enrol as a member of the fund, so as to enable it to fulfil its tasks completely in the present hard time and to help maintain all Jewish positions with the help of the free credits obtained.
The Moral — On the Signboard Tax

Whenever an economic matter on which there is no [—] [?] comes up for consideration, the Jewish economic activists arrive and each group wants to make sure that the law takes only its own group under protection, whether it concerns workers, craftsmen or small traders. Each has in mind only that the group he represents should not be [—] by the punitive [?] law; they never have an all-Jewish approach to such matters. There have indeed been times when the economic communal workers held that only they should be elected to the elected municipal bodies, and not representatives of social-political parties, which have an all-Jewish approach to economic matters and not a narrow economic-partisan one.
Some time ago the plenum of the Będzin city council dealt with the matter of the signboard tax. A Jewish ławnik [member of the municipal executive] and the writer of these lines spoke out against the project, pointing out that the project hits [?] only the Jewish poor, who must have large signboards because they mostly [?] live in side streets and in attic [?] rooms, whereas the richer enterprises make do with small signboards. We also pointed out that the project is not legal, if only because the industrial law [prawo przemysłowe] obliges every merchant or craftsman to have a signboard. All these arguments, however, had no effect, and when the concession was given to the craftsmen and small traders that holders of 8th-category craft patents [trade licences] and 4th-category trading patents would be exempt from the project — all the councillors, even the small traders' representatives (with the exception of the aforementioned Jewish ławnik and the writer of these lines), voted for the project, thinking that they had done their duty and defended their partisan interests.
But what turned out? The województwo [provincial authority] approved the statute [?] and struck out the amendment exempting holders of small patents from the said tax, and now the poor craftsmen and small traders, the wretches, run about with payment orders [nakazy] for larger sums, which they had not reckoned with at all.
The moral — when we deal with an economic matter that concerns the entire Jewish population, one must act in the interest of the whole of Israel, not of parties and groups. Had this been remembered then, many unpleasantnesses might have been spared the Jewish poor.
Councillor Ch. M. Zylberberg.
Sopot Miniatures

[Literature — short sketches; a seaside resort.] By P. Blumenkrants [P. Blumenkranc] (Częstochowa)
Revenge

She did not wait for someone to declare his love to her, to go out with her, to look into her eyes and count her fingers, as in Nadir's little story [Moyshe Nadir].

She took the initiative herself. And when he caught her fancy, she invited him to her room, treated him, showed him how far gone [?] she was, and watched the impression she was making.

When that did not help either, she just happened to need to take something down from the cupboard and was afraid to climb down; the young man helped her down, and she, straight away, without a moment's thought:
— Panie, już całować [?]! [Polish: "Sir, now kiss!" (?)]
But the young man was a naive one; he was embarrassed and begged her pardon. Had he been a bold one, he would have understood how he ought to behave from then on...
She, for her part, soon gave the first one to understand:
— Nic nie szkodzi! [Polish: "Never mind!"] You are young, after all, especially since [?] it is the accepted thing at a spa. But when she saw that this did not help either, she went over to an open offensive:
— Surprised [?], sir? I like to have a good time at a resort. I must have my friend to spend the time with. Last year I was at the sea too, got to know an interesting man, and we spent the time intimately.

And then she begins, for some reason, to "describe":
— Ah, how good it is to have a whole person with whom one can [spend time] always, to know that he is mine entirely. At home I already have one. I met him only a few days ago. I hope we shall become friends. I love him, but here I don't have him.

And when the naive young man cannot make sense of the whole matter, so strange to him, she gives him to understand more clearly:
— Let's go for a walk now; later we'll go home to your place, kochanie [Polish: darling] — you live alone, don't you?

* * *

This woman made a strange impression on me. I felt that her behaviour was not merely the result of lust, but on the contrary, as if she wanted to cover something up with it, to forget.
Later [?], seeing how she took an Aryan [i.e. a non-Jew] whom she had met by chance onto the "kopite" [?], I decided to ask [?] the reason for her behaviour.

She looked at me ashamed [?], her face grew sad, and she told me:
— It really does make a bad impression, my throwing myself from one to the next; it may seem that I crave the men I happen to meet, but it is not so. Perhaps I want to find in all these men a resemblance to the one who tramples me underfoot — and in the end I do not find it.

— We married — she went on — I was young; he awakened in me the desire for life. I clung to him, cut myself off from society, and held my duties as a wife sacred.
But soon after the wedding he began to ignore me. I sat at home, in noisy Warsaw, and he amused himself until late at night.

I kept silent about all of it; I was afraid I would lose him altogether. He invented the old banal excuses of meetings, conferences, transactions, and I pretended that I believed him.

But he became bolder in his conduct; he no longer even bothered to invent excuses, until one night he came home with a street woman.
He was staggering drunk and shouting in befuddled [?] voices. I lay frozen with fright, and he threw himself with the shikse [gentile woman] onto the other bed.
I jumped out of bed and in my terror could not utter a word; he wallowed with the shikse, and lust [—] from his mug.

I went into the other room, threw myself down and began to [sob (?)]. I saw my husband in all his loathsomeness. To run away from him — I decided; to run away as fast as possible, but how? I was not prepared for life, I could not do anything. I kept silent, and he began to repeat the orgies more often, came home drunk and brought women from the street.

I began to hate him with every fibre of my soul, but as soon as he came close to me I forgot everything.
And he trampled me with his conduct, like a [?] over a harem; he never noticed me at home; I had become superfluous to him, like a broken vessel.
And it may sound like something from a novel, but on one of those nights I went out into the street and gave myself to a man I happened to meet.
Yes, it is the story of the "Marguerites" [?], but I acted that way too. Since then I have conducted myself so. Every year I go away and betray my husband. Perhaps you will find [?] my conduct too loose [?], but I ask nobody and I do not reckon with the accepted forms. Besides, others do the same; with them the approach just takes longer, while I — if a young man pleases me, I tell him so, and [he (?)] wants me; one must make use of it as long as one can still please.
She spoke with heat; her face took on an expression of care; the wrinkles around her eyes stood out more sharply, and a strange feeling of pity awoke in me for this forsaken, ignored, spat-upon woman, who in her helplessness seeks revenge by trampling and spitting on herself, who wants through filth [?] to free herself from her tormenting double feeling: love and hate...
