Problems of Jewish Education

(In connection with the projected Jewish state in the Land of Israel).

We Jews are now entering a new epoch of history. Each of us feels that the way things have been until now cannot go on, and that all forms of life will have to change against our will, for such is our tragic fate in exile: we must always adapt ourselves to the conditions created by other factors with certain tendencies...

We Jews have indeed passed, through the whole two thousand years, the examination of adapting ourselves to the situations created for us, but it has cost us too dearly: in this way we forgot our language and adopted new languages from the peoples among whom we lived; we were forcibly transformed from an agrarian people, which loved to sit "under its vine and under its fig tree", into a people of "air-people" [luftmentshn] and other disreputable[?] livelihoods of the economy, which a [—] wind of decrees[?] can ruin...

And the most tragic thing of all is that during the long exile we also lost the "sixth" sense, the sense of a homeland of our own, which is very aptly expressed in Hebrew: "chush ha-moledet" (the sense of homeland).

They tell this story: a village Jew came home from town very agitated[?] and frightened: people in town are saying that the Messiah will come one of these days and lead the Jews, too, to the Land of Israel — and what will become of our fields, our cattle, our chickens and the debts the peasants owe us?!

His wife comforted him: don't worry, my husband — the Master of the Universe, who saved us from a Pharaoh, a Haman and other enemies, will surely save us from a Messiah too!.. And the daughter added: Daddy, good Jews will not allow it!..

Twenty years have already passed since the Balfour Declaration, and had the Jews possessed the "sense of homeland", they could have bought up the whole Land of Israel on both sides of the Jordan and settled several million people, and then we would not have come to all these misfortunes.

But now, when our future reveals itself to us in a real form in the Land of Israel, in the shape of a state of our own, we must already set about, here in the lands of exile, preparing the ground and organising a spiritual hachshara (training) among the broad popular masses, in the sense of reconquering what we lost in exile: for example, the Hebrew language, technical vocational training, and in general reawakening in the people the sense of a homeland of its own.

It goes without saying that we must make the beginning with our small children. We must organise our schools in such a direction that Judaic subjects stand in first place, with Hebrew as the language of instruction; carry on a strong campaign among Jewish parents that they educate their children in Jewish schools and prepare them for the new life opening before them in the Land of Israel; and also impose a national duty on all youth organisations that they learn the Hebrew language — just as it indeed was in former years, when the Hebrew language was cultivated and every young person knew that the organisation would train him to speak Hebrew.

Further, the school curriculum must also be reorganised to such an extent and in such a form that the treasures of Jewish culture are given as much as possible in the original, so that they reveal themselves to the pupils in their full splendour and with their brilliance uncover the dormant sense of homeland. And who[?] is[?] then able to awaken it like the fiery words of the prophets with their love of Zion, the sweet words of the aggadot and midrashim and the poems of Rabbi Yehuda Halevi, down to the new poets of the revived, rich Hebrew literature? And our whole history, too, is so rich in beautiful moments that can serve as material to wake the people from its lethargic sleep. — Yes, we must say with regret that our people is asleep, for when 80 per cent of its children are estranged from Jewish schools and Jewish education, or when even in most of the so-called Jewish schools the teaching is only superficial — one cannot call it anything other than a disease in the people's organism!..

So, things are not in order in our little Jewish world, and we must see to it in good time to win back our lost virtues of a normal people — with a love for its language, for labour, and a need for a land of its own — and then we shall have a Jewish state which even "good Jews will also allow"..

Elchanan Zyder.
Steel and Iron

If what scientists have calculated is true, then soon, very soon — if not in our generation, then at the latest in the next generation — we shall be left without metals.

Year in, year out, 220 million tons of iron are taken out of the earth, and to this day no means has been found by which that iron could again become useful. Where the iron is taken out, a hole remains for ever.

According to statistics of the Leipzig Fair we learn more precisely some interesting facts about steel and iron.

From the year 1870 to 1930, two thousand million tons of iron were dug out. Of these, rust laid waste 800 million tons; that is, forty per cent went to ruin.

From iron one makes steel. Some 10 thousand metric quintals of steel are used to manufacture — needles; from half a million metric quintals one manufactures — beds. 340 thousand metric quintals are used to make mattresses and bedsprings; three and a half million metric quintals of steel are used in the world to manufacture — automobiles; from one and a half million metric quintals one makes kitchenware; for "bar-danen"[?] six million metric quintals of steel are used; from thirteen thousand metric quintals of steel one makes — gramophone needles. For writing pens (nibs) 42 thousand metric quintals are consumed, and on razor blades a thousand metric quintals of steel are spent.

Interesting, too, are the prices of steel and iron.

A kilo of raw iron, as it is found in the earth, is worth four groszy. When the iron comes up from the mines, it already costs, with all expenses, fourteen groszy, and once it is processed into steel it costs eighteen groszy.

If razor blades are made from this material, the kilo of steel already costs seventy dollars; if fine scissors are made from the same material, the kilo costs a hundred and ten dollars; if springs for watches are made from the same steel, the kilo costs no less than a hundred and eighty dollars; if fine parts for very expensive watches are made from the same steel, the kilo costs from 40 to 200 thousand dollars. Then steel is already dearer than gold.

A great deal of metal is lost because old utensils that can no longer be used are thrown away; millions of dollars go to waste through broken tools and machines; every year some third of all metals perish in this way through [—].

It has been calculated, for example, that tin, which is so rare, is destroyed every year to the value of thirty million dollars by the throwing away of little boxes and tubes of various pharmaceutical goods.

As one sees — very interesting figures, worth pondering.

Z. Haber, Vienna.
Hoshana Rabbah at Night

[Poetry — Hoshana Rabbah.]
...For the thousandth time on this night,
when the heavens above split open
and silently there rise to the Throne of Glory
stray prayers, hidden for distant generations —
yet they do not reach the goal they long for,
though the heavens split open...

...For the thousandth time on this night
he now thirsts deeply for a brotherly heart —
and his hand stays stretched out in the air,
oh, like a beggar's, full of pain, full of sorrow;
and high above the moon looks smiling down —
and it seems that everything is dyed black.

...For the thousandth time on this night,
when I see here my shadow, without my knowing,
tangle at my feet upon the earth,
I am ready for life to go on —
and I look over there at the pale moon,
how broadly she smiles over my faith...

L. Bergson.
With Neighbours in the Sukkah (A Sketch)

[Feuilleton — Sukkot; a courtyard sketch.]
For the first time, this year I had the privilege of sitting with all my courtyard neighbours in one sukkah and getting to know them a little better over seven days. The age-old men of pedigree, the former courtyard magnates, who [—] year after year put up separate little sukkahs for themselves, covered them with specially prepared new "[—]", decorated them with a large electric lamp and shut themselves away[?] for the whole holiday, so that no one should disturb them at their meal or their dignity, God forbid, suffer from it — this year, poor things, they had to capitulate, shut themselves into the big courtyard sukkah and decided to lower themselves to the common "neighbour-folk" [a pun on shoykhn oylem, "He who dwells forever"].

"Yes!" Reb Henekhl rubbed his hands and with a little hammer knocked the walls together. "This year we'll have a big [—] sukkah, much bigger than last year. Everything has become equal, completely evened out, so why really split up into several little corners, and why knock about[?] so cramped in the narrow [—] sukkahs. [—] in people! Oy —" he sighed heavily, set about putting up the last wall and meanwhile hummed in his own hoarse voice: "Alas, Jewish troubles, Jewish suffering! What do you think — it tears at the heart!"..

When I went into the sukkah one evening[?], I did indeed find the whole courtyard of neighbours there; every last one[?] had turned up, even some "[—]" who had never in their lives sat in any sukkah and had never taken an interest in such Jewish things — this year they had become real [enthusiasts?] about the sukkah, sat down [—] like the chief in-laws at a wedding, and even sang lustily along with the zmires, keeping right in step with the whole "band".

In other respects, however, it was sad. The fine portions[?] of former times, alas, no longer appeared in the sukkah, and people had generally stopped being ashamed of poverty. More than one had exchanged last year's challahs for bread, the live carp for herring — and the cheapest at that — and above all they made do[?] with a few bits of dry potatoes, thanking God that they still had enough to still their hunger somehow. To make up for it, though, Jews sang many zmires, poured out their hearts without measure, sighed and wished themselves better times.

—

The whole company sat deep in thought, watching one another. Among the silent and grieving sat Reb Anshl[?] with his [—] grey beard, who less than a year ago had become impoverished and whose hair his troubles had indeed turned[?] silver. Suddenly he broke the prevailing silence and began to speak. He spoke very quietly, but boldly and with assurance. From time to time his hoarse voice trembled, as if he were about to weep, but paying no heed he went on speaking, mastering himself with all his strength and holding the whole company in suspense.

"A year ago I still had a fine Passover," he began to tell, "only not long ago I still kept a broad, wealthy household, kept a maid in the house, had the children educated and gave a nice couple of gulden to charity every week. Things began to go worse and worse, until, God spare us, I came down to my present state." Reb Anshl gave a heavy sigh and went on: "May it not happen to you — I was left with the 4 bare walls; they carried out the whole little bit of belongings. They made a ruin of my bright home and put me in such a position that right now, just before winter, I am threatened with eviction. My situation is truly unbearable and I no longer have the strength to bear it."

Reb Anshl suddenly broke off his speech and wiped away the sweat that was pouring down his face, stroked his beard and covered his face with his hands. For a short while a deathly silence reigned, until suddenly Reb Yisroelke, the Shir ha-Maalos singer, roused himself — he who for 20 years without a break has sung, every year before grace after meals, his Shir ha-Maalos to one and the same tune — and struck up with great fervour. The whole company leapt up as if from sleep and began singing along, each in his own way.

There were no needless worries about grace this year, because the former magnates, who for years had pined after various honours, this year voluntarily renounced everything of their own accord. This year Reb Henekhl received the leading of grace as a reward for his trouble in putting up the sukkah; nobody so much as grimaced, everyone felt that it was his by right, since he had been the first pioneer[?] of all the impoverished who now find themselves in the sukkah.

One by one, after grace, the company began to leave the sukkah. The candles started to go out and the sukkah grew darker and darker; the last little flames leapt up with their blue, dying tongues, now short for a minute, now long for minutes at a time, and a few minutes later the sukkah was already pitch dark.

—

In a [—] I sat deep in thought in the company of several persons who stay every year to spend the night on the hard, narrow benches in the sukkah. None of them slept. In a corner sat a neighbour who was sobbing hard, loudly bewailing the fate of his wife and children, who have not eaten their fill for several years. For the first time he had decided to spend the night in the sukkah; it is hard for him to go back home, he can no longer bear to watch the suffering of his wife and his young fledglings, who torment and torture themselves without end. The whole company instinctively began to weep, and among the tears, which for the first time this year flowed so thickly in the sukkah... [the sentence breaks off thus in print.]

—

Quietly and unnoticed I tore myself out of the sukkah, so as not to disturb my unhappy Jews as they wept themselves out until their hearts felt somewhat lighter. When I came into the house, I felt that my cheeks were wet and found on them two big round tears.

For the first time in my life I left the sukkah this year with such an embittered heart, and for a long time I could not calm myself, thinking of the bitter fate of my poor and helpless Jewish brothers...

Loyt[?].
In Honour of Sukkot. Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes about Sukkot

Collected and styled by Yehuda Yafet.
A) The pilgrimage.
Speaking of the commandment to make the pilgrimage on Sukkot, Passover and Shavuot, the Torah confirms it twice: "Three times a year shall all thy males appear before the Lord thy God in the place which He shall choose." The question arises: why should only males make the pilgrimage?
Dr. Shlomo Rubin gives an interesting explanation of this:
The ancient Greek writer Herodotus relates that in ancient Babylon every woman had, once in her life, to make a pilgrimage to the temple of the goddess Mylitta and there give herself up to a strange man. This was also considered a charm for barren women, and since this depraved custom was very popular in biblical times, the Torah expressly stressed that only males should make the pilgrimage to the Temple in Jerusalem..
*
In Prague there was a custom that all householders visited the rabbi on Simchat Torah. When the "Noda BiYehuda" was accepted as rabbi in Prague, he abolished the custom, because — so he reasoned — the custom derives from the saying of the Sages (Rosh Hashanah 16) "A person is obliged to greet his teacher on the festival", and — as he also rules in the "Noda BiYehuda", second edition, Orach Chaim, section 92 — in our time the commandment of greeting one's teacher on the festival does not apply, for if one cannot make the pilgrimage to God's house, one is not obliged to make a pilgrimage to a rabbi. The honour of flesh and blood must not be dearer than the honour of God..
B) Caught a chill in the sukkah
The Gaon R' Tzvi Kazner[?] fell ill in the sukkah, and the doctor told him that he had caught a chill in the sukkah because of the rain.
Says R' Tzvi Kazner[?] to him:
— True, I caught a chill in the sukkah, but not because of the rain — rather because I felt too little of the warmth of the commandment of sukkah..
C) Seven days.
"[Before] the Lord your God seven days" — but not in the outlying regions all seven. And after the Temple was destroyed, Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai ordained that the lulav be taken in the provinces seven days, in remembrance of the Temple. Torat Kohanim.
The four species — says the commentator[?] — are a symbol of unity, of binding together all the elements of the people, and therefore this commandment in the Temple applied to all seven days, until Shemini Atzeret, because the greater a place is, the holier the people are — the less unity reigns there..
And in our time, for our many sins, in this respect every place is like the Temple.. Yalkut Yehuda.
D) Chazak ve-nitchazek
When the reading of the Torah is completed on Simchat Torah, people call out "Chazak ve-nitchazek" (Be strong and let us be strengthened)! Because in Berakhot, folio 33[?], the Gemara says: Four things require strengthening, and these are: Torah etc. Sifrei Yanchi[?].
E) Simchat Torah customs.
Once, canopies were set up for the "bridegrooms", the Bridegroom of the Torah and the Bridegroom of Genesis; they were escorted from the synagogue with burning torches, and a special band of gentile musicians accompanied them home. Divrei Chachamim.
*
In Vilna, in the Great Synagogue, there was a custom that the one who "leads" the hakafot (processions) puts on a special splendid cloak with an old hat, worn hundreds of years ago, and thus he leads the congregation in the hakafot. Shulchan HaKri'a.
*
R' Chaim David Doktor, the famous penitent (ba'al teshuva) of Piotrków, used on Simchat Torah, during the hakafot, to run out into the street with a Torah scroll in his hand and shout:
— Jews, repent! Jews! Come with me into the circle! Come into the circle of the "sons of the Palace"! Awake, arouse yourselves, Jews, children of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob!..
*
In a letter from the Land of Israel of the year 5507 [1747] R' Gershon Kitover [of Kuty] writes that in Jerusalem he was Bridegroom of the Torah, and at night all the sages of Jerusalem as well as Arab neighbours came to dance at his place, who "clapped and danced together with the Jews and sang songs in Arabic".
F) The burial society on Simchat Torah.
On Simchat Torah the men of the Łęczyca burial society (chevra kadisha) held a kiddush and invited the rabbi, R' Chaim Auerbach. Being in their cups, they asked him to say a Simchat Torah-style Torah thought, and he said by way of a joke:
— The burial society has an old grievance against the Master of the Universe: why did He bury Moses Himself and not leave it to them? After all, they would at least once have got a glass of liquor for it.
The Master of the Universe answered them:
— For that reason the portion of Moses' burial will be read on a day when the burial society will drink and drink anyway.. (for on Simchat Torah the portion about the burial of Moses is read).
Drunkenness, Cards and Cultural Affairs

[Essay — society and morals; drink and gambling.] At a conference [?] of the "National Federation of Working [?] Women" in Atlantic City (United States) papers were read about the bad habits that women have taken over from men. People spoke and argued [?] about the truly epidemic form that drunkenness and card-playing have assumed among present-day women. One of the women speakers characterised the modern woman of today as follows:
"The women who after the wedding become sunk in card-playing call themselves modern, but if this stratum of women who play cards does nothing at home, for the child, but [= or? probably a misprint] for society — these are parasites, a curse to their own home and to the whole of human society. Our mothers and grandmothers at least worked for their families, and that brought benefit to all people; and here we see how a class of women-parasites is developing, who use their good opportunities in life to be card-players, to live on the labour of others and to bring abandoned children into the world, which will cost society dearly.
Certainly [?] misfortune comes when a man drinks, when a man gambles; it is still worse when the woman lets herself be drawn into it. The woman is the guardian of the family. When the guardian gets drunk, woe to society. When the woman sinks into brandy and cards, corruption and licentiousness grow in our life.
To learn the virtues of famous men takes time, takes much effort; the faults of men who drink and play [—] cards one learns, and when a woman does not play cards and does not drink brandy, she is laughed at."
A second speaker, P'o. [Prof.?] Studenski [?], who spent months studying the life of American university youth, established that brandy-drinking is increasing among youth in general, but that girl drinkers are becoming far more numerous than young men. Brandy-drinking has spread especially in the last few years. Most girls are still ashamed to drink in a tavern or restaurant, and when they drink they mix the brandy with fruit, with soda — but they drink.
To the question put to the girls why they drink, almost all give one answer: "I drink because everybody drinks." Also current [?] is the popular answer: "When you drink brandy you become merrier and it is more interesting."
And how is it with us? With us too no ball, no celebration passes without the "bitter drop", and girls, young women in general, do not lag behind the male youth in this respect. Even those who by their profession or by their social position ought to be a model for others drink brandy. The same can be said about cards and other games of chance.
This plague has not diminished even now, when we find ourselves literally in a state of siege, when from various sides and in various countries people lie in wait to destroy us, and we need exceptionally healthy nerves, an exceptional concentration of all our spiritual and physical forces, in order to live through the hardest of times.
With the greatest difficulty we manage to raise the smallest sum for important purposes. Not long ago there was a "Month of the Yiddish Book", and much ink, paper and drawing-paint [?] was spent on it. The effect (not the outward one, but the practical one) was, however, negligible, and the blame was laid on our poverty, on assimilation. Certainly they are to blame to a great extent — but is the swamp [?], the rot [?] that has eaten through all our limbs any less to blame? Is it not high time to combat the plague that kills off more than one initiative, that hurls a person down to the level of a beast, that dangerously weakens our power of resistance and endangers our national existence?
A. Z.
Simchat Torah, Hopenyu

[Feuilleton — Simchat Torah; by Eliash.]
It is good [?] that after the Days of Awe, with their sorrow and dread, comes the joyful festival of Sukkot, and after it the still more joyful Simchat Torah.
The festival of Sukkot gives us not only a symbol of our wandering of old in the desert, when we had to put up tents in haste; it is also a symbol of our present Jewish life.
In recent years we have had Sukkot constantly. Emigration to all countries has been stopped, so Jews have meanwhile built themselves sukkahs in every corner of the world, even in China and in Japan.
But... this thought I will not finish, because at this very moment I am reminded once again that it is the eve of Simchat Torah, and on Simchat Torah one must be merry.
True, these are times when we cannot sing the familiar little song, the Simchat Torah song we used to sing, but we can twist the song a little, and it will do for the present times too:
Simchat Torah, hopenyu,
Though [?] in the bottle and in our little head
There's not a single dropenyu!
We have reasons enough to be merry even without drink, and although our life is anything but merry.
Merry we must be that we have remained W E, despite all the persecutions, all the terrible oppressions and all the wanderings: "And they journeyed and they encamped, and they encamped and they journeyed."
Yes, brothers, we must be merry because — as another folk song goes:
Whatever we are, we are,
But Jews we are,
And kapores we swing
And "Vehu rachum" we say.
Whatever we are, we are,
But Jews we are,
And into the sukkah we crawl
And "Shema Yisrael" we cry.
Whatever we are, we are,
But Jews we are,
And the Torah we revere
And of mitzvot we think...
Yes, it is no small joy that after all the troubles we are still Jews, for to be a Jew is the greatest feat, the greatest heroism, the greatest act of daring!
What kind of bargain is it to be a gentile, a German or an Englishman, or a Frenchman, or any other nation?!
Nothing at all!
Is it a feat to be what one is while sitting in a comfortable home, with every comfort and a fat state treasury?
But to remain a people with no home of your own, persecuted on all sides — now that is an accomplishment!
The gentiles have fist-fighting champions. We are all champions — we have been fighting for two thousand years against the whole world, and we are the victors, the champions.
The whole world is our arena, our sports stadium, the sports grounds in which there is "boxing".
We are a people of Jack Dempseys.
But we do not "box" with fists. The world attacks us with fists, and we — we hit back with patience, with wisdom and with morality.
And our strength we draw from the Torah — that is why we fear no one, and if we are sometimes afraid after all, that does not matter either, as the rhyme goes:
They — fists,
We — the Torah,
Of punches [?]
Have no fear.
Where is Rome now,
Where is Babylon?
Only a dream now
On a tablet.
But — we, the Jews,
Our nation —
Lives in peace,
Has a revival!
For not force
Is our law —
But the brain,
Where the sense lies.
So dance, brothers,
Free, without fear —
Sing songs now
To the Torah!
To spite all our enemies we live, and we rejoice precisely with the Torah, for which we have suffered and still suffer.
And we march with flags! True, it is our children who carry the flags, but we stand behind them — long generations stand behind them...
For our flags
Remind and demand
Of the rulers on thrones
That not in cannons,
In the might of nations,
But in the — — — —
In the... in the Torah, in morality, in trust in God. We did not finish the last line of the song because we found no rhyme that would both express the idea we wanted and fit "kanonen" [cannons] and "tronen" [thrones].
Our frankness has surely aroused in the reader the suspicion that we (I, that is) are already tipsy even before Simchat Torah — and there is a bit of truth in that suspicion. Although we have not tasted a bitter drop, we have so immersed ourselves in the Simchat Torah mood and in memories of Simchat Torah of years gone by that our head too [?] is spinning.
So let us rejoice with the Torah, for whose sake our people has suffered so much — rejoice with it not only to spite our enemies, but also our — so-called — Bible critics, who take a morbid pleasure in destroying the beauty of the Bible.
A Bible critic will be bent on proving to you that the Torah was given not on Mount Sinai but next to Mount Sinai, that Pharaoh was a little calf and Haman — a Chinaman, just so that in the end [?] it comes out that the Torah made a mistake.
Therefore, dear Jews, when you dance with the Torah at the hakafot and triumph over our enemies, triumph at the same time over the foolish Bible critics, who are blind to true beauty.

(A poem.)
We circle round and round
and trade in the Torah.
We shout: buy, buy, customers!
The Torah is a tree of life
with living fruit!
It holds half of it in mitzvot
and also a lot of sins.

Hey, customers! Hey, young folk!
Barbarians, gluttons and drunkards!
Buy honesty, justice, mercy
and other good deeds!
We are selling everything off!
We leave ourselves not a crumb —
we have no more strength
to drag ourselves along with the bundle...

We have been trading in these goods
for many thousands of years.
To all the prayer-fairs
we run, hurry, ride!
At every market we shout
like true Jews:
buy humanity, you robbers!
buy love, freedom, peace!

But nobody wants to take
the mitzvot and commandments,
and our fine merchandise
is trampled underfoot.
They beat us and drive us away
instead of buying from us —
and on and on the shopkeeper must
run with new bundles.

How heavy the burden is,
the pack is breaking our shoulders.
What is to be done, good brothers?
How is one to manage?
We have precious goods,
but nobody wants to look at them,
and the merchant is already sick,
he has almost no back left...

Helper of the poor, save us now!
Oh, help us, Father in Heaven,
and send us as customers
the German, the Turk, the Tatar!
Oh, let them too
drag Your pack a little.
Oh, give them our troubles,
then they won't pester us.

Sukkot — the Joyful Festival.

["Der Kokh-lefl" — humour; feuilleton, Sukkot.]
Sukkot is the most joyful time of the year, and perhaps of life — so I hold, and you will agree with me.
I like Sukkot. Firstly, because getting a sukkah is not as hard as getting a flat.
When getting a place in someone else's sukkah you don't have to pass a hard examination in which you must answer, for instance, when you go to sleep, whether you live in peace with the neighbours, and above all how many children you have.
Getting a place in a sukkah won't harm you even if you had twelve little children, may they live and be well.
Another advantage of great importance: for the whole time you live there you don't set eyes on any landlord — and above all, for the whole Sukkot season that you sit there you need pay no rent.
Besides, there are still other rare advantages that make the sukkah dear and precious compared with the flat in which you live the rest of the year: there the collector from the power station will not come in[?] on you, and it won't go dark before your eyes when you see his bill.
Your wife does not force you at the start of every season "to paint and freshen up the sukkah", as she does with the flat; you need not buy coal and dread every coal strike, nor do you have to sift the coal and save[?] the coal dust [miał]...
In the sukkah there is always fresh air; there you will always see the blue sky with the stars — provided it isn't raining — things which in an ordinary dwelling are rare.
Moreover there is the greatest advantage of all, that there you will surely have something to eat: nobody goes hungry in a sukkah, whereas in many houses, in present-day times, people go hungry with great relish: there are houses, may it not befall you, where there is not a bite of bread.
The sukkah is one of the [?] [word uncertain] places where you will surely finish your meal in peace and meanwhile not have to listen to your wife's instructions, her constant complaints and demands that never stop.
Sukkot really is the most joyful time of the year, the true "season of our rejoicing".
What's more, it has the merit of reminding us of olden times, when we wandered in the desert after leaving Egypt and were free people, like birds in the forest and like men in town — when the wives go off in summertime to a summer resort.
There, in the desert, it was light and warm the whole year, and one was almost spared going to a "dacha", where, for that little bit of light and warmth, you sweat out your mother's milk [idiom: suffer and pay dearly].
A constant cloud rested on the Jewish camp, and a roof, so that nobody needed to buy an umbrella; in it [—] somewhere as if forgotten, a place, as [—] the testimony of the Torah — the clothes never wore out and the feet never swelled during all the 40 years that the Jews were in the desert.
And there, where hardly any new garments were needed, there were surely no tailors who work so long until they work their way up — to textile merchants or even manufacturers.
Consequently there were also no strikes, unemployment and other calamities there, and also no strife and brawls[?] between Right and Left...
And the feet did not swell — from the modern tight shoes, and women's feet were not squeezed by the tower-high heels, with whose help "the fair sex" wants to appear taller than it really is... and the feet did not swell among the shopkeepers and butchers going to their "good" customers to dun them for debts.
Because, you understand me, the manna that Jews received from heaven served as food, and from it one got the taste of meat, of fish, of onion, of milk and of everything one could wish to enjoy.
And what the manna [man] was for Jews in the desert, today's husband [man][?] is for women: they too make of him whatever they like — a breadwinner, a rent payer, a nanny for the children, a pram pusher in the street, a coal sifter, and even a good roast, which fries all summer in town while, for the wife's spa-cure bill, they tear pieces of flesh off him, and all winter long they gnaw his bones.
In the desert there was that manna from heaven which settled[?] on the ground every morning; today's husband comes home from work as if he lay 9 ells deep in the ground.
In remembrance of the Exodus from Egypt — a memento of the time when Jews went out of Egypt and strolled in the desert.
In the desert — where sukkot were put up and no tall houses, and therefore there were no fire insurances with arson trials...
There were no streets where the Angel of Death in the form of an automobile robs human lives right and left.
Once there were good times; only a memory remains.
That is the festival of Sukkot.
Ḥeker.
When One Hands a Child Over to Irresponsible Hands...

When the maidservant went out on Tuesday afternoon with the one-year-old[?] child for a walk, her employer, Mrs. D. of Będzin, told her to walk with it around the park on Sączewska[?] Street.
A few hours later Mrs. D. went to the park and took food along for the child, but on arriving there she did not find the maid with the child. She then began searching, thinking they were at acquaintances', but every single one gave the same answer:
— The maid with the child had not been here at all. Only then did Mrs. D. become alarmed and ran all over town looking for the child, but without success. Only towards evening did she learn that the maid and the child were by the water, at the „Nagaska“[?]. Mrs. D. went there and indeed found her child, which was starving, pale and shivering with cold..
— Perhaps this fact will serve as a moral lesson for today's „hot“ mothers, that they should not hand their children over to irresponsible hands!
Large Craftsmen's Meeting in Sosnowiec

On Tuesday, at the close of the first festival days of Sukkot, a meeting called by „Ḥalutz Ba'al Melakhah“ (the Artisan Pioneer) took place in the new premises of the Zionist Organisation in Sosnowiec.
The meeting was very well attended because the posters had announced that Messrs. Advocate Stawalski[?] and Dr. Melarista[?] would lecture on craftsmen's problems. The Jewish craftsmen did indeed come to hear a word of comfort for their sufferings, but in the lectures delivered — very instructive ones, by the way — they found no cure for the affliction..
After the lecturers were greeted by Mr. Kornhendler, Advocate Kazalski[?] takes the floor for his lecture, in which he gives statistics on the situation of the craftsmen in general and of Jewish craftsmen in particular; he comes to the conclusion that the craftsmen must improve their situation. By what means? By opening cooperatives.
Dr. Melarista[?] speaks of the brilliant period of Jewish craftsmanship in Poland, which was organised by Zionist activists, then of the period of decline, and stresses that the only way out at the present moment is — for the craftsmen to concentrate under the national banner.

On the Prices of Articles of Prime Necessity

[Poland — prices.]
An ordinance of the Minister of the Interior has appeared on regulating the prices of articles of prime necessity, containing a number of provisions concerning white rye flour and wheat flour.
The wholesale[?] prices of wheat and rye flour will in principle not be fixed; in special cases the voivode may apply to the Minister of the Interior with a proposal to fix the prices of rye flour.
The prices of pure rye-flour bread are to be officially fixed. As [—] it is stated that the price of this kind of bread made of “pytlowa” (sifted) flour, milled[?] at 65 per cent, may not exceed the wholesale price of that kind of flour plus 2 groszy. The prices of baked goods of mixed wheat and rye flour are to be treated like the prices of rye-flour breads.
No prices will be fixed for wheat-flour baked goods (white water baked goods).
• • •
Meat, too, is covered by this ordinance. Prices will be fixed only for the cheap kinds of meat products, such as podroby (offal), heads, feet, liver, kidneys, ordinary sausage and [plain] kinds of kishke.

Lecture by Prof. Dr. Fodor in Sosnowiec

[Sosnowiec — Zionism and culture.]
On the initiative of the Zagłębie branch of the Society of “Friends of the Hebrew University in Jerusalem” a lecture was given on Saturday evening by Prof. Dr. Fodor, professor at the Hebrew University in Jerusalem, on the subject “The Hebrew University and Its Cultural Tasks”.
The lecture, which took place at the premises of the Merchants’ and Industrialists’ Association, drew a large audience from Sosnowiec, Będzin, Dąbrowa, Strzemieszyce and Katowice.
Prof. Fodor was escorted into the hall by Messrs. P’en[?], Sofer and Dr. Melowista[?].
Dr. Melowista greeted the distinguished guest, pointing to the importance of the Hebrew University and also to the tasks of the Society of “Friends of the Hebrew University in Jerusalem”.
The speaker stressed that after a whole series of attempts they had nevertheless succeeded in creating in Zagłębie a society which is developing and can already point to substantial help that it has rendered to the University.
Prof. Fodor began his lecture in Hebrew, stressing that he feels especially bound to Polish Jewry and thanking the Society for giving him the opportunity to come into contact specifically with the Jews of Zagłębie.
He then went over to speaking German. In his brilliant lecture Prof. Fodor gave a precise analysis of the general cultural and especially the Jewish significance of the Hebrew University, and assured that even today one can write a study on psychoanalysis in fine Hebrew.
In the second part of his lecture the speaker pointed to the types[?] of scholars needed in this field: the teacher, the physician and the laboratory researcher. The teacher and the researcher already receive their proper training at the University; as regards the physician, the medical faculty is already being prepared by building hospitals.
Concluding his lecture, the speaker stressed that the Hebrew University is the symbol of our spiritual and cultural revival. (Thunderous applause.)
Dr. Melowista thanked Prof. Fodor for the pleasure he had given the gathering and assured him that the Jews of Zagłębie will do all they can to help the Hebrew University realize the age-old “For out of Zion shall go forth the Law”.

Now That's What You Call a Woman of Valour...

(Section: "Life in Kielce" — Friday, 19 Tishrei 5698 / Friday 24 September 1937.)
How a Kielce wife took her husband to cheder [i.e. taught him a lesson]..
If you are told that a Jewish wife is ready to perform kapparot with her husband — believe it; and not, God forbid, because she hates him, because she loves a "kochanek" [lover], or because he squanders the money carousing with other women and for his wife he has an empty pocket — but precisely because she is devoted to him body and soul, because his health is dearer to her than her own life, and because she trembles over her husband as only a true Jewish wife is capable of — and that is exactly why she performed kapparot with him.
It concerns a certain Nute G., once an ardent Hasid; lately he no longer goes to the shtibl. But it is not so terrible: he has merely become more "democratic" and prays in the beth midrash, and even misses[?] the shtibl; he has, however, taken off the little [Hasidic] cap and put on a "kapelusz" [a hat], and the Kielce Ger shtibl does not tolerate any "Daytshn" ["Germans" — modern-dressed Jews].
One sin leads to another: from the kapelusz Reb Nute went a step further and decided not to perform kapparot. If there must be a kapparah at all, he argued, he would like to perform it with somebody else and not with an innocent fowl.
His wife, however, holds that while the husband may well have been allowed to put on a kapelusz, she still wears her sheitel, she still considers herself the wife of a Ger Hasid, and if she lets him not perform kapparot — who knows where he will end up! You know, after all, that when a Hasid becomes an apikoros he eats bread with lard. So she took a rooster, and on the morning of Yom Kippur eve, while her husband was in the beth midrash, she went up[?] to him with a small prayer book in her hand, found[?] the "Bnei Adam" [the opening of the kapparot prayer] and in front of the whole congregation begged him:
— My soul, take the rooster, perform kapparot, and let it be an atonement for your sins, for my sins and for the sins of all Jews.
The crowd of Jews raised a little commotion, Reb Nute and his wife in the middle of it, and Reb Nute did not let himself be begged for long: he said "Bnei Adam"[?] and swung the rooster over his head — and a very contented one at that; and the little wife came out of the beth midrash happy, with tears of joy in her eyes, and off she went to the shochet.
For the sake of Yom Kippur eve, Reb Nute forgave his wife for coming to him in the beth midrash and even thanked her for her woman-of-valour deed.

Craftsmen's Cards of the Shoe-Upper Cutters in Kielce Being Withdrawn

As we are informed, the craftsmen's cards [karta rzemieślnicza] of a number of Jewish shoe-upper makers-cutters who do not run workshops of their own have lately been withdrawn.
In town it is said that the withdrawal of the cards from the shoe-upper cutters is the result of a lengthy effort on the part of the Jewish shoe-upper makers' guild, which wished to approach the competent authorities about this with a special letter against its former members, who had been expelled from the guild.
If this is true, it would be one of the greatest public scandals. We therefore await an explanation from the Jewish shoe-upper makers' guild.

What's New in Upper Silesia? — Natan Bistritzky in Katowice

(L.T.)[?] Last Wednesday morning [29 September 1937] the well-known Hebrew poet and leading figure of the KKL [Keren Kayemet LeIsrael, Jewish National Fund], Natan Bistritzky, arrived in Katowice.
The united committee of the Katowice Zionist organisations delegated a sizeable delegation which met the guest at the station, and already on the same day the well-known poet gave two lectures in the „B'nai B'rith" premises: in the afternoon for WIZO and in the evening for the members of the „Concordia" lodge.
On Thursday evening a large mass meeting took place in the great hall of the kehilla building. The topics were: „The liberation of woman in view of the Jewish renaissance", „Messianic dreams and a new meaning" and „The new act of the Jewish tragedy".
The programme of the Bistritzky days in Katowice from today on is: today, Friday, at 8 p.m., a large youth meeting in the kehilla hall on the subject „The history of the building of Eretz Israel in songs". Tomorrow, Saturday, at 4 p.m. in the kehilla hall, an „Oneg Shabbat"; Sunday the 3rd of this month[?] at 10 a.m., a meeting of the KKL workers in the Zionist premises; Monday the 4th at 8.30 p.m., a women's meeting in the kehilla hall on the subject „Heavenly Jerusalem — earthly Jerusalem"; Tuesday the 5th at 8.30 p.m., a public meeting on the subject „The Jewish people and the European spiritual crisis".
The great campaign for the redemption of Galilee has been organised and has already begun; all active Zionists have set themselves the task of raising the greatest possible sum — the maximum that Jewish Katowice can give.
Judging by the mood, good results can truly be expected.

Oneg Shabbat (Sabbath Delight)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly Torah portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Bereshit
—o—
a) "In the beginning God created" (1:1)
In Tractate Megillah, folio 9, the Gemara says that when the Torah was translated into Greek for King Ptolemy, they had to reverse the first verse and say "God created in the beginning," so that no one would interpret[?] "Bereshit" as the name of a god who created God (Elokim).
And this allows us to link the end of the Torah, "before the eyes of all Israel," with its beginning, "In the beginning God created."
Only "before the eyes of all Israel" — only for Jews does one read "Bereshit bara Elokim"; for strangers one must read it reversed: "Elokim bara bereshit"... Or Zahav[?].
—o—
b) "In his image; in the image of God He created him" (ibid., 27)
First man was created "in his image," in his own form, and only later "in the image of God" — for above all one must be a mentsh (a decent human being).. R. Mendele of Kotzk.
• • •
Many times — says the Midrash — God deliberated whether to create man. The question arises: why did He not deliberate thus when creating the snakes and scorpions, which bring nothing but harm to the world?
It is because man is the kind of creature that with one foot leans[?] [—] up to the seventh heaven, and with the other stands in the very depths of the netherworld. There is no limit to his baseness and vileness... Rer[?] Welbiner[?].
—o—
c) "And He sanctified it" (2:3)
The author of "Tiferet Shlomo" [R. Shlomo HaKohen of Radomsko] once came for the Sabbath to R. Yechezkele of Kuzmir [Kazimierz]. R. Yechezkele used to eat the Friday-night meal in seclusion. So the "Tiferet Shlomo" sent his attendant to ask whether he would permit him to eat the meal together with him.
R. Yechezkele of Kuzmir pondered and answered:
"It does not depend on me alone; I must ask the ministering angels, with whom I eat the meal."
When the attendant brings the "Tiferet Shlomo" the answer, he says jokingly, as was his way:
"If so, I shall ask the angels; they will be at my place first."
The attendant shrugs his shoulders:
"Rebbe, if the ministering angels come to you before they come to R. Yechezkele of Kuzmir, then after all it is you who have the say[?], our master[?]"
"Fool!" the "Tiferet Shlomo" answers him. "Why don't you understand? I make kiddush right after the prayers and immediately invite the ministering angels: 'Peace be upon you, ministering angels, angels of the Most High'.. R. Yechezkele, however, comes to the meal too late, so naturally the ministering angels come to him later..."
—o—
d) "And the Lord God commanded the man, saying" (ibid., 16)
"'Saying' — this refers to forbidden sexual relations."
Sanhedrin 56.
How can "saying" allude to forbidden relations? —
Because "saying" means: to tell another; and it is man's way to take up[?] an injunction[?] from his parents — what is handed down within the family, what a father passes on to a son, is sacred. Therefore: "'saying' — this is forbidden relations," for only when family purity is guarded[?] is what the father passes on sacred to the son. But when one does not know who the father is.. Ateret Tzvi.
—o—
e) "If you do not do well — sin crouches at the door" (4:7)
"If you do not do well" — if you do not become better, you become worse; one cannot stand still on one level. If a person does not grow better from day to day — "sin crouches at the door": the evil inclination already stands ready at the door, and as soon as you let go of the door handle, it is already here... the Vilna Gaon.
—o—
f) "Am I my brother's keeper?" (ibid., 9)
"Am I my brother's keeper?" — this is actually a simple answer: is he obliged to know where his brother is? But it is laced with insolence[?]: what does my brother matter to me? And beneath this insolence[?] the vilest things always hide, even murder... Ateret Tzvi.
—o—
g) "And in process of time Cain brought an offering to the Lord" (ibid., 3)
Every Cain, when he reaches old age, when he no longer has the strength to sin, becomes pious and brings offerings to God... Leket Amarim.
• • •
At the blessing of the new month we say: "a life in which there is fear of Heaven and fear of sin." Seemingly, fear of Heaven and fear of sin mean one and the same thing.
But "fear of sin" is present in a person in his youth; then there is still the lure of sin, the passion for sin — a kind of "fear," an awe of sin — but then the person lacks "fear of Heaven." In old age, on the other hand, a person has "fear of Heaven," but then he lacks "fear of sin": sin no longer holds any attraction for him. Therefore we pray: "a life in which there is fear of Heaven and fear of sin," that in our youth, when we possess "fear of sin," we should also be "God-fearing".. An old saying.
—o—
h) "Men of renown" (6:4–5)
"...men of renown. And the Lord saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually."
For it is mostly the men of renown, the "celebrities," the famous, who harbour such evil thoughts.. Imrei Chen.
On Public Oversight

Recent times have brought with them the enormously developed rationalisation of every kind of work, of every kind of production. Everyone strives to work with ever more perfected methods — cheaper, faster, more. Abroad, and here in Poland too, there exist special enterprises whose aim and purpose is to check the working methods and the output of factories and other economic bodies.
We have the same thing in the oversight of the work of state and municipal enterprises.
And now to the matter itself.
Our public budget in Zagłębie — I say "budget", because this is no longer charity and philanthropy but a stable, regular, normally working apparatus — our Jewish public budget alone amounts, in my opinion, not counting the kehilla and its institutions, to many hundreds of thousands of złoty a year.
That is a huge sum, but it is ever harder to squeeze the money out of the exhausted Jewish public.
It is ever harder to cover the budget, while at the same time the tasks and needs grow enormously. [—] For a long time [?] I have considered it necessary that a body of 5 to 7 persons be created in Zagłębie, experts in matters of public economy and costing, and that this body should systematically check the activity, the working methods, the output, the administrative costs etc. of the various, simply countless Jewish institutions in Zagłębie that live and exist on money collected from the public.
Such a body, which can and must be created, must stand in close contact with the kehilla bodies. I am convinced that an exact analysis of the life and work of a great many of our institutions would bring very large savings, would lead to rationalisation, to cheaper working costs, and together with that to an increase in our output in line with the growing demands.
I am convinced that seriously intended and honestly run institutions will gladly [?] submit [?] to the oversight of such an audit committee, and all the others will in one way or another surely [?] have to heed the committee's opinion, since publicising that this or that institution does not want to be audited would in consequence reduce the flow of money it receives from the public.
I consider the matter quite ripe, and if such an audit committee comes into being in Zagłębie, it will be an example for other towns as well.
It goes without saying that the committee would be exempt from auditing the institutions that are centralised and already possess the proper supervisory bodies, such as the gemilut-hasadim (interest-free loan) funds, the cooperative bank, etc.
Ts. M.
What Pays Better for the Tenants?

A group of tenants from Sosnowiec who occupy commercial premises in a certain house and turned to us for advice give us the following account.
Their landlord is about to rebuild the house and wants them to vacate the shops for him amicably. He offers them other premises, which, however, are not suitable for them; moreover, even if the landlord agrees [?] to leave them in place, the shops will be rebuilt in such a way that each one's share will come to barely half of the space they now occupy.
Should they accept one of the two offers or let themselves into a lawsuit?
The matter raised has an important significance, and not only for the several enquirers, therefore it is indeed worth shedding light on it in more detail.
It is hard to know on the basis of which patent (trade-licence) category the said tenants run their businesses, whether on the basis of a 4th or a higher category, and so we do not know whether their premises fall under the provisions of the tenants' protection decree or not.
Let us assume that they hold a 4th-category patent and consequently the tenants' protection decree does apply to the premises they occupy. In such a case the agreements with the tenants must be terminated 3 months in advance. Then the landlord must conduct a lawsuit and prove that the rebuilding is necessary not only for the interests of his pocket but also from a public standpoint: for example, the number of flats will be increased [?] and thereby the housing shortage will be eased, or a museum [?] will receive a home in the rebuilt building, or a school will be enlarged, or another important institution.
First the court must recognise the expediency of the rebuilding; an eviction is ordered, but then the landlord is obliged to pay the tenant monetary compensation in the amount of 7 months' rent.
Now, the opposite case: the premises are not covered by the tenants' protection. The landlord may then terminate the lease without grounds; as soon as [?] it concerns a tenant who has already been in the premises for longer than 5 years, the agreement must be terminated 2 months in advance.
After the 2 months the landlord obtains an eviction if he conducts a lawsuit. The tenant can only apply once, and that too for a term until 31 March 1939 at the latest.
That is how the legal side of the matter looks.
As for the practical situation, it is as follows:
By the court route you can obtain the possibility of staying in the premises at best until 31 March 1939. Of the two offers the landlord is making you in order to settle the dispute peacefully, the second can come into consideration, i.e. to stay in the same reduced shop. But you must take care [?] not to come off worse by the peaceful route than you could have achieved by the court route.
Since by court you can stay in the whole premises until 31 March 1939, i.e. another year and a half, you must see to it that the landlord concludes with you a written agreement concerning the halved premises for a term of at least 3 years.
In One Code

[Poland — economy and trade; legislation: the food-trade code.]
The government has drawn up a detailed code on the food trade, which will soon be dealt with in the Sejm and will be put into effect in the shortest possible time.
The text of the food code has already received [?] the approval of the Chamber of Commerce and of the economic organisations.
At present there are countless laws, decrees, ordinances and ministerial circulars concerning the trade in food products. This mass of regulations and provisions will now be unified into one code, which will regulate all branches of the food trade.
Indeed, there are now so many ordinances and circulars that the food merchants cannot cope with them. They are unable to remember and understand all the regulations and provisions, which are scattered [?] across the statute books of many years.
The food merchants constantly complain that they are subjected to a rather large number of inspection commissions, sent by various administrative bodies.
Thus the food merchant is subject to the control of the "shtayer-mekhes" (tax/excise authority), of [— illegible word: another supervisory body], of sanitary commissions, of a commission for combating the adulteration of foodstuffs, of the control over prices and invoices, and of yet other similar inspection commissions. In no branch do merchants incur as many fines as the food merchants, and this only because they are unable to master all the laws concerning the food branch.
Especially important for the food merchants is the question of the prices of foodstuffs. On this too there are many decrees, ordinances and ministerial instructions, which teach the officials when one must punish for charging excessive prices. Nevertheless, in practice it is hard to work out what "charging excessive prices" means, and how the merchant is to know that the price he charges is calculated according to the regulations, and which prices are already too high, so that he must be punished for them.
How much, actually, may a merchant in foodstuffs earn so that he cannot be punished for "likhte" [?] prices?
The merchant cannot find his way in these matters, because there are many laws on the subject, issued over the course of 20 years, and all are still in force — so that even lawyers find their way in them only with difficulty.
For the many thousands of food merchants it will therefore be of very great importance that all the regulations, laws and circulars will be concentrated in one "code", so that it will be easy for everyone to become acquainted with them and to guard against fines and lawsuits.
H. B.
The First Days

(Psychological sketches).

Adam and Eve

In the lower Garden of Eden a soft, gentle breeze is blowing. It plays with the just-sprouted grasses and leaves, from which there spreads a young, fresh scent of spring with an enticing, fragrant aroma.
The earth, a broad green carpet spread far[?] and wide; flower crowns of many colours peep out curiously from among the jumble of grass stalks of all kinds.
In the air drift the voices of all sorts of young beasts and cattle, birds of every kind, like the chirping of small children.
Above them the transparent blue sky [—], and the warm sun looks down with tender lovingness upon the creatures barely just created, with cheerful contentment, like a mother upon her firstborn who has only just been born. From the deep blue heavens come quiet songs of angels: "Holy, holy, holy".
On a thick, grassy carpet, among colourful[?] leafy flowers, lies Adam.
He plucks the grasses and little leaves around him, carries them to his mouth and chews them; a bitter, unpleasant taste spreads over his tongue; with a grimace he spits out what he has chewed and looks at it just as it is. The big human being with the childishly naive eyes contemplates and marvels at it all.
Adam[?] is not alone: around him various animals lie, stand and walk; flocks of birds fly over his head; all kinds of creeping things[?] buzz. Some of the young animals crawl up to Adam, stretch out their [—] little heads to him and lick his body, crawl about on him. He lets it all happen, and contemplating it all gives him peace and amuses[?] him.
After a short wander through Eden, Adam[?] comes upon shallow water, by which he stops. The first smile appeared on his lips: behind the mirror of the water he saw a second one like himself... To his great amazement he sees that the one in the water makes the same movements, and he wants to grab him; with a wild[?] cry he hurries out of the water and starts to run.
Running like this, a shout breaks out of him: "Kh-a-a-a-ch"! And the voice rings far[?] across the valleys of Eden.
— Kh-a-a-a-ch! — an echo answers back from the hilly places and rolls across the whole broad expanse, round and round in the void.
And again Adam now confirms that he is not alone: someone answers his call..
— That must surely be the one in the water — he thinks to himself — he must go and look for him.
Inspired[?] by the certainty that the one who answered his call is not far from here, all his newly-arisen senses awoke in him. He runs; a vapour[?] [—] out of his wide-open mouth, and from his forehead large drops of sweat roll down, gleaming in the sun like pearls.
Tired from running, the giant[?] [—] Adam[?] drops down onto a many-coloured carpet of grass, thickly overgrown with a hundred kinds of flowers and fragrant herbs.
* * *
A breeze carried hither the sharp fragrant scent of roses and other flowers of Eden. Adam[?] lies heavily tired on his back, and with open eyes he watches with wonder the setting of the mild, warm sun.
From the opposite horizon a laughing, pale moon floats up, draws near to him and smiles. Adam[?] thinks to himself: surely this is the face that answered his call. He keeps looking at the lightly smiling, laughing face; his eyes at long last grow tired, until finally they close. The first man fell asleep for the first time.
* * *
At dawn he awoke, and he was no longer alone: he sees some body lying beside him. Who is it? Perhaps the [—] from the sky with the pale face, which came smiling towards him? In the sky the face is indeed no longer there.. He wants to get up, but in one side of his body he feels a [—] pain that borders on a pleasant feeling; his ribs crack, as if something had torn itself away from that very spot and is moving. He cannot understand what has happened to him.
The flaming purple colours[?] in the sky have changed into a sea of deep blueness with [—] red-pink stripes; from the little clouds [—] curiously down; hosts of little angels peeled themselves out, fluttering[?] about and circling Adam and also the second figure. From the valleys of Eden come melodious voices of angels: Holy, holy, holy!
Suddenly Adam[?] noticed that the figure beside him was moving freely. Tired and weak, he tries to bend his head towards that body in his vicinity; it is hard for him. He sees a face, but[?] no[?], not at all like the one that had smiled in the sky.
Red lips, thick hair lying wildly[?] tossed over her shoulders and neck, black-[?] eyes sparkle and gaze ahead somewhere[?].
* * *
Adam[?], half asleep, not fully in his senses, looks around, listening to the song of the birds and to the ringing rustle of the palm leaves; it [—] to him that Eden is full of wonderful life; he feels that something touches him and moves. What[?] — he thinks to himself — is this the one from the water? He turns [—] round, and beside him lies a second human being; two beautiful feminine eyes look at him with an enchanting grace and with a smile. He cannot believe that the one from the water should[?] be here beside him. He wants to make sure, and calls again: "Kh-a-a-a-chu".
The feminine, childlike mouth, wanting to imitate Adam, let out a childish[?], childlike sound: "Z[?]-a-a-a-ch"!
Adam, repeating his call, added to it her "Z[?]-a-a-a-ch". And from the valleys of Eden there echoed back, rustling and soft, the called-out name of the first woman: "Chava [Eve]!"
With curious eyes Adam[?] peers closely at Eve's face. His head follows his gaze; he looks at her mouth, which had cried out the first word and from which a warm breath streams and breathes upon his face.
— This is the one who called back to me from afar — he thinks to himself.
He bends to her face, he feels the warm breath of her lips, which he touches with his mouth, wants to swallow her hot breath out of her mouth and — — —
Born was — — — the first kiss...
H. Salnik.
From the Holidays. (A Short Stroll).

The past festival of Sukkot did not stand here in Zagłębie in its finest splendour — no wonder, when economic life is so bitter. Besides, the "joyful" tidings from our neighbouring towns produced a pessimistic mood.
Still, our brethren the Children of Israel did not stint on a few more groszy for a fine etrog with a lulav, for a few bundles of schach; people also allowed themselves [?] to hold the "Simchat Beit ha-Shoeva", and Jews drank l'chaim.
In the batei midrash and in all the shtiblekh they beat the hoshanot hard and prayed with intent that the new year should at last be a year of redemption and salvation.
In many sukkahs heated discussions were held about the Jewish state.
There were those who pleaded in its favour, arguing that the Jews would make do with a small state, but the majority protested and raised a storm that such a thing must not be allowed — we must have a state on both sides of the Jordan.
There were cases where in some courtyards poor "yordim" [the come-down] were ashamed to sit in the sukkah and waited until late at night; only then, when all the sukkah-sitters had finished eating [?] and left the sukkah, did they go in to hold their "seudah" in the sukkah.
The Yiddish film "The Dybbuk" had a great success in the "Nowości" [?] cinema in Będzin. The crush recalled the former performances of the Vilna Troupe in Będzin.
The finale [?] of the holidays also did not turn out as lively [?] and tipsy as in former years.
There was no real, open joy this year; people sang a niggun, even tried to strike up a dance, but the enthusiasm "was missing", the real joy. Too few Jews were seen supposedly swaying in the street, but it was not hard to tell that these were not the genuine drunks and that there was more in the bottle than in the head. Indeed those who joked that they had got drunk on water, just so people would at least think so, were not satisfied [?]...
And so too the "pedigreed" householders gave up their claim to a "fine" hakafah, and precisely at "Ozer Dalim" Jews protested who once used to play first fiddle... Even among the simple, open "common folk" one could notice that the wish to really celebrate had suddenly been lost; what more do you need — even among the Hasidim, who feel themselves with the Torah "pan grest" [?, unclear expression], something was also not as with everyone: in the present crisis the aspirants to "Atah Hareta", "Chatan Torah", "Chatan Bereshit" made the deals cheaply, prices fell, it was ridiculously cheap and there was no need to haggle [?] long at the auctions.
The fat, open-handed "kaddishes" of former times were very lean this time; nevertheless the "95-proof Hasidim-drinkers" [i.e. drinkers of 95% spirit] took heart, and beside little barrels of beer at twilight they danced out the most heartfelt [?] joy in the shtiblekh. In some shtiblekh people even rejoiced, but on the whole [?] the worries [?] of a whole year began to bite again, and holding the glasses of beer not one Jew failed to beg those around him: — Jews, let us wish each other that the Jewish troubles should finally end.
And in one other particular the festival went bankrupt this year.
Usually in Zagłębie one always used to see the small-town Chol ha-Moed visitors promenading; Będzin in particular has had a claim to this since the six days of Creation: from the smaller towns around there used to come the dressed-up little grooms [?] in their small-town outfits [?], and there was a bustle in every corner; but today, only rarely did [?] a "caught" [engaged] lad stroll [?] with his prima donna. The general crisis has set its stamp on this field too, as the saying goes:
"Crisis over everything".
300 Years of Coffee.

We sit at home or in a coffee-house, drink our daily coffee and do not know that exactly 300 years will now have passed since the world got a new drink, which is more widespread in the whole world than any other drink except water.
We do not know how long the Turks and the Arabs have known coffee, which one gets at its best among them to this day. Already at the end of the 12th century there are signs of coffee plantations among the Arabs, but there is no exact information about it.
In our parts people began drinking coffee only in the year 1683, when the Turks withdrew after Sobieski's war before Vienna. They left behind in Vienna thousands of sacks of coffee; in Vienna no one knew what to do with them, until someone, a Turk who had lived in Vienna for many years already, hit on the idea of buying up the coffee for a pittance [?] and making a drink of it; he soon opened the first "coffee-house" in Vienna, in which the "noble [?] people" got a little of this drink for a lot of money.
But already in the year 1637, exactly 300 years ago, a Turkish merchant brought several sacks of coffee to the Leipzig fair, which no one wanted to buy. Since he did not want to take the coffee back, he handed the sacks over to a local merchant to sell them bit by bit until he would come to the next fair.
In the archive lies a letter from the Leipzig merchant to a customer of his in Merseburg, who used to order many goods from him. This Merseburg customer was sent a little coffee: his wife should cook it, and he would have a drink with a real "taste of Paradise".
The Merseburger's wife cooked the coffee exactly as she had been told, only instead of with water she cooked it "with a good, very fat beef broth"...
So the Merseburger wrote a letter to his Leipzig friend and gave him "his father's father" [cursed him roundly] for having sent him something from which he could easily have departed this world — he simply wanted to poison him; therefore he should send him no more goods, because he does not even want to know of him.
In the end he demands back 16 Kreuzer for medicines which he had to buy at the pharmacy to clean his stomach of the poison..
It is not known whether the two merchants made up afterwards, just as it is not known when people began drinking coffee in Merseburg.
Z. Haber, Vienna.
A Garment and a Name

[Note — Jewish identity, dress and name; economic antisemitism.]
(A note).
What is closer to a person — his garment or his name?
A strange question, eh?
But it is written somewhere that the Jews were redeemed from Egypt because they did not change their garments and their names.
And now we are, after all, supposedly facing some kind of redemption; one would like to know: by what merit does it come to us, and how do things stand with us regarding these two matters?
It would seem that the name is closer than the garment; the garment is on him, while the name is a part of him himself; a garment can be thrown off and changed, but a name cannot.
Nevertheless one sees that traditional, conservative, Orthodox Jews hold on more firmly to the garment than to the name.
Be he a Misnaged or a Hasid, a Mizrachist or an Agudist, even a Belzer and Munkacser Hasid — if only for business it is necessary to put a nicer, altered or concealed name on the firm, he will not hold back from it.
I have never yet seen a big firm, a factory, a trading house, a joint-stock company bearing in golden letters: Bezalel, Motl, Berish and the like.
But look for the owner of that very firm, and you will see a Jew in a long kapote, a yarmulke, a little beard — who has not departed by a hair's breadth from tradition.
And now an assault is being made on both things.
In "Nasz Przegląd" a Jewish assimilationist demands that the Jews throw off the Hasidic garments and dress "German" [in modern European clothes], so that the antisemites will not recognise them and will not know whom to hit over the head with the stick.
And the Polish merchants demand that a law be passed that a Jewish merchant may not display on his firm's signboard a Christian name, or a disguised half-name, so that a gentile customer should know whom one must boycott and avoid.
We can say with certainty that the simple Jew will be very angry if he is, God forbid, forced to display himself on the signboard under his own name, Chatzkel or Mendel; and he will be just as angry if he is told to take off his bekishe and his gartel.
Why, then, is the Jewish garment dearer to him than the Jewish name?
Is the name not closer, more a part of his own body and soul?
It remains a kushye [an unanswered question].
Avi-Ver.
Children (A Story)

[Short story.]
The old couple ate their modest supper. Today, exceptionally [?], they had to eat so late: they had been waiting for their youngest son, who was "on the road" on business and was supposed to be home, back from his trip, before supper. The old folks waited for him impatiently and decided not to delay any longer! The old man washed his hands; they even had many current matters to talk over, but whatever they started on, their conversation came round to the youngest son — what could it be, he is so punctual, he wrote to them that he would eat supper together with them, and he is still not here.

A hasty ring at the door interrupted their talk. The old woman hurried to open. On the threshold stood the postman — a telegram, he said, and held out his hand. The old woman, however, did not hurry; first she had to let her Yosl know — "Yosl, a telegram!"

The old man repeated the magic word a few times, but by no means wanted to ask whom it was from; until his impatience got the better of him — his urge to ask — and he asked hastily: from whom? Only then did the old woman consent to open the telegram, signed for it at the indicated place and... shut [?] the door behind the departing postman. The old man was already in the kitchen, snatched the dispatch from her and began to read — "Dearest parents, I could not do otherwise, I have stayed true to my brothers, wish me mazel tov, I have a bride."

The old couple stood there as if stunned, although it was nothing new to them: all their children had married for love and far from home, and only a short notice in the form of a telegram had reached them, and all they could do was wish the young couple mazel tov — but still — the youngest!

The eldest son had been in a third-class compartment of an ordinary passenger train. Next to him a young, pretty miss with a very interesting face had taken a seat. He looked for some pretext to get closer [?] to her, but when an opportunity presented itself she herself spoiled it. He stuck out his elbow more than is "socially" permitted, but that did not help either, until she dozed off, and when she opened her eyes he was already in the happy position of looking into her eyes. She all but ignored it, opened a book and became absorbed in reading. He tried to start a conversation with her: "You are surely reading an exciting book." Slowly she raised her eyes, measured him indifferently and went on reading. "Not bad" — she tossed out two words after a while, as if in passing. Her manner intrigued him even more; he had long since passed the town where he was supposed to meet the director of the firm in which he was employed as an agent; but he firmly resolved to travel on with her. — A week later he ran, a happy man, to the post office to give his parents the joyful news: "Dear parents and dear brothers! I have a bride, you are — in-laws! To you — much joy, wish me mazel tov, all of you." The old woman burst into sobs, the old man had a drink, and the brothers gave each other strange [?] looks.

The second son studied chemistry abroad; every two weeks he wrote long letters home, until one day... he fell in love. For over a month the old folks had received no word from him. He had made an excursion to Vienna and visited various sights, but of them all he liked best the art museum. There he first saw her, by a picture of Rubens. She admired the work of art, and he — her. Quickly an acquaintance was struck up between them. They went on talking, standing before the picture. She spoke about the picture, and he... about her, until she let herself be convinced — that she had wonderfully beautiful features resembling Rubens's glorious portrait of a maiden. Vienna no longer interested them; her family home received him warmly, he quickly settled in with the family, and after two months of romantic love he, contented, gave the servant a five-złoty note and a telegram to wire to his parents: "Dear parents! I am happy, already after the wedding, wish me even more happiness." This time the old man too wept, and the two remaining brothers went about the whole evening with strange thoughts.

The third son had a flair for public affairs and was very active in that field. To the annual conference, held in the capital, he was sent as a delegate. The conference had long ended and he was still there; he wrote home that he had to stay on for a while for various consultations that were still to take place. Meanwhile he sent his town newspaper a report on the conference, but he himself was still nowhere to be seen. At home they waited for him or for a second letter, and in public circles people were already whispering about him and his "future". In a letter he confided in a friend of his: "They like each other: he heard her speak at the conference. Never before had he heard anyone speak so easily and so convincingly; he was down to speak after her, but he had already given up — she had exhausted everything so thoroughly that nothing was left to him but to keep silent. From then on he sought to get closer to her. Their love grew on a spiritual [printed: "neystign"] foundation. The result was a jointly wired dispatch to his parents: "We have bound ourselves for ever, we to you, you to us — mazel tov."

The old woman no longer wept, she only sadly bowed her head and looked at her Yosl, and the old man... he found it very hard before God, and even more so because of people; he took heart and began to see God's hand in it.

And the youngest son went about nervously, as if he already wanted to know what his fate would bring him.

The old couple lived it all through once more as in a dream — four children, and all of them married far [?] from home, but still... the youngest — he had been their last hope, and he too... stayed true to them...

Goren
