What does the new draft law on crafts say?

A short time ago a number of deputies [to the Sejm] grouped around the present leadership of the Union of Chambers of Crafts introduced a draft law amending the President's decree of 7 June 1927, as amended on 10 March 1934. The draft contains a series of changes of principle, of which we give the most important, concerning the right to practise a trade independently and to teach it.
1) Chałupnicy [home-based outworkers], who had been excluded from the industrial law, are to come under the provisions of the decree; this is, however, to concern only those chałupnicy who employ outside workers.
2) The authorities may prohibit itinerant trade (przemysł okrężny) (both of a commercial and of a craft character) in the territory of certain powiats [districts] or of whole voivodeships.
3) All kinds of enterprises are to be counted as craft enterprises, except those which the Ministry of Commerce and Industry considers to be run on a factory basis.
4) The crafts are divided into licensed (concession), regulated and free ones. Over 30 trades are counted among the regulated ones, among others also some that until now were counted among the free industries, for example printing and milling. On the other hand, a number of trades with a larger number of workshops have been struck out, for example photography, brass founding, "vesk[?]" making, etc. The Minister of Commerce and Industry will be able to change the list of regulated trades.
5) One may practise a trade independently only after registering in the register of craftsmen. In the licensed and regulated trades only a person who holds the title of master in the given trade may be registered. For registering in the register of free craftsmen, on the other hand, it is enough to report that one runs a workshop.
6) Young people working in licensed and regulated trades are regarded by the law as apprentices (terminators).
7) In the licensed and regulated trades it is permitted to take payment for teaching the trade.
8) Only a master who has received the right to do so from the Chamber of Crafts may teach the trade.
9) An apprentice must, at the end of the term of apprenticeship, take an examination as a journeyman. Craftsmen in licensed and regulated trades may not employ any persons who have not passed this examination.
10) The master's title can be obtained after passing a master's examination. The following may be admitted to the examination: a) certified journeymen with several years of practice in the trade; b) persons who have run their own workshop for 3 years; c) chałupnicy who have run their own workshop for 8 years and have completed a vocational supplementary course; d) persons who had the right to teach a trade before 16 December ["grudnia"] 1927.
As can be seen from the points cited, the authors of the draft have gone in the direction of further restrictions (making the right to run a workshop dependent on the master's title). The aim is to subject the whole of small industry to the chambers of crafts and to compel the workers employed in the licensed and regulated trades to fulfil the provisions of the law (the condition of not employing workers other than apprentices and journeymen). In this way, the authors of the draft believe, broad areas of the crafts which until now lay outside the limits of their influence will be brought under their control.
Troubles from not registering children on time

Too much is simply[?] forgotten when one counts up how many troubles Jews bring on themselves by not registering their children on time.
How far not registering children on time is an accepted rule among Jews can be seen from the fact that the late classic Sholem Aleichem, in one of his humorous stories, described a Jew agonising over how he should register his newborn son — before the time or after the time — and it never occurred to him that he could simply register the child when it was actually born.
It is not only the registering of children on time that is neglected; the same applies to weddings, etc.
It is a fact that after the birth of a child the parents have still not completed their marriage records, and the child must be registered as illegitimate.
The Jews who do not complete the formalities on time know themselves what harm they do to themselves and later to their children.
For example: payment orders [nakazy] for income tax (podatek dochodowy) are sent out. The law provides that for every child 20 zł. is deducted from the income tax.
The Jew, having several children, lodges an appeal, quite sure that according to the number of children so many[?] times 20 zł. will be deducted for him. The tax office forwards all the appeals to the municipality [magistrat] to check whether the person who lodged the appeal actually has the stated number of children. In most cases it turns out that legally the number of children cannot be stated, because the children are registered under the mother's name, and for the most part they are not registered at all.
It is the same when registering a child at school: one meets great difficulties if one does not have a birth certificate [metryka].
As we have been informed, a heavy penalty threatens for not registering children on time, and in general for not registering at all the children not registered so far.
Until now penalties have been avoided, and if the Jewish population continues to neglect the matter in this way, the guilty will begin to be punished with fines and arrest.
It is therefore in the interest of each and every one to use the opportunity and register the children not yet registered, regardless of their age, and to put things in order so that they have legal documents.
When the penalties begin, nobody will then be able to help anyone, because it will already be too late.
For its own good the Jewish population must use the opportunity, in order to avoid unpleasantness and fines.
D. Z.
Dance.

(Reflections).
Dancing was the motto of 1937, and dancing will be the masterpiece ["shede-khr", probably "chef-d'œuvre"] of 1938.
Dances — an ancient custom, bound up with mysticism and cult. The wildest tribes approach their idols with dance and music.
The Orient has its own distinctive dances. Its kings, sultans and shahs have their ballets and dancing girls; the Negroes are masters of dancing. Dancing is now taught in the schools.
—
We now live in a time when dancing has become almost a spiritual nourishment, a refreshment.
The magic spell of the tango!
The chords of the fox[trot] make us light and nimble[?], drive away our melancholy.
The English waltzes lead us into a labyrinth of mirages and fata morganas — they create the loveliest illusions.
—
We are intoxicated[?] by the sounds of music. The emotion is strong! In grey everyday life one forgets that life is empty and foolish.
You dance, manoeuvring, you feel your partner's breath — her scent[?] — you are childlike and happy.
Opposite your table sits a young, beautiful lady; she is a regular guest at the balls[?], she is proud of her grace and beauty, she bids her admirers[?]: come, you handsome cavaliers, and dance with me; the world has much splendour and enchantment, a world of passion and pleasure; Eros will come and play his loveliest symphonies!..
—
He sits in a carriage[?]; his young wife is a passionate dancer, her blood is hot... He thinks:
Strange men will embrace her, she will smile at them, they will kiss her hand, press her to their chest: erotic, passionate feelings will flare up.
Jealousy gnaws at his heart, he sees wild orgies in his imagination, he suddenly understands that his great happiness is nothing more than a chimera.
He must be loyal. He must forbid her nothing; he is a cultured, intelligent person, he must be decent; society is watching, it could take him for a vandal. He looks at the clock — it is 12, midnight. He knows the call: "Panie, na tem kończymy dziś [nasz?] dancing i zapraszamy na jutro!" [Polish in Hebrew letters: "Gentlemen, with this we close today's dancing and invite you for tomorrow!"]
Where is his wife going now?
J. Reichenbach.

The Stingy Spinster.
That is what they called her.
The stingy spinster.
The neighbours said nothing bad about her, could not say anything, because the girl had worked hard her whole life; in her youth she studied, finished a secondary school, later a college; she had to provide for her own living, and so had no time to take life the way youth is entitled to. While her fellow students spent the hours strolling, at the theatre, at dancings, our heroine toiled over textbooks or at private lessons for a living, putting everything off until later — and the "later" came in the shape of a dental surgery. Again she had to work, to earn herself a professional name, again she put off her own life until later; and when you don't go out into society, have no colleagues and wage no love-rivalry with girlfriends, you have no ambition for a nice coat, an even nicer dress, a fine hat, a luxury handbag, etc. The fashion magazines are entirely superfluous for someone like her.
She lived in a small room, isolated from people, and gathered złoty by złoty, and the more the figures grew in her savings book, the more grew her ambition to have still more. She did not allow herself even a decent pair of shoes, and so the neighbours called her "the stingy spinster"; and although they said nothing bad, they did have grievances against her: who should allow themselves things, if not she?..
But she thought otherwise: she is gathering[?] a dowry; a girl who earns her own living and has capital besides — she will surely make the best match!
At first it was not so easy for the neighbours to win her consent[?]: whoever liked her — she did not like, and whoever she did like — was in no hurry for the stingy spinster.
Years upon years went by; the deposit in the bank grew, but at the same time so did the "little bit of years" — already over 40. With every day, with every hour the longing for a home of her own, for a husband, grows stronger; the matchmaker's task is now much easier.
The stingy spinster finally got married.
But the husband is no boor: a big-city man, a man who knows the world; he spent his youth differently from her. Everything he tells is so new to her; she swallows every word of his. Her eyes are already half extinguished, but in her heart burns a hellish fire, and the husband is a good 10 years younger than she. Every word of his is a command to her. She will keep working, saving, but heaven forbid he should lack anything; let him live even better than before; let him know that he has married, that she is his wife. That she slaved her whole life, that he is the dearest thing in the world to her, dearer than her money — of this she convinces him. "Here, take my savings book. Treat yourself, my dear, don't think, don't worry, I will go on working and paying."
Her husband is, heaven forbid, no swindler; an honest man, never took anything from anyone; but he married her because he was already in great trouble. The savings book with its several tens of thousands of złoty made him younger still; he is drawn and torn toward the world, toward life, gaiety, pleasure. She, the "stingy spinster", cannot be his partner in that; for her the surgery is enough — and the radio. He, however, likes to take life directly.
Trips begin under all sorts of pretexts, but each time to a different town, and suddenly she learns that, with her money, her husband has set up in Warsaw her[?] former technician, a young and pretty girl — — —
He has not run away from her, has not asked for a divorce; he comes home often; she listens to his stories, his excuses, accepts it all as truth, although she knows it is all lies. Her heart is torn, but the mind orders silence, and only now does she understand why the neighbours bore her a grudge for so many years: after all, she did them no harm — and yet they called her "the stingy spinster" with such bitterness.
Now she already understands her former sins.
Sins [avenge?] themselves.

Why Calculate?

[Humour — joke.] The husband sits gloomy and lost in thought; his wife comes up to him and gives him a tender stroke on the head:
— Why are you so downcast, my dear husband?
— Today I added up on the calculating machine all the expenses of our car — he answers with a sigh.
— But I told you not to buy it! — says the wife.
— What? You told me not to buy a car? — the husband jumps up.
— No — the wife calms him — I told you not to buy a calculating machine; then you would have been spared calculating the expenses the car costs you...

I’ll Have to Go Bust...

[Feuilleton — satirical monologue; Zagłębie, trade and the cost of the holidays.] (A monologue of a plain Jew).
Y. Oberżanes
And here I thought I would be the exception to the rule, that I alone would not go bankrupt, that my name would be inscribed in golden letters:
“The Wygania [?] business was the only one that did not go bankrupt.”
No small thing — one man in Zagłębie who fought the crisis so stubbornly, one man who “held out” [“geholtshet”] with all his strength and did not go bankrupt.
And truly they ought to have put up a “pomnik” [monument] to me, and perhaps even named a street after me — it would have been no injustice at all. For do you know how I have stayed on my feet until now? How I fought the crisis? Why I have not “gone into flight” [geyn pleyte — gone bust, fled the creditors] until now? — Why, I showed “narozhichive” [?] heroism, a heroism that ought to be described in the newspapers, and a hero like me ought to be immortalized in history!..
What, you ask, did I do so as not to go bust? I did such things as no Zagłębie merchant ever did.
I did not ride in a car [“samafar” — so printed, probably samochód] of my own, I did not keep a chauffeur for my wife’s sake, I went on foot, as my father and my grandfather did.
I did not buy houses in order to get a “pożyczka” [loan], I did not want to be called “Panie gospodarzu” [Mr. Landlord] at a time when not a single brick is mine...
I did not take “parcels” [goods] “oyf tshop” [?], I did not sign the business over to my mother-in-law, I did not give any “kugrishe” [?] bills of exchange, I did not keep [?] any books — I kept the bookkeeping in my pocket: one pocket was the “przychód” [income] and the other pocket the “rozchód” [expenditure], and — basta!
I did not spread myself out in 6 rooms with a kitchen, my wife did not hold any “przyjęcia” [receptions], no one played poker and bridge whole nights long, I did not travel to Merano or to Karlsbad, I did not have my blood pressure measured, and my wife did not get any “neforn” [?] and did not have any “zabiegi” [treatments]; if I had a złoty, I ate lunch, if I didn’t — I swallowed my spit. All this I did so that I would stay on my feet, so that I would not go bust.
Until now I have “held out”, until now I have not gone bust, but now I shall have to go bankrupt after all — and do you know why? Because of this year’s holidays! Because of the holidays I shall have to go bankrupt.
And what, I ask you, is the wonder? A whole month “bez przerwy” [without a break], holiday after holiday. From the 5th to the 29th of September we had holiday after holiday in a row.
— How so?
The 3rd of September was a Thursday, and you had already started to wonder: where does one get the money for Shabbat? Friday is Erev Shabbat, Shabbat is after all Shabbat, and on Sunday we had Erev Rosh Hashanah. You went around with a “tsuglisn” [?] head [—]: where does one get the money for Rosh Hashanah? Rosh Hashanah we had on Monday and Tuesday, Wednesday — the Fast of Gedaliah, and Thursday you again had nothing for Shabbat. Sunday is after all Sunday, on Monday your wife again needed money for kapores, and Tuesday was Erev Yom Kippur, on Wednesday we had Yom Kippur, and on the Thursday after Yom Kippur, while you were still weak from the fast, you again had to get money ready for Shabbat.
And now, gentlemen, take, if you please, the calendar and leaf on: no sooner had you lit a candle on Saturday night, right after Havdalah, and said “a good week”, than your wife at once said:
“My shining husband, my treasure [“mayn lekhtiker man treytl”], be so good and go over the purse [i.e. open your purse].”
— From where? We’ve only just lit a candle! So my wife showed me the calendar:
You know, my treasure, what tomorrow is? Tomorrow is Erev Sukkot, and a Sunday on top of it. True, they did “permit” trading on Sunday from 7 to 10 in the morning, but I don’t want to be killed for Kiddush Hashem: a hundred women tear at the tail of one fish.. and by the time one fights one’s way to a feather of a fowl — the women first tear their own skin off.
So my wife gave me to understand, and I did not know what to answer, for what can you answer when there is ḥaron kis [a shortage of cash], when, may it not befall you, there is a “przeciąg” [a draught] in your pocket! And where would you get money for Sukkot on Saturday night, right after Havdalah? Do you have your own “kshonzhestvo” [? — principality], your own little money machine?
And what about [“kbḥ” — ?] an etrog? A lulav? The Four Species and other little things?
So I had to grieve quietly [“unter der pakh” — lit. under the armpit, Pol. pacha], and it was bitter and [?] for me.
Now, gentlemen, do you think you are already done? If you think so, you have made a big mistake from the start; excuse me — and onward.
The first days of Sukkot we again had on Monday and Tuesday, Wednesday the first day of Chol Hamoed, and on Thursday one again needed money for Shabbat. You haven’t yet digested the fish from Sukkot, and already you need money for fresh fish — for Shabbat.
On Saturday night, before Havdalah had even been made, the very same conversation as a week before repeated itself:
“My dear husband, my treasure, excuse me and go over the purse.”
— What is it again?
— What do you know, what? Tomorrow is Hoshana Rabbah, with a Sunday as an extra; after Hoshana Rabbah is Shemini Atzeret, after Shemini Atzeret is Simchat Torah, and after Sukkot comes Shabbat again right away with a Sunday — and all this smells of “bigger things” [i.e. heavy expenses].
So once again I had to grieve quietly: Master of the Universe, where does one get so much money? Before one manages [?] to snatch through one holiday, the second holiday is already at the door. A whole month of holiday after holiday, a whole month of fish with “yoykhlekh” [broths], with poultry, with compotes, and what about [?] so much drink?
And here I thought that I would stay on my feet, that I would be the only one in Zagłębie who would not go bankrupt. And indeed I would not have gone bankrupt, were it not for today’s holidays. Because of this year’s holidays I shall have to “go into flight” — a whole month of fish with tsimmes, there’s no way I can hold out!

Foreign guests visit the Będzin synagogue.

[Będzin — community life.]
On Friday towards evening a car with passengers appeared in the Synagogue Street (Shul-gas) in Będzin, and they asked passers-by where the town synagogue was.
The passengers attracted attention, and it was not long before the car was besieged by men, women and children. Zamkowa Lane was seething with the quickly spread news that "American Jews" had come to Będzin to hand out money to the poor for the holiday...
With great effort the guests (2 men and 3 women) managed to get out of the car and into the synagogue, where they were received by the shammes Brachman, who answered the questions put to them.
As it turned out, these were German Jews. They live in Bavaria and own a coal mine near Piekary (Upper Silesia). Coming on business matters, they also paid a visit to the Będzin synagogue.

Dąbrowa

[Dąbrowa — kashrut.]
The treyf sheep "revealed" the secret...
Here things are seething as in a cauldron because of the brand-new kashrut scandal, which was discovered by chance.
The story is as follows: a local butcher had 2 sheep slaughtered, of which one sheep turned out to be treyf.
The butcher, who apparently could not bear to suffer the loss of the sheep that had become treyf, played a trick [?] and sold the meat as kosher.
By chance the matter was discovered, and the butcher was fined in that for 2 weeks he must [—] in his butcher's shop [wording unclear in the original].
The "severe" ruling has aroused great dissatisfaction in Hasidic circles, and the talk of the day in Dąbrowa is the story of the treyf sheep and the ruling that was issued.

At the Sosnowiec Chamber of Commerce

[Economy — chamber of commerce.] The proposal to introduce an educational qualification (census) for merchants has been adopted
Jewish councillors leave the meeting
On Wednesday a meeting of the trade section took place at the Chamber of Commerce in Sosnowiec. The most important item on the agenda was the question of a qualification census for merchants.
For various reasons 5 of the 9 Jewish councillors could not come to the meeting.
Before proceeding to this item, councillor Frenkel (Radom) took the floor and said: since the majority of the Jewish councillors were unable, for unavoidable reasons, to come to the meeting, the proposal should not be dealt with.
Councillor Aliner made a longer speech in which he described the sad situation of the Jewish merchant community because of the boycott, the pickets and so forth. The Chamber of Commerce, as an economic institution — he said — ought to have concerned itself with the economic situation of the Jewish merchants, and since this has not been done so far, the Chamber of Commerce must not be the factor in introducing new trade reforms that could worsen the economic situation of the Jewish merchants even further.
Both proposals were also supported by the member of the commission, councillor D. Gutensztajn.
When both proposals were rejected by the non-Jewish councillors, Mr. Frenkel declared that he was leaving the meeting; the same declaration was made by Messrs. Aliner and Gutensztajn.
Despite this the meeting was carried on, and the project of introducing an educational census was adopted.
A Merry Isru-Chag — Million Prize Falls in Będzin

[Będzin — local news.] On Wednesday morning it became known through the radio that the prize of one million złoty had fallen in Będzin. The news spread through the town as fast as lightning; the editorial office's telephone did not rest, hundreds of people called to ask whether the news was true.
The town was in a whirl [lit. "went on little wheels"], especially once it was already known who the winners in the lottery were — and indeed it pleased everyone that the greater part of the million was won by poor Jewish families. Particular attention was drawn by one of the winners, a Jewish package-carrier (porter), who won one hundred thousand zł. He was not at all "overcome" by having become a rich man so quickly, and went on carrying the packages of goods from the station.
One of the lucky ones, a poor resident of Wazarna [?] Lane, moved out on Wednesday night from his "apartment" of until now, because people simply besieged [?] him.
The talk of the day is the million prize, which fell on number 6424 at Kokoszka's [?] lottery agency in Będzin.

The Bistritzki Days in Katowice

[Katowice — Zionism; JNF; culture.]
For almost a whole week the festival lasted in the Katowice Zionist camp, and in Katowice Jewish society in general; in these Bistritzki days [it] was torn out of the everyday greyness and lived through hours of true spiritual elevation — and no wonder: Bistritzki [Natan Bistritzki (Agmon)] showed how great is the power of the wonderful magic word "Ge'ula" (redemption), Zionism, deliverance, the liberation of the Jewish people in its old-new home.
A cycle of serious lectures (apart from songs, [—?] etc.) for the Jewish intelligentsia, for the Jewish woman, for Jewish youth and for Jews in general [?] — this is what Bistritzki gave in Katowice; and how great such an effect is was shown by the banquet held last Saturday night at the "Concordia" Lodge [the B'nai B'rith lodge of Katowice], chaired by President Dr. Rappaport, who in his opening proposed that people speak about the influence Bistritzki had had on those present; and Rabbi Chameides [Rabbi Dr. Kalman Chameides] wittily and aptly characterised the poet's effect on the Jew's thought, on his feeling, his imagination and his admiration — with his songs. Rabbi Vogelmann: [?] Hasidim come to the Rebbe for the Melave Malka, and here too one hears songs of Zion, etc.
Further speakers: Perl [?], Neumann and Neugauer.
Bistritzki then takes the floor, and between one song and the next he deals with the problem of the Zionist next generation.
Bistritzki's last lecture, on Tuesday, on the topic "The Jewish People and the European Spiritual Crisis", made the strongest impression, and the audience presented the gentle poet-orator with warm applause.
The campaign to redeem the Galilee is in full swing.
A R U I [?].

Bistritzki Day in Chorzów

[Chorzów — Zionism; JNF; refugees; community; education; kashrut.]
On 3 October, at exactly 3 p.m., the Great Synagogue was already packed with people — men, women and youth — who had come to hear the beloved poet Natan Bistritzki [Agmon], who came on a mission from the JNF (KKL) Directorate in Jerusalem.
In a solemn silence the poet begins his lecture in Hebrew, in which he greets his listeners and conveys a greeting from the Yishuv in Eretz Israel. Everyone swallowed every word the poet uttered. The two-hour lecture was closed with Hatikvah.
In the evening a banquet took place.
Greetings in Hebrew were given by the P.A.S. [?] and the Hebrew teacher Kokot, with fine expressions, among which he says that Bistritzki has been the symbol of the building of Eretz Israel. Then the director of the KKL (Kraków) gave greetings, and then the closing word was given to the honoured guest, who expressed deep thoughts.

Last week a ball was organised by the Jewish refugees in Chorzów. The ball was impressively arranged by Messrs. Hochbaum, Steinitz [?] and Wiśnicer. Malka Moskower, of Blessed Memory

[Sosnowiec — obituary.]
At the age of 85 Mrs. Malka Moskower died in Sosnowiec, the wife of the long-serving Sosnowiec shochet Reb Yekl, may he rest in Eden.
The deceased was the eldest sister of the Będzin Rabbi, Rabbi Reb Yissachar Berish Graubart, of blessed and saintly memory, and was a rare type. She was versed in the entire Tanakh, knew the Tanakh literally by heart, and was also well versed in Midrash and in Gemara. A learned woman such as is rarely found, so that the loss of Malka Moskower is indeed a loss that cannot be restored.
Peace to her dust. May her soul be bound in the bond of life.

The Role of the Gemilut Hasadim (Free-Loan) Funds at the Present Moment

A part of Jewish society still regards the gemilut hasadim (free-loan) funds as charitable and philanthropic institutions. We therefore consider it important that the matter[?] be widely explained — the enormous role that the gemilut hesed funds play in Jewish economic life, and the great and responsible tasks that the funds have to fulfil in these hard times for Jews.
Jewish small trade and market-stall trade has lately become the target (literally "target-board") of all sorts of enemies of Israel. Against the impoverished and exhausted Jewish merchant a strong boycott agitation is being waged, which is often accompanied by shameful deeds. And let us not fool ourselves: it is not out of envy of the "fortunes" of the Jewish merchants that such a poisonous and malicious[?] campaign of incitement is waged against them; the enemies of the Jews also know only too well the gloomy life of the Jewish merchant and his hard struggle for the daily piece of bread. But the war of extermination against Jewish small and stall trade is only a means to the great goal: to push the Jews out of all their economic positions — out of wholesale trade, the crafts, industry, etc. The enemies of the Jews believe that as soon as they succeed in pushing the Jews out of small and stall trade, and the places are taken over by non-Jewish merchants, it will then be easy for them to go on and push the Jews out of all their economic positions, because with proper agitation and organisation the non-Jewish merchants will entirely shun Jewish wholesale trade and manufacturing, and that will lead to the ruin of all Jewish economic positions.
Jewish society must therefore take stock and understand that Jewish small and stall trade are strategic positions which must be protected and strengthened at any price. The whole of Jewish society must therefore contribute[?] its assistance to the defence of the embattled Jewish small and stall trade. In this it is important that the help should not bear the character of charity and philanthropy, which is in and of itself also a sacred duty. In this case, however, it is a matter of a general Jewish defence action, and the help given to strengthen and protect the economically weaker Jew at the same time protects and strengthens those who give the help.
The question arises: by whom and in what manner should the relief work for the benefit of Jewish small trade be conducted? The small-traders' associations conduct their activity only in the field of taxes and similar matters; in the field of helping the impoverished Jewish merchant in any way whatsoever, on the other hand, they do nothing. The Jewish cooperative banks are mercantile[?]-commercial institutions and neither want to nor can do anything for the Jewish merchants; and nothing remains in the field except the broad[?] network of the g"ch (free-loan) funds, which already have 10 years of successful activity behind them, and thanks to whose work thousands of Jewish livelihoods have already been saved from certain ruin and collapse.
In view of today's exceptionally hard times for Jews and the sad future foreseen for Jewish small and stall trade — and consequently also for the whole Jewish economy — the activity of the funds must be widened and enlarged tenfold. Because of the small and limited working[?] capital of the funds, not all needy Jews are served with credit; the size of the [—]granted loans is too small and the repayment terms are not easy ones — such loans are of little effect and do not reach their goal. The size of the loans must absolutely be increased and they must be issued on easy repayment terms, but for that it is necessary that the working capital of the funds be increased many times over.
In a great number of towns and shtetls the funds have already set about carrying out the so necessary constructive relief work, that is: creating new sources of livelihood for the Jews who have been pushed out, and giving livelihoods to the economically weakened Jews. It is possible that at first there will be failures and disappointment, but one can be sure that in the end the funds will find the right way and system, and the constructive relief work will be a blessing for the thousands of declassed and impoverished Jews. But here too is the first condition: money, and precisely large sums of money.
In order that the g"ch funds may be able to fulfil these great and responsible tasks, what is simply necessary is a mobilisation of the whole of Jewish society, which should support the funds morally and materially; no Jew may, at such a moment, in such a "time of trouble for Jacob", stand aside; every Jew must join the ranks of those who defend the Jewish economic positions; every Jew must be a member of the gemilut hasadim fund of his town.
S. Berg.
The Attitude of the Intelligentsia and of Well-to-Do Parents toward the Jewish Secondary Schools in Zagłębie

[Zagłębie — education; article.] Injustices, insults, restrictions, physical and moral blows — that is the daily fare for us Jews.
Our general human dignity (so say the Socialists), our national dignity (the Nationalists), our religious dignity (the Orthodox) demands that we react to all this ("we" means, of course, the community), but those very talkers and sayers themselves, wherever it is a matter only of their own egoistic interests, all spit in the face of the whole community.
The question of the employment of Jewish workers and Jewish clerks by Jewish manufacturers and business owners is for us Jews, in the present situation that has arisen, one of the most burning necessities[?] — and we encounter exactly the opposite phenomena.
It is quite an everyday thing that when these same manufacturers find themselves in any company whatsoever, they certainly[?] have complaints against the Jewish community that it has no society of its own — but they themselves spit in the community's face.
In Zagłębie there are two Jewish gymnasia. Materially, both have struggled a good deal[?], because the intelligentsia and the richer parents had no understanding for a Jewish secondary school. Although the humanistic gymnasia were set from the very first moment on a high pedagogical level, with matura results no worse than in the non-Jewish schools; although the Jewish environment and Jewish teachers create an entirely different atmosphere, suited to the Jewish child; although, thanks to the wealthier parents, a poor but capable child can also enjoy secondary education — all this did not help, and not even[?] because of their own interests, they "pushed" their children by various ways into the private non-Jewish secondary schools, and so constantly spat in the community's face.
It is, after all, known to everyone that a Jewish doctor, who to a certain extent himself made a living from the Jewish gymnasium, sent his son precisely to a non-Jewish secondary school.
The same sad phenomenon was seen (and today too...) when supposedly nationally-minded parents, religious ones too, who certainly[?] have complaints about treyf meat, and above all about any religious deviation whatsoever, give and send their daughters to a non-Jewish secondary school, where one receives no Jewish upbringing, where one makes friends with non-Jewish girlfriends or with non-Jewish boyfriends. And such facts can still be pointed to to this very day — is that not spitting in one's own face!
Now another practical question: can a Jew with the matura certificate of a non-Jewish secondary school more easily get into the university, and is one then already protected from all troubles..
If in the present time of boycott and pickets, at a time when the last sources of livelihood are taken from the Jew by force, and the last morsel is literally torn from his mouth, well-to-do and educated parents allow themselves to push their children into non-Jewish schools — is that not spitting in one's own face!
It would truly be worthwhile, therefore, to think this over quite seriously and honestly put an end to this situation.
L. T.
Our Panorama

[Satire — synagogue life in Zagłębie, Sukkot and Simchat Torah.] (The idyllic "Season of Our Rejoicing." — The petichah right lost. — An "angel" who grabs "Atah Hor'eita." — A strike by a caretaker[?] at the hakafot. — Hagbah is no commodity. — The troubles of a "scholar." — With the pitom pointing down. — [?] gabbaim. — "Kibini materi.")
The past "Season of Our Rejoicing" ought — in our opinion — to be immortalised in golden letters: something of a trifle — a whole month of holidays, and not one single "event" to record, as in former times. Even from the synagogue in Old Sosnowiec (Stary Sosnowiec), where the atmosphere used to be boiling like on a volcano, the holiday report is a pale one; it is truly hard to believe that such a "trifle" took place in such a "stormy republic" as the synagogue in Old Sosnowiec...
— What happened? A worshipper there always held the right (chazakah) to the petichah (opening of the Ark) at Ne'ilah; this year the petichah suddenly got "blocked." When the holder of the right went up to the Holy Ark, an outcry arose ("vayitz'aku"): "Get down!" — and having no choice he had to resign the right. True, it really is a pity: he came all the way[?] from "Nowy Targ" and did not get his portion; but it passed off hush-hush, quietly, as if nothing had happened...
—o—
Almost the same "event," only polished a little differently, took place in the "Mizrachi" minyan in Będzin. One of the worshippers in that minyan holds the right to say "Atah Hor'eita" on the eve of Simchat Torah; this year an "angel" came "from afar" and snatched the right. At that moment the congregation trembled with fear lest, God forbid, serious outbursts[?] break out, but the crisis passed and everything ended properly. Moreover, the injured holder of the right displayed his "consistency" and did not want to follow the "angel" who was conducting the hakafot. "Why[?], I can do it myself" — he said, and shouted aloud: "Ozer dalim hoshi'ah na!"
—o—
Quietly, too, passed the "strike" of a Sosnowiec caretaker[?] (dozorca?) during the hakafot in the synagogue. The "proletarian" caretaker[?] stood tensed[?] and watched how with the first hakafot they honour the presidents, vice-presidents and other similar "surigus"[?], and his name is not mentioned. Only at the third hakafah does the beadle call out his name. Then the pride of his "ego" awoke in him and he declared:
— I'm not going! I'm as much of a notable as the president and the vice-president — I[?] am not going!
And to his credit it must be said that the caretaker[?] was "consistent": he said "I don't want to," and indeed he did not go, and resigned the hakafah.
—o—
The same "strike" was played out in the Krymiłów[?] (Kromołów?) "shtibl" in Sosnowiec. The difference, however, is this: in the synagogue, where the worshippers are usually "prostaki" (simple folk), the "strike" was not taken into account — you don't want the hakafah, then don't; let's move on. The situation turned out differently in the above-mentioned "shtibl," because "Chassidim and men of deeds" do not tolerate one of them daring to declare publicly: "I don't want any hakafah! You have 'gobbled up' the aliyot — so keep the hagbah 'bargain' for yourselves too!"
And there was indeed a reaction. The culprit was brought before the "green table" and tried. The verdict: the sinner has to choose[?] — to pray[?] in the shtibl and not receive any aliyah for a whole year, or — outside the camp.
The condemned man accepted the second point and left the "shtibl."
—o—
The report from the "Chevra Tehillim" (Psalms society) in Sosnowiec will no doubt arouse the pity of every one of our readers, because the society suffers from a plague "not written in the Torah." Imagine: into the society's minyan has come[?] a "scholar" (lamdan) who finds new "laws," according to which all the versions and customs used until now become "void." Thus, for example, he — the "scholar," so to speak — has demonstrated that on Yom Kippur only 5 aliyot are read, and that during Hallel on Sukkot the etrog must be held with the pitom pointing down.
— Well, never mind — argue the Tehillim people — for the sake of peace we had one aliyah fewer and we held the etrogim with the pitoms down; but if it goes on like this, we shall come to the conclusion that at the Seder we will eat dairy blintzes and on Shavuot we will hold the Haggadah...
— A just complaint, upon my life; but it is quite surprising that the worshippers of the above-mentioned society do not know the well-known ruling:
— "A scholar — out of the society!"
—o—
With a hard question a group of worshippers of the Będzin synagogue turn to us, demanding an answer; and indeed the question is not one of the ordinary ones. It concerns clarifying whether the gabbaim of the synagogue go "with the stream" or backwards.
And there are symptoms both of the "stream" and of backwardness. Here — they argue — it is worth touching on the new system used this year at the hakafot: one no longer heard the call "So-and-so son of so-and-so is honoured with the honour of the Torah"; instead the calling was done in a modern manner, for example: "Moshe Gimpel Cukierkandel is honoured with a hakafah"; and if the person concerned was not a "local"[?], they immediately announced before the whole congregation from which town the honoree comes, etc., etc.[?]. Well, it is indeed fine and good that the "mouldy" system has been abolished thanks to certain gabbaim who are steeped in cultured civilisation. But Satan is the accuser, and within a few days the joy is completely spoiled.
This happened on Shabbat Bereshit, when someone in the synagogue wanted to speak about Sabbath observance. Since the speaker did not have the proper permission for it from the kehilla, the gabbaim did not allow him to speak.
And here the main thing begins. When the congregation agreed with the gabbaim, one of the gabbaim went up to the Holy Ark and protested against it. "Such gabbaim," he thundered, "must be 'doloi' (Russian: 'down with them!'), as the verse says:
'Ya[?] kibini materi'..." (a crude Russian curse, roughly "to hell with it").
Therefore the worshippers ask: do we have gabbaim who go with the stream, or backwards?...

New Houses and Tenant Protection

[Article — housing and tenant protection.]
In a few weeks' time, with the expiry of the year, the long-standing dream of the landlords will finally come true: tenant protection is being liquidated. True, for the time being not yet formally, but in fact all the same.
For what else, if not a liquidation of tenant protection, can one call the regulation under which, from the year 1938 on, tenant protection will no longer apply to new tenants, even of the smallest flats?
One must remember that because of the steady deepening of the crisis and the impoverishment of the population, the demand for smaller flats is growing feverishly, so much so that even now people fight[?] over the smallest hole, paying hundreds of złoty („gulden“) in key money and a year's rent or more in advance.
If tenant protection is completely abolished, there will certainly be a greater rise in the cost of flats; the appetites and the house-gouging („hoyz-shinderay“) of the landlords will grow even further.
It is also worth pointing to one more circumstance. Landlords carry around eviction verdicts („eksmisye-virkn“[?], from Polish wyroki eksmisyjne) against private tenants, and if to this day they have not made use of them, it is surely not so much out of humanitarianism as because a change of tenant would not have paid off for them.
Now, when tenant protection is abolished and a landlord can charge for a flat as much as his heart desires, he will no longer be such a tzaddik as to go on keeping the old tenant, of whom he can[?] so easily rid himself.
Most landlords will surely exploit the conjuncture and carry out the existing[?] evictions, in order to be able to squeeze a tidy sum[?] out of the new tenants.
Besides, once tenant protection is abolished, is it any trouble to obtain an eviction of a tenant? It is enough for the landlord to apply to the court and his request is granted at once. He need not cite any grounds and need not have any excuses.
So a veritable bonanza[?] will open up for the landlords, especially for the unscrupulous and greedy among them, who will keep changing tenants in order to snatch ever fresh „pidyonot“ [payments].
No tenant will be [sure of][?] the next day. On top of the countless troubles and worries that torment a poor Jew today, a further burden will now be added. He will constantly have to wander about the town looking for a flat, and above all rack his brains over how to put together the sum needed for such a flat.
And one must remember that under today's hard housing conditions barely two out of ten evicted[?] tenants will manage to get into a new flat. The rest will be condemned to share the bitter lot of a subtenant, or to drift about somewhere at a relative's.
And there is one more point that must[?] not be forgotten either, namely, that losing a flat means for many tenants losing at the same time the place to work, to earn a living, and consequently also to live and exist.
And yet the tenant masses relate to the matter with an unforgivable indifference and do not see the seriousness and magnitude of the situation that may be created for them by the abolition of tenant protection, even if only for new tenants.
While the demand to extend the validity of the rent reduction still attracts somebody's[?] attention, absolutely nobody is interested in the latter matter.
Such a passive attitude to the matter of excluding new tenants from tenant protection is perhaps[?] explained by the fact that its consequences are not yet directly felt by anyone for the time being. But this short-sightedness will take bitter revenge on the tenant community as a whole.
Therefore the tenants must [—][?] raise a demand for the postponement of the regulation under which tenant protection is not to apply to new tenants. The question must be placed at the head of the action now being conducted, and around it the broadest tenant masses of our towns and country must rally.
Y. A.
The Post and Other Trifles

[Miscellany — trifles: history of the post, small states, war debts.]
Today we complain that the post is too slow, that we cannot send off our letters quickly enough, and we forget how much patience our forefathers had to have when they had to send a letter.
Not to mention that most of them could not write, and those who did write took no small pains over it. But once the letter had been written, one still had to look for a special messenger by whom the letter could be sent... And even when the post had already been introduced, people almost never knew when and where one could[?] catch the postilion to whom one had to[?] hand the letter.
In the year 1, 2[?] drummers were introduced for the first time at the Leipzig fair; they went around with drums among all the merchants, and letters were handed to them to be sent.
These drummers were afterwards introduced in many places. Once or twice a week they would go around all the streets with drums and collect the post. Only later were postcards introduced.

Small States
It is worth taking a look at the small states that exist in the world. Andorra is a state of its own, has an area of 453 square kilometres and is inhabited by six thousand people. (In Vienna, for example, there is one single house in which almost six thousand people live —).
Liechtenstein, which lies between Austria and Switzerland and is ruled by a prince, is only 159 square kilometres in size and is inhabited by 11.500 people.
On an area of one and a half square kilometres in Monaco live 22 thousand people, who are also ruled by a prince. They pay no taxes, because the country is maintained from the income that comes in from the famous gambling casino of Monte Carlo, which is located there.
Thirteen thousand people live on an area of 61 square kilometres in the state of San Marino.
The smallest country is the "Vatican City", also a state of its own, which belongs to the Pope. All the gardens, churches and palaces belonging to the Pope are there. The state is not even half a square kilometre in size, and only 518 people live in it, who belong to the various services around the Pope's government.

How Much Is Still Owed for the War?
America still receives a great deal of money today that was left owing to it for war expenses in the years 1914 to 1918. England still owes four and a half billion dollars, France three billion, Belgium half a billion, Italy one billion, Yugoslavia four hundred million, Romania one hundred million and Greece 85 million dollars. Whether America will ever see this money back is very doubtful...
Z. Hoper[?], Vienna.

I Am a Jew

[Feuilleton — diary notes; antisemitism in Poland.] By P. Blumenkranz (Częstochowa[?]).
(Leaves from a Friend's Diary)

It is late in the evening[?]. An eerie stillness all around. I stand at the window and stare into the grey[?] darkness. Like a child in a fever[?], the broken-off[?] voices that come from somewhere only deepen the stillness and lend it something mysterious.
I feel very sad, strangely heavy at heart, like someone getting drunk for the first time. I look for a reason for this sadness, go back[?] in my mind over the course of the day, and have no event to record that might account for my present mood. On the contrary: my capricious boss, who takes out all his private troubles on me, and precisely in the presence of strangers, joked with me today, and I smiled and forgot all the insults (it is my nature to forget quickly).
Could the small incident at the cinema be the cause of my present mood? Yes, it would have been naive of me to take such episodes seriously; it would be proof of my hypersensitivity, which is especially[?] dangerous for oppressed people.
And what did the blond fellow actually say to me before? He did not even turn to me. He was talking[?] to his neighbour, a charming girl with platinum hair and large smiling eyes. Instead of a compliment he whispered to her:
— Panna Stefa, let's change seats. The Żyd [Polish slur for "Jew"] has spoiled the film for us[?]...
The girl gave him an enamoured[?] look, as if he had said something very clever, and coquettishly, at once, gave[?] a laugh, a smile.
And I, too, did not react at all and kept silent.
Yes, I really am over-sensitive. After so many insults, humiliations, shames and disgraces, I make a tragedy out of such words and dramatise because of such a "compliment" (the polite young man was a student) addressed to me.
If I intended to publish my diary, I would be ashamed to write this. It would make everyone smile: what is he babbling about[?]? After all, in Tsarist times Jewish daughters were raped in the presence of their parents, Jewish children had their little heads smashed[?] before their mothers' eyes. Sheets of Torah scrolls were desecrated, Jewish synagogues were given up to fire, thousands, tens of thousands of Jews were hanged, murdered, suffocated, burned, ordered to dig their own graves, fathers[?] cut[?] up alive, driven from one place to another — and you make an issue out of a few insulting words.
But I write all this only for myself, so I may speak about my sadness.
I feel that I am truly very badly off, worse than my grandfather and father.
My grandfathers were[?] [—] at the squire's (the "porets"). The squire went about idle and was bored. He had no sound film, the journey to Paris took too long, women had become tiresome, so they leased the tavern (karczma) to the Jew: a tremendous profit — and amused themselves rowdily[?] with him. The squires competed among themselves with ideas. One squire — an acquaintance told me — used to feed his Jew sweets, forcing him, and when the squire saw that the Jew was about to vomit, he tied the Jew's head together with the head of another Jew, so that they would vomit into each other's faces.
The grandfathers, however, were able to split their "I" in two. One "I" went to the squire, bowed to him with reverence, let the courtyard dogs tear at his coat-tails, kissed the hairy hand of "jaśnie wielmożny" [his lordship], bowed double and treble — and the second "I" sat together with the household[?] at the table.
My father too was better off than I. He, for his part, believed in the heaven-born Haskalah [Enlightenment], was convinced the Jewish question could be solved by learning grammar and trimming the beard[?]: "Be a Jew in your tent and a man when you go out."
I cannot make two "I"s of myself. The "I" that needs[?] a livelihood does not want to part from the other. They live in peace and torment me...
• • •
I pace about the room. I cannot settle down[?]. My shadow dances strangely on the ceiling and runs out. My steps knock eerily in the silence. A drunkard has burst into hoarse song in the street:
"Graj, skrzypko, graj, / graj całą noc[?]" [Polish: Play, fiddle, play, / play all night[?]].
A dog howled somewhere, and from various sides others answered him plaintively, as if they were lamenting the world.
And I say to myself:
— [?] that it is an honour to belong to a people that has given the world so much of value; to a people distinguished by such endurance, which in times of universal savagery preached social justice, which in the darkest times dreamed of world peace.
But how can one demand of an ordinary Jew that, when he is spat upon, he should remember the idea of the End of Days? How can one demand of a young man before whom all doors are shut that he should find[?] relief in the social justice preached by his people? And I, when I am insulted and cannot react, find no consolation in my lofty descent and in the other's, the insulter's, [?] the bully's backwardness...
Can one demand of a person who is hungry that he should then find consolation in the nothingness of life, in the "vanity of vanities" philosophy? Can one require of someone who lies evicted in the street that he console himself with the fact that his landlord, too, did not take his 4 houses with him to the grave?
Perhaps there are individuals capable of finding consolation, while still young, in the "vanity of vanities" that its author himself preached in his old age, being[?] already sated with everything... But I, as an ordinary Jew, feel that the words "I am a Jew" are bound up not only with the historical pride of a chosen[?] people, but also with the fact that every nobody can spit in my face and walk on.
• • •
At a neighbour's a child burst out crying; the mother wants to quiet it and [?]. Then it starts screaming again, louder and louder. The child's crying absorbs me completely; in my head stir[?] the words of Motl[?] Semiatitskin:
"Children in the nights scream blindly.
That they are[?] human — and they weep[?]
And mothers, sleepy, stop up —
stop up their mouths with the breast."
The child has fallen asleep.
The town clock struck three...

From the Culture Fair. (Notes.)

[Culture — Yiddish; obituary; news.] 1. After the Culture Congress.
A culture fair — our local Jews, here in Zagłębie, neither know [?] nor speak [?] of such a "fair", where one occupies oneself with culture; and perhaps — let us not sin with our words — people here do not even begin to grasp what folk culture is?..
Here one "lives" off fairs, plain, common ones, of tselnik [?], onions and... ts[—]h! One draws no vitality from our spiritual treasures, one does not live with, nor rejoice [?] in, the achievements of Jewish culture. Here people do not know that at this culture fair, too, a bitter struggle is being waged on the part of [?] reaction and of the whole world [?], and it is precisely on this point that we must concentrate all our national forces. For only on this battlefield can we fight and win. A worked-out [?] strategy as [—]: "Not by might, nor by power, but by My spirit" — a [—] formula: not the fist but the spirit.
And — what are we doing here in Zagłębie for this holy struggle?! Only the awareness that we are [?] Jews, a people with an old and a new culture, can harden [?] us against the spit in the face that we receive.
And what are we doing to instil [?] the pride of this very awareness into the souls of our youth? Do we open to them our Jewish fount [?] of knowledge? Do we lead them into our "pantheon"? Is our youth brought up in the spirit of the "sea of books" [?]? We must acquaint them with, and make them fall in love with, the old and the new literature — from the Prophets to H. N. Bialik and H. Leivick, from the beautiful Aggadah to I. L. Peretz and Sholem Asch, from Maimonides to Spinoza and Sigmund Freud — and that is indeed culture, cultural work. And only such a cultural awareness can save our youth from rotten assimilation and "shmendrikism" [empty pettiness].
And does anyone here know — that elsewhere something is indeed being done in this field?
In Paris there took place a World Jewish Culture Congress, which was called into life after severe birth pangs. Delegates came from twenty-odd countries. An imposing manifestation of Jewish culture. Colossal [?], significant resolutions were adopted.
In particular [?] this congress may be compared to the "Czernowitz Conference", which took place in 1908, where Yiddish was proclaimed the language of the Jewish people, and — now, at this world congress, it was established that Jewish culture lives, acts and creates.
2. Boris Kletskin.
In Wilno [Vilnius] there died, at the age of 61, the pioneer and builder of modern publishing — Boris Kletskin, the man who devoted his life and fortune to the Yiddish book.
Kletskin's publishing house issued the "Literarishe monatsshriftn" [Literary Monthlies], which at that time were truly a phenomenon. In the years 1912–1915 there appeared the very rich-in-content journal "Di yidishe velt" [The Jewish World]; the first Yiddish children's journal, "Grininke beymelekh" [Little Green Trees], began to appear at Kletskin's publishing house. After the World War the publishing house was reorganised, began a rich activity, mobilised a whole staff of writers and translators and published the finest and the best; all the works of Peretz, Sholem Aleichem, David Bergelson, [—] etc., and new books by our young writers appear(ed) [?] at the publishing house of B. Kletskin.
He occupied the finest place in the history of the expansion [?] of our modern book trade.
He was alert to general cultural life. He contributed much [?] to the creation of the "Yiddish Scientific Institute" [YIVO] and so on.
Boris Kletskin — over his grave flutter the leaves of the Yiddish book!
Heshl Dantsiger.

[Feuilleton — education; gymnasium.] A beautiful autumn morning; the children run with joy, with song, into the schools.
Among them a mother is taking her child to the first class of the public school. The child is laden with new things, the mother beams; she is full of pride and joy, she thinks to herself and smiles [?]: how I shall live to see my child finish school. The child looks with joyful eyes into its mother's face; it wants to know what Mummy is saying to herself. Mummy, what are you saying? The mother hugs the child, gives it a kiss. Later you will know everything. When? — asks the child. When you grow older! They kiss and part.
In another street a mother has taken her dressed-up [?] son to the gymnasium. Not because [?] he is going for the first time and does not know the way — no, the way he knows only too well. Simply so: the mother feels that she must fulfil her duty as her child's protector. The child feels uncomfortable; he is ashamed and keeps repeating: Mummy, it's a disgrace for me, go home! When I was little you didn't take me to school. I ran by myself with joy and eagerness, and now that I'm big you lead me like a small child.
— No, my child — the mother replies — it is not I who lead you, but the world that leads you, because they do not want to fulfil their motherly duty towards the grown-ups; therefore we must again take you by the hand and lead you like little children. It may be that when all mothers start again leading their grown-up children to school, the world will [?] take on a different face.
They kissed and parted.
On the way the two mothers met.
The mother who had taken her child to the public school speaks up: You are well off, your child has already achieved his [?]. For me it is still hard enough, until I live to bring my child to the level of your son.
The older mother: I would gladly and with pleasure be at your stage. Because it is hard to watch and to go through the sufferings of one's own child. Every morning, when he starts getting dressed and goes to school, I get [—] at heart. A trifle! — before I lived to raise him and bring him to his present level. Well, now I cannot even say how much I feel. I would give everything I own if my child could now be back in the first class. Back then he used to come home with joy, with song; like a little bird he would flutter about the rooms. Today, when he comes home, he is silent [?], careworn [?], just like one condemned to the severest punishment; nothing interests him, he only counts the pages of the calendar.
The younger one: And I always considered you the happiest mother in the world.
The older one: A mistake! All mothers live in error. Perhaps that is what keeps them going.
The younger one: As far as I can see — all mothers are destined for great troubles.
Shiele.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Noach)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Noach
—o—
a) "These are the generations of Noah" (Gen. 6:9)
"To teach you that his righteous deeds were better for him than sons and daughters." 
Pesikta Zutarta.
Reb Mendele of Kotzk had entirely torn the family feeling out of his heart. When he married off his son Reb Moshe and became related by marriage to the well-known magnate Reb Itshe Blas[?], Reb Itshe drank wine and held out his hand to him:
— L'chaim, mechutan!
The old Kotzker raised his eyebrows:
— With whom am I a mechutan here?
• • •
Once a brother of his came to the Kotzker and asked him to pray for him.
— What is your mother's name? — the Rebbe asks.
The other opens his eyes wide:
— But we are brothers...
The Kotzker answers angrily[?]:
— My own flesh I forgot long ago — how[?] should I know what your mother is called?..
—o—
b) "Noah was a righteous man" (ibid.)
The name tzaddik became especially popular in the times of Rebbe Elimelech of Lizhensk [Leżajsk]. Reb Chaim Rapoport, the famous rabbi of Lemberg [Lwów] and a mitnaged, then said:
— We do not find the title tzaddik given to anyone but Noah, because the title tzaddik refers to one who sustains the many, as the verse puts it: "You open Your hand and satisfy every living thing with favour; the Lord is righteous (tzaddik) in all His ways." And Noah, who sustained the many in the Ark, received the title tzaddik. Today's tzaddikim, however, do not sustain any many — rather the many sustain them..
—o—
c) "And Noah begat three sons" (ibid., 10)
Earlier the verse says that Noah was a righteous man, perfect;
he — as the homily says — did not rebuke the generation of the Flood, because "Noah begat three sons", and "whoever has children in the cradles leaves people in peace"... Ma'ayanei Melech.
—o—
d) "And the earth was corrupt before God" (ibid., 10)
Before God — but in the eyes of men it was all in perfect order; in the eyes of men it was not called robbery, but business... Reb Avraham Saba.
—o—
e) "For the earth is filled with violence" (ibid., 13)
"Their sentence was sealed only on account of robbery."
Rashi.
The Gemara says: "The Merciful One does not strike at lives first" — God first punishes a man through his money, before He turns to lives. But when "the earth was filled with violence", when the money was not theirs, when it was robbery — God could not punish them through their money, which was not theirs, and so He had[?] to turn at once to their lives.. That is the meaning of "their sentence was sealed only on account of robbery"...
Melo ha-Omer.
—o—
f) "And I, behold, I bring the Flood" (ibid., 17)
"Our Rabbis taught: the generation of the Flood grew arrogant only because of the bounty the Holy One, blessed be He, lavished on them." Sanhedrin 108.
The generation of the Flood was steeped in sexual immorality. Sin[?] comes from the fact that a man is well off. And for that one could still find an excuse: what can the son do and not sin?.. But if they were so well off, what excuse could they have for robbery, if they were not hungry and did not have[?] to rob for bread? That is the meaning: their sentence was sealed only on account of robbery... Yalkut Yehuda.
—o—
g) "And of the beasts that are not clean" (6:2 — as printed)
From the fact that the verse does not simply say "and of the unclean beasts", but lengthens[?] and says "and of the beasts that are not clean", the Gemara in Pesachim, folio 4 [as printed], infers that a person should speak in clean language.
The question arises: is it not said in the Torah "he is unclean"?
But when one sometimes has to write "he is unclean" — so-and-so is unclean — one need not be particular about clean language, not speak delicately and in disguise, but shout it out loud... The Dubno Maggid.
—o—
h) "For the inclination of man's heart is evil" (8:21)

[Humour — "Der Kokh-lefl": a matchmaker's monologue, and other items.] ...You understand? [—] What, to put it mildly[?], is a bachelor? Nothing with nothing, a ship without a rudder, a whip-handle[?] without a whip, an umbrella without a cover, simply a broken scrap[?]... Eating in restaurants — and what illnesses and ailments[?] do you get from the restaurants? Constipation, gallstones, [—][?], stomach ache, stitches[?], vomiting. And you say you don't want to marry. Do you know what you are saying? Can you even imagine the pleasure of a wife? However much I describe it to you, it is a thousand times more. Take me, for example. As you see me — a pauper, a poor wretch, I toil[?] like a dog, run around, sweat; more than once, may it befall the enemies of Zion, I am sick of life. But when I come home, I sit down at the table, my "wife" sits down opposite me. I talk to her, she talks to me; I say one word, she says ten; I get cross, she gets angry; I say and she says, I talk and she talks (angrily). Oh, how she talks! May she talk out the [—][?]!... A mouth, a sharp tongue, brimstone and pitch! May she go completely dumb. Master of the Universe, you understand, where does she get so many curses? Dear God, how she shortens my years!...
Young man! Why are you running away, what? What, you really don't want to marry at any price? Have you seen a slightly crazy man?...
Sar Alef [pen name].

At S. An-sky's grave.

The Cooking Spoon — A Menu for Banquets

[Humour — "Der Kokh-lefl": section heading and a satirical banquet menu.] Der Kokh-lefl ["The Cooking Spoon"]. Humour and satire by Amutsln[?].

Since the season of banquets, at which speeches must be made, is approaching, the "Kokh-lefl" proposes that banquet menus should list the dishes together with the speeches. Here we give a sample of such a menu.
Festive banquet in honour of the jubilarian Gensnfisl ["Goose-foot"].
Menu

2) Fish in cold aspic, small braided rolls; speech by Mrs. Rolmopsgiza[?] [a pun on "rollmops" herring] on the merits of the jubilarian.
3) Goose[?], liver, breast, salads, horseradish, mustard; speech by the poet Supan[?] in honour of the jubilarian, part two.

Biography of a Freshly Baked Sosnowiec 'Jewish' Communal Activist

[Humour — "Der Kokh-lefl": satire on an assimilated activist in Sosnowiec; a "biography" in broken Yiddish.] In Sosnowiec there has now surfaced a brand-new[?]... freshly baked "communal activist", a "zhidek"[?] [Polish żydek, "little Jew"] who chokes on a Yiddish word, and yet he has become a Jewish public figure, quite a big shot[?] in the kehilla. He has sent the "Kokh-lefl" his biography, written "in Yiddish"; here is what he himself writes:
"[Polish in Hebrew letters:] Although[?] I know that we are good brothers (az mir zenen gute brider [Yiddish: that we are good brothers]), I will write you my biography myself in pure 'jargon' [Yiddish]:
[Broken Yiddish:] When my mommy daddy had me, I was a little kiddie, later on me grew — grew. Knows not one word[?], when I became a big lad and didn't know even the alef-beys. Daddy to me soon[?] says[?]: you will be Jewish communal activist [spelled 'klal' wrongly]. Later in fact so it was. I turn little wheels among little Jews. [garbled line, not securely legible:] ikh veltn[?] lig 'eyn'[?] in mertshim[?] zayn a kile[?] a davir[?] ikh zayn.

Tragedy of a Modern 'Mężatka'

[Humour — "Der Kokh-lefl": an intercepted letter and other items.] An intercepted letter.
Mrs. Regina is a little "mężatka" [Polish: married woman], one of today's modern little married women who do not hold with the "one-husband system". This week she came home distraught, sat down at her writing desk and wrote the following little letter:
— Koshek[?] [a Polish pet name]! After what happened today I do not want to see you any more. Don't you dare show yourself before my eyes again. You scum! I do not even allow you to come to me tomorrow, 5 October 1937, at exactly 5 in the afternoon, when my husband is not at home and I am alone within my four walls.
With the deepest contempt,
I am[?] no longer your Regina.

A tip for pedlars. How do you take in money?
At a meeting of pedlars in the Sosnowiec Small Traders' Association, a member gave a lecture on how to get into a home easily and how to make sales.
— If you come into a home and the lady of the house opens the door, she may be an old granny, a [—], you should say:
— Excuse me, may I speak with your mummy?
If you put this question, you can be sure that you will make a sale, and a good one at that.
—o—
Tailors' Torah. Why does he make such trousers?
A tailor received an order from a local orphanage for a hundred pairs of little trousers. When he delivered them, the president says to the tailor:
— Reb Tsvok[?], these little trousers have no seats[?] at all!
The tailor smiled and answered:
— The trousers are for orphans, and the Gemara says: "Orphans are not capable of mechila [waiving]"... [a pun on "mechila"].

Without language.
At the last Esperanto congress it was resolved that, since it is hard for the whole world to learn Esperanto, people should communicate without any language at all.
As it turns out, this invention was introduced long ago in Zagłębie, and the public speaks with its limbs. Young men speak with their hands, women — with their eyes, girls at the dancings and [—][?] — with their feet. In markets and parks hooligans speak with their fists, and [—][?] one speaks with the thumb[?]. The "Polska Ka-ta"[?] speaks with bile.
A Fair Thing.

[Humour — “Der Kokh-lefl”; Będzin — kehilla and synagogue.] In the Będzin kehilla’s budget the “pension” for the choir has been struck out.

In the minyan of “Mizrachi” [?] in Będzin, on Simchat Torah, before the hakafot, a cloud of dust suddenly appeared, which thoroughly [?] roused [?] the worshippers.

In Better Company

In a company of Sosnowiec ladies, someone asks the poet Moyshe Broderzon:
— You are a poet?
— Yes.
— That is a ridiculous profession.
— Whence do you conclude that?
— Just imagine, panie Broderzon: you work a whole year on one book, while for 2 złoty one can get the best books by the greatest writers.

In the Middle of the Night.
Three o’clock at night, the night bell of the pharmacy rings. A quarter of an hour later the pharmacist comes out, half asleep.
— What do you want?
— I need a remedy for a stomach-ache, a Jew explains to him; my wife has severe cramps.

— Keep your remedy, it’s no longer needed — answers the Jew — I’d rather give her a glass of warm water... Good night!
