A Scene in a Doctor’s Surgery.

[Humour — “Der Kokh-lefl”; sketch.] Characters:
Patient (an old bachelor, a hunchback, a pensive, melancholic fellow, keeps blinking [?] with one eye).
Doctor (a doctor who does not believe in feeding a patient with prescriptions. A quite serious man).
Doctor (examining his patient with his eyes): You have never been to me before?
Patient: Never.
Doctor: Your name.
Patient: Leon Rernik [?].
Doctor: Your age?
Patient: Forty-two years.
Doctor: Married?
Patient: No.
Doctor: Ever been married?
Patient: Not so far.
Doctor: Do you weigh yourself sometimes?
Patient: Certainly.
Doctor: What is your weight?
Patient: Sixty-two kilos.
Doctor: Have you ever been seriously ill?
Patient: No, seriously I have never been ill; as far as I remember I was ill twice with typhus, three times I had dysentery; what one is supposed to have, I had as well. Only last winter I had whooping cough. I have not yet had measles, and so a serious illness I haven’t had either.
Doctor: So what is wrong with you?
Patient: Healthy.
Doctor: In what respect?
Patient: In all respects.
Doctor: What do you complain of?
Patient: As such I complain of nothing, only I always see black wheels before my eyes when I lend out a few złoty, my hands and feet tremble; and when I have to dun the złoty back, I sweat.
Doctor (examines his patient and speaks, already after the examination): I will not prescribe you any prescriptions; I don’t believe in stuffing a patient with herbs. But I will instruct you how to conduct yourself, and you really must obey me (notices cigarettes in the patient’s breast pocket). Young man, you must stop smoking at once!
Patient: I don’t smoke, never have smoked.
Doctor: Then what are these cigarettes in your pocket?
Patient: I lend money at interest; someone borrowed money from me to open a tobacco kiosk (trafika). Since [?] I come for the interest, I grab a few cigarettes from him.
Doctor: And what do you do with the cigarettes?
Patient: When a few more pile up, I sell them.
Doctor: That is good, for that you deserve a compliment. But I’m not finished with you yet; I have many things to instruct you.
You must not drink any schnapps, young man. Not even a drop of schnapps should you take into your mouth. Do you hear what I’m telling you? No schnapps!
Patient: Who drinks schnapps? I don’t even know the taste of schnapps. What more do you want, doctor: when I happen to be at a wedding and schnapps is served at the table, I always have a little bottle in my pocket; I pour my share into the little bottle and take it home with me.
Doctor: And what do you do with it at home?
Patient: It comes in handy. Sometimes a guest [?] comes; I rub my body with a bit of schnapps; it comes in handy.
— That’s good. Now tell me, young man, how do you stand with eating?
I mean, if you are not married, you probably have to eat in a restaurant, and I want to warn you that you must be very careful. As God is dear to you, avoid [?] the overly cheap restaurants!
Patient: I don’t eat in any restaurant.
Doctor: Where do you eat then?
Patient: Nowhere.
Doctor: What does that mean?
Patient: That I don’t believe in eating. All I need is a little milk and a stale roll.
Doctor: And how do you stand with love?
Patient: Love-shmove, who needs love?!
Doctor: You mean you never had any love affair in your life?
Patient: God preserve me! I have never spent even a grosz on a woman. Never even touched a woman — who needs it [?]!
Doctor (finally losing his patience): So if not drinking and not eating, and not smoking and not loving — for what black year do you need to live at all?! (The curtain falls, if there is a curtain.)
What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin: A Lawless Act against the Members of the Local Rabbinate

What's new in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 3 Cheshvan 5698 — Friday, 8 October 1937)
Będzin
A lawless act against the members of the local rabbinate.
On Monday morning the rabbinate, together with several members of the Kashrut Committee, stood in the street by Schwarzberg's butcher shop in the market halls[?] on Mandoszewer[?] Street and persuaded the customers not to buy the meat in the butcher shop, because the meat is not kosher.
At that moment Schwarzberg's wife came out of the shop, began to curse and doused the rabbinate with water.
It goes without saying that this disgraceful act caused great indignation among those who saw it, and they protested sharply against the insult to the rabbinate.
Then a brother of Schwarzberg came out of the shop and shoved the dayanim (moreh-tzedek) Lipszyc and Frajberg. That is what really inflamed the spirits of those assembled, and people came running from all sides, so that the place in front of the shop was black with people. Schwarzberg (the brother) then called a policeman, who drew up a report against the dayanim for preventing people from buying meat at Schwarzberg's.
In connection with this, larger meetings have already taken place at the rabbinate. As is reported, a series of resolutions was adopted on how to react to the insult to the rabbinate.
The kehilla board, too, has decided to take legal action against those guilty of this base[?] insult.
Conference at the Discount Bank

On Sunday a conference took place in the premises of the local Discount Bank attached to the Small Traders' Association, with the participation of a fairly large number of well-to-do merchants.
From the reports delivered by Messrs. B. Brama[?], G. Rechnic and Y. Rus it emerges that the bank is in a stage of development and is gaining[?] the confidence of merchant circles. Among other things it was also pointed out that the bank currently handles about 1000 bills of exchange a month for collection.
After the reports, those present declared their readiness to lend larger sums of money as a basis for the further development of the financial institution.
The German Synagogue Is Inscribed in the Golden Book of the JNF

On the initiative of the JNF (Keren Kayemet) representatives in the "German" synagogue, Messrs. Y. Gelbard and Y. Finer, the gabbaim decided to inscribe the A. D.[?] in the Golden Book of the JNF.
The worshippers received the decision with great enthusiasm, and during the holidays pledged larger sums for the JNF (over 400 zł.). This is the first synagogue in Zagłębie to be inscribed in the Golden Book. Other houses of prayer will surely not fail to follow this worthy example.
Accident to a Jewish Worker

On Tuesday an accident befell the worker Yekl Czeplak at the "Korona" brewery; he was busy loading[?] barrels on the hoist. For an unknown reason Czeplak lost his balance and fell from the third floor into a cellar. He was taken to hospital unconscious.
—o—
From the Hitachdut
In connection with the Party Council of the Hitachdut in Poland, which meets on the 8th and 9th of this month, a lecture by Mr. Eliezer Geller (Warsaw) on the subject "The important task of the Party Council" will be held today at 8.30 p.m. in the premises of "Gordonia".
Delegated to the Party Council from Będzin are Messrs. Dr. R. Rechtman and Y. Gersler.
—o—
In the Nick of Time.
On Friday around noon thieves got into the flat of Mr. Sanszajn (Satacka[?] 9) and began to make themselves at home. When the household goods and clothes were already packed, a neighbour arrived and disturbed the "work". The thieves then took 70 zł. in cash and fled.
—o—
Car Runs Over a Young Jewish Man.
Avremele[?] Honigman, walking along the road to Czeladź, was run over by a car. Honigman was taken to the local hospital.
The Town of Będzin Has Gained 75,000 Złoty — Interior Ministry Has Not Approved the Investment Tax

Interior Ministry has not approved the investment tax.
As is known, at the town council session held in May of this year, the statute on an investment tax amounting to 75 thousand zł. for school purposes was adopted with the votes of the "Workers' Club".
At that session the ławnik (alderman) Rubinlicht spoke out against the tax, for which he was branded in the Polish press as an opponent of building schools.
Although the majority adopted the tax statute, ławnik Rubinlicht did not give up and entered into the minutes a statement in which, with a series of factually grounded arguments, [he pointed] to the incorrectness of the investment tax.
Besides that, Mr. Rubinlicht, on behalf of the Merchants' Association, applied with a detailed memorandum to the Ministry of the Interior asking that the tax not be approved.
This week the magistrate received a reply from the Ministry of the Interior announcing that the investment tax has not been approved.
Tram Accident Involving a Warsaw Resident

On Saturday, at the tram stop on the corner of Kołłątaja and Santszewska[?] streets, an accident befell a certain Marczinkewski from Warsaw.
Marczinkewski wanted to board the tram when it was already moving, and he fell under the wheels, which cut off all the toes of his right foot.
He was taken to the local hospital.
Meeting of the policyholders of “Przyszłość”.

Under the chairmanship of Ch. Ch. Unger, a meeting of the policyholders of the “Przyszłość” company was held on Sunday[?] in the premises of the Merchants’ Union. About 60 people from Zagłębie and also from Upper Silesia took part in the meeting.
The meeting was informed that, through joint action by the insured members of the above-mentioned company, there is a possibility of recovering about 80 percent of the sums paid in so far on the policies.
For this purpose a provisional committee was elected, consisting of Ch. Unger, G. Herzinger, M. Lasker, Maurycy (Moris) Gertner and Ch. Frenkel.
—o—
Shop-window contest.
The local Merchants’ Union announces that the Chamber of Commerce in Sosnowiec is organising, in the Będzin area, a contest of shop windows. Firms wishing to take part in the event should register as early as possible.
—o—
15 and 25 groszy for opening the gate.
For the winter “season” the house caretakers have been permitted to charge the following fee for opening the gate during the night hours: until 24 o’clock — 15 groszy, later 25 groszy.
—o—
City council session.
Next Tuesday a city council session will take place, at which a number of economic questions are to be dealt with, as well as a number of tax statutes.
Sosnowiec — Festive opening of the premises of the Zionist Organisation.

Last Saturday night (motzei Shabbat) the Zionist Organisation in Sosnowiec celebrated the house-warming of its new, large premises at Chstolna[?] Street 4.
The celebration was attended by the chairman of the Zionist Organisation in Poland, Advocate Hartglas, Zionist activists from the neighbouring towns and a large number of invited guests.
The official part of the celebration began with the orchestra of the local Jewish gymnasium playing the Polish and the Jewish anthems, as well as a number of Land-of-Israel songs; then the president of the local organisation, Dr. Meladystag[?], opened the celebration. Invited to the presidium were the guest A. Hartglas and Messrs. G. Stachski[?], G. A. Gutman (Dąbrowa) and Y. Hinarucki[?] (Będzin).
In his opening speech Dr. Meladystag[?] stressed the importance of premises for Zionist and cultural work in general, and in particular of having a place to spend time in a comradely setting and a brotherly atmosphere, which is so necessary at the present moment; but the premises — he said — must not be merely an outward form, but filled with Zionist content.
Then came greetings. On behalf of the Zionist Organisation in Będzin, Mr. Higadzki[?] gave greetings; from the local “Mizrachi” — Mr. Ch. Kostermintz[?]; from the Będzin WIZO — Mrs. Husner[?]; from the local “HaNoar HaTzioni” — Kaszuk[?]; from the local WIZO — Mrs. Langer; greetings were also given by the activists Dr. Kachalski[?], A. Lichter (Będzin) and G. Stachski[?].
On behalf of the Central Committee Adv. Hartglas gave greetings. The Zionist Organisation in Sosnowiec — he said — has its fine pages in the history of the Zionist movement in Poland; in recent years the Zionist Organisation in Sosnowiec has indeed been neglected. On this I agree with the representative of “HaNoar HaTzioni”, who criticised the Zionist Organisation. But Sosnowiec is no exception: in every great movement there are moments of upswing and of decline.
Then he spoke about the project of a Jewish state and said: a League of Friends of the Jewish State will be created, and he thinks that the premises whose house-warming we are celebrating today will soon be turned into premises of the League “Friends of the Jewish State in Eretz Israel”.
Then Mr. Feder performed very successfully a monologue by Tunkeln[?], a recitation “The Blind Man”, and the mixed choir under the direction of Israel Herszkowicz sang a number of beautiful Land-of-Israel songs with musical accompaniment performed by Mr. Mandelbaum.
With this the official part was closed, and then the public enjoyed the richly laid tables.
At 3[?] o’clock at night the impressive celebration closed in an elevated mood.
The next day a lecture by Adv. Mr. Hartglas was held in the “Rialto” cinema, under the title “The present situation in Eretz Israel”.
The lecture was well attended, also by such elements as had not been at a meeting with a Zionist speaker for years.
Dr. Meladystag[?] welcomed the distinguished guest in Yiddish and gave him the floor. In his two-hour lecture (in Polish) he dealt with the question of the “yes” and “no” sayers regarding the Jewish state and came to the conclusion that one must agree to what “they want to give us”, only that on our side the forces must continue to be strained towards the realisation of the Jewish national home in Eretz Israel.
On behalf of the audience Dr. Meladystag[?] thanked the lecturer for his interesting exposition.
A new ławnik elected. — Jewish councillors did not take part in the vote

At Tuesday’s session of the local city council the agenda was — to elect a ławnik (member of the city executive board). As is known, when the city executive was elected an injustice was done to the Jewish population, which did not receive any ławnik.
At the present election too the Jewish councillors tried to have the injustice corrected, but things stayed as they were — the Jewish population, represented by 9 Jewish councillors, has no representative of its own on the city executive.
In this sense Councillor Aliner, at the last session, made a speech and delivered a declaration that the Jewish councillors would not take part in the election of the ławnik.
Elected was Mr. Szpigiter[?], president of the Legionnaires’ Union in Sosnowiec.
The one-year commercial school is already operating.

The one-year commercial school, founded here by the Merchants’ Union and the Small Traders’ Union, is already housed in its own large and comfortable premises at Puszpiaur[?] 1.
The school is organised according to the ministerial regulations, and the pupils will receive in it an excellent preparation for the merchant’s profession.
Enrolments have exceeded all expectations. As we are informed, there are still a few free places. It is therefore in the parents’ interest to hurry and register their children at the school.
We once again draw the attention of the merchants and small traders to the importance of the school, especially at the present moment, when the question of an educational qualification requirement in commerce is becoming ever more topical. It is therefore a sacred duty of the Jewish merchant class not to neglect the opportunity given to it by the above-mentioned Jewish merchants’ organisations to train the growing youth properly.
The murderers of the 5 Jewish martyrs of the village of Stawy before the Kielce District Court

[Kielce — Trial, murder.] As our readers already know, on 27 April of this year the Kielce District Court heard the trial of several Christians who were accused of murdering in a bestial manner the 5 Jewish martyrs of the village of Stawy, beyond Jędrzejów.
The accused — Józef Wszepecki[?], Jan Petras and Antoni Chmiel — were acquitted for lack of evidence.
A few days after the trial, by chance — as we already reported in our paper at the time — the real murderers of the 5 Jewish martyrs in the village of Stawy were discovered. The three Kaszyński brothers and two other murderers were then arrested and put in prison.
The 5 murderers, as we are informed, confessed immediately after their arrest to carrying out the gruesome murder. On Monday[?], 11 October, their trial takes place at the Kielce District Court.
Reorganising the Jewish District Merchants' Association

[Kielce — Commerce, associations.] The Jewish District Merchants' Association in Kielce, which was once known among the merchants of the Kielce voivodeship for its energetic work in all economic fields, has for several months not carried on any proper activity, and the Jewish merchants of the Kielce district have suffered greatly from this.
The Central Merchants' Association in Warsaw, striving[?] to reorganise the Kielce district association anew, has delegated to Kielce for a longer period its representative, Mr. Józef Rechtszaft, who has taken over the office of head of the association.
With the help of Mr. Rechtszaft — who for many years directed various associations in a number of larger provincial towns, possesses great knowledge in the field of commerce, is an expert in tax matters and a very capable and energetic organiser — the Central Merchants' Association in Warsaw believes it will succeed in properly organising the Kielce merchants' association and raising it back to its former height.
As we see, the Central Merchants' Association has so far made no mistake. Mr. Rechtszaft, who is also[?] a good, national-minded Jew, indeed possesses enormous energy and strong organising power. In the short time he has been staying in Kielce he has managed to revive the association and make it a merchants' organisation with a right to exist[?], which the Jewish merchant class needs so badly in the present difficult hour.
Mr. Rechtszaft's first task is to organise the separate merchants' sections and to bring about the general meeting, which takes place on the 31st of this month with the participation of the president[?] of the Central Merchants' Association in Poland.
500 dollars from America for the Kielce fire victims

[Kielce — Relief for fire victims.] The Rabbi of Kielce, Rabbi Rapaport, received this week a letter from the Kielce Relief Committee in America, in which they announce that they have sent to the rabbi's address 500 dollars for the benefit of the unfortunate Kielce fire victims. This sum was collected among the Kielce landsmen in America.
This sum, however, is but a drop in the ocean compared with the large funds that are absolutely necessary for the 400 poor burnt-out Jews who are wandering about under the open sky and perishing from want and hunger.
The really necessary sum must be given by the Jews of Kielce.

Police during the hakafot in the Białogon study house

[Kielce area — Community life, religion.] In the shtetl of Białogon, near Kielce, this past Simchat Torah was very "homely". The local "intelligent" youth, because of an "[?]" (agrafe) by the local rabbi Goldberg, decided to boycott the hakafot and to leave the "foolish [?]" to the old idlers[?]. The night-time hakafot of Simchat Torah they did indeed boycott; on the other hand they did not "boycott" scandals and brawls during the hakafot themselves — so that the worshippers left the study house in the middle of the hakafot.
Fearing that the second hakafot of Simchat Torah, in the daytime, would also be accompanied by a chorus of squealing and scandals, the Jews of Białogon, having no choice, invited the local police to the hakafot, and they stayed in the study house until after the "king's hakafa"..
Yes, happy are you, Jews of Białogon!..
Thieves pose as “police agents” and search Jewish homes.

On the night from Friday to the Sabbath several elegantly dressed young Christians came to the flat of one Moshe Meir Machsinger [?] (Piotrkowska 172), introduced themselves as “police agents”, carried out searches, drew up a report and left [?] a summons stating that Machsinger was to report to the Investigation Office. During the search the cunning [?] swindlers took [?] identity papers and trade-licence (patent) tokens [?].
When the next day the summoned man presented himself at the Investigation Office, it turned out that these were no “police agents” at all, but a few thieves. The police are investigating.
Propaganda campaign for “Ster” in Zagłębie.

From the 8th to the 18th of this month a campaign is being held in Zagłębie to recruit subscribers and readers for the weekly “Ster”. For this purpose the editorial office has specially delegated Mr. Apel from Warsaw, who together with the local Zionist activists will carry out the campaign.
We believe that the Jewish population of Zagłębie, appreciating the importance of this organ, will show a warm attitude to Mr. Apel’s work.

In connection with the report printed in the last issue of the “Kieltser-Zaglembyer Tsaytung” that at the last session of the Sosnowiec Chamber of Commerce, at which it was decided to introduce an educational qualification for merchants, only 5 of the 9 Jewish councillors were present — we have been asked to state that among the 5 present was also the Kielce councillor Mr. Chaim Pachel [?], who together with his colleagues left the session as a sign of protest.

His Father Enrolled Him in the Chevra as a Child... / An Interesting Din Torah Before the Będzin Rabbinate

[Będzin — Religious Life.]
An Interesting Din Torah Before the Będzin Rabbinate.
Two full brothers, Shmuel and Leib, both pray in the synagogue, and both were in the same chevra [society]. The devil's work: the brothers quarrelled, and Leib went and struck Shmuel off the chevra.
The epilogue of the story took place before the Będzin rabbinate. The wronged [?] Shmuel pointed to the magnitude of the injustice: when I was a little boy — he argued — my father enrolled me as a “son of the chevra,” and now my younger brother has dared to strike me off the society — how can this be, Rabbi?!
The rabbinate recognised Shmuel's claim as just and issued a ruling to enrol him in the synagogue chevra.

Open Letter to the Kehilla Representatives in Dąbrowa

[Dąbrowa — Kehilla; Letter to the Editor.]
At the kehilla council meeting of the 3rd of this month it was decided not to lodge any appeal (rekurs) against the subsidies struck out or reduced by the voivode, following the reasoning of the chairman of its [?] administration that, since the approved small subsidies will in any case not be paid out, just as until today, because the kehilla has no money.
As everyone knows, every kehilla budget consists of expenditures and revenues; that is, one makes a total of all the foreseen expenses, for which one seeks revenues, of which the main revenue is from the etat [communal tax]. But when drawing up the distribution (rozkład) of the etat, the expenses in the form [?] of subsidies for various institutions are taken into account — more correctly said, in every sum a few złoty are charged for philanthropic purposes, for if it were only for the salaries of the religious functionaries, the etat would have been much smaller. But when all the money of the etat is spent only on everything except the subsidies for the municipal [?] institutions, because “there is no money,” the question arises: by what right is the part designated for the institutions used for other purposes?
Were the institutions created to support the gabbaim, or must [?] the gabbaim support the institutions?
By what right are approved small subsidies used for other purposes?
— On the contrary, we await an answer to this.
Zelig Miodownik.

The Jewish Hospital Is Our Cause, a Cause of the Whole People! / Our proposal for rescuing the financial situation of the Jewish hospital in Sosnowiec.

The chaos[?] that was raised a few weeks ago around creating a fund that would maintain the existence of the Jewish hospital in Sosnowiec has died down.
Has the situation improved? No — perhaps it has even worsened. The hospital's debt is growing, a renovation is needed, and there is no money.
How does one get out of it?
The old trouble: there is nobody to go round (collecting).
And the local communal workers are racking their brains over how to collect the necessary sum in Zagłębie.
It seems this could be done quite easily: in Zagłębie there are only 8 thousand families, who should contribute through a public levy[?] of one day's hospital fee for a patient — every family should give, so to speak, a redemption-payment of one night[?] for one day of being ill, 5 zł. — and the round sum of 40 thousand gulden [złoty] would be collected.
For this one need not travel anywhere at all; it can be collected by paid collectors, as a small social tax which everybody would gladly pay.
For there is no doubt whatsoever that maintaining the Jewish hospital is a cause of the whole people.
Because the people gain a great deal from it;
the Jewish patient has ritually permitted food, Jewish treatment, and instead of a picture on the wall — a mezuzah on the door.
The Jewish kehilla has a gain and proprietorship[?].
The honour of the Jews is raised by presenting the city with such an important modern institution,
a post (placówka) for Jewish doctors and technical staff,
opportunities for clinical work and professional development for young Jewish medics.
Especially at the present time, when a process is under way of pushing us out of all kinds of positions we hold and pushing us into a medieval ghetto, every Jewish institution is turned into a Temple[?], at whose altar we cling and hold fast.
And we build new temples, temples of education, temples of work, in order to have more such altars for ourselves.
And the Jewish hospital is one of the finest and strongest Jewish temples, because it has long been recognised and adopted[?] by the city, to be kept at its own[?] expense; because here, just as in Solomon's Temple, the Christian is received together with Jews, but the Jew feels surrounded by homeliness and by what is his own, and takes pride in this Jewish gift[?] to the general good.
This pride the broad Jewish masses can acquire for themselves through small, merely insignificant sacrifices.
Someone has calculated that so far a total of 105 people have been drawn into the campaign; the whole town has still been left aside!
Now the turn has come for "all of Zagłębie": all the towns with their shepherds should gather together, climb down[?] into[?] the little cage[?].
And the kehilla?
After all, it is the natural[?] and actual, the real party concerned with the hospital; what weight does the required sum have for it, measured against the size of the undertaking!
Yes, we can be sure of this: the Jewish hospital will soon function again to its full extent!
Remarks. / Bread for the Hungry. Coal for the Frozen

1.
Winter is near, and with it — hunger and want in the houses of the poor population. There is no worse enemy of poverty than the winter months.
In summer the world is still open; it is easier to look for and also to find some kind of work, and at worst it is simply easier to go hungry in summer.
In winter, however, the world is closed: every kind of building activity stops, with all the work connected to it; public works are halted, and in the homes of those without a livelihood King Hunger and Queen Cold reign cruelly.
The picture of want is generally known;
a neglected[?], dark dwelling, windows stuffed with rags, and in these "prehistoric" caves human shadows huddle.
Especially hard in winter is the situation of the poor child who, having no clothes and shoes, is robbed of his only consolation — school, where he could have spent a few hours in a warm, bright room, played in the company of his peers and indeed also received a midday meal.
The government, as well as the communal authorities, will this year again undertake the winter-relief campaign for the unemployed.
But although the number of Jewish unemployed is, proportionally, perhaps greater than the Christian, in registration[?] they appear in a glaring[?] disproportion. Suffice it to say that the number of registered Jewish unemployed employed on public works is minimal.
Only some forty Jewish unemployed have any[?] prospects of receiving support from the winter relief, and even that only if the qualification commission does not disqualify them.
2.
In view of this state of affairs, Jewish society too must show[?] its interest and care, its help and winter support for all Jewish unemployed and those without a livelihood, even for those who have not registered their hunger-distress and suffering from cold anywhere.
For the precepts of social help of Jewish society, of Jewish tradition and world-view (as it is ridiculed by some "radicals" and decried as outdated "charity") know nothing of a qualification commission when it comes to a piece of bread for the hungry.
"One does not investigate those who ask for food" — one must not disqualify anyone who stretches out his hand for a piece of bread.
One must also care for those who are languishing from hunger and cold and are ashamed to say anything about it.
The Jewish kehillot in Zagłębie, especially the new kehilla representation of Sosnowiec, must in the first winter of its term set about organising a special winter-relief campaign for the large needy Jewish population in Sosnowiec.
The Jewish public will certainly cooperate with its elected representation for the success of this campaign.
A.

Letter to a Friend

First letter.
My friend and brother;
I do not know where [?] you are, to whom I am turning with these very words. True, I have never yet met you anywhere face to face, yet I believe in my heart that you must be somewhere, in one of the corners of the world. It cannot be that there is not a single person in the whole world whom I may call "friend and brother".
If there is such a one, here or there, he will seek me [?] out today or tomorrow, and then my intimate feelings will resound in his heart!
— And if two hearts feel the same thing, the most important thing in life, is not life itself hallowed thereby?...
I feel with all my nerves, with all my hidden senses, that a great and holy secret hovers around me, above my head, and penetrates into the depths of my soul — and the secret begs and strains to reveal itself, but the power of expression is lacking.
•
The people around me wander about life, but none of them dares to approach the centre, the highest point, the very substance of life. People content themselves with a minimum, with a weak impulse of life, with the reflected glow [?], with the mirror-image of so-called "life", but what is within them is very far from real, living life.
I seek words with which I might be able to designate the foundation, the true essence of real life, its very nature. But I have not yet succeeded in discovering the precise, the entirely exact word that would symbolise life. Had I found the right word for it, I would have reached the centre and thereby would have revealed the great secret. But I grope about in the darkness. If only a single bright ray would fall on my path, which is wrapped in a dense fog...
If only I were granted, in my whole life, one single higher revelation; if only I succeeded in perceiving [?], for just one second, the utterly quiet whisper of eternal existence...
My friend, or my future spiritual heir, my later one, the purified one — to you I send my words, so that you may know that I sensed you [?] beforehand, even before you were born...
I feel that a very thin, almost airy partition separates [?] me from the hidden life, from true life, for which my longing is so strong. I see how the people among whom I wander — the strong and also the weak, the professional people [?] and also the warm-hearted [?] people — still live in their simplicity and do not strive at all toward a higher and purer life. On the contrary: they are drawn to a coarser, a dirtier life... I hide from strange eyes the sorrow that lives in me, so as not to desecrate it. For the fighter and dreamer in me there is no place in society; he is without a fatherland [?], he lacks a human environment, any comrade, any friend.
Second letter.
My friend and brother:
And I have not yet stopped seeking your face among the human shadows that float past me. I seek my hidden brother, who, when he reads my words, will also be able to penetrate the spirit that hovers over the words and the soul that rests in them.
My friend, if you are among my contemporaries, then you surely have bundles of sufferings of your own, greater and smaller. I have no doubt, my friend, that you are wrapped up in your own world and wholly swallowed by your surroundings, by your milieu, by your own problems and your own riddles, which torment you, you alone. The air that you breathe in and the atmosphere in which I find myself; surely my sigh [?] is not your sigh, and the rhythm of your life is no doubt quite different from my life's rhythm. But I shall be content if only a part of my words penetrates your heart...
And perhaps the friend and brother whom I never stop seeking will never be found, will never answer. For seas and deserts [?] separate brother from brother, and even when both brothers speak their mother tongue, or their national tongue — they still speak two foreign languages, strangers to one another.
One way or another — I cannot bury in my heart all my thoughts and feelings.
I already stand on the threshold of my older years, and I would like, after all, to begin everything anew; I would not want to keep silent any longer about the secret of my life and the manner of my being. I feel and know that I have not lived as I ought to have lived, as my own will was to live. My life until now has been a waking dream, or a kind of superficial, short-sighted awakening from a deep sleep. I was pushed, dragged along by an external force, and even at the time when I believed that I had free will and was personally responsible for the conduct of my life, for all my deeds, it was nothing more than self-deception, a lying fantasy.
I said: "I would like to begin everything anew" — day after day, over the course of the last years, I say these words to myself. Each time I resolve to start anew and put an end to the error of my life — and yet I still drag behind me the old chain of my life's errors. I am hobbled [?] with ropes with which others have bound me since my childhood years.
In my adult years I myself, with my own hands, almost of my own will, bound myself in chains — silken ones, but chains.
I seek a friend, a brother in the wide world — but have I sought and found myself, my true essence? Did I not do in my younger years, and do I not do now as well, such deeds as even my worst enemy would not have demanded of me? Have I not ruined, through my own deeds, both my body and my spirit? Have I not always found myself in the condition of "Yossi slaughters [?] Yossi"?
Friend and brother: do not regard me as a penitent. I do not love the penitents with the lowered heads. Wailing mothers [?], those who repent because they are feeble-minded, or because of old age, or out of terror. I cannot bear the fanatical, the wild penitents, who deny and annihilate themselves. I do not tolerate those who become penitents after they have sated themselves with sins, with transgression to the point of disgust, to the most impossible swinishness.
I do not know the way of life that I should choose, although I show [?] this very way of life to others.
I know the contradictions, the conflicts between the opposites of my life, but I do not know how to reconcile them and bring them into harmony. Perhaps life and its essence are just like this. Just so is life, and so it must be: confused, blurred, full of contradictions and reversals.
Perhaps life is a bad business that God has given to the children of men, so that they should torment [?] themselves a little and withstand the hard trial. "That they should torment themselves a little" — for whose sake? For what?
It seems I lack the ability to become a penitent. Today I do not know which of my deeds are bad and which of them are good. I do not know at all what I should repent of today.
D. B-n.

The Jews of Eretz Israel Have Taken to Writing...

[Eretz Israel — a letter; air mail and the LOT airline.] (A letter from Palestine)

When you stand in the Tel Aviv post office on Sundays, Tuesdays and Thursdays, you get the impression that all the Jews in Eretz Israel have nothing whatever to do but write letters all day long.

If on these days you want to fight your way through to buy a postage stamp or attend to something else at the post office, you have to take a little trouble and steel yourself [?], stand in line a good long while and have patience... Sometimes you will find the end of the queue right out on Allenby Street, and in the last minutes before the post office closes — even a little further.

Naturally I tried to find out whether this "epidemic" of writing has been going on for long — and all of them, as with one voice, answered me that it is only since the LOT aeroplane began to run.

"You understand," an old Jew whom I know from back in Będzin argued to me [?], "in 'those days', when letters used to drag along on the way for a full ten days and two weeks, and sometimes even more, people wrote less. One made do with corresponding once a month; but today... by what miracles... a letter that I write today is read tomorrow there, at my home in Będzin — so how can one hold back and not write? So one does write, and one writes the latest news, about the latest fashion and about whatever you like..."

From reliable sources I have also learned that large commercial transactions, especially between Eretz Israel and Poland, are lately being concluded only thanks to this convenient connection.

It must also be added that the tariff is not significantly more expensive and is accessible to everyone. Indeed, the mail is sent by LOT not only by Polish citizens but also by Jews from Romania, Czechoslovakia, Lithuania, Latvia and Austria, because it is the most convenient and the best connection.

It is a real pity to watch how the two [?] workers at Lydda, poor things, drag themselves with the full sacks of letters to the aeroplane every Monday, Wednesday and Friday morning, smile at the Polish airmen and greet them in their "Polish":
"Dzień dobry!.."

Lately, however, rumours have been circulating in Eretz Israel that the LOT management in Warsaw intends to introduce certain changes in the flight schedule for the winter months as well and to reduce the number of trips to two a week. The inhabitants of Eretz Israel speak of this reduction with understandable dissatisfaction, and judging by my talks with many Jews, all express the opinion and the wish that the LOT management will not make this experiment and will keep the same number of aeroplanes for the winter too.

The LOT management has already [?] achieved a great deal in aviation between Poland and Eretz Israel, and it is to be hoped that it will meet this request.

The inhabitants of Eretz Israel are very satisfied with this connection, and Polish Jews, who have not lost their patriotism toward Poland even there, are proud that it was precisely a Polish company that brought about such a tremendous "revolution" in the local air [?] and postal service..

And when in the afternoon hours one sees the great, giant bird with the familiar letters "S. P." flying over the skies of Tel Aviv, Jewish children [ḥ'utsim — perhaps "ḥalutsim", pioneers?] stand in the streets, gaze after the great bird with enraptured looks and whisper quietly:
"A fresh little letter from Mother!"

And it truly is a fresh little letter, for only yesterday Father and Mother wrote it and perhaps shed a tear, and before the tear has dried the child is already reading the letter, and it seems to him that his parents are standing there speaking right into his ear..

Yes, mighty is technology — it even works on the feelings.
Wars over a Postage Stamp.

[Article — postage stamps and international disputes.]
We all know the story of Kamtza and Bar Kamtza, and of other petty causes over which, more than once, great and long wars broke out that laid waste whole cities and countries; and we mostly think that in our times no disputes at all can arise from such trifling little things.

Only a short time ago it was thought that a war would soon break out between the two South American states Honduras and Nicaragua over a postage stamp that Honduras had issued. On this stamp a map of Honduras was painted, and on the map a piece of land belonging to Nicaragua was marked.

An outcry ["va-yitz'aku"] arose in Nicaragua. The people there saw in it a provocation by Honduras, which presumably wanted to grab a piece of land from Nicaragua. In both countries there was already plenty of talk about mobilization, and on both sides money was indeed already being collected for war preparations... Meanwhile the stamp became dearer and dearer; people practically snatched it out of each other's hands, and stamp dealers earned good money. Luckily the dispute ended well and it did not come to war.

In the archive of the Leipzig Fair several such disputes over postage stamps are recorded, which caused serious upheavals.

In 1912, for example, the English post issued a new postage stamp for India with the picture of an elephant that had the head of a pig. Since the elephant is a holy creature in India, the Mohammedans felt insulted, and who knows what would have happened had the English post not withdrawn the stamp.

Eight years ago war nearly broke out between Haiti and Santo Domingo [the Dominican Republic]. In Santo Domingo, too, a postage stamp was issued with a map on which a piece of Haiti was marked. Both countries had indeed already mobilized, and the soldiers of both countries were already standing at the borders. At the last moment they made it up, and both countries earned good money from a stamp they issued in honour of the peace.

In 1927 Paraguay issued a stamp, also with a map, on which the "Chaco" was marked as belonging to Paraguay. In truth it belongs to Bolivia. Bolivia immediately issued a postage stamp too, in which it drew on a map a piece of land belonging to Paraguay. From this a real war indeed developed, in which tens of thousands of people were killed on both sides. That war ended only in 1935 with a victory for Paraguay.

This was in fact the first postage stamp that brought about a real war. Disputes over postage stamps are recorded in history hundreds of times, but actually to wage war over them — that we have had to live to see only now. Only today can we understand how people in earlier generations could wage wars over trifles at which we laugh today...

Z. Haber, Vienna.

I'll Forgo the Honour...

(Y. Oberżanek[?])
Last week I had a guest: my neighbour Reb Shmelke. He came to me at dawn, while my household was still sleeping soundly. He came into my bedroom, and before I knew what was happening he was already sitting on the bed.
— Reb Yankl, are you asleep?
— What has happened, Reb Shmelke, is there some news?
— You still ask what news?
— What is it then?
— The business with the "benk" [benches].
— And what business do I have with "benk" [banks]? If something has happened with the banks, let Gutman and Fürstenberg worry!..
— Reb Yankl, have you gone muddled?
— my neighbour Reb Shmelke got angry — I am talking about benches, not about — banks!
Here my neighbour Reb Shmelke took a newspaper sheet out of his breast pocket: here, take it, read, Reb Yankl:
— "The rectors of the universities have decided to introduce separate benches for Jewish students. The Jewish benches will be marked with the letter 'ח', and the benches for Poles with the letter 'ב'.
— Well, so I have come to you to hear your opinion about this "Jewish ghetto". How do you look upon it, Reb Yankl?
— It is a terrible thing, if you say so.
— Then listen, Reb Yankl, I will tell you what a discussion I had today. I barely got out[?] alive. My wife sent me to the devil. So I went straight to you.. Listen, Reb Yankl, how the discussion went:
Reading in the paper the report about the "Jewish ghetto" with the "ב" and "ח" benches, I called together my household, my wife and daughters, and read it aloud. There was an uproar: my wife screamed and the daughters screamed.
So I took the floor and spoke to them thus:
— What are you making such a scandal for? What is the calamity here, eh?
— Idiot — my wife interrupted me — don't you understand that this is only the beginning ("początek"); it will go further; elsewhere too there will be "separate benches".
— Where, for instance?
— Theatre, restaurants, "jeszcze[?] ..."[?] — she said — that there will even[?] be Jewish restaurants and non-Jewish restaurants, and where will I, an "intelligent woman" (inteligentna kobieta), find myself — "in a Jewish restaurant" (w żydowskim lokalu)!..
— Aha, "that's where it hurts you" (tu cię boli)!.. You are quite right, Yente Dhasha: how will you, an "intelligent woman", be able to find yourself in a "żydowski" restaurant! How does it befit your "pure Aryan" pudding-nose to show itself in a Jewish restaurant? How does it befit you, Yente Dhasha, to go "to the Jewish theatre" (do żydowskiego teatru) to hear "some" Ida Kamińska, some Maurice Schwartz play... How does it befit you, Yente Dhashi, to look into a "jargon"[?] booklet, who are the jargon writers there: "some" Peretz, some Mendele, some Sholem Aleichem, Sholem Asch... call these writers, "kompania [?]"[?]. Such an "intelligent person" (inteligentna osoba) as you, honoured lady (szanowna pani) Yente Dhashi, must read only Polish books, must go only "to the Polish theatre" (do polskiego teatru) and sit only in non-Jewish restaurants. Your "pure Aryan" pudding-nose demands it.
Having finished with my "pure Aryan" Yente Dhasha, I turned to my daughters:
— Well, and you, little misses ("panienki"), what is pinching you?
— "What!... What will become of my Staszek?.." (Co będzie z moim Staszkiem?) — sobbed the youngest.
— "Nothing will happen" (nic nie będzie).. [you'll][?] sit on separate benches...
— "How so?" (jak to?)
— Just so (tak to): you will sit on a bench on the New Market [Nowy Rynek], and Staszek on a bench — on Sanczewska[?] Street.
— "I won't bear it!" (nie wytrzymam) — she lamented with big tears.
— You'll bear it (wytrzymasz) — I answered.
Well, things got lively in my home. The end of it was that my wife sent me to the devil; I obeyed her and came to you... to hear your opinion about it. What do you say to it, Reb Yankl?
— And what do you say, Reb Shmelke? Do you think that introducing a "Jewish ghetto" will be good for Jews?
— Listen, Reb Yankl, to what I will tell you — my neighbour Reb Shmelke replied:
— You know me, not from today and not from yesterday. I am no Doctor Chajes, nor a dumb beast either. Nor am I a "[?]"; I am a [plain][?] Jew, I look at life soberly, and as such I see no great misfortune in the "separate benches" and in the marking with the letters "ב" and "ח". I imagine how it will look when everything that is Jewish will be marked with a "ח" and everything that is not Jewish — with a "ב".
— I picture it like this:
The depot (remise) of the tramway company will be marked with a "ב", that is, the management does not take on any Jewish conductors, any Jewish drivers or any Jewish inspectors.
The same at the mines ("grubes")[?]: the "Henolaze"[?] mine, the "Zhamieshgitshe"[?] mine and other "mines" will be marked with a "ב", meaning that no Jewish officials (urzędnicy), no Jewish secretaries etc. are taken on.
The same at the power station (elektrownia), the social-insurance office (ubezpieczalnia) and other offices: where there is a "ב", people will know that Jews have no foothold there.
On the other hand, the factory buildings of, let us say, Fürstenberg, the Schein Brothers etc. will be marked with a "ח", meaning that there are Jewish workplaces[?] there and that entry is strictly forbidden to any non-Jew whatsoever.
The same will be with the parks: special "Jews' days" will be arranged in the parks. On the "Jews' days" only Jews will be allowed[?] into the park. On such a "day" the narodowcy [nationalists] will hang around the park like dogs near a butcher's stall; they will want to make a riot, but they won't go in, because "pure" Aryans may not, after all, sit together with Jews...
Now, as regards the separate benches in the universities, I will tell you the truth, Reb Yankl: I'll forgo the honour!...
Heard and Seen

[Zagłębie — feuilleton.] By Ben Amotz.

"Ye wise men, be careful with your words"..
At the meeting on how to react to the insult to the Będzin rabbinate it was, among other things, also decided to decree a fast. We have no way of estimating to what percentage the proclaimed fast succeeded; incidentally, the whole fast affair does not interest us at the present moment, but[?] we only want to draw attention to the fact that matters of serious content are taken and deliberately made petty, reckless[?] — and precisely by those who are called to stand guard so as not to profane what is still wrapped in the mantle of holiness. Why[?], teach us, our master, what[?] has happened that one should decree a fast? True, everyone, even one who is not a hundred-percent religious Jew, condemns and despises such deeds as the wife of a Jewish butcher permitted herself, and the whole Jewish population of Będzin protested directly or indirectly against this lawlessness. But proclaiming a public fast, even until midday — that must be weighed. Beware! Do not overdo it, for firstly[?] no such calamity, God forbid, has occurred over which a fast must be decreed; and secondly[?], if respect for the Torah is so great among the initiators of the fast that a public fast is proclaimed over the slightest insult, then dozens of such fasts should already have taken place in Będzin.. After all[?], the local Sochaczew rebbe, the Koziegłowy rabbi, the Kromołów[?] rebbe and others — no lesser religious authorities than the Będzin rabbinate — [—], and when one saw [—], no fast was decreed; why[?]..
Therefore we hold that the proclaimed fast brought a negative result. May the initiators permit[?] — we shall remind them of the warning:
— "Ye wise men, be careful with your words"... Before going to call a public fast, one must first give an account of what one is about to do. It is not a matter like calling a ban on machine-made matzos... [—]. Therefore, once again:
— "Be careful with your words"..

Modern "Anusim"...
— "There is nothing new under the sun" — says Ecclesiastes. There is no new thing under the sun. Everything we take as something new — has already been; the difference is only in time..
We were sure that the era of the Anusim [forced converts, Marranos] already belonged to the past, but in our present time, when medieval methods and systems are coming back to life, secret types of "Anusim" have begun to appear.
The difference between the Anusim of old and those of today is this: the Anusim of old sacrificed themselves and endured troubles and torment for the sake of their faith. Outwardly, in appearance, they were kosher Christians, but in private, in secret, in dark cellars, they prayed to the Jewish God. Today's "Anusim", however, sell their national dignity for the clink of the coin and plant themselves behind the shoulders of a kosher Aryan, so that they should not be seen[?]..
The first "swallows" of today's "Anusim" have appeared in Sosnowiec. In that town there are two brothers, well-to-do Jews, partners in one business. And it came to pass one day — that is to say[?], it happened in August — that they were given to understand that they are Jews.. This greatly annoyed them, the "green" brothers. Is it possible? We do not yet belong to the "khalamshaushes"[?] — why are you picking on us?
We do not know what answer the brothers received to this question, and perhaps they were given no answer at all. One thing, however, became clear: the brothers became "Anusim"..
And one fine morning a new signboard appeared over the business. Besides a new name, the business has acquired[?] an Aryan partner, who is the whole "head and bulk" of the business, and them, the poor brothers, one hardly sees; they are barely mentioned by an "& Co." [S-ka][?], the poor things.
— Modern "Anusim"...
And just as the Aryan[?] "plays", the "Anusim must dance", and all the others must dance too, the Jewish patrons among them; and they, the Jewish patrons, keep silent and accept everything with love, even when a showing of a Yiddish film is scheduled for them at 11 o'clock[?]. They must come then too — do they have a choice? Better than nothing, for what would the Jewish patrons have done when the Aryan partner has no desire at all to take a Yiddish film. He even holds[?] [—] the motto[?] that "the Jew is treyf but his money is kosher"...
— Yes, dear readers, we have lived to see fine times: boycott, pickets, troubles, beatings and — "modern Anusim"...

A Story About a "Sroka"..
Long live the present kehilla council in Dąbrowa! It is truly a delight to be present at a meeting — the best revue — and a [—] for [—] single appearance of any parnas[?]: a brilliant programme consisting of "Yiddish-Polish" speeches and little stories, which are actually told, and the "gallery" is greatly amused.
There is among the parnasim one who is a great "expert" at telling little stories. No sooner does he take the "floor" than one already knows a "fine" story is coming..
And at the last meeting this same man told several stories, but the most important story was about the "sroka" [magpie].
The tale is this: he, the parnas, so to speak, bought a kuropatwa [partridge]. Afterwards it turned out to be a "sroka". Well, that I — says he — did not know the difference between a partridge and a "sroka" can still be forgiven; but worse is that the shochet did not know either, slaughtered the "sroka", and the parnas ate the "sroka" up...
At that moment there were people in the hall who shrugged[?] their shoulders and asked: "Mai ka mashma lan" — what is he telling us? Does the parnas intend to criticize the shochet, who cannot distinguish a partridge from a "sroka"? Or did he want the "broad public" to know that he had eaten the meat of a "sroka"? But be that as it may, the story was a fine one. Which story, you ask?
— The story of the "sroka"...
From Our Own "Little Parliament"...

[Dąbrowa — kehilla.] (The meeting of the kehilla council in Dąbrowa.)
On Sunday a meeting of the Dąbrowa kehilla council took place. The agenda consisted of: 1) a tariff for burial plots, 2) fees for the slaughter of fowl, 3) by-laws, and 4) free motions.
The first item was adopted after a discussion according to the board's draft, i.e. that the fees for burial plots are from 10 to 1000 zł.
More interest was aroused by the second item, because the matter of the slaughter of fowl, which had always been the "private property" of the shochtim, has, on the basis of an order of the supervisory authority, passed into the domain of the kehilla, and since the shochtim lose a certain income on account of this, the kehilla board decided that the shochtim should also perform the role of supervisors [ne'emanim], and for this each shochet receives 10 zł. a week.
Around this item a discussion developed which took on a comic character. The leading role was played by parnas Landner, who told no fewer than 2 stories (the chairman calls them parables[?]...): one story about an apostate-heretic, and the second an original one — rather, about himself: how he came to grief with a "sroka" [magpie] only because the shochet to whom he had sent the "fowl" to be slaughtered did not know the difference between a magpie and a partridge [kuropatwa].
— If so — the parnas concludes — it may well happen that the shochet will slaughter a dog[?] thinking it is a calf!
After the discussion this item too was adopted, and the fixed fees are: for a pigeon 10 gr., a kurczak [young chicken] — 20, a hen — 30, a goose — 50 and a turkey — 80 gr.
Parnas Miodaznik [Miodownik?] moves an "amendment" that "if a woman insists and says of a hen that it is a kurczak, this too should not be contested"...
At the by-laws item the artisans'[?] representatives declare that, because they have to travel to an urgent conference in Będzin, they must leave the meeting. The chairman is not satisfied with this and declares that the by-laws item will be placed only on the agenda of the budget[?] meetings.
Then it is decided to apply to the supervisory authority concerning a certain parnas who does not come to the council's meetings.
With this the meeting was closed.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Lekh Lekha)

[Oneg Shabbat — weekly Torah portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parshat Lekh
—o—
a) "And there was a famine in the land, and Abram went down into Egypt" (12:10)
Because if there is a famine in the land — whom will they blame if not the Jew? So Abraham at once set about uprooting himself from the land. Don Isaac Abarbanel.
b) "For their substance was great, so that they could not dwell together" (ibid., 6)
In the end it is property that divides friends and companions; the greater the property — the more envy and hatred... Or Torah.
c) "Let there be no strife, I pray thee, between me and thee... for we are brethren"
"And the Midrash Aggadah: they resembled each other in facial features." Rashi.
And that is why Abraham hurried to part[?] from Lot: the two looked alike, and when Lot robbed, people said that Abraham was doing it... Bikurei Aviv[?].
• • •
"Let there be no strife, for we are brethren."
How much misfortune, how many disputes has this "for we are brethren" — the cleverest peace formula[?] — already brought about[?], all so that, because of "for we are brethren", no dispute should arise... R' Yaakov Beg[?].
d) "And the Lord said unto Abram, after that Lot was separated from him" (13:14)
"As long as the wicked man was with him, the divine word kept away from him"; and although[?] Lot was with him, it is written: "And the Lord appeared unto Abram" — "at that time he was still worthy." Rashi.
How is it that Lot suddenly stopped being worthy and stopped being righteous? What happened to him in the meantime?
Precisely in the meantime — the Torah tells — "and Lot also, which went with Abram, had flocks, and herds, and tents." He suddenly grew rich, and wealth, as usual, made him no longer righteous and no longer a worthy man... Ktav Sofer.
• • •
A worthy man — said R' Nachman of Bratslav — cannot, in our times, possibly own money. "Va-tered[?] pela'im" ("she came down wonderfully") — these are the letters of "alafim" (thousands): to reach the thousands one must necessarily undergo a spiritual descent.
e) "For all the land... to thee will I give it... And I will make thy seed as the dust of the earth" (ibid., 15)
Eretz Israel is so small, it seems, that it will not take in even a tenth of the Jews; but the size of Eretz Israel depends on the number of children who come to her. When the Jews multiply in her, the borders of the land will widen too. Is it ever too crowded at one's own mother's? As many children as you like may gather there[?]... Pnei Yafot.
f) "And Melchizedek king of Salem brought forth bread and wine" (14:18)
R' Mattityahu Strashun once came to Königsberg together with the magnate Moshe Wolf[?] Polnadski[?], and the two went to pay a visit to the local rabbi, R' Zvi Hirsch Mecklenburg. R' Zvi Hirsch happened not to have at home refreshments fit for two such rich men, so he said to them with a witticism[?]:
— Do not be surprised at the meagre refreshments. Melchizedek honoured Abraham only with "bread and wine" — a piece of bread with wine. Do you know why? Because "he was the priest of the most high God." He was a rabbi, a holy vessel — and a rabbi who takes has no means to give... Zikaron la-Aharonim.
• • •
R' Levi Yitzchak of Berdichev went around collecting donations for an impoverished man of good family. He comes to R' Baruch of Medzhybizh and tells him about the dire situation of that poor man. The rebbe R' Baruch stands up, heaves a groan and gives him a blessing. Says R' Levi Yitzchak:
Of Melchizedek it is said "he brought forth bread and wine" and only afterwards "and he blessed him" — first he gave, and only later did he bless...
g) "Whereby shall I know that I shall inherit it?" (15:8)
Abraham asked: "Whereby shall I know that I shall inherit it" — what assurance do I have, Master of the Universe, that the children who will inherit me will follow my path, that they will not assimilate among the nations?
So the Master of the Universe showed him "a great darkness", the darkness of exile, and said: "Know of a surety that thy seed shall be a stranger in a land that is not theirs, and shall serve them; and they shall afflict them four hundred years" — this very pain they will suffer will be the best guarantee that they will have to remain Jews.
h) "And they shall afflict them four hundred years" (ibid., 13)
A rich man once asked R' Yitzchak Nalpuer[?]:
— You, Rebbe, wait so for the Messiah and are sure he will come any day now, while the Gemara says: "The son of David will not come until the last penny is gone from the purse" — and among Jews there are still so many rich men.
R' Yitzchakl answered:
— The Master of the Universe told Abraham that the Jews would be in the Egyptian exile 400 years, and in the end they sat there only 210 years. The reckoning doesn't add up? The commentators have already sharpened their brains[?] to reconcile the reckoning. So it is with this saying too: let the Messiah come first — even though the penny is not "gone from the purse" — and sharp minds will surely be found to reconcile it...

A Prayer of a Communal Worker (for a Flower Sale)

Master of the Universe! Hear my plea;
grant success to the little flower —
the sick need it for a full recovery,
the gabbai needs it to live...

You should not, God, punish all the
associations
that [line up(?)] before You in rows;
they help the sick with good remedies
and give the healthy(?) something to chew...

The first, it seems, is called
"Linat ha-Tzedek",
the second is called "Linat ha-Cholim",
the third — a new one, is called
"Malon Orchim",
the fourth: "Mishmeret ha-Cholim".

Do not put to shame, Father
in Heaven,
all the associations mentioned,
let not(?) heaven be filled with
lamentation,
let no one, God forbid, weep...

And let there lie in the charity boxes
no buttons,
nor ten-groszy coins worth a three-groszy piece...
but let a few złoty remain
in the till,
for the sick and the not-sick this year.

Y. Radoszycki(?).
Zagłębie Fashions

Summer — autumn — winter.

Fashions change. What is in fashion in Zagłębie today?

In the Sosnowiec kehilla presidiums are in fashion. And indeed they intend there soon to issue a printed manifesto about the "dictatorship of three".

Besides that, this year(?) committees are in fashion in Zagłębie — that is, "temporary" committees, which will never liquidate themselves.

Among the Jewish city councillors it has become fashionable to raise their hands.

In the Jewish banks it is the fashion to make the eve of a holiday into a holiday too.

Among the women gossip is in fashion today: about telephones, doctors and lawyers.
Diary of Modern Youth

Sunday. Slept till noon; in the afternoon dressed up elegantly and went to the "Sajf"(?) — for lack of anything better. That is, if a "depressed mood" reigns in the pocket, I made do with a game of cards or snatching a little dance to the radio music, and went to bed after midnight.

Monday. Studied the whole sports press, so as to be well versed in which club rose to a higher league in the Sunday matches and which suffered a defeat. In the evening went to the cinema, came home to sleep at a "normal" hour.

Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday — the same as Monday, only with the change that instead of losing myself in sport, I spent the days flirting, took a ride on a motorcycle, manicured my nails, had my hair waved, etc.

Friday afternoon went to "acquaintances" and came back for the Sabbath "supper" (kolacja).

Sabbath. In the forenoon a stroll, leading a dog with the right hand and holding a cigarette in the left. In the evening — to a ball until morning.
What Is the Father's Name? (The Man with a Weak Memory)

It is said of a Jew from Dąbrowa that he is a "brilliant" forgetter. He himself wishes he possessed all that he has already forgotten in his life. As a young man he signed betrothal contracts (tena'im) with three girls, and married the fourth, because he had forgotten the previous three.

When he stood under the wedding canopy, instead of "harei at" he said to the bride: "May you already be spared(?) from sorrow."

When his wife bore him twins, he went to the civil registry office to take out birth certificates, and when the official asked him what the father's name was, he answered that he did not remember, went to the telephone and asked his wife:
— Leah, what is the name of our children's father?
A Talmudic Twist

To my dear wife, may she live!
"I ask you, my dear wife, to be so kind as to send me at once your shirts, which I forgot to take with me. You must understand yourself that I do not, God forbid, mean your shirts, but mine. But if I write you 'my shirts', you will read 'mine' and you will think I mean yours. Therefore I write you 'yours'. Then you will already know that I mean not yours but mine, and I am sure that you will indeed send me my shirts."

Ben Aharon.
Just a Little Foot

A young man with a broken leg was brought to the Jewish hospital the other day. The doctor asks him:
— How did this happen?
— While playing.
— Football?
— No.
— From what, then?
— I was playing cards, and my wife gave me signals under the table.
Lech-Lecha...

Lech-Lecha is the most current sedra,
always topical in the extreme.
It is a sedra that is read constantly,
in all the weeks of the whole year...

The League of Nations argues with the Duce:
— Leave the poor Queen of Sheba alone!...
And Mussolini answers the League of Nations:
Today's sedra is — Lech-Lecha (get thee out)!...

A Jew slips illegally into the Land of Israel,
because on the [?] of the land — there is no place for him!...
The Englishman grabs him by the collar:
— Reb Jew, today's sedra is — Lech Lecha!...

You can run for months after a donation to a Sosnowiec magnate,
until the "pan" is, with luck, finally at home...
And in sum he answers you:
Uncle dear, you know(?), today's sedra is Lech-Lecha!...

A neighbour proposes a match to a young man,
a maiden — a real gem, but a dowry, alas, there is none...
The young man answers at once:
— Take, Reb neighbour, your maiden — and Lech-Lecha!

When I submit an application to the interest-free(?) loan fund,
the guarantors don't please them,
and when I come for the loan they answer me at once:
— Take back your application — and Lech-Lecha!

Y. Fridman.
Bitter Times

— I tell you, Mrs. Kandlzucker, these days are bitter times, unbearable.
— Really? You feel the crisis too?
— What a question! In the good times it was enough for me to faint once, and I already got the most beautiful silk dress from my husband; and today, for a silly hat costing a few złoty, I have to faint ten times and have spasms(?) at least twenty times.

Two Generations

[Serialized story — Odessa, 1905; Jews and Christian neighbours; apparently installment 1.]
Sh. Vaynitser [Sz. Wajnicer?].

An astonishing story of a pogromshchik [pogrom participant] who became an ardent friend of the Jews.

This is a story that spans two generations, and it began in Odessa.

Some thirty-odd years ago there lived in Odessa, on Tretetsky [?] Street, a Jewish family named Hirsh Ber Geyrof [?]. [He was] a smith; in a corner of the courtyard he had his smithy. His wife Sore Beyle was a simple, pious Jewish woman, but with a good heart, and although she herself could barely keep her household going, she helped the needy with whatever she could. Sore Beyle had two children, a boy and a girl. The boy was called Leybl and the girl Ester. Leybl was seven years older than Ester. Hirsh Ber wanted his Leybl not to have to work as hard as he did, and sent him to the "voraskais" [?; probably gorodskoye] uchilishche (municipal school), which Leybl finished at 16. Now the father had a great worry on his mind: he was looking for some occupation for his Leybl.

Opposite the Geyrofs, door by door, lived a Russian family, Zhelenetsky. The father of the family, Nikolai, worked in the port. The Christian family consisted of three persons [?]: the father, the mother, Katya, and a boy, Sergei. Both families, the Jewish and the Christian, lived very well together. The Zhelenetskys were very poor, and Sore Beyle took it upon herself as a duty to help them out. She often brought over a little flour, groats, [?] and the like. In winter she used to supply them with wood and kerosene. In this way both families became very close friends. Esterl, who was almost the same age as Sergei (he was all of half a year older), played with him constantly, just as with her own little brother. Thus a good few years went by.

And it was at the beginning of the year 1905. A niece of Nikolai's named Maria came to visit the Zhelenetskys at that time. She was a young girl from a village not far from Odessa. Maria's mother had died giving birth to her. Her father was a great drunkard and raised her with blows and curses. Her mother suffered much from him, from her father, and had it not been for the father's brother, Maria's uncle in America, who from time to time sent them a few dollars, she would long since have perished from hunger. As long as the father was alive, Maria stayed with him in the village. But when he died, she came to her uncle in Odessa. She went on receiving a few dollars a month from her uncle, and that money she now gave to [—] uncle, who gave her food.

Maria was all of a few months younger than Leybl, who was by now an 18-year-old young man. She was slender, a blonde with blue eyes and a very lovely smile on her lips. Since the Zhelenetskys received a few dollars every month, it paid them to keep her. The Jewish family, too, soon became close friends with her, and Maria was very often at the Geyrofs' house.

It did not take long before Leybl Geyrof grew very close to Maria. This was Leybl's first friendship with a woman, and he fell deeply in love with her. After a few months anyone could already notice that Leybl and Maria were not indifferent to each other.

The first to catch on was the mother, when she saw how Leybl could not take his eyes off Maria.

"What is this, Leybl? What is going on here [?] — are you in love with the shiksa? Tell me!" the mother asked him.

"I don't know!" he answered. "And if so, so what?"

"You are a Jewish child, and I don't want you to turn your head over a shiksa, do you hear!" the mother shouted at him.

"You won't tell me your opinion about whom I may like and whom not," Leybl answered angrily.

The father, Hirsh Ber, came in on the talk, and Sore Beyle poured out her bitter heart to him:

"Have you heard [?]: he wants to marry a shiksa! I'd sooner kill you dead. A shiksa, no less! It's no wonder, when a young man hangs around idle."

When Maria's uncle heard about the quarrel, and that it concerned his niece, he went into the Geyrofs' and started shouting:

"What, you still don't want it? People have long been telling me that I shouldn't allow Maria to be with your son. But I didn't listen to them; I answered them that you were fine people, not at all like Jews. And now you're making a fuss on top of it. Cursed zhidki!" [Russian slur for Jews]

That was the first time the Geyrofs quarrelled with the Zhelenetskys, and now both families burned with anger at each other.

But while all relations between the two neighbours were broken off, one thread [?] still tied together two members of both families — namely Leybl and Maria, who only now felt how much they loved each other. They now met in secret in side alleys, so that none of their own people would see them.

But there were neighbours who noticed Leybl with Maria in a dark side alley, and they told Leybl's father.

The father went to a rabbi and told him the story.

The rabbi, on hearing this, wrote a letter and said to Hirsh Ber:

"Drop your work and do what I tell you. Here is a letter to a good timber merchant, not far from Kiev. Go there with your son. There he will get a position in the forest. In time he will forget the shiksa completely. Do as I tell you."

And Leybl went along with his father into the forest.

On Her First Day the New Maid Committed a Theft

[Będzin — crime.] On Monday around midday a Christian woman presented herself at the apartment of S. Lasker (Szlachacka[?] St. 13) and declared that she wished to take the position of maid. When Mrs. Lasker asked for a document, the Christian woman declared that she would bring the document the next day, because „I have to run away from the place where I was, because the 'pan' [master] is pestering me“. At the same time she gave the address where she had served until then.
Mrs. L. believed her and took her on as maid. In the meantime[?] Mrs. L. went to the address given in order to inquire about the new maid she had hired, leaving the maid with the child.
It turned out, however, that it was „neither bears nor forest“ [a complete fabrication]: there was no such[?] name at all in the house indicated.
Mrs. L. then hurried home, as the matter had already become suspicious to her, but on arriving home she saw that the maid had taken from the apartment various goods worth several hundred złoty and had vanished.
As it turns out, she was a cunning thief. She had made the child drunk with spirit so that it would sleep soundly.
City Council Session Did Not Take Place

[Będzin — municipality.] On Tuesday a session of the city council was due to take place. The appointed time for city council sessions is 9 o'clock, but they never begin earlier than half an hour later. This time, however, the session was opened a quarter of an hour after the appointed time.
Before the agenda, councillor Segalski[?] takes the floor[?] and announces on behalf of the „Klub Naczarcz“[?] (formerly the B.B. [BBWR, the pro-government Nonpartisan Bloc]) that as long as the Rubinlicht affair has not been settled (as is known, Mr. Rubinlicht is accused of having allegedly used an insulting word about the councillors in a conversation with the Sosnowiec city president), the councillors of the „Klub“ will not take part in the session. After this declaration they left the session and no quorum remained.
(The Jewish councillors only arrived after the president had declared that the session would not take place.
It is rumoured that the Rubinlicht affair was exploited by the above-mentioned „Klub“ as a means of preventing the session from taking place, because the leaders of the „Klub“, Messrs. Director Błażejewicz[?] and Naza'a[?], have resigned as councillors.
Protest over the Insult to the Rabbinate

[Będzin — community and religion.] As we have already written, the local rabbinate was insulted in a shameful manner by a certain butcher on Modrzejowska[?] Street, because the rabbinate had alerted the Jewish customers not to buy in the butcher shops the meat that is not under its kashrut supervision.
In connection with this, last Sabbath all the minyanim and „shtiblekh“ were closed, and only „thousands“ of worshippers prayed in the synagogue, where Messrs. Shlomo Yitzchak Rinski and Nate Guter spoke about the vile deed. During N. Guter's speech many people wept bitterly.
Collision of a Taxi with a Cart

[Będzin — accidents.] On Thursday night, at the corner of Potocka–Małachowskiego[?] streets, a taxi collided with a cart. The collision was a strong one: all the windows of the taxi were smashed. Mr. Jakob Rafner[?] of Katowice[?] was injured by the pieces of glass.
Another „Millionaire“

[Będzin — people.] We have already reported that the owner of one quarter-ticket of number 6424, on which the prize of a million złoty fell in the 4th class of the 39th lottery, is Mr. N. Gotlib of Będzin. He made his living carrying around and selling satchels[?] for schoolchildren. Lately he had been left unemployed and only earned something from time to time as a broker.
Now, having won the 200 000 złoty, Mr. Gotlib intends to buy a house in Katowice[?] or in Kraków. He has of course already provided himself with a ticket for the first class of the 40th lottery.

Conference of Jewish Guilds

[Zagłębie — artisans.] In the premises of the local Artisans' Association a conference of all the Jewish guilds in Zagłębie took place under the chairmanship of President Goldsztajn.
The conference dealt with the latest amendment to the Industrial Law. After Mr. Goldsztajn's report a broad discussion developed, after which a commission was elected to deal with the points of the amendment and then to express its opinion.

[Będzin — community and religion.] At the meeting of the „Va'ad ha-Kashrut“ (kashrut committee) a resolution was adopted that a special „Va'ad ha-Kashrut“ consisting solely of women should also be founded, who are to check in which household [?] utensils are being used...
The men's „Va'ad ha-Kashrut“ places great hopes in the women's committee bringing the right result...

The Upper Silesian bus company has again renewed the regular bus service on the Chorzów–Będzin line and back. The bus runs through Czeladź, Siemianowice[?], Bańgów. Departure from Browarna Street in Będzin every 2 hours, starting from 7 in the morning.

Sosnowiec — General meeting of Jewish academics

In the Kehilla premises the annual general meeting of the Jewish academic association „Uniska“[?] took place on Sunday.
Before the agenda a protest resolution was adopted concerning the separate benches for Jewish students in the institutions of higher learning.
Chairman Plattner opens the meeting and hands the chair to Dr. K. Lieberman; to the presidium: Miss Szpigelman and Arnsztajn. From the report given by Mr. Plattner it emerges that the board did fruitful work in the field of the self-help fund and general and cultural matters; members' talks on various subjects and lectures were organised, among them also by the poet Broderzon.
After the discussion the board is granted an absolutorium [vote of approval], and the following board is elected by acclamation: Plattner (chairman), H. Bernstein (secretary), Z. Geier (treasurer), Miss Szpigelman, Miss Bajtner, Miss Solna, Miss Nachemias[?] and Mr. Ochsenhändler.

Wounded by a hooligan on the train — and fined for soiling the carriage

Travelling by train from Sosnowiec to Katowice, a quarrel broke out in the carriage between Mr. Chaim Fridman and a brawler (awanturnik); at a certain moment the brawler threw himself at Fridman and wounded him with a knife.
On arriving in Katowice, Fridman paid 1 złoty for soiling the carriage with blood.
