Verdict in the trial of the murderers of Jews.
Chief organiser sentenced to death.

Of the witnesses at the trial of the murderers of the 5 Jews from the village of Stawy[?], the first to be heard was the police senior constable (przodownik) of the Jędrzejów command, Julian Peszach[?]. He described exactly how the murder had happened.
The hearing of the constable's testimony lasted over an hour. Then the remaining witnesses for the prosecution and the defence were examined. Among other things, the wives and brothers-in-law of the accused related that they had been threatened with shooting if they would "shoot them"[?] [so printed; probably: if they betrayed them].
Prosecutor Lehman[?], in his indictment speech, demanded the highest penalty for the accused, [since] their "penalty"[?] [probably: guilt] had been proven, and for such a crime there can be no milder sentence than the death penalty.
Then the civil claimant, Adv. Cyter[?], made a forceful speech. He pointed out in his speech that Tadeusz Kraszyński's [—] had been [—] the [—] of the [—], and that in addition he had also [—] incited others to murderous attacks. He demanded the death penalty for all the accused.
The defence counsel, Advocates Chęciński, Stipczin[?] and Kradżyński[?], asked for a mild sentence for the accused and, for Władysław Kraszyński[?], an acquittal.
In their last word all the accused burst into tears and asked for a mild sentence. Mieczysław Kraszyński[?] declared in his last word, among other things: "I ask for a mild sentence. I did not go in order to murder but in order to rob[?]. But my brother Tadek talked me into murdering; he said the priest had preached that the Jews must be driven out of Poland and their property taken away, because they want to rule over us. I was naive and I believed it."
After a three-hour deliberation the court handed down the verdict, under which Tadeusz Kraszyński, the chief organiser of the murderous attack, is sentenced to death. His brother Mieczysław to life imprisonment, Stanisław Cichoń[?] to 15 years' imprisonment, Edward Kraszyński to 10 years' imprisonment.
All the accused, including Tadeusz Kraszyński who was sentenced to death, received the verdict with complete indifference.
You will be able to go on trips without a penny.

The Polish railways will shortly introduce an innovation that will give everyone the possibility, at least once a year, of making a holiday journey across the country without paying for a ticket.
The new possibilities will be provided by the "tourist vouchers", which the railways will issue thanks to the initiative of the League for the Promotion of Tourism.
The scheme consists in collecting small-value coupons, which will later be exchanged for tourist vouchers, for which one will receive at any railway ticket office a ticket for a corresponding number of kilometres.
The vouchers will be distributed by a number of firms which, for their own advertising purposes, will hand out kilometre coupons to their customers as free premiums for goods purchased.
A customer who buys, for example, food, haberdashery, cosmetics and the like will each time receive in the shop, as a free bonus, a voucher for half a kilometre, 1, 2, 3 or 5 kilometres, depending on the value of the purchase. Once one has collected from one firm vouchers for 20 kilometres, one will be able to exchange them for a standard tourist voucher, for which one will get a free railway ticket for a distance of 20 kilometres.
For a hundred-kilometre 3rd-class voucher one will be able to buy a second-class ticket for 65 km or 50 km in first class.

Several poor Jews who were travelling at night from Chmielnik to Kielce were attacked on the way by several hooligans. One of them, an elderly[?] beggar, a cripple, the hooligans dragged off the cart, beat him badly and robbed[?] [him of] money.

Income tax on devalued debts.
The Ministry of Finance has sent the tax offices a circular reporting[?] a ruling of the Supreme Administrative Tribunal, under which firms that keep commercial books are obliged to pay income tax on devalued debts in foreign currency. The New Regulations on the Sale of Tobacco

Hundreds of small traders are very worried because of the new regulations on the tobacco trade, which burden it with many formalities and rules that hit above all the small shopkeeper.
Because of the importance of the matter we shall pass on some details from the new implementing regulations to the law on the tobacco trade.
The tobacco trade is divided into 3 branches: 1) wholesale, 2) mixed retail and 3) retail. Wholesale businesses may sell only to shopkeepers and only in large quantities. Mixed retailers may sell both to shopkeepers in smaller quantities and to consumers. Retailers may sell only to consumers.
To run a tobacco trade one must conclude a special agreement with the Polish Tobacco Monopoly. For the wholesale storekeepers a special district is designated, belonging to the particular wholesale depot (hurtownia). The Tobacco Monopoly may also conduct the wholesale trade through its own authorised officials. Small sale (retail sale) is again divided into a) shop sale, where one sells either tobacco alone or tobacco together together with other goods; b) house sale, i.e. tobacco sale in dwellings, hotels and catering businesses; and c) street sale, i.e. for example in kiosks, railway stations and itinerant sale, by hand or from boxes in the streets. For all kinds of tobacco trade one must have an agreement with the Tobacco Monopoly; only for itinerant sale does one take a permit from the excise office.
It is worth noting here that if one obtains a permit and does not start the tobacco trade within 2 months, the permit loses its validity.
The discounts for the tobacco trade will be as follows: in wholesale trade for cut tobacco — 6 percent, cigarettes — 8 percent, half-wholesale also 8 percent. Retail sale 5 and 6 percent. Street, railway-station and itinerant sale — 5 and 7 percent, house sale — 6 and 7 percent.
Tobacco may not be traded by deputies, senators, state and municipal officials, military personnel [?], as well as by those against whom an investigation is being conducted and those who do not have Polish citizenship.
The new regulations come into force on 1 March 1938.

[Sosnowiec — crime.] Bloody love drama in Sosnowiec.
A groom shoots his bride, who had become unfaithful to him.
On Wednesday morning the tailor Abraham Englender of Sosnowiec came to the apartment of his bride Mila Bergsztajn. After a short, harsh exchange Englender fired at her three times and seriously wounded her.
Mil[a] Bergsztajn was operated on in the hospital.
After committing the deed Englender went to the police station (komisariat) and gave himself up to the police.
As is supposed, this was an act of revenge by Englender, because the bride, to whom he had been engaged for several years, had come to regret the match.

A Living Torch in the "Rialto" Cinema.
In the "Rialto" cinema the following tragedy took place on Sunday morning: a certain Laron[?] caught sight in the cinema of his wife, who had run away from him, and begged her to make peace with him and come back home. When the "woman of valour" refused his request, Laron doused himself with petrol and set himself alight. In a moment Laron was engulfed in flames, but thanks to the energetic rescue it was possible to save him from death. Badly burned, he was taken to hospital.
Weddings May Take Place Only in the Kehilla Premises

[Upper Silesia — Katowice; Kehilla.]
The board of the Jewish kehilla in Katowice has adopted a resolution that wedding ceremonies (chuppahs) may take place only in the premises of the kehilla, such as in the synagogue, at the rabbis', in the kehilla hall. Where necessary, chuppahs may be set up in private flats where the wedding is held, but the gmina (community) must first issue a permit to set up a chuppah. The purpose of the resolution is that no more chuppahs should take place in restaurants and other public places without the slightest knowledge of the kehilla or the rabbinate.
Life in Chorzów — From Artisans' Life

[Upper Silesia — Chorzów; artisans.]
On Sunday the general meeting of the artisans took place here. With 50 members present, the former president Teichbaum[?] opened the meeting and declared that, owing to the bad state of the association and the members' disregard, he was giving up his post[?] and resigning.
The chair was taken over by Mr. Izydor Rozenberg, who spoke about the oppressed situation of Jewry in general and of the Jewish artisan in particular.
A rich lecture was delivered[?] by the guest, Mr. Kaufman of Katowice, which made a good impression on those present. Mr. Fischer of Kraków (president of the Kraków artisans' association) also spoke and was greeted with long-lasting applause.
The meeting sent a telegram to Warsaw, joining the protest day.
Parents' Meeting of the "Gan Yeladim"

[Upper Silesia — education.]
A meeting took place at the "Beit Sefer Ivri" (Hebrew school) in the presence of 20 people[?]. The opening speech was given by the head of the school, Rabbi Mordechai Blumenfeld, who lectured on the question of education in general and among Jews in particular. The lecture made a very good impression on those present.
After the lecture a discussion developed, in which Messrs. Ehrlich, Strausberg, Balinger[?], Lipziger and others took part.
Then a board of trustees (curatorium) was elected, consisting of Messrs.: Ehrlich, Kanengiser, Strausberg, Balinger[?], Kleiner, Roth, Ringelheim, Klasner, Lipziger, Mrs. Drexler and Mrs. Breitkopf.
In conclusion Rabbi Blumenfeld greeted the curatorium, thanked the parents for their confidence in the head of the school, and appealed to the parents to help in educating their children in a religious-national spirit.
It is the parents' duty to take an interest in this important educational institution and to enrol their children aged 3 to 14. Places are limited.
Enrolment at the school office, Głowackiego 3, 1st floor.

Only "Sabina" is to blame...

[Everyday life — Zagłębie.] The little wife[?], he and "Sabina". The [—] in the [—] one meets young and old, modern girls and Jewish women in wigs, deeply absorbed in the tragic life story of the innocent "Sabina". "Sabina" has caused more than one family scandal. With one couple in Dąbrowa it nearly came to a divorce (get), because the husband, a worker, coming home for lunch, finds his wife sitting and reading.
— Why are you crying[?]? What has happened? — the husband asked in fright.
— Nothing has happened, God forbid[?]. It simply [—] me at the heart [—], why should "Sabina" suffer so much.
— Which "Sabina"? Somebody from our family?
— No family at all — answers the wife with tears in her eyes — I mean the "Sabina" from the booklet that I bought from the newspaper seller.
The husband, hungry as he was[?], hearing that his wife was crying over the fate of the "Sabina" from the booklet, made a real scandal, and had it not been for the intervention of the neighbours, his wife would have had to cry over her own fate and would no longer have remembered "Sabina"...
A similar story happened this week on Dekerta Street in Sosnowiec. Mrs. Ch., buying various articles at the market in honour of the Sabbath, on her way home went up to the newspaper seller who stands at the [corner?] of Man-dushever[?]–Dekerta, and bought several booklets of "Sabina". But she did not wait with the reading [—] at home; she walked along the street reading.
The more her thoughts were taken up with "Sabina", the less she noticed how the live carp she had bought for the Sabbath "took a stroll" out of her bag...
On coming home she began to unpack the parcels she had bought and — "woe is me!" — she cried out.
The household was badly frightened. No questions about a story — nowadays anything can happen. What has happened to you? the household asked with frightened looks.
— "The fish has jumped out of my bag" — Mrs. Ch. barely got out — but I am not to blame at all; she is the one to blame.
— Who do you mean[?]?
— Yes, she is to blame, that "Sabina"...

Apathy Is a Crime.

(On the role of the intelligentsia in Jewish life).
In every healthy people the intelligentsia is the seismograph of the people's life. When a danger hovers over the people and the masses become alarmed, the spiritual elite of the people — the intelligentsia — responds.
The Jewish intelligentsia of former times took an interest in the fate of the people. The rabbis, who were once the leading force in Jewish life, although they were isolated from day-to-day life, reacted to all phenomena.
The sufferings, woes and painful questions of the people's life were dealt with by the Council of Four Lands and the like.
Hasidism, as is well known, also fulfilled in its beginnings a certain mission of regeneration. The very fact that Hasidism raised the spirit of the masses, showing[?] them that one could hold a place without necessarily being a Talmudic scholar, affected the psyche of the simple person and pulled him out of the depression of those days.
While being far from enthusiastic about the attitude of the former — and today completely bankrupt — assimilation, one must nevertheless admit that within its whole naive attitude to the Jewish question there was at the same time[?] a concern for the needs of the Jewish masses.
True, they treated the poor in a purely philanthropic way; but there was an interest: they wanted to mingle with the gentiles, yet at the same time[?] they remembered that there exists a poor, rightless Jewish mass for whom something must be done.
We stress once more that some of their public activities[?] definitely arouse, because of their approach, aversion in today's Jew. But the phenomenon itself — that they wanted to do something — must not be underestimated.
And let us fool ourselves! [sic; presumably "let us not fool ourselves"] Almost all the important institutions in the Jewish communities of Poland were created by the assimilationist societies or by individuals.
And how does it look today? How does the intelligentsia react today to the needs of the masses? Does it also show great interest in the present bitter time, when the whole of Jewish life is tottering?
It is truly a disgrace that while the Jewish people suffers blow after blow and the Jewish masses sink from day to day deeper into the abyss of want and despair, the Jewish intelligentsia, in its great majority, lives in a kind of "splendid isolation", and that is how it looks[?] almost everywhere.
These intellectuals (we stress once more: in their great majority) push their way into non-Jewish associations, social and philanthropic, in order to belong by force to the "community" of another nation.
And when one reproaches[?] them for this, as we do[?] (explicitly or by hint), they create their own "clubs" with cards, dancing, balls[?] and a few other urgent things. For the sake of clarity:
Nobody objects that people want to create their own circle, in order to entertain themselves[?] there. Well, not everyone has democratic inclinations and not everyone is flexible; he finds it better to flirt with "his own", and a game of cards is also better with his "own" race.
But these "society clubs" surely cannot replace even the work of the former assimilationists, let alone the heavy tasks which lie today upon every conscious Jew who can, in the smallest measure, relieve the distress of the great, despairing masses.
• • •
We have no intention of moralizing. We only want to point out that apathy at the present time is a crime.
Jewish life, especially the upbringing of the young generation, must take other paths.
Jews must direct more attention to the productivization of the youth. The Jewish school system must be radically changed; one must begin to look at life more realistically and seek practical means so that other possibilities of livelihood will not be cut off.
The whole attitude of Jews to education and schooling must be revised. In view of the Endek [Polish nationalist] efforts to undermine Jewish livelihoods, and of the hell of our student youth, one must think about steering the education of the young onto[?] other, more practical paths. Economic defence is not organized among us; Jews are short-sighted and do not want to look far ahead.
The thousands of misfortunes[?] in the most varied times have not strengthened the Jews' memory at all.
But, to return to our point: what can the ordinary person do, even when he fully realizes the burning necessity of preparing the Jew for the economic defensive struggle?
These matters are, after all, bound up first of all[?] with great financial difficulties which he will not overcome; for can the Jew, impoverished and blackened, have perspective and think about the future generation when he has to pay his rent?
And here the intelligentsia, which is better situated and more versed in these matters, must come to help.
• • •
But not only on this question does the majority of the intelligentsia say not a word; no problem of Jewish life whatsoever interests them.
Not only in the movement are intellectual forces lacking; the same is noticeable in many public institutions, both general and local, and this must be changed. The Jewish intelligentsia that possesses a sense of public responsibility must give thought to this.
The Jewish intelligentsia in its majority must, however, remember that in a people's hour of destiny, isolation itself is a crime.
And if it is not able to change significantly the situation of the Jewish masses, it must go[?] to those who are struggling bitterly for their existence and help to consolidate their tottering livelihoods.
Indifference in some cases shows a lack of responsibility, of national feeling in the sublime sense of the word.
P. Blumenkranz.

The Grave That Was Desecrated

[Palestine — opinion piece; Jewish orange-growers and „Hebrew labour“.]
I have a little story to tell you. A little story that happened not in olden times, not in the dark Middle Ages, but in our own days, in the year 5698 since the Creation of the world, and not somewhere beyond the Mountains of Darkness, but in the very heart of the Land of Israel, not far from Jerusalem, during the bloody events — and the people did not shudder and the community did not rage.
In a rich land there lived a Jew, a great man of wealth, who made his living in comfort. The Jew lived quietly and free of care and thought he had already lived seventy years in contentment and honour. But, as they say, man plans and God — laughs. Bad times came upon the world. A storm passed in the year 5693 [1933] over the land of Ashkenaz [Germany]. A wicked regime came to power, and for the rich merchant the wheel of fortune turned. He began to feel the ground shaking under his feet... and when he looked around and saw that a crash was coming and that he would, God forbid, be left without a penny to his soul — he fell into melancholy.
Meanwhile a rumour reached our Jew that in the Holy Land there is abundance; pioneers, real mama's boys, had stood through the very hungriest years and drained swamps, plucked the wild [—] [?], broken stones and created a small place of refuge for persecuted Jews. Our Jew fell deep into thought.
And it came to pass one day, on a fine morning, that our diamond merchant says to his good lady:
— Sarah, my wife, I have heard that in the land of our forefathers Jews live quite freely; why should we stay here? Let us really set off there and in this way save our bit of property and goods.
Sarah was a simple woman who always did her husband's will — so she said: — What do I know? If it pleases you, it suits me; do, my husband, as you understand, and let us leave in a lucky hour.
No sooner said than done: R. arrived in the country in the days of the great „prosperity“. The times of the Second and Third Aliyah were already forgotten. He found everything ready-made. The country flourished, the orange groves — fit to be gilded, a plot of land — worth pure gold. Our diamond merchant did not think long, planted an orange grove and settled down, as the verse says: „under his vine and under his fig tree“ — as if in father's vineyard... But R. was no Zionist, „who only has his own interests [in mind]“, but truly a Jew with a warm heart, with humanitarian feelings; so he went out to his brothers — the children of Ishmael — and saw how the poor things were struggling; his compassion was stirred — his pity was aroused by their fate, and he took them in and gave them work in his grove.
When his own flesh-and-blood brothers came to him with complaints: — Give us too a bit of work, how can you hide from your own? — R. opened his eyes wide and with a God-fearing little face said this:
— Gentlemen, I am no Zionist; don't pester me with Hebrew labour. It is my grove, my money, my property, and every man shall do what is right in his own eyes — that is how I like it!
So several years passed, until 5696 [1936]. Wild, incited Arabs attacked Jewish fields, burned trees, destroyed human toil and murdered from ambush nurses, old people and children on the roads. Our grove-owner grew troubled in his soul; his workers left him. At night hundreds of trees were uprooted on his estate, and the Arab watchmen did not make a peep, but in the morning they looked [—] [?], and in their eyes smouldered a poisonous [—] little fire [?]...
Then the former diamond merchant remembered Zionism, the pioneers, and turned to the Jewish watchmen in these words: — Comrades, I have sinned. Forgive my sins and send me Jewish young men to guard our grove, our estate, our lives; from this day on I will be good and pious.
The Jewish watchmen, being children of Abraham our father, know that revenge is a disgraceful trait and that a Jewish grove is a Jewish grove; they did not hesitate at all, and in the very midst of the events they went to his estate, which was surrounded by the villages of Miska and Tayibe — the nests of the Arab murderers — and guarded his property.
Three watchmen they were, three comrades set out, and on the very first night one of them — Yechiel Chaimowicz — fell; three — went, two came back.
The watchmen took the clothes stained with the blood of their fallen comrade, dug a grave on the very spot where the Jewish pioneer had fallen, planted a tree and erected a holy gravestone with the inscription: „The blood of Yechiel Chaimowicz, who gave his life defending Hebrew property and the honour of the Yishuv“.
And the comrade watchmen thought: holy shall be this place where their comrade rests, and the stone shall be a sign and memorial to the Jewish grove-owner, which will not let his conscience rest, will forever call and demand: „Here my young life was cut off guarding your property, here I fell — and I loved life so much; let my [—] [?] reward be the Jewish worker — my brother-watchman — working here, where my blood flowed“.
Not much [time] passed; the little tree on the grave had not yet grown, the earth — not yet dried, the wounds — not yet healed, and the Jewish grove-owner turned to an English judge:
— Remove from my field the stone, the gravestone!
By chance he came upon a man with a heart and Jewish feelings, and that man answered him:
— Yes, by law you may demand it [?], but a judge with a conscience will not dare to pronounce such a verdict!
R., however, could not tolerate the gravestone; it was always to him a reminder of sin. And the year had not yet passed — when the grave of the young Jewish pioneer was destroyed, the gravestone — removed, and at once the grove filled up with Arab workers from the village of Miska, where the tracks of Chaimowicz's murderers had led...
And the grove-owner is now content. He can stroll openly and freely in his grove; the gravestone of the Jewish watchman does not cry out — hush, quiet...
• • •
It is no legend I have told you, no tale from the Thousand and One Nights that happened in the Middle Ages! But a true story, which happened in the year 5698, not somewhere beyond the Mountains of Darkness, but in the very heart of the Land of Israel, not far from Jerusalem the Holy City, during the bloody events, in the days of Wauchope, High Commissioner of Judea. And the pious, God-fearing Jews, who always take up the [—] of the Master of the Universe [?], who tremble in mortal fear lest Jerusalem, God forbid, fall into the hands of Zionists — all these Jews did not shudder and did not raise their voice, the bourgeois press was silent, the grove-owners did not see, and the people did not shudder at this deed of Sodom.
• • •
I have told you this little story because it is now a time of soul-searching, both for the individual and for the community. Perhaps someone will be found who will turn to the Jewish grove-owner — by the village of Miska — and write him a serious word about the Jewish grave that was desecrated...
Z. Buszastowiecki [?].

New Guilds — New Worries (On the Draft of the New Guild Law)

For long months now there has been debate about the direction in which the amendment [?] (nowelizacja) of the Industrial Law should go. Two conceptions are clashing [?]: one is represented by the president of the Central Union of Christian Craftsmen, Sgaczyński [?]; the other by the director of the Lublin Chamber of Crafts, Paszyński [?]. The first conception is meant to express the will of the Christian craftsmen; the second claims to be the expression of the country's objective economic and social needs.
—
It is interesting what exactly [?] the contending sides want.
Let us first of all dwell on the project of Director Paszyński, which aroused a tremendous storm [?] in Christian craftsmen's circles, and which, with some improvements, was practically accepted by the ministerial commission and is to serve as material for the government bill.
Under the Industrial Law in force, some 70 trades, which are enumerated in the law, are regarded as crafts. All other industrial occupations not enumerated in the law are regarded as free industries and may be practised without any hindrance.
The new project provides that all entrepreneurs who employ on average 20 workers in their workshops shall be regarded as craftsmen, regardless of whether they produce on their own account or on a merchant's account, whether they work the whole year or only in the season, and whether or not they use mechanical power. One condition is, however, set: the work must be carried on in one's own workshop. In this way home-workers (chałupnicy) too will be regarded as craftsmen and will be subject to all the provisions of the Industrial Law.
All trades subject to the Industrial Law are divided into 3 categories:
a) concessioned;
b) qualified;
c) free.
A. The concessioned craftsmen will include: installers of water mains, sewerage, gas, electricity and central heating; chimney sweeps; printers; persons engaged in repairing weapons; butchers (ritual); bricklayers and carpenters [?] (the last 2 trades only where they undertake all kinds of work; for smaller jobs no concession will be needed).
B) The following will be regarded as qualified craftsmen: tinsmiths, blacksmiths, locksmiths and mechanics, metal turners, joiners, saddlers, bakers, confectioners, butchers and sausage-makers, and hairdressers.
C) All the remaining trades, among them also some 50 trades that until now were regarded as crafts (tailors, shoemakers, painters, glaziers, hatters, milliners, furriers, brush-makers, upholsterers, goldsmiths, engravers, watchmakers, coppersmiths [?], gaiter-makers, bookbinders, photographers, etc.) will belong to the so-called free industries. Tailors and shoemakers may, on the basis of a special ordinance, be regarded as craftsmen in the larger towns.
A concession or a qualification certificate will be obtainable only on the basis of a master's or journeyman's diploma together with confirmation of 3 years of journeyman practice. In addition, a certificate of having completed a general school will be obligatory. In no case will it be possible to be exempted from the duty of presenting the said documents.
To be able to practise a trade that has been classed as a free industry, it is necessary only to register with the Chamber of Crafts, which may not create any difficulties in issuing registration cards. In general, the chambers of crafts become the only institutions entitled to qualify craftsmen and to issue craftsman's cards; their powers are considerably extended.
In principle, all craftsmen entitled to run independent workshops will be permitted to keep apprentices. The industrial authority may, however, at the guild's proposal, withdraw the right to keep apprentices if the workshop is not at a proper level. One may keep as many apprentices as adult workers. Every non-adult worker who does not hold a journeyman's diploma will be regarded as a "terminator" (apprentice). The "apprenticeship" may last from 2 to 5 years, depending on the trade. After that, passing the journeyman's examination will be obligatory. The master is obliged to pay the apprentice's examination fee. Young people who have completed a general school and are at least 14 years old may be accepted as apprentices (until now one had to be 15).
The bill provides for major legal changes in the organisational field of crafts and small industry. The guilds get back, and to an even greater extent, the right to concern themselves with the economic affairs of their members, which was taken from them in 1934. The most important thing, however, is that they are given the possibility of turning themselves into compulsory guilds. It is enough that 2/3 [printed "2—3"] of the members of a guild numbering, say, 15 members decide to turn the guild into a compulsory guild, for the Minister of Commerce, after hearing the opinion of the Chamber of Crafts, to be able to decree that all craftsmen running their workshops within the guild's area must belong to it. In that case only single [?] guilds of each nationality will be able to exist.
It is worth noting that Director Paszyński, in his report, spoke in favour of a quite different solution of the question, which would have been more acceptable to the Jewish craftsmen as well. Likewise he spoke against introducing concessions for some of the crafts.
Only craftsmen whom the law regards as concessioned or qualified may belong to the guilds; those, on the other hand, who belong to the so-called free trades will be able to organise themselves in special associations. The guilds and the associations are placed under the supervision of the chambers of crafts. Oversight over them will be exercised by the voivodeship and not, as until now, by the district offices (starostwa).
Guilds and associations active within the area of 1 voivodeship will be able to form a voivodeship union of guilds or associations.
Such a union will have great prerogatives. It is worth mentioning that the arbitration court at the union will have the right to forbid a craftsman to keep apprentices and even to expel him from the guild, which, where the guild is a compulsory organisation, will entail withdrawing his craftsman's card and forbidding him to run an independent workshop.
These are the most important provisions of the new bill.
The Jewish craftsmen must take a position on these questions, and this must be done as quickly as possible.
TOZ Activity in the Near Future

[Zagłębie — health and welfare; TOZ.]
This year's summer-colony campaign of „TOZ“ [Society for the Protection of the Health of the Jewish Population] was carried out with great success. Thanks to the devoted work of the women's committees at „TOZ“ it was possible to send 134 children from the poorest strata of the Jewish population on summer rest. What benefit the colony brought to the children's health need not be mentioned. It will suffice to stress that the average gain in the children's weight amounted to 2 and a half kilos.
After winding up the colony campaign, „TOZ“ is turning to other, very[?] important tasks. First of all the feeding campaign will be carried out, from which over 400 children of the „Talmud Torah“ and other schools benefit — schools attended by the children of the poorest parents. The breakfasts the children receive at school are often the almost only, or even the only, meal in the whole twenty-four hours. Together with the feeding the children receive cod-liver oil, which is very important for their development. The children are also systematically examined by a „TOZ“ school doctor, and those who need it are sent for treatment. Great attention is also paid to the children's hygienic condition, and for this purpose „TOZ“ has engaged a special school hygienist, who also administers irradiation with the quartz lamp.
Carrying out all these tasks requires considerable funds, but unfortunately the Jewish public in Zagłębie does not show proper interest in the activity of „TOZ“. This may be understandable given the strained situation in which we find ourselves, but the well-understood self-interest of the Jewish population demands that the activity of „TOZ“ finally be properly appreciated and properly supported.
Y. P—d.

Heard and Seen

[Feuilleton — „Heard and Seen“; Zagłębie: the doctors' association, the Będzin–Dąbrowa tram, „Bikur Cholim“ in Old Sosnowiec.]
By Ben Amotz.
Times change...
A short notice appeared this week in our Jewish press in Poland that the doctors' association in Zagłębie, too, has adopted the „Aryan paragraph“.
Reading the notice we thought to ourselves: well, „if there's a wedding, there's also an in-law“. Besides, „what did the sages achieve with their enactment“? Does one first have to bear the title of doctor for that? After all, even ordinary [—] have adopted the „Aryan paragraph“. But my neighbour, who has a strong memory, drew our attention, regarding the notice about the „Aryan paragraph“, to the fact that the resolution adopted deserves a few words about the chief speaker at that „historic“ meeting.
And he, my neighbour, reminds us that at the last Sejm elections a Jewish association in Zagłębie conducted a strong campaign for a certain candidate, a doctor, whom they presented not only as a great democrat but also as a lover of Israel. All these virtues were listed in a special leaflet (if I am not mistaken, also in Yiddish), in which the Jewish masses in Zagłębie were called upon to vote for their candidate, the great lover of Israel.
— Well, so what? What connection does that have with the resolution to exclude the Jewish doctors from the doctors' association? — we ask.
— What indeed? A great connection, one matter with the other — my neighbour answers, and hands me an Endek newspaper which reports at length on the meeting at which the above resolution was adopted.
The report says that „Dr. Reis [?] read a declaration in which it is said, among other things, that no discussion could be allowed on this matter, since it concerns only the benefit of our own, and the opinion of other elements has no significance whatever for him“.
It goes without saying that from a loyal standpoint we have no intention, God forbid, of reproaching the reader of the declaration for his conduct towards his hitherto Jewish colleagues, and perhaps the camp[?] even deserves a „yasher koach“ for the resolution — on the contrary. Let the majority of Jewish doctors, who have until now stood outside the camp, take stock and beat their breasts for not having „kept their own vineyard“. We only want to show how quickly times change: in 1935 the same man wanted to get into the Sejm with the help of Jewish votes, and in 1937 he lectures on the „Aryan paragraph“...
— Times change...
But Jews we are...
What we are telling [—] happened in the tram on the way from Będzin to Dąbrowa.
One of the passengers, a „kosher Aryan woman“, asked for a ticket for 20 groszy. When paying for the ticket she realised she was 10 groszy short, and so she found herself in great embarrassment.
In the carriage there were a great number of non-Jewish passengers, who paid no attention at all to the Christian woman's desperate situation over 10 groszy. The one who came to her aid was precisely a Jew, a complete stranger, who paid the 10 groszy for the ticket.
Seeing this, the well-known verse[?] came to my mind:
— „What we are — we are, but Jews we are! We are indeed „barbarians“, we are excluded from all the „fine“ societies, even the Polish hairdressers' guild no longer wants any dealings with its Jewish colleagues of the trade, but
— a high morality we possess...
Bread for the hungry...
We take part in a meeting of the „Beit Lechem“ section of „Bikur Cholim“ in Old Sosnowiec.
At the meeting a broad discussion is held, in the course of which the prevailing want among the broad Jewish masses comes to expression.
No one discusses broad plans, no stock speeches are delivered — just simply, practically, how to increase „the number of bread-givers“.
— Bread for hungry children.
And the official in charge of the bread vouchers relates:
„On Friday, a scant[?] hour before candle-lighting, I noticed a young man, a very respectable one, walking back and forth in front of my shop. Probably he is waiting — I thought to myself — for someone on business matters; he is[?] after all a merchant.
Only later did I see my great mistake. When I came to the house where I live, the same young man greeted me with a smile; he wants to say something, but [—] cannot, his tongue is as if [—].
— „I... — he barely stammers out — that is, I don't need a favour, but you understand me, I was supposed to get money from a customer, but it is late, I was told[?]; it is even hard for me to say it.
— Young man, speak plainly, it is already time for candle-lighting, say what you want — I said to him.
— You want plain words? It is very hard for me; yes, I only want to ask you to lend me 2 loaves of bread for my family for Shabbat. Well, the whole week one goes hungry [—], but it is Shabbat after all“...

How much does a king earn?

[World — the wealth of kings.] The old tales that kings and princes[?] possess money without measure have ceased. Today there may still be famous treasuries with great treasures among the Indian princes, about which we have no exact information. With today's kings one knows quite precisely how much they own, because their money lies in various factories or in various banks.
We once sat at a press meeting of the Leipzig Fair, and Mr. Stes[?], the editor of the London "Times", gave us certain information on the matter.
The richest of all monarchs is the English one; he received from his country a salary of no less than two million dollars a year, and in addition has an inheritance of about fifty million dollars left by the previous kings. Had the present Duke of Windsor not abdicated the throne, he would have been one of the richest people in the world. Today he must live in exile and has an income of "only" 425 thousand dollars a year, on which he, "poor thing", has to get by.
The former Spanish King Alfonso was in his time the greatest speculator in [—]ations[?]; in this way he made himself so great a fortune that he could buy more than a hundred large houses in America, from which he now draws his livelihood in exile.
The fortune of the Dutch Queen has grown fivefold in the last twenty years; today she holds[?] the greater part of all the rubber plantations and oil wells in the Indies [the Dutch East Indies], and earns a great fortune from them.
In addition, the Dutch royal family receives a salary of 160 thousand pounds a year.
The murdered[?] Yugoslav King Alexander left an inheritance of five million pounds. He was the largest vineyard owner and the largest partner in all the Yugoslav mines of gold, silver, copper and so on and so forth. The income from his businesses brings in up to two thousand pounds every day. In addition they receive a salary of 58 million dinars a year, of which they spend only a part.
The Egyptian King is there the largest milk supplier in the Near[?] East and has a lot of money lying in the Italian banks.
The Romanian King learned, while living in exile, to be a miser. From his salary and from small stock-exchange speculations he has already managed to save a million dollars, which lies in his name in the Swiss banks.
The Albanian King has a salary of only 12[?] thousand dollars a year, but he is a partner in several Italian companies, from which he has managed to accumulate[?] 300 thousand pounds in cash in the banks of Switzerland.
Only the Bulgarian King has no fortune and lives on his salary, which amounts to five thousand dollars a month, and on the interest[?] of his wife's [property?], which also brings in five thousand dollars every month. With these ten thousand dollars a month he has to get by.
Z. Haber. Chin[?].
"The Good Earth".

[Będzin — cinema; film review.] (Film review.)
The Chinese Wall, which has stood almost as long as the Jewish exile and which hid from us the true face of China — has fallen.
And we saw a horror, a terror to tell what we saw.
A terror, agitated[?] thoughts[?], floods our calm and our cold-bloodedness.
Tears choke, conscience stings. Questions arise.
But how does one clothe these thoughts in words?
You see thousands, tens of thousands of starving, languishing and benighted people, young and old, women and children, wandering from one region to another across distant fields dried out by the sun, fleeing from hunger. Many do not endure it, and indeed their road is strewn with the skeletons of those who fell on the way. Flocks[?] of birds of prey accompany the wanderers, impatient[?] but sure that sooner or later they will after all fall between their sharply curved beaks.
You see how a mother strangles with her own hands her newborn baby, so as not to see how it must[?] writhe[?] in the torments of hunger.
You see how people cook in pots... earth, yes, plain earth, to still their hunger.
You see how parents sell their daughters, to still the hunger, at least for a while, with the pennies they receive.
You see how a wife laments over the dead body of her husband, who could not endure the penal-servitude labour in the big city. The first question of those who share her grief is where the man worked — so as to snatch his place.
But if certain social moments of the film may still be doubted, it is impossible to count the numerous individual-psychological pearls of art that lie scattered literally at every step in this rare work of art. Just recall the scene with the ox, or the scene where the father catches his son in a love affair with his stepmother, and so on and so on. This we undoubtedly owe to the deep and spirited artistic performance of the two main heroes, Paul Muni and Luise Rainer.
A surprise, however, and a true, wonderful revelation for us is his partner in the picture — Luise Rainer as the slave and peasant woman O-Lan: as a quiet, submissive wife, as a silent, suffering mother. Such realism, such an artistic embodiment of lived experience[?] [—] the cinema has not yet given us until now. Her manner of acting in this film is so strong and genuine, so clear and convincing, that she takes first place in the picture. In Luise Rainer's acting there is no trace of overacting (charge), not a single cheap effect...
You feel how the actress lives in her role; you believe her, you trust her every caress[?] of her longing, frightened eyes, her every twitch of her thin, pointed shoulder... What artistic power one must possess in order, like Luise Rainer, to forget oneself completely and pour oneself body and soul into the role of an enslaved Chinese woman!
A [—] film, a film of full value in all its scenes from beginning to end, without any reservations or excuses.
The artistic value of the film is beyond all doubt.
Seeing the film "The Good Earth" at the "Nowości" in Będzin is much more than entertainment; it is a genuine, deep artistic experience.
Y. P.

Oneg Shabbat — Torah Sayings, Remarks and Anecdotes on This Week's Portion

[Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings and Hasidic tales on parashat Vayera.]
Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Vayera
—o—
a) "And he saw them, and ran to meet them" (18:2)
Hospitality is greater than receiving the Divine Presence. Shabbat 127.
The commandment of hospitality is greater even than receiving the Shekhinah, because — said R. Moshe Leib of Sasów — the Shekhinah is everywhere and one can always receive it, "the whole earth is full of His glory"; hospitality, however, cannot be fulfilled at every moment — not every moment offers the opportunity — and therefore hospitality takes precedence.
* * *
The Torah describes the commandment of hospitality in a way that is really no commandment at all: according to the midrash these were angels, who need nothing to eat. This teaches us that in charity and hospitality the main thing is only the good intention of wishing to help someone in need; and even if it turns out that the other person did not need the good deed at all, the commandment is a commandment. R. Yisrael, the Rebbe of Grodzisk.
—o—
b) "And they did eat" (ibid., 8)
R. Yisraelche of Ruzhin once met his in-law R. Chaim of Koziv [?]. R. Chaim ate as usual, while R. Yisraelche merely touched the food, tasted a little and immediately pushed it away, for that was his custom. R. Chaim asks him:
"Why does the in-law eat nothing?"
"Because," answers the Ruzhiner, "when we came down to this world we made a condition with the body that we would not let it enjoy anything..."
Hearing this, R. Chaim pushed away his food too. The Ruzhiner asks him:
"And you, in-law, why don't you eat? Did you, too, make some condition with the body?"
"No," answers R. Chaim, "we made no condition at all with our body; but this is why I don't eat: when Friday night comes, two angels accompany us home from prayers, and at home we welcome them with 'Shalom aleichem, ministering angels.' Right away we dismiss them with 'Go in peace,' because with angels who do not eat it is not pleasant to sit together at a meal..."
* * *
R. Naftali of Ropczyce once said in jest:
Ever since the angels transformed themselves into humans at Abraham's, we take leave of the angels on Friday night even before Kiddush: we say to them "Come in peace" and at once "Go in peace," because, God forbid, they might again transform themselves into humans and this time really eat, and not merely pretend to eat as at Abraham's...
—o—
c) "And Sarah laughed within herself" (ibid., 12)
The daughter of R. Shmuel of Kamionka was barren. Once the tzaddik R. Rafael of Bershad came to Kamionka; she went to him and asked him to pray for her that she be helped with children. He said:
"A charm (segula) for children is joy."
The daughter told this to R. Shmuel, and he said to her: the segula is found in the Torah, in the Prophets and in the Writings. In the Torah: "And Sarah laughed," and after the joy she bore Isaac; in the Prophets: "Sing, O barren one"; in the Writings: "a joyful mother of children."
The daughter asks R. Shmuel:
"If Sarah laughed for the sake of a segula, why then was God angry with her?"
R. Shmuel answers her:
"Because when a rebbe promises, one indeed needs a segula as well; but when God promises, she should not have had to resort to segulas first — and that was her sin..."
—o—
d) "The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah is great, and their sin is very grievous"
When a person commits a sin for the first time, there is still an excuse for him: "his inclination overpowered him" — he could not overcome the evil inclination. But when it is a case of "he sinned and repeated it," when he hardly has any pleasure from the sin any more and still does it ("once he sinned and repeated it, it becomes to him as if permitted" — he has no more pleasure from the sin than from something permitted), such a sin is far graver.
"The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah is great" — their sins were of the category of "he sinned and repeated it," and therefore "their sin is very grievous"; that is why their sin was heavy... R. Pinchas HaLevi Horowitz.
—o—
e) "And the two angels came to Sodom" (19:1)
"Earlier he called them men? With Abraham, whose strength was great and angels were as frequent with him as men, he called them men; and with Lot he called them angels." Rashi.
The only thing noticeable about the angels was "that they showed honour to one another" (see Bereshit Rabbah, section 48 [?]). For Abraham this was a simple matter, and he took them for decent people, "worthy persons"; but Lot, the judge of Sodom — he simply could not grasp how ordinary [?] people would show honour to one another, and therefore he took them for angels, for as plain humans he could not imagine them. Yalkut Yehuda.
—o—
f) "And Lot sat in the gate of Sodom" (ibid.)
That day they had appointed him judge over them. Rashi.
At the time when Jews were not allowed to live in Petersburg, many Jews kept themselves there by bribing the officials. And there was there a censor [?], an apostate, Wasman, who used to inform on the Jews who were in Petersburg.
Once R. Yitzchak Elchanan met him and rebuked him for informing on Jews.
"What do you mean, informing?" Wasman flares up. "You surely know, Rabbi, that 'the law of the kingdom is the law'; and if I tell the government that such-and-such a Jew gave an official a bribe, I am only fulfilling 'the law of the kingdom'..."
R. Yitzchak Elchanan answers him:
"On the verse 'And Lot sat in the gate of Sodom' Rashi says: 'That day they had appointed him judge over them.' What does Rashi mean by this? Well, the Torah tells that the people of Sodom were wicked and sinners and had barbaric laws — so how could one exist there at all? Only that there, just as in Russia, one bribed the high officials. But Lot, brought up at Abraham's in honesty and justice, who surely took no bribes — how could he govern in Sodom as a judge? To this Rashi says 'that day they appointed him judge': he was judge for only one day, and when Lot, the honest judge, began within one day to enforce Sodom's laws strictly, God immediately had to send an angel to overturn Sodom..."
In Zakopane.

A Jew with a Bundle

What's new? How's business?

[Humour and satire — “Der Kokh-lefl”; Sosnowiec.] Today's “Philanthropists”.
A true story about a Sosnowiec rich man.
The Sosnowiec rich man K. says to his wife:
— Look, today someone slipped me a counterfeit złoty.
— I have an idea, — the wife replied, — when a poor man comes, give him that złoty as alms.
— No less than that... a whole złoty as alms?! — the rich man grimaced.

[Humour and satire — “Der Kokh-lefl”.] A Question at the Doctor's.
A Jewish woman came to a doctor-rabbiner [a university-trained rabbi] with a ritual question about a slaughtered chicken in whose gizzard she had found a needle.

— I am not a rabbi, — the rabbiner replied, — I am a doctor.
Hearing these words, the woman said with a sour face:

[Humour and satire — “Der Kokh-lefl”; Będzin — winter relief.] The “Fortunate” Glaziers' Trade.

For the current winter-relief campaign at “Beys Lekhem” [the bread-for-the-poor society] statistics are being compiled of the trades from which the poor are recruited. While looking over the list, the secretary says to the chairman:

— It's a clear matter, — the chairman replied, — for a hundred years the glaziers haven't had as good a season as last winter.

Two Generations.

[Serialized story — the Odessa pogrom of 1905; installment 2.]
S. Winitzer.
An astonishing story of a pogromshchik [pogrom participant] who became an ardent friend of the Jews. (2)

The timber merchant, a Jew named Shrayber, read through the letter and gave Leybl a position — 25 roubles a month with full board. Leybl was to be an assistant to the forest clerk [„vald-shrayber“]. Hirsh Ber thanked the merchant warmly and went back home.
In the letter the rabbi had written to the merchant that he should keep an eye on the boy so that he could not travel home, at any rate not before a year had passed.
After Leybl left, Maria simply pined away with longing. Whole days she wept and lamented. Nikolai and his wife simply feared for her life, so he wrote to his American brother to send her a ship's ticket, so that she could go to America. A few weeks later a ship's ticket arrived for her. Weeping, Maria left the village[?] and went off to America. That was in the month of September 1905.
After Maria had left and Leybl too was not at home, the two families, the Jewish and the Christian, gradually made peace with each other; but Hirsh Leyb more than once told Sore Beyle that their neighbour Nikolai was quietly nursing a bitter hatred of them.
— The goy carries hatred for us in his heart — Hirsh Ber said to his wife — and as soon as he is able, he will take revenge on us. Listen to me, Sore Beyle, let us move away from here.
— What notions you get — Sore Beyle replied — so what if people quarrel sometimes! They quarrelled, and afterwards they made it up. I will not move to another flat because of that.
— I only hope I am lying[?] — Hirsh Ber said[?] to Sore Beyle.
It was in the stormy year 1905, when, right after the revolutionary uprisings, a series of pogroms against Jews began in Russia. The Jews of Odessa were also afraid of a pogrom. At the end of summer, after the High Holidays, the Jewish community of Odessa decided to do something and sent a delegation to the gradonachalnik [city governor]. But he would not receive them.
That was a definite sign that something was brewing in the city.
At once a Jewish self-defence of several hundred young Jews was organized. Many Poles[?] also signed up for the self-defence.
The days were very restless. All sorts of rumours spread through the city. The „Black Hundreds“ [„shvarts sotnikes“] even boasted that they would carry out a slaughter of Jews such as the world had never yet seen.
One evening Sore Beyle, pale as death, said to her husband:
— Hirsh Ber, I see that you were right. Today I saw something that filled me with terror. I went in to bring Katya a little barley, and I saw on the floor a whole pile of axes, hammers, knives and long pieces of iron. When Katya noticed me looking at it, she grabbed a rag and covered it all. She herself turned as pale as the wall. I said nothing[?] and handed her the barley. She did not want to take the food[?]. Before I left, she said to me:
— Be careful, Sore Beyle, they are preparing a pogrom. But you need not be afraid. They will not touch you.
Hirsh Ber and Sore Beyle had already decided to move out of the house. But they could not easily find a suitable flat, and before they knew it the 17th of October arrived, when the Tsar issued the constitution, and on that day the „Black Hundreds“ had organized[?] pogroms in many Jewish towns and in Odessa too.
On the 17th of October, early in the morning, the pogrom broke out. Hirsh Leyb shut the workshop, and he with Sore Beyle and Ester locked themselves in at home.
All day it was quiet in their courtyard. Only in the evening did they begin[?] to tear at the door. A gang of pogromshchiks broke the door open and came in. Their leader was none other than the neighbour Nikolai. Among the pogromshchiks were also Katya and Sergei.
Katya carried a big axe with her and at once set about plundering. Whatever came to her hand she put into a sack. Several bestial hooligans dragged Sore Beyle into the bedroom, and she did not leave their hands alive. They murdered her in the most bestial manner. In another corner, further on[?], Nikolai raised an axe at Hirsh Ber. Nikolai was drunk and wild with bloodlust.
But Hirsh Ber seized him by the hand and begged him:
— Nikolai, remember God, have mercy! Your neighbour, your friend!
— Ah, no mercy! — Nikolai, drunk, shouted — I have waited long for this day. You insulted my niece!
And he brought the axe down on Hirsh Ber's head. Hirsh Ber fell dead in a river of blood.
In the tumult Sergei grabbed little Esterl, hid her in the kitchen behind the stove and said to her:
— Stay here! Don't go out. Otherwise they will murder you. Don't scream and don't say a word. I will bring you food.
When Nikolai came in with the axe to finish off Sore Beyle, he found that his „friends“ had already done the job for him.
After three days of murder and robbery the pogrom subsided.
Sergei kept his word and for all three days smuggled in food and drink for Ester, each time warning her not to leave her hiding place.
When the pogrom was over, a committee to help the pogrom victims went round the pogrom-stricken houses. When they saw the devastation in Hirsh Leyb's house, they took Esterl away to an orphanage and prepared[?] for the burial of the murdered husband and wife.
But before the dead were taken away, Katya, by now sobered up, went in to take a look at the ruined flat of the Nayvarts[?], saw Sore Beyle lying on the floor with her belly slit open and stuffed with feathers, and was so terrified by the sight that she kept fainting the whole day.
In the evening, when Nikolai came home, Sergei told him what had happened. Nikolai said:
— The zhids [„zhides“, a slur for Jews] deserved it!
— But I saved one — Sergei barely stammered out.
— Whom?
— Esterl.
— What have you done? Who told you to? Now she will throw the blame on us.
(To be continued).

Sosnowiec — Doctors' Association in Zagłębie Adopts the "Aryan Paragraph"

[Sosnowiec — Physicians; antisemitism.]
Even converts may not belong as members...
On Thursday evening[?] an extraordinary meeting of the members of the Doctors' Association in Zagłębie took place.
On the agenda were point 7 of the statute concerning the "Aryan paragraph" and the election of delegates to the Polish[?] congress.
As we have learned, the "historic" meeting proceeded as follows:
The meeting opened at 8.30 sharp. The chairman reads out the agenda of the meeting and asks who wishes to sign up to speak. Then Dr. Weinzieher announces that he is signing up to speak. The floor, however, is given not to Dr. Weinzieher but to Dr. Weiss, who reads a declaration stating, among other things, that the amendment of point 7 of the statute should be adopted without any discussion, because "to hear the opinion of other elements has no significance whatsoever for us", and he proposes adopting the following amended wording of point 7 of the statute:
"A member of the Zagłębie Doctors' Association may be a doctor who is a Polish citizen and a Christian by birth. Doctors who do not meet these conditions may be admitted exclusively by the executive committee of the Main Board, on the proposal of the board of the district concerned."
After the declaration, in which [sic] Dr. Weinzieher was not given the floor, they proceeded to the vote. The vote was by roll call according to the list, and among the 58 non-Jewish doctors there was only one single one, Dr. Malicki, who had the courage to vote against the proposal together with the 27 Jewish doctors. It is interesting that among the doctors who declared themselves for the "Aryan paragraph" there is a convert from Zawiercie, who does not realise that he himself may not belong to the association, since he is not a Christian by birth...
As we are informed, among those who voted for the "Aryan paragraph" are some who have a considerable number of Jewish patients.

Conference on the Kashrut Question / and further Sosnowiec items

[Sosnowiec — Kashrut, community.]
In the kehilla premises a conference took place devoted to the kashrut question in our town. The purpose of the conference was to hear the opinion of the rabbinate as to whether it is necessary for the rabbinic decisors (morei hora'ah) to be present in the slaughterhouse during slaughter, and about engaging trusted supervisors (ne'emanim) in the licensed butcher shops.
The first to speak on the question was Rabbi Schwarz[?], who declared that he holds full supervision over kashrut in the slaughterhouse.
The moreh tzedek Gliksman says that he is the rabbi, the supervision in the slaughterhouse is due to him, and not to "him".
During the "discussion" a letter was read from the shochet Federman[?], who declared that in the whole fight over kashrut only those are involved who have their own interests and seek their own benefit.
The conference brought no positive results. It was decided to call a second meeting, to which representatives of the "shtiblekh" are to be invited.

[Sosnowiec — Trade; signboards.]
As is known, under pressure from the Polish economic organisations it has been decreed that the signboards of shops and other enterprises must state the first name and surname of the owner.
The decree was sent through the [?] Ministry [probably Industry and Commerce] to the merchants' organisations with a deadline: by 1 November [listopad] the signboards must be duly supplemented.

[Sosnowiec — Economic institutions.]

Campaign to Combat Begging

[Będzin — society and welfare.] At the premises of the Small Traders' Association a meeting was held devoted to the fight against street begging, which is a plague for Jewish society in general and for the merchants in particular. After councillor Mr. Kiwer gives a number of explanations on the matter, among them that the statutes have already been approved by the voivode, a committee is elected whose task is to carry out the technical work of the campaign. Information on the matter is given at the Small Traders' Association, and also at the House Owners' Association.
Courses for Bookkeepers

[Będzin — trade associations.] At the new premises of the Bookkeepers' Association (Modrzejowska 26) a larger members' meeting took place with the participation of representatives from Katowice, Chorzów, Mysłowice and Będzin. At the meeting the delegates to the second Bookkeepers' Congress in Warsaw gave a report on the resolutions adopted in connection with the bill that is to be dealt with at the next session of the Sejm.
Having heard the report, it is decided to introduce preparatory courses for members of the Bookkeepers' Association. Information on this and other questions is given every day from 20:00 to 21:30 at the premises.

Impressive celebrations in Kielce in honour of Marshal Rydz-Śmigły

[Kielce — state.] Last Saturday Marshal Rydz-Śmigły stayed in Kielce. Marshal Śmigły took part in the ceremony at which the city of Kielce presented a banner to the Second Artillery Regiment.
In honour of the visit of the distinguished guest a series of impressive celebrations took place, in which many thousands of people took part; they greeted the Marshal ceremoniously and gave him enthusiastic ovations.
In the course of Saturday various celebrations took place with the participation of the Marshal.
In the afternoon a ceremonial session of the city council was held, during which the Marshal delivered a longer speech and thanked the city for the honorary citizenship and for the honour that had been shown him.
At all the celebrations the Marshal was accompanied by the Kielce voivode Dr. Dziadosz, the city president Artwiński and others, and high military and administrative officials.
Marshal Śmigły also took part in the celebrations of Hetman Stefan Czarniecki in Czarnca, beyond Włoszczowa.
General meeting of the district merchants' association

[Kielce — economy.] On the 31st of this month a general meeting of the Jewish district merchants' association in Kielce will take place. The preparations for the general meeting are in full swing.
The reorganisation work of the association, as well as the organising of the various sections, is being directed by the head of the association, Mr. Józef Rechtszaft [?].
The Keren Kayemet committee in Kielce reorganised

[Kielce — Zionism.] In connection with the great propaganda campaign for the Keren Kayemet, which was recently proclaimed by Director Bistritzky, the well-known Zionist activist, editor Cyncynatus, stayed in Kielce this week.
Editor Cyncynatus held a series of meetings with all the Zionist groupings and informed them about the urgent tasks of the Keren Kayemet in the present hour, so fraught with responsibility for Zionism.
In the presence of editor Cyncynatus the local Keren Kayemet committee was reorganised. A new board was elected, to which belong the most important Zionist activists of all tendencies.
7 chalutzim arrested for calling for shops to close on the day of the protest strike against the ghetto

[Kielce — antisemitism.] On Tuesday, in the morning hours, the police arrested 7 chalutzim [pioneers] of the local Borochov kibbutz, who had called for the Jewish shops to be closed in protest against the introduction of the shameful ghetto in the institutions of higher learning.
As these lines are being written (Wednesday night) the seven arrested have still not been released.
Because a big market day takes place in Kielce every Tuesday, not all Jewish shops were closed. On the main street all the Jewish shops were closed.
Warsaw appoints a commissioner in the artisans' association...

[Kielce — artisans.] The central artisans' federation in Warsaw has dissolved the board of the Kielce artisans' association. A Kielce resident and former parnas [kehilla councillor] in Dąbrowa, Mr. N. Granatsztejn [?], has been appointed temporary commissioner of the Kielce artisans.
As we are informed, the legally elected artisans' board does not want to hand over power to the new commissioner. It will do so if it is compelled to by the authorities.
Just like that, upon my life, there was a plan that the Kielce artisans should elect a delegate and send him to Warsaw as commissioner of the Folkist artisans' federation...
In any case, Dąbrowa has luck. Once again a parnas has become commissioner in the voivodeship city, Kielce...
Mazel tov to you, Panie Komisarzu [Mr. Commissioner]!...

Why Is Nothing Further Being Done?

[Będzin — artisans — opinion.] (On uniting the artisans' organisations in Będzin).
Anyone who knows the history of the negotiations to unite the Jewish artisans in Będzin will admit that things had already reached the point where the negotiations were about to break a record; but, as it turned out, the talks ended in nothing. There were meetings, conferences and so on[?], and in the end... everything remained... as before.
People did believe, and everyone was sure, that the union was an accomplished fact. Unfortunately, however, the sad truth is that nothing further has come of the union, although nobody wants to believe what[?] is being said[?]; when two Jewish craftsmen meet, the first question is: what about the union, has it come about? Everyone is sure that the talks between the sides are still being conducted.
And it is indeed no wonder that nobody wants to believe any more that the union has remained, for the future too, a utopia. Even those who conducted the negotiations took the matter seriously, because they knew that the question can no longer be handled as it once was, that the union can no longer be a game for fooling somebody; everyone knows that the union of the Jewish craftsmen has now become a question of Jewish craft in Poland.
The so strongly organised Endek [National-Democratic] antisemitism has created a united front against the Jewish economic positions.
Day after day one hears more cries from the ruined Jewish artisan workshops in the provinces.
Hundreds of Jewish artisan workshops are forced to liquidate, and their owners with their families come into the town[?] to starve.
From all sides calls for help arrive at the Jewish artisans' organisation, and one is at a loss[?] how to help: can an organisation that is itself broken and splintered accomplish anything for the community? Can such an organisation have any outward influence whatsoever?
And yet, all the more[?], the question: how could it again be allowed that the union of the Jewish artisans in Zagłębie, which was supposed to serve as a motive for consolidation, should again come to nothing? Especially at a time when one sees[?] that the Christian artisans' organisations in the country have organised themselves into a single organisation, and that solely in order to create the front against the Jewish craftsman.
As it is explained to us, the union has not come about now because of fear. One organisation was afraid that the other would snatch the primacy from it, because they would carry[?] into it[?] — take over — the party influence.
For anyone who knows the situation of the Jewish craftsman at the present day, and who seriously intends to find the way out by which to improve it, this motive (and unfortunately it is the true one) is a ridiculous one, because, first, today, when any question whatsoever of the Jewish craftsman is being dealt with, the party question can no longer come into consideration; in this case only one party comes into consideration — the Jews in Poland.
The antisemitic wave makes no exception between the artisan who is a Zionist, a Folkist or of some other party affiliation, and therefore — in creating the general artisans' organisation — the party element can no longer come into consideration.
The fear of the primacy being seized is also almost[?] an excuse — greatly exaggerated, for who wants to take anything from whom, and who can here, if one may say so, gain or lose, and what? It is a simple question of Jewish craftsmen uniting, artisans with artisans, who have workshops and belong to two Jewish organisations, which likewise have nothing that anyone would want to take from them; or is it perhaps a matter of great fortunes that one wants to take from the other!
And therefore the negotiations must be continued, all the motives that hinder the work must be removed, and with a little seriousness and good will the union can be realised.
The Jewish Artisans' Union in Będzin, as one of the first in Poland, must continue to set the tone for good organisation, and the union in Będzin, too, will surely serve as an example and give the impetus for the union of all Jewish economic organisations in Zagłębie.
***
Union of the Two Merchants' Organisations

[Będzin — merchants — opinion.]
More than once we have touched, in the columns of our newspaper, on the question of the necessity of both Jewish merchants' organisations in Będzin. We hold that such a phenomenon is harmful in general, and particularly now, at a time of Endek [National Democratic] assault on the very existence of the Jewish merchant class — then a uniform line of union of all the active forces is surely absolutely necessary.
If the existence of two merchants' organisations perhaps still had some justification at the time when the tax commissions were active, to which both organisations sent their members and thus enlarged the representation of the merchant class on the commissions — that system has now been abolished, and the members of the appeal commissions are, after all, not sent by the merchants' organisations but are appointed by the Chamber of Commerce; thus this argument now falls away entirely.
There remain, then, other considerations which are, in our opinion, second-rate in comparison with the main task that such an organisation has to fulfil now.
Surely we cannot justify the existence of two organisations merely on account of the independent appearances at the various elections — beginning with the Sejm, the Chamber of Commerce, municipal self-government, the kehillas — or on account of ambition for representation, or interventions [?], or on account of second-rate motives. Surely the union of the economic interests of the merchant class, which forms so large a part of Polish Jewry, must not be put in the shade because of these personal ambitions — particularly now, at a time when the merchant class must fight against the means that threaten its existence.
This question is surely clear to everyone, and the fussing over the "darling son" only serves to diminish the role of the Jewish merchant class.
Besides, we have after all seen with our own eyes (on the 8th of this month, on the Day of the Polish Merchant) in Sosnowiec [?] the big Polish merchant marching together in one rank with the owner of the small shop, and the common intentions [?] of the two of them are surely so clear that they need no explanation; and indeed it was then that the question stood before us in all its nakedness: and now, too, shall the curse of disunity still reign among us?
This is not the time to look for the guilty; besides, such a search would not bring us nearer to the goal but, on the contrary, take us further from it.
One thing, however, is clear to us: never yet has the necessity of a union of the two merchants' organisations been as urgent as now, and therefore we want the leaders of the Jewish merchant class in Będzin to remember well that in unity lies strength.
Y. B.
