On the Far Side of Reason...

[Feuilleton / sketch — a visit to an asylum for the mentally ill.] (From a visit to an institution for the mentally ill in Brzozowice [?].)

We are among mentally ill people who have a particular weakness for questions of a philosophical-ethical and metaphysical character.

We have entered the first room, where the people deafen one another [?] with their strange droning.

It roars, it is tumult, it is clamour. One man declaims some poem “for himself”. A second delivers a speech, with pathos, with gesticulation; a third quietly murmurs some prayer, goggling his eyes toward heaven, and so too the rest. And I thought to myself meanwhile: all this pathos, which is being spent here on nothing, unproductively, could surely among us, the lucid ones, be put to quite productive use. How greatly, for instance, would our communal activists relish this enthusiasm!

Off to one side sits a young man, making notes in a copybook. I tried to take a look at his writing, but he at once asked me “to be polite”, and explained along with it why I have no right at all to look into “his thoughts”.

— I am — he says — the secretary of this ward, and I bear the whole responsibility. I must always record the most important occurrences, both those that happen in heaven and those that take place on earth. Just now I am recording the heavenly events. You want to know what is new up there? The angel Michael was shot dead yesterday because he wanted to desert to the earth and... become a human being... ha-ha-ha. Among you, “becoming a human being” [a mentsh] is a high rung, but in heaven it is one of the worst things. Perhaps you would like to read my latest poems?

And he began to declaim a kind of mishmash of half phrases, of scraps of lines, of bits of thoughts.

A few paces farther on we came upon an elderly Jew. He sat with his eyes closed and, never ceasing to sway, kept murmuring something quietly the whole time. I tried to draw near him and put my ear to him, to catch some word, but it was impossible.

A neighbour of his — also mentally ill, it goes without saying — explained to me that the old man is reciting Psalms and praying that the world should not overturn: as long as he recites Psalms, the world will hold; but the moment he stops reciting, the world will have to perish at once, be swallowed up in the earth, and so on.

We walk on and come into a second room. Here there are creatures of quite another kind.

— Tell me, my dear young man — one of the patients turns to me — have you perhaps met my only little son, my Nocheml? You know, don't you, that I had an only little son, a treasure — may I suffer in his stead, for his sick, cold little bones. Well, but God took him away from me; have you ever heard of such a murder? What does he have against me, that God of yours? Does he need to play with souls? Well, is he so short of souls up there in heaven, that he has to rob us down here of our dearest and most beloved little fledglings? Ah, he loves young flesh, the “Old One”; he wants only children's souls — but I will not give in, I will...

A horror seizes your soul when you come into this living hell. They seem to be people like everyone else: they talk, laugh, weep, eat, philosophise — and many of them speak with such sharp-wittedness, with such refined humour, with such biting satire, they show erudition in various fields of learning, and yet...

— I am — a young man introduces himself to me — the representative of the heavenly League of Nations on earth; I am the Messiah's little nephew [?], and I have an order “from above” to establish order on earth, among men, by fair means or foul. If you obey me, well and good; if not, woe and misery to you and to your children and children's children... I will send down upon you planets that spit human blood. Do you hear? And I will open the heavens, and whole oceans of light will flood you; wherever you turn, mighty waves of light will meet you and beat upon your weak eyes. I will annihilate the night, and you will long for a little twilight, for a bit of night-darkness, but — a fig for you! Ha-ha-ha! Night is what they fancy! Such fine, respectable people must have only light, only day!

And I will unlock the Palace of Honour and cast all the treasures down upon the earth; the earth will choke [?] on the abundance of honour. Be he a nobody, a little man, a good-for-nothing — he will bathe in honour, he will guzzle whole bowlfuls of honour, and all the while groan with pleasure and growl with contentment, like a beast when it devours its prey [?].

And the Treasury of Money I will open too, and gold coins will pour down on your heads, gold coins — big as stones, heavy — as your thoughts, and coarse as your hearts, and you will walk about pleased with yourselves, with the honour that you have; each one will think that the other has no honour at all [?], and as for the heaps of gold lying in his hiding-places — you will rummage and pry with your nasty little eyes. You will look for more honour, for more money, and when you do not find it you will flare up with rage and burn one another alive.

The young man sank down powerless, having been greatly weakened by his “prophecy”. His eyes, half closed, half open, gazed somewhere into a little world of which we, the lucid ones, presumably have no conception, and a faint smile slowly spread over his face.

Only — what difference does it make what a madman can think and see? The main thing, after all, is that we, the lucid ones, should not, God forbid, be infected with all these manias, with all these insane thoughts and moods; for say what you will — honour is not something one can wave away, and money is no trifle either...

Y. Weinstein.
The Great Man of Simplicity

[Będzin — in memoriam.]
By Yehuda Yefet.
(On the first yahrzeit (16 Tevet) of R' Yehoshele Telner of blessed memory, Ravad [head of the rabbinical court] in Będzin)
It is a great rung, simplicity. All kinds of blessed talents, such as sharpness of mind, a deep intellect and others, are only steps towards the highest peak, which only a few are privileged to reach: simplicity.
A Baal Shem Tov, who climbed[?] to such lofty heights, fathomed such depths and embraced such breadths, came at the edge of his earthly, spiritually stormy life to the conclusion that after all the greatest faith is: the simple faith, simplicity.
When one strays, when one is carried on restless waves under thick fogs — there comes brooding, which often leads to crippling[?]. But when one sees God and the world with the clear, washed eyes of a child, everything is so simple, so honest and so pure.
And such eyes that Jew possessed.
And that, after all, is what our Torah Jews lack: they have shunned simplicity, turned life into pilpul[?], and so the simple life has shunned them. That is their tragedy and ours.
* * *
R' Yehoshele of blessed memory was in his essence a misnaged.
Sh. Gorelik once wrote that unfortunately there is among us too much veneration for the Hasid, for the seething and the enthusiastic one, and that the misnaged is passed over in silence[?], with his calm and steadfastness, which have majesty in them.
And he is right, very right. The Divine Presence of majesty is found only where there is calm and steadfastness, where there is simplicity.
And just such a majestic calm looked out of his eyes. A misnagdic calm, at first sight — a dry one, but when you looked more closely into that calm, you found there a warmth of heart, a welling[?] warmth of heart.
* * *
And simplicity and honesty are sisters of one flesh. How R' Yehoshele could not bear any injustice! How his pure conscience seethed on hearing of some injustice. How he suffered physically from it! And how he could not imagine that a person should commit some wrong — out of his great faith in man he believed so little in injustice.
More than once, when I see the cynical human injustice that hems in[?] our whole life, I recall the holy trembling of the great man of simplicity and great upright Jew at the sight of some falsehood or wrong.
Not for nothing did Hasidim mark as a rung: "an erlekher yid" [an upright, God-fearing Jew].
A great upright Jew he was, R' Yehoshele of blessed memory!
* * *
When one remembers him — one remembers a bygone generation, a generation that will not come back. Beside such people one walked through life more calmly, more surely, and beside such people the world had a purer[?] face.
How Were Prices Regulated in Former Times?

[Feuilleton — economics and history.]
Today people already know what to do when they want to regulate prices on the world market; today it is already known that one can throw millions of sacks of coffee into the sea, so that no one should get any benefit from them. Today it is known that with wheat, for example, one can fire the boilers of the railways and of the ships, that cows which give a lot of milk must be slaughtered, and the carcasses thrown on the fields instead of manure.
Today people are already "civilised" and can employ all the "means of culture", so as not, heaven forbid, to bring about cheapness in the world.
But hundreds of years ago people still had to resort to other means.
In the archive of the Leipzig Fair there are records of how prices used to be regulated.
In the year 1512 many trees bearing cloves and all kinds of spices were found on several Portuguese islands. At that time spices were very expensive, because they grew only in the Dutch Indies, and the Dutch company [khavruse], to whom the spice fields belonged, used to demand a fortune for spices.
So the company at once founded a joint firm which was to occupy itself with the Portuguese spice forests and take care [?] that, heaven forbid, the prices not be spoiled. The King of Portugal, too, joined this partnership, so that the company could do with the forests whatever it pleased.
So they at once began to tear the spice trees out by the roots, to burn the spice forests, so that no trace of them should remain. In this way it would be possible to keep the prices high.
But the local population, the half-wild tribes, did not let their forests be burned. So the Portuguese governors who ruled there did indeed begin to wage a war against the inhabitants.
In the region of Ternate [?], for example (a Portuguese island), 35 thousand spice trees were burned. But at the same stroke 894 men of the local natives, who did not want to allow the spice trees to be burned, were slaughtered there.
In the year 1617 the governor of the Portuguese islands informed his king that he would not rest until all the spice forests had gone up in smoke, even if the last native should have to perish in the process.
That is how easy it was in those days to regulate the price of spices throughout the whole world...
Z. Haber, Vienna.
The Keren HaYesod Campaign in Progress

[Będzin — Keren HaYesod.] The Będzin campaign for Keren HaYesod reached, in the past week, the highest point of its development. Almost all of the most prominent wealthy men of our town have already given their declarations for this year, with significant increases over a year ago. But the medium and smaller declarations, too, have been greatly raised this year. It is reckoned that in the coming days the campaign will be completely finished. The success exceeds all expectations. It is owed in the first place to the unusual self-sacrifice of the communal workers, who have perhaps never worked with such devotion as now, when we stand [?] before a historic decision about the fate and future of the Jewish people and of the Land of Israel. For the first time President A. [?] Fürstenberg, the chairman of the local Keren HaYesod committee, himself took a significant active part in the work and made a great number of visits, which brought brilliant results. The same can be said of the work of Mrs. Cesia [?] Szajn and of the other members of the committee, among whom the ladies of WIZO particularly distinguished themselves.

The delegate of Keren HaYesod from Jerusalem, Mr. Gross-Zimmermann, who is directing the campaign, gave two brilliant lectures in the past week, in the premises of WIZO and of the "W. Sh. T. K." [?] The first evening was devoted to the problem of educating the Jewish people for national freedom. On the second evening Mr. Gross-Zimmermann spoke on the subject: "On the Threshold of the Jewish State." Both lectures drew a large, educated audience and left a strong impression in town.

As we learn, Mr. Gross-Zimmermann has also been invited by other groups to give lectures on political and literary subjects. This cultural work, in the best sense of the word, which is being done by the delegate of Keren HaYesod, is a truly festive uplifting of the Jewish population of our town.

An active part in the work for Keren HaYesod is also being taken by the inspector of the Warsaw head office of Keren HaYesod, Mr. Birns [?].
Encounters

[Feuilleton — Będzin.] Little pictures caught on the wing, by Sh. Libaszon.

"Ja rabina chcę..." [Polish in Yiddish letters: "I want the rabbi"]

The conversation takes place at the corner of Małachowskiego [?] and Modrzejowska streets in Będzin. A Jew, a Hasidic Jew of dignified appearance, is chatting with a non-Jew, a house-owner on Modrzejowska Street...

The manner of speaking, the gesticulation, give the impression that the Jew wants to convince the Christian; probably — we think — the Jew wants to explain that the better part of Polish society need not believe all the old wives' tales that the Endek press invents about Jews. But when we come closer we hear that we were greatly mistaken: the conversation is actually about the flat for the Rabbi of Grajewo, who is settling in Będzin.

"I am very much surprised [?] at you, Panie gospodarzu [Mr. landlord]; you are, after all, known in our town as a clever obywatel [citizen] and still more as a practical house-owner, and in the end I learn from my acquaintances that you have done such a foolish thing and let a flat to a rabbi. A rabbi for a tenant you want in your house? What is the matter with you, Panie gospodarzu?"

"Jak to? [How so?]" — the house-owner wonders — "is it bad to have a rabbi for a tenant? First, in that case I am sure of my rent, and second, I believe that to have a rabbi for a tenant is in fact a szczęście [a piece of luck]..."

"To prawda [That is true]" — the handsome Jew strokes his long beard — "but there is, after all" — he says — "a różnica [a difference] [?] what kind of rabbi. What more do you need: one of our own, a 'Żydek' of ours, who has only just built a house on Piłsudskiego Street, on hearing that his tenant was to be the rabbi, at once laid out [?] a few hundred gulden [złoty], just so as not to let him into his house."

But [?] this argument, too, did not convince the Christian house-owner, who after a short pause declared briefly and sharply:

"Ja rabina chcę"...

The only breadwinner...

A cold, wet autumn day; low, dirty clouds, driven by a cutting wind, cover the whole sky. A thick mud underfoot.

Children in worn-out and in new warm little coats hurry into school.

Out of Zawale lane there steals, like a shadow, a little boy with a prayer book under his arm. I look at his clothing: the little coat torn, the trousers patched, the shoes crooked, falling apart with age, open [?] at the toes.

He walks with quiet steps, lost in thought; his little eyes are as if extinguished, pity looks out of them. The little face pale, without a drop of blood, drawn...

His gait and bearing attract my attention.

"Where are you coming from so early, little boy?" I ask him.

"From prayers [?]; I say Kaddish for my father, who died only a short time ago."

"What did he do for a living, your father?"

"A shop assistant in a cloth shop; he became hoarse, so they dismissed him; he was ill for a long time, he had consumption of the throat..."

"And your mother?"

"Mother deals in vegetables; my brother works in an oil-press [?], he already earns a gulden [złoty] a day, and he gives it to Mother..."

"How old is he, your brother?"

"After Sukkot he turned thirteen."

And I think to myself: we really are the "most capable" people of all peoples, and the proof — a boy who is barely 13 years old is already the breadwinner of a family, or more correctly:

— the only breadwinner...

Little boots...

A fresh fashion — little boots.

The fashion is not a new one; our grandmothers in the small towns were wearing boots years ago. The only difference is that our grandmothers' boots were covered by their long dresses, and today the little boots are high and lacquered, and the dresses — short.

Our Stefcias and Zosias [?], with their red-smeared [?] little lips, parade in their little boots through the streets and fill the air with their laughter and frivolous behaviour.

We meet a communal worker of our acquaintance; he is sad and embittered.

"What is the matter with you, Reb ...?" we ask him.

"I am not" — he says — "a moraliser nor a preacher of morals, but — may it be no disgrace to us — we fall in our own eyes, and still more in the eyes of strangers, at the very time when we groan over our condition, over our sad situation, over our economic decline. We are going under from day to day, but the outside world does not see it — besides, it does not want to see it; the outside world also does not see the scenes that are played out in many Jewish homes because of the new fashion, the fashion of

— little boots..."

She dances, poor thing.

I ask Madame Szmeterling [?], an acquaintance of mine: "What is the matter with you, why does one not see you, Mrs. Szmeterling? Once you used to come to us on a visit almost every Saturday night, and now a long time has passed and one neither sees you nor hears from you, neither you nor your husband? Perhaps it no longer befits you to come? Perhaps you have become rich?"

"What rich, who rich? We were paupers, we are paupers now, and with God's help we shall remain paupers."

"Then why don't you come on a visit once in a while?"

"Who has time for that? The old man works, and after a day's work he feels like a broken potsherd. Who has a head for going visiting?"

"But on Saturday night there is no work! Then you can surely allow yourselves to go visiting!"

"Oh, woe is me!" my acquaintance cries out. "Saturday night is the worst time of the week for me. The whole Sabbath my poor Ruchele lies in bed and struggles [?] for her life [?]."

"What do you mean? Every Sabbath your Ruchele is ill?"

And the good, simple woman begins to pour out her heavy heart to me:

"You know my Ruchele, don't you? A weak girl, poor thing, barely alive; she has a weak heart and on top of that she has — may it not befall you — bad legs, but every Friday night she goes off dancing. Well, well, don't even ask: she comes back from the dancing broken, and on the Sabbath the poor thing lies in bed, truly, as they say, between death and life."

"Then who tells her to go dancing?" I begin to wonder.

"Ay, what are you saying! She has to dance, poor thing, woe is me; does she dance for pleasure? She is, no evil eye, no longer a young girl; one must get married some time, so the poor thing has to go dancing. When you dance you get a bridegroom — all her girl friends did so: Sara [?] with the swollen blue [?] veins got a bridegroom while dancing, Rajzl the hunchback got a bridegroom at the dancing; well, so my Ruchele has to dance too. But, a calamity upon her mother — does my Ruchele have the strength to dance? Only one must, so the poor thing sacrifices herself and dances somehow through a Friday night; but afterwards, on the Sabbath, when [?] she lies in bed and screams with pain, the old man and I are no longer human beings: we have to keep on putting hot compresses on her legs and one on her head; every moment she faints. Do we have Sabbaths any more? On Friday night our poor Ruchele dances, and the whole Sabbath we have to dance around her. Now do you understand why we cannot leave the house on the Sabbath?"

"Yes, I understand."

"Ruchele has to dance, poor thing; such is the world, oh, woe is me!" the good, simple woman heaved a heavy sigh. "Can she, may she? But she has to dance, poor thing."
They Threaten with Denunciation

[Będzin — kehilla, the rabbinate affair.] Yet another "pretty little flower"[?] of the "great" activity of the present rulers of the kehilla — the Jewish public had the opportunity to make its acquaintance last Friday, from the letter published in the "Zaglembier Tsaytung". For the sake of the Rabbi of Grajewo we have found it important to make the following clear to the public:

When the Rabbi of Grajewo was in Będzin, in connection with the rabbinical competition, a very large number of Jewish inhabitants, among them the notables of the town, turned to him asking that he agree to settle in our town. After long negotiations and great effort, by applying various kinds of patronage and interventions, it proved possible to obtain the consent of this great Torah scholar and noble personality to live in our town.

It is really not worthwhile, and it is beneath the dignity of the esteemed Rabbi of Grajewo, to argue with the gentlemen of the Agudah–Ger "cheder", or to take a position on the content of the hypocritical threatening letter, in which the "innocent"[?] Ger politicians wrap themselves in the cloak of born[?] preachers of peace, who are interested only in the troubles of the community... And precisely because of this we cannot keep silent and we must tell you that your deeds and dealings in Jewish life are only too well known to the Jewish public, and you should know, gentlemen Agudah board members ("dozors")[?] with your "captive" president[?], that no sly tricks and hypocritical stunts will help you any more; we have too bitter an experience from the past, which constantly rouses us and reminds us that we must be on guard, so that what happened 17 years ago should not repeat itself in Będzin...

Now, gentlemen Agudah politicians, with what moral and formal right do you drag the Jewish population of Będzin into your threatening letter with its veiled insults? And whence do you get the impudence and insolence to accuse anyone of strife? For when, against[?] the whole of public opinion and the intervention of various local personalities, you announced a rabbinical competition and prepared[?] the fire of strife, and when it seemed to you that you already had victory in your pocket, you cynically rejected every peaceful way out. Ask your leaders, who conducted negotiations about peace and quietly prepared war... You do know the truth, after all!

But fortunately the victory you had prepared by announcing a rabbinical competition — whose aim was to "favour" our town with a rabbi who in no way befits that dignified office — you lost; and then you suddenly remembered the "difficult Jewish situation", "strife", "kashrut", and you weep, poor things[?], crocodile tears. Whom do you mean to fool? Is your hypocrisy still not conspicuous enough? You speak of the difficult Jewish situation, which concerns you at all times as much as last year's snow, and you have the audacity to mention strife. You, who[?] kindle the greatest fire and desecrate God's name[?] when it is a matter of installing someone of your dynasty in a town — and in spite of that you still have the impudence to talk about morality; whom do you want to dazzle?

Finally we draw your attention to the fact that the esteemed Rabbi of Grajewo has exactly the same right to live in Będzin as your candidate, and we ask you to take note that Jewish society will no longer let itself be dictated to and directed[?] by you; your hegemony must be broken; it is the Jewish public that will decide about the candidates' qualifications. At the present time we have no intention whatsoever of waging a fight over the rabbinate. But let it be known to you that to all the various kinds of public sallies[?] or attacks we shall react properly and with dignity, in order to defend the honour and good standing[?] of the Jewish population of Będzin.

Org. "Mizrachi", Będzin.
Org.[?] "Torah va-Avodah", Będzin.
A Provincial Delegation (Reportage)

[Feuilleton — reportage: small-town Jews and the question of a Jewish representation.]
The slow train on which the delegation from the provincial shtetl travelled to Warsaw dragged along all night and kept making stops. At the tiniest station, a mere hint of a hut, the locomotive halted, coughed itself out like an old man, and went on puffing.
The five householders, the emissaries of the community (kahal), sat in the railway compartment as if on hot coals. They sat down and got up, looked at one another with mute glances; they are waiting, back home — the burden drove each of them — a shtetl is waiting on our mission.
— Oh, how this thing goes [?]. How it drags [?]! — the apothecary spoke up — half German, half Yiddish — on top of our troubles we had to get a slow train. With a [—] as well [?] we had to travel!
— Well, yes — sighed Pinchas, the head of the community — had you gone collecting from house to house for the travel expenses [?], you would have seen how hard, with what green gall every grosz came to us. The community is poor and tormented [?]; the artisans wanted to give and have nothing; the rich, so to speak, are warming [?] their last bit of sweets [?]. What gives me no rest is this: will our journey bring anything? Will our effort at least be worth it...
— I am thinking the same — said Zelig the tailor — to whom shall we really [?] turn in Warsaw? Who are our representatives? There is some talk of a People's Congress (folks-kongres); unfortunately it does not exist yet, and things are indeed [?] very bad..
— What do you mean? — Leyb the iron-merchant, a dark Jew with a pitch-black [?] beard, waved his hand — we shall go to my [?] “Central”; they will tell us what to do.
— There is more than one “Central” [?] — Chanina the market-trader let his squeaky voice be heard — do you read newspapers or not? There would be an address if, say, a Jewish representation were created by a People's Congress, a good and a “sure” [?] address — that would be something else; but as it is we are groping in the dark either way...
In the last hours of the journey the five emissaries sat like that, deliberating, conferring without pause and seeking counsel. When the train, with luck, arrived in Warsaw, they still had no decision; broken and unslept they stepped out into the strange city.
A tram took them from the station to Nalewki, from where, for provincial Jews, the roads of the big city part. They went into an inn, drank a glass of tea and fell into talk with other harried [?] Jews, provincials too; each of them told of his own bundle [of troubles]..
Hour chased hour and the delegation sat with what it had come with. When the waiter had overheard what they were tormenting themselves about, he said in his own manner, boldly:
— Let each one go to whomever he trusts; if it does no harm, it will certainly not help.
B. K. [?]
Home-workers (chałupnicy) Are Exempt from Trade Licences (“Patents”)

[Taxes — law: a Supreme Court ruling.]
A ruling of principle by the Supreme Court.
A woman sewed trousers in her own home for shops selling ready-made clothing, and her sister helped her with it [?].
The tax authority fined her for not having bought a “patent” (trade licence); she took the matter to court, which acquitted her. Against that judgment a cassation appeal was lodged by the public prosecutor, who found [?] that by recognising that home-workers (chałupnicy) are exempt from buying licences, the court had violated the article of the law on the turnover tax.
The Supreme Court established that the work of the accused [masculine in the print] bears the marks of home-work (outwork); that home-work, unlike handicraft, does not fall under the Industrial Law; that the provisions of the turnover tax, being provisions that impose obligations on citizens, must be interpreted strictly; and since the law on the turnover tax likewise nowhere mentions home-workers, one must come to the conclusion that no licence is required for the work of home-workers.
The ruling of principle of the Supreme Court, which is printed in the December issue of “Przegląd Skarbowy”, is of great importance for many home-workers. The cited ruling of the Supreme Court, in which it was decided that a home-worker is not a producer [?], but a worker in a special sense, who stands in an employment relationship to his employer. [Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings on the weekly portion.]
Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes around this week's portion
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Shemot

a) "And the land was filled with them" (1:7)
"...Another interpretation [?]: after the theatres and circuses were filled with them, it was at once decreed upon them that they keep away from them." Yalkut Shimoni 162.
A maskil [enlightened secularist] once argued before R' Moshe Mordechai of Slabodka [?]:
— It is not right that pious Jews do not go into the theatre. Theatre — the maskil argued — has an educational significance, it elevates a person and can also serve the religious idea...
R' Moshe Mordechai answers him:
— I will tell you a story. A certain theatre director, who had great merits on behalf of the theatre, died. When he came before the Heavenly Court he claimed that Paradise was due to him. When he was asked why Paradise was due to him, he answered that he had accomplished much for the theatre, which educates people and makes them more honest. They answer him in Heaven: Good, wait here by the door of Paradise; if a person comes here who became more pious and more honest through the theatre, the two of you will go into Paradise together. And to this day — says R' Moshe Mordechai — that man is still sitting by the door of Paradise and waiting...

b) "And He made them houses" (ibid., 21)
"'And He made them houses' — Yocheved received as her reward priesthood and kingship, Moses and Aaron; what did Miriam receive — her reward was wisdom, as it is said: 'Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom.'"
Of a pious person people are accustomed to say that he is not overly clever; therefore God gave Miriam, as reward for her piety — wisdom...
Yalkut Yehuda.

c) "And she sent her handmaid and took it" (2:5)
"...And our Rabbis expounded it in the sense of 'hand'... and they expounded: 'her amah' — her hand, and her arm stretched out many cubits."
According to the homiletic reading it emerges that Pharaoh's daughter stretched out her hand toward the floating little box with the child. Although [?] the box was many cubits farther away from her, yet through a miracle her hand became a few cubits long and she reached the child.
The question arises: but how did Pharaoh's daughter know that the miracle would happen to her?
One should indeed learn from Pharaoh's daughter that when it is a matter of rescuing a person, one must first of all act; although at first glance the rescue looks hopeless, first of all a person must act, and then sometimes a miracle happens as well...
Nifla'ot Chadashot.

d) "And the child grew, and she brought him to Pharaoh's house" (ibid., 10)
A hasid of the opposing camp once needled R' Yisroeltshe of Ruzhin [?] as to why he keeps such a royal household. R' Yisroeltshe answered him:
Moses, the saviour of Israel, had to be brought up in a house of kings. Having a royal habit and knowing what wealth is, he also took pains that the Jews should go out of Egypt "with great substance", for he knew that one needs money to live. Had he, however, come from a poor home, himself content with a kav [?] of carobs from one Sabbath eve to the next, he would have insisted that the Jews go out of Egypt with the shirt on their back; that too would have been enough for him...

e) "And he looked on their burdens" (ibid., 11)
In the Sabbath prayer we say: "Moses rejoiced in the gift of his portion." The question arises: in what way is the Sabbath, more than all the commandments, Moses' gift?
But the Midrash, Shemot Rabbah 1, relates: "'And he looked on their burdens' — he saw that they had no rest; he went and said to Pharaoh: One who has a slave — if he does not rest one day in the week, he dies; and these slaves of yours, if you do not let them rest one day in the week, they will die. He said to him: Go and do for them as you say. Moses went and instituted for them the Sabbath day to rest." Thus Moses was the first in Egypt to win the Sabbath for the Jews, and therefore it is called by his name.
Shibbolei HaLeket.

f) "Surely the thing is known" (ibid., 14)
The Jews in Egypt had many sins, but all those sins were toward Heaven. For such sins God would not have let them be punished by Pharaoh. For such sins He Himself, as it were, exacts [?] payment; but if He handed them over to a wicked man as punishment, it is a sign that their sins were between man and his fellow — informing — and therefore they are judged [?] also by human hands...
Ktav Sofer.

g) "Out of the midst of the bush" (3:2)
The Divine Presence did not rest upon Moses — neither when he was with Pharaoh in the royal palaces, nor when he was king in Kush — but only when he found himself a lonely man in the desert, because every lordship distances one from the revelation of the Divine Presence...
Abravanel.

h) "Cast it on the ground" (4:3)
When Moses went to the Jews with a stick, God said to him "Cast it on the ground" — throw it away onto the ground. One does not go to Jews with a stick...
Leket Amarim.

And young and old are killing themselves — mortal danger — to see how "moykers"[?]...

After him[?] Lolek,

Reb Yekl the Matchmaker

[Humour and satire — “Der Kokh-lefl”.] His chat with the bridegroom before the “look”[?] (the viewing of the bride)..
— Have you got some decent bride for me?
— A question, whether I have? Just take a look at the photograph. Milk and honey, eh?
— But she is so small, and so skinny besides.
— This is merchandise sold by the piece, not by the kilo. What did you want — should I perhaps give you an elephant?
— But she looks so old.
— What are you talking about? A year ago she was still playing with dolls, may we both[?] be so healthy!
— An idiot?
— Eh, she was a saleswoman in a toy shop. And secondly, one can after all take a look. Looking costs no money.
— Does she have an education, too?
— Ah, how do you come to that? Her enemies or jealous girl-friends must have gossiped that about her.
And how much dowry does she have?
— Twice as much as you.
— I have a zero.
— Then she has the second one; together you will have “two zeros” [“00” — the usual sign for a lavatory]. In a flat that sometimes comes in handy..
— And what do her parents do?
— The father sits and the mother lies.
— What does that mean?
— The father is sitting [in prison] because of a “pleyte” (a fraudulent bankruptcy), and the mother is lying — in childbed.. But why are you conducting an investigation (śledztwo) here with me — what are you, an examining magistrate, or what the devil? You came to get married, after all. So come along for a “look”... My merchandise, you understand me, cannot lie long in the warehouse...
— What, does she go bad?
— No, she gets wiser, and fault-finders[?] like you she sends[?] to all the black years. Enough — take your overcoat and come.
The two[?] of them go off “to look”[?].

A Boycott of the “Zagłębie Ladies”

[Humour and satire — “Der Kokh-lefl”; feuilleton.] A carnival-eve “narada” (conference). By Y. Oberzhanek [J. Oberżanek[?]].
This week a “narada” [Polish: a conference] took place at my home. Not, heaven forbid, to discuss the Jewish situation; nobody spoke about the series: pickets, boycott, benches [the “ghetto benches”], Madagascar. The narada was a women’s one, and there was one question on the agenda: where does one go for the winter?
Although the “narada” was a confidential one, purely of women, behind “closed doors”, I nevertheless managed to find out details — for what reasons the narada had been called.
Hear, gentlemen, what women think about and of, what their worries are at the present time.
It was last winter. The little wives of Zagłębie set off — as every winter — for the mountains, to Zakopane. Each wanted to outdo the other with her outfits, the sporting ones and the drawing-room ones. Each took along packed suitcases with all sorts of trousers, sweaters, boots, hats, dresses, coats and other rags. For a whole month they sat at the dressmaker’s, at the milliner’s — the work went at full steam.
My little wife did not sit with “folded hands” either. She too was preparing to “conquer” Zakopane. For whole days she sat in front of the mirror trying things on: navy-blue trousers with pompoms and black trousers without pompoms, out of one pair of trousers and into a second pair; for each pair of trousers she had a separate sweater, a separate little cap; after the trousers came a series of dresses — which dress she would wear at the “five” [five-o’clock tea dance] and which at the dancing. Now coats: when the wool[?] fur coat and when the “niebieski lis” [blue fox]; and when I saw her with the suitcases on the other side of the door, I breathed more easily. A mountain came off my shoulders, I was rid of a trouble. A yoke off my head.
Having arrived in Zakopane, the “Zagłębie ladies”, with my missus at their head, set out to “conquer” Zakopane. First they made for the “Morskie Oko” [a dance-restaurant in Zakopane]. Dressed up in vinegar and honey [= dressed to the nines]. Each one separately was preparing to “reign” [królować]. To vanquish the Warsaw and the Zakopane[?] men. So they sat down at the little tables and waited to be “asked to dance” [poprosić do tańca]. They sat, drank a “pół czarnej” [a small black coffee]. Another pół czarnej, smoked cigarettes, crossed the right leg over the left, the left leg over the right, sat an hour, two — and a “yesterday’s day” [= and nothing came of it].
They left the “Morskie Oko” as if spat upon[?], insulted. Without a crumb of “powodzenie” [success with the men]; the affair vexed them greatly. How can it be? How come? We, the Zagłębie ladies, who have always reigned in Zakopane? So they went off to “Trzaska” [a Zakopane restaurant], perhaps there they would have more luck. They went there, again dressed up in vinegar and in honey, again drank pół czarnej, again smoked cigarettes, crossed one little leg over the other, again sat through two or three hours. All the little wives from other towns — the Częstochowa wives, those from Kielce, from Lublin — have powodzenie, they are literally torn to pieces, they are asked to dance, and they, the Zagłębie ladies, sit, poor things, in waxed[?] trousers, and nobody so much as looks round at them.
So they left “Trzaska” too — as if slapped[?].
The same thing was repeated later on the promenade, in the valleys (doliny), even in the “Dolina za Bramką”. On “Gubałówka”, by “Giewont” — everywhere the same: all the little wives have powodzenie, they are literally torn to pieces. People go sledging and fly on skis, “z górki na pazurki” [downhill]. They clamber up the mountains, creep for half the night “w towarzystwie” [in company] through the snows, break their necks “w towarzystwie”... go[?] strolling[?] “w towarzystwie”... “shelter”[?] in the “schroniska” [mountain huts] “w towarzystwie”... All the women have powodzenie, only they are waxed and polished, and nobody so much as looks round at them. The lads (chłopcy) avoid them like a plague, Heaven preserve us,
So the Zagłębie ladies began to investigate and inquire: what has happened? What is different this year from all other years? And it was found out that the men had declared a boycott of the Zagłębie ladies.
After a week I receive a telegram from my missus;
“Natychmiast przyjechać” [come at once].
Having received the telegram, everything went dark before my eyes: what has happened? Perhaps a catastrophe? Perhaps she turned a somersault (koziołek) off Giewont? Perhaps she has been buried by snow? Perhaps a piece of mountain broke off? There’s no questioning a tale — it is Zakopane, after all!...
I did not think long, grabbed the suitcase and — hayda — off to the train.
I come to the train, take a look — what is this? Somehow so many acquaintances with little suitcases, somehow they are all so sad; we all get into one carriage, they are all mute as the wall. They do not utter a word. I grew curious, and I ask one of them:
— Panie [Mr.] Pistikchl[?]. Where are you travelling?
— To Zakopane, and you?
— Also to Zakopane.
— Why are you so sad?
I show him the telegram “Natychmiast przyjechać”, and he too takes out a telegram with the same words: natychmiast przyjechać.
A third man overhears our conversation, and he too takes out a telegram with the same “Natychmiast przyjechać”. A fourth, a fifth, a sixth — they all have telegrams from their wives.
— What is this? What can this mean? Has there been an earthquake in Zakopane, a cloudburst, or what the devil? Why all at once?
Yet I felt a little easier; as they say[?], the trouble of many is half a consolation — as long as I am not alone in the trouble.
The same story happened a few hours later in Zakopane at the train. The first to come to the train was my missus with a bouquet of flowers — she had come to meet her husband. A minute[?] later came Mrs. Wiener (Wienerowa), also with a bouquet of flowers, and she [my wife] asks her friend:
— Pani Wienerowa, whom are you waiting for?
— My husband, and you?
— My husband.
Within 10 minutes the platform was full of little wives from Będzin and Sosnowiec, all with flowers in their hands, all of them had come to meet their husbands; and when the train arrived, it turned out that what had come was a train of men from Zagłębie.
The wives with flowers and the men — with telegrams.
That same evening all the Zagłębie ladies came to the “Morskie Oko” “do pary”[?] [in pairs] with men, all “paraded” out of spite, sat down at the little tables, drank coffee, smoked cigarettes; as the saying goes: where there is no man, a herring is — a fish. When there is no strange man, one’s own husband is also merchandise...
The next morning the Zagłębie ladies gathered for a “narada” in order to consider the situation that had arisen. What is the point of sitting in the “Morskie Oko”, in “Trzaska”, with one’s own husband? What flavour is there in walking in the valleys with one’s own husband, and what sense is there in creeping about the mountains at night with one’s own husband, in crawling away with one’s own somewhere into a “schronisko” for a night’s lodging? Why, that is terrible! One has one’s husband at home the whole year, after all; for that one did not need to travel to Zakopane!
After a lengthy “narada” it was agreed: to swap husbands!.. The “wniosek” [motion] was adopted “jednogłośnie” [unanimously]; the men too voted for the “wniosek”, and in this way the matter was solved: both the men had a good time in Zakopane, and the little wives did not have to be bored with their own shlimazls.
* * *
That, gentlemen, was the reason for the “narada” which took place this week; it was a matter of the “serious” question: where does one go?
That is what the “fair sex” thinks about and of, and what sort of worries it has: who thinks about pickets, boycott, the market-stall [stragan], Madagascar, benches — and who about “dokąd jechać” [where to go]!...
What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin — The Gymnastics and Sports Association "Hakoach" Must Be Rebuilt

[Będzin — Sport.] [At the head of the page, the section banner "What's New in Zagłębie?"; date boxes: Friday, 20 Tevet 5698 — piątek, 24 grudnia 937; sub-section heading: Będzin.]
So resolves the extraordinary general meeting.
On the premises of the society Ż.T.K.[?] [probably Żydowskie Towarzystwo Krajoznawcze, the Jewish Sightseeing Society] an extraordinary general meeting took place on Monday evening[?] concerning the present sad state of "Hakoach".
The meeting aroused very wide interest; the hall, which holds close to 200 people, was full.
Mr M. Plessner opens the meeting, and at the general demand the chair is taken by Mr M. Lancman[?] of Sosnowiec. Messrs Herman Pinkus, H. Hirsz and Lancman[?], as secretary, are invited to the presidium table.
On the present state of "Hakoach" Mr Plessner reports; he says that the extraordinary meeting must elect a suitable board, which is to take the fate of "Hakoach" into its hands.
A very lively discussion developed about the causes that brought about the present decline of "Hakoach"; a series of proposals is put forward, among them a proposal by M. Openheim to elect a commission which is to audit the activity of the board that has served until now and at the same time to express a protest against those who led to the present situation. All the proposals are rejected, but it is resolved to hand the matter over to the Bielsko [Bielitz] "Maccabi", which is to investigate the whole affair around "Hakoach".
Then a provisional committee is elected, consisting of Dr Rechtszaft, Natan Gutman, Pinkus, Inwald, Lachman[?] [perhaps again Lancman], Hirsz, M. Sercarz, M. Plessner and S.[?] Barenblat.
The committee, which has set itself the task of rebuilding the only Jewish gymnastics and sports association in our town, has already set about a series of work plans.

Sosnowiec. Simcha Glicksman in the dock

[Sosnowiec — court; press.] Sosnowiec
Simcha Glicksman in the dock.
Last Friday the local District Court heard the case against Sz. Glicksman (Simchowicz), editor of the “Zagłębier-Szlezisz Folksblat”. He was brought to judicial account for insulting the editors of the “Zagłębier Cajtung”, Messrs. L. Szpigelman and Sz. Lewkowicz.
At the request of the defence counsel of the accused side, the judge proposed a settlement. To this the counsel on behalf of the editorial office, Dr. Rechtman, agreed on condition[?] that his side, the insulted parties, receive full moral satisfaction.

Glicksman apologises to the editors of the “Zagłębier Cajtung”, who were insulted in his little paper without his knowledge. The apology must be printed on the first page of the “Zagłębier-Szlezisz Folksblat”, the “Zagłębier Cajtung” and “Haynt”.
If all these points are not carried out, the charge remains in force.

The Jews of Kielce Must Set Up a Tombstone on the Grave of Sh. H. Kirschenbaum

[Kielce — antisemitism / charity.]
[Page head: “Life in Kielce” — Friday, 20 Tevet 5698 / 24 December 1937.]
In two or three weeks falls the first yahrzeit [anniversary of death] of the poor Jewish village trader Shlomo Hirsh Kirschenbaum [Szlama Hersz Kirszenbaum], who was severely wounded outside Kielce by a group of hooligans and died a few days later.
His wife, a forlorn, unfortunate widow who is perishing from want and from hunger, runs around to all the institutions (the kehilla among them) and begs that a tombstone be set up on her husband's grave. She knocks on the doors of all the communal workers, she does not rest, and she wants the tombstone of her husband, the martyr, to be set up on the day of his first yahrzeit.
In the name of the widow we appeal to the Jews of Kielce that each one should, in the course of the coming week, donate a few złoty for this purpose. Everyone should pay in the donation at the Rabbi of Kielce, Rabbi Rapoport.

Bandit Attack on a Jewish Merchant in Suchedniów

[Kielce district — crime.]
On Monday, at 4 o'clock before dawn, 3 armed bandits burst into the dwelling of the Jewish merchant Abraham Birnbaum in Suchedniów and began shooting at the members of the household. Birnbaum was severely wounded in the left arm.
In the dwelling were Birnbaum's wife and a maidservant. The two women threw themselves on their knees before the bandits and begged them to have mercy and to let them live. The bandits ransacked the whole dwelling, taking with them several dozen złoty. Then they looked at Birnbaum lying there and, thinking that he was already dead, expressed their condolences to the women; afterwards they warned that the police should not be notified, and fled.

Economic News.

[Kielce — economy / taxes.]
Important information on tax matters.
Edited by advocate Dr. Wajnberg [Weinberg] and advocate-trainee Feldman

On the grounds of tax assessment.
In accordance with Art. 101 of the Tax Ordinance, every taxpayer has the right to apply to the tax office with a request to state to him the grounds of the tax assessment, and the tax office is obliged to state [?] the grounds. A request for the grounds must be made within the same term in which an appeal can be lodged. One may apply for the grounds in writing and orally.
A question thus arises: can the taxpayer also demand written grounds after the tax office has already once stated oral grounds?
Paragraph 95 of the executive regulations to the Tax Ordinance explains that besides oral grounds the taxpayer may also demand written grounds. For written grounds one must file a request at the tax office; the request must bear a stamp duty of 3 zł.
The circular of the Ministry of Finance of 16 May 1935 explains that the tax office is obliged to state written grounds even when the request bears no duty at all; the 3 zł. are afterwards collected by way of execution.
From the moment a request for the grounds has been filed at the tax office, the limitation period (przedawnienie [?]) of the appeal is interrupted; i.e., if the tax office stated the grounds on the 20th, one has a fresh 20 days in which to lodge an appeal.
This circular is of great importance for taxpayers.
